title: Detailed Judgment on Riba PLD 2000 SC 225
citation: PLD 1975 Pesh. 161; Islamia University Bahawalpur through its Vice-C
explainer:
This case, decided by the Shariat Appellate Bench of the Supreme Court, is the well-known landmark ruling on Riba (interest) in Pakistan, often cited as PLD 2000 SC 225. It brought together dozens of appeals filed by banks (including Allied Bank, United Bank, Habib Bank, National Bank, MCB, ABN AMRO), government bodies (the Federation of Pakistan, Punjab government), and individual borrowers, all arising from earlier Federal Shariat Court rulings that had declared interest-based banking transactions un-Islamic and contrary to the injunctions of the Quran and Sunnah.

The banks and government argued they should be allowed to continue charging and paying interest on loans, while individuals and petitioners supported the Federal Shariat Court's findings that all forms of interest, including bank interest, amount to Riba, which is strictly prohibited in Islam. The appeals were consolidated because they raised the same core legal and religious question: whether existing laws permitting interest-based financial transactions violate Islamic injunctions under the Constitution.

While this excerpt does not contain the court's final reasoning or ruling in detail, it confirms the Supreme Court's Shariat Appellate Bench examined this massive, consolidated set of appeals together. The case matters because its outcome shaped Pakistan's ongoing debate over Islamic banking, affecting how financial institutions, government bodies, and courts approach interest-based transactions under Islamic law.

title: Pakistan Limitation Act, 1908
explainer:
This entry reproduces part of Pakistan's Limitation Act, 1908, along with case notes summarizing how Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Pakistani courts have interpreted it, rather than a single court judgment deciding one dispute.

The core legal point highlighted concerns how limitation periods apply to appeals from Family Court decisions. The Family Courts Act prescribes a specific 30-day period for filing appeals against a Family Court's judgment, which differs from the general limitation periods listed in the First Schedule of the Limitation Act, 1908. The cited ruling (PLJ 1996 AJK (FSC) 179) clarifies that when a special law like the Family Courts Act sets its own distinct limitation period, that specific period governs, rather than the general provisions of the Limitation Act. However, Section 29 of the Limitation Act still applies to such appeals, meaning certain general principles of the Limitation Act (such as rules on computing time or condoning delay) continue to operate alongside the special period, unless expressly excluded.

This matters because it establishes a clear rule of statutory interpretation: specific laws override general ones on matters they specifically address (such as timeframes for appeals), while general procedural safeguards under the Limitation Act can still supplement specialized statutes where not inconsistent. This principle affects how litigants calculate deadlines for appeals in family law disputes and ensures consistency in how Pakistani and AJK courts handle conflicts between general and special limitation laws.

title: FIA shall act in accordance with provisions of FIA Act and Rules of 2002
explainer:
This case involved a man who repeatedly complained to the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) alleging corruption, fake nursing college approvals, and financial irregularities within the Pakistan Nursing and Midwifery Council (PNC). He filed a petition in the Islamabad High Court asking the court to direct the FIA to register a formal criminal case (FIR) based on his complaints, arguing that the agency was taking too long and had been evasive.

The court explained that under the FIA Act and its 2002 Rules, the agency is required to first conduct an inquiry into complaints and is not legally obligated to immediately register an FIR before that process is complete. The judge found that the petitioner had failed to provide solid evidence backing his allegations, and that many of the issues raised actually fell within the PNC's own regulatory authority to handle internally.

More importantly, the court found the petitioner had not come to it with "clean hands." He had filed contradictory cases in different courts about the same PNC affairs, concealed earlier related litigation from this bench, and could not explain how he obtained certain official documents he submitted as evidence. The judge concluded he acted in bad faith, possibly as a proxy for other interests, and had misused the court's process.

As a result, the petition was dismissed, and costs were imposed on the petitioner for his conduct. The case underscores that courts expect honesty and transparency from litigants and won't force agencies to bypass their standard investigative procedures without solid justification.

title: Conflicting Judgments on Section 4 MFLO
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over inheritance under Islamic family law in Pakistan, specifically how to calculate the share of a granddaughter whose mother died before the grandmother (the person whose estate is being inherited).

The family involved was: Mst. Daulan (grandmother), her daughter Mst. Lalan (who died before her mother), and Mst. Lalan's daughter Mst. Manzooran. Since Mst. Lalan died before Mst. Daulan, Section 4 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 treats her as if she were still alive when the inheritance opened, so she would notionally receive her share (one-third of the estate).

The dispute was over how much of that one-third share should then pass to her daughter, Mst. Manzooran. The petitioner (another family member) argued that Manzooran should only get half of her mother's notional share (one-sixth), with the rest going to other relatives, based on a Lahore High Court ruling. The lower courts, however, had awarded Manzooran the entire one-third share, following a Peshawar High Court ruling that said the full notional share passes to the deceased daughter's children.

Since the Lahore High Court and Peshawar High Court had given conflicting interpretations of Section 4, the Supreme Court decided the matter needed a final, authoritative ruling. It granted leave to appeal so this legal question could be settled definitively, while allowing partial interim relief to the petitioner pending the final decision.

title: Consistency of PWs during Cross Examination
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with issuing a cheque that bounces due to insufficient funds or a closed account, essentially dishonest cheque issuance. He had been sentenced by a trial court in Khushab to three years of simple imprisonment plus a fine, and his appeal against that conviction had already been dismissed by an Additional Sessions Judge. He then filed a criminal revision petition before the Lahore High Court.

Notably, the petitioner's lawyer did not challenge the conviction itself, only asking for a reduced sentence, citing that the petitioner was a first-time offender who had already spent about one year, five months, and twenty-three days in jail. The prosecution and complainant's lawyers did not object to this request.

The High Court reviewed the evidence and found that the prosecution had clearly proven the offense occurred, and that the key witnesses, including the complainant, gave consistent testimony even under lengthy cross-examination, with no major contradictions. Because of this, the court upheld the conviction as correctly decided.

However, considering the time already served, the court reduced the sentence to match the period the petitioner had already spent in jail, while keeping the fine and default punishment unchanged. This case illustrates how courts balance upholding valid convictions with showing leniency in sentencing based on time already served and witness credibility.

title: While computing period of limitation, Intervening period of summer vacations has to be excluded
explainer:
This is an explainer about a civil procedure case from the Peshawar High Court.

The dispute began when a man sued another for Rs. 40,000 over a property sale, claiming he had paid for the land but the seller never transferred it to his name. The trial court proceeded against the defendant without his presence (ex-parte), assuming he had been properly notified, and ruled in favor of the plaintiff. The defendant later discovered this decree during execution proceedings and tried to get it set aside, but both the trial court and the district court on appeal rejected his request, partly on the grounds that he had filed his application too late.

The High Court found serious flaws in how the case was handled. The court summons had not been served according to the proper legal procedure, there was no clear record of how or why the defendant was served at an unusual location instead of his home address, and the trial court had never examined the process server under oath as required by law before proceeding ex-parte. Additionally, the lower courts miscalculated the deadline for the defendant's application by failing to exclude the summer court vacation period from the limitation period, as required under the Limitation Act.

Because of these procedural failures, the High Court set aside the previous judgments and sent the case back to the trial court to be decided fresh, with both parties given a proper chance to present their case. This ruling reinforces that courts must strictly follow service-of-summons rules and correctly calculate limitation periods, including excluding vacation time, before deciding cases without a party's participation.

title: Filing of Appeal during Summer Vacations
explainer:
This case arose from a family dispute over maintenance payments for two minor children. After the dissolution of his marriage, the children's mother filed a suit seeking maintenance, reimbursement of delivery expenses, and return of dowry articles. The Family Court ordered the father to pay interim maintenance, but when he failed to pay on time, the court struck off his defence and passed a decree against him granting monthly maintenance to the children.

The father then tried to appeal this decision, filing his appeal on 21 August 2010, during the courts' summer vacations. The Additional District Judge dismissed his appeal as time-barred, reasoning that it was filed too late.

The Lahore High Court disagreed. It held that under Section 4 of the Limitation Act, 1908, a person has the choice to either file an appeal during court vacations or wait until the courts reopen and file it then. Since the father could have validly filed his appeal as late as 1 September 2010 (when courts reopened), his filing on 21 August 2010 was actually within time, not late.

The High Court therefore set aside the order dismissing the appeal and directed the Additional District Judge to hear the appeal on its merits. This case matters because it clarifies that litigants are not penalized for filing appeals during court vacations, protecting their right to a fair hearing rather than losing cases on technical timing grounds.

title: Post Arrest Bail granted in Dubai Visa Case
explainer:
This case involved a man named Muhammad Aslam who was accused of fraud related to fake visa promises. According to the complainant, Aslam took Rs. 700,000 in two installments in October 2016, promising to arrange employment visas to Dubai for the complainant and his brother. He allegedly never delivered the visas or returned the money, leading to an FIR being registered against him under the Emigration Ordinance, 1979, which deals with illegal emigration-related offences.

Aslam was arrested and sought post-arrest bail from the Lahore High Court (Multan Bench). The court noted several weaknesses in the prosecution's case: there was a significant and unexplained delay of about a year between the alleged incident and the filing of the FIR, and the complainant failed to specify exact dates for the payments. The court found these gaps sufficient to warrant "further inquiry," a legal standard under Section 497(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code that allows bail when the case against the accused is not clearly established.

The court also considered that Aslam had no prior criminal record, had cooperated with the investigation, and was not needed for further questioning. Since his trial was unlikely to conclude soon, the court ruled that keeping him in jail indefinitely served no purpose.

The court granted him bail, requiring a bond of Rs. 200,000 with one surety. This case illustrates how delays and lack of specific evidence in a complaint can support a bail application, even in fraud-related cases.

title: PLJ 2021 Islamabad 40 - Withholding of Outstanding Dues
explainer:
Getz Pharma, a pharmaceutical company, had employed several individuals as sales managers. These employees either resigned or were dismissed after the company accused them of breaching their contracts and violating a conflict-of-interest policy by setting up a rival business, Sun Health Care, while still employed. As a result, the company withheld their final dues, including gratuity, relying on a rule that denies gratuity to employees dismissed for misconduct or who resign under such circumstances.

The employees filed claims under Section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, before the Assistant Commissioner/Magistrate, who ordered the company to pay the outstanding dues and compensation. Getz Pharma challenged this order before the Islamabad High Court through writ petitions, arguing that the employees were not "workmen" under labour law, that the dispute should be handled in Karachi courts as per their contracts, and that the National Industrial Relations Commission, not the Payment of Wages authority, had jurisdiction.

The High Court dismissed the petitions. It held that since no labour court functions in Islamabad, the writ petition was the only available remedy and was maintainable. However, it found that the Assistant Commissioner had properly considered all evidence and arguments before ruling. In writ proceedings, the court's role is limited to checking for legal or jurisdictional errors, not re-examining factual findings. Since Getz Pharma failed to show any such error, the original order directing payment stood, reinforcing that courts generally won't disturb factual findings of lower author

title: Judgment on Punjab Partition of Immovable Property Act 2012
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over a house in Karachi left behind by a woman who died in 1993, with her two sons as heirs. After one son also passed away, his many children (the appellants) and the other son (respondent) could not agree on how to divide the property, so a partition suit was filed. Since the property could not be physically divided among so many heirs, the court appointed a Nazir (court officer) to arrange its sale, first by private agreement among the family, then by auction if needed.

Disputes arose over the property's value. The respondent offered to buy it for Rs. 3 crore, but the appellants insisted it was worth more and demanded over Rs. 4 crore. The court gave them repeated chances to either match that price, deposit the money, or bring in another buyer willing to pay more. They failed to do any of this. As a result, the single judge confirmed the sale to the respondent at Rs. 3 crore.

The appellants challenged this decision before a larger bench, asking for more time to find a better buyer. The High Court rejected their appeal, finding that they had already been given ample opportunity and had not fulfilled any of the court's conditions. The judges upheld the original order, confirming the sale at Rs. 3 crore and dismissing the appeal as meritless.

This case illustrates how courts handle property disputes among multiple heirs when physical division is impossible, emphasizing that parties must act on opportunities given by courts rather than indefinitely stall proceedings.

title: Public Functionaries are bound to obey direction of Wafaqi Mohtasib
explainer:
This case involved a citizen who applied to the telephone department for a new connection but never received one, even though he was billed for a number that was never actually installed. Frustrated, he filed a complaint with the Wafaqi Mohtasib (federal ombudsman), who investigated, found the telephone department guilty of maladministration, and ordered it to install the connection free of cost within 30 days. The department neither complied nor challenged this order through the legal channels available to it, such as appealing to the President of Pakistan or approaching the courts. Instead, it simply ignored the ombudsman's direction.

The petitioner then went to the Lahore High Court asking it to enforce the ombudsman's order. The department argued that installing the connection required erecting 14 poles, calling it a policy matter beyond the court's jurisdiction, and suggested the petitioner should have filed a contempt case instead.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It held that public functionaries are legally bound to obey directions of the Wafaqi Mohtasib unless they formally challenge them before the President or the courts. Since the department did neither, its failure to act showed bad faith. The court ordered the telephone department to implement the ombudsman's order in letter and spirit within four months.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that government agencies cannot simply ignore ombudsman rulings; they must either comply or formally contest them through proper legal avenues.

title: Responsibility of NHA in road Accidents
explainer:
This case involved a woman who, while traveling with her husband and others from Karachi to Larkana on a national highway, met a serious accident when her car hit small crash stones scattered on the road near Tando Masti. There were no warning signs or cautionary boards, even though several similar accidents had reportedly happened at the same spot before. The petitioner and her companions were injured and her car was badly damaged. She approached the Sindh High Court asking that the National Highway Authority (NHA) and other authorities be directed to take proper safety precautions on highways and to compensate her for the losses suffered.

The court examined the NHA Act, 1991 and the National Highways Safety Ordinance, 2000, holding that NHA, as the body controlling and managing national highways, has a mandatory duty to ensure road safety, including placing proper traffic and warning signs, maintaining speed checks, and enforcing rules, not merely on paper but in practice. Since NHA collects toll tax on such roads, it cannot avoid its safety obligations. The court directed NHA to provide round-the-clock patrolling, establish emergency medical aid and ambulance facilities at toll points, and report compliance within a specified time.

However, the court held that it could not determine the actual compensation or damages in a constitutional petition, since that requires evidence-based findings. It therefore allowed the petitioner to approach a civil court for compensation.

This judgment is significant because it clarifies that highway authorities have an enforceable duty to ensure road safety, not just collect tolls.

title: Prosecution must establish that chain of custody was unbroken, unsuspicious, indubitable, safe and secure
explainer:
This Supreme Court judgment deals with several narcotics cases together because they raised the same important legal questions about how drug evidence must be handled before someone can be convicted.

Under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, once police seize a suspected narcotic substance, a sample must be sent to a Narcotics Testing Laboratory for analysis. The Government Analyst's report is given strong evidentiary weight in court and is treated as conclusive unless rebutted. Because so much weight rests on this report, the Court examined the rules governing how samples are collected, preserved and tested.

The Court held that the "chain of custody" - the unbroken record of who handled the sample from the moment of seizure until it reaches the laboratory - must be safe, secure, and free of suspicion. Any gap or irregularity in this chain undermines the reliability of the final report.

The Court also analysed the Control of Narcotic Substances (Government Analysts) Rules, 2001, distinguishing between rules that are merely "directory" (good practice, non-compliance doesn't invalidate the report) and those that are "mandatory" (essential, non-compliance invalidates the report). It ruled that the requirement to record full testing protocols in the analyst's report is mandatory, while other procedural requirements like multiple signatures or copies are merely directory.

This judgment matters because it sets clear standards protecting accused persons from convictions based on unreliable or improperly documented drug testing.

title: PLJ 2017 Lahore 720
explainer:
This case involved a father seeking custody of his young son through Pakistan's family courts. The father, Shabir-ul-Hassan, had divorced the child's mother, Tanveer Zaidi, back in 2008. Years later, concerned that the mother was unable to properly care for the boy, possibly due to financial difficulties, health issues, and the fact that the child was actually being raised by his paternal aunt rather than his mother, the father filed a petition asking the court to give him custody.

The trial court heard evidence from both sides but rejected his request. When he appealed, the appeals court simply upheld that decision in a very brief, half-page ruling without properly explaining its reasoning.

The father then approached the Lahore High Court, arguing that the lower courts had mishandled the evidence and failed to think the matter through carefully.

The High Court agreed that something had gone wrong, not with the trial court, which had analyzed the evidence thoroughly, but with the appellate court, which had dismissed the appeal too quickly without explaining its reasoning or properly discussing the evidence. The judge emphasized that courts must always give clear reasons for their decisions, even when upholding a lower court's ruling, especially in sensitive matters like child custody.

As a result, the High Court set aside the appellate court's judgment and sent the case back for a fresh, more careful decision. This case highlights the importance of thorough, reasoned judicial decision-making, particularly in cases affecting children's welfare.

title: Parsi Divorce Case Law
explainer:
This case involved a divorce petition filed by Geeti Mahyar Dhatigara against her husband, Mahyar Mehrwan Dhatigara, under the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936. The couple were Parsis, a community governed by this special law rather than general divorce law, and their case was heard by the Sindh High Court, which appointed a judge along with "delegates" (community representatives) to assist, as required under the Act.

The wife sought divorce under Section 32(g) of the Act, which allows dissolution of marriage when a couple has not lived together for a specified period. She did not pursue earlier allegations of cruelty against her husband, relying instead simply on the fact that the couple had been separated for more than three years. The husband, appearing in person, confirmed this separation and stated he had no objection to the divorce, saying he did not want his wife to remain in a marriage against her will.

The delegates present also agreed that the couple should not be forced to stay married against their wishes. The court held that the legal requirements for divorce under Section 32(g) were satisfied, given the prolonged separation and mutual lack of objection. It therefore dissolved the marriage and ordered that a divorce decree be prepared and sent to the Registrar of Marriages.

This judgment illustrates how Pakistan's Parsi community has its own distinct marriage and divorce law, and shows a straightforward, consent-based dissolution of marriage based on long-term separation.

title: Statement on Holy Quran in a Family Case
explainer:
This case involved a husband who challenged a family court's decree ordering him to pay his former wife dower in the form of gold ornaments, Rs. 500,000 under a special condition in their marriage contract (Nikah Nama), and maintenance during her waiting period (iddat) after divorce.

During the trial, the husband himself proposed a special oath procedure: he offered that if his wife's grandfather swore on the Holy Quran that the conditions written in the Nikah Nama matched what the couple had actually agreed to at the time of marriage, then the case should be decided against him. The grandfather took this oath, and the husband and his lawyer acknowledged this with their thumb impression and signature. The Lahore High Court held that under the Oaths Act, 1873, this amounted to a binding admission that could not later be challenged, so the findings on the dower and ornaments stood.

However, the court drew a distinction regarding the Rs. 500,000 payment tied to wrongful divorce or expulsion from the house. It ruled that this amount was not dower or personal property, and therefore did not fall within the Family Court's jurisdiction—it was a civil matter that should be decided by a civil court instead. The special oath procedure could not expand the Family Court's powers beyond what the law allows. As a result, the petition was partly accepted, meaning this specific claim was set aside while the rest of the decree remained intact. The judgment highlights that courts must stick to their statutory jurisdiction even when parties agree to alternative methods of proof.

title: PLJ 2018 Cr.C. 664
explainer:
This case involved a young domestic servant, Tayyaba Bibi, who was under ten years old and worked as a maid in the home of Mst. Maheen Zafar and her husband Raja Khurram Ali Khan, who was an Additional District and Sessions Judge. The child was allegedly beaten, burned, confined, and mistreated while in their care, leading to an FIR and criminal charges including wrongful confinement, causing hurt, criminal intimidation, child abuse under section 328-A of the Pakistan Penal Code, and causing the disappearance of evidence to shield a co-accused.

After examining testimony from sixteen witnesses, medical evidence, and photographs of the child's injuries, the Islamabad High Court found that some charges were not proven beyond reasonable doubt, including wrongful confinement, criminal intimidation, and causing disappearance of the child to protect a co-accused, due to insufficient direct evidence.

However, the court found both accused jointly guilty under section 328-A, which criminalizes willful assault, ill-treatment, neglect, or abandonment of a child causing harm. The court held that as the employers responsible for the child's care in their household, both the husband and wife bore joint responsibility for the harm she suffered, relying on circumstantial and medical evidence forming a complete and credible chain.

This case is significant because it reinforced legal protections for child domestic workers and clarified that circumstantial evidence, when forming an unbroken chain, can support a conviction even without direct eyewitness testimony.

title: Jurisdiction is important in guardian cases
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute over an 11-year-old boy, Amaan Hassan, between his parents. The mother had filed a petition in the Guardian Judge's court in Islamabad seeking custody of the child under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890. The father objected, arguing that the Islamabad court had no jurisdiction to hear the case, since the family had never actually lived there together. The couple had lived in Peshawar, then Lahore, and eventually settled in Abu Dhabi.

The Guardian Judge in Islamabad rejected the father's objection, reasoning that courts where a wife resides generally have jurisdiction over such matters. The father challenged this decision before the Peshawar High Court.

The High Court examined the relevant law, particularly Rule 6 of the Family Courts Rules, 1965, which says jurisdiction belongs to the court where the cause of action arose, or where the parties reside or last resided together. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the Chief Justice held that since the mother never lived in Islamabad and the family had no connection to that city, the Islamabad court had no jurisdiction to hear the custody case.

As a result, the court set aside the Islamabad Guardian Judge's order and directed that the mother's petition be filed instead before a court that actually has proper jurisdiction. This case highlights that in custody and guardianship disputes, choosing the correct court based on where the parties actually lived is a crucial legal requirement, not a mere technicality.

title: Quashment of FIR on the illegality of Police
explainer:
This case involved a petition filed before the Lahore High Court, Rawalpindi Bench, seeking to quash an FIR registered against Muhammad Munir under Section 216 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with harbouring an offender. The FIR alleged that Munir helped his two sons, who were wanted in a separate case, escape from police custody when officers tried to arrest them.

The petitioner argued that there was no real evidence proving his sons were ever legally declared proclaimed offenders, and that no proof existed connecting him to the alleged act of harbouring them. The police had relied only on the original complaint and a site plan, without properly verifying the sons' status as proclaimed offenders or establishing any concrete evidence against the petitioner.

The court examined the legal definitions of harbouring under Section 52-A and the offence under Section 216 of the PPC, and found that the essential elements of the offence were missing. Since there was no credible evidence linking Munir to the crime, the court held that forcing him to stand trial would be a futile and unjust exercise, likely to end in acquittal anyway. It emphasized that while offenders must be punished, individuals also have a constitutional right to protection against false or baseless charges, and courts should resolve such matters early rather than let innocent people suffer the ordeal of a trial.

The court ruled that the police had committed a clear illegality in registering the FIR, making the entire proceeding void

title: There is difference between Power of Attorney and Will
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Karachi. A father had given his son an irrevocable General Power of Attorney, allowing the son to deal with a plot of land. The son sold the property to a buyer (the applicant in this case) for Rs. 36,000, and the buyer built on it and took a bank loan against it. Later, the father claimed he had actually intended the document to be a "will," not a power of attorney, and that he had since cancelled it. He filed a suit for declaration, cancellation, and possession, and won at the appellate level, with the buyer being dispossessed without ever having been properly notified of the case.

The Sindh High Court overturned that decision. It clarified a fundamental legal distinction: a power of attorney and a will are completely different instruments. A power of attorney authorizes an agent to act on someone's behalf during their lifetime, while a will only takes effect after death. The document in question was clearly meant to operate during the father's lifetime, so it was a valid, functioning power of attorney, not a will. The court also noted that the alleged "cancellation" was neither signed by the attorney (the son) nor properly registered, making it legally ineffective.

As a result, the son's sale of the property was valid, and the buyer's ownership and possession were restored. The case matters because it reinforces that powers of attorney and wills serve distinct legal purposes and cannot be reinterpreted after the fact to undo transactions already carried out in good faith.

title: There are four ingredients of Benami Transaction
explainer:
This case was about a property dispute between Musa Khan, who claimed he had secretly funded the purchase of a plot in Islamabad while living in the UK, and Ashram Bibi, in whose name the plot was officially registered. Musa Khan argued this was a benami transaction, meaning the property was only held in Ashram Bibi's name on paper while he was the real owner, because he had sent the purchase money through a jointly operated bank account and she had acquired the property through misrepresentation. The trial court agreed with him and declared him the owner. Ashram Bibi appealed to the Islamabad High Court.

The High Court overturned the trial court's decision. It explained that anyone claiming a property is benami must prove four things: the source of funds used to buy the property, who held custody of the original title documents, who was actually in possession of the property, and the motive behind disguising the real ownership. The court found that Musa Khan had only argued that he provided the money, but failed to address or prove the other three essential elements, particularly possession and custody of documents, which were shown to be with Ashram Bibi. The court also noted that such claims often surface only after relationships sour, which undermines their credibility.

This judgment matters because it reaffirms the strict evidentiary standard required to prove benami ownership claims in Pakistani law, protecting registered property owners from claims based on incomplete or weak evidence.

title: Termination of Agency of Contract
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between an advertising agency and a bank over a terminated advertising agreement. The agency had been appointed as the bank's exclusive advertising agent, with the contract set to run for an initial period and then automatically renew, and with a clause requiring two months' advance notice for termination by either side. The agreement also contained an arbitration clause requiring disputes to be resolved by arbitrators rather than through ordinary litigation. When the bank sought to end the relationship, the agency approached the Sindh High Court, arguing the termination was premature and that its agency was a special kind called an agency coupled with interest, which under the Contract Act cannot be revoked without honoring that interest.

The court held that genuine disputes about whether proper notice was given had to go to arbitration, as the parties had agreed. On the substantive point, the judge found that this agency was not coupled with interest, since it lacked any pre-existing interest of the agent in the subject matter being protected, so it did not qualify for special protection against revocation. Even if termination was premature or improper, the court said money damages, not an order forcing the bank to continue the relationship, was the appropriate remedy. The court allowed the matter to proceed to arbitration while declining to grant the injunction sought.

This matters because it clarifies that most commercial agency agreements can be ended by payment of damages rather than forced continuation, and that arbitration clauses will generally be enforced over court intervention.

title: Possession can be restored to Tenant
explainer:
This case involved a landlord-tenant dispute in Islamabad. The landlord sought to evict her tenant from a house, claiming she needed it for personal use—specifically, to accommodate her mother-in-law, a cancer patient who required frequent treatment in Rawalpindi/Islamabad, making travel back and forth from Wah Cantt inconvenient. The tenant argued, among other things, that a similar eviction petition had previously been filed and withdrawn, so the second petition should not be allowed without special permission, and that although the lease had expired, it had been orally extended.

The Rent Controller initially dismissed the landlord's eviction request, but an appellate court reversed this and ordered the tenant to vacate within 60 days. The tenant then challenged that decision before the Islamabad High Court.

The High Court upheld the eviction. It ruled that since the earlier petition was withdrawn without any final decision on its merits, filing a fresh petition was legally permissible. The court also clarified that under the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance, a landlord's genuine statement of personal need is generally sufficient to justify eviction, especially since the law protects tenants by allowing them to reclaim possession if the landlord doesn't actually occupy the property within six months. Additionally, since the lease had expired and wasn't formally renewed, the tenant was liable to vacate. The petition was dismissed, reinforcing landlords' rights to reclaim property for genuine family needs.

title: Non Compliance of 265-C shall vitiate Trial
explainer:
This case involved a married woman, her alleged lover, and a third person who were convicted by an Additional Sessions Judge in Multan under Pakistan's Offence of Zina (Enforcement of Hudood) Ordinance, 1979. The allegations centered on a woman accused of disguising her identity under a false name to remarry while still legally married to the original complainant, leading to charges of adultery (zina) and related fraud offences. The accused received lengthy prison sentences, whipping, and fines.

On appeal, the defense argued that the trial court had failed to follow a mandatory legal requirement: before trial, the accused should have been given copies of the complaint, witness statements, and other key documents under Section 265-C(2)(d) of the Criminal Procedure Code. This failure meant the accused couldn't properly cross-examine witnesses or prepare their defense. Notably, both the complainant's lawyer and the state prosecutor agreed that this requirement had not been met, and they consented to sending the case back for retrial.

The Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) accepted the appeal, relying on earlier Supreme Court precedent establishing that compliance with Section 265-C is mandatory, not optional - and that failing to follow it invalidates the entire trial. The court set aside the conviction and ordered a fresh trial after the missing documents are properly supplied, directing the lower court to resolve the matter within three months.

This case matters because it reinforces a fundamental fair-trial safeguard: accused persons have a legal right to see the evidence

title: New Owner Naturally Becomes Landlord
explainer:
This case concerns a landlord-tenant dispute over a shop in Jinnah Super Market, Islamabad. The new owners of the shop filed for eviction of the tenant, Nadeem Younas, claiming the lease had expired and rent had gone unpaid since 2011. They said they had bought the property from its previous owners and had notified the tenant of the change in ownership, though the tenant denied receiving such notice and disputed that any landlord-tenant relationship existed at all.

The case went through multiple rounds of proceedings, including an attempt by the tenant's son to intervene, claiming he was the actual tenant, which was rejected. Eventually the Rent Controller and the Appellate Court both ruled in favor of eviction, partly because the tenant repeatedly failed to appear and present evidence, leading to his right to cross-examine or present a defense being closed.

The Islamabad High Court dismissed the tenant's petitions. It held that when ownership of a rented property changes hands, the new owner automatically becomes the landlord, and defects in the previous ownership documents do not concern the tenant. The filing of the eviction case itself was considered sufficient notice of the change in ownership. Since the tenant continued to not pay rent during the proceedings, he was found to be a willful defaulter.

This case matters because it clarifies that tenants cannot use technical objections about ownership documents to avoid rent obligations, and that buyers of rented property step into the landlord's shoes without needing elaborate formalities.

title: Formal Preliminary Decree is mandatory at times
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between three brothers over property left by their father, a retired judge. One brother filed a suit asking the court to divide ("partition") property that had been gifted by their father to all three sons in equal shares through a registered gift deed. One brother contested the suit, while another agreed with it.

The brother challenging the suit tried to get the case thrown out by arguing that the plaintiff had not properly filed a list of witnesses as required by law. The trial court rejected this attempt and, since all parties had effectively admitted that the property was jointly owned in equal one-third shares (based on the admitted gift deed), the trial court went ahead and issued an order equivalent to a "preliminary decree" declaring the shares, without taking further evidence.

The challenging brother approached the High Court, arguing that a preliminary decree could not be passed without first recording evidence after issues were framed. The High Court disagreed, holding that when parties have already admitted the key facts (joint ownership in equal shares), no evidence needs to be recorded, and a preliminary decree can validly be passed at that stage.

However, the High Court noted one technical flaw: the trial court had not prepared a formal, properly drafted preliminary decree document. It dismissed the petition but directed the trial court to prepare this formal decree to fix that procedural gap. The case clarifies that while courts can decide partition shares based on admissions without full trials, they must still formally document the decree.

title: Suspension of Sentence on Medical Ground
explainer:
This case involved a petition before the Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) seeking suspension of sentence and bail for a convicted prisoner named Yasin, pending the outcome of his criminal appeal. Yasin had been convicted by a trial court for house-trespass and kidnapping/abduction offenses and sentenced to seven years' imprisonment and life imprisonment respectively, to run concurrently.

The petition was filed on medical grounds, as Yasin was suffering from AIDS. Two other petitioners initially named in the case, Zafar and Ashiq Hussain, were dropped from the petition by their own counsel and their case was dismissed as not pressed.

The court examined medical reports from jail and hospital doctors. These showed that Yasin's health was steadily worsening - he had lost over 15 kg in weight, suffered recurring critical episodes requiring hospital transfers, and needed continuous specialist supervision that the jail could not provide. The state opposed the petition, arguing adequate treatment was available in jail, but the court found the medical evidence persuasive.

The court accepted the petition, suspended Yasin's sentence, and ordered his release on bail with bond conditions, pending final decision of his appeal.

This judgment matters because it illustrates how courts can use their discretion under Section 426 of the Criminal Procedure Code to suspend sentences when a prisoner's serious illness cannot be adequately managed within jail facilities, balancing humanitarian medical concerns against the state's interest in enforcing pun

title: Right of cross examination in a family suit
explainer:
This case involved a family court dispute in Taunsa Sharif, where a wife, Mst. Shaheen Bibi, had filed a suit against her husband, Muhammad Irfan, for jactitation of marriage (a declaration that no valid marriage existed), or alternatively for dissolution of marriage through khula.

During the trial, the wife and one other witness gave their statements in court, but the husband's lawyer could not cross-examine them right away because he was busy in another court. The next two hearing dates were disrupted because lawyers were on strike. When the case came up again, the Family Court judge refused to let the husband's counsel cross-examine the witnesses and closed his right to do so, even though his lawyer was present in court that day.

The husband challenged this decision in the Lahore High Court, arguing the order was passed in haste and unfairly denied him a basic right. The wife's side argued he had already had enough chances and only had himself to blame.

The High Court agreed with the husband. It held that the right to cross-examine witnesses under Section 11(3) of the Family Courts Act, 1964 is a valuable legal right that cannot be taken away without strong justification. Since the delays were due to genuine reasons, not bad faith, and the lawyer was present and willing to proceed, the court struck down the Family Court's order and sent the case back, allowing cross-examination to proceed, with clear conditions to avoid further delay. This case reinforces that courts must have solid grounds before denying a party's right to cross-examine witnesses.

title: Bail Granted on 8 days delay in FIR
explainer:
This case involves two petitioners, Muhammad Imran and Muhammad Asif, who sought post-arrest bail in a theft case registered under Sections 381-A and 411 of the Pakistan Penal Code, relating to the alleged theft of a tractor. The complainant said his tractor went missing overnight while parked on a farm, but the FIR was lodged eight days after the incident without any explanation for the delay.

The petitioners were not named in the original FIR and there was no direct evidence against them. They were implicated only later, through a supplementary statement by the complainant. The court noted that recovery of the stolen property was allegedly made jointly on the pointing out of the petitioners along with a co-accused, who had already been granted bail by a lower court, a decision the complainant never challenged.

The Lahore High Court held that since the offenses did not fall under the prohibitory clause of Section 497 of the Criminal Procedure Code, bail is generally the rule rather than the exception. Given the unexplained delay in the FIR, the lack of direct evidence, the reliance on a later supplementary statement, and the fact that investigation was complete with no trial yet started, the court found the matter required further inquiry into the petitioners' guilt. It granted bail, emphasizing that denying bail indefinitely serves no real purpose for persons not yet convicted. This case illustrates how delays and weak initial evidence can support bail in non-serious offense categories.

title: Ex-Parte Decree in a Guardian case can be set-aside
explainer:
This case concerns minors whose property rights were at stake in a civil suit for specific performance of an agreement. When their father died during the lawsuit, the minors were brought into the case as his legal heirs. Since they were minors, the trial court appointed court officials, a reader and later another court employee, as their guardian ad litem, meaning someone to represent their interests in court. However, this appointed guardian failed to properly defend the minors, most critically by not cross-examining key witnesses whose testimony formed the basis of the decree against them. As a result, an ex parte decree was passed against the minors. When they later asked the trial court to set aside this decree, citing the guardian's negligence and fraud, the trial court refused.

The Lahore High Court disagreed with the trial court. It held that a guardian ad litem is a trustee of the minor's rights and must actively protect their interests. If a decree is obtained because the guardian failed in this duty, even without proving intentional fraud, the minor should not be bound by it. The court also noted it was improper to appoint a court official as guardian when the children's mother was alive and had not been properly asked whether she wished to take on that role.

The High Court therefore set aside the trial court's dismissal and ordered the ex parte decree set aside, allowing the minors to defend the case properly, with their mother's involvement. This case matters because it reinforces that courts must ensure minors are genuinely and competently represented in litigation, not just formally assigned a guardian.

title: Scope of FIR during Civil Litigation
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between two people who ran a carpet business together. One party, Muhammad Younas, claimed that a sum of money was owed to him and that an agreement to sell had been signed, and he registered a criminal case (FIR) under Section 406 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with criminal breach of trust, against Muhammad Abbas.

However, Abbas had already filed a civil suit earlier, challenging that very agreement, claiming his signature had been obtained by force. He argued that only after the complainant received court notices about this civil suit did the criminal case suddenly get registered against him, suggesting it was done to pressure him into dropping the civil case rather than because a real crime had occurred.

The Lahore High Court examined the FIR and the timeline of events and agreed that the criminal case appeared to be a tactic to turn a civil/business dispute into a criminal matter, apparently driven by bad faith and ulterior motives. While the court did not fully quash the FIR, it ruled that the criminal proceedings should be put on hold until the civil suit was finally decided.

This judgment matters because it reinforces a legal principle: when a dispute is essentially civil in nature (like unpaid debts or contested agreements) but someone tries to use criminal law as a pressure tactic, courts can pause the criminal case until the underlying civil matter is resolved, preventing misuse of the criminal justice system.

title: Judgment on Quashment by Justice Athar Min Allah
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between parties who had entered into property exchange agreements in 2012. After disagreements arose, one party filed a civil suit to stop property transfers, and shortly after, also got an FIR (criminal case) registered against the petitioners under Sections 406 and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code, accusing them of criminal breach of trust.

The petitioners asked the Islamabad High Court to quash the FIR, arguing that the underlying dispute was purely civil in nature, arising from property exchange agreements, and that the essential ingredient of criminal breach of trust, namely entrustment of property, was not even made out from the agreements themselves. They also pointed out that the FIR was filed over a year after the alleged incident and only after the civil suit had already been initiated.

The respondents opposed this, arguing that quashing an FIR is an extraordinary remedy to be used sparingly, that alternate remedies already exist under the Criminal Procedure Code for the petitioners to seek discharge at trial, and that a pending civil case does not automatically bar criminal proceedings.

The court decided not to quash the FIR itself. Instead, it held that the question of whether property was truly entrusted should be examined by the trial court, which has proper mechanisms to decide this. The High Court exercised judicial restraint, directing the petitioners to pursue alternate remedies before the trial court rather than deciding the factual dispute itself. This shows courts' cautious approach to using constitutional powers to stop criminal cases prematurely.

title: Appointment on Contract Bases Case Law
explainer:
This judgment from the Islamabad High Court deals with a challenge to the appointment of the Chairman of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR). A petitioner, who was an FBR employee, challenged two notifications: one appointing Respondent No. 1 as Chairman FBR, and another giving him additional charge as Secretary of the Revenue Division. The petitioner argued that the appointment process was flawed, non-transparent, and failed to follow objective criteria or open competition, despite the position being a key public office requiring specialized expertise in taxation and economics. He claimed the appointment violated principles of good governance, equality of opportunity, and due process under the Constitution.

The respondents raised preliminary objections, arguing the court lacked jurisdiction because service matters fall under the Federal Service Tribunal, and that the petitioner lacked standing since he wasn't personally harmed by the appointment.

The court rejected these objections, holding that the petitioner, as an FBR employee, was not a stranger to the organization and had legitimate concerns about unqualified appointments. It also noted that in matters of public interest, a petitioner need not show personal grievance.

On the merits, the court found the appointment was made through a colourable exercise of authority, lacking due process, transparency, fairness, and merit-based selection. It set aside both notifications and allowed the petition. The case highlights judicial scrutiny over appointments to important public offices and emphasizes transparency and merit in government appointments.

title: Constitutional Jurisdiction of High Court
explainer:
This case involved a petitioner who approached the Lahore High Court asking it to quash an FIR (a criminal complaint) registered against him, using the Constitution's writ jurisdiction under Article 199.

The judge did not rule on the merits of the FIR itself. Instead, he used the occasion to clarify the proper limits of the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction. He explained that the Constitution exists to provide a governing system and to protect people's fundamental rights, and that Articles 184(3) and 199 exist specifically to safeguard those rights when violated. However, this power is not meant to bypass other legal and statutory mechanisms, nor to interfere with the normal functioning of institutions like the police. Criminal investigation is a statutory police function, and the High Court is not meant to act as a "super investigator." The Court should only intervene when police authorities fail to perform their duties or exceed their powers - not immediately after an FIR is filed, as increasingly seen in many petitions rushing to court before investigation even begins.

The judge also criticized the growing trend of filing frivolous constitutional petitions that burden the High Court and delay more serious appellate and constitutional matters, reminding lawyers of their duty to avoid misusing court time.

Ultimately, the petitioner was directed to approach the Superintendent of Police (Investigation) with his grievance, rather than have the High Court intervene. The petition was disposed of accordingly.

This judgment is significant because it reinforces boundaries on when constitutional courts should intervene in police investig

title: Transaction with Pardanesheen Ladies
explainer:
This case was about a disputed land sale agreement dating back to 1966, allegedly signed by several pardanasheen (secluded, illiterate) women. A buyer sued for specific performance of the sale agreement, claiming the women had agreed to sell land to him, while later purchasers of the same land, including the appellant, disputed the validity of that original agreement.

The central legal issue was whether proper procedures had been followed in verifying that the women actually understood and consented to the transaction, as required under Section 38 of the Registration Act and prior Supreme Court precedent (Janat Bibi v. Sikander Ali). Witnesses who were supposed to confirm the women's identities and execution of the document gave contradictory or doubtful testimony, and some denied the women's signatures or thumb impressions were genuine.

The Supreme Court held that when pardanasheen women are involved in a transaction affecting their property rights, the person claiming the benefit of that transaction must affirmatively prove the women understood what they were doing and had independent advice. Since this had not been properly established, and since the lower courts had decreed the case without carefully weighing the evidence, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, overturning the earlier decisions.

This case matters because it reinforces strong legal protections for vulnerable parties, particularly illiterate or secluded women, ensuring they cannot be bound by major property transactions without clear proof of informed consent.

title: Contempt Proceedings against Chief Secretary Sindh
explainer:
This case concerns a major Supreme Court review of how civil servants were appointed, transferred, and absorbed into government service in Sindh. The petitions challenged various laws and practices, including the Chief Minister's power to appoint officers to posts like Assistant Commissioner by transfer beyond his prescribed quota, and laws allowing employees from other organizations to be "absorbed" into civil service cadres with backdated seniority, bypassing the normal competitive examination process.

The Supreme Court found these practices unconstitutional. It held that appointments made in excess of the Chief Minister's quota disrupted the legitimate seniority of officers who had earned their positions through competitive examinations, and ordered such officers reverted to their original posts. The Court also struck down legislation (including the Sindh Civil Servants Regularization of Absorption Act and related ordinances) that allowed non-civil servants to be absorbed into government service with backdated seniority without competing through proper recruitment. The judges reasoned that this deprived genuine civil servants of their constitutional rights to status and reputation, encouraged nepotism and corruption, and violated principles of equality under the Constitution.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that government appointments and promotions must follow merit-based, transparent processes rather than political patronage. It protects the rights of civil servants who qualify through proper competitive procedures and sets limits on executive power to manipulate civil service rules for favoritism, reinforcing constitutional safeguards against arbitrary governance.

title: Strong grounds are required for cancellation of bail
explainer:
This case from the Peshawar High Court dealt with a request to cancel bail that had already been granted to an accused person. The accused, Respondent No. 1, had been named in a criminal case involving allegations of theft, criminal intimidation, kidnapping, and related offences. He had been granted pre-arrest bail by a trial court. The complainant then approached the High Court asking that this bail be cancelled, arguing that the accused was specifically named in the police report, that the offences were serious in nature, and that he was still needed for further investigation.

The High Court refused to cancel the bail. It explained that cancelling bail already granted requires much stronger justification than what is needed to grant bail in the first place, since the two situations involve different legal considerations. If bail is wrongly refused, the wrongly jailed person cannot be compensated even if later found innocent, whereas if bail is wrongly granted, the situation can still be corrected through conviction after trial. The court noted there was an unexplained delay in filing the police report, no independent witnesses, no recovery of evidence from the accused, and no proof that he had misused his bail or was likely to flee, especially since he was a government servant. Simply being named in the FIR was not enough to deny bail. The petition was dismissed, reaffirming the principle that courts should rarely interfere with bail once properly granted.

title: Professional Misconduct Judgment
explainer:
This case was heard by the Tribunal of the Pakistan Bar Council and dealt with a professional misconduct complaint filed by Mst. Razia Begum against an advocate, Sardar Muhammad Ishaq.

The complainant alleged that the advocate had charged large sums of money from her family for arranging her son's marriage at his own residence, for filing a restitution of conjugal rights case, and for defending her son in a criminal case under the Hudood Ordinance. She also claimed he secretly took money from the opposing party and gave bad advice that harmed her son's interests, eventually leading to a divorce.

The Tribunal examined the evidence and found that most allegations, including claims that the advocate was bribed by the opposing side or deliberately mishandled the case, were not proven. However, it did find two things established: first, that the advocate had allowed his own home to be used for the marriage and had charged a fee of Rs. 10,000 for this, which was improper; and second, that he had acted as defense counsel in the Hudood case despite being himself a prosecution witness in that same case, a clear conflict of interest he should have avoided from the start.

Based on these findings, the Tribunal reprimanded the advocate, ordered him to pay Rs. 12,000 in costs to the complainant (including reimbursement of the improperly charged fee), and directed that the reprimand be recorded in the official rolls of advocates. The case highlights the importance of lawyers avoiding conflicts of interest and acting with transparency regarding fees.

title: Proceedings for attachment of Property
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute between co-sharers (described as sisters and their representatives) who were fighting over possession of a house in Kotli. After police reported possible breach of peace, a magistrate attached (took control of) the disputed property under Section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code, appointing a receiver to manage it. This order was upheld by the Sessions Judge but later challenged before the High Court, which quashed it. The matter then reached the Supreme Court of Azad Jammu and Kashmir.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeal. It found that the magistrate had attached the property without properly applying his mind or following the legal requirements of Section 145. The police report did not show any real emergency justifying attachment, and the magistrate failed to hold a proper inquiry before acting. The court also noted that since the magistrate had already taken action to prevent breach of peace under separate provisions (Sections 107, 150, 151), that concern had effectively been addressed, making the attachment unnecessary. Additionally, the court observed that when a civil court is already handling a property dispute, criminal attachment proceedings become largely unnecessary, since civil courts have broader powers to protect property during litigation.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that magistrates cannot attach property as a matter of routine or convenience, they must genuinely assess whether an emergency exists, and it clarifies the relationship between civil and criminal proceedings over the same property dispute.

title: Presumption of Correctness: Article 100 of QSO
explainer:
This case concerns a long-running property dispute over a small house in Charsadda, District Peshawar, involving competing claims based on a gift deed and inheritance rights.

Muhammad Israr claimed ownership of the house through a registered gift deed, allegedly executed in his favour by his maternal grandmother, Mst. Kishwara, in 1997. Jehanzeb and other relatives disputed this, arguing the house actually belonged to one Masaib Shah and should be divided among his legal heirs according to Islamic inheritance shares. After multiple rounds of litigation, including a case reopened under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code due to procedural irregularities, the trial court ruled in favour of Jehanzeb and the heirs, but the appellate court reversed this and upheld Israr's claim based on the gift deed.

The Peshawar High Court, hearing a revision petition, examined whether old or registered documents automatically deserve a "presumption of correctness" under Article 100 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order (Pakistan's law of evidence). The Court held that merely being registered or old does not automatically prove a document's authenticity, especially when its execution is seriously challenged. The beneficiary of such a document must still prove it was properly executed, including requirements like offer, acceptance, and delivery of possession for a valid gift. Since Israr failed to produce key witnesses or sufficiently prove these elements, the High Court found the appellate court's reasoning flawed.

title: Personal guarantee of a dead person cannot be used against his legal heirs
explainer:
This case is about whether a bank can recover a loan guarantee from the heirs of a man who had personally guaranteed a company's debt but died before the bank filed its recovery suit.

Meezan Bank sued Focus Apparels and others for recovery of over 84 million rupees under a finance agreement. One of the guarantors, Defendant No. 3, had died before the suit was filed, so his name was removed from the case. The bank then asked the court to add his legal heirs as defendants, arguing that the guarantee document itself stated his successors would be liable after his death, and that under the law, death of a surety only ends a guarantee if there is no agreement saying otherwise.

The heirs argued they never knew about any such guarantee, were not parties to it, and that a personal guarantee is a personal obligation that should not automatically pass on to them.

The Sindh High Court agreed with the heirs. It held that a personal guarantee is tied to the individual who gave it and does not bind his legal heirs, since no contract existed between the bank and the heirs themselves. The court also noted that no demand or legal proceeding had been initiated against the guarantor during his lifetime, and the guarantee was effectively revoked by his death. The bank's application to add the heirs was therefore dismissed.

The case matters because it clarifies that banks cannot automatically pursue the heirs of a deceased guarantor for debts unless those heirs had separately agreed to take on that liability.

title: No inheritance of wife if she dies first
explainer:
This case was about who should inherit the land of a deceased man, Muhammad Razaq. After his death in 1982, a mutation (official land record change) listed his wife, daughter, and sister as his legal heirs. However, the petitioners, who were other relatives claiming a share of the inheritance, argued that the wife and daughter had actually disappeared 16-17 years earlier and their whereabouts were unknown, meaning they were presumably already dead before Muhammad Razaq died. If that were true, they would not be entitled to inherit from him, since a person cannot inherit from someone who outlives them.

The respondents countered that the wife and daughter were alive, pointing to a power of attorney document supposedly signed by them in favor of a third relative after the husband's death.

The Lahore High Court found serious problems with this power of attorney document, including inconsistent dates suggesting it had been fabricated or manufactured after the fact. Because the document was unreliable, the Court held that the respondents had failed to prove the wife and daughter were actually alive at the time of the husband's death. The Court ruled that a wife who dies before her husband cannot inherit from him. Since the respondents could not prove the women were alive, the petition was allowed, meaning the lower courts' decisions were overturned in favor of the petitioners.

title: Judgment on construction of Signal Free Junction
explainer:

title: All owners in Shamlat Deh land are necessary party to the suit
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute over forest land in Village Sehr Mandi, District Kotli, which was originally government-owned "crown land" (Khalsa Sarkaar). A plaintiff, Muhammad Sabir, claimed that this land had been converted into communal village land (Shamlat Deh) through a mutation entry, and that forest department entries in the revenue record claiming the land as forest were wrong. In 2000, the trial court issued a consent decree in favor of Sabir and another person, declaring them owners. The Forest Department and other parties appealed, and the appellate court set aside this consent decree and sent the case back for fresh trial. Both sides then approached the High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision to overturn the consent decree. It found that such decrees transferring crown land or Shamlat Deh land through sale, gift, or private compromise, without including all necessary parties, are not valid in law. It also noted that disputes about correcting revenue records concerning crown land fall outside the jurisdiction of civil courts. Importantly, the court held that when crown land becomes village common land (Shamlat Deh), all landowners of that village are necessary parties to any suit concerning it—not just select individuals. Since the original case excluded other village landowners, the decree could not stand. This ruling reinforces protections against improper private deals over public and communal land.

title: No maintenance to wife if she doesnt wish to live with perfect husband
explainer:
This case from the Peshawar High Court dealt with a woman who sought dissolution of her marriage, return of dowry items, and maintenance allowance shortly after her wedding in 2008. The marriage was never consummated. The trial court dissolved the marriage through khula (a wife-initiated divorce) because she could not prove that her husband was cruel or impotent, but she had expressed extreme hatred toward him and an unwillingness to continue living with him. Since she was the one refusing to fulfill marital obligations, the court denied her maintenance allowance. The trial court also ordered return of her dowry articles but did not require her to return gold ornaments given to her at the time of rukhsati (sending the bride to the groom's house). On appeal, the appellate court ordered that the gold ornaments be returned to the husband, since in a khula divorce where the wife is ending the marriage without fault on the husband's part, he is entitled to recover what was given as dower.

The High Court upheld both the khula divorce and the return of the gold to the husband. It reasoned that when a wife says she cannot live within the bounds set by God due to hatred for her husband, courts must grant khula even without an explicit plea, and in such cases it is fair for the husband to recover the dower he gave. This case clarifies that courts can grant khula based on the wife's expressed hatred alone, but that such wives who aren't at fault-free may lose both maintenance and retained dower.

title: Burden of Proof in case of non custom paid vehicle
explainer:
This case is about a Mitsubishi Pajero Jeep that was stopped in Quetta in 1999 because its chassis number appeared to have been tampered with. Customs officials, acting on intelligence, seized the vehicle after examination suggested it had been smuggled into the country and its chassis number altered to avoid detection. The Additional Collector of Customs ordered the vehicle confiscated, and this decision was upheld by the Customs Appellate Tribunal. The vehicle's possessor then challenged this before the Balochistan High Court.

The main legal question was who bears the burden of proving a vehicle was legally imported: the customs authorities, or the person possessing the vehicle. The applicant argued customs had failed to prove the vehicle was fake or smuggled, and also claimed the show-cause notice was issued late.

The High Court rejected both arguments. It held that under Section 187 of the Customs Act, 1969, once someone is found in possession of goods and a question arises about lawful authority or import, it is that person's responsibility to prove they lawfully imported the item and paid applicable customs duties and taxes - not the other way around. The court also found that the notice had in fact been issued within the legally required time frame. As a result, the confiscation order was upheld, and the reference was decided against the applicant.

This case is significant because it clarifies that individuals possessing vehicles suspected of being smuggled must prove legal ownership and importation, rather than requiring customs authorities to prove illegality.

title: What are the Functions of Justice of Peace?
citation: PLD 1960 SC (Pak) 85; Shahnaz Begum v. The Hon'ble
explainer:
This Lahore High Court judgment explains the role and powers of a "Justice of the Peace" and "ex-officio Justice of the Peace" under Pakistan's Criminal Procedure Code, particularly sections 22, 22-A, 22-B and 25. The court traced the historical origins of the concept from England, noting that while some countries gave Justices of the Peace judicial powers over minor cases, in the Indo-Pak subcontinent their role remained limited because an elaborate system of Magistrates already existed to handle judicial matters.

The court clarified that in Pakistan today, an ordinary Justice of the Peace can make certain arrests, call on police for help in preventing crime, and certify or attest documents, but mainly serves as an assistant to the police in keeping peace. An ex-officio Justice of the Peace, which includes Sessions Judges, has the additional power (added in 2002) to direct police on complaints about refusal to register a case, transferring an investigation, or police neglect or misconduct.

Crucially, the court held that none of these powers are judicial in nature. They are purely administrative and ministerial functions, not an exercise of judicial authority to dispense justice.

This matters because it clarifies the limits of what Justices of the Peace can legally do, preventing them from overstepping into judicial territory and ensuring the proper separation between administrative assistance to police and actual judicial decision-making.

title: Shahbaz Sharif's Case Judgment
explainer:
This case involved a legal challenge over whether Mian Muhammad Shahbaz Sharif could validly contest and hold office as Chief Minister of Punjab, based on questions about his qualifications under the Constitution and election laws. A citizen had raised objections during the nomination process, arguing that Shahbaz Sharif had made statements prejudicial to the judiciary's independence and had submitted an incorrect declaration, which could disqualify him under Articles 62 and 63 of the Constitution. These objections went through the Election Tribunal and Election Commission, and eventually to the Lahore High Court, which ruled in his favor and allowed him to continue functioning as Chief Minister. The Federation and others then challenged that High Court decision before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court examined technical questions about election law, particularly the difference between two provisions, Section 14(5) and Section 14(5-A), of the Representation of the People Act, 1976. It held that ordinary citizens have the right to bring information about a candidate's disqualification to an Election Tribunal, that such challenges are not bound by the strict time limits meant only for formal appeals, and that the word source in the law covers both individuals and organizations. The Court also confirmed that a citizen could challenge a candidate's qualifications through a writ petition even before elections were completed. Ultimately, the Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's reasoning and upheld its decision, reinforcing accountability and transparency in the electoral process.

title: Are the employees of Statutory Corporation entitled for promotion?
explainer:
This case was about whether Telephone Operators working in Pakistan Telecommunication Company Ltd (PTCL), a statutory corporation, were entitled to promotion from BPS-8 to BPS-11. A group of employees had been denied promotion despite meeting educational and experience requirements they believed qualified them, while a colleague in a similar position, Muhammad Akram, had earlier won a case before the same tribunal and was granted the promotion, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court.

The employees argued that PTCL's own notifications from 1992, 1995, and 1997 set out clear rules for promotion to BPS-11, and that these rules applied to all Telephone Operators across the company's system, not just those working in specific overseas exchanges. They contended that since Akram had been granted relief, they deserved the same treatment under identical rules.

The Federal Service Tribunal examined the relevant notifications and found that promotion to BPS-11 was indeed available to Telephone Operators throughout the PTCL system, based on either experience and qualifications for promotion, or separately through direct recruitment limited to overseas exchange postings requiring graduate qualifications and an English test. The tribunal directed PTCL to re-examine all the appellants' cases under this interpretation and decide on their eligibility for promotion within six months.

This case matters because it clarifies that employees of statutory corporations can claim promotion rights created by internal company notifications, and that such rights must be applied consistently across similarly situated staff.

title: Oral Gift by the Plaintiff

title: When complaint for illegal dispossession is not competent
explainer:
This case was about a woman, Mst. Neelam Parveen, who filed a criminal complaint claiming she had been illegally dispossessed of land that belonged to her late husband. She said she stayed connected to the property until 1995, after which the accused persons took it over with the help of the land's previous owners. The accused, on the other hand, claimed they were genuine buyers of the land, having purchased it through a properly sanctioned mutation (an official land transfer record).

The Lahore High Court examined whether this dispute could be pursued as a criminal complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, which is meant to punish land grabbers and criminals who forcibly dispossess people of their property. The court found that this was essentially a civil property dispute, not a criminal matter of forcible dispossession. Importantly, the complainant herself admitted she was not in physical possession of the land, which contradicted her claim that she was forcibly dispossessed. Since the accused held a valid mutation and did not fit the profile of land grabbers or criminals targeted by the Act, the court ruled that the proper remedy was to file a civil suit to reclaim ownership or possession, not a criminal complaint.

The court dismissed her petition, finding no legal error in the lower court's decision. This case clarifies that the Illegal Dispossession Act is meant for genuine criminal land-grabbing, not for resolving ordinary ownership or title disputes, which belong in civil courts.
