title: Sanctity of DNA test under the law
explainer:
This is an explainer of a Lahore High Court decision from 2008 dealing with how Pakistani law treats DNA testing when a father disputes his child's legitimacy.

In this case, a mother and her minor son filed a maintenance suit against the father, who denied the child was his and asked the Family Court to order a DNA test. The Family Court refused, and the father challenged that refusal before the High Court.

The High Court dismissed the father's petition. It held that legitimacy of a child is a serious matter with far-reaching consequences and cannot be decided casually. Under Pakistani law, a child born within a lawful marriage is presumed legitimate, following the principle that the "child follows the bed." A father cannot defeat this presumption through mere denial or accusation; he must provide solid proof and credible evidence, or pursue the formal legal procedure known as Liyan (a special court process for disowning paternity), which the father in this case had not done.

Since there was no real evidence to support the father's claim that the child was illegitimate, the court ruled the child, born during the marriage, must be treated as legitimate and was entitled to maintenance from the father.

This judgment matters because it shows that Pakistani courts protect children's legitimacy strongly, requiring solid legal grounds and proper procedure—not just a father's unsupported denial or a DNA test request—before paternity can be challenged.

title: Case of a girl raped by Father
explainer:
This case, decided by the Federal Shariat Court (2012 YLR 847), involved an appeal by a man named Zulfiqar Ali against his conviction for raping his own daughter.

The victim testified that her father had sexually assaulted her on three occasions. She did not report the crime immediately, explaining that she feared the consequences for her father and was conscious of her family's honour, only going to the police once she could no longer bear his behaviour. The court found her testimony credible and consistent, noting she had complained to her mother each time the abuse occurred. Her account was backed up by medical evidence, a Chemical Examiner's report, and DNA evidence. There was no evidence suggesting she had a bad reputation or ulterior motive, and the court dismissed the defence's claim that she was involved with another man as baseless and unsubstantiated.

The court held that a delay in filing a police report does not automatically weaken a prosecution's case if the delay is reasonably explained and other evidence is strong. It emphasized that a daughter would not fabricate such a serious accusation against her own father without real cause. Given the severity of the crime, the court ruled that the father deserved exemplary punishment and upheld his conviction and sentence.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that courts should sensitively consider the psychological and social pressures victims of familial sexual abuse face, rather than treating delayed reporting as automatically suspicious.

title: What if name of accused in column no 2 of challan
explainer:
This case involved a man accused of murder under sections 302, 34, and 109 of the Pakistan Penal Code, arising from a violent incident during a village meeting where two people were shot dead. The complainant's original FIR named the petitioner as one of the shooters, firing at one of the deceased.

However, several things undermined the prosecution's case. The complainant kept changing and expanding his account over time, giving fresh statements that added more and more accused, eventually implicating 17 people in a later complaint, while the deceased's brother filed a separate complaint naming 12 accused. This inconsistency raised doubts about the reliability of the allegations.

More importantly, six different police officers investigated the case at various stages, and each one independently concluded that the petitioner was not present at the scene and was innocent. Based on this, the police placed his name in Column No. 2 of the police report (challan), meaning he was not recommended for prosecution despite being named in the FIR.

The Lahore High Court held that while police opinions are not admissible as evidence in court, they are still relevant when deciding bail, especially since the police report is the basis on which courts take cognizance of a case. Given the repeated findings of innocence and the inconsistent complainant versions, the court ruled this was a case requiring further inquiry and granted the petitioner bail, setting surety at Rs. 50,000.

title: How to deal with a case of unseen occurrence?
explainer:
This case involved two men, Tahir Mehmood and Sajid Ali alias Sajjad Ali Munna, convicted by a trial court in Jhang for murdering two women, Mst. Ferhat Bibi and her maid Mst. Hajran Bibi, and for robbery. Both were sentenced to life imprisonment for murder and additional rigorous imprisonment for robbery. They appealed to the Federal Shariat Court challenging their convictions.

title: Burden of Proof in case of benami transactions
explainer:
This case was about a husband, Din Muhammad Wagan, who claimed that properties registered in the name of his deceased wife, Mst. Farkhanda Khatoon, actually belonged to him alone. He said these were "benami" transactions, meaning the properties were bought with his own money but registered in his wife's name only for convenience, while he remained the real owner. After his wife died, her sister, Mst. Rashida Khatoon, claimed a share in the properties as a legal heir. The husband sued to have the court declare him the true owner of several properties, a bank locker's contents, and a loan receivable, and to block his sister-in-law from claiming any share.

The Sindh High Court ruled against the husband. It held that in benami claims, the burden of proof lies on the person asserting that the property, though registered in someone else's name, was actually bought with his own funds. The court found that all the documents were in the wife's name, and the husband failed to provide any evidence that he had actually paid for the properties from his own resources. Because he could not prove the benami claim, the properties were treated as genuinely belonging to the wife. As her legal heirs, her sister was entitled to inherit half the share, while the husband would inherit the remaining half as her surviving spouse.

This case matters because it clarifies that merely claiming a transaction is benami is not enough—concrete proof of payment and intent is required, protecting the inheritance rights of other legal heirs.

title: Suit for recovery of dowry articles
explainer:
This case involved a husband, Muhammad Imran, who challenged where his wife's lawsuit for recovery of dowry articles was being heard. After a family court in Bahawalpur had already decided the couple's divorce case and rejected the wife's maintenance claim, a separate suit by the wife to recover her dowry items remained pending in the same court. The husband argued that the Bahawalpur court had no territorial jurisdiction to hear this dowry suit, claiming his wife actually belonged to Khanewal district, where the marriage had also taken place. The family court rejected his objection, and he then approached the Lahore High Court to overturn that decision.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It explained that under a 2002 amendment to the Family Courts law, along with the Family Courts Rules, a wife is entitled to file a suit for recovery of dowry articles in the family court located wherever she ordinarily resides, regardless of where the marriage occurred or where dissolution and dower cases are filed. The court also noted the husband had not objected to the same court's jurisdiction when it handled the earlier divorce and maintenance cases, making his sudden objection in the dowry case inconsistent.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that family courts must prioritize convenience for wives seeking recovery of dowry items, allowing them to sue in their own place of residence rather than forcing them to travel to where the marriage was performed.

title: Orally gifted property in Nikahnama doesn't require registration
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over whether property pledged as surety in a court case could actually be seized to pay off a debt, given that it had earlier been given away as a gift through a marriage contract.

A man named Muhammad Hafeez stood as surety for someone else's debt, offering a house as security. When the debt wasn't repaid, the court ordered the property attached and sold to satisfy the decree. However, Hafeez's wife objected, arguing the house was not his to pledge because he had already given it to her at the time of their marriage, as recorded in their Nikahnama (marriage contract), in lieu of her dower rights. The trial court rejected her objection and allowed the attachment to proceed.

On appeal, the Lahore High Court sided with the wife. It held that an entry in a Nikahnama recording the transfer of property to the wife is sufficient legal proof of that transfer, and no separate registration or additional documentation is needed to make the gift valid. Since the husband had already given up his ownership rights over the property before offering it as surety, he had no legal right to pledge it, and the property could not be attached for the debt.

This ruling matters because it confirms that property gifted to a wife through a Nikahnama is legally hers, protecting such transfers from being treated as still belonging to the husband, including shielding them from his creditors or legal obligations.

title: Limitation in case of Shufa
explainer:
This case concerned a dispute over the right of pre-emption, a legal right that allows certain persons, such as co-sharers or neighbors, to buy property before it is sold to someone else, or to claim it after sale by filing a lawsuit within a strict time limit.

The petitioner, claiming superior pre-emption rights as a co-sharer and neighbor, filed a suit for possession of land that had been sold to Respondent No. 3 through a registered sale-deed dated 28.12.2005. He argued he only learned of the sale on 19.07.2006 because the vendee kept it secret, and since the Revenue Officer never issued the notice required under Section 31 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1991, the four-month limitation period should run from his date of knowledge rather than the registration date. His suit, filed 31.07.2006, would then be within time.

The trial court initially agreed, but the Additional District Judge reversed this on revision, rejecting the plaint as time-barred. The Lahore High Court upheld that decision. It ruled that under Section 30 of the Act, the limitation period starts from the date of registration of the sale-deed itself, which is treated as public notice. Section 31's notice requirement is a separate, independent provision and failure to issue it does not extend the limitation period. Since the suit was filed more than four months after registration, it was rightly dismissed as time-barred.

title: Jurisdiction of High Courts to issue writs
explainer:
This case concerns a petition filed in the Lahore High Court by a citizen who wanted a criminal investigation transferred from one police officer to another. He approached the High Court under Article 199 of the Constitution, which allows courts to issue writs such as directions, declarations, habeas corpus, or quo warranto.

The court dismissed the petition at the outset. It explained that before a High Court can use its special constitutional powers under Article 199, it must be satisfied that no other adequate legal remedy exists. This is a basic requirement, not optional. In this case, the petitioner had another clear remedy: if unhappy with how an investigation was being conducted, he could complain to a higher-ranking police officer, since the police force has its own internal hierarchy under the Police Act and Rules to handle such matters.

The judge also explained the legal framework governing police investigations under the Criminal Procedure Code, noting that investigating crimes is the statutory duty and right of the police, not something courts should interfere with except in limited circumstances. Quoting earlier Privy Council and Supreme Court rulings, the judge stressed that courts and police perform complementary but separate functions, and that courts stepping into police investigation work would disrupt the proper functioning of the justice system.

This judgment matters because it reinforces the principle that constitutional writ jurisdiction is a last resort, not a substitute for available administrative remedies, and that police investigations should generally proceed without premature judicial interference.

title: Every Corporation is liable to pay tax
explainer:
This case involved a government irrigation department (Lower Jehlum Canal Quarry Sub-Division) that supplied stones for flood protection and development works to other parts of the Irrigation Department in Punjab. It had been filing sales tax returns and paying sales tax for years. After an audit covering 2001 to 2005, the tax department found that the division had been miscalculating its sales tax by failing to include royalty, excise duty and other incidental charges in its tax base, as required by law. A tax demand of over one crore rupees was raised, and this was upheld by lower appellate forums.

The petitioner argued it was really just an arm of the Provincial Government, operating on a no-profit, no-loss basis, so it should not be taxed like a commercial entity. The Lahore High Court rejected this argument. It held that Article 165-A of the Constitution makes clear that government-owned or controlled corporations and bodies are still separate legal entities liable to tax on their income or business activities, regardless of who ultimately benefits from that income. The court also noted the petitioner's own conduct, filing returns and seeking a tax exemption, contradicted its claim of being exempt. However, the court did limit the tax department's power by ruling that under Section 36(2) of the Sales Tax Act, notices could only be issued for the three years before the notice, not further back.

The case confirms that government-linked entities cannot escape sales tax merely by claiming to be part of the state, while also protecting taxpayers from open-ended retrospective tax claims beyond the statutory limitation period.

title: Divorce Happens even when legal requirements are not met properly
explainer:
This case involved a husband working in Germany and his wife in Pakistan, who sued for maintenance allowance for herself and their son, and for her dower money. The wife claimed her husband had stopped supporting them after moving abroad and had hidden the fact that he was already married with children in Germany. The husband argued he had divorced her in March 2000 under Islamic law, and so owed nothing further.

The Family Court ruled in the wife's favor, ordering him to pay maintenance for her during her iddat period (the waiting period after divorce) and for the child until custody changed. On appeal, the wife's claim was extended to cover the period from 1997 to 2000. The husband then challenged these decisions before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions. It noted that the husband himself admitted in his written statement that he had divorced his wife without notifying the local Union Council Chairman, as legally required under the Muslim Family Law Ordinance, 1961. Despite this procedural lapse, the divorce was still treated as having taken effect, triggering the wife's entitlement to maintenance through her iddat period. The court also found the husband had substantial financial resources, including property and foreign benefits, making the maintenance amount reasonable rather than excessive.

This case matters because it illustrates that a divorce can be recognized as valid in practice even when the legal notification requirement is not fulfilled, while still carrying financial obligations like maintenance and dower for the wife.

title: A dismissed Petition can be restored
explainer:
This case was about whether an election petition that had been dismissed because the petitioner failed to appear in court could later be restored and heard on its merits.

Syed Fakhar Imam had filed an election petition, but it was dismissed on 20 June 2008 when neither he nor his lawyer was present, due to a mix-up about when the case would be called by the Tribunal. He then applied for restoration, explaining through affidavits that his counsel had been misinformed about the timing and had come to court both before and after the case was actually taken up.

The key legal question was whether the Election Tribunal, under the Representation of the People Act, 1976, had the power to restore a petition dismissed in default, even though the Act does not expressly provide for this. The petitioner's lawyers argued that since the Tribunal has all the powers of a civil court, and since general legal principles allow courts to do what is necessary to further justice even without express provision, restoration should be permitted. They also argued the petition could not have been validly dismissed under Section 76 because the trial had not yet begun.

The Tribunal accepted these arguments, noting the returned candidate never contested the restoration application despite being served, the explanation for the absence was genuine, the petition for restoration was filed promptly, and the case was still at an early stage. The petition was restored, confirming that Election Tribunals can revive dismissed election petitions when there are genuine and sufficient reasons, protecting litigants from losing their case over procedural mishaps.

title: Controversial Judgment of Iftikhar Chodhary Regarding Master and Servant Doctrine
explainer:
This Supreme Court decision dealt with a series of appeals by Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (PTCL) against rulings from several High Courts that had ordered reinstatement of employees or granted them benefits like the Voluntary Separation Scheme after their contracts were terminated or they were otherwise let go.

The central legal question was whether PTCL, a partly privatized company (with the federal government still holding a majority 62% stake), could be taken to court through constitutional petitions, and whether its employees had enforceable statutory rights or were simply governed by ordinary contract law, known as the "master and servant" principle.

The Supreme Court held that since the government retained majority ownership, PTCL remained subject to the High Courts' constitutional jurisdiction. However, because PTCL had no statutory service rules, its employment relationships were governed by ordinary master-servant principles rather than public law protections. This meant contract employees had no vested right to continued employment or regularization once their contracts ended; the employer had discretion to end their service, subject only to standard notice requirements under labor law. The Court set aside the High Court judgments that had reinstated employees, ruling that such terminations were lawful, though affected employees remained entitled to one month's notice or pay in lieu, as applicable to workmen.

This judgment matters because it clarified the limits of judicial protection for employees of partially privatized state enterprises lacking formal statutory service rules.

title: Can trial court recall its own order
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute where a buyer sued a seller for specific performance of a sale agreement after the seller allegedly failed to complete the sale. During proceedings, the seller's representative made a statement conceding the case, but the seller later changed his position, disputed the authority of his attorney, and sought to be added as a party to contest the matter on merits. The trial court initially accepted the seller's applications, which the buyer challenged. Later, the trial court actually signed and announced a judgment decreeing the suit in the buyer's favor based on a compromise statement, but then, on the very same day, recalled its own judgment.

The Lahore High Court held that once a judge signs and pronounces a judgment, the court becomes functus officio, meaning it loses the authority to alter or recall that judgment on its own. The proper procedure would have been to file an appeal or a formal review, not for the trial court to simply reverse itself on a verbal request. The court also found that the seller's conduct did not amount to an unconditional admission, so Order XII Rule 6 of the Civil Procedure Code, which allows courts to decree cases based on clear admissions, did not strictly apply. The High Court ruled that the matter required proper evidence and formal issues to be framed, and sent the case back to the trial court for a fresh decision on merits. This case clarifies that courts cannot casually undo their own final orders after pronouncing them.

title: Writ Petition by Civil Medical Officer
explainer:
This case involved a government doctor, a Civil Medical Officer at Sheikh Zaid Hospital in Muzaffarabad, who wanted to pursue specialized training in pulmonology at a medical college in Abbottabad. He had obtained a no-objection certificate from that institution, but the health department rejected his application to be released for this training. He challenged this rejection through a writ petition filed in the Azad Jammu and Kashmir High Court.

The court dismissed the petition on two main grounds. First, the petitioner had failed to include the Director Health Services, the official who actually issued the rejection order, as a party to the case. The court held that a writ cannot be issued when a necessary party has not been included in the proceedings. Second, and more fundamentally, the court ruled that since the petitioner was a civil servant, challenges to orders affecting his terms and conditions of service could not be brought through a constitutional writ petition at all. Such matters fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Service Tribunal, not the High Court. The court relied on a Supreme Court of Pakistan precedent establishing that any order affecting an employee's service conditions, whether a general policy or an individual decision, qualifies as a departmental order that must be challenged before the appropriate Service Tribunal.

This case matters because it reinforces an important jurisdictional principle: civil servants seeking to contest decisions about their employment, training, or deputation must use the specialized Service Tribunal system rather than filing writ petitions directly in the High Court.

title: Fugitive from law loses some of his rights
explainer:
This case involved a bail application before the Peshawar High Court by a man named Azizur Rehman, who was accused of murdering Suleman Shah. According to the First Information Report, the complainant, the victim's mother, witnessed the accused shoot her son with a pistol in broad daylight during a confrontation rooted in a pre-existing blood feud between the families. The accused had already been refused bail twice by lower courts and approached the High Court seeking the same relief.

His lawyers argued there was a delay in filing the police report, that medical evidence contradicted the complainant's account, that no independent witnesses existed, and that a separate police report suggested the killing may have resulted from crossfire between rival groups since the victim was allegedly a drug dealer.

The court rejected these arguments. It found the complainant's account direct, consistent, and supported by physical evidence like a bullet casing and bloodstains. It also noted that the alternative police theory was unsupported by actual evidence and that courts are not bound to accept police claims at face value. Significantly, the accused had evaded arrest for over a year, was declared a proclaimed offender, and the trial had already begun with witnesses testifying in his absence.

The court held that a person who flees from the law loses certain normal legal protections, and bail can be refused simply because of this absconding, regardless of the case's other merits. The bail petition was dismissed.

title: Revision Petition in Bhoja Air Case
explainer:
This case arose from the tragic crash of Bhoja Air flight B4-213 on 20 April 2012 near Islamabad, in which all 127 people on board, including crew, died. Two FIRs were registered over the incident, initially citing Section 302 of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder/qatl-e-amd) along with other offences. Before framing charges, the trial court examined whether the accused should face trial under Section 302 (murder) or the lesser charge of Section 322 (qatl-bis-sabab, causing death indirectly through an act), and concluded that only Section 322 applied. The complainant challenged this decision before the Islamabad High Court.

The High Court did not decide which section ultimately applied. Instead, it found that the trial court's order lacked proper reasoning. The judgment emphasizes a long-standing principle from Pakistani case law that any judicial decision must clearly state the points for determination, the decision itself, and the reasons supporting it, especially important material like the official Commission report that had held the airline responsible for endangering passengers' lives. Without such reasoning, an order is merely administrative, not a valid judicial verdict.

Because the trial court's order fell short of this standard, the High Court set it aside and sent the matter back for fresh determination, directing the trial court to properly consider all evidence and hear both sides again. This case highlights the judiciary's insistence on reasoned decisions, particularly in matters involving mass casualties and serious criminal liability.

title: Fake Bank Accounts Case
explainer:
This Supreme Court case deals with the "Fake Bank Accounts" scandal, in which the Court took up the matter on its own initiative (suo motu) under Article 184(3) of the Constitution after reports surfaced of numerous fictitious bank accounts allegedly used for money laundering, bribes, kickbacks, and other illegal financial dealings involving large sums of money.

The Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) identified individuals and companies, including the Omni Group, linked to these accounts. A Joint Investigation Team (JIT) was formed because specialized expertise in banking, corporate transactions, and cyber-tracing of funds was needed—expertise the FIA alone lacked. The JIT's investigation implicated several high-profile individuals, including Bilawal Bhutto Zardari and Murad Ali Shah, whose names were placed on the Exit Control List, along with others like Hussain Lawai, who was arrested.

The Court found that the funds had been layered through fake accounts to hide the real beneficiaries and legitimize questionable money. title: Suit for Recovery of Marriage Expenses
explainer:
This case was about whether a father is legally required to pay for his daughter's wedding expenses, in addition to her regular maintenance.

A man divorced his wife, and their daughter grew up in her mother's custody. When the daughter got married, the mother paid Rs. 300,000 for the wedding and then sued the father to recover this amount. A Family Court ordered him to pay Rs. 150,000, and an appellate court reduced this to Rs. 100,000. The father challenged this in the Lahore High Court, arguing that since he had regularly paid maintenance for his daughter until her marriage, he should not have to pay additional marriage expenses.

The Lahore High Court dismissed his petition and upheld the Rs. 100,000 award. The court explained that under Islamic law, "maintenance" is not limited to just food, clothing, and shelter but also covers other necessary expenses for a person's wellbeing, including education, medical costs, and marriage expenses. A father's duty to maintain his daughter continues until she marries, and this includes helping bear reasonable marriage costs according to his financial means. The court also noted the father had successfully supported five other daughters from an earlier marriage without hardship, so the amount ordered was not excessive given his financial status.

This judgment matters because it clarifies that a Muslim father's financial responsibility toward his daughter extends beyond routine living expenses to include contributing to her wedding costs, reinforcing protections for daughters under family law.

title: Recovery of Minor Children through Habeas Corpus
explainer:
This case concerns a mother's petition before the Lahore High Court seeking the recovery of her two minor children, a daughter and a son, from the custody of their paternal uncle and grandmother. She alleged that after her husband disappeared (following an abduction in 1997), his relatives took her dowry items and the children away to Rawalpindi, later pressured her to marry her brother-in-law, and threw her out without the children when she refused.

The respondents countered that they took responsibility for the mother and children after the husband's disappearance, enrolled the children in good schools, paid for their education, and that the children were thriving and happy in their care. They also noted that a separate guardianship case was already pending before the Guardian Court.

The court examined the facts and concluded that the children had not been forcibly or recently snatched from the mother, were not in illegal or unsafe custody, and were doing well academically while being cared for affectionately by their grandmother and uncle. It held that habeas corpus petitions under Section 491 of the Criminal Procedure Code are meant for emergency situations involving illegal custody or danger to a child's life, not for resolving ordinary custody disputes. The final determination of custody and the children's welfare, the court ruled, must be made by the Guardian Judge. The petition was therefore dismissed, leaving the custody matter to the pending guardianship proceedings.

title: Suit for Cancellation of Partition
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land in Quetta district. The plaintiffs (respondents in this petition) had filed a suit seeking declaration, cancellation of partition, transfer of mutation, specific performance, and related relief, claiming their predecessor had purchased the disputed land through a 1995 agreement that was never fully acted upon, leaving the property still recorded in the name of the defendants predecessor.

The defendant (petitioner here) asked the trial court to reject the plaint outright under Order VII Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code, arguing the agreements did not match the property's survey numbers and that disputes over revenue record entries could only be handled by revenue authorities, not civil courts. The trial court agreed and rejected the plaint. On appeal, the appellate court overturned that decision and sent the case back for a full trial. The defendant then challenged that reversal before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision, dismissing the defendant's petitions. It held that a plaint can only be rejected if it is clearly barred by law based on its own contents, not by considering the defendant's objections or the merits of the case. Since genuine, serious factual disputes existed, particularly about ownership and the authenticity of the agreement, these could only be resolved through evidence and a proper trial, not by dismissing the case at the outset. The ruling reinforces that civil courts have jurisdiction to protect legal rights and that factual disputes must go to trial rather than be cut short procedurally.

title: Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act 2013 explained in a Judgment
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between separated parents over their minor child, Kian Munir. The mother filed a petition under the Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act, 2013, alleging domestic abuse, and the Magistrate issued a notice directing the father to produce the child in court. The father challenged this order, arguing that the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction and that custody matters should instead be handled under the Guardian and Wards Act. After losing before the Sessions Court in revision, he approached the Sindh High Court.

The High Court dismissed his application and upheld the lower courts' orders. The judge explained that the Domestic Violence Act was specifically created to protect the most vulnerable members of society, women and children, who often cannot speak up about abuse due to fear of being hurt, abandoned, or thrown out of their homes. The court noted that the Act allows an aggrieved person to file a complaint before a Judicial Magistrate, who can issue notices and even grant temporary custody of the victim. Since the mother had made specific allegations of abuse, the Magistrate was right to take up the case under this law.

The court held that the father still had full opportunity to defend himself and prove his innocence before the Magistrate, and that his challenge was merely an attempt to stall proceedings early on. This case matters because it reinforces that courts should not allow procedural objections to undermine the protective purpose of domestic violence legislation.

title: Women Rights Judgment on Article 25 clause (3)
explainer:
This Supreme Court order concerns Mst. Fazal Jan, an elderly woman who, without a lawyer, had pursued a civil suit claiming inheritance rights over land she said came down from her grandfather, Fazal Din, through either her father or an uncle. Her suit for declaration had been dismissed by the trial court, the appellate court, and finally by the Peshawar High Court in a civil revision, partly because her own statements about her family connection to Fazal Din were inconsistent.

The Supreme Court, after hearing her in person, found that she was clearly unable to present her complicated case coherently, and that the confusion in her statements likely stemmed from her inability to express herself clearly rather than dishonesty. It also noted that the opposing side's claim, based on a woman called Mst. Piari, was equally unclear, and that the property had passed through several suspicious transactions, including gifts, sales, and a pre-emption decree, raising the possibility that Fazal Jan's vulnerability had been exploited.

The Court granted her leave to appeal and ordered that she be provided a competent lawyer, holding that this assistance was required under Article 25(3) of the Constitution, which mandates special protection for women. It clarified that such protection covers not just physical safety but also property rights, and that courts themselves fall within the "State's" duty to protect women. This case is significant for recognizing that constitutional protection of women extends to ensuring fair access to justice and safeguarding their property rights.

title: Complaint before Ombudsperson during pendency of Suit
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over inheritance rights under the Punjab Enforcement of Women's Property Rights Act, 2021. A widow and her daughters filed a complaint with the Punjab Ombudsperson, alleging that their rightful shares in the deceased husband's property had been fraudulently taken from them through a fake gift deed in favor of the sons. However, before filing this complaint, the women had already filed a civil suit in court seeking to have the same gift declared invalid, and that suit was still pending when the Ombudsperson took up the complaint.

The sons challenged the Ombudsperson's decision, arguing she had no authority to decide the matter while the civil suit was still pending, and that she failed to follow the specific procedure required by law, which mandates that when a related case is pending in court, the Ombudsperson must file a report with that court and wait for permission before proceeding further.

title: Acting Charge according to NHA Appointment and Promotion Rules 1995
explainer:
This case involved multiple employees of the National Highway Authority (NHA) who challenged a seniority list prepared under the NHA's service rules. The employees, represented by several senior lawyers, disputed how seniority was calculated, particularly regarding appointments made on an acting-charge basis and the status of regular versus work-charge employees.

The Federal Service Tribunal examined the legal history behind NHA's employment rules, tracing them back to the earlier National Highways Board Employees Services Rules of 1974, and clarified that even though no law explicitly repealed the 1974 rules, they were effectively superseded once the newer 1995 Rules were enacted, since two sets of rules on the same subject cannot operate simultaneously.

On the substantive issue, the Tribunal ruled that being appointed on an acting-charge basis does not automatically entitle an employee to regular promotion or seniority rights. It also found that seniority is correctly counted from the date of regular appointment, following the principle of seniority-cum-fitness, and that an employee appointed later cannot be made senior to one appointed earlier. Since the appellants were found to be junior to the respondents under the rules, their appeals against the seniority list were dismissed as not legally sustainable.

title: Re-investigation of decided case is not allowed
explainer:
This case concerned how police investigations can be transferred between officers under the Police Order, 2002. An FIR had been lodged over a death, and during investigation the police cleared some accused of involvement. The main accused then successfully applied to have the investigation transferred to a different officer, and later the petitioner and the accused jointly got it transferred again to another officer, with approval at the Regional Police Officer level. Later, the complainant also approached the Regional Police Officer and got the investigation changed a second time by that same officer. The petitioner challenged this latest change in the Lahore High Court, arguing the Regional Police Officer had no power to order a second transfer, and that the new team's composition also violated the law's rank requirements.

The court examined Article 18-A of the Police Order, which allows a district police chief to transfer investigation once, and the Regional Police Officer to do so a second time if asked to review that first transfer - but no provision allows repeated, open-ended transfers of investigation. The court also noted that by the time of the disputed order, a challan (charge sheet) had already been filed and the trial court had taken cognizance of the case. At that stage, reinvestigation is not legally permissible; police lose authority to reinvestigate once a court is seized of the matter. The court therefore quashed the impugned order allowing a second change of investigation.

This matters because it clarifies limits on police power to repeatedly change investigating officers, especially after a case has reached court, protecting the integrity and finality of judicial proceedings from administrative interference.

title: Re-Examination after Final Arguments
explainer:
This case comes from the Sindh High Court and deals with a civil dispute originally about specific performance of a property sale agreement. During the trial, after both sides had presented their evidence and the case was pending final arguments, the defendant asked the trial court for permission to further cross-examine the plaintiff, explaining that his lawyer had been unavailable due to illness and other court commitments, so the earlier cross-examination had been incomplete. The trial court allowed this request. The plaintiff challenged this decision before the High Court, arguing that there was no legal basis to reopen cross-examination once both parties had closed their respective sides, and that the request was simply an attempt to cover gaps in the defendant's case.

The High Court disagreed and dismissed the challenge. It held that even without an explicit law permitting it, courts have inherent power to recall witnesses for further examination or cross-examination at any stage of proceedings, whether on their own initiative or at a party's request, if justice and fairness require it. This power exists under Order XVIII Rule 17 of the Civil Procedure Code, and courts may also use Section 151 CPC when parties make such requests. The guiding principle is that courts must strive to uncover the truth rather than rigidly enforce procedural closure.

This judgment matters because it clarifies that procedural technicalities should not prevent courts from ensuring a fair and complete examination of evidence, especially in exceptional circumstances.

title: Locus Poenitentiae--In appointment of Person

Despite being the top candidate, she was effectively denied the appointment without valid justification.

The High Court ruled in her favor, holding that once she was selected on merit through a lawful, transparent process, the authorities created a legitimate expectation and legal right in her favor. title: Powers of Higher Education Commission
explainer:
This case was about an educational institution called the Open International University for Complimentary Medicine, claiming to be based in Sri Lanka, which challenged its inclusion on a list of illegal or fake universities published by Pakistan's Higher Education Commission (HEC). The petition was filed by someone claiming to be its Vice Chancellor in Pakistan, who asked the Islamabad High Court to remove the university's name from the list and stop HEC from taking action against it.

The court examined HEC's powers under the Higher Education Commission Ordinance, 2002, and found that HEC has broad authority to collect and publish information about educational institutions, both within Pakistan and abroad, especially when such institutions solicit admissions from Pakistani students. The court noted that the petitioner failed to provide credible proof that the university actually existed, was a genuine degree-awarding institution, or that the person filing the petition had authority to do so. It also noted inconsistencies, such as a recognition letter referring to a differently named institution.

The court ruled that HEC acted within its lawful authority in publishing the list after conducting inquiries. However, it gave the university the option to approach HEC directly, or through Sri Lanka's regulatory authority, to prove the published information was incorrect, in which case HEC would be required to correct the list.

This case matters because it clarifies HEC's regulatory power to protect students from fraudulent or unrecognized institutions, including foreign ones operating in Pakistan.

title: Litigation is notice to public at large
explainer:
This case was about a land dispute in Bahawalpur. Faiz Ahmed had made an agreement in 2006 to buy a piece of land from Muhammad Ahmed and Muhammad Younas, paying earnest money and later more, with possession handed over to him. However, the sellers refused to formally execute the sale and later, while the court case was still pending, sold the same land to a third person, Muhammad Afzal, through a registered sale deed. Faiz Ahmed sued for specific performance of the original agreement and asked the court to cancel the later sale to Afzal.

The trial court and the lower appellate court ruled in favour of Faiz Ahmed, and the sellers and Afzal challenged this in the Lahore High Court through second appeals.

The High Court dismissed the objection that evidence recorded through a commission was defective, holding that since neither party had raised this procedural issue earlier, they could not raise it now. More importantly, the court rejected Afzal's claim that he was an innocent buyer unaware of the earlier agreement. It held that ongoing litigation is treated as public notice, and anyone buying property should be careful to check whether it is already under dispute. Since the agreement and lawsuit existed before Afzal's purchase, he could not claim to be a bona fide purchaser without notice.

This case reinforces an important property law principle: buyers must verify the legal status of land before purchasing, as pending litigation binds subsequent purchasers too.

This case involved a woman, Surraya Bibi, who claimed that land she owned was taken from her through a fraudulent sale deed. She sued for cancellation of the sale deed, declaration of ownership, and possession. The trial court initially ruled in her favor, but after the case was sent back for more evidence, it was dismissed, and her appeal also failed. She then approached the Lahore High Court.

The High Court examined whether the sale deed met the legal requirements to be valid, particularly whether it was properly witnessed. Under the law of evidence, such documents involving financial transactions must be attested by at least two genuine marginal witnesses. The court found that one of the supposed witnesses had merely acted as an identifier of the illiterate seller, not as a proper attesting witness, which made the document legally defective.

The court ruled that even though lower courts had reached the same conclusion (a "concurrent finding"), it could still intervene because the earlier decisions were based on misreading and ignoring evidence, and violated clear legal requirements. It held that the sale deed was inadmissible and wrongly relied upon, and ruled in favor of Surraya Bibi.

This case matters because it reinforces that courts can overturn even consistent lower-court rulings when there are serious legal errors, and it clarifies that proper witnessing of property documents is essential for their validity.

title: PLJ 2017 Sh.C. (AJ&K) 74
explainer:
This case involved a husband-wife dispute over dowry articles and maintenance payments in the Azad Jammu and Kashmir High Court. The wife and her children had sued for recovery of dowry items given at marriage and for unpaid maintenance, claiming the husband had thrown them out and kept the dowry goods. The husband denied mistreating her and claimed he had already divorced her in 2008.

The trial court had dismissed the dowry claim for lack of proof but awarded modest monthly maintenance to the wife and children. Both sides appealed, the wife wanting more dowry items and maintenance, the husband wanting the amounts reduced or the claim dismissed entirely because of the divorce.

The High Court found that the trial court had wrongly rejected the dowry claim. It held that witness testimony about the dowry items was unrebutted and should have been accepted, and that simply because 16 years had passed did not mean the goods had become worthless without actual evidence to that effect. The court ordered the proven dowry articles returned to the wife.

On maintenance, the court clarified an important principle: a divorce only becomes legally effective, for maintenance purposes, from the date the husband formally states it in court, not from an earlier claimed date. The wife remained entitled to maintenance up to that point, plus three months of iddat (waiting period) expenses afterward. The appeal was accepted accordingly, correcting how both dowry and maintenance claims had been assessed.

title: Two months delay in lodging FIR
explainer:
This Supreme Court case involved a doctor, Dr. Samina Matloob, who was charged after a new-born baby died during delivery, allegedly due to her negligence. An FIR was registered against her and two others under Section 322/34 of the Pakistan Penal Code (offences relating to causing death without intent to kill). She sought pre-arrest bail, which was refused by the lower court and the Lahore High Court, so she approached the Supreme Court.

Her lawyer argued there was no real evidence of negligence, that the complaint was filed two months after the incident, and that under Section 29 of the Punjab Healthcare Commission Act, 2010, such medical negligence matters should fall under the Commission's jurisdiction rather than being investigated or prosecuted under ordinary criminal law. The state's prosecutor did not contest these points.

The Supreme Court noted that the two-month delay in reporting the case, combined with the police's failure to exhume the baby's body to gather medical evidence, meant crucial evidence was lost. It also agreed that such matters, involving a registered healthcare facility, should be handled by the Healthcare Commission rather than ordinary criminal courts. Since the investigation itself had also cleared the petitioner, the Court confirmed her pre-arrest bail, converting her petition into an appeal and allowing it.

The case highlights how delays and poor investigation can undermine prosecutions, and clarifies that medical negligence cases involving registered healthcare providers may fall outside normal criminal law under special legislation.

title: PLJ 2018 Islamabad 28
explainer:
This case involved newly appointed Civil Judges-cum-Judicial Magistrates in Islamabad who challenged a requirement that they pass a departmental examination before their services could be confirmed. The judges had been appointed in September 2012, but nearly three years later, in 2015, the Islamabad High Court amended its service rules and adopted Punjab's examination regulations, applying them retrospectively to these officers. The petitioners argued this was unfair and unlawful because no such exam requirement existed when they were appointed, they had never been given the mandatory prior training, the examination committee was improperly constituted with only two judges instead of the required three, an outside examiner wrongly both set and graded the papers, and the exam schedule crammed four attempts into ten months instead of the two years allowed under the rules. They also claimed discrimination, since similarly placed judges in other provinces (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh, Balochistan) had this examination requirement waived, and other Islamabad judicial officers were not required to sit similar tests.

The court examined the relevant service rules and emphasized that completing training and passing the prescribed departmental examination is mandatory before confirmation, and that rules must be interpreted harmoniously and sensibly according to their plain meaning. This judgment matters because it clarifies how procedural rules governing judicial officers' confirmation must be properly and fairly applied, protecting judges from arbitrary or retrospective changes to their service conditions.

title: PLJ 2018 Islamabad 124
citation: PLD 2008 SC 673). Paragraph 9 of the said report is reproduced herei
explainer:
This case involved Park View Enclave (Private) Limited, a company developing a housing scheme called Park View City in Zone-IV of Islamabad, on land it had purchased for the project. The Capital Development Authority (CDA) had approved the layout plan in 2013 and later issued a No Objection Certificate (NOC) in 2014 allowing development, subject to several conditions, including following the approved layout and transferring land for roads, parks, and public buildings to CDA free of charge.

CDA later cancelled the NOC, finding that the petitioner had failed to comply with the conditions attached to it. The company challenged this cancellation in the Lahore High Court, asking that the cancellation be declared illegal and the NOC restored.

The court dismissed the petition. It found that despite repeated warnings from CDA to stop unauthorized construction, the petitioner continued development work in violation of the approved terms, essentially taking a calculated risk. The court held that such conduct did not entitle the petitioner to relief under the High Court's discretionary constitutional jurisdiction. It also noted that compliance with CDA's NOC requirements could not be excused merely because of the scheme's size or the financial stakes involved, and that courts could not validate construction carried out while the NOC was cancelled.

The judgment reinforces that developers in Islamabad must strictly follow CDA regulations and warnings, and that courts will not reward parties who proceed with construction despite clear notice that they are acting outside legal approval.

title: Custody Case of a British Child
explainer:
This case concerned a custody dispute between a divorced couple over their minor son, Ibrahim Khan, who holds British nationality as he was born in the United Kingdom to both parents. The mother had earlier been given custody by the Family Court, but the appellate court ruled that once the child reached age seven, custody should pass to the father, following the traditional rule that mothers' custody rights (hizanat) end at that age for boys. When the father later sought custody under this ruling, courts eventually ordered the child handed over to him, which the mother challenged before the Peshawar High Court.

The High Court noted that the father actually lived in the UK with his parents, and the custody application had instead been filed through an attorney unrelated to the family. The judges found this arrangement unacceptable, stating that handing a child's custody to an attorney is not recognized under either English law or Islamic law. They also found that the mother's financial situation and character were not in question, and that minor school attendance issues during one term did not prove neglect, especially since the child was doing well in a good school afterward.

The court emphasized that the child's welfare, not rigid application of personal law, must be the deciding factor in custody cases. Noting the child's own preference to stay with his mother, the High Court ruled in the mother's favor, overturning the lower courts' decisions. This case highlights that courts can look beyond technical legal rules to protect a child's actual best interests.

title: Sale on the basis of Irrevocable Power of Attorney
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land that had been sold using a power of attorney. The petitioner, Abdul Rahim, had given an irrevocable general power of attorney to Mukhtar Ahmad, who then used it to sell the land to other people. Abdul Rahim later filed a lawsuit claiming the power of attorney itself was invalid, and therefore the sale made under it should also be cancelled.

The trial court initially ruled in his favor, but the first appellate court overturned that decision after re-examining the evidence, finding that the power of attorney had genuinely been given in exchange for Rs. 20,000, which Abdul Rahim had admitted receiving. The High Court upheld this reversal, and Abdul Rahim then asked the Supreme Court for permission to appeal further.

The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. It noted that the sale deeds executed by the attorney were for an amount close to the consideration already paid for the power of attorney, suggesting the transaction was genuine and that Abdul Rahim had effectively sold the land through this arrangement because he needed money. The Court also rejected the argument that a witness's testimony should be disregarded simply because he was related to a party, holding that relationship alone does not discredit a witness if the testimony is otherwise credible and disinterested.

This case matters because it confirms that an irrevocable power of attorney given for real consideration can validly support a subsequent sale, and that courts will not disturb consistent factual findings of lower courts unless there is clear misreading of evidence.

title: Contents of Plaint are important for Rejection of Plaint
explainer:
This case was decided by the Sindh High Court and involved a company, Sunley Developers, suing Mumair Associates over a housing scheme called Gulshan-e-Rumi in Karachi. Sunley claimed it had signed an agreement in 1998 to buy land for 950 residential plots, paid a large sum of money, and was given possession, but the defendant failed to obtain necessary approvals, complete development work such as roads and boundary walls, and honor the agreement. Sunley sued for specific performance of the contract, declaration, and injunction. The defendant asked the court to reject the plaint outright, arguing the suit was time-barred and that the plaintiff had no valid cause of action.

The court explained that when deciding whether to reject a plaint, it must assume the plaint's contents are true and can only reject it if the plaint itself clearly shows the claim is barred by law, such as limitation. Here, the court found the agreement, despite being called an "agreement to sell," was actually a complete transfer of the land with full power of attorney given to the plaintiff to sell plots itself. Since all the obligations complained about were actually duties of the plaintiff, not the defendant, there was no real grievance against the defendant. The court also noted the agreement failed to clearly identify the land's lease details. As a result, the court allowed the application and rejected the plaint. The case highlights how courts closely examine the actual wording and substance of an agreement, not just its title, when deciding whether a lawsuit can proceed.

title: Victory of a MBBS Student in a Case
explainer:
This case is about a student, Raza Hassan, who applied for admission to the first year MBBS program at Khyber Medical College, Peshawar, for the 1997-98 session. He applied under both the regular merit category and the self-finance category before the official deadline, took the required entry test, and passed it. Only the interview stage remained.

However, after the deadline had passed and the entry test results were already out, the government changed the admission rules through a letter from the Health Department, allowing children of doctors who had missed the original deadline to compete for self-finance seats as well. This reduced the number of available seats and resulted in some candidates with lower merit than the petitioner getting admission, while he was left out.

The Peshawar High Court examined whether this late change in policy was valid. It found that the change was not properly made through an official notification, as required when altering rules in the admission prospectus, but was instead communicated through an informal letter. Since the petitioner had already fulfilled all requirements before the deadline, the Court held that he had earned a vested right to be considered fairly.

The Court ruled in his favor, directing that he be admitted to the first year MBBS class, without disturbing the admissions already granted to other students. The case highlights the importance of due process and fairness in changing admission rules after students have already met existing requirements.

title: Supreme Court's Judgment on Forged Documents
explainer:
This case was about a land dispute involving allegations of fraud. Ghulam Muhammad claimed that someone forged a general power of attorney in his name, and that a person calling himself his attorney, Basharat Ali, used this fake document to sell his land without his knowledge or consent. Based on this, several sale transactions and mutations (official land transfer records) followed over the years. Ghulam Muhammad sued to cancel these transactions and recover possession of his land.

The trial court and first appellate court ruled that the sale was indeed fraudulent, since the defendants could not produce the power of attorney document itself, failed to produce Basharat Ali as a witness, and failed to call any witnesses who had seen the document signed. However, these courts still dismissed the suit on the technical ground that it had been filed too late, beyond the legal time limit for such cases. The High Court disagreed and ruled in favor of the original owner's heirs.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeal. It held that when a document (like the power of attorney) is proven to never have been validly executed in the first place, it is void from the very beginning, not merely questionable. Such void documents and all transactions based on them have no legal existence at all. Therefore, the stricter three-year time limit for cancelling documents does not apply; instead, a longer limitation period applies to void transactions. This matters because it protects people from losing property rights due to forged documents, even if they discover the fraud years later.

title: Powers of a Civil Judge in Ex-Parte Suits
explainer:
This case involved a contractor who had done repair and construction work for the Punjab government. After a dispute over a stopped payment cheque, he sued the government for "rendition of accounts," asking the court to make the government disclose records showing what was owed to him. Because the government did not appear in court, the trial judge passed an ex-parte preliminary decree in the contractor's favor, appointed an accountant to examine the records, and later issued a final decree awarding him a specific sum based on that report.

The government then appealed to the High Court, which overturned both the preliminary and final decrees, ruling that since the relationship between the parties was contractual rather than fiduciary, the government was never obligated to "render accounts," and the contractor should have simply sued for a specific amount.

The Supreme Court restored the contractor's decree. It held that the trial judge did have jurisdiction to hear the case, and that the government's absence from the original proceedings amounted to waiving its right to object to that jurisdiction. More importantly, since the government never appealed the preliminary decree within the legal time limit (as required under Section 97 of the Civil Procedure Code), it could not later attack that decree indirectly by appealing only the final decree. Allowing this would let parties bypass limitation laws. The case clarifies the limits of a civil judge's authority in ex-parte suits and reinforces that procedural deadlines for challenging decrees must be respected.

title: Quashment Dismissal Judgment
explainer:
This case involved Murad Gul, who was booked under narcotics law after police allegedly caught him with 650 grams of chars (hashish) in Peshawar. He threw away a shopping bag containing the drugs and fled when a police patrol stopped him, according to the FIR.

Gul asked the Peshawar High Court to quash the FIR against him, arguing that the complainant had acted out of malicious intent and that there was nothing connecting him to the crime, and that he had no prior criminal history.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It explained that its special inherent power to quash cases (under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code) is meant only for extraordinary situations, not as a routine alternative to a full trial. The court noted that police had already completed their investigation and filed a formal charge sheet, and the case was already before a trial court. It held that allegations of bad faith by police cannot be used to shut down a case before the prosecution gets a chance to present its evidence, since deciding whether evidence is reliable is the trial court's job, not the High Court's. The judge pointed out that Gul still had the option to seek acquittal during the trial itself if the evidence turned out to be insufficient.

This case illustrates how Pakistani courts are generally reluctant to stop criminal trials early, preserving that power only for truly exceptional circumstances.

title: Reinstatement is inevitable on acquittal of civil servant
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Zafran, a former Warder at Central Jail Rawalpindi, who was dismissed from service after being implicated in a narcotics smuggling case. He was initially dismissed under one law, the Punjab Removal from Service (Special Powers) Ordinance, 2000. He appealed, and the tribunal earlier ordered reinstatement with a fresh, proper inquiry. However, during the new proceedings, the authorities switched to a different law, the PEEDA Act, 2006, and dismissed him again.

The Punjab Service Tribunal found several problems with this fresh dismissal. First, switching between different laws partway through the process was improper, following established Supreme Court precedent. Second, the inquiry officer never gave Zafran a chance to cross-examine the witnesses against him, making it an incomplete and unfair inquiry. Most importantly, the criminal court had already acquitted Zafran of the narcotics charges, and this acquittal was never challenged or overturned by the prosecution, so it was final.

The Tribunal held that once a civil servant is acquitted by a competent criminal court, the department cannot lawfully refuse to reinstate him. The authorities had ignored this acquittal while rejecting his appeals.

As a result, the Tribunal set aside all the dismissal orders and ordered Zafran's full reinstatement with all back benefits. This case reinforces an important protection for government employees: a criminal acquittal generally entitles them to get their job back.

title: Placement of name in E.C.L. Judgment
explainer:
This case involved a Pakistani citizen, Riaz Ahmad, who had worked as an auto mechanic in Doha, Qatar since 1995, returning home once a year to see his family. In September 2012, when he arrived in Pakistan, authorities stopped him at the airport because his name had been placed on the Exit Control List, which prevents people from leaving the country. His passport was taken and he was investigated by intelligence agencies, but nothing incriminating was found against him; a local army-constituted committee even issued a character certificate in his favor. Despite this, his name remained on the list, his passport was not returned, and his repeated appeals went unanswered. The government claimed his name was added based on an intelligence recommendation alleging involvement in terrorist activity during a military operation in Swat, but provided no evidence or formal charges.

The Islamabad High Court ruled in his favor, holding that the right to travel is a fundamental constitutional right that cannot be taken away without due process. Since no trial had been held and the petitioner had not been cleared either, keeping him in limbo indefinitely was unlawful. The court ordered his name removed from the Exit Control List and his passport returned immediately.

This case matters because it reinforces that government authorities cannot restrict citizens' fundamental rights, like freedom of movement, based on vague or unproven allegations, and must act fairly and within a reasonable time.

title: The surety is confiscated if accused absconds
explainer:
This case from the Azad Jammu & Kashmir High Court deals with what happens when a person who stood surety (guarantor) for an accused fails to produce that accused in court.

An accused facing trial for minor offences absconded and went abroad after someone (the respondent) had furnished a surety bond of Rs. 50,000 guaranteeing his appearance. When the accused could not be produced for nearly two years, the trial Magistrate forfeited the entire surety amount. On appeal, the Sessions Judge reduced the forfeited amount to Rs. 30,000. The surety's relative who had originally sought full forfeiture then challenged this reduction before the High Court, arguing the full amount should be confiscated since the surety had been given ample time and failed to comply.

The High Court upheld the Sessions Judge's reduced order. It explained that when forfeiting a surety bond under Section 514 of the Criminal Procedure Code, courts must strike a balance between being too harsh and too lenient. Noting that the accused had since surrendered and appeared before the court, and that the reduced amount had already been deposited in the government treasury, the Court found the Sessions Judge's order fair and just. It dismissed the petition seeking restoration of the full forfeiture.

This case matters because it illustrates how courts weigh fairness and proportionality when sureties fail to produce an accused, rather than automatically imposing the harshest penalty.

title: Shia Law Inheritance Judgment
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the inheritance of Syed Hassan Asghar Taqvi, a police officer (SIP) who was killed in a terrorist attack in 2004. His mother and his wife both claimed shares in his estate, including his service benefits, death compensation, and salary that would have been paid until he turned 60.

The mother argued that the wife should be excluded from inheritance because the deceased had allegedly divorced her before his death, with the divorce supposedly taking effect by the time he died. She relied on affidavits from two witnesses claiming to have witnessed the divorce.

The trial court had already ruled that under Shia law, the widow and children were not excluded from inheritance, and that the mother was entitled to a one-sixth share while the rest went to the widow and children. The trial court also ordered the police department to pay salary arrears and continuing pension to the widow, deposit death compensation and other dues with a court official for distribution, and invest the minor children's shares until they came of age or married.

On appeal, the Sindh High Court rejected the mother's divorce claim as fake, pointing out the suspicious fact that the witness affidavits were dated the very day of the alleged divorce, which made no logical sense. The court upheld the trial court's order as legally sound, confirming the shares under Shia inheritance law and the entitlement of the widow and children to the deceased's benefits. The appeal was dismissed.

title: Section 195 and 476 do not bar police to lodge FIR
explainer:
This case is from the Lahore High Court, Rawalpindi Bench, dealing with whether a criminal case could be registered by police over an allegedly forged document that had been used as evidence in an earlier civil lawsuit.

The background: Rashid Javed had sued Aamir Shahzad for recovery of money, relying on a document called an "Iqrarnama" (agreement) dated 2006. The civil court found this document to be forged and dismissed the suit. The complainant, Aamir Shahzad, then got an FIR (police case) registered against Rashid Javed and others for fraud and forgery under the Pakistan Penal Code. Javed challenged this FIR, arguing that under Section 195(1)(c) of the Criminal Procedure Code, only the court before which the forged document was produced could authorize such prosecution - not the police directly.

The High Court disagreed and dismissed the petitions. It held that Section 195(1)(c) only restricts courts from taking cognizance of such offences without proper authorization; it does not stop the police from registering an FIR and investigating. More importantly, since the forgery was allegedly committed in 2006 - before the lawsuit was even filed in 2009 - this legal restriction didn't apply at all, because the restriction only covers forgery committed during or in relation to ongoing court proceedings, not before them.

This ruling clarifies that victims of document fraud can approach police directly for an FIR when the forgery predates any court case, without needing special court permission first.

title: Right of Daughter usurped in mutation challenged
explainer:
This case was about a woman, Mst. Zainab, who was denied her rightful share of inheritance from her father, Muhammad Ramzan. When her father died, a mutation (an official land revenue record change) was sanctioned in 1918 giving the entire property only to her brother, Allah Wasaya, leaving her out entirely. Her brother later gifted parts of this land to his own sons. Zainab, who was a pardah nashin (secluded) woman unfamiliar with legal and property matters, eventually sued through her son acting as her attorney, seeking a declaration that she was entitled to her Islamic (sharai) share of the inheritance. The defendants argued her claim was time-barred and that a local custom called pagwanda justified excluding daughters from inheritance.

The Lahore High Court ruled in Zainab's favor. It found no evidence proving the custom of pagwanda actually existed in that area, so it could not be used to deny her inheritance rights. The court also held that a mutation is not itself a document of title, inheritance automatically vests in heirs the moment someone dies, and such vesting does not depend on revenue authorities' actions. Since the original mutation was obtained through fraud and concealment, it was void from the start, meaning no limitation period could block her claim. The court ordered a fresh mutation be sanctioned giving Zainab her proper Islamic share. This case matters because it reinforces that daughters cannot be deprived of their lawful inheritance through fraudulent or unproven customary claims, and that technical limitation rules should not

title: Power of Attorney holder has to produce attesting witnesses
explainer:
This case was heard by the Peshawar High Court, D.I. Khan Bench, concerning a long-running property dispute originating from a 1972 civil suit. Hussain Bakhsh had obtained a decree in 1972 against Abdul Majid, who appeared in that case through a general power of attorney holder. Based on this decree, Bakhsh became the owner of the disputed land. Decades later, in 1992, Abdul Majid's legal heirs filed an application under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, claiming the original 1972 decree was obtained through fraud and misrepresentation because, they alleged, no one had actually appointed the attorney who appeared on Abdul Majid's behalf.

The trial court initially dismissed this challenge twice, but an appellate court eventually set aside the old decree and allowed the heirs to contest the suit, prompting Bakhsh's heirs to file this writ petition.

The High Court examined whether the attorney's power of attorney had been properly proven. title: Reference to High Court in a case decided by Member Customs Appellant Tribunal
explainer:
This case involved a Toyota Land Cruiser Jeep that had been registered with the Motor Vehicle Registration Authority in Karachi back in 1996. In 2005, customs officials intercepted the vehicle and seized it, alleging it was smuggled because one of the documents produced by its owner, a photocopy of a Bill of Entry, did not actually match the vehicle when customs checked their records. The vehicle was confiscated, though the owner was given the option to pay a redemption fine plus duties and taxes to get it back. The case went through multiple rounds of appeals, including to the Supreme Court, which sent it back to the Customs Appellate Tribunal for a fresh decision. The Tribunal again ruled against the vehicle owner, prompting this reference to the High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the applicant (the vehicle owner). It found that the registration authority had already verified the vehicle's registration as genuine, and the customs authority had never properly checked whether the registration itself was lawful or whether the documents were fake. Since the owner had produced several genuine-looking documents, including the original registration book and proof of duty payment, the burden of proof shifted to the customs authority to prove the vehicle was smuggled, under Section 187 of the Customs Act. The Tribunal had ignored this and relied on guesswork instead of evidence.

This case matters because it reinforces that once a vehicle owner provides reasonable documentation, authorities bear the responsibility of proving smuggling with solid evidence, not assumptions.

title: When Qazf Proceedings can be initiated?
explainer:
This case concerns Qazf, the Islamic law offence of falsely accusing someone of adultery (zina) without producing the required evidence. The Pakistan Shariat Appellate Bench of the Supreme Court heard a petition from a husband, Haji Bakhtawar Said Muhammad, challenging a Federal Shariat Court decision against him.

After divorcing his wife, Dur-e-Shahwar Begum, the husband allegedly told her relatives and notables who came to arrange reconciliation that she was of bad character and that their three children were illegitimate, the result of adultery. He repeated similar allegations in written statements filed in separate maintenance and dower-recovery court cases. His wife filed a criminal complaint accusing him of Qazf under Pakistan's Offence of Qazf Ordinance, 1979.

The husband argued that since she was his wife, any such accusation should instead fall under separate legal rules for spouses (li'an), not ordinary Qazf, and that his later statements were merely repetitions of an earlier claim. The Court rejected this argument, holding that by the time he made these accusations, the couple was already divorced, so they were no longer husband and wife. This meant the special spousal provision did not apply, and his conduct squarely fell under the general Qazf provisions (Sections 6 and 7), since he was accusing a woman who was no longer his wife of adultery without proof.

The Court upheld the Federal Shariat Court's order directing that formal Qazf charges be framed and the case proceed to trial.

title: No one shall be allowed to commit financial murder of another person
explainer:
This case concerns a bail application filed by Muhammad Imran, who was accused of issuing a dishonoured cheque under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code. According to the complainant, the accused owed him Rs. 1,250,000 and had issued a cheque for that amount, which bounced because there was insufficient money in the account. Lower courts had already rejected the accused's bail requests, prompting this petition before the Peshawar High Court.

The petitioner argued he was a government servant whose job could be jeopardized, that there was no written proof of the loan, and that the offence did not fall under the strictest category of crimes where bail is normally denied. The State and the complainant opposed bail, pointing out that the accused admitted owning the bank account, had gone into hiding after the cheque bounced, and had not genuinely denied issuing it.

The High Court dismissed the bail application. It held that even though the offence wasn't in the category where bail is automatically barred, that alone doesn't guarantee bail—each case must be judged on its own facts. The judge emphasized that dishonoured cheques are a growing problem eroding public trust, and that issuing worthless cheques amounts to a kind of "financial murder" of another person. The court ordered the trial to be completed within four months, clarifying that its remarks were preliminary and shouldn't influence the actual trial.
