title: Khawaja Mateen V. The State
explainer:
This case concerns a bail application filed by Khawaja Mateen Yousaf before the Lahore High Court. He had been arrested under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with issuing a cheque that is dishonoured when the person had no intention of honouring it or insufficient funds in the account. The complainant alleged that he had given the petitioner over Rs. 64 lakh for business purposes, and while some amount was returned along with several cheques, one cheque worth Rs. 300,000 bounced.

The petitioner argued that this was essentially a business dispute between partners rather than a criminal matter, that he had no prior convictions, that investigation was complete, and that he had already secured bail in six similar cases filed by other business associates of the complainant.

The court agreed to grant bail. It relied on established legal principles: where a genuine business relationship is admitted between parties, bail should generally not be refused. It also noted that since the offence carries a maximum punishment of three years, it does not fall under the serious offences where bail is restricted, meaning bail is the normal rule rather than the exception. Considering the petitioner's clean record, completed investigation, and the business nature of the dispute, the court granted him bail upon furnishing bonds and a surety. This case illustrates how courts distinguish genuine business disputes from criminal fraud in cheque dishonour cases.

He sought post-arrest bail, arguing that the cheque was actually issued as a guarantee for business dealings rather than for a loan, and that it had been misused. His lawyer also pointed out that the offence did not fall under the category of crimes where bail is normally restricted, and that he was no longer needed for further investigation.

This case matters because it confirms that a large cheque amount does not automatically disqualify someone from bail in dishonoured cheque cases.

title: Masood Ahmad Bhatti V. Federation of Pakistan
explainer:
This case concerns employees who originally worked for the government's Telephone and Telegraph Department, which was later converted into Pakistan Telecommunication Corporation and eventually privatized into Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (PTCL). Three employees had disputes with PTCL over matters like pensions, promotions, and a voluntary separation scheme. One of them had already won a case before the Service Tribunal, but PTCL did not implement that ruling.

When the employees went to the Sindh High Court seeking enforcement of their rights, the High Court dismissed their petitions, reasoning that PTCL's employment rules were not "statutory rules" and therefore courts had no jurisdiction to intervene under Article 199 of the Constitution.

The Supreme Court disagreed. It held that under the Pakistan Telecommunication Corporation (Reorganization) Act, 1996, employees who were transferred from the government corporation to the new company retained protection for their existing terms and conditions of service, which could not be changed to their disadvantage by either the company or the Federal Government. Because this protection stemmed directly from the law, the Court ruled these employees' terms of service were indeed governed by statutory rules. However, employees who joined PTCL after the transition did not have this same protection, since their employment was contractual.

The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and sent the case back for proper implementation of the employees' rights, reinforcing that transferred government employees retain legal protections even after privatization.

title: Who can file suit for Jactitation of Marriage?
explainer:
This case concerned a dispute over an allegedly fake marriage (jactitation of marriage), where one party, who lived in England, sued to have a marriage between the appellants declared forged and fraudulent, and sought an order preventing one defendant from claiming the other as his wife.

The appellants challenged the case on several technical grounds: that certain photostat (photocopied) documents, including a divorce deed and certificates, had been wrongly relied upon despite not being properly proven in court; that the suit was filed in the wrong location since the plaintiff lived abroad; that the lawsuit was filed before the power of attorney authorizing it was even signed; and that only a wife, not a husband, is legally allowed to bring such a suit.

The Supreme Court of Azad Jammu and Kashmir rejected these objections. It held that photocopied documents cannot be relied upon as evidence unless properly proven, and the people who attested them had not testified in court. It ruled that minor procedural issues, like the plaint being signed by a lawyer rather than the plaintiff personally, do not invalidate a case unless the law specifically says so. Importantly, the court clarified that a suit for jactitation of marriage is not limited to wives alone; husbands, wives, or even third parties can file such suits, and Family Courts have exclusive jurisdiction over them.

This judgment is significant because it clarifies who can legally challenge a disputed marriage and confirms that courts should focus on substantive justice rather than rejecting cases over technical defects.

title: What is the concept of bonded labor?
explainer:
This Supreme Court of Pakistan judgment deals with the problem of bonded labour at brick kilns, where workers became trapped in cycles of debt owed to kiln owners. The case reached the Court through a telegram alleging that labourers were being held against their will and forced to work off loans (peshgis) advanced by owners, sometimes through intermediaries called Jamadars/Jamadarnis who controlled payments on workers' behalf.

The Court ruled that the old peshgi system, where owners gave large advances that trapped workers in debt, must end going forward. Only small advances (not exceeding seven days' wages) could be given under fair, agreed terms. The Jamadar/Jamadarni middleman system was abolished entirely, requiring direct dealings between owners and workers. Past unpaid loans remained legally recoverable, but only through courts and legal process, never through coercion or police force. Smaller emergency loans given for events like weddings or funerals were to be treated as forgiven if workers voluntarily returned to work. Workers were given freedom to leave or change employers, with protection from forced retention. The Court also clarified its own broad powers under Article 184(3) of the Constitution to issue whatever orders are necessary to enforce fundamental rights, including acting on information like telegrams.

This case matters because it addressed exploitative labour practices affecting vulnerable workers, using constitutional fundamental rights protections to curb forced labour while balancing legitimate debt recovery through lawful means rather than coercion.

title: Constitution Petition is maintainable if petitioner is deprived anyway
explainer:
This case was about a university teacher, Ihsanullah Bajwa, who was denied an overseas scholarship under the Central Overseas Training Scheme, even though his department head had initially recommended him as the top candidate over a colleague, respondent No. 6. The university later reversed this recommendation and put the colleague forward instead. After an earlier court challenge succeeded on procedural grounds (he had not been given a hearing), the matter was reconsidered by a committee, which again rejected him. He then filed this constitutional petition challenging that decision.

The authorities argued the petition could not be heard because a scholarship is discretionary, not a legal right, and that the petitioner was ineligible since he had already received a scholarship before. The Lahore High Court rejected these objections. It held that a person does not need a strict legal right to approach the court under Article 199; it is enough that he has been deprived of a benefit through a public authority's failure to follow its own rules. The court also found that the official criteria only barred candidates who had received a scholarship within the last three years, and since more than three years had passed since the petitioner's earlier scholarship, he was wrongly excluded. Since his merit score was higher than the other candidate's, the court ruled the decision was arbitrary and violated the constitutional guarantees of equal treatment, and accepted the petition.

title: Can the protective bail be granted without touching merits?
explainer:
This case concerns a man named Muhammad Jamal who was outside Pakistan when a criminal case (FIR) was registered against him by Customs authorities in Karachi, alleging offences under the Customs Act, Sales Tax Act, and Income Tax Ordinance relating to tax and customs violations. Fearing arrest upon his return to Pakistan, he approached the High Court seeking what is called protective bail, essentially a short-term legal safeguard allowing him to travel back into the country and present himself before the trial court without being arrested immediately on arrival.

The court, without examining the actual merits of the criminal allegations against him, granted this protective bail for a limited period of 15 days. During this time, he was required to surrender before the trial court that would actually handle his case. The bail was conditional on him providing a solvent surety of one million rupees along with a personal bond of the same amount, to the satisfaction of the court. The judges made clear that this was a one-time concession: if he failed to surrender within the 15-day window, he would forfeit the surety money, and no extension would be granted regardless of circumstances.

This type of ruling matters because it illustrates how courts balance an individual's right to return home safely with the state's interest in ensuring accused persons face trial, using financial guarantees and strict deadlines rather than ruling on guilt or innocence at this stage.

title: When talaq proceedings start?
explainer:
This case explains the rules for when a divorce (talaq) legally takes effect under Pakistan's Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961.

A husband pronounced talaq against his wife and sent the required notice to the Chairman of the local Arbitration Council, as mandated by Section 7 of the Ordinance. Before the 90-day waiting period expired, however, the husband changed his mind, telling the Chairman he had only pronounced the talaq due to a misunderstanding, and formally withdrew it. The couple reconciled and resumed living together. Despite this, under pressure from the wife's family, the Chairman later issued an order declaring the talaq effective anyway, even though his own earlier record showed the husband had revoked it in time.

The husband challenged this order in the Lahore High Court. The court examined Section 7, which states that a talaq does not become effective until 90 days after notice is given to the Chairman, and that it can be revoked before that period ends. Since the husband had clearly revoked the talaq within the 90-day window, and the Chairman's own order acknowledged this, the court held that declaring the talaq effective afterward was illegal and contradictory.

The court set aside the Chairman's order, ruling it had no lawful authority. This case clarifies that a talaq can be validly cancelled within the 90-day period, and once revoked, it cannot later be treated as effective.

title: There are rules of Prison in Pakistan
explainer:
This case was decided by the Federal Shariat Court, which has the power to review laws and rules to check whether they conform to Islamic teachings. The issue concerned Rule 84 of the Pakistan Prisons Rules, 1978, which restricted prisoners' ability to issue cheques, including requiring permission from a District Co-ordination Officer for any cheque amount exceeding Rs. 5,000.

The court examined this rule in light of numerous verses of the Holy Qur'an and held that it violated Islamic injunctions. It reasoned that every person, including a prisoner, has the right to use his lawful income and is religiously obligated to support his wife and children. No prison regulation can take away this responsibility. The court said that while authorities could keep a prisoner's chequebook in safe custody and have prison officials countersign cheques to confirm authenticity, the strict permission requirement for larger amounts was an unnecessary and unjustified barrier, contrary to the Islamic principles of easing hardship (Usar and Yusar) and ensuring a person's right to lawful earning (Rizk-e-Halal). It clarified that prisoners whose money was linked to offences like theft or fraud would not get this concession.

As a result, the court declared Rule 84 would cease to have effect from 1 December 2009, giving authorities time to amend or remove it. This case matters because it shows how courts in Pakistan can strike down administrative rules that unduly burden fundamental rights, even for prisoners, by testing them against Islamic law.

title: Judgment in the case of Phillips (Respondent) v Mulcaire (Appellant)
explainer:
Nicola Phillips worked as an assistant to Max Clifford, the publicist. She sued Glenn Mulcaire, a private investigator who had pleaded guilty to phone-hacking offences, alleging he unlawfully intercepted her voicemail messages, which contained private and commercially confidential information about her clients. As part of the case, a court ordered Mulcaire to disclose information about how the interceptions happened. Mulcaire refused, claiming the privilege against self-incrimination, since answering could expose him to further criminal prosecution for conspiracy.

Phillips argued that a specific law, section 72 of the Senior Courts Act 1981, removed this privilege in cases involving intellectual property rights, because the confidential information at issue counted as technical or commercial information under that law's definition of intellectual property. The lower courts agreed with Phillips, ordering Mulcaire to disclose the information.

The Supreme Court had to decide two things: whether this kind of private and confidential information actually fell within the law's definition of intellectual property, and whether any resulting criminal prosecution would count as a related offence exempt from protection.

This case matters because it addresses how far people can be forced to hand over information in civil lawsuits even if doing so might incriminate them criminally, particularly in the context of the wider phone-hacking scandal involving tabloid journalism in the UK.

title: When property cannot be partitioned its sold
explainer:
This case was about a house in Gulshan-e-Iqbal, Karachi, registered in the name of Wilayat Hussain, who died in 1993. His grandchildren and daughter-in-law (the plaintiffs) sued for partition of the property, arguing it formed part of his estate and should be divided among his legal heirs.

The relatives of his other son, Anwar (the defendants), argued that although the house was registered in Wilayat Hussain's name, he was only the "ostensible" owner, while the real owner was Anwar, who had paid most of the purchase price and funded the construction. They claimed Wilayat Hussain had verbally given up his rights in the property in Anwar's favor.

The Sindh High Court rejected this argument. It held that under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, any transfer of immovable property worth more than Rs. 100 must be done through a registered document. Since the property could not practically be divided among the heirs according to their shares, the court ordered it to be sold through public auction by the Official Assignee, with proceeds distributed among the rightful heirs. title: Court can declare a document null and void
explainer:
This case concerned a dispute over land in Pakistan where the original owner, Ghulam Muhammad, claimed that a sale deed and related land mutations were the product of fraud. He alleged he never appointed one Basharat Ali as his general attorney, yet Basharat Ali had purportedly sold his land on his behalf starting in 1972. The buyers argued the lawsuit was filed too late, beyond the three-year limitation period that normally applies to suits seeking cancellation of documents.

The trial court and first appellate court dismissed the suit on limitation grounds, even though they found in the owner's favor on the merits, concluding the power of attorney was never proven to be genuine. The High Court reversed this, and the Supreme Court upheld that reversal.

The Supreme Court explained that when a document like a power of attorney is never validly executed, everything built upon it legally does not exist at all, it is void from the start, not merely voidable. Such void transactions are not subject to the short three-year limitation period under Article 91 for cancelling documents. Instead, they fall under Articles 142 or 144, which deal differently with possession and void transactions. Since the defendants never produced the power of attorney or its witnesses, the court treated the entire chain of sales as void. The appeal was dismissed, affirming that the original owner's suit was not time-barred.

title: Admiralty Jurisdiction of High Court
explainer:
This case was heard by the Sindh High Court under its admiralty jurisdiction. The plaintiff, Aslo Marines Limited, sued the vessel M.T. Magda and its owners for over Rs. 13 lakh in damages, claiming that cargo shipped on the vessel between Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Karachi was short-landed and delivered late, causing financial loss due to price increases in the market.

The key legal issue was whether the plaintiff, who was merely the charterer of the vessel (not the owner, consignee, or assignee of the bill of lading), had the right to bring such a claim under the court's admiralty jurisdiction. This depended on Section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, which specifically limits such claims to owners, consignees, or assignees of a bill of lading.

The court found that the plaintiff did not fall into any of these categories, being only a charterer under a charter-party agreement. Relying on precedent and the specific wording of the 1861 Act—which continues to govern admiralty jurisdiction in Pakistan despite later reforms in English law—the judge ruled that charterers have no standing to sue under this provision.

As a result, the suit was dismissed as not maintainable. The case is significant because it clarifies the limits of who can bring cargo damage claims in Pakistani admiralty courts, confirming that charterers, unlike owners or consignees, cannot use this specific legal route for such claims.

title: Validity of General Power of Attorney
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute between family members. A woman, Asghari Begum, had leased her agricultural land to her brother, Abdul Haq, for several years. When the lease ended and she sought to renew it, she discovered that her brother claimed she had earlier given him a general power of attorney, which he then used to gift the land to his own son. Asghari Begum denied ever executing this power of attorney, calling it fraudulent, and sued to have it, the gift deed, and related land records cancelled.

The trial court and the first appellate court both ruled in her favor, cancelling the documents. The brother and his relatives challenged this before the Lahore High Court, arguing that the power of attorney was validly signed and registered, with witnesses present when she put her thumb impression on it, and that registered documents carry a presumption of truth.

The High Court found that the lower courts had failed to properly examine the central issue, whether the power of attorney was genuine. Despite this being framed as a specific issue in the case, no real discussion or independent findings had been made on it. Because of this gap, the High Court set aside the appellate court's decision and sent the case back for a fresh decision, suggesting that the authenticity of the woman's thumb impression on the document be properly compared and verified. This case highlights how courts must thoroughly examine disputed signatures or thumb impressions before deciding property rights based on them.

title: Rape is not possible with wife
explainer:
This is a bail case from the Lahore High Court, Multan Bench. The petitioner, Ashiq Muhammad, was in custody over an FIR lodged by his ex-wife, who alleged that he and eight others abducted her daughter and handed her over to accomplices, who then arranged her forced marriage, during which another man allegedly committed rape under the guise of a nikah ceremony.

The petitioner's lawyer argued that the real issue was a long-running family dispute between the petitioner and his divorced wife, not a genuine abduction. He pointed out contradictions: the daughter herself had earlier approached a Justice of Peace for protection from harassment, naming her mother (the complainant) as the main person to be restrained, not the petitioner. At that time, she was living with her father, the petitioner, and had never denied or challenged the marriage arranged by him.

The court found that the daughter's own conduct and statements contradicted the abduction and rape narrative in the FIR, and that the case required further investigation. Since the marriage itself was admitted and never disputed by the daughter, the judge found sufficient grounds for bail.

The court granted bail, ordering the petitioner's release upon furnishing bail bonds of Rs. 50,000 with one surety, pending further inquiry into the conflicting claims.

title: Principle of Trichotomy of Powers
explainer:
This Supreme Court judgment arose from appeals challenging decisions of the Lahore High Court, which had struck down the Punjab Undesirable Co-operative Societies (Dissolution) Ordinance, 1992. The Ordinance allowed the Punjab government to dissolve co-operative societies it considered "undesirable," particularly those operating like unregulated financial institutions taking deposits from the public. Several affected co-operative societies had challenged the law, and the High Court agreed it was unconstitutional, finding it violated citizens' fundamental rights, lacked clear guidelines, amounted to a "legislative judgment" condemning specific societies without trial, and breached the constitutional separation of powers (trichotomy) between legislature, executive and judiciary.

The Supreme Court disagreed with most of this reasoning. It held that the Ordinance did provide adequate safeguards, since affected societies could seek redress before a co-operative judge and then through writ petitions in the High Court—satisfying requirements of due process even without a prior hearing. The Court also held that the existence of other laws like the Co-operative Societies Act and Banking Companies Ordinance did not prevent the legislature from enacting this special law, and that the Ordinance did not declare anyone guilty of an offence. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgments and upheld the Ordinance's validity, except confirming that one specific section (Section 22) was indeed unconstitutional. This case clarifies limits on separation-of-powers challenges

title: Possession can not be restored through illegal dispossession act
explainer:
This case from the Lahore High Court dealt with a dispute over agricultural land in Okara. The land owner had filed a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, alleging that the people farming his land under a lease agreement refused to vacate and had illegally taken possession after their lease period ended. While that complaint was pending, the parties reached a compromise before the Additional Sessions Judge, extending the lease until 30 June 2011 with payment through post-dated cheques, and the complaint was formally disposed of.

Later, after the lease period ended, one of the cheques was dishonoured. The land owner then filed a fresh application before the same judge, who ordered the original occupants to hand back possession, backed by police assistance. The occupants challenged this order in the High Court.

The High Court ruled that once the original complaint was disposed of through compromise, the judge became "functus officio," meaning he no longer had any jurisdiction over the matter. Since no case under the Illegal Dispossession Act was still pending, the judge had no legal power to pass a fresh order restoring possession based on an alleged breach of the compromise. The Act contains no provision allowing such restoration after a case is already closed. The court therefore declared the order illegal and without jurisdiction, and allowed the petition.

This case clarifies that courts cannot reopen settled disputes to enforce compromise terms unless specific legal authority exists for it.

title: PLJ 2012 Lahore 259  Present: Muhammad Farrukh Irfan Khan, J.
explainer:
This case involved railway police employees who had been served with a charge sheet and show-cause notices accusing them of misconduct and inefficiency, specifically alleged embezzlement of case property for which they had also been arrested and faced criminal proceedings. The employees went to the Lahore High Court asking it to stop the departmental disciplinary proceedings, arguing that since a criminal case on the same facts was already pending in court, the department should wait for the criminal case to conclude before taking any departmental action against them. They also claimed the department was acting with bad intent to remove them from service.

The court rejected this argument and dismissed the petition. It held that a writ petition is not maintainable against a mere charge sheet, since no final adverse order had yet been passed against the employees. It further ruled that departmental and criminal proceedings serve different purposes and can run simultaneously: criminal courts examine whether a crime was committed under the Criminal Procedure Code, while departmental authorities assess whether an employee is guilty of misconduct under service rules. There is no legal bar preventing both processes from proceeding in parallel. The court said the proper course for the employees was to respond to the charge sheet and raise their defenses before the departmental authority itself, not to approach the High Court prematurely.

This judgment reinforces an important principle in Pakistani administrative law: employees cannot bypass internal disciplinary procedures by rushing to court before any final decision is made, and pending criminal cases do not automatically suspend an employer's right to conduct disciplinary proceedings.

title: Order 23 Rules 3 CPC
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between the Income Tax Department (appellant) and four employees who had been promoted on an acting-charge basis to Inspector posts after passing a departmental promotion exam in 2004. The employees complained that, unlike colleagues in other zones who received the salary of the higher post they were officiating on, they were being paid only according to their original lower grade. They filed a writ petition seeking promotion and the corresponding salary.

The single judge of the Lahore High Court disposed of their petition based on a consent order, agreed to by lawyers for both sides, directing that the employees be paid according to the pay scale of the acting post they were working on, and that their promotion case be decided following a relevant Supreme Court precedent.

The department later tried to appeal this consent order. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that once both parties agree to a settlement in court, they give up their right to challenge it later through appeal, as established under Order 23 Rule 3 and Section 96(3) of the Civil Procedure Code. The court also rejected the argument that the order violated constitutional provisions on service tribunals, noting the real issue was discriminatory salary treatment, not improper promotion by the court.

This judgment reinforces the principle that consent orders are final and binding, discouraging parties from going back on agreements they voluntarily made in court.

title: Judgment on Revisional Jurisdiction
explainer:
This case concerns a family land dispute from Pasroor. The petitioners sued claiming ownership rights over property that had been gifted by their relative to his daughters through a mutation in 1987. During the trial, the petitioners were repeatedly given chances—eleven in total—to produce evidence, but on 18.7.2008 their evidence was again absent, so the trial court closed evidence and dismissed the suit under Order XVII, Rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code.

The petitioners appealed, but filed it late, well beyond the thirty-day limitation period prescribed under the Limitation Act. They asked the appellate court to excuse the delay, citing confusion over the next hearing date caused by court staff, but the appellate court rejected this explanation and dismissed the appeal as time-barred.

The High Court, hearing the petitioners' further challenge, upheld both lower court decisions. It calculated the limitation period precisely, found the appeal was filed months too late, and ruled that the explanation offered did not amount to sufficient cause for condoning the delay. The court also clarified that its special revisional powers could only be used where a lower court had wrongly assumed, refused, or exercised jurisdiction illegally or with serious irregularity—conditions not met here.

The petition was dismissed, meaning the original dismissal of the suit stood. The case highlights how strictly limitation periods for appeals are enforced, and that mere administrative confusion is often insufficient to excuse delay.

title: Is Gratuity a deducible expense
explainer:
This case involved a private limited company that published newspapers and was in a tax dispute with the Income Tax Commissioner over several assessment years (1977-78 to 1986-87). The tax authorities had disallowed the company's claimed expenses for employee gratuity payments, as well as certain administrative expenses like telephone, travel, and entertainment costs that were certified by the company's directors.

The Lahore High Court addressed four legal questions referred by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. On the gratuity issue, the court ruled in favor of the company, holding that gratuity amounts calculated and set aside each year are a legitimate deductible business expense, even though actual payment to employees depends on a future event and had not yet become due. This followed an earlier Supreme Court ruling on the same principle.

However, on the question of whether expenses verified only by company directors should automatically be treated as valid business expenses, the court ruled against the company. It held that any expense must meet two legal tests: it must have actually been incurred, and it must have been incurred wholly for business purposes. Mere certification by a director does not satisfy these requirements.

This judgment matters because it clarifies two important tax principles: companies can claim gratuity provisions as deductible expenses even before actual payment, but they cannot escape proper documentation requirements for other expenses simply by having a director sign off on them.

title: Forthwith means without further adjournment
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over agricultural land where the respondent, Nazir Ahmed, had filed a civil suit claiming a right of pre-emption to purchase land that Muhammad Aslam had acquired. During the trial, the plaintiff repeatedly failed to produce his evidence due to various delays, including judges being transferred and adjournment requests. Eventually the trial court invoked Order XVII, Rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code to close the plaintiff's evidence and dismissed the suit with costs. On appeal, the Additional District Judge set aside this dismissal and sent the case back for a fresh decision, and the Lahore High Court upheld that decision. Muhammad Aslam then challenged this before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, clarifying an important legal point: when a law says a court must proceed to decide a matter forthwith, this does not mean the court must immediately dismiss the suit. It only means the court should proceed without further adjournment to take the next appropriate step. In this case, since the plaintiff himself was present in court on the relevant date, the trial judge should have called him to testify directly instead of dismissing the entire suit. This ruling matters because it protects litigants from losing their case outright due to procedural technicalities when alternative, fairer options were available to the court.

title: Family suits should be filed seperately
explainer:
This case involved a husband, Chan Zeb, who had earlier obtained an ex-parte decree from a Family Court in Haripur for restitution of conjugal rights, meaning the court had ordered his wife to return to the marriage. His wife, Mst. Khalida Shaheen, later filed a separate suit seeking recovery of her dower (money or property owed to her under the marriage contract). The husband challenged this separate suit, arguing that under the Family Courts Act, 1964, all disputes between spouses, including claims like dower, should have been raised together in the same case as the restitution suit, not filed separately.

The Peshawar High Court rejected this argument. It clarified that the law only requires that claims for restitution of conjugal rights and dissolution of marriage be combined and decided together, so that one spouse cannot block the other by filing separate competing suits on those two specific issues. However, other matters such as dower, dowry, maintenance, and recovery of a wife's personal property are not required to be combined with those suits and can be filed and decided independently in separate proceedings.

The court held that the law is meant to help spouses get justice quickly, not create hurdles. Since there was no legal bar to filing a separate dower suit, the petition was dismissed. This ruling clarifies which family-related claims must be joined together in family court litigation and which can proceed separately.

Two other men initially accused in the same incident had already been acquitted at trial after police found no evidence linking them to the crime and no recoveries were made from them.

The prosecution's case against the appellant rested heavily on recovered crime-scene evidence, including spent cartridges, and a positive report from the Forensic Science Laboratory supposedly linking a recovered pistol to the shootings. title: Can police raid without search warrants?
explainer:
This case involved Arshad Mahmood, who was convicted under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997 for possession of charas (hashish) and sentenced to life imprisonment with a heavy fine. Police had raided his house in Islamabad in 2000 based on secret tip-off information, without first obtaining a search warrant from a magistrate, and recovered over 21 kilograms of charas from the courtyard. His wife, who was present at the time, was arrested on the spot but later acquitted, while the appellant himself was said to have fled before police arrived.

The Supreme Court examined whether such warrantless raids on private homes violate Article 14 of the Constitution, which protects the dignity and privacy of citizens. The Court held that police and similar agencies do not have unlimited power to search a person's home without satisfying legal requirements, even when a magistrate accompanies the raiding party. The presence of a magistrate does not excuse police from the mandatory legal duty to obtain a search warrant when there was time and opportunity to do so.

The Court also found no proof that the house was in the appellant's exclusive possession, and noted the inconsistency of acquitting the wife while convicting the husband based on the same recovery. As a result, the conviction and sentence were set aside.

This judgment is important because it reinforces that constitutional protections of privacy limit police search powers, and that procedural shortcuts cannot override an individual's fundamental rights.

title: Jurisdiction of Returning Officer in case of involvement in criminal cases
explainer:
This case involved Malik Ahmad Usman Nawaz, a candidate for a Punjab Assembly seat (PP-254, Bahawalpur), whose nomination papers were rejected ahead of the 2024 general elections. The Returning Officer rejected his papers claiming his signature on the nomination form did not match the one on his CNIC. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal upheld the rejection but for a different reason—that he was a proclaimed offender in a criminal case and thus a fugitive from law. The Lahore High Court later dismissed his petition, agreeing with the Tribunal's reasoning. The matter reached the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court found both grounds for rejection flawed. First, the alleged signature mismatch was not legally sufficient grounds for rejection, since the law only allows rejection for mismatched signatures of a proposer or seconder, not the candidate himself, and in any case the mismatch was not shown to be "material." Second, the petitioner had already obtained protective pre-arrest bail, undermining the claim that his status as a proclaimed offender barred him from contesting. title: Conviction in absentia by Anti Terrorism Court
explainer:
This case involved a man named Khanzado, who was tried in absentia (in his absence, since he was declared an absconder) by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Jacobabad. He had been accused, along with others, of kidnapping a six-year-old boy for ransom, under charges including Section 365-A of the Pakistan Penal Code and anti-terrorism laws. At the end of the trial, all accused, including Khanzado, were acquitted of the main kidnapping-related charges due to lack of evidence. However, the trial court separately convicted Khanzado under Section 21-L of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, which deals with absconding from trial, sentencing him to five years in prison and ordering forfeiture of his property.

Khanzado appealed to the Sindh High Court, arguing that this conviction was unlawful since he was never even formally charged with the Section 21-L offence, no evidence was presented on it, and he was punished without a hearing. The government's lawyer agreed with this argument.

The High Court found serious legal flaws: no charge had been framed for Section 21-L, no evidence was recorded on it, and the trial court gave no reasoning before convicting him. This violated his constitutional rights to be heard and treated fairly under Articles 9 and 10(1) of the Constitution. Since he had already been acquitted of the main charges, the court set aside his conviction entirely, ruling that a retrial was unnecessary.

They asked the High Court to order the FIA to drop the inquiry and to stop allegedly harassing bank employees, arguing no proper legal procedure was followed.

The court focused first on whether the petition was even maintainable, given that Section 22-A(6) allows an "ex-officio Justice of Peace" (a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge) to issue directions to police authorities about non-registration of cases, improper transfer of investigations, or excesses committed during investigations. The court held that FIA officials, who exercise the same powers as provincial police under the law, do qualify as "police authorities" under this provision. Therefore, aggrieved persons can approach a Justice of Peace for complaints against FIA conduct, just as they could against provincial police.

Since this alternate remedy existed and was adequate, the court ruled that the writ petition under Article 199 of the Constitution was not maintainable, and dismissed it accordingly. title: Opinion of minor has to be considered if minor was old enough to form an intelligent preference
explainer:
This case was about who should have custody of two young children after their mother died. The children's maternal grandmother applied for custody, arguing that since the father had remarried, the children's welfare would be better served living with her rather than with a stepmother. The father opposed this, saying that as the natural guardian he was entitled to custody, that he had enrolled the children in a good English-medium school, and that they had been living with him for over four years since their mother's death.

Both the trial court and the Shariat Court had already ruled in favor of the father, and the grandmother appealed further. The Supreme Court of Azad Jammu and Kashmir upheld these earlier decisions and dismissed her appeal.

The court explained that the central issue in custody matters is always the welfare of the minor, which includes moral, spiritual, and material well-being. Judges must weigh factors such as kinship, character and capacity of the proposed guardian, home environment, and the age, sex, and religion of the child. Importantly, the court found that the children were old enough and intelligent enough to express a meaningful preference, and that their views should not be lightly ignored. Given that the father was financially stable and could provide better education, while the elderly grandmother was herself dependent on relatives and might struggle to raise the children, the court ruled that custody should remain with the father.

title: Mother's right of custody after second marriage
explainer:
This case was about who should have custody of two young children, a girl and a boy, after their parents' marriage broke down. The children's grandmother had applied for custody, arguing that the mother had remarried a man outside the family and the father was in prison over unpaid maintenance. The family courts had sided with the grandmother, removing the children from their mother's custody mainly because the mother had remarried.

The Lahore High Court overturned these decisions. It held that the mother remarrying a stranger, by itself, is not automatically a valid reason to deny her custody of her children. The court also clarified an important legal point: the usual order of preference for custody (mother, then mother's mother, then other relatives) only applies when the father is deceased or absent, not while the real father is alive and capable of claiming custody. Since the father never actually came forward to seek custody or support his own mother's claim, the grandmother's petition was essentially filed on her own initiative, which the court found insufficient grounds for taking children away from their mother.

The court also noted the children had never actually lived with the grandmother, so there was no bond to protect, while the father had failed to pay maintenance for his children.

Ultimately, the court ruled that the children's welfare was best served by remaining with their mother, restoring her custody rights. This case reinforces that remarriage alone does not disqualify a mother from custody under Pakistani law.

title: Medical evidence was prima facie in contradiction with the version of victim
explainer:
This case involved a father, Shabbir Hussain, accused under Section 376 of the Pakistan Penal Code of committing rape against his own minor daughter. The complaint was filed by the girl herself, alleging the assault occurred while she was alone at home. The accused sought post-arrest bail, arguing he had been falsely implicated due to a family dispute: he claimed the real issue was that the girl had developed an inappropriate relationship with a relative's son, and to protect that young man, the girl's grandmother and aunt orchestrated a false case against him.

The Lahore High Court, Multan Bench, examined the record and found several reasons to doubt the prosecution's version. The medical evidence did not clearly support the victim's account, and chemical examination results were still pending. The father had seven children living in the same house, making it seem improbable he would commit such an act in their presence. Notably, the victim had refused to meet her own mother and preferred staying with her grandmother and aunt, the very relatives suspected of pressuring her to make the allegation. The court noted that a young, poorly educated girl could easily be influenced by relatives.

Given these contradictions, the court ruled the matter required further inquiry rather than definite guilt, and granted bail since the accused had already been detained for six months. The court also ordered police protection for the victim and directed an independent inquiry into the allegations.

title: Guardian Judge  has parental  jurisdiction over minor
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute over two young children after their father died. The mother had left the matrimonial home due to strained relations with her husband before his death by suicide. After his death, she attended the funeral but was later made to leave the household without her children, who remained with the paternal family. She approached the Guardian Judge seeking custody under the Guardian and Wards Act, 1890, and also asked for interim (temporary) custody while the main case was pending. The trial court granted her interim custody, and this was upheld on appeal. The paternal side then challenged this before the Lahore High Court, arguing there was no urgent need to change custody and that they were better off financially.

The High Court dismissed the challenge. It held that a Guardian Judge does not need to show urgency before granting interim custody under Section 12 of the Act; the law should be interpreted liberally, and the judge has broad parental jurisdiction to act in the child's interest at any time. The paramount consideration is always the welfare of the minor, taking into account factors like age and sex. The court emphasized that young children need their mother's love and care, especially since she had not remarried, and that a mother's bond cannot be substituted by a grandmother's care. It also ruled that interim custody arrangements should not be disturbed without compelling reasons. The court directed the main custody case to be decided quickly, within one month.

title: After death of mother maternal grandmother has preferential right of hizanat
explainer:
This case concerns a father who filed a constitutional petition in the Lahore High Court seeking custody of his young son, roughly one and a half years old, after the child's mother passed away. Following the mother's death, the child had been living with his maternal grandmother. The father approached the court under the habeas corpus-type jurisdiction (Section 491 of the Criminal Procedure Code and Article 199 of the Constitution), seeking to have the child removed from the grandmother's custody and handed over to him.

The court held that under Islamic law (Mohammadan Law), after the death of a child's real mother, the maternal grandmother has a preferential right to custody (hizanat) of young children. Since the child was already settled with his grandmother and had not been recently or wrongfully taken from anyone's custody, this was not a case of urgent "snatching" that would justify the High Court stepping in to change custody immediately. The judge noted that disturbing the child's current, stable living arrangement would harm his normal life.

The court therefore declined to interfere and allowed the child to remain with his maternal grandmother. However, it clarified that the father is not without recourse: he can file a proper guardianship petition before the relevant family court to seek interim or permanent custody through the normal legal process, rather than through this emergency constitutional remedy. This case reinforces the principle that such emergency powers are reserved for urgent custody disputes, not for settling long-term custody questions, which belong before specialized guardian courts.

title: Status of medical evidence is always corroborative in its nature
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Moeen, who was convicted by a trial court in Dir Upper for a 1999 incident in which he and several co-accused allegedly broke into a house armed with firearms and abducted a woman, Mst. Naiba, to force her into marriage. When she resisted, she was shot and injured in both arms. The appellant absconded for over 21 years before being arrested in 2020 and tried. He was convicted under multiple sections of the Pakistan Penal Code and the Offence of Zina Ordinance, receiving various prison sentences and fines.

On appeal before the Federal Shariat Court, his lawyer argued that some witness statements used against him had been "transposed" (carried over) from earlier related trials of his co-accused without their supporting documents being formally re-exhibited, so they should not be relied upon.

The Federal Shariat Court rejected this argument. It held that once a statement is properly recorded and exhibited in one trial, those exhibits become part of that statement and do not need to be separately re-exhibited when transposed into a co-accused's later trial, provided the legal conditions under Section 512 of the Criminal Procedure Code and Article 47 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order are met. The court found the victim's testimony credible and well-supported by eyewitnesses, noting that medical evidence only serves a supporting role rather than being essential on its own. The conviction was upheld, reinforcing how courts handle evidence transposed from earlier related trials.

title: Re-Investigation can be permitted under special circumstances
explainer:
This case involved the National Accountability Bureau's attempt to reopen a corruption investigation against Abdul Hakeem, a General Manager at Pakistan State Oil, and other officials, long after it had been officially closed. NAB had investigated the respondents in 2002, found no evidence against them, and formally closed the case with court approval in 2005. Years later, in 2009, NAB sought permission to reinvestigate the same matter. That request went through a lengthy legal back-and-forth, eventually landing back before the Accountability Court, which rejected NAB's application in 2019. NAB then challenged that rejection before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed NAB's petition, upholding the trial court's refusal to allow reinvestigation. The court explained that while re-investigation is legally possible even after a case is closed, it can only happen if genuinely new evidence has emerged that was not available earlier. Courts should not simply rubber-stamp an investigator's request; they must be satisfied there are valid reasons. In this case, the same allegations had also been examined through four separate administrative inquiries by the Customs Department, and the respondents were cleared each time. Given that 17 years had passed with no fresh evidence presented, the court found that continuing to pursue the respondents would be unfair and amount to misuse of the legal process.

This ruling matters because it sets a check on investigative agencies like NAB, preventing indefinite harassment of individuals through repeated investigations without solid new justification, reinforcing fairness and finality in legal proceed

title: Conviction under section 22 of Emigration Ordinance 1979
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Naeem-ul-Haq, who was convicted by a trial court for posing as an unauthorized overseas employment promoter. He had taken Rs. 700,000 from a complainant, promising to send the complainant's son to America for employment, but failed to deliver on this promise. He was convicted under the Emigration Ordinance, 1979, receiving four years' imprisonment under Section 17 and another four years under Section 22 (running concurrently), along with fines and compensation to the complainant.

Naeem-ul-Haq appealed to the Lahore High Court, but his lawyer did not contest the conviction itself-only asked for a reduced sentence, citing that this was his first offense and he had already served over a year in custody. The complainant's lawyer did not object to this request.

The High Court upheld the conviction, finding the prosecution's evidence credible and consistent. However, it agreed to reduce the sentence to time already served, while keeping the fine and default sentence intact. The appellant was given one month to pay the fine.

This case illustrates how courts balance punishment with rehabilitation, particularly for first-time offenders. The judgment emphasizes that criminal justice aims not just to punish, but to allow individuals the chance to reform, provided this doesn't undermine the seriousness of the offense or society's interests.

title: Clerical Mistake in Evidence
explainer:
This case comes from the Lahore High Court, Multan Bench, and deals with a murder trial. A prosecution witness, Manzoor Ahmad, had testified under oath that it was co-accused Riaz who fired the shots that killed the victim. Weeks later, the witness filed an application claiming this was a clerical mistake and that he actually meant to name Ejaz, the petitioner, as the shooter. The trial judge allowed the witness to be re-examined and change his testimony, and then refused the defence lawyer's request for time to challenge this decision, forcing the defence to cross-examine immediately without that opportunity.

Ejaz challenged this in the High Court. The Court ruled in his favour, holding that the law governing evidence (Article 133 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984) only allows a witness to be re-examined to explain something raised in cross-examination, or to address a genuinely new matter with court permission. It does not allow a witness to go back and effectively change or "correct" testimony to fix a problem in the prosecution's case. The Court also stressed that criminal trials must follow fair procedure, especially in serious cases where an accused may face the death penalty, and that an accused must get a meaningful chance to defend himself before being convicted.

As a result, the trial court's order allowing the re-examination was cancelled, along with everything that followed from it. This case matters because it reinforces that procedural fairness and safeguards for the accused cannot be bypassed even to accommodate a complainant's shifting evidence.

title: Jurisdiction of Court of Protection matters for supervising care of mentally disordered person
explainer:
This case is about who can get court protection and appointed as a manager for the property of a mentally disordered person under Pakistan's Mental Health Ordinance, 2001.

The petitioners, whose mother was allegedly suffering from a mental disorder and living abroad, sought to be appointed managers of her property. Before approaching the Court of Protection, the law required them to first get written consent from the Advocate General, Punjab. That consent was refused because the mother did not reside within the territorial jurisdiction of the relevant Court of Protection, and neither she nor the petitioners appeared before the Advocate General's office in person. The petitioners argued that the Advocate General's consent was merely a clerical formality and that he had wrongly taken over powers belonging only to the Court of Protection, especially since the mother could not travel to Pakistan.

The Lahore High Court disagreed. It held that the Advocate General's consent is a substantive, meaningful check, not a rubber stamp. Its purpose is to confirm that there genuinely is a mentally disordered person, that the person and the relatives seeking guardianship live within the court's jurisdiction, and that the application is genuine. The court reasoned that since the Court of Protection must continuously supervise the person's care and property, both the disordered person and the manager must reside within its jurisdiction. The petition was dismissed, meaning the refusal of consent stood.

title: Suspension of Registration of Sales Tax Registered Person
explainer:
This case was about whether tax authorities could suspend a business's sales tax registration without giving it prior notice or a chance to be heard. The petitioner, a lubricants company, challenged Rule 12 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006, which allowed the Commissioner to suspend a registered person's tax registration immediately, without notice, based on suspicions like fake invoices, tax evasion, or fraud, pending further inquiry.

The Lahore High Court ruled that this part of Rule 12 was unconstitutional. The court held that suspending a business's registration effectively stops it from operating, which infringes on the constitutional right to conduct lawful trade or business (Article 18) and violates the right to a fair trial and due process (Article 10-A). Since the allegations involved serious, almost criminal-type accusations like fraud and evasion, the affected person deserved an opportunity to be heard before such a drastic action was taken, not just afterward. The court also found that an administrative rule cannot go beyond what the main law (the Sales Tax Act) actually permits, and that natural justice principles require fairness whenever a decision could seriously affect someone's rights or livelihood.

As a result, the court struck down the part of Rule 12 allowing suspension without prior notice, ruling that tax authorities must give notice and a hearing before suspending anyone's sales tax registration. This decision reinforces that due process protections apply even in tax administration and businesses cannot be punished before being heard.

title: Dispute regarding Territorial Jurisdiction of Family Court
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over which Family Court had the legal authority to hear a custody and visitation case involving a married couple and their infant son. The husband, an army officer, filed a suit for restitution of conjugal rights and sought visitation of his son before the Family Court in Mardan. The wife, who lived and worked in Quetta with the child, challenged this, arguing the Mardan court had no territorial jurisdiction over the matter since she and the child resided in Quetta. Lower courts repeatedly rejected her objections, treating related orders as interlocutory and not appealable, and her defense in the case was eventually struck off.

The Peshawar High Court examined the Family Courts Act, 1964 and its rules, which say a family court's jurisdiction depends on where the cause of action arose, where the parties reside or last resided together, or, in marriage dissolution/dower cases, where the wife resides. Relying on these provisions and a Supreme Court precedent, the High Court held that for custody and guardianship disputes, jurisdiction lies with the family court where the wife resides. Since the wife and child lived in Quetta, the Mardan court lacked proper territorial jurisdiction over the custody matter.

This case matters because it clarifies that in child custody disputes, the location of the mother (and child) determines which family court can hear the case, protecting against forum misuse by the other spouse.

title: PLJ 2015 Lahore 951
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over the recovery of dower (money owed to a wife under Islamic marriage law) that was filed in a Family Court twenty-three years after the husband's death.

Mst. Sakina married Allah Wassaya in 1980. The husband's family claimed he divorced her in December 1981, with the divorce becoming effective in March 1982, and that he died in October 1982. Decades later, in 2005, Mst. Sakina filed a suit for recovery of her dower. The Family Court ruled in her favor, and this decision was upheld on appeal by the Additional District Judge. The husband's heirs then challenged both rulings before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court examined the Limitation Act, 1908, which sets a three-year deadline for filing dower claims, starting either from when payment is demanded and refused, or from when the marriage ends through death or divorce. Based on the evidence, the marriage had ended either in March 1982 (divorce) or October 1982 (death). Either way, the three-year limitation period expired by 1985, decades before Sakina filed her suit.

The court held that both lower courts had failed in their basic duty to first check whether the suit was time-barred before proceeding to decide it on merits. Since the suit was clearly filed too late, the judgments of both lower courts were declared invalid and without jurisdiction. The petition was allowed, and the earlier decisions were set aside. This case underscores that courts must address limitation issues before examining a case's substance.

title: Death of Husband during Talak Case
explainer:
This case from the Lahore High Court dealt with a dispute over whether a divorce (talaq) had legally taken effect before a husband's death, which determined whether his widow retained her status as a wife and heir, or whether the father of the deceased could claim property as if she were divorced.

The deceased husband allegedly sent a notice of talaq to his wife on 14 June 2011. He died just six days later, on 20 June 2011, from a cardiac arrest. His father then petitioned the court to compel the local administrator to issue a formal divorce certificate, arguing that under the Muslim Family Law Ordinance, 1961, the 90-day waiting period should still run its course and the talaq should be treated as effective. The wife argued the notice was fabricated and backdated, pointing out that it was purportedly signed in August, weeks after the husband had already died.

The court found serious doubts about the authenticity of the notice, given the impossible dating. But more importantly, it ruled that even assuming the notice was genuine, a talaq only becomes final after 90 days, during which the husband retains the right to revoke it. Since the husband died within that period, the divorce never became effective. The court suspected the father was attempting to manipulate the process to seize the deceased's property, especially since the couple had four minor daughters. The petition was dismissed, affirming the widow's status as a lawful widow and heir.

title: Custody of Minor Remains with Mother till 7 Years of Age
explainer:
This case concerns a custody dispute over a young boy between his father, Attique Ahmed, and his mother, Adla Noreen, who had been divorced. The father filed a case in the Family Court seeking custody, but both the Family Court and the Shariat Court ruled against him, allowing the child to remain with his mother. He then appealed to the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the father's appeal. It noted that the child, about three and a half years old, had lived with his mother since birth, while the father had been living abroad and had remarried. The court relied on Islamic legal principles, citing precedent that under Muslim law, custody of a young son may remain with the mother until he reaches seven years of age, unless there is clear evidence that this would harm the child's welfare. The court emphasized that the paramount consideration in custody cases is the welfare of the minor, taking into account the child's age, sex, and personal law, rather than automatically favoring either parent.

This judgment reaffirms an important principle in family law: young children, especially those who have been with their mother since birth, are generally best served by remaining in her care during early childhood, absent compelling reasons otherwise. It highlights how courts balance religious legal traditions with the overriding duty to protect a child's best interests.

title: Doubt regarding Prosecution Case is sufficient to give Benefit of Doubt to Accused
explainer:
This case involved two men, Umar Draz and Muhammad Nawaz, who were convicted by a trial court of murdering Gulbaz and sentenced to death. The prosecution's story was that Umar Draz called the victim away from a gathering, and later the complainant and a witness found both accused strangling him with a noose in the dark, after which the accused fled.

On appeal, the Lahore High Court found the case full of doubts. The alleged motive, that the victim had an illicit relationship with one appellant's mother, was based only on hearsay, as the complainant admitted he only "learnt" of this from an unnamed person who was never produced as a witness. The court also noted the mother was an elderly woman, much older than the victim, making the motive implausible. Additionally, one appellant was sixty-seven years old, yet supposedly outran younger witnesses who claimed to catch him in the act. No weapons or incriminating evidence were recovered from the accused. The court concluded the murder likely happened unwitnessed at night, and the accused were implicated merely on suspicion because the body was found near their home.

Applying the principle that even a single reasonable doubt is enough to benefit the accused, the court acquitted both men, setting aside their conviction and death sentences. The judgment highlights how courts must guard against convictions based on weak motive evidence, hearsay, and implausible circumstances, especially in capital cases.

title: At bail stage it is neither permissible nor desirable to make a deep scrutiny
explainer:
This case is about a wife accused of attacking her husband and seeking anticipatory (pre-arrest) bail in a criminal case. The husband alleged that his wife cut off his penis with a sharp weapon while he slept, motivated by a marital dispute. Police registered charges under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with causing hurt. The accused was initially granted pre-arrest bail by a lower court, but this was later withdrawn. She then filed a revision petition before the Azad Jammu and Kashmir High Court challenging that withdrawal, arguing the case was fabricated, inconsistent, and malicious, and also citing poor mental and physical health.

The High Court explained key legal principles: at the bail stage, courts should not conduct a deep examination of evidence; pre-arrest bail is an extraordinary remedy that must be used cautiously, especially in serious offences carrying heavy punishment; and a good ground for bail after arrest does not automatically justify bail before arrest. The court also noted that bail on medical grounds can be granted only if the illness is serious enough that proper treatment isn't possible in custody.

In this case, the accused had already received the extra time she requested for treatment, failed to appear in court even when summoned, and avoided appearing in person during the hearing. Because of this conduct, the court refused her pre-arrest bail and dismissed her petition, reinforcing that pre-arrest bail is a limited remedy not meant for routine use or to avoid accountability.

title: PLJ 2018 SC 391
explainer:
This case involved a petition by Mst. Sughran Bibi, whose son Mohsin Ali was killed in what police described as an encounter. After the police version of events led to an FIR being registered, investigation completed, and a formal challan (charge sheet) submitted to the trial court, the mother filed her own private complaint giving a different account of how her son died, naming different circumstances around the police action. She then sought registration of a separate, second FIR based on her version of the incident. The Supreme Court examined a recurring legal question: can multiple FIRs be registered for different versions of the same occurrence, or must a new version be handled differently under the law.

The Court ruled that only one FIR can exist for a single incident involving a cognizable offence. Any alternate account of the same occurrence, given later, should ordinarily be recorded as a statement during investigation, not as a fresh FIR. However, a separate FIR becomes permissible if the new version concerns a genuinely different occurrence, a different set of accused persons, or discloses a distinct cognizable offence.

Since an FIR already existed, investigation had concluded, a challan was filed, and the petitioner's private complaint was already being tried in court, the Supreme Court held that registering a second FIR for her version of the same incident was not legally justified. The petition was dismissed. This judgment clarifies how Pakistani courts should handle competing narratives of the same crime, ensuring consistency in the FIR system while still protecting victims through alternative legal remedies like private complaints.

title: Police is not statutory prohibited for reinvestigating a case
explainer:
This case involves an appeal against a conviction under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. Abdul Jabbar was caught driving a vehicle containing 170 kilograms of charas hidden in secret compartments, and a trial court sentenced him to life imprisonment and a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The key issue was how the evidence was handled. Initially, only small samples from 10 of the 140 recovered packets were sent for chemical testing. Later, after the prosecution's witnesses had already testified at trial, the investigating officer sent additional samples from all the remaining packets for testing without getting the trial court's permission first. The appellant's lawyer argued this was procedurally improper, and the state's own counsel admitted the investigator had no authority to send samples for testing after the case had already gone before the court.

The High Court agreed that this was a problem. It held that when the law requires something to be done in a specific way, that procedure must be followed exactly, and no shortcuts are allowed. Because the second chemical report was obtained improperly, the court ruled it inadmissible as evidence. However, the court also clarified an important principle: police are not legally barred from reinvestigating a case multiple times or filing a fresh charge-sheet based on new investigation. Despite finding the second report inadmissible, the court ultimately dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction based on other valid evidence.

title: Ex-Parte Proceedings in a Civil Suit
explainer:
This case comes from the Lahore High Court, Multan Bench, and deals with a dispute over property partition. The respondents had filed a suit to divide property they jointly owned with the petitioner, Zubaida Begum, who was named as a co-sharer in the case. She did not appear in court, and proceedings went ahead without her (ex-parte) starting in 1998. A preliminary decree was issued in 2004, which protected her share of the property. However, it was only in 2010, about 12 years after being declared ex-parte, that she filed an application asking the court to set aside those ex-parte proceedings, claiming she never received proper notice.

Both the trial court and the appellate court rejected her application because it was filed far too late. She then approached the High Court through a civil revision petition, also asking for condonation of a short delay in filing that revision, which the court allowed in the interest of justice.

On the main issue, however, the High Court ruled against her. It noted that her share in the property had already been protected in the preliminary decree, and since the property could not be physically divided, an auction had been ordered with her entitled to receive her share of the proceeds. Given the enormous 12-year delay in challenging the ex-parte order, the court held that the lower courts were right to dismiss her case as time-barred. The revision petition was therefore dismissed, reinforcing that legal challenges must be made within a reasonable time, even when rights are otherwise valid.

title: Constitutional Ejectment Petition
explainer:
This case concerned a dispute between a landlord and a shopkeeper over a rented shop in Sukkur. The landlord, Muhammad Rafi, claimed the petitioner was his tenant under a written rent agreement and sought eviction, partly to use the shop himself for his own business. The tenant, Muhammad Aslam, denied any landlord-tenant relationship with Rafi, claiming instead that he was a tenant of the Municipal Corporation on municipal land, with his own separate lease and rent arrangement with that authority. He argued the rent agreement produced by Rafi was fake. The Rent Controller ruled against the tenant, and the Appellate Court upheld that decision, though with some modification favorable to the tenant regarding his municipal allotment. The tenant then challenged this before the Sindh High Court under Article 199 of the Constitution.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that its constitutional jurisdiction is narrow: it cannot re-examine factual findings or act as a substitute for an appeal or revision, which are not available in such rent matters beyond the first appeal. The Court can only intervene if the lower courts acted without jurisdiction or their findings were legally perverse. Since the tenant had not challenged the appellate court's modified order and no jurisdictional error was shown, the Court upheld the eviction order.

This case matters because it clarifies the limited scope of High Court review in rent disputes, preventing such petitions from becoming backdoor appeals.

title: Nine Months Delay in FIR : Bail Granted
explainer:
This case is about a bail application in a cheque-dishonour case from Muzaffargarh, Punjab. The petitioner, Muhammad Nawaz, was accused under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with issuing a cheque that bounces due to dishonest intentions. The complainant alleged that Nawaz issued a cheque for Rs. 700,000 that was dishonoured when presented to the bank. Nawaz had been arrested and was in custody, and he applied to the Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) for post-arrest bail.

His lawyer argued that the cheque was given only as a business guarantee, that the FIR (police complaint) was filed nine months after the cheque was dishonoured without any explanation for the delay, that the maximum punishment for this offence is three years, and that police no longer needed him for investigation.

The court agreed with these arguments. It noted that the offence did not fall under the "prohibitory clause" of the bail law (which restricts bail for more serious crimes), and that the long unexplained delay in lodging the FIR raised doubts. Relying on earlier Supreme Court and High Court precedents, the judge granted bail, requiring Nawaz to submit a bond of Rs. 50,000 with a surety.

This case illustrates how courts weigh delay in reporting a crime and the severity of potential punishment when deciding bail requests.

title: Denial of Relationship in a Family Suit
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over whether a family court or a civil court had the authority to decide a marriage case. A woman had filed a suit for dissolution of marriage, claiming to be the wife of the petitioner. In his written response, the petitioner denied that any marriage existed between them and argued that since there was no valid marriage to dissolve, the Family Court had no jurisdiction to hear the case at all - he claimed such a dispute should go to a civil court instead.

The Family Court rejected this objection and proceeded with the case, prompting the petitioner to challenge that decision before the Islamabad High Court.

The High Court ruled against the petitioner. It explained that when one spouse denies the existence of a marriage, this is legally called "jactitation of marriage," and Pakistani law specifically places such disputes within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Family Court, not the civil courts. The court distinguished this situation from cases the petitioner cited, which involved disputes over inheritance where a third party (not one of the spouses themselves) questioned whether a marriage had existed. In those situations, civil courts were appropriate because the people disputing the marriage weren't the spouses themselves.

Since this case was a direct disagreement between two people claiming to be spouses, the Family Court was the correct venue. The petition was dismissed, meaning the case would continue in the Family Court as originally decided.

title: Bail Granted on Medical Ground
explainer:
This case involved Pir Muhammad Azam, who was facing accountability proceedings before the National Accountability Bureau on corruption-related charges. His first bail request had already been rejected by the Peshawar High Court in an earlier case. He then approached the court again, this time seeking bail purely on medical grounds, pointing out that in a separate but related criminal case, the same court had already granted him bail because of his serious health condition.

Medical reports showed that the petitioner suffered from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), with severe breathing difficulty requiring urgent treatment, ideally in an intensive care unit. A prison medical officer's report confirmed that the jail hospital lacked the specialized facilities and equipment needed to properly treat his condition, despite repeated hospital referrals.

The National Accountability Bureau opposed bail, arguing the jail could provide adequate care, but could not dispute that the petitioner had already been released on bail on identical medical grounds in another case.

The High Court held that once it is established that an illness cannot be properly treated inside jail and requires specialized care, the accused is entitled to bail regardless of the seriousness of the alleged offence. Relying on established Supreme Court precedents, the court ruled that gravity of illness can outweigh gravity of the charges, and granted bail on medical grounds, noting prosecution could later seek cancellation if the petitioner's health improved.
