title: Bail Confirmed because FIR was lodged after two days delay
explainer:
This case involved four petitioners—Nazir Ahmad and three others—who were accused of forcibly entering a complainant's house armed with weapons and injuring him and a woman, under various sections of the Pakistan Penal Code relating to causing hurt, house-trespass, assault, and rioting. They had already been granted temporary pre-arrest bail and were now asking the Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) to make that bail permanent.

The court confirmed their bail. Several factors influenced this decision. First, there was an unexplained two-day delay in filing the police report (FIR), which raised doubts about the complainant's account. Second, the investigating officer himself found that the location of the alleged incident actually belonged to the accused's family, and that the real event was just a minor quarrel between women of the two families—not the serious attack described in the FIR. Third, the two sides were relatives with an ongoing civil property dispute, suggesting a possible motive for false accusations. The investigating officer also confirmed that the accused had cooperated with the investigation, which was complete, and that their continued custody was unnecessary. Additionally, the petitioners had no prior criminal record, and the charges did not fall under the most serious category of offenses that normally bar bail.

This case illustrates how courts scrutinize delays in reporting crimes, investigative findings, and family disputes when deciding whether bail should be granted, especially where malicious prosecution is suspected.

title: Bail After Discharge Judgment
explainer:
This case from the Lahore High Court concerns a bail application filed by Bakht Nawaz, who was accused in a robbery-murder case. According to the original police report (FIR), two unknown armed men on a motorbike tried to rob the complainant and his companions after they withdrew cash from a bank. When the deceased, Irshad Hussain, resisted the robbery attempt, he was shot and killed.

Bakht Nawaz was not named in the original FIR. He was implicated later, nearly nine months after the incident, when the complainant gave a supplementary statement accusing him of being a facilitator or abettor. After his arrest, police investigated and actually found him innocent, recommending his discharge from the case. However, the local magistrate disagreed and kept him in custody.

The High Court noted several weaknesses in the case against him: no identification parade was conducted, the FIR mentioned only two unknown attackers while the later application suddenly named five accused including Nawaz, and his alleged role was limited to conspiracy rather than the actual shooting. The court found the prosecution had not gathered sufficient evidence linking him to the crime and that his guilt required further investigation.

Based on this, the court granted him post-arrest bail, requiring bail bonds of Rs. 100,000. The judgment clarifies these findings are preliminary and won't affect the actual trial, illustrating how courts grant bail when evidence against an accused appears weak or incomplete at this stage.

title: Personal Need of Landlord in Islamabad Rent Law Case
explainer:
This case from the Islamabad High Court involved a dispute between a tenant, Nadeem Asghar, and his landlords over rented commercial premises in F-7 Markaz, Islamabad. The landlords had filed an ejectment petition seeking to evict the tenant on several grounds, including non-payment of rent, personal need, subletting, property damage, and expiry of the lease. The Rent Controller initially ordered eviction based on default in rent payment and the landlord's personal need. On appeal, the Additional District Judge overturned the default finding but upheld the eviction on the ground of personal need, since the landlord, a doctor, wanted the premises to build a hospital for himself and his daughter, also a doctor. The tenant then challenged both decisions through this writ petition, arguing the landlords had not clearly specified how the space he occupied was needed, especially since another portion of the building was already vacant.

The High Court upheld the eviction, ruling that it is a landlord's legal right to reclaim property for genuine personal need, and courts should not interfere with that prerogative when the need is shown to be bona fide. However, the court clarified an important safeguard: if the tenant is evicted but the landlord does not actually use the premises for the stated purpose, the tenant can apply to the Rent Controller under Section 17(6) of the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance to be reinstated. This decision reinforces landlords' rights while protecting tenants from misuse of eviction orders.

title: Report of Handwriting Expert Obtained by High Court in a Writ Petition
explainer:
This case involved a petitioner, a retired Brigadier, who filed a writ petition in the Lahore High Court asking for registration of a criminal case (FIR) against several respondents. He alleged that his signature and that of another individual on an agreement to sell property in a Defence Housing Authority area had been forged, claiming the respondents had digitally copied his signature using computer scanning technology.

To resolve the dispute, the High Court itself took an unusual investigative step: it directed the respondents to appear in court with the original agreement to sell and the General Power of Attorney, which was an admitted document bearing genuine signatures and thumb impressions. The court then collected fresh specimen signatures and thumb impressions from the petitioner and the other individual in the presence of both parties, and sent all the material to the handwriting expert at the Federal Investigation Agency for comparison.

The expert's report concluded that the thumb impressions and signatures on the disputed agreement matched the specimen samples, based on ten identified points of similarity. Given this positive scientific finding contradicting the forgery claim, the court held there was no merit in the petition and declined to exercise its writ jurisdiction to order an FIR. The petition was dismissed, though the petitioner was left free to pursue other legal remedies such as a civil suit. The case illustrates how courts can use forensic evidence to test factual claims even in constitutional writ proceedings.

During investigation, it emerged that the material she was carrying was actually a partially burnt Namaz (prayer) book, not Quranic pages, and there was no witness who actually saw her burning anything. One of the prosecution's own witnesses, a cleric named Qari Muhammad Khalid Chishti, was found to have planted fake evidence and was himself later charged. Medical and investigative reports showed the girl was a minor, uneducated, with a mental age below her actual age, and essentially unaware of religious teachings in either Islam or Christianity.

The court found no evidence of criminal intent (mens rea), which is necessary for a blasphemy conviction, and noted apparent ulterior motives behind the complaint, possibly linked to tensions aimed at pushing the local Christian community out of the area. The judge ruled that forcing her through a trial would amount to abuse of the judicial process and quashed the FIR entirely.

title: Perjury is a heinous offence
explainer:
In this case, the Peshawar High Court dealt with a man named Haji Umar Khan who had originally filed a police report (FIR) accusing certain people of murdering his relative with firearms. The case went to trial, but when Umar Khan was called to testify under oath, he suddenly reversed himself, claiming he had never actually witnessed the murder and had not voluntarily lodged the FIR. He suggested he had been pressured by police and by the complainant's brother to sign a false report.

The trial court did not believe this reversal. It found that Umar Khan had indeed filed the original report of his own accord and signed it correctly, and that his later denial under oath was false. He was convicted of perjury under Section 193 of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to three years of rigorous imprisonment plus a fine of Rs. 10,000.

Umar Khan appealed the conviction, while the deceased's brother separately sought a harsher sentence. The Peshawar High Court reviewed the trial record and upheld the conviction, finding the trial judge's reasoning sound and not arbitrary. The High Court emphasized that lying under oath in court is a serious offense, since it can destroy an innocent person's reputation or freedom by falsely implicating them in a crime. Such conduct, the court said, deserves no leniency.

This case matters because it reinforces that witnesses who contradict their own sworn statements without credible justification can be prosecuted and punished for perjury, protecting the integrity of judicial proceedings.

title: Railway Accident Contributory Negligence Case Law
explainer:
This is a 2011 Supreme Court of Pakistan decision in a railway accident case, where the heirs of persons killed in railway accidents sued for compensation under the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855. The High Court of Sindh had ruled in favour of the victims' families, and the Railways appealed, arguing that the deceased themselves were partly to blame (contributory negligence) and so compensation should be denied or reduced.

The Supreme Court dismissed the Railways' appeals. It held that railways cannot escape liability for accidents caused by their own failure to maintain safety measures, such as keeping crossing gates closed, simply by claiming the victim should have been more careful. The defence of contributory negligence only applies if the railway proves it had taken all proper safety precautions and the victim deliberately bypassed them, for example by climbing a fence or opening a closed gate. Since the gate was admittedly open at the time of the accident, the fault lay with the Railways, which is also vicariously liable for its employees' negligence.

The judges further explained that tort law exists both to compensate victims' families and to deter negligent behaviour by institutions, and that delayed justice undermines its purpose. The court also discussed guidelines for estimating a deceased person's likely working life for compensation purposes, and noted that exemplary damages could be considered in cases of serious negligence.

title: Court can issue warrants or resort to sureties for appearance of accused
explainer:
This case from the Peshawar High Court dealt with the question of who is responsible for ensuring an accused person shows up in court. The accused, Sher Afzal, had been charged in a case registered under the Zina (Enforcement of Hudood) Ordinance and was granted bail by a magistrate. The complainant, Noor Muhammad, later asked the Sessions Court to cancel that bail, apparently because the accused was not appearing. The Additional Sessions Judge refused to cancel the bail, reasoning partly that the complainant had failed to point out or help locate the accused, who belonged to a different area.

The High Court found this reasoning flawed. It held that it is never the complainant's job to secure the attendance of an accused person in a criminal case. That responsibility lies with the State, and specifically the police, who must trace and produce the accused when summoned. The court also noted that when an accused cannot be found, the proper legal tool is to proceed against the sureties who guaranteed his appearance, not to blame the complainant.

Because the Sessions Court had wrongly placed this burden on the complainant and never even issued notice to the sureties, the High Court set aside its earlier order and sent the bail-cancellation matter back for a fresh decision on its actual merits. This judgment is significant because it clarifies that complainants should not be penalized for the State's failure to produce an accused, reinforcing that police and sureties bear that responsibility.

title: Wrong transfer of Shares in Property
explainer:
This case from the Peshawar High Court dealt with a family dispute over inheritance shares under Islamic law. The petitioners claimed they were descendants of a woman named Zeenat Bibi, daughter of the late Syed Rasan, and that they were entitled to their rightful shares in his estate (legacy). However, the entire property had been wrongly transferred into the names of Syed Rasan's two sons, cutting out the daughters' descendants from their inheritance.

The trial court had initially ruled in favor of the petitioners, but an appellate court reversed that decision and dismissed their case. The petitioners then brought this revision petition to the High Court.

The High Court held that under Sharia law, rightful heirs cannot be denied their due inheritance shares once their blood relationship to the common ancestor is established. It clarified that the petitioners' mother was entitled to a 1/6 share in Syed Rasan's estate, and each petitioner (as her children) was entitled to a 1/12 share. The court also addressed inheritance from another deceased relative, Mst. Zain Noora, directing how her share should be distributed among her nieces and other heirs.

Ultimately, the court found no legal error in the appellate court's judgment and dismissed the revision petition. This case highlights how Pakistani courts apply Islamic inheritance principles to ensure legal heirs, including women and their descendants, are not deprived of their rightful shares through improper property transfers.

title: Oral Sale Transaction Judgment
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land in Narowal after the death of Din Muhammad, the original owner. A mutation (record of land transfer) dated 12 April 1995 showed that Din Muhammad had orally sold his land to Muhammad Asghar shortly before his death. After Din Muhammad died, his legal heirs filed a lawsuit claiming he was mentally unwell at the time and lacked the capacity to make such a transaction, and that the sale was fraudulent and without real payment.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled against the person claiming to have bought the land, finding that the deceased was mentally disordered and that the sale was not genuinely proven. The buyer then approached the Lahore High Court, also asking for permission to bring new witnesses (two local lumberdars) to prove the deceased had identified himself as the person making the sale.

The High Court refused to allow this late additional evidence, holding that such evidence is meant to help the court reach a fair decision, not to let a losing party fix gaps in their original case long after the opportunity had passed. Since the buyer failed to produce solid proof of payment or of the deceased's free consent, and since two lower courts had already agreed on the facts, the High Court upheld their decisions and dismissed the case, confirming the land rightfully belonged to the deceased's heirs.

title: One Co-Sharer cannot deprive others to inherit
explainer:
This case involved a long-running family inheritance dispute from what is now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. When a man named Sarfraz died in 1931, local custom at the time excluded his daughters from inheriting, leaving his land only to his two sons. One son, Muhammad Afzal, died in 1935 without children, and his share was passed entirely to his brother Muhammad Nawaz under the same custom, again excluding Afzal's sisters, including Mst. Ayesha. Decades later, in 1993, Ayesha sued, arguing that by the time her brother Afzal died, the North-West Frontier Province Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1935 had replaced customary law with Islamic inheritance law, meaning she was entitled to a 1/3rd share of his estate as a legal heir. Over the years, Nawaz and his heirs had sold parts of the inherited land to outside parties, complicating her claim. The trial court dismissed her suit as filed too late, but the appellate court and later the High Court partly ruled in her favor.

title: Inheritance is distributed according to Sect
explainer:
This case from the Lahore High Court dealt with a family inheritance dispute that hinged on an unusual question: what religious sect did the deceased landowner belong to at the time of his death?

A man named Shukar died in 1941, leaving land that was initially given to his widow as a life estate. Later, under personal law reforms, this life estate ended and revenue authorities transferred the property to his widow and two daughters, after determining that Shukar was Shia by faith (which affects how inheritance shares are calculated under Muslim law). Distant relatives of Shukar, who stood to inherit a share only if he was Sunni, challenged this in civil court, claiming he was actually Sunni.

The trial court agreed that Shukar was Shia and ruled against the distant relatives, but the first appellate court reversed this, saying there wasn't enough proof of his sect and that evidence from earlier mutation proceedings shouldn't have been considered.

The High Court restored the trial court's decision. It held that documentary proof of someone's religious sect isn't required, and that people can change their sect during their lifetime. Crucially, a relative who himself stood to gain by claiming Shukar was Sunni had earlier testified, against his own interest, that Shukar was Shia. The court found this kind of admission highly credible. It also ruled that evidence from mutation proceedings could properly be considered by civil courts, reinstating the widow and daughters' full inheritance rights.

title: PLJ 2017 Lahore 875
explainer:
This case concerns a Christian citizen's constitutional challenge over divorce rights under Pakistani law. In 1981, during a non-democratic era, a military regime's Federal Laws (Revision and Declaration) Ordinance deleted Section 7 of the Divorce Act, 1869, which had allowed courts to grant divorce relief to Christians based on principles similar to those in UK divorce law. After this deletion, Christians in Pakistan were left only with the limited divorce grounds listed in Section 10 of the Act, such as adultery combined with other specific faults, making divorce very difficult for Christian couples compared to the broader relief previously available.

The petitioner argued this repeal violated fundamental rights guaranteed to religious minorities under the Constitution, including equality, dignity, and protection of minority interests, and that it was done without any democratic deliberation or consultation with the Christian community.

The Chief Justice clarified that the court was not examining or ruling on biblical or canonical Christian teachings, but purely reviewing whether a State law (the 1981 Ordinance) was constitutional. The judgment traces how divorce law has evolved globally, including the "no-fault" divorce movement recognizing irretrievable breakdown of marriage as sufficient grounds, reflecting changing understanding of marriage and family relationships.

This matters because it addresses the legal rights of Pakistan's Christian minority to obtain divorce fairly, scrutinizing whether laws imposed during military rule unjustly restricted minority rights without

title: Judgment on Sindh Local Government Ordinance
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a no-confidence (recall) motion against the Zila Nazim (district mayor) of Sukkur under the Sindh Local Government Ordinance, 2001. Two council members had issued a recall notice against the Zila Nazim, alleging he was acting against public interest. When the council meeting was convened to consider the motion, it had to be adjourned because there was no quorum present. The Zila Nazim argued that since the law did not require a quorum for such a meeting, the adjournment meant the recall motion should be treated as automatically considered and rejected, which would have let him keep his position without further challenge. The High Court of Sindh had rejected this argument, and he appealed to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision. It ruled that a recall motion must actually be put to a vote as required by Section 24(3) and (4) of the Ordinance; if a meeting is adjourned without voting, the motion remains pending rather than being deemed rejected. The Court also held that internal council bye-laws cannot override the clear requirements of the Ordinance, and that courts should generally avoid interfering in the internal business of elected local bodies unless there is a genuine legal violation.

This decision mattered because it clarified the correct legal procedure for handling no-confidence motions against local government heads, ensuring that recall motions are properly voted on rather than dismissed on technical grounds, thereby protecting the democratic process of accountability within local councils.

title: Impleading Minister as a Party in a suit
explainer:
This Supreme Court judgment, reported as PLJ 1990 SC 543, dealt with a dispute over the registration of the Islamabad Stock Exchange under the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969. Applicants had sought registration of a new stock exchange, but their application was effectively refused, partly through an order attributed to a Minister of State. The High Court had earlier found that the Minister's order was vitiated by malafide (bad faith), even though the Minister had not been formally made a party to the case, relying instead on principles of natural justice.

The Supreme Court majority disagreed with this approach. It held that Article 248 of the Constitution, which protects the President, Governors and Ministers from being personally blamed for acts done in their official capacity, cannot be bypassed simply by invoking natural justice. Courts cannot record adverse findings of personal bad faith against a Minister unless he has been properly impleaded as a party or has appeared as a witness. However, the Court still found the refusal of registration unlawful because the statutory procedure was not followed properly—no hearing was given, no reasons were recorded, and the decision was not communicated correctly, violating mandatory requirements of the law.

The Court dismissed the appeals, upheld that the registration process must be reconsidered afresh, and ordered adverse remarks against the former Minister to be removed from the judgment. The case is important for clarifying the limits of constitutional immunity for public officeholders and the right to a fair hearing in administrative decisions.

title: Evidence Act: Correctness of document test
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute from Mardan district. The plaintiffs claimed ownership of agricultural land, arguing their title stemmed from a 1926 compromise decree in an old pre-emption lawsuit, which they said was later confirmed through a 1964 agreement. The trial court and the first appellate court both ruled in the plaintiffs' favor, relying heavily on the age of these documents, treating them as presumptively genuine under the thirty-year-old document rule in the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order (Pakistan's evidence law).

The Peshawar High Court overturned these decisions. It held that merely because a document is old does not automatically make it reliable or true. Courts must also examine whether the document actually came from proper custody and whether it was genuinely signed by the person it claims to be from. More importantly, the court pointed out that the lower courts failed to actually read and understand what the documents said. The 1926 decree was from a pre-emption suit that was dismissed by compromise—it did not establish ownership or title at all. The 1964 agreement contradicted the 1926 decree and was not even a public document, so it couldn't automatically enjoy the same presumption of genuineness.

The High Court found the plaintiffs' suit was actually time-barred and essentially a retaliatory lawsuit. It set aside both lower court decisions, ruling they were legally and factually unsustainable. This case highlights that courts cannot blindly apply presumptions of correctness to old documents without examining their actual content and context.

title: Decree of Khula on unregistered Nikahnama
explainer:
This case from the Sindh High Court dealt with a husband's challenge to an ex-parte khula (wife-initiated divorce) decree granted by a Family Court in favor of his wife.

The wife had filed for dissolution of marriage, stating the Nikah was unregistered, that her Haq Mehr (dower, fixed at two tolas of gold) was never paid, and that her husband mistreated and eventually expelled her. The husband did not appear in court despite being summoned through multiple means, including newspaper publication, so the Family Court granted the divorce in his absence. The husband later challenged this in the High Court, claiming the Nikahnama was actually registered, that he was condemned unheard, and that the law required restoration of dower before khula could be granted.

The High Court dismissed the husband's petition. It held that the law requiring return of Haq Mehr applies only when the wife herself offers to surrender it in exchange for an expedited khula decree. Since the wife's dower was never paid to her in the first place, there was nothing to restore, and no violation occurred. The court also noted that the husband already had a pending application before the Family Court to set aside the ex-parte decree under the Family Court Rules, making the High Court petition premature and not maintainable. Any dispute about property allegedly transferred to the wife would have to be resolved separately in civil court.

This ruling clarifies that dower restoration rules protect husbands only when wives voluntarily give up already-received dower for quick khula, not in every khula case.

title: Restitution of Conjugal Rights  Decree
explainer:
This case involved a husband, Muhammad Shiraz, who had filed a suit for restitution of conjugal rights against his wife, while the wife had filed her own suit seeking maintenance and enforcement of certain conditions written into their Nikah Nama (marriage contract), specifically clauses 17 and 20, which dealt with gold ornaments and a lump sum payment of Rs. 50,000 in case of desertion by the wife.

The Family Court had granted the husband's suit for restitution of conjugal rights, while also awarding the wife and daughter maintenance, but had refused her claims for the gold ornaments and the Rs. 50,000 payment. On appeal, the Additional District Judge reversed this partly and awarded her the gold ornaments and the money. The husband challenged this before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court held that since the wife had deserted the husband and a decree for restitution of conjugal rights existed in the husband's favor, the contractual condition triggering payment upon "desertion" could not be enforced against him. It also ruled that such a condition in the Nikah Nama did not qualify as an "actionable claim" under the Transfer of Property Act. However, the Court held that since the wife still legally carried the husband's name as his wife, she remained entitled to basic maintenance as an acknowledgment of that status.

The petition was therefore partly allowed, setting aside the ornaments and Rs. 50,000 award, while upholding the maintenance granted to the wife.

title: Judgment on confiscation of non custom paid vehicles
explainer:
This Lahore High Court judgment dealt with dozens of customs appeals (87 cases decided together) concerning vehicles that had been seized by anti-smuggling authorities because no customs duty had been paid on them. The vehicle owners had applied to pay the required duties and fines to get their vehicles released, but Customs officials refused, citing a government notification (SRO 1374/1998) that barred such release for certain vehicles after a specified cut-off date. A lower appellate tribunal had sided with the owners, ordering the vehicles released on payment of fine and duty. The Customs Department challenged this before the High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of Customs. It held that since the vehicles exceeded Rs. 50,000 in value and no duty had been paid, they qualified as smuggled goods under the law. While Section 181 of the Customs Act normally allows owners the option to pay a fine instead of losing their goods, this right is subject to exceptions that the Board of Revenue can specify—meaning certain goods can be excluded from that option altogether. The tribunal had ignored this restriction. The court also rejected the claim that a buyer was protected as an innocent purchaser, since there was no proof of a genuine purchase, and the burden of proving good faith lay on the possessor, which was not met.

As a result, the High Court set aside the order releasing the vehicles and restored their confiscation. The judgment matters because it clarifies that authorities' power to allow fines instead of confiscation is not absolute and can be restricted by official regulations.

title: Two sisters cannot be married to one man at the same time
explainer:
This case involved a man, Wajid Hussain, who married two sisters in a way that violated Islamic marriage rules. He had married the elder sister, Shahida Parveen, in April 2010, then claimed to have divorced her in June 2010. Just 40 days later -still within the woman's mandatory waiting period (iddat) after divorce, during which a divorce is not yet legally final- he married her younger sister, Adeela Bibi. Adeela's father filed a police complaint (FIR) alleging his daughter had been enticed away for an improper purpose, and the couple approached the Islamabad High Court asking for the FIR to be thrown out, claiming their marriage was consensual and valid.

The court examined Islamic law and the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961, noting that a divorce (talaq) only becomes effective after the 90-day waiting period ends, not immediately when pronounced. Since the second marriage happened before the first divorce was finalized, the man was effectively married to both sisters simultaneously, which Islamic law strictly forbids. The court found this conduct contrary to social and religious norms and noted that other criminal offences beyond the one mentioned in the FIR might apply.

The court refused to use its special constitutional powers to cancel the FIR, ruling that the normal criminal justice process should continue instead. The petition was dismissed, meaning the case would proceed through regular trial.

title: Refusal of Bail in 489-F is an exception
explainer:
This case involved a man named Sajjad Haider who was accused of issuing a dishonoured cheque worth Rs. 300,000 to a complainant, an offence under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code. He was arrested and sought bail from the Lahore High Court after his arrest, known as post-arrest bail.

The prosecution argued that he had defrauded the complainant of a large sum and that he had previously been named in two other similar cheque-dishonour cases, so he should not get bail. The defence argued that the cheque was issued only as security for a business arrangement, that there was a 13-day delay in filing the police complaint, and that he had no prior convictions.

The court noted that offences under Section 489-F do not fall within the "prohibitory clause" of Section 497 of the Criminal Procedure Code, a legal category of serious offences where bail is normally refused. For offences outside this category, bail is the rule and refusal is the exception. Since the petitioner had never actually been convicted in his earlier cases, mere involvement in similar cases wasn't enough to deny him bail. The court also noted he could not be kept in jail indefinitely while his trial remained unfinished. Bail was therefore granted. This case reinforces the principle that for less serious offences, courts should favour granting bail unless exceptional circumstances justify refusal.

title: What to do if police detains someone wrongly?
explainer:
This case is about two people, Aamir, a 12-year-old student, and his father Nazir, who were detained by police in Nankana Sahib without proper legal procedure. Police had raided their home seeking a proclaimed offender, Nazir's other son, and in the process took away the boy, his father, two women, and two cows. The women were released, but Aamir and Nazir were held in illegal custody for days without their arrest being recorded or being produced before any court, as required by law.

The Lahore High Court sent a bailiff to recover them. Medical examination showed clear signs of brutal torture. The court found that although Aamir was technically named in an FIR, both detentions were illegal since proper procedures were ignored. Importantly, Nazir himself was not even accused of any crime; he was held merely to pressure information about his absconding son, which the court said was unacceptable because no one can be punished or tortured for a relative's alleged crimes.

The court ordered both detainees released, converted the habeas corpus petition into a bail matter for Aamir, and awarded compensation to be paid by the responsible police officers for illegal detention and torture. It also directed the Inspector General of Police to take disciplinary action against the officers involved under relevant police accountability rules, emphasizing that illegal detention and torture violate fundamental constitutional rights and international human rights standards.

title: What is case of sudden arrest?
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a conviction under Pakistan's Arms Ordinance, 1965. The appellant, Naik Amanullah Khan, had been found by police patrolling an area in Karak carrying two Kalashnikov rifles with ammunition, without any valid license. He was arrested on the spot, and the weapons were seized and documented. He was later convicted by a trial court and sentenced to three years' rigorous imprisonment with a fine, though because he was young and a first-time offender, the court showed leniency and placed him on probation instead of requiring him to serve time in custody.

He appealed to the Peshawar High Court, arguing the conviction was flawed. The High Court reviewed the testimony of the police officers involved, including the officer who made the arrest, a witness to the seizure, and the investigating officer who obtained an expert report confirming the weapons. The court found their testimony consistent, credible, and unshaken by cross-examination, with no evidence of bias or personal grudge against the appellant. It reaffirmed the legal principle that police officers are valid witnesses just like ordinary citizens, and their evidence shouldn't be dismissed simply because they work for the police.

The court concluded this was a case of sudden, on-the-spot arrest rather than a pre-planned raid based on prior tip-off, and that the prosecution had proven its case convincingly. Finding no error in the trial court's judgment, the High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction and probation.

title: What happens iIf police makes a strong and true case?
explainer:

On appeal, the defense argued that all witnesses were police officials, that police had entered the house without a magistrate's permission, that no identification parade was held since the appellant was unknown to police beforehand, and that no evidence linked the house to the appellant.

The Lahore High Court rejected these arguments and upheld the conviction. The court held that police witnesses are just as credible as any other public witnesses, citing Supreme Court precedent. It found the two police witnesses' testimony consistent and credible, with no major contradictions. The court also noted that ordinary members of the public are often reluctant to testify in such cases out of fear of retaliation from accused persons, which explained the absence of independent witnesses. Since the defense could not show any enmity motivating the police to falsely implicate the appellant with such a large quantity of narcotics, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction and life sentence. This case matters because it reinforces that police testimony alone, if credible and consistent, can sustain a narcotics conviction.

title: Judgment in HH v. Deputy Prosecutor of Italian Republic Genoa
explainer:
This Supreme Court decision concerns extradition cases where parents facing extradition have young children in the UK. One case involved an Italian warrant against two British parents convicted of drug trafficking, with children aged 11, 8 and 3. The other involved Polish warrants against a mother accused of dishonesty offences, with children aged 21, 17, 13, 8 and 3. No one disputed that removing these parents, as primary carers, would seriously harm the children.

The central legal question was how much weight courts must give to children's rights under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to family life) when deciding whether to extradite a parent. The court had to reconcile its earlier ruling in Norris, which held that extradition should only be blocked where the human rights consequences are "exceptionally serious," with a later case called ZH (Tanzania), which emphasized that children's best interests must be a primary consideration in decisions affecting them.

The judgment reviews the Norris precedent in detail, noting that extradition carries strong public interest weight, and only exceptionally compelling circumstances—potentially including serious harm to dependent family members—can outweigh it. The excerpt ends before the court's final conclusions, but the case matters because it shapes how UK courts balance international extradition obligations against the welfare of children whose parents are extradited, affecting many future extradition decisions involving families.

title: Time period for appeal in kashmir
explainer:
This case involved a husband, Muhammad Javaid, who was appealing against two ex-parte court decisions against him involving his wife, Mst. Zarria Begum. She had filed two cases, one seeking recovery of dower money and another seeking dissolution of the marriage. When the husband did not respond, the Family Court decided both cases against him without his participation and issued decrees on 24.11.2005.

The husband later tried to appeal these decisions, but he filed his appeals on 5.1.2006, well after the deadline. Under the AJ&K Family Courts Act, 1993, and related procedural rules, appeals against Family Court decisions must be filed within 30 days, though time spent obtaining certified copies of the judgment can be excluded from that count.

The husband argued he was not at fault because of delays in receiving copies of the decisions. However, the court calculated that even after deducting the two days he spent obtaining copies, his appeals were still filed nine days too late.

The AJ&K High Court, relying on an earlier Supreme Court interpretation of what counts as time "requisite for obtaining copies," ruled that the appeals were filed well beyond the permitted period. As a result, the court dismissed both appeals as time-barred, without even examining the merits of the husband's case.

This case is significant because it reinforces strict adherence to limitation periods in family law appeals, showing that even valid grievances cannot be heard if procedural deadlines are missed.

title: Suit for Pauperis can be filed without court fee
explainer:
This case was about a man who filed a civil suit for damages after being wrongly prosecuted and later acquitted. Unable to afford court fees, he applied to sue as a "pauper" (an exemption allowing poor litigants to file without paying court fees upfront). This application was rejected by the courts, including on revision. He then asked the trial court for more time to pay the required court fee instead, which was granted, and his suit was admitted for hearing.

The opposing party later argued that once his pauper application was rejected, his case no longer had a valid "cause of action" and the suit should be thrown out. The trial court disagreed, but a revisional court sided with the opposing party and rejected the plaint entirely.

The Sindh High Court overturned this, ruling that the rejection of a pauper application and the existence of a cause of action are two completely separate legal issues. Being refused fee exemption does not erase someone's underlying right to sue; it simply means they must pay the court fee like any other litigant. Since the petitioner was given time to pay the fee and did so, his suit was properly before the court. The High Court held the revisional court had misunderstood the law and sent the case back for proper proceedings.

The ruling matters because it protects poor litigants' access to justice, clarifying that fee disputes should not be used to wrongly kill genuine legal claims.

title: Shia widow cannot inherit husband's property
explainer: This case is about a property dispute between two families claiming to be heirs of Ahmad Ali, a man who died in the 1940s without children. His land passed to his widow, Mst. Hajran Bibi, as a limited owner under customary law. After customary law was abolished, officials transferred the land back to Ahmad Ali's side of the family rather than to the widow's heirs, on the basis that Ahmad Ali was Shia by faith. Under Shia inheritance law, a childless widow does not inherit her husband's immovable property (land), though she may get a share of movable property and household goods. The widow's relatives argued that Muslims in undivided India should be presumed Sunni Hanfi by default and that the claim was filed too late. The trial court initially dismissed the suit, but the appellate court reversed that decision and ruled in favor of Ahmad Ali's relatives. The High Court, in this revision petition, upheld the appellate court's ruling, confirming that since Ahmad Ali was Shia and died without children, his widow had no right to inherit his land, and the land rightly reverted to his blood relatives after her death. This case matters because it shows how a person's religious sect can significantly affect inheritance rights for surviving spouses under Pakistani law, particularly regarding childless widows.

title: Poor remarks against judiciary can result in contempt of court
explainer:
This case is about contempt of court proceedings brought against the Editor-in-Chief of a daily newspaper, Lashkar, after it published a news headline on 28 November 1997 that the court found to be false, scandalous, and damaging to the reputation of judges and the judiciary as a whole. The Chief Justice initially flagged the offending headline, and a single judge of the High Court took up the matter, eventually finding the editor guilty under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1976, and sentencing him to six months' imprisonment plus a fine.

The editor appealed to a larger bench, explaining that he had been away in Rawalpindi when the item was published, that he immediately sacked the Chief News Editor responsible once he learned of it, and that he had tendered an unconditional and sincere apology without contesting the case or hiring a lawyer.

The appellate bench upheld the finding of guilt, agreeing that the publication did amount to contempt. However, considering his genuine remorse and unconditional apology, the court reduced his punishment, ruling that the time he had already spent in custody was enough to satisfy justice. He was ordered released, subject to paying the fine.

The case matters because it shows how courts balance protecting judicial dignity from scandalous reporting with recognizing genuine remorse and apology as grounds for leniency in sentencing.

title: Decision should be on merits
explainer:
This case involves a government employee, Syed Tahir Abbas Shah, who worked for the Oil and Gas Development Company Limited (OGDCL) and had a service-related grievance. He filed a constitutional petition in the Islamabad High Court seeking relief, but that court dismissed his petition, ruling that it had no jurisdiction over the matter and that he should instead approach the Federal Service Tribunal.

The Supreme Court disagreed. It traced through a series of earlier rulings dealing with the question of which forum, the High Court or the Service Tribunal, has jurisdiction over grievances of employees working in corporations connected to the federal government. The key principle that emerged is that if an employee's service conditions are governed by statutory rules, the High Court can hear their case under its constitutional jurisdiction. If, however, the employee's terms are governed only by contract or internal regulations rather than statutory rules, the ordinary master-servant principle applies and a different remedy is required.

The Supreme Court noted that in a related case involving OGDCL employees, it had already been held that OGDCL employees are governed by statutory rules, meaning the High Court, not the Service Tribunal, has jurisdiction over their grievances. Based on this, the Supreme Court found that the High Court's earlier dismissal was wrong, granted leave to appeal, and sent the case back to the Islamabad High Court to decide the petitioner's grievance on its actual merits rather than rejecting it on jurisdictional grounds.

title: Constitution petition dismissed in illegitimate child case
explainer:
This case was about a father, Zaheer Ahmad, who was ordered by the Family Court to pay monthly maintenance for a minor child, a decision upheld by the Appellate Court. The father challenged this before the Lahore High Court, arguing he should not have to pay because the child was illegitimate. His reasoning was that the child was born on 7 November 2004, about eleven months and five days after his wife had already left him in desertion on 2 December 2003, implying the child could not be his.

The High Court rejected this argument and dismissed the petition. It held that questions of a child's legitimacy carry serious, far-reaching consequences and must not be decided lightly or merely on a husband's accusations. A child born within a lawful marriage is presumed legitimate, and this presumption is strong under Islamic law, summarized in the principle that "the child follows the bed." Mere denial by the father, without strict and credible proof to the contrary, is not enough to displace this presumption. The court also noted that the father had never pursued the proper legal procedure of Li'an (the formal process for a husband to disown a child by oath) in a competent court.

Since there was no solid evidence proving illegitimacy, the court upheld the lower courts' rulings, affirming the child was legitimate and entitled to maintenance from the father. This case reinforces how strongly Pakistani law protects children's legitimacy and maintenance rights.

title: Term ‘police authorities’ used in Section 22-A(6), Cr.P.C. is wide enough to include FIA
explainer:
This case involved the National Bank of Pakistan and one of its officers, who were being investigated by the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) over allegations of illegally issuing loans and money laundering. The bank went to the Lahore High Court asking it to use its constitutional writ jurisdiction (Article 199) to stop or quash the FIA inquiry, claiming the agency was exceeding its authority and harassing its employees.

Before examining the merits, the court had to decide whether the petition was even allowed to be filed directly in the High Court, given that the law provides another remedy: under Section 22-A(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code, a person who feels wronged by "police authorities" (such as through non-registration of a case, unfair transfer of investigation, or excess of power) can complain to an "ex-officio justice of peace," usually a Sessions Judge.

The key legal question was whether the FIA counts as a "police authority" under this section. The court held that it does, since FIA officers are given the same powers, duties, and status as provincial police officers under the law that created the agency. Therefore, people with complaints against the FIA can and should go to the justice of peace first, rather than directly to the High Court.

Since this alternate remedy existed, the court ruled the writ petition was not maintainable and dismissed it, directing the bank to pursue its complaint through the justice of peace instead. This decision clarifies that FIA actions are subject to the same local judicial oversight mechanism as regular police, rather than requiring direct High Court intervention.

title: Granting Custody while granting visitation
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute over an eight-year-old boy, Waliyaan, following the breakdown of his parents' marriage. His mother had moved to the UK for higher education, originally with the father's agreement that she could take Waliyaan with her, provided his visa was approved. However, the boy's visa application was rejected, so he stayed in Pakistan with his maternal grandparents while his mother went abroad alone. The couple later divorced. The father then sought custody, while the mother and her parents fought to retain guardianship and custody.

The Family Court and the Appellate Court both ruled in favor of the father, granting him custody, while setting up a visitation schedule for the maternal grandparents and allowing the mother custody whenever she visited Pakistan. The mother and her parents challenged these decisions before the Islamabad High Court.

The High Court upheld the custody award to the father, reasoning that since the child could not join his mother in the UK, awarding custody to the father was not improper, especially as there was no finding that he was unfit to care for his son. However, the Court objected to one part of the lower court's ruling, that barred the mother from ever seeking permanent custody if she returned to Pakistan. The High Court struck down this restriction, holding that any future custody claim must be decided afresh based on the child's best interests at that time. The petition was therefore partly allowed.

title: Condition of Non Counting Contractual Service
explainer:
This case involved a government employee, Wali Muhammad, who worked on a contractual basis at the Prime Minister's Literacy Commission starting in 1996. His job was eventually regularized in 2018, but only with effect from 2013, giving him about four years of regular service before he retired in 2017 upon reaching retirement age. When he applied for pension, he was denied because the rules required a minimum of ten years of regularized service to qualify, and he argued his earlier years of contractual work should count toward that total.

The Federal Service Tribunal rejected his appeal. It explained that government office memorandums from 2013 and 2014, along with the Civil Service Regulations, clearly state that contractual service does not count toward the ten-year minimum needed to become eligible for pension. The Tribunal relied on Supreme Court precedents which established that while contractual service can be used to calculate the amount of pension once someone is already eligible, it cannot be combined with regular service just to meet the eligibility threshold in the first place. A special provision in the regulations that deals with counting temporary service was found not to override this requirement.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that many government employees who spent years on contract before being regularized cannot use that contractual time to make up for a shortfall in the ten years of permanent service required for pension eligibility, even if their total years of work exceed ten.

title: 302(b) - Modification in Quantum of Sentence
explainer:
This case is about a double murder appeal from Dera Ghazi Khan. Ghulam Akbar was convicted by a trial court of killing his relatives' parents (Naseer Muhammad and Musarrat Wazeer) and sentenced to death on two counts, after the complainant alleged a family dispute over marriages had turned violent. Three co-accused were acquitted. Akbar appealed his conviction and death sentence, while the case also went before the High Court as a Murder Reference, which is required whenever a trial court imposes a death sentence.

The Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) examined the evidence, including eyewitness testimony from the complainant and his brother, medical evidence, and a forensic report. It found the eyewitness accounts credible and consistent, supported by medical evidence, and rejected the defense's claim that the real culprits had been substituted. However, the court noted that the prosecution had only produced a photocopy of the forensic report, not the original, making it inadmissible evidence.

The court upheld Akbar's conviction for murder but decided his case did not warrant the death penalty, citing certain mitigating ("extenuating") circumstances in his favor. It reduced his sentence from death to life imprisonment, applying the principle that doubt or weaknesses in a case can benefit an accused specifically on the question of sentence, even where conviction itself stands.

title: Dower Amount can be enhanced by Husband during subsistence of Marriage
explainer:
This case involved a husband and wife whose marriage ended in divorce, which was later revoked after they agreed to reconcile. As part of that reconciliation, the wife claimed, the husband signed an agreement raising her dower amount from Rs. 500 to Rs. 100,000 and promising monthly maintenance for her and their son. When the husband later failed to pay, the wife sued for the dower and maintenance. The Family Court ruled in her favor, and her husband's subsequent appeal was also dismissed. He then challenged these decisions before the Lahore High Court, arguing that the agreement enhancing the dower was forged.

The High Court rejected his petition. It noted that the wife had produced the written agreement and witnesses to support it, and that handwriting comparisons by the lower courts found his signatures on the agreement matched his admitted signature elsewhere. The husband never sought expert verification to challenge this despite having opportunities to do so, which the court viewed as suspicious. Importantly, the court held that under Islamic law, a husband can voluntarily increase the dower amount at any time during the marriage, not just at the time of the nikah.

The ruling matters because it confirms that dower agreements made after marriage are legally enforceable, and courts will uphold a wife's right to such enhanced amounts when properly proven, protecting women from husbands who later try to deny commitments made to preserve the marriage.

title: Power of Review exercised by Wafaqi Mohtasib
explainer:
This case involved a company, Kasur Oil Mills, that had taken a complaint to the Wafaqi Mohtasib (a federal ombudsman set up under a 1983 presidential order) seeking redress for its grievance. The Mohtasib initially dismissed the complaint, but after the company filed a review petition, the Mohtasib reversed course and ruled in its favor. The opposing party then challenged this reversal before the President of Pakistan, who accepted their representation and set aside the Mohtasib's revised decision. The company then went to the Lahore High Court, arguing that the President's order lacked proper reasoning and had been passed without giving it a personal hearing.

The High Court rejected these arguments and dismissed the petition. It held that the Wafaqi Mohtasib never had the legal power to review its own earlier decisions in the first place, since the governing law contained no provision allowing this. The court explained that the power of review is not a mere procedural matter but a question of jurisdiction, and such power must be expressly granted by law before it can be used. Since no such power existed, the President was right to set aside the Mohtasib's review order, and this itself counted as a valid reason. The court also held that the President was not legally required to grant a personal hearing in such appeals.

This ruling reinforces the principle that administrative bodies cannot assume powers, like reviewing their own decisions, unless explicitly authorized by statute.

title: Judgment related with redressal of grievance petition of employee
explainer:
This case involved a Pakistan Railways employee, Said Muhammad, who joined as a Pointsman in 1969 and was gradually promoted over the years, eventually reaching the post of Guard Gr-1 in 1994 after completing a required training course. He retired in 1997 with his retirement benefits sanctioned. However, after his retirement, Railways authorities launched an inquiry into several Guards' matriculation certificates, which was a prerequisite qualification for that post. Said Muhammad allegedly could not produce his original certificate, and in March 1998, seven months after his retirement, the department reverted him to his earlier, lower post, which would reduce his pension benefits.

Said Muhammad complained to the Wafaqi Mohtasib (Ombudsman), who ruled in his favor, holding he was entitled to full pension based on the higher post he held at retirement. Railways then challenged this decision in the Peshawar High Court.

The High Court dismissed the Railways' petition. It found that an employee cannot be reverted to a lower post after retirement, that Railways had failed to use the proper legal remedy of appealing to the President as required by law, and that another employee in a similar situation had been treated differently, meaning Said Muhammad faced discrimination. The court also noted Railways' negligence in not checking his service record earlier. It upheld the Ombudsman's authority to intervene in cases of maladministration, even for railway employees, and refused to interfere with that decision.

title: Misconduct of a Judicial Officer
explainer:
This case involved a civil judge who was removed from service after a surprise inspection found 356 of his case files incomplete. In 226 of these files, judgments or orders had been dictated and typed but never signed by him. In another roughly 50 files, no judgment or order existed at all. Despite this, he had issued succession and guardianship certificates and robkars (court orders) to release criminal offenders based on these unsigned or non-existent judgments. A departmental inquiry was held, and he was ultimately dismissed from judicial service. He appealed to the Punjab Subordinate Judiciary Service Tribunal, arguing the punishment was too harsh given his otherwise clean record, that no litigant had actually been harmed, and that staff failures (an inefficient stenographer) were partly to blame for missing orders.

The Tribunal rejected these arguments. It held that there is no legal concept of an oral or unsigned judgment being valid or enforceable, and that issuing certificates and release orders without proper signed judgments was a serious illegality, not a mere technical lapse. It found the judge had effectively invented his own improper procedure for granting relief without legal authority to do so. Given the sensitive and important nature of judicial work, the Tribunal ruled that such inefficiency and dereliction of duty deserved an especially strict standard, higher than for ordinary government employees. It upheld the removal from service as a proportionate penalty, dismissing the appeal.

title: Once divorce is pronounced it is divorce
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over inheritance rights following the death of Syed Gulzar Hussain Shah. Mst. Asghar Bibi and another petitioner filed a suit claiming a share in his property through partition, but the respondents argued she was not entitled to inherit because Gulzar Hussain Shah had divorced her back in 1971, meaning she was no longer his wife when he died. Both the trial court and the appellate court had ruled against her on this point, finding that she had indeed been divorced, based on a written divorce deed (talaqnama) supported by witness testimony, including an admission from her own relative that she had been divorced.

On revision before the Lahore High Court, her lawyer argued the divorce was invalid because it was never formally reported to the local Union Council as required under Section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961. The court rejected this argument, holding that Islamic law does not require any specific procedure for pronouncing divorce - it can be oral or written, and a written divorce becomes irrevocable. Failure to send the required notice to the Union Council does not undo a divorce that has actually taken place, since requiring such notice to invalidate a divorce would conflict with Islamic principles.

The court also noted that the evidence strongly supported the divorce and that she had never properly denied it in her own testimony. The revision was dismissed, confirming she could not inherit as a wife.

title: Allocation of Category to Ad Hoc Teacher
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the regularization of a government school teacher's employment status. Mrs. Zakia Latif had been appointed as a Senior English Teacher on an ad hoc basis in 1989 at an Islamabad Model School. Although she was later selected for a regular position, a government ban on appointments meant she continued working on an ad hoc basis. In 1994, the Federal Government introduced a policy to regularize ad hoc employees hired between 1981 and 1990, sorting them into two categories. The Ministry of Education reviewed her case and placed her in Category 1, the more favorable category for regularization. However, the Federal Public Service Commission (FPSC) overruled this and placed her in a different category, which led to her being denied regularization.

Mrs. Latif challenged this before the Lahore High Court, which ruled in her favor, directing that she be treated according to the category assigned by the Ministry of Education. The FPSC then appealed to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, refusing the FPSC leave to appeal. It reasoned that since the regularization policy was made by the Government, and the Ministry of Education was a part of that same Government, the Ministry was better positioned to decide which category its own employees belonged to. The FPSC had failed to justify its authority to override the Ministry's categorization.

This case is important because it clarifies that when implementing government policies affecting employees of a specific ministry, that ministry's assessment of its own staff should generally be respected over an external body's contrary classification.

explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a petrol pump and CNG station site in Islamabad. The appellant had leased the plot from the Capital Development Authority's Staff Welfare Organization for thirty years starting in 1973, building the facility at his own expense. When the lease neared expiry, the authority offered only a five-year extension at a much higher rent, which the appellant did not outright refuse but instead asked for a full thirty-year renewal, similar to what the Authority itself enjoyed under its own arrangement. Without properly resolving this, officials dispossessed him and sealed his premises, despite an earlier court undertaking that he would not be removed except through due legal process.

The Lahore High Court held that this dispossession was illegal because it violated mandatory requirements of prior notice and fair procedure. The court emphasized that public authorities must act justly, fairly, and without arbitrariness, and that courts can intervene under Article 199 of the Constitution when such fairness is breached, even in matters touching contracts, if public functionaries act unreasonably or with mala fide intent.

The court found the rejection of the appellant's extension request arrogant and improper, especially since the authority had granted itself similar long-term benefits. It ordered that possession be restored to the appellant and directed that his lease be extended for thirty years, applying principles of equity and fairness.

This case matters because it reinforces that government bodies cannot bypass fair procedure or act arbitrarily against citizens, even in contractual or quasi-contractual relationships.

title: PLJ 2018 Tr.C. (Services) 147
explainer:
This case involved a police department employee who had originally been appointed as a Cook in 1999 on a family-support quota, following his father's death during service. In 2004, after applying for recruitment, he was appointed as a Driver Constable by the CCPO, Lahore, and served in that role for over a decade with a clean record.

In 2016, the CCPO withdrew his 2004 appointment order, claiming it was illegal because changing his cadre from Cook to Driver Constable violated rules, citing a Supreme Court of Pakistan judgment that had nullified out-of-turn and ante-dated promotions (often linked to gallantry awards).

The Punjab Service Tribunal disagreed. It held that the Supreme Court's ruling specifically addressed out-of-turn or ante-dated promotions and cases of officials transferred or deputed outside their proper cadre - not straightforward appointments like this one. Since the appellant was never promoted out of turn, nor was his case about deputation or transfer, the Supreme Court judgment did not apply to him. The Tribunal found that the department had wrongly relied on and misapplied that precedent to cancel a legitimate appointment made 12 years earlier.

As a result, the Tribunal set aside the 2016 withdrawal order and restored the appellant to his position as Driver Constable. This case matters because it shows courts scrutinizing whether government departments are correctly applying higher court rulings, protecting employees from having legitimate, long-standing appointments overturned based on precedents that don't actually fit their situation

title: PLJ 2018 SC 66
explainer:
This case was about tenants in Islamabad who were ordered to vacate rented properties because their tenancy periods had expired. The landlords used this expiry as the ground for eviction under the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance, 2001, and the lower courts, including the Islamabad High Court, agreed and ordered eviction. The tenants appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that even after the tenancy period ended, they remained "tenants" in the legal sense and could only be evicted on the specific grounds listed in Section 17 of the Ordinance (like non-payment of rent, subletting, or personal need of the landlord) — not simply because the lease term had ended.

The Supreme Court disagreed. It held that Section 6 of the Ordinance clearly states that a tenancy is no longer valid once its term expires. Reading this together with Section 17, the Court ruled that continuing to occupy the property after the tenancy period ends, without the landlord's written consent, amounts to a violation of the tenancy terms — which is itself a valid ground for eviction under Section 17. The Court rejected the argument that this made Section 6 redundant, saying such an interpretation would instead ignore it entirely and let tenants occupy property indefinitely despite having no legal right to do so.

The appeals were dismissed, meaning the eviction orders stood. The decision clarifies that landlords in Islamabad can seek eviction simply because a tenancy agreement's term has expired, without needing to prove another separate ground.

title: PLJ 2018 Peshawar 104
explainer:
This case involved a wife who had filed a family court suit against her husband seeking dissolution of marriage, dower, maintenance, dowry articles, and a sum of money. The Family Court partially ruled in her favor, granting dissolution of marriage through khula (in lieu of unpaid dower) along with maintenance during the iddat period, but rejected her claims for dowry articles and Rs. 50,000 she said she had given her husband. Her appeal against this partial decision was dismissed by the Additional District Judge, prompting her to file a writ petition before the Peshawar High Court.

The High Court also dismissed her petition. It found that she had failed to provide convincing evidence for her remaining claims. Regarding the dowry articles, she only submitted a typed list prepared on the day she filed the suit, with no receipts or supporting witnesses to verify it was genuine. Regarding the Rs. 50,000, she could not show any evidence of when or where she gave this money to her husband. The court held that mere unsubstantiated statements are not sufficient proof in law.

Since both lower courts had reached the same conclusions based on proper evaluation of evidence, and no legal error was found, the High Court held there was no basis to interfere. This case illustrates that in family law disputes, claims for dowry items or money must be backed by solid, verifiable evidence such as receipts or witness testimony, not just personal assertions or self-prepared lists.

title: To Prevent Abuse of Process of Court 561-A, 265-K and 249-A are remedies
explainer:
This case involved a woman, Farzana Siddique, who was caught in a legal dispute after marrying a man of her own choice. A complaint was filed against her, her husband, and others, leading to an FIR (police case) under laws dealing with abduction-related offences. The complainant alleged wrongdoing, but the woman insisted she was an adult who married by her own free will, and she had already given a statement to this effect before a civil judge.

She approached the Azad Jammu & Kashmir High Court asking that the FIR be quashed, arguing the case was false and that the registration of the complaint was delayed and unexplained.

The High Court explained that its inherent powers under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code exist to prevent misuse of the courts and to ensure justice, even without waiting for the trial court to decide the matter through other legal routes like Sections 249-A or 265-K. These powers should be used sparingly, but are appropriate when continuing a case would amount to unnecessary harassment.

The judge found that since the woman clearly and voluntarily confirmed her marriage, and Islamic law considers the free consent of an adult, sane couple sufficient for a valid marriage, no criminal offence was actually established. The court therefore quashed the FIR, emphasizing that such cases must be judged on their own specific facts, and distinguishing this case from another precedent where similar relief had been denied by the Supreme Court.

title: Suit for Correction of Parentage in Revenue Record
explainer:

The respondent, Abdul Hameed, filed a suit asking the court to correct his father's name in official land records, claiming his father was actually Mehr Khan, though records showed the name as Qutab Khan. The defendant, Abdul Latif, contested this, denying the respondent was Mehr Khan's son at all, effectively disputing his legitimacy and inheritance claims.

The trial court dismissed the suit, but on appeal, the District Judge sent the case back for retrial, directing that the plaintiff be allowed to amend his plaint, bring in all of Mehr Khan's legal heirs as parties, and properly raise the issue of legitimacy so the real dispute could be fully examined with evidence.

title: Procedure in case of Joint Trial of Challan and Complaint Case
explainer:
This case concerns a murder trial where the person who filed the original police complaint (FIR) also filed a separate private complaint containing the same allegations against the same accused persons. The trial court decided to hold a joint, single trial covering both cases together, rather than trying the private complaint first and keeping the police case on hold, which is the procedure normally recommended by courts.

The accused were acquitted by the trial court, and the High Court upheld that acquittal. The complainant then approached the Supreme Court, arguing that the acquittal should be overturned because the trial court had wrongly combined the two cases instead of trying the complaint case first.

The Supreme Court agreed that the law generally requires the complaint case to be tried first when the same complainant brings both an FIR and a private complaint on identical allegations against the same accused. However, it held that a procedural irregularity like this does not automatically invalidate a verdict. Under Section 537 of the Criminal Procedure Code, a conviction or acquittal cannot be reversed merely because of an error in the mode of trial unless it actually caused a failure of justice. Since the petitioner never objected to the joint trial at any stage, and since the evidence against the accused (last-seen evidence, motive, and an alleged extra-judicial confession) was weak regardless of how the trial was conducted, the Court found no failure of justice had occurred. The petition was dismissed, and the acquittal stood. The case clarifies that procedural irregularities only matter if they genuinely affect the fairness of the outcome.

title: Duty of Care is Legal Duty owed by employer towards employee
explainer:
This case, decided by the Islamabad High Court, dealt with a wave of petitions filed by employees of the Capital Development Authority (CDA) and similar organizations, who were asking the court to step in and resolve disputes over their terms and conditions of service, such as disciplinary actions and service grievances. Since these employees were not civil servants, they could not approach the Federal Service Tribunal and had no other effective forum, so they were forced to invoke the High Court's extraordinary constitutional jurisdiction under Article 199.

The court held that employers, including government-controlled bodies like CDA, owe a legal "duty of care" to their employees, similar to duties recognized between doctors and patients or lawyers and clients. This duty requires employers to protect employees from harm and to provide fair, affordable, and quick ways to resolve workplace disputes. Failing to provide such mechanisms, the court said, breaches this duty of care and violates employees' fundamental rights, particularly the right to access justice, which is tied to the right to life under Article 9 of the Constitution.

The court noted that forcing employees to seek relief only through High Court litigation is neither affordable nor accessible, especially for lower-grade staff. It directed the government and its organizations to justify why they haven't created independent, affordable, and impartial tribunals for employees, and praised CDA's steps toward establishing such a grievance-redressal forum, calling it a move in the right direction.

title: Judgment on Article 4 of Constitution
explainer:
This case involved landowners (encroachers) in Faisalabad who had been occupying land since 1947 and built construction on it in 1995. When revenue authorities earlier tried to demolish their construction, the petitioners went to court, and in 1997 the Lahore High Court directed the Collector to decide their claim in accordance with law. That order was never complied with. Instead, in 2009, the Deputy District Officer (Revenue) issued an order under the Colonization of Government Land Act, 1912, directing officials to forcibly retake the land and seize crops, trees, or building material without compensation and without giving the petitioners any notice or hearing.

The petitioners challenged this order, and the Lahore High Court ruled in their favor. The court held that even people who are encroachers or trespassers still have a constitutional right under Article 4 of the Constitution to be treated in accordance with law. Article 4 was described as Pakistan's "due process clause," guaranteeing fairness, natural justice, transparency, and the right to be heard before any action harmful to a person's property is taken. Since the 2009 order was passed without notice, without a hearing, and without complying with the earlier court directive, it violated Article 4 and could not stand.

The judgment matters because it reaffirms that government authorities cannot take action against anyone's life, liberty, or property—even against illegal occupants—without following fair legal procedure, reinforcing due process as a core constitutional protection for everyone in Pakistan.

title: Maintainability of Petition after notices are duly served
explainer:
This case involved a long-running property dispute. Muhammad Younas had filed a suit against Shabbir Hussain for possession of property through specific performance of a 1998 sale agreement. When Hussain failed to appear in court, he was proceeded against ex-parte in 2000. His application to have that ex-parte order set aside was rejected, and so was his subsequent appeal. He then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging those rulings, but crucially, he never obtained any order from the High Court pausing or suspending the trial court proceedings. While his writ petition was still pending, the trial court went ahead, recorded evidence, and issued a decree against him. Instead of appealing that decree, he wrongly filed another application under Order IX Rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code to have the decree set aside, which was also dismissed.

The High Court ruled against Hussain, holding that since he had been properly served with court notices, an application under Order IX Rule 13 was not the correct legal remedy for challenging the decree itself—he should have filed a regular appeal instead. The court also noted that Hussain had secretly sold the disputed property through a registered deed without informing the trial court, indicating an intent to delay proceedings and mislead the court. The petition was dismissed. This case clarifies that ex-parte orders and ex-parte decrees are separate legal matters requiring separate remedies, and that pending higher court petitions don't automatically pause lower court proceedings unless a stay is explicitly granted.
