title: Complaint for separation of share in Father's Legacy
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the inherited property of the late Alam Khan. Some female heirs filed a civil suit before a Civil Judge in Mardan seeking declaration, partition, and recovery of profits from their share. While that suit was still pending, they also filed a separate complaint before the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Ombudsman (Women's Property Rights) under a 2019 law meant to protect women's property rights, asking for their share to be separated. The Ombudsman ordered that the entire disputed property be attached and sealed until the complaint was decided. The other heirs, who were already contesting the civil suit, challenged this sealing order, arguing it was illegal and deprived them of income from the property.

The Peshawar High Court examined whether the Ombudsman had the authority to order such attachment and sealing while a civil court was already handling the same property dispute. The Court held that sealing property is not supported by law, and that attachment must follow proper procedures under the Civil Procedure Code. It ruled that once a matter is already pending before a competent civil court, the Ombudsman should generally step back, since proceeding otherwise could conflict with the constitutional separation of powers between the judiciary and executive bodies like the Ombudsman. The sealing order was set aside, though the earlier attachment order was allowed to continue. The case clarifies the limits of the Ombudsman's powers when courts are already seized of the same dispute.

title: Commercial and Service Activities of Civil Aviation Authority
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute between the Sindh Revenue Board and the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) over whether the Sindh government could charge sales tax on services CAA provides at airports, such as facilities for airlines and passengers. CAA challenged this tax in the Sindh High Court, which ruled in its favour and struck down the provincial tax as unconstitutional. The Sindh Revenue Board then appealed to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeal. It held that CAA performs functions that fall under subjects reserved exclusively for the federal government under the Constitution's Federal Legislative List, such as aviation, airports, and related regulatory matters. Although CAA charges fees for facilities like airport services, this does not transform its constitutionally mandated functions into "services" that a province can tax. The Court explained that CAA is structurally and financially controlled by the Federal Government: its governing board is dominated by federal appointees, its accounts are audited by the Auditor-General, its funds come largely from federal grants and loans, and it cannot even be wound up except by federal order. Allowing provinces to tax such federal functions would let them reach into other exclusively federal domains too, like railways, highways, or passports, which the Constitution does not permit. The ruling reinforces the boundary between federal and provincial taxing powers in Pakistan's federal system.

title: Fixation of increase in fee for Academic Year
explainer:
This case involved City School Private Limited challenging a Punjab government law that limited how much private schools could increase their tuition fees each year, capping the raise at 5 percent (later increased to 8 percent) and applying it in some instances retrospectively. The school argued this restriction violated its constitutional rights to conduct business and trade freely under Article 18 of the Constitution.

A full bench of the Lahore High Court rejected the challenge and upheld the fee-capping law. The court reasoned that the right to run a business or profession under Article 18 is not absolute and can be reasonably regulated by law, especially when such regulation serves public interest. It noted that private schools have always operated under a licensing and registration system, and that fee regulation has historically been part of that framework even before the challenged amendment. The court also emphasized that education is closely tied to the right to life and dignity, and after the 18th Constitutional Amendment, education became an independent fundamental right under Article 25-A. Given this, the state has a legitimate interest in preventing commercialization and profiteering in education by regulating fee increases.

This judgment matters because it affirms the government's authority to regulate private school fees in the public interest, balancing business freedoms against the fundamental right to accessible, affordable education for children.

title: Additional Charge of Chairman CDA
explainer:
The Islamabad High Court decided a petition challenging how the Chairman of the Capital Development Authority (CDA) had been appointed. The Federal Government had nominated the Mayor of the Islamabad Metropolitan Corporation as an ex-officio member of the CDA Board, and then, through a separate notification, directed him to additionally perform the duties of Chairman on a part-time basis.

The petitioner argued this arrangement was illegal because the CDA Ordinance, 1960 requires the Chairman and members to be formally appointed for fixed terms (five years for the Chairman, four years for members), following specific qualifications and disqualification criteria set out in the law. Simply nominating an elected Mayor as an "ex-officio" member and then assigning him additional charge of the Chairman's role did not meet these legal requirements.

The court agreed, holding that the appointments violated Sections 6 and 8 of the CDA Ordinance. It ruled that positions of Chairman and member of the CDA Board are "public offices," meaning the court could examine their legality through a quo warranto petition. The notifications were declared illegal, ultra vires, and without lawful authority.

This case matters because it reinforces that senior public appointments must strictly follow statutory procedures—fixed tenure, proper qualifications, and absence of conflicts of interest—rather than being filled through informal administrative arrangements, even temporarily. The petition was allowed.

title: PLJ 2017 Islamabad 370
explainer:
This case was about a dispute over elections for the managing committee of the Islamabad Farming Cooperative Housing Society. Several groups of petitioners challenged different aspects of the election process in four separate petitions heard together by the Islamabad High Court.

The core dispute was whether the Registrar of Cooperative Societies had the legal authority to scrap the entire election process. One petitioner argued the Registrar had no power to do this on his own initiative, since neither the Cooperative Societies Act, 1925 nor the election rules explicitly granted such suo moto authority. Other petitioners raised separate issues, including whether nomination papers were properly scrutinized, whether certain candidates were valid members of the society, and whether the election schedule was issued by the proper authority.

The court found that the election schedule had been issued solely by the Election Commissioner rather than by the full three-member Election Commission as required by the rules, making it unlawful. It also found that the Election Commission failed to prepare and notify a list of eligible voters within the required ten-day period, a serious irregularity. The court held that the Registrar did have authority under Section 64-A of the Act to examine the legality of the election process and was within his rights to scrap it. The court ordered fresh elections to be held within 45 days, with compliance reported back to the court. This case matters because it clarifies regulators' oversight powers over cooperative society elections and reinforces that procedural rules must be strictly followed.

title: Dower cannot be taken from the share of brother of husband
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute in Kohat. A woman, Respondent No. 1, had filed a lawsuit claiming her share of an ancestral house inherited from her father, which was also to be divided among her sister and brother, Sahib Gul. The trial court and the appellate court both ruled in her favor, granting her share of the property.

Years later, Zubaida, who was Sahib Gul's ex-wife (and the mother of the other contesting parties in the case), tried to overturn this final judgment. She filed an application claiming the decision was obtained through fraud and misrepresentation, arguing that part of the house had been given to her as dower (a mandatory payment owed to a wife under Islamic marriage law) by her ex-husband Sahib Gul, and that she should have been included as a party since she was a co-owner.

The lower appellate court rejected her application, and she challenged that rejection before the Peshawar High Court. The High Court dismissed her petition too. It found no evidence of fraud, noted that she had waited 22 years after her 1991 divorce to raise this claim, and concluded she was only brought in after the other family members lost their case. Importantly, the court clarified that even if she was owed dower, she could only claim it from her ex-husband Sahib Gul's own share of the property, not from his sister's separate inherited share.

title: A Sui Juris Woman cannot be kept in Darul Aman against her consent
explainer:
This case involved a habeas corpus petition filed by a husband asking the court to recover his wife, Mst. Shaista, whom he claimed was being wrongfully confined by her brothers. He said he had married her with family consent, was later pressured by his own parents to divorce her, signed a divorce paper under duress but never actually pronounced the divorce, and later obtained religious opinions supporting that such a forced divorce was invalid. The wife's brothers disputed this, claiming the husband had validly divorced her and that he was now harassing the family.

The Sindh High Court held that it could not, in a habeas corpus proceeding, determine whether the divorce was legally valid or effective, since that required separate legal proceedings. Instead, the court focused on the woman's own wishes. Since she was an adult, mentally competent woman ("sui juris"), the court ruled she could not be forced to live with her brothers, her husband, or in a shelter home (Darul Aman) against her will. Citing earlier Supreme Court precedents, including the Rinkle Kumari case, the judgment emphasized that a major woman has full legal capacity to decide her own future, and Article 9 of the Constitution guarantees personal liberty, meaning no one can be detained without consent. The court ordered her release to live wherever she chose, with police protection if needed. The case reinforces that courts must respect an adult woman's autonomy over disputes about marriage, custody, or shelter.

title: Delay in conclusion of Trial is ground for Bail
explainer:
This case concerns Muhammad Hussain, who was arrested in July 2015 under narcotics laws after police allegedly recovered 10.5 kilograms of opium from a jeep he was travelling in, with a co-accused allegedly carrying a similar quantity. He was charged under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, an offence that normally carries strict restrictions on bail.

He had already applied for bail once before and been refused on merits. This time, he sought bail on a different basis: that his trial was taking far too long through no fault of his own. Court records showed that from March 2016 to October 2017, prosecution witnesses repeatedly failed to appear, even after the court issued arrest warrants to compel their attendance. The prosecution then filed an application that the court suspected was simply meant to drag the case out further.

The Lahore High Court held that the right to a speedy trial is a fundamental right, and that this principle applies especially strongly in special courts like those handling narcotics cases, where prolonged delays can effectively punish an undertrial prisoner without conviction. The court criticized the trial judge for failing to actively manage the case and for leaving the prisoner's fate to chance. Since there was no realistic prospect of the trial concluding soon, and the delay was not the petitioner's fault, the High Court granted him bail. The case reinforces that unreasonable delay in trial, not just the nature of the charge, can be valid grounds for bail.

title: PLJ 2018 SC 95
explainer:
This Supreme Court order dealt with a dispute over whether an appeal by the Capital Development Authority (CDA) against Hashwani Hotels was filed too late. The case originated from a suit by Hashwani Hotels seeking declaration, possession, and specific performance relating to a lease, which the trial court dismissed but the Islamabad High Court later decided in the hotel's favour. CDA appealed to the Supreme Court. Hashwani Hotels then asked for the appeal to be dismissed, arguing that under the Supreme Court Rules, an appeal must be filed along with a certified copy of both the judgment and the decree, and since CDA only attached the decree-sheet weeks later, the appeal was effectively 44 days late.

CDA argued that the decree-sheet simply did not exist yet when they filed their appeal, since the High Court had not prepared it immediately after the judgment, and the delay was not their fault.

The Supreme Court examined when a decree actually comes into existence and found there was no clear record of when the decree-sheet was finalized by the High Court. Since this date was unclear and not caused by the appellants, the Court held the appeal could not be confidently said to be time-barred, and even if it were, the delay deserved to be condoned. The application to dismiss the appeal was therefore rejected. The case matters because it clarifies how limitation periods are calculated when procedural delays in preparing court documents are not the fault of the appealing party.

title: PLJ 2018 Lahore 606
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over maintenance allowance and recovery of gold ornaments. A wife and her two minor children had filed a suit against the husband, claiming monthly maintenance and the return of gold ornaments allegedly taken from her. The Family Court at Depalpur partly granted the claim, awarding maintenance only to the two children but rejecting the wife's personal claims. On appeal, the Additional District Judge overturned this entirely, ruling that the Depalpur court had no jurisdiction to hear the case in the first place, since evidence showed the wife was actually residing with her parents in Lahore, not Depalpur as claimed in the suit. The appellate court dismissed the whole suit, though it allowed the family to refile in the correct court.

The wife then challenged this dismissal before the Lahore High Court through a constitutional petition, arguing that she did reside in Depalpur and that court had jurisdiction.

The High Court examined the law on jurisdiction under the Family Courts Act, 1964, noting that a person can be deemed to reside at more than one place if they have both a permanent and temporary residence, and that even a short period of residence can establish jurisdiction for a wife's convenience. This principle is important because family law cases often hinge on where the wife or family actually lives, and the ruling reinforces that such jurisdictional rules are meant to protect the convenience of wives seeking maintenance.

title: PLJ 2018 Islamabad 302
explainer:
Rashid Ameer, a constable in Islamabad Police since 2007, wanted to apply for the post of Assistant Sub-Inspector (ASI) in the Counter Terrorism Force. The advertised age limit was 25 years, and he was over-aged by about four years. He asked the Inspector General of Police for age relaxation, citing rules allowing relaxation for government employees with continuous service and for children of civil servants who died during service (his father, a DSP in Sindh Police, had died while in service). The IG Police rejected his request, saying the Establishment Division's relaxation rules did not apply to Islamabad Police, and that allowing relaxation would disrupt the recruitment process which was already underway.

The Lahore High Court disagreed. It examined the Establishment Division's 1993 Rules on relaxation of upper age limits and a later 2010 office memorandum clarifying that government employees with two years of continuous service get a 10-year age relaxation, while general relaxation of 5 years applies to all citizens. The court found these rules did apply to Islamabad Police and that the petitioner, who was 29 at the time and had about 10 years of service, qualified for relaxation. It held that he could not be denied this right which had already accrued to him. The court allowed the petition, meaning his application for age relaxation should be accepted.

title: Change of Investigation after submission of Challan
explainer:
This case involved a petitioner whose cousin and father had been arrested in two narcotics cases registered under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, allegedly after drugs were planted on them due to a bribery dispute with police. The petitioner asked the Lahore High Court to direct the City Police Officer, Multan, to decide his application seeking a change of the police investigation into these cases, claiming the original probe was unfair.

By the time the matter reached court, however, the police challan (charge sheet) had already been submitted to the trial court, charges had been framed against the accused, and the trial was actively underway. The District Standing Board had also already reviewed the matter and disposed of the petitioner's application.

The High Court examined Article 18-A of the Punjab Police Order (Amendment) Ordinance, 2013, which allows transfer of investigation to a different officer under certain procedures. However, relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the Court held that requesting a change of investigating officer at such a late stage—after the challan was filed and trial had begun—was not legally sustainable.

The petition was therefore dismissed. The case clarifies that requests to change investigators under police law must generally be made early, before trial proceedings have advanced, and courts will not disturb an ongoing trial to revisit the investigation stage.

title: Interpretation of Sections 5 and 14 of Limitation Act
explainer:
This case from the Azad Jammu & Kashmir High Court dealt with a long-running property dispute and an important legal question about deadlines for challenging court decrees obtained through fraud.

The background: a woman obtained a compromise decree for land, which she later gifted to her minor son. Some other claimants, who said the land actually belonged to them, challenged the compromise decree, first through a regular lawsuit alleging fraud, which was rejected by the trial court and upheld on appeal as being legally barred. They then tried a different legal route, filing an application under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code (a special, faster remedy for cancelling decrees obtained by fraud). The original decree-holders argued this new application was filed too late and that the claimants, having already lost their earlier suit, had no standing to try again.

The High Court held that since the claimants were never made parties to the original compromise decree, they were legal strangers entitled to use the Section 12(2) remedy. It clarified that no specific limitation period is fixed by law for such applications, but Article 181 of the Limitation Act (a three-year general limitation) would apply, counted from when the party learned of the decree. The Court also explained when delay can be excused under Sections 5 and 14 of the Limitation Act - only if the wrong forum was chosen carefully and in good faith, not through gross negligence. This ruling clarifies how fraud-based challenges to decrees and limitation rules interact.

title: Appellant court can modify charge in a criminal case
explainer:
This case involved Mst. Kausar Bibi, who was convicted by a trial court for causing a fatal injury that led to the death of Muhammad Amin, her husband. She was sentenced to pay Diyat (compensation) to the victim's heirs and also received fourteen years of rigorous imprisonment under Section 308 of the Pakistan Penal Code. The prosecution's case relied on her own confession, recovery of the body and weapon from her house, and medical evidence showing death from a blunt-weapon head injury. She appealed her conviction and sentence to the Lahore High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence and found that while the exact circumstances didn't conclusively prove she committed murder as originally charged, the evidence did support that she was involved in concealing the body of the deceased, an offence under Section 201 of the Penal Code. Importantly, the trial court had never formally charged her with this specific offence. The High Court ruled that appellate courts have the power, under various provisions including Section 561-A and related Criminal Procedure Code sections, to convict and sentence a person for an offence even if it wasn't separately charged at trial, as long as the evidence supports it and no injustice results. The court modified her conviction to Section 201 PPC and reduced her sentence to time already served.

This case matters because it clarifies that appellate courts can amend or add charges based on trial evidence, and that minor procedural gaps like non-framing of a charge don't automatically invalidate a conviction.

title: A person may be owner but not a landlord
explainer:
This case from the Peshawar High Court dealt with a dispute between a man claiming to be a landlord and another he wanted evicted for allegedly defaulting on rent. The landlord filed for eviction under the Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959, but the tenant denied that any landlord-tenant relationship existed between them at all.

The Rent Controller initially sided with the tenant and dismissed the eviction petition, finding no proof of a tenancy relationship. However, an appellate court reversed this, relying heavily on a decision from an informal mediation body called a Musalehati Committee, where the tenant was said to have admitted he was indeed a tenant.

The High Court disagreed with the appellate court's reasoning. It found that the landlord's witnesses could not produce any rent receipts, utility bills, or even a tenancy agreement, nor could they recall specific details of alleged rent payments. The Court also noted that no one from the mediation committee was called to testify about what actually happened there, so the claim that the tenant admitted tenancy remained unproven.

The Court emphasized an important legal principle: owning a property does not automatically make someone a "landlord" in the legal sense, and the real issue in eviction cases is whether a landlord-tenant relationship exists, not who holds title to the property. Since this relationship wasn't proven, the High Court restored the original ruling dismissing the eviction case.

title: 249-A can be decided after giving opportunity to complainant
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over an alleged land sale deal between the appellant and the respondents. The appellant claimed he had entered into agreements to purchase agricultural land and paid large sums of money in cash, totaling over Rs. 28 lakhs, to Respondent No. 1, who was acting on behalf of himself, his mother, and his sister. When the deal allegedly fell through, the appellant filed a criminal complaint. The trial Magistrate, using powers under Section 249-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, acquitted the respondents before completing the full trial, finding the complaint groundless. The appellant challenged this acquittal in the Sindh High Court.

The High Court rejected the appeal. It held that an application under Section 249-A can be decided at any stage of proceedings, not only after all witnesses have testified, so long as both sides are given a hearing and the magistrate records clear reasons. The court found the appellant had been given full opportunity to argue his case, that his supporting documents (receipts) appeared forged or tampered with, that his witnesses gave hearsay or interested testimony, and that he had concealed a related civil suit. The court also noted that long, unexplained delay in filing a criminal complaint weakens its credibility.

This ruling clarifies that magistrates can dismiss weak criminal complaints early, provided fairness is maintained, preventing misuse of criminal courts to pressure parties in what are essentially civil disputes.

title: Fundamental Right of Accused is Fair Trial
explainer:
This case involved a man on trial under narcotics laws before the Special Judge, Anti-Narcotics Force, Multan. During the trial, when two prosecution witnesses, including the investigating officer, appeared to give evidence, the accused's chosen lawyer was unavailable because he was engaged in another murder case. Instead of granting an adjournment, the trial court immediately appointed a different lawyer at state expense, who cross-examined the witnesses the same day without ever consulting the accused or studying the case file. When the accused later asked the court to recall these witnesses so his own lawyer could properly cross-examine them, the trial court refused.

The Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) found this unacceptable. It held that under Article 10(1) of the Constitution, every arrested or detained person has the right to a lawyer of their own choice, and under the newly added Article 10A, everyone is entitled to a fair trial and due process. The court also noted that Section 340(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code guarantees an accused the right to be defended by counsel. A court cannot force a different lawyer onto an accused who has already chosen one, since genuine representation is central to a fair trial.

The High Court allowed the petition, directing that the witnesses be re-summoned for proper cross-examination by counsel of the accused's choice, as a final opportunity. This judgment reinforces that the right to counsel of one's own choice is a core part of fair trial guarantees in Pakistan's justice system.

title: Judgment on Section 8 of Code of Civil Procedure
explainer:
This case involved a long-running land dispute over property in Nodeh Bala, Pakistan. The appellants (descendants of Qudratullah) claimed ownership based on a 1938 sale deed through which their father bought land from Mst. Marjan, plus a 1944 mutation recorded in his favor. However, Mst. Marjan had earlier, in 1939, filed a separate suit for possession of the same land, and in 1940 obtained an ex-parte decree (a ruling made without the other side appearing) granting her possession, since Qudratullah had been proceeded against ex-parte and failed to contest.

The core legal question was whether this 1940 possession decree remained valid and binding, given that the sale deed itself was never directly challenged in that earlier suit, and whether the appellants could still rely on the sale deed to claim ownership.

The Supreme Court held that an ex-parte decree is just as legally valid and binding as a contested one, differing only in the methods available to challenge it. Since the appellants never took direct legal action to set aside the 1940 decree, it became final and binding on them. The Court further explained that in suits for possession under Section 8 of the Specific Relief Act, a declaration of entitlement to possession inherently includes a declaration of title. Therefore, even though the sale deed wasn't explicitly challenged, the possession decree effectively overrode it, rendering the sale deed legally ineffective. The appeal was dismissed.

Two co-accused were acquitted at trial, and one died during proceedings.

Maryam Bibi had filed a private complaint alleging she was abducted at gunpoint from her home, drugged, and held captive for about a month, during which she was repeatedly sexually assaulted. title: Personal Bonafide Need
explainer:
This case was about a landlord-tenant dispute between Al-Hadeed Enterprises, a partnership firm, and Allied Bank of Pakistan, which was renting commercial shops and a basement in Islamabad to run a bank branch. When the lease expired, the landlord sought a higher rent, but after the bank did not agree, the landlord filed for eviction, claiming it needed the property for personal use and that the bank had defaulted on paying an enhanced rent. Both the Rent Controller and the Additional District Judge ruled in favor of the landlord and ordered the bank to vacate the premises.

The bank challenged this before the Lahore High Court, arguing that the lower courts had misread the evidence, that the landlord's real motive was to extract a higher rent rather than genuine personal need, that no proper notice of rent increase had been served to establish default, and that the eviction petition was invalid because it was filed by an unregistered partnership firm, which is barred under the Partnership Act.

The High Court agreed with the bank. It found that the claim of personal need was actually a pretext to force a steep rent hike, and that no notice of rent enhancement had been given, so no default could be proven. It also held that an unregistered firm cannot legally file an eviction case. The court therefore reversed the eviction order, protecting tenants from eviction based on improperly proven claims and procedural defects.

title: High Court cannot Quash FIR once challan is presented in Trial Court
explainer:
This case involved a murder FIR lodged against several accused, including Muhammad Asghar, who was alleged to have instigated and abetted the killing of a man and his wife. After the police investigation, the trial court took up the case, framed charges against some accused, and the complainant testified, naming the petitioner as the instigator. Due to a clerical or typographical slip, the petitioner's name was accidentally left out of an earlier summoning order, though it was later included and he was eventually charged along with the others.

The petitioner approached the Lahore High Court asking it to quash the proceedings against him, arguing that he had never been properly summoned and that no clear charge had been framed against him, so the case should be dropped.

The High Court refused to quash the FIR or the proceedings. It held that once a challan (police report) has been submitted and the trial court has taken cognizance of the case, the High Court should not interfere using its inherent powers under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, relying on a Supreme Court precedent. Instead, the court said the petitioner could seek relief by applying to the trial court itself for premature acquittal under Section 265-K of the Cr.P.C.

This case matters because it reinforces the principle that once a criminal trial is underway in the trial court, higher courts should generally not intervene to quash cases; such matters should be resolved within the trial process itself.

title: Judgment on S.R.O 499(I)/2009 dated 13-06-2006
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over imported goods (described as Polypropylene) where customs authorities had allegedly mis-declared the goods' value and quality, and imposed a fine in lieu of confiscation based on rates set out in a government regulation, S.R.O. 499(I)/2009. The importer, Global International, challenged this regulation before the Sindh High Court, arguing that the Federal Board of Revenue did not have the legal authority to fix such fines, since the relevant provision of the Customs Act (Section 32) had been excluded from Section 15 after an amendment made through the Finance Act, 2011. The importer wanted the regulation struck down and the goods released.

During the hearing, the petitioner's lawyer conceded that the regulation had actually been issued before the 2011 amendment, at a time when the FBR did have the power to set such fines. So the original challenge could not succeed. Instead, the lawyer asked for an alternative relief, arguing that after the 2011 amendment, the regulation's provisions had become ineffective and should not be applied going forward.

Since the importer already had an appeal pending before the Collector of Customs (Appeals) against the original order, the court did not decide this new legal argument itself. Instead, by agreement between both sides, the court disposed of the petition and directed the importer to raise this specific legal argument before the Collector of Customs (Appeals), who was instructed to consider it and decide the appeal on merits within a reasonable time.

title: Contempt of Court Judgment against Lawyer
explainer:
This case from the Lahore High Court's Bahawalpur Bench dealt with a writ petition filed by a young woman, Mst. Tahira Kausar, who had married a man of her own choice against her father's wishes. Her father, a police official, had lodged a criminal case against her under the Hudood laws, and she asked the court to quash it to protect her marriage. While hearing this petition, the court became concerned about the conduct of an advocate, Mr. Riaz Hanif Rahi, who was representing her father. The judge found that instead of following proper legal procedures to seek transfer of the case to another bench, the advocate behaved in a disrespectful, aggressive, and intimidating manner in court, tried to dictate proceedings, referenced a prior unrelated order to pressure the judge into recusing himself, and generally attempted to overawe the court rather than make legitimate legal arguments.

The judge issued a detailed order describing the kinds of advocate misconduct that undermine judicial independence, including threats, disrespect, and manipulation of proceedings. The court held that such behavior potentially amounted to contempt of court. As a result, a show-cause notice was ordered to be issued to the advocate, requiring him to explain his conduct and why contempt proceedings should not be formally initiated against him under Article 204 of the Constitution and the Contempt of Court Ordinance, 2004.

This case matters because it highlights the judiciary's effort to safeguard courtroom dignity and ensure lawyers do not use intimidation or improper tactics

title: Punishment of Qazf is Eighty Stripes
explainer:
This case involved a woman convicted by a trial court in Layyah for the offence of Qazf, which means falsely accusing someone of unlawful sexual intercourse (zina). The trial court sentenced her under Section 11 of the Offence of Qazf (Enforcement of Hadd) Ordinance, 1979 to two years rigorous imprisonment, 40 stripes of whipping, and a fine of Rs. 50,000 as compensation to the complainant, with six months imprisonment in default of payment.

On appeal, the Federal Shariat Court found a fundamental legal flaw: Section 11, under which she was convicted, had actually been removed from the law back in 2006, before the alleged incident, the complaint, and the trial court's judgment ever took place. The correct provision in force was the amended Section 7, which only prescribes a punishment of 80 stripes for Qazf, with no provision for imprisonment, fine, or compensation. The court also noted that whipping as a tazir (discretionary) punishment, as opposed to whipping as hadd, had been abolished altogether since 1996.

Because the trial court convicted and sentenced her under a law provision that no longer existed, the entire judgment was declared to be without jurisdiction. The Federal Shariat Court set aside the conviction and acquitted the woman honourably, releasing her from her bail obligations. This case highlights the importance of courts applying the correct, currently valid law rather than outdated or repealed provisions.

title: Bank cannot lodge FIR under section 489-F
explainer:
This case involved a bank customer who was accused of issuing a dishonoured cheque for repayment of a loan. The bank reported the matter to police, who registered an FIR under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, a provision dealing with dishonestly issuing a cheque that bounces. The customer approached the Islamabad High Court asking for the FIR to be cancelled, arguing that since the dispute arose from a bank loan, it should be handled under a special law, the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001, rather than through ordinary criminal proceedings.

The court agreed with the customer. It noted that the complainant was a financial institution and the cheque in question related to repayment of a loan facility, a routine banking matter. The judge held that the 2001 Ordinance is a special law that specifically covers situations where a cheque issued for loan repayment is dishonoured, and it provides its own penalties and procedure, including filing a complaint before a Banking Court. Because this special law overrides the general criminal law, the bank could not use Section 489-F of the Penal Code against the customer. Doing so was ruled an abuse of court process. The FIR was therefore quashed.

This judgment matters because it clarifies that banks and financial institutions must pursue loan-related cheque disputes through banking courts under the specific ordinance, not by lodging criminal FIRs against borrowers.

title: Lahore Cantt Cooperative Housing Society Case Law
explainer:
This case involved a contempt of court petition filed against the Lahore Cantonment Cooperative Housing Society (now Defence Housing Authority) and its alleged Secretary, Col. (R) Ghulam Jafar. The petitioner, Amjad Ikram, claimed that the society and its secretary had defied court orders dated 11.11.2002 and 14.11.2002, which required maintaining status quo, by refusing to unlock the gate of a school as directed. He sought punitive action against the respondents for disobeying the court.

During proceedings, the housing society itself was removed from the case since it was a juristic entity, leaving only the individual named as Secretary, Ghulam Jafar, to respond. He denied ever holding that position or disobeying any court order. To verify the facts, the court had sent a bailiff to inspect the site, and also summoned the local police officer (SHO) for a statement.

The court found that none of the key evidence, the bailiff's report, the police daily diary entry, or the SHO's statement, actually named Ghulam Jafar as the person who obstructed the court's orders. Instead, they identified two different individuals, a Major and another Colonel, as responsible.

Since there was no evidence directly implicating Ghulam Jafar, the Lahore High Court held that the petitioner had failed to establish a prima facie case of contempt against him and dismissed the application. The case highlights that contempt charges require clear, specific evidence linking the accused person to the alleged violation.

title: Judgment on Conflict of Interest
explainer:
This case was about the appointment of the Chairman of the National Accountability Bureau (NAB), Pakistan's top anti-corruption body. The petitioners challenged the appointment, arguing it violated the Constitution and the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999.

The Supreme Court found that the law requires the President to appoint the NAB Chairman only after genuine consultation with the Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly, aimed at building consensus rather than just going through the motions. In this case, no such consultation had taken place before the Chairman was reappointed on 9 February 2011, making the appointment unlawful.

The Court also ruled that the law's requirement of a "non-extendable" four-year term means a person can only ever be appointed once to that office. Even a fresh appointment made before completing an earlier term would not get around this restriction, since allowing that would let an incumbent's term be artificially cut short and renewed, defeating the law's purpose of limiting tenure.

The Court further held that such petitions, filed under Article 184(3) of the Constitution, were a matter of public importance because the NAB Chairman's decisions affect thousands of people through inquiries, arrests and trials. It also noted that the Chief Justice of Pakistan could appropriately play a role in resolving disagreements over such appointments, given the Chief Justice's constitutional role as guardian of citizens' rights.

The ruling reinforced safeguards ensuring transparent, consultative, and legally compliant appointments to powerful public offices.

title: Ex-Parte Proceedings in absence of necessary party
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over government land. A person (the respondent) had filed a civil suit for possession and a permanent injunction against the provincial Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and others over certain property. The government defendants initially appeared through a representative but later failed to attend, leading the trial court to proceed ex-parte and pass a decree against them. The government later sought to have this ex-parte decree set aside, but both the trial court and the appellate court rejected that request, so the government approached the Peshawar High Court.

The High Court found serious problems with how the case had been handled. There was no proper proof on record that summons had actually been served on the government officials for the hearing date in question. The written statement in the case had been filed by a lawyer acting as a "special government pleader," but he had not been properly authorized by the government to represent it, since the government had never even been formally made a party to the suit and no official sanction had been given for its defense. The court also held that trial judges have a duty to add necessary parties like the government to a case, and that ex-parte proceedings conducted on a date not actually fixed for hearing are void from the start.

Because of these defects, the High Court set aside the lower courts' decisions and allowed the revision petition, emphasizing that such fundamental procedural failures cannot be cured by technical objections like limitation periods.

title: Suit for Damages on Malicious Prosecution can be filed within one year
explainer:
This case involves a suit for damages for malicious prosecution, filed against Habib Bank Ltd and others by two plaintiffs. The plaintiffs claimed their prosecution had been malicious, and they sought compensation after being acquitted. However, the law sets a strict one-year time limit for filing such suits, counted from the date of acquittal. The trial court had dismissed the suit as time-barred, since it appeared to have been filed more than a year after the plaintiffs were acquitted.

The plaintiffs later asked the Sindh High Court to recall and review that dismissal, arguing that the court had overlooked an important legal protection: Section 4 of the Limitation Act. This provision allows a suit to be validly filed on the very first day a court reopens after being closed, if the limitation period expired during the closure. The plaintiffs argued their suit was filed on the first working day after summer court vacations, meaning it was not actually late.

The Court agreed. It held that Section 4 does not extend the limitation period, but it does protect suits filed on the first reopening day when the deadline fell during vacation. Since this point had been missed earlier, the dismissal judgment and decree were recalled and reviewed.

This case matters because it clarifies that litigants who file on the first day courts reopen after a vacation should not be unfairly penalized for court closures beyond their control.

title: Writ Petition dismissed when filed with delay of 4 years
explainer:
This case concerns a wife, Mst. Aamna Abdullah, who filed a family court suit against her husband seeking dissolution of marriage, dower, maintenance, and dowry articles. When reconciliation efforts failed, the Family Court in Multan granted her a divorce on the basis of khula (a wife-initiated divorce) but ordered her to return the dower she had received, Rs. 500 and five tolas of gold, as required under the law when a marriage ends in khula. This decree was passed on 31.1.2007.

The wife did not challenge this order for four years. In 2010, she finally filed a constitutional petition before the Lahore High Court, arguing that the order to return the dower was illegal since her husband had never specifically asked for it back, and that her delay in approaching the court should be excused because of bad legal advice and illness.

The High Court rejected her petition primarily on the ground of laches, meaning excessive, unexplained delay. It held that constitutional jurisdiction is an equitable remedy, and a party who sleeps on their rights for four years without adequate justification cannot expect relief. The court found her delay amounted to negligence and dismissed the petition without deciding the merits of her dower argument.

This case is a reminder that even valid legal grievances can be lost if not pursued promptly, since courts exercising constitutional/equitable jurisdiction expect timely action.

title: Hidayatullah V. Federation of Pakistan
explainer:
This case concerns a petitioner, Hidayatullah, who was hired in 1996 on a "daily waged contract basis" by Telecom Foundation, a project linked to Pakistan Telecommunication Company Ltd. (PTCL). His appointment letter did not specify any fixed contract period, though it referred to separate terms and conditions supposedly agreed and signed by him. His employment was terminated shortly after, in December 1996. Many years later, after the government passed the Sacked Employees (Re-instatement) Act, 2010 to restore jobs to certain workers removed during earlier political periods, he filed a petition seeking reinstatement and back benefits under this law.

PTCL argued the case wasn't valid in court because PTCL's rules aren't government-backed (statutory), and that the petitioner had waited too long (delay, or "laches") to file his claim. The Sindh High Court rejected both objections: since the petitioner was asserting rights created by the 2010 Act itself—not just internal company rules—the petition was allowed, and since this right only came into existence in 2009-2010, there was no unreasonable delay.

On the merits, since PTCL could not produce any document proving a fixed contract term, and the petitioner denied signing one, the court held he qualified for reinstatement under Section 4(a) of the Act. The court ordered his reinstatement within two weeks, along with the benefits the law provides. This case clarifies how courts apply the Sacked Employees Act to contract workers lacking clear contract terms.

title: Who has to check the status of case at High Court?
explainer:
This Supreme Court of Pakistan judgment deals with a landlord-tenant dispute from Quetta. The landlord, Malik Muhammad Qasim, had sought eviction of his tenants, Ghulam Siddique and another, from a shop and house, citing rent default, personal need, and subletting. The Rent Controller ordered the tenants' eviction in 2007. The tenants appealed to the Balochistan High Court, but their appeal was dismissed because it was filed late, and the High Court refused to excuse (condone) the delay.

The tenants then approached the Supreme Court, arguing that their late appeal should have been excused and the case decided on its merits rather than being thrown out on a technicality. They suggested the delay was not really their fault.

The Supreme Court disagreed and refused to grant leave to appeal, upholding the High Court's decision. The Court emphasized an important principle: litigants cannot simply hire a lawyer and then walk away from responsibility for their own case. Even if a lawyer fails to keep a client updated, that negligence does not automatically excuse delays, especially once the opposing party has gained valuable rights through the passage of time. It is the litigant's own duty to stay informed about what is happening with their case in court.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that clients, not just their lawyers, bear responsibility for diligently pursuing legal proceedings, and that missed deadlines can have serious, irreversible consequences. The tenants were given nine months to vacate the premises.

title: Permission to appear and defend is required in Order XXXVII Suit
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over an unpaid loan documented through a pro-note, where the lender filed a special summary suit for recovery of Rs. 100,000 under Order XXXVII of the Civil Procedure Code, a procedure used for quick recovery of money on negotiable instruments like promissory notes.

The trial court initially allowed the borrower to defend the suit, but only on condition that he submit a surety bond for the amount claimed by a set deadline. The borrower failed to file his written statement or provide the surety bond, so the court proceeded against him ex-parte, meaning without his participation. He later tried to get this ex-parte order set aside but did not pursue that application diligently either, and it was dismissed for non-appearance. The trial court then recorded the lender's evidence alone and ruled in his favor, decreeing the suit.

The borrower appealed to the Lahore High Court, arguing he was never properly heard and that the judgment unfairly relied only on the lender's evidence. The High Court rejected this appeal, noting that the borrower had never complied with the original condition to furnish a surety bond and had been consistently negligent throughout the proceedings. Finding no legal or jurisdictional flaw in the trial court's decision, the High Court dismissed the appeal outright.

The case illustrates that courts will not reward parties who ignore procedural requirements and conditions attached to their right to defend a case, especially in summary suits designed for speedy resolution of debt claims.

title: Writ related with illegetimate child
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over whether a father had to pay maintenance (financial support) for a child he claimed was not his own.

The father, Zaheer Ahmad, had been ordered by a Family Court, and then by an Appellate Court, to pay monthly maintenance for a minor child. He challenged this before the Lahore High Court, arguing that the child could not be his because the child was born on 7 November 2004, while his wife had allegedly been living separately from him since 2 December 2003 - meaning the child was born about eleven months and five days after the couple separated. He therefore claimed the child was illegitimate and that he should not be responsible for maintaining him.

The High Court rejected this argument. It held that questions of a child's legitimacy are extremely serious and must not be decided lightly, based merely on a husband's denial or accusation. Under Islamic law, a child born within a lawful marriage is presumed legitimate - "the child follows the bed" - and courts always lean towards upholding legitimacy unless there is strong, convincing evidence to the contrary. The father had provided no real proof of illegitimacy, and importantly, he had never gone to the appropriate court to invoke "Li'an" (the specific legal procedure for disowning paternity).

As a result, the court upheld the lower courts' decisions, confirmed the child as legitimate, and ordered the father to continue paying maintenance. The case is significant because it reinforces strong legal protection for children's legitimacy and rights to support, placing a heavy burden on anyone trying to deny paternity.

title: Teachers lost case against PAF

The colleges received no public funding and each was treated as a separate employer with no transfers of staff between institutions. The Manual's rules were administrative guidelines, not government law, and teachers had signed undertakings to follow them.

The relationship between teachers and the colleges was an ordinary employer-employee one, not government service. title: Confirmation of death sentence in law
explainer:
This case, decided by the Lahore High Court's Rawalpindi Bench in 2009, involved Muhammad Sarfraz, who had been convicted by a trial court of murdering his nephew (his sister's son, Mumtaz Khan) and attempting to murder two other nephews during an argument over a money dispute. The trial court had sentenced him to death for murder, along with separate additional sentences for the attempted murders and various injuries caused to the surviving victims. The High Court was reviewing both his appeal and the mandatory reference for confirmation of the death sentence.

The High Court upheld his conviction for murder but refused to confirm the death penalty, converting it instead to life imprisonment. The judges found several mitigating factors: there was no prior enmity between the appellant and his nephews, who were in fact on cordial terms with him; the shooting occurred as a sudden, unexplained emotional outburst during a friendly conversation about an old business debt; and the record did not clarify what specifically triggered the violence. The court also held that since all the injuries occurred during a single continuous incident, the appellant could not be separately punished for each injury - only the most serious one counted.

This judgment matters because it illustrates how Pakistani courts weigh mitigating circumstances - such as the absence of premeditation, family relationship, and sudden provocation - when deciding whether a death sentence is truly warranted, even after a murder conviction is confirmed.

title: Is the court bound to serve notices before passing withdrawal order?
citation: PLD 1990 SC 596) and Ismail vs. Fida Ali and Syyed Iqbal Shabbir (PL
explainer:
This case concerns a property dispute where the plaintiff had filed a suit for specific performance of a contract. The trial court had ordered the plaintiff to deposit the remaining sale consideration with the court as a condition for an interim stay order, but the plaintiff repeatedly failed to do so despite multiple opportunities. Just before a scheduled hearing where the defendant sought to have the stay vacated, the plaintiff suddenly applied to withdraw the suit, with permission to file a fresh one, citing vague "legal defects" in the plaint. The trial court granted this withdrawal the same day, without issuing any notice to the defendant and without giving proper reasons.

The defendant challenged this before the Lahore High Court, arguing that by the time of withdrawal, certain rights had already accrued to him through the earlier court orders, and that the trial court should have given him a hearing before allowing the plaintiff to escape the suit and start over.

The High Court agreed. It held that once rights had accrued to a defendant during litigation, the court could not simply allow withdrawal and permission for a fresh suit without notifying the other side and recording proper reasons. The order was found to be vague, lacking specifics about the alleged defects, and issued without a hearing—violating principles of natural justice. The court set aside the withdrawal order and revived the original suit.

This case matters because it clarifies that withdrawal of a suit isn't a mere formality when the other party's rights are already affected—courts must ensure fairness and transparency before granting such permissions.

title: Critereon for determining Benami Transaction
explainer:
This case involved a husband suing his wife, asking the court to declare that he was the real owner of a house and plot registered in her name, claiming she held it only as a "benamidar" (a nominal owner holding property on behalf of someone else who actually paid for it).

The couple married in 1956. The husband claimed that in 1967-68 he sold an earlier house he owned, used the proceeds plus his savings to buy the disputed plot and build a house on it, but registered it in his wife's name out of mutual trust. He later remarried, and when relations with his wife deteriorated and she refused to let him move back into the house, he sued her for ownership, possession, and related relief in 1989.

The wife denied this, saying she bought the property herself using her own earnings as a teacher and later a bank employee, along with loans she had taken out.

The court explained that in benami cases, the person claiming ownership must prove it, based on factors like who actually paid for the property, who held the original title documents, who possessed the property, and what motive existed for structuring it as benami. The husband failed to produce evidence supporting his claims, while the wife showed she had sufficient income and means to purchase the property herself. The court also found the suit was filed too late, well beyond the six-year limitation period. The suit was dismissed with costs.

title: What happens when a suit is hit by Section 11 of CPC
explainer:
The case was about a land dispute in District Killa Abdullah, where several people filed a suit claiming ownership and possession of specific plots of land, saying revenue records had wrongly listed the land in the names of other people (the respondents) during a settlement carried out in 1963-64. The respondents argued that this new suit should not be allowed to proceed because the same land and the same ownership questions were already being litigated in an earlier case between largely the same parties, including a partition suit pending before revenue authorities.

A trial court initially rejected the plaint, but an appellate court sent the case back for a full trial. The High Court then stepped in during an earlier revision petition and set aside that remand order. In the present revision, the Balochistan High Court examined whether the suit could still continue, given that the core issues had already been decided in the earlier civil suit and in a related revision petition.

The Court held that the suit was barred under Section 11 of the Civil Procedure Code, which prevents courts from re-deciding matters that have already been conclusively settled between the same parties in earlier litigation. Since this legal objection can be raised and decided at any stage, and since the earlier case had already resolved the same issues, the present suit had become pointless. The petition was dismissed.

This case illustrates how Pakistani courts use Section 11 CPC to prevent repeated litigation over issues already judicially settled, promoting finality and preventing wastage of court time.

title: Value of Dying declaration in a criminal case
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a death sentence handed down for murder. The complainant, Ali Gul, had been shot and later died, naming his brother-in-law and two others, including the appellant Mumtaz, as his attackers. He claimed the motive was a family dispute: his sister had left her husband, one of the accused, and was living with her brothers. At trial, eyewitnesses testified that Mumtaz actually fired shots at the deceased, but the deceased's own dying declaration, recorded by police in the presence of a doctor, did not say Mumtaz had done anything violent or was even carrying a weapon.

The Balochistan High Court found this contradiction crucial. Since the dying declaration and the eyewitness accounts told different stories about Mumtaz's role, the court could not safely rely on either piece of evidence to convict him. The judges also noted a well-known pattern in such cases: relatives are sometimes falsely implicated alongside the real culprit, especially where family tensions already exist. Given the strained relations between the families over the marital dispute, the court could not rule out that the absconding brother-in-law alone committed the murder, with others wrongly added to the case.

Because the prosecution failed to prove the charge against Mumtaz beyond reasonable doubt, the court set aside his conviction and death sentence, acquitting him. The case highlights how inconsistent evidence, especially between a dying declaration and witness testimony, can entitle an accused to acquittal.

title: Revision in case of partition suit
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over jointly owned agricultural land in village Bhaun, District Chakwal. Ghulam Haider, whose legal heirs later became the respondents, claimed that the jointly held land had been formally partitioned between him and the other co-owners (predecessors of the petitioners), that a specific share of over six kanals had been allotted to him, and that he had been in possession until the petitioners illegally dispossessed him. He sued for recovery of possession.

The trial court dismissed his suit, finding no proof of partition or possession. On appeal, the District Judge reversed this and ruled in favor of the respondents. The petitioners then challenged that appellate decision before the Lahore High Court through a civil revision.

The High Court examined the evidence and found it lacking. The respondents could not produce the actual partition order, revenue records showing delivery of possession, or supporting documents proving the claimed division of land. The mutation entries relied upon were not properly signed or countersigned by competent revenue authorities, and one key document even contradicted the respondents' own claims about ownership shares.

The court ruled that mere unverified entries in revenue registers carry no legal weight without proper authentication. Since the respondents failed to prove partition or transfer of possession, the High Court set aside the appellate court's decision and restored the trial court's original dismissal of the suit. This case underscores that claims of property partition must be backed by properly authenticated official documents, not just informal or unverified revenue entries.

title: Order 41 Rule 27 CPC related with Additional Evidence
explainer:
This case involved a long-running land dispute between the legal heirs of two deceased men, Muhammad Tufail and Nazir Hussain, over agricultural land in Nankana Sahib district. Tufail had claimed ownership of land through a 1975 sale deed from a man named Murad, arguing certain revenue entries made in favor of the opposing party were illegal and done without notice to him. Both the trial court and the first appellate court rejected his claim and dismissed his suit.

Tufail then filed a civil revision petition in the Lahore High Court, which was initially dismissed in 2003. He appealed to the Supreme Court, which sent the case back, directing the High Court to specifically rule on his pending application to introduce additional evidence (under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Civil Procedure Code) before deciding the revision again.

On reconsideration, the High Court held that while courts do have power to admit additional evidence at later stages, including during revision, if doing so is essential for justice, the documents Tufail wanted to introduce were not relevant to the actual land dispute, and he had failed to explain why he didn't produce them earlier when he had the opportunity during the appeal. Since the lower courts' factual findings were well-reasoned and based on proper evidence, the court declined to disturb them and dismissed the revision petition.

This case clarifies when courts can allow additional evidence late in litigation and confirms that such evidence must be both relevant and justified by genuine necessity, not just convenience.

title: No appeal lies against Khula
explainer:
This case involved a husband and wife whose marriage ended in dissolution through khula (a wife's right to end her marriage), granted by a Family Court. The trial court had ordered dissolution of the marriage, return of dowry articles, and maintenance for the wife during her iddat period, but did not award her the dower amount since the marriage ended through khula.

The wife appealed, and the appellate court reversed course, awarding her the dower amount of Rs. 150,000 along with maintenance. The husband then challenged this appellate decision before the Peshawar High Court, arguing that a khula-based dissolution cannot be appealed, and that by awarding dower, the appellate court was effectively overturning the khula itself.

The High Court agreed with the husband. It held that no appeal lies against a judgment dissolving a marriage, whether based on cruelty or khula. Since the question of dower was closely tied to the basis of the khula, the appellate court could not grant dower without indirectly interfering with the dissolution itself. The High Court ruled that the appellate court had wrongly acted like a religious judge (qazi) rather than staying within its proper appellate role, and that its order granting dower was without jurisdiction.

The High Court therefore set aside the dower award but upheld the maintenance allowance. This case clarifies an important principle in Pakistani family law: decisions dissolving marriages via khula are final and cannot be appealed, even indirectly through related financial claims.

title: Judgment under Order 17 Rule 3 of CPC
explainer:
This case involved a property partition dispute among the legal heirs of the late Sher Mohammad Dar in Lahore. The plaintiffs, his granddaughters, sought a one-third share of family property that their deceased father would have inherited. During trial, after several adjournments, neither the plaintiffs nor their lawyer appeared on the scheduled hearing date to present evidence. As a result, the trial court closed their evidence and dismissed the entire suit for lack of proof, without specifying which procedural rule justified this harsh step.

The plaintiffs appealed, arguing that the dismissal was wrongly made under a rule that didn't apply to their situation, and that the trial court had acted too harshly given the circumstances, including confusion over whether they and their witnesses were actually present but simply not called into the courtroom.

The Lahore High Court examined two possible legal provisions: Order XVII Rule 3, which allows a court to decide a case on existing evidence when a party fails to do something it was specifically given time to do, and Order XVII Rule 2, which deals with simple non-appearance. The court ruled that Rule 3 did not apply here because the strict conditions for its use were not met. Instead, this was essentially a case of default of appearance, properly falling under Rule 2. Since dismissal for mere non-appearance should allow the losing party a chance to apply for restoration, the court set aside the dismissal and ordered the suit restored for proper hearing. This clarifies when courts can decide cases outright versus allowing parties a second chance.

title: Judgment against proclamation of emergency on 3rd November
explainer:
This case was decided by the Supreme Court of Pakistan (Chief Justice Iftikhar Muhammad Chaudhry and thirteen other judges) in response to petitions filed by the Sindh High Court Bar Association and others challenging the Proclamation of Emergency imposed by General Pervez Musharraf on 3 November 2007.

On that date, Musharraf, then Chief of Army Staff, had suspended the Constitution, issued a Provisional Constitution Order, dismissed judges who refused to take a new oath under his Oath of Office Order, and made other sweeping changes affecting the judiciary, including altering judges' pensions and court structures. These actions were preceded by a letter from the Prime Minister to the President describing concerns about terrorism, militancy and alleged judicial interference with executive functions.

The Court held that this letter did not constitute constitutional advice under Article 48, was not addressed to the Army Chief, and gave no authority for imposing emergency rule or removing judges. It found that neither the President nor the Army Chief had any constitutional power to proclaim emergency, suspend the Constitution, or dismiss judges in this manner. Doing so violated constitutional protections for judicial independence and tenure under Articles 2A and 209.

The judgment matters because it declared the 2007 emergency and all related actions unconstitutional, reaffirming that no individual, however powerful, can override the Constitution or judiciary without lawful authority.

title: Habib Bank Limited Versus Judge Banking Court Lahore
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between Habib Bank Limited and a customer who had taken an auto lease finance facility to buy a Honda City car. When the customer defaulted on his monthly installments, the bank repossessed the vehicle under a clause in the lease agreement that allowed it to do so. The customer then filed a suit before the Banking Court seeking rendition of accounts and return of the vehicle, claiming he had paid most of the loan and only a small amount remained outstanding.

The Banking Court ordered the bank to return the vehicle to the customer, relying on a letter in which the customer had asked the bank to waive early settlement charges. The bank challenged this order in the Lahore High Court, arguing that the Banking Court had misread the letter, which actually only refused to waive the settlement charges and did not confirm how much the customer had paid or still owed.

The High Court agreed with the bank. It found that the customer's claim about owing only a small amount was not supported by the case record and had not even been raised in his original suit. Since the bank had validly repossessed the vehicle under the lease agreement due to default, the Banking Court's order returning the vehicle was set aside. The case was sent back to the Banking Court to be decided properly and promptly, within one month.

This case highlights how courts scrutinize evidence carefully before overturning a lender's contractual right to repossess property upon default.

title: Criminal Case cannot be stayed for civil litigation
explainer:
This case involved a criminal complaint arising from a property dispute. Khadim Hussain and others were accused of trespassing on a field, damaging crops, and stealing fertilizer and wheat, leading to an FIR being registered against them in 1997. The accused argued that the land was theirs and that a related civil suit over ownership and possession was still pending between the parties. Based on this, a magistrate had adjourned the criminal case indefinitely to wait for the outcome of the civil litigation, without deciding the accused's application for acquittal under Section 249-A of the Criminal Procedure Code. An Additional Sessions Judge later set aside that order and directed the trial to proceed, prompting the accused to challenge this decision before the High Court.

The Lahore High Court dismissed the petition, ruling that criminal cases cannot be put on hold simply because a related civil case is ongoing. The court explained that civil and criminal proceedings are separate in nature and must be decided independently, based on the evidence presented in each. The accused could still present ownership documents as part of their defense during the criminal trial, but this did not justify stalling the criminal proceedings altogether.

However, the court noted that the magistrate had never actually decided the accused's acquittal application on its merits, and the sessions judge had overlooked this. So while the criminal trial was allowed to resume, the trial court was directed to first decide the pending acquittal application before moving forward. This case clarifies that pending civil disputes cannot be used as grounds to indefinitely delay criminal trials.

title: Article 25 of constitution gives equal rights to citizens
explainer:
This case involved a challenge by newspaper publishers to the Newspaper Employees (Conditions of Service) Act, 1973, which regulates wages and conditions for both working journalists and other newspaper employees. The petitioners argued the law was unconstitutional, claiming it unfairly grouped different categories of employees together, violated the right to equal treatment under Article 25, and denied due process under Article 10-A because it provided no right of appeal against decisions of the Wage Board, which sets employee wages.

The Supreme Court rejected these challenges. It held that working journalists and non-journalist newspaper employees work closely together toward common goals, so treating them alike under one law was a reasonable classification, not discrimination. The newspaper industry was also found distinct from other media like radio and television, justifying separate legislation. On the appeal issue, the Court explained that the Wage Board performs a legislative, not judicial or quasi-judicial, function—it sets general wage rules for an entire industry rather than deciding individual disputes between opposing parties. Since no individual right was being adjudicated, the absence of a right of appeal did not violate due process; affected parties could instead challenge Wage Board decisions through writ petitions if the Board acted unreasonably.

The judgment matters because it upholds protections for newspaper employees' wages and clarifies when due process requires a right of appeal, distinguishing legislative rule-making from adversarial judicial decision-making.

title: Judgement Related with PMDC
explainer:
This case involved medical students challenging the University of Health Sciences Ordinance, 2002, which required medical colleges to affiliate with the newly created University of Health Sciences instead of the University of the Punjab. Only four students out of roughly 6000 affected challenged the law, and none of the medical colleges themselves objected.

The students argued that the Ordinance conflicted with the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council Ordinance, 1962, violated their fundamental rights to equality under the Constitution, operated unfairly by exempting two colleges from affiliation, and defeated their legitimate expectation of being examined by the University of the Punjab as before.

The Supreme Court rejected all these arguments and refused to grant leave to appeal against the High Court's earlier judgment. It held that the Ordinance was a valid law and not unconstitutional. The exemption given to two colleges was temporary, using the phrase "for the time being," so it did not amount to permanent discrimination. The Vice-Chancellor's letter was simply informational and did not conflict with the law. Students had no vested right to stay affiliated with Punjab University, since college prospectuses always reserved the government's right to change rules. Importantly, the Court noted students would still get the same MBBS degree, and the new university existed to raise educational standards and was duly recognized by the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council.

This case matters because it confirmed the government's authority to restructure medical education oversight without violating students' rights.

explainer:

The victims had died in an unseen occurrence, meaning no one directly witnessed the killing, so the prosecution relied entirely on circumstantial evidence, including witnesses who claimed to have seen the accused near the scene (called "Wajtakar" evidence) and recovered items allegedly belonging to the deceased.

The court found serious flaws in this evidence. The witnesses who claimed to have seen the accused could not properly establish their own presence at the relevant time and place, their account of events was vague, and the investigating officer failed to verify their claims through phone records or travel tickets. Other witnesses were "chance witnesses" whose presence at the scene was never justified. The identification of recovered articles, including mobile phones, was not properly conducted before a Magistrate as required by law, making the recovery evidence unreliable. There was also no medical evidence of rape, contrary to allegations.

The court explained that circumstantial evidence must form an unbroken chain linking the crime directly to the accused, and any gap destroys its value. It also clarified the legal procedures police must follow when sending evidence to forensic labs under the Police Rules and the Punjab Forensic Science Agency Act, emphasizing that police, not forensic experts, bear responsibility for maintaining evidence custody.

title: A female child between the age of 10 to 15 needs her mother the most
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute between divorced parents over their young daughter, Hareem Fatima. The father, a Pakistan Army Colonel, had initially won custody from the Guardian Court in Mianwali, partly because the child herself expressed a preference to live with him. The mother, a doctor, appealed, and the Additional District Judge reversed that decision, awarding her custody instead while giving the father a visitation schedule. The father then challenged this reversal before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court upheld the mother's custody, dismissing the father's petition. The judge reasoned that while the child's preference and her bond with her father were genuine and noteworthy, a child's stated preference alone cannot be the sole basis for custody decisions, especially when the mother has not remarried and has no competing family obligations besides raising the child. The court emphasized that a girl between ages 10 and 15 undergoes significant biological and emotional changes during which she especially needs her biological mother, rather than a father, stepmother, or grandmother. It also noted the mother's professional stability as a doctor made her well-suited to provide care.

The case matters because it reinforces that in custody disputes, courts must weigh the holistic welfare of the child, particularly daughters at sensitive developmental stages, rather than relying solely on a child's expressed preference, and affirms that a mother's remarriage status—not her career—is the key factor weighed against her custodial rights.
