title: Benefit of Summer Vacations can be taken if appeal filed on 1st September
explainer:
This case from the Lahore High Court dealt with a long-running property dispute in which a family contested a gift of land made through a mutation (land record entry). During the trial, the plaintiffs repeatedly failed to produce their evidence despite being given eleven opportunities. When their evidence still wasn't presented on 18 July 2008, the trial court closed the evidence and dismissed their suit. The plaintiffs then appealed, but filed that appeal late, also asking the court to excuse the delay.

The key issue before the High Court was whether the appeal was filed within the legal time limit, and if not, whether there was sufficient reason to excuse the delay. The law required an appeal to be filed within thirty days of the judgment, which meant the deadline fell during the summer court vacations. The court held that even allowing for the vacation period, the plaintiffs should have filed their appeal on 1 September 2008, the day courts reopened — but they did not file until 31 October 2008, far too late. The court also rejected their excuse of confusion over hearing dates as unconvincing.

Because the appeal was hopelessly delayed with no valid justification, the High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the lower courts' decisions. The case clarifies how limitation periods are calculated when deadlines fall within court vacations, confirming that vacation benefits only extend the deadline to the day courts reopen, not further.

title: Application for Summoning of Record Keeper
explainer:
This case involved two connected land disputes over property in Raiwind, Lahore, both seeking specific performance of agreements to sell. During the proceedings, the petitioner produced an agreement to sell as evidence, but questions arose about the authenticity of the stamp paper used in that document.

The respondents wanted to summon the Record Keeper of the Treasury Office along with official records about that stamp paper, to verify whether it was genuine. However, they had not included this witness in their original list of witnesses, which under the Civil Procedure Code must normally be filed within seven days of the court framing the issues in a case. A trial court judge refused to allow this evidence because no "sufficient cause" was shown for the delay. On appeal, the Additional District Judge reversed that decision and allowed the record to be produced.

The petitioner challenged this reversal before the Lahore High Court, arguing that the rule requiring timely filing of witness lists is strict, and that the respondents could not bypass it, especially since the petitioner himself had earlier been denied a similar request.

The High Court dismissed the petition and upheld the decision to allow the treasury record. It reasoned that the document was already mentioned in the respondents' list of reliance, so there was no real surprise to the petitioner, and allowing this evidence served the broader goal of finding the truth and ensuring complete justice between the parties. The court found no legal error in the lower court's decision.

title: Authority of Selection Board cannot be Challenged
explainer:
This case involved candidates who had applied for positions as Civil Judge/Judicial Magistrate and Qazi (BPS-18) in Balochistan, following a 2014 advertisement. The petitioners argued that their appointments should have followed the Government of Balochistan Recruitment Policy of 1991, which they claimed required zonal (district-based) allocation of posts, rather than being decided purely on merit. One petitioner also complained that candidates ranked lower than him on the merit list had been selected ahead of him.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It explained that Article 27 of the Constitution bars discrimination in public appointments based on things like race, religion, caste, sex, residence or place of birth, but allows authorities the option, not an obligation, to reserve posts for certain areas to ensure fair representation. Since this reservation is discretionary, no candidate has an automatic right to demand a zonal quota system.

On the merit list complaint, the court found that although the petitioner ranked higher in the written exam, he scored lower marks overall after the interview, which placed him further down the list.

The court held that the Judicial Selection Board, composed of three High Court judges, is best positioned to judge candidates' abilities, and its decisions should not be overturned unless there is bad faith or the assessment has nothing to do with the candidate's actual competence. Both petitions were dismissed.

title: Second FIR of the same incident is barred
explainer:
This case, decided by the Supreme Court of Pakistan, dealt with a police encounter in which the petitioner's son, Mohsin Ali, was killed by local police. An FIR had already been registered about that incident, the police had completed their investigation, and a challan (police report) had been submitted to the trial court. The petitioner, Mst. Sughran Bibi, also filed a private complaint giving her own version of events, and that complaint had led to accused persons being summoned, with the trial already underway. She wanted the police to register a separate, second FIR based on her account of the same incident.

The Supreme Court refused this request and dismissed the petition. It held that only one FIR can exist for a single incident. If someone comes forward with a different version of the very same occurrence, that version should be recorded as a statement under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code during investigation, or pursued through a private complaint, not treated as a fresh FIR. A second FIR can only be registered if the new version concerns a genuinely different occurrence or reveals a separate cognizable offence altogether.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the law on multiple FIRs for the same incident, preventing confusion, duplication, and potential misuse of the FIR process, while still protecting victims' rights through investigation procedures and private complaints.

title: Relaxation of Upper Age Limit
explainer:
The case involved a police constable, Rashid Ameer, who applied for a promotion-related post of Assistant Sub-Inspector (ASI) in the Counter Terrorism Force of Islamabad Police. The advertised age limit was 25 years, and he was over-age by about four years. He sought relaxation in the upper age limit, citing rules made by the Establishment Division in 1993 and a later office memorandum that allowed extra years of age relaxation for government employees with continuous service, and additional relaxation for children of civil servants who died during service (his father, a DSP, had died while in service). The Inspector General of Police rejected his request, arguing that the Establishment Division's rules did not apply to Islamabad Police and that allowing relaxation would disrupt the completed recruitment process.

The Islamabad High Court disagreed. It held that the 1993 rules and the related office memorandum clearly entitled serving government employees with at least two years of continuous service to a 10-year age relaxation, and this benefit could not be denied to the petitioner. The court found that the authorities had failed to properly apply these rules and ruled in favor of the petitioner, allowing his writ petition.

This case matters because it reinforces that government employees have a legally protected right to age relaxation benefits under established rules, and administrative authorities cannot arbitrarily deny such entitlements by claiming non-applicability without proper justification.

explainer:
This case concerns a woman, Mst. Shayan Afzal, who had been given the right to divorce her husband under Column 18 of their marriage contract (Nikahnama). She exercised this right in 2013 by sending talaq notices and applied to the Chairman of the Arbitration Council in Islamabad for a certificate confirming the divorce had taken effect. The husband never appeared despite repeated notices, and reconciliation attempts failed. Before the certificate was issued, however, Shayan died in the UK in 2015. Her father then asked the Arbitration Council to issue the divorce certificate in her name, but his application was dismissed. He challenged this dismissal in the Islamabad High Court.

The court ruled in the father's favor. It held that once a wife has been validly delegated the right of divorce, she can exercise it without needing anyone's permission, and the Arbitration Council has no authority to refuse or withhold the certificate once reconciliation fails and 90 days have passed. The court clarified an important legal principle: if the person who pronounced talaq dies before the 90-day period ends, the divorce does not take effect; but if they die after the 90 days have passed, the Council is legally bound to issue the certificate confirming the divorce was effective.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the rights of women who hold delegated divorce power and limits the discretion of Arbitration Councils to delay or deny recognition of valid divorces, reinforcing procedural fairness under the Constitution.

On appeal, the Lahore High Court (Multan Bench) found the prosecution's case riddled with doubts. No witness had actually seen the victim with the accused. title: Re-Investigation could not be debarred after submission of Challan
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over the police investigation of a murder arising from a shooting incident at a hotel in Murree, which also involved anti-terrorism charges. After the initial police investigation, one accused was arrested and sent for trial while two others were cleared. Dissatisfied with this outcome, the complainant sought a change of investigation, and a new team found the two previously cleared men guilty. Those two accused then challenged this finding, leading to a Provincial Standing Board recommending yet another re-investigation, which the Inspector General of Police approved. The original complainant then challenged this second change of investigation in the Lahore High Court, arguing that once a challan (police report) had already been submitted to the trial court, the investigation could not legally be reopened, and alleging that the repeated changes favored the influential accused party.

The court dismissed the petition. It held that under Article 18(6) of the Police Order, 2002, a duly constituted board has the legal power to recommend re-investigation, and this power is not barred merely because a challan has already been filed. The court emphasized that an investigating officer's job is only to gather evidence, not to decide guilt or innocence, leaving that determination to the magistrate or trial court. It also noted the complainant could pursue a private complaint as an alternative remedy.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that police investigations can be reopened even after formal charges are filed, provided proper institutional procedures are followed, balancing thorough fact-finding against concerns about delay or misuse.

title: Stay of Execution in Rent Matter
explainer:
This case involved a landlord-tenant dispute that had already been fully decided through the courts. A Rent Tribunal in Sargodha had ordered the eviction of a tenant in 2010. The tenant appealed repeatedly, losing at every stage, including before the Lahore High Court and eventually withdrawing an appeal before the Supreme Court. This meant the eviction order had become final.

Afterward, the tenant filed a fresh civil suit claiming ownership of the property and got a temporary status quo order from a civil judge. Using this, he asked the court executing the eviction order to pause the eviction proceedings, arguing that an ownership dispute was pending. When this request was denied, he challenged that denial before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It explained that the legal rule allowing execution to be paused while another suit is pending (Order XXI Rule 29 of the Civil Procedure Code) only applies when someone is executing a civil court decree, not an eviction order from a Rent Tribunal, which operates on a different legal basis concerning landlord-tenant relationships. The court also noted that the tenant had concealed the existence of the final eviction order in his new ownership suit, which was dishonest and disqualified him from equitable relief.

This case reaffirms that final eviction orders by Rent Tribunals cannot be stalled through unrelated ownership suits, and that courts will not assist litigants who conceal important facts.

title: Eviction Order under Cantonment Rent Restriction Act 1963
explainer:
This case was about a landlord-tenant dispute under the Cantonment Rent Restriction Act, 1963, which deals with eviction and rent matters for properties in cantonment areas. The Lahore High Court had earlier dismissed the tenants' appeal against an eviction order, but also directed them to pay rent from August 2001 until they vacated the premises, at Rs. 5,000 per month, before handing over possession.

The tenants challenged this part of the order before the Supreme Court, arguing that while a Rent Controller does have the authority to order eviction when the landlord-tenant relationship itself is disputed, no provision of the 1963 Act actually gives the Rent Controller or any higher court the power to also order payment of specific rent arrears as a condition for vacating the property. The landlord's side argued that such an order was permissible when there was no real dispute about the amount of rent owed.

The Supreme Court examined the Act and could not find any provision supporting the power to impose such a rent-payment condition, and the landlord's lawyer could not point to any legal provision or precedent either. As a result, the Court partly allowed the appeal, removing the condition requiring payment of rent arrears before vacating the premises. However, it clarified that the landlord could still separately claim any unpaid rent through proper legal proceedings. This case matters because it clarifies the limits of a Rent Controller's powers under the cantonment rent law.

title: Previous Non Convict Bail Confirmed
explainer:
This case comes from the Lahore High Court, Multan Bench, and concerns a petitioner named Ghulam Qadir who sought post-arrest bail in a criminal case registered under the Pakistan Penal Code for offences related to theft and dishonestly receiving stolen property (cattle allegedly taken forcibly from a complainant). He was initially accused of robbery, but that charge was later dropped during investigation and replaced with lesser theft-related offences.

The court noted several important factors in deciding the case. First, there was an unexplained nine-month delay in filing the police report (FIR), which cast doubt on the prosecution's version of events. Second, the allegation that the petitioner had abetted the crime was not backed by any independent evidence. Third, the offences he was ultimately charged with did not fall under the more serious category of crimes that automatically restrict bail. The investigation was complete, the formal charges (challan) had been submitted to the trial court, but the trial itself had not yet begun. The petitioner also had no prior criminal record.

Given these circumstances, the judge ruled that keeping the petitioner in jail indefinitely served no real purpose and granted him bail, requiring him to post bail bonds and a surety. The judgment highlights how delays in reporting crimes and weak evidence can influence bail decisions, and that bail can be granted even in non-bailable offences when the case requires further inquiry.

title: Alienation of Property Judgment
explainer:
This case was about a family dispute over inheritance after the death of Haji Muhammad Zakir. His heirs filed an "administration suit" to determine and distribute his estate among them. One of the heirs, Ghazala Zakir, claimed that a particular property in North Nazimabad, Karachi had been gifted to her by her father before his death, so it was no longer part of his estate and should not be examined in the administration suit. Another heir, Muhammad Zahid, argued that since the property dispute was between the heirs themselves, its validity could and should be decided within the administration suit.

The trial judge had ruled that such gifts, especially where no registered document was challenged, generally fell outside the scope of an administration suit. On appeal, the Sindh High Court disagreed with this rigid approach. The appellate judges held that the real test is not whether the transfer was through a registered document, but whether deciding the issue would disturb the relative shares of the heirs. If resolving the dispute would upset the balance between heirs or give one of them an unfair advantage, then it falls within the scope of an administration suit and can be decided there.

Because of this, the court set aside the earlier decree and sent the case back to the trial court for fresh consideration. The judgment is significant because it clarifies how far administration suits can go in deciding disputed property claims among family members.

title: Constitutional Petition in a Rent Case
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a tenant, Muhammad Younas, and his landlord, Rana Muhammad Zahid, over a shop and basement in Blue Area, Islamabad. The landlord had sought the tenant's eviction after their lease agreement expired, claiming he needed the premises for his own personal use and also alleging rent default. The Rent Controller initially rejected the landlord's eviction request, but on appeal, the Additional District Judge sided with the landlord and ordered the tenant to vacate within two months. The tenant then challenged this decision before the Islamabad High Court.

By the time the matter reached the High Court, the rent default allegation was no longer being pursued, so the only issue was whether the landlord's claim of personal bona fide need was genuine. The tenant argued that the landlord had never clearly explained why he needed the shop. However, the court found that during cross-examination, the landlord had revealed he intended to start a vegetable business after returning from Saudi Arabia, which was sufficient to establish genuine need, even though it wasn't spelled out in the original application.

The court dismissed the tenant's petition, upholding the eviction order. It clarified that courts exercising constitutional writ jurisdiction generally don't disturb factual findings of lower courts unless there's clear misreading of evidence or legal error. The court also noted that if the landlord's claimed use later proves false, the tenant could pursue separate legal remedies for that violation.

title: To secure the ends of Justice High Court can pass any order
explainer:
This case from the Peshawar High Court dealt with a long-running dispute over a private criminal complaint. The petitioner, Mir Qasim Khan, had accused the respondents of using a forged special power of attorney to drag him into a fabricated civil lawsuit. The complaint bounced between a Magistrate, a Sessions Judge, and an Additional Sessions Judge multiple times, with disagreements over which criminal sections applied and which court had jurisdiction, particularly regarding forgery under Section 467 PPC, which must be tried by a Sessions Court.

Eventually a Magistrate found the complaint maintainable and ruled that the forgery allegations did fall under Section 467 PPC, sending the case for trial before the appropriate Sessions Court. The respondents challenged this, but the High Court examined its own inherent powers under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, explaining that these powers allow it to make any order necessary to prevent abuse of court process or to secure justice, even without a formal application, and even on matters not directly raised by the parties.

The court also clarified that restrictions under Section 195(1)(c) of the Cr.P.C, which require special permission before prosecuting certain offences, do not apply to forgery under Section 467 PPC. Based on this reasoning, the court allowed the quashment petition, effectively permitting the criminal case to proceed. The judgment matters because it reinforces the High Court's broad inherent authority to ensure fair process and correct procedural errors in criminal cases.

title: Judgment on Ejectment of Tenant
citation: PLD 1980 SC 298; Inayat Ullah v. Zahoor ud Din 1987 SCMR 1313; Muham
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant dispute in Islamabad concerning eviction of a tenant from a shop-cum-flat. The landlady, Mst. Jahanzeba Begum, had filed an eviction petition claiming the tenant defaulted on rent payments, violated the lease agreement, and failed to pay increased rent as required under the tenancy agreement and law. Both the Rent Controller and the Additional District Judge ruled in favor of the landlady and ordered the tenant to vacate.

The tenant challenged these orders before the Islamabad High Court. The Court found that the eviction orders were largely based on the tenant's failure to pay a Rs. 500 per day penalty for late rent payments, and on his failure to pay an automatic rent increase. The Court held that this penalty clause violated the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance, 2001, which specifically prohibits such penalties, making that part of the agreement void from the start. The Court also found that the landlady had never issued a proper notice demanding the increased statutory rent, nor had she applied to strike off the tenant's defence, so she could not rely on that ground either.

As a result, the High Court set aside both lower rulings and dismissed the landlady's eviction petition. This case is significant because it clarifies that landlords cannot evict tenants based on contractual penalty clauses that conflict with rent laws, and that proper legal procedure must be followed before claiming rent increases as grounds for eviction.

title: Quashment in Qazf Case
explainer:
This case involves a complaint filed by Dr. Maqsood Hussain against 36 people, asking the court to convict them for qazf (false accusation of zina, or unlawful sexual intercourse, under Islamic criminal law) for allegedly spreading claims that he had committed zina-bil-jabr (rape). This stemmed from an earlier case where a woman, injured in the 2005 earthquake and being treated in Lahore, had accused Dr. Maqsood of assault, leading to an FIR against him. She later said media persons had pressured her into making the complaint and asked that it be withdrawn; the original case against the doctor was eventually cancelled.

When Dr. Maqsood later filed his qazf complaint, the Additional Sessions Judge handling it adjourned the case repeatedly, often without proper reason, and eventually issued arrest warrants against the accused persons without properly following the law. The High Court found that the trial judge had violated Section 200 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which requires a magistrate to examine a complainant under oath and record the statement properly before proceeding. This had not been done.

The High Court also found that, based on the complaint and the woman's own statement, no actual offence of qazf had been established against the accused. For these reasons, the court declared the lower court's proceedings and warrants illegal and quashed them.

This case highlights the importance of following proper procedure before issuing serious orders like arrest warrants, and clarifies that criminal accusations must be backed by clear evidence of an actual offence.

title: Permission to produce documents under order 13 rule 2
explainer:
This case concerns a civil suit filed by Kohinoor Tobacco Company against S.M. Idrees Allawala, seeking declaration, injunction, and delivery of title deeds. While the case was at the stage of the plaintiff presenting evidence, the plaintiff filed an application asking the court's permission to produce 28 additional documents that had not been submitted earlier, relying on Order XIII Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code along with Section 151.

The plaintiff explained that these documents were part of old records that had gotten mixed up with other papers and were only recently retrieved. The defendant opposed this, arguing the request was a delay tactic since years had passed since issues were framed and evidence had already begun, including testimony from official witnesses.

The Sindh High Court ruled in favor of allowing the documents to be produced. The judge explained that whether "good cause" exists for late production is not governed by rigid rules but depends on the facts of each case, left to the court's discretion. Importantly, mere delay in filing such an application is not, by itself, sufficient reason to refuse the documents. The purpose of the relevant procedural rule is to keep out forged or fabricated documents and ensure speedy trials, not to block genuine, relevant evidence. Since the authenticity of the documents was not seriously in doubt, the court allowed them to be produced, emphasizing that procedural rules should serve justice rather than obstruct it.

title: Compulsory Retirement of a Civil Servant
explainer:
This case concerns a police constable, Tariq Mahmood, who was dismissed from service in 1992 after being implicated in a criminal case involving fraud and forgery charges. He was also briefly absent from duty around the same time. He filed a departmental appeal and later a revision petition, but the revision was kept pending for roughly 17 years while the related criminal case and a civil suit were decided. He was eventually acquitted of the criminal charges in 2010, and his revision petition was then allowed, meaning his dismissal was effectively reversed.

The dispute before the Supreme Court was whether he was entitled to back pay and benefits for the long period he was out of service, and whether the Punjab Service Tribunal had wrongly modified his punishment.

The Supreme Court held that a person is presumed innocent until proven guilty, so the department could not deny him benefits merely because of a pending criminal case. It ruled that reinstated employees are normally entitled to back benefits unless proven to have been gainfully employed elsewhere during that period. Since the long delay in deciding his revision petition was caused by the department, not by him, he could not be blamed for it. The Court directed a committee to calculate his entitlement, excluding only the short period of unexplained absence, and dismissed the department's appeal.

This case matters because it reinforces that civil servants should not suffer financially due to delays caused by the government's own administrative processes, and it clarifies principles on reinstatement and back-pay entitlements.

title: Powers of a court under Order I Rule 10(2) of CPC
explainer:
This case involved a civil suit filed by Kashmir Steel Mills against electricity department officials, seeking a perpetual injunction. During the proceedings before the District Judge, Mirpur, the defendants failed to appear on a hearing date, so the court proceeded against them ex-parte, meaning the case continued without their side being heard, and the plaintiff was allowed to present evidence. The defendants later applied to have this ex-parte order set aside, but their application was dismissed for being improperly filed and lacking sufficient justification for their absence.

The AJK High Court examined the record and found serious problems with how the ex-parte order was made. It noted that the defendants were still in the process of being served summons and had not all been properly notified, and that the date in question was not actually a hearing date for the main suit but for a related application. The application to set aside the ex-parte order, though filed on time, was presented by an unauthorized clerk and lacked a supporting affidavit.

The Court also addressed whether the Superintending Engineer, who was not originally a party to the suit, could be added as a defendant. Relying on Order I Rule 10(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, it held that he was a necessary party whose presence was required for the court to fully resolve the dispute, and directed him to apply to be impleaded.

Ultimately, the High Court found the ex-parte proceedings unwarranted and illegal, set them aside, and allowed the petition, emphasizing that lower courts and lawyers had mishand

title: Judgment on Recovery Proceedings by Customs Authorities
explainer:
This case involves Dewan Cement Limited, which challenged customs authorities' attempts to recover outstanding duty and taxes from the company. The customs department had issued a warrant of attachment to recover about Rs. 86.8 million in unpaid dues.

The company's dispute over this demand was already pending before the Customs Appellate Tribunal, which had earlier refused to stay the recovery and instead ordered the company to deposit the amount within 15 days via a bank guarantee. When the company failed to comply, it went to the High Court instead, which also ordered it to submit a bank guarantee for 50% of the demand. The company again failed to comply with this order too.

Rather than following either the Tribunal's or the Court's directions, the company filed yet another petition, this time also claiming it was entitled to sale proceeds from its own goods that customs had auctioned, asking for these to be refunded or adjusted against its tax liability.

The High Court found that the company had repeatedly ignored binding orders from both the Tribunal and the Court itself, seemingly to avoid paying its admitted tax liability altogether. It held that such conduct was dishonest and contemptuous, disqualifying the company from receiving any discretionary relief under the Court's constitutional jurisdiction. Since there was no valid stay order protecting the company and it had failed to honor the consent order, the Court dismissed the petition. This case underscores that courts will not reward parties who disregard prior judicial directions while seeking fresh relief.

title: Case in which defendant is not made party in Appeal
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over property, where the District Council Tharparkar had filed an appeal against a judgment involving Syed Muhammad Wali and the Government of Sindh. When the appeal reached the District Judge, the Government of Sindh, which had been a defendant in the original suit, was not made a party to the appeal. A preliminary objection was raised before the Sindh High Court arguing that this omission made the entire appeal legally defective and therefore the revision petition arising from it should be dismissed.

The High Court examined Order XLI, Rule 20 of the Civil Procedure Code, which allows an appellate court to add a person as a respondent if that person was party to the original suit and is interested in the outcome of the appeal. The court noted that this rule does not specify any automatic penalty for failing to implead such a person, and that the matter is left to the court's discretion based on whether the omitted party is genuinely necessary and affected by the outcome.

The court found that the Government of Sindh had no real stake in the dispute, had not claimed ownership of the property, had never objected during nearly five years of proceedings, and had not appealed itself. The real contest was between the plaintiff and the other defendant. Since the Government was merely a formal party and not genuinely affected, the court held that its non-joinder did not invalidate the appeal, and the objection was rejected.

This case clarifies that not every missing party automatically defeats an appeal; courts must assess whether that party was truly necessary to the dispute.

title: Wife cannot be forced to live with her husband
explainer:
This case involved a habeas corpus petition under Section 491 of the Criminal Procedure Code, filed by a husband who claimed his wife, Mst. Shaista, was being wrongfully confined by her brothers. He said he had married her, was pressured by his own family into signing divorce papers, but insisted he never actually pronounced the divorce, making it invalid under religious rulings he obtained. The brothers countered that a valid divorce had indeed taken place and been formally conveyed.

The Sindh High Court, however, found that it could not resolve the dispute over whether the divorce was valid within a habeas corpus proceeding, since that required separate legal determination. Instead, the court focused on what it could decide: the woman's personal liberty. Since Mst. Shaista was an adult (sui juris) capable of managing her own affairs, she could not be forced to live with her husband, her brothers, or be kept in a shelter home (Darul Aman) against her wishes. The court explained that under Islamic law, a woman cannot be compelled to live with her husband if she disagrees, and her husband's only recourse would be to file a separate suit for restitution of conjugal rights.

The court ultimately ordered that she be set free to live wherever she chose, emphasizing her constitutional right to liberty under Article 9. This case matters because it reinforces that adult women have the legal right to make their own choices about where and with whom they live, regardless of pressure from husbands or family members.

title: Mechanism for trial of matrimonial and family dispute between spouse
explainer:
This case is about a wife who sued for dissolution of her marriage, dower, maintenance, and dowry articles, claiming her husband was cruel and infertile, and had hidden his infertility from her before marriage. The Family Court dissolved the marriage, reasoning that concealing infertility amounted to cruelty, and awarded her part of her dower and maintenance. On appeal, the Additional District Judge disagreed with that reasoning but still dissolved the marriage, changing the basis from cruelty to khula (a wife-initiated separation), while also granting her the dowry articles she sought. The matter eventually reached the Supreme Court, which sent it back to the Peshawar High Court for a fresh decision.

The High Court held that the wife herself admitted she knew about her husband's infertility before marriage, and she could not prove ongoing cruelty or that infertility was still an issue. Since infertility is not a recognized ground for divorce under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939, and is simply a natural condition beyond human control, it could not justify dissolution on that basis. However, the court reaffirmed that even if a wife fails to prove the specific grounds she claims, she can still be granted separation through khula if she is unwilling to continue the marriage, since Islamic law does not compel spouses to remain in a marriage devoid of harmony.

This judgment matters because it clarifies that family courts can grant khula as a fallback remedy even when a wife's stated grounds for divorce (like cruelty or infertility) aren't pro

title: Child born after two years of divorce is legitimate
explainer:
This case is about who has to pay maintenance for a child, and whether that child was legally legitimate. A wife left her husband's home and later gave birth to a son about eleven months after their separation. She filed a family court case seeking dissolution of marriage, return of her dowry items, and maintenance for herself and the child. The husband denied the child was his, claiming the timing proved the boy was illegitimate, and also disputed handing over some dowry items.

Both the trial court and the appellate family court ruled against the husband, granting dissolution of marriage, ordering return of dowry articles, and awarding maintenance to both the wife and child. The husband then challenged these decisions before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' rulings. It explained that under Islamic law, a child born within two years of a marriage's dissolution is presumed legitimate, and a father cannot simply deny paternity to avoid paying maintenance—he must follow a strict legal procedure (called Liyan) before a competent court to formally disown a child, which the husband never did. The court also rejected his objections to the dowry articles, since he had not raised these issues properly earlier and the items were established to be in his possession.

The case matters because it reinforces that children's rights to maintenance and legitimacy are strongly protected by law, and fathers cannot evade responsibility through mere denial.

title: Quashment Petition in case of Tempered Vehicle
explainer:
This case involves a dispute over the custody of a vehicle whose identity had been questioned by police. The petitioner, Iftekhar Ali, was driving a car that police stopped and seized because he could not produce valid ownership documents. An investigation revealed that the vehicle's chassis number appeared to have been tampered with, and its registration book was not genuine according to the registering authority. A criminal case was registered against the petitioner, though he was eventually acquitted of the criminal charges. However, the courts ordered the vehicle itself to be confiscated by the State rather than returned to him.

The petitioner claimed he was a genuine buyer who had purchased the car for nine lakh rupees and produced witnesses to support the sale. However, he could not produce the actual seller or the people who had prepared and witnessed the sale document, leaving key facts about the purchase unverified. Forensic reports from two laboratories confirmed the chassis number had been altered, and there was no valid transfer letter or original registration book in his name.

The Peshawar High Court held that given tampered vehicle identification, lack of genuine ownership documents, and absence of credible proof of purchase, the lower courts were right to refuse returning the vehicle and to confiscate it to the State. The petition to quash these decisions was dismissed. The case highlights that mere acquittal in a criminal case does not automatically entitle a person to recover property suspected of being linked to fraud, especially when ownership documents cannot be authenticated.

The vehicle's owner challenged this order, arguing that Customs Courts do not have the legal authority to order confiscation and auction of seized goods. Instead, that power belongs to customs adjudicating authorities and the Customs Appellate Tribunal under specific provisions of the Customs Act, 1969.

The Sindh High Court agreed with the appellant. Relying on an earlier Supreme Court ruling, the judge explained that criminal proceedings before a Special Judge (to punish smuggling) and adjudication proceedings before customs officers (to decide whether goods should be confiscated) are separate and independent processes, even though they arise from the same law. The court found it was especially wrong for the Special Judge to order confiscation and auction when adjudication proceedings over the same vehicle were already pending before customs authorities and an appeal was pending before the Customs Appellate Tribunal.

The court therefore set aside the Special Judge's order regarding confiscation and auction of the vehicle. However, it did not order the vehicle released outright. Instead, it allowed the owner to apply for release of the vehicle to the proper authority, the customs adjudicating officer or the Appellate Tribunal, who were directed to decide the request within two weeks.

title: Delay in FIR in 489-F matter
explainer:
This case involves a man named Malik Irfan who was accused of issuing a dishonored cheque worth Rs. 200,000 under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with cheques issued dishonestly without sufficient funds. He was arrested and sought post-arrest bail from the Lahore High Court.

His lawyer argued that there was an unexplained delay of five months and ten days between the alleged incident and the filing of the FIR, that the dispute was essentially a civil financial matter rather than a criminal one, that he had no prior criminal record, and that since the police investigation was already complete, there was no need to keep him in custody.

The court agreed with these arguments. It noted the significant, unexplained delay in registering the FIR and found that the underlying dispute appeared to be civil in nature. It also pointed out that since the maximum punishment for this offense does not exceed three years, the case did not fall under the stricter bail provisions reserved for more serious crimes. Citing earlier Supreme Court precedent, the judge noted that for offenses not punishable by death, life imprisonment, or ten years in prison, granting bail should be the normal rule rather than the exception.

As a result, the court granted bail, requiring the petitioner to submit bail bonds of Rs. 50,000 with a surety. This case illustrates how delays in filing FIRs and the civil nature of financial disputes can be significant factors favoring bail in cheque dishonor cases.

title: Aslam Parvaiz V. The State
explainer:
This case involved Aslam Pervaiz, who was accused of issuing a dishonoured cheque worth Rs. 442,000 under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, a crime related to fraudulent cheques. The cheque had reportedly been issued as part of a land purchase deal, but the land was never actually transferred to him.

The complainant's side argued that the petitioner should be denied bail because he had around 25 similar cases against him, suggesting he was a habitual offender, and that the land had instead been transferred to another person named Qamar supposedly on the petitioner's instructions.

The Lahore High Court disagreed with denying bail on these grounds. It noted that having other pending cases does not automatically disqualify someone from bail if they otherwise qualify on merit, and the petitioner had no prior convictions. Importantly, the sale deed produced in court showed Qamar, not the petitioner, as the buyer, and police had never recorded any statement from Qamar confirming he acted on the petitioner's behalf. The court also pointed out that this type of offence does not fall under the restrictive "prohibitory clause" that normally makes bail harder to get, and that the matter required further inquiry before guilt could be established.

As a result, the court granted bail, requiring the petitioner to submit bail bonds of Rs. 100,000 with one surety. This case illustrates how courts assess bail based on concrete evidence rather than general allegations or an accused's reputation.

title: What happens if probation period ends?
explainer:
This case was a service law dispute about what happens to a government employee's probation status when various administrative actions occur during that period.

Dr. Waqar-ur-Rehman Qureshi was appointed as a Lecturer and later provisionally appointed as Assistant Professor at Ayub Medical College, Abbottabad, subject to a two-year probation period. Under the applicable rules, if no confirmation letter was issued after two years, the probation would automatically be considered extended for one more year, after which he would become a regular employee. While still within this probation period, he was granted unpaid leave to work abroad in Saudi Arabia through the Overseas Employment Corporation, with the understanding that he would complete his remaining probation upon return. However, before his leave ended, the Chief Executive of the institution repatriated him back to his parent department without any hearing.

The Peshawar High Court ruled in his favor, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision, refusing the institution's request for leave to appeal. The Court held that probation periods can be suspended, postponed, or extended, and that the employee's repatriation was done unilaterally without giving him any opportunity to be heard, violating principles of natural justice and the service rules governing medical institutions.

This case matters because it confirms that employers cannot unilaterally terminate or alter an employee's service status during probation without following proper procedure and affording a fair hearing, reinforcing protections for employees even during probationary periods.

title: If the abductee doesn't resist then offense is not attracted
explainer:
This case involved a man, Muhammad Yar alias Allah Yar, accused of forcibly abducting a woman named Mst. Shazia Nasim for illicit purposes, along with stealing cash and gold ornaments, under charges including abduction and rape (Sections 380, 365-B, and 376 of the Pakistan Penal Code). He sought bail while awaiting trial.

The Lahore High Court granted him post-arrest bail. The court reasoned that the complainant was not an eyewitness, and no one from the area came forward to confirm that the woman had resisted or that force was used during the alleged abduction. Since there was no evidence of restraint or resistance, the court held that the offence of abduction was not clearly established at this stage—suggesting the case looked more like elopement, especially since the woman had appeared before various courts admitting she had married the petitioner (Nikah). The court also noted a suspicious one-month delay in filing the police report, and that the Nikah reportedly took place before the FIR was lodged. A related case questioning the validity of the marriage was still pending, and a co-accused had already been granted bail and cleared during investigation.

This judgment matters because it reinforces a legal principle: for abduction charges to apply, there must be evidence of force or resistance by the alleged victim. Mere allegations, without supporting proof of coercion, may not meet the threshold required to deny bail, especially when conflicting narratives and procedural delays raise doubts about the prosecution's case.

title: An innocent person cannot be tortured or detained illegally
explainer:
This case involved a habeas corpus petition filed by Azmat Bashir on behalf of his brother, Mazhar Bashir, who had been illegally detained by police. Mazhar was arrested from his home in Okara by a police sub-inspector, not because he had committed any crime, but because his two brothers were allegedly involved in criminal cases and one was absconding. He was held for 20 days without being produced before any court, was not named in any FIR, and his arrest was never officially recorded. Medical examination confirmed he had been physically tortured, apparently to force him to reveal his absconding brother's whereabouts.

The Lahore High Court, acting under Section 491 of the Criminal Procedure Code, ordered the detenu's recovery through a court bailiff, who found him hidden at a police station. After hearing the police officers involved, who could not justify their actions, the court ordered Mazhar's immediate release. It ruled that no person can be punished or tortured for a crime committed by a relative, and that such treatment violates both the Constitution's guarantees of life and liberty and international human rights law.

The court awarded compensation of Rs. 50,000 and Rs. 25,000 to be paid personally by the two police officers responsible, acknowledging that no sum could truly compensate for lost freedom and suffering. It also directed the Inspector General of Police Punjab to take disciplinary action against the officers, emphasizing that illegal detention and torture of innocent citizens cannot be tolerated.

title: Effectiveness of Talaq
explainer:
Here is a plain-language explainer.

This case involved a husband and wife whose marriage had broken down. The husband pronounced divorce (talaq) and sent notices about it, but there was confusion and dispute over where the wife actually lived, since she had moved between different addresses in Lahore after leaving the matrimonial home. The wife argued that the divorce notices were sent to the wrong Union Council, one that did not have jurisdiction over her actual residence, and that this made the divorce proceedings legally ineffective.

After earlier litigation clarified her correct address, the husband issued a fresh divorce notice to that address and informed the relevant Union Council, the wife, her brothers, and other parties. The wife still did not respond or appear before the arbitration council, and the case shows a pattern of her repeatedly challenging procedural technicalities to delay the divorce taking effect.

The Lahore High Court dismissed her petition, holding that the legal requirements under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance to notify the Union Council are directory, not mandatory, since no penalty exists for failing to follow them. Failure to serve notice correctly is merely an irregularity and does not invalidate a divorce that has already been properly pronounced and communicated.

This case matters because it clarifies that technical lapses in notifying authorities about a divorce cannot be used to block or delay a divorce that has already validly taken place, preventing parties from exploiting procedural loopholes to prolong marital disputes.

title: Personal Injury Case Azad Kashmir
explainer:
This case concerns a UK Supreme Court decision (Jones v Kaney) that was cited and reported in Pakistani legal citation (SCMR 1298). The case arose from a personal injury claim after a road traffic accident. The claimant's solicitors hired a consultant clinical psychologist to examine him and prepare an expert report for his compensation case. She initially diagnosed him with post-traumatic stress disorder, but later signed a joint statement prepared by the opposing side's expert without reviewing or amending it properly. This joint statement undermined the claimant's case, suggesting he was being deceptive about his symptoms. As a result, the claimant was forced to settle his claim for far less money than he otherwise would have received.

The claimant then tried to sue his own expert witness for negligence, but she argued that expert witnesses are legally immune from being sued for how they perform in court proceedings. The court examined whether this traditional immunity should continue.

The court ruled that expert witnesses should no longer be immune from lawsuits for breach of duty related to their court participation. It reasoned that experts must testify honestly regardless of whether this helps or hurts their clients, and there is no real conflict between duties owed to the client and to the court. Removing immunity would not discourage honest experts, only penalize negligent ones. This ruling matters because it makes expert witnesses accountable for careless or negligent work, strengthening the integrity of expert evidence in legal proceedings. However, experts still retain protection from defamation claims.

title: Judgment must discuss each and every issue in evidence
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between Allah Ditta and Muhammad Sharif over a suit for possession of property. The trial court and the first appellate court had both dismissed the suit. The matter then went to the High Court on second appeal, which sent the case back (remanded it) to the appellate court, directing it to decide the case afresh. The losing party challenged this remand before the Supreme Court of Azad Kashmir.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to remand the case. It explained that under Order XLI, Rule 31 of the Civil Procedure Code, an appellate court is legally required to properly discuss the evidence and record findings on each issue raised in a case. As a court of facts, the appellate court cannot simply give a short, bare-bones ruling without engaging with the evidence - unless deciding just one or two key issues is enough on its own to resolve the whole case.

In this particular case, the appellate court had only addressed the question of limitation but failed to decide whether the suit was barred under Order II, Rule 2 of the CPC (a rule about splitting claims), and had not even framed that issue properly. Since this unresolved issue was crucial to deciding the appeal, the appellate court's brief, incomplete judgment was inadequate.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that courts must give reasoned, issue-by-issue judgments, ensuring fairness and transparency, rather than deciding cases in a cursory or incomplete manner.

title: Wrongful termination of police officer
explainer:
This case involved a police officer, an Assistant Sub-Inspector, who was dismissed from service in 1994 over a charge of being absent from duty. His appeal to the Service Tribunal was rejected. However, in 2005 the Chief Minister accepted his mercy petition and directed his reinstatement. The authorities implemented this directive, and the officer went on to complete required training, get his name entered into the promotion list, and was eventually promoted twice, first to Sub-Inspector and later to Inspector.

Two years after reinstatement, the government issued a show-cause notice claiming the reinstatement itself had been illegal, but later withdrew this notice while a court case challenging it was pending. Despite this, years later in 2002 the authorities dismissed the officer again, this time retroactively, treating his service as having ended back in 1994. The Service Tribunal ruled in his favor, and the government appealed to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court refused to grant leave to appeal, upholding the officer's reinstatement. It held that dismissal cannot be made retrospective unless a law specifically allows it, and that a wrong cannot be corrected at any time, especially after someone has served diligently and earned promotions over many years. The Court also noted that once the government withdrew its show-cause notice, the matter was closed and could not be reopened without lawful justification. This case highlights protections against arbitrary retrospective punishment and the importance of finality in administrative decisions affecting employees' careers.

title: Judgment on legitimacy of child in case filed by uncle
explainer:
This judgment, from the Lahore High Court in 2009, deals with a dispute over inheritance in which an uncle tried to challenge the legitimacy of his deceased brother's children in order to claim their share of property.

The court found strong evidence against the uncle's claim. He had consistently referred to his deceased brother as the father of these children in his own court filings, from the trial court all the way up. He had also raised no objection to their paternity when the inheritance mutation was first recorded in their favor. There was no proof that the children were born after their mother's divorce or that she had engaged in adultery. Notably, the uncle even offered a deal: he would accept the children as legitimate if they gave up their inheritance rights, a stance the court found hypocritical and contrary to Islamic legal principles (Fiqa).

The court applied the Sunni school's presumption that a child born six months after marriage, or within two years of its dissolution, is presumed legitimate. The uncle had also failed to use the proper Islamic legal procedure (Liyan) of swearing before a Qazi to formally disown the children as illegitimate. Since the deceased father himself never denied or disowned these children during his lifetime, the court ruled they were legitimate and entitled to inherit his estate.

This case matters because it protects children's inheritance rights against opportunistic relatives and reaffirms established legal presumptions of legitimacy.

title: Interpretation of Section 235(2) of CRPC
explainer:
This judgment explains an important rule about how courts must decide whether to impose the death penalty in criminal cases. Under Section 235(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, after convicting an accused, the court must give them a genuine opportunity to be heard on what punishment should follow. The judgment clarifies that this is not a mere formality - courts must actively try to bring out any facts, circumstances, or evidence relevant to sentencing, even if the accused stays silent or simply denies guilt. This hearing requirement works together with Section 354(3), which requires courts to record "special reasons" when awarding a death sentence instead of a lesser punishment.

The case involved Ajay Pandit, a dentist who deceived people with promises of sending them abroad for better opportunities; some victims were murdered and others barely escaped. The trial court had given him a life sentence, but the matter came up for possible enhancement to death. The court found that the lower courts had merely recorded the accused's bare denial without making any real effort to explore factors that might weigh against a death sentence.

title: What makes a transaction benami under the law?
explainer:
This Supreme Court case involved a husband and wife, Ghulam Murtaza and Asia Bibi, who jointly purchased several properties during their marriage, some of which were later transferred into the wife's name. After the couple separated, the wife sued claiming ownership of the properties, while the husband filed competing suits arguing that his wife was merely a "benami," meaning she held the properties only in name while he was the true owner because he had paid for them. The trial court and first appellate court agreed with the husband, but the Lahore High Court reversed those decisions, finding the evidence had been misread. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's ruling.

The Court explained that a transaction is not automatically "benami" just because one person paid the money while property was registered in someone else's name. Key factors include the source of funds, who holds the title documents, who possesses and controls the property, and most importantly, the motive behind the arrangement. If a person deliberately places property in another's name intending genuinely to transfer ownership, it is not benami, even if that person provided the money. The Court found the husband failed to prove his wife was a benami titleholder, especially since she managed the properties and paid for one deed herself. The judgment matters because it clarifies that spouses cannot later claim sole ownership of jointly acquired property simply because a relationship breaks down, protecting the genuine intentions behind family property arrangements.

title: Reported case on partition by lahore high court
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute between family members over the partition (division) of jointly owned land in Attock. The respondents had filed a partition suit, and after a preliminary decree was passed, a local commission (a court-appointed lawyer) was tasked with working out the practical division of the property. The parties reached a compromise before the commission, and based on that, the trial court passed a final judgment and decree for partition. The petitioner, Karam Elahi, challenged this outcome, first before the District Court, which dismissed his appeal, and then before the Lahore High Court through this civil revision petition.

The petitioner argued that he never agreed to the compromise, that the property had already been informally divided decades earlier, and that the partition would lead to demolition of his house. The High Court rejected these arguments. It held that since the petitioner had not challenged the original preliminary decree, he could not now argue that the property was already divided or indivisible, citing Section 97 of the Civil Procedure Code. The court also found that he had in fact signed the compromise agreed before the commission, which involved an equitable exchange of passages between the parties' properties.

Since two lower courts had already agreed on the facts and the arrangement seemed fair, the High Court declined to interfere and dismissed the petition. This case illustrates how courts enforce procedural rules requiring timely objections and respect compromises reached during partition proceedings.

title: Principle of Audi alteram partern
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between the PASTIC Employees Union and the Registrar of Trade Unions, heard on appeal before the Punjab Labour Appellate Tribunal in Rawalpindi.

A Labour Court had earlier ordered the cancellation of the union's registration, ruling that PASTIC was not an "industry" and therefore its employees had no right to form a trade union. However, the Labour Court reached this conclusion only after hearing arguments from both sides, without actually inviting or recording any evidence on the crucial question of whether PASTIC qualified as an industry. It also never asked the parties whether they wished to waive their right to present evidence on this point.

The union appealed, arguing that it had wanted to present oral and documentary evidence to prove PASTIC was indeed an industry, but was never given the opportunity to do so, causing it serious prejudice.

The Appellate Tribunal agreed. It held that whether PASTIC was an "industry" was a mixed question of fact and law, and parties have the right to decide for themselves whether to lead evidence on such a point. Wanting to produce evidence on a genuine factual-legal issue cannot be treated as an attempt to unnecessarily delay proceedings. Since the lower court failed to give this basic opportunity, it violated the principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem - the right to be heard).

The Tribunal set aside the Labour Court's decision and sent the case back, directing that both parties be given proper opportunity to present evidence before the matter is decided afresh. This

title: Justice Malik Qayyum's Judgment over Benami Transaction
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land that had originally been bought in 1956 by a father in the names of his two minor sons, including the petitioner. Years later, in 1967, the father sold half of that land to another party. The petitioner then sued, asking the court to declare that his father had no right to sell the land because it legally belonged to him, not his father.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court rejected his claim, finding instead that the petitioner was merely a benamidar, meaning his name was used on paper, while his father remained the true and beneficial owner who had actually paid for and controlled the property. The petitioner then challenged this finding before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the petition. It noted that the petitioner, who was a minor at the time of purchase, could not show any independent income or that he had personally paid for the land. His own evidence even contradicted his written claim, since he first said his father bought the land, then claimed his mother had purchased it. The court reaffirmed that Pakistani law does not recognize the English doctrine of advancement, meaning property bought by a father in a child's name is presumed benami unless proven otherwise. Since the petitioner failed to rebut this presumption, his suit was rightly dismissed.

title: In a benami transaction the property is not owned by title holder
explainer:
This case was a family dispute over the estate of a deceased army officer, Major Aziz-ur-Rehman Khan, who died in 1992 leaving behind sons, a widow, and various properties. Two of his sons filed a suit asking the court to administer and divide their father's estate, claiming that several properties, though registered in other family members' names (including their mother's and brother's), were actually "benami" transactions, meaning the real owner was their father, not the person whose name appeared on the documents. The trial court partly ruled in their favor, ordering partition of six properties while dismissing claims over three others. The brother who held some properties in his name appealed.

The Lahore High Court examined key legal principles. It explained that in a benami transaction, true ownership belongs not to the person named on paper but to whoever actually owns the property in substance. The court also addressed gifts under Muslim law, finding no proof that a valid gift had been made by the father to the respondent, since the essential legal conditions for a valid Islamic gift were not established. However, the court upheld an oral family settlement, ruling it did not need formal registration because it merely acknowledged existing facts about the father's estate rather than transferring new rights.

This case matters because it clarifies how courts determine real versus nominal ownership in family property disputes, and the legal requirements for valid gifts and family settlements under Pakistani law.

title: Determination of Benami Transaction
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute over a house and plot in Abbottabad. Dr. Asif Ali Khan had a plot registered in his name through a 1983 sale deed and later built a bungalow on it. He sued his brothers to evict them, claiming they were trespassers after being allowed to live there as licensees. His mother then joined the case, arguing that the property was actually purchased by her husband (Dr. Asif's father) using his own money, with the title merely placed in her son's name as a "benami" (nominal) arrangement to avoid taxes, while the real ownership remained with the father.

The trial court dismissed the son's suit, but the Peshawar High Court reversed this and declared the son the exclusive owner, ordering the family to vacate. The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's ruling. It found that the High Court had misread the evidence, particularly ignoring a witness's admission that payment for the property had come from a bank draft issued from the father's account, not the son's. The Supreme Court emphasized that determining who actually paid for a property, and who possessed it, are key factors in deciding whether a transaction is benami. Since the son's case relied mainly on the registered sale deed without solid supporting evidence, the Supreme Court restored the trial court's dismissal of the suit. This case illustrates how courts examine real financial contribution and possession, not just paperwork, when deciding true ownership in benami property disputes.

title: Writ not maintainable when matter is sub-judice
explainer:
This case was about a man, Ch. Abdur Rehman, who went to the Lahore High Court asking it to order the FIA (Federal Investigation Agency) to launch a criminal inquiry against various bank officials. He alleged they had prepared fake revenue records and a bogus passbook, and issued dummy loans for their own private business.

The bank officials opposed the petition, arguing it was premature and improper because the petitioner had several other legal routes available to him: complaining to the Banking Ombudsman, filing a complaint before the Special Court under banking law, approaching a Justice of Peace under the Criminal Procedure Code, or suing under the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance. In fact, he had already filed a recovery-related suit in the Banking Court at Sargodha, which was still pending (it had been dismissed, then an appeal was accepted and the case sent back for fresh decision). They argued he was simply trying to avoid repaying his loans by pressuring the bank through this petition.

The High Court agreed with the respondents. It held that courts cannot order registration of a criminal case or inquiry under their constitutional writ jurisdiction when other adequate legal remedies exist, and especially not when the same matter is already pending (sub-judice) before another court. Since the underlying dispute was still before the Banking Court, the petition was dismissed as not maintainable.

This ruling reinforces the principle that writ petitions are a last resort, not a shortcut when other legal avenues are open or already in use.

title: Use of Weopons and Firearms on Marriages
explainer:
This case concerns a police raid on a private wedding function in Hassan Abdal, Attock district. The SHO led 30 police officials into the house of the petitioner, Iftikhar Ahmad, acting on a tip that dancing girls were performing inside during a marriage ceremony. The police arrested the two dancers and 23 male guests, registering a criminal case under Section 294 PPC (obscene acts in public) read with abetment provisions, and also invoking marriage-function laws that restrict ostentatious wedding displays.

The Lahore High Court, Rawalpindi Bench, quashed the FIR and declared the arrests and entire police action illegal. The court held that the marriage-function laws only prohibit things like fireworks, illumination of public areas, and excessive meals, not private dancing inside a home. It also ruled that Section 294 PPC applies only to obscene acts committed in or near a public place, and since the event occurred inside a private, walled house, the law did not apply. The court further noted the SHO's allegations were vague, with no actual evidence of obscenity presented.

Importantly, the judgment emphasized that privacy of the home is a fundamental right under Article 14 of the Constitution and under Islamic law, and criticized the police for intruding into private family life without legal justification, calling such conduct an abuse of authority deserving condemnation.

title: Rule of consistency is not applicable in all criminal cases
explainer:
This case involved a bail application by Yousaf Khan, who was accused in a shooting that killed a police constable and injured another during a police patrol in Lakki Marwat in June 2010. According to the FIR, police chasing a suspicious vehicle were ambushed by armed men who opened fire, killing one constable and wounding another, before the attackers fled with police weapons.

Yousaf Khan sought bail, arguing that a co-accused, Niaz Ali, had already been granted bail, so he deserved the same treatment under the principle of consistency. He also argued he wasn't properly identified since his father's name was missing from the FIR, and that a witness statement conflicted with the FIR account.

The Peshawar High Court rejected these arguments. It found that the FIR named two groups of accused: five identified persons and five unknown persons. The co-accused who got bail belonged to the unknown group, while Yousaf Khan was specifically named and directly charged with firing the fatal shots. Since his situation was factually different, the rule of consistency did not apply to him.

The court also noted the FIR was filed within thirty minutes of the incident, eyewitness evidence linked him to the crime, and he had remained a fugitive without adequately explaining his absence. Based on these findings, the court dismissed his bail petition, ruling him ineligible for release pending trial.

This case matters because it clarifies that bail granted to one co-accused doesn't automatically entitle others to bail when their roles and evidence differ significantly.

title: Presence of prosecution witnesses is important in criminal case
explainer:
This case from the Federal Shariat Court involved a man, Saeed Ullah, who was convicted of murder and sodomy of a six-year-old boy, the son of his landlord. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and ordered to pay compensation. Two co-accused, his wife and minor son, had been acquitted by the trial court. Multiple appeals arose: Saeed Ullah appealed his conviction, the complainant appealed against the acquittals of the other two accused, and the state sought enhancement of Saeed Ullah's sentence to death.

The Federal Shariat Court examined the evidence closely and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. The complainant's initial report and the police inquest report did not mention key witnesses who later claimed to have seen the accused near the scene, raising suspicion about their credibility. The recovery of the child's body was not properly proven, and a key witness who claimed to have seen the accused carrying a sack was found to be a "chance witness" whose presence at the scene was doubtful. The court noted the incident was unseen by anyone, and there was no solid evidence linking Saeed Ullah to the crime beyond unreliable testimony.

The court ruled that the prosecution had failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and acquitted Saeed Ullah. This case highlights the importance of reliable witness testimony, proper documentation like inquest reports, and the principle that convictions cannot rest on suspicion or weak evidence.

title: New Plea in Constitutional Petition is not permitted
explainer:
This case involved a husband and wife whose marriage was performed in 1990. The wife filed a family court suit seeking recovery of her dower (29 tola of gold ornaments), maintenance allowance, recovery of dowry articles, and dissolution of marriage, claiming her husband had divorced her in April 2003 and turned her out of the house. The husband denied pronouncing divorce. The trial court ruled in the wife's favor, granting the dower, maintenance, dowry articles, and dissolution of marriage, relying on the wife's own statement that she had been divorced. The appellate court upheld most of this but modified the list of dowry articles she was entitled to recover.

The husband then challenged this in the Peshawar High Court, arguing for the first time that the wife's claim for dower was filed beyond the three-year limitation period, and also asking that the dissolution be treated as Khula (so he wouldn't have to pay dower) rather than divorce.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It held that a party cannot raise a brand-new legal plea, like limitation, for the first time in a constitutional petition if it was never raised in the pleadings, never made an issue at trial, and never argued in the lower courts or the appeal. The court also noted that even in Khula cases, the law does not require a wife to return the entire dower received. This case matters because it reinforces the principle that courts will only consider issues that were properly raised and contested at earlier stages, preventing parties from introducing surprise arguments later.

title: Jurisdiction lackness in a family suit can be addressed at initial stages
explainer:
This case is about a husband, Muhammad Naeem, challenging a family court decision that dissolved his marriage to Robina Kausar on the basis of khula (a wife-initiated divorce). The wife had sued for dissolution of marriage, dower, maintenance for herself and her minor daughter, and dowry articles. The family court granted the divorce, denied her dower claim, awarded maintenance for her and the child, and ordered return of dowry articles. The husband challenged the divorce decree in the Lahore High Court, arguing the court lacked territorial jurisdiction and that since the wife's jewelry (Haq Mehr) hadn't been returned to him, the divorce decree was unlawful.

The High Court rejected both arguments. First, it held that jurisdictional objections must be raised at the earliest possible stage of a case, and since the husband had actually admitted in his written statement that the court had proper territorial jurisdiction, he could not raise the objection later. Second, the court explained that under amended family law provisions, return of dower to the husband is only required when a divorce is granted immediately after failed reconciliation attempts. Since this case went through full evidence and trial rather than an immediate decree, the wife was not obligated to return her gold jewelry. The petition was dismissed, upholding the divorce.

This case matters because it clarifies two important procedural rules: jurisdiction objections cannot be raised belatedly, and the law aims to protect wives from prolonged litigation in divorce cases.

title: Entitlement of Maintenance of Wife and Child
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over maintenance after a marriage broke down. The wife and her minor child had filed a suit seeking monthly maintenance, delivery/medical expenses, and recovery of dowry articles. The Family Court awarded the wife maintenance only for her iddat period (a short post-divorce waiting period), granted the child monthly maintenance of Rs. 1200 until he reached adulthood, allowed Rs. 20,000 for delivery expenses and Rs. 4500 for the child's treatment, and ordered return of dowry articles (excluding gold ornaments) or their cash value.

Both the husband and wife appealed. The appellate court increased the child's maintenance to Rs. 3000 per month and raised the value of the dowry articles slightly. The husband then challenged these decisions before the Lahore High Court, arguing the amounts were excessive.

The High Court dismissed his petition, upholding both lower court rulings. It reasoned that Rs. 3000 per month was barely adequate given inflation and the real costs of raising a school-going child. On the delivery expenses, the court clarified an important point: such expenses are not limited to hospital birth costs but also cover preparing for the baby's needs afterward, including clothes, bottles, formula, and bedding. The court emphasized that a father, as provider, is responsible for these basic necessities before and separately from ongoing maintenance payments. This judgment reinforces fathers' financial responsibilities toward children and clarifies what "delivery expenses" legally include.

title: Concept of gift in Shia Law
explainer:
This case was about a dispute over agricultural land and a house in Multan, inherited from Syed Hussain Ahmad Shah, a Shia Muslim. His daughter filed a lawsuit claiming she was entitled to a share of the property, arguing that an earlier gift made by her father to his daughter-in-law in 1945 was conditional and only transferred usage rights, not full ownership, meaning the core property should eventually have passed to his legal heirs, including her.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court rejected her claim, and she challenged this before the Lahore High Court.

The High Court examined the original 1945 gift documents along with a later 1947 settlement deed in which the father himself confirmed that he had made a complete and unconditional gift. The court held that under Islamic law, once a gift of property is validly made and its corpus (the actual ownership) is transferred, any conditions attempting to control what happens after the recipient's death are void. The father could not create a new line of inheritance outside recognized legal or Islamic rules. Since the recipient had already dealt with the property for years without objection from any family member, the gift was valid and complete.

The court ruled there were no legal grounds to interfere with the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the revision petition, upholding the earlier rulings.
