title: A civil suit should have whole claim at once
explainer:
This case was about whether the Sindh High Court had the authority to hear a lawsuit involving land that was physically located outside Karachi. A man whose shops and school building in Naushahro Feroze district were allegedly bulldozed by local officials and political opponents sued in the Sindh High Court, seeking declarations that the demolition was illegal, along with damages for the destroyed property, loss of reputation, and recovery of items taken from the site.

The Court examined the rules governing where civil suits can be filed. It explained that the High Court's ordinary original civil jurisdiction is limited to the district of Karachi only, and does not automatically extend across the whole province of Sindh, even though certain sections of the Civil Procedure Code dealing with territorial jurisdiction don't technically apply to the High Court's original side. Since the disputed property was located in Naushahro Feroze, not Karachi, and the core relief sought concerned rights over that immovable property, the suit should have been filed in the court having jurisdiction over Naushahro Feroze.

The Court also emphasized that a plaintiff must bring all claims arising from one cause of action in a single suit rather than splitting them up, and that claims for damages are not independent of claims about the property itself.

This matters because it clarifies that filing a case in the wrong court makes the entire proceeding legally defective, and such cases must be returned for filing in the proper court rather than decided on their merits.

title: All Pakistan Newspaper Society Versus Federation of Pakistan
explainer:
This case concerns a challenge by the All Pakistan Newspapers Society against the Newspaper Employees (Conditions of Service) Act, 1973, which governs wages and working conditions for both working journalists and other newspaper employees. The petitioners argued the law was unconstitutional on several grounds: that treating working journalists and non-journalist newspaper staff under one law violated equal treatment guarantees under Article 25, that singling out the newspaper industry (as opposed to electronic media) was discriminatory, and that the law's Wage Board, which fixes wages, violated due process under Article 10-A since no right of appeal existed against its decisions.

The Supreme Court rejected these challenges. It held that courts should generally presume laws are constitutional unless clearly proven otherwise, and that classifying newspaper employees together was reasonable since journalists and other staff work collaboratively toward common goals, justifying similar treatment. The Court also found newspapers sufficiently distinct from other media to justify separate regulation. On the appeal issue, the Court explained that the Wage Board performs a legislative/executive function (setting general wage rules), not a judicial one resolving disputes between parties, so the absence of a right of appeal doesn't violate due process. However, Board decisions could still be challenged in court if shown to be arbitrary or perverse.

This judgment matters because it upholds protections for journalists' fair wages while clarifying when due process requires a right of appeal, distinguishing between law-making bodies and courts deciding individual disputes.

title: Muhammad Saleem V. Investigation Officer Levies Station Hanna, Quetta,
explainer:
This case arose from a murder FIR lodged by Muhammad Saleem after his brother's body was found in the mountains in Balochistan. After police completed their investigation, a challan (formal charge sheet) was submitted to the trial court, and the accused began facing trial, though one accused remained absconding. The complainant then asked the trial court to transfer the investigation to the Balochistan Crimes Branch, arguing the original investigating officer wasn't making serious efforts to arrest the fugitive accused. The Additional Sessions Judge rejected this request, and the complainant challenged that rejection before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower court's decision and dismissed the petition. It held that once a challan has been submitted and the court has taken cognizance of the case, the special provisions allowing citizens to seek police accountability (Sections 22-A and 22-B of the Criminal Procedure Code) can no longer be used to interfere with ongoing judicial proceedings. The court noted that the petitioner had not shown any bad faith by the investigating officer or any connection between the officer and the absconding accused. It also observed that the trial court had already issued arrest warrants and initiated proceedings to secure the fugitive's arrest.

This judgment clarifies the limited scope of the "Justice of Peace" powers under the law, confirming they are meant to address police misconduct before trial begins, not to second-guess courts once a case is already under judicial consideration.

title: Imran Rahim Durrani V. Province of Balochistan through Chief Secretary Civil Secretariate, Quetta and 8 others ,
explainer:
This case involved employees of the Irrigation Department in Balochistan who filed a petition asking the High Court to stop the Public Health Engineering (PHE) Department from constructing dams. The petitioners argued that under the Government of Balochistan Rules of Business, 2012, building dams was exclusively the job of the Irrigation Department, and that assigning dam projects to PHE in the Public Sector Development Program (PSDP) was illegal and encroached on their department's mandate. They pointed to the Irrigation Department's past experience building dams and argued PHE lacked the expertise.

The court dismissed the petition without even examining the merits of the dispute. It held that the petitioners, as ordinary employees, did not have the legal standing ("locus standi") to challenge this government decision. To file such a constitutional petition, a person must show that their own legal or fundamental rights were violated, making them an "aggrieved person." The court noted that the PSDP assignment had already been approved by the Cabinet and the Provincial Assembly, and importantly, the Secretary of the Irrigation Department itself had not objected to the decision. Since the petitioners were not personally affected and had no authority to question internal government business allocation decisions, their petition failed on this threshold issue of maintainability. title: Mst. Khair Bibi and 4 others V. Ghulam Sarwar and 17 others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running land dispute. In 1969, the appellants' predecessor allowed another family to irrigate his land under a share-cropping arrangement. The appellants claimed that, taking advantage of their illiterate predecessor, the other side fraudulently got the land mutated into their name and later sold it in 1997, with revenue officials colluding in the fraud. After the original owner died in 2012, his heirs discovered the mutation and sale deed, and filed a suit seeking a declaration, correction of land records, cancellation of the sale deed, and a permanent injunction.

The trial court dismissed the suit as time-barred. The appellants then filed an appeal in the wrong court (the District Court), which returned it for lack of jurisdiction. After their review petition was also dismissed, they eventually approached the High Court, converting their revision petition into an appeal.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the suit itself was filed decades late, and no satisfactory explanation was given for the enormous delay—both in filing the original suit (more than 40 years after the transaction) and in pursuing appeals afterward. The court emphasized that litigants must explain every day of delay, that courts must examine limitation issues even if not raised by parties, and that mistakenly approaching the wrong forum does not automatically excuse delay unless done diligently and in good faith. The ruling reinforces strict adherence to limitation laws in property disputes.

title: Chairman, NAB through Prosecutor General Accountability NAB V. Sarfaraz Hussain Mughal and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by Pakistan's National Accountability Bureau (NAB) against the acquittal of three men accused of corruption related to government wheat purchases and the sale of gunny sacks (Bardana) in Balochistan. The accused included an Assistant in the S&GAD Department and a Deputy Director of the Food Department, who were alleged to have taken illegal commissions and bribes from wheat farmers, with the money allegedly funneled through a bank account.

After a trial, the Accountability Court in Quetta had acquitted all three accused, finding the prosecution's evidence insufficient. Key witnesses who had filed the original complaint backed away from their allegations in court, with one stating he never made any statement to NAB and had no knowledge of the accused. No witnesses could prove that bribes were actually paid, and one accused provided documentary evidence showing the money in his account came from a legitimate property sale.

NAB appealed this acquittal, but the Balochistan High Court upheld the trial court's decision and dismissed the appeal. The High Court reasoned that an acquittal creates a strong presumption of innocence that can only be overturned with compelling evidence, and that courts should not interfere with a trial court's careful evaluation of evidence simply because another judge might interpret it differently.

This case matters because it illustrates the high legal threshold required to overturn an acquittal and underscores that accountability prosecutions must be backed by solid, consistent evidence rather than complaints that fall apart under scrutiny.

title: Baboo V. The State,
explainer:

Footprints near the body led towards the house of the applicant, Baboo, who was then charged with murder along with others under the Pakistan Penal Code. There was a history of tension between the two, as the deceased had earlier filed a complaint against Baboo before a magistrate.

Baboo sought bail, arguing there were no eyewitnesses, nothing was recovered from him, and the case against him was weak and based on suspicion rather than solid evidence. The Balochistan High Court agreed. It noted the crime occurred at night with no witnesses, that fingerprints on the recovered weapons (iron rods and sticks) were never examined despite being available, and that there was a contradiction between the medical evidence (showing sharp-weapon injuries) and the weapons actually recovered (blunt objects). The court also held that an alleged confession made to police was not legally admissible since no new evidence was discovered because of it.

Given these weaknesses, the court ruled the case needed further inquiry and granted bail, emphasizing the legal principle that even courts hearing ongoing trials can grant bail if the accused qualifies, and that wrongly detaining an innocent person can never truly be undone.

title: Abdullah Khan V. Ghulam Jan and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a father, Abdullah Khan, whose son Sajid Ali was found murdered in Quetta in 2014. He accused several relatives, with whom his family had a prior dispute over relationships, of killing his son. After years of investigation, these accused persons were arrested in May 2019 and granted bail by the trial court. The father then approached the Balochistan High Court asking for that bail to be cancelled.

The High Court refused to cancel the bail. It noted that no one had actually witnessed the murder, the accused were implicated purely on suspicion and past enmity, and no weapon or other evidence had been recovered from them. On a preliminary assessment, the case appeared to need further inquiry, meaning the evidence wasn't strong enough to clearly connect the accused to the crime. The court also held that proving motive is the prosecution's job, not something the accused must disprove, and that simply having evaded arrest for years doesn't by itself prove guilt.

The judgment is useful because it lays out the specific, limited grounds on which bail can be cancelled, such as misuse of bail, threatening witnesses, or an arbitrary bail order, and clarifies that these grounds are different and more demanding than the grounds needed to deny bail in the first place. Since none of those grounds were shown here, the request to cancel bail was dismissed.

title: Rasool Bakhsh V. The State,
explainer:
Rasool Bakhsh was a post office employee accused of embezzling government funds. The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) filed a reference against him, and when he could not be found to receive court notices, the trial court declared him a proclaimed offender and convicted him in his absence under Section 31-A of the National Accountability Ordinance, which punishes absconding to avoid legal proceedings.

Years later, after being arrested, Bakhsh challenged this conviction before the Balochistan High Court, arguing he was never properly served notice and had no real chance to defend himself.

The High Court agreed with him. It found that the trial court had not followed the proper legal procedure for declaring someone a proclaimed offender: warrants were not reissued for new dates after failing, they were not affixed at his residence, and no report was obtained from police confirming genuine service attempts. The prosecution also never proved the key requirement of Section 31-A, that the accused deliberately and intentionally avoided being served in order to escape trial.

The court also ruled that since Bakhsh was convicted without his knowledge, the time limit for appealing only began once he actually learned of his conviction, not from the date of the original order. This meant his appeal, filed after his arrest, was not too late.

The High Court set aside his conviction and sentence, holding that mere failed attempts to serve notice are not sufficient grounds to convict someone in absentia. This case underscores that even in accountability cases, basic fair-trial safeguards must be strictly followed.

title: Muhammad Essa Rooshan V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns a petition to quash a criminal case (FIR) registered against Muhammad Essa Rooshan at Pishin police station. The FIR accused him of making speeches during a political protest that allegedly used inappropriate language against state institutions and security agencies, provoking public sentiment against the state. He was charged under several sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with sedition-type offences, including promoting hatred between groups and condemning the state, along with a provincial sound-system regulation law.

The Balochistan High Court quashed the FIR. The key reason was procedural: under section 196 of the Criminal Procedure Code, courts cannot take cognizance of offences like these unless a formal complaint is filed with the authorization of the Federal or Provincial Government, or an officer specifically empowered to do so. In this case, the FIR was simply lodged by a police sub-inspector on his own initiative, without any such government sanction. The court held this requirement is mandatory, not optional, and its violation made the entire investigation and proceedings legally invalid.

This matters because it reinforces that certain serious offences against the state cannot be prosecuted through ordinary police action alone—government oversight is required to prevent misuse of these laws, particularly against political speech and protest. The judgment highlights the court's role in using its inherent powers sparingly, but decisively, to stop abuse of legal process when mandatory procedures are ignored.

title: Muhammad Hussain and 17 others V. Abdul Hameed and 4 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a civil suit that had been dismissed by a trial court for "non-prosecution" after the plaintiffs failed to appear on a hearing date. The twist was that the date in question had not been fixed by the judge himself, but by the court reader (clerk), after the judge was on leave. The plaintiffs' later attempts to have the suit restored were also rejected by the trial court and the appellate court, leading them to approach the High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners on several grounds. First, it held that a date adjourned merely by a court reader's note, rather than by the presiding judge, does not count as a proper "date of hearing" under the law, making the dismissal order invalid from the start. Second, since the case had already finished trial and was fixed only for final arguments, the correct legal procedure (under Order XVII, Rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code) required the court to either decide the case on available evidence or reschedule arguments—not dismiss it outright. Third, the restoration application was filed within the proper three-year limitation period, so it wasn't time-barred.

The Court set aside the lower courts' orders, restored the suit, and sent it back for a fresh decision on merits. The judgment is significant because it protects litigants from losing years of litigation effort due to procedural technicalities and clerical errors rather than substantive issues.

The complainant alleged that during an engagement ceremony, the accused abused and threatened his brother, then opened fire, injuring the brother and two other relatives. An FIR was registered, but after trial, the accused was acquitted, prompting the complainant to appeal.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the acquittal. It found serious inconsistencies in the prosecution's evidence: witnesses who were closely related to the complainant gave accounts that conflicted with those of independent, impartial witnesses, and the injuries described did not match the medical evidence, such as missing blackening or exit wounds expected from close-range firing. The court also noted that the accused had separately filed his own FIR about the same incident, suggesting it was actually a chaotic mutual brawl rather than a one-sided attack, making it unsafe to rely on the complainant's version.

Importantly, the court also ruled that the complainant himself was not injured in the incident, so under the law only an injured, aggrieved person could file an appeal against acquittal—not the complainant. Since the actually injured relatives did not appeal, the complainant's appeal was deemed legally incompetent.

The case highlights core criminal law principles: the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, acquitted persons enjoy a double presumption of innocence, and only genuinely aggrieved parties can challenge an acquittal.

title: Muhammad Ayub and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved seven appeals arising from a corruption scandal in Balochistan's education department. Government officials, including the District Education Officer and Deputy District Education Officer of Pishin, were accused of making 39 fake teacher appointments and misappropriating government funds. They were charged with criminal breach of trust, cheating, forgery, and misconduct under the Pakistan Penal Code and the Prevention of Corruption Act. On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found a serious procedural flaw: when the trial court questioned the accused under Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code (which requires courts to give accused persons a chance to explain evidence against them), it failed to properly put all the incriminating evidence to them. Important pieces of evidence, such as inquiry reports, statements of absconding co-accused, and specimen signatures, were relied upon by the trial court for conviction without ever being specifically put to the accused for their response.

The High Court held this was mandatory, not optional, under the law, and that evidence not put to the accused in this manner cannot be used to convict them. Because this requirement was violated, the court set aside the convictions and sent the case back to the trial court to properly re-record the accused's statements. This case highlights the importance of fair procedure and an accused person's right to respond to evidence before being convicted.

title: Kaazim Hussain V. The state,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Kaazim Hussain who was arrested in Balochistan after police allegedly found 1600 grams of charas (hashish) and 200 grams of ice (crystal meth) in his possession during a motorcycle check. He was charged under Section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and after his bail application was rejected by the trial court, he approached the Balochistan High Court seeking post-arrest bail.

His lawyer argued that he was innocent and falsely implicated, and pointed out that no independent or private witnesses were present during the recovery, only police officials.

The High Court rejected this argument and refused bail. It held that the law governing narcotics cases (Section 25 of the CNS Act) specifically excludes the usual requirement under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code to involve independent witnesses during searches. The court also noted that ordinary citizens are often reluctant to get involved as witnesses in criminal cases, so their absence doesn't automatically make the prosecution's case weak. Police witnesses, the court said, are presumed credible unless shown to be lying or acting with malicious intent.

Given the large quantity of narcotics recovered and the serious, "heinous" nature of drug offences, the court ruled that the accused did not qualify for bail. This judgment reinforces that in narcotics cases, courts apply a stricter standard before granting bail, and police testimony alone can be sufficient to sustain a case at this stage.

title: Kamaluddin and 13 others V. Abdullah and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over inherited land in Quetta. The respondent (Abdullah) claimed he owned certain properties inherited from his ancestors, but the land had never been formally partitioned among the co-sharers. He argued that while he was a minor, relatives managed the property, and some of it was later sold off by other family members without giving him his rightful share. He sued in civil court for a declaration of ownership, cancellation of mutation entries, possession, and a permanent injunction. The trial court ruled in his favor, and the other relatives appealed.

The main legal question was whether the civil court even had the authority to hear this case, given a provision in the Balochistan Land Revenue Act that generally bars civil courts from deciding partition disputes, leaving such matters to revenue authorities instead.

The High Court held that this bar does not apply when a genuine question of ownership (title) is involved, as opposed to merely how to divide an already-agreed share. Since the dispute here was fundamentally about who owned the property, not just how to split it, the civil court had proper jurisdiction. The court also found that a private partition among family members could itself create ownership rights. Finding no fault in the trial court's decision, the High Court dismissed the appeal, affirming that the respondent was indeed the owner of the disputed land. This ruling clarifies when civil courts, rather than revenue officials, can resolve property disputes rooted in inheritance.

title: Chairman, NAB through Prosecutor General V. Munawar Masih and another,
explainer:
This case involved Munawar Masih, a former postmaster accused of misappropriating over Rs. 14 lakh in money order funds. After years as a fugitive, he was eventually brought to trial before the Accountability Court in Quetta under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999. During trial, he applied for acquittal under Section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, arguing he had repaid the misappropriated amount. The trial court, however, treated this application as a plea bargain request and approved it, releasing him on that basis.

The Chairman of NAB challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing the trial court had acted improperly. The High Court agreed. It explained that under Section 25(b) of the NAB Ordinance, only the Chairman of NAB has the power to negotiate and approve a plea bargain, including deciding how much money the accused must return. Courts can only approve or reject a plea bargain already arranged by NAB, not create one on their own. Since the accused never applied for a plea bargain through NAB, and the Chairman NAB never approved any deal, the trial court had no authority to invent one and fix the liability itself.

The High Court set aside the trial court's order and sent the case back to the stage before the irregular conversion occurred.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that procedures laid down by law must be strictly followed, and reaffirms that only NAB's Chairman—not courts—can authorize plea bargains in corruption cases, preserving the intended checks against misuse of this process.

title: Haji Ashraf and 2 others V. Khan Muhammad and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute between neighbours or business parties that turned into a criminal complaint. Khan Muhammad claimed he had leased a property for a car-parking business, and alleged that the petitioners, along with 20 to 22 armed men, forcibly entered the premises, broke locks, and stole valuable items. He asked the Additional Sessions Judge, acting as Justice of Peace, to order police to register a criminal case (FIR) against the petitioners. The Justice of Peace granted this request, and the accused challenged that order before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court set aside the order directing FIR registration. It found the complaint doubtful because it did not mention a date for the alleged incident or name any witnesses. The police report itself confirmed that the dispute was essentially civil, over property, and that a civil suit was already pending between the parties. The court also noted that the petitioners were not given a chance to be heard before the order was passed, and found signs that the complaint may have been filed in bad faith to pressure the other side in the ongoing civil litigation.

The judgment clarifies that a Justice of Peace must not act as a rubber stamp when deciding whether to order registration of an FIR. They must independently verify that there is genuine supporting material, especially in cases that appear to stem from civil disputes, and should ideally hear the accused unless there's urgency or risk of evidence being destroyed. This protects people from criminal cases being misused as tools in civil disputes.

title: The State through Regional Director Anti-Narcotic Force Balochistan V. Abdul Wahab and 11 others,
explainer:
This case is about a government appeal challenging a trial court's refusal to let prosecutors reopen an already-completed narcotics trial to introduce new documents. The Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF) had filed cases against several accused persons, and by the time the trial reached its final stage, all prosecution evidence had been presented and the accused had given their statements. At that point, prosecutors tried to recall the investigating officer to submit detailed laboratory analysis reports from the Federal Government Analyst, reports that had been prepared years after charges were framed and were never shown to the accused earlier. The trial court rejected this request, and the state appealed.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the trial court's decision and dismissed the appeal. It explained that while Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code allows courts to summon or recall witnesses, this power exists to help the court discover truth, not to let the prosecution fix gaps or weaknesses in its own case after the fact. The court also stressed that accused persons must be given all evidence and documents against them before trial, so they can properly defend themselves; introducing new material at a late stage violates fair trial principles.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that prosecutors cannot use procedural tools to patch up an incomplete case late in proceedings, protecting the fairness and integrity of criminal trials, especially in serious narcotics cases.

title: Mirwise V. Mohib-Ur-Rehman, SI/SHO Police Station Saddar, Loralai and another,
explainer:
This case is about how courts should determine whether a criminal accused is a juvenile or an adult when the evidence on his age conflicts. The petitioner, Mirwise, was facing charges and claimed to be a minor at the time of the alleged offence, relying on his birth certificate and school leaving certificate, which showed his date of birth as 2000, making him under 18. However, NADRA family tree records showed a different date of birth, in 1998, suggesting he was already an adult. The trial court rejected his request to transfer the case to a juvenile court and also refused his later application to have his age determined through a medical board, relying instead on the NADRA record. This refusal was upheld by the Sessions Court on appeal.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that when there is a genuine conflict between documents about a person's age, NADRA records alone are not conclusive proof, since they are based on information supplied by individuals rather than independent verification. The court explained that under the Juvenile Justice System Act, 2018, whenever a real question arises about an accused's age, the trial court must conduct a proper inquiry, which should include examining documents, witness statements, and especially medical evidence such as an ossification test, since medical opinion is preferred when documents conflict.

The court therefore set aside the lower courts' orders and sent the case back to the trial court, directing it to conduct this inquiry and determine the petitioner's correct age through a medical board. This decision matters because it protects the rights of young accused persons to be properly treated as juveniles when their age is genuinely in dispute.

title: Razia Bibi V. Muhammad Younas Bhatti and 4 others,
explainer:
This case was about whether a woman involved in a civil lawsuit could avoid testifying in court in person and instead have her statement recorded through a local commissioner, because she claimed to be a pardanasheen (veil-observing) woman who should not appear in public.

The underlying dispute was a suit for declaration, where a woman was seeking to be legally recognized as the daughter of a certain man. The petitioner, one of the defendants in that suit, applied to have her statement recorded privately through a local commission rather than appearing before the trial court, citing purdah and her husband's illness. Both the trial court and the district court (in revision) rejected her request, and she challenged these rejections before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed her petition. It explained that simply claiming to be a pardanasheen lady is not enough; this status must be proven with evidence. The court noted that the petitioner had already executed a power of attorney and filed legal documents through processes that did not appear to have happened at her residence, undermining her claim. The court also stressed that judges cannot hand over decisions on important factual issues to a local commissioner when direct evidence before the court is required.

This case matters because it clarifies that exemptions for pardanasheen women from appearing in court are not automatic and must be backed by proof, balancing tradition with fair trial requirements.

title: Jalat Khan alias Jalo V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Jalat Khan, who was convicted and sentenced for the murder of the complainant's brother, allegedly shot while the complainant's cousin survived the attack. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court against his conviction and death sentence, which the trial court had referred for confirmation.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the accused, finding the prosecution's case riddled with doubt. The three eyewitnesses were all close relatives of the deceased, yet behaved unnaturally: they did not rush the victim to hospital, did not accompany the body, did not raise an alarm, and were not even named in the initial police report. There was an unexplained two-and-a-half hour delay in filing the FIR, and witness statements were recorded late without justification. Medical evidence describing a "hard and blunt" weapon contradicted the prosecution's firearm theory. The recovered rifle was found in a stranger's house with no connection to the accused, and crucially, the weapon and bullet casings were not sent to the forensic laboratory until eight months after recovery, undermining the reliability of the forensic report. Two key witnesses who could have supported the prosecution's version were never produced in court.

The court held that when related witnesses' testimony is not corroborated by surrounding circumstances or natural conduct, it can be discarded. Given these cumulative doubts, the accused was given the benefit of the doubt and acquitted, illustrating how procedural delays and inconsistencies can defeat even serious criminal charges.

title: Sanaullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a death sentence for murder. The appellant, Sanaullah, had been convicted by a trial court of qatl-i-amd (murder) under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, based largely on allegations that he kidnapped the deceased for ransom, was last seen with him, and later confessed.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the accused. First, it found that the accused was actually a juvenile (around 17 years old) at the time, as confirmed by a medical board. Under the Juvenile Justice System Act, 2018, juveniles cannot be sentenced to death or ordinary imprisonment with adults, so the trial court's death sentence was unlawful on this ground alone.

Separately, the court found the evidence itself unreliable. The "last seen" testimony was uncorroborated and appeared to be an afterthought, since the witness delayed reporting it for days. The alleged ransom call was never substantiated with phone records, and the people allegedly present when the call was received never reported it either. There was also an unexplained two-day delay in filing the police report (FIR), further undermining the prosecution's case.

This judgment matters because it reinforces two important principles: children must be tried and sentenced under special juvenile protections, not ordinary criminal law, and convictions—especially for capital offences—cannot rest on weak, uncorroborated, or suspicious evidence. The benefit of the doubt must go to the accused when the prosecution's case is unconvincing.

title: Pure Mineral (PVT.) Limited through duly Authorized Attorney V. Province Of Balochistan through Secretary, Mines and Mineral Development Department, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a mining company, Pure Mineral (Pvt.) Limited, which was granted an exploration license in 2011 by Balochistan's Mines and Minerals Department to explore copper, gold, and other minerals in an area of Chaghi district. Just weeks later, the government withdrew the allotment letter, saying it had been issued by mistake. The area was later formally acquired for the Balochistan Copper-Gold Project through an official notification in December 2012. The company challenged this acquisition notification in court, arguing it was illegal and issued without proper authority.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the company had never actually been given possession of the land or a prospecting license, and its original three-year license period had already expired without the company applying for an extension. The court held that extending or refusing a license is entirely the government's discretion, so the company had no vested right to the area. Separately, the court noted the company waited more than five years to challenge the 2012 notification, far beyond the normal three-month window for such challenges, and offered no explanation for the delay.

The judgment matters because it reinforces that mining licenses don't create permanent rights unless formalized through possession and proper legal steps, and that people challenging government decisions in court must act promptly or explain serious delays, or risk losing their case regardless of its merits.

title: Ghungar Khan V. The State ,
explainer:
This case involves an appeal against a murder conviction. Ghungar Khan and co-accused were accused of killing the complainant's brothers and nephew by stoning them after forcibly catching them, with charges including murder, rioting, and terrorism offences. The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the appellant.

The court found multiple serious problems with the prosecution's case. First, there was an unexplained delay of over a month in filing the police report, and the complainant's explanation for this delay was found implausible. Second, the three eyewitnesses, all close relatives of the deceased, behaved unnaturally—they claimed to have witnessed the killings but suffered no injuries themselves, made no attempt to intervene or rescue the victims, and even left the bodies at the scene for over a month before they were recovered. Third, the prosecution failed to produce two other named witnesses mentioned in the complainant's initial statement, which the court said suggested their testimony would have contradicted the official story. Finally, there was a direct contradiction between the medical evidence, which showed the victims died from firearm injuries, and the original police report, which only mentioned stoning—with witnesses later dishonestly changing their statements at trial to match the medical findings.

Because of these doubts and contradictions, the court held the witnesses were unreliable and acquitted the appellant, highlighting how delayed reporting, implausible witness conduct, withheld witnesses, and shifting testimony can undermine a criminal case.

title: Muhammad Khan Kurd V. Arbab Muhammad Hashim,
explainer:
This case involved a man who sued for 3 crore rupees in damages, claiming he had been maliciously prosecuted. Years earlier, the respondent had an FIR registered against the appellant and others for allegedly occupying property through fraud, breaking walls, and illegal possession. The criminal court framed charges, but after only two witnesses were examined, the appellant was discharged under section 249-A Cr.P.C. He then filed a civil suit claiming this prosecution was malicious and damaged his reputation. The trial court rejected his plaint, and he appealed.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the dismissal. It explained that to win a malicious prosecution case, a plaintiff must prove the prosecution was based on malice and lacked any reasonable or probable cause, and that it ended in his favor. Here, a related civil property dispute was already pending between the parties, showing there was a genuine basis for the complaint. The court also noted an important legal distinction: the appellant was "discharged," not "acquitted" on merits -- his case ended on a technical ground, not because he was found innocent. Additionally, the suit was filed four years after the criminal case ended, far beyond the one-year limitation period for such claims under the Limitation Act. Since the suit was both legally unfounded and time-barred, the appeal was dismissed, confirming the original judgment.

title: Sadiq V. The State through Prosecutor General, Quetta,
explainer:
This case involved an appellant named Sadiq who was tried alongside several co-accused for a violent incident in Chaman in 2008, arising from a dispute over an earlier theft. The original complaint alleged qatl-i-amd (murder), attempted murder, and armed rioting, with one person dying after being shot. During the trial, Sadiq remained absconding and was declared a proclaimed offender, while his co-accused stood trial and were ultimately acquitted by the Anti-Terrorism Court.

Despite acquitting the other accused, the trial court separately convicted Sadiq and sentenced him to ten years' imprisonment under Section 21-L of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, a provision that punishes people who abscond to avoid arrest or court proceedings.

The Balochistan High Court found this conviction unlawful. It noted that Sadiq had never actually been charged under Section 21-L, no evidence had been recorded to prove the specific ingredients of that offence, and the trial court had not even framed a proper legal question about it in its judgment. There was also no finding that his absconding was deliberate or that he was genuinely evading justice. Because the conviction was based on a flawed, informal process rather than a proper trial, the High Court set it aside and acquitted Sadiq.

The case matters because it reinforces that even absconding accused persons cannot be convicted through shortcuts—formal charges, evidence, and proper legal reasoning are required before punishing someone under anti-terrorism absconder provisions.

title: Ameer Bakhsh V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a pre-arrest bail application filed by Ameer Bakhsh, who was accused of instigating the murder of a man named Liaqat Khan in a case registered in Dera Murad Jamali, Balochistan. The actual shooting was allegedly carried out by other co-accused who fired upon the deceased, while Ameer Bakhsh was said to have instigated them to commit the murder, though he was not present at the scene.

The Balochistan High Court granted him pre-arrest bail, confirming the earlier ad-interim bail he had already been given. The court reasoned that there was no evidence on record showing the co-accused had conspired with or acted on the instigation of Ameer Bakhsh, and since he was absent from the spot, the case against him required further inquiry rather than immediate arrest. The court also rejected the state's objection that he should have approached the trial court first, noting that tribal enmity between the parties and a pending application to transfer the case to another district justified his direct approach to the High Court.

The judgment reaffirms important bail principles: pre-arrest bail exists to protect innocent people from harassment and humiliation by police, it must be exercised judiciously based on case-specific facts, and an accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty with a right to defend himself at trial. This case illustrates how courts assess abetment allegations distinctly from direct involvement in a crime.

title: Muhammad Nadeem and others V. Anjuman-E-Nasir-Ul-Aza through General Secretary,
explainer:

The landlord had filed an eviction petition seeking to reclaim three shops, stating it wanted to demolish walls and incorporate the shops into the Imam Bargah complex for use as a library, storage, and staff residences. The tenants resisted, arguing that an earlier eviction petition filed by the same landlord had already been dismissed, and that this should bar a fresh attempt.

The Balochistan High Court rejected this argument, clarifying that under the Rent Ordinance, a new eviction petition is only barred if the earlier one was decided on its merits. Since the first petition had been dismissed merely for non-prosecution (meaning it was never actually examined or decided), the landlord was free to file again on the same grounds.

The court also addressed other issues raised by the tenants, including payment of pagri (a premium paid by tenants), ruling that such payment does not create permanent tenancy rights or prevent eviction. It found that the landlord had demonstrated a genuine, bona fide need for the premises, and that the eviction application filed through an authorized attorney was valid.

Ultimately, the court upheld the lower court's decision ordering the tenants to vacate within two months, emphasizing that an owner's property rights take precedence over a tenant's occupancy rights. title: Aman Ud Din V. Muhammad Khan and others,
explainer:
This case involved a bail cancellation request in a criminal matter from Balochistan. The complainant alleged that the accused men had tried to forcibly take their uncle away while he was at a NADRA van getting his identity card processed. When the complainant and others intervened, one accused allegedly opened fire, injuring the complainant's ankle, while others beat him with fists and kicks. The accused were charged under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code including attempted murder (324), rioting, and acting with common intent. After their arrest, a trial court granted them bail, and the complainant then asked the High Court to cancel that bail.

The High Court refused to cancel the bail. It reasoned that cancelling bail requires much stronger grounds than granting it in the first place, since courts are reluctant to take away someone's liberty once bail has already been given, unless the original decision was clearly wrong or illegal. Here, the judge noted the accused fired only one shot, did not continue shooting when the victim was helpless, and the injury was not to a vital body part — suggesting no clear intent to kill. Since investigation was complete, no additional evidence needed recovering, and there was no misuse of the bail, the court found no reason to interfere.

This case illustrates the legal principle that bail, once granted, should not be revoked lightly, and matters like intent and exact criminal charges are to be sorted out at trial, not through bail cancellation.

title: Bibi Moashara V. Sahib Jan and 10 Others,
explainer:
This case concerns a family property dispute in Ziarat, Balochistan. Bibi Moashara, a descendant of one Khalo, filed a lawsuit seeking declaration of ownership, possession, and cancellation of a 1978 mutation (land transfer record), claiming it was fraudulent since no signatures or thumb impressions appeared on it. She argued that certain respondents had wrongly started leveling and excavating ancestral land in 2012 and only then claimed they had purchased it decades earlier through the disputed mutation.

Both the trial court and the appellate court dismissed her suit, and she then filed this civil revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal, focusing primarily on limitation (time-bar) rules. It held that a declaratory suit must be filed within six years, but the petitioner challenged the mutation more than thirty-four years after it was recorded, without explaining the delay or stating when she first learned of it. Her predecessor-in-interest, who was alive for decades after the mutation, never challenged it either. The court reiterated that a suit barred by time must be dismissed even if no party raises the limitation issue, and that courts cannot assume jurisdiction over time-barred claims. Finding no fraud proven and no error in the lower courts' concurrent findings, the High Court dismissed the revision petition, emphasizing that such findings cannot be overturned without clear illegality or evidence of misreading.

title: Nahida Jabeen V. Agha Muhammad and 6 others,
explainer:
This case was an appeal by a widow, Nahida Jabeen, against the acquittal of seven men accused of killing her husband and injuring her, her son, and her daughter during an attack with sticks and iron rods. The trial court had acquitted the accused, but the High Court found this decision was wrong and based on a misreading of evidence.

The High Court addressed several issues. First, it ruled that a two-hour delay in filing the police report was not suspicious, since the incident occurred in a remote area under Levies (local police) jurisdiction, and the family had to wait for the officer in charge to arrive before the report could be lodged. Second, the court found the eyewitness accounts of the widow, son, and injured daughter to be consistent, natural, and credible, especially since these witnesses were also injured in the attack, confirming their presence at the scene. Their testimony matched the medical evidence. The court also held that being close relatives of the victim did not automatically make their testimony unreliable, that failure to recover the weapons used did not disprove the prosecution's case, and that proving a motive was not essential when direct eyewitness and medical evidence was strong.

Since no specific witness could say which attacker caused the fatal blow, the court convicted the accused but reduced their sentence to life imprisonment rather than death. title:
Chairman National Accountability Bureau through Prosecutor General, NAB, Islamabad V.
Abdul Hakeem, General Manager Export, PSO, Karachi and 3 others
,
explainer:
This case involved a 17-year-old inquiry by the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) against officials of Pakistan State Oil. NAB began investigating the respondents in 2002 but found no evidence, so the case was formally closed in 2005 by the Accountability Court. Years later, in 2009, NAB sought permission to reopen the investigation, which the trial court initially granted. The High Court set that order aside and sent the matter back for a fresh decision. In 2019, the Accountability Court again refused to allow reinvestigation, prompting NAB to challenge that refusal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed NAB's petition, ruling that while agencies can seek reinvestigation after closing a case, this is only permitted if genuinely new evidence has emerged that was not available earlier. NAB must approach the relevant court and justify the need for reinvestigation; the court should not simply rubber-stamp the request. The judges emphasized key differences between ordinary police investigations and NAB investigations, noting NAB has far greater resources and time, so closure of a NAB case effectively amounts to a "clean chit" for the accused.

In this case, the accused had already endured 17 years of inquiry and investigation, with some even dying during the process. The court held that prolonging proceedings further, without new evidence, would be an abuse of process. This ruling reinforces protections against indefinite harassment of citizens under accountability laws and clarifies the legal standard required before reopening closed investigations.

title: Nisar Ahmed alias Chaloo V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Nisar Ahmed alias Chaloo, convicted under Section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code for committing sodomy with a young boy, his neighbour's nephew. The trial court had sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment and a fine, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court challenging his conviction.

The prosecution's case rested on the testimony of the complainant (the victim's uncle), who heard the child crying and saw the accused fleeing the scene, and the victim himself, a young schoolboy, who gave a clear and consistent account of being lured away with a promise of birds and then assaulted. Medical evidence corroborated the assault on the child, and a separate medical exam confirmed the accused was physically capable of the act. The court noted that despite lengthy cross-examination, nothing undermined the credibility of either witness, and there was no evidence the child had been coached by relatives.

The High Court held that related witnesses are just as credible as any other witnesses, provided they have no personal grudge against the accused. It also reaffirmed that in cases of sodomy or rape, even a single confidence-inspiring statement from the victim can be enough to convict. Finding no legal errors or contradictions in the evidence, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction, reinforcing how courts evaluate victim testimony and medical evidence together in such sensitive cases.

title: Muhammad Siddique alias Qurban Ali V. The State through Prosecutor General, Balochistan,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a man convicted of robbery under Pakistan's Penal Code. According to the prosecution, the petitioner and an accomplice snatched a motorcycle at gunpoint from the complainant and his relative near Dera Allah Yar. The victims reported the crime immediately, and police chased the suspects, catching the petitioner on the spot along with the stolen motorcycle and an illegal pistol. A trial court convicted him, sentencing him to three years in prison plus a fine, and an appellate court upheld this conviction. The petitioner then challenged both decisions through a criminal revision petition, arguing the evidence had been wrongly assessed.

The High Court reviewed the testimony of the complainant, his relative, and police witnesses, along with physical evidence like the recovered motorcycle and weapon. It found the eyewitness accounts credible, consistent, and corroborated by prompt reporting and recovery of stolen property. The court also noted there was no evidence of enmity or motive for false accusation, since the petitioner was a stranger to the area.

The court explained important legal principles: eyewitness testimony must be convincing beyond doubt, and supporting evidence only matters if the core eyewitness account is credible. Finding no errors in the lower courts' reasoning, the High Court dismissed the petition and upheld the conviction. This case illustrates how courts evaluate the reliability of eyewitness testimony alongside physical evidence in criminal cases.

title: Quetta Development Authority through Director General, Q.D.A V. Sajjad Khan and 10 others ,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute between the Quetta Development Authority (QDA) and a group of landowners whose property had been acquired in 1993 to build the Sraghudgi Housing Scheme. Under the Land Acquisition Act of 1894, an award was made fixing compensation for the land, with QDA promising to pay the remaining balance within six months. When QDA failed to pay the outstanding amount, the landowners sued for the unpaid compensation plus 15 percent additional charges as allowed under the law.

The trial court ruled in favor of the landowners, and QDA appealed. The case eventually went to the Supreme Court, which sent it back to the Balochistan High Court for a decision on the merits.

The High Court rejected QDA's argument that the lawsuit was filed too late, finding it was filed within the three-year legal deadline since the clock started when QDA failed to pay after the six-month grace period. The court also examined whether QDA had actually taken possession of the land, hearing testimony that QDA officials had indeed taken over the property and even held a public inauguration ceremony for the housing scheme.

Ultimately, the High Court upheld the landowners' right to compensation, but recalculated the 15 percent additional compensation to run specifically from the date of the award (March 1993) until the date the outstanding amount was actually paid (February 2001). The appeal was dismissed, meaning QDA had to honor its payment obligations to the original landowners, with interest calculated for the full delay period.

title: Rozi Khan and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a murder conviction from the Sessions Court in Pishin, Balochistan. The accused, Rozi Khan and others, had been convicted of murdering the complainant's brother and damaging solar panels at a garden, with Rozi Khan sentenced to life imprisonment.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the accused, finding serious flaws in the prosecution's evidence. The court noted a suspicious four-hour delay in reporting the crime, especially since a Levies checkpoint was located closer than the station where the report was eventually filed. It also found troubling inconsistencies: witnesses left the dead body unattended at the crime scene, then left it overnight at the Levies station before taking it for post-mortem examination the next day - a delay of seventeen hours. The medical report describing the injuries (head wounds and firearm injury) did not match the original account given by witnesses, prompting the complainant to later add a supplementary statement about knife and stick attacks to align with the medical findings. The court also found it implausible that none of the witnesses, who were relatives of the deceased, suffered any injuries despite allegedly being present during a violent attack by an equal number of attackers.

The court held that these unexplained inconsistencies created reasonable doubt, and under criminal law, even a single reasonable doubt is enough to acquit an accused. title: Ali Nawaz Shahwani and Brothers through Proprietor and another V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary C&W Department, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between construction contractors and the Balochistan government over a tender for school construction work. The petitioners, who are registered government contractors, had submitted bids in response to a public tender notice in May 2019. They claimed that when the time came to open the tenders in June, the authorities did not open them publicly as promised. Instead, they alleged the contract was secretly awarded to another contractor of the authority's choosing, without proper explanation or transparency, in violation of public procurement rules.

The contractors approached the Balochistan High Court asking it to declare the award illegal, cancel the rival contractor's work order, and allow them a fair chance to compete for the tender.

The government side argued that proper procedures had actually been followed, that other contractors did participate in the bidding process, and that the petition involved disputed facts not suitable for this type of court proceeding.

The High Court agreed with the government's position on procedure. It held that the case involved serious factual disputes - particularly around the authenticity of documents submitted by both sides - that could not be resolved through the court's constitutional jurisdiction, which is meant for clear-cut legal violations, not detailed factual investigations. Such disputes, the court said, require a full civil trial with evidence and cross-examination. Since an alternate remedy (a civil suit) was available, the constitutional petition was dismissed as not maintainable. This case illustrates the limits of High Courts' constitutional powers when genuine factual disputes exist.

title: Bashir Ahmed V. Director General, National Accountability Bureau through DPGA, NAB(b), Quetta,
explainer:
This case involved Bashir Ahmed, a government official who served as District Food Controller and Incharge of a wheat storage facility (godown) in Quetta. The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) began investigating him over allegations of misappropriation and wastage of stored wheat, after a large shortage and damage to wheat stocks was discovered. Facing possible arrest, Ahmed asked the Balochistan High Court for pre-arrest bail.

The record showed that the godown had capacity for only 238,000 bags, yet over 514,000 bags had been stored there, many left out in the open due to lack of space. Ahmed had repeatedly written to his superiors warning about deterioration, insect damage, and the need for fumigation and repairs, but his warnings went unheeded. An earlier government inquiry had already cleared him, finding the losses were due to overstorage, weather, and poor conditions rather than his wrongdoing.

The High Court found that singling out Ahmed, a lower-grade official, while higher officials who ignored his warnings faced no scrutiny, appeared unfair and suggested he was being made a scapegoat. Since he had cooperated with NAB and the allegations needed further investigation, the court granted him pre-arrest bail, while directing him to continue cooperating with the inquiry.

This case matters because it highlights how accountability proceedings can unfairly target junior employees while shielding senior officials, and shows courts using bail powers to prevent such unjust targeting.

title: Khurshid Alam and others V. Aneel Masih and 10 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land in Quetta between two sets of parties who were, for the most part, the same people but in different legal roles. One group had earlier filed a suit asking the court to stop certain parties from building a wall over property they claimed, identified by specific khasra (land survey) numbers. Later, another group filed a separate suit asking the court to restrain others from occupying what they said was Christian community graveyard land, identified by different khasra numbers.

The petitioners asked the trial court to pause the second suit, arguing it was essentially about the same dispute as their earlier suit and should not proceed while their original case was pending, relying on Section 10 of the Civil Procedure Code, which prevents courts from trying a case if the same matter is already being litigated between the same parties elsewhere. Both the trial court and the appellate court rejected this request, and the petitioners challenged those decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions. It explained that for Section 10 to apply, several conditions must all be met, most importantly that the subject matter of both suits must be identical. Here, the land parcels (khasra numbers), the cause of action, and the relief sought in the two suits were different. Since the core requirement of identical subject matter was not satisfied, the law did not apply, and the petition was dismissed. The case clarifies how courts determine whether two lawsuits are genuinely the same dispute for purposes of staying proceedings.

title: Tauk Ali V. The Additional District Judge-Vi, Quetta and 3 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a custody dispute over a young girl, Maria Ali, following the murder of her mother. Both the child's father and her maternal grandmother sought legal guardianship and custody under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890. The father (petitioner) argued he should have custody since the law generally favors a living father, while the grandmother argued she was already caring for the child and had done so since the mother's death.

Importantly, the father, his brother, and the child's stepmother had all been named as suspects in the FIR for the mother's murder, though the father was later acquitted after a compromise with the deceased mother's heirs. That compromise explicitly stated the child would stay with her maternal grandmother. The father also traveled abroad frequently for business, meaning the child would effectively be raised by her stepmother, who remained a fugitive in the murder case.

The trial court denied both the father's and grandmother's applications, but the appellate court sided with the grandmother. The father then challenged this in the High Court.

The High Court ruled that while fathers are normally preferred as guardians, this case's facts - the father's frequent absence, his association with the murder case, and the risk of leaving the child with an absconding stepmother - justified placing the child with the grandmother instead. The court upheld the trial court's original decision and dismissed the father's petitions, emphasizing that the child's welfare outweighs the normal legal preference for paternal custody.

یہ مقدمہ ایک کمسن بچی، ماریہ علی، کی تحویل کے تنازع سے متعلق ہے جو اس کی والدہ کے قتل کے بعد پیدا ہوا۔ بچی کے والد اور نانی، دونوں نے گارڈینز اینڈ وارڈز ایکٹ 1890 کے تحت قانونی سرپرستی اور تحویل کے لیے درخواستیں دائر کیں۔ والد (درخواست گزار) کا موقف تھا کہ چونکہ قانون عمومی طور پر زندہ باپ کو ترجیح دیتا ہے، اس لیے تحویل اسے ملنی چاہیے، جبکہ نانی کا کہنا تھا کہ وہ والدہ کی وفات کے بعد سے بچی کی دیکھ بھال کر رہی ہے۔

اہم بات یہ ہے کہ والد، اس کے بھائی، اور بچی کی سوتیلی ماں، تینوں کو والدہ کے قتل کی ایف آئی آر میں بطور مشتبہ نامزد کیا گیا تھا، تاہم بعد ازاں مقتولہ کے ورثاء سے صلح کے نتیجے میں والد کو بری کر دیا گیا۔ اس صلح نامے میں واضح طور پر درج تھا کہ بچی اپنی نانی کے پاس رہے گی۔ اس کے علاوہ والد اکثر کاروباری سلسلے میں بیرون ملک سفر کرتا رہتا تھا، جس کا مطلب یہ تھا کہ عملی طور پر بچی کی پرورش

title: Abdul Khaliq V. Additional District Judge-V, Quetta and another,
explainer:
This case involved a father and mother who had divorced after a Muslim marriage, with a daughter from their union. The mother had earlier won a court case for the child's maintenance, and the Family Court fixed the amount at Rs.5,000 per month with a 5% annual increase. Later, she filed a fresh case asking for the maintenance to be further enhanced. The father argued that this new case should not be allowed, claiming it was barred by the legal principle of res judicata, meaning the same issue could not be litigated twice between the same parties. The trial court agreed with him and dismissed the new suit, but on appeal, the Additional District Judge sent the case back for a decision on its merits.

The father then challenged this before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision, ruling that the earlier case was only about recovery of maintenance, not about its enhancement, so the two were not the same issue. The court explained that circumstances like a child's growth, inflation, and changing needs can create a fresh basis for seeking increased maintenance, meaning such claims can be filed again without being blocked by res judicata.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that parents are not permanently locked into an initial maintenance amount and can return to Family Courts for increases as a child's needs change over time, ensuring maintenance remains fair and realistic.

title: Abdul Khaliq V. Additional District and Sessions Judge-IV and 2 others,
explainer:
This case was about a father, Abdul Khaliq, who filed a petition asking to be made the legal guardian of his minor daughter after his marriage to the child's mother ended. The daughter remained in the mother's custody. The Family Court (Guardian Judge) dismissed his guardianship petition as not maintainable. He then appealed to the Additional District and Sessions Judge, but that appeal was also dismissed on the ground that, under Section 47 of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, any appeal in guardianship matters should go to the High Court, not the District Judge.

The Balochistan High Court examined how the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 interacts with the Family Courts Act 1964. It held that although guardianship and custody cases must follow the procedure set out in the 1890 Act, such matters fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of Family Courts, which are deemed District Courts for this purpose under Section 25 of the Family Courts Act. Since the original guardianship petition was decided by a Family Court judge who did not hold the rank of District Judge, the correct appellate forum was the District Judge, not the High Court, as specified under Section 14 of the Family Courts Act 1964.

The High Court therefore allowed the petition and directed the appellate court (District Judge) to hear and decide the appeal on its merits, clarifying the correct appeal route in guardianship disputes.

title: Akhtar Muhammad alias Ghani V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved the murder of a woman, Fouzia, whose brother-in-law Sardar Muhammad was accused of shooting her, while his brother Akhtar Muhammad was accused of helping hide the crime and giving false information to the police. The trial court had convicted Sardar Muhammad of murder, sentencing him to life imprisonment, and convicted Akhtar Muhammad of lesser offenses related to concealing evidence and misleading the investigation. Both men appealed their convictions, and the complainant separately asked the court to increase the punishment.

Since there were no eyewitnesses, the case relied heavily on circumstantial evidence and a judicial confession made by one of the accused, which he later retracted. The High Court examined this confession closely and found serious problems with how it was recorded, including unexplained delays, allegations of torture during investigation, and procedural lapses by the magistrate that cast doubt on whether the confession was truly voluntary. The court also noted a significant and unexplained delay of nearly two years in sending the weapon and bullet casings for forensic testing, which further undermined the prosecution's case.

The High Court ruled that these doubts were serious enough to require acquittal, emphasizing that even a single substantial doubt is sufficient to benefit the accused as a matter of right, not leniency. It overturned the convictions and acquitted both appellants, rejecting the complainant's request to increase the sentence. This case highlights how Pakistani courts scrutinize confessions and evidentiary

title: Muhammad Wali V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Wali, who was convicted by a trial court for possessing 10 kilograms of charas (hashish) under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and sentenced to ten years in prison along with a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The police claimed they stopped a passenger van and found the drugs in a bag on the appellant's lap. However, the High Court found serious flaws in how the prosecution handled the case. First, although the arrest happened at 10:00 a.m., the police did not file the official report until six hours later, with no explanation for the delay. Second, and more critically, the drug samples were supposed to be sent to the government forensic laboratory within 72 hours under the relevant rules, but they were not received by the lab until eleven days later - again with no explanation. The prosecution also failed to present the official who personally carried the sample to the laboratory, so there was no way to verify who had custody of the evidence during that unexplained gap.

Because of these failures, the court could not be confident that the evidence had not been tampered with or that the chain of custody was reliable. Since any doubt in such cases must benefit the accused, the court ruled that the prosecution had not proven its case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, and the conviction and sentence were set aside. This case highlights how strict procedural rules around evidence handling in drug cases protect defendants from unreliable convictions.

title: The State through District and Sessions Judge, Kalat V. Assistant Commissioner and others,
explainer:
This case arose after an Assistant Commissioner, during a raid, arrested a Qazi (a judicial officer) and then had him dragged, manhandled, and beaten in public view. This caused outrage across the judiciary in Balochistan, with judicial officers feeling humiliated and insecure, and several Bar Associations going on strike in protest. The matter was treated as a contempt of court case under the Contempt of Court Ordinance, 2003, because such treatment of a judicial officer was seen as an attack on the dignity and authority of the courts themselves.

The Balochistan High Court held that while judicial officers are not above the law and can be lawfully arrested like any citizen, the manner of this arrest—public humiliation and physical assault—went far beyond a mere procedural arrest and amounted to a deliberate attempt to undermine the judiciary. The court found the Assistant Commissioner guilty of contempt but took a lenient view because he had tendered an unconditional apology early on, sentencing him to a nominal fine and token imprisonment till the rising of the court.

Importantly, the court laid down detailed guidelines for how judicial officers must be arrested in the future—such as prior intimation to the District Judge or High Court, no handcuffing except in genuine emergencies, and safeguards during any arrest—to protect the judiciary's independence while still upholding equality before the law.

title: Gulzar Khan V. Mst. Rahima and 3 others,
explainer:
This case was about a custody dispute between a father, Gulzar Khan, and a mother, Mst. Rahima, over their three children after their marriage broke down. The father had filed an application seeking custody of his two sons and one daughter. The trial court gave him custody of the two boys but ruled that the young daughter, aged about five, should stay with her mother until she reached puberty. The father appealed this decision, and when the appeal was dismissed, he brought the matter to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the father's petition. The judges explained that under Muslim personal law, a mother is entitled to custody of her daughter even after puberty until marriage, while a father can only claim custody of sons after they turn seven. The court stressed that the welfare of the child is the most important factor in custody cases, including their mental, emotional and intellectual development. Since the father worked as a contractor and was frequently away from home, he could not show who would care for the young girl in his absence. The court also noted that a mother's limited financial means does not disqualify her from having custody, and that a mother's bond with a young daughter is especially important for her upbringing.

This case highlights how Pakistani courts prioritize children's overall wellbeing, guided by Islamic family law principles, over a parent's financial status when deciding custody matters.

title: Amanullah Khan V. The State,
explainer:
The case involved Amanullah Khan, a National Bank of Pakistan officer who worked as a pension-disbursing officer at the bank's city and cantonment branches in Quetta between 1996 and 2005. He was accused under the National Accountability Ordinance of fraudulently misappropriating over 10.8 million rupees meant for pensioners, mainly military pensioners under the Controller of Military Pension Accounts. He allegedly prepared fake pension bills in his own handwriting, forged pensioners' signatures, and withdrew money without proper verification. After the fraud was detected, he repaid about 8.5 million rupees, leaving roughly 2.258 million rupees unaccounted for.

An Accountability Court convicted him in 2010, sentencing him to over four years in prison, a fine equal to the outstanding amount, removal from public office, and a ten-year ban from holding public positions or obtaining bank loans. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court reviewed extensive evidence, including bank records, pension files, and testimony from twenty prosecution witnesses, whose accounts were found to be consistent and unshaken despite lengthy cross-examination. The Court found that Khan, as custodian of pension records, had committed serious forgery and abused his official position for personal gain. Finding no reason to disturb the trial court's findings, the High Court upheld his conviction and sentence, dismissing the appeal.

This case illustrates how courts handle financial corruption by bank officials entrusted with disbursing

title: Ghulam Nabi V. The State,
explainer:
Ghulam Nabi was convicted by a trial court for killing his daughter, Sehrish, after she and her husband beat the girl with shoes over a dispute involving a mobile charger. The girl died the next day, and the mother, who was the appellant's wife, eventually lodged an FIR after the body was exhumed for a post-mortem. The trial court convicted the father under section 302(c) of the Pakistan Penal Code (qatl-i-amd, intentional murder with lesser punishment) and sentenced him to ten years in prison plus compensation.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined whether the delay in filing the FIR and the fact that the complainant was the accused's own wife should weaken the case. The court held that delay alone does not make an FIR unreliable, especially given the family lived together and the wife observed purdah, explaining her hesitation to report immediately. The court also found no evidence of premeditation or serious enmity between the parties, and noted the weapon used (shoes) and circumstances did not show clear intent to kill.

Based on this, the High Court decided the case did not meet the threshold for murder under section 302(c), but instead fit the lesser offense under section 315/316 PPC (qatl-shibh-i-amd, unintentional killing with harmful intent). The court modified the sentence accordingly, while still dismissing the appeal, meaning the appellant remained convicted, but for a lesser offense reflecting the absence of premeditated intent to kill.

title: Rafaat Shah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves Rafaat Shah, who was convicted by a trial court for killing a man named Muhammad Nawaz by allegedly hitting him on the head with a stone during a quarrel. He was sentenced to ten years' rigorous imprisonment under section 302(c) of the Pakistan Penal Code, along with a compensation order. He appealed this conviction to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the appellant, giving him the benefit of the doubt. The judges found multiple serious problems with the prosecution's case. The eyewitnesses, who were close relatives of the deceased, behaved unnaturally - they neither took the injured man to hospital nor informed the nearby Levies Station, despite being right across from it, and instead let the injured man ride home alone on a motorcycle. There was also an unexplained 26-hour delay in filing the police report, even though the deceased had been medically examined within two hours of the incident. Additionally, the medical evidence contradicted the eyewitness account: doctors found only a single swelling injury with no broken skin, while the complainant claimed repeated blows, and the stone allegedly used as the weapon had no blood on it.

The court reaffirmed the important legal principle that even a single reasonable doubt is enough to acquit an accused person - prosecutors don't need multiple doubts to exist. This case illustrates how courts carefully scrutinize witness credibility, conduct, and consistency between evidence types before allowing a serious conviction to stand.
