title: Zia Ul Haq V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a bus driver, Zia Ul Haq, who was convicted by a trial court for causing the death of a police constable in a road accident, under laws dealing with unintentional killing through rash or negligent driving. The constable was struck by the appellant's minibus at a checkpoint at night and died of his injuries. The trial court sentenced the driver to prison and ordered him to pay compensation (Diyat) to the victim's family.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined whether the prosecution had actually proven that the driver was being rash or negligent, since mere involvement in an accident is not enough to secure a conviction. The court found serious gaps in the evidence: the only two prosecution witnesses admitted during cross-examination that they had not actually seen the accident happen. There was no proof of speeding, no tire marks indicating hard braking, no examination of the bus's brakes, and no statements taken from other passengers or nearby residents who might have witnessed the incident. The scene was also dark, and the sketch map lacked key details.

The court held that negligence cannot be measured by any fixed formula and must be judged from surrounding facts, and that speed alone does not establish rashness. Since the prosecution failed to provide reliable evidence proving rash or negligent driving, the court gave the accused the benefit of the doubt and overturned the conviction. This case highlights that criminal convictions require solid, direct evidence, not assumptions.

title: Yar Muhammad V. National Bank of Pakistan through Manager,
explainer:
This case involved a bank loan recovery dispute. Yar Muhammad had borrowed over 13 lakh rupees from National Bank of Pakistan but allegedly failed to repay it. The bank sued him in the Banking Court, which decided the case in the bank's favor and ordered him to pay the money, since he never filed an application seeking permission to contest the case, as required under the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001.

Yar Muhammad appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the bank had not properly attached required financial statements to its claim, that he was never properly notified of the case, and that his lawyer simply missed a hearing date due to being busy elsewhere, which shouldn't have cost him the chance to defend himself.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It found that notice had been properly published in newspapers as the law required, and that the bank had included all necessary documents with its claim. Crucially, the law gives a defendant only thirty days after such publication to apply for permission to defend the suit. Yar Muhammad missed this deadline by over a month, and never showed a valid reason for his absence or his lawyer's absence on the hearing date.

The High Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the lower court's decision. The judgment reinforces that borrowers must strictly follow procedural deadlines when challenging bank recovery suits, since the law is designed to ensure quick recovery of unpaid loans.

title: Habib Adm Limited through General Manager V. Executive Engineer Canal Irrigation Division Hub and another,
explainer:
This case was about a dispute between a company, Habib ADM Limited, and the Canal Irrigation Department over water rates. The company had built a new pipeline to supply water to its plant and claimed that officials had assured it the water charge would stay fixed at Rs.11 per unit. When the department later raised the rate several times, eventually to Rs.73 per unit, the company sued, arguing the increase was unjustified and unlawful, and asked the court to cancel the enhanced bills.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court rejected the company's claim, finding no proof that any binding promise had been made to keep the rate fixed forever. The company then filed a second appeal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions. It held that the company failed to produce any document proving the alleged assurance of a permanent rate, and that under the relevant law (the Balochistan Canal and Drainage Ordinance, 1980), water supplied without a written contract is subject to prescribed rates set by the authorities. The court also noted that in a second appeal, it cannot disturb concurrent factual findings of lower courts unless there is a clear legal or procedural error, which was not shown here.

The case highlights that government bodies can revise utility rates in the absence of a formal contract, and that courts give strong weight to consistent factual findings from earlier courts.

title: Maqbool Ahmed and others V. Secretary, Revenue Department, Government of Balochistan and others,
explainer:
This case was about the renaming of two places in Balochistan - Mangochar Sub-Division in District Kalat was renamed Khaliq Abad Mangochar, and Tehsil Phelawagh in District Dera Bugti was renamed Tehsil Qadirabad, through government notifications issued in 2014 and 2018. Local residents challenged these renamings in the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the government had no legal authority to change the historical names of these places, that the changes seemed aimed at honoring political families rather than serving public interest, and that no public consultation or objections process had been carried out before the names were altered.

The High Court agreed with the petitioners. It found that the Balochistan Land Revenue Act, 1967, which the government cited as its basis for the notifications, contained no provision actually allowing the renaming of a district or tehsil. Since there was no law empowering the executive to take such action, the notifications were declared illegal, without lawful authority, and void from the start. The court restored the original names.

The judgment also clarified important constitutional principles: courts can intervene when public officials act beyond their legal powers, even if the challenger doesn't have a strict personal legal right, as long as they have genuine public interest at stake. Government policies can be reviewed by courts if they violate the law or fundamental rights. This case matters because it reinforces that public authorities must act strictly within powers granted by law, and arbitrary administrative decisions affecting communities can be struck down when no legal basis supports them.

title: Sher Zaman Ex-Assistant Excise and Taxation Officer (B-16) V Board of Revenue BALOCHISTAN (Excise and Taxation Branch) through Member Board of Revenue-II/Secretary Excise and another,
explainer:
This case concerns Sher Zaman, a retired Assistant Excise and Taxation Officer in Balochistan, whose pension was withheld by the Board of Revenue because of a pending NAB (National Accountability Bureau) reference against him. He challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that denying him pensionary benefits without any legal basis was unjust.

The court ruled in his favor. It held that pension and gratuity are not discretionary favors or bounties but benefits an employee earns through years of honest, continuous service. Importantly, there was no provision in the Pension Rules allowing authorities to withhold pension simply because departmental or criminal proceedings were pending. The court also noted that the right to receive pension is protected as a property right under Article 9 of the Constitution, meaning no one can be deprived of it except through lawful authority. Since the petitioner had already been acquitted by a competent court, there was no justification for continuing to withhold his pension.

The judgment drew on precedent, including a Supreme Court ruling, emphasizing that people are presumed innocent until proven guilty and should not be punished administratively for accusations that may never result in conviction. It also highlighted the broader problem of retired government employees suffering hardship due to bureaucratic delays in pension processing.

The court allowed the petition and directed the authorities to release the petitioner's pensionary benefits, reinforcing that pension rights deserve strong legal protection and cannot be arbitrarily suspended.

title: Allah Dina and 21 others V. Ikhtiar Khan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Sibi, Balochistan, over shared agricultural land described as shamilat (common village land). The plaintiffs, who owned shares in the land, claimed that one co-owner, the respondent, had occupied far more land than his actual share and asked the civil court for a declaration of ownership, partition of the property, and an injunction against the respondent.

The trial court, after hearing evidence, decided it did not have jurisdiction to hear the case and returned the plaint, directing the plaintiffs to instead approach the Revenue Court, since partition of land was already pending before the Assistant Commissioner. The appellate court upheld this decision, prompting the plaintiffs to file this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that under the Balochistan Land Revenue Act, 1967, matters of partitioning shared land fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of Revenue Officers, not civil courts. The law specifically bars civil courts from hearing partition-related disputes once the matter is before revenue authorities. The court also clarified that revenue officers themselves have full power to resolve questions of ownership or title when deciding partition cases, so there was no need for a separate civil suit.

This ruling reinforces that disputes over partitioning jointly-owned land in Balochistan must go through revenue authorities rather than civil courts, especially when such proceedings are already underway, ensuring the specialized revenue law mechanism is respected over general civil litigation.

title: Bilal V. Abdul Karim and 6 others,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Bilal who claimed he owned agricultural land that had been illegally taken over by Abdul Karim and others while Bilal was living abroad. He filed a complaint under Pakistan's Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, a special law meant to criminally punish land grabbers, people who forcibly or unlawfully seize property without any legal title. The trial court dismissed his complaint, finding the dispute was essentially civil in nature, not criminal land-grabbing. Bilal challenged that dismissal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court first addressed a technical objection: since the Act does not specifically mention a right of appeal or revision, could Bilal even challenge the order this way? The Court clarified that the law's silence didn't eliminate appeal rights, because Section 9 of the Act applies the general Criminal Procedure Code to such cases, allowing revision petitions.

On the merits, however, the Court ruled against Bilal. It held that the Illegal Dispossession Act only applies in specific situations, such as when the accused has no title to the land, took it by force, acted outside legal process, or belongs to a land-grabbing gang. Since Bilal failed to show his case fit this criteria, and the matter appeared to be a civil property dispute, the Court upheld the trial court's dismissal and rejected his revision petition. The judgment reinforces that civil disputes cannot be disguised as criminal cases under this special law.

title: Muhammad Yousaf V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a fatal shooting on a road near Mastung. The complainant, Nazar Muhammad, and his nephew were riding a motorcycle when the appellant, Muhammad Yousaf, along with another man, intercepted them and opened fire. The nephew died at the scene, and the complainant himself was wounded. A trial court convicted Yousaf of murder, attempted murder, and causing injury, sentencing him to life imprisonment plus additional jail terms and fines. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing mainly that the FIR (police report) had been filed a day late, which he claimed cast doubt on the prosecution's story.

The High Court rejected this argument, finding that the delay was caused by police procedure (officers first took the injured complainant to hospital) rather than any attempt to falsely implicate the accused. The court emphasized that the complainant was an injured eyewitness with no prior enmity against the accused, that his account was consistent and detailed, and that medical evidence supported his version of events. The judges reiterated established legal principles: a solitary witness's testimony can be enough for conviction if credible; relationship to the victim doesn't automatically discredit a witness; and delay in filing an FIR alone is not grounds to disbelieve a case.

Finding the prosecution's evidence reliable and well-corroborated, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction and sentence. The case illustrates how courts evaluate witness credibility and procedural delays in serious criminal cases.

title: Abdul Nafey V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Nafey, who was convicted of murdering a man named Jelani after an argument outside Jelani's house. According to the prosecution, the accused was standing in front of the victim's home, and when challenged by the deceased, he pulled out a pistol and shot him. The trial court in Pishin convicted the appellant of murder under the Pakistan Penal Code, sentencing him to life imprisonment and ordering him to pay compensation to the victim's family. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, though the appeal was filed five months late.

The High Court examined the evidence, which relied mainly on one eyewitness (the deceased's brother) whose account matched the FIR, filed promptly after the incident, and was consistent with the medical evidence showing a fatal gunshot wound. The court held that a single eyewitness's testimony can be enough to convict if it is credible and consistent, since what matters is the quality of evidence, not the number of witnesses. It also ruled that being related to the victim does not automatically make a witness unreliable, especially when there's no evidence of enmity toward the accused that would motivate false testimony. The court further noted that absence or weakness of a motive doesn't matter when strong direct and medical evidence proves the crime.

Finding the prosecution's case solid and well-corroborated, the High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction and sentence. The case reinforces important principles about evaluating eyewitness credibility in murder trials.

title: Janan alias Janak V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a murder conviction. Janan alias Janak was convicted by a trial court for killing Nabiullah, son of the complainant, and was sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine as compensation under the law. He appealed his conviction, while the complainant filed a separate petition asking the court to enhance the punishment.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness testimony, medical reports, and the police investigation. Two eyewitnesses had seen the attack, correctly described how and when it happened, identified the accused in court, were not relatives of the victim or enemies of the accused, and had given consistent statements to police on the very day of the incident. Their account matched the medical evidence showing the victim died from sharp weapon injuries. The FIR was also filed promptly, naming the accused.

The court noted that the recovered weapon was not useful as evidence since it was never forensically tested, had no blood on it, and wasn't found exclusively with the accused. It also held that even though the motive for the killing was never established, this did not matter because strong direct and medical evidence already proved guilt—motive is not essential when other solid evidence exists.

Given all this, the High Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and life sentence, and did not increase the punishment either. The case illustrates how Pakistani courts rely on credible eyewitness and medical evidence to sustain murder convictions, even without proof of motive or forensic weapon analysis.

title: Director General Civil Aviation Authority through Airport Manager, Quetta V. Muhammad Dawood,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between the Civil Aviation Authority (Quetta Airport) and a contractor, Muhammad Dawood, who had been awarded a parking contract for three years starting in 2008. The contractor claimed that the Airport Authority's construction work next to the parking area damaged his business, causing him a loss of Rs. 300,000, and he sued for declaration, an injunction, and damages. The Authority, in turn, claimed the contractor owed it Rs. 193,000 in unpaid license fees and had adjusted his security deposit against this amount.

The trial court dismissed both claims, finding neither side had proven its case, and the Airport Authority's appeal against this decision was also dismissed by the Additional District Judge. The Authority then filed this civil revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions. It found that the Authority had never specified or documented how it calculated the Rs. 193,000 it claimed was owed, and had produced no evidence to support this figure. The Court also noted that the Authority's appeal before the lower appellate court had been filed late, and its explanation for the delay (that time was needed to obtain official sanction) was unsupported by any documentation, so the delay could not be excused under the Limitation Act.

Finding no legal error in the concurrent findings of the lower courts, the High Court dismissed the revision petition. The case highlights the importance of providing documentary evidence to support monetary claims and meeting appeal deadlines with properly justified reasons for delay.

title: The State through Prosecutor General Balochistan V. Muhammad Ashfaq,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by the State of Balochistan against the acquittal of Muhammad Ashfaq, who had been charged under the Arms Ordinance, 1965 for possessing an unlicensed pistol. The allegation was that police recovered a TT pistol, magazine, and two live rounds based on Ashfaq's pointing out the location while he was in custody in a separate murder case.

The trial court had acquitted him, and the State challenged this acquittal before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court upheld the acquittal, finding serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The weapon was allegedly recovered from a running water drain twenty-five days after the murder it was supposedly used in, yet a lightweight bullet casing had supposedly stayed put in flowing water that long—something the court found implausible. The recovery also happened in a populated area where independent witnesses could easily have been brought in to verify the process, but police made no such effort. There were also unexplained delays in sending evidence for forensic examination. Additionally, Ashfaq had already been acquitted in the original murder case this weapons charge stemmed from.

The court reaffirmed key legal principles: even a single significant doubt in the prosecution's case entitles the accused to benefit of the doubt as a matter of right, not mercy. It also stressed that once a person is acquitted, they gain a "double presumption of innocence," meaning appellate courts need strong, compelling evidence to overturn such a verdict. Finding no such evidence here, the court dismissed the State's appeal

title: Abdul Hadi V. The State,
explainer:

A search revealed ten kilograms of charas hidden beneath the driver's seat mat. He was tried and convicted under section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and sentenced to life imprisonment with a fine.

On appeal, his lawyers argued the case was fabricated, that no independent witnesses (as required under section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code) were present during the search, and that there were delays and irregularities in sending drug samples for chemical testing.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that section 25 of the Narcotics Act specifically excludes the requirement for private witnesses in such searches, so their absence did not invalidate the case. The court also found no evidence of enmity between police witnesses and the accused, and confirmed the samples reached the laboratory within the permissible 72-hour window, with proper testing confirming the substance was charas. The court reaffirmed that a driver is legally responsible for narcotics found in the vehicle he is driving.

However, since the quantity (10 kg) did not meet the higher threshold requiring mandatory life imprisonment under the law's proviso, the court reduced his sentence while upholding the conviction. The appeal was otherwise dismissed. This case clarifies how courts treat police-only searches in narcotics cases and how sentencing depends

This case involved an appeal against a death sentence given to Mohibullah, who was convicted of shooting and killing Naib Risaldar Hayatullah, a levies official, in Killa Saifullah district in 2018. The official had responded to reports of a quarrel between groups at a bazaar and was attempting to arrest the accused when he was shot dead. The trial court had convicted the accused under murder laws and also under the Anti-Terrorism Act, sentencing him to death.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the conviction for murder, finding the evidence solid, including a promptly filed police report naming the accused, and ballistic evidence matching the recovered pistol to the shooting. However, the court reduced the death sentence to life imprisonment, citing several mitigating factors: there was no proof the original quarrel had been reported to police, no witnesses from the other group involved in the altercation were produced, the attack appeared spontaneous rather than premeditated, the deceased official was not wearing his uniform at the time, and the accused fired only a single shot rather than repeatedly shooting the victim.

Importantly, the court also overturned the terrorism conviction entirely, ruling that since only the official was targeted, no one else was injured, and the legal requirements for an act to qualify as "terrorism" were not met. This case illustrates how courts carefully distinguish between ordinary crimes and terrorism charges, and how specific case circumstances can lead to reduced sentences even after guilt is established.

title: Mohibullah V. The State,
explainer:
Mohibullah was convicted by a trial court in Pishin for the murder of Zainullah and for causing serious injuries to Muhammad Ashraf during an attack near a petrol pump, allegedly carried out along with two other men armed with daggers and sticks. He was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, plus additional jail terms and fines for the injuries caused, under relevant sections of the Pakistan Penal Code. He appealed his conviction, while the complainant separately sought enhancement of his sentence.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence, including testimony from an independent eyewitness unrelated to the complainant, and from the injured victim himself, both of whom supported the prosecution's account of events. The court noted that although the complainant himself was not present during the attack and had only lodged the FIR based on information received by phone, this did not weaken the case, since his role was simply to report the crime, not to witness it. The court also held that failing to name the eyewitness in the FIR did not make the prosecution's case doubtful.

Finding that the accused and his companions had arrived at the scene armed and acted with shared intent, the court ruled that the prosecution had proven its case beyond reasonable doubt. It upheld the trial court's conviction and sentence, dismissing the appeal. This case illustrates how courts assess witness credibility and procedural technicalities like FIR omissions when deciding serious criminal cases.

title: Saleem Iqbal and another V. Muhammad Ashiq and others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of two men accused of murdering a woman's husband by shooting him. The complainant (the deceased's wife) claimed to be an eyewitness, but she herself had initially been named as an accused during the investigation, raising serious questions about the reliability of the prosecution's account. No independent witness came forward, making this essentially an unwitnessed crime relying on circumstantial and confessional evidence.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the trial court's acquittal, finding multiple serious flaws in the prosecution's case. The confessional statements recorded under the law were found to be unreliable because proper procedures weren't followed: the accused weren't given adequate time for reflection before confessing, co-accused weren't properly given opportunities to cross-examine each other as required, and the investigating officer improperly handled the accused after their statements were recorded. There was also an unexplained eight-day delay before one confession was recorded. Additionally, the recovery of the murder weapon was questionable—it was allegedly found in a water drain weeks after the crime, with no proof the drain even had running water, and forensic testing was delayed by five months without explanation.

The court emphasized that confessions alone cannot support a conviction without strong corroboration, and that any genuine doubt in the prosecution's case must benefit the accused as a matter of right. This ruling reinforces important safeguards protecting the fairness of criminal confessions and evidence in Pakistani law.

title: Naseebullah and others V. The State through Prosecutor General Balochistan and others ,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal before the Balochistan High Court arising from a shooting incident in which the complainant's father was injured and his brother was killed. Two accused were tried: one alleged to have fired the shots, and a co-accused allegedly present with him.

The court examined the delay in filing the police report (just over an hour) and found it was lodged promptly, given that witnesses first rushed the victims to hospital. It also reviewed eyewitness testimony from the complainant, the injured father, and another relative, finding their accounts consistent, credible, and well-corroborated by medical evidence and forensic analysis matching recovered bullet casings to a pistol linked to the main accused.

The court held that being related to the victims did not make witnesses unreliable, since their testimony was independent and truthful. However, regarding the co-accused, the court found the prosecution had only shown he was present at the scene, with no evidence he fired a weapon or shared a common intention to commit the crime. Mere presence alongside the shooter was not enough to establish joint liability under Section 34 of the Penal Code, which requires proof of shared intention, not just similar circumstances.

Consequently, the court upheld the conviction of the main accused but acquitted the co-accused, highlighting the legal principle that criminal liability for common intention requires more than mere association with an offender.

title: Mir Dost alias Kiraro and others V. The State ,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court concerned three men convicted for killing five members of a family, including a pregnant woman, after accusing two of the victims of adultery (declaring them "Siahkar"). The attackers opened fire on a sleeping household, allegedly to avenge a refused marriage proposal and to seize property. The trial court had sentenced the appellants to death for three of the murders and ordered compensation to the victims' families. The convicts appealed, and while the appeal was pending they reached a compromise with some of the surviving legal heirs, who pardoned them and waived their right to demand retribution (Qisas), asking the court to accept the settlement and acquit the accused.

The High Court refused to accept the compromise. It held that under the law, when a murder is committed in the name of honour—such as "Karo Kari" or similar customs—courts are not bound to allow such settlements, especially when the crime is particularly brutal, cruel, and shocking to society. The judges stressed that killing in the name of family honour or religion cannot be justified or sanctified by law. Because this case involved the slaughter of an entire family while they slept, for no real justification beyond honour and property, the court dismissed the compromise application.

This ruling reaffirms that courts can and should reject private compromises in extremely heinous honour-based killings, prioritizing justice and public interest over family settlements.

title: Asmatullah V. The State,
explainer:
The case involved Asmatullah, who was convicted by a trial court for the murder of Munir Ahmed and the attempted murder of his companion, following an altercation stemming from a prior dispute between the complainant's brothers and the accused's father. The trial court sentenced him to death, along with fine and compensation, and also convicted him under Section 324 PPC for attempted murder.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence closely. It found that none of the prosecution's witnesses, including the complainant, actually saw the accused at the scene. The key evidence was a statement given by the injured eyewitness, Syed Tawab Shah, but this was recorded earlier under Section 512 Cr.P.C. during proceedings against a co-accused, without the appellant present or able to cross-examine him. Before the fresh trial could properly record his testimony, the witness died in an unrelated road accident, and the trial court simply relied on his old, untested statement to convict Asmatullah.

The High Court held that such an uncross-examined statement could not be used against the appellant, and that the remaining witnesses were closely related to the deceased, requiring cautious scrutiny. With no weapon recovery, no independently proven motive, and no corroborating evidence, the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond doubt. The Court acquitted Asmatullah, highlighting the importance of reliable, tested evidence before convicting someone of murder.

title: Yar Muhammad and 4 others V. Muhammad Ali and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Quetta, Balochistan. The petitioners (plaintiffs) claimed ownership of certain settled agricultural land as well as a large tract of 2,500 to 3,000 acres of unsettled land, which they said belonged exclusively to their tribe. They filed a suit for declaration and permanent injunction against the respondents, alleging illegal interference with their property. The trial court initially ruled in the petitioners' favor, but the appellate court overturned that decision, prompting this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision and dismissed the petition. It noted that the land in question was officially unsettled land registered in the name of the Government of Balochistan, and neither side had produced solid evidence proving personal ownership. Crucially, the petitioners had named only government officials, such as the Member Board of Revenue and the Tehsildar, as defendants, but had failed to include the Provincial Government through its Secretary, as legally required under Article 174 of the Constitution and Section 79 of the Civil Procedure Code when government land or interests are involved.

Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the Court ruled that a suit concerning government-owned unsettled land is not legally valid unless the government itself is properly made a party. Since this procedural requirement was not met, the suit was rightly dismissed, reinforcing the principle that proper government representation is essential in disputes involving state land.

title: Secretary Communication and Works Department, Government of Balochistan, Quetta and another V. Abdul Majeed and 7 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between the Balochistan government and a private landowner, Abdul Majeed. In 2009, Majeed had given a piece of his land to the Communication and Works Department for building a rest house, based on an agreement that in return, the department would give a class-IV government job to a person he nominated. When the government did not honor this promise, Majeed waited six years and then filed a lawsuit in 2015 asking the court to either enforce the agreement or grant him a declaration in his favor.

The trial court dismissed his suit, but on appeal, the Majlis-e-Shoora (appellate court) ruled in his favor and ordered the agreement to be enforced. The government then challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court sided with the government. It found two major problems with Majeed's case. First, the lawsuit was filed too late, well beyond the three-year legal deadline for seeking enforcement of an agreement, and no explanation was given for the delay. Second, and more importantly, the agreement itself was illegal: government jobs cannot be given out based on private recommendations or as payment for land, since this violates the constitutional guarantee of equal treatment and amounts to effectively selling a public office, which is unlawful under contract law.

As a result, the High Court set aside the appellate court's ruling and restored the trial court's dismissal of the suit, reaffirming that public employment cannot be bought, sold, or promised through private deals.

title: Dr. Muhammad Arif V. Muhammad Anwar and 3 others ,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Dr. Muhammad Arif, who filed a criminal complaint (FIR) alleging that four men broke into his house at night, tried to attack his brother, and shot him when he intervened, causing a bullet injury. During the trial, after the prosecution had presented some witnesses but before all evidence was recorded, the accused persons applied under Section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking the trial court to acquit them early based on a medical board report suggesting the complainant's injury was self-inflicted rather than from gunfire. The trial court accepted this application and acquitted the accused without letting the prosecution complete its evidence. The complainant appealed this acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court set aside the trial court's order. It held that while judges do have power under Section 265-K to acquit an accused early to prevent abuse of the judicial process, this power should only be used when it is obvious from admitted facts that no offence is made out. Here, there was still oral and documentary evidence, including a disputed medical certificate, that needed to be properly tested through trial. Fairness required giving the prosecution a full opportunity to present its evidence before deciding the case, rather than cutting the trial short. The court emphasized that normal trial procedures should be followed unless truly exceptional circumstances exist, and sent the case back for a fair, complete trial.

title: Sher Muhammad V. Bibi Safia and 4 others ,
explainer:
This case concerns a landlord-tenant dispute under the Balochistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959. A landlord filed an eviction application against his tenant, Sher Muhammad, citing rent default and his own personal need for the property. The tenant resisted eviction by denying that any landlord-tenant relationship existed at all, claiming instead that he occupied the house as the tenant of a different person who, he argued, was the real owner.

The Rent Controller in Quetta ordered the tenant to vacate, and the tenant appealed to the Balochistan High Court. The High Court upheld the eviction. It found that the tenant's claimed alternate landlord had actually sued in civil court to establish his ownership claim, and that case had been dismissed and never appealed, so it was legally settled against him. Meanwhile, the actual landlord produced official mutation records proving ownership, while the tenant produced no documents proving his own claimed right to possession.

The court also rejected the argument that rent receipts or written agreements were necessary to prove tenancy, holding that a verbal agreement is sufficient under the law. Importantly, the court ruled that when a tenant denies the landlord's title without proof, and is found to actually be a tenant, he effectively becomes a trespasser and forfeits his tenancy, making eviction automatic. This case clarifies that tenants cannot escape eviction merely by disputing ownership unless they can back up that denial with solid evidence.

title: Abdul Aziz and others V. Town Municipal Officer Hub through Administrator Civic Centre Hub and others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute between tenants (shopkeepers) and the Town Municipal Committee, Hub, over rented shops. Earlier, the Balochistan High Court had disposed of an appeal between the parties through a consent order in 2016, which set out three things: the municipal committee would issue allotment letters to the tenants under an existing agreement, the monthly rent would be increased from Rs. 500 to Rs. 2000, and any dispute over previous unpaid rent could be taken to the appropriate court.

The tenants later filed an execution petition asking the Rent Controller to enforce this consent order, particularly the part about issuing allotment letters. The municipal committee objected, and the Rent Controller dismissed the execution petition, reasoning that no landlord-tenant relationship existed when the earlier appeal was filed.

The High Court held that this was wrong. Although the ordinary procedural rules of the Civil Procedure Code do not strictly apply to rent proceedings, the Rent Controller could still use its equitable principles. More importantly, an executing court must act strictly within the terms of the decree it is enforcing, not go beyond it or question its basis. Since the tenants had secured a valid consent decree, the Rent Controller was obliged to enforce it, including resolving the rent arrears issue mentioned in the order, rather than dismissing the execution outright.

The court allowed the appeals and sent the case back to the Rent Controller to decide the execution and objections strictly according to the terms of the original consent order.

title: Muhammad Akram V. Muhammad Khalid,
explainer:
This case was about a landlord-tenant dispute over a shop in Quetta. The landlord, Muhammad Khalid, had rented a shop to tenant Muhammad Akram and later sought to evict him, claiming he genuinely needed the shop for his own personal use—to demolish and rebuild it and start a business, since he could no longer practice law due to illness. The Rent Controller accepted the eviction request and ordered the tenant to vacate. The tenant appealed, arguing among other things that an earlier eviction case on similar grounds had already failed.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the eviction. It clarified that a fresh eviction case is only barred if an earlier case on the same issue was decided on its merits; since the earlier petition had merely been withdrawn (not decided on merits), a new petition was allowed. The court also addressed what happens when a landlord dies during proceedings—ruling that his legal heirs can continue the case, since rights and obligations pass to them and the matter does not end with death.

The court found the landlord's evidence credible and genuine, and held that ownership rights are protected under the Constitution and take precedence over tenancy rights. The tenant was ordered to vacate within two months after paying due rent. The judgment is significant for clarifying procedural rules on repeat eviction cases and continuation of legal proceedings after a party's death.

title: Muhammad Shafiq V. The State ,
explainer:
Muhammad Shafiq was convicted by a trial court in Killa Saifullah for murdering Gul Shah Khan, who was shot while walking toward the National Highway with his son. The trial court sentenced him to death under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, and the case also came before the court as a murder reference for confirmation of the death sentence.

The High Court examined the evidence carefully. The complainant had promptly named the accused in the FIR, and two witnesses, including the deceased's son, gave consistent, truthful, and unshaken accounts of the shooting despite lengthy cross-examination. Their testimony was supported by medical evidence and the recovery of the victim's blood-stained clothes. The court noted that although a pistol was recovered from the accused, it was not sent for forensic testing against the bullet casings found at the scene, so this recovery did not help the prosecution. The court also found no proven motive, but ruled that absence of motive alone does not create doubt when direct eyewitness evidence is strong.

However, considering the lack of established motive and the overall circumstances, the court held that the death penalty was not appropriate. It upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to life imprisonment. This case illustrates how appellate courts in Pakistan can reassess sentencing even while confirming guilt, particularly when circumstances surrounding motive remain unclear.

title: Deputy Commissioner (Revenue)/Collector, Quetta and another V. begum jamila daud and 15 others,
explainer:
This case was about a dispute over how much compensation the government should pay to landowners whose property was taken to widen a road in Quetta (connecting Mastung Road/Arbab Karam Khan Road to Hazar Ganji). The Land Acquisition Collector had awarded compensation based on an average land price calculated over just one year before the acquisition notice. The landowners felt this was too low and challenged it in a reference before the Additional District Judge, who increased the compensation significantly, setting higher rates for commercial land, residential land, and construction costs, plus statutory additions for compulsory acquisition and delayed payment.

The government appealed this increased award to the Balochistan High Court, arguing the original, lower valuation was correct.

The High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the increased compensation. It ruled that using a simple one-year average price is not an adequate or absolute method for valuing acquired land, especially given rising property prices. Citing a Supreme Court precedent, the court held that landowners who sacrifice their property for public projects must be compensated fairly and realistically, considering the land's location, potential, and market value, not through a mechanical formula. Since the acquired land was prime, well-located property, the court found the trial court's enhanced compensation reasonable, not excessive.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that compensation for government land acquisition must reflect true market value and fairness to citizens, not just bureaucratic averages.

title: Ali Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by Ali Muhammad, who had been convicted by a trial court in Lasbela and sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, after being accused along with a co-accused of shooting the complainant's brother and injuring his cousin. The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him, finding the prosecution's evidence riddled with doubt.

The court identified multiple serious problems with the case. The eyewitnesses contradicted each other about who actually fired the shots, and their accounts of the incident did not match. One witness was not even mentioned in the initial police report, suggesting his testimony was added later to patch up the story. There was an unexplained three-hour delay in filing the police report, and the injured witness only sought medical treatment a week after the alleged shooting, despite supposedly having gunshot wounds, which the doctor did not confirm at the first point of contact. Medical evidence also conflicted with witness accounts of how the attack occurred. Additionally, the alleged murder weapon was recovered 19 days after the incident, and it took 24 days to send it for forensic testing, raising serious doubts about its authenticity as evidence. Since a co-accused with a similar alleged role had already been acquitted and not challenged, the court found it unjust to convict this appellant on the same weak evidence.

This case reinforces the principle that even a single reasonable doubt must benefit the accused, and that prosecutions must independently prove their case beyond doubt, not rely on shaky, contradictory evidence.

title: Messrs Ghazi Rice Mills, Sole Proprietorship Ghazi Khan Lashari V. National Bank of Pakistan through Manager,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between Ghazi Rice Mills and the National Bank of Pakistan over an unpaid loan. The mill had obtained financing from the bank in 2008, using its property as security, and later renewed the facility. When the mill defaulted on repayment, the bank sued for recovery of over 12.4 million rupees plus costs. The Banking Court in Quetta ruled in the bank's favor, and the mill appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court rejected the appeal on two grounds. First, under the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001, a defendant seeking permission to contest a recovery suit must specifically detail the loan amount, payments made, dates of payments, and amounts still owed. The mill's defense merely made vague denials and claimed a fire damaged its stock, without properly addressing these legal requirements, so its request to defend the case was rightly rejected by the trial court.

Second, the appeal itself was filed very late - the legal deadline was 30 days after the judgment, but the mill filed after more than 45 days beyond that deadline, offering no credible excuse. The court explained that delays can only be excused if a party shows the delay was unavoidable and not due to negligence, and every day of delay must be justified. Since the mill failed to do this, the court refused to excuse the delay and dismissed the appeal, upholding the bank's right to recover the loan.

title: M. Khalid Aziz V. The State through Director General NAB, Balochistan,
explainer:
This case was about whether a man convicted under Pakistan's anti-corruption law, the National Accountability Ordinance (NAB Ordinance), could get extra time to file his appeal after missing the deadline.

Khalid Aziz, a trader, was accused of colluding with others to fabricate shipping documents and customs paperwork, causing financial loss to the government and a foreign company. He admitted wrongdoing and agreed to voluntarily return around 10 million rupees in illicit gains, but he only paid part of it and kept delaying payment of the rest. He was eventually tried and, on 13 July 2015, disqualified from holding public office for ten years under the relevant provision of the NAB Ordinance after being released on the condition that he return the money.

The law required any appeal against such a decision to be filed within ten days, but Aziz filed his appeal two months late, claiming he was too ill to travel and file on time.

The Balochistan High Court rejected this excuse, noting he was present in court when the judgment was announced, suggesting the delay was deliberate. More importantly, the court ruled that because the NAB Ordinance sets its own specific appeal deadline, the general law allowing courts to excuse delays for good reason (Section 5 of the Limitation Act) does not apply here, due to another provision (Section 29(2)) of the same law. The court therefore refused to excuse the delay and dismissed the appeal, reinforcing that strict, non-extendable deadlines apply to NAB appeals.

title: Abdul Rauf and others V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Services and General Administration Department and others,
explainer:
This case involved a group of job applicants who had applied for various government posts in the Mines and Minerals Department of Balochistan after advertisements in 2017 and 2018. The petitioners sat written tests and interviews conducted by a properly constituted Selection/Recruitment Committee, cleared them, and were placed on a merit list recommending them for appointment. However, instead of issuing appointment orders, the government re-advertised the same posts in 2019, citing delays in completing the recruitment process as the reason.

The petitioners challenged this re-advertisement in the Balochistan High Court, arguing it unfairly denied them jobs they had rightfully earned through a fair and completed selection process.

The High Court ruled in favour of the petitioners. It held that the recruitment process had already been substantively completed, with all key steps—tests, interviews, and recommendations—properly finished. The delay in finalizing appointments was an administrative lapse, not something the candidates were responsible for, and such a minor procedural delay could not be used to cancel the entire selection and start over. The court found no irregularity in how the Selection Committee was formed or how it conducted the process. Citing precedent, it held that once a selection process is validly completed, the authorities lose the power to retract or reverse it arbitrarily. The court ordered the government to verify the petitioners' credentials and issue them appointment orders. This judgment reinforces protection for job candidates against arbitrary government reversals after a fair selection process.

title: Aadil V. The State and another ,
explainer:
This case involved Aadil, who was convicted by a trial court in Turbat under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, for possessing 15 kilograms of charas (a narcotic drug) found during a police raid on his house. The trial court sentenced him to 15 years imprisonment plus a fine, citing mitigating factors such as the police not involving independent witnesses or obtaining a search warrant.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the relevant law closely. Under Section 9(c) of the Act, possession of narcotics exceeding one kilogram can attract punishment ranging from 14 years imprisonment up to death or life imprisonment. However, a proviso to this section specifically states that if the quantity exceeds 10 kilograms, the punishment cannot be less than imprisonment for life.

Since Aadil was caught with 15 kilograms, well above the 10-kilogram threshold, the law mandated a minimum sentence of life imprisonment. The trial court had overlooked this mandatory legal requirement and imposed a lesser sentence of 15 years instead.

The High Court held that this was an error of law that the trial court had missed. As a result, it set aside the trial court's judgment and sent the case back for the sentence to be decided afresh in line with the correct legal requirement. This case highlights how courts must strictly follow mandatory minimum sentencing provisions in narcotics cases, especially for large quantities of drugs, regardless of other circumstances considered during sentencing.

title: Messrs Abaseen ORE through Azmat Khan V. Director General (Licensing Authority) Mines and Minerals, Balochistan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a mining contractor, Abaseen ORE, whose contract for collecting royalty on minor minerals in District Pishin and Killa Abdullah had been terminated by the Mines and Minerals authorities in Balochistan. The contractor had earlier filed a constitutional petition challenging the termination, but the Balochistan High Court dismissed it, finding that the matter involved disputed factual questions (including allegations of foul play) that could not be resolved through constitutional jurisdiction without detailed evidence and investigation.

Unsatisfied with that outcome, the petitioner filed this review application, arguing that the court had overlooked certain constitutional provisions, a section of the General Clauses Act, and some of his counsel's arguments.

The High Court rejected the review application. It explained that review is a very limited remedy, available only when there is an obvious, self-evident error on the face of the record, or when new and important evidence has come to light that could not have been produced earlier. It is not meant to allow re-arguing a case or getting a second opinion on points already decided, even if the original decision might have been wrong. Since the court found that it had already carefully considered all the petitioner's arguments, there was no manifest error justifying review, and the application was dismissed.

This case is useful for understanding how limited the scope of judicial review is in Pakistani law, reinforcing that courts will not reopen settled matters absent a clear, obvious mistake.

title: Attaullah and 9 others V. Zainullah and 20 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over inherited property in Pishin, Balochistan. The plaintiffs (who became petitioners before the High Court) sued their relatives claiming shares in ancestral property left by their late father, seeking declarations of ownership, partition, cancellation of a mutation entry, and other relief. While the suit was pending, the plaintiffs asked the trial court to appoint a receiver to take control of the property and also asked to add a Telenor company official as a party to the case. The trial court rejected both requests, and the District Judge upheld that decision on revision. The plaintiffs then challenged these rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition, agreeing with the lower courts. It explained that appointing a receiver is a serious, drastic remedy that courts should use cautiously, only when it is truly just and convenient to protect property during litigation. A party seeking a receiver must show a strong prima facie case, prove their claim to the property, and demonstrate real risk of loss or misuse of the property - mere apprehension of mismanagement is not enough. Here, the property was already in the defendants' possession, officially recorded in their names, and the plaintiffs had not yet proven their ownership claims at trial, nor shown any urgent emergency. Finding no legal error in the lower courts' decisions, the High Court dismissed the petition outright, reinforcing that receivership is an exceptional remedy, not a routine one.

title: Abdul Bari V. Amir Muhammad and 3 others,
explainer:
This case was about a property dispute under Pakistan's Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005. The petitioner, Abdul Bari, had filed a complaint against the respondents claiming they had illegally dispossessed him of his immovable property. During the trial, he asked the court to summon the local police officer (SHO) to produce a report as evidence, using his right under Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows courts to call witnesses whose evidence is essential for a just decision. The trial court rejected this request, so Abdul Bari challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in his favor. It explained that under Section 540, a court must summon a witness if that person's evidence is material and essential to fairly deciding the case, regardless of whether the witness was named earlier in the investigation or witness list, or when the request is made during the trial. The trial court had failed to properly assess whether the SHO's report was material and necessary, and had wrongly dismissed the application without applying these legal principles. The High Court therefore set aside the trial court's order and directed it to summon the SHO so the document could be formally placed on record.

The case matters because it reinforces that courts cannot arbitrarily refuse to examine potentially crucial evidence, and clarifies when and how parties can request additional witnesses during a trial to ensure a fair and just outcome.

title: Abdul Wadood and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Abdul Wadood and Muhammad Rafiq, who were convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Pishin for a violent incident in 2009 in which gunfire was allegedly exchanged, several vehicles and shops were set on fire, one person was killed, and others were injured. Abdul Wadood was sentenced to death for the murder, while Muhammad Rafiq received a life sentence for causing critical injury to a prosecution witness. Both appealed to the Balochistan High Court, which also reviewed the death sentence as required by law.

The High Court found serious flaws in how the case was investigated and prosecuted. There was unexplained delay in recording witness statements, which courts treat as unreliable. Investigators never confirmed that the burned vehicles and shops actually belonged to the complainant's side, never questioned independent witnesses despite the crowded location of the incident, and failed to send recovered bullet casings for forensic testing. The FIR itself was lodged only after medical and postmortem reports were already available, suggesting the story may have been constructed afterward. The court also noted that abscondence alone cannot prove guilt without solid supporting evidence.

Because the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the High Court set aside both convictions and sentences, acquitting both men. This judgment reinforces important principles in criminal law: investigations must be thorough and impartial, and any genuine doubt in evidence must benefit the accused rather than the prosecution.

title: Abdul Ghafoor and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Abdul Ghafoor and Sher Ahmed, arrested together in a car after police found 2 kilograms of charas and 100 grams of heroin hidden beneath the driving seat. They were charged under Pakistan's narcotics law and sought bail after a lower court had already refused it.

The Balochistan High Court treated the two applicants differently based on their roles. Abdul Ghafoor was the driver of the vehicle at the time of recovery. The court held that a driver cannot escape responsibility when contraband is found being transported in the vehicle he is driving, relying on an earlier precedent. Finding a strong prima facie case against him, the court refused his bail.

Sher Ahmed, however, was merely a passenger sitting in the front seat. He was not driving, and the drugs were not found in his exclusive possession. The court found his situation required further inquiry at trial, a recognized ground for bail, and noted he had already been in custody since February 2020. He was granted bail upon furnishing bonds of Rs. 200,000.

The judgment matters because it illustrates how courts distinguish between a vehicle's driver and its passengers when drugs are discovered in hidden locations within a car, basing bail decisions on possession and control rather than mere presence. It also reaffirms that bail observations are preliminary and do not bind the trial court's final decision on the merits.

title: Iltaf Qadir V. Mst. Mehar Nigar and another,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over the Islamic law right of pre-emption, known as Shufa, which allows certain people—such as co-owners, neighbours, or those sharing rights in a property—to claim priority to purchase land that has been sold to someone else. The petitioner, Iltaf Qadir, claimed this right over land sold by one respondent to another, arguing his own property was adjacent to the disputed land. His suit was dismissed by the trial court and the appellate court, leading him to file this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found two major problems. First, the petitioner failed to properly describe or prove that his land was actually adjacent to the disputed property; in fact, record evidence suggested the properties were in different, non-adjoining areas. Second, pre-emption claims require strict compliance with specific legal formalities: an immediate first demand (Talb-i-Muwathibat) made right after learning of the sale, followed by a formal second demand (Talb-i-Ishhad) made before witnesses, explicitly referencing that the first demand had already been made. The petitioner's plaint lacked essential details—names of witnesses, and the exact date, time, and place these demands were made—making it impossible to prove he had followed the required procedure.

The court ruled these technical requirements are mandatory, not optional, and since they were not met, the suit was correctly rejected. The case reinforces how strictly courts enforce procedural formalities in pre-emption claims under Islamic law.

title: Syed Habibullah V. Syed Abdul Khabeer,
explainer:
This case involved a landlord-tenant dispute under Balochistan's rent laws. The landlord, Syed Abdul Khabeer, sought to evict his tenant, Syed Habibullah, from a shop, claiming the tenant was a bad payer and that the landlord and his brothers genuinely needed the shop to start their own business. The Rent Controller sided with the landlord and ordered the tenant to vacate within thirty days. The tenant appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the eviction order. It found the landlord had failed to prove his claimed need was genuine. Notably, the landlord was simultaneously trying to evict 22 tenants from separate shops on the same personal-need claim, yet he had not obtained municipal permission for any reconstruction or alteration of the building. His brothers, for whom the shops were supposedly needed, were not even named in the eviction application, lived abroad, ran independent businesses, and rarely visited Pakistan. Additionally, the property was actually registered in the landlord's father's name, yet the father was not the one who filed the eviction case.

The court held that while landlords generally have a stronger right to use their own property, tenants cannot be thrown out merely on a landlord's unproven assertions, whims, or desire to raise rents. Genuine "need" must be distinguished from mere "greed." Finding no real proof of bona fide necessity, the High Court accepted the tenant's appeal and dismissed the eviction application.

title: Mir Hussain V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a murder appeal before the Balochistan High Court. The accused, Mir Hassan, had been convicted of killing the complainant's cousin by firing, along with a co-accused, and was appealing that conviction.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the appellant, giving him the benefit of the doubt. The judges found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The eyewitnesses' presence at the crime scene was questionable, since the medical officer said the victim was brought to hospital by twenty unnamed members of the public, not by the complainant or witnesses as claimed. There was also an unexplained two-hour delay in filing the police report, despite the victim dying within minutes and the police station being only six kilometers away, suggesting the complaint may have been crafted after deliberation. Additionally, a key witness's statement was recorded two days late with no explanation, and the prosecution failed to produce the pickup driver who allegedly witnessed the event and drove the victim to hospital, nor did police interview the twenty people who accompanied him.

The court also noted it was implausible that armed attackers firing repeatedly from close range would hit only the victim while sparing nearby witnesses who could identify them.

This case matters because it illustrates how Pakistani courts scrutinize delays in reporting crimes, inconsistencies in witness testimony, and missing evidence to prevent wrongful convictions based on unreliable evidence.

title: Abdul Wahid and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a criminal appeal arising from a firing incident in which one person was killed and several others were injured, allegedly by a group of fourteen accused persons belonging to a rival family. The trial court had convicted some of the accused of murder, attempted murder, and related offences. The convicted persons appealed, while the state also filed an appeal against acquittals of others, and a criminal revision was filed as well.

The High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. It noted that during alleged indiscriminate firing by fourteen armed men, it was implausible that witnesses who were shot in the back could still specifically identify and attribute individual roles to each accused. The complainant and injured witnesses also failed to mention each other's injuries in their statements, further undermining credibility. The FIR was lodged nearly seven hours after the incident, which the court found suspicious, suggesting it was filed only after medical reports were obtained and names were deliberately selected. Additionally, there were unexplained delays and contradictions regarding when witness statements were recorded.

Based on these doubts, the court concluded that the case appeared to be an attempt to falsely implicate as many male members of the rival family as possible. It allowed the appeal against conviction, acquitting the accused.

This judgment reinforces important principles in Pakistani criminal law: unexplained delays in filing FIRs and recording statements, along with implausible eyewitness accounts, can create reasonable doubt sufficient to overturn convictions, even in serious cases involving death.

title: Muhammad Sultan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves Muhammad Sultan, who was arrested after police found 4000 grams of charas (hashish) in a vehicle he was driving, along with two other passengers. He was charged under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, for transporting narcotics.

Sultan had already applied for bail once, and the Balochistan High Court rejected that application on its merits, finding that as the driver of the vehicle, he could not escape liability at that stage of the case. About a month and twenty days later, he filed a second bail application before the same court, essentially repeating his request.

The court dismissed this second application, holding that a repeat bail application can only be filed if there is a genuinely new ground that did not exist when the first application was decided. Since Sultan's lawyer could not point to any fresh ground, and all his previous arguments had already been considered and rejected on merits, the second application was deemed meritless and not maintainable. The court relied on a Supreme Court precedent (State v. Zubair, PLD 1986 SC 173) which clarified that judges need not address every argument separately in detail, and that a prior rejection on merits covers all grounds raised, barring repeat applications without new grounds.

This case matters because it reinforces an important procedural rule: courts will not allow litigants to repeatedly seek bail on the same grounds already rejected, preventing misuse of the judicial process.

title: Asif Khan V. Anti-Terrorism Court Dera Allah Yar and another,
explainer:
This case concerns Asif Khan, who was accused of abducting two men, Mahram Ali and Allah Dina, for ransom along with co-accused, allegedly armed with rocket launchers. An FIR was registered against him under the Pakistan Penal Code for kidnapping for extortion. After investigation, the case was sent for trial before the Anti-Terrorism Court (ATC) in Dera Allah Yar. The accused sought to have the case transferred to an ordinary criminal court instead, arguing it should not be tried as a terrorism case. The trial court rejected this request, and Asif Khan challenged that rejection before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the FIR, investigation records, and statements of the victims, which indicated the abduction was carried out to demand ransom. Under the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, kidnapping or abduction for ransom is specifically listed as an offence that must be tried exclusively by Anti-Terrorism Courts, not ordinary courts. Since the facts of the case fit this definition, the High Court held that the trial court had correctly assumed jurisdiction and framed charges accordingly.

The High Court dismissed the petition, finding no merit in the challenge. This judgment reinforces that cases involving kidnapping for ransom fall squarely within the special jurisdiction of Anti-Terrorism Courts, regardless of attempts to shift them to regular criminal courts, due to the serious and specific nature of the offence as defined by law.

title: Asif Khan V. Anti-Terrorism Court, Dera Allah Yar and another,
explainer:
This case was about which court should hear a kidnapping-for-ransom case: a special Anti-Terrorism Court or an ordinary criminal court. The petitioner, Asif Khan, was accused along with others of forcibly abducting two men from a house in Jhal Magsi district while armed with rocket launchers, demanding a ransom of two million rupees. After the police completed their investigation and the case went to the Anti-Terrorism Court for trial, Khan asked that court to send the case to an ordinary court instead, arguing it did not qualify as terrorism. The Anti-Terrorism Court rejected his request, so he challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower court's decision. It explained that to decide which court has jurisdiction, judges must look tentatively at the FIR, investigation report, and the final police report. Here, the complainant's FIR described an armed abduction for ransom, and the victims themselves, in statements given to police and a magistrate, confirmed they were kidnapped for ransom. The court held that such facts fall squarely within the legal definition of kidnapping for ransom under the Anti-Terrorism Act, which the law specifically assigns to Anti-Terrorism Courts rather than regular courts. The petition was therefore dismissed.

This case matters because it clarifies how courts determine jurisdiction in kidnapping-for-ransom cases, reinforcing that such offenses are treated as terrorism-related and must be tried exclusively in Anti-Terrorism Courts.

title: Abdul Qadeer V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Public Health Engineering and 2 others,
explainer:
This case was filed by Abdul Qadeer, a farmer, asking the Balochistan High Court to cancel a government tender for installing a water supply scheme near Dalbandin, which he claimed was on agricultural land belonging to him and his forefathers. He wanted the land acquired properly under the Land Acquisition Act before any work was done, arguing the tender was illegal and harmful to local people.

The court did not examine the merits of his complaint. Instead, it focused on whether Abdul Qadeer had the legal right to bring such a petition at all. Under Article 199 of Pakistan's Constitution, only an "aggrieved person" whose own legal or fundamental rights have been affected can approach the High Court. After reviewing the land mutation records submitted with the petition, the judge found that Abdul Qadeer was not listed as the owner of the land in question, nor was his name recorded anywhere in the relevant entries. Since he could not show any personal, legal connection to the property, he did not qualify as an "aggrieved person."

Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the court held that a valid constitutional petition requires a genuine, justiciable personal right that has been violated - mere concern or indirect interest is not enough. Because Abdul Qadeer failed to establish this, his petition was dismissed outright without going into the actual dispute over the tender or the land.

This case illustrates an important procedural principle: courts will not hear constitutional complaints unless the person filing has a direct, provable legal stake in the matter.

title: Sanaullah V. Station House Officer Police Station Nushki and 3 others ,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute between the petitioner, Sanaullah, and some private respondents. Sanaullah claimed the respondents were interfering with his property, threatening him, and had damaged his motorcycle, even though a civil court had already ordered the parties to maintain the status quo. When police took no action on his complaint, he approached the Ex-Officio Justice of Peace (the Sessions Judge) under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking for police action. The Sessions Judge directed the police officer (SHO) to place the complaint before a Judicial Magistrate rather than ordering registration of a criminal case (FIR). Sanaullah challenged this direction before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the Sessions Judge's order and dismissed the petition. It explained that the alleged offences, causing damage to property and intentional insult to provoke a breach of peace, are classified as non-cognizable offences under the law. For such offences, police cannot automatically investigate or register a case; instead, under section 155 of the Criminal Procedure Code, they must record the complaint in the police diary and refer the complainant to a Magistrate, who alone can authorize investigation or arrest.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the distinction between cognizable and non-cognizable offences and confirms that for minor offences like property damage or verbal insults, citizens must seek permission from a Magistrate rather than expecting direct police investigation.

title: Muhammad Ismail V. Haji Ghulam Hussain and others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Balochistan. The petitioner, Muhammad Ismail, claimed to be a lawful co-owner of a piece of land called Khushkaba Bazigir, which he said his ancestors purchased from another tribe around 125 years ago under an agreement written in Farsi. He alleged that certain respondents had illegally interfered with the property, dumped construction material on it, and attempted to build a boundary wall. He also claimed that local authorities failed to act against them due to influence. He asked the High Court to declare the interference illegal and order the respondents to stop and remove the material.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition without going into its merits. The judge held that the case involved serious factual disputes, particularly about the authenticity of the old ownership documents, which could not be resolved through the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction. Such questions require detailed evidence and a full trial, which only a civil court can properly conduct after hearing both sides. The court also noted that a party seeking constitutional relief must show a clear, undisputed legal right, which was not the case here since ownership itself was contested.

This case reinforces an important legal principle: the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction is not meant to resolve disputed facts or substitute for ordinary civil litigation, especially in property disputes where alternate remedies exist.

title: Muhammad Ashraf V. The State,
explainer:
Muhammad Ashraf was convicted under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with dishonestly issuing a cheque that later bounces. The complainant, a manager at a trading company, claimed Ashraf had entered into a business partnership with the company, accumulated a large outstanding debt, and issued three cheques to settle it that were later dishonoured due to insufficient funds. Both the trial court and the appellate court convicted Ashraf, sentencing him to three years in prison and a fine.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction on revision. It found serious weaknesses in the prosecution's case: the complainant produced no written partnership agreement or any documents proving the business relationship existed, and could not give basic details about it. The complainant admitted he himself filled in the cheque amounts, undermining the claim that the accused had intentionally issued them. There was also an unexplained six-month delay in filing the FIR, and evidence suggested the complaint was filed only after legal consultation. Additionally, the actual owner of the trading company and his brother were never produced as witnesses, even though their testimony would have been crucial to prove the alleged partnership and debt.

The court held that mere dishonouring of a cheque is not automatically a crime unless dishonest intent is proven. Given these gaps and doubts, the court acquitted Ashraf, setting aside both lower court judgments. The case underscores that cheque-dishonour convictions require solid proof of intent and underlying transactions, not just an unpaid cheque.

title: Asif V.T he State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Asif who was arrested in Hub City, Balochistan, after police allegedly caught him carrying a black bag containing four kilograms of opium. He was charged under Section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, a provision dealing with possession of large quantities of narcotics. After the trial court refused to release him on bail, he approached the Balochistan High Court seeking post-arrest bail.

The High Court dismissed his bail application. The judges noted that Asif was allegedly caught red-handed with the drugs, and that the quantity recovered exceeded the threshold that places the offense in the more serious category under the law. The court emphasized that narcotics offenses are treated as particularly serious because they harm society as a whole, which is why the law itself (Section 51 of the Act) urges caution before granting bail in such cases. The court stated that someone accused of distributing a substance it described as a "deadly poison" to society does not easily qualify for bail unless they can show they meet the specific legal conditions for it.

This case is a useful example of how Pakistani courts generally treat narcotics cases—especially those involving large quantities—more strictly than ordinary offenses when deciding bail applications, reflecting the law's built-in presumption against easy release in such circumstances.
