title: Mohammad Iqbal V. Mohammad Hussain and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta. Mohammad Iqbal claimed ownership of a plot of land and alleged that Mohammad Hussain had illegally occupied it and built shops on it. Iqbal had earlier filed a civil suit in 2014 over the same property and cause of action, but that suit was withdrawn unconditionally through his lawyer. Later, in 2017, Iqbal filed a fresh suit seeking the same reliefs - declaration, possession, and permanent injunction - against the same opponent over the same property. The trial court initially allowed this second suit to proceed, but on appeal, the Additional District Judge rejected the plaint, ruling that filing a second suit after an unconditional withdrawal of the first was not legally permissible.

Iqbal challenged this rejection before the Balochistan High Court, arguing his lawyer had withdrawn the earlier suit without his authority and through fraud. The High Court dismissed his petition. It held that under Order XXIII, Rule 1(3) of the Civil Procedure Code, once a suit is withdrawn unconditionally, it is treated as dismissed, finally disposing of the matter and barring any fresh suit on the same cause of action between the same parties. The court also noted that if Iqbal believed the withdrawal was fraudulent or unauthorized, his proper remedy was to file an application under Section 12(2) of the CPC before the trial court, not a fresh suit. This case underscores an important procedural rule: withdrawing a suit without permission to refile

title: Rehmatullah and 5 others V. Aziz Ullah and another,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of a man named Azizullah, who had been accused of murdering Attaullah by stabbing him with a knife. The incident occurred at Azizullah's house, where the deceased was reportedly a guest. The victim's brother filed the murder case after being told his brother was found injured and later died from his wounds.

The prosecution had no direct eyewitness to the stabbing itself. The case relied entirely on circumstantial evidence. Notably, witness testimony showed that it was Azizullah himself who alerted a neighbor about the injured man and actively helped transport the victim to the hospital, even staying there afterward without attempting to flee. The court found it illogical that someone who had just committed a violent murder in his own home would then seek help to save the victim's life rather than escape. There was also no evidence of any motive or enmity between the accused and the deceased.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the trial court's acquittal, emphasizing key legal principles: in cases based on circumstantial evidence, the chain of proof must be complete and point unerringly to guilt, leaving no room for innocence. Courts must give the "benefit of doubt" to an accused when the prosecution's case has gaps. Additionally, an acquittal carries a "double presumption of innocence," meaning appellate courts should only overturn it in cases of serious injustice, not merely because another view is possible. The appeal was dismissed.

title: Muhammad Jamshed Khan V. Alamgeer and another,
explainer:
This case was an appeal against an acquittal in a murder case from Balochistan. The complainant alleged that his brother Javed was shot dead by two men, Din Muhammad and Alamgeer, who were hiding near a mosque, during a land dispute. The trial court acquitted Alamgeer (and earlier, other co-accused including Din Muhammad, Lal Muhammad and Sher Muhammad had also been acquitted). The complainant challenged Alamgeer's acquittal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. It noted that the complainant himself was not an eyewitness, and the two eyewitnesses who testified had attributed the same role to both Alamgeer and Din Muhammad, who had already been acquitted by the court on the very same evidence. The judges applied the legal principle "falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus" (false in one thing, false in everything), holding that if witnesses were disbelieved regarding one accused, their testimony could not selectively be trusted against another accused facing identical allegations, without independent corroboration. The court also noted that mere absconding by an accused is not enough to prove guilt unless supported by other evidence.

The court reaffirmed that an acquittal carries a double presumption of innocence and can only be overturned if it is clearly perverse or leads to a miscarriage of justice—not simply because another view is possible. The appeal was dismissed, reinforcing protections against inconsistent treatment of co-accused based on the same evidence.

title: Abdul Khaliq V. Sher Ali and 3 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a criminal appeal in Balochistan arising from a dispute between the complainant, Abdul Khaliq, and four accused persons. The complainant alleged that during a civil dispute, the accused attacked him and his companion, Bashir Ahmed, causing injuries. A trial court acquitted three of the accused, finding contradictions between witness statements and medical evidence, and Abdul Khaliq appealed against this acquittal.

The High Court dismissed the appeal outright. It found two major problems. First, the evidence itself was weak and contradictory: the injured witness claimed fractured hands, but the medical certificate did not record this; and the complainant claimed he suffered deep injuries, but the doctor testified she found no injuries on his body at all. Second, and more importantly, the court ruled that Abdul Khaliq had no legal right to bring this appeal in the first place. Under the law, only a "person aggrieved" can appeal an acquittal in injury cases, and this must be the actual injured victim (unless that person is a minor or insane). Since Abdul Khaliq himself was not injured, he could not file the appeal — only Bashir Ahmed, the injured party, could have done so, and he chose not to.

The judgment reinforces an important principle: acquittals carry a "double presumption of innocence" and should not be overturned unless clearly unjust, and only the actual aggrieved victim has standing to challenge such acquittals in hurt cases.

title: Abdullah Umar V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns Abdullah Umar, who was arrested for collecting donations for a banned organization, Falah-e-Insaniat Foundation. He was caught after a police constable, acting on a tip-off, gave him money which he accepted and for which he issued a receipt. He was charged under the Anti-Terrorism Act for supporting a proscribed organization. At trial, he pleaded guilty and confessed, and despite being warned of the consequences, he stuck to his confession. The trial court convicted him and gave relatively lenient sentences of six months imprisonment with small fines.

He then tried to appeal, but filed his case late - about five months behind the fifteen-day deadline set by the Anti-Terrorism Act for such appeals. He asked the court to excuse this delay under the general Limitation Act.

The Balochistan High Court rejected both his conviction appeal and his request to excuse the delay. It held that since he had pleaded guilty, the law only allowed him to challenge the fairness of his sentence, not his conviction itself. It also ruled that the Anti-Terrorism Act, being a special law with its own strict appeal deadline, overrides the general Limitation Act, and since the Anti-Terrorism Act contains no provision allowing delays to be forgiven, the court could not extend the deadline. The appeal was dismissed.

title: Jan Muhammad V. Humaira Allah Dita and another ,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a dispute over dower, dowry articles, and maintenance. The wife had filed a family suit against her husband seeking these claims. The husband contested the suit and, during the evidence stage, filed an application asking the Family Court to send a document called the Qabeen Nama (a marriage-related document dated 31.12.2011) for expert examination, alleging that its back portion had been tampered with in the wife's favor. He relied on Article 59 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order (the law of evidence) and Section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code.

The Family Judge dismissed this application, and the husband challenged that dismissal before the High Court through a constitutional petition.

The High Court upheld the Family Court's decision. It explained that the Family Courts Act, 1964 was specifically designed to resolve family disputes quickly and simply, cutting through technical legal procedures. Under Section 17 of that Act, the normal rules of the Civil Procedure Code and the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order do not strictly apply to family court proceedings. Citing a Supreme Court precedent, the Court reaffirmed that this exclusion exists precisely to avoid technical delays and ensure speedy justice in family matters.

As a result, the petition was dismissed, confirming that family courts have discretion to bypass such technical evidentiary applications in the interest of swift resolution of family disputes.

explainer:

title: Muhammad Yasir Nazeer V. Lubna Kosar and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a marriage dispute. The wife had sued for dissolution of her marriage along with recovery of dower, dowry articles, and maintenance, alleging cruelty, misconduct, and non-maintenance by her husband. The Family Court ruled in her favor, dissolving the marriage on grounds of cruelty and ordering payment of dower, maintenance, medical expenses, and return of gold ornaments and other items. The husband appealed, but the appellate court returned his appeal, saying it had no jurisdiction to hear it.

The husband then approached the Balochistan High Court. The key legal question was whether an appeal against a marriage dissolved on the ground of cruelty was allowed, given that the Family Courts Act generally bars appeals against dissolution decrees except in one specific situation involving a husband's inability to maintain his wife due to impotence. The High Court held that appeals against dissolution of marriage are barred except in that narrow circumstance, so the husband could not challenge the dissolution itself. However, the court found that the appellate court had wrongly refused to hear the parts of the appeal relating to dower, maintenance, gold ornaments, and medical expenses, since those issues were not covered by the same bar. The court also clarified that cruelty under the law includes mental and behavioral mistreatment, not just physical violence. The petition was partly allowed, restoring the appeal on the financial matters.

title: Saleh Muhammad V. Executive Engineer Irrigation and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a piece of land in Quetta. The petitioner, Saleh Muhammad, claimed he had purchased the property from its previous owner, Rasool Bakhsh, and was living on it. He filed a lawsuit asking the court to declare his ownership and to issue a permanent injunction stopping the Irrigation Department and other officials from interfering with his property. Along with the suit, he asked for a temporary injunction to maintain the status quo while the case was being decided.

The Irrigation Department opposed this, arguing that the land had actually been acquired by the government back in 1991 for use as a flood/rain drainage channel, and that compensation had been paid to the original owners at that time, even though the acquisition was never formally updated in the official revenue records.

Both the trial court and the appellate court refused to grant the temporary injunction, and the petitioner then approached the Balochistan High Court. The High Court upheld these decisions. It explained that simply having an arguable case is not enough to get an injunction; courts must also weigh whether the balance of convenience and risk of irreparable harm favor the person seeking it. Since government records showed the land had already been acquired and paid for, the court found the petitioner failed to establish a strong enough case or convenience in his favor, and dismissed his petition.

title: Akbar Harifal and another V. Zahid Noor and 3 others ,
explainer:
This case came from the Balochistan High Court, where two petitioners (levies officials) challenged an order directing police to register a criminal case against them. The dispute arose after a road accident: a passenger van collided with the petitioners' official vehicle. One petitioner said the respondent forcibly stopped their vehicle, got into an argument, and tore a levies official's shirt, after which the respondent was arrested and an FIR was registered against him the same day. The respondent, however, claimed he was forcibly abducted, tortured, and wrongfully confined for ten hours by the petitioners before being handed over to police on a false FIR. He got a lower court (acting as Ex-officio Justice of Peace) to order registration of a criminal case against the petitioners, without giving them a chance to be heard first.

The High Court set aside that order. It found no medical evidence supporting the respondent's torture claims, noted that the FIR against him was lodged and he was arrested the very same day (undermining his wrongful confinement claim), and concluded his application appeared aimed at harassing the public servants rather than seeking genuine justice.

The judgment reaffirms an important principle: a Justice of Peace cannot mechanically order FIR registration just because someone alleges wrongdoing. They must apply judicial mind and ensure there's credible supporting material, since the power under Section 22-A Cr.P.C. is discretionary ("may," not "shall") and meant to prevent misuse of the criminal justice system to harass people.

title: Naseebullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns a criminal trial arising from an attack in which a man and his group allegedly injured the complainant's party and damaged property. During the trial, after six prosecution witnesses had already testified, the complainant asked the trial court to allow four additional people to be examined as witnesses, even though they had not been listed in the original calendar of witnesses or had their statements recorded by police during investigation. The trial court allowed this, and the accused's revision petition against that decision was also dismissed by the Additional Sessions Judge. The accused then challenged both orders before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the lower courts' decisions. It explained that under Section 265-F of the Criminal Procedure Code, courts are legally required to take all evidence offered in support of the prosecution, and there is no rule limiting the prosecution to only those witnesses already named. A witness can be refused only if summoning them would cause unnecessary delay or defeat justice. The court also clarified that failing to record a witness's statement during police investigation does not bar that person from later testifying at trial, for either side. This ruling reinforces that trial courts have limited grounds to refuse witness testimony and that technical omissions during investigation do not automatically exclude relevant evidence from being heard.

title: United Bank Ltd. Through Regional Chief Executive UBL through Manager Shara-e-Hali Quetta V. Fareedullah Khan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a bank employee, Fareedullah Khan, who worked as a cashier at United Bank Limited. After being transferred from Quetta to Sohbat Pur, he failed to report for duty, citing illness and domestic problems. Following an inquiry, the bank terminated his employment in 2007 for continuous absence.

He appealed internally and then through the labour courts. The Labour Court upheld his termination, but on appeal, the Labour Appellate Tribunal partly sided with him, reducing the penalty from termination to compulsory retirement instead. The bank was unhappy with this reduction and challenged it before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the Tribunal's decision and dismissed the bank's petition. The judges reasoned that while the employee's absence from duty was indeed proven, there was no evidence that he was a habitual offender who repeatedly absented himself. Given his long service of 19 years and an otherwise clean record, outright termination without any benefits was too harsh a punishment. The court emphasized the legal principle that punishment should be proportionate to the wrongdoing, citing precedents that recognize mercy as the rule and severe punishment as the exception, especially for first-time or less serious infractions.

This case matters because it reinforces worker protections against disproportionate disciplinary action, affirming that employers and tribunals must weigh an employee's overall service record and the severity of misconduct before imposing career-ending penalties like termination without benefits.

title: Zahid and other V. Mst Sadia and others,
explainer:
This case involved a landlord-tenant dispute under the Balochistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959. Mst. Sadia, the landlady, owned five shops in Quetta that had been rented out for decades to several tenants, including the appellants. She filed an application to evict them, stating she needed the shops for her personal residential use. Her plan was to close the shops and convert them into rooms to be joined with her adjacent house, since her current living situation with her husband's family was cramped and she had no independent accommodation.

The tenants opposed this, arguing the eviction request was made in bad faith to pressure them, that the shops were in a commercial area unsuitable for conversion to residential use, and that losing their long-established businesses would cause them serious harm. They also argued the landlady had not obtained official permission to convert the property's use.

The Rent Controller ruled in favor of the landlady and ordered eviction. The tenants appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the eviction order. It held that the law only requires permission to convert a residential property into a commercial one, not the reverse, so the landlady did not need prior approval. It also found her testimony credible and consistent, and that the tenants failed to disprove her genuine need during cross-examination. The court further emphasized that an owner's property rights outweigh a tenant's rights, and tenants cannot dictate whether an owner's need is sufficient. Both appeals were dismissed.

title: Wahid Bakhsh V. Achar,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a landlord and an alleged tenant over a grocery shop in Hub, Balochistan. The landlord, Achar, filed an application to evict Wahid Bakhsh, claiming he was his tenant who had defaulted on rent and was needed for personal use. Wahid Bakhsh denied that any landlord-tenant relationship existed between them at all. The Rent Controller sided with the landlord and ordered eviction, relying on documents such as mutation entries, a map prepared by a government official, a Tehsildar's report, and a land revenue decision, which supposedly proved the landlord's ownership and the tenancy relationship.

The Balochistan High Court overturned this decision. It found that these crucial documents were never properly proved in court, as required by law. Nobody who had signed or issued the documents was called as a witness, and no other evidence confirmed their authenticity. The court explained that simply having documents on file isn't enough; they must be formally proved, especially when their authorship or origin is disputed, so the other side can test them through cross-examination.

Since the eviction order rested entirely on unproven documents, the High Court ruled it was legally unsound. It set aside the ejectment order and sent the case back to the Rent Controller to be decided again, this time following proper legal procedure for presenting and proving evidence. The appeal was allowed, reinforcing that courts cannot rely on documents that have not been properly authenticated in legal proceedings.

title: Syed Bakhtiar Ahmed V. Rana Muhammad Osaf and 2 others ,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over bail conditions in a cheque dishonour case. The respondent had been accused of issuing a dishonoured cheque worth Rs. 50,00,000, an offence under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code. After his arrest, he was granted bail by a magistrate, but only on condition that he furnish surety equal to the full cheque amount. He later applied to reduce this amount and was allowed to deposit a smaller cash surety of Rs. 300,000 instead. However, the trial court subsequently tried to make him submit the remaining surety amount as well. He challenged this before the Sessions Court, which set aside the trial court's orders demanding the additional surety. The petitioner, who had originally filed the case against him, then approached the High Court to have the Sessions Court's order overturned.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition and upheld the Sessions Court's decision. It ruled that there is no fixed rule requiring surety amounts to automatically match the cheque amount in such cases. The purpose of surety is only to ensure the accused attends court hearings, not to punish him or make bail unaffordable. Courts must set reasonable surety based on the facts of each case, considering the nature of the offence.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that bail conditions should not be used as a tool to penalize or financially burden the accused, protecting the fundamental right to reasonable bail.

title: Hadayatullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Hadayatullah who was accused of selling a stolen Honda City car to a complainant for Rs. 850,000. The car was later discovered to have been stolen in an earlier case registered in Punjab, and its registration book turned out to be forged. Based on these allegations, a police case (FIR) was registered against him in Quetta under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with forgery, using forged documents, and cheating.

The applicant sought pre-arrest bail, meaning protection from arrest while the case proceeded, after a lower court had already refused him such protection. The Balochistan High Court examined the timeline of events and noted that the FIR was lodged more than three months after the complainant first approached police, and that police had conducted a preliminary inquiry before registering the case. The court found this delay suspicious, suggesting possible bad faith or mala fide intent behind the prosecution.

The judge also noted that the offenses involved did not fall under the "prohibitory clause" of the bail law, meaning they were not among the most serious crimes where bail is harder to get, and that investigation had already been completed. Given these circumstances, the court decided the matter required further inquiry rather than immediate arrest, and confirmed the pre-arrest bail earlier granted to the applicant.

This case illustrates how courts weigh delays in filing police complaints and signs of possible misuse of the criminal process when deciding bail applications.

title: Hatim Ameer Baloch V. Shahbana Khuda Bakhsh and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over who was entitled to receive the pension of a deceased government employee, Khuda Bakhsh, who had worked as a Section Officer in the Civil Secretariat in Quetta. After his death, his widow, Shahbana Khuda Bakhsh, applied to the District Judge in Mastung for a succession certificate to claim his monthly pension. The trial court granted her request but rejected a competing claim made by the deceased's son, Hatim Ameer Baloch, who then appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The son argued that his mother was not truly dependent on his late father, since she herself was a government employee earning a salary. The High Court examined the relevant pension rules and a Supreme Court precedent, which clarified that certain benefits like pension, gratuity, and insurance payable after a government servant's death are meant for the family left behind, rather than being treated as the deceased's personal assets to be divided among all heirs under normal inheritance rules.

Based on these pension rules, which specifically identify the widow as the primary recipient of family pension, the High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It found no legal error in granting the pension to the widow and dismissed the son's appeal.

This case matters because it clarifies that pension benefits for deceased government employees are governed by specific pension rules favoring the surviving spouse, rather than ordinary inheritance law.

title: Shaban Khuda Bakhsh V. Hatima Ameer and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a family dispute over money left in a deceased man's bank account. After Khuda Bakhsh died, his son applied for a succession certificate under the Succession Act, 1925, so that the money in his father's National Bank account could be legally distributed among the heirs. The deceased's widow objected, claiming that a large part of the amount did not belong to the estate at all, arguing it was actually proceeds from the sale of two plots that she co-owned with her husband, and that only a smaller amount should be divided among the legal heirs.

The trial court examined the claims and issued a succession certificate dividing the full amount among the son, widow, and daughter according to their Islamic inheritance shares. The widow challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision and dismissed the appeal. It explained that succession certificate proceedings are meant to be quick and summary, not detailed trials. Complicated questions about who actually owns disputed property, such as the widow's claim over the sale proceeds, cannot be properly resolved in this limited process. Such ownership disputes must instead be decided through a full civil lawsuit where evidence can be thoroughly examined.

This case is important because it clarifies the limited scope of succession certificate proceedings and confirms that real estate or property ownership disputes among heirs require a separate, full court suit rather than being settled in summary inheritance proceedings.

title: Muhammad Naseem V. Vice-Chancellor Bolan University of Health Sciences, Quetta through Registrar and another,
explainer:
This case involved a student, Muhammad Naseem, who had passed the MDCAT entrance test for medical college admission with over 71% marks and expected his name to appear on the district merit list for MBBS admission at Bolan University of Health Sciences, Quetta. When the tentative merit list was published, his name was missing, even though students with lower marks were included. He claimed he had tried repeatedly to contact and visit the university office but was blocked by a staff strike and then by heavy snowfall on the roads. By the time he submitted written objections, the admission process was already complete, so he approached the Balochistan High Court asking it to order the university to include his name on the merit list.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It found that merely passing the MDCAT test was not enough: candidates also had to separately apply online, submit hard copies of their application, pay the required fee, and appear for interview by the university's set deadline. The record showed the petitioner had done none of this, and he only raised his objection weeks after the final deadline had passed. By then, the admission session had already started and other candidates had been lawfully selected. The court held that it could only intervene under Article 199 of the Constitution to correct genuine jurisdictional errors or illegality, and since the university had followed proper procedure, there was no error to correct. A person's own carelessness cannot justify displacing students who were validly admitted.

title: Bibi Quresh V. The Government of Balochistan, through Secretary Home and Tribal Affairs Department and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta. Bibi Quresh filed a constitutional petition before the Balochistan High Court, asking it to stop government authorities from dispossessing her from a piece of property she claimed was disputed. She also wanted the court to declare that officials had acted illegally by treating the property as undisputed and potentially favoring another private party in the matter.

However, the court discovered that Bibi Quresh had already filed a separate civil suit for declaration and permanent injunction over the same property before a Civil Judge in Quetta, and that case was still pending. Additionally, her lawyer repeatedly failed to appear in court on multiple hearing dates, suggesting a lack of interest in pursuing the constitutional petition.

The High Court ruled that since she already had an adequate alternate legal remedy through her pending civil suit, it was not appropriate for her to also seek relief through the High Court's special constitutional jurisdiction. Citing Supreme Court precedents, the judges reaffirmed the principle that constitutional petitions should not be entertained when a party is already pursuing the same issue through ordinary civil litigation. As a result, the petition was dismissed outright.

This case matters because it reinforces an important legal principle: courts expect people to use the normal legal channels available to them (like civil suits) rather than jumping straight to higher constitutional remedies, except in cases where no other adequate remedy exists.

title: Sadia Gill V. Vishal Masih and another,
explainer:
This case involved a married Christian couple, Sadia Gill and Vishal Masih, whose marriage was breaking down. The husband, Vishal Masih, filed a suit in the Civil Court at Muslim Bagh seeking judicial separation and divorce on the ground that his wife had deserted him. The wife challenged this, arguing that she was now living in Quetta and that the dispute arose there too, so the Muslim Bagh court had no authority to hear the case. She asked for the plaint to be returned so the case could be refiled in Quetta.

The trial court rejected her request, and she challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the Divorce Act, 1869, which specifically defines which court has jurisdiction in such matrimonial cases: either the court where the husband and wife last resided together, or the court where both currently reside, even if separately. The evidence showed the couple married in Quetta but last lived together in Muslim Bagh, so that location qualified as proper jurisdiction under the first option.

The court also clarified that the general rule under the Civil Procedure Code, which normally allows a suit to be filed where the defendant resides, does not apply when a special law like the Divorce Act already specifies jurisdiction. Special laws override general procedural rules.

The High Court therefore upheld the trial court's decision and dismissed the wife's petition, confirming that Muslim Bagh was the correct venue for the case.

title: The State V. Syed Amir Muhammad,
explainer:
This case involved an application by the state, through the Anti-Narcotics Force, to cancel bail that had been granted to Syed Amir Muhammad, who was accused of carrying 4 kilograms of methamphetamine (ice) in a bag. He was arrested in Kuchlak, Balochistan, after officials received a tip that he was selling the drug near schools and language centers.

The trial court had granted him post-arrest bail after seven months in custody, reasoning that prosecution witnesses had failed to appear for several hearings, that no private witnesses such as teachers or students were associated with the case despite allegations of selling drugs near schools, and that a forensic report was doubtful.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed and cancelled the bail. It held that the absence of private witnesses was not a valid ground for bail in narcotics cases, since the law governing such cases specifically excludes the usual requirement of associating independent witnesses with searches. The court also found that the trial court had gone too far by deeply evaluating the evidence at the bail stage, when only a preliminary assessment is appropriate. Additionally, the High Court noted that courts should be cautious about granting bail when a trial is near its final stage.

This judgment reinforces that in serious narcotics cases, bail should not be granted based on technical evidentiary gaps that are meant to be examined at trial, not at the bail stage.

title: Ghulam Dastagir alias Dodo V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case concerns Ghulam Dastagir, who had been sentenced to death for murder, a sentence later reduced to life imprisonment by the Balochistan High Court and upheld by the Supreme Court. While in prison, he pursued education and, on that basis, asked the court to direct prison authorities to grant him special remission in his sentence, specifically the remission announced by the President of Pakistan under Article 45 of the Constitution.

The government pointed out that presidential notifications granting such special remissions explicitly excluded certain categories of prisoners, including those convicted of murder, espionage, terrorism, kidnapping, and similar serious offences. Since the petitioner was convicted of murder, he fell into the excluded category and was not entitled to this particular remission, even though he had already received other remissions available to ordinary prisoners.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the government. Relying on a Supreme Court ruling, it held that the President can lawfully classify prisoners and withhold remission benefits from those convicted of heinous crimes, as this distinction is reasonable and not discriminatory under the Constitution. Since such prisoners are not in the same position as ordinary convicts, excluding them from special remission does not violate equality rights.

The court therefore dismissed the petition, confirming that prisoners convicted of murder and similar serious crimes cannot claim special presidential remissions when they are expressly excluded by the relevant notifications.

title: Muhammad Ashraf Magsi V. Mst. Shafiqa Akbar and another,

The wife had filed a suit seeking dissolution of her marriage on grounds of cruelty, stating she was willing to give up her dower rights, along with a claim for return of a laptop. The husband contested the suit and filed a written statement, but despite being given several opportunities by the Family Court to appear for mandatory pre-trial reconciliation proceedings, he repeatedly failed to show up. As a result, the trial court struck off his right to defend the case and proceeded to hear only the wife's evidence, eventually granting the divorce.

The husband challenged this before the High Court, arguing that the family court had no specific legal power to strike off a defendant's right to defend simply for not attending reconciliation hearings.

The High Court disagreed and dismissed his petition. title: Jahanzaib V. The State,
explainer:
This appeal concerns a man convicted by the Anti-Terrorism Court in Turbat for allegedly supplying goods to members of a banned organization, the Baloch Liberation Army. He had pleaded guilty to charges under the Anti-Terrorism Act, and the trial court convicted and sentenced him to prison terms and fines based solely on that guilty plea, without a trial.

The Balochistan High Court found serious problems with how this conviction was obtained. The accused had no lawyer, and the trial court never asked him whether he wanted one. There was no record showing he had been given copies of key documents, such as the FIR and witness statements, which the law requires be provided to an accused person before trial. The court also found that the charge itself was not properly framed as required by law, and that it failed to spell out the essential elements of the specific offenses he was accused of.

The High Court held that when someone pleads guilty, the charge must be read and judged strictly, and a conviction cannot stand if facts necessary to prove the offense are missing, even if the accused admits guilt. It also clarified that while someone who pleads guilty generally cannot appeal their conviction, higher courts still retain the power to examine whether that conviction was lawful.

As a result, the court set aside the conviction and sentence and sent the case back for a fresh trial, ensuring the accused gets a fair process, including proper legal representation and access to case documents.

title: Naseer Ahmed V. Sumeyya and another,
explainer:
This case is about a family dispute before the Balochistan High Court involving a wife's suit for dissolution of marriage. Originally, the wife had filed her case seeking divorce on the ground of cruelty, along with claims for dower, dowry articles, and maintenance. After reconciliation efforts between the spouses failed and the case moved toward evidence, the wife asked the Family Court for permission to amend her suit, changing the basis of her divorce claim from cruelty to khula (a wife's right to seek dissolution of marriage). The Family Court allowed this amendment and also directed the couple to appear again for reconciliation. The husband challenged this decision, arguing the Family Court should not have allowed such a change.

The High Court dismissed the husband's petition, ruling that the Family Court had acted within its powers. It held that Family Courts have broad authority to manage their own proceedings to ensure the quick and fair resolution of family disputes, especially since the Family Courts Act does not cover every possible situation. Allowing the amendment served the best interests of both parties by avoiding a fresh, time-consuming lawsuit. The court also emphasized that reconciliation efforts can be ordered at any stage of the case, not just at the beginning.

This decision matters because it confirms that Family Courts have flexibility to adapt proceedings practically, prioritizing speedy resolution and reconciliation in sensitive marital disputes over rigid procedural technicalities.

title: Rakhshanda Jamal V. Shahid-Ul-Hassan and 2 others ,
explainer:
This case was decided by the Balochistan High Court on a petition filed by Rakhshanda Jamal, who was seeking reinvestigation of a case involving the alleged abduction of her two daughters. The accused had already been tried: police had completed their investigation, submitted the charge sheet, the trial court framed charges, and prosecution evidence had already been recorded. At that late stage, while the case was awaiting defense evidence, the petitioner asked the trial court to order a fresh investigation by the Crimes Branch. The trial court rejected this request, and she challenged that rejection before the High Court.

The High Court dismissed her petition, holding that the legal provisions she relied on (sections 22-A and 22-B of the Criminal Procedure Code) exist to give citizens a remedy against police failures, such as refusal to register a case or improper investigation. However, these provisions are not meant to be used to interfere once a case has already gone to trial and reached an advanced stage. The court noted that reinvestigation is permissible before a case is finally decided, but not as a tool to disrupt ongoing trial proceedings, especially when no new facts had been presented to justify it.

This ruling matters because it clarifies the limits of using police-oversight provisions to interfere with judicial proceedings already underway, reinforcing that courts, not reinvestigation requests, should determine the outcome once trial has progressed significantly.

title: Para Din V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Para Din, who was accused of abducting four young children belonging to his brother's wife, Bibi Sira. The complainant alleged that her husband was a drug addict, that she lived separately with her children at her father's house, and that the petitioner, along with relatives, forcibly took her four children, aged between one and seven years. The children were later recovered by police from a room in a dairy farm in Quetta, not a residential home.

The trial court convicted Para Din under Section 363 of the Pakistan Penal Code (kidnapping) and sentenced him to three years' imprisonment plus a fine. His appeal was dismissed, and he then filed this criminal revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The petitioner argued that the children's own father had taken them, claiming lawful guardianship. However, evidence showed the father was actually in jail at the time of the abduction and had multiple prior narcotics convictions, discrediting this defense. The court held that being the children's uncle did not entitle Para Din to their custody, and that only a father could claim the legal exception under Section 361 PPC, and only if acting in good faith for lawful purposes.

Finding the complainant's and witnesses' testimony consistent and credible, and no legal errors in the lower courts' judgments, the High Court dismissed the revision petition and upheld the conviction. The case reinforces that only legitimate guardians can claim exceptions to kidnapping charges, and relatives have no automatic right to take children from their lawful custodian.

title: Abid Ali and another V. Muhammad Tahir and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over property left by a deceased man, Ghulam Sabir, between his children. Some of the legal heirs (the petitioners) claimed they were the rightful owners of certain properties based on a Will their father had made during his lifetime, which they said gave them exclusive rights. Other legal heirs (the respondents) disputed this, saying they had never agreed to such a Will and that it did not comply with Islamic law. They wanted the property divided among all heirs according to Sharia inheritance shares.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled against the petitioners, finding that the Will could not override the rights of heirs who never consented to it. The Balochistan High Court, hearing the case in its revisional jurisdiction, upheld these decisions.

The High Court explained a key principle of Islamic law: a person can only bequeath up to one-third of their property through a Will, and any bequest to a legal heir beyond that is invalid unless all other legal heirs voluntarily consent to it. Since the other heirs here did not consent and actively contested the Will, it could not be enforced in the petitioners' favor. Instead, the property had to be distributed through normal inheritance rules among all heirs.

This case reinforces an important protection in Islamic inheritance law: a parent cannot sideline some legal heirs in favor of others through a Will unless everyone agrees, ensuring fairer distribution of inherited property.

title: Muhammad Ibrahim V. Mahrban Khan and 5 others,
explainer:
This case was heard by the Balochistan High Court on a civil revision petition filed by Muhammad Ibrahim against Mahrban Khan and others. The dispute arose from a lawsuit about an agricultural land-sharing agreement, where the original plaintiff (respondent No.1) had sued seeking cancellation of an agreement, alleging that his partner had taken over jointly cultivated land and crops instead of sharing proceeds as agreed.

The defendant had earlier filed an application asking the trial court to reject the plaint, but the trial court dismissed that request. While an appeal against this dismissal was pending, the plaintiff suddenly asked the appellate court for permission to withdraw his suit with the right to file a fresh one. The appellate court granted this request the very same day, without giving detailed reasons.

The High Court found this improper. Under Order XXIII of the Civil Procedure Code, a court can only permit withdrawal-with-liberty-to-refile if it is satisfied there are genuine, sufficient grounds, and it must explain those reasons in a reasoned order. This safeguards against misuse of the withdrawal process to gain unfair advantage or harass the opposing party. Since the appellate court gave no such justification, the High Court set aside its order and sent the case back for a proper decision on the original appeal regarding rejection of the plaint.

The case highlights that courts must give reasoned decisions when allowing withdrawal of lawsuits, protecting defendants from tactical or unfair litigation maneuvers.

title: Muhammad Owais V Aawal Khan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a murder complaint where the complainant, Muhammad Owais, alleged that the accused, Awal Khan, and others shot and killed his brother. Medical examinations by two doctors concluded the victim died from firearm injuries to the skull. During investigation, the accused was arrested and requested the court to exhume the victim's body for a fresh post-mortem to verify the cause of death. The trial magistrate allowed this, and a revision petition against that order was also dismissed. The brother then approached the Balochistan High Court to quash the exhumation order.

The High Court ruled in favor of quashing the exhumation order. It held that exhumation was not necessary since the cause of death had already been clearly established through medical certificates from two doctors and a police investigation report, all consistently pointing to firearm injuries as the cause of death. The court explained that if the accused doubted the medical findings, the proper remedy was to challenge the doctors through cross-examination during trial, or present rebuttal expert testimony-not to seek physical exhumation of the body. The court also noted the request came six months after the death, making it more of an academic exercise than a genuine investigative necessity, and that the law on exhumation primarily concerns deaths occurring in police custody, which was not the situation here.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the limited circumstances under which courts should order exhumation, protecting the dignity of the deceased and preventing misuse of such requests as a delaying tactic in criminal trials when cause of death is already medically established.

title: Mujeeb-Ur-Rehman V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted separately in two different trials for stealing two different cars, based on two separate police complaints filed months apart. In each case, he was convicted under Section 381-A of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to three years' rigorous imprisonment plus a fine. His appeals against both convictions were dismissed by the Sessions Judge, after which he filed revision petitions before the Balochistan High Court.

Before the High Court, his lawyer did not contest the convictions themselves but asked that the two sentences be allowed to run concurrently (at the same time) rather than one after the other, relying on provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code. The State did not object.

The court explained that one provision (Section 35) only allows concurrent sentences when a person is convicted of multiple offences in a single trial—which was not the situation here, since these were separate trials for separate thefts committed at different times and places. However, another provision (Section 397) gives courts discretion to order sentences from different trials to run concurrently. Using this discretion, the judge dismissed the appeals on merit but directed that the sentences in both cases run concurrently, meaning the man would not have to serve the two three-year terms back-to-back. This clarifies how courts handle multiple convictions from separate trials.

title: Abdul Hadi V. Jafar khan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal filed by Abdul Hadi, the complainant in a criminal case, against the acquittal of three accused persons. The accused had been charged under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with causing injuries (shajjah and jaifah) with common intention, after allegedly attacking Abdul Hadi's uncle, Rehmatullah, with a stick and stones on a roadside in Loralai district in 2018. The trial court had acquitted the accused before full evidence was recorded, accepting an application filed under section 249-A of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the appeal on two independent grounds. First, it found the appeal was filed late. Under the law, an appeal against acquittal must be filed within thirty days, but this appeal was filed fifty-eight days after the trial court's order, and no proper explanation was given for the delay, despite an application seeking condonation of it. Second, and importantly, the court held that Abdul Hadi himself was not legally entitled to file the appeal because he was not the injured person, only a witness and relative. The law requires that only the actual injured victim, if not a minor or of unsound mind, can challenge such an acquittal. Since the uncle who was actually injured did not file the appeal himself, the complainant's appeal was incompetent.

This case highlights strict procedural limits on who can appeal acquittals and the importance of timely legal action.

title: Rifat Bibi V. Abid Shah and another ,
explainer:
This case involved a criminal appeal against the acquittal of a man accused of committing an unnatural offence (sodomy) under Section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code, allegedly against the complainant's young nephew. The complainant's aunt, Rifat Bibi, filed an appeal challenging the trial court's decision to acquit the accused.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the appeal on two grounds. First, it was filed late. The law required such appeals to be filed within thirty days of the trial court's judgment, but this appeal was filed fifty-three days later, and no application was made to excuse the delay, nor was the delay properly explained.

Second, even looking at the merits, the court found the acquittal was justified. There was no eyewitness to the alleged act, and the medical evidence was inconclusive. The doctor's examination did not follow proper medical procedure for such cases, found no real injuries, and could not confirm penetration, which is legally required to prove the offence. Forensic test results on clothing samples were never produced in court. The court also noted both the accused and victim were very young children. Given these gaps, the court held that an acquittal carries a presumption of innocence that can only be overturned if the original decision was clearly unreasonable, which was not the case here. The appeal was dismissed, reinforcing how strictly courts require proof before overturning acquittals.

title: Rehmatullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a 17-year-old boy convicted of robbery under Section 394 of the Pakistan Penal Code for allegedly tying up a 36-year-old complainant, injuring him, and trying to steal his motorcycle at knifepoint. The Balochistan High Court heard his appeal against conviction.

The court found serious problems with the prosecution's case and gave the accused benefit of the doubt, allowing the appeal and overturning the conviction. Several issues undermined the case: it seemed physically implausible that a slim 17-year-old student could overpower and tie up a grown man; the complainant's account of events, including how he got help while supposedly tied up, did not make logical sense; and the accused had actually filed his own complaint claiming the older complainant tried to molest him, suggesting a possible scuffle rather than a robbery.

The court also found major contradictions between witnesses about timing of events and the FIR registration, inconsistencies about how and when the alleged knife was recovered, lack of forensic testing on the knife, and no corroboration from other witnesses about the recovery. Additionally, the accused's confessional statement did not match the complainant's version of events.

This judgment matters because it reinforces important principles of criminal law: the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, contradictions among witnesses can be fatal to a case, physical evidence must be properly corroborated, and courts must critically scrutinize confessions and recovery evidence rather than accepting them at face value.

title: Ubaidullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about Ubaidullah, who applied to the Balochistan High Court for pre-arrest bail after being named in a murder case. The FIR alleged that he was present with his father and brother when they confronted the complainant's party over a land dispute, and that gunfire from the group killed one man and injured another. However, the FIR and witness statements specifically attributed the fatal and injury-causing shots to the co-accused, not to Ubaidullah himself, even though he was allegedly also carrying a weapon and firing.

The court noted that since Ubaidullah had not been shown to have caused any injury to the deceased or the injured witness, his role required further inquiry at trial rather than immediate arrest. It also pointed out that one of his co-accused had already been granted bail by the court, so under the "rule of consistency," Ubaidullah deserved the same treatment.

The judge explained that pre-arrest bail exists to protect innocent people from humiliation at the hands of police, especially where the case appears to need further investigation, and that such relief should be granted based on each case's specific facts. The court ultimately confirmed pre-arrest bail for Ubaidullah. This judgment is important because it reinforces how courts balance serious criminal allegations against an individual's actual proven role, and ensures fairness between co-accused in similar situations.

title: Ali Bakhsh V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Ali Bakhsh, who was convicted by a Special Judge under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, for possessing 40 kilograms of charas (hashish). He was sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution's case was that police, acting on a tip-off, stopped a pickup truck driven by Ali Bakhsh and found 40 one-kilogram packets of charas hidden in secret compartments of the vehicle. Police witnesses testified consistently about the recovery, and their testimony held up even under detailed cross-examination.

The appellant argued he was innocent and had been falsely implicated due to a dispute with the police officer, but he offered no evidence to support this claim. The court noted that merely making general denials isn't enough to overcome strong prosecution evidence, especially since he was admittedly driving the vehicle and therefore would have known about the hidden drugs.

The defense also raised concerns about delay in sending drug samples for chemical testing and about police witnesses being the main evidence. The court rejected both arguments, finding the delay had been properly explained by the investigating officer and that there was no proof the evidence had been tampered with. It also reaffirmed that police officers' testimony cannot be disregarded simply because they are police officers.

The High Court upheld the conviction and dismissed the appeal, finding the prosecution had proven its case beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Muhammad Hanif and 6 others V. Syed Zakir Hussain Shah and 8 others,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and concerns a long-running land dispute in Quetta. The petitioners were recorded as owners of certain land, while the respondents' father had allegedly been wrongly entered in revenue records decades earlier as a "lathband buzgar" (a type of cultivator) over the same property during a 1985 settlement exercise. The respondents filed a revision petition before the Senior Member, Board of Revenue, asking that these old entries be corrected and their names restored as owners. The Senior Member accepted their revision and sent the case back to the Deputy Commissioner for fresh decision.

The petitioners challenged this order, arguing they were never issued notice or given a hearing before the decision was made, and that the Senior Member had no authority to directly entertain a revision over entries that were more than 34 years old, bypassing lower revenue forums. The High Court agreed, noting serious procedural defects: no proper notice, no hearing, and no order from subordinate authorities before the matter reached the Senior Member. It also held that since the dispute involved the title of the property, only a civil court—not revenue authorities acting through mutation proceedings—could decide it. The Court set aside the Senior Member's order and quashed the proceedings.

This case matters because it reinforces that revenue officers cannot decide disputed ownership questions through summary mutation processes, and that due process (proper notice and hearing) must be followed before altering decades-old property records.

title: Mst. Arbab Khatoon V. Imam Bakhsh and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of four men accused of murdering the complainant's brother through firing. The trial court had acquitted the accused, and the victim's relative (the complainant) challenged that acquittal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal, finding the prosecution's case riddled with serious doubts. First, the FIR was lodged with an unexplained one-and-a-half-hour delay despite the police station being only four kilometers away. Second, the eyewitnesses claimed to have identified the attackers using light from an electric bulb, but no such bulb appeared in the site plan or was recovered by investigators, making identification doubtful. Third, the witnesses were "chance witnesses" who did not actually live at the scene and gave no convincing explanation for being there overnight. Fourth, the witnesses claimed the accused fired from extremely close range with automatic weapons for two to three minutes, yet the witnesses standing nearby escaped completely unharmed—an implausible scenario. Finally, medical evidence showed the deceased had shotgun pellet wounds, while witnesses and recovered evidence pointed to Kalashnikovs and pistols, creating a direct contradiction between medical and ocular evidence.

Given these cumulative weaknesses, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove any fault in the trial court's judgment, and dismissed the appeal, meaning the acquittal stood. The case illustrates how courts require consistent, credible evidence before overturning an acquittal.

title: Sabir Hussain V. The State ,
explainer:
This case involved a man accused of murdering the son of the complainant, allegedly along with a co-accused, under Pakistan's Penal Code provisions on murder and common intention (sections 302 and 34). There were no eyewitnesses to the killing, making it an unseen occurrence that relied entirely on circumstantial evidence.

The prosecution's case rested mainly on three things: a witness who claimed to have last seen the accused taking the victim away on a motorcycle, physical items like a rope, slipper, and motorcycle recovered based on the accused's statements to police, and the accused's own disclosure made while in custody. The Balochistan High Court found serious problems with all of this evidence. The "last seen" witness only came forward three days after the victim went missing, despite being the complainant's own nephew, making his story appear fabricated and unreliable. The FIR itself was filed four hours after the body was discovered, raising further doubt. The recovered items were not properly sealed by investigators and were commonly available objects, not found in any hidden location, so they didn't qualify as meaningful discoveries. The accused's disclosure to police came 14 days after arrest and wasn't made before a magistrate, reducing its legal weight.

Given these gaps, the court ruled the prosecution failed to build the complete, unbroken chain of evidence required to prove guilt beyond doubt in a circumstantial case. The conviction was overturned and the appeal allowed, reinforcing that weak, delayed, or uncorroborated evidence cannot justify a murder conviction

title: Ghulam Mustafa alias Raja Buledi and others V The State,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court (Sibi Bench) involved an appeal against convictions for murder. The accused were charged with shooting and killing the complainant's brother, allegedly motivated by prior threats and an earlier dispute involving the complainant's shop. One accused was also accused of acting in common intention by standing armed nearby while the murder took place.

The defense raised several points to challenge the prosecution's case: a three-hour delay in filing the police report (FIR), alleged discrepancies in witness testimony, and questions about whether witnesses were reliable given their relationship to the deceased. The court rejected these arguments. It found the delay was reasonably explained by the time taken to rush the injured victim to the hospital before reporting the crime. It held that minor inconsistencies in testimony don't undermine a case unless they damage its core elements. It also clarified that being related to a victim doesn't automatically make a witness "interested" or unreliable - what matters is whether they have a motive to falsely implicate someone.

The court found the eyewitness accounts, medical evidence (multiple gunshot wounds matching the ocular testimony), and recovered weapons and cartridges all corroborated each other. It also held that the armed companion who prevented resistance could be held equally liable, not merely as a facilitator, since his presence showed shared criminal intent.

The appeals were dismissed, upholding the convictions. This case is useful for showing how courts evaluate delayed FIRs, witness credibility, and shared criminal responsibility in murder cases.

title: Waheed and another V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case involved two men accused of robbing and murdering a police official, with the main evidence being a dying declaration allegedly made by the victim identifying the attackers before he died. The trial court had convicted the accused, but they appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction, finding serious doubts throughout the prosecution's case. First, the court questioned why the FIR was not registered based on the victim's own oral report at the crime scene, and noted that the police officer supposedly present when the dying declaration was made never had his statement recorded. Second, the timeline did not add up: the shooting occurred at 8:45 pm, but the body reached the hospital by 9 pm, leaving an implausibly short window for the dying declaration to have been made and relayed. Third, medical evidence showed the victim's injuries were to vital areas of the skull and abdomen, making it doubtful he could have spoken at all. Additionally, the recovered motorcycle could not be reliably linked to the accused's house, and bullet casings found at the scene did not match the number of wounds and were never forensically tested.

The court emphasized that even a single serious doubt is enough to acquit an accused, as a matter of right rather than mercy. This judgment underscores how courts scrutinize dying declarations and circumstantial evidence carefully before upholding murder convictions, especially when timelines and corroboration are weak.

title: Abdul Hameed Khan and 6 others V. Nasrullah and others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta over land identified as Khasra No. 1226 and related plots. Two separate lawsuits had been filed in the civil court concerning the same property: one by Abdul Hameed Khan and others (the petitioners) seeking declaration, possession, and injunctions against certain defendants, and another by Muhammad Naeem (respondent No. 5) against largely the same parties over the same land.

The defendants in the first suit asked the trial court to consolidate both suits into one proceeding, arguing they involved the same property and overlapping parties. The trial court agreed and merged the cases. The petitioners challenged this through a civil revision petition, which was dismissed, and then approached the Balochistan High Court under its constitutional jurisdiction, asking that the consolidation be undone.

The High Court dismissed the petition and upheld the consolidation. It explained that although the Civil Procedure Code does not explicitly provide for consolidating suits, courts have inherent power to do so when the parties and subject matter overlap, in order to prevent conflicting judgments and promote efficient justice. Relying on Supreme Court precedents, the court held that consolidation is a matter of judicial discretion aimed at avoiding multiple, possibly contradictory rulings on the same dispute, as long as no litigant is prejudiced.

This ruling reaffirms that Pakistani courts can combine related lawsuits over the same property or issue, even without explicit statutory authority, in the interest of judicial efficiency and consistency.

title: Chairman Nab through Prosecutor General Accountability, NAB HQ Shahrah-e-jumhuriat, G-5/I, Islamabad V. Zahoor Taj and another,
explainer:
This case involved a corruption reference filed by the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) against Zahoor Taj and others, accused of staging a fake tendering process for a government contract in connivance with department officials, amounting to corruption under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999.

Before any prosecution evidence was recorded, the accused filed an application under Section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking the trial court to acquit him early in the proceedings. The Accountability Court accepted this application and acquitted him without hearing any evidence. NAB challenged this acquittal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court held that while there is no time limit for filing such an early-acquittal application, fairness requires that the prosecution be given a genuine opportunity to present its evidence before a case is decided. The court noted that other co-accused were still facing trial on the same evidence, so it was improper for the trial court to make findings on credibility and reliability of evidence at such an early stage, effectively deciding the case without hearing the prosecution.

The High Court ruled that in corruption and misappropriation cases especially, courts must proceed with extreme caution and should not hastily acquit the accused without a full trial. It set aside the acquittal and sent the case back to the trial court for a proper trial, with evidence to be recorded before any decision is made. This judgment reinforces that corruption cases deserve thorough scrutiny rather than premature dismissal.

title: Muhammad Tufail and another V. Samina Tabasum and another,
explainer:
This case was about the custody of an eight-year-old girl, Farheen, after the death of her father. Her mother, Samina Tabasum, filed a case seeking custody and also an application for interim custody while the main case was pending. The paternal grandparents, who had been keeping the child, opposed this. The Family Judge in Quetta granted interim custody of the minor to the mother, and the grandparents challenged this order before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the Family Judge's decision. It explained that under the Guardians and Wards Act, a Guardian Judge has the power to make temporary custody orders for a minor's protection even without proof of urgency. The court noted that the mother is the minor's natural parent, while the grandfather could not be considered a substitute for a mother's care and affection. It also held that custody should not be allowed to swing back and forth between parties once a court has granted interim custody, unless there are strong reasons to change it. Such interim orders remain subject to the final decision in the main custody case.

The court dismissed the grandparents' petition but directed the trial court to ensure the grandparents could still visit and spend time with the child, without disrupting her education. This case highlights how courts prioritize a child's welfare and a mother's custodial rights in guardianship disputes, while still allowing extended family involvement.

title: Ghulam Sarwar and 19 others V. Muhammad Naseem and 5 others ,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running family land dispute over inherited property in Quetta, Balochistan. The petitioners, descendants who inherited land through a recorded mutation, claimed they owned and possessed the property but that their relatives, the respondents, had illegally trespassed on it after a boundary wall was built. The respondents argued they had been in proprietary possession of the land since 1971, claiming it came to them through a private property exchange with the petitioners' predecessors, and that the suit was time-barred.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court had ruled against the petitioners, favoring the respondents' version based on oral testimony. The Balochistan High Court, however, found this to be an error. It held that the petitioners held documented ownership through an inheritance mutation, which carries a legal presumption of truth. The respondents failed to produce any documentary evidence proving forty years of cultivation or possession, and could not even specify when their claimed "adverse possession" began. The lower courts had ignored this missing evidence and wrongly relied on oral claims instead.

The High Court ruled that mere possession, however long, does not create ownership rights, especially since Pakistani courts have held that adverse possession claims conflict with Islamic legal principles. It declared the petitioners the lawful owners entitled to possession and allowed their revision petition, overturning both lower court decisions. The case highlights the importance of documentary land records over unsupported oral claims in ownership disputes.

title: Ghulam Sarwar and 19 others V. Muhammad Naseem and 5 others ,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over agricultural land in Quetta between neighboring families. The petitioners claimed they inherited the land from their forefathers and that neighboring landowners (the respondents) had wrongly trespassed onto their property after jointly building a boundary wall between the two plots. The respondents argued they had privately divided the inherited property decades earlier, had been in continuous possession of the disputed land for about 40 years, had dug a tube-well, grown crops, built walls, and constructed a house on it.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled against the petitioners, finding that the respondents had proven long, uninterrupted possession while the petitioners failed to prove theirs.

The Balochistan High Court reversed these decisions. It held that the petitioners had produced official mutation (land record) entries and witness testimony establishing their ownership, and the respondents never proved these records were fake or fraudulent. Under the law, such revenue records carry a presumption of truth unless disproved. The court also noted that mere possession, even if long-standing, cannot defeat the rights of the true, documented owner, and that oral evidence cannot outweigh official documents. Citing Islamic legal principles, it added that long possession alone (akin to adverse possession) cannot create ownership.

The court allowed the revision petition, set aside the lower courts' rulings, and restored the petitioners' ownership and possession rights, reinforcing that documentary land records take precedence over claims based solely on physical possession.

title: Muhammad Naseem Javed V. Anjuman-E-Asna Ashria and another,
explainer:
This case was about a dispute over an Imam Bargah (religious congregation hall) property in Quetta. The petitioner, Muhammad Naseem Javed, sued seeking a declaration that the original name of the institution was "Anjuman-e-Asna Ashria Hazara," challenging an official letter that had removed the word "Hazara" from its registration, and asking for cancellation of related documents plus a permanent injunction preventing removal of the word "Hazara" from the building's signage.

The trial court initially ruled in his favor, but on appeal the Additional District Judge reversed that decision and dismissed the suit entirely. The matter then came before the Balochistan High Court in revision.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the petitioner himself had admitted the property in question was waqf property (a charitable or religious endowment). Under Section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code, lawsuits involving public charitable or religious trusts require prior permission from the Advocate General before they can be filed in court. Since Javed had not obtained this permission, and his claims fell within the type of relief covered by Section 92, his suit was not legally maintainable from the outset.

The court explained that this rule exists to protect public religious and charitable trusts from being misused for private disputes, ensuring such institutions are not harassed by individuals pursuing personal interests under the guise of protecting public trust property. The revision petition was therefore dismissed, and the appellate court's decision stood.

title: Meeran Bakhsh alias Matru V. The State ,
explainer:
This case concerns Meeran Bakhsh alias Matru, who along with another person was accused of murdering a woman named Mst. Razul, as recorded in a 2015 FIR. Because the accused had absconded and could not be arrested, the Anti-Terrorism Court at Dera Allah Yar declared them proclaimed offenders and, without a full trial, convicted them under Section 21-L of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, which punishes a person for evading arrest or court proceedings. They were sentenced to five years' imprisonment with a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious legal flaws in this conviction. No formal charge had ever been framed against the appellant under Section 21-L, no evidence was recorded to prove the elements of that offence, and the trial court had not even determined whether the absconding was intentional. The High Court held that convicting someone under this provision requires following proper trial procedure, including giving the accused a fair opportunity to be heard, as guaranteed by Articles 9 and 10(1) of the Constitution. Convicting someone in their absence without these safeguards amounted to condemning them unheard.

Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the High Court declared the conviction illegal, allowed the appeal, and sent the case back to the trial court to properly frame charges and conduct a lawful trial. The judgment reinforces that even proclaimed offenders are entitled to fair trial protections before being convicted and punished.

title: Taj Muhammad V. National Bank of Pakistan through Manager,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a borrower, Taj Muhammad, and the National Bank of Pakistan over an unpaid loan of Rs. 15 lakh. The Banking Court in Quetta had ruled against the borrower and ordered him to repay the bank, since he never appeared in court or contested the case. He later tried to appeal this decision to the Balochistan High Court, but filed his appeal more than a year late. He asked the court to excuse the delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, claiming he did not know about the judgment against him.

The High Court rejected this request. It explained that the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001, which governs bank recovery suits, is a special law that sets its own 30-day deadline for filing appeals. Under the Limitation Act's own rules, when a special law provides its own limitation period, general provisions like Section 5 (which allows delays to be excused for good reason) do not automatically apply unless the special law says so. Since the Ordinance did not allow for such exceptions, the court held it had no power to condone the delay.

The court also noted that the borrower's excuse was unconvincing, since he filed the appeal more than a month after receiving the judgment, not immediately as claimed. As a result, the appeal was dismissed as time-barred. This case clarifies that strict deadlines in special banking laws leave little room for delay in challenging court decisions.

title: Messrs Amir Jan Oil Mill through Proprietor and another V. National Bank of Pakistan through Manager,
explainer:

The National Bank of Pakistan sued Amir Jan Oil Mill and its proprietor to recover Rs. 20,45,042 under a financing arrangement. However, their application failed to meet the specific legal requirements set out in Section 10(4) of the Ordinance, which requires defendants to clearly state details such as the amount borrowed, payments made, amounts still owed, and any specific amounts being disputed along with supporting facts.

Because the borrowers did not provide this required information, the Banking Court rejected their request to defend the case and ruled in favor of the bank. The borrowers appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing they should have been allowed to contest the suit.

The High Court upheld the Banking Court's decision. It found that the borrowers had partly admitted taking the loan but failed to rebut the bank's documentary evidence or show any repayment, and their appeal did not satisfy the mandatory disclosure requirements of the law. The court also noted unfavorably that the appellants failed to deposit a required surety or court fee during the appeal process.

This case illustrates how strictly courts enforce procedural requirements under banking recovery laws, meaning borrowers who wish to contest a bank's recovery suit must provide detailed, specific information, not vague
