title: Abdul Saleem and another V. Abdul Aziz and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a family property dispute in Quetta. A son and grandson (plaintiffs) sued their relatives, claiming rights to an ancestral house left by their grandfather, which had passed down through the family. During the trial, after evidence was recorded, the plaintiffs asked the court to amend their plaint under Order VI, Rule 17 of the Civil Procedure Code, to add clearer wording about the property being ancestral and to specifically ask for possession of the house, since they were not actually living in it.

The trial court refused to allow this amendment, but when the plaintiffs challenged that refusal before the Additional District Judge, the amendment was allowed. The defendants then approached the Balochistan High Court, asking it to overturn that decision.

The High Court upheld the lower appellate court's order. It explained that amendments to a plaint are allowed unless they introduce a completely new and different cause of action. Here, the proposed changes simply clarified the ancestral nature of the property and added a request for possession, something already implied by the facts already pleaded. This did not change the fundamental nature of the case or bring in a new claim.

The court dismissed the petition, meaning the amendment stands and the case will proceed with the clearer pleadings. title: Muhammad Arif and others V. State through Prosecutor General Balochistan Quetta ,

A separate FIR (No. 66), lodged by one of the accused, alleged that the complainant's side had entered his house and opened fire on his brother. These are known as "cross" or "counter" cases, since they stem from the same event but present opposing versions.

Because this fair procedure was not followed, the court partly accepted the revision petition, recognizing the importance of considering both sides' evidence before convicting anyone in such intertwined disputes.

title: Dr. Muhammad Arif V. Muhammad Anwar and 3 others ,
explainer:

Before the prosecution could complete its evidence, the accused applied under Section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking the trial court to acquit them early. The trial court agreed and acquitted them, relying heavily on a medical board report suggesting the complainant's injury was self-inflicted rather than caused by a firearm, even though no evidence had actually been recorded to verify that medical report's authenticity.

The High Court found this acquittal flawed. It held that the trial court acted hastily by accepting a questionable medical report without examining the doctors involved or testing its genuineness through evidence. Since the prosecution had not been given a fair chance to prove its case, the complainant was effectively condemned unheard. The High Court emphasized that courts must decide cases on merits, giving both sides a chance to present evidence, and that justice requires protecting the innocent while also punishing the guilty. The acquittal was partly set aside, and the case was sent back to the trial court for proper proceedings based on full evidence.

title: Muhammad Ayub V. Additional Sessions Judge-VII/Justice of Peace, Quetta and others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved Dr. Muhammad Ayub, who had been a complainant in a criminal case (FIR for attempted murder and related offences) against several respondents. During the trial, a dispute arose over a medical report dated 11.07.2018 issued by a medical board, which the petitioner's brother claimed was fake, since two doctors named as board members later denied ever issuing such an opinion. The petitioner wanted the police to register a case against those responsible for the allegedly fabricated report and approached the Ex-Officio Justice of Peace (an Additional Sessions Judge) under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, but his application was dismissed. He then challenged that dismissal before the High Court.

The High Court explained the proper scope of a Justice of Peace's powers under section 22-A: such powers are quasi-judicial, not merely administrative or mechanical. The Justice of Peace cannot simply accept one party's version of events but must independently verify that there is genuine supporting material before ordering registration of an FIR or transfer of investigation. The court relied on a Supreme Court precedent warning that these powers are often misused to harass opponents or convert civil disputes into criminal cases, and must therefore be exercised with discretion and proper hearing of all parties.

This judgment matters because it reinforces safeguards against misuse of the FIR-registration process, ensuring that judicial officers scrutinize evidence carefully rather than rubber-stamping complaints.

title: Najeebullah and others V. The State ,
explainer:
This case involved three men arrested together in a vehicle near Pishin, Balochistan, after police stopped the Surf van they were traveling in. Officers recovered five kilograms of hashish from the vehicle's trunk, along with Rs.535,000 in cash. All three were tried together and convicted under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, with the driver, Wali Muhammad, and two passengers, Najeebullah and Naseemullah, each sentenced to seven years imprisonment and fines.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court upheld the driver's conviction, holding that the person driving a vehicle carrying narcotics is responsible for transporting the contraband, and that the prosecution's evidence—consistent witness testimony, proper recovery procedure, and an intact chain of custody for the forensic sample—was credible and unshaken by cross-examination. The court also rejected arguments that the absence of independent civilian witnesses during the search invalidated the case, noting that a specific provision of the narcotics law excludes the usual requirement for private witnesses, and that reluctance of ordinary people to get involved in such cases is a recognized reality.

However, the court overturned the convictions of the two passengers, finding no evidence they knew about the hidden hashish or had any connection to the vehicle beyond merely riding in it. Since the drugs were concealed in the trunk and not visible to them, mere presence was insufficient to prove guilt.

This case highlights the principle that criminal liability in narcotics cases requires proof

title: Babar Jahangir and another V. Nadir Ali,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over unpaid debt. Nadir Ali filed a summary suit against Babar Jahangir and another person under a special fast-track procedure (Order XXXVII of the Civil Procedure Code) used for recovery based on cheques. Jahangir had allegedly borrowed money and given cheques that later bounced due to insufficient funds, with the second appellant acting as surety.

Under this summary procedure, a defendant must seek the court's permission ("leave to defend") within ten days of being served, otherwise the suit is automatically decreed against them. The trial court ruled that the appellants' application for leave to defend was filed too late and accordingly decreed the suit in the respondent's favor without a full trial.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the record and found that one appellant had only received a copy of the plaint (the document containing the claim) on 16 March 2018, and the leave to defend application was filed on 26 March 2018 - exactly ten days later, counting correctly. The court held that a defendant cannot be expected to apply for leave without first having a copy of the plaint, and that the ten-day period should be counted excluding the date of service itself. Therefore, the application was actually filed within the legal deadline.

As a result, the High Court set aside the trial court's judgment and sent the case back for fresh consideration of the leave to defend application, on merits, within two months. This case highlights how strict procedural deadlines must be fairly calculated to ensure defendants get a genuine chance to defend themselves.

title: Ali Ahmed and 2 others V. Ghulam Mustafa and others ,
explainer:
This case was about a request to transfer a civil lawsuit from one court to another. The petitioners, Ali Ahmed and two others, had filed an ejectment suit against Ghulam Mustafa and others before a civil court in Pishin. While that case was ongoing, they asked for it to be moved to a different court, claiming the presiding judge was biased against them. Their main evidence was that the opposing side had allegedly said they would get favorable treatment from the court. The District Judge rejected this transfer request, and the petitioners challenged that rejection before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the decision to deny the transfer. It explained that bias can take different forms, such as a judge having a personal stake in the case, a financial interest, or personal hostility toward a party. However, simply alleging that someone claimed to have influence with the court, without any solid evidence or actual conduct by the judge showing unfairness, is not enough. The court stressed that mere suspicion or apprehension cannot substitute for real proof, and cases should not be transferred routinely or based on a party's personal whims.

This ruling matters because it reinforces an important safeguard for the justice system: confidence in courts requires that transfer requests be based on genuine, demonstrable grounds like proven bias or financial interest, not vague fears or unverified claims, which helps prevent misuse of the transfer process to delay or manipulate proceedings.

title: Abdul Mateen through guardian/father V. Bibi Khadija and others ,
explainer:
This case was about a request to correct what the petitioner claimed was a clerical mistake in a civil court judgment. In 2015, a trial court in Quetta decided a suit filed by Abdul Mateen (through his father) regarding an injunction over a shared wall between shops. In its judgment, while deciding one of the legal issues, the trial court referred to an earlier ruling (from a separate eviction case) that had gone in favour of the "defendants." The petitioner argued that this word should actually have read "plaintiff," and that it was simply a typing or clerical slip, asking the court to fix it under Section 152 of the Civil Procedure Code, a provision meant for correcting minor clerical or arithmetical errors.

The trial court rejected this request, finding that the wording was not a mistake at all, but reflected the actual outcome of the earlier litigation between the parties, which had indeed favored the respondents. This rejection was upheld in a subsequent revision petition, leading to the present case before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition, explaining that Section 152 can only be used to fix genuine accidental or clerical errors that are obvious on their face. It cannot be used to reopen or change a court's deliberate findings or correct what a party feels is an unfair or wrong decision. Since the trial court had used the word "defendant" deliberately and correctly, there was nothing to correct, and the petition was dismissed.

title: Mehrab-Ud-Din V. Moula Bakhsh and 8 others ,
explainer:
This case was an appeal by a complainant against the acquittal of nine people accused of murdering his relative. The accused had allegedly opened fire on the victim during a property dispute, killing him. After trial, the Sessions Judge acquitted all the accused, and the complainant challenged that acquittal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. It found the prosecution's case riddled with doubt. The FIR was lodged two hours after the incident without any explanation, even though the police station was close by, raising suspicion of deliberation or false implication. The eyewitnesses, including the complainant himself, failed to explain why they were present at the scene, and it seemed unnatural that they escaped unharmed despite being right next to the shooting. The identification of accused at night using torch light was considered weak evidence, and witness statements contained major contradictions. The postmortem was also delayed by 15 hours without explanation, suggesting time may have been used to fabricate witnesses or a false story. Additionally, no forensic report linked the recovered weapon to the crime, making that evidence inconclusive.

The court reaffirmed that in appeals against acquittal, conviction is only reversed if the original judgment is clearly perverse or unjust. Since the trial court's reasoning was sound and multiple doubts existed, the accused deserved benefit of the doubt, and the appeal was dismissed, keeping the acquittal intact.

title: Muhammad Ameen V. The State ,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Muhammad Ameen, who was convicted under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997 for possessing 520 grams of charas (hashish). Police claimed they acted on a tip-off, found him in an empty quarter near a railway colony, and recovered the drugs from his possession. He was convicted by a Special Judge in Dhadar and sentenced to one and a half years' rigorous imprisonment plus a fine, with benefit given for time already served. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the prosecution's four witnesses, including the arresting officer and investigators, and found their testimony consistent, credible, and unshaken by cross-examination. The court rejected the defense argument that no independent (private) witnesses were present during the arrest, ruling that the law specifically exempts narcotics cases from the usual requirement of involving private witnesses during searches.

The defense also argued that a four-day delay in sending the seized drugs for chemical testing cast doubt on whether the sample was tampered with. The court held that the relevant testing timelines are only directory, not mandatory, and since there was no evidence of tampering, the delay did not undermine the case. The chemical report confirmed the substance was charas.

Finding no reason to doubt the prosecution's evidence, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction and sentence. The case clarifies that minor procedural delays and absence of private witnesses do not automatically invalidate narcotics prosecutions in Pakist

title: Saeed Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Saeed Ahmed, who was stopped while driving an Alto car at a police checkpoint in Sibi. Police searched the vehicle and found 8,000 grams of charas (hashish) concealed in secret cavities. He was charged and convicted under section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and sentenced by the trial court to ten and a half years of rigorous imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence, including testimony from the arresting officer, witnesses to the recovery, the officer who stored the drugs in police custody, the officer who transported the samples to the forensic laboratory, and the investigating officer. The court found their statements consistent and credible, noting that the sample had been sent for forensic testing within 72 hours, ruling out tampering, and the lab confirmed it was charas. The defense argued that no private witnesses were included in the search, only police officials, which would normally be required under section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The court rejected this, pointing out that narcotics law specifically excludes that requirement.

The court also relied on precedent holding that whoever is driving a vehicle is responsible for whatever is found inside it, since the driver controls the vehicle. Finding no reason to doubt the prosecution's case, the court upheld the conviction and dismissed the appeal. The case reinforces that drivers can be held liable for narcotics found in their vehicles, and that police-only searches are valid in drug cases.

title: Hameedullah V. The State ,
explainer:
Hameedullah was convicted by a trial court under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act and sentenced to life imprisonment after 300 kilograms of charas (hashish) were allegedly recovered from the car he was driving near Dera Murad Jamali. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him, citing serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, there was an unexplained two-hour delay in registering the police report (FIR) after the alleged recovery, which the court said raised doubts about whether the case had been genuinely reported promptly or was later concocted. Second, and more critically, the drug samples were sent to the government forensic laboratory ten days after recovery, far beyond the 72-hour limit required by law. The prosecution offered no explanation for this delay and failed to produce key witnesses, such as the constable who transported the samples or the officer responsible for storing them, to show the samples remained securely handled throughout.

Because the court could not be sure the substance analyzed was the same material taken from the accused, it held that the chain of custody was broken, creating reasonable doubt. Under criminal law, any such doubt must benefit the accused. The court therefore allowed the appeal and acquitted Hameedullah.

This case highlights how strict procedural safeguards, like timely reporting and reliable evidence handling, are essential to secure a valid conviction in narcotics cases.

title: Danish Ali and 2 others V. National Bank of Pakistan through Manager,
explainer:
This case involved a bank loan dispute. The National Bank of Pakistan sued three individuals to recover about Rs. 8.76 lakh they allegedly owed. The borrowers tried to defend themselves by applying for leave to defend the suit, but the trial court (Banking Court, Quetta) rejected their application because they failed to properly specify details required by law, such as the amount borrowed, payments made, and dates of payment. The trial court then ruled in the bank's favor.

The borrowers appealed to the Balochistan High Court, but they filed the appeal late, about two months after the deadline. They asked the court to excuse the delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, explaining that one appellant's father had died during that period.

The High Court rejected this request. It held that the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001 is a special law that sets its own 30-day deadline for appeals, and such special laws override the general Limitation Act unless they specifically allow its provisions to apply. Since the Ordinance did not permit delay condonation under Section 5, the court ruled it could not be used to excuse the late filing. The court also found that the appellants had failed to meet the legal requirements for defending the suit in the first place and had not disputed the loan or shown repayment.

The appeal was dismissed, upholding the trial court's decision in favor of the bank. This case clarifies that deadlines in special banking laws are strict and cannot be relaxed by general limitation rules.

title: Aurangzaib and another V. The State ,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Aurangzeb and Asfand Yar, who were stopped by police at a checkpoint near Sibi while traveling in a car from Quetta. Police found 68 kilograms of baked charas (hashish) hidden in secret cavities of the car's tank and doors. Asfand Yar was driving, while Aurangzeb was a passenger in the front seat. Both were convicted by a trial court under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act and sentenced to over ten years in prison.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence carefully. It found that the prosecution witnesses, all police officials, gave consistent and credible testimony about the arrest, the recovery location, and the handling of the narcotics, and the defence could not shake their account or show any enmity that might explain a false charge. The court also ruled that a six-day delay in sending drug samples for chemical testing was not fatal to the case, since such time limits are guidance rather than strict law, and there was no evidence of tampering.

However, the court drew a key distinction for the passenger, Aurangzeb. Since the drugs were hidden in the vehicle's structure and not on his person, and there was no evidence he knew about them, merely sitting in the car was not enough to prove guilt. His conviction was overturned, while the driver's conviction was upheld. The case highlights that physical presence alone cannot establish criminal responsibility—actual knowledge or control over contraband must be proven.

title: Bevergh Khan V. Surat Khan and 7 others ,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute in Balochistan involving the Islamic law right of pre-emption, which allows certain people, such as neighboring landowners or co-sharers, to claim first right to purchase land when it is sold to someone else.

The appellant, Bevergh Khan, claimed that land adjacent to his property had been sold by the respondents without informing him, and that he was entitled to claim it under the right of pre-emption since his land shared a water source with it. His pre-emption suit was dismissed by the trial court, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal for several reasons. First, the appellant failed to properly describe his property or clearly prove that his land was actually adjacent to the disputed land, a claim the respondents disputed. Second, under Islamic law as codified in the Muhammadan Law applicable in Balochistan, a person claiming pre-emption must immediately assert this right upon learning of the sale, a formal step called Talab-i-Muwathibath, and then promptly repeat the demand before witnesses, referencing the first demand, known as Talab-i-Ishhad. The appellant's plaint and evidence did not specify the date, time, or place when he made this immediate first demand, which is a strict legal requirement.

Because these essential technical and procedural requirements were not met, the court ruled that the appellant had not established his right to pre-emption, and the appeal was dismissed.

title: Nozo V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves Nozo, who was arrested on 10 February 2020 and accused of possessing an improvised explosive device and other explosive materials. He was tried under the Explosive Substances Act and the Anti-Terrorism Act, and convicted by a Special Judge of the Anti-Terrorism Court. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him, giving him the benefit of the doubt. The judges found multiple serious flaws in the prosecution's case: the FIR was lodged eight hours after the alleged incident with no explanation, raising suspicion of manipulation; the recovered explosives were not sealed at the scene but six hours later; no one recorded how much explosive material was actually recovered; the sample sent for forensic testing arrived eighteen days late with no explanation, and the officials responsible for its custody and transmission were never produced as witnesses; and crucially, the law required prior government permission (sanction) before prosecuting someone under the Explosive Substances Act, which was never obtained.

Because sanction is a mandatory legal requirement, its absence made the entire trial void. Combined with the unexplained delays and broken chain of evidence, the court concluded the prosecution had failed to prove guilt beyond doubt.

This case highlights how procedural safeguards—prompt FIR registration, proper evidence handling, and legal permissions—protect individuals from wrongful conviction, even in serious terrorism-related cases.

title: Abdul Ghani V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of raping a ten-year-old girl while she was out grazing goats with her younger sister. The trial court had found him guilty and sentenced him to ten years in prison. Both the convicted man and the state appealed - he sought acquittal, while the state sought a harsher sentence through a criminal revision.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the conviction, rejecting arguments about a thirteen-hour delay in filing the police report, since the father was out of town and acted promptly once informed. The court relied on strong medical evidence showing recent sexual assault, and on the detailed, consistent testimony of the victim and her younger sister, who were both found competent child witnesses despite their young ages, after the trial judge properly tested their understanding. The court noted that DNA testing is not legally required to prove rape when other evidence is sufficient.

Importantly, the court found that the trial judge had made a legal error: under the law applicable at the time (as amended in 2016), rape of a minor carried only two possible punishments - death or life imprisonment - not a ten-year term. Since the accused was himself a juvenile (16-17 years old) at the time, the death penalty was barred by juvenile justice law, leaving life imprisonment as the only proper sentence.

The court dismissed the man's appeal and enhanced his sentence from ten years to life imprisonment.

title: Syed Naseem Agha and 3 others V. Shuja Ud Din Kasi and others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta where the respondents claimed ownership of land through a mutation entry and sought possession from the petitioners, who were occupying the property. During the lawsuit, the petitioners asked the trial court to appoint a local commissioner to visit the site and determine who actually possessed the property compared to the ownership map (tatima) presented by the respondents. The trial court agreed and appointed a commissioner, but the respondents challenged this in revision before the District Court, which overturned the trial court's order, saying it was improper to gather such information before evidence was formally recorded.

The Balochistan High Court was asked to review this decision. It ruled that civil courts have broad powers under the law to order local investigations or demarcations to clarify disputed facts, especially in matters involving possession and encroachment, since such issues often cannot be resolved without an on-site inspection. However, the court agreed that at this very early stage of the case, before any issues were framed or evidence recorded, the genuineness of the mutation entries could not be settled merely through a commission's visit, only a full trial with evidence could establish that. The court also clarified that a commission's report is not binding evidence but only assists the judge, and parties may still object to it. Importantly, the court noted the petitioners could reapply for a local commission later, and dismissed the current petition.

title: Rehmatullah V. Mst. Bibi Zenora and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a husband, Rehmatullah, challenging a family court decision that favored his wife, Mst. Bibi Zenora. The wife had filed a suit seeking dissolution of her marriage on grounds of cruelty, along with recovery of dower, custody of her children, and return of educational certificates. The Family Court partially granted her requests. The husband then tried to appeal, first before the Member, Majlis-e-Shoora (a local appellate forum), which said it had no jurisdiction, and then before the District and Sessions Judge, who dismissed his appeal for being filed too late.

The Balochistan High Court upheld these decisions. It clarified that under the Family Courts Act, appeals from family court decisions should go to the District Judge, and explained how old Kalat-era judicial structures fit into this framework. It also found the husband's appeal was filed beyond the 30-day limit set by law, with no valid request made to excuse the delay.

On the substance, the court agreed that the wife had proven cruelty, noting evidence of physical and mental mistreatment and the husband's failure to support her for years. The court emphasized that cruelty isn't limited to physical violence and can include emotional harm. It also reaffirmed that the law generally does not allow husbands to appeal dissolution-of-marriage decrees, as this protects wives from prolonged, costly litigation. The petition was dismissed.

title: Muhammad Hussain and another V. Muhammad Bashir and another,
explainer:
This case is about an appeal filed by the complainant against the acquittal of a man accused of being involved in his brother's murder, which took place in 1995. The main accused in the shooting was separately convicted, and that conviction was upheld all the way up to the Supreme Court. However, the respondent in this appeal was accused only of abetment and sharing common intention with the shooter, not of firing the fatal shots himself.

The trial court acquitted the respondent, finding that no specific role, weapon, or motive had been clearly attributed to him by the complainant or witnesses. Crucially, the only eyewitness to the crime had died before he could testify against this particular respondent, and his earlier statement (given in relation to the main accused) could not be used against the respondent because the respondent never had a chance to cross-examine him.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the acquittal, agreeing that the prosecution failed to prove the respondent's involvement, motive, or common intention beyond doubt. It reaffirmed the important legal principle that an acquittal carries a "double presumption of innocence," meaning appellate courts should only overturn it in cases of serious and obvious error, not simply because another view of the evidence is possible. The appeal against acquittal was therefore dismissed.

title: Noor Ahmed alias Ahmed Agha V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Noor Ahmed, who was convicted of murdering the complainant's brother and sentenced to death under Pakistan's murder laws. The prosecution's case rested on circumstantial evidence, a confessional statement, and recovery of a pistol allegedly used in the crime.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the accused. It found several serious weaknesses in the prosecution's case. First, the circumstantial evidence was weak: witnesses only said the victim told them by phone he was going to meet the accused to collect money, but no one actually saw the two men together before the murder. Second, the accused's judicial confession was unreliable because the magistrate who recorded it did not give him adequate time for reflection, did not confirm his handcuffs were removed, and improperly administered an oath to him in violation of the Oaths Act—making the confession inadmissible. Third, there was an unexplained fifteen-day delay before the confession was recorded. Finally, the recovery of the weapon and matching ballistic evidence was also found unreliable due to delays and procedural lapses in handling the crime evidence.

The court held that retracted confessions can support a conviction only if corroborated by strong independent evidence, especially in death penalty cases—which was lacking here. This judgment underscores the importance of proper procedure in recording confessions and the high standard of proof needed before someone can be convicted of murder, particularly when facing a death sentence.

title: Kazim Ali V. Ishaq Ali ,
explainer:
This case is about whether a defamation lawsuit could proceed after the plaintiff had already tried and abandoned earlier attempts to sue over the same issue. Kazim Ali sued Ishaq Ali for defamation and damages of Rs. 10 million, claiming a 2011 newspaper publication had harmed his reputation. The trial court dismissed his suit at the outset, under a procedural rule allowing rejection of a plaint without a full trial, and Kazim Ali appealed.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that Kazim Ali had previously filed two earlier suits over the same defamatory publication and the same facts - one of which he withdrew without court permission to refile, and another which was already rejected by a different court. He concealed these facts from the trial court in his new suit, approaching it with "unclean hands." Under civil procedure rules, once a suit is withdrawn without permission to file afresh, the plaintiff cannot bring a new suit on the same cause of action. The court also noted that the Defamation Ordinance, 2002, sets its own strict time limits for filing such claims, requiring notice within two months of learning of the defamatory material - here, the legal notice was sent eight years late, far beyond that limit.

The judgment matters because it reinforces that courts can dismiss repetitive, time-barred, or concealment-tainted lawsuits early, without a full trial, protecting the judicial process from abuse through repeated litigation on the same grievance.

title: Syed Mohsin Ali V. The State through Deputy Prosecutor General (DPG), National Accountability Bureau (NAB), Balochistan ,
explainer:
Syed Mohsin Ali was convicted by an Accountability Court in Quetta for running a housing scheme called "Pine Town Housing Scheme" and allegedly defrauding members of the public who paid money for plots that were never allotted or handed over. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment, a heavy fine, and disqualification from holding public office or getting bank loans for ten years.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. The court found that out of 412 people who had booked plots, only ten testified, and two of them admitted they had not even paid the full amount owed. The investigating officer himself admitted the scheme failed because of civil litigation between the accused and the original land seller, not fraud. The court held that to prove corruption under the National Accountability Ordinance's provision on defrauding "the public at large," the prosecution must show the fraud affected the public at a broad, macro level—not just a small handful of individuals. Ten witnesses did not meet that threshold.

The court also explained that criminal breach of trust and cheating require proof that the accused intended to deceive from the very beginning, and that merely taking investment money for a business venture that later failed does not automatically amount to criminal breach of trust. It concluded this was essentially a civil contractual dispute, not a criminal case, and set aside the conviction and sentence. This case clarifies the high bar prosecutors must meet when alleging large-scale public fraud under accountability laws.

title: Abdul Nasir and others V. The State and another,

The High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness testimony from the complainant and his brother, both sons of the deceased, and medical evidence confirming the firearm injuries. The court found their accounts credible, consistent, and unshaken despite cross-examination, and ruled that being related to the victims did not automatically make their testimony unreliable. The court upheld the convictions, finding the prosecution had proved its case.

However, the court identified problems with the prosecution's case regarding sentencing: the recovered weapon was never scientifically matched to the crime, making it unreliable evidence of the sequence of events, and the alleged motive for the killings was never proven or even questioned to the accused during trial. As a result, the High Court maintained the convictions but reduced the sentence from death to life imprisonment. This case illustrates how courts can accept guilt based on strong eyewitness evidence while still showing leniency in sentencing when doubts remain about motive or supporting forensic evidence.

The court found that the FIR was lodged within an hour of the incident, suggesting it was genuine and not the result of false implication, since the parties already knew each other. It also held that the dying declaration made by the deceased to his brother, naming the accused as the shooter, was credible and could alone support a conviction since nothing in cross-examination discredited it.

Regarding the confessional statement recorded under section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the court found it voluntary and reliable, noting that the recording magistrate had followed proper legal procedures and that no evidence showed torture or coercion. Although there was a fourteen-day delay before the confession was recorded, the court held this delay alone was not enough to discard it, since no universal rule requires confessions to be recorded immediately.

Based on all this evidence, the court concluded that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt. However, considering the circumstances, the court converted the death penalty into life imprisonment, while otherwise dismissing the appeal. This case illustrates how Pakistani courts assess dying declarations, confessions, and sentencing in murder cases.

title: Baz Muhammad Kakar V. Syed Abdul Rasheed and another ,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running property dispute in which the petitioner, Baz Muhammad Kakar, had filed a civil suit for declaration, specific performance, and permanent injunction against the respondents. The trial court dismissed his suit because he repeatedly failed to produce his evidence and witnesses, despite being given fifteen opportunities to do so. He challenged this, and the High Court initially gave him another chance, setting clear conditions: pay court fees, pay costs to the opposing party, and complete his evidence by a fixed deadline, warning that failure to comply would result in automatic dismissal of his suit. Despite this, the petitioner again failed to meet these conditions, and the trial court dismissed his suit a second time. His appeal against this was also rejected by the appellate court.

When he brought this revision petition to the Balochistan High Court, neither he nor his lawyer showed up for hearings, even after being given a final opportunity to appear. The High Court found that the petitioner had shown a pattern of delay and non-compliance throughout the case, which amounted to contumacious (willfully defiant) conduct. The judge held that courts cannot allow endless opportunities when a party disregards directions and causes delay, since delayed justice is denial of justice. Finding no legal error in the lower courts' decisions, the High Court dismissed the revision petition, emphasizing that a litigant who does not act in good faith cannot expect leniency or equitable relief from the court.

title: Sheikh Arsalan V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Sheikh Arsalan who was convicted by a trial court in Quetta for murder (qatl-i-amd) and robbery, after being accused of snatching a mobile phone and shooting a man named Najeebullah, who later died of his injuries. The trial court sentenced Arsalan to life imprisonment plus additional jail time and fines.

Arsalan appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing his conviction was flawed. The High Court agreed. It found several serious problems with how the trial was conducted. First, the trial court never properly examined or made findings about how the victim actually died. Second, when Arsalan was questioned under section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code (a step where the accused must be confronted with the evidence against him), he was never asked about key evidence like the recovered pistol or the allegedly snatched mobile phone, even though the trial court used this evidence to convict him. Third, the witnesses who witnessed the recovery of the weapon and phone were never properly examined in court, and the actual case property (weapon and phone) was never formally presented as evidence.

Because of these fundamental procedural failures, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence entirely and sent the case back to the trial court to be decided fresh, this time properly examining the recovery witnesses and evidence. The case highlights how strict evidentiary and procedural fairness rules in criminal trials must be followed before someone can be convicted.

title: Sharaf-Ud-Din V. Abdul Wadood and 3 others ,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over land in Kuchlak, Balochistan. A man who ran a school filed a civil suit asking the court to declare his ownership of certain land and to stop his neighbours from building shops on adjoining land that he claimed encroached on his property. The defendants contested the suit and filed their written response. While the case was ongoing, the plaintiff tried to withdraw his suit, seeking permission to file a fresh one later. The trial court allowed this withdrawal, but the defendants appealed, and the appellate court reversed that decision, refusing to let the plaintiff withdraw with the right to refile. The plaintiff then challenged this in the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision and dismissed the plaintiff's petition. It held that under the law governing withdrawal of suits (Order XXIII of the Civil Procedure Code), a plaintiff cannot withdraw a case and get permission to refile it just because he wants to—he must show either a formal legal defect in the original suit or some other genuine, sufficient reason, and the court must be satisfied this isn't being done to harm the other side or misuse the legal process. Here, the plaintiff gave no real justification, a court-appointed inspection had already taken place, and allowing withdrawal would unfairly disadvantage the defendants. The ruling clarifies that withdrawal with permission to refile is not an automatic right but requires proper judicial scrutiny.

title: Asad Javed V. Ahmed Shah ,
explainer:
This case was about a civil dispute over a dishonoured cheque. Ahmed Shah (the plaintiff) claimed he had given Asad Javed (the defendant) a loan of Rs. 20,80,820 for business purposes, and in return received a crossed cheque dated 20.08.2014. When Shah tried to cash the cheque, it bounced due to insufficient funds. He sued for recovery under a special summary procedure for negotiable instruments. Javed denied taking any loan and claimed the cheque had actually been stolen by the plaintiff's brother, to whom he said he had given a much smaller amount.

The trial court sided with the plaintiff and ordered Javed to pay the amount. Javed appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the decree. It reasoned that under Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, a cheque is presumed to have been issued for valid consideration, and the burden falls on the person denying this to prove otherwise. The court found Javed's "theft" defense self-contradictory and unsupported by evidence—he could not credibly claim the cheque was stolen while also admitting dealings involving it. Since he never proved the cheque didn't belong to his account or wasn't signed by him, mere denial was insufficient.

This judgment reinforces that cheque issuers face a strong legal presumption of liability, and vague or inconsistent defenses will not overcome that presumption.

title: Shah Muhammad V. Allah Bakhsh,
explainer:
This case involved a civil appeal before the Balochistan High Court. The appellant had earlier filed a suit seeking cancellation of an agreement dated 24.06.2007 relating to a plot of land, along with recovery of Rs. 3,30,000, but the trial court (Majlis-e-Shoora, Chaghi) dismissed his suit on 09.10.2018. He obtained certified copies of the judgment soon after, but did not file his appeal until 04.03.2020, roughly one and a half years later, far beyond the 90-day limitation period prescribed under Article 156 of the Limitation Act, 1908.

Neither the appellant nor the respondent appeared before the High Court despite repeated notices and several hearing dates, so the court decided the matter based on the available record. The High Court held that the appellant failed to provide any reasonable explanation for the long delay in filing the appeal, noting that a party seeking condonation of delay must account for every single day of delay and show that the delay was caused by circumstances beyond their control. Since no such justification was given, the court ruled that the law of limitation is mandatory, not a mere formality, and exists to protect vigilant litigants, not those who neglect their rights. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed as time-barred.

This judgment reinforces the strict approach Pakistani courts take toward limitation periods, emphasizing that delays in legal proceedings must be properly justified, or claims risk being dismissed regardless of their underlying merits.

title: Mehtab alias Methoo V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves Mehtab, also known as Methoo, who was accused of breaking into a house at night and stealing two mobile phones. He was convicted by a trial court based on his own guilty plea and sentenced to several years in prison, a sentence later upheld on appeal. The matter reached the Balochistan High Court through a jail petition.

The High Court found serious problems with how the case was handled. First, the trial court had earlier suspected the accused might be mentally ill and had asked the jail superintendent for a medical report, but no report ever came back, and the court went ahead with the trial anyway, never resolving the question of his mental fitness to stand trial. Second, the accused had no lawyer, and the court never properly checked whether he wanted one or ensured he received required case documents before recording his guilty plea. Third, the formal charge against him was incomplete and failed to include key legal elements of the offense, and there was no eyewitness or identification parade linking him to the crime beyond recovered phones.

Because of these failures, the High Court ruled that the conviction could not stand. It set aside the judgment and sent the case back to the trial court, instructing it to first determine whether the accused was mentally fit to defend himself before proceeding further. This case highlights the importance of protecting the rights of potentially mentally ill defendants and following proper legal procedure before convicting someone, even on a guilty plea.

title: Changaz Khan V. Mian Khan and 2 others ,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and deals with a civil dispute over a right of pre-emption, where the plaintiff (petitioner) had sued to claim priority rights over a property sale, along with seeking a declaration and injunctions.

The trial court dismissed the petitioner's suit for non-prosecution because he failed to produce evidence to support his case, relying on Order XVII, Rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code. The appellate court upheld this dismissal. The petitioner then challenged both decisions before the High Court, arguing that he was never given a genuine opportunity to present his evidence or his own testimony, and that his witnesses' absence was not deliberate but due to them being out of town.

The High Court agreed with the petitioner. It held that before closing a party's right to produce evidence under this rule, courts must ensure certain conditions are met, including that a previous adjournment was granted at that party's own request and that there is some material already on record to justify deciding the case. Since the trial court's order did not show this had happened, and the petitioner was never even given a chance to make his own statement, the dismissal was improper and a denial of fair process.

The High Court set aside the lower courts' orders and sent the case back for retrial, directing the trial court to give the petitioner two more opportunities to present his full evidence, on condition that he pay costs of Rs. 30,000 to the other side. This case underscores that courts must not let procedural technicalities override a litigant's fundamental right to a fair hearing.

title: Suleman and another V. The State ,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Suleman and Rehmatullah, who were convicted of murdering a man named Zakir by shooting him at night in Pasni, Balochistan. The alleged motive was that the deceased had entered a neighbor's house at night, prompting threats from one accused's mother, leading to the shooting later that night.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction, finding the prosecution's case riddled with doubt. The incident happened at midnight in complete darkness, yet the eyewitnesses never mentioned any source of light that would have allowed them to identify the attackers or see who fired the fatal shots. The court also found unexplained delays - witness statements were recorded two days late without justification, weakening their credibility.

Further doubts arose over the recovery of the murder weapon: the investigating officer claimed to be at the crime scene until 1:35 a.m., yet another witness said the weapon was recovered from the accused at 2:30 a.m., at a location 135 kilometers away - making his presence at both places physically impossible. There was also an unexplained delay of nearly two months before sending the pistol for forensic testing, and the alleged motive was never corroborated by any witness.

The court ruled that recovery of a weapon alone, without reliable direct evidence, cannot support a conviction. Because the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the appeal was allowed and the convictions were set aside, highlighting how courts scrutinize identification, timelines, and evidence handling in criminal cases

title: Saadat Khan V. Ali Sher and 2 others,
explainer:
This case explains the legal doctrine of res judicata, meaning that once a court has finally decided a dispute between parties, the same dispute cannot be litigated again. The petitioner, Saadat Khan, had filed an earlier civil suit claiming rights over certain property. He then filed a fresh suit over the same property, seeking cancellation of an agreement and a no-objection certificate, and asking the court to enforce a different, earlier agreement in his favor. The defendants objected, arguing that this new suit was barred because the same property, the same parties, and essentially the same cause of action had already been the subject of previous litigation.

Both the trial court and the appellate court agreed, rejecting the plaint under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code, read with Section 11 (the res judicata provision). Saadat Khan then challenged these decisions through a civil revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions, explaining in detail the purpose of res judicata: to prevent repeated litigation over matters already decided, protect parties from harassment, and ensure finality of judgments. It also discussed "constructive res judicata," meaning that even issues which could have been raised earlier but were not are treated as decided. Finding that the property, parties, and cause of action were identical to the earlier suit, the court dismissed the revision petition, ruling that the new suit was legally barred and that the petitioner was also stopped by his own conduct from reopening the matter.

title: Noor Jan and 5 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application in a murder case from Balochistan. Six people (Noor Jan and five others) were accused of firing on and killing a man named Nawab Khan in his field. The deceased's mother filed a police report naming eight accused persons and unidentified others, alleging they all fired on her son. The accused had been denied bail by the trial court and approached the High Court seeking release on post-arrest bail.

The High Court granted bail. It found several weaknesses in the prosecution's case: there was a two-and-a-half-hour delay in reporting the incident despite the police station being only 12 kilometres away, suggesting the complainant may have had time to deliberate or consult others before naming suspects. The FIR vaguely described the incident without specifying which accused caused which injury, and did not even identify the weapons used. Although eight people were accused of firing, the victim had only one gunshot wound, and no witnesses were injured despite the open setting of the alleged attack. The court also noted that another person had filed a competing report about the same incident, resulting in two separate police challans (charge sheets) reflecting conflicting versions of events. No weapons were recovered from the accused during investigation.

Given these inconsistencies, the court held that the case fell under the provision allowing bail due to doubtful evidence, and granted the accused post-arrest bail.

title: Abdul Rauf V. Government of Balochistan, through Chief Secretary and 3 others,
explainer:
Abdul Rauf, a civil servant working as Executive Engineer in the Public Health Engineering Department, challenged his transfer order through a constitutional petition filed in the Balochistan High Court. He argued that the notification transferring him from his post was illegal and asked the court to set it aside and let him complete his tenure.

The High Court dismissed the petition without examining its merits, holding that it had no jurisdiction to hear the case. The judge explained that matters relating to the terms and conditions of service of civil servants, including transfers and postings, fall exclusively within the domain of the Balochistan Service Tribunal. While Article 199 of the Constitution allows High Courts to hear constitutional petitions, Article 212 specifically bars courts from intervening in matters that fall under the jurisdiction of Administrative Courts or Tribunals like the Service Tribunal. Since Article 212 overrides Article 199 in such cases, the court said it could not even consider issues like whether an alternate remedy existed or whether the transfer was made in bad faith, because the jurisdictional bar prevented the court from acting at all.

The case matters because it reaffirms a key constitutional principle: civil servants seeking to challenge service-related decisions such as transfers must go through the Service Tribunal and departmental appellate channels, not the High Court, reinforcing the clear separation of jurisdiction between ordinary courts and specialized service tribunals.

title: Muhammad Ishaque Notezai V. Government of Pakistan, establishment division, cabinet Secretariat, islamabad through Secretary and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Ishaque Notezai, a Member of the National Industrial Relations Commission (NIRC) posted at the Quetta Bench in Balochistan. He went to court because he discovered he was being paid significantly less than a counterpart Member serving at the NIRC's Multan Bench, even though both held the same rank (BPS-21) and performed identical duties.

The petitioner had signed a contract agreement when appointed, which stated his pay and allowances would be fixed in line with Members of NIRC working in other provincial benches. However, pay records showed a large gap: he received about Rs. 224,812 per month, while his counterpart in Multan received about Rs. 362,586.

The Balochistan High Court found that although the petitioner was not automatically entitled to pay equal to a High Court Judge (since he had agreed to BPS-21 terms), he was entitled to equal treatment with other NIRC Members under his own contract terms. Since he performed the same function as Members elsewhere and had been appointed on identical terms, paying him less amounted to unjustified discrimination, violating Article 25 of the Constitution, which guarantees equality before the law.

The court allowed the petition and directed the authorities to pay him salary and allowances equal to those paid to the Member of the Multan Bench. This case highlights that government employees doing the same job under the same terms must be treated equally, regardless of which province they serve in.

title: Muhammad Yahya Khan and others V. Akram Shah and other,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute over land in Quetta district. The plaintiffs (respondents in this appeal) claimed that their predecessor had purchased the disputed land through an agreement in 1995, but the agreement was never acted upon and the property remained registered in the name of the sellers' side. The plaintiffs sued for declaration of ownership, cancellation of records, partition, enforcement of the sale agreement, and related relief.

While the suit was ongoing, the defendants asked the trial court to reject the plaint outright, arguing the agreement had nothing to do with the actual land in question and that disputes over revenue entries could only be handled by revenue authorities, not civil courts. The trial court agreed and dismissed the case without a full hearing. On appeal, the appellate court reversed this and sent the case back for a proper trial. The defendants then challenged that reversal before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It held that when a case involves genuinely disputed facts, such as whether an agreement is genuine or relates to the property in question, the court cannot simply throw out the case at a preliminary stage. Instead, it must let the parties present evidence and decide the issues on merit. The court also rejected the argument that civil courts lacked jurisdiction, noting that civil courts can hear such disputes unless a law specifically bars them. The revision petitions were dismissed, meaning the case will now proceed to trial.

title: Dad Muhammad V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against convictions for murder, attempted murder, and rioting arising from a 1995 incident in which several people, including the complainant's brother, nephews, and a labourer, were killed or injured due to alleged prior enmity. The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence closely and found serious flaws in the prosecution's case.

The complainant, who was not an eyewitness, never appeared in court to testify despite summons, and his original police report showed he was uncertain about the identity of the attackers when the FIR was filed. A key injured witness changed his account dramatically over the years, naming the accused only after a nineteen-year gap, contradicting his earlier statement describing masked attackers. Two other witnesses claiming to be eyewitnesses were found to be interested and biased relatives of the victims, and their account was implausible because they claimed to be present during heavy gunfire yet were untouched despite being obvious targets given their relationship to the deceased.

Based on these inconsistencies, dishonest improvements in testimony, and the implausible nature of the witnesses' accounts, the court concluded the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, and the conviction was overturned.

This case matters because it demonstrates how courts scrutinize witness credibility, delays in testimony, and implausible narratives to protect the fundamental principle that the prosecution must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt before someone can be convicted of a serious crime.

title: Munir Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted and sentenced to death by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Pishin for the kidnapping, murder and attempted sodomy of a ten or eleven-year-old boy who had gone missing in 2019. The accused was convicted under multiple sections of the Pakistan Penal Code and the Anti-Terrorism Act, with the trial court also awarding ten years imprisonment for attempted unnatural offence.

On appeal to the Balochistan High Court, the convict argued he was actually a juvenile at the time of the crime, and that the state-appointed defence lawyer at his trial had failed to properly represent him by not cross-examining prosecution witnesses, and that no inquiry into his age had ever been conducted.

The High Court agreed this was a serious failure of due process. It held that when there is conflicting evidence about a person's age, medical opinion should generally be preferred. It also emphasized that lawyers appointed at state expense owe the same duty of diligent representation as any other counsel, and that an accused's right to a fair, properly prepared defence is constitutionally protected.

As a result, the Court set aside the conviction and death sentence entirely and sent the case back to the trial court. It ordered that the accused be given a genuine opportunity to choose his own lawyer or have a senior lawyer appointed, that witnesses be recalled for proper cross-examination, and that a formal inquiry into his age be held under the Juvenile Justice System Act before the trial continues.

title: Taweez Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves an appeal by Taweez Khan, who was convicted and sentenced for the murder of the complainant's son and another person, allegedly killed by firing. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court challenging his conviction.

The court examined the evidence closely and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. First, the complainant was not an eyewitness and learned of the killings from a relative, who was never produced in court or questioned by investigators, even though this relative was clearly important to the case. Courts can treat withholding such a key witness as suggesting the evidence would not have supported the prosecution. Second, there was an unexplained delay of over three and a half hours in filing the police report, raising suspicion that time was used to deliberately decide who to name as culprits. Third, the sole eyewitness refused to identify the accused in court and was declared hostile, with no identification parade ever conducted. Fourth, the mobile phone call records used as evidence were unreliable, not properly verified, and could not even be confirmed as belonging to the accused. Finally, bullet casings found at the scene were never sent for forensic testing, making them unreliable corroborative evidence at best.

Given all these weaknesses, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and allowed the appeal, overturning the conviction. This case highlights how courts scrutinize witness credibility, evidence handling, and investigative shortcuts before upholding serious criminal convictions.

title: Murtaza V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves Murtaza, who was convicted by a trial court in Balochistan and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine for allegedly possessing 26 kilograms of charas (hashish), an offence under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. The drugs were supposedly found hidden in his car during a checkpoint search.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him, citing serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, the chain of custody for the drug samples was not proven: the police official responsible for storing evidence (the Moharrar) was never produced or questioned, and there was an unexplained three-day gap between the recovery of the drugs and when the samples reached the laboratory, raising the possibility of tampering. Second, there was an unexplained five-hour delay in filing the police report (FIR), which the court said increases the risk of false implication and requires a credible explanation that the prosecution failed to provide. Third, the witnesses gave contradictory accounts about key details, such as exactly where in the car the drugs were found, who searched the vehicle, and what time they arrived at the scene.

Because of these unexplained gaps and inconsistencies, the court held that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and the appellant deserved the benefit of the doubt. This case illustrates how strict evidentiary standards, especially around evidence handling and witness consistency, are essential to prevent wrongful convictions in narcotics cases.

title: Gulzar and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal before the Balochistan High Court by two men, Gulzar and another, who had been convicted of murder and attempted murder. The prosecution's case was that the accused fired upon two brothers, killing one and injuring the other. The complainant, who was the injured brother, lodged the FIR within thirty minutes of the incident, naming the accused and describing their specific roles.

The court examined the eyewitness testimony from the complainant and the injured brother, both of whom were present at the scene and gave consistent accounts despite lengthy cross-examination. This testimony was supported by medical evidence confirming the cause of death and the nature of injuries, as well as physical evidence like blood-stained soil, clothing, and recovered bullet casings matched by forensic analysis. The court rejected the defense's argument that the witnesses, being brothers of the deceased, were unreliable, ruling that relation alone does not discredit testimony when it is credible and no enmity is shown.

However, the court found problems with the recovery of weapons from the accused, noting contradictions between the Head Constable and Investigating Officer about when and how the recovery happened, and ruled that since the weapons were recovered jointly from both accused rather than individually, this evidence was not admissible.

Ultimately, based on the strength of eyewitness and medical evidence, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the convictions, reinforcing that reliable eyewitness testimony from related witnesses can be sufficient to prove guilt even without flawless corroborating evidence.

title: Mir Wais V. Naseebullah and 3 others,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and deals with how police complaints are handled when someone approaches a Justice of Peace to get a criminal case registered against another person.

The petitioner, Mir Wais, had an FIR registered against him under injury-causing provisions of law, and separately was arrested in a narcotics case involving a vehicle with two different number plates. The complainant in the original injury case then filed an application asking a Justice of Peace (an Additional Sessions Judge acting in that capacity) to direct police to register a further criminal case against the petitioner. The Justice of Peace accepted this request and ordered registration of the case without giving detailed reasons.

The petitioner challenged this order, arguing it was issued mechanically and was intended merely to harass him.

The High Court agreed. It held that a Justice of Peace must not act as a rubber stamp by simply accepting one party's version of events. Instead, the judge must genuinely examine whether there is actual supporting material before directing registration of a case, since such proceedings are quasi-judicial, not routine administrative acts. Relying on earlier Supreme Court guidance, the Court found the complaint here appeared aimed at harassing the petitioner rather than seeking genuine justice, showing mala fide intent. It therefore set aside the Justice of Peace's order and allowed the petition.

The case highlights safeguards against misuse of police-complaint powers to settle personal scores through criminal proceedings.

title: Muhammad Yaqoob V. Zahir Shah,
explainer:
This case is about a civil appeal filed before the Balochistan High Court by Muhammad Yaqoob, who had earlier sued Zahir Shah for defamation and damages of Rs. 2 crore under the Defamation Ordinance, 2002. Yaqoob claimed that Shah had made defamatory allegations against him while recording a statement before NAB authorities during an inquiry into land dealings in Gwadar. The trial court had dismissed his suit, and he challenged that dismissal before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that Yaqoob's plaint failed to specify crucial details required by law, such as when and where the alleged defamatory statements were made, who heard them, what exact words were defamatory, and how financial loss was calculated. The court noted these are mandatory requirements under the Civil Procedure Code's rules on pleadings. It also found the suit was filed too late: the legal notice to Shah was sent nearly eleven months after Yaqoob learned of the allegations, even though the Defamation Ordinance requires notice within two months and sets a six-month limitation period for filing such suits, which applies instead of the general Limitation Act since this is a special law.

The judgment matters because it clarifies that defamation claims require precise, detailed pleadings and must be filed within strict time limits, otherwise vague allegations without specifics cannot succeed in court, even if genuine reputational harm is claimed.

title: Meer Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court, deciding an appeal by Meer Muhammad against his conviction for murder (qatl-i-amd), abetment, and acting with common intention under the Pakistan Penal Code. He had allegedly fired at the deceased on the instigation of a co-accused.

The court examined the evidence of the complainant and two eye-witnesses, who were cousins of the deceased, and found it unreliable for several reasons. The witnesses' conduct was unnatural: instead of taking the dead body and injured person to the hospital themselves, they simply waited at the scene for Levies officials. The FIR was lodged with an unexplained delay of seven hours and forty minutes, despite the witnesses supposedly being present at the scene, suggesting it was prepared only after consultation rather than being a spontaneous report. The complainant did not even name the eye-witnesses in the FIR, and the two eye-witnesses' statements contradicted each other and failed to mention each other's presence. The court also found it implausible that the accused would spare the eye-witnesses, who were unarmed and defenseless, while killing their cousins with whom there was no clear motive.

Based on these doubts, the court held that the prosecution failed to prove the case with reliable, trustworthy evidence and gave the accused the benefit of the doubt, allowing the appeal and setting aside the conviction. The case highlights how courts scrutinize witness credibility, delays, and inconsistencies to prevent wrongful convictions.

title: Asadullah V. Allah Dad and 2 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a murder trial (FIR under sections 302, 337-ADF, 504, 506 and 34 PPC). During the trial, an eyewitness (PW-4) testified but only named one accused as responsible, even though in his earlier police statement he had implicated two accused persons. The complainant's lawyer and the public prosecutor asked the trial court to declare this witness "hostile" so they could cross-examine him, but the trial court refused. The petitioner challenged that refusal before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It explained the important legal difference between a "hostile" witness and an "unfavourable" witness. A hostile witness deliberately lies, changes his story, or shows bias against the party who called him. An unfavourable witness simply gives testimony that doesn't help the prosecution's case, without any deceit or hidden motive. The court found that this witness had consistently supported the main story of the incident but had genuinely not implicated the other two accused - there was no evidence he was lying or suppressing truth. Since declaring someone "hostile" is a discretionary power courts must use cautiously, and no grounds for hostility were shown here, the High Court dismissed the petition.

This case matters because it clarifies that simply giving testimony unfavourable to one's own side is not enough to brand a witness "hostile" - actual deceit, inconsistency, or bias must be shown first.

title: Muhammad Ameen V. Deputy Commissioner Panjgur,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Muhammad Ameen, whose land was partly taken by the government for a road construction project in Panjgur, Balochistan. He had already received compensation for date palm trees located on the affected land, but he wanted additional compensation for about 700 square feet of actual land that was absorbed into the road. When the Deputy Commissioner's office failed to decide his compensation application, he approached the Balochistan High Court directly under Article 199 of the Constitution, asking the court to order the authorities to process his claim and pay him.

The court dismissed the petition. The key problem was that Ameen could not prove he actually owned the land. He never produced any title documents, and when given a chance to submit evidence, he only provided an old court judgment from a dispute between other parties, which did not establish his ownership. The government's lawyer confirmed the land was officially government property.

The court explained that its special constitutional powers can only be used when someone's legal right is completely clear and beyond doubt. Since ownership here was disputed and unproven, the matter required a full civil trial with evidence, not a quick constitutional petition. This case illustrates an important principle: courts will not use their extraordinary writ jurisdiction to resolve property ownership disputes that need detailed factual investigation—such claims must go through ordinary civil courts instead.

title: Samiullah V. Special Judge Anti Rape/Sessions Judge, Sariab Division and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal trial involving a charge under Section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code. During the trial, the accused, Samiullah, asked the trial court to recall the victim, who had already testified and been cross-examined, so that he could be cross-examined again. The accused argued that his earlier lawyer had not asked proper questions and that a fresh cross-examination was necessary for justice. The trial court refused this request, and the accused challenged that refusal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision and dismissed the petition. It explained that Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code allows courts to summon or recall witnesses, but this power has two parts: one discretionary, and one that applies only when further evidence is truly essential for a just decision. The court clarified that simply hiring a new lawyer is not a valid reason to recall a witness who has already testified and been cross-examined. Allowing parties to reopen cross-examination merely because they are dissatisfied with previous counsel's performance would let trials drag on indefinitely and would misuse the law to fix gaps left by the parties themselves.

This ruling matters because it reinforces the principle that recalling witnesses is meant to serve justice, not to give either side a second chance to redo their case, helping ensure criminal trials proceed efficiently and fairly.

title: Khaliq Dad V. Nadir Khan and others,
explainer:
This case involved a clash between two tribes, the Mandokhail and Babar, over a disputed piece of land (viala) where one side was building a mosque. The fight involved 25-40 people from each side using cudgels and stones, and people on both sides were injured. Police lodged an FIR, and after investigation, separate criminal cases (challans) were filed against accused persons from both tribes, since each side blamed the other for starting the violence.

In one of these cases, the trial court accepted an application under section 249-A of the Criminal Procedure Code and acquitted the accused before the prosecution had even finished presenting its evidence. The complainant, Khaliq Dad, appealed this acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found this was improper. Although courts can review evidence in acquittal appeals, it noted that acquittals granted early under section 249-A don't carry the same weight as acquittals reached after a full trial. Since these were cross-cases arising from the same incident, the court held that both cases should have been tried side by side by the same court, with judgments announced together. This is because determining who was the real aggressor requires looking at evidence from both sides together, and deciding one case in isolation risks unfair or inconsistent results.

The court partly allowed the appeal, cancelled the acquittal, and sent the case back for trial to continue properly alongside the related case, with both judgments to be delivered simultaneously. This ruling reinforces fair procedure in cases involving rival versions of the same incident.

title: Maryam and others V. Nazuk and others,
explainer:
This case explains a property dispute about cancelling mutation entries (land ownership records) where the plaintiffs' suit was dismissed by the trial court for non-prosecution, meaning they failed to appear and present evidence. Their appeal was also dismissed. They then challenged both decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The key issue was that the case had been rescheduled not by the actual judge, but through a note from the court's Reader (clerical staff), after the original judge was transferred. On the new date, neither the plaintiffs nor their lawyer appeared, so the suit was dismissed.

The High Court found this procedurally improper. It held that a hearing date fixed only through a court clerk's note, rather than by the presiding judge himself, cannot be legally treated as a proper "date of hearing." Therefore, the dismissal based on that date was void and without jurisdiction. The court also noted that the trial court had wrongly used the law (Order XVII Rule 3 CPC, meant for failure to produce evidence) instead of the correct procedure, and had failed to give the plaintiffs a fair opportunity to testify.

The High Court ruled that such technical lapses should not be used to defeat people's genuine legal rights. It accepted the petition, effectively reviving the case so it can be decided on its merits rather than on a procedural technicality. This judgment reinforces that courts must follow proper procedure and protect litigants' fundamental right to a fair hearing.
