title: Alamzaib Khan V. Kasi Behria Town Main Jinnah Road, Quetta through CEO,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta. A buyer, Alamzaib Khan, had agreed to purchase two plots from a housing scheme called Kasi Behria Town under an installment plan, paying an advance of Rs. 40,000 plus monthly installments of Rs. 10,000. By the time of the dispute, he had already paid more than half the total price of Rs. 800,000. He filed a lawsuit seeking specific performance of the sale agreement (that is, forcing the seller to complete the sale) along with a declaration and permanent injunction, and asked the court for a temporary injunction to stop the housing scheme from cancelling his allotment or transferring the plots to someone else while the case was pending.

Both the trial court and the appellate court refused to grant this temporary injunction. Khan then challenged those refusals before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court explained that to get a temporary injunction, a person must show a prima facie case, risk of irreparable loss, and that the balance of convenience favors them. Reviewing the facts, the judge found that since Khan had already paid over half the purchase price under a valid agreement, he clearly had a strong prima facie case, and he risked serious loss if the property were sold to someone else. The High Court ruled that the lower courts were wrong to deny the injunction, set aside their orders, and granted the temporary injunction in Khan's favor, protecting his claim to the plots until the main case is decided.

title: Muhammad Rafique V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns a bail application in a murder case registered in Noshki, Balochistan. According to the First Information Report, the complainant's brother was shot and killed by a co-accused, Kaleemullah, who fired a pistol inside a shop. The applicant, Muhammad Rafiq, was also named in the FIR as having arrived at the scene with Kaleemullah on a motorcycle, but no act of firing was attributed to him. His earlier bail request had been rejected by the Sessions Judge, prompting this application before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court granted bail, reasoning that mere presence at a crime scene is not enough to establish guilt unless the prosecution shows the accused shared a common intention with the actual shooter or helped him in some way. The FIR did not even clarify whether the applicant was armed or empty-handed, and the co-accused's confession named a different person as being with him, not the applicant. The weapon was recovered based on the co-accused's disclosure, not the applicant's.

The court held that since no specific role was attributed to the applicant, his case required "further inquiry," a recognized ground for bail. It emphasized that even if trial proceedings have begun, courts retain power to grant bail where warranted, and wrongful detention of an innocent person cannot later be compensated. Bail was granted upon furnishing sureties worth Rs. 500,000.

title: Shah Jan Kareem and another V. Bashir and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over land in Turbat, Balochistan. The petitioners (Shah Jan Kareem and another) claimed their late father had purchased the property in 1986 and built boundary walls on it. They alleged that Respondent No. 1 fraudulently obtained an NOC from the local Municipal Corporation in 2018, transferred the property into his name, and later began illegal construction on it. The petitioners filed a lawsuit seeking a declaration of ownership, a permanent injunction, and cancellation of the fraudulent property transfer (mutation).

However, both the trial court and the appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora Mekran) rejected the plaint, pointing out that the petitioners had already filed an earlier, nearly identical lawsuit over the same property against the same parties, which had been rejected. When they appealed that earlier rejection, they withdrew the appeal without seeking permission to refile the case later.

The High Court upheld these decisions, applying the legal doctrine of res judicata, which prevents the same parties from re-litigating issues that have already been decided by a competent court. The judge explained that allowing a second suit on the same matter would be unfair, encourage endless litigation, and undermine the finality of court decisions. As a result, the court dismissed the petitioners' revision petition, meaning they could not pursue the same property dispute again.

title: Hassan Ali and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved three men—Hassan Ali, Bilal Khan, and Zafrullah—convicted of robbing a shop in Sibi in December 2020. During the robbery, the shop owner's son and a laborer present at the scene were shot and injured when one tried to resist the robbers. Police, alerted by the gunfire, arrived quickly and arrested all three men at the scene, recovering a pistol, the stolen money, and a motorcycle used in the crime.

A trial court convicted the men under Pakistan's Penal Code provisions dealing with robbery involving attempted murder or grievous harm, sentencing each to seven years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The men appealed to the High Court.

The High Court upheld the convictions. It found the First Information Report (FIR) had been filed promptly—within 25 minutes, given the short distance to the police station—which supported the credibility of the complainant's account and ruled out any chance that witnesses had fabricated the story. The court noted that four witnesses, including the injured parties and police officials, gave consistent testimony that withstood cross-examination. Forensic evidence and medical reports also matched the eyewitness accounts. Since the accused were caught red-handed with the weapon and stolen cash, the court found no grounds to doubt their identification. The appeals were dismissed, and the original convictions and sentences were upheld, reinforcing how prompt reporting and strong corroborating evidence can secure a robbery conviction.

title: Dilawar V. The State,
explainer:
Dilawar vs. The State (reported as part of a combined judgment with Pervaiz vs. The State) arose from a 2019 shooting in Gwadar district, Balochistan, in which one man was killed and another injured. The trial court had convicted the appellant Pervaiz of murder and attempted murder, sentencing him to life imprisonment and additional punishment for causing injury, while acquitting two co-accused. Three connected matters came before the Balochistan High Court: the convicted man's appeal against his conviction, the victim's widow's petition seeking a harsher sentence, and her separate appeal against the acquittal of the other two accused.

The High Court examined the evidence carefully, including eyewitness testimony from the deceased's brother and the surviving injured friend, who both consistently identified the appellant as the shooter. This was backed by medical evidence confirming firearm injuries, and forensic evidence showing that recovered bullet casings matched a pistol seized from the appellant, along with blood-stained material confirmed by laboratory testing.

The court held that being related to the victim does not automatically make a witness unreliable, especially when the testimony is consistent and withstands cross-examination. Finding the prosecution's case proven beyond reasonable doubt, the court dismissed the appeal against conviction. This case illustrates how courts weigh eyewitness accounts alongside forensic evidence to determine guilt in serious violent crimes.

title: Muhammad Rahim V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Rahim, who was convicted of murder (qatl-i-amd) for allegedly shooting the complainant's brother. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, along with a related reference confirming his death sentence.

The court examined the evidence closely and found serious doubts about the prosecution's case. The deceased was shot around 5:30 p.m. but only reached the hospital at 7:45 p.m., with a constable—not the supposed eyewitnesses—bringing the body. The court found it unnatural that injured persons would be left bleeding for over two hours instead of being rushed for treatment, suggesting the witnesses were not actually present.

The court also noted contradictions: despite claims of heavy indiscriminate firing (seven to nine shots at close range), only the deceased was hit while the other two people on the motorcycle were completely unharmed—an implausible outcome. It was also suspicious that the accused spared the eyewitnesses despite them being able to identify him later. Additionally, police failed to recover the motorcycle supposedly involved, and witnesses' clothes had no bloodstains, undermining the claim that the deceased was riding with them. Finally, the prosecution failed to produce any independent local witnesses from the area, despite dozens of people reportedly gathering at the scene.

Given these inconsistencies, the court ruled the prosecution had not proven guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, the conviction overturned, and the death sentence reference rejected. This case highlights how

title: Mir Muhammad V. Naeemullah and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a request to transfer a murder trial from one court to another. The applicant, involved in an FIR registered under section 302 of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder), asked the Balochistan High Court to move the case away from the Sessions Judge, Kalat, claiming that the judge was biased against him.

The High Court rejected this request. It explained that bias can take different forms, such as a judge having a personal stake in the case, a financial interest, or personal hostility toward a party. However, simply alleging bias is not enough, there must be solid, trustworthy evidence showing a real likelihood that the judge's conduct would unfairly affect the outcome of the trial. The court noted that the applicant's claim rested only on an alleged remark by the opposing side that they would receive favorable treatment from the court, something the judge said did not amount to proof of actual bias.

Since no concrete evidence was provided and the allegations were vague, the court dismissed the application outright, meaning it was rejected without even going into a detailed hearing of the merits.

This ruling reinforces an important principle: courts cannot be casually transferred just because a party feels suspicious or uneasy. Doing so would undermine judicial stability and allow parties to manipulate the system through baseless complaints. Genuine evidence of bias is required before such a serious step is taken.

title: Muhammad Anees and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two brothers, Muhammad Anees and another man, who were convicted of possessing narcotics - 800 grams of ice (crystal meth) and 450 grams of charas - allegedly recovered from a residential house. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court against their conviction.

The court overturned the conviction and acquitted the appellants. It found several serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, there was no proof the accused actually owned or occupied the house where the drugs were found, and witnesses admitted other people also lived there, meaning conscious possession was never established. Second, the story itself was implausible: police claimed both brothers together tried to hide a small bag of drugs in the bathroom, but no witness explained which one did it, and it seemed physically odd for two people to jointly hide one small bag. Third, no independent witnesses from the neighborhood were included during the raid and arrest, despite people being available nearby, raising doubts about transparency. Fourth, there were contradictions among police witnesses, suggesting a sloppy investigation. Finally, police failed to obtain a search warrant for the house as generally required by law, despite having prior information and time to get one.

This judgment matters because it reinforces important safeguards in narcotics cases: police cannot convict someone merely for being present near drugs, must prove actual ownership or control, should involve independent witnesses, and must follow proper search procedures to prevent false implication.

title: Bashir Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This is a Balochistan High Court appeal by Bashir Ahmed, who had been convicted of murdering the complainant's son by throwing him from a mountain. The High Court overturned the conviction, finding the prosecution's evidence unreliable and insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

The judgment identified several major flaws in the case. First, there was an unexplained eighteen-day delay in filing the police report, even though the complainant could have traveled from Sindh to Balochistan in about twenty hours and had allegedly learned of the murder claim much earlier -- raising suspicion of deliberation or fabrication. Second, the prosecution relied on an alleged extra-judicial confession, where a witness claimed the accused admitted guilt casually. The court found this confession inherently weak and suspicious, noting the witness was an ordinary person with no reason to receive such an admission, and that courts treat such confessions as having almost no evidentiary weight unless strongly corroborated. Third, key witnesses to the alleged confession and a video recording were never produced in court, and a forensic report could not confirm the video's authenticity, triggering a legal presumption that the withheld evidence would have hurt the prosecution's case. The sole eyewitness's account was also questioned as unreliable.

title: Muhammad Saleem V. The Assistant Commissioner Turbat and another,
explainer:
This case was about a land dispute in Turbat involving a cell phone tower. Ufone, a mobile company, had leased land from Muhammad Saleem to install a communication tower, and a local land official (Patwari) had confirmed the land belonged to him. However, another party claimed ownership of the same land and filed a complaint with the Assistant Commissioner Turbat, who ruled in their favor, declaring that the land belonged to them instead.

Saleem challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the Assistant Commissioner had no authority to decide such a dispute.

The High Court agreed with him. It held that when a genuine dispute over property ownership exists, especially involving allegations of fraud, only a civil court can resolve it, because civil courts have full ("plenary") power to examine evidence and hear both sides properly. Revenue authorities, like the Assistant Commissioner, only handle matters in a summary, limited way and cannot settle complicated ownership disputes. The court explained that a "question of title" arises whenever someone denies another person's ownership claim, and such questions must go to a civil court, not be decided administratively.

Since both parties claimed ownership and denied each other's rights, the Assistant Commissioner's order was declared unlawful and set aside. The case highlights that ownership disputes must be resolved through proper civil litigation, not through quick administrative decisions.

title: Pervaiz V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an applicant named Dilawar, accused in a 2021 FIR of entering a complainant's house with others and firing on the complainant's son, causing bullet injuries, under charges of attempted murder and robbery/dacoity with intent to cause death or grievous hurt. He had earlier been granted bail by the trial court, but that bail was cancelled by the High Court on merits. He later applied again for bail, this time arguing that he had already spent a long time in jail without his trial concluding, and that the delay was not his fault.

The Balochistan High Court examined the law under section 497 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which states that if an accused is detained for more than one year in a non-death-penalty case, and the delay in trial is not due to the accused's own actions, the court must grant bail. The record showed the applicant had been in custody for one year and nine months, prosecution evidence was still incomplete, and both his lawyer and the state's counsel agreed the delay was not his fault.

Based on this statutory ground, the court granted him bail, requiring sureties worth Rs. 500,000. This case illustrates how prolonged pretrial detention without progress in trial can itself become a valid legal ground for bail, reinforcing the principle that personal liberty should not be indefinitely restricted due to court delays beyond the accused's control.

title: Kashmir alias Soba Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by a man convicted of murdering his brother along with the brother's wife, a crime also involving rioting charges. The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence against him and found serious problems with the prosecution's case.

First, the FIR (police report) was lodged 22 hours late, even though the distance to the police station could have been covered in 8-9 hours, and police had actually arrived at the crime scene before the FIR was even filed-suggesting time was taken for deliberation about who to accuse rather than reporting spontaneously.

Second, the complainant mentioned a police official who informed him of the murder, but that official was never produced as a witness, creating doubt.

Third, the court found the alleged eyewitness's account implausible-questioning why the attackers would spare him if he could identify them, and noting his statement was oddly recorded only after the FIR, not before.

Fourth, the crime occurred at 3:00 am, yet no evidence was presented showing any light source existed to allow identification of the attackers.

Finally, both the complainant and the eyewitness had significantly changed their statements between two different court appearances, first implicating one set of accused and later excluding an already-acquitted co-accused while still naming the appellant-damaging their credibility.

Given these cumulative doubts, the court allowed the appeal and overturned the conviction, highlighting how delay, unreliable witnesses, and inconsistent testimony can undermine a murder case.

title: Abdul Aziz V. The State,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court, deciding a criminal appeal alongside an automatic reference on a death sentence. Abdul Aziz was convicted of murdering his father-in-law and wounding his mother-in-law during a family dispute. The incident occurred when the appellant insisted on taking his wife and children with him, but his father-in-law asked him to wait a day since his mother-in-law was unwell. The appellant responded by opening fire with a pistol, fatally wounding his father-in-law and injuring his mother-in-law.

The court examined the evidence carefully, including the dying declaration made by the father-in-law (recorded by police before he died), eyewitness testimony from the injured mother-in-law, and corroborating testimony from the couple's son, along with medical reports confirming firearm injuries. The court explained that dying declarations carry special weight since a dying person is unlikely to lie, but still require scrutiny; here, medical certification confirmed the victim was conscious and fit to make his statement. The court also addressed the defence argument that witnesses were "interested" because they were relatives, ruling that family relationship alone does not disqualify a witness's credible testimony.

Finding the prosecution's case proven beyond reasonable doubt, the court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence from death to life imprisonment due to mitigating circumstances, dismissing the appeal with this modification. The case illustrates how Pakistani courts evaluate dying declarations and witness credibility in serious crimes.

title: Syed Muhammad Tasleem Shah V. Government of Pakistan through Ministry of Religious Affairs and Interfaith Harmony Islamabad and others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute over a shop in Quetta originally allotted by the Evacuee Trust Property Board. The petitioner's father had occupied the shop for decades, while the predecessor of the private respondents claimed to be the registered tenant. Over the years, both sides went through multiple rounds of civil litigation. The private respondents' earlier suit for possession was dismissed, and that decision became final after being upheld through appeal and a constitutional petition. Later, the petitioner himself filed a civil suit seeking a declaration of title and an order directing authorities to issue the rent receipt in his name. That suit was initially partly decreed in his favor, but on appeal, the Additional District Judge reversed the decision and dismissed the petitioner's suit entirely.

Months later, after officials locked the shop and issued an eviction notice, the petitioner approached the High Court under Article 199 of the Constitution, asking it to declare the locking unlawful and to direct authorities to act on his pending applications, including transferring the rent receipt to his name.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that since the petitioner's claim to title had already been rejected by the civil courts, he was effectively trying to relitigate a settled matter through writ jurisdiction. The court emphasized that constitutional relief is equitable in nature, available only to those who approach with clean hands, and cannot be used to achieve what courts have already denied. This case reinforces that writ jurisdiction cannot override final civil court findings or assist litigants seeking unjust outcomes.

title: Basit Ali V. Higher Education Commission (HEC) and others,
explainer:
This case was heard by the Balochistan High Court after a law graduate, Basit Ali, challenged the way the Higher Education Commission (HEC) selected candidates for a foreign scholarship program for LLM studies. The petitioner had taken HEC's scholarship test twice, in 2021 and 2022, but was not selected either time. He argued that the eligibility criteria, which combined test scores with academic credentials like LLB grades, unfairly disadvantaged graduates from the University of Punjab, Lahore, because that university's grading system resulted in lower scores compared to other institutions. He asked the court to direct HEC to prepare the merit list based solely on test scores rather than academic credentials.

The court dismissed the petition. It found that the petitioner had voluntarily participated in the HEC test under the known criteria, and only complained after failing to secure a scholarship. Applying the legal principle of estoppel, the court held that someone who willingly takes part in a selection process cannot later challenge its fairness simply because they did not succeed. The court also emphasized that courts should not interfere in policy and technical decisions made by expert bodies like HEC unless there is clear evidence of bad faith or illegality, which was absent here. The judgment reinforces that educational institutions have discretion to set evaluation criteria, and dissatisfaction with results alone is not grounds for judicial intervention.

title: Dr. Chakar Riaz V Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary Civil Secretarait, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:

He later challenged his transfer out of the post and the appointment of another person as the new CEO, arguing the government's actions were illegal.

The Balochistan High Court examined the Pak-Oman Hospital Pasni Act, 2021, which clearly lays out that the CEO must be appointed by the Hospital's Board of Governors, based on a panel of three candidates recommended by a Special Selection Committee after a proper merit-based process. The court found that neither the petitioner's original appointment nor the respondent's subsequent appointment followed this legal procedure—both were made through the Health Secretary on the Chief Minister's recommendation, bypassing the Board entirely.

Because both appointments violated the law, the court ruled that neither man could claim a vested right to the post, since rights to public office can only arise from lawful, properly conducted appointments. The court emphasized that when a law specifies a particular procedure, it must be followed exactly, and that temporary or stopgap postings don't create permanent entitlements.

The petition was disposed of by directing the Board of Governors to appoint a new CEO strictly in accordance with the procedure set out in the 2021 Act, reinforcing the principle that public appointments must follow statutory process rather than political recomm

title: Muhammad Rafique V. The State,

Three eyewitnesses testified, but their accounts showed that Rafique himself was unarmed and did not cause any injury to the victim.

The court noted that two other co-accused, facing identical allegations based on the same evidence, had already been acquitted and given the benefit of the doubt. It held that evidence disbelieved for some accused cannot suddenly become credible against another accused in the same trial. The alleged motive—a dispute over the deceased visiting his father-in-law's house before marriage—was also found unproven, as the witnesses' accounts were inconsistent and improbable. Additionally, the trial court had relied on evidence that was never properly put to the accused during his statement under Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code, denying him a chance to explain it.

The High Court also emphasized that mere presence at a crime scene, without any proven common intention or overt act, cannot justify convicting someone under principles of shared or vicarious liability.

Concluding that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the High Court acquitted Rafique and allowed his appeal, reinforcing important safeguards against convictions based on weak or inconsistent evidence.

title: Muhammad Ilyas V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court, deciding an appeal by Muhammad Ilyas, who had been convicted of murdering the complainant's brother by shooting him. Ilyas challenged his conviction, arguing weaknesses in the prosecution's evidence, including a retracted confession.

The court examined several pieces of evidence: the FIR was filed the same day as the murder, before the parties could have conspired to falsely implicate anyone; the complainant's testimony about last seeing his brother was consistent and could not be shaken under cross-examination; and most importantly, the accused's judicial confession recorded under Section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

Although the accused later retracted his confession during trial, the court found it was made voluntarily, after he had time to reconsider, and the magistrate who recorded it followed all proper legal procedures. The court noted that a twelve-day gap between arrest and confession did not automatically make it unreliable, since no fixed time limit exists for this as long as it falls within legal custody, and there was no evidence of coercion. The medical evidence confirming firearm injuries to the head matched details in the confession, adding further corroboration.

Based on this combination of prompt reporting, credible witness testimony, a voluntary and corroborated confession, and supporting medical evidence, the court concluded the prosecution had proven guilt beyond reasonable doubt and dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction. This case illustrates how retracted confessions can still support convictions when properly corroborated.

title: Mir Shams Ud Din V. Mir Zia Ud Din and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute between Mir Shams Ud Din and Mir Zia Ud Din, with two connected civil suits pending before a Senior Civil Judge in Quetta. During the proceedings, the petitioner, Shams Ud Din, asked for both suits to be transferred away from the trial judge, claiming the judge was biased against him. His main evidence was that the opposing side had allegedly said they would get a favourable outcome from that particular court. The appellate court (District Judge) rejected this transfer request, and Shams Ud Din then challenged that rejection before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower court's decision and dismissed the petition. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, it explained that bias can take different forms, such as a judge having a personal stake in the case, a financial interest, or personal hostility toward a party. However, simply claiming that the other side boasted about getting favour from the court, with no concrete evidence of improper conduct by the judge, is not enough to prove bias. The court stressed that transfer of cases cannot be granted on mere suspicion or convenience of a party; there must be solid, trustworthy evidence of actual bias or interest.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that courts will not easily permit parties to shop for different judges based on unsubstantiated fears, protecting the integrity and stability of ongoing trials.

title: Waheed Khan V. Naseebullah and another,
explainer:
This case involved Waheed Khan, who was convicted by a Sessions Court in Harnai, Balochistan, for attempted murder after his brother allegedly shot and injured a man named Asadullah. According to the prosecution, Waheed and his absconding brother Ahmed arrived together on a motorcycle, Waheed called the victim out of his shop, and Ahmed then opened fire, wounding him. Waheed was convicted not for firing the shot himself but under the legal principle of common intention, meaning he was held equally responsible for sharing a plan with his brother to commit the crime.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined whether simply accompanying his brother and calling the victim outside was enough to prove Waheed shared a common intention to commit murder. The court found no evidence of prior enmity between the families, no proof of planning between the brothers, and crucially, that Waheed was unarmed at the time. The court reasoned that if he had known his brother intended violence, he likely would have carried a weapon too. The investigation was also weak, failing to even verify ownership of the motorcycle used.

The court explained that convicting someone for sharing common intention under the law requires strong, convincing evidence of prior agreement, not just presence at the scene. Since the prosecution failed to meet this standard, the High Court allowed the appeal and overturned Waheed Khan's conviction. The case highlights how courts guard against punishing people merely for being present during a crime committed by a relative.

title: Bibi Fareeda V. Jan Bibi,
explainer:
This case arose from a property dispute. Jan Bibi had won a civil suit against Ali Dost over declaration, partition, and possession of property. When Ali Dost died during execution proceedings, the court ordered the property to be auctioned. His widow, who should have been named Bibi Fazila, filed an appeal against the auction order, but due to a clerical error by a typist (steno), her name was mistakenly written as Bibi Fareeda in the appeal's title. The appeal itself was successful in 2021, but two years later, when she sought to correct her name in the appeal's title, the appellate court refused, saying the request came too late.

The Balochistan High Court overturned that refusal. It held that courts have the power under Sections 151 and 152 of the Civil Procedure Code to fix genuine clerical mistakes, and a two-year delay alone is not a good enough reason to deny such a correction, especially when the error was an honest typing mistake and did not harm the other party. The court stressed that procedural rules exist to serve justice, not to create technical obstacles that defeat genuine claims. It ordered the appeal's title corrected to reflect the correct name, Bibi Fazila.

This case matters because it reinforces that courts should prioritize substantive justice over rigid technicalities, especially for minor, honest errors that don't prejudice anyone.

title: Sanaullah V. Cantonment Executive, Officer, Quetta Cantt and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a civil dispute over Bungalow No. 24-C, Model Town, Quetta. The petitioner, Sanaullah, had filed a suit seeking a declaration of ownership and transfer of the property, but the trial court dismissed his suit after a full trial. He then appealed to the District Judge, Quetta. While the appeal was pending, he asked the appellate court for permission to introduce certain additional documents as evidence, something allowed only in limited circumstances under Order XLI, Rule 27 of the Civil Procedure Code. The appellate court refused, and Sanaullah challenged that refusal before the Balochistan High Court through this civil revision petition.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision and dismissed the petition. It held that the documents in question were irrelevant to the case, were not mentioned anywhere in the original plaint, and predated the filing of the suit, meaning the petitioner must have known about them earlier. He gave no credible explanation for why he could not produce them during the trial. The court emphasized that the law allowing additional evidence at the appeal stage is meant for exceptional situations, not to let a losing party patch up weaknesses in their case after the fact. Citing a Supreme Court precedent, the judge found no new evidence had genuinely surfaced and ruled the petitioner's attempt amounted to a "fishing inquiry," reinforcing that courts should use this power sparingly to maintain fairness and finality in litigation.

title: Syed Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a bail application before the Balochistan High Court by Syed Muhammad, who was accused of murder under Pakistan's Penal Code. He was charged along with two other men for allegedly shooting and killing a man named Azizullah in December 2022. The trial court had earlier refused him bail.

The key issue was that all three accused were said to have played the same role in the shooting. However, one co-accused had already been acquitted by the trial court after being given the benefit of the doubt, and another co-accused had been granted bail. Since the applicant was accused of the identical role as these two men, the High Court applied what is called the rule of consistency or doctrine of parity, meaning that when accused persons face the same allegations, they should generally be treated the same way unless there is a clear difference in their roles.

The prosecution argued that the applicant should be denied bail because he had been absconding after the incident, but the court held that mere absconding is not proof of guilt and does not automatically block bail if the case otherwise qualifies on its merits.

The court concluded that keeping the applicant in custody would serve no purpose, since the matter would ultimately be decided through trial evidence. Bail was therefore granted.

This case is important because it reinforces how fairness and consistency between co-accused must be considered at the bail stage, and clarifies that absconding alone is not sufficient reason to refuse bail.

title: Umer Khayam Jogezai and 4 others V. Mumtaz and 22 others,
explainer:
This case arose from a property dispute in which the petitioners had filed a civil suit seeking declaration of ownership, possession, and a permanent injunction over disputed land. During the trial, after the petitioners had already presented four witnesses, they sought to introduce additional documentary evidence, specifically a map of the disputed property, through a representative of the revenue authority. They filed this request under Order XIII, Rules 1 and 2 of the Civil Procedure Code. The trial court rejected this application, apparently because it came late in the proceedings.

The petitioners challenged this rejection before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court ruled in their favor, holding that a mere delay in filing an application to produce documents is not, by itself, sufficient reason to refuse it. The law allows courts to admit such evidence at any stage if there is a good cause and if the authenticity of the documents is not genuinely in doubt. Since the document in question was a public record held by the revenue department, there was little risk of tampering or manipulation, and the opposing side would still get a chance to question it during cross-examination.

The Court emphasized that procedural rules exist to serve justice, not to create technical obstacles, and that cases should be decided on their merits. As a result, the High Court set aside the trial court's order and allowed the petitioners to produce the document. This case reinforces that courts should prioritize fair, complete fact-finding over rigid procedural timing.

title: Allah Dad V. Maqbool Ahmed,
explainer:
This case was about a landlord-tenant dispute that had already been decided, but a new issue came up during the enforcement of that decision. The landlord (respondent) had won an eviction case against the tenant (appellant), and the court ordered the tenant to vacate two shops and pay outstanding rent. This decree became final after appeals were exhausted, and possession of the shops was handed back to the landlord.

However, after the case was fully decided, the landlord filed a new application asking the execution court to also order the tenant to pay unpaid utility bills, claiming his previous lawyer had mistakenly left this out of the original eviction case. The execution court agreed and ordered the tenant to pay the utility arrears.

The Balochistan High Court overturned this decision. It ruled that an execution court's job is only to enforce the decree as written, not to add new reliefs or re-examine issues that were never raised or decided during the original trial. Since the utility bills issue was never pleaded, argued, or ruled upon in the original case, it could not be introduced later at the execution stage. Courts must execute decrees exactly as they are, since allowing new claims afterward would mean decrees never truly become final. The appeal was therefore accepted, and the order requiring payment of utility bills was set aside.

title: Mir Ahmed Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which punishes dishonestly issuing a cheque that later bounces. The complainant claimed the accused owed him Rs. 58,00,000 for purchasing a house and had issued a cheque to settle the debt, which was dishonored because the bank account was dormant. The trial court convicted the accused, sentencing him to three years imprisonment and a fine, and an appellate court upheld this conviction. The accused then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction. It found serious problems with the complainant's case: during cross-examination, the complainant admitted the house actually belonged to a third party who had mortgaged it to a bank, raising doubts about how the complainant could have sold it at all. This key witness was never produced in court, and his absence allowed the court to presume his testimony would have contradicted the prosecution's story. The complainant also changed his account midway, first claiming the debt was for a house, then switching to claim it was for vehicles—a shift the court viewed as a deliberate, dishonest improvement rather than innocent memory lapse.

The court emphasized that merely issuing a cheque that bounces isn't a crime; there must be proof of a genuine underlying debt and dishonest intent. Since the complainant failed to prove any real transaction existed, the conviction could not stand, and the accused was acquitted. This case highlights how courts scrutinize the credibility and consistency of evidence before upholding cheque-dishon

title: Rab Nawaz V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by a man convicted of raping an eight or nine-year-old girl, the daughter of the complainant, in Balochistan. The trial court had sentenced him to death, and the matter came before the High Court both as his appeal and as a mandatory reference to confirm or reject the death sentence.

The defense raised several objections: an eight-day delay in reporting the crime, gaps in medical evidence, reliance on a child witness's testimony, and the absence of DNA testing. The High Court rejected each objection. It found the delay understandable given the family's poverty, lack of transport, difficult terrain, and the social stigma attached to reporting sexual assault. It held that the medical evidence, including findings of hymen penetration and vaginal bleeding from a credible, unbiased doctor, supported the prosecution's case, and that DNA testing was not legally required once rape was otherwise established. The court also held that child witnesses can testify and even support a conviction alone, provided the trial judge is satisfied they understand the nature of testifying, and found this child's detailed, consistent testimony reliable.

Ultimately, the court upheld the conviction, concluding guilt was proven beyond doubt. However, due to unspecified mitigating circumstances, it reduced the death sentence to life imprisonment, dismissing the appeal with that modification. The case illustrates how courts assess delayed reporting and child testimony in sexual abuse cases while still exercising sentencing discretion.

title: Shahmeer V. The State,
explainer:
This case was an appeal before the Balochistan High Court by a man named Shahmeer, who had been convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Sibi for the murder (qatl-e-amd) of a man named Abdul Razzak. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and ordered to pay compensation (diyat) to the victim's family.

The conviction largely rested on a "disclosure statement" the accused allegedly made to police, supposedly leading to recovery of the dead body, plus testimony from witnesses who were later declared hostile by the prosecution.

The High Court found serious problems with this evidence. It noted that police already knew about the murder and had already found the body before the accused supposedly made his disclosure—meaning nothing new was actually discovered because of his statement. Under the law of evidence (Qanun-e-Shahadat Order), a mere statement to police like this is not admissible in court, since confessions to police officers are legally excluded to prevent misuse. The Court also found that the complainant's testimony was based on hearsay, and that the other witnesses had not actually implicated the accused in their direct testimony, only after being confronted with earlier police statements, which also cannot be used to secure a conviction.

Concluding that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt using only inadmissible or unreliable evidence, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted Shahmeer, ordering his release. The case highlights important safeguards against convictions based on improper evidence.

title: Muhammad Aslam and 7 others V. Mira Jan and others,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over a rented property in Quetta. The landlords (appellants) sought to evict their tenant, Mira Jan, under the West Pakistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, citing default in rent payment, illegal subletting, and their own genuine need for the premises. The tenant, however, denied any landlord-tenant relationship, claiming he had purchased the property and thus owed no rent or obedience to the landlords. The Rent Controller initially sided with the tenant and dismissed the eviction application, prompting the landlords to appeal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the tenancy history, including an original 1990 tenancy agreement, later property transfers, and conflicting claims by the tenant and another party who also claimed ownership. The court found that the tenant could not provide solid evidence proving he owned or independently possessed the property. It also noted that an agreement relevant to the ownership claim was never specifically denied by the opposing party, which under law amounts to an admission of its execution. Based on this, the court concluded that a landlord-tenant relationship did exist.

The High Court set aside the Rent Controller’s judgment, accepted the eviction application, and ordered the tenant to vacate the premises within two months. This case highlights how courts assess competing claims of ownership versus tenancy, and reinforces the principle that an unchallenged document’s execution can be treated as admitted in landlord-tenant disputes.

title: Zafar Iqbal V. Moula Dad and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta. Zafar Iqbal claimed he owned a plot of land, but alleged that someone had forged a power of attorney in his name and used it to fraudulently sell his property, which was then transferred through a sale deed and recorded in official mutation records in favor of another person. The trial court dismissed his lawsuit, partly because he hadn't specifically asked for cancellation of a second power of attorney that the defendant mentioned during the case.

The Balochistan High Court overturned this decision. It found that courts can grant necessary relief even if not specifically requested, especially to do complete justice. Crucially, the defendant never actually produced the original power of attorney in court, nor proved it was lost or destroyed, which are legal requirements before a copy can be used as evidence. Since these conditions weren't met, the photocopied power of attorney was inadmissible and couldn't prove any transfer of ownership. The court also noted no witnesses to the document were presented.

Finding the trial court's judgment was based on misreading of evidence and reliance on legally inadmissible documents, the High Court ruled in favor of Zafar Iqbal, declared him the rightful owner, and cancelled the fraudulent sale deed and mutation entries.

This case matters because it reinforces an important evidence law principle: parties cannot rely on copies of crucial documents like powers of attorney without proving the original was genuinely lost, destroyed, or unavailable, protecting property owners from fraud based on unverified paperwork.

title: Abdul Rehman V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Rehman, who was convicted by a trial court in Quetta under Section 412 of the Pakistan Penal Code for dishonestly receiving stolen property, specifically a vehicle allegedly stolen during a dacoity (armed robbery). He was sentenced to seven years imprisonment and a fine. Rehman appealed, arguing he was a genuine purchaser of the vehicle and had proper documentation to prove it.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. Most importantly, there was no evidence showing Rehman knew the vehicle was stolen, which is a required element to prove the offense under Section 412. The court also noted that the prosecution's own evidence undermined its case: it had obtained a verification letter from the Excise and Taxation Officer confirming the vehicle's registration, which supported Rehman's claim of being a legitimate buyer. Additionally, a key document suggesting the vehicle wasn't found in official records had never been shown to Rehman during his formal examination, as required by Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code, so it couldn't be used against him.

Finding that the trial court had misread and overlooked evidence, the High Court ruled the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It overturned the conviction and acquitted Rehman. This case highlights the importance of proving criminal knowledge or intent, and the requirement that all evidence against an accused be properly presented to them during trial.

title: Yar Muhammad V. Provincial Transport Authority, Balochistan through Chairman and 3 others,
explainer:
This case dealt with a dispute over a bus route permit in Balochistan. The petitioner, Yar Muhammad, held Route Permit No.2 of 2007 for a route between Aeri and Sibi. A rival operator challenged his permit and timetable before the Provincial Transport Authority (PTA). Earlier, the PTA itself had ruled in the petitioner's favour, directing the Regional Transport Authority to let him operate his bus and issue a timetable. That order went unenforced, and the petitioner had to approach the High Court to get it implemented. Later, however, the PTA Chairman passed a fresh order cancelling not just the disputed permit but four other route permits belonging to the petitioner, without conducting any inquiry or examining the official record, relying instead on verbal claims made by the opposing party.

The High Court found this cancellation order legally flawed. It held that under the Provincial Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1965, only the Transport Authority that originally granted a permit can cancel or suspend it, and only after following proper procedure, including inquiry through the concerned authority. The PTA had no jurisdiction to cancel permits based on unverified assertions without record or investigation, especially when it conflicted with its own earlier order favouring the petitioner.

The court set aside the cancellation order and sent the matter back to the Transport Authority to be decided afresh in accordance with law. The case highlights the importance of due process, proper inquiry, and consistency in administrative decisions affecting people's livelihoods.

title: Habibullah and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about an appeal against a murder conviction. Two men, Habibullah and another appellant, were convicted of murdering Fida Hussain and sentenced to life imprisonment by a trial court in Quetta. They challenged this conviction before the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution's case relied mainly on two eyewitnesses, who were nephews of the deceased. The High Court found serious problems with their testimony: these witnesses lived more than 100 kilometers from where the murder happened, and their explanation for why they were present at the scene was unconvincing. The person who first reported the crime to police was not even an eyewitness himself but had only heard about the murder secondhand. Additionally, other important witnesses, including an independent eyewitness and an injured victim of the same attack, were never brought to testify, which the court said allowed it to assume their testimony would have hurt the prosecution's case. The accused also presented documentary evidence supporting their claim that they were elsewhere when the crime occurred, and the prosecution failed to disprove this alibi.

Given these weaknesses, the High Court ruled that the prosecution had not proven its case beyond reasonable doubt. It overturned the trial court's judgment, acquitted both appellants, and ordered their release.

This case illustrates an important principle in criminal law: even a single reasonable doubt can be enough to acquit an accused person, and courts must carefully scrutinize witness credibility and the prosecution's failure to produce key evidence before upholding a conviction.

title: Nasrullah V. Muhammad Rasool and 7 others,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute involving the Islamic law doctrine of pre-emption, which allows certain people (like neighbours) to claim the first right to buy land when it is sold, provided they follow strict legal formalities. Nasrullah claimed this right over land adjacent to his property after it was sold and later exchanged between several respondents. To succeed, a pre-emption claimant must make specific demands called "Talbs," including an immediate assertion of the right as soon as he learns of the sale, known as Talb-e-Muwathibat.

The trial court dismissed Nasrullah's suit, finding he had not properly made this demand. On appeal, the Balochistan High Court agreed. It found serious inconsistencies between what was stated in the plaint and what Nasrullah and his witnesses testified in court, including conflicting dates about when he learned of the sale, missing details about witnesses present at the time, and a mismatch between the pleaded version of events and the evidence given later. The court held that a party cannot introduce a new version of facts during trial that was not part of the original pleadings. Since the plaint did not properly describe an immediate, witnessed assertion of the right, the claimed demand did not meet the legal requirements of Talb-e-Muwathibat.

As a result, the High Court dismissed the appeal, reaffirming that strict compliance with pleading requirements and the correct legal procedure is essential for a valid pre-emption claim.

title: Abdullah and another V. Mst. Farzana,
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant rent dispute decided by the Balochistan High Court under the West Pakistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959. The landlady, Mst. Farzana, sought eviction of her tenants from a small shop (Cabin/Khoka) in Quetta, claiming they had stopped paying monthly rent since January 2012. The tenants argued they had actually paid rent for an earlier period through a receipt, that the landlady later refused to accept rent, and that whatever default existed should be treated as a condonable "first default" under the law.

The trial court (Rent Controller) had already ruled in the landlady's favor, ordering the tenants to vacate for wilful default in rent payment. On appeal, the High Court upheld this decision. It found that the tenants never actually produced the rent receipt they claimed existed during the trial, nor questioned the landlady about it when she testified—merely attaching a document to the appeal later was not valid proof. The Court also rejected the argument that occasional lump-sum rent payments created a habit of flexible payment timing; tenants were legally required to pay monthly, and failing to deposit rent within 60 days of it falling due amounted to wilful default.

This judgment reinforces a key rent-law principle: tenants must strictly prove rent payments through proper evidence at trial, and irregular or delayed payment practices do not excuse legal default, reaffirming landlords' strong protection against non-paying tenants.

title: Shah Muhammad and 3 others V. Abdul Samad and 6 others,
explainer:
This case was about a dispute over land in Mastung district, Balochistan. The petitioners claimed that certain property, which they said was part of their shared village land (Shamilat Deh), had been wrongly transferred into the name of the respondents' father through a fraudulent mutation entry, with the help of revenue officials. They sued for cancellation of several mutation entries and a declaration of their rights. The trial court ruled in their favor, but on appeal, the Majlis-e-Shoora (appellate court) reversed that decision and dismissed the suit.

The petitioners then approached the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition. The High Court found serious procedural flaws in how the case had been handled by both lower courts. Specifically, no proper issue had ever been framed on whether the disputed mutation was valid, and the courts had not required parties to produce clear evidence on this central question. The High Court also noted that since the land was shared village property (Shamilat Deh), all co-owners (Patadaran) of that land should have been made parties to the case, which had not been done properly.

Because of these gaps, the High Court set aside both the trial court's and the appellate court's judgments entirely and sent the case back for a fresh decision, with proper issues framed and all necessary parties included. This case highlights the importance of correctly framing legal issues and including all relevant parties, especially in disputes involving communal or shared land.

title: Mst. Bibi Zohra and 7 others V. Habib-Ur-Rehman and 12 others,
explainer:
This case concerned a family property dispute among the heirs of a deceased man, Gul Muhammad, who died in 1993. He left behind two sons and two daughters. After his death, the sons recorded the property solely in their own names through inheritance mutations, later selling part of it to another person. The daughters' children (the plaintiffs) claimed they were being paid their rightful share of rent/income from the property for years, but only discovered in 2012 that the mutations had excluded their mothers' shares through alleged fraud and misrepresentation. They sued for a declaration of ownership, cancellation of the fraudulent mutations, and partition of the property.

The defendants argued the suit was filed too late and that the daughters had accepted cash payments instead of a share in the property, so the plaintiffs were barred by their own prior conduct (estoppel) and limitation law.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the trial court's decision in favor of the plaintiffs. It held that since the defendants themselves admitted they had been regularly paying shares to the daughters and later their children, this admission defeated any claim of estoppel. The court also ruled that the 12-year limitation period for claiming a share in joint family property starts running only from exclusion from the property, and since the mutations were products of fraud, no limitation period could protect them. The daughters were confirmed as rightful co-owners.

This case reaffirms that fraudulent property transfers remain challengeable regardless of time lapse, and that family admissions of shared ownership carry strong legal weight.

title: Muhammad Yousaf V. Director, Culture Balochistan 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about two government job appointments in Balochistan's Culture Department that were challenged in court for being made unfairly. In one petition, a man contested the appointment of two people as Art Teachers, arguing they lacked the required qualification (a B.A. in Fine Arts) and two years' experience, and that their names did not even appear on the official merit list, while his own name topped it. In the other, petitioners challenged appointments to lower-grade posts of Mali (gardener) and Farash (orderly) on similar grounds of being bypassed despite ranking higher on merit.

The High Court found serious irregularities. The Chairman of the Departmental Selection Committee was on leave at the time, so a Deputy Director, who had no authority to do so, advertised the posts, convened the meeting, and signed the recommendations and merit list himself. This violated the Balochistan Civil Servants (Appointment, Promotion and Transfer) Rules, 2009. The court also found the appointed candidates lacked the required qualifications, experience, and artistic skill for the Art Teacher posts.

The court ruled that these appointments were illegal and tainted by bad faith on the part of the selection committee members. It struck down the appointments and ordered disciplinary action against those responsible. The case highlights the importance of following proper procedure and merit in public sector hiring, and shows courts will intervene when recruitment processes are manipulated.

title: Shahab-Ud-Din and 9 others V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved ten petitioners who wanted to apply for Pharmacist/Drug Analyst and Drug Inspector posts advertised by the Balochistan Public Service Commission in a local newspaper. The advertisement set a closing date of 7th April 2014 for submitting applications, but the petitioners' final year Pharm-D results were only announced on 12th April 2014, after the deadline had passed. They asked the university Vice-Chancellor to request an extension on their behalf, but the Public Service Commission did not grant one. The petitioners then went to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that fixing a strict deadline had no legal backing and that the date should be extended to accommodate them.

The High Court dismissed the petition at the outset. It found that the petitioners had never actually deposited the required application fee or submitted any application form, so they could not genuinely claim they were ready to apply but were merely blocked by the late results. The court also noted they could have submitted their qualifications later, before any test or interview, but failed to do so. Relying on earlier precedents, the court held that setting deadlines for applications is a policy matter within the Public Service Commission's discretion and has statutory backing, so courts should not interfere absent a violation of rules or bad faith. Since no such violation was shown, the petition was rejected. The case underlines that courts generally will not second-guess administrative deadlines in recruitment processes.

title: Muhammad Akbar through Attorney V. Government of Pakistan and 2 others,
explainer:
In 1994, Muhammad Akbar was intercepted by customs officials at Gwadar airport with foreign-origin gold found on him, and he was charged under the Customs Act. A special customs court tried him and acquitted him in December 1994, finding that the prosecution had not proven its case, partly because he claimed he intended to declare the gold and pay duty on it. However, the acquittal only cleared him of criminal liability; it said nothing about ownership or return of the seized gold itself.

More than sixteen years later, in 2010, Akbar filed a constitutional petition in the Balochistan High Court asking that the customs authorities be directed to return the gold to him upon payment of the applicable customs duty.

The High Court dismissed the petition outright. It held that the matter was barred by extreme delay (laches), since 16 years had passed since seizure. More importantly, the Customs Act itself provides a complete process for dealing with confiscated goods: adjudication by customs authorities under section 179, followed by appeal and revision under sections 193 and 196. Akbar never used these remedies. The court clarified that a criminal trial court's acquittal does not extend to deciding the fate of confiscated goods, which falls exclusively within the customs authorities' jurisdiction. Since no order of the customs adjudicating authority was ever challenged, and an effective alternate remedy existed, the constitutional petition was not maintainable and was dismissed.

title: Allauddin V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Allauddin who was caught driving a pickup truck carrying 306 kilograms of charas (a narcotic substance) near Taftan, close to the Afghanistan-Iran border. Acting on secret information, anti-narcotics force (ANF) officials intercepted his vehicle at night, and after he tried to flee, they recovered the drugs hidden in sacks in the vehicle. He was arrested, charged under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, and convicted by a trial court, receiving a life sentence and a fine.

Allauddin appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that there was a seven-hour delay in registering the police report (FIR) and recording witness statements, and that there were contradictions in witness testimony, which he claimed should invalidate his conviction.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It found the delay was reasonable because the arrest happened at 3am in a remote area, making it impractical to immediately reach a police station. The court also held that minor inconsistencies in witness statements were not serious enough to undermine the prosecution's case, and that testimony should be assessed as a whole rather than picking out isolated phrases.

The court upheld the conviction and life sentence, dismissing the appeal. This case illustrates how courts handle common defense arguments in narcotics cases—procedural delays and minor contradictions—showing that such issues alone usually won't overturn a conviction if the core evidence is credible.

title: Dad Karim and 12 others V. Ishaq and 20 others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Gawadar, Balochistan, between relatives descended from a common ancestor named Aboo. The appellants claimed their branch of the family had been wrongly recorded with fewer shares of ancestral land than they were entitled to. They first filed a suit in 2006 to correct this, but withdrew it unconditionally in 2007. Later, in 2009, they filed a fresh suit claiming that on the very day they withdrew the first suit, the parties had actually reached an out-of-court compromise agreeing to transfer them additional land shares, and that compensation from government land acquisition based on that agreement was wrongfully kept by the other side.

The High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the trial court's rejection of the suit. It held that if such a compromise genuinely existed, the plaintiffs should have disclosed it when withdrawing their first suit rather than withdrawing unconditionally. Because they withdrew the earlier suit outright, filing a new suit on a cause of action that already existed at that time was barred under the Civil Procedure Code. The court also found that the person who allegedly signed the agreement on behalf of the other side was not properly authorized to do so, and the plaintiffs failed to legally prove the agreement itself.

This case reinforces an important procedural principle: parties cannot withdraw a lawsuit outright and later file a new one based on facts or agreements they knew about but failed to disclose earlier.

title: Rizwan Ahmad Baloch V. Arshad Khan and 2 others,
explainer:
This appeal arose from a property dispute in Gwadar. The appellant claimed he had agreed to buy about 13 acres of land from respondent No.1 in December 2004 for Rs.5,200,000, paid the full price, but the seller instead transferred the land to respondent No.2 through a mutation entry, breaching the agreement. He sued for specific performance of the contract. Since the defendants did not appear despite being served through courier and newspaper publication, the trial court proceeded ex parte and recorded the appellant's own evidence. Even so, the trial court dismissed the suit, prompting this appeal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the appellant's own evidence contradicted his pleadings, particularly regarding how the property was transferred. His affidavit revealed that he himself had used a general power of attorney to transfer the land to respondent No.2, which amounted to a novation (replacement) of the original agreement. This meant he was legally stopped, or "estopped," from now claiming the original contract should be enforced, since his own actions showed he had accepted a different arrangement.

The court reaffirmed the legal principle that a party's evidence must match what was stated in the pleadings, and parties cannot introduce new facts not pleaded. Since the appellant's evidence departed from his pleaded case, the court could not rely on it to decree the suit in his favor. The appeal was therefore dismissed, reinforcing that courts strictly require consistency between pleadings and evidence in civil litigation.

title: Mst. Alim Taj V. Mst. Sahib Jan and 2 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a family property dispute. A daughter (the appellant) sued her stepmother and others, claiming that a house registered in her stepmother's name was actually purchased by her late father and only put in the stepmother's name as a "benamidar" (a nominal or front owner) out of love and affection because the stepmother was childless. The daughter wanted the property declared as her father's actual asset, so that she and her stepmother could inherit shares in it according to Islamic inheritance law, and she also sought cancellation of a later mutation transferring the house to a third party.

The trial court dismissed her suit, and she appealed. The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the daughter failed to prove the essential elements of a benami transaction - particularly that her father actually paid for the house. Her witnesses did not personally witness any such payment, and she herself admitted she wasn't present during the purchase. The court also noted that her father never claimed during his lifetime that his wife was merely holding the property on his behalf, and he did not object when the stepmother later transferred the house to someone else.

The case matters because it illustrates how Pakistani courts handle benami property claims: the burden of proof lies heavily on the person alleging a sham ownership, and vague oral claims cannot override documented transactions and years of inaction.

This case concerned a family dispute over inherited land. The plaintiffs claimed they were entitled to a 1/7 share of property left by their ancestor and sought declaration, partition, and possession of the land. The trial court ruled in their favor and ordered the property divided, which the defendants then challenged before the Balochistan High Court through an appeal and revision petition.

The High Court found two major legal problems with the lower court's decision. First, part of the disputed land had been dedicated as a trust (waqf) for religious or charitable purposes. Under the law, any lawsuit concerning trust property of this kind requires prior permission from the Advocate General, and no such permission had been obtained here. Because of this, the trial court had no legal basis to decide the case in the plaintiffs' favor.

Second, the land was classified as "Shamilat Deh," meaning common village land. The Court explained that civil courts have very limited power over such land, and no individual share can be declared or awarded unless the land is formally partitioned by revenue authorities according to the ancestral shares of recognized proprietors. Ordinary residents, tenants, or occupants without such ancestral rights cannot claim a share.

Based on these findings, the High Court set aside the earlier judgments and decrees as unsustainable, allowing the revision petition. The ruling highlights important procedural safeguards protecting trust property and clarifies that village common land disputes must go through revenue authorities, not ordinary civil courts.

title: Imdad Ali V. The State,
explainer:
This is a criminal appeal decided by the Balochistan High Court. Imdad Ali had been convicted by a trial court for murder (under section 302(b) read with section 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with acts done with common intention) and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine, for allegedly helping another man, Bahadur Khan, who shot and killed Faqir Muhammad. The prosecution's case was that Bahadur Khan fired the fatal shot while Imdad Ali stood nearby with a running motorcycle, then both fled together.

The High Court found serious problems with the evidence. The only eyewitness testimony merely showed that Imdad Ali was present at the scene and left with the shooter afterward—it did not prove he shared a common intention to commit murder. The court noted that mere presence at a crime scene is not enough to convict someone under the "common intention" provision; there must be clear proof of shared intent. The court also found that a supposed "disclosure" statement by the accused didn't reveal anything new, since police already knew those facts from the original complaint, so it couldn't count as valid evidence of discovery. Relying on established Supreme Court precedents, the judges ruled that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted Imdad Ali, ordering his release.

This case matters because it reinforces the principle that criminal liability cannot rest on mere presence or association with an offender—concrete evidence of shared criminal intent is required.

title: Sabzal and 9 others V. Deputy Commissioner/Collector and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land acquired by the Government of Pakistan in 2006-2007 in Gwadar for a Joint Defence Complex. The landowners (petitioners) received compensation for their land without raising any objections at the time, and possession was handed over to the government. However, in March 2010, years later, they filed a reference with the Deputy Commissioner/Collector, challenging the valuation of their land and alleging irregularities in the acquisition process. The Collector rejected this reference as time-barred, since it was filed long after the legal deadline.

The landowners then challenged this rejection in the High Court, arguing that the Collector had no authority to reject their reference and should have forwarded it to the District Court for a decision on merits.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It held that under the Land Acquisition Act 1894, a person objecting to an award must file a reference within six weeks of the award if they were present or served notice, or within six months if they were not served notice. Since the petitioners had accepted compensation without objection and filed their reference years late, without even seeking condonation of the delay, the Collector was legally entitled to reject it as time-barred.

This judgment clarifies that strict limitation periods apply to land acquisition disputes, and landowners who accept compensation without objection, then delay challenging the award, risk losing their right to contest it in court.

title: Noor Agha alias Abdullah V. The State,
explainer:

The defense argued there were contradictions in witness statements, that medical certificates and inquest reports for the victims were missing, that there was a suspicious gap between arrest and the recorded confession, and that the alleged motive wasn't proven.

The High Court rejected all these arguments. It found that the accused's confession was voluntary, lawful, and credible, and that it matched eyewitness accounts from the father and brother of the victims, as well as an independent shopkeeper who witnessed the shooting. This case matters because it illustrates how Pakistani courts assess the reliability of confessions and eyewitness testimony in murder cases, and what evidentiary gaps (like missing medical reports) do or do not affect a conviction.

title: Bakhtiar V. Nasrullah and 12 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over 40 acres of land in Mouza Padua, Tehsil Hub, District Hub, Balochistan. The recorded owners of the land had allowed certain individuals (including Bakhtiar) to cultivate it, with an understanding that the cultivators would share produce with the owners. A dispute arose when the cultivators began unauthorized construction and stopped sharing produce, leading the owners to seek repossession, including through proceedings under the Illegal Dispossession Act.

Bakhtiar claimed he had actually purchased the land through an unregistered agreement for Rs. 70,000 and sought declaration of ownership, while the landowners filed a separate suit seeking possession. The trial court ruled against Bakhtiar and in favor of the landowners, prompting two connected appeals before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It held that a mere agreement to sell does not itself transfer ownership or create legal title in immovable property; only a registered sale deed can do that under the Registration Act. Since Bakhtiar's agreement was unregistered and its execution was not properly proved (the witnesses to it were never produced), it could not establish ownership. The court also noted that mutation records carry a presumption of truth, supporting the original owners' claim. The appeal was dismissed, with the occupiers ordered to vacate and pay compensation.

This judgment reinforces the legal principle that unregistered sale agreements cannot override formal, registered ownership records in Pakistan.

title: Muhammad Khan V. Ch. Abdul Rahim and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over "pre-emption," an Islamic law right that lets a neighbouring landowner claim first option to buy adjoining property when it is sold. Muhammad Khan claimed that his neighbour's land, sold to another buyer for Rs. 18,00,000, should instead go to him because he exercised his pre-emption rights properly. To succeed in such a claim, the law requires the buyer to perform certain formal steps called "Talbs" immediately upon learning of the sale, and to prove this was done exactly as described in the original court filing (the plaint).

The trial court had dismissed Khan's suit, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court. The High Court examined his evidence and found that his testimony and witness statements about when he learned of the sale and how he performed the required Talbs did not match what he had originally stated in his pleadings. There were also contradictions within his own evidence. Since pleadings and evidence must align, and a party cannot introduce new facts not mentioned in the original pleadings without formally amending them, the court held that Khan failed to prove he had properly performed the legal requirements for a pre-emption claim.

As a result, the High Court upheld the trial court's decision and dismissed the appeal. The case highlights the importance of consistency between pleadings and evidence in pre-emption lawsuits, and the strict procedural requirements for such claims under Islamic law as applied in Pakistan.

title: Khan Muhammad and others V. The State,
explainer:

The case arose after a large quantity of arms and ammunition, including rifles, submachine guns, and ammunition rounds, went missing from the arms storage room (Kot) at Police Lines, Barkhan. One applicant was the designated in-charge of the storeroom who had remained absent from duty before the shortage was discovered, while the other was a line officer who had reported the absence to senior officials.

It held that even when charges do not fall under the strict "prohibitory clause" that normally blocks bail, courts can still refuse bail in exceptional situations. The missing arms had not been recovered, raising serious concerns they could be misused, and there was enough preliminary evidence linking the applicants to the offence.
