title: Khuda Bukhsh and 3 others V. Hamza and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over water rights from a water channel called Wangoee Dhora, which flowed through land in Lasbela district. The original plaintiff, Wadera Lakho (father of the petitioners), claimed he had long irrigated his land from this water source and that the respondents had wrongfully blocked and diverted the flow onto their own land. He sued for a declaration of his rights and a permanent injunction.

The respondents argued that this very dispute had already been resolved through arbitration, with an award approved by the Assistant Commissioner, Hub Division, making the lawsuit legally barred. The trial court initially ruled in favor of the plaintiff, but on appeal, the Majlis-e-Shoora overturned that decision and dismissed the suit. The petitioners then challenged this reversal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It found that an arbitration award already existed covering the same dispute, and under Section 32 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, no separate civil suit can be filed to decide the existence or validity of such an award. Instead, a party disputing an award must specifically challenge or seek to set it aside through the proper legal process, not file an ordinary suit. The court also noted that the petitioners' witnesses failed to provide solid evidence supporting their water rights claim.

This ruling reinforces an important legal principle: once an arbitration award exists, parties cannot bypass it by filing fresh lawsuits—they must use specific remedies under the Arbitration Act to challenge

title: Ghulam Qadir V. Governor of Balochistan through Personal Secretary, Quetta and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a government school teacher, Ghulam Qadir, whose service was terminated in 2000. He filed repeated representations against his termination over several years, but these went undecided. Eventually, after a delay of about nine years, he filed a complaint with the Provincial Ombudsman of Balochistan, who ruled in his favour and set aside the termination. The Governor of Balochistan, acting as the appellate authority, later overturned the Ombudsman's decision. The teacher then challenged the Governor's order before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that the Ombudsman had no legal authority to hear complaints relating to a civil servant's terms and conditions of service, such as termination from employment - such matters fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Service Tribunal under the Balochistan Service Tribunal Act. Since the Ombudsman lacked jurisdiction from the outset, his decision condoning a nine-year delay without any formal application or valid justification was void, and the question of limitation became irrelevant. The court clarified that a civil servant aggrieved by termination must seek relief from the Service Tribunal, not the Ombudsman.

This judgment matters because it reinforces the boundary between the Ombudsman's complaint-resolution powers and the specialized jurisdiction of Service Tribunals over civil servants' employment disputes, ensuring such disputes are routed to the correct forum.

title: Jamal Khan V. Secretary Home Department and 6 others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running land dispute in Zhob, Balochistan. The petitioner, Jamal Khan, claimed that other parties had forged an arbitration agreement from 2000 by falsely putting his thumb impression on it, and that this forged document was later used in court proceedings. He asked a Sessions Judge, acting as Justice of the Peace, to order police to register a criminal case (FIR) against the other parties for cheating and forgery. The Sessions Judge refused, and Jamal Khan challenged that refusal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the real issue was a civil dispute over partition of shared (Shamilat) property, and that the petitioner was trying to turn this civil matter into a criminal case simply to keep possession of a piece of land. The court noted that the petitioner waited 13 years after the agreement was signed before alleging forgery, and that none of the other people who signed the agreement supported his claim. Since the law already provides a specific remedy for challenging arbitration agreements or awards, through the Arbitration Act, the petitioner should have pursued that civil remedy rather than seeking criminal proceedings.

The case matters because it reinforces that courts will not allow criminal law, particularly FIR registration, to be misused as a tool for resolving essentially civil property disputes when proper civil remedies exist.

title: Zulikha Bibi V. Election Commission of Pakistan through Secretary and another,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a challenge to the eligibility of a candidate who had won a local government election. The petitioner, also a candidate in the same local body elections, argued that the winning candidate (respondent No.2) should not have been allowed to contest because he was simultaneously a government contractor and the Chairman of the District Zakat Committee, Lasbela. She claimed this violated eligibility rules under the Balochistan Local Government Act, 2010, which bars certain government-linked persons from contesting local elections.

The respondent argued that he had resigned from the Zakat Committee post before filing his nomination papers and that he received only an honorarium, not a salary, so he should not be treated as a government servant. He also argued the petition was filed too late and that the petitioner had no standing to challenge his election.

The court rejected these defenses. It held that the Chairman of a District Zakat Committee, being nominated by the government, qualifies as a public servant and is therefore disqualified from contesting local body elections. It also ruled that delay (laches) does not bar this type of petition—called a "quo warranto" petition, which questions someone's authority to hold public office—because such challenges involve a continuing legal issue. The court accepted the petition, set aside the respondent's election notification, and directed the Election Commission to remove his name from the list of validly elected candidates. The case clarifies eligibility rules for public officeholders contesting local elections.

title: Rahim Bakhsh and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Rahim Bakhsh and another appellant, who were booked in a murder case and declared absconders by a trial court in 2009. Because they allegedly failed to appear, the court attached their immovable property under the law dealing with proclaimed offenders. The men were eventually tried and acquitted in 2012. Two years later, in 2014, they asked the trial court to return their attached property, but the court refused, saying their request came too late, since the law requires such applications to be filed within two years of the attachment.

The Balochistan High Court overturned this decision. It examined the legal procedure the trial court had followed when declaring the men absconders and attaching their property, and found it was seriously flawed. The law requires a proper public proclamation giving the accused at least thirty days to appear, along with a written court record confirming when and how that proclamation was published. In this case, no such valid proclamation or written confirmation existed, and the court had issued both the proclamation and the attachment order on virtually the same day, making the process legally defective from the start.

Because the original proceedings were conducted without proper legal authority, the High Court ruled they were invalid altogether, meaning the two-year time limit for seeking restoration never properly applied. The appeal was allowed, the attachment order was cancelled, and the men's property was ordered returned to them. The case highlights the importance of strict procedural compliance before the state can seize a person's property.

title: Bibi Babo V. Muhammad Aslam and another,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute over a house in Quetta between Bibi Babo (the plaintiff) and Muhammad Aslam (the defendant). Bibi Babo claimed she owned the house, backed by revenue records (a mutation entry in her name), and alleged that while she was away in Karachi caring for her ailing husband, Aslam broke in and illegally occupied it. Aslam argued he had lived there for 28 years, paid the utility bills, and that an earlier complaint Bibi Babo filed under the Illegal Dispossession Act had already been dismissed.

The trial court sided with Aslam, dismissing her suit for possession, reasoning that his long possession and utility bills proved his claim, and that her case was also time-barred and vaguely described.

The Balochistan High Court reversed this decision. It held that a mutation entry in revenue records carries a legal presumption of truth, which Aslam failed to disprove. Utility bills, the court said, can show who lived in a property but cannot establish legal ownership, especially when there is a recorded owner. The court also found the property was adequately identified, the earlier dismissal of her Illegal Dispossession Act complaint didn't give Aslam any ownership rights, and her suit was filed within the legal time limit. The appeal was allowed, and the house was awarded to Bibi Babo. The ruling reinforces that mere long-term possession or paying bills cannot defeat the rights of a documented, true owner.

title: Dilmurad Diljan alias Dilo V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns Dilmurad Diljan alias Dilo, who was convicted by a Sessions Court in Turbat for murdering Shakir Ali and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court through jail authorities.

According to the prosecution, the victim was found severely beaten and burned, and before dying he allegedly told his brother and police that the appellant and others had assaulted him. This statement, recorded by police as a dying declaration, was the main evidence against the appellant.

The High Court found serious problems with this evidence. No eyewitness had direct knowledge of the assault, and the so-called dying declaration was not properly verified. There was no doctor's certificate confirming the victim was conscious and fit to give a statement when it was recorded, the doctor never testified to support it, and there were inconsistencies about when the victim actually arrived at the hospital. The court also noted that another key witness, the victim's brother Zareef, was never produced, raising suspicion that his testimony might not have supported the prosecution.

Given these gaps, the court ruled that a dying declaration can only support a conviction if it's shown the person was conscious, coherent, and medically certified fit when making it. Since none of this was established, the evidence was too weak and doubtful to sustain a murder conviction. The court acquitted the appellant, releasing him, emphasizing the importance of reliable proof before convicting someone of a capital offense.

title: Government of Balochistan through Additional Chief Secretary, Planning and Development Department V. Messrs Enterprise and Development Consulting (Pvt.) Ltd.,
explainer:
This case involved a contract dispute between the Government of Balochistan and a private consulting firm, Enterprise and Development Consulting (Pvt.) Ltd., hired for a resource management project. When a payment dispute arose over about US$23,794, the company sought arbitration under the Arbitration Act, 1940, as provided in their contract. The trial court appointed an arbitrator, who eventually issued an award in the company's favor, and the trial court made this award a rule of court, effectively enforcing it.

The government challenged this, arguing the trial court had acted beyond its powers and ignored the specific arbitration procedure laid out in the contract when appointing the arbitrator.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the government. It held that before appointing an arbitrator, a court must first determine whether it even has jurisdiction over the dispute, and must follow the method for selecting an arbitrator specified in the agreement itself. Since the trial court appointed an arbitrator unilaterally, without properly considering the contract's arbitration clause or its own jurisdiction, the resulting award was void from the start. The court set aside the trial court's order, rejected the award, and sent the case back for the trial court to first decide whether it had authority to appoint an arbititor outside the contract's own procedure.

This case matters because it reinforces that courts and parties must strictly follow agreed contractual procedures for resolving disputes through arbitration, rather than taking shortcuts.

title: Shah Jahan V. Muhammad Noor and another,
explainer:
This case involved a murder appeal from Balochistan High Court. Nizam-ud-Din was found dead with bullet injuries in January 2009. Initially, no one came forward to identify a suspect, and police closed the case after several months. Almost a year later, the deceased's son, Shah Jehan, applied to reopen the case, naming his own brother as the killer, claiming he and another brother had witnessed the shooting but stayed silent out of fear.

The accused brother was arrested, and police recorded a disclosure statement from him leading to recovery of a Kalashnikov rifle. The trial court acquitted him, and the complainant appealed against the acquittal.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. It found that the accused's disclosure statement and the weapon recovery were not legally significant under Article 40 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, since the facts and location had already been known to police before the accused ever spoke. There was also no forensic match or recovered bullet casings linking the weapon to the crime. Crucially, the court noted the witnesses' highly suspicious behavior: as the deceased's own sons, they neither took their dying father to hospital nor informed police for nearly a year, and during cross-examination admitted that after implicating their brother, they inherited his substantial land, orchard, and cattle. This raised strong doubt about false implication, so the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the acquittal, emphasizing that courts should not disturb a well-reasoned trial court acquittal without compelling reason.

title: Haji Abdul Qadir and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two brothers, Abdul Qadir and Abdul Hadi, convicted by a trial court in Killa Abdullah of murder (qatl-i-amd) and causing injuries during a violent confrontation in 2008, after a complainant and his companions were allegedly attacked near a group of houses, resulting in one death and several injuries. The trial court sentenced them to life imprisonment plus fines and compensation. The appellants challenged the conviction, while the complainant separately sought enhancement of their sentence.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence and found serious weaknesses in the prosecution's case: witnesses claimed firing occurred, but no bullet casings were recovered from the scene; no clear motive was established; and the prosecution failed to prove that the accused shared a "common object" as a group, which is required to hold multiple people collectively responsible under the law of unlawful assembly. The court noted the encounter appeared to be a chance meeting rather than a planned, coordinated attack, so merely holding knives did not prove common intent.

As a result, the court acquitted the appellants of murder and the more serious injury charge, since those required proof of shared criminal purpose that was missing. However, it upheld their conviction for a lesser injury offense, since individuals can still be personally liable for their own actions even without proof of group conspiracy. The complainant's request for harsher punishment was rejected. The case highlights how courts must carefully distinguish individual guilt from collective blame in group violence cases.

title: Muhammad Ali Khan Paracha V. Mst. Binish and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a husband (Muhammad Ali Khan Paracha) challenging court decisions that required him to pay dower (Haq Mehr) and maintenance to his former wife, Mst. Binish.

The couple married in 1998, with dower fixed at Rs. 500,000 payable on demand. In 2002, the wife was divorced and left the husband's home with their daughter. She filed suit in 2009 seeking the unpaid dower, maintenance for herself during the waiting period after divorce (iddat), and maintenance for the child, plus some gold jewelry.

Both the Family Court and the appellate court ruled in her favor on the dower and child maintenance (the appellate court removed the iddat maintenance). The husband then approached the High Court, arguing he had already paid the dower and that the claim was filed too late, beyond the three-year limitation period under the Limitation Act.

The High Court rejected both arguments. It found that the husband's own witnesses admitted during cross-examination that the dower had never actually been paid. On the limitation issue, the court clarified that the three-year clock for dower claims starts only when the wife demands payment and the husband refuses it - not simply from the date of divorce. Since the husband never clearly refused payment until he denied owing it in his written statement during the lawsuit, that was the actual starting point for limitation, making the 2009 suit timely.

The petition was dismissed, and the lower courts' rulings stood. This case clarifies how limitation periods for dower claims are calculated under Pakistani law.

title: Abdul Zahir V. Khuda-E-Dad and others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute over land that had been jointly owned. One party, Abdul Zahir, claimed he had purchased a share of the land from the predecessor of the other side and had it formally recorded through a mutation entry in the revenue records. The other side, Khuda-e-Dad and others, claimed this mutation was fraudulent and obtained through collusion with revenue officials, and they sued to have it cancelled, along with seeking possession of the land. The matter went through a trial court, which ruled in favour of Zahir, and then an appellate court, which reversed that decision in favour of the other side. Both parties then approached the Balochistan High Court through separate revision petitions.

The High Court ruled in favour of Abdul Zahir. It found that the opposing side's claim to cancel the mutation was filed too late, beyond the three-year limitation period, and that they failed to prove their allegations of fraud, especially since they had withdrawn those specific claims during the case and failed to produce key witnesses. The court held that revenue records carry a legal presumption of truth that can only be rebutted with solid evidence, not mere verbal claims. It also found that the appellate court had wrongly allowed a delayed appeal without good reason. As a result, the High Court restored the trial court's original decision favouring Zahir.

This judgment is significant because it reinforces the evidentiary weight given to official land records and clarifies limitation rules and standards for proving fraud in property disputes.

title: Zahir Khan and Brothers, Engineering and Constructors through Partner V. Federal Board of Revenue through Member and 4 others,
explainer:
This case was about a company that imported steel strand from China and declared its customs value at a certain price. Customs officials rejected that declared value, saying it was too low, and instead assessed duty and taxes based on an official Valuation Ruling (No. 370 of 2011) issued by the customs authorities, which set a much higher price per kilogram. The importer disagreed, arguing that customs should have followed the standard step-by-step valuation process under Section 25 of the Customs Act rather than relying on the ruling, and complained it was not given a hearing before the final assessment.

The company approached the Balochistan High Court directly under its constitutional jurisdiction, challenging the valuation ruling and the resulting assessment.

The court dismissed the petition. It held that assessment orders made under Section 80 of the Customs Act are appealable, and valuation rulings themselves must be challenged through the specific remedy provided under Section 25-D of the Customs Act, with further appeals available under Section 193. Since the law already provided proper channels to contest both the valuation ruling and the assessment, the importer should have used those remedies instead of coming straight to the High Court.

The judgment reinforces an important principle: constitutional petitions are not meant to bypass normal legal procedures. Courts will only intervene directly when an order is clearly without jurisdiction, contrary to settled law, or likely to cause a miscarriage of justice—none of which applied here.

title: The State through Public Prosecutor, ATA and others V. Abdul Bari and others,
explainer:
This case involved a shootout in March 2012 between security forces (Levies, Anti-Terrorism Force, and Frontier Corps) and a group of armed men in Killa Abdullah, Balochistan. During the operation, some accused allegedly opened fire, injuring a soldier and damaging a vehicle, while one of their own companions died from the crossfire. Several accused were arrested along with weapons and explosives, leading to multiple FIRs under the Pakistan Penal Code, the Anti-Terrorism Act, and the Arms Ordinance.

At trial, the Anti-Terrorism Court acquitted all the accused. The prosecution appealed this acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious flaws in how the trial was conducted. Crucially, the prosecution's Special Prosecutor had been negligent: important witnesses who had signed the recovery memos (documenting the seized weapons) were never examined in court, and the actual seized weapons and explosives (the "case property") were never produced as evidence. The trial court had ignored its power under Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows courts to summon material witnesses necessary for a fair decision, and failed to check whether the prosecution had presented all necessary evidence.

Because of these gaps, the High Court set aside the acquittal and sent the case back to the trial court, directing it to record statements from the recovery memo witnesses, produce the seized weapons as evidence, and let both sides present further evidence before deciding the case afresh. This case

title: Jamal Ud Din and 9 others V. Syed Faizullah Shah and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Chagi district, Balochistan, over property known as Khaskhain Nali. The respondents, belonging to the Syed Kalani tribe, claimed historical ownership of the land, arguing that the appellants and their ancestors were merely tenant farmers (bazgars) who had fraudulently gotten revenue entries changed into their own names decades earlier. After an earlier suit against a related tribe, the respondents withdrew part of their claim and filed a fresh suit against the present appellants in 2004, which the trial court (Majlis-e-Shoora) decided in their favour in 2008.

The appellants challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court, arguing the suit was time-barred, lacked proper evidence of fraud, relied on unproven documents, and failed to include the Government of Balochistan despite involving unsettled land.

The High Court agreed with the appellants. It held that merely withdrawing an earlier suit and filing a new one does not create a fresh cause of action or reset the limitation period. Since the disputed revenue entries dated back to 1967-68, and the respondents could not explain this long delay, the suit was barred by time. The court also found no evidence proving fraud, and noted that suits concerning unsettled government land must include the government as a party.

As a result, the High Court set aside the trial court's judgment and dismissed the original suit, allowing the appeal. The case highlights the strict application of limitation laws and procedural requirements in property disputes.

title: Muhammad Hanif V. National Accountability Bureau Islamabad through Chairman and 2 others,

He was accused of acquiring assets and property worth tens of millions of rupees between 1987 and 2014 that were disproportionate to his known income, allegedly with the help of a co-accused who used his own name and bank accounts to hide illicit commission payments and properties on Hanif's behalf. A formal reference was filed against him, and charges including corruption, forgery, and using forged documents were framed in April 2015.

Hanif had already sought bail multiple times before this petition. His pre-arrest bail was refused, he was arrested, and two separate post-arrest bail applications were also dismissed by the Balochistan High Court, with one appeal to the Supreme Court also failing. Witness testimony recorded so far had neither cleared him nor supported his release. Finding no fresh grounds, the court dismissed his petition.

This case illustrates how courts in accountability matters are reluctant to grant bail repeatedly on identical grounds, emphasizing that delay alone, without new circumstances, is insufficient to justify release in serious corruption cases.

title: Qadir Bakhsh V. Mst. Hazaan and 50 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a long-running dispute over agricultural land in Kachhi, Balochistan, originally held as "jagir" (a feudal land grant). Under a 1959 Martial Law Regulation (MLR 64), all such jagir lands in the area were abolished and reverted to the Provincial Government free of any claims. The petitioner, Qadir Bakhsh, and others had been recorded as occupants of this land and were later declared full owners through a 1983 mutation order. The original jagirdars (the respondents) challenged this, arguing they were not really jagirdars and that their land did not fall under the abolition law. After years of litigation, the Supreme Court ruled that the land was indeed jagir land that had reverted to the government, and sent the case back to the Deputy Land Commissioner to determine what rights, if any, the parties had going forward.

Following this, the Deputy Land Commissioner cancelled the 1983 mutation entries favoring the petitioner and directed the original jagirdars to submit declarations so their entitlement under the law could be properly determined. The petitioner challenged this cancellation through several appeals, all of which were dismissed, leading to this petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court held that the officials' orders correctly followed the Supreme Court's directions and the relevant law (Paragraph 21 of MLR 64). Finding no illegality in how the matter was handled, the court dismissed the petition. The case illustrates how historic land reform laws continue to affect property rights and ownership disputes in Pakistan

title: Muhammad Ibrahim and another V. Abdul Salam and 9 others,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute between a landlord and a tenant over a shop in Quetta. The landlords sought the tenant's eviction, claiming he had defaulted on rent payments from 2007 to 2013 and that the shop was needed for the personal use of two of the landlords' family members who were unemployed. The tenant argued he had not defaulted, that he had deposited rent with the local Bazar Union, and that the landlords were acting in bad faith since they had other shops available.

The Rent Controller in Mastung ruled in favor of the landlords, ordering the tenant to vacate the shop. The tenant appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the eviction order. It held that a landlord's sworn statement about needing the property for personal use is sufficient evidence to justify eviction, and a statement made through an attorney counts the same as one made by the landlord personally. The fact that the family members who needed the shop didn't personally testify did not undermine the landlords' case. The court also found that the tenant had failed to pay the legally required periodic rent increases, which amounted to wilful default, making him liable for eviction even though he later paid the arrears. The landlord was also found to have the right to choose which of his properties to reclaim for personal use. The tenant was given six months to vacate while continuing to pay rent, and the appeal was dismissed.

title: Aziz Jan V. Ayaz and others,
explainer:
This case was about a man, Aziz Jan, who claimed he had bought agricultural land from another person through three agreements made in 1991 and 1993. He later discovered that the land had instead been transferred to someone else (respondent No.3) through official mutation entries, and eventually gifted further. He sued for specific performance of the sale agreements, cancellation of these mutations, and declaration of his ownership.

The trial court dismissed his suit, and the appellate court upheld that dismissal. Aziz Jan then filed this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court also ruled against him. It held that he had failed to properly prove the agreements to sell, since the required attesting witnesses were not produced in court, and testimony from the scribe who wrote the documents was not enough on its own. The court also noted that an admission made by one co-defendant (the seller's heirs) could not be treated as binding on the other contesting defendant, especially since the plaintiff himself had disputed the validity of the agreement in the framed issues. Additionally, no evidence was presented to show that the land transfers to respondent No.3 were fraudulent or that any revenue official acted improperly. Because of this lack of proof, the court found the plaintiff had no standing to challenge the mutations as forged.

This case highlights how strictly Pakistani courts require formal proof—like witness testimony—before enforcing property agreements, and that one defendant's admission cannot automatically bind others in a dispute.

title: Abdul Ghafoor V. Province of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a government employee dispute in Balochistan concerning whether a telecom company employee could be transferred to a government department on deputation ahead of a sitting employee's promotion prospects.

Abdul Ghafoor, a government officer eligible for promotion to the post of Assistant Director/Planning Officer, challenged the government's decision to instead bring in Fareedullah, an employee of Pakistan Telecommunication Company (PTCL), on deputation to the same post. Ghafoor argued this violated the Balochistan Civil Servants Deputation Policy 2012 and blocked his own promotion.

The Balochistan High Court ruled in Ghafoor's favor. It held that PTCL employees are not civil servants, so Fareedullah's deputation into a civil service post was legally invalid from the start. The court further found that the deputation had been arranged not out of genuine public interest or administrative necessity, but because a Minister personally directed it - which the court said ministers have no authority to do. It emphasized that secretaries of departments must follow proper rules and resist ministerial directions that violate law or policy, rather than simply complying.

The court declared the deputation notification unlawful and of no legal effect, and directed the authorities to make a regular appointment or promotion to the post following proper legal procedure. The judgment reinforces that government postings must follow established civil service rules and policies, not personal preferences of officials, and protects the promotion rights of eligible civil servants against improper outside appointments.

title: Amanullah V. Sadia Shah and others,
explainer:
This case was about a family dispute over dower (money or property promised to a wife at marriage) and maintenance after divorce. A wife, Sadia Shah, sued her husband, Amanullah, for unpaid dower of Rs. 500,000 and for maintenance for herself and their children. The husband argued he had already paid the dower by transferring a property to her name instead of cash.

The trial court agreed with the husband, finding he had proven the dower was paid through the property transfer, and limited the wife's maintenance to her iddat period (the waiting period after divorce). On appeal, the District Judge reversed this, ruling the husband still owed the dower money and that the daughter should get maintenance until she reached adulthood rather than until marriage.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed both rulings together. It found that the wife herself had admitted during cross-examination that the property was transferred to her, and this was also recorded in the divorce deed. The appellate court had wrongly dismissed this evidence just because the divorce deed itself wasn't formally presented in court, even though both sides agreed it existed and its contents were undisputed. The High Court restored the trial court's decision that the dower had already been paid through the property.

However, it corrected the appellate court on one point: the daughter's maintenance should continue until she gets married, not just until she turns 18, following Islamic family law principles. This case clarifies that undisputed facts don't need formal re-proving and reaffirms daughters' maintenance rights extending to marriage.

title: Gul Baran V. Umer Khan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a murder appeal from Balochistan. Sher Zaman was killed in a shooting near Cinema Galli, Zhob, in 2009. The main shooter, Ali Shah, was convicted by the trial court. However, another person present at the scene, Umer Khan, was acquitted by the trial court, and the complainant's father appealed this acquittal to the High Court.

The complainant argued that Umer Khan, along with the others present, shared a common intention to commit the murder under Section 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which allows people acting together with a shared criminal purpose to be held equally liable, even if only one person physically committed the act.

The High Court disagreed. It found that the eyewitnesses only showed Umer Khan standing nearby when Ali Shah opened fire - there was no evidence he did anything (no overt act), had any motive, or helped the shooter in any way. The court emphasized that mere presence at a crime scene, especially when the encounter itself appeared to be a chance meeting rather than something planned, is not enough to prove common intention. Citing earlier Supreme Court rulings, the judges stressed that criminal liability under common intention requires actual participation or a role in planning, not just being nearby.

The appeal was dismissed, and Umer Khan's acquittal was upheld. This case reinforces an important principle: simply being present when a crime occurs does not automatically make someone criminally responsible for it.

title: Muhammad Kaleemullah V. Mst. Rehana Naseer and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a husband (petitioner) challenging a family court decision ordering him to pay his former wife dower, dowry articles, and maintenance allowance worth over Rs. 650,000. The wife had filed a suit after their marriage ended in divorce, and the trial court ruled in her favor based partly on receipts for dowry items that she produced during her own testimony.

The husband appealed, but the appellate court dismissed his appeal solely because it was filed three days late, without examining the actual merits of the case, including his objection that the receipts used as evidence were not properly admissible since his ex-wife was not the author of those receipts nor had she personally issued them.

The Balochistan High Court found that the appellate court should not have thrown out the case purely on a technical delay of a few days without considering whether the evidence was properly admitted and whether the delay could be excused given the circumstances. Relying on Supreme Court precedents, the High Court held that courts can take up delayed matters when the merits of the case warrant it.

As a result, the High Court set aside the appellate court's judgment and sent the case back for a fresh decision on the actual merits, including the question of whether the receipts were legally admissible evidence, giving both parties a chance to be heard again.

This case matters because it reinforces that procedural technicalities like minor delays should not override substantive justice, especially in family law disputes involving financial claims after divorce.

title: Sain Dad Khan V. General Manager HR and Admn. (NTDC) Wapda, Lahore and 4 others,
explainer:
This case is about a government employee, Sain Dad Khan, who worked as an Assistant Line-Man for WAPDA/NTDC. When he joined service in 1980, his date of birth was recorded as 1st July, 1956. Years later, the record showed signs of alteration, with the date of birth changed to 21st December, 1961 after some cutting or editing in the service book. The petitioner wanted this later date, 1961, to be officially recognized, since it would delay his retirement by several years. He relied on documents like his school certificates and local certificates to support his claim.

The department had already rejected his request for this correction back in 2009, and he did not challenge that decision at the time. It was only in 2015, when he was informed he was nearing retirement based on the 1956 date, that he raised the issue again. The department again refused, citing that there was no rule allowing review of an already-settled date of birth.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It held that under civil service rules, once a date of birth is recorded at the time of joining service, it becomes final and cannot be changed later. The court also noted that the special WAPDA rules allowing correction for clerical errors did not apply to him, since he had joined before 1994. Because he waited 26 years and never challenged the 2009 decision, his case was also barred by unreasonable delay.

title: Aqeel Ahmed and others V. Lasbella University of Agriculture and others,
explainer:
Two job applicants, Aqeel Ahmed and Abdul Latif, applied for the post of Deputy Registrar (BPS-18) at Lasbella University of Agriculture, Water and Marine Sciences after it was advertised in 2014. They passed the written NTS test and were called for interviews. Instead of finalizing their selection, the university promoted a departmental employee, Faisal Khan, to the same post through an internal promotion notification. The petitioners challenged this promotion before the Balochistan High Court, arguing it violated the university's own rules, which set a 50/50 quota between promotion and direct recruitment, and that the promotion quota had already been filled earlier through another officer's promotion.

The court examined the recruitment rules and found that the first Deputy Registrar post rightly belonged to the promotion quota, already filled by that earlier appointment. The second post was meant for direct/initial recruitment through public advertisement, for which the petitioners had applied and competed. Since the advertisement for that post was never withdrawn, promoting Faisal Khan to it instead was improper, especially since he also lacked the required five years' experience. The court declared his appointment notification void and of no legal effect, setting it aside. It directed the university to decide the outcome of the advertised post based on the merit list from the test already conducted. The case highlights the importance of following proper recruitment procedures and honoring merit-based public competitions in government institutions.

title: Muhammad Iqbal and another V. Deputy Commissioner District Lasbella and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a father and daughter whose domicile certificates for Lasbella district had been cancelled by the Deputy Commissioner. Domicile certificates are official documents confirming a person's residence in a particular area, and they matter because they can affect rights like job quotas, admissions, and other benefits tied to residency.

The Deputy Commissioner cancelled the certificates after an inquiry suggested the petitioners did not actually live permanently in the area in question. However, the petitioners challenged this cancellation, arguing they were never given a proper chance to defend themselves before their certificates were revoked.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the petitioners. It found that although an Assistant Commissioner had been asked to investigate the matter, there was no evidence that the petitioners were notified or allowed to participate in that inquiry. The Deputy Commissioner's own order only mentioned a personal visit to the area, without clarifying whether official land records were examined. The court held that since domicile certificates create legal rights for their holders, those rights cannot be taken away without following fair procedure.

Relying on established legal principles, including the rule that no one should be condemned unheard, the court ruled that the cancellation violated natural justice. It set aside the cancellation order and sent the case back for a fresh decision, this time requiring that the petitioners be given a genuine opportunity to present their case before any final ruling is made.

title: Bahadur Khan and 6 others V. Muhammad Anwar and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute. The respondents had filed a suit seeking declaration and possession through partition of inherited property from their predecessor, Mehrban. The trial court (Civil Judge) decided in their favor. When the petitioners (the losing side) tried to appeal, they filed before the District Judge in Quetta. However, the appellate court returned their appeal, saying it lacked jurisdiction because the property's value exceeded Rs. 500,000, which would mean the appeal should go to the High Court instead.

The petitioners challenged this, arguing that the suit had been valued at only Rs. 37.50 for jurisdiction and court-fee purposes in the original plaint, and that this figure—not any later estimate of the property's worth—should determine which court hears the appeal.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the petitioners. It held that the forum for appeal must be based on the value stated in the original plaint, not on the property's market value as it may have grown during the case or come out through evidence later. Since neither the defendants had challenged this valuation during the trial, nor had the trial court formally revalued it through proper legal procedure, the original figure of Rs. 37.50 stood. The District Judge, not the High Court, was the correct appellate forum. The High Court set aside the order returning the appeal and directed the District Court to decide the case within two months, reaffirming that appeal rights should follow the plaint's stated value, protecting litigants from losing their proper forum due to later property valuation disputes.

title: Messrs Mandokhail Brothers Commercial Trading and Government Contractor V. Chairman Civil Aviation and 4 others,
explainer:
This case was about a construction tender for a Staff Mess and APM residence at Zhob Airport, invited by the Civil Aviation Authority. The petitioner, Mandokhail Brothers, submitted the lowest bid and was listed as such after bids were opened. However, no work order was issued for three months, and the authority eventually cancelled the tender and re-advertised it, citing various ambiguities found in the bids during scrutiny, such as unclear rate entries, unauthorized word changes, and inconsistent markings.

The petitioner argued that being declared the lowest bidder gave it a vested right to be awarded the contract, and that cancelling the tender violated principles of natural justice and procurement rules. The respondents countered that no final contract had ever been concluded and that the authority retained the right to cancel tenders for valid reasons.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It held that merely being the lowest bidder does not create a concluded contract or a vested legal right to be awarded the work. Since no final contract existed, the principle of natural justice did not apply, and the authority was within its rights to cancel the tender and call for fresh bids.

This judgment matters because it clarifies that in public procurement, being the lowest bidder only makes someone a potential contractor, not an automatic winner, until a formal contract is finalized by the competent authority.

title: Murad Bakhsh and 4 others V. Mst. Syeda Ashraf Jahan and 4 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a land dispute between two families over property recorded in revenue records as mutations (ownership transfers) dating back to 1979. The plaintiffs claimed their predecessor originally owned the land and that the defendants had fraudulently transferred it into their own names through false mutations. They only filed suit challenging this in 2009, three decades later, after discovering the alleged fraud when they tried to partition the property.

The trial court and appellate court both dismissed the suit as time-barred, since Pakistani law requires declaratory suits to be filed within six years of the cause of action. The High Court upheld this dismissal, emphasizing that anyone seeking legal relief must act diligently, and if a suit is filed late, every day of delay must be explained. Here, the plaintiffs failed to specify exactly when they learned of the disputed mutations, so their decades-long delay went unexplained. The court also clarified that even if limitation isn't specifically raised as a defense by the opposing side, courts must still dismiss suits filed beyond the limitation period.

The judgment also discussed the legal principle of restitution under the Civil Procedure Code—meaning that if a lower court's decision is later overturned, parties must be restored to their original position, with any wrongly received benefits returned.

This case matters because it reinforces the strict application of limitation laws in property disputes and reminds litigants that delays in asserting legal rights, especially regarding land records, can be fatal to their claims.

title: Muhammad Umar and others V. Hamid Hamza and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Gwadar, Balochistan. A man named Syed Muhammad had won a court case in 2009 for declaration, possession, and other relief concerning certain land. Later, a person (Respondent No.4) who was not included as a party in that original lawsuit challenged the judgment, arguing it was obtained through fraud and misrepresentation, since he had rightful interest in the same land through earlier dealings that were concealed from the court. The trial court agreed, accepted his application, and cancelled the 2009 judgment and decree, restoring earlier property records. The petitioners (successors of the original winning party) challenged this cancellation, arguing the trial court decided the matter without properly examining evidence or holding a full hearing.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the trial court's decision to set aside the 2009 judgment, agreeing that there was sufficient documentary evidence showing concealment of facts and fraud, and that the challenger was indeed a necessary party who had been wrongly left out. However, the High Court found an error: once a judgment is cancelled under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, the original lawsuit should be revived and reheard on its merits, with the challenger properly included as a party. Since the trial court had not done this, the High Court ordered the case sent back for a fresh, complete trial. This clarifies that cancelling a judgment for fraud doesn't end the case—it must be retried fairly with all rightful parties included.

title: Eid Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murder under Pakistan's Penal Code after stabbing another man with a knife during an argument, resulting in the victim's death. The trial court had sentenced him to death, and the matter came before the Balochistan High Court both as an appeal by the convicted man and as a reference for confirmation of the death sentence.

The defence argued several points: that required procedures for recording the accused's statement were not properly followed, that the witnesses had not been named in the initial police report, and that they were "chance witnesses" who hadn't justified their presence at the scene.

The High Court rejected these objections. It found that the procedural certificate, though typed rather than handwritten, still satisfied legal requirements and caused no unfairness. It held that witnesses not being named in the FIR did not discredit their testimony, especially since the incident happened in public and people naturally gathered. Their accounts were also consistent with medical evidence about the fatal wound.

However, the court found mitigating circumstances: there was no prior enmity between the men, only a single knife blow was struck following a verbal dispute, and no clear motive was established. Because of these factors, the court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence from death to life imprisonment, illustrating how courts can lower the harshest punishment even while confirming guilt, based on the specific circumstances of how the crime occurred.

title: Muhammad Ramzan and 2 others V. Chugair and 3 others,
explainer:
This case explains which court has the power to hear a challenge to a judgment when the challenge is based on fraud or misrepresentation under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code.

A trial court (Qazi Lasbela) had issued a judgment in 2009, which was then challenged in appeal and upheld on its merits by the appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora) in January 2010. Later, one party filed an application under Section 12(2) CPC before the original trial court, alleging the 2009 judgment was obtained through fraud. The trial court agreed and set aside its own earlier judgment. However, the appellate court overturned this, ruling that since it had already affirmed the judgment on its merits, any fraud-based challenge should have been filed with the appellate court, not the trial court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It clarified that under Section 12(2), such applications must go to whichever court issued the "final" judgment, meaning the last court that actually examined the case on its merits (facts and law). If a higher court confirms a lower court's decision after fully reviewing it, the lower court's judgment merges into the higher court's ruling, which then becomes the proper forum for any fraud challenge. Since the petitioners filed in the wrong court, their revision petition was dismissed.

This case matters because it clarifies procedural rules about which court has jurisdiction to reopen a judgment alleged to be tainted by fraud, preventing confusion when judgments pass through multiple levels of appeal.

title: Rahim Muhammad alias Rohi Muhammad V. Syed Noor Shah,
explainer:
This case involves a landlord-tenant dispute over a shop (Cabin) in Quetta. The landlord, Syed Noor Shah, had earlier obtained an eviction order against his tenant, Rahim Muhammad, from the Rent Controller for default in rent and personal need, fixing the monthly rent at Rs. 16,000. That eviction order was upheld all the way up to the Supreme Court. Following this, the landlord filed a separate civil suit to recover arrears of rent amounting to over Rs. 1.4 million, which the trial court largely granted.

The tenant appealed, arguing that the rent amount had never been properly proven through documents or evidence, that the civil suit was not competent, and that recovery for rent older than three years was barred by the Limitation Act.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that since the Rent Controller had already determined the landlord-tenant relationship and the rate of rent, and these findings had been upheld through the appellate process up to the Supreme Court, they could not be reopened or challenged again in a civil suit. The court also held that under Article 110 of the Limitation Act, 1908, the three-year limitation period runs from when each installment of rent falls due, so the suit filed in 2014 was within time.

The appeal was dismissed, reinforcing the principle that final findings of a Rent Controller on landlord-tenant relationship and rent rate are binding in later civil proceedings.

Syed Noor Shah, the landlord, had previously won an eviction case against his tenant, Rahim Muhammad, over a rented cabin in Quetta, a decision upheld all the way to the Supreme Court. The Rent Controller had noted in that earlier ruling that the landlord could separately approach a civil court to recover unpaid rent at Rs. 16,000 per month from June 2007 onward. The landlord then filed a civil suit for recovery of arrears amounting to over 1.4 million rupees, and the trial court partially decreed the suit in his favor for about 1.39 million rupees.

The tenant appealed, arguing there was no documentary proof of the rent rate, that the rent amount had never been properly determined, and that the claim was time-barred under the Limitation Act.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that the rent rate and landlord-tenant relationship had already been conclusively determined by the Rent Controller and upheld through the Supreme Court, so they could not be re-litigated in a civil suit. It also ruled that the three-year limitation period under Article 110 of the Limitation Act had not expired when the suit was filed. Finding no error in the trial court's evaluation of evidence, the High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the recovery decree.

title: Muhammad Hussain V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Hussain, who was convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Quetta for his role in a shooting that killed two men and injured another, following a business dispute. He was initially tried in absentia and sentenced to death. After his arrest, an earlier appeal succeeded in getting that conviction set aside, and the case was sent back for a fresh trial.

During the retrial, a key witness who had survived the shooting but later died had her earlier statement (recorded during the absentia trial) placed on record under a law that allows such statements when a witness has since died. The defense argued this evidence shouldn't count because it came from a trial that had already been overturned, but the High Court disagreed, noting the earlier proceedings were still valid judicial proceedings and the defense lawyer had cross-examined the witness at the time.

The Court also found that a different witness, who only came forward three months after the incident with no good explanation for the delay, could not be trusted. However, the statement of the deceased injured witness, backed by medical evidence and recovered physical evidence, was reliable enough to sustain the conviction.

Because the prosecution failed to prove the alleged motive, the Court treated this as a mitigating factor. It upheld Hussain's conviction but reduced his sentence from death to life imprisonment.

title: Naseebullah Khan V. Abdus Samee Babar,
explainer:
This case involved a defamation lawsuit in which a former Customs and Sales Tax official sued a man for 5 billion rupees in damages. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant, falsely claiming to be Vice Chairman of a business council, held a press conference in 2008 accusing him of wrongdoing. These allegations were reported in several newspapers and broadcast on television. The plaintiff later showed that the defendant was not actually affiliated with the business organizations he claimed to represent, as confirmed by various chambers of commerce.

The defendant denied the allegations in his written statement, but the trial court closed his opportunity to produce evidence or record his own statement after he missed a few hearing dates, and then decreed the full 5 billion rupee claim against him without properly examining the evidence or discussing the issues framed in the case.

The Balochistan High Court found this improper. It held that even when a defendant fails to appear, a court cannot simply decree a case without evaluating the evidence already on record, especially in a case involving such a massive damages claim. The court stressed that both regular and ex-parte decrees must be based on proper appreciation of evidence, otherwise they are legally void. The appeal was partly allowed, meaning the trial court's decision was reconsidered rather than upheld outright. This case highlights the importance of fair hearing and evidence-based decision making in civil litigation.

title: Naseebullah Khan V. Abdus Samee Babar,
explainer:
This case involved a civil suit where a government customs official sued a businessman for 5 billion rupees in damages, claiming the man had held a press conference making false, defamatory allegations against him that were published in several newspapers and aired on television. The defendant denied making any defamatory statements and contested the suit.

During the trial, the defendant submitted a list of witnesses but failed to produce them on the scheduled dates. The trial court closed his right to present evidence and, without properly examining the plaintiff's evidence or recording any reasons, decreed the full 5 billion rupee claim against him under procedural rules governing adjournments.

The Balochistan High Court found this approach improper. It clarified that under the Civil Procedure Code, a court asked to "decide the suit forthwith" must still base its decision on the evidence actually on record - it cannot simply decree a case as a penalty for a party's absence without reasoning or evaluation of proof. Given the enormous sum involved, the court held that the defendant was not given fair opportunity to present his case or record his statement, and the trial court's decree lacked any discussion of evidence or justification.

As a result, the High Court set aside the trial court's judgment and decree and sent the case back for a fresh decision, ensuring both parties get a proper hearing based on evidence rather than procedural technicalities.

title: Abdul Hadi and 9 others V. Abdul Hanan and 17 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute in Balochistan over land left behind by a man named Malik Mehmood, who died in 1954 leaving four daughters. The plaintiffs, descendants of some of these daughters, claimed that other relatives had fraudulently transferred the entire inherited property into their own names, falsely claiming to be the only legal heirs, and had deprived the rightful heirs of their Islamic inheritance shares.

The defendants argued that the plaintiffs' mother had never challenged the original property transfers during her lifetime, and also produced a photocopied "Will" claiming the original owner had named them as his heirs. They later also argued, for the first time at the appeal stage, that local custom excluded daughters from inheritance.

The High Court rejected these defenses. It held that heirs automatically become co-owners of property the moment inheritance opens, regardless of whether official records are updated, and that one heir's possession benefits all co-sharers. The unregistered, unproven photocopy of the Will was inadmissible and could not establish any claim to inheritance. The court also rejected the "custom excluding daughters" argument because it was never raised in the original written statement and contradicted earlier admissions by the defendants that shares had partly been paid out.

The court upheld the trial court's decision recognizing the daughters and their heirs as rightful co-sharers entitled to their Islamic shares, dismissing the appeal. The case reinforces that inheritance rights arise automatically by law and cannot be defeated by unproven documents or late-raised customary claims

title: Ghousia Rice Mills through Proprietor V. National Bank of Pakistan through Manager and 2 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved Ghousia Rice Mills, which had a cash finance arrangement with the National Bank of Pakistan secured against mortgaged property and pledged stocks of rice and paddy. Two connected disputes arose. First, the mill owner sued the bank and its insurance company, claiming that floods in 2010 had destroyed the pledged stock (which was kept under the bank's control) and sought a court declaration that the insurance company should pay out on the policy. Second, the bank separately sued the mill owner for failing to repay the finance facility it had taken out, worth over fifteen million rupees.

The trial court dismissed the mill owner's suit against the bank and insurer, but ruled in favor of the bank in its recovery suit. The mill owner appealed both decisions together since they stemmed from the same financial relationship.

The High Court upheld both rulings. It found that the insurance policy itself required disputes over loss amounts to go to arbitration, and since the mill owner skipped this step and went straight to court, the suit was barred by law. On the bank's recovery suit, the court found the bank had properly documented everything required, including loan agreements, account statements, and mortgage papers, satisfying legal requirements for such claims. Finding no errors in how the evidence was handled, the High Court dismissed the appeals, reinforcing that contractual arbitration clauses must be followed before approaching courts.

title: Abdul Majeed V. President National Bank of Pakistan through President Head Office and 3 others,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves two employees of the National Bank of Pakistan who were issued charge sheets and show-cause notices as part of disciplinary proceedings against them. The employees challenged these notices directly in court, arguing they were issued in violation of the bank's internal disciplinary policy, were time-barred, and were unfair since they claimed no personal fault for the issues raised (which stemmed from a special audit covering a period before one of them had even taken charge of his position).

The court dismissed both petitions. It held that a mere charge sheet or show-cause notice does not by itself harm anyone's legal rights, since it is only a preliminary step in disciplinary proceedings, not a final decision. Courts can only intervene under their constitutional writ jurisdiction when a final order imposing punishment, or some other adverse decision, actually affects a person's rights. Until then, there is no real "grievance" to complain about. The judges also noted that questions about violations of procedure, timing, or factual innocence should first be raised before the inquiry officer conducting the disciplinary proceedings, not before the High Court.

This judgment matters because it reinforces an important principle in Pakistani administrative and service law: courts will not interfere prematurely in internal disciplinary processes, and employees must first use available internal remedies before approaching the High Court.

title: Shaukat Ali V. The State,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court, hearing an appeal by Shaukat Ali against his conviction for rape (zina-bil-jabr) under the Pakistan Penal Code.

The prosecution's case was that Shaukat Ali and a co-accused, Shehzad, forcibly picked up a minor girl, Habiba, and a boy, Yasir, in a vehicle and drove them to a remote area, where Shaukat committed the offence against the girl. The girl's mother filed the FIR, and at trial the victim, her mother, and the boy who accompanied her gave evidence. Medical examination supported the allegation, and the doctor's findings, including injuries on the victim's body, indicated she had resisted. The co-accused, Shehzad, was acquitted on the same evidence, but Shaukat was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to life imprisonment with a fine.

On appeal, the defence argued there were contradictions in witness statements and lack of independent corroboration. The High Court found the victim's and witness's accounts credible and consistent with medical evidence, noting minor contradictions were understandable given the long delay (the accused had evaded arrest for years) and the victim's age. However, the court found that the trial court had wrongly applied the rape provision when the facts actually matched the unnatural offence provision, and therefore reduced the sentence from life imprisonment to three years, while upholding the conviction and reducing the fine.

This case illustrates how appellate courts review both the evidence and the correct legal classification of offences

title: Zarghoon Shah and others V . Dilawar Khan and others,
explainer:
This case concerns a long-running property dispute in Quetta over land that was originally leased to the predecessors of the private respondents. Years later, an unregistered 1995 lease agreement surfaced, reportedly giving the tenants certain rights, including a claim that the property could not be sold to anyone else without first offering it to them. Based on this, a court had earlier decreed that the owner must honor the agreement. Subsequently, the property changed hands through gifts between family members, and a new owner eventually obtained a court decree confirming his ownership. The original tenants then challenged that decree using Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, which allows a judgment to be set aside under specific legal grounds, and both the trial court and the appellate court sided with them, canceling the decree and the related property mutation.

The Balochistan High Court found that the lower courts had acted improperly by deciding the matter without framing proper legal issues or giving the parties a chance to present evidence on crucial points, especially regarding whether the unregistered lease was legally valid under the Transfer of Property Act, the Registration Act, and the Contract Act. Because these important legal and factual questions were never properly examined, the High Court set aside both lower court orders and sent the case back to the trial court to be decided afresh, with proper procedure. This case highlights the importance of due process and thorough legal examination before overturning property rights.

title: Haji Abdul Wahid V. Abdullah and 5 others,
explainer:
Haji Abdul Wahid filed a suit against Abdullah and others seeking a mandatory injunction, recovery of mesne profit, and permanent injunction, claiming a share in the income of a flour mill business run on his family's property and rent arrears for shops and a godown. The defendants were in possession of the premises under an arrangement where they ran the flour mill business and were supposed to share income and pay rent to the plaintiff's family, but allegedly stopped paying after 1990.

Earlier, the plaintiff had filed an eviction petition which was dismissed, followed by an earlier suit for mesne profit and mandatory injunction. When he later filed a fresh suit for ejectment, the lower courts dismissed it, holding it was barred under Order II, Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code, which prevents a party from splitting claims arising from the same cause of action into multiple suits.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that the earlier suit concerned mesne profit and injunction, while the new suit concerned ejectment, a different cause of action that had not fully matured earlier. Since the defendant's possession was permissive (based on the business and rent arrangement) rather than wrongful, the claims were distinct, and the bar under Order II, Rule 2 did not apply. The court set aside the lower courts' orders and sent the case back for trial on merits, allowing the revision petition. This clarifies that procedural bars against repeat litigation apply only when the same cause of action is involved, not simply because related disputes involve the same

title: Government of Balochistan, Industries Department V. Muhammad Yousaf and others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute over compensation for land acquired by the Balochistan government to build a rainwater drain in Hub. In 2001, a civil judge set the compensation rate, which was later increased by the High Court in 2008. The government appealed to the Supreme Court, but that appeal was dismissed in 2015 for being filed too late, and a subsequent review petition was also dismissed in 2016.

Meanwhile, the landowners had already filed an execution application back in 2000 to recover the compensation, but it was put on hold because the Supreme Court had issued a stay on the judgment while the appeal was pending. After the Supreme Court finally dismissed the appeal and review, the landowners filed a fresh execution application in 2016. The government argued this was filed too late and objected to the execution process.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the government's objections. It held that since the first execution application had been pending and was only adjourned due to the Supreme Court's stay order, and since there was no evidence that the stay was lifted before the final 2015 decision, the new execution application was filed within the legal time limit. Relying on earlier Supreme Court precedents, the court ruled that the execution proceedings were valid and dismissed the government's appeal, meaning the landowners could proceed to recover their compensation.

title: Azeem Khan and 2 others V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case involved a murder near Killa Saifullah, Balochistan, where a man named Mehboob Khan was shot dead while traveling home with relatives. The complainant alleged that two accused men attacked the group, one engaging in a physical fight while the other, Azeem Khan, pulled out a pistol and shot the victim, who later died in hospital. A third person was also tried as a co-accused for allegedly sharing the common intention to commit the crime. The trial court had convicted the accused and sentenced them to death.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the eyewitness testimony, medical evidence, and forensic reports. It found the ocular evidence credible and consistent, supported by medical findings of a gunshot wound and by forensic matching of recovered cartridges to the pistol seized from the accused. The court held that being related to the victim did not automatically discredit the witnesses, since their accounts were reliable and corroborated.

However, the court found that the prosecution had failed to prove the alleged motive (old enmity), which it treated as a mitigating factor, and reduced the death sentence to life imprisonment for the main accused. For the co-accused allegedly sharing common intention, the court found no evidence of any overt act, weapon, or instigation, and acquitted him, giving him the benefit of the doubt.

This case highlights how Pakistani courts weigh eyewitness, medical, and forensic evidence together, and how failure to prove motive can reduce punishment even when guilt is otherwise established.

title: Mst. Popalzai and others V. Muhammad Asif Khan and 33 others,
explainer:
This case concerned a long-running dispute over agricultural land in Quetta that had originally belonged to a Hindu landowner and was treated as evacuee property after Partition. The government had allotted portions of this land to certain allottees in 1960-62, and the land was officially mutated in their names, though physical possession was never handed over. Separately, descendants of one Khan Bahadur Khudai Rahim claimed their ancestor had purchased the same land back in 1947, before Partition, through unregistered sale documents, and sought formal confirmation of that sale from the Custodian of Evacuee Property. This application was filed decades late, only against one of the two allottees, and without properly establishing the claimant's authority to act on the deceased purchaser's behalf. The Member, Board of Revenue rejected the request for confirmation of sale, and the purchaser's heirs challenged that rejection in the High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that the application for confirmation of sale was filed well beyond the legally prescribed thirty-day period, that the allottees whose rights were affected had never been properly made parties or challenged through valid legal proceedings, and that no proper inquiry by the Custodian of Evacuee Property was shown on record. The court also noted that disputed factual questions like these cannot be resolved through constitutional petitions. It ruled that the original Board of Revenue decision was properly reasoned, and the purchaser's heirs lacked standing to pursue the claim at this stage, though it left open other appropriate legal remedies for them to pursue

title: Ghulam Farooq V. Dolat Khan,
explainer:
This case involved a landlord, Ghulam Farooq, trying to evict a tenant, Dolat Khan, from a property in Quetta under Balochistan's rent laws. The landlord claimed the premises were rented out verbally for Rs. 2,000 per month, and that the tenant had stopped paying rent since August 2015. The tenant denied being a tenant at all, claiming instead that he had bought the property from the landlord's brother for Rs. 300,000 and held possession as its owner, relying on an agreement signed years after the alleged sale.

The trial court initially dismissed the eviction case, finding no landlord-tenant relationship existed. On appeal, the Balochistan High Court disagreed. It found that the tenant failed to prove his brother-in-law seller actually had any legal authority to sell the property or transfer ownership, since records showed the property remained registered in the landlord's name and mortgaged to a bank by him. The court held that mere claims of a prior purchase, unsupported by proper documentation or authority, could not override the established ownership and tenancy relationship.

The court ruled that ownership itself helps establish the landlord-tenant relationship, and since the tenant could not prove a valid purchase, he must vacate first and pursue any ownership claims separately through proper legal channels. The eviction was allowed, and the tenant was ordered to hand over possession within two months after paying due rent. This case reinforces that tenants cannot resist eviction merely by alleging an unproven sale.

title: Mst. Mah Khatoon and 3 others V. Feroz and another,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute in Quetta. A father, Muhammad Ameen, owned land along with constructed shops. He had one son and several daughters. In 2009, he executed a disinheritance deed against his son, Feroz, accusing him of disobedience, and published this in a newspaper. Shortly after, he gifted the entire property to his three unmarried daughters through a mutation, excluding his son and married daughters.

After the father's death, the son sued for declaration, possession, partition, and cancellation of the mutation, arguing the gift was actually meant to cut him out of his rightful inheritance. The trial court and the appellate court both ruled in his favor, declaring the gift invalid.

The daughters challenged this before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions, ruling that disinheriting an heir through a so-called Aaq-Nama (disinheritance deed) has no legal or religious sanctity under Islamic law. A gift made with the real intention of depriving a legal heir of their rightful share is invalid, regardless of the formal requirements of a gift being met. The court did note that since the daughters had paid Rs. 200,000 to their father as part of the gift arrangement (making it a Hibba-bil-Awez, a gift for consideration), the son was required to return that amount to them.

This judgment reaffirms that parents cannot lawfully disinherit legal heirs under Islamic inheritance law simply by framing a transfer as a gift, protecting the inheritance rights of children.

title: Mst. Mah Khatoon and 3 others V. Feroz and another,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over inherited property in Quetta. Muhammad Ameen owned land which, before his death, he transferred through a gift mutation to his three unmarried daughters, excluding his son Feroz. The father had earlier published a notice disowning his son, apparently over disobedience, and the defendants argued this justified cutting him out of inheritance. After the father's death, the son sued to have the gift mutation cancelled, seeking his rightful share of the property along with possession and partition.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled in the son's favor, declaring the gift mutation invalid and holding that all legal heirs were entitled to their shares. The daughters challenged this before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the revision petition. It held that disobedience is not a valid ground under Islamic law to disinherit a legal heir, and that a gift made specifically to deprive an heir of their rightful inheritance share is void, even though Muslims are generally free to gift property to anyone during their lifetime. The court noted that since this was a gift made in exchange for Rs. 200,000 (Hiba-bil-Iwaz), the son would have to return that amount to the daughters.

This ruling reinforces that parents cannot use gifts to bypass Islamic inheritance rules and punish heirs for perceived disobedience, protecting the fixed inheritance rights guaranteed under Islamic law.
