title: Mst. Saeeda Begum and 4 others V. Mst. Habib-U-Nisa and others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running family property dispute in Quetta. A plot had originally been allotted to Abdul Karim, who built a house and shops on it. After his death, one of his sons, Raja Muhammad Sabir, got the entire property transferred into his own name through a settlement department order in 1971, rather than it being divided among all of Abdul Karim's legal heirs. Years later, the property was redeveloped into a shopping center and hotel, and Raja Sabir exchanged it with other parties for different properties and cash, who then sold part of it onward.

The other children of Abdul Karim sued, arguing they were co-sharers (joint owners by inheritance) and that the exchange deal was illegal since it ignored their shares. The trial court agreed and cancelled the exchange. On appeal, the High Court upheld this decision. It held that once a father dies, his children automatically become co-owners of his property, and each co-sharer is treated as having a stake in every part of the land until a formal partition occurs. The court also examined whether the later buyers could be protected under a legal principle (Section 41, Transfer of Property Act) that shields good-faith purchasers who took reasonable care before buying. However, since the buyers never claimed or proved they acted in good faith or investigated the sellers' ownership properly, this protection did not apply.

The ruling reinforces that property transfers ignoring rightful heirs' shares are void, and that buyers must verify ownership claims carefully to claim good-faith protection.

title: Mir Shoaib Nosherwani V. Mir Muhammad Ismail Peerakzai and 5 others,
explainer:
This case concerned a man whose nomination papers for Balochistan's Provincial Assembly election in 2013 (constituency PB-46 Kharan) were rejected by the Returning Officer, a decision later upheld by the Election Tribunal. The rejection was based on findings that in the 2002 general election, he had falsely declared possession of a Bachelor's (BA) degree, when in fact he had failed his BA examination at Punjab University. Investigation at the time revealed that his answer sheets had been tampered with during a rechecking request, leading a university disciplinary committee to bar him from taking exams for three years. He never challenged that disciplinary ruling. Instead, he later took and passed a BA exam from the University of Balochistan in 2006 under a different roll number.

The petitioner argued that since the 2002 election petition against him was withdrawn without a final decision on merits, and since no objection was raised when he contested in 2008, the old findings should not be used against him in 2013.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that his failure to challenge the disciplinary committee's decision meant it stood as final, and his repeated reliance on a false claim of holding a BA degree showed he was not "honest, righteous, and Ameen" as required by the Constitution for contesting elections. The court dismissed his petition, upholding rejection of his nomination papers. The case underscores that candidates making false educational claims can be permanently disqualified, regardless of later unrelated qualifications.

title: Kausar Ali and another V. Javed Anjum and 6 others,
explainer:
This case involves a property dispute in Quetta over a house originally owned by one Noor Zaman, who had two sons, Anjum Qazalbash and Ramzan Ali Qazalbash. Anjum gifted his half-share to his brother Ramzan Ali in 1982. Ramzan Ali later willed the entire property to his wife, Ruqayya Begum, who then sold it to Kausar Ali. After Anjum's death, his children (the plaintiffs) sued, claiming the original 1982 gift and subsequent transfers were illegal, and that they were entitled to a share of the property as legal heirs.

The trial court and the first appellate court both ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, cancelling the sale to Kausar Ali and awarding them a share of the property.

The Balochistan High Court overturned these decisions. It held that Anjum Qazalbash, the plaintiffs' father, never challenged the 1982 gift during his own lifetime, even though all the relevant property transfers happened while he was alive. The court ruled that since he did not dispute these transactions himself, his children could not later claim a right to challenge them after his death. The court found that the lower courts had misread the evidence and ignored this crucial timeline.

As a result, the High Court set aside the earlier judgments and dismissed the plaintiffs' suit entirely. This case reinforces an important legal principle: if a person directly affected by a property transfer does not contest it during their lifetime, their heirs generally lose the right to challenge it later.

title: All Pakistan Land Route Custom Agent Association through Secretary General and others V. The Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Ministry of Commerce and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns two trade associations in Balochistan that challenged a federal law and rule governing elections of trade organizations and chambers of commerce. Under the Trade Organizations Act 2013 and its accompanying rules, new members of a chamber or trade association must wait two years after enrolment before they can vote in elections, while old members who re-register after a lapse only need to wait one year. The petitioners, who had recently obtained their trade licences, argued this two-year waiting period was discriminatory and violated their fundamental right to equality under Article 25 of the Constitution, especially since it would prevent them from voting in an upcoming election where, by rotation, Balochistan was due to have representation.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petitions. It held that courts must exercise judicial restraint when reviewing policy matters, and that under Article 30(2) of the Constitution, laws cannot be challenged merely on grounds of policy. The court also explained that Article 25's equality guarantee allows reasonable classification, meaning people in different situations can be treated differently, and persons similarly situated are to be treated alike. Since new and old members are not identically situated, the differing waiting periods were a valid classification rather than unconstitutional discrimination. The law was presumed constitutional, and the petitioners failed to show any clear violation of constitutional principles.

This case matters because it illustrates how courts balance individual rights claims against legislative policy choices, reaffirming that not all differential treatment amounts to unconstitutional discrimination.

title: Syed Abdul Manan and others V. Malik Asmatullah and others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Balochistan over roughly 14 acres of agricultural property. Two groups of people each claimed ownership: one side said their ancestors bought the land back in 1932 through an informal agreement, and that a later official land settlement in the 1940s had mistakenly recorded ownership under the other family's name. The other side, recorded as the official owners in revenue records, said they had merely lent four acres of the land to the first group in 1993 for six years so they could dig a tube-well and farm it, in exchange for a share of the crops.

The trial court initially dismissed the claim of the family seeking declaration and correction of records, but the appellate court reversed that and ruled in their favor. The matter eventually reached the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court sided with the recorded owners (the respondents). It held that an old, undated arbitration award—produced to support the other side's claim—was invalid because the attorney who agreed to it had no authority to do so, and the arbitration had bypassed the court entirely, making it legally worthless. The court also ruled that long-standing official revenue entries are presumed true unless strongly disproven, and that mere possession of land doesn't override documented ownership. It also clarified that the time limit for filing such suits starts when the other side formally denies ownership in their written reply, not earlier.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that official land records carry strong legal weight, and that informal agreements or arbitration without court approval cannot be used to override documented ownership.

title: Shah Bakhsh and others V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and others,
explainer:
This case involved teachers and education staff from Balochistan who had been given higher pay scales, known as time scale grants, after completing certain years of service, under government policies issued in 2007 and 2012. These grants allowed employees to receive a higher salary scale without being formally promoted to a higher post. The dispute arose over how much Group Insurance money (payable at retirement or death under the Balochistan Provincial Employees Group Insurance Act) the employees were entitled to. The petitioners argued they should receive insurance benefits based on this higher time-scale pay, treating it as equivalent to a promotion.

The Balochistan High Court rejected this argument. It held that a time scale grant is different from a promotion: promotion means moving to a higher rank or position, while a time scale grant only raises an employee's pay to relieve long-service stagnation, without changing their actual post or rank. Since the employees had voluntarily accepted the financial benefits of the time scale policy, the court said they could not later challenge the same policy to claim additional insurance benefits as if they had been promoted. The court ruled that insurance payouts must be based on the employee's actual last pay scale or grade, not an assumed higher one. All the petitions were dismissed.

This case matters because it clarifies the legal distinction between "promotion" and "time scale" grants in Pakistani civil service law, affecting how retirement and insurance benefits are calculated for many government employees.

title: Agha Construction Company through Proprietor V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary, Mineral and Mines Deptt. and another ,
explainer:
Agha Construction Company challenged how Balochistan's Mines and Minerals Department handled a contract for collecting royalty on minerals across several districts. The department had auctioned the contract, but the first highest bidder failed to meet the contract terms, so his security deposit was forfeited. The contract was then offered to the petitioner, the second highest bidder, who was supposed to sign the agreement within ten days. When he too failed to do so, his security deposit was also forfeited, and his later appeal to the Secretary of the department was dismissed.

The petitioner argued he never actually received the offer letter and was never given a chance to explain before his deposit was forfeited. The High Court examined the relevant mining rules and the official offer letter, and found that the letter did not show the required government approval and that the department produced no evidence proving the petitioner had been given an opportunity to respond before the forfeiture decision.

The Court also noted that the department had improperly extended royalty collection arrangements between auctions for about a year without proper authority, which could harm government revenue if left unchecked.

As a result, the Court partly allowed the petition, set aside the Secretary's order, and sent the appeal back to be decided afresh—emphasizing that administrative forfeiture decisions affecting money and rights require fair process and proper authorization.

title: Khurshid Ashraf through Attorney and 3 others V. Aftab Ashraf and another,
explainer:
This case is about a long-running family property dispute in Quetta over land that was to be divided among relatives. An earlier partition suit had already been decided in favour of the plaintiffs, upheld all the way to the Supreme Court, but the decree was never executed within the legal time limit. So the plaintiffs filed a fresh partition suit for the same property.

During this new suit, one of the defendants asked the trial court to add two more people and a housing cooperative as parties, claiming the plaintiffs had sold a related house in Karachi to them, making them necessary parties. The trial court agreed and ordered the plaintiffs to amend their claim to include these new parties. The plaintiffs challenged this order before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court set aside the trial court's order. It held that a plaintiff is "dominus litis," meaning they have the right to choose whom to sue and cannot be forced to add parties they don't wish to sue, unless those parties are truly "necessary" (essential for an effective decree) or "proper" (useful for complete adjudication). Here, the request to add new parties was not supported by any documents proving the alleged sale, so it was premature and based on mere assertion. The court dismissed the impleadment application, while allowing the other side to reapply later with proper evidence. This case clarifies courts' limited discretion to force additional parties into a lawsuit without solid proof.

title: Asad Mahmood and another V. Federation of Pakistan and others,
explainer:
This case involved two petitioners who had originally worked for the erstwhile T&T Department, which was later converted first into the Pakistan Telecommunication Corporation and then into Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (PTCL). They went to the Balochistan High Court seeking relief on several issues: increased pay, pension benefits, promotion, transfer, and the legal status under which they could be subjected to disciplinary proceedings.

The court examined the relevant laws governing the transformation of the T&T Department into a corporation and then a company, which contained provisions protecting the terms and conditions of service for employees who were transferred. However, the court found that one petitioner was not actually an original T&T Department employee—he had joined after the Corporation was already established, and later accepted promotion under the company's own terms, meaning he could not claim the special protections meant for original transferred employees. For both petitioners, the court also found procedural problems: their pension claims were premature since they were still in service, their promotion claims failed because they had not included the relevant comparator employees as parties to the case, and for other grievances, they had not first approached the proper departmental authorities, who offered an effective alternate remedy.

As a result, the court dismissed the petitions. This case matters because it clarifies that protections for former government employees absorbed into a corporatized entity depend on actual employment history, and reinforces that courts expect people to exhaust other available remedies before seeking constitutional relief.

title: Balochistan University of Information and Technology and Management Sciences, Quetta V. Nawab brother (pvt.) Limited,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a Quetta university and a private construction company over unpaid work. The company filed a claim, and both sides agreed to appoint an arbitrator to settle the matter. The arbitrator reviewed the evidence, rejected the university's counter-claim as unsupported, and awarded the company roughly 48 million rupees plus interest and costs, while disallowing a large portion of the company's original claim for lack of contractual support.

The university objected to the award in the trial court, but the objections were rejected and the award was confirmed. The university then appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that its evidence and counter-claim had not been properly considered.

The High Court dismissed the appeal. It held that courts reviewing arbitration awards do not act as appellate courts and cannot re-examine evidence to look for errors unless such errors are clearly visible on the face of the award itself. Since the university could not point to any specific mistake or misconduct by the arbitrator, and the award was based on documented evidence, there was no legal basis to overturn it. However, the court did modify one part of the award, ruling that the arbitrator had no authority to grant interest on the award amount from the date of the award until actual payment, since this went beyond his powers.

This judgment reinforces the limited role courts play in reviewing arbitration awards, emphasizing finality and respect for arbitrators' decisions unless clear errors appear on record.

title: Eng. Saeed Ahmed and others V. Chairman National Highway authority, Islamabad and others ,
explainer:
This case involved three employees of the National Highway Authority (NHA) who had originally been hired on contract in 1996 and were later terminated. Under the Sacked Employees (Re-instatement) Act, 2010 (SERA), NHA reinstated them in 2011 into regular positions one grade higher than before, treating them under section 4(a) of the law, which applies to regularly appointed staff.

However, in a separate case, the Sindh High Court had ruled that contract employees like these petitioners should actually be dealt with under section 4(b) of SERA, not 4(a), since they were originally hired on contract, not on a regular basis. Following that ruling, NHA issued a fresh order in 2013 demoting the petitioners back down one grade. The employees challenged this demotion before the Balochistan High Court, arguing it was unfair, done without hearing them, and went beyond what the Sindh High Court had actually ordered.

The Balochistan High Court held that it could not use its constitutional writ jurisdiction to overturn or sit in judgment over an order passed by another High Court (the Sindh High Court) acting in its judicial capacity. One High Court cannot issue a writ against another High Court's judicial order. Because NHA's demotion order was simply implementing the Sindh High Court's binding decision, the Balochistan High Court found it had no power to interfere, highlighting an important limit on the scope of High Courts' authority over each other's judgments.

title: Messrs Jeeand Coal Company through Managing Partner and others V. Appellate Authority/Secretary, Mines and Minerals Development Department and other,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and deals with a long-running dispute over coal mining rights in Dukki, District Loralai. Jeeand Coal Company had obtained a prospecting licence and later a 20-year mining lease covering 1,920 acres. Several local landowners objected, claiming parts of that area overlapped with their agricultural land, homes, or other property, and filed applications and appeals asking for their land to be excluded from the lease or for the licence to be cancelled altogether.

The Appellate Authority/Secretary of the Mines and Minerals Development Department issued various orders on these competing claims - sometimes excluding specific acreage from the company's lease, sometimes directing that mining stay a set distance from homes, mosques, schools and graveyards, and sometimes rejecting requests to cancel the licence outright. Both the mining company and the landowners challenged these decisions before the High Court through several petitions, which were heard together.

The High Court found that the authorities below had not properly examined the relevant legal provisions or clearly determined what the landowners were actually seeking - whether a prospecting licence/no-objection certificate or outright exclusion of land from the lease. Because these crucial issues were left unresolved, the Court set aside the earlier orders and sent the matter back to the authorities to decide afresh, in accordance with law, including resolving the licensing questions properly. This case matters because it highlights how competing claims over mineral and agricultural rights must be carefully and transparently adjudicated before land is leased out for mining.

title: Shams-Ud-Din V. Salah-Ud-Din and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute between brothers over inherited business and mining assets left by their late father. After their father died in 1992, his properties, including shares in two mining companies, had never been formally divided among the heirs. The matter was referred to a private arbitrator, who issued an award in April 2019. One brother, the petitioner, then asked a civil court to confirm this award as an official court order and also sought a temporary injunction to maintain status quo over a house he was occupying.

The trial court initially granted the injunction, ordering the parties to preserve the existing situation regarding the house. However, on appeal, the Additional District Judge overturned that order. The petitioner then challenged this reversal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision and dismissed the petition. It explained that courts cannot grant temporary injunctions merely because a party has a prima facie case; they must also weigh whether the balance of convenience and risk of irreparable harm favor the applicant. Since any loss the petitioner might suffer could be compensated financially if he ultimately won the case, it did not qualify as irreparable harm. The court also noted that the case involved complex factual and legal questions, including disputes about who was bound by the arbitration agreement, which required full evidence and trial rather than an injunction at this early stage. This ruling reinforces established principles on when courts should or should not grant temporary injunctions.

explainer:
This case was about a family property dispute. After Karam Khan died in 1980, his descendants through his daughters claimed a share of his property through a suit for declaration, partition, possession and other relief. The defendants disputed that these women were actually Karam Khan's daughters.

During the trial, the plaintiffs asked the court to let them produce official family registration records (RTC forms) through NADRA to prove the disputed family relationship, even though these documents had not been filed earlier in the case. The trial court refused, but on appeal the Additional District Judge partly allowed the request, letting the plaintiffs obtain these records through NADRA, while rejecting a related request about calling additional witnesses. The defendants then challenged this appellate decision before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's order and dismissed the petition. It explained that the legal requirement of showing "good cause" for late production of documents under the Civil Procedure Code should be interpreted liberally, in the interest of justice, rather than used to punish parties for technical delays. Since there was no fraud or doubt about the authenticity of the NADRA documents, and such records are public documents presumed genuine, they could be allowed in as evidence. The court also clarified that someone who merely produces a document in response to a court summons does not thereby become a witness.

This ruling is significant because it clarifies how courts should balance procedural strictness with fairness when parties seek to introduce important evidence, especially genuine public records, later in a trial.

title: Syed Muhammad Ali V. Syed Fasahat Hussain and 5 others,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute over a house in Quetta. The petitioner (Syed Muhammad Ali) claimed he bought the house in 1985 from respondent No.1 through sale agreements and an irrevocable power of attorney, and that possession was handed over to him. He said he later rented the house out, but the tenant (respondent No.2) fraudulently obtained a second power of attorney from the original owner and transferred the property to himself, who then transferred it to respondent No.3. The petitioner claimed he only discovered this in 1997 and filed a suit for specific performance seeking enforcement of his purchase.

The respondents argued that the petitioner himself had sold the house to respondent No.2 shortly after buying it, and asked the original owner to issue the second power of attorney to allow transfer and loan adjustment with the House Building Finance Corporation. Both the trial court and the appellate court dismissed the petitioner's suit, finding it was filed too late (barred by limitation) and that he failed to prove he still possessed the property or to disprove the documents against him.

The High Court upheld these decisions. It ruled that limitation is not a mere technicality - courts must dismiss time-barred suits even if the issue isn't specifically raised as a defense. Since no real legal error was found in the lower courts' reasoning, the revision petition was dismissed, meaning the petitioner lost his claim to the house.

title: Lal Jan V. Kamalhan and others,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and concerns a claim of pre-emption, a right under Islamic law that lets certain people (such as neighbors or co-sharers) step in and purchase property when it is sold, ahead of other buyers, provided a valid sale actually took place.

The petitioner, Lal Jan, claimed that Kamalhan had purchased land from another person and that he had a preferential right to acquire that land instead. He said he learned of the sale through a witness and then followed the proper legal steps to assert his pre-emption claim. The respondents denied any sale occurred, insisting the land had only been leased (Ajara) for seven years, not sold.

The trial court dismissed the suit because the petitioner failed to prove a sale had actually happened. On appeal, the High Court agreed. It explained that pre-emption rights only arise from a genuine, complete sale, not from leases, gifts, inheritance, or similar arrangements. The witnesses presented by the petitioner had no direct knowledge of any sale; their testimony was based on hearsay, which the law does not accept as valid evidence. Since no direct, admissible evidence of a sale existed, the core requirement for pre-emption was missing.

The High Court therefore dismissed the appeal, upholding the lower court's decision. The case highlights that courts require solid, direct proof of a sale before granting pre-emption rights, and secondhand information is not enough.

title: Fayyaz Ahmed and 2 others V. Muhammad Azam,
explainer:
This case involved a landlord-tenant dispute over half a house in Quetta. The landlord, Muhammad Azam, sought to evict tenants (the Fayyaz Ahmed family) for non-payment of rent since January 2014 and because he needed the property for his own personal use. The tenants denied that any landlord-tenant relationship existed, arguing there was no written rental agreement and no rent receipts proving they paid rent to the landlord.

The Rent Controller originally ruled in favor of the landlord, ordering the tenants to vacate and pay back rent. The tenants appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the eviction order. It found that the landlord had proven ownership of the property through mutation (land record) entries and utility bills, while the tenants could not produce any document proving their own right to possess the premises. The court held that a tenancy does not need to be in writing - it can be oral or implied through conduct, especially where parties are closely related, as was claimed here. Since the landlord's ownership was unchallenged by any proof from the tenants, the law presumes the person in possession is a tenant. The court also found the tenants had deliberately avoided paying rent.

This judgment matters because it confirms that Rent Controllers can decide landlord-tenant relationships based on circumstantial evidence like ownership records, and that oral tenancies are legally valid even without formal written agreements.

title: Mst. Nuzhat Gulzar and 10 others V. Shamim Gul Durrani and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running family property dispute in Quetta over a house at Satellite Town. Years earlier, a widow's suit claiming sole ownership of the house was dismissed, and that decision was upheld all the way to the Supreme Court. Later, other family members (the petitioners) successfully sued for partition and possession of their Sharia-based shares in the same house, which was recorded in court records as measuring 5400 square feet. This partition decree was also upheld through the appellate courts and Supreme Court.

When it came time to actually divide the property, the decree-holders discovered that the house's real area, according to the original allotment order from the Quetta Development Authority and the site plan, was actually 7065 square feet, not 5400 as mistakenly written in the earlier court papers. They asked the court to correct this clerical error under Section 152 of the Civil Procedure Code, but the executing court refused, and the family brought the matter to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners, holding that since ownership shares had already been conclusively settled, the wrong area figure was simply an inadvertent mistake that could and should be corrected to match the official allotment order, which was the true foundation of ownership. Citing Supreme Court precedent, the judge allowed the correction, subject to verifying the area against the allotment order. This matters because it confirms that courts can fix honest factual errors in decrees without reopening settled ownership rights.

title: Criminal Appeal and Criminal Revision Petition ,
explainer:
This case is about the murder of Faqir Muhammad, who was allegedly shot while walking with his son, the complainant, along a road in Quetta in 2010. The complainant claimed his father was shot by the appellant, Bahadur Khan, while a co-accused stood nearby with a motorcycle ready for escape. That co-accused was earlier tried, convicted, but then acquitted on appeal. Years later, after his arrest, Bahadur Khan was tried separately, convicted of murder by the trial court, and sentenced to life imprisonment plus compensation to the victim's family.

Bahadur Khan appealed his conviction, while the complainant separately asked the High Court to enhance the sentence. The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence, which relied mainly on the complainant's eyewitness account, statements the accused and co-accused allegedly made to police, and medical evidence.

The court found serious problems with this evidence. The so-called disclosure statements merely repeated facts already known from the initial police report, so they did not count as genuine new discoveries under the law of evidence. More importantly, the court doubted the complainant's claim of being present when the shooting happened, noting that the victim's body was actually brought to the hospital by a police officer, not by the complainant himself, which raised doubts about his story.

Because the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the court acquitted Bahadur Khan, overturning his conviction, and rejected the complainant's request to increase the sentence.

title: Ghulam Ali V. The State,
explainer:
This case was about who should get custody of a truck that had been intercepted carrying a large quantity of narcotics, after the driver who was initially convicted was ultimately acquitted on appeal.

Under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, vehicles used to transport drugs can be confiscated by the court. However, the law also says a vehicle cannot be confiscated unless it is proved that the owner knew it was being used to commit the crime. The trial court had ordered the truck confiscated, but the appellant, who claimed ownership (or co-ownership) of the truck, challenged that part of the judgment, arguing he was never prosecuted and no evidence showed he knew about the drug smuggling.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the appellant. It found that the case record was silent on whether the prosecution ever investigated or proved that the truck's owner had knowledge of the narcotics being transported. Since the burden of proving such knowledge lies on the prosecution, and that burden was not met, confiscation could not stand.

The court allowed the appeal, set aside the confiscation order, and sent the case back to the trial court to release the truck, subject to verifying actual ownership through the vehicle registration authority. This case matters because it reinforces that innocent vehicle owners should not automatically lose their property just because it was misused by someone else without their knowledge.

title: Syed Muhammad Ilyas V. Syed Muhammad Shafi and 7 others ,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running family property dispute between brothers over inheritance left by their late father. The appellant had earlier filed a suit for partition of family properties, which was dismissed after the defendants' attorney took a special religious oath explaining how the property had already been divided among the brothers. That dismissal was upheld on appeal. The appellant also tried, separately, to have an arbitrator's award on the same property partition made enforceable through the courts, but that attempt was dismissed too.

Years later, the appellant filed a fresh suit, this time asking for declaration, possession through partition, and cancellation of certain mutation entries, concerning essentially the same inherited properties. The trial court threw out this new suit, ruling that it was barred by the legal principles of res judicata (a matter already decided cannot be relitigated) and under Order II, Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code, which prevents a person from splitting a single cause of action into multiple lawsuits.

The High Court agreed. It held that since the earlier partition suit and the arbitration matter had already been conclusively decided, the appellant could not bring the same dispute back to court under a different label. The court emphasized the core principle that no one should be sued or vexed twice over the same cause of action, and litigation must eventually end. The appeal was dismissed.

This case reinforces important procedural rules preventing repeated litigation over settled disputes, promoting finality in legal proceedings.

title: Muhammad Imam-Ud-Din V. Mst. Saira Bano and 2 others ,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over dowry articles worth over 1.3 million rupees. A wife filed a suit against her husband for recovery of these items. Rather than contesting the suit on its merits, the husband offered a settlement: he proposed that if the wife took a special oath on the Holy Quran swearing that the articles had not been returned to her, he would pay the full amount claimed. The wife accepted this offer and took the oath in court. Based on this, the Family Court decided the case in her favor, and an appeal by the husband was also rejected.

The husband then challenged the decision in the High Court, arguing that the oath procedure violated Article 163 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order (Pakistan's law of evidence), since technically it should have been the plaintiff making the offer of oath, not the defendant, and that this law didn't even apply to Family Court cases.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It held that the Qanun-e-Shahadat law does not apply to Family Court proceedings, which can set their own procedures. However, nothing stops a Family Court from resolving a dispute through a special oath if the parties agree to it. Since the husband himself had proposed the oath and the wife had acted on it, he could not later back out of the agreement. The court applied the principle that one cannot accept the benefits of an arrangement and later reject it. This case clarifies that voluntary oath-based settlements in Family Court are valid and binding, even without strict adherence to evidence law.

title: Muhammad Usman and another V. Bibi Amina and others,
explainer:
This case is about a land dispute in Lasbella district, Balochistan. A plot of land was originally owned by two people (respondents Nos. 2 and 3). Someone claiming to act under a power of attorney sold the land through an unregistered sale agreement to Muhammad Usman, and mutation entries (official land record changes) were made in his favour, and later transferred again to two other petitioners. The original owners challenged these mutations before revenue authorities, who cancelled them and restored ownership to the original owners. This decision was upheld through multiple levels of appeal, eventually reaching the Board of Revenue, and then the Balochistan High Court.

The petitioners argued that only a civil court, not revenue officials, could resolve such disputed questions of fact and fraud, and that they were denied a chance to present evidence.

The High Court disagreed. It held that under the Balochistan Land Revenue Act, 1967, mutations based on unregistered documents (rather than inheritance, registered deeds, or court orders) are not valid unless proper identification and inquiry procedures are followed, which had not happened here. Since the error was obvious from the record itself, correcting it fell within the revenue authorities' own powers, not the civil court's. The court dismissed the petition, meaning the land stayed with the original owners, while noting that if the petitioners wanted to claim title, they would need to approach a civil court instead.

This case matters because it clarifies when revenue authorities, rather than civil courts, can correct land records, especially regarding unregistered property transfers.

title: Naseer Ahmed and another V. Ghafoor Khan,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a landlord-tenant dispute under the Balochistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959. The landlord (respondent) sought to evict a tenant and his son from a shop, claiming the tenant had stopped paying rent since 2012 and that he genuinely needed the shop for his own son's business. The tenant argued he had paid a large sum as "pagri" (a form of premium or key money) when renting the shop, and that the landlord hadn't come to collect rent, so he shouldn't be blamed for non-payment.

The Rent Controller had already ruled in the landlord's favor, ordering eviction. The tenant appealed, but the High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the eviction order.

The court held that tenants have a legal duty to pay rent proactively - if a landlord refuses or fails to collect rent, the tenant must send it by money order or deposit it with the court, rather than simply waiting. The law does not require landlords to chase down tenants for payment. The court also found that the tenant could not prove the pagri payment with any documents, and that paying pagri does not protect a tenant from eviction when the landlord genuinely needs the property. The landlord had provided sufficient evidence of his son's real need for the shop.

This case clarifies tenants' ongoing responsibility to pay rent and confirms that informal payments like pagri don't override a landlord's legitimate right to reclaim property for personal use.

title: Eduard Bilyayev through Attorney and 4 others V. M.V. "Figaro" (Ex-Free Goddess) through Messrs Commercial Metal,
explainer:
This case involved foreign sailors who worked on the vessel M.V. "Figaro" but said they were never paid their full wages. They sued in the Balochistan High Court's admiralty jurisdiction, seeking to recover outstanding salaries, arguing the company operating the ship was its beneficial owner and should pay what was owed. However, by the time the case reached court, the ship had already been sold to a new buyer, Messrs Commercial Metal, through a bill of sale showing the vessel was purchased free of all encumbrances via a leasing company. The new owner asked the trial court to throw out the lawsuit, and the single judge agreed, rejecting the plaint.

On appeal, the High Court explained the legal concept of "action in rem," which allows a claim to be brought directly against a ship (rather than its owners) when a maritime lien exists, such as unpaid wages. Normally this right travels with the ship until the vessel is destroyed. But the law also requires certain conditions to be met before such a claim can be enforced against a ship that has changed hands. Since the sale document was never specifically challenged when the suit was filed, and because the ship had since been demolished, the court found those conditions were not satisfied.

The High Court dismissed the appeals, upholding rejection of the sailors' claims. The case highlights how maritime wage claims can be extinguished once a ship is validly sold and later destroyed, limiting workers' ability to recover unpaid dues through admiralty action.

title: Muhammad Saddiq and another V. Ghulam Sarwar and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute over a land sale agreement from 2009. Earlier, the High Court had ruled that the buyer (decree holder) could get the land transferred to his name, but only if he paid the remaining sale price of over Rs. 32 lakh within two months, otherwise the agreement would automatically stand cancelled.

The sellers (judgment debtors) later argued in execution proceedings that since the buyer failed to pay within the two-month deadline, the agreement had lapsed and he could no longer enforce the decree. The case went through multiple rounds, including a Supreme Court order asking the executing court to determine whether payment had actually been offered on time.

The High Court found that the buyer had repeatedly tried to pay through cheques on several occasions, but the payments could not go through either because the sellers were absent or unwilling to accept them, or because court proceedings were stayed. The court also held that delays caused by the court's own scheduling, summer vacations, or litigation should not be held against the buyer, since the court itself had failed to direct him to deposit the money directly into the court's account.

The High Court ruled that the buyer should not suffer because of these external delays and ordered him to deposit the balance sale amount within 15 days, allowing the transaction to proceed. The case highlights that genuine, repeated attempts to comply with a court decree count even if technical deadlines slip due to circumstances beyond a party's control.

title: Almas Mandokhail V. Ainuddin and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over ownership of a house in Quetta after the original owner died and the property passed to his children as legal heirs. One of the heirs, Mouzam Iqbal, allegedly sold his share through an unregistered sale agreement to another man, Tariq Mehmood, who allegedly sold it again through another unregistered agreement to the petitioner's father. Later, the father reportedly gave the house to the petitioner through an affidavit. Separately, the other legal heirs sold the house through proper mutation to a different buyer, Ainuddin. The petitioner sued for declaration of ownership, cancellation of that mutation, and an injunction, relying on the chain of unregistered sale agreements.

The trial court ruled in the petitioner's favor, but the appellate court reversed this and dismissed the suit. The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision and dismissed the petitioner's revision.

The court explained that under the Registration Act and the Transfer of Property Act, any document transferring ownership of immovable property worth more than a certain value must be registered. An unregistered sale agreement does not transfer ownership or create title in the property; it only gives a right to seek enforcement of the agreement through a court (specific performance). Since the petitioner's claim rested entirely on unregistered agreements, it could not establish legal ownership, making the suit for declaration unsustainable.

This case reinforces an important principle in property law: informal or unregistered sale agreements, even with possession or partial payment, do not make someone the legal owner of property. Only

title: Dr. Muhammad Akbar V. Mst. Safia Kakar and 9 others,
explainer:
This case arose from a family property dispute in Balochistan. A man had married twice; his children from both marriages, along with other relatives, became entangled in a lawsuit over inherited property after his death in 1991. The plaintiffs (children from the second wife) sued for declaration, partition of property, mesne profits (compensation for use of property), and a permanent injunction, targeting a doctor (the petitioner, also from the second wife) and other relatives. The disputed property included over 200 acres of agricultural land in Pishin, allegedly in the possession of children from the first wife, as well as a separate plot later sold to outside buyers.

During trial, the judge ordered that the children of the first wife and the buyers of the sold land be added as defendants, since the case involved property claims affecting them too. The doctor challenged this, arguing a 1996 family settlement had already divided the properties, so these people had no stake in the case.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that since the plaintiffs sought partition of the Pishin property, the first wife's children were "necessary parties" without whom the court could not grant an effective, complete decision. Citing Supreme Court precedent, the court ruled that although technically a case cannot be thrown out merely for missing parties, if a truly necessary party is left out, the suit cannot succeed until they are included. The petition was dismissed, upholding the trial court's order to add these parties.

title: Malik & Company through Proprietor V. Chairman Pakistan Tobacco Board, Peshawar and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a government cess (tax) collection contract. Malik & Company won a bid to collect cess on Rustica Tobacco in Balochistan for 2002, agreeing to pay Rs. 89 lakh to the Pakistan Tobacco Board in installments. A dispute arose when the Board first exempted certain tobacco by-products from the cess, then withdrew that exemption and demanded the contractor pay outstanding installments. The contractor invoked the arbitration clause in the contract instead of paying, seeking relief through arbitration.

After a long legal history involving multiple arbitration awards, court challenges, and a prior High Court order sending the matter back for fresh arbitration, the Chairman of the Pakistan Tobacco Board, acting as sole arbitrator, issued a new award in 2015. Lower courts upheld this award as binding, and the contractor's appeal was dismissed.

The Balochistan High Court examined whether this arbitration award should be overturned. It held that the arbitrator had properly considered the contractor's losses from the exemption issue, and that courts should not substitute their own interpretation for an arbitrator's decision when reasonable people could disagree about it. Since the grounds for setting aside an award are limited, and no clear misconduct or error was shown, the High Court refused to interfere and dismissed the petition.

This case illustrates the limited scope courts have to review arbitration awards, reinforcing that arbitration decisions are generally final unless clear legal grounds for interference exist.

title: Abdul Raziq V. Muhammad Rafiq and others,
explainer:
This case is about a property pre-emption dispute from Quetta, Balochistan. Under pre-emption law, a person claiming the right to buy adjoining property must make a timely declaration called talb-i-muwathibat, and the exact date, time, and place of this declaration are legally crucial.

The plaintiff, Abdul Raziq, had stated in his plaint that he learned about the sale and made his declaration at 12:26 AM at the tehsil office. The buyers pointed out in their written statement that this timing was implausible, since a patwari would not be present at a government office at that hour. After this objection was raised, the plaintiff applied to correct AM to PM, claiming it was an accidental typing error. The trial court allowed the correction, but on revision, the Additional District Judge reversed this, and later also rejected the plaintiff's attempt to reopen that decision.

The High Court upheld the rejection of the correction. It ruled that even an interim order can be treated as a final "case decided" under the law if it affects the merits of the case, so revision was properly available. It also held that because the correction was sought only after the defendants specifically challenged the timing, and because it would change the fundamental character of the suit and erase the defense already raised, it was not a genuine clerical fix but an attempt to manipulate the case. The petition was dismissed, reaffirming that precise time details in pre-emption claims cannot be casually altered once challenged.

title: Mai Mithan and 67 others V. Banda-E-Ali and 94 others,
explainer:
This case was about a property dispute in Balochistan. A group of people filed a civil suit asking a court to cancel certain revenue entries (land records) and to declare their rights over disputed land, along with seeking a permanent injunction. The people being sued had initially tried to get the case thrown out early using a procedural rule (Order VII, Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code), arguing the suit was filed too late and had no valid legal basis. The trial court (Qazi Bhag) rejected that request, saying the issue of limitation needed to be decided only after evidence was presented. However, on appeal, the Majlis-e-Shoora overturned that decision and dismissed the plaintiffs' case outright, ruling it was filed way too late.

The plaintiffs then challenged that dismissal before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that whether their suit was time-barred was a mixed question of fact and law that needed a full trial with evidence, not an early dismissal.

The High Court disagreed with the plaintiffs. It explained that when deciding such early dismissal applications, courts only look at what is written in the plaint itself, assuming it to be true. Here, the plaintiffs' own pleadings showed that their predecessor had known about the disputed land entries for 48 years but never challenged them. Because of this long, unexplained delay, the court held the suit was clearly barred by limitation just from reading the plaint, so no trial was needed. The petition was dismissed, reaffirming that courts can and should screen out clearly time-barred or baseless suits

title: Bahadur Khan V. Karim Gul and 4 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a land dispute from Quetta, Balochistan. A buyer (respondent No.1) sued, claiming he had purchased a plot of land partly from Bahadur Khan (the petitioner) through an attorney (respondent No.2), who he said held power of attorney to sell Khan's share. The buyer claimed he paid most of the price and would pay the rest at the time of mutation (official transfer of ownership records). Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled in the buyer's favor and ordered the land transferred to him.

Bahadur Khan challenged this in the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the buyer never actually produced the written sale agreement or the power of attorney he relied on, and that the case was instead decided based on oral testimony that went beyond what had been stated in the original pleadings.

The High Court agreed with Khan. It held that under the Qanun-e-Shahadat (Pakistan's law of evidence), agreements to sell immovable property and powers of attorney involving property rights must be properly attested by witnesses and proved through those witnesses in court. Since neither document was produced or proved, and the buyer's own testimony contradicted his written claims, the lower courts' decisions were legally flawed. The High Court set aside the earlier judgments and dismissed the suit, emphasizing that such important property documents cannot simply be assumed or proved through inconsistent oral statements.

title: Commissioner Inland Revenue Zone-I, Regional Tax Office, Quetta V. M/s. Saindak Metals Ltd. Quetta, Tax Year 2006,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over whether the tax authorities could amend an income tax assessment years after the original return was filed, based on a change in the law governing time limits.

Saindak Metals Ltd, a government-owned company, filed its tax return for the 2006 tax year in December 2006, declaring a loss. This was treated as a deemed assessment. In June 2012, the tax department issued an amended assessment creating a substantial tax demand of over Rs. 404 million, arguing the original assessment was erroneous and harmful to revenue. The company successfully appealed to the Appellate Tribunal, which ruled the 2012 amendment was issued too late and was therefore invalid.

The key legal question was about limitation periods. Originally, the law gave tax authorities five years from the date an assessment was issued to amend it. A 2009 amendment changed this slightly, making the five-year period run from the end of the financial year in which the assessment was issued, rather than from the exact issuance date. The tax department argued this amendment should apply retrospectively to extend their deadline. The company argued the amendment could only apply going forward.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the company. It held that once a limitation period begins running under old law, it becomes a "closed transaction" for the taxpayer, and changes affecting such substantive rights cannot be applied backward unless the law clearly says so. Since the five-year deadline (calculated under the original law) had already expired before the 2012 amendment order, it was time-barred. The appeal by tax authorities was dismissed, reinforcing that

title: Muhammad Amin and others V. Haji Abdul Wahid and others,

This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves a long-running dispute over land that had already been decided in favour of the respondents, Haji Abdul Wahid and others, in earlier court proceedings dating back to 2003 and 2015. The petitioners, led by Muhammad Amin, repeatedly tried to block enforcement by filing an application to set aside the judgment, then a separate civil suit, then objections during execution, and then a challenge against orders freezing official bank accounts to realize the decree. Each of these attempts had already been rejected by the trial court, the appellate forum, or the High Court itself in earlier rounds.

The High Court held that under the Civil Procedure Code, once a court decree is final, questions about rights or claims over the property must be raised and settled within the execution proceedings themselves, not through fresh separate lawsuits. Since the petitioner's objections had already been heard and rejected multiple times, and his separate suit had also failed, there was no legal basis to interfere again. The court ruled that the government officials, as judgment debtors, could not avoid their legal obligation to satisfy the decree. Both petitions were dismissed, meaning the respondents could proceed with enforcing their decree.

title: Innayatullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Inayatullah, accused of storming a house with armed companions and shooting several people, killing two and injuring three others. The motive was a family dispute over marriage. During trial, the victims families and injured persons filed a compromise with the accused, and the trial court acquitted him of murder and related charges but still convicted him separately under a law dealing with offences classified as fasad fil ard, meaning crimes considered a serious disturbance to public peace, sentencing him to fourteen years in prison plus payment of compensation.

Both sides appealed. The accused wanted his conviction overturned despite the compromise, while the father of one victim argued the compromise itself was invalid because it had been obtained through pressure, coercion, and ongoing threats from the accused, who was allegedly a dangerous habitual criminal controlling the area through fear.

The Balochistan High Court agreed that something was wrong. It held that whenever there is a possibility that a compromise was not genuine but forced through intimidation, courts must carefully examine its authenticity, including observing the accused's conduct and background. Since the trial court failed to do this, the judgment was flawed. The High Court dismissed the accused's appeal, accepted the father's appeal, set aside the trial court's judgment, and sent the case back for a fresh trial with full opportunity for evidence from both sides.

title: Deputy Commissioner/Collector, Quetta and others V. Habib-Ur-Rehman and others,
explainer:
This case is about how much compensation the government must pay when it forcibly acquires private land for a public project. The Deputy Commissioner of Quetta acquired land from several owners to widen Joint Road from Dukani Baba Chowk to Chaman Phattak. The government's award fixed compensation at Rs.700 to Rs.800 per square foot. The landowners were unhappy and challenged this before a Referee Court (District and Sessions Judges), which raised the compensation significantly, up to Rs.7000 per square foot for land and Rs.200 per square foot for construction, plus additional costs. The Deputy Commissioner and other government officials then appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing the lower courts relied only on witnesses' verbal statements without proper documentary proof of market value.

The High Court disagreed. It explained that under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, compensation must reflect the true market value of the land at the time of acquisition, considering factors like nearby land sales, the property's development potential, and past transactions. Since the land was in a busy urban part of Quetta and similar nearby land had earlier fetched much higher prices in a comparable acquisition, and since the landowners had presented documentary evidence that the government failed to rebut, the court upheld the Referee Court's decision. The appeals were dismissed.

This case matters because it reinforces that citizens whose land is taken for public projects are entitled to fair, evidence-based compensation reflecting real market value, not arbitrary government rates.

title: Khrum Shezad Zafar and 2 others V. Razia Begum and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a woman, Razia Begum, who filed a lawsuit seeking two things: cancellation of a gift mutation through which she had transferred property to her nephews, and restoration of her possession over two rooms she claimed to have built on that property, from which she said she was forcibly and unlawfully dispossessed. The defendants (her nephews) asked the trial court to reject the entire plaint, arguing it disclosed no valid cause of action since the gift and mutation were admitted facts. The trial court agreed and rejected the plaint outright. On appeal, the District Judge partly disagreed, ruling that while the cancellation claim might be weak, the second claim about forcible dispossession from the rooms deserved to be heard on evidence, and sent that part of the case back for trial.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It held that when deciding whether to reject a plaint, courts must look only at the plaint's averments, and each case must be judged on its own facts. Since the plaintiff's claim about forcible dispossession from the rooms raised a genuine factual dispute requiring evidence, that portion of the suit could not be dismissed at the outset. Importantly, the court ruled that a plaint cannot be partially rejected—if one part of a suit raises a valid triable issue, the whole application for rejection must fail on that count. The revision petition was dismissed, allowing the dispossession claim to proceed to trial.

title: Sheikh Ameen-Ur-Rasheed V. Shaikh Mamon Ur Rasheed and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over an ancestral house in Quetta among siblings who were declared co-owners by a trial court, which ordered the brother in possession to either buy out his siblings' shares or let the house be sold and proceeds divided. During execution of this decree, the court sent the property to public auction, and an outside bidder won with the highest offer. However, the brother who had possession of the house had also expressed willingness to buy it, and he objected to the auction process, arguing it violated legal procedure and that he was not properly notified or heard.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with him. It found multiple serious flaws in the auction: no proper notice was given to the co-owners, no reserve price was fixed as required by law, the sale proclamation wasn't displayed on the court notice board, and crucially, the winning bidder failed to deposit the remaining 75% of the purchase price within the legally mandated 15 days. Since the sale was never formally confirmed and the payment rules weren't followed, the court ruled the entire auction was invalid under the Civil Procedure Code's rules governing execution sales.

The High Court set aside the lower courts' orders and ruled in favor of the brother in possession, allowing him to purchase the house himself provided he deposits the full sale amount plus a required 5% penalty. This case underscores that courts must strictly follow procedural safeguards in auction sales to protect co-owners' rights and ensure fairness.

title: Bandenawaz (Private) Limited through Director V. Federation of Pakistan through Deputy Director Ministry of Defence and others,
explainer:
This case involves a boundary dispute between two neighbouring landowners in Hub, Balochistan, whose properties were affected by the construction of a government bypass road. Each side accused the other of encroaching on their land and filed separate civil suits seeking declarations that the other party was a trespasser, along with directions for the government to survey and demarcate the disputed property. The trial court combined both suits but then returned the plaints, ruling that it had no jurisdiction to hear the matter because such disputes fall under the Balochistan Land Revenue Act, which assigns demarcation issues to Revenue Authorities rather than civil courts.

The appellant challenged this before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It explained that neither party disputed actual ownership as recorded in revenue records; the real issue was about where the boundary line fell after road construction, which is fundamentally a demarcation question. Under the law, civil courts cannot decide demarcation disputes unless the Revenue Authorities have already carried out an official demarcation. Since no such demarcation had occurred, and neither party had approached the Revenue Officer first, the proper venue was the revenue system, not the civil court. The court also clarified that while courts can declare pre-existing rights, they cannot create new rights, and demarcation is not something a civil court can order from scratch.

The appeal was dismissed. This ruling reinforces the principle that boundary and encroachment disputes over agricultural land must first go through revenue authorities, with civil courts stepping in only after demarcation

title: Dr. Rashid Tarin V. The Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary, Civil Secretariat, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns the appointment of the Chief Executive Officer of the People's Primary Health Initiative Balochistan (PPHI-B), a public sector company that manages basic health units in rural Balochistan under the Companies Act, 2017. The petitioner, a member of the company's Board of Directors, challenged the government's notification appointing a new CEO, arguing that the proper legal procedure and eligibility criteria had not been followed.

The government first argued that the petitioner had no standing to bring the case. The Balochistan High Court rejected this, holding that when a petition seeks a "writ of quo warranto" (challenging someone's authority to hold a public office), the person raising the challenge does not need to be personally aggrieved.

On the merits, the court examined the Companies Act 2017, the Public Sector Companies (Corporate Governance) Rules 2013, SECP guidelines, and the company's own Articles of Association. These required the Board to evaluate candidates, recommend at least three names to the government, and only then have the government's chosen nominee formally appointed by the Board. The court found that this required process had not been properly followed in appointing the private respondent as CEO.

As a result, the court struck down the appointment notification and ordered the authorities to conduct a fresh, merit-based selection process in accordance with the law. The ruling reinforces that appointments to public sector company leadership must strictly follow prescribed legal procedures, not just government preference.

title: Syed Matiullah Agha V. Haji Muhammad Hussain alias Haji Muhammad Hassan,
explainer:
This case is about a money dispute over cheques between two individuals in Quetta. The respondent claimed he had given Rs. 80 lac to the appellant, who allegedly repaid part of it and issued several cheques for the remaining amount. When these cheques were dishonored, the respondent filed a summary suit for recovery of over Rs. 77 lac, and the trial court decreed the full amount in his favor.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence closely. It found that out of nine cheques claimed, only two (worth Rs. 5 lac each, totaling Rs. 10 lac) had actually been presented to the bank and dishonored, with proper evidence including bank witness testimony. The remaining seven cheques were never shown to have been presented to the bank at all—they were simply produced by the plaintiff himself during his court statement.

The court explained that under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, presenting a cheque to the bank is a mandatory legal requirement before a person can sue on it. Without presentment, no right to recover money arises, and such a suit cannot be maintained under the summary procedure used here.

As a result, the High Court set aside the decree regarding the seven cheques and dismissed that part of the suit, while upholding the decree for the two properly proven cheques (Rs. 10 lac). The appeal was thus partly allowed, reinforcing that mere production of a cheque in court is not enough—proper presentment to the bank is essential to claim payment.

title: Syed Matiullah Agha V. Haji Muhammad Hussain alias Haji Muhammad Hassan,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over money allegedly owed through post-dated cheques. The respondent (plaintiff) claimed he had given Rs. 80,00,000 to the appellant in 2016, of which only a small amount was repaid, and that the appellant issued cheques to cover the remaining balance. When those cheques bounced, the respondent filed a summary suit for recovery of Rs. 77,39,300 under Order XXXVII of the Civil Procedure Code, a fast-track procedure typically used for cheque and negotiable instrument cases. The trial court had ruled in the respondent's favor and decreed the full suit.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence closely. It found that out of nine cheques relied upon, the respondent could only prove, through a bank representative, that two cheques (worth Rs. 5 lakh each) had actually bounced and were properly presented to the bank. For the remaining seven cheques, there was no evidence that they had ever been formally presented to the bank branch for payment. The court held that presentment of a cheque to the bank is a mandatory legal requirement before a payee can sue the drawer, especially under the summary procedure of Order XXXVII. Since this wasn't proven for seven cheques, the suit couldn't succeed on those.

The court therefore partly allowed the appeal, upholding the trial court's decision only for the two cheques that were properly proven, while rejecting recovery based on the other seven. This case reinforces that proper proof of presentment is essential in cheque-based recovery

title: Ameer Muhammad and another V. State,
explainer:
This case involved a violent land dispute between two tribes, Shamozai and Badezai, in Quetta that ended in death and injuries. During the confrontation, gunfire was exchanged between both sides. Muhammad Farooq of the Badezai tribe was killed, and members of both groups were injured. Police registered separate cases based on each side's version, and the trial court proceeded with the Badezai group's version.

The trial court convicted Ameer Muhammad of murder under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, sentencing him to life imprisonment, while his co-accused Jan Muhammad was convicted for attempted murder and given a prison term. Both men appealed.

The defense argued that the complainant's side had actually come armed to the appellants' property, tried to occupy their land, and initiated the firing, causing serious injuries to the appellants themselves. They claimed this was a case of self-defense and that the trial court failed to properly assess who was the aggressor.

The High Court examined the evidence, including circumstantial details like property documents and the sequence of events, and concluded that the complainant party had approached the disputed land and stopped Appellant No. 1 from construction, which triggered mutual firing. Because of this, the court found the killing did not amount to the more serious offense under Section 302(b), but instead fell under Section 302(c), a lesser category of culpable homicide. The appeal was partly allowed, reducing the conviction and sentence accordingly. This case highlights how courts weigh conflicting versions of events and circumstantial

title: Nafeesa Rehman V. The Election Tribunal Balochistan, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a woman who tried to contest for a reserved seat for women in the 2024 general elections but missed the deadline for filing her nomination papers.

The Election Commission of Pakistan had set 24 December 2023 as the cut-off date for submitting nomination papers. The petitioner, Nafeesa Rehman, filed her application six days late, on 30 December 2023, asking the Returning Officer for permission to submit her papers anyway. Her request was rejected. She then challenged this rejection through several rounds of litigation, including two earlier constitutional petitions and an appeal to the Election Tribunal, all of which went against her. She finally approached the Balochistan High Court, arguing she had been denied a fair opportunity and that the failure was due to the Returning Officer not properly displaying the required priority list, not her own fault.

The High Court dismissed her petition. It held that Section 104 of the Elections Act, 2017 lays down a strict procedure and timeline for filing nomination papers for reserved seats, and this must be followed exactly as prescribed. Since she had missed the deadline, her later application could not be entertained. The Court also emphasized that election processes are time-bound and, once started, cannot be interrupted by courts at intermediate stages; complaints about the process must instead go through the proper tribunal at the right time. This case reinforces that strict compliance with election deadlines is essential and courts will not relax them for individual candidates.

title: Mehmood Khan Achakzai V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case is about whether a criminal case (FIR) filed against Mehmood Khan Achakzai, a sitting National Assembly member and political party leader, should be cancelled. The complainant had alleged that unnamed family members of the petitioner had illegally occupied a government residential plot, and authorities recovered possession in March 2024. However, the FIR was registered five years after the original complaint was made to land authorities, and it did not even name the specific family members supposedly involved, let alone accuse the petitioner directly.

The Balochistan High Court examined the relevant criminal trespass laws and found that the property was merely a residential plot, not a "house," so charges of house-trespass did not apply. It also found that the FIR failed to show any intent by the petitioner to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy the person in possession of the property, which is required to prove criminal trespass. Since no evidence supported these essential elements, and the case appeared to be based on vague allegations with an unexplained five-year delay, the court ruled that continuing the trial would be pointless and an abuse of court process.

The court quashed the FIR and declared the resulting proceedings against the petitioner unlawful. This case matters because it reinforces that courts can step in early to stop unfounded criminal cases from proceeding, protecting individuals from harassment through weak or belated prosecutions, especially when legal elements of the alleged crime are clearly missing.

title: Collector, Collectorate of Customs (Enforcement), Khuzdar, Camp Office at Customs House, Gaddani V. Muhammad Ali and another,
explainer:
This case involved a legal dispute over whether a truck used to transport smuggled goods should be permanently confiscated or could be released back to its owner after paying a fine.

Customs officials in Khuzdar intercepted a truck carrying plastic shopper bags hidden in a cavity near the front of its container, in violation of customs and import control laws. The Customs Collectorate confiscated the vehicle outright, arguing the goods were hidden in a specially designed secret compartment, which under customs rules (SRO 499(I)/2009) would bar release of the vehicle even on payment of a fine. However, the Customs Appellate Tribunal disagreed and ordered the vehicle released upon payment of a 20% redemption fine, finding that the vehicle did not actually have a false or secret cavity.

The Collectorate challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court. The Court dismissed the challenge, holding that "liable to confiscation" under the Customs Act does not automatically mean a vehicle "must be confiscated" — the law also allows for fines instead of outright confiscation, unless specific goods are exempted by the tax authorities. The Court also noted that the official notice against the owner did not clearly describe a "secret" cavity, and the Tribunal's factual finding on this point could not be re-examined by the High Court in this type of case.

This ruling clarifies that customs authorities cannot automatically seize vehicles without properly proving hidden compartments, protecting vehicle owners from overly harsh confiscation.

title: Muhammad Ikhlas V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Ikhlas, who was convicted for allegedly attacking and injuring a complainant and his companion during a fight, facing charges including attempted murder and rioting under the Pakistan Penal Code. He appealed his conviction to the Balochistan High Court.

The court overturned the conviction, finding multiple serious problems with the prosecution's case. First, there was an unexplained ten-hour delay in filing the police report (FIR), even though the police station was only about a mile and a half from the crime scene. The court noted such delays often allow time for complainants to falsely add names to a case, and indeed the accused's brothers had been named but were acquitted at trial. Second, medical evidence contradicted witness testimony about how and when injuries occurred. Third, there was an unexplained one-day delay in recording the injured witness's statement, which courts treat as seriously undermining reliability. Fourth, the key eyewitness behaved unnaturally—claiming to have witnessed the attack yet not taking the injured for treatment or promptly reporting the crime, and his account didn't match hospital records. Fifth, this witness had no credible reason to be present at the scene. Finally, the prosecution failed to produce another witness without explanation, which the court said should be held against it.

Given these cumulative doubts, the court ruled the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant, reinforcing that shaky evidence and unexplained delays can be fatal to criminal cases.

title: Muhammad Akber V. The Secretary, Education Government of Balochistan and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved a job dispute in the Balochistan Education Department. The petitioner, Muhammad Akber, held a religious qualification called Shahadat-ul-Aalia (considered equivalent to a B.A.), along with a teaching certificate and intermediate qualification. He applied for two advertised posts, Junior Arabic Teacher and Mo'alam-ul-Quran, took the NTS test, and scored highest among applicants for both positions, placing first on the merit lists.

Despite this, the department refused to issue him an appointment letter, ruling that his academic degrees did not meet the specific qualification requirements for these posts. Instead, appointment letters were given to two other candidates who had scored lower marks. The petitioner challenged this decision, arguing it violated merit and was discriminatory, but his internal appeal was also rejected on the same grounds.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed his petition. It held that the department had not acted illegally, since the competent authority, after review, had determined his degree was invalid for these specific posts, a decision applied uniformly to all candidates without discrimination. The court emphasized that under Article 199 of the Constitution, it cannot interfere in policy matters or resolve factual disputes about degree validity, which require detailed investigation and evidence rather than constitutional review. Since no fundamental right was violated, the petition was dismissed.

This case illustrates the limited scope of judicial review over administrative and policy decisions, even when a candidate has topped a merit list.
