title: Mian Khan V. Inspector General Police Balochistan and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a police constable, Mian Khan, whose employment was dismissed in 2014. He appealed to the Balochistan Service Tribunal, which ruled in his favor, but nearly two years passed without the police department implementing that decision. Frustrated by the delay, he approached the Balochistan High Court under Article 199 of the Constitution, asking it to order the authorities to reinstate him and carry out the Tribunal's judgment.

The High Court dismissed the petition, not because it disagreed with the merits, but because it found this was not the right legal avenue. The court explained that under the Balochistan Service Tribunal Act, 1974, the Service Tribunal itself is treated as a civil court when deciding appeals, and therefore has all the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, including the power to enforce its own judgments. This means an employee seeking to enforce a Tribunal ruling should go back to the Tribunal to have it executed, rather than filing a fresh constitutional petition in the High Court.

The judgment matters because it clarifies the proper channel for enforcing Service Tribunal decisions, discourages unnecessary litigation in the High Court, and prevents the High Court from being turned into an "executing court" for Tribunal orders. It reinforces that Tribunals must develop their own mechanisms to ensure compliance with their rulings, protecting the efficiency of the service dispute resolution system.

title: Jalal Khan V. Abdul Rauf and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of four men accused of murdering a teenage boy, Zafarullah, whose throat had been cut near a watercourse in Balochistan in September 2014. When the crime was first reported, the killers were unknown, and the FIR named no suspects. Eleven months later, the boy's father suddenly gave a new statement naming the respondents as the killers, based on two "eyewitnesses" who claimed to have seen the murder happen but had never come forward before.

The trial court acquitted the accused, and the father appealed. The Balochistan High Court upheld the acquittal, finding the prosecution's case deeply suspicious. The court noted that genuine eyewitnesses would not stay silent for eleven months, especially when they claimed to be relatives of the victim, did nothing to stop the attack, never reported it, and did not even help move the body to a hospital. This unnatural, unexplained delay suggested the witnesses had been "planted" later after deliberation, rather than being truthful accounts of what actually happened.

The court reaffirmed a basic principle of criminal law: the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and any doubt must benefit the accused. Since the evidence here was unreliable and uncorroborated, the doubt could not be resolved against the accused. This case illustrates how courts scrutinize delayed evidence and witness credibility, protecting individuals from convictions based on suspicious, after-the-fact testimony.

title: Ahmed Khan Floraid Company through Owner V. Secretary Mines & Minerals, Government of Balochistan and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over mining rights in Balochistan. The petitioner, Ahmed Khan Floraid Company, wanted the government to issue him a No Objection Certificate (NOC) so he could obtain a prospecting license to mine fluorite in a particular area. He claimed he was qualified and entitled to the NOC, and that a rival company (Respondent No. 3) had obtained its own mining rights through fake and tampered documents, which had already been cancelled through earlier legal proceedings, yet that company was still illegally mining in the area.

The petitioner asked the High Court to declare him deserving of the NOC, to order the government to issue it to him, and to stop the rival company's ongoing mining activity.

The court did not rule on the merits of these claims. Instead, it dismissed the petition on procedural grounds, finding that the petitioner had not exhausted the alternate remedies available to him. Specifically, there were two administrative forums, the Secretary of Mines and Minerals and another department, where he could have sought redress but had not done so. The court explained that a constitutional petition can only be filed when no other effective remedy exists, citing Article 212(2) of the Constitution, which limits courts from intervening in matters that fall under the jurisdiction of administrative tribunals.

The petition was dismissed, but the petitioner was left free to pursue his grievance through the proper administrative channels first.

This case involved a mining business, Ahmed Khan Floraid Company, which had applied for a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the Balochistan government's Mines and Minerals department in order to seek a prospecting license for mining fluorite in an area in Loralai. The petitioner claimed the NOC had been issued to him but the authorities failed to take further action on it, while a rival party (respondent No. 3) was allegedly continuing illegal mining despite having his own allotment and work orders cancelled earlier due to fraud and tampered documents. Frustrated by the inaction, the petitioner approached the Balochistan High Court directly, asking it to declare him entitled to the NOC, expose the rival's fraud, and stop the illegal mining.

The High Court did not examine these claims on their merits. Instead, it held that the petition was not "maintainable," meaning it should not have been filed in this form at all. The court found that alternate remedies existed - the petitioner could have approached the Secretary of Mines and Minerals or other departmental authorities to resolve his grievance before rushing to court. Under Pakistani law, courts can only be approached directly through a constitutional petition when no other effective remedy is available. Since such remedies existed here, the petition was dismissed, though the petitioner was allowed to pursue his complaint through the proper administrative channels.

This case highlights an important principle: courts generally expect parties to exhaust available administrative remedies before seeking judicial intervention.

title: Liaqat Ali and 2 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved three men, Liaqat Ali and two others, who were convicted by a trial court in Jaffarabad, Balochistan, for attempted murder and causing injuries during an alleged incident of cattle theft. The prosecution claimed that around 4:30 a.m., the accused came to steal two bullocks from the complainant's home, and when resisted, opened fire, injuring the complainant and his son. Police later claimed to have arrested the accused after a thirty-minute encounter.

The Balochistan High Court, however, found the prosecution's case riddled with doubts. The FIR named the accused with full parentage despite the incident occurring in darkness, yet no proof was offered that there was adequate light to identify them. Although both sides allegedly exchanged fire for half an hour, no one was hurt and no property damaged, raising suspicion about the encounter story. There were also contradictions between witnesses about hospital visits and the filing of the FIR, a mismatch between the injured person named in police records and the medical certificate produced in court, and an unexplained three-month delay in sending weapons and shells for forensic examination.

Given these serious inconsistencies, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. It acquitted all three appellants, setting aside their convictions and sentences.

title: Allah Dina V. The State ,
explainer:
This case involved Allah Dina, who had been convicted and sentenced for murdering a man and injuring another during a shooting incident in 2012. His conviction had already been upheld on appeal. After that, the parties reached a compromise, and Allah Dina asked the trial court to accept it and acquit him under the law allowing victims' heirs to pardon an offender.

The trial court refused to accept the compromise, finding that material facts had been hidden. On revision, the Balochistan High Court agreed with that decision and dismissed the petition.

The court found serious problems with the compromise. The deceased had six legal heirs, but the compromise was signed only by the father, a brother (who was not actually a legal heir), and a minor son around 14-15 years old, too young to give valid consent. Two other heirs, a wife and daughter, were claimed to have died, but their death certificates had been issued based merely on information given by the deceased's brother, not properly verified. Another surviving wife was said to have been divorced before the deceased's death, but no official divorce record from the Union Council was produced. It also emerged that this "divorced" wife was the convict's own sister, a fact deliberately concealed.

The court held that anyone seeking judicial relief must approach with clean hands, and that courts, as protectors of all heirs' rights, cannot ignore suppressed facts or irregularities. The petition was dismissed, keeping the conviction intact.

title: Shafi Muhammad and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court concerned a violent dispute over an extortion demand. According to the prosecution, the accused had demanded Rs.400,000 from the complainant in exchange for allowing renovation work on a canal to continue, threatening to stop the work otherwise. When the complainant refused to pay, the accused opened fire the next day, killing his two sons and injuring his driver. The trial court convicted several appellants of murder, attempted murder, and rioting, sentencing them to life imprisonment plus fines, five years for attempted murder, and two years for rioting.

On appeal, the defense argued that the eyewitnesses were closely related to the victims and therefore biased, that there were contradictions between the medical and eyewitness evidence, and that no weapons were recovered from the accused.

The High Court rejected these arguments and upheld the convictions. It held that testimony from relatives can still be relied upon if it is consistent, credible, and supported by medical and circumstantial evidence. The court found the witnesses' accounts firm and unshaken, matching the medical evidence, and noted that failure to recover the weapons did not clear the accused, especially since they had fled and were later arrested elsewhere. The court concluded the prosecution had built a complete and trustworthy chain of evidence, and dismissed the appeal, affirming that the accused did not deserve leniency for such a serious crime.

title: Regional Election Commissioner, Naseerabad at Dera Murad Jamali V. Tariq Magsi,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by the Regional Election Commissioner, Naseerabad, against the acquittal of Tariq Magsi, who had been accused of submitting forged educational degrees along with his nomination papers when he successfully contested the 2013 General Election. A complaint was filed alleging violations of the Representation of the People Act and provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code relating to false statements and using forged documents as genuine. During the trial, the respondent applied for acquittal under section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, and the trial court granted it, finding the prosecution's case weak.

The Balochistan High Court upheld this acquittal. It found that the complainant had failed to specify which particular degree was fake, and more importantly, had not produced any witnesses from the relevant educational boards or universities to prove that the degrees were actually forged. Without such evidence, the court held that guilt had not been proven beyond doubt.

The judgment reinforces important legal principles: that even a single reasonable doubt entitles an accused to acquittal as a matter of right, not leniency; that acquittals carry a "double presumption of innocence" that appellate courts are reluctant to overturn unless the original decision was clearly flawed; and that courts apply less strict scrutiny when reviewing appeals against acquittals compared to appeals against convictions. The appeal was therefore dismissed.

title: Sajjid Ahmed and others V. National Accountability Bureau, through Director General and another,
explainer:
This case concerns several public officials in Balochistan accused of corruption under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999. The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) alleged that the petitioners had conspired to appoint seven fake ("bogus") teachers in Quetta and then unlawfully activated their salaries, causing a financial loss of over 43 lakh rupees to the government. Some petitioners were accused of making the fraudulent appointments, while others, including officials from the Accountant General's office, were accused of processing the salary payments improperly.

The petitioners sought pre-arrest bail, arguing that they were innocent, had cooperated fully during the inquiry, and that the case against them was weak. Some pointed out inconsistencies, such as one petitioner having retired years earlier or being abroad during the alleged offence, while another argued he did not even have the authority to approve salaries. Importantly, in earlier, similar cases arising from the same investigation, the High Court had already granted bail to other accused persons facing the same allegations.

The Balochistan High Court held that since it had already confirmed bail before arrest for other accused in connected cases based on identical allegations, fairness and consistency required that these petitioners be treated the same way. The court therefore confirmed pre-arrest bail for the petitioners, emphasizing the principle that similarly situated accused persons should receive similar treatment from the courts.

title: Haji Muhammad Umar V. Taj Muhammad and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a sale of buffaloes between two parties in Quetta. The complainant, Haji Muhammad Umar, alleged that Taj Muhammad, along with his brothers, had issued him four cheques as payment for the buffaloes, but the cheques bounced due to insufficient funds. A criminal case was filed under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with dishonestly issuing a cheque that gets dishonoured.

The trial court initially convicted Taj Muhammad while acquitting his brothers. However, on appeal, the Additional Sessions Judge overturned this conviction and acquitted him too. The complainant then challenged this acquittal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence and found that the cheques had actually been presented to the bank about two years after they were issued, far beyond the legally required six-month window for cashing a cheque. A written agreement (iqrarnama) between the parties did not even mention these cheques. The court also noted there was an ongoing civil dispute between the parties, raising doubts about whether the criminal case was filed to pressure the accused rather than to pursue a genuine criminal complaint.

Applying the principle that acquittals carry a double presumption of innocence and should not be overturned unless clearly flawed, the High Court found no such flaw here. title: Malik Wali Muhammad etc. V. AC/SDM and Collector Saddar Sub-Divisional, Quetta and another,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over compensation for land acquired by the government near Hanna Lake in Quetta under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. In 1994, authorities issued a notice to acquire land belonging to the appellants, and in 1995 an award fixed compensation rates ranging from Rs. 9,000 to Rs. 46,000 per acre depending on land type. The appellants felt this undervalued their land and sought a reference to the District Judge for higher compensation. The trial court dismissed their claim, finding the original valuation fair and the appellants' evidence insufficient. They appealed to the High Court, which upheld the dismissal, and then to the Supreme Court, which found that both lower courts had failed to properly examine key documentary evidence (sale deeds) presented by the appellants and only focused on oral testimony. The Supreme Court sent the case back to the High Court to reconsider the matter using the existing evidence, without needing new proceedings.

In this judgment, the High Court re-examined the case, including the documentary evidence such as sale records of comparable land. Ultimately, it concluded that the compensation originally awarded was proper and consistent with prevailing market rates, and that the appellants had not provided adequate proof to justify a higher amount. The appeal was dismissed.

This case matters because it illustrates how courts evaluate compensation disputes in land acquisition cases, emphasizing the importance of properly considering documentary evidence like sale deeds, not just witness testimony, in determining fair market value.

title: Malik Wali Muhammad and 40 others V. AC/SDM and Collector Saddar Sub-Division, Quetta and another,
explainer:
This case involved a group of landowners near Hanna Lake in Quetta whose land was acquired by the government in 1994 under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Collector fixed compensation rates for different types of land, but the landowners felt these rates did not reflect the true market value of their property. They asked for the matter to be referred to the District Judge, who upheld the Collector's valuation and rejected their claim for higher compensation. They appealed to the High Court, which also dismissed their case, and then to the Supreme Court, which sent the matter back to the High Court because the lower courts had not properly examined the documentary evidence (sale deeds and revenue records) the landowners had submitted.

On reconsideration, the High Court found that the landowners' own documents actually showed land values lower than what they were now claiming, undermining their case. It also noted that the trial judge had personally visited the site and found the land uneven, mountainous, and never cultivated, unlike other lands used for comparison. The court held that landowners can object to an award even after accepting compensation under protest, but in this instance the evidence still supported the original valuation. Finding the trial court's decision well-reasoned and free of legal error, the High Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the compensation originally awarded.

title: Niaz Ali V. The State ,
explainer:
The case involved Niaz Ali, who was convicted of attempting to commit robbery under sections 392 and 511 of the Pakistan Penal Code. According to the prosecution, Niaz Ali and a co-accused, armed with pistols, tried to snatch a motorcycle from the complainant at gunpoint on a highway near Dera Murad Jamali. The complainant resisted, and Niaz Ali was caught on the spot while his companion escaped. A trial court convicted him and sentenced him to three years' rigorous imprisonment plus a fine, and an appellate court upheld this conviction, although his co-accused was acquitted on appeal due to benefit of the doubt.

Niaz Ali then filed a revision petition before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the evidence had been wrongly appreciated and that it was unfair for him to remain convicted when his co-accused, tried on the same evidence, was acquitted.

The High Court examined the testimony of the complainant, an eyewitness, and police witnesses, finding their accounts consistent, credible, and unshaken by cross-examination, with no evidence of false implication due to enmity or grudge. The court therefore upheld the conviction, finding no reason to disturb the finding of guilt. However, it found the three-year sentence too harsh given the circumstances and reduced it to eighteen months.

This case illustrates how appellate courts can reassess evidence and adjust sentences without overturning a conviction, balancing accountability with proportionality in punishment.

title: Mukhtiar and anohter V. The State and anohter,
explainer:
This case is about how far a trial court can go in allowing new witnesses to be called during a criminal trial. Two men, Mukhtiar and another, were accused in a murder case where the victim's death was initially reported as a road accident but later alleged to be murder by strangulation. During the trial, the prosecution's key eyewitnesses refused to testify, reportedly out of fear of the accused. The complainant then asked the trial court, under Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code, to summon additional witnesses to replace those who would not appear. The trial court granted this request. The accused challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that these additional witnesses had never been named in the police challan or in earlier statements recorded under Section 161 of the CPC, so introducing them now was really an attempt to patch up gaps in the prosecution's case rather than a genuine search for truth.

The High Court agreed with the accused. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent (Shahbaz Masih v. State), it held that witnesses whose names do not appear in the list of witnesses and whose statements were never recorded under Section 161 or 164 cannot simply be summoned later to strengthen a weak case. The court therefore set aside the trial court's order allowing these witnesses.

The case matters because it clarifies limits on courts' power to summon witnesses, protecting the fairness of criminal trials by preventing prosecutors from introducing new, unvetted witnesses late in proceedings simply because earlier witnesses failed to cooperate.

title: The State through Regional Director/Force Commander, Anti-Narcotic Force Balochistan V. Muhammad Bakhshal and another,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by the state, through the Anti-Narcotics Force Balochistan, against the acquittal of two men, Muhammad Bakhshal and Noor Muhammad. They had been travelling in a pickup truck along with the driver, Saffar Khan, when the vehicle was stopped and 102 packets of charas (a narcotic substance) were found concealed in its floor. The driver was convicted and sentenced, but the trial court acquitted the two passengers, finding no clear evidence linking them to the hidden drugs. The state challenged this acquittal, arguing that since the men were present in the vehicle and did not deny this, they should be treated as equally responsible.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed and upheld the acquittal. It noted that the two respondents had claimed from the start that they were merely hitching a ride, and the prosecution's witnesses gave no evidence showing they knew about or controlled the concealed contraband. Only the driver, as custodian of the vehicle, could reasonably be held responsible for what was hidden inside it.

The court reaffirmed important legal principles: prosecutors must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, any doubt benefits the accused, and acquittals carry a "double presumption of innocence" that appellate courts should not disturb unless the decision is clearly unreasonable or against evidence. Finding no such flaw here, the court dismissed the state's appeal, keeping the acquittal intact.

title: Abdul Rahim and another V. Chief Secretary Balochistan, Government of Balochistan and 2 others,
explainer:
The case involved two contractors, Abdul Rahim and another person, who had been awarded a government contract to build a 10-kilometer road in Balochistan. They claimed that during construction, militants attacked their workers and machinery with rockets, kidnapped their laborers, and forced them to pay ransom, ultimately halting the project. They sued the Balochistan government for over 14 million rupees in damages, arguing the government had assured them it would cover such losses.

The trial court dismissed their suit, and they appealed to the Balochistan High Court. The appellants argued the lower court had ignored their evidence and misapplied the law, including a provision they said meant the government had already admitted their claim.

The High Court disagreed. It found that the contractors could not go beyond the terms of the contract they had voluntarily signed, and that any law-and-order problems should have been addressed through local administration rather than by suing the government for damages outside the contract's scope. The court also noted the plaintiffs failed to prove their claims with credible evidence and had withheld important facts about the actual contract awarded. Notably, the appellants and their lawyer had stopped appearing in court for over a year, suggesting delay tactics.

The court upheld the trial court's dismissal, ruling that contractors cannot claim damages beyond what their contract allows, especially without solid proof and honest disclosure to the court.

title: Noor Ahmed and another V. Deputy Commissioner, Kharan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a young woman who took the entry test for admission to Bolan Medical College and topped the merit list. However, when she went to check her result, she discovered that her local residency certificate for Kharan district had been cancelled by the Deputy Commissioner, acting on a recommendation from another official. This cancellation meant she could lose her spot despite her top ranking, potentially benefiting another candidate who had placed fourth on the merit list.

The petitioners, the young woman and a relative, challenged this cancellation in the Balochistan High Court. They argued that they were genuine, longtime residents of Kharan, supported by decades-old identity documents showing their family's residence there since the 1970s and 1990s, including local certificates issued in 1994. They also argued that they had never been given a chance to defend themselves before their certificates were cancelled, and that notices about the proceedings had been sent to an address where they did not actually live.

The court found that the cancellation process was flawed and unfair. It noted that notices were deliberately sent to the wrong address, effectively ensuring the petitioners could not respond, and that an influential private individual appeared to have pushed hard to get them declared non-residents. The court criticized the Deputy Commissioner for acting hastily and illegally without giving the petitioners a hearing. Concluding that the petitioners had proven their genuine residency, the court accepted the petition, effectively restoring their local certificates and protecting the woman's rightful admission based on merit.

This case involved a dispute over residency status affecting a medical college admission. The petitioners, a girl seeking admission to Bolan Medical College and her father, had obtained local certificates confirming they were permanent residents of Kharan district in Balochistan. After the petitioner scored first on the merit list for the entrance test, the Deputy Commissioner of Kharan cancelled the family's local residency certificates based on a recommendation, effectively disqualifying her for admission on the basis that she was not actually a local resident.

The petitioners challenged this cancellation in the Balochistan High Court, arguing they had been condemned without a hearing and that the cancellation was driven by malicious intent to benefit another candidate who ranked lower on the merit list.

The court found that the petitioners had strong evidence proving generations-long residency in Kharan, including old identity cards issued to the petitioner's father and mother decades earlier, and an existing local certificate issued to the petitioner's brother in 1994. The court also noted that official notices had been sent to an address where the petitioners did not live, suggesting an intentional effort to cancel their certificates without their knowledge. The court concluded that authorities acted illegally and in haste, without due process.

The court set aside the cancellation order and restored the petitioners' local certificates. This case highlights the importance of due process and protects citizens from arbitrary denial of identity and residency rights, especially when it affects access to education opportunities.

title: Messrs Saindak Metals Ltd. through Managing Director V. Chairman, Federal Board of Revenue and 3 others,
explainer:
Saindak Metals Limited, a company involved in mining and metallurgical processing at Saindak, Balochistan, had leased its project to a Chinese company and received income as rent and a share of profits. In its tax returns, Saindak Metals classified this income as "income from business," which allowed it to claim benefits from past business losses. The tax authorities initially accepted this classification but later realized it was a mistake, since the income was actually from renting out the project rather than from carrying on business itself. The Commissioner issued a rectification notice under section 221 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, reclassifying the income as "income from other sources," which meant the company could no longer offset its brought-forward business losses. Saindak Metals challenged this, arguing that the correction was time-barred and exceeded what rectification under section 221 could achieve, and that such changes should only have been made through the amendment procedure in section 122, which has stricter time limits.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the company's arguments. It explained that section 122 deals with amending a taxpayer's return, while section 221 allows tax authorities to correct their own clear, apparent mistakes in earlier orders. Since the original acceptance of "business income" was a fundamental error that helped avoid proper tax payment, correcting it fell squarely within section 221, not section 122. The court found no illegality and upheld the rectification, meaning the company's income was correctly reclassified and it could not claim the disputed loss benefits.

title: Abdul Haq alias Abdullah V. Muhammad Naseem Achakzai,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of a man accused of cheating under Section 420 of the Pakistan Penal Code. The complainant alleged that a vehicle was purchased and later sold through a chain of transactions involving several people, and that the vehicle turned out to belong to someone else, who reported it missing. The complainant claimed that the accused, along with others, conspired to have the vehicle released to them through court proceedings (superdari) while the last buyer was reimbursed by the appellant, leaving the complainant cheated.

The trial court had acquitted the accused, and the complainant appealed. The Balochistan High Court upheld the acquittal, dismissing the appeal. It found the case highly suspicious because the police complaint was filed nearly four years after the alleged cheating took place. The court held that the dispute appeared to be a civil matter over a vehicle transaction rather than a criminal offense, since there was no evidence of dishonest intention at the time the property changed hands, which is essential for a cheating charge to succeed.

The judgment reaffirms important legal principles: an accused enjoys a stronger presumption of innocence after acquittal, courts should be cautious about overturning acquittals unless there is a clear error, and any reasonable doubt must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not favor. This case is significant for reinforcing how criminal cheating charges are distinguished from ordinary civil disputes.

title: Pakistan Railways Employees Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. through General Secretary, Quetta V. Haji Ghulam Haider and 3 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a housing society for Pakistan Railways employees in Quetta, which held a 99-year lease over railway land for residential development. The society filed a civil suit seeking declarations that it was the lawful lessee of the land, that certain individuals had no right to build on it, and seeking a permanent injunction against alleged encroachers, along with an order for proper demarcation of the property. The respondents contested the suit, with one claiming the land was actually used by a livestock research project (CASVAB) and another alleging the society itself had encroached on his property.

During trial, a local commission was appointed to inspect the disputed site. The commissioner's report noted irregularities, including the absence of the relevant land record official (Patwari) during the visit, which the society objected to at the time. Despite these objections, the trial court decided the case without resolving the objections or framing proper legal issues, and dismissed the suit. The appellate court upheld this decision without deeper scrutiny.

The Balochistan High Court found that both lower courts had acted hastily and failed to follow proper procedure, given that valuable property rights were at stake. It held that such cases must be decided on merits, after issues are properly framed and both sides given full opportunity to present evidence. The High Court set aside both earlier decisions and sent the case back to the trial court for a fresh, lawful decision. This judgment underscores the importance of procedural fairness in civil property disputes.

explainer:
This case is about a housing society for retired railway employees in Quetta, which had leased about 47.77 acres of railway land in 1990 for building residential colonies. The society claimed that some individuals had wrongfully encroached on this land and asked the court for a declaration confirming its lawful lease rights, an injunction against illegal construction, and an order for demarcation of the property.

Instead of properly conducting a trial, the lower court appointed a Local Commissioner (a lawyer) to visit the site and report on the boundaries. Based solely on that report, the trial court decided the case without formally framing legal issues or giving both sides a real opportunity to present evidence. The appellate court upheld this decision without properly examining whether that process was fair.

The Balochistan High Court found this approach improper. It ruled that both lower courts had failed to follow correct legal procedure - they relied on an unexamined and objected-to report instead of holding a proper trial with evidence and arguments from both sides. This, the High Court said, caused a miscarriage of justice.

As a result, the High Court set aside the earlier decisions and sent the case back to the trial court, directing it to conduct proper proceedings, frame issues, and allow both parties a fair chance to present evidence before deciding the matter afresh. The case highlights the importance of following due process, rather than shortcuts, in resolving property disputes.

title: Zonal Manager Canteen Store Department, Quetta Cantt V. Abdul Rehman,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a shop at the Canteen Store Department (CSD) in Quetta Cantonment. Abdul Rehman claimed he had been running the shop under an agreement since 1997 and, due to old age, had his nephews help manage it. The CSD sent him a notice in January 2015 stating it had learned he had died and that whoever was running the shop was doing so illegally, ordering them to vacate. Rehman sued for a declaration that he was alive and that the eviction notice was unlawful, along with an injunction to stop interference with his business.

The CSD asked the trial court to reject the plaint under the Civil Procedure Code, arguing the suit had no valid basis since Rehman had violated his agreement, including by subletting the shop. The trial court agreed and rejected the plaint. On appeal, the Additional District Judge overturned this and sent the case back for a full trial with evidence from both sides.

The Balochistan High Court, hearing CSD's revision petition, sided with the original trial court. It held that the trial court had correctly examined the record and found the suit meritless, and that courts should dismiss such incompetent suits early to save time and resources. The High Court ruled the appellate court had wrongly interfered, set aside its order, and restored the trial court's rejection of the plaint. This case highlights how courts can screen out weak lawsuits early rather than letting them proceed to full trial.

title: Zonal Manager Canteen Store, Department CSD Quetta Cantt. V. Abdul Rehman,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a shop at the Canteen Store Department (CSD) in Quetta Cantt. A shopkeeper, Abdul Rehman, had been allotted a shop under an agreement in 1997. Years later, CSD management sent him a notice claiming he had died and someone else was running the shop illegally, ordering the shop vacated. Rehman filed a civil suit seeking a declaration that he was alive and that the notice was unlawful, along with an injunction stopping CSD from interfering with his business.

CSD, the defendant, argued the suit itself was not legally maintainable because Rehman had violated his tenancy agreement by subletting the shop to others and had not renewed his tenancy after it expired. The trial court agreed and rejected the plaint (dismissed the suit at the outset) without going into a full trial. On appeal, the Additional District Judge sent the case back for a full trial on the merits, disagreeing with that dismissal.

CSD then challenged this remand order before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court sided with CSD, ruling that the appellate court had erred. It found that Rehman had approached the court with unclean hands—giving inconsistent figures for renovation expenses—and had also filed his appeal before the wrong forum given the value of the suit. The High Court restored the trial court's original decision rejecting the plaint, emphasizing that meritless or legally incompetent suits should be dismissed early to save judicial time and resources.

title: Noor Zaman V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about the murder of Gul Zaman, who was allegedly shot dead by his brother Noor Zaman following a property dispute. According to the prosecution, the accused came to the family's house at night, took the victim outside, and fired several shots that proved fatal. He was arrested after being a fugitive for some time. The trial court convicted him under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced him to death, along with a fine payable to the victim's heirs.

The case had a complicated procedural history: an earlier appeal led to the case being sent back to the trial court for witnesses to be re-examined, and after a further judgment, the Supreme Court sent the matter back to the Balochistan High Court to decide the appeal on its merits.

The High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness accounts from family members present at the scene and medical evidence, and found them consistent and credible. The court held that testimony from relatives should not be automatically disregarded simply because of their relationship to the victim. It also ruled that lack of a strong motive does not undermine a conviction if eyewitness evidence is solid, and that a lengthy trial or time spent on death row is not sufficient reason to reduce a death sentence. The court ultimately dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction and death sentence, reinforcing that death is the standard punishment for murder unless clear reasons justify leniency.

title: Khair Muhammad alias Khario and another V. The State and anohter,
explainer:
Khair Muhammad was tried for shooting and killing Younas Masih over a dispute about payment for medical treatment. Masih had treated the accused for piles; when he later asked for money to buy medicine ingredients, the accused left, then confronted him the next morning near his house and shot him. Masih's sons heard the gunfire, saw the accused fleeing with a pistol, and their father told them what happened before dying in hospital. Based on this, the trial court convicted the accused under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced him to death, plus compensation to the victim's heirs.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court upheld the conviction and death sentence. The court found that minor contradictions in witness statements were not serious enough to create doubt about the prosecution's case. The eyewitness account from the victim's sons matched the medical evidence and recovered items like bullet casings and blood-stained articles. Being relatives of the deceased did not automatically make their testimony unreliable, since cross-examination did not reveal any false implication due to enmity or grudge. The court also held that lack of a clear motive did not matter given strong eyewitness evidence, since motive and intent are different things. It ruled the killing was premeditated, not a sudden reaction, so there were no grounds for a lesser sentence. The court reaffirmed that death is the normal punishment for murder unless there are good reasons to reduce it, and dismissed the appeal, confirming the death sentence.

explainer:

The appellant, Mujeeb-ur-Rehman, had been convicted by a Sessions Court and sentenced to life imprisonment for allegedly desecrating pages of the Holy Quran during a dispute over an unpaid "tax" (bhatta) he demanded from a street vendor selling copies of the Quran.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. Only one witness, the complainant, actually claimed to have seen the incident, while the other six witnesses offered only indirect, circumstantial evidence. Crucially, the cart vendor—the person most directly involved and best positioned to know what happened—was never produced as a witness, with no explanation given for his absence. The court also noted that the complainant had a prior personal grudge against the accused, raising doubts about his motives for testifying.

Given these gaps, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. Applying the well-established legal principle that any genuine doubt in a criminal case must benefit the accused as a matter of right, the court acquitted Mujeeb-ur-Rehman, overturning his conviction and life sentence. title: Zulfiqar Ali Bakhtiari and others V. Mst Khalida Bakhtiari and anohter,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over inheritance. After Sajjad Ali Bakhtiari died in 1985, his children were entitled to shares in the movable and immovable property he left behind, including shops that were generating rental income. One daughter, Khalida Bakhtiari, filed a lawsuit claiming that her siblings (who were in possession of the properties) were denying her rightful Islamic inheritance share and had failed to distribute the estate, including years of accumulated rent from twelve shops.

The trial court heard evidence from both sides and ruled in favor of the daughter, granting her a declaration of her inheritance share. The family members who lost appealed to the District Judge, but that appeal was also dismissed. They then approached the Balochistan High Court through a revision petition, arguing that the lower courts had misread the evidence and wrongly favored the daughter's claims.

The High Court dismissed the revision petition. It explained that when two lower courts have already agreed on the facts of a case (called "concurrent findings"), the High Court's revisional powers are limited. It cannot re-examine the merits of the case as if it were an appeal; it can only step in if the lower courts' decisions were clearly illegal, based on misreading of evidence, or so unreasonable as to be shocking or perverse. Since neither court's reasoning suffered from these defects, the High Court upheld the original decision favoring the daughter's inheritance claim. This case illustrates the limited scope of High Court revision powers over factual findings already agreed upon by two courts.

title: Abdul Manan and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Abdul Manan and Zain-ud-Din, convicted by a trial court for the murder of the complainant's father, allegedly shot after a dispute. They were sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The complainant claimed he witnessed the accused catch hold of his father while another fired the fatal shot. However, the High Court found serious problems with this account. It was suspicious that the accused themselves, rather than the complainant who claimed to be present, took the injured man to the hospital. An important eyewitness had been questioned by police on the very first day but was never listed as a prosecution witness, suggesting the police may have hidden testimony unfavorable to their case. Another witness's statement was recorded five days late without explanation. No fingerprint tests were done on the accused or the weapon. There was also no prior enmity between the accused and the deceased to explain a motive for murder.

Given these unexplained gaps and contradictions, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It reaffirmed the legal principle that even a single reasonable doubt entitles an accused to acquittal as a matter of right, not leniency. The court overturned the convictions and allowed the appeal.

This case highlights how flawed police investigation and unreliable witness testimony can undermine a criminal case, reinforcing the fundamental principle that doubt must benefit the accused.

title: Abdul Samad and 3 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved four men convicted of murdering Attaullah, the brother of the complainant, following a property dispute between the two families. The prosecution alleged that on the night of the incident, the accused, armed with daggers, knives, and sticks, attacked the victim, who died from his injuries at the hospital. The trial court had found the appellants guilty and sentenced them to life imprisonment, along with compensation to be paid to the victim's family.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court re-examined the evidence, particularly the testimony of the three eyewitnesses, including the complainant. The court found serious contradictions between their accounts, such as disagreement over what weapons different accused carried, confusion over how many vehicles were used to flee the scene, and even disagreement over the time the incident occurred. The court also noted it was suspicious that none of the eyewitnesses, despite being present and closely related to the victim, sustained any injuries themselves during an attack by eight armed men.

Given these inconsistencies, the court ruled that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Applying the well-established legal principle that any genuine doubt in a criminal case must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not favor, the court overturned the convictions and acquitted all four appellants, setting aside their life sentences. This case highlights how inconsistent witness testimony can undermine even serious criminal prosecutions.

title: Chief Secretary, Government of Balochistan, through EDO (Revenue), Kalat and another V. Bibi Ruqia (Widow of Late Shahzada Mehmood Khan) and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land in Kalat, Balochistan. A man claimed his grandfather had gifted him nine acres of land through a gift deed dated 1984, and he had been in continuous possession of it. Part of that land, however, was recorded in government records as belonging to the Provincial Government and the Frontier Corps. He sued for a declaration of ownership, a permanent injunction, and cancellation of the government's revenue entries.

The trial court (Qazi Kalat) dismissed his suit, but on appeal, the Majlis-e-Shoora Mastung reversed that decision and ruled in his favor. The government then challenged this appellate decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court sided with the government and restored the trial court's dismissal. It found that the suit was legally flawed because a necessary party, the Secretary of the Board of Revenue, had not been included in the case. More importantly, the alleged gift failed to meet the basic requirements of Islamic law: a valid gift needs an offer, acceptance, and actual delivery of possession. Here, physical possession was never proven to have been transferred. The court also noted a serious contradiction: the grandfather who supposedly made the gift had died in 1983, a year before the gift deed was dated. Additionally, the suit was filed 35 years late without justification.

This case reaffirms that Islamic gift law requires strict compliance with its essential conditions, and that courts must scrutinize the timing and evidence behind claimed property transfers, especially against government-recorded land.

title: Bibi Kalsoom V. The General Public and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family pension dispute after the death of a government schoolteacher in Balochistan. His children, including his unmarried daughter Bibi Kalsoom, applied to the courts for a succession certificate to claim his pension dues and other benefits. While the lower courts granted the siblings their share of the dues, they denied Bibi Kalsoom's specific claim to receive her father's monthly pension, reasoning that since she was above 21 years of age, she was not entitled to it as an unmarried daughter.

Bibi Kalsoom challenged this decision, first in an appeal before the District Judge, Pishin, which was also rejected, and then through this civil revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined a 1998 government notification that amended the Balochistan Civil Services Pension Rules, 1989. This notification stated that an eldest unmarried daughter of a deceased government servant is entitled to family pension until she marries, without mentioning any age limit or cutoff at 21 years. The court found that the lower courts had misunderstood the law and wrongly imposed an age restriction that did not exist in the actual rules, causing injustice to the petitioner.

The High Court set aside both lower court orders and directed the relevant government department to process her pension claim properly. This judgment clarifies that unmarried daughters remain eligible for their deceased father's family pension regardless of age, as long as they remain unmarried, protecting their financial rights under pension rules.

title: Mst. Jamila Kakar V. Mst. Surriya Nasreen and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a police officer's estate after his death. His widow obtained a succession certificate identifying herself and her minor son as legal heirs. The deceased's sister and other relatives then challenged this, claiming the minor son was actually adopted and therefore had no right to inherit. The trial court, based on this factual dispute, cancelled the succession certificate and told the parties to go to civil court to resolve the parentage question. The widow's appeal against this was dismissed on limitation grounds, so she approached the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found that both lower courts had erred. It noted that the boy's parentage as the deceased's son was supported by official records from NADRA and a passport issued by the Ministry of Interior. Under the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order (Pakistan's law of evidence), such official and public documents carry a legal presumption of truth and genuineness unless someone proves otherwise. The relatives had not rebutted this presumption; the court viewed their claim as a fabricated attempt to grab money from a vulnerable widow.

The High Court set aside the orders of both lower courts and restored the original succession certificate in favor of the widow and her son. The case highlights how courts must respect official documentary evidence like NADRA records and passports unless properly disproved, protecting vulnerable heirs from baseless challenges to inheritance rights.

title: Dr. Muhammad Jamal and another V. Sultan Muhammad,
explainer:
This case arose from a property dispute where a plaintiff sued for possession through pre-emption, claiming a right to purchase adjacent land that had been sold without informing him, as required under pre-emption law. During the trial, the plaintiff had already introduced a revenue official as a witness who produced land records as evidence. Later, the plaintiff filed another application asking to bring the very same document onto the record again and re-examine the witness. The trial court allowed this request, and the defendants challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the defendants, holding that once a document has already been placed on the court record, it cannot be introduced again simply to fix gaps or weaknesses that emerged during cross-examination. The purpose of re-examining a witness is only to clarify genuine confusion created by cross-examination, not to give a party a second chance to strengthen or improve their case. The court found that the trial judge had made a legal error by permitting the same document to be produced again without valid justification.

The High Court set aside the trial court's order and sent the case back for the trial court to proceed and decide the matter properly within two months. The judgment reinforces an important principle in civil procedure: courts must apply the law correctly and fairly to both sides, and cannot become a tool that lets a party patch up weaknesses in their evidence after the fact.

title: Muhammad Hashim and others V. Syed Kalimullah and others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running landlord-tenant dispute in Balochistan. The landlords had won an eviction order against the tenants back in 2009 from the District Judge, Pishin. The tenants challenged this decision through a revision petition in the High Court and then the Supreme Court, but both were dismissed, with the Supreme Court finally rejecting the case in January 2018.

The landlords then filed an execution petition in October 2018 to enforce the 2009 eviction decree. The tenants objected, arguing that too much time had passed and the execution request was barred by limitation law, which generally requires such petitions to be filed within three years of a decree. The lower courts rejected this objection, reasoning that the pending appeals had effectively kept the matter alive.

The High Court disagreed. It held that simply appealing or filing a revision petition does not automatically pause or stay a judgment unless a court specifically grants a stay order, which had not happened here. Since no such stay existed, the three-year clock started running from 2009, meaning the execution petition filed in 2018 was nine years late and time-barred. The court also rejected the landlords' excuse that they mistakenly believed pending appeals blocked execution, stating that ignorance of the law is not a valid excuse.

As a result, the High Court overturned the lower courts' rulings and dismissed the execution petition entirely, ruling in favor of the tenants on procedural grounds. This case reinforces the importance of timely legal action and clarifies that appeals do not automatically freeze enforcement deadlines.

title: Dr. Aziz Ur Rehman and others V. Noor Bibi and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute in Balochistan. A daughter (the plaintiff) sued her brothers and others, claiming she had been unlawfully deprived of her rightful inheritance share in her deceased father's property. She argued that certain mutations (land record transfers) and a gift claimed by the defendants were illegal, and that the property had later been sold or exchanged to other people without her consent.

The trial court and the appellate court both ruled in her favor, finding that the alleged gift was never properly proven and that mere transfer of possession does not make a gift valid. Several petitioners then challenged these decisions before the Balochistan High Court through revision petitions.

The High Court dismissed the revisions, upholding the lower courts' findings. It held that a legal heir's right to inherit does not expire with time, since limitation does not apply to void transactions. It also ruled that co-sharers cannot transfer more property than their own share, and that anyone who bought land from such co-sharers could only claim rights from the sellers' shares, not from the rightful heir's portion. The court emphasized that concurrent findings of fact by two lower courts cannot be disturbed unless clearly unjust or unlawful.

This judgment reinforces protections for women's inheritance rights under Islamic law and clarifies limits on property transfers by co-owners and the responsibilities of purchasers to verify ownership before buying land.

title: Asadullah alias Sado V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a shooting in Quetta in 2009 in which a man, Asadullah alias Sado, was accused of killing four members of one family, his father, uncle, and two cousins, and injuring a labourer, allegedly over a previous enmity between the families. The trial court had convicted him of murder and sentenced him to death, along with additional punishments for attempted murder and causing injury, and referred the death sentence to the High Court for confirmation.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence carefully. Four eyewitnesses, including the complainant, gave consistent accounts naming Asadullah as the person who fired the shots, and their testimony was supported by medical evidence. The court held that being relatives of the deceased did not make these witnesses unreliable, since their presence at the scene was natural, and that even weak motive evidence does not undermine a strong eyewitness case.

However, the injured labourer who survived the attack never testified, and no proof was given for why he was unavailable, such as a death certificate. Because his own account of his injuries was missing, the court set aside the conviction and sentence specifically related to injuring him, while upholding the murder conviction and death sentence.

This case matters because it shows how courts weigh eyewitness testimony, medical evidence, and gaps in the prosecution's case to ensure convictions meet the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Muhammad Saleem V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Saleem, who was convicted by a trial court for the murder of Naqeebullah and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine payable to the victim's family. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The background was a dispute over a sewerage system between neighbors. The victim confronted the appellant about the issue, and the appellant attacked him with scissors, causing fatal injuries. The victim's brother witnessed the attack, and two other men caught the appellant at the scene with the scissors still in hand. Medical evidence confirmed the cause of death matched the injuries described. Notably, the appellant himself had earlier admitted to the incident in a statement to a magistrate, though he claimed it was unintentional.

The High Court examined whether this killing qualified as "qatl-i-amd" (intentional murder) under Pakistan's Penal Code. It explained that murder does not require a specific intention to kill - it is enough if someone causes an injury they know, in all likelihood, could cause death, especially when striking a vital part of the body. Since the appellant struck the victim with scissors in a highly sensitive area, the court found he must have known this could cause death.

Given the consistent eyewitness accounts, supporting medical evidence, recovery of the weapon, and the appellant's own admission, the court upheld the conviction and dismissed the appeal, affirming the life sentence.

title: Amjad Ali and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Amjad Ali and Nawaz Hussain, who were convicted by a trial court in Panjgur and sentenced to life imprisonment under Section 376(2) (rape) read with Section 34 (common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code. They had allegedly abducted two young women while the women were fetching water, and committed rape.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence and found the prosecution's case unconvincing. Several inconsistencies raised doubt: the alleged abduction happened in a densely populated area, yet no one witnessed or reported it at the time; the victims did not report the incident themselves and stayed silent, which the court found unnatural; the FIR was not filed by the victims or their close family members; medical examination showed no signs of violence; and the victims failed to correctly identify the accused during trial. The court also noted contradictions and improvements in witness statements, and found that police claims about confessions or recoveries from the accused led nowhere.

Based on all this, the court held that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and ruled that even a single reasonable doubt entitles the accused to acquittal as a matter of right, not leniency. The appeal was allowed and the men were acquitted.

This case reinforces important criminal law principles: serious punishments require strong, reliable evidence, and courts must guard against wrongful convictions based on inconsistent or exaggerated prosecution stories.

title: Muhammad Imran V. Muhammad Afzal and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involves a landlord-tenant dispute in Quetta under the Balochistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959. Muhammad Imran, who owned two commercial shops (gifted to him by his brothers), sought to evict his tenants—one running a barber shop and two others selling vegetables—claiming he needed the shops for his own business since he was unemployed. He also alleged the tenants had illegally sublet the front platform of the shops and stopped paying rent to him after he became the owner.

The Rent Controller initially dismissed his eviction application. Imran then appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court noted this was actually the third round of litigation over these shops—an earlier application had been settled by compromise, and a second one was dismissed and later withdrawn on technical grounds, meaning the principle of res judicata (which normally bars repeated litigation on the same issue) did not apply here.

The High Court found that Imran had proven through his testimony and documents that he genuinely owned the shops and needed them for his own use, and that this evidence was never disproven or shaken during cross-examination. It held that a landlord's own sworn statement, if consistent and unchallenged, is strong proof of genuine personal need, and that landlords cannot be permanently denied the right to use their own property just because it was once rented out. The court also found the tenants guilty of willfully not paying rent. The appeal was allowed, and the tenants were ordered to vacate the shops.

title: Malik Muhammad Ameen V. Mst. Saeeda Maqbool and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a house in Quetta. The petitioner claimed he had purchased the house from Maqbool Ahmed, one of several co-sharers who inherited it, through a 2008 agreement where he paid half the price upfront, with the rest and formal transfer due later. He said he continued paying rent to the seller and his widow after his death. When the property was later transferred through inheritance to another relative and then sold to a third party, the petitioner sued for a declaration of ownership, cancellation of the mutation records, and enforcement of the sale agreement.

Both the trial court and the appellate court rejected his claims, finding no credible evidence that the sale agreement was genuine or that any payment was ever made. His own witnesses could not confirm they were present when the agreement was signed or money changed hands. The courts also noted the petitioner kept paying rent for years after supposedly buying the house, undermining his ownership claim. Crucially, one co-sharer could not sell the entire jointly-owned property without the consent of the other co-sharers.

The High Court upheld these findings, explaining that in revision it could not overturn concurrent factual findings of lower courts unless they were clearly illegal, irrational, or unsupported by evidence. It also ruled that a tenant cannot challenge his landlord's title without first giving up possession. The petition was dismissed, reinforcing protections for co-owned property and limits on tenants disputing ownership while still occupying the premises.

title: Abdul Khaliq V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary, Civil Secretariat and 3 others,
explainer:
This case was decided by the Balochistan Service Tribunal. Abdul Khaliq, a government school teacher who had earned his B.A. and B.Ed. degrees, challenged a government notification that changed the promotion rules for Secondary School Teachers. Under the original rules, half the promotion posts were to go to qualified subordinate staff based on seniority and merit, judged on a province-wide basis. The new notification restricted eligibility to teachers who had served continuously for three years within the specific district where a vacancy existed, ranked by district-based seniority rather than provincial seniority.

The appellant argued this change was designed to favor certain favored individuals ("blue-eyed" candidates) by letting less experienced or less qualified teachers jump ahead simply because they happened to be posted in the right district, while sidelining more deserving, senior candidates like himself.

The government argued the Tribunal had no power to examine the validity of such rules since that was a constitutional matter beyond its jurisdiction.

The Tribunal rejected this objection, ruling that it does have the authority to examine whether departmental service rules are lawful, especially when they affect civil servants' fundamental rights and terms of service. It found the amended rule unreasonable, made in bad fainted faith, and inconsistent with the purpose of the law authorizing it. As a result, the Tribunal declared the notification invalid and struck it down.

This case matters because it confirms that service tribunals can review and invalidate discriminatory or arbitrary civil service rules that unfairly affect employees

title: Shazia Azeem V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Education Department, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a school teacher, Shazia Azeem, who had been appointed as a Secondary School Teacher (SST) in 2003 and later worked as an Assistant District Education Officer (ADEO) in Chiltan Town, Quetta. She was suddenly transferred out of her post, with another employee, who had not even joined her original posting, being placed in her position instead.

Azeem challenged the transfer before the Balochistan Service Tribunal, arguing it was not a genuine administrative decision but the result of political pressure, since letters and directives from the Chief Minister, a senator, and a provincial minister had influenced the decision. She argued this made the transfer mala fide, meaning it was done in bad faith for improper reasons rather than for legitimate service needs.

The Tribunal agreed with her. It acknowledged that transferring and posting civil servants is normally within the government's discretion under the Balochistan Civil Servants Act, 1974. However, it held that this discretion cannot be used arbitrarily or to favor politically connected individuals. Transfers must be based on fairness, the needs of the department, and an employee's capability, not on outside political influence. The Tribunal criticized the common practice of government employees using political contacts to secure favorable postings.

Because the transfer order was found to be driven by political pressure rather than genuine administrative reasons, the Tribunal set it aside and allowed Azeem's appeal. The case is significant because it reinforces that civil service transfers must be fair, merit-based, and free from political interference.

title: Mehmood Khan v. Muhammad Ibrahim,
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant dispute under Pakistan's rent laws. A shop owner (the landlord) applied to evict his tenant from a shop, claiming he needed the premises for his own personal use after retiring from government service, and also alleging the tenant was a poor rent-payer. The Rent Controller in Pishin accepted the eviction application and ordered the tenant to vacate within three months. The tenant appealed, arguing that the landlord hadn't specified what kind of business he planned to start, that the landlord was too old (about 75) to run a business, that he had four sons already employed as government servants, and that he owned other properties besides this shop, suggesting he really just wanted to sell the shop at a higher price rather than use it himself.

The Balochistan High Court rejected all these arguments and dismissed the appeal. It ruled that a landlord doesn't need to specify the exact nature of the business he intends to start, nor prove where his capital will come from. Old age alone doesn't disprove genuine need, especially since the landlord could be assisted by his sons. The court also held that even if a landlord wants to eventually sell a property, that doesn't invalidate a genuine claim for personal need. Finally, it confirmed that landlords owning multiple properties can choose which one they want for personal use, and tenants cannot dictate which property the landlord should keep for himself. This case reinforces landlords' rights to reclaim property for bona fide personal use.

title: Zamin Ali v. the State,
explainer:
This case concerns Zamin Ali and Asif Ali, who were accused of taking large sums of money from people promising to arrange jobs abroad, but the individuals sent overseas were never heard from again. A complainant, Muhammad Essa, had earlier filed a private complaint against them, resulting in their conviction and one-year sentence under sections 406 and 420 of the Pakistan Penal Code (criminal breach of trust and cheating). Separately, the FIA registered another case against the same petitioners under section 22(b) of the Emigration Ordinance, 1979, based on the same facts.

The petitioners asked the Balochistan High Court to quash this second case, arguing it amounted to punishing them twice for the same conduct. The High Court agreed. It held that under Article 13 of the Constitution, section 403 of the Criminal Procedure Code, and section 26 of the General Clauses Act, a person cannot be tried or punished twice for the same offence. Since the emigration law charge could have been included in the original trial but wasn't, it was too late to prosecute it separately now. The court also noted the petitioners had already gone through lengthy civil and criminal litigation, had reached a compromise with the complainant, and had been acquitted by the High Court on that basis, making that acquittal final.

The court quashed the pending FIA proceedings, emphasizing that reopening a closed matter would serve no purpose and would amount to abuse of legal process. This case reinforces the principle against double jeopardy in Pakistani law.

title: M/s Allied Precision Engineering v. Jhanda Khan Maree,
explainer:
This case involved workers who were terminated from their jobs at a company manufacturing auto parts. The company claimed these workers were actually employed by an outside contractor, not directly by the company, so labour laws protecting employees didn't apply to them. The workers filed grievance petitions, and both the Labour Court and the Appellate Tribunal ruled in their favor, finding they were genuine employees of the company and ordering their reinstatement with full back pay. The company then challenged this before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the finding that the workers were indeed company employees, not contractor employees. It laid out key factors for making this determination: who has administrative control over the worker, who has power to hire and fire, whether the work is permanent and tied to the manufacturing process, who pays wages, and whether the contractor is a genuine business or merely a sham to avoid labour law obligations. Evidence showed the company controlled these workers, paid them directly, and kept them on staff even as different contractors came and went - proving they were the company's real employees.

However, the court modified the back-pay award. It ruled that such compensation isn't meant to punish employers but only to make up for the worker's actual job loss. Since the workers hadn't proven they remained unemployed throughout the entire period after termination, the court reduced full back-benefits to just three months' pay, presuming that's a reasonable time to find alternate work.

This case matters because it clarifies how courts determine true employment relationships despite contractor arrangements, protecting workers from being wrongly excluded from labour law protections through disguised contracting.

title: Dr. Saba Durrani v. Chairman House Allotment Committee,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over a government-allotted house in Quetta. Dr. Saba Durrani had been officially allotted House No. C-3 in Wahdat Colony after it became vacant following Abdul Sattar Khajjak's retirement from government service. Khajjak had initially been allowed to keep living in the house for six months post-retirement, but instead of vacating it, he obtained another order from the Chief Minister extending his retention for a full year, even though the applicable rules did not allow this.

Dr. Durrani challenged this extension in court, arguing that under the Residential Accommodation at Quetta (Procedure of Allotment) Rules, 2009, retired civil servants cannot keep official housing beyond six months, and that the Chief Minister had no authority to override this rule.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with her. It held that while the Chief Minister generally has power to relax certain rules, this power did not extend to letting someone occupy government housing indefinitely in violation of clear, specific rules. The court also rejected Khajjak's argument that he could keep the house until alternate accommodation was found for his son, noting the son's grade did not qualify him for that type of house.

The court declared the extension order illegal and void, and directed that vacant possession of the house be handed over to Dr. Durrani. The case reinforces that government authorities cannot bypass clear housing rules through discretionary orders, and that civil servants are not obligated to follow illegal directives.

title: Abdul Jabbar V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Jabbar, who was convicted by a Special Judge in Quetta under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine, after 170 kilograms of charas was allegedly found hidden in secret cavities of a pickup truck he was driving. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found problems with how the prosecution handled the evidence. Although 170 kilograms was allegedly recovered in 140 packets, only small samples (10 grams each from 10 packets, totaling 100 grams) were initially sent for chemical testing. There was no proof that samples were taken from every packet to confirm the entire recovery was actually charas. Samples were also sent to the Chemical Examiner about seven months after arrest, with no explanation of where the drugs were kept meanwhile, breaking the chain of custody. The court also noted that any additional evidence the investigators later tried to introduce should have gone through proper legal procedure under the Criminal Procedure Code, not informally.

Because of these gaps, the court ruled the prosecution had only proven possession of 100 grams of charas, not the full 170 kilograms. Since the accused had already been in custody since January 2008, the court ordered his sentence be treated as already served.

This case matters because it highlights the importance of proper evidence handling and chain of custody in narcotics cases, and shows courts will not convict based on incomplete or improperly obtained forensic evidence.

title: Shafi Muhammad and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Shafi Muhammad and Akbar, who were convicted by a trial court for murder and sentenced to life imprisonment after allegedly killing a man during a nighttime attack near a canal in Balochistan. The prosecution's case rested mainly on eyewitness testimony from relatives of the deceased, an alleged extra-judicial confession, an identification parade, and recovered weapons.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted both men. The judges found serious problems with the evidence. The witnesses were closely related to each other and hostile toward the accused, making their testimony unreliable without independent support. They also failed to name the accused until five days after the incident, despite claiming to have recognized them that night - raising doubts about whether they actually saw the attackers. The alleged joint confession was legally inadmissible, and the identification parade was contradictory, since witnesses admitted it was too dark to identify anyone yet still picked out the accused. Medical evidence didn't match the witness accounts, and weapons were recovered ten days later in a manner (joint recovery) not permitted by law.

The court emphasized that supporting evidence like recoveries or medical reports cannot substitute for solid, direct evidence of guilt. Since the core evidence was too weak and contradictory, the men could not be lawfully convicted, and their life sentences were set aside.
