title: Ali Muhammad v. the State,
explainer:
A five- or six-year-old girl went missing from her home in Dera Murad Jamali. Her family searched for days, and eventually her dead body was found hidden in a drain at their own guesthouse, showing she had been murdered with a sharp weapon. Two men, Ali Muhammad alias Baboo and Rasool Bakhsh, were later named as suspects by the girl's father and were tried under the Anti-Terrorism Act and the Pakistan Penal Code. The trial court convicted them, sentencing both to life imprisonment plus fines.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. It found that the prosecution's case rested mainly on police testimony about the accused supposedly confessing and pointing out where a knife was hidden. Confessions made to police are not legally admissible as evidence, and while the recovery of the knife itself could be considered, the knife wasn't even proven to have blood on it, and no forensic report was presented to confirm this. The court stressed that such recovery evidence is only "corroborating" and cannot substitute for real, direct proof of guilt. It also noted that the complainant admitted he suspected the accused only based on their reactions during "Balochi Hal-o-Ehwal," a traditional greeting custom, which is not proof of a crime. Because the case did not meet the standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt, the court gave the accused the benefit of the doubt and acquitted them.

title: Master Mukhtiar Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Mukhtiar Ahmed who was denied bail by a Sessions Court in a case where he and three co-accused were alleged to have intercepted the complainant on a motorcycle, fired at him with Kalashnikovs, and caused a single bullet injury to his leg. He was booked under section 324 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with attempted murder, a serious offense that normally makes bail harder to get.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the case and granted bail. The judge reasoned that if the accused truly intended to kill the complainant, they had ample opportunity to do so after he fell to the ground, yet they stopped firing. The fact that only one bullet struck a non-vital area like the leg, despite three armed men firing, suggested there was no clear intention to kill. The court found the charge of attempted murder was not firmly established at this stage and that the facts more likely fit lesser, often bailable, offenses under other sections of the Penal Code. The court also noted the prosecution had failed to record a statement from an eyewitness who was present, raising doubts about the case.

This judgment matters because it illustrates how courts assess intent and evidence at the bail stage, without conducting a full trial, and reaffirms that doubts in the prosecution's case and incomplete evidence can justify granting bail even in serious-sounding charges.

title: Bashir Ahmed and another V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by a man convicted of murder under section 302(b) read with section 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code, alongside a revision petition seeking a harsher sentence for another accused. The murder allegedly arose from a family dispute over property between brothers, with one brother killed. The trial court had convicted the appellant to life imprisonment, while acquitting a co-accused.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence and found it seriously deficient. The prosecution relied almost entirely on the testimony of the deceased's widow, the sole eyewitness, whose account was uncorroborated by any independent evidence. No weapon was recovered from the accused, there was no forensic report, and the body had never been medically examined, so no medical evidence supported her version either. The court also noted the witness had a personal interest in the outcome due to an ongoing property dispute, and had improved her testimony over time to strengthen the case. The prosecution's argument that the accused's absconding proved guilt was rejected, since absconding alone does not establish guilt.

The court also stressed that any evidence not put to the accused during his examination under section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code cannot be used against him. Since the co-accused had already been acquitted on the same evidence, the court found no basis for convicting this appellant either. It set aside his conviction and ordered his release, highlighting the importance of solid, corroborated evidence in murder cases.

title: Ghulab Khan and others V. The State and others,
explainer:

title: Moulvi Naqal-ud-Din v. Abdullah,
explainer:
Naqal-ud-Din sued to claim pre-emption rights over two plots of land in Muslim Bagh, Balochistan, arguing that he had a superior right to acquire the land because of his adjoining property rights and that he had properly performed the legally required demands (Talbs) needed to claim pre-emption. Under Islamic pre-emption law as applied in Balochistan, a claimant must make two specific demands quickly and correctly: Talb-e-Muwathibat, an immediate assertion of the right upon learning of the sale, and Talb-e-Ishhad, a follow-up demand made before witnesses referencing the first demand. The trial court had dismissed his suit, and he appealed.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the appellant failed to prove he had properly performed either demand: the person who allegedly informed him of the transaction was never produced as a witness, his own witnesses gave contradictory accounts of when and how the demands were made, and he never even mentioned the first demand while describing the second. The court also noted that the appellant had admitted during cross-examination that the transaction was actually an exchange of properties, not a sale, and only sales (not exchanges) can be subject to pre-emption claims.

This case matters because it reinforces that pre-emption rights are not automatic or informal privileges but require strict, timely, and well-evidenced compliance with procedural requirements, and that only genuine sales—not property exchanges—qualify for such claims.

title: Ghulam Rasool v. the State,
explainer:

This case matters because it illustrates how courts protect individuals from abuse of the criminal justice system in cases where families file abduction complaints against men who marry women of their choice.

title: Shah Nawaz and 2 others V. The State,

The prosecution's case relied mainly on the testimony of two eyewitnesses, one the deceased's cousin and the other his brother. The court also noted that the alleged murder weapon was never sent for forensic testing, so there was no scientific proof it was actually used in the killing. Additionally, the prosecution failed to prove the motive it had itself alleged.

Given these serious gaps, the court ruled that the evidence was not strong enough to sustain a conviction, especially for such a serious charge carrying capital punishment. The court set aside the convictions and sentences, acquitting and ordering the release of all three appellants. This case highlights how Pakistani courts require solid, corroborated evidence before convicting someone of murder, particularly when witnesses have personal relationships with the victim that could affect their reliability.

title: Ghulam Rasool v. the State,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves a man named Ghulam Rasool who was accused of abducting a woman, Mst. Ghazala, under Pakistan's Penal Code provisions on abduction. Her father had filed a police report (FIR) claiming she was enticed and abducted while Ghulam Rasool was working as a driver for a government health project vehicle.

Ghulam Rasool asked the court to quash the FIR, arguing that Ghazala was an adult who married him of her own free will, without any pressure. The evidence supporting this included a signed affidavit from Ghazala stating she was 21 years old and had chosen to marry him freely, a registered marriage certificate (Nikah Nama) confirming the marriage with witnesses and a dower amount, and her personal appearance in court where she refused to support her father's abduction claim and instead asked for the FIR to be cancelled.

The court ruled in favor of Ghulam Rasool, quashing the FIR. It reasoned that since Ghazala was a legal adult capable of making her own decisions, and the marriage was valid under Islamic law, no crime of abduction had actually occurred. The judge emphasized that Pakistan's Constitution protects a person's right to do what is not prohibited by law, and nothing prevented two consenting adults from marrying.

This case matters because it reinforces that adult women have the constitutional right to choose their own spouse, and that courts can intervene to stop investigations that amount to harassment when no real crime exists.

title: Shahid Hakeem V. Altaf Hussain Agha and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over agricultural land in Lasbella, Balochistan. Altaf Hussain Agha, who had purchased property through a court auction, complained that Bolan Casting Limited and its representatives had illegally occupied part of his land. He filed a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005. The trial court convicted Shahid Hakeem, who was associated with the company, sentencing him to two years imprisonment, a fine, and compensation.

Hakeem appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that he had joined the company only after the alleged encroachment took place, and that mere continuation of managing land already enclosed by boundary walls did not prove criminal intent on his part, which the law requires.

The High Court examined the evidence and agreed that while some encroachment onto the complainant's land had indeed occurred, the case had originally been filed against the company's Managing Director, and Hakeem's name was added later without proper justification, even though he was not present when the encroachment happened. The court clarified that under the Illegal Dispossession Act, a conviction requires proof of both an unlawful act and criminal intent to grab property, not just occupation or encroachment. Since Hakeem lacked the necessary intent, his conviction could not stand.

The court set aside his conviction and sentence, acquitting him. This case is significant because it clarifies that criminal liability under the Illegal Dispossession Act requires clear proof of intent, and individuals cannot be held liable merely for administering property they inherited control of from others.

title: Muhammad Ali alias Khamisa V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal appeal filed by Muhammad Ali alias Khamisa, who was convicted by a trial court in Balochistan for murdering two people, Muhammad Aslam and Mst. Amiran, in December 2005. According to the prosecution, the appellant and two other accused ambushed Aslam with firearms and killed him, and shortly afterward also shot and killed Mst. Amiran, allegedly because of her suspected illicit relationship with the deceased Aslam. The appellant was convicted under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to life imprisonment on two counts, along with fines payable to the victims' heirs.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence, including eyewitness testimony from the complainant (father of one victim), medical reports, recovery of the murder weapon from the appellant, and a positive ballistic expert report. The court found the complainant's testimony credible and consistent despite cross-examination, and ruled that being related to the victim did not automatically make him an unreliable witness, since he had no personal grudge against the accused. The court also noted the appellant never testified to explain his side.

The High Court upheld the trial court's conviction, finding no grounds to interfere with the judgment. This case illustrates how courts evaluate eyewitness credibility, corroborating forensic evidence, and the significance of an accused's silence when assessing guilt in serious criminal cases.

title: Malik Jaffar and 2 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved three applicants, Malik Jaffar Khan, Haji Abdul Hakeem, and Saleemullah, who sought bail after being arrested in a murder case registered under Pakistan's Penal Code. They were accused, along with several companions, of attacking a complainant and two others with firearms during a tribal dispute, resulting in one death and one injury.

The applicants argued they should get bail because rival cross-cases had been filed by both sides, making it unclear who was the aggressor, and because no specific individual role had been assigned to each of the many accused named in the case.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It found that the applicants were clearly named in the initial police report, that witnesses including the complainant and the injured victim had given supporting statements, and that medical evidence confirmed the cause of death matched the allegations. The court also noted that under Section 149 of the Penal Code, when a crime is committed by an unlawful assembly of five or more people pursuing a common objective, every member can be held equally responsible—so the lack of individually specified roles did not help the applicants' case. The court also pointed out that the rival case had been filed hours after the original complaint, suggesting it was a defensive afterthought.

The court therefore refused bail, while clarifying its comments were preliminary and should not influence the trial court's independent judgment on the merits.

title: Gul Muhammad v. Dost Muhammad,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the registration of a criminal case. The petitioner, Gul Muhammad, alleged that respondents came armed to a village, opened fire, killing one man and injuring another. He claimed he reported this to the police, but the station house officer refused to register an FIR. He then approached the Sessions Judge, acting as Justice of Peace, under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking that police be directed to register the case. The Sessions Judge dismissed his application, and Gul Muhammad challenged that dismissal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that a Justice of Peace has limited power: only to check whether the information given discloses a cognizable offence, not to investigate the truth of the allegations. However, the Court found the Sessions Judge's order was well-reasoned, noting that neither the deceased's family nor the injured person had come forward to support the petitioner's version, that the petitioner himself had no direct connection to the incident, and that he filed his application after an unexplained three-month delay while concealing relevant facts, including that those involved were linked to prior criminal cases.

The judgment clarifies the limited, non-investigative role of the Justice of Peace and confirms that courts will not interfere with well-reasoned orders unless there is a clear failure to apply judicial mind, especially where the applicant appears to be acting with delay or hidden motives.

title: Zahoor Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved the murder of Haji Muhammad, who was shot dead in broad daylight along with an injury caused to another bystander, Zahid Hussain. According to the prosecution, the appellant Zahoor Ahmed, along with two co-accused, opened fire on the deceased following a dispute linked to a matrimonial matter. The complainant, the deceased's son, promptly reported the incident to police, and the appellant was later arrested with a pistol that forensic experts linked to the crime.

The trial court convicted Zahoor Ahmed and sentenced him to death, along with additional punishment for the injury caused to the other victim. He appealed, seeking acquittal, while the case was also sent to the High Court for confirmation of the death sentence.

The Balochistan High Court examined the eyewitness accounts, medical evidence, and recovery of the weapon, and found the prosecution had proven his involvement in the killing beyond doubt. However, since three men were accused of firing and it could not be established whose bullet actually caused death, the court held that awarding the death penalty to only one accused was not justified. The court also noted the prosecution failed to prove the alleged motive despite claiming one.

As a result, the death sentence was converted to life imprisonment, with credit given for time already spent in custody. This case highlights how courts distinguish between proving guilt and justifying the harshest punishment when multiple people share responsibility for a single act.

title: Qadir Bakhsh and 2 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved three men, Qadir Bakhsh, Moula Bakhsh, and Shah Muhammad, who were convicted by a Sessions Court in Sibi for murder under sections 302(b) and 149 of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to life imprisonment plus compensation payments. The prosecution's case relied mainly on one eyewitness, Wazir Khan, who claimed the accused had attacked the victim, Abdul Nisar, with sticks, causing injuries that later proved fatal.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The sole eyewitness had made dishonest improvements to his story during trial, lived far from the scene without a credible reason to be there, and behaved in ways inconsistent with normal human conduct. There was also an unexplained two-and-a-half-hour delay in filing the police report, suggesting the story may have been fabricated. Medical evidence contradicted the eyewitness account, and the prosecution failed to produce another eyewitness mentioned in the initial report, who later testified for the defense that the accused were not the actual culprits. The recovered sticks, allegedly used as weapons, were not proven to have human blood on them.

Given these doubts, the court ruled that the benefit of the doubt must go to the accused as a matter of right, not favor. The convictions were overturned and all three men were acquitted. This case highlights the importance of reliable eyewitness testimony and thorough investigation in securing a fair murder conviction.

title: Amanullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves an appeal by three men, Amanullah, Attaullah, and Hidayatullah, who had been convicted by a trial court in Quetta for possessing explosive material and illegal weapons, including a pistol, cartridges, and a hand grenade, allegedly recovered after their car was stopped at a checkpoint. They were sentenced to seven years imprisonment under the Explosive Substances Act, with two of them receiving an additional two-year sentence under the Arms Ordinance.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court closely examined the evidence and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. Key witnesses gave contradictory accounts about the timing of the arrest and when the police arrived at the scene, undermining the credibility of the arrest and recovery story. No site plan of the location was ever prepared. Additionally, the prosecution failed to properly prove that the expert reports on the explosive material and weapons were actually issued by government-authorized experts, as legally required, and no bomb disposal or crisis management official testified to confirm the authenticity of these reports.

Because of these gaps, contradictions, and procedural failures, the court concluded that the prosecution had not proven its case beyond reasonable doubt. The court acquitted all three appellants, ordering their release unless wanted in another case.

This judgment matters because it reinforces the principle that criminal convictions, especially those carrying severe punishment, must rest on credible, consistent evidence and proper legal procedure, not just police allegations.

title: Nizam-Ud-Din V. The State,
explainer:

The allegation was that sugar meant for public distribution through the Utility Stores Corporation, at subsidized rates for poor communities in Sibi district, was instead diverted and sold in the open market—and possibly smuggled to Afghanistan—for higher profits. The applicant allegedly bought this subsidized sugar cheaply by colluding with officials of the Trading Corporation of Pakistan and Utility Stores Corporation, causing major financial loss to the government and depriving needy people of their rightful benefit.

The Balochistan High Court refused to grant bail. It found there was sufficient material on record, including recovered sugar from the applicant's godown and evidence of payments made to a USC employee, suggesting his involvement in the scheme. The court rejected his claim of being an innocent buyer, noting witness statements contradicted this. It described the case as a clear example of "mega corruption" involving collusion between government officials and private individuals, calling for strict action against such corruption. Since a co-accused's bail had already been denied on similar grounds, and the alleged offences fell under a category of law where bail is generally restricted, the court dismissed the application. This case highlights how courts treat corruption cases involving public welfare resources and government funds seriously at the bail stage.

title: Bagan Khan and another V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court in 2011, involved a shooting incident that took place way back in 1993 in a village in Jhal Magsi district. According to the prosecution, a group of armed men attacked a village, killing two shepherds, Mumtaz and Sikandar, and injuring two women, Mst. Sukhan and Mst. Khanzadi. One accused, Pandhi alias Bagan, was tried years later and convicted by the trial court, sentenced to death for the murders and to further imprisonment for the injuries and rioting-related offences. He appealed his conviction, and the trial court also sent the case for confirmation of the death sentence.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the appellant. It found the prosecution's case deeply flawed: the eyewitnesses were all relatives of the deceased or of each other, one witness was not even named in the initial police report, and other witnesses' statements were recorded after an unexplained 17-year delay. No weapon was recovered from the accused, no ballistic report existed, and no medical or autopsy evidence supported the witnesses' account. The court also noted that a co-accused had already been acquitted on the same evidence, so it would be unfair to convict this appellant on it.

The judgment matters because it reinforces that in serious criminal cases, especially those carrying the death penalty, courts must be extremely cautious about relying solely on interested witnesses without independent, credible corroboration.

title: Abdul Rehman V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man accused of murdering his wife after allegedly finding her with another man. The prosecution's story was that the accused confessed to strangling his wife to companions at a gathering, and the wife's body was later found at her family's home. He was convicted by a trial court in Dera Allah Yar and sentenced to life imprisonment for murder, plus a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the accused. The court found the prosecution's case riddled with serious problems: the two main witnesses were closely related to each other and hostile toward the accused; their accounts contradicted each other on important points; one witness's testimony was pure hearsay since he hadn't witnessed anything himself and only learned of events six days later without explanation; and the deceased's own father had separately accused different people (not this appellant) of the murder in a formal complaint. A key prosecution witness who was declared hostile did not actually testify against the accused. The alleged motive was never proven, and medical evidence alone could not identify who committed the crime. The court also noted that withholding key evidence creates a legal presumption that it would have been unfavorable to the party withholding it.

This judgment matters because it reinforces important legal principles: convictions must rest on credible, consistent evidence beyond reasonable doubt; motive, once alleged, must be proven; and courts must critically scrutinize witness credibility, especially in cases relying on circumstantial or interested testimony rather than direct evidence.

title: Majeed and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a murder trial from Jhal Magsi, Balochistan. According to the prosecution, the complainant and his two brothers were grazing cattle when four armed men opened fire on them, killing one brother (Afzal Khan) and wounding another (Sohrab Khan). One of the accused, Majeed, was arrested and tried, while the others remained unidentified or unavailable for trial. The trial court convicted Majeed of murder and related offences and sentenced him to death, along with lesser sentences for the injuries caused and orders to pay compensation to the victims.

Majeed appealed, but his lawyer did not ask for a full acquittal. Instead, he argued that since four people were accused of firing, it could not be proven exactly whose bullet killed the deceased, so the death penalty was too harsh.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with this narrower argument. It found that the eyewitnesses were credible and consistent, their presence at the scene was natural, and the accused's flight after the incident supported his guilt. However, because it could not be established which of the four assailants actually fired the fatal shot, the court held that a death sentence was not justified. It upheld Majeed's conviction but reduced his sentence from death to life imprisonment.

This case matters because it illustrates how courts handle uncertainty about individual responsibility in group crimes, especially when deciding between life and death sentences.

title: Shafi Muhammad v. the State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Shafi Muhammad and Akbar, who had been convicted and sentenced under the Pakistan Arms Ordinance. They had appealed these convictions to the Balochistan High Court, but their lawyer withdrew the appeals, telling the court they were "not pressed," apparently under the mistaken belief that the men had already served their sentences (having been acquitted separately in a related murder case). Later it turned out they still had significant jail time left, so they asked the High Court to review its own order dismissing their appeals, hoping to have the appeals heard properly or get reduced sentences.

The High Court refused. It explained that under Section 369 of the Criminal Procedure Code, once a court signs and pronounces a judgment, it cannot alter or review it, except to fix minor clerical mistakes. This rule applies even to the High Court. The court also rejected the argument that its inherent powers under Section 561-A could be used to get around this bar, clarifying that those powers help enforce the law or prevent injustice but cannot be used to change a final decision already made.

This matters because it reinforces the important legal principle of finality in criminal judgments—once a court rules, that decision generally stands, even if a lawyer's mistake led to an unfavorable outcome, except in narrow circumstances involving genuine clerical errors.

title: Abdul Sattar v. the State,
explainer:
This case is about Abdul Sattar, who was convicted by a trial court in Dera Murad Jamali for the murder of Abdul Qadir and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution's story was that Abdul Qadir was shot dead by four men, including the appellant, following a dispute over marriage—the deceased had married a woman who had divorced the appellant's brother. A co-accused was caught at the scene with a pistol and separately convicted, but the appellant was arrested and tried later.

The High Court found serious problems with the case against the appellant. The witnesses were all closely related to the deceased and hostile to the accused, and their testimony was not independently corroborated. No weapon was recovered from the appellant, and forensic evidence showed the bullets came from the gun recovered from the co-accused, not from any weapon linked to the appellant. One independent witness did not even mention the appellant's presence. The court also noted that the appellant's alleged absconding could not be held against him since he was never questioned about it during his trial, and flight alone does not prove guilt.

Because the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the High Court gave the appellant the benefit of the doubt, overturned his conviction, and ordered his release. The case highlights the importance of independent, credible evidence in murder trials, especially when witnesses have personal stakes in the outcome.

title: Ali Gul V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a murder in Balochistan where a man named Ali Gul was accused of shooting his cousin Zulfiqar Ali dead and injuring the victim's elderly father, Abdul Sattar, while they were harvesting a mustard crop in April 2005. The motive alleged was a matrimonial dispute, as the deceased's wife was the accused's cousin.

The trial court convicted Ali Gul, sentencing him to death for murder under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, along with a separate sentence for attempted murder under Section 324 for injuring the father. Ali Gul appealed from jail, and the case also came before the Balochistan High Court as a mandatory reference for confirmation of the death sentence.

The High Court upheld the conviction and death sentence. It found the eyewitness testimony of the injured father and the complainant brother credible, noting their close relationship to the deceased did not automatically make them unreliable witnesses, since they had no personal grudge against the accused. The court also relied on strong supporting evidence: the weapon recovery, ballistics report matching the rifle, bloodstained evidence, and the fact that the FIR was filed promptly and named the accused.

Importantly, the court ruled that a weak or insufficient motive alone is not grounds to reduce a death sentence when other evidence strongly proves guilt. The appeal was dismissed, and the death sentence was confirmed.

title: Shah Mir and 6 others V. Ghulam Hussain,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over tenants living in houses in Quetta since 1965. In 1993, Ghulam Hussain bought the property and later filed a petition to evict the tenants, claiming they had stopped paying rent since the purchase and that he genuinely needed the houses for his own family's use. The tenants argued the sale was fraudulent, that he never properly notified them of the change in ownership, and that he did not truly need the property, especially since he was not the sole owner.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the eviction order. It found that the landlord's need was genuine, as he was living in a crowded joint household with his brothers and five grown children, and the tenants failed to disprove this. On the notice issue, the court ruled that even without formal notice, the act of filing the eviction petition itself served as notice, making the tenants liable for rent from the date ownership changed hands - and since they admittedly hadn't paid, they were in default. The court also clarified that questions of ownership or title are not the concern of rent proceedings; what matters is the landlord-tenant relationship. A co-owner can file for eviction without needing permission from other co-owners.

This judgment reinforces settled principles under rent laws: tenants cannot use ownership disputes to escape eviction once a landlord-tenant relationship and rent default are established, and silence on notice does not shield tenants from consequences of non-payment.

title: Mst. Kubra Khanum v. Anjuman-e-Imamia Assn-e-Ashria,
explainer:

The Rent Controller ordered eviction, and the tenants appealed, claiming they weren't given a fair hearing and that the landlord didn't really need the shops.

Importantly, the court held that property ownership rights, protected under Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution, are superior to tenancy rights, meaning tenants cannot dictate whether a landlord's need for the property is sufficient. This case reinforces that landlords' bona fide personal need, especially for religious or charitable purposes, can override tenant occupancy, provided it is properly proven in court.

The court rejected the appellant's attempt to escape anti-terrorism jurisdiction, ruling that killings carried out under the guise of "honour" or "siyahkari," where a person takes the law into his own hands, create fear and panic in society and therefore properly fall under the Anti-Terrorism Act. The court also held that even though the parties had reached a compromise, private individuals cannot compound such offences under this special law because they are considered crimes against the State, not just the victim's family. The court emphasized that honor-based killings are un-Islamic and illegal, and cannot justify reduced punishment. This case matters because it reinforces that "honour killings" cannot be treated as private family matters or escape strict anti-terrorism accountability through compromise.

title: Ameer Bakhsh alias Mumtaz Ali and 2 others V. The State,
explainer:
This is a murder appeal from the Balochistan High Court. Three men, Ameer Bakhsh, Inayatullah, and Ahmed Sultan, had been convicted by a trial court and sentenced to life imprisonment for the murders of three people, allegedly killed by gunfire during a nighttime incident in December 2006. They appealed their conviction.

The High Court re-examined the evidence and found it seriously lacking. The main prosecution witnesses were close relatives of the deceased, making them potentially biased, and their accounts were inconsistent and uncorroborated. Several key witnesses, including the complainant himself, had turned hostile and did not support the prosecution's version. One witness could not even establish that he was present at the scene. The FIR was filed 4-5 hours after the incident without explanation, and it did not name the witnesses who later testified. No weapons were recovered from the accused, and no ballistic report linked them to the crime.

Given these gaps, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. It held that even a single reasonable doubt must benefit the accused, and acquitted all three men, setting aside their convictions and ordering their release.

This case matters because it reinforces a fundamental principle of criminal justice: the burden of proof lies entirely on the prosecution, and convictions cannot stand on weak, interested, or unsupported testimony, especially in serious cases carrying life sentences.

title: Muhammad Hayat V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved the murder of Abdul Nabi, a schoolteacher, who was allegedly lured away by three men including Muhammad Hayat under the pretext of a tea party and then shot dead with a Kalashnikov. The trial court in Dera Allah Yar convicted Hayat under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced him to death, also ordering him to pay compensation to the victim's family. Hayat appealed his conviction, while the trial court simultaneously referred the death sentence to the High Court for confirmation, as required by law.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness testimony, the recovery of the murder weapon from the accused, and a positive firearms expert report. Although the witnesses were relatives or close to the deceased, the court held that this alone did not make their testimony unreliable, especially since the crime occurred in daylight and the witnesses' accounts were consistent with medical and forensic evidence. The court therefore upheld the conviction, ruling that the prosecution had proven its case beyond reasonable doubt.

However, the court found that the motive alleged in the initial police report had not been proven with solid evidence. Because of this gap, the judges decided that the death penalty was not justified, and instead converted the sentence to life imprisonment. The compensation order remained in place, and Hayat was given credit for time already spent in custody. This case illustrates how Pakistani courts distinguish between confirming guilt and deciding on the severity of punishment.

title: Niaz Muhammad Khoso v. Government of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved a government employee, Niaz Muhammad Khoso, who had won an appeal before the Balochistan Service Tribunal in March 2010. The Tribunal had set aside the order removing him from service and directed the relevant government authority to reconsider the withdrawal action against him after giving him a hearing, within one month. However, the government did not comply with this order, so the petitioner approached the Balochistan High Court asking it to direct the authorities to implement the Tribunal's judgment and reinstate him with back benefits.

The High Court did not rule on the merits of his reinstatement claim. Instead, it examined whether the petitioner had another proper legal route to get the Tribunal's order enforced. The Court noted that under Section 5(2) of the Balochistan Service Tribunals Act, 1974, the Service Tribunal is treated as a civil court when deciding appeals, and therefore has all the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, including powers to enforce its own judgments. This meant the petitioner could go back to the Tribunal itself and ask it to enforce compliance with its earlier order, rather than seeking a fresh remedy through a constitutional petition in the High Court.

Because this alternate and effective remedy existed, the High Court disposed of the petition, advising the petitioner to approach the Tribunal directly for enforcement. This case clarifies that Service Tribunals have enforcement powers akin to civil courts, guiding civil servants on the correct forum for enforcing tribunal judgments.

title: Abdul Sattar v. Federation of Pakistan,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Sattar, who claimed he had been interviewed and declared qualified for the post of Assistant Lineman at the Quetta Electric Supply Company (QESCO). He alleged that after the Director of Human Resources passed away, his appointment letter was withheld so that other, favored candidates could be given the job instead. He asked the Balochistan High Court to direct QESCO to issue him an appointment letter.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the petitioner could not produce any document proving he had actually participated in the interview, let alone that he had been declared qualified or selected. The interview call letter itself contained a clear disclaimer stating that merely being called for interview did not create any right to a job, and that eligibility would only be finally decided after interview, medical examination, and verification of documents. The court also noted that the petitioner had waited almost two years after the interview before filing his case, without explaining this delay.

The judges held that to invoke the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction under Article 199, a person must show an existing legal or fundamental right that has been violated. Since no law or rule gave the petitioner a right to appointment, and he failed to prove any such right was infringed, he had no standing to bring the case. The petition was dismissed at the initial stage.

title: Lal Muhammad V. Abdullah and others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of two men, Abdullah and Lal Muhammad, who had been accused of murdering a man named Jehangir during a violent incident in Balochistan. According to the prosecution, the deceased and others were chasing people who had stolen a tractor when a group of accused persons opened fire with Kalashnikovs, killing Jehangir. The motive alleged was a dispute over a marriage between the appellant's son and the daughter of one of the accused.

After trial, the Additional Sessions Judge acquitted both respondents, and the complainant, Lal Muhammad, challenged these acquittals before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence and upheld the acquittals. It noted that although eight people were named as accused, the actual fatal shooting was attributed only to one absconding accused, not the respondents. No weapons were recovered from the respondents to support the eyewitness accounts, and despite claims of heavy firing by multiple attackers, only four bullet casings were found at the scene, raising doubts about whether the witnesses had truly seen the event as described.

The court explained that appeals against acquittal are treated with extra caution, and interference is only warranted where there is clear error or injustice. Since the prosecution's case suffered from significant doubt, the court applied the principle that such doubt must benefit the accused, and dismissed the appeals, confirming the acquittals.

title: Mst. Khan Bibi and others V. Abdul Malik and others,
explainer:
This case involved the murder of a young man, Ghulam Nabi, who was shot and killed near Quetta in 2005. His mother, Mst. Khan Bibi, filed the initial police report, but it named different suspects based on suspicion arising from an earlier dispute over stolen goats. Later, three men, Abdul Malik, Muhammad Arif and Saleh Muhammad, were tried for the murder but were acquitted by the trial court, prompting the complainant to appeal against their acquittal.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the acquittals. It found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence: the eyewitnesses were closely related to the deceased, appeared at the scene under questionable circumstances, and had added exaggerated details to strengthen the case, undermining their credibility. Their account also did not match the medical evidence, and they behaved unusually for people supposedly witnessing a murder, doing nothing to help the victim or catch the attackers. The court also noted the prosecution failed to properly prove any motive, despite trying to establish one.

The judgment reinforces an important principle in criminal law: when the prosecution chooses to allege a motive, it must prove it convincingly, and courts must critically scrutinize eyewitness testimony, especially when witnesses are relatives of the victim and their conduct or accounts raise doubts. This case highlights how weak or inconsistent evidence can lead to acquittal even in serious crimes like murder, and why appellate courts are cautious about overturning acquittals without strong justification.

title: Abdul Wahid v. the State,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Wahid, who was convicted by a trial court in Khuzdar, Balochistan and sentenced to death for the murder of Hussain Bakhsh, who was shot while sleeping under a mosquito net in his home at night. The complainant, the victim's father, initially said in his police report that it was dark and he could not identify the shooter, but later the prosecution presented eyewitnesses claiming they had identified the appellant. Co-accused in the same case had already been acquitted by the trial court.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found the prosecution's case deeply flawed. Since all witnesses agreed there was no electric light and no other light source such as a torch or moonlight was mentioned, the court held it was not actually possible to identify anyone in the darkness, making the witnesses' claimed identification unreliable. The original FIR did not even name the appellant as the culprit, suggesting he was implicated later based on suspicion arising from prior family enmity. The court also found major contradictions regarding recovery of the alleged murder weapon, undermining the ballistics evidence, and noted medical evidence could not identify the actual perpetrator.

Applying the principle that any reasonable doubt must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not favor, the court set aside the conviction and death sentence, acquitting Abdul Wahid entirely. title: Haji Ghous-ud-Din v. The state through NAB authorities,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted by an Accountability Court in Quetta for corruption offenses under the National Accountability Ordinance. He was sentenced to prison and fined a large sum of money, with his properties to be auctioned to recover the fine if it wasn't paid. His appeal to the High Court reduced the fine amount, and his further petition to the Supreme Court was dismissed. He then served the alternative prison sentence for non-payment of the fine and later asked the Accountability Court to release his attached properties, arguing that since he had already served extra jail time in place of paying the fine, the authorities could no longer seize his property to recover it. The trial court rejected his request and instead allowed the authorities to auction his properties to recover the fine, and he appealed that decision.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed his appeal. It held that serving imprisonment in default of paying a fine does not cancel the obligation to pay the fine itself; the two are separate. The fine could still be recovered as arrears of land revenue under the relevant law, since the amount had been clearly fixed by the Supreme Court. The court also clarified that in NAB cases, a "fine" isn't just punishment but is meant to recover misappropriated public money and compensate the state. It further explained that recovery proceedings were within the legal time limit, counted from the Supreme Court's final order. This case matters because it confirms that convicts in corruption cases cannot escape repaying looted public money simply by serving extra jail time instead.

title: Haji Rehmatullah v. the State,
explainer:
This case concerns two petitions filed by Haji Rehmatullah and another person after the death of Ghulam Sarwar and injuries to Khan Jan during an incident on the Taftan border. According to Frontier Corps personnel, Sarwar died and Khan Jan was injured when their vehicle, allegedly smuggling narcotics, was fired upon after failing to stop. The petitioners gave a different account, claiming Sarwar was a bird trader who was shot without cause or justification by FC personnel. When police refused to register a case (FIR) against the FC personnel, the petitioners approached an Additional Sessions Judge acting as Justice of the Peace under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, seeking an order for registration. The Justice of the Peace dismissed their request.

The Balochistan High Court found this dismissal improper. It held that a Justice of the Peace has only limited powers under section 22-A and should not weigh disputed facts or decide the truth of allegations at that stage. If the complaint discloses a cognizable offence, the police (or Tehsildar in this area) are legally bound to register an FIR without first investigating who is right. The Court noted the Justice of the Peace's order gave no valid reasons and ignored the unnatural, unjustified killing described. It set aside the order and directed the Tehsildar to register the FIR and proceed according to law. The case reinforces that FIR registration is a mandatory first step, not something to be blocked by discretionary gatekeeping.

title: Fida Hussain V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves Fida Hussain, who was convicted by a Sessions Judge in Kalat, Balochistan, for possessing an unlicensed Kalashnikov rifle under the Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965, and sentenced to three years in prison plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The background was that Hussain had originally been arrested during an alleged encounter with a Levies (police) party while they were investigating a separate robbery case. He was acquitted in those original cases. The arms case was essentially a spinoff of that earlier incident.

The High Court found several serious problems with how the case was handled. The same person, a Naib Tehsildar named Ghulam Haider, acted as both the complainant and the investigating officer, even though he was allegedly involved in the encounter itself. The trial court had already disbelieved his testimony in the related cases. Additionally, despite the arrest happening in a populated area with many bystanders present, no independent witnesses from the public were included in the recovery process, violating a legal requirement meant to ensure fair investigations. There was also no forensic report confirming the weapon was operational.

Given these serious procedural failures and the lack of credible, independent evidence, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitting Hussain. The judgment underscores that police or officials involved in disputed encounters should not investigate their own actions, and that recoveries must be properly witnessed to ensure fairness.

title: Mst. Perveen Kousar and others V. Shakil Ahmed and others,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murdering his brother-in-law with a dagger. He was sentenced by a trial court in Quetta to life imprisonment under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, along with a fine payable to the deceased's heirs. He appealed the conviction, while the complainant separately sought enhancement of his sentence.

The Balochistan High Court found a serious procedural flaw in the trial. During the trial, the defence lawyer had tried to cross-examine the Investigating Officer about earlier statements made by prosecution witnesses to the police, pointing out contradictions and improvements in their court testimony. The trial judge had refused to allow this line of questioning, which the High Court held was a clear violation of Article 140 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (the law of evidence), which lays down a specific procedure for confronting witnesses and investigators with prior statements to test their credibility.

The High Court ruled that skipping this required procedure was not a minor irregularity but a fundamental unfairness that prejudiced the accused's right to a fair trial. It set aside the conviction and sent the case back to the trial court, directing it to re-examine the Investigating Officer and give the defence a proper opportunity to cross-examine him according to law. The complainant's request to increase the sentence was dismissed.

This case matters because it reinforces those accused of crimes have a legal right to properly challenge witness credibility, and courts must follow prescribed evidentiary procedures strictly.

title: Abdul Lateef V. The State,
explainer:
Abdul Lateef was convicted by a Special Judge in Balochistan under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, for possessing 40 kilograms of heroin, and was sentenced to life imprisonment along with a fine. Police, acting on secret information, raided his house and recovered the heroin from beneath the bedding of a cot he was sitting on. He appealed his conviction to the Balochistan High Court.

His lawyer argued that the investigation was invalid because it was carried out by Criminal Investigation Agency (CIA) staff, who are not legally authorized to investigate such cases, and that other procedural requirements were not followed, including that only a small sample of the heroin (40 grams) was sent for chemical testing rather than the whole quantity.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It held that while CIA personnel technically lack power to investigate cognizable offences, this was only a procedural irregularity since the case had properly been registered at a police station and the police station's own officer had filed the formal charges. Since no actual prejudice or injustice resulted, and the accused hadn't objected during trial, this did not invalidate the proceedings. The court also confirmed that sending only a sample for chemical analysis is legally sufficient, and found the defence's claims implausible. The appeal was dismissed and the conviction upheld.

This case matters because it clarifies that minor procedural lapses in narcotics investigations do not automatically void a conviction if no real harm was caused to the accused.

title: Samiullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns a man named Samiullah who was convicted for drug trafficking under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. He was stopped at a checkpoint in Quetta while driving a car, and police found 40 kilograms of hashish hidden behind the rear seat. He was arrested and later convicted by a Special Judge, sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine.

On appeal, his lawyer argued the prosecution's evidence was contradictory and unreliable, that no private witnesses were involved in the recovery (as normally required under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code), and that the defence evidence was more credible.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments and upheld the conviction. It clarified an important legal point: while Section 29 of the Act creates a presumption of guilt once the prosecution proves recovery of narcotics, this does not remove the prosecution's basic duty to first prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The presumption only shifts the burden to the accused after that initial proof is established.

The court also held that Section 103 Cr.P.C. (requiring independent witnesses during searches) does not apply to narcotics cases, so police testimony alone can be sufficient if credible. Since Samiullah was driving the car and controlled it, he was deemed to be in conscious possession of the drugs found inside. Finding the police account credible and the defence story implausible, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld his conviction and sentence.

title: Bibi Hanifa V. Dr. Jamila Gynaecologist, Civil Hospital Pishin,
explainer:
This case involved a woman, Bibi Hanifa, who underwent surgery at a government hospital in Pishin during a difficult childbirth. She later accused the doctors involved of negligence, alleging that her baby died due to their carelessness and that two surgical sponges were left inside her abdomen after the operation, causing her pain. She filed a private criminal complaint against the doctors under a section of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with causing hurt through rash or negligent acts. The trial court acquitted the doctors, and she then sought leave to appeal against that acquittal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court refused to grant leave to appeal, upholding the acquittal. It noted that the complaint was filed nine months after the operation with no explanation for the delay, and that the doctor who actually performed the surgery had not even been named as an accused. The evidence showed the operation was carried out in an emergency situation with the husband's consent and was successful in delivering a live baby, who died later of natural causes. The alleged sponges were never mentioned during the initial inquiry or trial, undermining that claim. The court reaffirmed the legal principle that an acquittal carries a strong presumption of innocence that should not be disturbed unless the original decision was clearly unreasonable or unjust, which was not the case here.

title: Mst. Jamila Nargis v. Secretary to the Government of Pakistan,
explainer:
This case concerns a long-running dispute over a shop built on a plot in Quetta that had originally been allotted to the petitioner's father-in-law by the Evacuee Trust Property authorities after the property was left vacant following Partition. He built a shop there and rented it to a tenant. Years later, in 1976, authorities wrongly allotted the shop itself to that tenant's family without proper survey. This transfer was challenged through the courts, and in 1998 the Supreme Court of Pakistan finally ruled in favour of the original allottee's side, dismissing the tenant family's claim.

After her husband died in 1992, the petitioner applied to have the tenancy of the shop restored in her name, and this was granted. However, nearly a decade later, the tenant's successors objected, arguing that under the 1977 Scheme governing evacuee trust properties, the tenancy could not legally be transferred to her. Government authorities accepted this objection, cancelled her tenancy, and ordered the shop to be auctioned instead.

The Balochistan High Court found that this reversal ignored the Supreme Court's earlier binding decision and had no legal basis, since the matter had already been conclusively settled. The court set aside the orders cancelling her tenancy and directed that the shop be vacated from the private respondents and handed back to the petitioner. The judgment reinforces the principle that disputes should be decided on their merits, and that parties should not be allowed to exploit technicalities to defeat settled judicial decisions.

title: Muhammad Asif V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a murder appeal from Balochistan. Muhammad Asif was convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Khuzdar and sentenced to death for killing Munawar Shahwani by shooting him in the forehead with a pistol, during a gathering at a university hostel lawn. The complainant, a friend who witnessed the shooting, promptly reported the incident, naming only the accused. The accused fled but was later arrested by police in Mastung along with the vehicle he had used to escape.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence and upheld the conviction and death sentence. The court found the eyewitness accounts credible, detailed, and consistent, noting that friendship between the witnesses and the victim did not undermine their credibility since there was no evidence of any motive to falsely implicate the accused. The daylight setting and familiarity between the parties ruled out mistaken identity. The eyewitness testimony was also supported by medical evidence confirming the fatal gunshot wound.

Importantly, the court clarified that the absence of a recovered murder weapon or unclear motive does not automatically weaken a prosecution's case if there is strong direct evidence, such as credible eyewitness testimony. This judgment reinforces the principle that Pakistani courts prioritize consistent, corroborated eyewitness accounts over technical gaps like weapon recovery when deciding serious criminal cases like murder.

title: Zaffar V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Zaffar who was convicted by a Sessions Judge for the murder (qatl-e-amd) of a person named Aqeel and sentenced to life imprisonment along with a fine to be paid to the deceased's family. He appealed this conviction to the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution had no eyewitness to the killing and relied entirely on circumstantial evidence: a judicial confession by the accused, an axe allegedly recovered based on his disclosure, and the fact that the victim's body was found near or connected to the accused's location. However, the High Court found serious problems with this evidence. The confession appeared to have been obtained through torture rather than given voluntarily. Witnesses last saw the deceased with a co-accused, not with Zaffar himself. The blood-stained axe was sent for forensic testing after an unexplained one-and-a-half month delay, and even the lab report did not confirm the blood matched the victim's blood group. The court noted that recovery of a weapon is only supporting evidence and cannot by itself justify a conviction without stronger direct proof. Similarly, merely finding the body near the accused's house did not prove he committed the murder.

Given these gaps, the court held that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, emphasizing that any doubt must benefit the accused. As a result, Zaffar was acquitted. The case highlights how convictions cannot rest on weak, delayed, or coerced evidence, reinforcing the fundamental principle that guilt must be established

title: Tor Jan alias Jag V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Tor Jan, who was convicted by a trial court in Killa Abdullah and sentenced to life imprisonment for allegedly kidnapping his neighbor's sister, Bibi Rabia, who was later found dead with gunshot wounds. The prosecution claimed he broke into the family's house at night and abducted the woman, whose body was eventually found and identified in Afghanistan.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted Tor Jan. The judges found serious flaws in the prosecution's case: the FIR was filed thirteen days after the incident with no explanation for the delay, despite the police station being only four kilometers away. The witnesses were all closely related to the complainant and had personal animosity toward the accused. Since the abduction allegedly happened at night in darkness, the court doubted the witnesses could reliably identify the culprit. No medical or official documents were produced to prove how the woman died. The trial court's own reasoning was contradictory, first saying death by shooting wasn't proven, then treating it as proven anyway.

The High Court emphasized that in criminal cases, the prosecution must prove guilt beyond doubt, and any reasonable doubt must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not favor. This case matters because it reinforces important legal safeguards: unexplained delays in reporting crimes, biased witnesses, and weak evidence cannot justify a conviction, protecting individuals from wrongful punishment based on suspicion rather than solid proof.

title: Khudai Dad alias Pehlwan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Khuda-e-Dad alias Pehalwan, convicted of murdering Miran Jan and injuring another man, Muhammad Khan, by firing at them near Refugee Camp No.5 in Quetta on 1 June 2006. The trial court sentenced him to life imprisonment for murder, plus additional sentences for attempted murder and causing injury. He appealed his conviction, while the complainant separately sought enhancement of his sentence to death.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence, including testimony from two prosecution witnesses who were relatives of the deceased. The court held that being related to the victim does not automatically make witnesses unreliable, especially when their account is consistent, supported by medical evidence, recovered weapons, and forensic lab reports, and when the crime occurred in broad daylight, ruling out mistaken identity. Finding no serious contradictions in the evidence, the court upheld the conviction and dismissed the appellant's appeal.

On the question of enhancing the sentence to death, the court noted the killing was not premeditated, the accused had not initiated the encounter, and the real motive was never disclosed by the prosecution. Given also a six-year delay in the case, the court declined to increase the punishment and dismissed the complainant's revision petition.

The judgment matters because it reaffirms two principles: relatives' testimony can still be credible if corroborated by other evidence, and death sentences should not be imposed where premeditation and motive remain unclear.

title: Nasrullah alias Nasro and another V. The State and another,

His conviction under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code was appealed to the Balochistan High Court, which also had to confirm or set aside the death sentence referred by the Sessions Judge.

Two eyewitnesses, relatives of the deceased, testified to seeing the murder. The defense argued they were "interested witnesses" due to their family connection and pointed to some inconsistencies with medical evidence and the exact location of the crime scene. The court rejected these arguments, holding that mere relationship to the victim does not make a witness unreliable unless there is actual hostility toward the accused. It found the witnesses' accounts credible and well-supported by other evidence, including the accused's pistol being recovered based on his own disclosure, a positive ballistic report matching the weapon, and the fact that the accused had fled and remained absconding for two months without any reasonable explanation, which the court treated as evidence pointing to guilt.

The court also ruled that even though the prosecution failed to prove a specific motive, this alone was not enough to avoid the death penalty, since death remains the normal punishment for murder unless mitigating circumstances exist. Finding none here, the High Court upheld the conviction and confirmed the death sentence, dismissing the appeal. The case reinforces principles about evaluating witness credibility and the weight given to absconding as corroborative evid

title: Syed Muhammad Javed Ahmed V. The State and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a lawyer who stood as a surety, on humanitarian grounds, for an alien accused facing minor charges under the Foreigners Act and Foreigners Order for issues related to his registration documents. When that accused later jumped bail and could not be produced, the trial court ordered forfeiture of the entire surety amount of Rs.40,000, and this order was upheld on revision by the Sessions Judge. The surety then approached the Balochistan High Court through a constitutional petition, seeking to have the forfeiture set aside or reduced.

The High Court held that standing surety for someone, especially a foreigner with no local connections, is an act of generosity and should not be punished harshly unless there is clear evidence that the surety acted with an ulterior motive or helped the accused escape. Courts must balance fairness with deterrence: sureties for serious crimes like murder, kidnapping, or terrorism deserve strict treatment, but those involved with minor offences should be treated leniently, since undue severity could discourage people from ever standing bail for others.

Finding no evidence that the surety had colluded with the absconding accused, and noting the accused's offence was minor, the court reduced the forfeited amount from Rs.40,000 to Rs.20,000. The judgment is significant because it sets out guidelines on how courts should decide the extent of forfeiture of bail bonds, distinguishing between serious and minor offences.

title: Ghous Bakhsh and others V. The State,
explainer:
Ghous Bakhsh had been convicted in three separate trials before the Sessions Judge, Kalat Division at Mastung, arising from three different FIRs involving separate incidents: an attempted motorcycle snatching with firing, a daylight robbery in which shepherds were tied up and 250 sheep stolen, and a firing incident that injured a man. He received different sentences in each case, including under sections dealing with attempted robbery, robbery, and causing hurt.

On appeal, his lawyer argued that under Section 35 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the sentences should run concurrently rather than one after another, since this would reduce his overall time in prison.

The Balochistan High Court rejected this argument. It explained that Section 35 only allows concurrent sentences when a person is convicted of multiple offences in a single trial. Since Ghous Bakhsh was convicted in three separate trials for distinct crimes committed at different times against different victims, this provision did not apply. The court distinguished this from Section 397, which deals with sentences imposed in different trials, and noted that even under its inherent powers, it could not order concurrent sentences for unrelated offences committed at different times.

The court also emphasized that sentencing serves both to deter crime and reform offenders, and must be neither too harsh nor too lenient. Since the appellant had already received minimum sentences and credit for time served, his appeals were dismissed as without merit.

title: Shah Jahan and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Nasrullah and Shah Jahan, convicted by a Sessions Court in Mastung for murdering Abdul Waheed and sentenced to life imprisonment plus compensation. Both appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution's case rested largely on circumstantial evidence: a witness had seen the deceased last in the company of one accused, and during police interrogation that accused led officers to a well where the victim's body was recovered after he admitted killing him with a knife. Medical evidence supported the cause of death.

The High Court examined the two appellants differently. For the accused who was seen with the deceased before his disappearance and who led police to the body, the Court held that this chain of circumstances - last-seen evidence, recovery of the body on his pointing it out, and medical evidence - was strong enough to prove guilt beyond doubt. His conviction was upheld.

For the second accused (co-accused), the only evidence was his own statement implicating himself, made during interrogation. The Court ruled this amounted to an inadmissible confession under the law of evidence, since it did not lead to discovery of any new fact - the location was already known to police. With no independent evidence connecting him to the crime, he was given the benefit of the doubt and acquitted.

The judgment illustrates how courts evaluate circumstantial evidence and confessions, and how the same set of facts can lead to different outcomes for different accused persons.

title: Faiz Muhammad Jaffar v. the State,
explainer:
This case involved corruption charges under Pakistan's National Accountability Ordinance, 1999, relating to a government procurement scheme where tenders were called for supplying school materials like furniture and books under a World Bank-assisted education project. A contracting firm was allegedly awarded contracts despite quoting higher rates than competitors, and payments were made based on fake receipts even though goods were never actually supplied to schools. Officials were accused of accepting bribes or commissions in exchange for releasing payments to the contractor.

The trial court convicted three accused persons—Faiz Muhammad Jaffar, Sikandar, and Muhammad Rasheed Anjum—sentencing them to varying prison terms and heavy fines. They appealed, arguing that the witnesses who paid commissions were themselves complicit in illegality and thus untrustworthy accomplices.

The Balochistan High Court rejected this defense, holding that the witnesses had been forced to pay commissions only because officials withheld payment otherwise, so they weren't willing accomplices. The court also explained that once bribery is alleged, the burden shifts to the accused to prove any payment was legitimate remuneration—a burden the appellants failed to meet.

The court upheld the convictions and fines but reduced the prison sentences to time already served. It also clarified that if a convicted person dies, their fine can still be recovered from their estate, since criminal liability ends with death but financial liability does not. This case reinforces how corruption cases involving public funds are evaluated and how accountability continues even

title: Bohair Qazi and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Bohair Qazi, who was accused in several criminal cases involving robbery and related offences under the Pakistan Penal Code. He was in jail custody but had suffered a severe leg injury that led to gangrene, a serious and potentially life-threatening condition where body tissue dies due to poor blood supply. His leg had already been partly amputated, and doctors recommended further specialized treatment, including possible surgery in Karachi or abroad, which was not available in the jail hospital.

His bail applications had earlier been rejected by the trial court on the ground that he had not surrendered and was considered a "fugitive from law." He then approached the Balochistan High Court seeking bail purely on medical grounds.

The High Court examined medical certificates confirming the seriousness of his condition and ruled that continued detention in jail, where proper treatment was not possible, posed a direct threat to his life. Relying on precedents from the Supreme Court, the judge held that bail cannot be treated as punishment, and that when an accused suffers from a disease that cannot be treated in jail and endangers his life, he is entitled to bail on medical grounds.

The court granted him bail in all the connected cases. This judgment reaffirms the principle that health and human life must be protected even for undertrial prisoners, and that bail on medical grounds is a legitimate legal remedy, not an exception to punishment.

title: Khalil Ahmed and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved three men, Khalil Ahmed, Muhammad Ali alias Heera, and Mumtaz Brohi, convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Turbat for kidnapping for ransom. The victims, two brothers traveling from Gwadar to Karachi, were abducted and their family was contacted demanding Rs. 5 crore in ransom. The trial court sentenced Muhammad Ali and Mumtaz Brohi to life imprisonment for abduction for ransom under the Penal Code and Anti-Terrorism Act, and Khalil Ahmed to life imprisonment for abetting the crime.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found a serious procedural flaw. When one of the accused was arrested later and joined the trial, the earlier prosecution witnesses were only recalled for cross-examination based on their previously recorded testimony, instead of having their full examination-in-chief repeated in his presence. The law requires that a witness's main testimony be recorded in the presence of every accused person, not just that they be made available for cross-examination. The court also noted that crucial mobile phone call-location data used to convict the accused had never been formally presented as evidence in court, which unfairly prejudiced the defense.

Because of these violations, the High Court set aside the convictions and sent the case back to the trial court for the witnesses to be properly re-examined. The judgment stresses that speedy justice must not come at the cost of fair and lawful trial procedure.

title: Khadim Hussain v the State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Khadim Hussain and Ghulam Sarwar, who were accused of murdering Juma Khan and Mst. Bakhtawar in Quetta in 2006, allegedly on the pretext of siyahkari, meaning suspected illicit relations, often described as an honour killing. They were charged under Section 302 (murder) read with Section 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code. A trial court had earlier refused them bail. They then approached the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the families of the victims had forgiven them and reached a compromise outside court, so they should be granted bail.

The High Court rejected this argument and refused bail. It held that no one has the right to take the law into their own hands and kill people in the name of honour or ghairat, calling such killings un-Islamic, illegal, and unconstitutional, violating the right to life protected under Article 9 of the Constitution, with customs justifying such killings being void under Article 8(1). The court clarified that while such offences can sometimes be compounded, any compromise is not automatically valid just because families agree privately outside court; it must be formally sanctioned by a court, which retains discretion to refuse it based on the case's circumstances. Since the accused were named in a promptly filed FIR, had been absconders, and were involved in taking two lives under the guise of honour, they did not qualify for bail.

This judgment matters because it firmly rejects honour as a legal justification for murder and limits misuse of private compromises to escape prosecution.

title: Fazal Mir alias Zallai and another V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a murder conviction from the Balochistan High Court. The accused, Fazal Mir alias Zallai, had been sentenced to death by a trial court for shooting and killing Saleh Muhammad, who was making ablution near a disputed piece of land. The dispute arose because the accused claimed ownership of the land and had, a day before the killing, tried to stop the deceased from working on it. When the deceased continued using the land, the accused fired at him and also allegedly fired shots toward the complainant and a witness.

The accused argued that the prosecution had not proven its case beyond reasonable doubt, pointing to issues like witness relationships with the deceased, a delay in filing the police report, and failure to recover the murder weapon. The High Court rejected these arguments, finding that relatives of a victim are not automatically "interested witnesses" unless they have a personal motive to falsely accuse someone, and that the failure to recover the weapon or minor delays in reporting did not undermine an otherwise credible, consistent account of the crime.

However, the Court found mitigating circumstances: the accused had fired only a single shot despite having the chance to fire more, and the killing followed provocation from a property dispute. Because of this, while his conviction was upheld, his death sentence was reduced to life imprisonment. The case highlights how courts weigh witness credibility and use mitigating factors to moderate sentencing in murder cases.

title: Haji Abdul Majeed and others V. Amjad Khan and others,
explainer:
This case was about a decades-old land dispute in Loralai, Balochistan, involving several plots of agricultural land. The dispute traced back to a 1958 agreement in which the defendants' predecessor sold land to the plaintiffs' predecessor for a set price, part of which was paid upfront with the rest due in installments. The defendants argued the buyer failed to pay the remaining installments, so the agreement was cancelled and the land reverted to them. The plaintiffs, however, claimed ownership and possession, alleging the defendants had illegally interfered with their land by digging wells and installing a transformer. Lower courts had ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, and after an earlier appeal, the Supreme Court sent the case back to the High Court for a fresh, more thorough hearing on all the issues raised.

The Balochistan High Court examined several legal points: how much weight should be given to original land-revenue records (very strong evidentiary weight, hard to overturn), whether time was strictly essential in property contracts (not necessarily, especially where substantial performance already occurred), and rules about proving the execution of documents through witnesses. These principles guided how the court evaluated the competing claims of ownership and the validity of the 1958 agreement.

The case matters because it clarifies important evidentiary and contract-law principles applicable to long-running property disputes in Pakistan, particularly regarding revenue records and specific performance timelines.
