title: Muhammad Alam V. Noor Muhammad and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over whether a Justice of the Peace could order police to directly register a criminal case (FIR) against someone, even after officials had already investigated and found the allegations to be false.

A man named Noor Muhammad had filed a complaint against Muhammad Alam. A Tehsildar (local official) investigated and reported that the allegations were baseless. Despite this, the Sessions Judge, acting as Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace, ordered the Tehsildar to register an FIR against Alam anyway. Alam challenged this order before the Balochistan High Court, arguing it was improperly issued without following the law and that it unfairly prejudiced him despite the earlier finding that the complaint was false.

The High Court agreed with Alam. It explained that under the law, a Justice of the Peace only has the power to ensure police properly entertain a complaint and investigate it if it discloses a cognizable offence—not to directly order an FIR's registration as if guilt were already established. Since the word "may" is used in the law, this power is discretionary, not mandatory, and should not be exercised automatically or bindly.

Because the Tehsildar had already found the complaint false, the court ruled there was no justification for directing an FIR. It set aside the earlier order and instead directed the Tehsildar to properly examine the complaint and register a case only if a genuine cognizable offence was found. This judgment reinforces protections against misuse of the FIR process and clarifies the limited role of a Justice of the Peace in criminal complaints.

title: Suleman and others V. Pir Bakhsh and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family land dispute in Gwadar, Balochistan. The petitioners claimed they were the rightful owners of certain land inherited from their grandfather, but said the respondents, with help from revenue officials, had fraudulently transferred the land records (mutation) into their own names. The trial court dismissed the petitioners' suits after hearing evidence. When the petitioners appealed, the appellate court refused to even hear the appeal, returning it on the technical ground that the case's value exceeded its pecuniary jurisdiction, partly based on a compensation amount reportedly paid by the Civil Aviation Authority for the land.

The High Court found this approach wrong. It held that if a court believes a suit is undervalued, it must give the plaintiff a chance to correct the valuation before rejecting the case, which had not happened here. It also clarified that for deciding which court has jurisdiction, the value stated in the suit itself matters, not the property's market value or any compensation figure, unless that valuation is formally challenged and a proper issue is framed. The High Court also noted that courts can add necessary parties with an interest in a case, such as the Civil Aviation Authority here, using their inherent powers.

As a result, the High Court set aside the appellate court's order and sent the case back for fresh proceedings, directing that proper issues on valuation and court fees be framed first. This case matters because it reinforces that technical jurisdictional objections cannot be used to deny litigants a fair hearing without following proper procedure.

title: Abdul Qahir alias Sadiq v. Bibi Aisha,
explainer:
This case is about a legal dispute over possession of a house in Quetta. Bibi Aisha, a widow, filed a complaint claiming that her late husband's property was forcibly occupied by Abdul Qahir and three others. Since her husband had died, the property legally passed to her and her heirs under Islamic inheritance rules, even though it was still officially recorded in her deceased husband's name. While she and her son were away, her watchman was staying at the house and was forcibly removed by the accused. A trial court used the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005 to order that possession be restored to her.

The accused challenged this in the Balochistan High Court, arguing the complainant's documents were fake, that she wasn't the legal owner or occupier, and that she therefore had no right to bring the complaint.

The High Court dismissed their petition and upheld the trial court's order. It ruled that a widow inherits her husband's property automatically upon his death, making her a lawful owner even before formal transfer of records. It also held that having a watchman live in the property counted as her "possession," since possession under the law includes constructive possession—meaning control through another person—not just physical occupation. The court further clarified that filing a police report (FIR) doesn't block someone from also seeking remedy under the Illegal Dispossession Act, and doing so doesn't amount to double punishment for the same offense. The judgment emphasizes the State's duty to protect the property rights of widows and orphans.

title: Muhammad Majid V. Gul Muhammad and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about whether police in Pakistan can register a First Information Report (FIR) against a Pakistani citizen for an offence that actually took place outside Pakistan. The petitioner, Muhammad Majid, was accused under section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code (dishonestly issuing a cheque) after cheques he issued to the complainant bounced at a bank in Dubai. He asked the Balochistan High Court to quash the FIR, arguing that local police had no jurisdiction over an offence committed abroad, and that section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code requires special government or political-agent certification before such a case can even proceed.

The court explained that Pakistani law does allow citizens to be tried in Pakistan for offences committed abroad, under sections 3 and 4 of the Penal Code and section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code. However, the requirement to obtain certification or sanction under section 188 only applies before the case can be formally "inquired into" or tried in court, not before an FIR is registered or investigated by police. This sanction can be obtained later, even after the police complete their investigation and file charges.

Since the bar in law applies only to trial/inquiry stage and not registration, the court refused to quash the FIR. It ruled that the complainant and police could proceed to seek the necessary government sanction while continuing the investigation, and dismissed the petitioner's application.

title: Baloch Khan V. Haji Ahmed Shah and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a land sale dispute that turned into a criminal complaint. Haji Ahmed Shah sold 50 acres of land to Baloch Khan for a total price of over three crore rupees. Only part of the payment (fifty lakh rupees) was made, and the buyer allegedly backed out of the agreement without paying the rest. Instead of pursuing this as a civil matter, the seller got a police FIR registered against the buyer under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with cheating and fraud.

The buyer approached the Balochistan High Court directly, asking for the FIR to be quashed, arguing the dispute was purely civil in nature and did not amount to any criminal offence. The respondents argued he should have first approached the trial court under a different legal provision before coming to the High Court.

The High Court held that while it is normally proper to approach the trial court first, the High Court is not barred from directly using its inherent powers to prevent abuse of court process or to secure justice. Examining the facts, the judge found that the dispute was essentially a civil disagreement over an unpaid sale amount, wrongly dressed up as a criminal case. Since the FIR did not disclose any real criminal offence, the police had no jurisdiction to register it, making the whole proceeding invalid. The FIR was therefore quashed, reinforcing that civil disputes over contracts should not be misused as criminal cases.

title: Khadim Hussain V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about Khadim Hussain, who was accused of murder and related offences and had been in jail since December 2009 awaiting trial. His trial had dragged on for over two and a half years without conclusion. He had earlier applied for bail, which the High Court had refused, but with a direction that the trial court finish the trial within one month. That deadline passed without progress, so he applied for bail again.

The trial court had earlier refused bail by calling him a dangerous and desperate criminal because of his alleged involvement in a previous murder case. The High Court found this reasoning flawed, since he had actually been acquitted in that earlier case, so he could not fairly be labelled dangerous or desperate.

The High Court examined a 2011 amendment to section 497 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which entitles an accused to bail if trial is delayed beyond a fixed period, unless the delay is his own fault or he falls into excluded categories like repeat offenders or dangerous criminals. Since neither exception applied here, the court held he had a statutory right to bail.

The prosecution promised to finish the trial within one month. The court ordered the trial to conclude within that time, failing which the accused would automatically be deemed granted bail. This case highlights the constitutional right to a fair and speedy trial and limits on prolonged pretrial detention.

title: Ajab Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves Ajab Khan, who was convicted by a trial court for causing death and injuries through rash and negligent driving, an offense classified under Pakistan's Penal Code as qatl-e-khata (unintentional killing). He was sentenced to 10 years imprisonment along with orders to pay diyat (compensation for death) of Rs. 500,000 per victim and daman (compensation for injury) of Rs. 20,000 per injured person. The trial court had also ordered that he remain imprisoned until the diyat and daman amounts were paid.

Khan appealed and asked the Balochistan High Court to suspend his sentence and release him on bail while the appeal was pending, arguing that his offense was legally bailable and that he had already been out on bail during the original trial.

The High Court agreed to suspend the sentence and grant bail. It reasoned that since the offense was both bailable and compoundable (meaning the parties could reach a settlement), keeping Khan in jail would actually prevent him from earning money to pay the compensation he owed. The court felt that releasing him would give him a realistic chance to arrange the funds and could also open the door to a compromise between the families involved, promoting reconciliation.

This case matters because it illustrates how courts balance punishment with practical considerations, particularly in cases involving financial compensation to victims, favoring outcomes that could lead to compensation being paid and relationships being restored rather than pure incarceration.

title: Secretary C&W v. Dad Bakhsh,
explainer:
This case involved a contractor, Dad Bakhsh, who sued the Communication and Works Department of the Balochistan Government and its officials, claiming they owed him money he had spent on their verbal instructions, including expenses incurred during a visit by senior officers and for extra construction work. The government officials were served with the lawsuit but failed to properly defend it: their written statement was signed only by their lawyer instead of by them personally, they did not clearly deny the contractor's claims, and they later stopped appearing in court altogether. Based on this, the trial court passed an ex parte (one-sided) judgment against the government without ever recording evidence or examining witnesses, and this decision was upheld on appeal. The court then allowed the government's own Rest House to be auctioned off to satisfy the decree.

The Balochistan High Court found serious flaws in this process. It ruled that pleadings alone are not evidence, that the decree was issued on a date that wasn't even a proper hearing date, that summons was never properly served on the key official, and that government property cannot be sold based on such a legally void decree. The court suspected collusion between the contractor and the officials who failed to defend the case properly, causing loss to public funds. It set aside the earlier decisions, sent the case back for a proper trial with evidence, and ordered the government to investigate and hold the responsible officials accountable. The case highlights the importance of due process and safeguarding public money from careless or collusive litigation.

title: Arab v. State,
explainer:
This case involves Arab, convicted of murdering Bashir Ahmed in Loralai in 2008. The dispute arose over vacating a rented shop. Bashir Ahmed was shot with a Kalashnikov near a mosque and later died from his injuries. Arab confessed to the crime before a judicial magistrate a day after his arrest, having voluntarily surrendered to police along with the weapon used. He later retracted this confession during trial, but the trial court convicted him of qatl-e-amd (intentional murder) under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, sentencing him to life imprisonment plus compensation to the victim's family.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court upheld the conviction but reduced the charge to section 302(c), a lesser category of murder, and cut the sentence from life imprisonment to fourteen years. The court found the confession voluntary, properly recorded following legal procedure, and supported by medical evidence and motive, even though the murder weapon's forensic report was unavailable due to a lab accident. Importantly, the court noted that before the shooting, the deceased had entered the accused's house and misbehaved, suggesting the victim's own conduct contributed to the fatal confrontation, which justified leniency in sentencing.

This judgment matters because it clarifies how courts evaluate confessions that are later withdrawn, confirms that a voluntary, credible confession alone can support conviction, and shows how provocation or victim conduct can influence sentencing even when guilt is established.

title: Saleh Muhammad alias Hashim Marri v. State,
explainer:
This case is about a shooting that took place at a fruit shop in Hub, Balochistan, on 14 April 2010. According to the complainant, an argument over Rs. 20 change escalated when the accused, Saleh Muhammad alias Hashim Marri, left the shop threatening revenge, then returned about 20-25 minutes later with two armed companions and opened fire on the shopkeeper and others present. Two people, the complainant's cousin and brother, were killed, and three others were injured. Police registered an FIR shortly after the incident and recovered a pistol from the accused at the scene.

The trial court convicted Saleh Muhammad under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder) and sentenced him to death. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, and the case also came up for confirmation of the death sentence.

The High Court upheld the conviction and confirmed the death sentence. It found the FIR was lodged promptly, the eyewitness account matched the medical evidence, the motive (the argument over money) was credible, and the recovered weapon was forensically linked to the crime. The court also clarified important legal principles: a single witness's testimony can be enough for conviction if trustworthy; being related to the victim doesn't automatically make a witness unreliable; and failure to recover bullet casings or weak motive evidence doesn't necessarily undermine an otherwise solid prosecution case. The appeal was dismissed, and the death sentence stood confirmed.

title: State v. Noor-ud-Din,
explainer:
This case involved the killing of a man, Nazeer Ahmed, and a woman, Mst. Zubaida, on allegations of "Karo Kari" (so-called honour killing). title: Aftab Iqbal Khilji v. State,
explainer:
This case involves a police officer, Aftab Iqbal Khilji, who was convicted in two separate criminal cases: one for possessing illegal arms and another for accepting a bribe (illegal gratification). His appeals against both convictions were dismissed by the Balochistan High Court in 2002 and 2004. Years later, in 2009, he filed review petitions asking the High Court to reconsider those earlier judgments, arguing his lawyer had not properly argued his case and that he had already suffered hardship, including losing his job.

The High Court examined whether it had the power to review its own criminal judgments, noting that while the law does not explicitly allow review of criminal judgments, courts can use their inherent powers to correct clear errors or jurisdictional mistakes if leaving them uncorrected would cause serious injustice.

The Court found no such error here. It noted the review petitions were filed nearly five years after the original judgments, with no reasonable explanation for the delay, and suspected the petitions were filed mainly to create grounds for his reinstatement in the police force, which had occurred shortly before the review petitions were filed. The Court called this suspicious and indicative of bad faith by both the petitioner and police authorities.

The Court refused to interfere with the convictions and sentences, dismissing the review petitions. The case highlights limits on using court review powers to reverse settled convictions long after the fact, especially when motivated by service-related benefits rather than genuine legal errors.

title: The State through Prosecutor General Accountability, Pakistan V. Tariq Nouman and another,
explainer:
This case involved allegations of corruption after a 2004 attack on a Moharram procession in Quetta caused deaths and destruction of property. The government released about 180 million rupees in compensation, but complaints arose that officials had approved payments to undeserving people instead of genuine victims. A National Accountability Bureau reference was filed against several accused, including public officeholders, under corruption-related provisions. Before trial evidence was fully examined, the Accountability Court accepted applications filed by the accused under section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code and acquitted them without a full trial. The State appealed this early acquittal.

The Balochistan High Court held that acquittals granted under section 265-K (or the similar section 249-A) do not carry the same weight as acquittals reached after a complete trial, since they short-circuit the normal evidentiary process. The court stressed that in corruption cases involving public money, trial courts must be especially cautious before acquitting the accused early, and prosecutors must be given a full opportunity to prove their case. Noting that witness testimony existed, that many claims were suspicious, and that some accused had returned large sums of allegedly embezzled money, the court found this evidence needed proper explanation rather than dismissal. It set aside the acquittals and sent the cases back to resume full trial proceedings.

title: Ali Ahmed Baloch v. the State through NAB authorities,
explainer:
Ali Ahmed Baloch, a retired provincial secretary, was convicted under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999 for holding assets far beyond his known income. He was sentenced to seven years imprisonment, a large number of his properties were confiscated, and he was also ordered to pay a fine. His appeal against the conviction was dismissed by the Supreme Court, after which NAB filed proceedings to recover the fine as arrears of land revenue. While that recovery case was pending, Baloch applied for a plea bargain under section 25 of the Ordinance, and his family members applied to be added as parties. The trial court rejected both applications and allowed NAB's recovery application, and these rulings were challenged before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the appeals and petition. It held that serving a prison sentence for defaulting on fine payment does not cancel the obligation to actually pay the fine, especially in corruption cases where the fine represents public money that must be recovered. It also ruled that a plea bargain can only be requested before an accused is investigated, or during trial or a pending appeal, not after the courts have already given a final verdict. Since Baloch's conviction had already been upheld by the Supreme Court, the trial court had no power left to consider a plea bargain. NAB was found entitled to auction his remaining property to recover the fine. This case clarifies that accountability courts cannot be used to bypass final convictions through last-minute plea bargains, and that fines in corruption cases remain enforceable even after imprisonment is served

title: Mir Hamayun Aziz Kurd and another V. Provincial Election Commissioner, Balochistan and another,
explainer:
This case involved Mir Hamayun Aziz Kurd, who wanted to contest Pakistan's 2013 general elections for both a National Assembly seat and a Provincial Assembly seat from constituencies in Balochistan. His nomination papers were rejected by the Returning Officers because he had earlier been prosecuted under election and forgery laws for using what appeared to be a fake educational degree, allegedly from "Eire International University," to qualify as a graduate candidate in the 2008 elections under rules then requiring candidates to hold a bachelor's degree.

The appellant argued he should be allowed to contest because a criminal court had acquitted him in the forgery case. The Balochistan High Court's Election Tribunal rejected this argument. It held that a criminal court acquittal does not prove someone actually holds a valid, recognized degree — only the Higher Education Commission has authority to determine whether an institution and its degree are legitimate. Since the Higher Education Commission had found his degree invalid, his declaration that he was a graduate was a false statement, amounting to "corrupt practice" under election law, regardless of his acquittal.

The court dismissed his appeals, upholding rejection of his nomination papers.

This matters because it clarifies that criminal acquittals don't automatically restore election eligibility, and reinforces that only proper academic authorities—not courts—can certify degree validity, protecting the integrity of candidates' qualifications in Pakistan's electoral process.

title: Mustafa Ali V. The State,
explainer:
Mustafa Ali, a manager at an NGO in Quetta, was accused of creating a fake Facebook profile in the name of a woman he knew from university, using her photos, and sending her obscene and threatening messages. He was booked under the Electronic Transactions Ordinance, 2002 and various sections of the Pakistan Penal Code covering cheating, criminal intimidation, and insulting a woman's modesty. After his arrest in March 2014, a trial court refused him bail, so he approached the Balochistan High Court seeking post-arrest bail.

The High Court granted him bail. It reasoned that since the investigation was already complete and the challan (police report) had been submitted to the trial court, there was no longer any need to keep him in custody for further questioning. It also noted that the criminal offences he was charged with under the Penal Code did not fall under the category of serious crimes where bail is normally denied, so granting bail is the norm rather than the exception. Additionally, the court pointed out that the Electronic Transactions Ordinance offences allowed for either imprisonment or a fine as punishment, and since it's uncertain which penalty a trial court would eventually impose, this uncertainty itself justified bail.

This case illustrates how Pakistani courts apply established bail principles, particularly regarding cybercrime offences with alternative penalties, and reaffirms that bail is generally granted unless a case falls into specific serious-offence categories.

title: Noor Uddin V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about the murder trial of Noor Uddin, who was convicted by an Additional Sessions Judge in Killa Abdullah, Balochistan, for killing his cousin Haji Muhammad Siddique with a Kalashnikov. He was sentenced to death under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, along with a fine to be paid as compensation to the deceased's family. The case came before the Balochistan High Court both as an appeal by the convict and as a mandatory reference for confirmation of the death sentence.

The defence argued that Noor Uddin was insane at the time of the crime, suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, and should be excused from criminal liability under Section 84 of the Penal Code, which protects people who cannot understand the nature of their actions due to unsoundness of mind. The court explained that raising insanity as a defence requires the accused to show real evidence of mental incapacity, not just a mental disorder in general. Reviewing the medical opinion and the accused's behavior before, during, and after the killing, the court found no proof of insanity - his conduct showed he acted deliberately after being angered by the deceased.

The court also found the evidence of eyewitnesses, medical reports, and forensic recovery of the weapon fully consistent and credible, rejecting defence attempts to discredit the witnesses simply because some were related to the deceased. The court upheld the conviction and confirmed the death sentence, showing how Pakistani courts assess insanity pleas and evaluate eyewitness reliability in

title: Juma Khan V. The State and another,
explainer:
Juma Khan, the complainant in a firing case, went to the Balochistan High Court asking it to cancel the pre-arrest (anticipatory) bail granted to Sher Ali, the accused, in a case registered under section 324 PPC (attempt to commit qatl-e-amd). The FIR alleged that Sher Ali opened indiscriminate fire, injuring the complainant's two nephews and two passersby, and that medical evidence supported this account. The trial court had granted anticipatory bail mainly because two of the injured persons had given affidavits exonerating the accused and because there was a property dispute between the parties.

The High Court found these grounds weak. It noted that one of the affidavit-givers had actually confirmed the time, place, and manner of the attack, while the other was not even an eyewitness. It also held that a pre-existing civil or property dispute cannot automatically justify anticipatory bail, since such a dispute could just as easily be the motive for the crime rather than a reason to doubt the accusation.

Relying on Supreme Court precedent, the High Court reaffirmed that pre-arrest bail is an extraordinary remedy meant only for cases of malicious prosecution or false implication, not a routine alternative to regular bail. Since the accused failed to show any such ulterior motive and the evidence suggested a genuine, serious offence, the court set aside the trial court's order and cancelled the bail, emphasizing that fairness requires courts to correct bail orders that are perverse or unjustified.

title: Abdul Karim V. The S.H.O. Sariab Police Station Quetta and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Karim, who was injured during a shooting incident on land where he worked as a watchman. He wanted the police to register a separate FIR (First Information Report) telling his own version of events, but the police had already registered an FIR about the same incident describing it as a land dispute between rival groups. A trial court refused his request, reasoning that a second FIR for the same occurrence was not permissible, especially since multiple people were injured in the same firing.

Abdul Karim challenged this refusal before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court ruled that there is no absolute legal bar against registering a second FIR for the same incident when the aggrieved party gives a genuinely different account of what happened, so long as it is not merely repeating or expanding on the first version. The court found that Abdul Karim's account, that he was performing lawful duties and was attacked, differed materially from the police version portraying both sides as land-grabbing groups exchanging fire. Since this suggested a distinct criminal offense against him, the police should have registered his complaint too. The court also noted that accused persons named in a complaint have no right to be heard at the FIR registration stage.

The High Court set aside the trial court's order and sent the matter back for fresh decision, allowing the petition. This case matters because it clarifies that victims are not automatically barred from having their own version recorded, even if police have already filed a report describing the same event differently.

title: Altaf Hussain and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about two men, Altaf Hussain and Abdul Majeed, who were travelling as passengers on a bus intercepted by police near Hub, Balochistan. Police, acting on a tip about stolen motorcycles, stopped the bus and found five motorcycles, dismantled into parts, hidden in packages on board. Several passengers, including the petitioners, were arrested and charged under section 411 of the Pakistan Penal Code for dishonestly receiving or retaining stolen property. They were convicted by a magistrate and later by a Sessions Judge on appeal, each getting three months' imprisonment.

The petitioners challenged this in the Balochistan High Court, arguing they were merely passengers with no knowledge of the hidden stolen goods, and that the prosecution failed to prove they had actual, conscious possession of the stolen parts.

The High Court agreed with them. It explained that under section 411, simply being near or on the same vehicle as stolen property isn't enough for conviction. The prosecution must prove the accused knowingly and dishonestly received or retained the stolen goods. Since the motorcycle parts were recovered from the bus itself, driven by a co-accused, and not from the personal possession of the petitioners, the prosecution failed to establish conscious possession or knowledge.

The court set aside the convictions of both lower courts and acquitted the petitioners, emphasizing that courts can and must correct clear miscarriages of justice even when lower courts agreed on the facts.

title: Jalal Ud-din V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Jalal-ud-Din and Gul Dad, who sought bail after being arrested when police intercepted their vehicle near Kuchlak, Quetta, and found 80 sacks of potassium chlorate (2,000 kg total). They were booked under the Explosive Substances Act, 1908, along with a general criminal conspiracy provision.

Their lawyers argued that potassium chlorate is not itself an explosive and that no evidence showed intent to use it for causing an explosion, so the men should not be held under sections 3 or 4 of the Act, which deal with actually causing or intending explosions.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed with granting bail, though it accepted that potassium chloride alone is not explosive. It noted the substance found was potassium chlorate, a chemically derived compound that produces heat and oxygen when it decomposes, is highly reactive, and is commonly used in explosives, including improvised bombs. A Bomb Disposal Commander and an official police certificate confirmed the material was dangerous and recommended for destruction.

The court held that even without proof of bad intent, simply possessing such explosive material under suspicious circumstances is punishable under section 5 of the Act, which carries up to 14 years imprisonment. Since this fell within the "prohibitory clause" of the bail law, meaning serious offenses where bail is harder to get, the court refused bail, clarifying its remarks were tentative and would not bind the trial court's final decision.

title: Shahid Hakeem V. Altaf Hussain Agha and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over farmland near Hub, Balochistan. The complainant, Altaf Hussain Agha, said he had legally purchased a large property through a court auction and had been given vacant possession, but that Javed Sikandar, associated with Bolan Castings Limited, illegally occupied a portion of the land. When the accused person named in the complaint was replaced by the appellant, Shahid Hakeem, in his role managing the company's affairs, the trial court convicted Hakeem under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, sentencing him to two years' imprisonment, a fine, and compensation to the complainant.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined whether Hakeem's actions actually amounted to "illegal dispossession" under the law, or merely encroachment. The court clarified that illegal dispossession requires both a wrongful act and criminal intent to grab someone's property, whereas simple encroachment lacks that intent and is legally different. The court also noted that the Act does not apply retroactively to occupation disputes that were already pending before another forum when the law came into force, but does apply if no such prior case existed.

The judgment is significant because it draws a clear legal distinction between encroachment and illegal dispossession, emphasizing that criminal liability under this Act requires proof of deliberate intent to seize property, not just continued occupation of previously encroached land. This protects individuals from criminal conviction merely for managing or occupying land inherited administratively, without proof of dishonest intent.

title: Haji Abdul Hameed V. Raz Muhammad and another,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves a murder trial arising from the death of Abdul Qayyum, allegedly killed by Raz Muhammad and others in 2011. Medical evidence showed the victim died from sharp weapon injuries, severe blood loss, and shock. During the trial, the accused asked the trial court to allow exhumation of the deceased's body so a sample could be taken for DNA testing to match against bloodstained knives recovered as evidence. The trial court granted this request, and the victim's brother challenged that decision in the High Court.

The High Court overturned the trial court's order. It held that the legal provisions on inquiries into cause of death and exhumation exist only to determine whether a death resulted from a crime, not to help identify the specific weapon used or to serve the defense's evidentiary strategy. The court also noted the relevant law technically applies to deaths in police custody, which was not the situation here. Since the request came 18 months after the incident and appeared to be an academic exercise rather than a genuine need to resolve doubt about the cause of death, exhumation was not justified. The court emphasized that Islamic and cultural values require respect for the dead, so exhumation should only be permitted in serious, well-explained circumstances. The accused could instead challenge the medical evidence through cross-examination or expert testimony rather than digging up the body.

title: Khan Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man arrested for allegedly stealing electricity by connecting directly to a power pole and misusing a domestic electricity connection for commercial purposes. He was charged under theft laws, an electricity theft law, and an anti-corruption law, and had been in custody since July 2013. His bail request had earlier been refused by a Special Judge, so he approached the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court granted him bail. It reasoned that the investigation was already complete, so there was no longer any need to keep him in custody for questioning. It also found that the corruption law provision did not really apply to his situation, and that the remaining offences he was charged with allowed for punishment of imprisonment or fine, or fine alone. The court explained that if someone could ultimately be punished with only a fine, keeping them locked up during trial could amount to unfair double punishment, since time spent in jail cannot later be compensated if the final penalty is just a fine. The court linked this to constitutional protections against being punished twice for the same matter.

This judgment matters because it reinforces the principle that bail should normally be granted, not refused, in cases where offenses are not extremely serious, and that pretrial detention should not be used as a form of premature punishment before guilt is proven.

title: Bibi Feroza and 5 others V. Abdul Hadi and another,
explainer:
This case involved a woman, Bibi Feroza, whose marriage to Abdul Hadi was dissolved by a Family Court in 2011 on the basis of khula, at her request, after reconciliation efforts failed. She later remarried a man named Nasrullah. Her former husband, Abdul Hadi, then had a criminal case registered against her, alleging she had committed bigamy since, according to him, the khula-based divorce had not fully taken legal effect because she hadn't returned certain marital benefits or waived her rights, as required under family law.

Bibi Feroza and others approached the Balochistan High Court asking it to quash the FIR, arguing it was filed out of malice and that she had legally remarried after a valid divorce.

The High Court agreed with her. It explained that a wife's right to khula is equivalent to a husband's right to pronounce talaq, and that once a Family Court grants a khula decree, the marriage is dissolved immediately - it does not have to wait until the wife returns any benefits received during the marriage. Any obligation to return such benefits is a separate civil matter, not something that delays or undoes the divorce itself.

Since the marriage had been validly dissolved before she remarried, there was no legal basis for the criminal charge of bigamy. The court found the case baseless and quashed the FIR, ruling that continuing the prosecution would amount to unnecessary harassment. This judgment reinforces that a khula divorce takes immediate effect regardless of unresolved financial matters between former spouses.

title: Azad Khan V. The Station House Officer, Police Station Satellite Town Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about who gets to have their version of events officially recorded by police after a violent incident. The petitioner, Azad Khan, said his father was killed and he and his cousin were seriously injured during a daytime attack. Although the matter was reported to the police station promptly by the injured cousin, the Station House Officer did not record the incident based on that account. Instead, the SHO filed his own version, which the petitioner believed distorted the facts and unfairly protected the accused by lumping victims and attackers together in a single case. When Azad Khan asked a Sessions Judge, acting as Justice of the Peace, to order a proper case to be registered based on his account, that request was dismissed without real examination of his complaint.

The Balochistan High Court found that there is no legal bar on registering a second police report about the same incident, as long as it presents a genuinely different account rather than just repeating the first one. The court rejected the argument that the petitioner's only option was to file a private complaint in court, noting that police involvement is often essential to gather evidence, especially in serious crimes. It also dismissed fears that allowing second reports would lead to endless competing versions, pointing out that the law already punishes anyone who knowingly gives false information to police.

The court ordered the SHO to register a fresh report based on Azad Khan's version against the accused persons, in accordance with law. This case matters because it clarifies that victims have a right to have their own account officially recorded when the initial police report appears inaccurate or biased.

title: Mir Sanad Khan and 6 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a criminal revision petition against a trial court order allowing the complainant to summon a Judicial Magistrate as a witness under Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The Magistrate had earlier conducted an inquiry into the incident and formed an opinion about the accused's alleged negligence, based on statements from witnesses who had already testified before the trial court.

The petitioners argued that the Magistrate's evidence would be hearsay, inadmissible, and not binding on the trial court, and that summoning him would serve no real purpose since the same witnesses had already been examined at trial.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the petitioners. It explained that an "inquiry" and a "trial" are legally distinct processes, and a Magistrate's opinion formed during an administrative inquiry is not evidence of fact but merely an opinion, which is inadmissible except in specific circumstances under the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order. The court held that convictions must rest only on evidence properly recorded by a competent court, not on opinions formed elsewhere. It also clarified that Section 540 gives courts discretion to summon witnesses only when genuinely necessary for justice, not to fill gaps in the prosecution's case or prolong proceedings.

Since the Magistrate's testimony would add nothing admissible or essential, the court set aside the trial court's order and dismissed the application. This ruling reinforces limits on when courts can call additional witnesses and clarifies the distinction between inquiry and trial evidence.

title: Muhammad Ayub V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man accused of murder, robbery, and dacoity in Quetta. According to the prosecution, he and a companion, armed with weapons, robbed a student of his motorcycle, shot and injured the student, and also fatally shot his own companion during the incident. He was caught on the spot by locals and handed to police. He was charged under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with murder and robbery, along with a provision of a special law dealing with property offences.

The accused sought bail, arguing that he had reached a compromise (compensation/forgiveness agreement) with the victim's side, and that courts should treat all murders as compoundable under Islamic law regardless of the circumstances.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the bail application. It held that while compromises can sometimes be a factor considered in deciding bail, they cannot by themselves entitle an accused to bail as a matter of right, especially in serious non-compoundable offenses like murder committed during robbery or dacoity. The law specifically bars compounding such offenses. The court also noted that the accused was caught red-handed with the weapon, and that this was a serious crime involving both murder and an attempt to kill another victim, making bail unjustified on the merits.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that a private compromise between an accused and a victim's family does not override criminal law protections meant to serve the wider interest of society, particularly in violent crimes.

The tenants did not deposit rent on time, instead paying it in delayed lump sums over many months. Because of this, the Rent Controller struck off their defense and ordered their eviction. title: Muhammad Akram Baloch V. Akbar Askani and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the 2013 general election result for a Provincial Assembly seat (PB-50 Kech-III) in Balochistan. The losing candidate, Muhammad Akram Baloch, filed an election petition alleging that the declared winner, Akbar Askani, won through massive rigging and illegal practices, allegedly with help from the district administration. Specifically, he claimed that at two polling stations no actual voting took place and no election staff were present, meaning the results there were fabricated.

To prove this, the petitioner asked the Election Tribunal to send the counterfoils (vote stubs) from those polling stations, along with the voter lists, to NADRA for scientific verification of thumbprints, to check whether real voters had actually cast those votes or whether impersonation occurred.

The Tribunal ruled in favor of allowing this verification. It held that while ballot secrecy is important and inspection of ballots should not be allowed routinely, courts can use modern technology like NADRA's biometric data as evidence when serious, specific allegations of rigging are made. It found that a voter's right to ballot secrecy is not absolute and can be waived to ensure fair elections. The Tribunal allowed the NADRA verification report to be produced as evidence, with both sides free to raise objections to it.

This case matters because it shows courts using modern technology to investigate serious election fraud claims while balancing it against the constitutional principle of ballot secrecy.

title: Muhammad Akram Baloch V. Akbar Askani and others,
explainer:
This case comes from an election dispute in Balochistan. After Akbar Askani won a Provincial Assembly seat by 54 votes from Constituency PB-50 Kech-III, the losing candidate, Muhammad Akram Baloch, challenged the result before the Election Commission, alleging rigging and corrupt practices. When that petition was dismissed, he filed a formal election petition before the Election Tribunal.

The specific issue decided here was procedural: while the petitioner had listed his proposed witnesses' names in the petition, he had not attached their sworn affidavits, as required by the Representation of the People Act, 1976. He argued this requirement was merely directory, not mandatory, and asked the Tribunal to still allow him to produce these witnesses, claiming they had been inaccessible at the time of filing.

The Tribunal rejected this request. It held that although filing affidavits is not backed by a specific penalty making it strictly mandatory, a party who fails to submit them—or omits witnesses from the list—must show "good cause" before being allowed to call such witnesses. Simply asserting that witnesses were unavailable was not enough to meet this standard. The Tribunal emphasized that affidavits serve an important purpose: informing the opposing side in advance what evidence to expect, enabling proper cross-examination and preventing fabricated testimony.

The case matters because it clarifies the evidentiary discipline required in election petitions and limits attempts to introduce witnesses without proper justification.

title: Payo Khan alias Kakay V. The State,
explainer:
Payo Khan was convicted by a trial court in Quetta for possessing an unlicensed rifle, a pistol, ammunition and a handgrenade, and sentenced to seven years plus three years imprisonment under the Explosive Substances Act and Pakistan Arms Ordinance. The prosecution's case was that police acted on secret information and raided his house, recovering the weapons.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious flaws in how the case was handled. No one had actually asked the accused to produce a license for the weapons before charging him, and simply possessing arms is not itself illegal unless a person fails to produce a license when asked. The recovery process was also questionable: the memo documenting what was seized was supposedly prepared at the scene at 3:50 a.m., but records showed it was actually written up nearly sixteen hours later at the police station, after the case had already been registered. The witness to the recovery admitted he wasn't even present at the raid and gave his statement later at the police station, not on the spot as required. No independent, respected member of the community was included in the raid, as normally expected in such proceedings.

Given these serious doubts about whether the recovery was genuine and properly documented, the High Court ruled that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. It set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitting Payo Khan. The case highlights why courts insist on strict, honest procedure in police recoveries — sloppy or fabricated paperwork can undermine even serious criminal charges.

title: Registrar, High Court Of Balochistan, Quetta V. Mazar Khan and others,
explainer:
This case involved civil servants who had gone to civil or Qazi courts and obtained decrees allowing them to change their officially recorded dates of birth, without making the Balochistan government a party to those lawsuits. The High Court took up the matter on its own initiative (suo motu), using its revisional powers under Section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code, after concerns emerged about such practices.

The court held that date-of-birth and other service-record matters for civil servants fall under the special jurisdiction of Service Tribunals, not ordinary civil courts. Since the government was never made a party to these suits, any decrees obtained were not binding on it. The court also noted the civil servants had waited decades (36 years and 5 years in these cases) before challenging their recorded dates of birth, which undermined the credibility of their claims and suggested they had earlier accepted the correct record.

The court ruled that such decrees, passed without proper jurisdiction, were nullities and could be challenged at any stage. It set aside the judgments and decrees altering the dates of birth, and directed the government to review all similar cases, take action against affected employees (including possible dismissal, retirement, and recovery of extra salary paid), consider criminal cases if forged documents were used, and discipline any officials who were negligent or complicit. This judgment matters because it protects the integrity of government service records and limits misuse of civil court decrees to gain undue service benefits.

title: Abdul Qadir Shah V. Muhammad Qasim and 2 others,
explainer:
This case dealt with whether Pakistani courts could investigate and try a murder allegedly committed outside Pakistan's borders, near the Afghan frontier. The victim, a mechanic from Quetta, had gone to Chaman to run a garage with men who later sent his body back after he was killed with knives and screwdrivers. His brother filed a complaint, and a magistrate acting as Justice of Peace ordered police to register an FIR against the accused. The accused challenged this, arguing that since the offence occurred beyond Pakistani territory, and beyond the local police station's jurisdiction, the police had no authority to investigate without prior certification from the Federal Government or a Political Agent, as required under Section 188 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The Balochistan High Court rejected this argument. It held that Pakistani law extends to citizens who commit offences abroad, under Sections 3 and 4 of the Pakistan Penal Code. While formal sanction under Section 188 is indeed needed before a court can "inquire into" the charge at trial, this requirement does not block the earlier step of registering an FIR or conducting a police investigation. Such sanction can be obtained later, even after the police have completed their investigation and filed a charge-sheet. Since both parties were Pakistani nationals residing in Quetta, the Court found no reason to stop the investigation and dismissed the petition, allowing the case to proceed.

title: Muhammad Ayaz Khan Jogezai and 2 others V. Government of Pakistan States and Frontier Regions Division, Islamabad and 31 others,
explainer:
This case concerned recruitment into the Federal Levies Force in Balochistan. The provincial government had advertised about 3,000 vacancies, but the petitioners challenged this, arguing that appointments were being made under outdated 1954 Instructions issued by the Federal Government, which conflicted with constitutional guarantees of equality, non-discrimination, and fair employment opportunities under Articles 25, 27 and 33. They also argued the old rules relied on consultation with tribal sardars, even though Balochistan had abolished the sardari (tribal chief) system through a 1976 law.

During hearings, both the provincial Advocate-General and federal counsel conceded that the 1954 Instructions were outdated and impractical, and that no proper service rules existed for the Levies Force, making transparent recruitment difficult.

The Balochistan High Court acknowledged that Balochistan faced severe security challenges, including terrorism, target killings, and bomb blasts, creating an urgent need for more manpower in law enforcement. Recruiting local youth, the court noted, would both improve security and provide employment opportunities.

Since no valid rules existed, the court did not stop recruitment altogether. Instead, it allowed the provincial government to proceed on a temporary, stop-gap basis using a proposed recruitment formula, while laying down specific terms and conditions for making these appointments fairly until proper rules were framed. This ensured urgent recruitment could continue without violating constitutional principles.

title: Miss Gulnaz Baloch V. Registrar, Balochistan High Court, Quetta and others,
explainer:
This case involved Miss Gulnaz Baloch, who applied for the post of Civil Judge/Judicial Magistrate in Balochistan after a 2011 advertisement. She passed the written exam and was called for an interview conducted by a panel of four High Court Judges led by the then Chief Justice. She scored only 54 out of 200 interview marks and was not selected. She filed a constitutional petition arguing that the interview marks seemed unfair and inconsistent, suggesting bias, and asked the court to order fresh interviews, disclose how marks were awarded, and set aside the appointments of successful candidates.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed her petition at the outset, holding it was not maintainable. The court explained that the notification she challenged was issued by the Registrar acting on the Chief Justice's orders, and such actions taken on behalf of the High Court cannot be challenged under Article 199 of the Constitution, which grants courts immunity from constitutional petitions against their own judicial and administrative decisions. The court emphasized that a Selection Committee's judgment about candidates' abilities deserves deference, and the High Court should not override such assessments unless there is proof of bad faith, which was not shown here.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that High Courts cannot be sued under Article 199 for decisions made by the Chief Justice or on his authority, reinforcing the constitutional immunity of court actions from judicial review by another court.

title: Pwd Employees' Union, Balochistan through Vice-President and others V. Secretary, Communication and Works Department, Government of Balochistan Quetta and others,
explainer:
This case concerned Rule 12 of the Balochistan Civil Servants (Appointment, Promotion and Transfer) Rules, 2009, which reserved certain government jobs specifically for the widows or children of civil servants who had died while in service. Employees and petitioners challenged this rule before the Balochistan High Court, along with related contempt and other connected petitions, arguing that reserving posts for a specific privileged category of citizens was unfair and unconstitutional.

The court held that while classification of citizens for legitimate purposes is not automatically forbidden, any such classification must have a reasonable connection to the goal being pursued. Since the object of government recruitment is to secure the best available talent through merit, reserving posts for relatives of deceased civil servants had no logical link to that goal. The court found this arrangement discriminatory, saying it unfairly advantaged one class of widows and children over others in society, could result in less qualified candidates being appointed over better qualified ones, and risked creating an impression that government jobs were hereditary.

The court ruled that Rule 12 violated the constitutional guarantees of equality, non-discrimination, and the right to pursue lawful occupations through open, transparent competition. It declared the rule unconstitutional and directed the government to reconsider such discriminatory reservations. The judgment matters because it reinforces that public employment must be merit-based and open to all citizens equally, rather than reserved for favored groups.

title: Haroon Ahmed and others V. Secretary Communication and Works Department and another,
explainer:
This case involved two applications asking the Balochistan High Court to restore constitutional petitions that had been dismissed for non-prosecution after the applicants' lawyer failed to appear in court. The lawyer explained that he had been granted leave by the Chief Justice to travel abroad for a specific period (late September to mid-October 2014) to appear as a witness in an international arbitration case in Paris, but the petitions were dismissed on 10 November 2014, after his approved leave period had already ended.

The applicants sought restoration under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, arguing the dismissal order should be recalled. The court examined the law and found that Section 12(2) applies only to situations involving fraud, misrepresentation, or lack of jurisdiction, none of which were present here. It then considered whether it could use its general inherent powers under Section 151 CPC to restore the case, noting that such powers require the applicant to show due diligence and sufficient cause for missing the hearing.

The court found that the lawyer's approved absence had ended weeks before the actual dismissal date, meaning there was no valid explanation for the failure to appear on the day the case was actually dismissed. Concluding that the applicants had not shown sufficient cause or due diligence, and that restoring the case would serve no useful purpose, the court dismissed the restoration applications. The case illustrates how strictly courts apply the requirement of genuine justification when parties seek to reopen dismissed cases.

title: Dr. Asadullah Khan Tareen V. Government of Balochistan Health Department and another,
explainer:
This case involved a civil servant, Dr. Asadullah Khan Tareen, who approached the Balochistan High Court through a constitutional petition seeking implementation of a judgment previously passed in his favour by the Service Tribunal, in a dispute connected to his employment terms with the Government of Balochistan's Health Department.

The core legal question was whether the High Court had jurisdiction to order implementation of a Service Tribunal's judgment. The Court held that it did not have this power. It explained that under the Constitution, the High Court's authority is limited to what is specifically granted to it by the Constitution or by law, and matters concerning the terms and conditions of civil servants' service fall exclusively within the domain of Service Tribunals, not ordinary courts. The Service Tribunal itself functions like a civil court and has full power, including under the Code of Civil Procedure, to enforce its own orders if they are disobeyed. The High Court's constitutional jurisdiction is meant to address questions of law, not to resolve factual disputes or enforce another tribunal's rulings.

The Court also discussed the importance of respecting separation of powers among the legislature, executive, and judiciary, and noted that while government authorities must promptly comply with Tribunal judgments or appeal them, that process falls outside the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction.

As a result, the petition was dismissed. The case reinforces that civil servants must seek enforcement of Service Tribunal decisions through proper channels, not through the High Court's constitutional powers.

title: Talal Haleem and 3 others V. Principal Bolan Medical College, Quetta and 4 others,
explainer:
This case concerns admissions to Bolan Medical College, Quetta for the 2014-15 academic year. Four male students who had passed the entry test challenged a rule in the college prospectus reserving 50% of MBBS seats for female candidates and 50% for male candidates. They argued this quota system was discriminatory, arbitrary, and violated their constitutional rights, disadvantaging male applicants who had qualified on merit.

The college and health authorities defended the policy, arguing it was meant to address practical problems such as female doctors being reluctant to serve in rural areas, women leaving the profession after marriage, and the high cost of training doctors who might not practice.

The Balochistan High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners. It held that while Article 25 of the Constitution allows reasonable classification between groups if there is a rational and justifiable basis, the authorities in this case failed to provide credible justification for assuming women wouldn't ultimately work in medicine. The Court noted women already serve across many professions including law enforcement and administration. It concluded the gender-based quota amounted to unconstitutional discrimination rather than a reasonable restriction, and ordered the disputed provision removed from the prospectus, directing that admissions instead proceed under the college's earlier admission policy.

This decision matters because it reinforces that gender-based quotas must be backed by solid justification and cannot rest on generalized assumptions, upholding constitutional equality principles in access to professional education.

title: Muhammad Nadeem and 3 others V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Home and Tribal Affairs Department and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over government job appointments in Balochistan. In 2004, several candidates, including the petitioners, applied for the post of Assistant Investigating Officer in the Home and Tribal Affairs Department after tests and interviews were conducted by a Departmental Selection Committee. The petitioners claimed they topped the merit list but were later bypassed when a 2007 notification appointed other candidates (the private respondents) instead.

The petitioners challenged this notification in the High Court, seeking to have it declared illegal and asking that they be appointed according to the merit list. However, the court found that these appointments were actually made in compliance with an earlier Division Bench judgment from 2007, which had already resolved a related case (filed by some of the private respondents) and directed the government to appoint those selected candidates.

The court ruled that the petitioners' case was barred by the principle of "constructive res judicata," meaning the same issues had already been decided and could not be relitigated using different arguments. It also held that courts should not interfere with selection committee decisions absent bad faith, and noted the private respondents had already served over eight years without complaints, making it unjust to disturb their positions now.

The petition was dismissed. This case reinforces that final court decisions cannot be reopened indefinitely, and that long-serving employees should not be displaced without strong legal justification.

title: Mst. Razya Ghulam and another V. The General Public,
explainer:
This case is about a widow seeking a succession certificate after her husband, a government sweeper, was killed by terrorists in 2013. She wanted authority to collect his compensation, cash payment, and salary dues, totalling over Rs.50 lakh. No other heir objected to her claim. The trial court agreed she was the sole legal heir entitled to the certificate but insisted she provide two sureties equal to the certificate's value before it would be issued. When she asked to be excused from this requirement, the trial court rejected her request with a one-line order, giving no reasons at all.

The Balochistan High Court found this one-line dismissal unacceptable because a judicial order must show that the judge actually considered the arguments raised, not just announce a conclusion. The court also clarified the law: under the Succession Act, courts must demand sureties only in specific situations involving summary proceedings; in other cases, requiring a surety is discretionary. Since all heirs agreed, there was no dispute over entitlement, and the purpose of a surety (protecting other possible claimants) did not apply here, the High Court ruled sureties were unnecessary.

The High Court set aside the trial court's order and directed that the succession certificate be issued to the widow, subject only to a personal surety bond from a government official, not the heavier requirement originally imposed. This case highlights that courts must give reasoned orders and shouldn't impose unnecessary burdens on undisputed heirs, especially vulnerable claimants like a widow.

title: Tahir Humayun and others V. High Court of Balochistan through Registrar and others,
explainer:
This case concerns the seniority of judicial officers in Balochistan. Several judges, magistrates, civil judges and additional district and sessions judges had been appointed on an ad hoc basis in 1997-1999. Later, the Provincial Cabinet and the High Court's Administration Committee regularized their services, but backdated their seniority to their original ad hoc appointment dates. Other officers, including the appellants, who had been appointed on a regular basis through the Public Service Commission before this regularization, argued that this retrospective backdating unfairly pushed them below officers who were actually junior to them in regular service.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the appellants. It held that ad hoc service, before being formally regularized, cannot count toward seniority - seniority should instead run from the date of substantive (regular) appointment. The Administration Committee had no authority to grant seniority retrospectively from the ad hoc appointment date, and doing so was an arbitrary and unreasonable exercise of power that harmed regularly appointed officers. The court emphasized that illegal actions do not become legal simply through the passage of time, and that void orders can be challenged without any limitation period.

The court declared the appellants and similarly placed officers senior to the respondents whose ad hoc service had been retrospectively regularized, and directed that their promotion cases be reconsidered accordingly. This ruling matters because it protects merit-based, regularly recruited employees from being unfairly overtaken in seniority by administrative shortcuts.

title: Muhammad Ewaz Zehri (Baloch) V. Chairman Selection Committee For Appointment of District and Sessions Judges and 10 others,

He failed the test and filed a constitutional petition claiming the results were the product of favouritism, nepotism, and discrimination based on his caste and tribe. He asked the court to have his answer sheet re-evaluated by a third party, sought disqualification of some successful candidates, and wanted an upcoming interview stayed.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition outright. It found no evidence of bias or unfair treatment, noting that answer sheets were coded to hide candidates' identities during marking, ensuring confidentiality and fairness. Experienced judges of proven integrity had evaluated the papers. The court itself rechecked the petitioner's answer sheet and found the marking accurate, with no errors in totals or unmarked sections. It also noted that candidates who succeeded included people from the petitioner's own ethnic background, undermining his discrimination claim.

The judges strongly criticized the petitioner for making unfounded allegations against them, saying he was trying to dress up his personal failure as institutional bias. The court held that unsuccessful candidates often believe they performed better than they actually did, and that re-evaluation cannot be ordered without genuine grounds. title: Najeebullah and others V. Director Nadra, Balochistan, Quetta and others,
explainer:
This case involved a group of petitioners from Quetta who claimed to belong to indigenous tribes long settled in the area and who had previously held manual and computerized national identity cards (CNICs). When they approached NADRA to obtain new CNICs or renew existing ones, they were asked to produce supporting documents. Despite submitting these documents, NADRA declined to issue or renew their CNICs, prompting them to file constitutional petitions asking the High Court to direct NADRA to issue the cards.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petitions as not maintainable. It found that the petitioners' cases had merely been sent to verification committees, and no formal orders cancelling, impounding, or confiscating their CNICs had been issued under the relevant law, nor had they been given show-cause notices. Since no final adverse order existed, the petitions were premature. The Court also noted that if such an order were eventually passed, the proper remedy was an appeal to the Federal Government, not a constitutional petition. Additionally, NADRA alleged some documents were fraudulently obtained, meaning the case involved disputed facts requiring detailed evidence and inquiry—something better suited to a civil court than constitutional jurisdiction.

This case matters because it clarifies the limits of the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction, emphasizing that it cannot be used to bypass proper administrative procedures or resolve factual disputes, and reaffirms the specific legal channels available to challenge NADRA's decisions regarding identity documents.

title: Quetta Metropolitan Corporation through Administrator, Quetta and 2 others V. Abdul Wasay and others,
explainer:
The Quetta Metropolitan Corporation (QMC) had leased out shops to several tenants over decades. After the lease terms expired, the tenants continued paying rent monthly, but QMC decided to raise rents significantly and asked tenants to sign new agreements at the higher rates. The tenants sued, claiming the increase was arbitrary and that QMC should have gone through the Rent Controller under rent-control law instead of unilaterally raising rents. Two lower courts agreed with the tenants and ruled against QMC.

QMC challenged these rulings before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court found that government notifications specifically exempted properties belonging to local bodies like municipal corporations from the Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance when used for shops or commercial purposes. It held that QMC, as a public body, had the right to manage its properties, set rents according to market rates, and increase rent to reflect fair value especially since tenants had occupied the shops for around 50 years while paying very low rent. The court ruled that such decisions by public authorities could only be challenged if they were arbitrary, discriminatory, or made in bad faith, none of which was shown here.

The court set aside the lower courts' decisions, ruling in favor of QMC's right to enhance rent, while allowing tenants to keep their shops if they paid the new rates; otherwise, QMC could pursue eviction. This case clarifies that public bodies have broad authority to manage and monetize their properties in the public interest.

title: Haji Mullah Noor Ullah V. Secretary Mines And Minerals and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a petitioner, Haji Mullah Noor Ullah, who had been granted a Prospecting License for limestone crushing near Quetta. After local residents complained, his No Objection Certificate was suspended, and eventually his license was cancelled by mining authorities. He challenged this cancellation through a constitutional petition, and separately, a related civil suit he had filed for declaration and injunction was rejected by lower courts.

The Balochistan High Court examined the case not just as a licensing dispute, but through the lens of public health and environmental rights. It held that the right to life under Article 9 of the Constitution includes the right to clean, pollution-free air, and citizens can approach the High Court under Article 199 to protect against environmental harm like air pollution. At the same time, the court recognized that the right to conduct business or trade under Article 18 is not absolute and can be reasonably restricted to protect public welfare, especially when an industry poses health risks.

Balancing these rights, the court ruled that stone-crushing businesses could no longer operate within Quetta city limits. It ordered the government to identify safer zones, away from highways, schools, hospitals, and residential areas, for relocating these businesses within set deadlines, ensure pollution control measures, and conduct regular inspections. This judgment is significant because it prioritizes environmental and public health protections over unrestricted business operations, while still allowing affected businesses a path to relocate and continue operating safely.

title: Mujeebullah Gharsheen and another V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 3 others,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court, dealt with the question of whether government employees and civil servants have an unrestricted right to go on strike, hold demonstrations, or stage sit-ins (dharnas), particularly ones that block public roads or disrupt essential services like education and healthcare.

The court held that while civil servants have the right to form associations, this right is not absolute and is subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law, particularly to protect public order. Strikes and sit-ins by civil servants are not recognized or protected under existing law and are, in fact prohibited. The court ruled that any civil servant or employee of a statutory body (except those legally classified as "workmen") who participates in such strikes or demonstrations is guilty of "misconduct" and should face departmental disciplinary action.

The judgment emphasized that disrupting schools, hospitals, and public thoroughfares through strikes violates the fundamental rights of ordinary citizens to education, healthcare, and free movement. It directed the Chief Secretary of Balochistan to consider amending the relevant conduct rules, and warned that if authorities failed to take disciplinary action against striking employees in the future, those responsible officials could themselves face contempt of court proceedings.

This ruling matters because it clarifies limits on public employees' right to protest and reinforces that government inaction against disruptive strikes can itself be held accountable by the courts, protecting the broader public's access to essential services.

title: Abdul Ghaffar V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man accused of murder and other serious offences, who claimed during his trial that he was mentally unsound and asked the court to send him to a medical board for examination before proceeding further. The trial court examined him personally, questioned him about everyday matters like his family, hobbies, and past events, and concluded he was mentally fit and was faking insanity simply to delay the trial. His application was rejected, and he challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It explained that under the law, a court is only required to formally investigate an accused's mental state if it genuinely appears, from the court's own observation or other evidence, that the person cannot understand or conduct his defence. Simply filing an application claiming unsoundness of mind is not enough to trigger such an inquiry. The burden of proving insanity rests on the accused, and what matters legally is his mental state at the time of the offence, not merely at trial. Medical reports showed the petitioner suffered from bipolar disorder, but the court held that bipolar disorder, though a real mental illness involving mood and energy fluctuations, does not amount to legal "unsoundness of mind" that would excuse criminal responsibility.

The case is significant because it clarifies that a mental illness diagnosis alone does not automatically qualify as legal insanity, and courts can reject insanity pleas they find to be tactics to stall proceedings.

title: Muhammad Jan & others V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and another,
explainer:
This case involved employees of the Zakat and Ushr Department, Government of Balochistan, who had worked on contract for around 10 to 12 years without their jobs being made permanent. They approached the Balochistan High Court, arguing that although they were hired as contract staff to audit Zakat funds, they had continued serving for over a decade with satisfactory performance, and their positions were effectively permanent since the work was still needed. They also pointed out that six new posts of Junior Auditor had actually been created to accommodate and regularize them, but instead of doing so, the department advertised these posts for fresh, open recruitment, which would force the long serving employees to compete again despite many of them now being overage and unable to seek other jobs.

The government argued the employees had accepted contract terms and had no automatic right to permanent status.

The High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners. It held that since their appointments followed proper selection procedures, their work was needed by the department, no one questioned their qualifications or performance, and posts were specifically created for them, re-advertising those same posts made no sense and unfairly punished experienced workers. The court allowed the petition, effectively protecting their right to continue in these regularized posts.

This case matters because it reinforces that long-serving, competent contract employees performing necessary government functions cannot be arbitrarily displaced through repeated re-advertisement, especially when posts were created specifically for their regularization.
