title: Muhammad Jan and 3 others V. The Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and another,
explainer:
This case is about workers of the Zakat and Ushr Department in Balochistan who had been employed on contract, and later temporary, basis for around ten to twelve years as Audit Officers, effectively performing what they said were permanent duties. Instead of regularizing their long service, the government advertised the same posts (including newly created posts meant for their regularization) for fresh appointments. The petitioners asked the High Court to declare this advertisement unlawful, to stop treating their positions as contractual, and to direct the government to regularize their employment against sanctioned posts, counting their years of service.

The Balochistan High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners. It held that although they were technically contract employees, the nature of their jobs was permanent, since they had served for over a decade without any complaints of misconduct or incompetence, and their work remained continuously necessary to the department. The re-advertisement of the same posts, the court noted, actually proved the ongoing need for these roles. Relying on earlier Supreme Court precedents on long-serving contract employees, the court directed the authorities to regularize the petitioners' services, though without back benefits, in accordance with the law.

The case matters because it reinforces the principle that long-term contract workers performing essential, permanent functions cannot indefinitely be denied job security, and government departments cannot bypass regularization obligations by re-advertising the same positions.

title: Mrs. Tahira Parveen Baloch V. Chief Justice, High Court of Balochistan, Quetta through Registrar,
explainer:
This case involved a District and Sessions Judge in Balochistan who was compulsorily retired from service after being found guilty of misconduct. She faced allegations including withdrawing over three lakh rupees in cash without proper procedure after being transferred from one post, complaints of bribery through a court stenographer while posted elsewhere, and allegedly pocketing money collected from a contractor meant for purchasing air conditioners for the court. A departmental inquiry, conducted by a sitting High Court judge, found her guilty on these counts, and the recommendation of major penalty was accepted by the Chief Justice acting as the disciplinary authority, resulting in her compulsory retirement.

She challenged this decision before the Service Tribunal, arguing the punishment was unjustified. The Balochistan High Court, sitting as the tribunal, dismissed her appeal. The court held that judicial officers must be held to a higher standard than ordinary civil servants because their integrity must be beyond doubt to preserve public confidence in the justice system. It noted her service record was already full of prior complaints, warnings, and show-cause notices, and that sufficient evidence supported the misconduct findings. The court clarified that compulsory retirement, unlike dismissal, still entitles the officer to proportionate pension benefits, making it a comparatively lesser though still serious penalty.

This case matters because it reinforces that judges are held to stricter accountability standards, and courts will uphold disciplinary action where corruption allegations against judicial officers are substantiated through proper inqui

title: Zakir Hussain V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Zakir Hussain, who was convicted by a trial court in Quetta and sentenced to four years imprisonment plus a fine for allegedly possessing an unlicensed Kalashnikov rifle and fifteen live cartridges, under the Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965. Police had raided a house looking for his brother, Karar Hussain, who was wanted in a separate attempted murder case, and the house itself belonged to the brother. Zakir Hussain was not named or wanted in that case, nor did he own the house. He argued he had been falsely implicated because his brother was absconding.

The Balochistan High Court accepted his appeal and acquitted him, overturning the trial court's conviction. The court found several serious flaws in the prosecution's case: there was no evidence that police ever asked him to produce a license or permit for the weapon, which is necessary before mere possession becomes a crime. More importantly, the police failed to follow Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which requires searches to be conducted in the presence of independent, disinterested witnesses to prevent false implication. No such witnesses were involved despite their availability.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that procedural safeguards during police searches exist specifically to protect citizens from wrongful implication, and courts must give the accused the benefit of the doubt when these legal requirements are ignored.

title: Mubashar Mehmood and another V. Home and Tribal Affairs through Secretary Civil Secretariat and others,
explainer:
This case involved several petitioners whose domicile certificates had been cancelled by Deputy Commissioners in different districts of Balochistan. These certificates matter because people rely on them to claim jobs and admissions to educational institutions under the quota system for various districts and departments. The petitioners argued that the authorities cancelled their certificates without following the proper legal procedure set out in the Pakistan Citizenship Act, 1951 and the Citizenship Rules, 1952, and that officials wrongly confused two separate concepts: domicile and permanent residence.

The Balochistan High Court, sitting as a larger bench to settle recurring confusion on this issue, clarified that domicile is a legal status that does not automatically change just because a person moves to another province to live there permanently, whereas permanent residence is simply a factual matter of where someone lives. The court held that domicile certificates can only be cancelled by following the specific procedure under Rule 26 of the 1952 Rules, including proper inquiry, especially since cancellation on grounds of fraud or misrepresentation carries serious consequences, potentially amounting to a denial of a person's citizenship rights. Since the authorities had cancelled the certificates without holding proper inquiries, the court set aside those cancellation orders and restored the petitioners' domicile certificates. This ruling matters because it protects citizens from having such important rights taken away arbitrarily, without due process.

title: Mohibullah and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a motorcycle seized by police after its owner, Muhammad Umar, was booked in a criminal case involving alleged use of a firearm and obstruction of law enforcement. He and a co-accused, Mohibullah, were convicted by a magistrate, and the motorcycle was ordered confiscated by the state. Their conviction was upheld on appeal, but the Balochistan High Court later acquitted both men on revision, giving them the benefit of the doubt, though the judgment did not specifically address what should happen to the motorcycle.

The applicant then filed a separate application asking the court to release the motorcycle to him. The State argued he had delayed too long and that acquittal based on benefit of the doubt was not a full or clean acquittal, so he wasn't entitled to get his property back.

The High Court disagreed. It held that once the conviction was overturned and the accused acquitted, the acquittal was unconditional and complete, regardless of it being based on benefit of the doubt. The court noted the motorcycle was never proven to be stolen or actually used in committing the offence. It also clarified that applications for return of property under the Criminal Procedure Code are not subject to any limitation period. Consequently, the court ordered the motorcycle be returned to the applicant, affirming that acquitted persons are entitled to recover property seized from them unless it is proven to be linked to a crime.

title: Sadullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two accused persons facing murder trials in Balochistan whose cases had stalled because key prosecution witnesses could not be located or produced in court. Instead of proceeding to a verdict or dismissing the charges, the trial courts ordered that the proceedings be kept dormant or in abeyance indefinitely, to be revived whenever the missing witnesses became available.

The accused challenged these orders before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that indefinitely suspending a criminal trial violated their right to a fair and speedy trial.

The High Court agreed. It examined Section 249 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows magistrates to stop proceedings, and found this provision applies only to magisterial trials, not to trials before Sessions Courts, which are governed by a different chapter of the law that contains no concept of keeping cases dormant or adjourning them indefinitely. The court held that judges cannot invent such powers where the law is silent; any gap in legislation must be filled by Parliament, not by courts. While Sessions Courts can adjourn cases for specific, reasonable periods with recorded reasons, they cannot suspend trials indefinitely.

The High Court set aside the lower courts' orders and sent the cases back for decision according to law based on available evidence, emphasizing that indefinite suspension undermines the constitutional guarantee of a fair and timely trial and prevents cases from ever reaching a real conclusion.

title: Church Missionary Trust Association through Authorized representative V. Federation of Pakistan through Ministry of Religious Affairs, Islamabad and others,
explainer:
This case concerns disputes over church-owned communal properties belonging to the Christian community in Balochistan. The Deputy Commissioner of Quetta had issued an order restraining revenue authorities from issuing property documents to anyone except one specifically authorized individual, in an attempt to stop fraudulent groups and land grabbers from falsely claiming ownership of Christian community properties using fake powers of attorney. The Church Missionary Trust Association challenged this order before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court disposed of the petition by laying down clear rules: communal property meant for a minority community's collective use cannot be bought, sold, or transferred by anyone; any minority community member can obtain certified copies of revenue records regarding such property, but cannot purchase it; the Deputy Commissioner has no authority to approve transfers of communal minority property; and even the petitioner organization or church diocese representatives themselves cannot sell or transfer such properties. The Court declared the Deputy Commissioner's original letter unlawful and void, and directed all judges in the province to decide pending property disputes involving minority communal land according to the Balochistan Protection of Communal Property of Minorities Act, 2018.

The judgment also discussed constitutional protections for religious minorities, Islamic legal traditions of religious tolerance, and international human rights obligations. It matters because it strengthens legal safeguards against land mafias exploiting vulnerable minority communities and clarifies that communal properties are protected from private sale altogether.

title: CORRUPTION IN PAKISTAN STEEL MILLS CORPORATION AND OTHERS MATTERS
explainer:
This Supreme Court of Pakistan case involved a suo motu inquiry, meaning the court took up the matter on its own initiative after a newspaper report revealed corruption and mismanagement at Pakistan Steel Mills Corporation during 2008-2009, which allegedly caused billions of rupees in losses to the government. The Chief Justice and two other judges examined whether officials had misused their positions and whether investigating agencies had properly looked into the allegations.

The judgment found that the Federal Investigation Agency and the Ministry of Industries failed to conduct a serious or professional investigation. Directors General of the investigating agency were repeatedly transferred before they could make progress, cases registered against accused persons resulted in bail with no effort made to cancel it, and a forensic audit report showing losses of over 26 billion rupees was ignored while the Ministry deliberated instead of acting. The court noted the agency could not even establish clear links between certain business dealings and the people who benefited from underpriced transactions with the Steel Mills.

The court discussed corruption broadly, citing constitutional duties of citizenship and the UN Convention against Corruption, emphasizing that corruption undermines democratic institutions, the rule of law, and economic stability, and that the state has a duty to investigate and prevent it effectively.

title: Munir Ahmed Khan Kakar and another V. Province of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 7 others,
explainer:
This case is about whether the Balochistan government was following Supreme Court rulings and its own official rules when transferring and posting civil servants. A member of the Balochistan Bar Council petitioned the High Court, arguing that instead of the department Secretary handling transfers as required by law, a provincial minister had been given this power through a 2012 notification, and that transfers were being made on verbal orders and for political reasons, including apparent retaliation against officials in areas where lawmakers had moved a no confidence resolution against the government.

The High Court agreed this was improper. It held that under the Rules of Business, only the Secretary, as administrative head of a department, can handle transfers and postings, not a minister, and that the 2012 notification delegating this power to the minister was illegal and void from the start. The court also stressed that Supreme Court judgments are binding on all government bodies, and no executive action can undermine them. It directed that all future transfers follow proper procedure, requiring formal written summaries rather than verbal instructions, and warned that any official who violates Supreme Court directions could face contempt proceedings.

This matters because it reinforces that civil servants should be protected from political interference and arbitrary transfers, helping ensure a more professional, independent bureaucracy rather than one subject to political victimization.

title: Mir Mujib-Ur-Rehman Muhammad Hassani V. Returning Officer PB-41 Washuk and 16 others,
explainer:
This case is about a challenge to the results of the 2018 provincial assembly election for constituency PB-41 Washuk in Balochistan. The petitioner, who lost by 219 votes, filed an election petition claiming the results should be overturned because of rigging and corrupt practices. He alleged that his polling agents were expelled before counting, some polling stations continued voting late at night without electricity, workers supporting the winning candidate intimidated voters and blocked his supporters from entering polling stations, and that bogus votes were cast in favor of the winner.

The Balochistan High Court, acting as an Election Tribunal, examined the evidence, including witness testimony, but found that the petitioner failed to provide specific details or concrete proof of these allegations. He could not name who committed the illegal acts, had made no written complaints at the time, and relied only on vague, general claims. The court explained that recounting of ballots is not something a losing candidate can demand automatically-it requires solid, specific evidence suggesting real irregularities, not just suspicion or unproven claims. Since the petitioner failed to meet this standard, his request for recounting and his overall petition were dismissed.

This case matters because it reinforces the legal principle that election results, reflecting the will of voters, cannot be overturned or reinvestigated without concrete proof, protecting elections from being challenged on flimsy or unsubstantiated grounds.

title: BARAM KHAN V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerned Baram Khan, who challenged his continued detention under the West Pakistan Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960. He had originally been detained by the Deputy Commissioner of Killa Abdullah after being linked to a criminal case, though that criminal case had already been suspended by the High Court. Despite an order for his release after he furnished surety for good conduct, authorities withdrew that release order before he could actually be freed, and later extended his detention further, citing vague references to "anti-social activities" without specifying any actual incidents.

The Balochistan High Court ruled in his favor. It held that detention under the Public Order Ordinance can only be justified when a person's actions genuinely threaten public peace and safety at large - not merely based on suspicion or unspecified allegations tied to an individual. The court emphasized that personal liberty is constitutionally protected, and any order curtailing it must be backed by concrete, reasonable evidence, not speculation. Since the authorities failed to provide any specific grounds or material justifying the extended detention, and had arbitrarily reversed a release order without new evidence, the court declared the detention order illegal and without lawful authority, ordering Baram Khan's immediate release.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that preventive detention powers cannot be used loosely against individuals without demonstrable threats to public order, and courts will scrutinize such actions to protect constitutional rights to liberty.

title: Obaidullah and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This Balochistan High Court case involved multiple appeals arising from a murder trial. Two men, Zubair Ahmed and Obaidullah, were convicted for killing a person: Zubair was sentenced to death, and Obaidullah to life imprisonment. A third accused had been acquitted by the trial court, and the complainant filed a petition seeking harsher punishment, while the acquitted man's release was challenged separately.

There was no direct evidence of the murder. The case relied on circumstantial evidence, including the accused's disclosures leading to recovery of the murder weapon, forensic ballistic reports confirming the weapon matched crime scene evidence, and confessions recorded by a judicial magistrate. Although the confessions were later retracted, the court found them voluntary, truthful, and corroborated by other evidence, so they could still support conviction.

The court upheld the guilty verdicts against both men, finding the evidence excluded any reasonable possibility of innocence. However, it reduced Zubair's death sentence to life imprisonment, since the confession had been recorded six or seven days after arrest—an irregularity urging caution—and because the crime appeared to have been committed under the influence of an absconding co-accused with whom he had a personal involvement.

Regarding the acquitted man, the court upheld his acquittal since the only evidence against him was an extra-judicial confession made while in police custody, which is not legally admissible.

explainer:

title: Nasar Ud Din V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Nasar Ud Din who was stopped while driving a vehicle, which police allegedly searched and found 67 packets of charas (a narcotic drug) weighing 80 kilograms hidden in secret compartments. He was convicted under Pakistan's narcotics law and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine by a trial court.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction, finding serious flaws in how the prosecution built its case. Instead of testing a sample from each of the 67 packets separately, authorities combined everything into one 670-gram sample and tested only that, which the court said violated established legal requirements, citing prior Supreme Court rulings that each packet must be sampled and tested individually. The laboratory report also failed to properly document the technical protocol behind its chemical testing, making it legally insufficient to prove the substance was actually charas. Additionally, the prosecution could not prove the recovered material had been safely stored and transported to the lab without tampering, and failed to produce a key witness (the police record-keeper) to establish this chain of custody. Most strikingly, the witness who claimed to have found the drugs in secret compartments of the vehicle admitted during cross-examination that no such hidden compartments actually existed.

Given these failures, the court ruled the prosecution had not proven its case beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant, highlighting how procedural shortcuts in narcotics cases can undermine convictions.

title: Wazir Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns Wazir Muhammad, who was convicted by a trial court in Killa Abdullah, Balochistan, for the murder of his wife, Mst. Bibi Gul Dasta, who was killed inside their home. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and fined under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code.

The prosecution's case rested on an FIR lodged by the complainant, the victim's brother, who was not an eyewitness and did not explain how he knew the appellant was responsible. Two other witnesses, the couple's sons, also had not seen the crime themselves; they only repeated information told to them by their uncle, who was never produced or examined in court. The prosecution argued that since the wife died unnaturally inside the husband's house, some burden fell on him to explain her death, and his absconding after the incident suggested guilt.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that hearsay testimony from witnesses who didn't witness the crime cannot reliably identify the real culprit. While the husband's failure to explain his wife's death inside their home was suspicious, this alone did not amount to the level of proof required for a murder conviction. The court also ruled that mere absconding is not proof of guilt, since people flee for many reasons. Finding the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the court acquitted the appellant, extending him the benefit of the doubt and overturning his conviction and sentence.

title: Ahmed Shah and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about two men, Ahmed Shah and Abdul Wali, convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Loralai for possessing explosive substances found in a vehicle they were traveling in. They were sentenced to five years in prison. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

First, the police officer who filed the complaint also conducted the entire investigation himself, which raised concerns about bias, especially since he was of a rank (Assistant Sub-Inspector) below what the law requires for investigating such offenses under the Anti-Terrorism Act. Second, instead of calling independent, respectable witnesses from the area to observe the search and recovery of evidence, as required by law, the officer chose only his own subordinates as witnesses. Third, the prosecution failed to prove the evidence had been safely stored or properly handled after recovery. Finally, there was no proof that one of the appellants was even aware of the explosives hidden in the vehicle's trunk.

Because of these serious lapses, the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. This case highlights the importance of independent witnesses, unbiased investigation, and proper evidence-handling procedures in criminal trials, especially in serious cases involving explosives and terrorism charges

title: Muhammad Essa and another V. The State and another,
explainer:
A man named Muhammad Essa was accused of murdering his wife inside their home at night, allegedly over a strained marriage. His wife's father lodged an FIR naming Essa and another man as suspects. The trial court convicted Essa and sentenced him to death, while acquitting his co-accused. Essa appealed to the Balochistan High Court, and the case also came before the court as a mandatory murder reference.

The High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's case. The FIR was filed over two hours after the crime, raising suspicion that the story may have been deliberated and fabricated rather than reported immediately. The murder happened at night, unwitnessed, inside the house, and Essa was named mainly on suspicion.

The court also found the confession unreliable: it had been recorded under oath by the magistrate, which is legally improper because it effectively forces the accused to testify against himself, violating constitutional protections. There was no record that his handcuffs were removed or that he was given time to reflect before confessing.

Additionally, medical evidence contradicted the prosecution's theory, since the doctor could not have concluded the cause of death before receiving chemical analysis results, yet did so anyway.

The court ruled that a wife's death in her husband's house does not by itself prove his guilt; the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Finding the evidence unreliable, the High Court acquitted Essa, allowing the appeal and rejecting the death sentence.

title: Najeebullah V. The State through Prosecutor General, Balochistan,
explainer:

Given these doubts, the court ruled the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted Najeebullah, highlighting how delayed reporting, contradictory statements, and withheld evidence can undermine a criminal conviction.

title: Khushhal V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a murder conviction. The prosecution alleged that the appellant, along with several co-accused, tried to steal two bullocks from the complainant's home at night. When the complainant tried to catch them, the accused allegedly opened fire, fatally wounding the complainant's brother. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, sentencing him to life imprisonment and a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction, finding the prosecution's case riddled with doubt. Key problems included an unexplained eight-hour delay in filing the police report, raising suspicion of fabrication; the complainant being the only eyewitness, while other claimed witnesses were never produced in court; and a stark contradiction between the ocular account and medical evidence, since the postmortem was conducted eleven hours after death despite the incident happening at 1:30 a.m. The court also noted the implausibility of identifying attackers in darkness, since no light source (like an electric bulb) was ever recovered as evidence, despite claims of available lighting.

The court reaffirmed the principle that any reasonable doubt in a criminal case must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not leniency, and that circumstantial factors like absconding cannot substitute for solid direct evidence. Given these serious inconsistencies, the court acquitted the appellant, allowing the appeal.

title: Rahim Bakhsh V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Rahim Bakhsh, who was arrested at a police checkpoint in Turbat after two kilograms of charas were found in a bag he was carrying, plus another 200 grams from his pocket and 26 grams of crystal (a narcotic substance) recovered from his person. He was charged under section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and applied for bail after the trial court refused it.

His lawyer argued that the case fell into a "borderline" category between lesser and more serious narcotics offences, and that courts should consider the likely actual sentence rather than the maximum possible punishment when deciding bail.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It noted that courts have granted bail in genuine borderline cases where the recovered quantity only slightly exceeds the one-kilogram threshold separating offence categories. Here, however, the amount recovered (2000 grams of charas plus 26 grams of crystal) was far beyond any borderline range. The court also relied on a Supreme Court ruling (Socha Gul v. State) holding that in serious narcotics cases, courts should not speculate about likely sentences at the bail stage, as this would interfere with the trial court's sentencing discretion.

The bail application was dismissed. This case matters because it clarifies that bail in narcotics cases is assessed strictly based on the quantity recovered and established legal thresholds, not on guesses about eventual punishment, especially for large-scale recoveries.

title: Sewa Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Sewa Khan, who was convicted by a Sessions Judge in Kohlu for illegal possession of weapons under the Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965. According to the prosecution, Levies personnel tried to arrest him on an outstanding case, and he allegedly opened fire to resist arrest, wounding a constable, before being overpowered and found with an SMG rifle, three magazines, and 35 live cartridges. He was convicted and sentenced to three years' imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. The court found serious gaps in the prosecution's evidence: the injured constable was never produced in court, nor was any medical certificate presented to prove he was shot; no bullet casings (empties) were recovered from the scene despite claims that firing occurred from both sides; the FIR did not mention whether the accused was asked for a weapons license or confirmed to lack one; and, crucially, the recovered weapon was never sent to a ballistics expert to confirm it was even functional.

The court emphasized that in criminal cases, guilt must be proven firmly through solid evidence, not assumptions. Since the prosecution failed to establish basic facts—like the weapon's working condition or the absence of a valid license—the conviction could not stand. The appeal was allowed, and Sewa Khan was acquitted and ordered released unless wanted in another case. The judgment highlights the importance of forensic verification and complete evidence in arms possession cases.

title: Bismillah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Bismillah who was charged under section 324 of the Pakistan Penal Code (attempted murder) after an incident where a pistol was used. During his trial, the parties reached a compromise, and the trial court accepted this compromise under section 345(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, acquitting him of the charge. However, despite acquitting him, the trial court ordered his licensed pistol to be confiscated by the State and directed the cancellation of his arms license.

Bismillah appealed this part of the order, arguing that once he was acquitted, he was entitled to get his property, including the pistol, back, and that the trial court had no legal authority under the West Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965 to cancel his license, since that power belongs only to specific licensing or judicial authorities defined in the law.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with him. It held that an acquittal is an acquittal, whether it results from a full trial, an early dismissal of charges, or a compromise between parties, and all such acquittals carry the same legal consequences. Therefore, Bismillah was entitled to the return of his property. The court set aside the confiscation order and directed that the pistol be returned to him, subject to verification of his license by the appropriate authority. This case clarifies that people acquitted through compromise are entitled to the same rights as those acquitted on merits, including recovery of seized property.

title: Muhammad Ajmal and 3 others V. Province of Balochistan through Secretary Irrigations and others,
explainer:
This case is about farmers near Quetta who had, for generations, irrigated their crops using untreated sewage (black/grey) water flowing through the Nohsar channel. Earlier, in 2014, the court had allowed them to continue this practice on condition that the sewage water be diluted with purified water at a fixed ratio. When authorities later blocked the channel at several points, cutting off water to about 1,000 acres, the farmers went back to court, arguing this violated their fundamental right under Article 18 of the Constitution to freely carry on their trade and livelihood.

The Balochistan High Court examined official reports showing the "sewage" water actually contained hazardous waste from households, hospitals, and factories. Crops, especially leafy vegetables, grown with this contaminated water were absorbing toxic chemicals and metals, posing serious health risks to consumers in the local market. The court held that while Article 18 protects freedom of trade and business, this right only extends to lawful business, not one that endangers public health. It ruled that cultivating crops with contaminated sewage water is an unlawful business and directed authorities to stop it, relying on the earlier Shehla Zia case on environmental rights.

The judgment matters because it shows courts can use their constitutional powers to protect public health and safety, even when this restricts an economic activity that people have depended on for their livelihood.

title: Muhammad Ajmal and others V. Province of Balochistan through Secretary Irrigation and others,
explainer:
This case is about a request to review an earlier ruling by the Balochistan High Court concerning the use of contaminated sewage water for farming near Quetta. In the original judgment, the court had ruled that irrigating crops with contaminated, arsenic-laced wastewater was dangerous to human and animal health and ordered this practice stopped, declared void an agreement that allowed farmers to mix wastewater with clean water for irrigation, and directed authorities to enforce the ban, including through criminal law if necessary.

Some farmers then filed a review application, asking the court to reconsider its decision specifically regarding the cultivation of wheat, barley, and fodder. They argued that the government had not produced any laboratory reports proving that these particular crops were actually harmful to humans or animals.

The court rejected this review application. It explained that a review is not the same as an appeal, it can only correct clear, obvious errors on the face of the record, not allow parties to reargue their case or seek a different outcome. The judges found that the farmers had not identified any real legal error or irregularity in the original ruling. They noted that the earlier judgment had already relied on scientific studies showing that while sewage water contains nutrients that can boost plant growth, it also introduces harmful heavy metals into crops, soil, and the environment, posing risks to human and animal health. Since these concerns were already properly addressed, the review was dismissed. This case highlights the limited scope of judicial review and reinforces protection of public health and environmental safety.

title: Mst. Sameena Anwar and 2 others V. The Manager, United Bank Ltd. and others,
explainer:
This case involved a woman and her two daughters seeking release of money from a bank account belonging to their husband and father, Abdul Ghaffar, who had gone missing in 2009 after leaving home and never returning, despite an FIR and complaints to the Commission for Enforced Disappearance. The bank refused to release the funds, insisting that his death first be legally confirmed and that a succession certificate be obtained from a court.

The Balochistan High Court examined whether a missing person can be declared dead by a court, and whether a succession certificate was mandatory before releasing funds. The court held that life cannot be ended by legal declaration just as it is not created by law, so a missing person cannot simply be declared dead. It distinguished between natural death and civil death, noting Islamic law treats a missing person as alive until 90 years from birth. However, relying on Section 124 of the Contract Act on indemnity, the court ruled that the wife could obtain the funds by furnishing an affidavit or personal indemnity bond, protecting the bank if the missing person later reappeared. The petition was allowed, and the bank was directed to release the money to the wife upon such indemnity, without requiring proof of death or a succession certificate.

This judgment matters because it provides a practical, humane solution allowing families of missing persons to access frozen funds for survival, without forcing an artificial legal declaration of death.

title: Dr. Ilyas and another V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and others ,
explainer:

The Balochistan High Court held that this arrangement was unconstitutional. Under Article 105 of the Constitution, the Governor of a province is generally bound to act on the advice of the Chief Minister, except in specific situations where the Constitution expressly allows independent discretion. The court rejected the argument that a Governor acting under a special statute (rather than directly under the Constitution) could bypass this requirement, saying no such distinction exists in law. Since the Governor has no powers beyond what the Constitution grants, a law cannot give him unchecked personal authority to appoint university heads.

The court also explained the background of the 18th Constitutional Amendment, which shifted education mostly to provincial control, while matters of standards in higher education remained under joint federal-provincial jurisdiction.

As a result, the court struck down the relevant sections (15(1) and 15(2)) of the university law, declaring them void for violating Article 105. This case matters because it reinforces the principle of constitutional government—Governors must act on ministerial advice—and limits the ability of provincial laws to hand unchecked personal power to a Governor in university appointments.

title: Commissioner Inland Revenue Zone-I, Regional Tax Office, Quetta V. M/s. Quetta Electric Supply Company Limited, Quetta,
explainer:
This case is about how Quetta Electric Supply Company (QESCO) should be taxed on money it receives from the Government of Pakistan known as the Tariff Differential Subsidy (TDS). QESCO sells electricity to consumers at a rate lower than the tariff fixed by the power regulator NEPRA, and the Government pays it the difference. The tax department treated this TDS amount as part of QESCO's "turnover" or sales, making it subject to minimum tax under Section 113 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. QESCO argued the TDS was a subsidy from the Government, not sale proceeds, and should be tax-exempt. A tax tribunal ruled in favor of QESCO, and the tax department challenged that ruling in the High Court.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed with the tribunal. It held that the TDS is not truly a "subsidy" or bailout grant, but simply the balance price of electricity that the Government pays on behalf of consumers to give them relief. Since it represents payment for electricity actually supplied, the full amount, including the TDS, counts as gross revenue from the sale of electricity and is subject to minimum tax unless a specific legal exemption exists. The court also found the tribunal had wrongly relied on an exemption clause that only applies to total income, not to minimum tax exemptions, which fall under a different part of the law.

This decision matters because it clarifies that electric supply companies cannot avoid minimum tax on government-paid subsidy amounts tied to electricity sales,

title: Sardar Muhammad V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Home and Tribal Affairs Department, Quetta and 5 others,
explainer:
This case is about a man, Sardar Muhammad, who complained to the Balochistan High Court that police were harassing him, raiding his house without warrants, and pressuring him to pay off a debt that was not his own. The alleged debt had actually been taken by his brother, whom the family had publicly disowned, from a private lender (respondent No.6). Instead of taking action against the lender, police repeatedly summoned and pressured the petitioner to repay the money.

The court noted that private money lending is itself illegal under the Balochistan Prohibition of Private Money Lending Act, 2014, and that the police, through their Complaint Redressal Cell, had wrongly used their authority to force repayment on behalf of the lender rather than investigating him for the illegal lending. The judges held that police had no jurisdiction to act as debt collectors and that such financial disputes must be resolved by a proper court after evidence is examined, not through police pressure.

The court also made broader observations about the separation of powers, stressing that only constitutionally recognized courts and tribunals can exercise judicial functions, and that bodies like police complaint cells cannot assume that role. It ruled in favor of the petitioner, ordering the police to stop interfering in the private dispute. The judgment matters because it reinforces limits on police power and protects citizens from being misused as pressure tools in private financial disagreements.

title: Masooma and another V. Federal Government through Ministry of Interior Pak Secretariat and another,
explainer:
This case concerns two women whose ancestors migrated from Afghanistan to Pakistan, and who themselves were born in Pakistan and later married Pakistani citizens. They applied for Computerized National Identity Cards (CNICs) after meeting the required conditions, but their applications were rejected by NADRA. They challenged this refusal before the Balochistan High Court, arguing they were entitled to CNICs as citizens.

The court examined the Pakistan Citizenship Act, 1951, particularly the provisions on married women (Section 10) and certificates of domicile (Section 17). It found that under the law, a foreign woman married to a Pakistani citizen can be registered as a Pakistani citizen, but only after obtaining a Certificate of Domicile from the Federal Government and taking an oath of allegiance. The court noted that this special route is available only to female foreign nationals, not males. Since the petitioners had not obtained such domicile certificates, NADRA lacked the legal power to issue them CNICs, even though the women appeared otherwise entitled to citizenship by birth and marriage.

Recognizing the hardship caused by their lack of identity documents, the court did not dismiss the petitions outright. Instead, it directed the petitioners to apply to the Federal Government for Certificates of Domicile through the proper process, after which their citizenship and CNIC status could be resolved. The case highlights procedural requirements foreign-born spouses must satisfy to gain recognition as Pakistani citizens.

Swati asked the Balochistan High Court to quash all these FIRs, arguing it was unfair and legally wrong to prosecute him multiple times, in multiple cities, for one and the same act.

The High Court agreed. It held that registering several FIRs across different jurisdictions for the same incident, under the same legal provisions and against the same person, violated constitutional guarantees against double jeopardy (Articles 4 and 13) as well as provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code and General Clauses Act. The law intends a single trial for a single offence, not parallel prosecutions in different courts. Relying on Supreme Court precedent, the judge ruled that pursuing multiple simultaneous cases amounted to harassment and misuse of legal process.

The court therefore quashed all the FIRs and ordered Swati's release. The judgment reinforces the principle that a person cannot be tried repeatedly for the same conduct merely by lodging cases in different locations.

title: Abdul Wai and 2 others V. State,
explainer:
This case involved three men convicted of robbery under Sections 392/34 of the Pakistan Penal Code for allegedly snatching a motorcycle, mobile phone, and cash at gunpoint. They were sentenced to three years imprisonment by a trial court, and that conviction was upheld on appeal. They then challenged their conviction before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious flaws in the prosecution's case. The FIR was lodged 24 hours after the incident with no explanation for the delay, raising suspicion that the story may have been fabricated in the meantime. The complainant also gave contradictory statements about the distance between the crime scene and the police station, which affected the question of whether the police even had jurisdiction to investigate. His account of the incident also included details not mentioned in his original statement to police. Additionally, the recovery of the motorcycle was not properly witnessed by independent people, ownership documents were never verified, and the complainant failed to specify what role the accused actually played in the crime, relying merely on identification.

Given these gaps and contradictions, the Court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. It accepted the petition, meaning the conviction was overturned.

This case matters because it reinforces important legal principles: delays in filing police reports, inconsistent testimony, and weak evidence collection can all undermine a criminal case, and courts must give the benefit of the doubt to the accused when such doubts exist.

title: Waqas Ahmed V. Arshad Mehmood and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal appeal against acquittal decided by the Balochistan High Court. Waqas Ahmed had accused Arshad Mehmood and others of murdering his brother, Waqar Ahmed, in an armed ambush. According to the complaint, six men on motorcycles stopped the family's vehicle, dragged the brother out, and shot him on the instructions of one of the accused. A trial court had already acquitted the accused under a legal provision allowing early acquittal when the evidence is weak, and the complainant appealed against that decision.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. It found serious problems with the prosecution's case: the FIR was filed seven hours after the incident without a good explanation, raising suspicion that the complainant may have consulted others before naming suspects. The complainant's story that he walked to the police station despite having a vehicle available also seemed implausible. Additionally, the key eyewitness failed to identify the accused in court, no identification parade was conducted, and physical evidence like bullet casings and blood-stained soil was collected fourteen days late. The witnesses were also close relatives of the victim, raising questions about bias.

The court explained that once someone is acquitted, they gain a "double presumption of innocence," meaning strong evidence is needed to reverse that finding on appeal. Since the trial court's reasoning was sound and not based on any misreading of evidence, the High Court dismissed the appeal, confirming the acquittal of the accused.

title: Abdul Qudoos V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Qudoos, who was convicted by a Special Judge in Dalbandin under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, for allegedly possessing 38 packets of charas found during a police raid on a house. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him. The court found several serious problems with the prosecution's case. First, the police never actually proved that the house where the drugs were found belonged to or was controlled by the accused—no documents, land records, or neighbor testimony were presented to establish this, and witnesses admitted other people also lived there. Since mere recovery from a house doesn't prove guilt unless ownership and conscious possession are established with solid evidence, this gap was fatal to the case.

Second, the drug samples were sent for chemical testing 35 days after seizure, an unexplained and unusual delay that raised doubts about whether the samples were properly stored and safely transported to the laboratory. The court relied on Supreme Court precedent holding that when safe custody and transmission aren't proven, lab reports become unreliable. Additionally, the laboratory report itself lacked complete testing protocols required by law.

This case highlights how narcotics convictions require the prosecution to prove not just recovery of drugs, but also possession, ownership, and proper handling of evidence—procedural shortcuts can result in acquittal even in serious drug cases.

title: Abdul Raheem V. The State,
explainer:

He was accused of carrying 2 kilograms of hashish on his person, while another 3.4 kilograms of opium was allegedly recovered from beneath the seat of the rickshaw he was traveling in, along with a co-accused.

The Balochistan High Court granted him bail. The judges found that the evidence connecting him to the opium found in the rickshaw lacked independent supporting proof, and it was not yet established that he had knowledge of the opium's presence. This meant the case required further inquiry rather than being a clear-cut matter. The court also noted that for the hashish recovery, the amount involved meant he likely would not face the maximum possible sentence, and courts deciding bail should consider the sentence realistically expected in the circumstances, not just the harshest penalty theoretically available under the law. Since he had already completed the investigation phase and been moved to jail custody, keeping him detained further served no real purpose.

This case is a useful illustration of how courts approach bail in narcotics cases, showing that weak or uncorroborated evidence linking an accused to recovered substances, combined with the principle that bail should reflect the likely rather than maximum sentence, can justify release even in serious drug cases while the trial proceeds.

title: Mst. Sahiba V. Dr. Akbar and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of two men accused of beating a woman and her sisters with sticks in Quetta in 2013. The complainant had filed a case under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with causing hurt. During the trial, after only four prosecution witnesses had testified, the accused applied for early acquittal under Section 249-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows a magistrate to acquit an accused at any stage if the charge appears groundless or conviction seems improbable. The trial court granted this acquittal, and the complainant appealed.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the acquittal. It found serious problems with the prosecution's case: the FIR was lodged more than ten hours after the alleged incident without any explanation, raising suspicion that the complainant may have deliberated or consulted others before filing it. Even more significantly, evidence showed that some witness statements were recorded by police before the FIR was even registered, suggesting investigation began before the formal complaint was made, which undermines the FIR's credibility. Additionally, the medical evidence contradicted the witnesses' claims of injury, including an alleged fractured finger that medical examination did not confirm.

The court reaffirmed that convictions require solid, credible evidence, and any doubt must benefit the accused. It also noted that acquittals carry a "double presumption of innocence" that appellate courts are reluctant to disturb unless there is a clear miscarriage of justice. Finding none here, the court dismissed the appeal.

title: Atta Muhammad V. Aurangzaib and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of two men accused of murdering a young man named Muhammad Rafique. The victim's father, who was the complainant, alleged that during a quarrel between his neighbors and his brother-in-law, the accused held him and his brother-in-law down while another person (not one of the two respondents) stabbed his son to death. The father challenged the trial court's decision to acquit the two respondents, arguing the evidence against them was strong and had been wrongly dismissed.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed with the appellant and upheld the acquittal. It found that none of the prosecution's eyewitnesses had accused the two respondents of actually inflicting any injury, and all witnesses agreed the respondents were unarmed at the time. The court also noted that all the eyewitnesses were close relatives of the complainant, even though independent bystanders were reportedly present, raising doubts about the reliability of the testimony. Mere presence at the scene, the court held, does not prove participation in a crime, and there was no solid evidence that the respondents shared a common intention to kill.

The judgment reinforces an important legal principle: when a person is acquitted by a trial court, that acquittal carries a strong presumption of innocence that appellate courts should not overturn unless the original decision was clearly unreasonable or unsupported by evidence. Here, the High Court found the trial court's reasoning sound and dismissed the appeal.

title: Nasibullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Nasibullah who was convicted by a trial court in Pishin for possessing an unlicensed pistol under the Arms Ordinance, 1965, and sentenced to three years imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the police failed to follow proper legal procedure when arresting him and recovering the weapon.

The High Court found several serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, although the investigating officer had recorded a statement from a private witness (someone from the public, not police) at the scene, the prosecution never brought that witness to testify at trial, without any explanation. The court held that failing to produce this witness raised a legal presumption that his testimony would have gone against the prosecution's version of events. Second, the law requires police to involve independent local witnesses when conducting searches and recoveries, and the prosecution did not adequately show why this wasn't done. Third, there was an unexplained 27-day delay before the seized weapon was sent for forensic testing, further undermining confidence in the evidence.

Because of these gaps, the court ruled that the prosecution had failed to prove its case against Nasibullah beyond reasonable doubt. It set aside his conviction and sentence and acquitted him.

This case highlights how procedural safeguards, like producing independent witnesses and avoiding unexplained delays in evidence handling, are essential to ensuring fair trials, especially in cases involving police-led arrests and recoveries.

title: Alamgir V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a vehicle seized by Pakistan Coast Guards after narcotics, 3.9 kg of charas and 10 kg of opium, were found in its toolbox. The vehicle's registered owner, Alamgir, was not the driver and was not accused in the criminal case. He applied to the trial court for temporary custody of the vehicle (called superdari) while the case proceeded, but the trial court rejected his request.

Alamgir appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing he was the undisputed owner, had no connection to drug trafficking, was unaware the vehicle was being misused, and that the vehicle was deteriorating while sitting unused at the police station, harming his family's livelihood. The state opposed this, saying releasing such vehicles would encourage narcotics transportation.

The High Court sided with Alamgir. It noted he was not an accused, the prosecution had presented no evidence showing he knew about the narcotics, and the drugs were found in an ordinary toolbox rather than a hidden compartment built into the vehicle. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the court held that a vehicle cannot be confiscated unless it is proven the owner knew it was being used for crime. Since no evidence of such knowledge existed and Alamgir held valid ownership documents, the court set aside the trial court's order and directed the vehicle be released to him on furnishing a surety bond of Rs. 500,000.

title: Lal Bibi and 10 others V. Abdul Rehman and 8 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute in Quetta over land left behind by a deceased government officer, Abdul Hayee, whose heirs disagreed over how various properties, allegedly purchased under other people's names (benami transactions), should be divided. Two civil suits were filed and later combined, and after trial, the court decided the matter based on a compromise agreement reached between the parties in 2004.

Later, some of the heirs who felt shortchanged by the compromise filed an application under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, arguing that the compromise decree should be set aside because it was obtained through fraud and misrepresentation, and that they had not received their fair share of the inheritance. The trial court rejected this application, but on appeal, the Additional District Judge sent the case back to the trial court, ruling that evidence should be recorded and the matter reconsidered.

The petitioners then challenged this remand order before the High Court, arguing it was wrongly decided and that the application was filed too late without proper explanation.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It ruled that since specific allegations of fraud and misrepresentation had been raised and denied, the parties deserved a fair opportunity to present evidence before any final decision was made. The petition was dismissed, meaning the case would go back for a proper hearing with evidence, ensuring fairness in resolving the inheritance dispute.

title: Lal Bibi and 10 others V. Abdul Rehman and 8 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over inheritance property left by a deceased man, Abdul Hayee, who allegedly purchased various properties in Quetta and Mastung through "benami" (nominal) transactions. His heirs filed civil suits seeking declaration, correction of revenue records, partition, and injunctions regarding these properties. The two related suits were consolidated by the trial court, and eventually both suits were decided based on a compromise between the parties, following an earlier remand caused by an appeal from an outside party (intervener).

Some heirs, however, later challenged that compromise decree by filing an application under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, arguing they had not received their rightful shares. The trial court dismissed this application, but on revision, the Additional District Judge sent the matter back to the trial court, directing that issues be framed and evidence recorded before deciding the application afresh.

The petitioners then approached the High Court, arguing this remand was improper. The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition, holding that while framing issues is not always mandatory in Section 12(2) applications, in cases like this one, where facts are disputed, parties must be given a fair chance to present evidence before a decision is made. Finding no illegality in the lower court's order, the High Court upheld the remand, emphasizing the importance of due process and fair hearing in resolving property and inheritance disputes.

title: Abdul Aziz and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves two men, Abdul Aziz and another appellant, who were caught by Excise Police in Sibi after their car was intercepted based on a tip-off. Police found five kilograms of charas (a narcotic substance) hidden in secret cavities of the vehicle. A trial court convicted them under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, sentencing each to life imprisonment and a fine.

On appeal, their lawyer argued that the forensic laboratory report used to prove the substance was indeed narcotics was legally defective. The report did not follow the mandatory format required by law, failed to describe the complete testing protocol, and did not explain how the sample was safely transported to the laboratory for testing. The officer who handled the sample was also never questioned in court.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the defense, relying on Supreme Court precedents establishing that such analyst reports must strictly follow prescribed rules to be considered valid evidence. Since the report in this case failed to meet these legal requirements, the court ruled it had no evidentiary value.

As a result, the High Court overturned the convictions and allowed the appeal, meaning the men were not proven guilty based on the flawed evidence presented.

This case matters because it reinforces that in narcotics cases, technical compliance with forensic testing and reporting procedures is not a mere formality—it is essential to protect the rights of the accused and ensure convictions are based on reliable scientific evidence.

title: Muhammad Ismail Khan V. Yar Muhammad and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal appeal filed by a father after the men accused of beating his son were acquitted by a trial court in Kharan, Balochistan.

Muhammad Ismail Khan's son, Noor Ahmed, was allegedly attacked and beaten by Yar Muhammad and two others while performing ablution near a tank. The father lodged an FIR, and the accused were tried for causing hurt under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code. After hearing eight prosecution witnesses, the trial court acquitted all three accused. The father then filed an appeal against this acquittal under Section 417(2-A) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows a "person aggrieved" to appeal an acquittal.

The Balochistan High Court did not examine the merits of the beating allegations at all. Instead, it focused on a threshold legal question: was the father legally entitled to file this appeal? The court held that "person aggrieved" in hurt cases means the actual victim who suffered the injury, not just any relative or family member. Since the father was not present at the scene, was not himself beaten, abused or threatened, and only learned of the incident afterward, he did not qualify as an aggrieved person under the law. The court distinguished murder cases, where legal heirs of a deceased victim can pursue appeals, from hurt cases, where only the injured person themselves generally has that right. As a result, the appeal was dismissed as not maintainable, without any ruling on whether the accused were actually guilty.

title: Ghulam Nabi V. Mir Muhammad Ali Rind,
explainer:
This case concerns a lawsuit for 250 million rupees in damages, filed by Mir Muhammad Ali Rind against Ghulam Nabi over alleged false accusations of corruption and running terrorist camps. During the proceedings, Ghulam Nabi stopped appearing in court. After repeated failed attempts at notifying him through ordinary means, the trial court ordered notice by newspaper publication (substituted service). However, the publication was submitted late and did not correspond to the actual hearing date on which Ghulam Nabi was ultimately declared absent (ex-parte). The court then decided the case against him and awarded damages without his participation.

Ghulam Nabi later asked the trial court to set aside this ex-parte decree, arguing he was never properly informed of the case. The trial court refused, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found that the trial court had not followed the proper legal procedure for substituted service, such as pasting notice at his home or business, or confirming through a process server that ordinary summons had failed. It also found that he was declared ex-parte on a date for which no valid publication existed. The High Court held this was a serious legal error and ruled that cases should be decided on their merits, not technical shortcuts. It allowed the appeal, effectively giving Ghulam Nabi a chance to defend the case properly.

title: Ali Akbar V. Mst. Samina and another,
explainer:
This case involved a husband and wife whose marriage lasted only seven months before breaking down. The wife filed a suit in the Family Court seeking dissolution of marriage, return of her dowry articles (or their value), and unpaid maintenance, alleging that her husband and his family mistreated her, that he was a drug addict who tortured her while intoxicated, and that she was eventually thrown out of the house. The husband contested the case, but the Family Court ruled in the wife's favor, granting dissolution of marriage and ordering return of dowry articles and maintenance. The husband challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court, arguing the trial court had ignored evidence and wrongly accepted the wife's claim of cruelty.

The High Court dismissed the husband's petition. It held that the trial court was right to dissolve the marriage since genuine hatred had developed in the wife's mind, which is a valid ground for such relief, and courts must assess this based on the facts of each case. On the dowry issue, the husband's own witnesses admitted the wife had brought the articles, shifting the burden to him to prove otherwise, which he failed to do. The court noted that in practice, brides are rarely able to keep receipts or signed lists of dowry items. This case matters because it reinforces that courts can rely on the overall circumstances and testimony, rather than strict documentary proof, when deciding dowry and divorce disputes.

title: Chief Executive Officer QESCO and another V. Azizullah, Commercial Superintendent and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute between QESCO (Quetta Electric Supply Company) and three of its employees, working as Commercial Superintendents, over pay upgradation. The employees had been promoted through the ranks over decades of service and, based on an official government memorandum dated 22 April 2013, claimed they were entitled to a two-step time scale up-gradation. This memorandum stated that employees in a certain pay grade (BPS-15) should receive this benefit. When QESCO did not grant it, the employees filed a grievance, which was upheld by the Labour Court and then by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. QESCO challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed QESCO's petition. It found that QESCO had failed to produce any documentary evidence to counter the employees' claim, relying only on a verbal statement from a company representative. Although QESCO cited other official memorandums in its written defense, it never actually proved them in court, and the law requires documents to be properly proved, not just mentioned in pleadings. Since the employees met the qualifications set out in the 2013 memorandum, the court held they were rightly entitled to the upgradation.

This case matters because it reinforces a basic evidentiary principle: government departments cannot simply assert facts or cite documents in written statements—they must formally prove them in court, or risk losing the case, even against their own employees.

title: Attaullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a bail application filed by Attaullah, who was arrested and charged under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, after five kilograms of narcotics were allegedly recovered from his possession during a routine check of a passenger coach by Coast Guard personnel in Uthal, Balochistan.

Attaullah's lawyer argued for bail on the grounds that the investigation had dragged on for over six months without witness statements being recorded, that no independent or public witness was present during the search, and that the challan (charge sheet) had already been submitted, meaning the accused was no longer needed for further investigation.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that the requirement under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code for independent witnesses during a search does not apply to narcotics cases, since this requirement is specifically excluded by Section 25 of the CNS Act. The court also noted that law enforcement officers are considered credible witnesses unless the accused can show bias or ill will, which was not demonstrated here. Since the offence carried a punishment of life imprisonment or death, it fell under the category of serious offences where bail is generally restricted under Section 497 of the CrPC. The court further explained that bail should not normally be granted at the early stage of a trial when evidence is still being presented.

This judgment reinforces how Pakistani courts treat narcotics cases seriously, limiting bail where large quantities of drugs are involved and the recovery process appears procedurally sound.

title: Noor Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a request to move a criminal trial from one court to another. Noor Muhammad, a sitting minister in the Balochistan Provincial Assembly, was an accused in a murder case registered in 2011, in which he and two others were alleged to have attacked and killed a young man named Abdul Qayum. Muhammad had already obtained pre-arrest bail, which was later confirmed. He then asked the Balochistan High Court to transfer his trial from the Sessions Judge in Loralai to a court in Quetta, arguing that as a provincial minister he had received serious threats of dire consequences from the complainant and feared for his safety.

The High Court rejected the request. It noted that the applicant failed to provide any actual evidence of the alleged threats, such as copies of threatening messages or a report to any authority. Mere claims of danger, without supporting proof, were not enough to justify transferring a case. The court also pointed out that being a minister does not automatically entitle someone to special treatment in court, and that the government, not the courts, is responsible for a minister's personal security.

The judgment reaffirms an important legal principle: cases can only be transferred from a competent court if there are strong, convincing reasons showing that a fair trial isn't possible there - not simply because a party requests it or claims vague apprehensions.

title: Haji Muhammad Amin V. Hafiz Abdul Malik and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a land dispute in Kharan, Balochistan. Two brothers (respondents) claimed ownership of land called Cheedai, saying it originally belonged to their maternal grandfather, was gifted to their mother, and then passed to them. They sought a court declaration confirming their ownership and cancellation of a conflicting land mutation record, plus a permanent injunction. The trial court initially dismissed their suit, but after an appeal and remand, dismissed it again. The brothers appealed again to the Majlis-e-Shoora (appellate forum), which this time ruled in their favor and reversed the trial court's decision.

The losing party then challenged this appellate decision before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court found that the appellate court's judgment was legally flawed because it failed to follow mandatory procedure under Order XLI, Rule 31 of the Civil Procedure Code. This rule requires an appellate court to clearly identify the specific points in dispute, give its decision on each point, and explain its reasoning—especially when reversing a lower court's ruling. The appellate court had not done this, and had also failed to rule on the specific request to cancel the land mutation.

Because of these gaps, the High Court set aside the appellate court's judgment and sent the case back for a fresh decision that properly follows the required legal procedure. This case highlights the importance of appellate courts providing clear, reasoned judgments rather than simply reversing decisions without proper analysis.

title: Ghulam Muhammad and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Ghulam Muhammad and another appellant, who were convicted by a trial court in Mastung for possessing narcotics under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. Levies personnel had stopped their motorcycle at a checkpoint and allegedly recovered packets of charas (cannabis) weighing several kilograms, hidden in the vehicle's saddlebags. Based on this recovery, both men were sentenced to eight years' rigorous imprisonment plus fines.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the forensic evidence closely. It found that the Government Analyst's report, which was central to proving the substance was actually a narcotic, did not comply with mandatory rules requiring full protocols and test details to be documented. Without this, the report had no real evidentiary value. The court also noted that the prosecution failed to produce the process-server who supposedly carried the drug samples to the laboratory, meaning there was no proof the samples were safely and reliably transmitted without tampering or mix-up.

Relying on Supreme Court precedents, the High Court held that these gaps created serious doubt about the prosecution's case. Since the benefit of doubt in criminal cases must go to the accused, the court allowed both appeals and set aside the convictions.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that narcotics convictions cannot rest on incomplete or improperly verified laboratory reports, protecting individuals from wrongful convictions based on weak forensic and chain-of-custody evidence.

title: Rizwan V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns a bail application filed by Rizwan, who was arrested after police on routine patrol allegedly recovered 1300 grams of charas and 300 grams of crystal (a narcotic) from his possession. He was booked under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and his earlier bail request had been rejected by the trial court.

The Balochistan High Court granted him bail. The key reasoning was that the recovered quantity of charas only marginally exceeded 1000 grams, placing the case on the borderline between two different punishment categories under Section 9 of the Act (clauses b and c). Courts have consistently held that in such borderline cases, bail should generally be granted, and where a law provides two possible sentence ranges, the lesser one should be considered for bail purposes. This meant the exact punishment applicable was uncertain and required further inquiry during trial, which is itself a valid ground for bail under Section 497(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The court also noted that since the witnesses were only police personnel and the applicant was already in judicial custody, there was no risk of him tampering with evidence or needing further investigation. Additionally, medical records showed he was suffering from cancer, and keeping him in custody without proper treatment could endanger his life.

The court granted bail on furnishing sureties, clarifying that its observations were tentative and would not affect the final trial outcome. This case illustrates how borderline drug quantities and health concerns can influence bail decisions.

title: Sher Ali Kakar V. Station Head Quarters, through Umair Hameed,
explainer:
This case involved a landlord-tenant dispute over property damage. The Station Head Quarters (representing military authorities) sued Sher Ali Kakar, a former tenant of a rented house in Quetta Cantonment, claiming he had damaged the property extensively before vacating it and demanding over 57 lakh rupees in compensation.

The defendant tried to get the case dismissed early on through a legal application, which the trial court rejected, ordering him instead to file his formal written response (written statement). However, the defendant failed to appear on the scheduled dates for various reasons, including a lawyers' strike. The trial court eventually closed his right to file a written statement due to his repeated absence, and after hearing only the plaintiff's evidence, decided the case against him without his side being heard, awarding damages to the plaintiff.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found that the trial court had not given the defendant genuine, fair opportunity to defend himself. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, it held that deadlines for filing written statements are procedural guidelines meant to speed up cases, not rigid rules allowing courts to punish parties without proper notice. The High Court ruled that the trial court should have formally summoned the defendant before shutting him out. It set aside the judgment and sent the case back for a fresh, fair hearing on merits. This decision reinforces that courts must prioritize substantive justice over technical procedural strictness, especially before deciding cases in a party's absence.

title: Umar Mukhtar V. The State through Director General Regional Accountability Bureau and others,
explainer:
This case is about three officials of Balochistan's Food Department, along with a flour mill owner, who were convicted by an Accountability Court for embezzling wheat meant to be sold as subsidized flour (atta) through fair price shops to the public. The Regional Accountability Bureau alleged that the flour mill lifted more wheat than it converted into flour for distribution, and that the responsible Assistant Directors of Food failed to prevent this, causing loss to the government treasury. The trial court had sentenced them each to ten years' imprisonment, heavy fines, and disqualification from public office.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the convictions. It found that the prosecution had not properly investigated the matter: officials from the administration who were supposed to monitor sales were never questioned, the fair price shop owners were never examined, and no evidence showed wheat was actually misappropriated or sold illegally. There was also no proof that the accused received any financial benefit. The court held that the case was built on assumptions rather than solid proof, and that under the law, misuse of authority and criminal intent must be clearly established before an accused can be asked to prove innocence.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that in corruption and accountability cases, the burden of proof lies strictly with the prosecution, and convictions cannot rest on suspicion or incomplete investigation. The appeals were allowed and the accused were acquitted.
