title: Muhammad Khan Durrani through Attorney V. Abdul Ali Durrani and 4 others,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute in Quetta, Balochistan. Muhammad Khan Durrani claimed he originally bought a large piece of land, distributed portions of it to his father and brothers, and kept 13 poles for himself, on which he built a house. He alleged that he later asked his relatives to vacate the house for his son's use, but they refused, and his mother claimed the property mutation was actually in her name. He sought a court declaration that he was the rightful owner, that certain mutations (official land records) were fraudulent and should be cancelled, and that he be given possession of the house.

The trial court dismissed his suit, and he appealed. The Balochistan High Court upheld that dismissal. The judges found that the appellant failed to prove his ownership claim with solid evidence — his testimony was contradictory and unconvincing, he provided no witnesses to the original purchase, and he did not adequately rebut the documents produced by the other side, which carried a legal presumption of truthfulness. The court also held the suit was filed too late (barred by limitation) and reiterated the legal principle that anyone alleging fraud must prove it with real evidence, not just verbal claims. The court also noted that a plaintiff must win on the strength of his own case, not merely because the defendants' evidence was weak.

This case illustrates how Pakistani courts require strong, credible proof — not just allegations — in property and fraud disputes, and it reinforces that delays in filing suits can be fatal to a claim.

title: Sabzal Khan and 9 others V. Muhammad Akbar and 10 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over agricultural land in Mastung, Balochistan. The petitioners claimed they were the rightful owners of certain land, both settled and unsettled, based on ancestral possession, purchase deeds, and old land grants (sanads). They filed a suit seeking a declaration of ownership, a permanent injunction against interference, and correction of revenue records. The trial court dismissed their suit, and on appeal, the appellate court partly allowed it only regarding the settled land, not the unsettled land. The petitioners then challenged this outcome before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the petitioners' case. It found that the land mutation had been carried out back in 1962-64 in the presence of the petitioners, who raised no objection at the time and effectively accepted it. Since they waited more than fifty years to challenge it—far beyond the six-year limitation period for declaratory suits—their claim was time-barred. The court also noted they failed to explain this long delay or provide strong evidence proving ownership of the unsettled land. Under the law, unclaimed forests and wasteland are presumed to belong to the government unless proven otherwise.

This judgment reinforces two important legal principles: parties must challenge property records promptly, and unsettled or waste land is presumed government property unless private ownership is clearly established through solid evidence.

title: Nasrullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Nasrullah, who was convicted by a trial court in Loralai for illegal possession of a pistol under the Arms Ordinance, 1965, and sentenced to two years' imprisonment plus a fine. The pistol had allegedly been recovered based on information he gave during investigation of a separate, unrelated murder case.

Nasrullah appealed to the Balochistan High Court, and the court overturned his conviction, acquitting him. The judges identified several serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, the pistol was recovered from an open place accessible to the public, not somewhere under Nasrullah's exclusive control, and no independent private witness was present during the recovery—only police officials. Second, the weapon was sent to the forensic laboratory without the spent cartridges (empties), meaning the lab could only confirm the gun was in working condition, not that it was actually used in any crime or exclusively linked to the accused. Third, there was an unexplained two-month delay before the weapon was even sent for forensic testing, and the prosecution never explained who had custody of the weapon during that gap or presented evidence of its safe-keeping.

Given these gaps, the court ruled the evidence was too weak and doubtful to sustain a conviction, and under legal principles requiring recoveries to be free of doubt, the benefit of that doubt had to go to the accused. This case illustrates how Pakistani courts scrutinize the reliability and chain of custody of physical evidence, especially in weapons cases, before allowing a conviction to stand.

title: Nasrullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court, deciding an appeal by Nasrullah, who had been convicted of murdering the complainant's brother during an alleged robbery, along with related charges of attempted murder and causing grievous hurt.

The court found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The complainant was not an eyewitness, and the FIR was initially lodged against unknown persons. The accused was only arrested later based on a co-accused's confession in another case, not because he was identified at the scene. The identification parade used to link him to the crime was conducted in a police lockup after a magistrate had refused to hold it due to missing documentation, making it unreliable. The two witnesses who claimed to have seen the incident gave contradictory and inconsistent accounts about basic facts, such as how the body was transported and the exact timeline of events, and their presence at the scene was not confirmed by other evidence like the site plan. There was also an unexplained four-hour delay in filing the FIR, and the medical evidence about the timing of the victim's death did not match the witnesses' testimony.

Given all these inconsistencies and unreliable evidence, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, and Nasrullah's conviction and sentence were set aside, resulting in his acquittal. This case highlights how flawed identification procedures and contradictory witness testimony can undermine a criminal conviction.

title: Muhammad Raheem V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man convicted for allegedly evading arrest, under a special anti-terrorism law provision (Section 21-L of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997), which punishes someone who deliberately hides or avoids court proceedings to obstruct justice.

The appellant was not originally named in the FIR (the initial police complaint) about a violent armed attack that killed two people and caused other serious harm. He was only implicated later, after the main accused were tried and mostly acquitted, when the complainant filed a supplementary statement naming him. The trial court then declared him a proclaimed offender and convicted him in his absence, without ever formally charging him with the specific offence of evading arrest, and without holding the legally required inquiry into whether his absence was truly deliberate.

The Balochistan High Court found this process deeply flawed. The law requires courts to properly investigate and prove that an accused deliberately absconded before convicting them in absentia. Since no such charge was framed, no evidence of willful absconding was presented, and the complainant himself knew the appellant lived elsewhere, the court held that his fundamental rights to a fair trial and due process (under Articles 9, 10, and 10-A of the Constitution) were violated.

The court set aside the conviction and sent the case back for retrial, reinforcing that even in terrorism cases, basic fair trial safeguards cannot be bypassed.

title: Director General, Pakistan Coast Guard Head Quarter, Karachi through Deputy Attorney General V. Sikandar,
explainer:
This case involved an oil tanker seized after 900 kilograms of charas (hashish) were found hidden in secret compartments during a checkpoint search in 2016. The two men driving the tanker, Sana Ullah and Sajid, were later convicted of narcotics trafficking. Sikandar, who claimed ownership of the tanker, was acquitted in the main case. Since no verdict had been issued regarding what should happen to the tanker itself, Sikandar applied to the trial court for its temporary release (superdari) into his custody, producing valid ownership documents that were verified by the Excise and Taxation Department. The trial court granted his request, and the Pakistan Coast Guard challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the release of the vehicle. It explained that under Section 32 of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, a vehicle used to transport drugs can only be confiscated if the prosecution proves the owner knew it was being used for that purpose. Here, there was no evidence Sikandar had any knowledge of or connection to the crime, and no one else came forward to claim the tanker. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent with similar facts, the High Court ruled that an innocent owner with valid documents and no link to the offence is entitled to recover his vehicle. The petition was dismissed.

This judgment matters because it clarifies that owners uninvolved in drug trafficking should not automatically lose their property, protecting innocent third parties from unjust confiscation.

title: Juma Gul V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about the murder of Barat Khan, who was allegedly shot by Juma Gul during a quarrel while packing vegetables in an orchard. The trial court had convicted Juma Gul under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced him to death, along with a compensation order to the victim's family. Juma Gul appealed to the Balochistan High Court, and the case was also sent for confirmation of the death sentence.

On reviewing the evidence, the High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's case. Witnesses gave contradictory accounts, and it appeared the complainant may not even have been present at the scene. The site plan did not match witness testimony about where the shooting occurred, and no eyewitnesses were marked on it. Medical evidence about how close the shooter stood contradicted the physical findings on the body. The recovered weapon and bullet casing were never sent for forensic testing, weakening that evidence further. Additionally, blood-stained clothing was handed over to police two days after the incident, raising further doubts. The eyewitnesses were all close relatives of the deceased and had existing enmity with the accused, making independent corroboration necessary but lacking.

Given these unresolved doubts, the court ruled that the benefit of doubt must go to the accused, acquitting Juma Gul and overturning his death sentence. This case highlights the importance of consistent, corroborated evidence, especially in cases involving the death penalty and testimony from interested witnesses.

title: Shafi Muhammad V. Sessions Judge, Lasbela at Hub and 3 others,
explainer:
This case concerns an accused person's right to present defense evidence during a criminal trial. The petitioner, Shafi Muhammad, had asked the trial court to summon a representative of a company called Gatron to verify an attendance sheet as part of his defense. The trial court rejected his application, and when he challenged this before the Sessions Judge in revision, that court also upheld the rejection. He then approached the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in his favor. It held that under Section 265-F of the Criminal Procedure Code, once an accused expresses intent to present defense evidence, the trial court is legally obligated to allow it—the word "shall" in the law does not give judges discretion to refuse. A court can only deny such a request if it believes the accused is trying to cause delay or defeat justice, and even then, it must record specific reasons in writing.

The High Court found that the lower courts had no valid grounds to refuse the petitioner's request, since the authenticity of the disputed document could only be properly assessed after hearing the witness testify. By denying this opportunity, the trial court had violated the petitioner's right to a fair trial guaranteed under Article 10-A of Pakistan's Constitution.

The High Court set aside both lower court orders and directed the trial court to summon the company representative as requested. This judgment reinforces that courts must respect an accused person's fundamental right to present a full defense.

title: Aziz-Ur-Rehman V. Mst. Bibi Jameela and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute after a divorce between Aziz-ur-Rehman and his former wife, Mst. Bibi Jameela, over dowry articles, dower money, and maintenance. The wife had sued for recovery of Rs. 300,000 as dower, dowry articles worth Rs. 472,800, and maintenance for the Iddat period. The Family Court ruled in her favor, and this decision was upheld on appeal. The husband then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

He argued that the dowry articles had already been returned to his wife through a government official, but he could not produce any receipt or proof of this claim, and the official he presented as a witness did not confirm it either. The court held that since he failed to prove his claim, the wife's version stood. It also noted that wives generally cannot be expected to maintain detailed purchase records or get signed lists of dowry items, so her own statement was sufficient proof.

On the dower amount, since it was admitted that the marriage was never consummated, Islamic law entitles the wife to only half the fixed dower, with the rest returnable to the husband unless he voluntarily gives it up. The court therefore modified the lower courts' decisions by reducing the amount related to dowry articles and adjusting the dower accordingly, while otherwise upholding the decisions. This case clarifies evidentiary standards in dowry disputes and reaffirms dower entitlement rules when a marriage is unconsummated.

title: Feroz Shah V. The Secretary Education Department, Government of Balochistan Civil Secretariat Quetta and others ,
explainer:
This case is about a government job applicant who challenged the withdrawal of his recommended appointment. Feroz Shah applied for the post of watchman in the Education Department of Balochistan after seeing an advertisement, appeared in the interview, and was placed on a merit list of successful candidates recommended for appointment. However, the department later noted that appointment orders could only be issued against clearly sanctioned vacant posts, and it turned out that the original advertisement had only listed one vacant post, that of a driver, not watchman. No watchman post had actually been advertised. The department subsequently cancelled the earlier approval and issued a fresh merit list for Class-IV posts, which did not include Shah, as all recommended candidates in the new list were for the post of Naib Qasid.

Shah went to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that he had been wrongly excluded due to political influence and favoritism, and asked the court to direct his appointment.

The High Court dismissed the petition, holding that since no vacant post of watchman was ever advertised, Shah had not applied for a properly sanctioned post, and therefore the court could not direct the department to appoint him to a position that did not exist in the advertisement. The court relied on a Supreme Court ruling emphasizing that public appointments must follow proper advertisement of actual vacancies to protect citizens' fundamental right to fair recruitment. This case highlights that courts will only enforce appointment claims based on genuinely advertised, sanctioned vacancies.

title: Muhammad Rafique V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a bus and an oil tanker collision on a highway that killed seven passengers and injured eleven others. The bus driver, Muhammad Rafique, was convicted by the trial court under Pakistan's Penal Code for culpable homicide and causing hurt through rash and negligent driving, and was sentenced to pay compensation (diyat and daman) to the victims and their families, along with imprisonment.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted Rafique. The court found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The only eyewitness contradicted his own earlier statement to police, first saying someone else was driving the tanker, then claiming at trial that he himself was driving it. The court considered this a dishonest improvement that undermined his credibility. The court also noted the investigation appeared to have started before the FIR was even officially registered, which is not legally permitted. Crucially, no mechanical inspection of the bus was conducted and no expert evidence was presented to establish whether the crash was caused by speeding or a mechanical fault. The court emphasized that simply driving at high speed is not itself a crime, the prosecution must specifically prove rash or negligent driving.

Since the prosecution failed to provide solid, convincing evidence of negligence, the court gave the benefit of the doubt to the accused and acquitted him. This case highlights the importance of proper investigative procedure and the need for concrete evidence, not just assumptions, in criminal convictions.

title: Usman Ali and 17 others V. The Secretary, Religious Affairs and Inter-Faith Harmony Department, Government of Balochistan and another,
explainer:
This case is about a group of job applicants challenging the government's refusal to appoint them after they had already qualified for posts.

The Religious Affairs and Inter-Faith Harmony Department, Government of Balochistan, advertised vacant posts of Stenographer and Junior Clerk in 2018. Eighteen petitioners, including Usman Ali, applied, took the written test and interview, and were recommended for appointment by the department's Recruitment/Selection Committee. However, before their appointment letters were issued, the Chief Minister imposed a general ban on recruitment across departments. Later, this ban was lifted, and departments were told to complete pending recruitment processes. Instead of issuing appointment letters to the petitioners, whose selection process had already been completed, the department decided to re-advertise the same posts, partly citing concerns that some candidates had crossed the age limit.

The petitioners challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that since they had already qualified and been recommended before the ban, they were entitled to appointment, and that other candidates for different posts (like Naib Qasid and Chowkidar) had already been appointed on the same basis.

The High Court agreed with the petitioners, finding no valid justification for withholding their appointment orders after their selection process was complete. It held that denying them appointment violated their constitutional rights under Articles 4 and 5, and directed the authorities to issue their appointment orders. The petition was allowed.

title: Muhammad Sharif V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Muhammad Sharif who was stopped by police in Hub, Balochistan, and allegedly found carrying 1800 grams of charas (hashish). He was charged under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act. Although he initially pleaded not guilty and demanded a trial, midway through the proceedings he admitted his guilt and asked for leniency. The trial court recorded this admission under Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code and convicted him, sentencing him to two years' rigorous imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined whether this conviction was proper. The court clarified that admitting guilt during a Section 342 statement is not the same as formally "pleading guilty," so the appeal was legally permissible. More importantly, the court found serious flaws in the prosecution's case: the drugs were sent to the forensic laboratory more than 20 days after being seized, with no explanation for the delay; the police official who transported the sample was never questioned during the investigation; and only one witness was examined at trial. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the "safe custody" and secure handling of the seized narcotics.

Because these are essential requirements to trust the evidence in narcotics cases, the court set aside the conviction and acquitted Muhammad Sharif, ordering his release. This case highlights how procedural lapses in evidence handling can lead to acquittal, even when a defendant admits guilt.

title: Mor Khan and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Mor Khan and another accused, who were convicted of murdering the complainant's uncle following a shooting on 19 December 2017. The prosecution's case was that the accused, armed with pistols, ambushed the complainant, his uncle, and cousin while they were on their way to irrigate farmland, and opened fire, killing the uncle on the spot. The motive was said to be longstanding enmity between the families. The trial court convicted the accused under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced them to life imprisonment plus compensation to the victim's heirs. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the conviction. It found the eyewitness testimony of the complainant and his cousin to be consistent, credible, and mutually corroborating, noting that the witnesses knew the accused personally, making misidentification unlikely. The FIR had been lodged promptly, within an hour, undermining any suggestion of fabrication through delay. The court also rejected the defence argument that the witnesses were unreliable simply because they were relatives of the deceased, clarifying that relationship alone does not make a witness "interested" unless there is evidence of bias or motive to falsely implicate someone. Additionally, forensic evidence—recovered pistols and cartridge casings matched by a firearms report—supported the prosecution's case. The appeal was dismissed, reinforcing key principles about evaluating eyewitness credibility and the weight of forensic corroboration in murder trials.

On appeal, the High Court examined the evidence closely and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. The witnesses who claimed to have seen the killings were closely related to the deceased, making them "interested" witnesses whose testimony needed independent support that was missing here. Given these unresolved doubts, the court applied the principle that any reasonable doubt must benefit the accused. It set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitting Muhammad Bakhsh. title: Muhammad Ramzan and another V. Bismillah Khan and 7 others,
explainer:
This case is about a land dispute in Quetta. The buyers, Muhammad Ramzan and another person, claimed they had agreed to purchase a portion of land from a seller in 2006 through a sale agreement, paying earnest money, with the balance to be paid in installments. They alleged the seller later secretly sold the same land to other people through official mutation entries, so they sued for specific performance of the contract, cancellation of those mutation entries, and a permanent injunction. The trial court dismissed their suit, and they appealed.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the buyers failed to properly prove their case: their witnesses gave no clear evidence about the sale price or date, only one witness to the agreement was produced instead of the legally required two marginal witnesses, and the sale consideration payment was not proven. The court also noted that such agreements involving property over Rs.100 need registration, that merely signing an agreement to sell does not create ownership rights, and that the buyers never deposited the remaining sale price with the court, which is required when seeking enforcement of such an agreement.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that courts require solid, consistent proof and proper legal procedure before enforcing property sale agreements, and clarifies that an unregistered agreement to sell does not by itself grant ownership or legal rights over land.

title: Fazal Khan and 2 others V. Additional Sessions Judge/Model Criminal Trial Court, Barkhan at Rakhni and another,
explainer:
This case is about whether false testimony given by prosecution witnesses in a murder trial should be punished. A man was killed, and an FIR was lodged accusing several people of murder. After a full trial, the Additional Sessions Judge acquitted the accused, and separately ordered that a Magistrate initiate proceedings against three prosecution witnesses for giving false evidence, an offence under sections 193, 194 and 195 of the Pakistan Penal Code.

The witnesses (through the complainant and others) then approached the Balochistan High Court, asking it to use its special inherent powers under section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code to quash the trial court's order and stop the Magistrate's proceedings against them.

The High Court refused. It held that these inherent powers cannot be used to override clear legal provisions, and can only be invoked to prevent misuse of court processes or to secure justice, not routinely whenever someone claims evidence was false. It also rejected the old legal principle that if a witness lies about one part of their testimony, all of it must be disbelieved, saying this idea does not fit Pakistan's legal or Islamic framework, since lying under oath is itself a serious crime with penal consequences. The court found the trial judge was right to refer the matter for prosecution of the witnesses, and dismissed the petition seeking to stop that action.

The eyewitness's account also conflicted with medical evidence, and the site plan failed to even show where he was supposedly standing. The investigating officer had started investigating and collecting evidence before the FIR was formally registered, casting doubt on the case's foundation. title: Faiq Ali and others V. The State and others,

The convicted men appealed for acquittal, while the complainant filed a separate petition asking the court to increase their sentences.

The eyewitnesses gave contradictory accounts of how the shooting happened and when the victims died, yet strangely, only one person was hit despite several people sitting close together. Witnesses' calm behavior during a violent attack also seemed unnatural. There was a major mismatch between eyewitness claims about firing distance and the doctor's medical findings. title: Gul Hassan V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns a bail application before the Balochistan High Court in a murder case. The applicant, Gul Hassan, was accused, along with absconding co-accused, of shooting and killing the complainant's brother at Dera Murad Jamali following a dispute rooted in prior enmity. He was charged under Pakistan Penal Code provisions dealing with murder, abetment, and common intention, and had already been denied bail once by a trial court.

Before the High Court, his lawyer argued that no specific role had been assigned to him individually, suggesting the matter required further inquiry, which under the law could justify bail.

The court rejected this argument and refused bail. It noted several factors weighing against the applicant: the FIR was lodged promptly after the incident, he was specifically named in it, a weapon was recovered based on information he provided, eyewitnesses implicated him, and medical evidence supported the allegations. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the judge held that the mere possibility of further inquiry exists in almost every criminal case and does not, by itself, entitle an accused to bail.

This judgment illustrates how Pakistani courts assess bail requests in serious offenses like murder, emphasizing that strong prima facie evidence, such as prompt FIRs, recoveries, and eyewitness testimony, can outweigh defense arguments about ambiguous individual roles, reinforcing a cautious approach to bail in grave criminal cases.

title: Ali Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted for allegedly possessing twenty liters of alcohol in violation of the Prohibition (Enforcement of Hadd) Order, 1979. He was originally sentenced by a Magistrate to two years imprisonment plus a fine, and on appeal an Additional Sessions Judge reduced the sentence to one year. The man then challenged his conviction before the Balochistan High Court through a criminal revision petition.

The High Court found serious flaws in how the prosecution handled the case. The alcohol sample reached the forensic laboratory seven days after seizure, with no explanation of where it was kept or who had custody of it during that time. The police official who actually transported the sample to the lab was never produced as a witness to confirm it hadn't been tampered with. Additionally, the witnesses gave contradictory accounts of basic facts, such as when the investigating officer arrived at the scene and who prepared the sealed sample parcels.

Relying on Supreme Court precedents, the High Court held that when the chain of custody of evidence is broken or unexplained, the forensic report becomes unreliable and cannot support a conviction. The court also reaffirmed the principle that legal procedures must be followed exactly as prescribed, or they are considered not followed at all.

As a result, the court accepted the revision petition and acquitted the accused, highlighting how failures in evidence-handling and witness reliability can undermine even seemingly straightforward criminal cases.

title: Muhammad Alamgir V. Baha-Ud-Din and another,
explainer:
This case is about an attempt to cancel bail that had already been granted to an accused person in a serious criminal case.

The background: an FIR was registered against the accused under sections dealing with dacoity (armed robbery) and abetment, alleging that he and his companions had forced the complainant's uncle out of a dumper truck at gunpoint, tied him up, and stole the vehicle. After his arrest and completion of investigation, the accused applied for bail, which was granted by an Additional Sessions Judge. The complainant was unhappy with this decision and approached the Balochistan High Court asking that the bail order be declared illegal and cancelled, and that the accused be re-arrested.

The High Court dismissed the complainant's request. It explained that once bail has been granted by a court with proper authority, it cannot simply be cancelled later unless there are strong, exceptional reasons to do so. Cancelling bail is legally different from deciding whether to grant it in the first place. The court noted that the complainant had not shown that the accused misused his bail in any way after being released, such as tampering with evidence, threatening witnesses, or fleeing. Simply disagreeing with the earlier decision, or presenting an alternative view of the evidence, was not enough to justify cancellation.

This case matters because it reinforces an important principle in Pakistani criminal law: bail once granted is protected from casual reversal, ensuring stability and fairness in the justice process, unless genuine misuse of that liberty is demonstrated.

title: Shahida Yasmin V. The State,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a woman, Shahida Yasmin, whose late husband had stood as a surety (guarantor) for an accused person, Fazal Rehman, to secure his bail in a criminal case. As part of the surety arrangement, her husband deposited Rs. 50,000 in cash and submitted property documents.

After being released on bail, the accused later jumped bail and stopped appearing before the trial court. The husband who had acted as surety had already died before this happened. Despite his death, the trial court forfeited the full surety amount of Rs. 300,000. When the petitioner requested relief on humanitarian grounds, the trial court only reduced the forfeited amount by 25 percent, which she felt was insufficient, prompting her to approach the High Court.

The High Court ruled in her favor, relying on Section 514(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which clearly states that if a surety dies before the bond is forfeited, his estate is automatically discharged from all liability under that bond. Since the husband died before the accused absconded, the forfeiture proceedings themselves were invalid from the start.

The court declared the forfeiture order void and ordered the full cash deposit and property documents returned to the petitioner. This case reinforces that legal liability under a surety bond cannot survive the surety's death if it occurs before forfeiture, protecting the deceased's estate and heirs from such financial obligations.

title: Bibi Maryam and 8 others V. Government of Balochistan, through Secretary Education department and 9 others,
explainer:
This case is about a group of petitioners from District Noshki who applied for Class-IV (support staff) jobs in a government school after donating land on which the school buildings stood. They took the recruitment test and interview, but the District Recruitment Committee did not select them. They complained to a Complaint Redressal Cell, which recommended they be given preference in appointment because they had donated the land, and the Provincial Ombudsman also asked the government to implement this recommendation. However, the education department did not appoint them, so they approached the Balochistan High Court.

The petitioners argued that there had been an understanding with the education department that in exchange for donating the land, they would have the right to recommend who gets appointed to these posts. The court rejected this argument. It held that no government post can be filled based on a private person's recommendation, and any such agreement is illegal and against public policy. Trading land for a job amounts to effectively selling a public office, which violates the law and the constitutional guarantee of equality (Article 25). The court also cited Section 23 of the Contract Act, which makes agreements void if their object is unlawful. Since the underlying agreement had no legal validity, the petitioners could not demand its enforcement. The petition was dismissed.

This case matters because it reinforces that public employment must be based on merit and lawful procedure, not private deals or favors, even when land or resources are donated for public infrastructure.

title: Government of Balochistan through Collector Kachhi and another V. Hazar Khan and others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Kachhi, Balochistan, where a group of plaintiffs sued for declaration, permanent injunction, and correction of revenue records over a piece of land. The trial court decided in favor of the plaintiffs after the government defendants failed to properly pursue their defense and were eventually proceeded against ex parte. The government then tried to appeal, but filed that appeal over three years and eleven months late, without ever submitting an application explaining the delay. The appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora, Sibi) dismissed the appeal for being time-barred, and the government challenged that dismissal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It explained that the law of limitation exists to protect the rights of the opposing party once a deadline has passed, and that anyone seeking extra time to file an appeal must formally request condonation of delay and give solid reasons for it. Courts do have discretion to excuse delays under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, but this discretion must be used carefully and cannot be granted automatically. Importantly, the court stressed that government agencies are not entitled to special treatment in matters of limitation and must follow the same strict rules as private citizens. Since the government failed to explain even a single day of the lengthy delay, the court ruled that the appeal was rightly rejected, reinforcing that limitation laws must be strictly enforced regardless of who the litigant is.

title: Haji Abdul Sattar and 2 others V. Mst. Mehnaz and 7 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over agricultural land in Naseerabad district, Balochistan. The plaintiffs claimed they had never gifted their land to one of the defendants, but their brother had secretly transferred the property into his son's name through a fraudulent gift mutation, without their knowledge. The land was then sold onward to other buyers. The trial court and the appellate body (Majlis-e-Shoora) both ruled in favor of the original owners, cancelling the fraudulent transfer, and the buyers challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions. It found that the person claiming the gift had the burden of proving when and how the oral gift was made, but failed to do so. There was no evidence showing the actual owners had appeared before revenue officials or signed the mutation documents. Since the transfer was done fraudulently and without the owners' knowledge, the court held that no legal protection could be given to such an act, and importantly, that the normal time limits for filing a lawsuit do not apply when the underlying act itself was illegal.

The court also reaffirmed that when reviewing lower court decisions in this type of petition, it cannot re-examine the facts of the case freely, but only step in if there was a clear legal error or if evidence was ignored or misread. Finding no such error, the court dismissed the petition, meaning the land stayed with its rightful owners.

title: Khaeri Khan and 5 others V. Muhammad Siddique Alias Siddiqo and 8 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute where the petitioners had filed a civil suit seeking declaration, possession, mesne profits, and a permanent injunction against the respondents. The respondents contested the suit and applied to have it rejected under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code, a legal provision allowing plaints to be thrown out at an early stage without full trial if they suffer from specific defects, such as failing to disclose a cause of action or being legally barred.

During the proceedings, a local commissioner was appointed to visit the disputed land and submit a report. Based largely on this report, the trial court rejected the plaint. The petitioners appealed, but the appellate court dismissed their appeal on the technical ground that it was filed a day or two late.

The Balochistan High Court found both lower court decisions flawed. It held that rejecting a plaint under Order VII, Rule 11 requires courts to examine only the plaint itself at face value, not external reports like that of a local commissioner. If a report is used, the commissioner must be formally examined and both parties must get a chance to cross-examine before it forms the basis of any decision. The court also criticized the appellate court for dismissing the case on a minor delay rather than deciding it on merits, emphasizing that technicalities should not obstruct justice.

The High Court accepted the revision petition, set aside both lower court orders, and sent the case back to the trial court to properly frame issues, allow evidence from both sides, and decide the matter on its actual merits.

title: Toor Jan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Toor Jan who was convicted under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with dishonestly issuing a cheque that later bounces. The complainant alleged that in a vehicle business deal, the accused handed over cheques worth over 80 lakh rupees, which were later dishonored due to insufficient funds. A trial court convicted the accused to six months imprisonment and a fine, and an appellate court upheld this conviction. The accused then challenged both decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the accused. It found serious flaws in the prosecution's case: key witness statements, including that of the bank's operations manager, were recorded with an unexplained delay of over a month, which the court said seriously undermined their credibility. More importantly, the complainant failed to produce any documentary evidence proving that a genuine vehicle sale transaction actually took place—no agreement, no vehicle registration or ownership documents, and no proof of purchase. One prosecution witness even testified that no transaction occurred in his presence.

The court clarified that merely issuing a cheque that bounces is not automatically a crime; the prosecution must first prove an underlying obligation existed and that the cheque was issued dishonestly. Since reasonable doubt existed, the accused was entitled to acquittal as a matter of right, not favor. This case reinforces important safeguards protecting the accused from convictions based on weak or unproven evidence in cheque-dishonor cases.

title: Ghulam Nabi V. Saifullah and others,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute in Khuzdar, Balochistan, involving competing claims over land whose mutation records had changed over time. Ghulam Nabi filed a fresh suit seeking declaration, correction of revenue entries, cancellation of mutation entries, and a permanent injunction. Some defendants asked the trial court to dismiss the suit on the ground that the same matter had already been litigated and settled between the same parties years earlier, through a compromise decree in 1986 and a further decree in 1998 that was never appealed. The trial court agreed and rejected the new suit, applying the legal principle of res judicata under Section 11 of the Civil Procedure Code, which prevents parties from relitigating issues already decided by a competent court.

Ghulam Nabi challenged this rejection before the Balochistan High Court, arguing he was denied a chance to present evidence and that factual disputes needed a full trial. The High Court disagreed, finding that the earlier litigation between the same parties over the same subject matter had already conclusively settled the dispute, and allowing a new suit would unfairly force the parties to fight the same battle twice. The court also clarified a technical procedural point: whether such rejection orders should be challenged by appeal or revision depends on whether a formal decree sheet was drawn up. Finding no merit in the challenge, the High Court dismissed the revision petition, upholding the trial court's decision. The case reinforces how res judicata protects finality of court decisions and prevents repeated litigation over settled matters.

title: Abdul Karim and others V. Secretary Health Department Government of Balochistan and others,
explainer:
This case concerned employees hired on one-year contracts by the Health Department, Government of Balochistan, under a Vector Borne Disease Control Program. After passing tests and interviews, they received official offer letters and some were also issued posting orders, with a few actually joining duty. However, before most could be properly posted or paid, the Director General Health Services cancelled their appointments through a letter, without giving any reasons or issuing show-cause notices. Salaries were also withheld even for those who had joined. The employees challenged this cancellation and non-payment before the Balochistan High Court.

The court found that the employees had been recruited lawfully, through a proper process approved by the competent authority. Any delay or failure in issuing posting orders was the department's fault, not the employees'. Since employees cannot start work without being formally posted, they could not be blamed for not reporting for duty. The court also held that cancelling their appointments without notice or explanation was unlawful, and denying them salaries violated Article 3 of the Constitution, which guarantees economic justice and protection from exploitation.

The court declared the cancellation order void, and directed the department to pay the employees' salaries from the date of their offer letters until the expiry of their contract terms. This judgment reinforces that government departments cannot arbitrarily cancel lawful appointments or withhold pay without due process and valid reasons.

title: Shafi Muhammad V. Muhammad Gul and another,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Shafi Muhammad, who was allegedly attacked and injured by the respondents. An FIR was first registered against the accused over the same incident, and after trial they were acquitted. Instead of appealing that acquittal properly, the complainant later filed a fresh private complaint before a magistrate, repeating the same allegations against the same people over the same incident. Both the trial magistrate and the sessions court (in revision) dismissed this private complaint, reasoning that the matter had already been tried and decided once.

The Balochistan High Court upheld these decisions and dismissed the constitutional petition. It explained that Article 13 of the Constitution and Section 403 of the Criminal Procedure Code protect a person from being tried twice for the same offence once they have been convicted or acquitted by a competent court, as long as that verdict stands. The court invoked the legal principle "nemo bis punitur aut vexatur pro eodem delicto" - no one should be punished or harassed twice for the same offence - similar to the common law doctrines of "autrefois acquit" and "autrefois convict." Since the respondents had already faced trial and been acquitted for the same allegations in the earlier FIR case, they could not be tried again through a new private complaint. This case reinforces the fundamental legal safeguard against double jeopardy in Pakistani law, ensuring finality once a competent court has ruled on a matter.

title: Dr. M. salah-Ud-Din Mengal and another V. Government of Balochistan through Board of Revenue and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Quetta where the government took over property, including a poultry farm business, to build a police station. The landowners sought compensation through a reference filed under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, before the Collector (Deputy Commissioner). After an award was made, disagreements arose over the compensation amount, with the landowners arguing the land and structures were undervalued and that additional costs owed to them had not been paid. The Deputy Commissioner forwarded their reference to the District Court for adjudication. However, the trial court (Additional District Judge-V, Quetta) dismissed the reference, ruling that it had been filed too late, that is, barred by limitation.

The landowners appealed this dismissal to the Balochistan High Court. The High Court held that the trial court was wrong to dismiss the case on limitation grounds. It explained that under the law, the question of whether a reference was filed within the time limit is something the Collector must decide before forwarding the case to court, not something the court itself can reconsider afterward. Since the Collector had sent the reference to the court without raising any objection about it being late, the issue of limitation was no longer open for the court to examine.

As a result, the High Court allowed the appeal, set aside the trial court's dismissal, and sent the case back for a proper decision on its actual merits, giving both parties a fair opportunity to present their case.

title: Fazal Ur Rehman V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Home and Tribal Affairs and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a citizen challenging the government's decision to list his name as a "proscribed person" under anti-terrorism law. Fazal Ur Rehman had been arrested in connection with several FIRs (police cases) in Quetta but was granted bail and later acquitted by the courts. Despite this, the Balochistan government placed his name in the Fourth Schedule of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, a list reserved for people suspected of terrorism-related activities, first in 2015 and again in 2019. He petitioned the Balochistan High Court to have his name removed.

The police officer investigating his case reported that Rehman was not involved in any anti-state activities and was not a member of any banned organization. Based on this, the court found that the government had added his name without proper evidence or valid reasons. It held that merely being named in criminal cases is not sufficient grounds to restrict someone's liberty, and that Article 4 of the Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to be treated according to law. Keeping someone on such a list indefinitely without justification violates this fundamental right.

The court allowed the petition and ordered authorities to remove Rehman's name from the Fourth Schedule. The judgment matters because it reinforces that the state cannot restrict citizens' liberty through terrorism-related blacklists without solid evidence, protecting individuals from indefinite, unjustified restrictions.

title: Muhammad Mohid-Din V. Director General, NAB (Balochistan) and another,
explainer:
This case involved a person, Muhammad Mohid-Din, who was not a party to a corruption reference filed by NAB (National Accountability Bureau) in 2014, but who wanted the court to let him appear and record his own statement as a prosecution witness or court witness in that case. He filed an application before the Accountability Court under Sections 265-F and 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code, but the court returned it without deciding it. He then approached the Balochistan High Court through a constitutional petition asking to be allowed to testify and present material he claimed supported the corruption case.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that the law under Section 265-F Cr.P.C. allows the complainant or accused to ask the court to summon witnesses acquainted with the facts of the case, but the petitioner was neither the complainant nor otherwise connected to the case. He had never given a statement to the investigating officer and had stayed silent for five years after the reference was filed, without explaining his delay. While courts do have wide discretionary power under Section 540 Cr.P.C. to call any witness whose evidence is essential to a just decision, this power must be used judiciously and not to fill gaps in a case after such a long, unexplained delay. The court noted that if the petitioner had a personal claim against the accused, his proper remedy was to approach a civil court instead. This ruling clarifies limits on outsiders trying to insert themselves into ongoing criminal trials.

title: Tooba Saeed V. Chairman, Admission Committee Bolan University of Medical and Sciences Quetta Balochistan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a student, Tooba Saeed, who wanted admission to MBBS at Bolan University of Medical and Health Sciences (BUMHS), Quetta. To be eligible, candidates had to pass the Medical and Dental College Admission Test (MDCAT) with at least 50 percent marks, a threshold that had already been reduced from the usual 60 percent specifically for Balochistan due to low pass rates in the province. The petitioner scored 99 out of 200 marks, which is 49.5 percent, just short of the required 50 percent. She argued that 49.5 percent should be rounded up to 50 percent by international standards, and asked the court to direct the university to consider her application on special grounds, citing her background from a remote area of Balochistan.

The Balochistan High Court rejected her petition. It held that admission criteria set by universities are administrative policies that must apply equally to all candidates, and courts should not interfere in academic matters unless there is clear injustice. Since the reduced 50 percent threshold had already been approved by the university's Syndicate and endorsed by the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council, and the petitioner had not challenged that decision itself, she could not claim admission through special consideration. The petition was dismissed, reaffirming that eligibility rules for professional admissions must be applied uniformly and objectively.

title: Arsala V. Special Judge, Anti-Terrorism Court and another ,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Arsala who had originally been sentenced to death for murder under Pakistan's Anti-Terrorism Act. After appeals, the Supreme Court acquitted him of the murder charge but upheld his conviction under the terrorism law, reducing his sentence to life imprisonment with a fine. Once in prison, he asked for the benefit of special remissions (sentence reductions) that the government routinely grants to other prisoners, plus credit for time already spent in custody before trial. Prison authorities refused, citing Section 21-F of the Anti-Terrorism Act, which specifically bars remissions for anyone convicted under that law, except children.

The Balochistan High Court ruled in Arsala's favor. It held that the Constitution's Article 25 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection for all citizens, including prisoners. The court reasoned that while different laws may set different courts or harsher punishments, once someone is convicted, they should be treated like any other prisoner under prison rules. Denying remissions only to those convicted under anti-terrorism law, while granting them to others, amounted to unfair discrimination with no reasonable justification. Relying on earlier rulings from Balochistan, Lahore, and Sindh High Courts, the court found Section 21-F's blanket denial of remissions unconstitutional as applied here, and ordered authorities to give Arsala all remissions he had been denied. The case reinforces that constitutional equality rights extend to how prisoners are treated, regardless of which law they were convicted under.

title: Nabi Bakhsh V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a road accident where a passenger vehicle overturned, killing three women and injuring several others. The driver, Nabi Bakhsh, was tried and convicted by a trial court for causing death by rash and negligent driving and for causing injuries to passengers, and was sentenced to pay compensation (Diyat, Daman, and Arsh) as well as imprisonment.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious flaws in how the trial court had reached its verdict. None of the witnesses who were actually present at the accident testified that the driver had been negligent, and the complainant himself was declared a hostile witness. Instead of properly weighing this evidence, the trial court had convicted the driver mainly based on his own statement during questioning, where he admitted the accident happened but blamed it on a mechanical failure (a broken tie-rod). The trial court rejected this explanation partly by inspecting the vehicle itself many months after the accident, without any proper mechanic's report confirming its condition right after the crash.

The High Court held that courts must first independently assess whether prosecution witnesses are credible before turning to the accused's own statement, and cannot selectively accept only part of that statement. Since no witness supported the claim of rash or negligent driving, and speeding alone isn't enough without proof of negligence, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitting the appellant. The case highlights the importance of proper procedure and solid evidence, not assumptions, in criminal convictions.

title: Dawood Khan and another V. Sultan Muhammad,
explainer:
Dawood Khan and another challenged a decision of a Rent Controller in Quetta who had thrown out their eviction case against their tenant, Sultan Muhammad. The dispute involved a shop that had originally been rented out by one family member. After the original landlord died, the shop passed to his heirs through inheritance, and the new owners sought to evict the tenant, both for non-payment of rent and because they wanted to use the shop themselves. The tenant argued there was no landlord-tenant relationship between him and the new owners, claiming he had actually bought the shop from a third party who had earlier purchased it from a relative of the landlords. The Rent Controller sided with the tenant, ruling that the new owners had failed to prove they were his landlords, and dismissed the case entirely.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It found that the tenant had originally been inducted into the shop by a relative of the new owners, and that ownership had since passed to the new owners through a proper inheritance mutation. The court held that simply denying the landlord-tenant relationship does not change a tenant's legal status, and that a co-owner is fully entitled to file an eviction case. Because the tenant's denial was found to be deliberate and unjustified, the court ruled he must vacate the shop immediately and pay three years of unpaid rent, with any further arrears to be pursued separately in civil court. The appeal was allowed, reversing the Rent Controller's decision.

title: Muhammad Wassay Tareen V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved the former Provincial Ombudsman of Balochistan, who sued the provincial government for refusing to pay him a "Superior Judicial Allowance." When he was appointed in 2013, his terms of service did not include this allowance, and an earlier court petition on the same issue was dismissed in 2018 on the grounds that an Ombudsman is not a judicial officer and therefore not entitled to an allowance meant for judges.

However, the situation changed: the Governor of Balochistan later approved payment of this allowance specifically in the petitioner's favor, and it emerged that previous Ombudsmen had, in fact, been receiving this same allowance. Despite the Governor's approval, the Chief Minister rejected the summary authorizing payment.

The Balochistan High Court found that denying the allowance to this petitioner, while past Ombudsmen had received it, amounted to unjustified discrimination with no rational basis or reasonable distinction to explain the different treatment. The Court held that the Chief Minister had erred both factually and legally in rejecting the Governor's approved summary, and that the Governor's order to pay the allowance was lawful.

The Court allowed the petition and directed the provincial government to release the Superior Judicial Allowance to the petitioner as originally approved by the Governor. The case highlights how constitutional guarantees against discrimination (Article 25) can require equal treatment among people in similar official positions, even when procedural or contractual technicalities are raised as objections.

title: The Collector of Customs, Model Customs Collectorate, Quetta V. Fazal Muhammad and others,
explainer:
The Collector of Customs challenged a decision by the Customs Appellate Tribunal that had ruled in favour of Fazal Muhammad, a passenger who was caught at Quetta Airport carrying 50,000 Australian dollars while boarding a flight to Dubai. Customs officials had seized the money and imposed a heavy fine, accusing him of smuggling foreign currency because he could not show lawful authority for possessing it. The Tribunal had overturned this penalty, prompting Customs to bring the matter before the Balochistan High Court.

The respondent's position was that the money did not belong to him alone. He said at the time of his arrest that four other people had also contributed to the amount, each around 10,000 dollars, and this was supported by receipts and affidavits filed with the Pakistani Embassy in Dubai confirming their share of the currency. However, the customs investigating officer never questioned these four people to verify the claim, despite having legal power to examine witnesses during such inquiries.

The High Court held that when hearing a customs reference, its role is limited to deciding legal questions, not re-examining facts already decided by the Tribunal, unless those findings are clearly wrong or contrary to the record. Since the investigation was found to be incomplete and the Tribunal's factual findings were not shown to be flawed, the High Court dismissed the Customs Department's reference, upholding the relief granted to the respondent. The case highlights the importance of thorough investigation before penalizing individuals for currency-related offenses at airports.

title: Director General, Provincial Disaster Management Authority (PDMA), Balochistan and others V. Amirullah and others,
explainer:
This case is about compensation claims for houses destroyed in the 2008 earthquake in District Ziarat, Balochistan. The government had classified earthquake-affected houses into four categories, ranging from totally collapsed (Category A, entitled to Rs. 350,000) to minor damage (Category D, entitled to Rs. 15,000). The plaintiffs claimed their houses were completely destroyed and should be compensated under Category A, but they were left out of the official list of affectees.

A local commission appointed by the court inspected the houses and confirmed they were collapsed and unrepairable. The trial court accepted this and awarded full compensation. However, the appellate court partly overturned this, downgrading some plaintiffs to a lower compensation category based on a survey report the defendants said was conducted by the Army.

The Balochistan High Court restored the trial court's decision. It found that the defendants never produced the original Army survey report or called any Army witness to prove it — they only submitted a photocopy, which has no legal value as evidence unless the original is proven lost. The court reaffirmed that documents must generally be proved through primary evidence, and unproven photocopies or mere statements in a written statement cannot substitute for actual evidence.

This case matters because it reinforces basic evidentiary standards in civil litigation: claims and defenses must be backed by properly proved documents, not unverified copies or unsupported assertions, especially in cases involving public compensation for disaster victims.

title: Kamal Ud Din V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a death sentence handed down by a trial court in Killa Abdullah, Balochistan. The accused, Kamal-ud-Din, along with co-accused, was alleged to have blocked a road and, during a scuffle with the complainant's party, fired a shot that killed the complainant's cousin, while also injuring others using pistols, knives, and daggers. He was convicted under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder) and sentenced to death, along with a compensation order to the deceased's heirs.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined several defence arguments, including delay in recording witness statements, the fact that eyewitnesses were relatives of the deceased, minor inconsistencies in testimony, and the absence of recovered weapons since the accused was arrested twelve years after the incident. The court held that none of these issues were serious enough to undermine the prosecution's case. It found the eyewitness accounts credible and consistent, noting the witnesses had no prior enmity with the accused and were not shown to have any motive to falsely implicate him.

However, the court found that the incident occurred suddenly, arising from a dispute over passage on a blocked road, without any premeditated motive, and involved a single gunshot. Given these circumstances, the court held that a death sentence was not appropriate and reduced it to life imprisonment. This case illustrates how courts evaluate eyewitness reliability and the significance of premeditation versus sudden provocation in determining the severity of punishment for murder.

title: Noor Ur Din and 4 others V. The Secretary Board of Revenue Department and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over 5 acres of land in Ziarat, Balochistan. A group of petitioners had applied for allotment of this land under the Land Lease Policy of 1988. Their application was rejected by the Additional Commissioner (Revenue). Rather than fully disclosing what happened with their application, they filed a civil suit asking the court to declare that they were entitled to the land and to stop the government and other parties from interfering with it.

The government and other respondents argued that the petitioners already had a pending appeal against the rejection before the Commissioner, and could not pursue two remedies for the same issue at the same time. They also pointed out that the petitioners had not been fully honest in their court filing about the status of their land application. The trial court agreed and threw out the case, and the appellate court upheld that decision.

The High Court examined a technical but important legal distinction: the difference between "rejecting" a plaint (which allows a person to refile a fresh suit) and "dismissing" a suit (which is a final decision after a full trial, leaving no option to refile). The lower courts had used dismissal, but the High Court found this was actually a case that should be treated as rejection of the plaint. It corrected the record accordingly, but still ruled against the petitioners, and their revision petition was dismissed. This clarifies how courts should classify such decisions and what remedies remain open to litigants.

title: Mst. Abida Khanum and another V. Sarfaraz and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the estate of a deceased police officer, Hussain Ali, and who among several claimants qualified as his legal heirs entitled to a share of his property and pension. His first wife and others applied for a succession certificate, but a woman named Zaib-un-Nisa intervened, claiming she was his third wife and therefore also a legal heir. The trial court and the appellate court both accepted her claim, declared her a legal heir, and divided the estate accordingly among the widows, sons, and daughters. The other heirs challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that Zaib-un-Nisa had failed to properly prove her marriage and that the courts had wrongly shifted the burden of proof onto them instead of her.

The High Court examined Islamic law principles on marriage, noting that even if a woman remarries before completing her mandatory waiting period (iddat) after a divorce, this makes the marriage merely irregular, not void, and such marriages are not against Islamic law. The court also clarified that proceedings for a succession certificate are meant to be simple and summary in nature. They are not the proper venue for resolving complicated factual disputes about heirship or property title, which should instead go to a civil court through a full trial.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the limited scope of succession certificate proceedings and reaffirms Islamic law principles distinguishing irregular marriages from void ones, protecting the rights of parties in inheritance disputes while directing complex heirship questions to proper civil litigation.

title: Muhammad Jaffar Magsi V. Sanaullah and 2 others,

When the Levies police did not register an FIR, Sanaullah approached the Additional Sessions Judge acting as Ex-officio Justice of the Peace, asking for an order directing registration of the case.

The judge sought a report from the Tehsildar (a local official overseeing the Levies police), who investigated and found that no such incident had actually occurred in the area. Despite this report clearing the accused, the judge still ordered the FIR to be registered, without any supporting evidence from the complainant to contradict the official report.

If an official report contradicts the complaint, the judge must give solid, tangible reasons for rejecting that report before ordering registration of a case. Since no such reasons were given here, the court set aside the order.

title: Shabbir Ahmed V. Muhammad Muzamil Hussain and another,
explainer:
This case involves a property dispute over a house allotted on a government plot in Dera Allah Yar, Balochistan. The original plaintiff had sued the defendant seeking a declaration that he was the lawful allottee of the house and an order directing the defendant to vacate and hand over possession, claiming the defendant had illegally occupied it.

The trial court partly decreed the case, ruling that the plaintiff was the lawful allottee but finding that since both parties were living in separate portions of the property, the defendant's occupation could not be called illegal, so possession was not ordered to be handed over. The plaintiff appealed, and the District Judge overturned this, declaring the plaintiff the legal allottee and ordering the defendant to vacate and hand over full possession. The defendant then challenged that appellate decision before the Balochistan High Court.

During the High Court proceedings, both the petitioner and the respondent passed away, and their legal heirs did not come forward to be substituted as parties. The court explained that under Order XXII, Rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code, if no application is made to bring in legal representatives within the limitation period, the case does not automatically end (abate) - the court can still proceed and decide the matter, and such a decision remains valid even though a party has died.

This case is significant because it clarifies that the death of a litigant does not stall justice indefinitely, and courts can and must decide pending cases using the existing record when heirs fail to step in, ensuring disputes are not left unresolved.

title: Muhammad Noor V. Muhammad Usman and 4 others,
explainer:
This case is about a civil lawsuit filed by Muhammad Noor seeking a court declaration and cancellation of a sale deed involving certain land. During the trial, Noor produced one witness but then failed to bring further evidence. The trial court dismissed his suit for lack of interest and non-prosecution under a specific procedural rule, Order XVII, Rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code. His appeal to a higher trial-level court was also dismissed, this time on the separate ground that the land in question was in an unsettled area, meaning no formal government land settlement had been conducted there, and therefore Noor could not claim ownership.

The Balochistan High Court found problems with both decisions. It explained that Rule 3 can only be used to decide a case immediately if there is already enough evidence on record to reach a decision on merits; here, the trial court dismissed the suit without properly considering the available material, which was legally improper. The High Court also rejected the appellate court's reasoning, holding that there is no law stating that residents of unsettled areas automatically lose their property rights simply because the government has not yet conducted a formal land settlement. Title to property must be proven through evidence, not assumptions.

As a result, the High Court set aside both lower court decisions and sent the case back to the trial court, directing that Noor be given two more opportunities to present his evidence. This matters because it protects a litigant's right to a fair hearing and clarifies how procedural dismissals for non-prosecution should be handled.

title: Taj Muhammad V. Noor Ud Din and another,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute in Quetta. Taj Muhammad claimed he was the rightful owner of a piece of land, saying a mutation entry (record of property transfer) had been fraudulently created without his knowledge or signature. He sued to cancel that mutation, regain possession, and secure declarations confirming his ownership. Both the trial court and the first appellate court rejected his suit, so he brought the matter to the Balochistan High Court.

The key legal issue was about how expert evidence, specifically a handwriting and fingerprint analysis report, had been used in the case. The report suggested his signature on the disputed mutation was not genuine, though the thumb impression matched his. However, the expert who prepared this report was never called to testify in court or be cross-examined; the trial court simply placed the report on record as evidence.

The High Court ruled this was improper. It held that expert opinions are only legally relevant if the expert is produced in court to explain and defend the findings, allowing the other party to cross-examine them. Simply filing or 'exhibiting' a report without the expert's testimony does not make it valid evidence, even if both sides initially seemed to accept it. The court also clarified that any document, not just expert reports, must be proven through a witness, not just placed on file.

This case matters because it reinforces basic fairness in legal proceedings, ensuring that evidence, especially technical expert findings, is properly tested and not accepted blindly.

title: Zia Ud Din V. Khan Muhammad and 7 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Pishin, Balochistan. The petitioner, Ziauddin, had earlier filed a civil suit (No. 09/2006) claiming his father's legacy property, which was decreed in his favor and fully acted upon. Later, he filed a fresh suit seeking possession of other portions of land connected to the same property and inheritance dispute, along with mesne profits (compensation for wrongful use of property) and a permanent injunction.

The defendants argued this second suit was barred by law because it was based on the same cause of action as the earlier, already-decided suit. Both the trial court and the appellate court agreed, dismissing the case under Order II, Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code, which prevents a person from splitting up a single claim into multiple lawsuits. If someone leaves out part of their claim in an earlier suit, either by choice or oversight, they cannot come back later and sue for that leftover portion separately.

The Balochistan High Court upheld these decisions, agreeing that Ziauddin's second suit was essentially trying to claim something he should have included in his first case back in 2006. Since he did not do so, and that earlier suit had already reached finality, he was legally barred from raising it again. The court dismissed his revision petition, finding no error in the lower courts' rulings.

This case matters because it reinforces an important procedural rule protecting defendants from repeated litigation over the same underlying dispute, ensuring that all claims from one dispute are settled together rather than split across multiple lawsuits.

title: Abdul Kareem V. Sultan Badshah,
explainer:
This case involved a money recovery dispute between Abdul Kareem and Sultan Badshah. Sultan Badshah had originally sued Abdul Kareem for recovery of Rs. 8,000,000 based on a negotiable instrument, using a summary procedure under Order XXXVII of the Civil Procedure Code. The trial court initially decreed in the plaintiff's favor, but the High Court reversed this on appeal. The plaintiff then approached the Supreme Court, which sent the case back to the trial court, directing both parties to produce additional evidence about their business dealings, payments made, and account settlements, since the existing evidence on these points was scant.

After the case returned to the trial court, the plaintiff sought permission to submit a ledger document that had not been part of the original case file. The defendant objected, arguing the document was filed late and without proper justification. The trial court allowed the document to be added, and the defendant challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It explained that the rule governing late submission of documents (Order XIII, Rule 2, CPC) exists to keep out forged or fake documents and to keep trials moving quickly, not to block genuine evidence. If there is no real doubt about a document's authenticity, courts should not reject it just because it was submitted late, especially when it is important for reaching a fair decision. The revision petition was dismissed, meaning the ledger could be used as evidence in the ongoing trial.

title: Muhammad Nawaz V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns a police officer, Muhammad Nawaz, who was convicted for allegedly allowing a drug suspect to escape from police custody due to negligence while on duty. A First Information Report had been lodged after the suspect broke the lockup and fled during the night. Eight police employees were initially arrested; five were later released for lack of evidence, and two co-accused were acquitted by the trial court. Only Muhammad Nawaz was convicted and sentenced to one year's rigorous imprisonment plus a fine, a decision upheld on appeal before he brought this revision petition to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found the prosecution's case seriously flawed. None of the witnesses who saw events firsthand testified that Nawaz was actually in charge of guarding the lockup, and the prosecution never produced the duty register that would have proven who was responsible for security that night. His conviction rested mainly on an inquiry report, but the court held that such administrative findings are not binding on a criminal court, which requires actual evidence of negligence, not assumptions.

The court explained that to convict someone under this law, prosecutors must prove actual negligence causing the escape, not merely that the accused was on duty. Since real doubt existed about the case, and doubts must benefit the accused, the court acquitted Muhammad Nawaz. This judgment matters because it reinforces that criminal convictions require solid evidence and cannot rest on suspicion, presumption, or unproven administrative reports.
