title: Fatima V. National Database and Registration Authority through Director General,
explainer:
Fatima went to court after the National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) refused to renew her expired computerized national identity card (CNIC), telling her the card had been blocked. She had originally obtained a manual identity card and then a CNIC after her marriage in 1984, and had also secured her children's B-Forms through NADRA. When renewal was refused, she sued for a declaration and related relief. The trial court ruled in her favor, but an appellate court later overturned that decision and dismissed her suit. She then challenged that appellate ruling in the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court sided with Fatima. It held that since NADRA itself had earlier registered her and issued her a CNIC after verifying all legal requirements, the authority could not later block her card without proof that she was not a Pakistani citizen. As someone who was a citizen by birth, she was automatically a citizen of Pakistan, and the burden was on NADRA to prove otherwise rather than rely on vague verbal claims. The court emphasized that blocking a CNIC without notice or hearing was arbitrary and violated fundamental rights, since a blocked CNIC effectively strips a person of access to education, health, employment and other basic rights protected under the Constitution. The court restored the original decree in Fatima's favor.

This case matters because it reaffirms that identity card blockages cannot be done arbitrarily or without due process, and that citizenship rights, once recognized, cannot be stripped away by unsupported administrative action.

The petitioner claimed ownership, saying his father had purchased the property, and he sought a court declaration of ownership, cancellation of a mutation and a Deputy Commissioner's order in favor of another party, and a permanent injunction against transfer of the property. Both the trial court and the appellate court dismissed his suit, finding he failed to prove his claim. He then approached the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions. It held that simply attaching a sale deed to the plaint does not prove that the document was validly executed. Under Article 79 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat, a document requiring attestation must be proved by producing at least two attesting witnesses; without this, the document cannot be treated as legally proved. Since the petitioner failed to produce any attesting witness to the alleged sale deed, or explain why they couldn't be produced, he failed to discharge the burden of proof resting on him as the plaintiff. The Court explained that this witness requirement exists to prevent fraud and fabricated evidence.

Because both lower courts had reached the same factual conclusion and no legal error was shown, the High Court declined to interfere and dismissed the revision petition. The case highlights the strict evidentiary standard required to prove property documents in Pakistani courts.

title: Qudratullah V. Bakht Muhammad alias Qari and another,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta. The petitioner (plaintiff) filed a lawsuit seeking declaration of rights, enforcement of a property distribution agreement dated July 2013, partition, possession, and other relief against the respondents. He claimed the agreement entitled him to a share of property that had allegedly been distributed among the parties. Both the trial court and the appellate court dismissed his case, finding he failed to properly prove the agreement.

The Balochistan High Court, hearing his revision petition, upheld these decisions. The court explained that under the law of evidence (Qanun-e-Shahadat Order), any document requiring attestation—like the agreement in question—must be proved by calling at least two witnesses who actually witnessed its signing. The plaintiff's witness had not witnessed the agreement being signed and gave contradictory testimony, so this requirement was not met. Meanwhile, the other side produced a registered sale deed for the property, and registered documents carry more legal weight than oral testimony; oral evidence alone cannot disprove a registered document. Since the plaintiff could not produce any competing document to challenge the sale deed, his case failed.

The court also noted that its revisional powers are limited—it can only step in for major legal errors or clear misreading of evidence, not to re-decide factual findings that lower courts have already agreed upon. Finding no such error here, it dismissed the petition, leaving the earlier rulings intact.

title: Muhammad Sarfaraz V. Najeeb Ullah and another,
explainer:
This case involved two lawsuits arising from the same land dispute. One party (the petitioner) sued for a declaration, cancellation of mutation entries, and a permanent injunction, while the other party had already filed a separate suit over the same matter. The trial court combined both cases, dismissed the petitioner's suit, and decreed in favor of the other side. The petitioner appealed, but the appellate court dismissed the appeal for non-prosecution under a rule (Order XVII, Rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code) that applies to trial-level suits, not appeals.

The High Court found this was a legal error. It explained that Order XVII, Rule 3 uses the word "suit" and only governs trial proceedings, not appeals. Appeals can only be dismissed for a party's absence under a different rule, and only on a date actually fixed for hearing. Here, the date the appeal was dismissed was not a proper hearing date, and worse, the record showed that notices to the appellant had never been properly served—they came back marked "unserved" or "refused," which cannot be treated as valid service.

The court held that people's legal rights should not be lost due to procedural technicalities or administrative errors by the court itself. It set aside the appellate court's dismissal order and sent the case back for a proper hearing on the merits. This decision reinforces that appellate courts must follow the correct procedural rules and ensure proper notice before dismissing an appeal.

title: UK law judgment in HTC v Apple case
explainer:
This UK patent judgment (though the prompt mislabels it as Pakistani) concerns a High Court dispute between HTC and Apple over four Apple-owned European patents relating to smartphone technology. HTC sought to have three of Apple's patents revoked, arguing they were invalid, while Apple sued HTC Corporation for infringing those patents plus a fourth. HTC counterclaimed for revocation of that patent too. Essentially, the two tech giants were fighting over whether Apple's patents were valid and whether HTC's products infringed them.

Justice Floyd's judgment sets out the legal framework the court applied to decide these questions: how to interpret patent claims (based on what a skilled person would understand the patentee to mean), how to assess whether an invention was genuinely new (novelty), whether it involved an inventive step (not obvious to a skilled person), whether the patent improperly added new subject matter after filing, and whether the invention fell into excluded categories like computer programs or presentations of information, which cannot be patented under UK and European law.

This case matters because it was part of a broader global patent war between HTC and Apple over smartphone and tablet technology, a dispute reflecting intense competition in the mobile device industry. The judgment demonstrates how UK courts apply established legal tests to determine whether tech patents are valid and enforceable, decisions with significant commercial consequences for what companies can and cannot do with competitors' patented innovations.

title: Zainullah V. Hizbullah and others,
explainer:
This case involved two civil disputes over ownership and possession of the same piece of land in Quetta, filed by the same plaintiff against different sets of defendants. He sought court declarations confirming his ownership and orders stopping others from interfering with the property. During the trial, a local commissioner (a court-appointed person, here an advocate) was sent to inspect the site and measure the land, with the consent of both parties. Based largely on that commissioner's report, the trial court dismissed both suits, and the appellate court upheld those dismissals.

The plaintiff challenged this in the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the lower courts wrongly treated the commissioner's report as if it were a binding arbitration decision, while ignoring the actual evidence presented by the parties. He also complained that his pending applications to amend or withdraw parts of his case had never been decided before judgment.

The High Court agreed with him. It clarified that a local commissioner appointed under the Civil Procedure Code is meant only to clarify specific factual matters, like measuring land, not to act as an arbitrator whose findings replace the court's own evaluation of evidence. Consent to appoint a commissioner does not mean the parties made him the final decision-maker. The Court also held that pending applications must be decided before the main case, and each legal issue must be addressed separately. As a result, the High Court accepted the revision petitions, meaning the lower courts' decisions were set aside for reconsideration in light of proper procedure.

title: Abdul Wahid v State,
explainer:
This case is about two men, Abdul Wahid and Irshad, who were caught driving a truck carrying 600 kilograms of charas (hashish) hidden in secret compartments in the petrol tank. They were tried under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act and convicted by a trial court, receiving life imprisonment and heavy fines.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined how the evidence was handled. The contraband was in the form of 500 packets of rods, but only 12 small samples (10 grams each, totaling 120 grams) were taken for laboratory testing to confirm the substance was actually charas. The problem was that the prosecution could not show from how many of the 500 packets or rods these 12 samples were actually drawn, since not all packets were opened and tested.

The court ruled that because the law must be applied strictly in narcotics cases, and because there was no proof the untested rods actually contained charas, this created reasonable doubt. Following the principle that any reasonable doubt should benefit the accused, the court held that the prosecution had only proven the presence of 120 grams of charas, not 600 kilograms. As a result, the more serious charge under Section 9(c) was reduced to the lesser charge under Section 9(b), and the appellants were sentenced only to the time they had already served in custody, rather than life imprisonment.

title: Messrs Noor Flour Mills v Judge Banking Court,
explainer:
This case involved a bank recovery suit under the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001. A bank had sued a flour mill and its guarantor for recovery of a loan, claiming they defaulted on repayment after availing financing facilities. The defendants applied for leave to defend the suit, raising various factual and legal objections and submitting supporting documents. However, the Banking Court in Quetta dismissed their application without properly examining these objections or the documents, and went ahead to decree the suit in the bank's favor for a substantial amount.

The defendants appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the Banking Court's judgment was inadequate. The High Court agreed, holding that a proper judgment must clearly state the case, identify the points for determination, and give reasoned decisions on each issue - especially in commercial disputes where documents defining the parties' rights and obligations must be carefully considered. The Court found that the Banking Court's order was not a "speaking judgment" because it failed to address the legal and factual arguments raised by the defendants or discuss the documents they filed.

As a result, the High Court set aside the judgment and decree, and sent the case back to the Banking Court to properly decide the leave-to-defend application. This case matters because it reinforces that courts, especially specialized tribunals handling fast-track commercial disputes, must still provide reasoned, well-considered judgments rather than brief, unexplained rulings - ensuring fairness even in expedited recovery proceedings.

title: Qaisar Khan v Chief Secretary,
explainer:
This case was brought by employees of the Balochistan High Court, working as Private Secretaries and Readers, on behalf of the Court's establishment staff. They asked the court to declare it illegal and discriminatory that the provincial government had refused to pay them a Special Judicial Allowance equal to three times their initial basic pay, backdated to 1 July 2009, even though similar staff at the Supreme Court, Federal Shariat Court, and the High Courts of other provinces (Sindh, Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) had already received this allowance from that date. The provincial government resisted, citing financial constraints and the province's poor fiscal position.

The Balochistan High Court ruled in favour of the petitioners. It held that denying the allowance to Balochistan High Court staff, while granting it elsewhere, amounted to unjustified discrimination under Article 25 of the Constitution, which guarantees equal treatment to persons similarly situated. The court said financial difficulty cannot override constitutional guarantees of fundamental rights, and that arbitrary or unreasonable distinctions between similarly placed employees are unconstitutional. It directed the government to pay the Special Judicial Allowance to Balochistan High Court establishment staff at the same rate and from the same date as other courts, and to issue the necessary notification.

The case matters because it reinforces that budgetary excuses cannot justify unequal treatment of government employees performing similar roles across provinces.

title: Ikramullah v State,
explainer:
Ikramullah was convicted by a trial court for the murder, kidnapping, and robbery-related killing of Saat Muhammad, and sentenced to life imprisonment along with a heavy fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The case arose after the victim disappeared while traveling with the appellant, who was his vehicle's conductor. Ten days later, the victim's brother filed a police report. During investigation, the victim's pickup truck was found near the appellant's family orchard, and after his arrest, the appellant led police to a spot where the victim's buried body was recovered.

On appeal, the defense argued the ten-day delay in filing the police report was suspicious and that the prosecution had not proven murder, suggesting at most a lesser offense of concealing evidence. The court rejected this, finding the delay adequately explained and noting there was no motive for the family to falsely accuse the appellant. The recovery of the vehicle and the body, based on the appellant's own disclosure, was undisputed by the defense.

The court held that the evidence formed an unbroken chain of circumstances linking the appellant to the crime, even though he may not have personally fired the fatal shots. Because the killing was carried out with common intention shared among the accused, the appellant was held equally and vicariously liable for the murder. The conviction was upheld, reinforcing the legal principle that all participants in a crime committed with shared intent bear equal responsibility, even if only one person carries out the fatal act.

title: Rahim Khan v State,
explainer:
This case involves an appeal by two men, Rahim Khan and Karim Khan, convicted under the Explosive Substances Act and the Anti-Terrorism Act after police raided a house in Quetta at night and allegedly recovered 49 hand grenades from one appellant's room and 40 kilograms of explosive material, along with detonation equipment, from the other's room. They were sentenced to eight years' rigorous imprisonment by the Anti-Terrorism Court.

On appeal, the defence argued that no independent witnesses were involved in the search as required under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code, that the investigating officer was not produced at trial, and that the expert opinion on the recovered material was inadmissible.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that, given the raid happened at 2:25 a.m., it was understandable that private witnesses could not be arranged, especially since efforts had been made to find them. The court reaffirmed that police officers are competent and credible witnesses unless there is specific evidence of malice or false implication, which the defence failed to show. It also noted that the defence never objected to the expert report when it was presented at trial, so they could not challenge it later.

Finding that the prosecution had proven the explosives were recovered from the appellants' exclusive possession, and noting the legal presumption of guilt under Section 27-A of the Anti-Terrorism Act once such possession is shown, the court upheld the conviction and sentence, considering the punishment already lenient.

title: Ghulam Ahmed v Muzafara Begum,
explainer:
Ghulam Ahmed sued to establish that he co-owned a house in Quetta with the family of Muzafara Begum and others. He said the house was jointly purchased in 1920 by his father and the defendants' great-grandfather through a registered sale deed, giving each side a 50% share. However, during a later settlement operation and subsequent revenue corrections, the property was wrongly recorded as being solely owned by the defendants' predecessor, cutting the plaintiff out entirely. The trial court had dismissed his suit, so he appealed.

The Balochistan High Court ruled in his favor. It held that a mutation entry in revenue records does not itself create ownership rights—it only creates a rebuttable presumption of ownership, which can be challenged and overturned with better evidence. Here, the 1920 registered sale deed clearly proved joint ownership, and the defendants could not produce any document showing how their ancestor became sole owner. The court found the mutation record naming him as exclusive owner was the product of fraud, which meant it was void from the start—and fraud-tainted entries don't get protection from the law of limitation, since the clock only starts running from when a plaintiff's rights are actually denied.

As a result, the court set aside the trial court's decision and ruled that the plaintiff was a half-owner of the property, also entitled to inherit further shares through his mother and wife, with the property to be properly corrected, partitioned, and possession handed over accordingly. title: Haji Abdul Rahim v State,

His defense was found to be inconsistent and untrustworthy, with no evidence of false implication. The court therefore upheld the conviction and life sentence.

title: Rasheed Tareen v Chairman Workers Welfare Board,
explainer:
This case concerns a government engineer, Rasheed Tareen, who was sent on deputation from his parent department, Communication and Works (C&W), to the Workers Welfare Board Balochistan, where he served as Director (Works). His deputation was extended for a fixed period, but before any further extension or permanent absorption was formally approved, the Welfare Board issued a notification sending him back to his parent department. Tareen challenged this, arguing that recommendations from the provincial government and a No Objection Certificate meant he had effectively been permanently absorbed into the Welfare Board and could not be returned.

The Balochistan High Court rejected his petition. It explained that a deputationist remains an employee of his parent (lending) department unless he is formally and validly absorbed into the borrowing department through proper procedure, such as approval by the relevant Selection Committee or Board under the applicable service rules. Mere recommendations or an NOC, especially one later withdrawn, do not amount to permanent absorption. The court held that deciding whether someone is permanently absorbed involves terms and conditions of service, an issue that falls under Article 212 of the Constitution, which bars the High Court from intervening under Article 199. Since the petitioner's lien with his parent department remained intact, he was not an "aggrieved person" entitled to relief, and the petition was dismissed.

This case clarifies that deputation does not automatically become permanent employment and reinforces limits on constitutional courts interfering in civil service matters governed by specialized service tribunals.

title: Khan Muhammad v State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by Khan Muhammad, who had been convicted by a Sessions Court in Turbat for murdering his elder brother Yar Muhammad and his nephew Naveed, and for seriously injuring his niece Mst. Gulshan, following a dispute over ancestral property. He was sentenced to death for the murders, along with additional prison terms and fines for the other offences. The trial court referred the death sentence to the Balochistan High Court for confirmation, and the convict separately appealed against his conviction.

The High Court examined the evidence, which included eyewitness testimony from people who were inside the house at the time of the killings, medical evidence confirming the injuries, and physical evidence such as a recovered Kalashnikov rifle, spent cartridges, and a bullet, all matched to the weapon through a firearms expert's report. The defense argued that witnesses were biased relatives and that some statements were recorded late without explanation, but the court found the witnesses consistent and credible, noting that being related to the victims does not automatically make testimony unreliable if the witness is otherwise truthful and was present at the scene.

The court concluded that the prosecution had proven its case fully, that the accused acted in a brutal and calculated manner, and that no circumstances justified leniency. It upheld the conviction and sentence, emphasizing that courts have a duty to victims and society to impose punishments that deter serious crime.

title: Muhammad Jamil v State,
explainer:
This case is about two employees of a pharmaceutical company, Messrs Chas-A Mendoza, who were prosecuted under Pakistan's Drugs Act, 1976 for allegedly manufacturing and supplying a misbranded and substandard medicine capsule called Ronuvit. A drug sample was tested by the Central Drug Laboratory, which found it substandard, and the company received sanction for prosecution. However, only two employees—the Quality Control Incharge and the Warrantor—were charged, while the company itself was never prosecuted.

The employees sought acquittal before the trial court, which was rejected, prompting them to approach the Balochistan High Court to quash the proceedings entirely.

The High Court ruled in favor of the employees. It held that without first prosecuting the company itself, its employees could not be held liable under the Drugs Act. The court also found serious procedural flaws: the lab report was submitted nine months late instead of within the required sixty days, the report failed to disclose the testing method used as legally required, and the trial court's order was passed only by the Chairman without the required two additional Members, making it improperly constituted. The order was also non-speaking, meaning it failed to address the arguments raised.

Given these violations, the court concluded there was no chance of conviction even if the trial continued, so it quashed the proceedings and acquitted the accused. This case highlights how strict procedural compliance and proper legal targeting of responsible parties are essential in drug law prosecutions.

title: Patoo v State,
explainer:
This case involved two brothers, Patoo and Moula Baldish, who were convicted by a trial court in Lasbela and sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder of a man named Din Muhammad in 1986. The prosecution's case rested mainly on a dying declaration (the victim naming the accused before he died), alleged confessions recorded before a magistrate, and recovery of weapons like an axe and knife.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted both men. It found the prosecution's evidence riddled with serious problems: the main witness contradicted his own police statement and improved his account in court; no identification parade was held to confirm who the attacker was; a key witness never actually identified the accused; and the dying declaration, which is inherently weak evidence needing independent support, had none. The recovery of the weapons was not properly linked to the accused, there was no chemical report confirming blood on the axe, and the motive was never clearly established.

Most importantly, the confessions were recorded far from where the accused were held, with no explanation for moving them, and the magistrate failed to follow the mandatory legal procedure under the Criminal Procedure Code for recording confessions safely and voluntarily.

Because of these combined doubts, the court ruled the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and the accused deserved the benefit of that doubt. This case underscores the strict safeguards required for confessions and dying declarations to be legally reliable.

explainer:

Years later, two daughters from the deceased's second marriage applied to have this certificate revoked, arguing they were entitled to a share of the money as legal heirs. The trial court agreed and revoked the certificate, also ordering that the appellant's surety would be responsible for paying the other heirs their Islamic law shares if the appellant failed to do so.

The Balochistan High Court overturned this decision. It found that the revocation application was filed very late, was not properly signed, and was never supported by evidence or affidavits. More importantly, the High Court held that succession certificate proceedings are meant only to protect whoever collects a deceased person's debts or securities, not to determine actual ownership or inheritance shares. Courts handling such certificates cannot decide who is entitled to what, or order payments—that must be pursued through a separate civil suit. Since the certificate itself doesn't establish final title, revoking it served no real purpose. title: Nasir Mehmood V. Director Education (Colleges), Balochistan, Quetta and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a lecturer position at a government college in Balochistan. The petitioner, Nasir Mehmood, had applied for a Lecturer in English post at Balochistan Residential College Turbat and stood fourth on the merit list. Separately, another candidate, Adnan Riaz, was appointed as a lecturer at Cadet College Panjgur based on a "hope certificate" from his university, which predicted he would pass his final Master's exam, even though he had not yet completed his degree. When it became clear his results would be delayed, his appointment was cancelled, and the college decided to re-advertise the post. The petitioner argued that since he was next in line on the merit list, he should be given that position instead.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the petitioner had never applied for the Cadet College Panjgur post in the first place, only for the Turbat position, so he had no claim to the vacancy created by Adnan Riaz's removal. The court held that the decision to re-advertise the post was lawful and not something requiring judicial interference, though it left the petitioner free to apply when the position was re-advertised.

Importantly, the court strongly criticized the practice of appointing candidates based on "hope certificates" - documents merely predicting future exam success. It ruled that required qualifications must be completed before applying for a job, and disapproved of any government or institution accepting such certificates in the future.

title: Sardar Haider Khan Nasir and another V. Sardar Dur Muhammad Nasir,
explainer:
This case involved two election petitions challenging the 2013 election of Sardar Dur Muhammad Nasir to the Balochistan Provincial Assembly from constituency PB-14 Loralai-I (Dukki). Two losing candidates, Sardar Haider Khan Nasir and Muhammad Shafique Tareen, separately alleged that the winning candidate had engaged in corrupt or illegal practices affecting the results at numerous polling stations, and asked the Election Tribunal to declare the election void and instead declare them elected.

The Balochistan High Court, sitting as an Election Tribunal, dismissed both petitions. It held that anyone challenging an election bears the burden of proving corrupt or illegal practices through clear, cogent, and convincing evidence, similar to the standard required in a criminal trial. Vague affidavits, interested witness testimony without corroboration, or the mere filing of a police complaint on polling day were not enough. The court found no proof that polling was rigged, that result forms were forged, or that the winning candidate was responsible for lapses like unsealed election material or poor-quality ink, since those were failures of election officials, not the candidate. The court also noted that even excluding all disputed votes, the winning candidate still led by 234 votes.

This case matters because it reinforces the strict evidentiary standard for overturning election results in Pakistan and confirms that candidates cannot be blamed for administrative failures of election officials.

title: Hifeeza and 5 others V. General Public,
explainer:
This case involved a family from Turbat, Balochistan, seeking a succession certificate after their relative died in an accident while working as a farmer in Sharjah, UAE. Such a certificate was needed to collect compensation and dues owed to the deceased. The District Judge at Turbat had dismissed their application, ruling that it lacked jurisdiction because the deceased was considered domiciled in Sharjah at the time of death, and the money owed was located there.

The family appealed, arguing that their relative was actually a permanent resident of Turbat who had only gone abroad temporarily to earn a living, and had not given up his Pakistani domicile.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the family. It explained that under the Succession Act, 1925, succession to a deceased person's movable property is governed by the law of the country where the person was domiciled at death. Since "domicile" is not defined in the Act, the court relied on standard legal dictionaries and treatises, which define domicile as a person's true, permanent home to which they intend to return, even if currently living elsewhere. The court found no evidence that the deceased intended to permanently abandon Pakistan. Therefore, the trial court had wrongly interpreted "domicile" and wrongly refused jurisdiction. The High Court set aside that order and sent the case back for a decision on its merits. This ruling clarifies that working abroad temporarily does not change a person's legal domicile.

This case involved a long-running family property dispute over a house in Quetta. Family members had jointly inherited the property, and one group first sued for partition in 1994. That earlier suit was successful, and courts at every level, including the Supreme Court, upheld the decision that the plaintiffs were entitled to a share of the property. However, the winning parties never took the legal step of formally executing that court decree to actually divide the property, and too much time passed for them to do so under the law.

Years later, in 2012, some family members filed a fresh lawsuit asking again for partition and possession of the same property. The trial court dismissed this second lawsuit, reasoning that the matter had already been decided (the legal principle of res judicata, meaning the same issue cannot be litigated twice) and rejected the plaint.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It found that although the earlier case had been decided in the plaintiffs' favor, since the decree was never executed within the legal time limit, it became unenforceable. Because the property remained jointly owned and unpartitioned, and one plaintiff was not even covered by the earlier decree, there was no valid bar to filing a new suit. The trial court had wrongly dismissed the case. The High Court set aside that dismissal and sent the case back for a full hearing on its merits.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that an unexecuted court decree does not permanently settle ownership if it was never enforced in

title: Syed Fateh Agha V. Accountability Court and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute between a citizen, Syed Fateh Agha, and the National Accountability Bureau (NAB). Years earlier, the petitioner had been allotted and compensated for land by the Quetta Development Authority, built shops and flats on it, and obtained a completion certificate. NAB later took up a complaint about the pricing of the land allotment. The petitioner applied for a voluntary return, NAB accepted it, and he paid the entire agreed amount of about Rs. 2.18 million. NAB and QDA then issued No Objection Certificates, and the petitioner sold the property through a registered sale deed. Despite this settlement, NAB later issued a fresh order freezing the very same property, which was subsequently confirmed by the Accountability Court.

The petitioner challenged this freezing order in the High Court, arguing it amounted to punishing him twice for the same matter. The authorities argued he should have filed an appeal instead of a constitutional petition. The High Court found that the law did not actually provide any appeal against this type of freezing order, so the petitioner was right to come directly to the High Court. On the merits, the Court held that freezing property that had already been cleared through the voluntary return process violated the constitutional protection against double jeopardy. It declared NAB's freezing order and the Accountability Court's confirmation of it null and void, and ordered the property de-frozen. The case matters because it reinforces that once a matter is settled through legal process, authorities cannot reopen it against the same person over the same property.

title: Uma Gul V. Gul Bibi and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over property and money in Quetta. The respondents' predecessor had allegedly agreed to buy a house from the appellant for Rs. 34 lakhs, paying most of the price upfront, but before the property could be formally transferred, he was murdered. His legal heirs then sued the appellant, seeking to be declared owners of the house, to have it transferred and possession handed over, and to recover Rs. 11 lakhs they claimed was separately invested in the appellant's fruit business. The appellant denied owing anything, claiming the original purchase agreement had been mutually cancelled and only a smaller forfeited deposit was ever paid.

The trial court had decreed the suit in favor of the respondents, and the appellant appealed. Rather than deciding who was right on the facts, the Balochistan High Court found a basic procedural flaw: the trial court had never properly framed the necessary legal and factual issues arising from the parties' pleadings, as required by the Civil Procedure Code. The High Court held that this was the trial court's own duty, regardless of whether the parties raised it, and that a court's failure to do its job should not unfairly harm any party's case.

As a result, the High Court set aside the trial court's judgment and sent the case back for the issues to be properly framed and decided afresh. This case underscores that courts must independently ensure procedural fairness, since parties should not suffer for a judge's oversight.

title: Merck (Private) Limited through Notified Factory Manager V. Member Labour Appellate Tribunal and 24 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between Merck (Private) Limited, a pharmaceutical company, and workers who claimed they had been employees of the company and were wrongfully terminated. The workers said they had been hired on a permanent basis after a probation period but were never given formal appointment letters, and were later barred from entering the factory by police. They filed a grievance claiming unlawful termination and sought reinstatement.

Merck denied any employer-employee relationship, arguing the workers were actually hired by a separate contractor or consultant engaged to provide services at the factory, not by the company itself. The Labour Court agreed with Merck and dismissed the workers' grievance, finding no proof they were company employees. However, the Labour Appellate Tribunal reversed this decision and ordered the company to reinstate the workers with permanent appointment letters.

Merck challenged the Tribunal's ruling before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court found that there was no evidence, such as appointment letters or payroll records, showing the workers were employed by Merck. Instead, records showed they were on the payroll of the consultant/contractor, with whom Merck had a service agreement. The Court ruled that the Tribunal had wrongly assessed the facts and law, and restored the Labour Court's original decision dismissing the workers' claims.

This case matters because it clarifies that companies using contracted labor through third-party consultants are not automatically responsible as "employers" under labor law, especially when no direct employment evidence exists.

title: Syed Bibi V. Naib Tehsildar Levies Bostan and 10 others,
explainer:
This case involved a mother, Syed Bibi, seeking justice for her son, Hafiz Muhammad Jan, who died during what police described as an armed encounter with Levies personnel in Bostan. Police had registered an FIR claiming Muhammad Jan and another man opened fire on a patrol, prompting a shootout in which he was killed. The mother alleged instead that her son had been tortured and killed while in police custody, not in an exchange of gunfire, and she applied to have a second FIR registered against the police officials involved. A Sessions Judge, acting as Justice of Peace, rejected her request, so she approached the High Court.

The High Court found serious contradictions in the prosecution's version, including unexplained multiple injuries and a skull wound caused by blunt force that didn't fit the "encounter" story, and the absence of any medical certificate despite claims the injured man was taken to hospital. Since the mother's account described a materially different time, place, and manner of death, the Court ruled that this amounted to a distinct version disclosing a separate offense, which legally required registration of its own FIR and investigation.

The Court set aside the lower court's order, directed police to register the second FIR based on the mother's allegations, and ordered that this new case be investigated and tried alongside the original case. This decision matters because it reinforces that when family members present a credible, conflicting account of a death involving police, courts must allow that version to be formally investigated rather than dismissed outright.

title: Messrs United Agro Chemicals through authorized dealer and another V. Government of Pakistan through Collector Customs House and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerned three trucks carrying imported DAP fertilizer that were stopped by Pishin levies at a checkpoint in Balochistan and handed over to the Frontier Corps, on suspicion that the fertilizer was being smuggled out of Pakistan into Afghanistan. Customs authorities seized the trucks and fertilizer and later issued a legal notice to the transporter under the Customs Act, 1969.

The company that imported the fertilizer from Australia, along with its authorized dealer who was transporting it to local farmers, challenged this action in the Balochistan High Court. They argued the fertilizer was legally imported, was meant for agricultural use in nearby villages, and was seized deep inside the country, far from the Pak-Afghan border, not while attempting to cross it.

The court agreed with the petitioners. It held that since the fertilizer was lawfully imported and the trucks were intercepted in the interior of the country rather than at the border, no smuggling offense under the Customs Act had actually occurred. Mere suspicion that the goods might eventually be smuggled across the border was not sufficient legal ground for seizure or for initiating customs proceedings. The court ruled that the interception, seizure, and subsequent notice were without lawful authority, ordered the trucks and fertilizer released to the petitioners, and quashed the proceedings. This case highlights that authorities cannot punish people based on assumptions about future illegal acts; actual violation of law at the relevant place (the border) is required.

title: Muhammad Shafiq and 6 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a bail-before-arrest application from seven applicants accused in a violent altercation in Chaman that resulted in one death and several injuries. Two rival First Information Reports (FIRs) were lodged over the same incident, each side accusing the other of attacking first. Under FIR No.32, the applicants were accused of causing the death of a man named Haji Dad Muhammad and injuring others. Under FIR No.33, filed by the opposing side, the original complainant and his relatives were accused of assaulting the applicants and their relatives.

Notably, the accused in FIR No.33 (the complainant party in FIR No.32) had already been granted pre-arrest bail by the trial court. The applicants argued there were serious doubts about the case against them, including inconsistencies in the medical evidence about the cause of death, irregularities in the postmortem process (the body was initially buried without autopsy, then exhumed), and missing forensic samples sent for analysis.

The Balochistan High Court found that, given the cross-versions of the incident and the doubtful evidence, the case required further inquiry rather than immediate arrest. It held that mere absconding is not enough to deny bail if the case genuinely raises doubts, and that possible false implication due to malice could not be ruled out. The court granted pre-arrest bail to the applicants, emphasizing fairness when both sides of a violent dispute file competing criminal complaints against each other.

title: Abdul Haleem V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murder and attempted murder over a family dispute involving his sisters and their allegedly abusive husbands. The trial court had found Abdul Haleem guilty of killing Ahmed Ali and injuring his brother, sentencing him to life imprisonment plus additional jail time and fines. He appealed the conviction, while the complainant separately sought a harsher sentence, including the death penalty.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. The eyewitnesses claimed to have been present during a shooting but were not themselves hit by any bullets, which the court found suspicious. The police site plan failed to show where the witnesses or accused were standing during the incident, raising doubts about whether they were actually there. There were also unexplained delays in sending the weapon and bullet casings for forensic testing, which undermined the reliability of that evidence. Additionally, a key witness statement was recorded three days after the crime, further weakening its credibility. The accused also presented evidence supporting an alibi.

Given these gaps and inconsistencies, the court ruled that the prosecution had not proven its case beyond reasonable doubt. It set aside the conviction, acquitted Abdul Haleem, and ordered his release. This case highlights how Pakistani courts scrutinize forensic delays, witness credibility, and physical evidence like site plans to ensure convictions are based on solid, trustworthy evidence rather than assumptions.

title: Muhammad Arif V. The National Accountability Bureau through Director-General, Cantt., Quetta,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Arif, who was accused by the National Accountability Bureau of participating in a fraud scheme involving fake lottery draws for cars, and specifically of using ATM cards belonging to other account holders to withdraw and benefit from proceeds of the crime, amounting to millions of rupees. He was arrested in March 2013 and had been in custody for over two years by the time this petition was filed. He asked the Balochistan High Court for bail, arguing that his trial had been unreasonably delayed and that under the law, prolonged detention without conclusion of trial should entitle him to bail.

The court rejected this argument. It held that offences under the National Accountability Ordinance are non-bailable, and the normal statutory right to bail for delay under the Criminal Procedure Code does not automatically apply to such cases. While the High Court can still grant bail using its special constitutional powers in appropriate situations, this is discretionary, not a right. Here, much of the delay was caused by the conduct of the accused's own lawyer, and the accused had earlier been a fugitive who did not cooperate with investigators. Given the strong evidence against him, the court found no justification to grant bail. Instead, it dismissed the petition and directed the trial court to hold hearings weekly and finish the trial quickly. The case highlights how accountability law limits bail rights for corruption accused, even amid delays.

title: Abdul Khaliq Mandokhel and 2 others V. Chairman, Balochistan Public Service Commission and another,
explainer:

After completing their papers, BPSC withheld results and later disclosed, through meeting minutes, that it had cancelled the Revenue Law-II paper based on an Inquiry Committee's recommendation. That committee had re-evaluated only about 10% of answer sheets, chosen at random, and apparently suspected copying, though no candidate was ever accused specifically, summoned, or given a chance to explain. The petitioners challenged this cancellation before the Balochistan High Court.

The court first addressed whether the petition was even allowed to be filed in the High Court, given that civil servants normally must appeal to the Service Tribunal. It held that BPSC is not a "departmental authority" and its actions during recruitment are not covered by that appeal route, so the petitioners rightly came directly to the High Court.

On the merits, the court found no evidence of cheating—correct answers alone cannot prove copying, and suspicion or presumption cannot substitute for proof. Since candidates were never given notice or a hearing before their paper was cancelled, this violated natural justice. The court also noted BPSC's own rules did not permit re-evaluation of competitive exam answer sheets in this manner.

title: Lafarge Pakistan Cement Ltd. through Attorney V. Messrs Decent Coal Company through Managing Director,
explainer:
This case involves a business dispute between Lafarge Pakistan Cement Ltd and Decent Coal Company over payment for a coal supply contract. The coal company sued in Quetta for recovery of about 15.2 million rupees, claiming the cement company had withheld payment for coal already delivered and caused additional losses. The cement company, based in Islamabad, argued that the Quetta court had no jurisdiction since it does not do business there, and asked for the case file to be sent back so the suit could be filed in Islamabad instead. The trial court rejected this request, and the cement company challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined how the contract was actually formed. The parties had communicated by email and fax: an offer was sent from Islamabad, but it was accepted by the coal company from Quetta and communicated back. The court explained a key legal principle: when contracts are made through letters or electronic correspondence, the contract is considered complete at the place and time the acceptance is sent, not where it is later received. Since acceptance was dispatched from Quetta, that is where the cause of action arose, giving Quetta courts jurisdiction. The court dismissed the cement company's appeal, confirming the suit could proceed in Quetta. This ruling clarifies how jurisdiction is determined in disputes arising from contracts formed through email and fax communication.

title: Naseebullah Khan Bazai V. Dr. Ummar Khan Babar and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about whether a court judgment can be reversed after it was discovered that the person who won the case had hidden important facts from the court.

The High Court ruled in his favor on 30 August 2017. However, Naseebullah Khan Bazai, another officer who was senior to Dr. Babar and would be affected by this decision, filed a review application asking the court to reconsider its own judgment. He argued that he had not even been made a party to the original case despite having a direct interest in the outcome, and that Dr. Babar had concealed a crucial fact: he was facing a pending criminal case under the National Accountability Ordinance over alleged embezzlement of over 40 million rupees. Under the applicable promotion rules, an officer facing such pending criminal proceedings was not eligible for the promotion in question.

The High Court held that its constitutional jurisdiction is a discretionary power meant to serve justice, available only to those who approach the court with clean hands. Since Dr. Babar had concealed a materially important fact affecting his eligibility, the judgment obtained was tainted. The court ruled that it has the inherent power to review its own orders in such circumstances, and since the original judgment had not yet been implemented, it recalled that judgment and dismissed the original petition entirely.

title: The Collector of Customs, Model Customs Collectorate, Quetta V. Messrs Al-Habib Enterprises and Engineering and others,
explainer:
Naeem  Akhtar  Afghan,  J. 

This case concerned six used concrete transit mixer trucks imported from China into Pakistan through Quetta. The importer submitted pre-shipment inspection certificates stating the trucks were no more than five years old. Customs officials assessed and charged duties based on these documents, and the trucks were cleared and released after payment. Later, on inquiry with the manufacturer, customs discovered that the trucks were actually older than declared, some manufactured as far back as 2004. Based on this, the Additional Collector of Customs (Adjudication) issued show-cause notices and imposed heavy penalties on both the importer and the inspection company for misdeclaration.

The importer appealed, and the Customs Appellate Tribunal set aside these penalty orders. The Collector of Customs then challenged the Tribunal's decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the Tribunal's decision and dismissed the Collector's references. It held that once goods have been assessed under Section 80 of the Customs Act, duties paid, and goods cleared under Section 83, the proper remedy for the customs department to challenge that assessment is to file an appeal under Section 193 of the Act—which was not done here. The Additional Collector (Adjudication) had no jurisdiction to issue a fresh show-cause notice or penalize the importer after clearance without following this route. Since no legal question warranting the High Court's intervention arose, the references were dismissed.

title: Messrs Riegn Nutro Pharma (Pvt.) Ltd. and 2 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Riegn Nutro Pharma and its officials, who were accused of selling an unregistered drug, a zinc-based syrup called Maxzin, in violation of Pakistan's Drugs Act, 1976. A Drug Inspector had taken a sample of the syrup, and while lab testing showed it was not substandard, authorities pursued a criminal case against the company because the product had not been registered as a drug. The company argued the syrup was actually a food or nutritional supplement, not a drug, and therefore should be regulated under a different law, the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan Act, 2012, not the Drugs Act.

The trial court had rejected the company's request for acquittal, so the matter came before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court examined the relevant rules defining food supplements, health products, and nutritional supplements, and found that zinc supplements clearly fall into these categories. It noted that after the 2012 DRAP Act and related 2014 rules came into force, authority over such supplements shifted to the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan, not the provincial bodies enforcing the Drugs Act.

As a result, the court ruled that the Provincial Quality Control Board had no legal authority to sanction prosecution against the company for failing to register the syrup as a drug. The court quashed the pending case and acquitted the accused, clarifying that supplements like this must be handled under the newer, specialized regulatory framework rather than general drug laws.

title: Messrs City Marketing Service and 2 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about who can be criminally prosecuted when a substandard or spurious drug is found being sold. Drug inspectors recovered a substandard cough syrup (XAMOL) from a medical store, which had been supplied by City Marketing Service, the distributor, under a written warranty from the actual manufacturer, Macquin's International Pharmaceutical Manufacturers of Karachi. The distributor and its associates were put on trial under the Drugs Act, 1976, even though the manufacturer itself was never prosecuted.

The Balochistan High Court held that under the Drugs Act, a distributor who is not the manufacturer or the manufacturer's agent cannot be held liable for a defective drug if it relied on a proper written warranty from the manufacturer confirming the drug's compliance with the law. The liability of the manufacturer and its distribution agent is meant to be joint, but since the manufacturing company was never charged, the distributor alone could not be convicted. The court found there was no possibility of conviction even if the trial continued, so it quashed the pending proceedings against the distributor and its owners and acquitted them.

This judgment matters because it clarifies that distributors who act on a manufacturer's warranty are legally protected from prosecution, and that authorities must pursue the actual manufacturer responsible for a defective drug rather than only the seller or distributor down the supply chain.

title: Abdul Qayyum and another V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Abdul Qayyum, who was placed under preventive detention by the Balochistan government under Section 3(1) of the Balochistan Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960. He was first detained for 30 days by the Deputy Commissioner of Loralai, and this detention was later extended for another 30 days by the Additional Chief Secretary (Home), Government of Balochistan. The stated reasons were that he was considered a potential threat to public safety, likely to create a law-and-order situation, and was allegedly provoking people against the State. A second petitioner, initially also detained, was released after completing his 30-day detention and did not pursue the case further.

The Balochistan High Court examined whether the government's satisfaction in ordering the detention was based on real evidence or was arbitrary. The court held that such satisfaction must be objective, backed by concrete material, not just vague or general assertions. It found that the grounds given for detaining Abdul Qayyum were generic and unsupported by any actual evidence.

As a result, the court declared the detention orders null, void, and without legal effect. This ruling matters because it reinforces that no citizen's liberty can be restricted without lawful justification, and that courts have the power to review and strike down preventive detention orders that lack proper evidentiary basis, safeguarding fundamental rights under the Constitution.

title: Abdul Jabbar and another V. Sardar Khan Rind and another,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal shooting incident from 2010 in Quetta, in which three unidentified men on a motorcycle allegedly opened fire, and later the complainant added a supplementary statement claiming additional attackers arrived in a Prado vehicle, naming several people including one respondent. That respondent was not named in the original FIR but was implicated later through this improved version of events. He surrendered before the Anti-Terrorism Court and was granted pre-arrest bail, which was later confirmed by the trial court.

The complainant then asked the Balochistan High Court to cancel this bail, arguing the respondent had been absconding for a long time and that the trial court had wrongly exercised its discretion in granting bail.

The High Court rejected this request and upheld the bail. It found no evidence that the respondent even knew he had been implicated, since he was named only in a later supplementary statement rather than the original FIR. The court held that such circumstances fall within the scope of "further inquiry," which can justify granting or confirming pre-arrest bail. It also noted there was no sworn evidence (affidavit) showing the respondent had misused his bail.

This decision matters because it reaffirms that bail decisions depend on the specific facts of each case, and that late, unsupported implication of an accused through a subsequent statement can be legitimate grounds for courts to grant or maintain bail rather than automatically canceling it.

title: Sajjad Haider Tareen, PDSP, Quetta and 10 others V. The Provincial Police Officer, Balochistan Quetta and 12 others,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court, concerned a long-running dispute over how Deputy Superintendents of Police (DSPs) belonging to the police prosecution branch should be treated in seniority lists compared to DSPs from other branches of the Balochistan Police.

Originally, a joint seniority list covering DSPs from all branches, including prosecution, was maintained until 2000. After that, the department began excluding prosecution branch DSPs from the joint list without issuing any separate list for them either. As a result, DSPs from other branches who were junior to prosecution branch officers were promoted to Superintendent of Police ahead of them. Prosecution branch DSPs challenged this exclusion as illegal and discriminatory.

The court examined the relevant service rules and found that while different branches of the police service were organized as separate units, they were not formally designated as distinct "cadres" requiring separate seniority lists under the Balochistan Civil Servants Act, 1974. It also noted that although lower-ranked prosecution staff could not transfer to other branches, DSPs of the prosecution branch faced no such restriction and could serve in other branches after promotion.

The court accepted the petitions, ruling that the department must maintain one joint seniority list for all DSPs regardless of branch, rather than separate lists that disadvantaged prosecution branch officers in promotions. This decision reinforced fair treatment and equal promotion opportunities for civil servants across branches within the same service cadre.

title: Sher Zaman and 4 others V. Government of Balochistan, Secondary Education Department Civil Secretariat, Quetta through Secretary and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a challenge to parts of the Balochistan government's 2019 recruitment policy for teaching staff (BPS-09 to 15). The petitioners, who were candidates seeking appointment, objected to specific clauses of the 2019 policy and wanted the government to instead follow an earlier, more favorable rule from the 2014 recruitment policy. They argued the older policy's method of filling vacancies would give them a better chance of appointment if selected candidates failed to join their posts.

The government's side argued that the 2019 policy was updated deliberately, based on a Supreme Court ruling that the earlier 2014 policy hadn't accounted for, and that recruitment rules already protect district and zonal-based allocation of posts, so there was nothing improper about the change.

The Balochistan High Court examined the disputed clauses closely and compared them with the earlier policy and the relevant civil service rules. It found that the 2019 policy's method of ranking candidates by village, union council, tehsil, and district was actually consistent with the earlier policy and with the established recruitment rules. The court held that government policies cannot be struck down by courts unless they are shown to be made in bad faith, arbitrarily, or as an abuse of power. Since there was no evidence of that here, and the petitioners suffered no real prejudice, the court dismissed the petition. This case is significant because it reinforces how much deference courts give to government policy-making decisions, intervening only when there's clear misuse of power.

title: Messrs A&B Petrol Urunleri Pazarlama through Authorized Attorney V. MV Nazlican and others,
explainer:
A Turkish company that supplied fuel and bunker services to two ships sued in the Balochistan High Court to recover unpaid bills totaling tens of thousands of US dollars. By the time the suit was filed, the ships had already been sold and were being broken up at the Gadani ship-breaking yard in Balochistan. The plaintiff sued not just the companies that owed the money, but also the vessels themselves, the new purchaser, the ship-breaking association, and the yard, invoking the court's special "admiralty" jurisdiction, which allows claims directly against a ship (an action "in rem") in addition to claims against the person who owes the debt (an action "in personam").

The court explained that under the Admiralty Jurisdiction of High Courts Ordinance, 1980, a claim for supplies like fuel can only turn into a lien enforceable against the ship itself if, at the time the lawsuit was filed, the ship was still beneficially owned by the same person or company who owed the money. Here, the ships had already been sold to a new owner before the suit was filed, so the necessary ownership link was broken.

Because this key requirement was not met, the court held that the suit was not maintainable under admiralty jurisdiction and dismissed it. The case clarifies the strict ownership timing rule for enforcing maritime supplier claims against a ship in Pakistan.

title: Messrs Meerab Enterprises, through Authorized Attorney V. The Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Federal Board of Revenue and 3 others,
explainer:
Meerab Enterprises imported two consignments of pistachios from Iran through a land route and declared their value for customs purposes. The customs appraising officer assessed a slightly higher value and the company paid duty and taxes accordingly. However, before the goods could be released, officers of the Directorate of Intelligence and Investigation seized the consignments, alleging that a Valuation Ruling had not been properly applied and that this caused revenue loss to the government.

The company challenged the seizure in the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the Directorate had no authority to seize goods on this basis. The court examined the relevant law, particularly a 2007 government notification defining the powers of the Directorate. It held that intelligence officers can only intercept and seize goods when there is misdeclaration of the description, quality, or quantity of goods leading to revenue loss. They have no jurisdiction to seize goods merely because a Valuation Ruling was allegedly not applied correctly or was wrongly applied, since that determination falls outside their domain.

Based on this reasoning, the court accepted the petition and declared the seizure report void and legally ineffective.

This case matters because it clarifies the limits of power of customs intelligence agencies, ensuring they do not overstep into valuation disputes that belong to other authorities, thereby protecting importers from arbitrary seizures based on disagreements over customs valuation methods rather than genuine misdeclaration.

title: Sher Zaman and 2 others V. Syed Abdul Sadiq and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a family land dispute in Quetta that had been stuck for years over a technical procedural issue: could the plaintiff amend his original lawsuit, or did he need to withdraw it and start over?

Sher Zaman had filed a civil suit seeking declaration, specific performance of an agreement, possession, and injunction, based on an agreement (iqrarnama) from 2012. His original plaint had drafting problems, including unclear description of the property and an incomplete account of the cause of action. He later asked the trial court to allow amendments to fix these issues. The trial court allowed the amendments, but the District Court reversed that decision, ruling that the changes were so significant they would alter the entire nature and cause of action of the suit, which is not permitted under ordinary amendment rules.

The Balochistan High Court agreed that such fundamental changes could not be made through a simple amendment. However, it held that the defects in the original plaint, poor drafting, missing facts about the agreement, and unclear property description, qualified as formal defects or other sufficient cause under Order XXIII, Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code. Since the case was still at an early stage with no evidence recorded, the court ruled that the plaintiff should not be denied justice over technicalities. It allowed him to withdraw the suit and file a fresh, properly drafted one. This shows courts favoring substance over procedural technicality when a genuine claim exists.

title: Abdul Ghani Khetran and another V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Irrigation Department and another,
explainer:
This case is about a challenge to how the Balochistan government awarded contracts for building water dams. The Irrigation Department had invited pre-qualified contractors to bid on 23 dam projects across different districts under Package-IV of a 100 Dams program. After receiving applications, the Project Director proposed merging or packaging ten of these dams (located in four districts) into just four combined contracts, arguing this would attract stronger, better-resourced firms and improve construction quality, based on lessons learned from earlier packages where progress had lagged. This plan was approved by the Secretary of the Irrigation Department.

The High Court agreed with the petitioners. It held that government contracts involving public money and public interest must be fair, transparent, and free from arbitrary or biased decision-making, and that such actions are subject to judicial review under Article 199 of the Constitution. The court declared the merging of the ten dams into four contracts, along with the related pre-qualification summary, null and void. Since financial bids had not yet been opened, the court cancelled them and directed authorities to invite fresh bids for all ten dams as separate, individual projects, restoring the original competitive process for the previously pre-qualified companies.

When they moved the timber into Balochistan, the provincial Forest Department also charged them tax. The importers challenged this, arguing they were being taxed twice, which they claimed violated Article 163 of the Constitution, and also arguing that the Forest Act, 1927 had never been formally adopted by the Balochistan Government, so the Forest Department had no legal power to collect any tax.

The matter had a long history: a Balochistan High Court had earlier ruled in the importers favor, but the Supreme Court set that decision aside and sent the case back for fresh examination of whether prior permission from forest authorities was needed to move timber through Balochistan, and whether the place of loading mattered.

On reconsideration, the High Court held that the Central Laws (Statute Reforms) Ordinance, 1960 had extended the Forest Act, 1927 to the whole of Pakistan, including Balochistan. Under Section 39 of that Act, the provincial government was legally authorized to levy duty on timber and forest produce through official notification. Since the Forest Department had acted within this legal authority, its tax collection was valid and not illegal. The court dismissed the petitions and ordered the importers to release the disputed tax amounts, along with accrued profit or interest, to the Forest Department. This clarified that provincial forest taxes on imported timber were legally valid even after federal customs duty had been paid.

title: Habib-ur-Rehman v. State,
explainer:
This case involved Habib-ur-Rehman, who had been convicted by a trial court for possessing an unlicensed .22 bore pistol and two cartridges under the West Pakistan Arms Ordinance. The trial court had sentenced him to three years' imprisonment and a fine of Rs.50,000. On appeal, the Balochistan High Court reduced his prison sentence to time already served, since he had no prior criminal record and had already spent over four months in custody. However, that earlier appellate order was completely silent about the fine, neither confirming nor cancelling it.

Habib-ur-Rehman then filed an application asking the court to clarify or correct this gap, since he had already deposited the full Rs.50,000 fine and wanted it addressed given his reduced sentence.

The High Court held that although criminal judgments are normally final, courts retain inherent power under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code to review or rectify their own orders when something has been mistakenly omitted, especially if it affects a party's rights. Using this power, the court corrected its earlier order, reducing the fine from Rs.50,000 to Rs.5,000, and directed that the excess amount of Rs.45,000 already deposited be refunded to him.

This case matters because it confirms that courts can revisit and fix genuine omissions in their own judgments to ensure fairness, even after a decision has technically been finalized.

title: Jamal Shah Khilji v. State,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and concerns a man arrested under Pakistan's narcotics law for alleged possession of drugs. During the police investigation, he asked the investigating officer to record statements from two witnesses he believed would support his case, but the officer refused. He then asked the Judicial Magistrate to order the police to record these statements, but the Magistrate refused too, saying courts cannot direct how police conduct investigations. When he challenged this before the Special Judge through a revision petition, the judge agreed the Magistrate's reasoning was flawed but still dismissed the plea because the trial had already begun and the case had moved to the court stage. The judge instead told him he could present evidence himself during trial.

The petitioner then approached the High Court, arguing the witnesses' statements were crucial and should have been recorded during investigation. The High Court explained that while trial courts have power to summon important witnesses who were missed during investigation, once a trial has actually started, the High Court should not interfere by ordering re-investigation, as this would disrupt the normal trial process. It also clarified that a Sessions Court cannot use its revisional powers to review purely administrative orders passed by a Magistrate. For these reasons, the High Court dismissed the petition.

This ruling matters because it clarifies the boundaries between police investigation, magisterial oversight, and trial court powers, and confirms that courts should generally let ongoing trials proceed rather than send cases back for further investigation.

title: Liaquat Ali v. Sabrullah,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Muhammad Islam who was shot and killed in Washuk in December 2006. The complainant, Liaquat Ali, filed a criminal case against nine people, accusing them of murder and rioting under the Penal Code. After trial, the Additional Sessions Judge acquitted all the accused, finding the evidence insufficient. The complainant then appealed this acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the acquittal. It found that none of the prosecution witnesses actually saw the named accused fire the fatal shots; instead, they blamed an absconding accused who was not part of this appeal. No weapon was recovered from the accused, and there was no independent evidence supporting the complainant's version. The court also noted there was no proof the accused shared a common purpose or formed an unlawful assembly, which is required for group liability in such cases. It found it suspicious that as many as nine people were implicated for a single killing, suggesting possible false implication of some accused.

The judgment reaffirms an important principle: when reviewing an acquittal, courts must presume innocence twice over and should not overturn it just because another view of the evidence is possible. Acquittals are only reversed if the original decision was clearly perverse or ignored crucial evidence. This case illustrates how Pakistani courts protect the acquitted from being punished twice through appeals based on weak or exaggerated evidence.

title: Karim Bakhsh v. State,
explainer:
This case involved a devastating train accident in Balochistan on 26 September 2002, when the Quetta Express derailed near Bridge 130/B, killing eight people and injuring around 114. A government inquiry blamed several railway employees for negligence, and they were tried and convicted by a trial court under multiple laws, including murder-related provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code, causing hurt, damaging property, and endangering passenger safety under the Railways Act. They received sentences ranging up to fourteen years.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence, including the official Railway Inspector's report, and found that while the employees were indeed negligent, there was no evidence of intent to kill or cause harm. The court ruled their actions amounted to "qatl-e-khata" (death caused by mistake or negligence, not intentional murder), reducing their conviction from murder to this lesser charge and cutting their sentence to five years. Some other charges, like causing hurt and terrorism-related offenses, were dropped for lack of evidence, though the conviction for property damage was upheld.

Importantly, the court also ruled that since individual employees couldn't be blamed alone, the Railway Department itself was responsible for compensating victims, ordering it to pay Rs. 500,000 to the families of each deceased passenger. This case matters because it clarifies the legal distinction between negligence and intentional crime, and it reinforces those public bodies like railways have a duty to compensate passengers harmed due to systemic or employee failures.

title: Zafar Masood v. Chief Secretary Govt: of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute among civil servants in Balochistan over their seniority ranking. After an earlier ruling by the Balochistan Services Tribunal, the Provincial Selection Board was told to redo the seniority list properly, considering relevant rules and appointment dates. A final seniority list was issued in March 2009, listing the petitioners favorably. However, some other officers (the private respondents) felt the list ignored their claims, so they appealed to the competent government authority. That authority agreed with them and issued a corrigendum in November 2009, revising the seniority list in their favor. The original petitioners then challenged this corrigendum in the High Court, arguing it was issued in bad faith and violated the Tribunal's earlier directions.

The High Court disagreed. It clarified that the Tribunal's earlier ruling had not favored any specific individual—it simply required the Board to follow proper procedure. Since the revised list was the result of a lawful appeal process available to civil servants, and since disputes over service seniority fall under matters that must go to the Service Tribunal (not the High Court) due to Article 212 of the Constitution, the High Court ruled it had no jurisdiction to hear the case. The petition was dismissed without examining its merits.

This case highlights an important principle: seniority and service-related disputes among civil servants must be resolved through the proper appellate channel—the Service Tribunal—not through the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction.

title: Muhammad Akram v. Muhammad Qahir,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between Muhammad Akram and Muhammad Qahir over a piece of land in Quetta. Akram claimed he owned the land and that Qahir, who had been his tenant, had handed over possession to him under a private settlement, after Qahir received Rs. 200,000. Akram alleged that Qahir later illegally re-entered and occupied the land, so he filed a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005. The trial court dismissed the complaint and acquitted Qahir, saying there was no direct evidence that Qahir had actually given up possession.

Meanwhile, a related civil suit filed by Qahir over the same property had been decided against him at every level, including the High Court and the Supreme Court, all of which found that possession had indeed been transferred to Akram and that Qahir's reoccupation was illegal.

The Balochistan High Court held that the trial court had ignored these consistent civil court findings and the substantial oral evidence (ten witnesses) presented by Akram, amounting to misappreciation of evidence. It set aside the acquittal, convicted Qahir under Section 3 of the Illegal Dispossession Act, sentenced him to one year's imprisonment plus a fine, and ordered police to restore possession of the land to Akram within a week.

The case matters because it shows courts using prior civil litigation outcomes to inform criminal proceedings on illegal dispossession, and it reinforces protection against forcible land-grabbing after lawful settlements.
