title: The State through Deputy Prosecutor General V. Muhammad Kaleem Bhatti,
explainer:
This case involved a corruption conviction under the National Accountability Ordinance. Muhammad Kaleem Bhatti had been convicted and sentenced to five years imprisonment along with a fine of Rs. 1,50,00,000. As part of the sentence, his properties were ordered forfeited to cover the fine amount, but the judgment also specified that if the fine was not recovered or paid, he would serve an additional two years in prison.

Bhatti served his original sentence and, since the fine was not recovered, also served the additional two years in default of payment. He then applied to the trial court asking for his properties to be released, arguing that since he had already served the extra sentence in lieu of paying the fine, the forfeiture no longer applied. The trial court agreed and ordered the release of his properties.

The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) appealed this decision to the Balochistan High Court, arguing the order was illegal and reopened a matter already settled by the Supreme Court.

The High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that once Bhatti served the additional sentence in place of paying the fine, the punishment had been fully carried out. The law does not allow double punishment, so his properties could not remain forfeited once he had served time instead of paying. The court also noted that the trial court, having issued the original judgment, was best placed to interpret its own order.

title: Muhammad Ali Satakzai v. Appointing Authority of the Addl. D&S Judges,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and deals with how judges of the rank of Additional District and Sessions Judge should be appointed. A group of petitioners, who were working on an ad hoc basis in that post, challenged a letter through which the Balochistan Public Service Commission had invited applications, conducted tests, and interviews for these judicial posts. They argued that the Commission had no constitutional authority to be involved in appointing judicial officers, since this power under the applicable service rules conflicted with Article 175 of the Constitution, which requires separation of the judiciary from the executive. The petitioners also asked the court to regularize their ad hoc appointments.

The court agreed that letting a government-influenced body like the Public Service Commission control appointment of judges undermines judicial independence and lowers the dignity of judicial office. It held that under the Constitution, such appointments should instead be handled directly by sitting judges of the High Court, not the Commission. As a result, the letter sent to the Commission for recruiting these judges was declared legally ineffective.

However, the court rejected the request for regularization of ad hoc appointments, ruling that no rule allowed automatic confirmation of ad hoc judicial officers, and that ad hoc service does not create any right to permanent appointment, seniority, or promotion.

This judgment matters because it reinforces the principle of judicial independence by removing executive-controlled bodies from the process of appointing judges.

title: Khalo v. State & Abdul Qayyum v. State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Khalo and Abdul Qayyum, who were arrested at a graveyard in Quetta at night based on a tip-off from a police informant. Police found unlicensed pistols and cartridges on them, and they were charged with making preparation to commit dacoity (armed robbery) under sections 399, 400, and 401 of the Pakistan Penal Code. A trial court convicted them, sentencing each to seven years in prison plus a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined whether the prosecution had actually proven the legal requirements for the offence of preparing to commit dacoity, which requires showing both intention and concrete preparation. The court found that none of the prosecution witnesses gave any evidence about the accused's actual intentions, and there was no proof of any overt act suggesting they were preparing for a robbery. The case rested merely on the informant's tip and the fact that armed men were found in a graveyard at night. The court held that simply being present somewhere unusual at an unusual hour, even with an illegal weapon, does not by itself prove intent to commit dacoity, since no law restricts when or where people may move about.

Finding the prosecution's case highly doubtful, the court ruled that this doubt should have benefited the accused, something the trial court failed to do. The convictions were set aside and the men were acquitted, highlighting that vague suspicion and informant tips alone cannot substitute for concrete evidence of criminal intent.

title: Muhammad v. Dad Rahim,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves a dispute over land ownership in Gwadar. The petitioners (Muhammad and 15 others) claimed they were the rightful owners of a piece of land, but during official settlement proceedings, the land was recorded in the name of a private respondent, Dad Rahim. The petitioners said they were abroad at the time and only learned of this mutation later, prompting them to sue for a declaration of ownership, a permanent injunction, and correction of the land records.

Both the trial court and the appellate court had already dismissed their case, and they brought a revision petition to the High Court challenging those decisions.

The High Court also dismissed the petition. It found that none of the petitioners' witnesses actually supported their claim of ownership, and one of their own witnesses admitted the petitioners were present in the area during the settlement proceedings, contradicting their claim of being abroad and unaware. The court noted that settlement proceedings are conducted openly on the spot, and objections must be raised within six years, which the petitioners never did. Since they were neither the recorded owners nor in possession of the land, they had no legal standing under the Specific Relief Act to bring such a suit. The court also emphasized that settlement entries carry a strong legal presumption of correctness, which the petitioners failed to rebut with solid evidence.

This case highlights how important it is to timely challenge land record entries and how courts give strong weight to official settlement records unless clearly disproven.

title: Abdul Sattar v. State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Abdul Sattar, who had stood as a guarantor (surety) for an accused person, Noor Ali, allowing him to be released on bail. Sattar deposited Rs. 2,00,000 in cash as security to guarantee that the accused would appear in court. When the accused failed to appear and could not be produced, the trial court forfeited Rs. 1,50,000 of the surety amount as a penalty. Sattar challenged this before the Additional Sessions Judge, who upheld the forfeiture, so he approached the Balochistan High Court asking for the amount to be reduced.

The High Court held that standing surety for someone is generally an act of goodwill, and a guarantor should not be punished harshly unless there is evidence he acted for personal gain or with bad intent in helping the accused get bail. Since there was no proof that Sattar benefited financially or acted with ulterior motives, and the trial court had not properly justified such a heavy penalty as required under Section 514 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the forfeiture was excessive.

The Court reduced the fine from Rs. 1,50,000 to Rs. 80,000 and ordered the remaining Rs. 1,20,000 to be returned to Sattar. This case matters because it clarifies that courts must balance fairness and proportionality when penalizing sureties, rather than automatically imposing maximum penalties.

title: Naseer Kakar v. State,
explainer:
This case involved Dr. Naseer Kakar, a doctor at Helper Eye Hospital, Quetta, who was accused of misappropriating medicines worth over Rs. 82 lakh while allegedly serving as Incharge of the hospital's Medical Store between 1994 and 1997. He was convicted by the Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Balochistan on charges of criminal breach of trust by a public servant, forgery, falsification of accounts, and criminal misconduct, and sentenced to multiple years of imprisonment with heavy fines.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him. The court found that the prosecution never proved he was actually appointed Medical Store Incharge, since no official notification supporting this claim was produced, only a vague claim that he was given charge orally. The court noted such an important post could not be assigned informally, and no one could explain who supposedly gave him this responsibility. Additionally, key documents like indents showed alterations that the Medical Superintendent disowned in court, and the crucial Stock Register that could prove whether medicines were actually received and misused was never presented. The court also noted others responsible for managing medicines, like the Medical Superintendent and Store Incharge, were not held accountable.

This case matters because it highlights how criminal convictions require solid, direct proof of a person's official role and actions, not assumptions or informal arrangements, especially when serious corruption charges and heavy penalties are involved.

title: Abdul Sattar v. Fateh Khan,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over how to properly finalize a court decree after a lawsuit had already been decided. The plaintiffs had won their case in the trial court, and since no one appealed, that decision became final. Later, the losing party (the judgment debtors) noticed that the written decree did not clearly spell out what relief the winning party was actually entitled to, even though the judgment itself had explained it. They asked the trial court to clarify the decree under Section 152 of the Civil Procedure Code, and the trial court agreed, adding the missing details so the decree matched the judgment. The original winning party then challenged this clarification, arguing the trial court had no power to alter the decree after it was issued.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed and upheld the clarification. It explained that a judgment and a decree are two different documents, and it is the decree that must be enforced. Therefore a decree needs to be complete and precise on its own, without needing to refer back to the judgment. If a decree does not match the judgment or is unclear, courts have the power under Section 152 CPC to correct it and bring it in line with the judgment. Since the original decree lacked necessary details making it hard to enforce, the correction was proper. This case clarifies that courts can fix incomplete or ambiguous decrees so they accurately reflect the judgment and can be executed.

title: Munir Akhtar Awan and others V. Khalid Mansoor and others,
explainer:
This case involved a group of students who obtained LLB degrees from a Quetta campus of Al-Khair University, a university originally established in Azad Kashmir. When they applied to the Balochistan Bar Council to be enrolled as advocates, their applications were rejected because the Pakistan Bar Council had passed a resolution declaring that Al-Khair University was not recognized for enrolment purposes. The students challenged this refusal in the Balochistan High Court.

The court noted that Al-Khair University's degrees had been recognized as equivalent by Pakistan's Higher Education Commission. However, since the university had no territorial jurisdiction within Pakistan, its Quetta campus needed proper affiliation with the local University of Balochistan, which had not actually happened. The University of Balochistan had merely issued a No Objection Certificate, which the court clarified is not the same as formal affiliation.

Despite this technical shortfall, the court found that the students had enrolled and completed their degrees in good faith, reasonably believing the campus was properly affiliated, before the Pakistan Bar Council's resolution was passed. The fault lay with the two universities, not the students. Penalizing the students for this institutional failure would be discriminatory. The court therefore directed the Bar Council to accept and process their enrolment applications, allowing the petitions.

This case matters because it protects students who acted in good faith from being punished for administrative failures by educational institutions beyond their control.

title: Shams-Ullah v. State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Shamsullah who was convicted by a Sessions Judge in Loralai for causing explosions and attempted murder, receiving seven years imprisonment under the Explosive Substances Act and two years under Section 324 of the Pakistan Penal Code, to run concurrently. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution's case was that the complainant heard three explosions outside his house at night, saw two people running away, identified the appellant using torchlight, and claimed the appellant fired a pistol at them before fleeing. Police recovered a piece of burnt wire and earth from the scene as evidence of the explosion.

The High Court found serious flaws in the prosecution's case. The burnt wire did not meet the legal definition of an explosive substance, and it was never even sent to a ballistic expert for testing. No pistol, bullets, or shell casings were recovered or tested either. Witnesses only saw the accused running away, not actually causing any explosion. Despite the incident happening in a populated area, no independent witnesses were brought forward. The court also noted a civil dispute existed between the complainant and the accused, raising the possibility of false implication, and ruled that a delayed, uncorroborated statement by the accused could not be used as evidence.

Because the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the court overturned the conviction and acquitted Shamsullah, highlighting the importance of solid forensic evidence and independent witnesses in criminal cases.

title: Chakar Khan v. Azad Khan,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute between two families over agricultural property in Sibi, Balochistan. The respondents claimed they were the rightful owners and that the petitioners' predecessor had been given possession of the land only as a tenant under a cultivation arrangement, but had failed to pay the agreed share of produce. They sued for declaration of ownership and possession. The petitioners denied any landlord-tenant relationship and claimed ownership through long possession. During the case, the petitioners also filed a separate suit to cancel mutation entries recording the land in the respondents' names. The two suits were consolidated and tried together by the trial court, which ruled in favor of the petitioners. On appeal, the district judge reversed both decisions, ruling for the respondents instead.

The petitioners challenged this in the High Court, arguing that a single appeal could not validly cover two separate judgments and decrees, and that their suit was wrongly deemed time-barred.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It held that once two suits are consolidated and decided through one common judgment, they lose independent existence, so a single appeal is valid and proper. The court also held that mere long possession does not create ownership, and since the petitioners denied the respondents' title, the respondents were entitled to sue in civil court rather than revenue court. The revision petition was dismissed, meaning the appellate court's decision favoring the respondents stood. The case clarifies procedural rules on consolidated suits and reaffirms that possession alone cannot defeat ownership rights.

title: Muhammad Anwar v. State,
explainer:
This case involved five men accused of kidnapping the complainant's son under Pakistan's Penal Code provisions on abduction. The complainant alleged that on 2 October 2010, the applicants forcibly abducted his son in a vehicle, but he only filed the police report two days later, despite the police station being just one kilometer from the scene.

The accused had initially been granted bail by a Judicial Magistrate, but this was later cancelled by an Additional Sessions Judge after the complainant objected. The applicants then approached the Balochistan High Court seeking bail again.

The High Court found several weaknesses in the prosecution's case: the unexplained two-day delay in filing the FIR, the absence of any specific role attributed to each accused, and the fact that no eyewitnesses were named in the FIR. It also emerged during investigation that there was a property dispute between the parties, suggesting a possible motive for a false implication. Importantly, the alleged victim had still not been recovered, meaning the actual facts remained unclear. The court also found the lower judge's claim that the victim was in the accused's custody to be unjustified, since there was no evidence to support it.

Since investigation was complete and the accused were no longer needed for questioning, the court held that bail should not be denied as a form of punishment. It granted bail, emphasizing that its observations were tentative and should not influence the trial court's final judgment.

title: Muhammad Khalil v. Executive District Officer,
explainer:
This case is about whether a district revenue officer could cancel domicile certificates that had already been issued to two petitioners, a father who was a police constable and his son.

The father had worked as a constable in Pishin since 1984 but only applied for a domicile certificate from Pishin in 2006. His son later got a separate certificate issued in his own name in 2008. After someone raised an objection, the Executive District Officer investigated and cancelled both certificates in 2009, finding that the family actually lived permanently in Dera Ghazi Khan and had only used a Pishin address to gain benefits meant for people from that backward district.

The petitioners argued that once a domicile certificate is granted, it creates a right that cannot be taken away. The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It explained that a domicile certificate is only prima facie proof of where someone permanently lives, and authorities can investigate and cancel it later if it was obtained through fraud, misrepresentation, or concealment of facts. Since the evidence showed the petitioners had concealed their true permanent residence and misrepresented facts to get the certificates, the cancellation was lawful.

The court dismissed the petition, finding no illegality in the officer's decision. The case matters because it clarifies that domicile certificates are not permanent, unchallengeable rights and can be revoked if obtained dishonestly, protecting the certificates' purpose of accurately reflecting genuine residence.

title: Muhammad Saleem v. State,
explainer:
This case concerns Muhammad Saleem, an Executive Engineer in Balochistan's C&W Department, who was accused of misappropriating Rs.30 million. He was tried before the Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, and convicted of criminal breach of trust, cheating, forgery, and corruption, receiving lengthy prison terms and heavy fines, including a fine of Rs.30 million recoverable from his property.

He appealed, but died while the appeal was pending. Normally a criminal appeal ends automatically when the accused dies. However, the Balochistan High Court explained that under Section 431 of the Criminal Procedure Code, an appeal against a fine does not abate on death because it affects the deceased's estate and property, not just his person. Since Saleem's fine was to be recovered from his property, and his conviction would also affect his pensionary benefits as a government employee, the appeal survived his death and had to be decided on merits.

On the merits, the court found that no witness had actually supported the misappropriation allegations, and official reports actually showed the funds were properly spent. The prosecutor had even asked the trial court to withdraw the case for lack of evidence, but the trial judge refused without giving any reasons. The High Court held this was illegal and that the evidence was insufficient. It therefore set aside the conviction and sentence.

The case matters because it clarifies when appeals survive an accused's death and stresses that courts must give reasoned decisions when prosecutors seek to withdraw weak cases.

When they refiled before the Banking Court, the bank again objected, this time arguing that the depositors did not qualify as "customers" and their claims did not involve "finance" as defined under the law, so the Banking Court itself lacked jurisdiction. Similarly, "finance" refers to loans and similar financial accommodations, not ordinary deposits. Since the appellants were merely account holders trying to recover deposited money rather than borrowers challenging a loan-related dispute, their claims did not fall within the Banking Court's specialized jurisdiction. title: Attiq Ahmed Khan v. Noor-ul-Saba,
explainer:
This case is about a husband and wife whose marriage had been dissolved through a court decree of Khula, granted to the wife by the Family Court in Quetta. The husband challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court, but his petition was dismissed in 2009. Later, both parties came back to court together, telling the judges they had reconciled and wanted to reunite as husband and wife, and asked the court to set aside its earlier judgment through a review application.

The High Court refused to reopen or set aside its earlier ruling. It explained that a Khula granted by a court amounts to a single, irrevocable-type divorce called Talaq-ul-Ba'ayen, since the husband never agreed to it voluntarily. Importantly, the court clarified that Islamic law does not require the practice of Halala (marrying another person first) before a couple can remarry after such a Khula. The couple can simply remarry by performing a fresh Nikah. However, since reuniting depends on a new marriage contract rather than undoing the old one, there was nothing wrong with the original judgment to correct, so no legal ground for review existed. The court also stressed that a review of a judgment cannot be granted simply because the parties later reach a compromise; review is only allowed for genuine errors or new evidence, not to accommodate a change of heart. The application for review was therefore dismissed, though the court confirmed the couple could still remarry through a new Nikah without any religious or legal barrier.

title: Muhammad Saleem v. Abdul Samad Khan,
explainer:
This case involved railway employees who filed a contempt of court application against Pakistan Railways officials, claiming they had disobeyed a 1985 Supreme Court order. That earlier Supreme Court ruling had held that certain railway service rules did not prevent the employees from receiving specific financial benefits under a government notification. Railway authorities paid these benefits for years but eventually stopped, prompting the employees to argue this amounted to willful defiance of the Supreme Court's decision, punishable as contempt.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It found that the Supreme Court's 1985 order only clarified the employees' rights in general terms and did not issue any specific, enforceable direction ordering the authorities to make payments. Since there was no concrete command to disobey, stopping the payments could at most be seen as a denial of the employees' rights, not contempt of court. The court explained that for a contempt application to succeed, there must be a clear, executable order that was violated, and that condition was not met here.

As a result, the court dismissed the contempt application as legally not maintainable. However, recognizing that the case had been pending since 2004 through no fault of the applicants, the court allowed them 60 days to pursue the correct legal remedy elsewhere, such as filing a proper civil claim for their unpaid dues.

title: Shakil Ahmed Baloch v. Returning Officer,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the 2010-15 election for the Balochistan Bar Council. The petitioner and another candidate tied with 41 votes each, so the Returning Officer resolved it by drawing lots, as allowed under election rules, and the other candidate won. The petitioner challenged this outcome, arguing that two votes counted in his opponent's favor should have been invalid, one cast by a government servant who wasn't eligible to vote, and another marked with a tick instead of the required cross.

However, before examining these merits, the court had to decide whether it even had jurisdiction to hear the case. The respondent argued the Election Tribunal was improperly formed since the Bar Council never requested its creation. The judge rejected this objection, clarifying that under the applicable rules, the Chief Justice must appoint a High Court judge as Election Tribunal for such disputes, and no formal request from the Bar Council is legally required.

Despite confirming jurisdiction, the court found a different procedural flaw: the petitioner had filed his complaint directly with the Election Tribunal, bypassing the required step of first submitting a written objection to the Chairman of the Provincial Bar Council, who should have then forwarded it to the Tribunal. Because this mandatory procedure was skipped, the court ruled that proper legal process wasn't followed and returned the petition, allowing it to be refiled correctly rather than deciding the underlying vote-counting dispute.

title: Shah Muhammad v. State,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal appeal filed by Shah Muhammad, who had been convicted by a Sessions Judge in Loralai for helping another person escape from police custody, an offence under Section 225 of the Pakistan Penal Code. He was sentenced to one year of rigorous imprisonment.

The background was that a man named Ahmed Din had allegedly been arrested by police, and Shah Muhammad and others were accused of using force to free him, in the process supposedly firing on police and damaging a police vehicle. Shah Muhammad appealed his conviction to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found major problems with the prosecution's case. Most importantly, the police never proved that Ahmed Din's arrest or detention was actually lawful, since no officer from the police station that supposedly first arrested him testified. The court explained that Section 225 only applies when someone helps a person escape from lawful custody, meaning custody backed by a valid warrant or legal authority. Since lawfulness was never proven, no offence under this section could stand even if the rescue happened.

The court also noted the FIR was filed eight hours late without explanation, contradictions between witnesses, and failure to produce the supposedly damaged police vehicle, all suggesting the story was fabricated and the accused falsely implicated because he was the escaped man's brother.

As a result, the High Court set aside the conviction and acquitted Shah Muhammad, reinforcing that proving lawful custody is essential before someone can be punished for helping another escape from it.

title: Mahesh Kumar Chawala v. Abdul Karim,
explainer:
This case involved a landlord, Haji Abdul Karim, who sought to evict his tenant, Mahesh Kumar Chawala, from a shop under the Balochistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959. The landlord's eviction application relied on two grounds: that the tenant had illegally sublet the shop to someone else, and that the landlord needed the shop for his own son's personal use, since the son was unemployed. The Rent Controller initially ruled in the landlord's favor and ordered the tenant to vacate.

The tenant appealed to the Balochistan High Court, which reversed the decision. The Court found serious flaws in the landlord's case. First, the landlord never even named which son needed the shop, and that son never appeared in court to testify about his own need for the property, making it impossible to verify the claim or later enforce any eviction order. Second, on the subletting claim, the landlord failed to name the alleged sublessee as a party to the case or specify when the subletting occurred, which meant this ground could not be properly argued or proven. The Court also noted that the tenant had a legitimate partnership agreement with the person allegedly occupying the shop, and that the landlord's witnesses gave unreliable, essentially copied testimony.

As a result, the High Court set aside the eviction order and dismissed the landlord's application entirely. The case highlights that landlords must provide specific, verifiable evidence and follow proper procedure when seeking to evict tenants for subletting or personal need.

title: Mussa Kaleem v. State,
explainer:
This case is about how prison remission (sentence reduction) should be calculated when a convict's sentence changes on appeal. Mussa Kaleem was convicted under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act and sentenced to 14 years' rigorous imprisonment. While his appeal was pending, the President of Pakistan granted a special remission of one-fourth of the total sentence to mark the passing of the 18th Constitutional Amendment. Later, the High Court reduced Kaleem's sentence from 14 years to 10 years after he chose not to contest his conviction on merits and only sought a lighter sentence. Kaleem argued he should get one-fourth remission based on his original 14-year sentence, since that was his sentence when the President's order was issued. Jail authorities disagreed, calculating the remission based on the reduced 10-year sentence, which meant he had not yet served enough time to be released.

The Balochistan High Court sided with the jail authorities. It explained that under the Pakistan Prison Rules, "sentence" means the sentence as finally fixed after appeal, not the original trial court sentence. Since Kaleem's appeal resulted in a reduced sentence of 10 years, that became his final sentence, and the one-fourth remission had to be calculated on 10 years, not 14. The petition was dismissed.

This case matters because it clarifies how courts and prison authorities should compute remissions when sentences are altered on appeal, ensuring remission calculations follow the final legal sentence rather than the original one.

title: National Highway Authority through General Manager V. Mehrullah Khan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over compensation for land acquired by the National Highway Authority to build a road. The landowner, unhappy with the compensation awarded by revenue authorities, filed a reference before the Additional District Judge, Kalat, who increased the compensation. The National Highway Authority then appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the trial court's decision was flawed because it did not follow proper procedure under the Civil Procedure Code.

Two issues arose. First, the landowner argued the Authority had no legal right to appeal, claiming only the Provincial Government could do so under the Land Acquisition Act. The High Court rejected this, noting that a 2000 amendment to the law in Balochistan extended the right to appeal to the Federal Government, Provincial Government, companies, or local authorities acting as acquiring bodies - so the Authority's appeal was valid.

Second, on the merits, the High Court found that the trial court had failed to frame proper legal issues or record evidence before deciding the case, as required by procedural rules (Order XX, Rule 5 of the Civil Procedure Code). This made the trial court's judgment legally defective.

As a result, the High Court set aside the trial court's order and sent the case back for a fresh decision, directing that issues be properly framed, evidence recorded, and parties heard, ideally within six months. The case highlights the importance of following proper court procedure even in land compensation disputes.

title: Pakistan Mobile Communication Ltd. v. Niamatullah Achakzai,

title: Kala Khan v. State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Kala Khan who had earlier been convicted of criminal breach of trust by a public servant and criminal misconduct, offenses related to sections 409 of the Pakistan Penal Code and 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. In an earlier appeal, the Balochistan High Court had upheld his conviction but reduced his sentence to time already served, while ordering that fines totaling ten lac rupees be recovered from his property.

Kala Khan then asked the court to clarify that judgment. He argued that the order did not specify what should happen if he failed to pay the fine, and pointed out that he owned no property from which the fine could be recovered.

The High Court explained that under section 386 of the Criminal Procedure Code, a fine can be recovered either by seizing and selling the offender's property or through civil execution proceedings against his movable or immovable assets. Importantly, the law only allows arrest or imprisonment for non-payment if the original sentence specifically ordered imprisonment in default of payment. Since the court's earlier judgment contained no such order for imprisonment, Kala Khan could not be jailed for failing to pay the fine.

However, the court clarified that the fine obligation itself does not disappear. If he currently owns no property, the debt remains outstanding and can be recovered later if and when he acquires property in the future. With this clarification, the petition was dismissed.

title: Vice-Chancellor, University of Balochistan v. Chancellor,
explainer:
This case is about a legal dispute over the tenure of a university's Vice-Chancellor. The petitioner had been appointed Vice-Chancellor of the University of Balochistan in 2010, under a notification that set his term at two years. He accepted those terms and served without objection. When his two years were about to end, he himself wrote to the Chancellor noting his contract was expiring, and was then appointed as an Acting Vice-Chancellor on a temporary basis. Only afterward did he challenge the original notification, arguing that the University of Balochistan Act, 1996 actually guarantees a four-year term, making the two-year limit illegal.

The Balochistan High Court rejected his petition. It held that since he had voluntarily agreed to the two-year term, worked under it without protest, and only raised the issue after his tenure ended, he had effectively waived his right to claim a longer term. The court explained that waiver occurs when someone knowingly gives up a legal right through their actions or silence rather than enforcing it. It also found the petition was filed too late (barred by "laches"), since he raised the issue only after two years had passed.

This case matters because it reinforces the legal principle that a person who accepts and acts under certain terms cannot later challenge those same terms after benefiting from them, especially after significant delay.

He later filed a petition arguing that under Section 12(1) of the University of Balochistan Act, 1996, a Vice-Chancellor's term should legally be four years, so the two-year limit in his appointment notification was illegal, and he should be allowed to serve out the remaining two years.

It found that although the law allowed for a four-year term, the petitioner had voluntarily accepted a two-year term, never objected during his tenure, and even acted as caretaker after it ended. By his conduct, he had waived any right to challenge the shorter term. The court also noted he raised the issue too late, after already completing his two years, which amounted to unreasonable delay (laches).

This ruling matters because it reinforces that a person who knowingly accepts and acts under certain contractual terms cannot later challenge those terms once they no longer suit him, especially after significant delay.

title: Datsun Motors v. Ain Ullah Agha,
explainer:
This case is about a shop rental dispute in Quetta. The landlord filed for eviction of his tenant, a business called Datsun Motors, claiming he genuinely needed the shop for his own personal use. The Rent Controller agreed and ordered the tenant to vacate. The tenant appealed.

While the appeal was pending, the landlord died. The tenant's lawyer argued that since the landlord had died, his legal heirs could not benefit from the eviction order because the personal need was specific to the deceased landlord, not his heirs. The tenant also argued on the merits that the landlord hadn't genuinely needed the shop, and separately claimed he had paid goodwill money (Pagri) to a previous owner, so the eviction shouldn't be allowed.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It explained that a decree (the court's formal order) creates a legal right, and once that right belongs to a person, it automatically passes to their legal heirs when they die - the heirs step into the deceased's shoes and can defend the decree in court. So the death of the landlord did not cancel or weaken the eviction order. The court also rejected the Pagri argument, since such informal goodwill payments aren't a legal transaction, and that issue was between the tenant and the previous owner, not the landlord's family.

The appeal was dismissed, meaning the eviction order stood, and the landlord's heirs could enforce it. This case clarifies that legal rights won through court decrees survive a person's death and pass to their heirs.

title: Manzoor Hussain v. State,
explainer:
This case is about a man, Manzoor Hussain, who had filed a criminal complaint alleging he and his driver were abducted. During trial, his driver's testimony did not support the allegations, and the trial court acquitted the accused, declaring the original complaint false. The trial court also directed that proceedings be started against Manzoor Hussain himself for making a false complaint. Based on this direction, police registered a new case against him under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with giving false information and making false charges, and the matter proceeded to trial.

Manzoor Hussain challenged both the acquittal of the original accused and the new case against him through a constitutional petition in the Balochistan High Court. The court ruled that he could not challenge the acquittal this way because the law already provides a specific right of appeal against acquittals, which he had not used.

However, regarding the new case against him, the court found serious legal flaws. The relevant offences could only be prosecuted following specific procedures - requiring a written complaint from a police officer or from a court - and these procedures were not followed. Instead, police registered the case simply on a letter from a District Attorney. The court held that skipping these mandatory legal steps made the entire case unlawful and without jurisdiction. It therefore quashed the case against Manzoor Hussain, while leaving the earlier acquittal untouched. This shows the importance of following proper legal procedure before prosecuting someone.

title: Muhammad Azam Kasi v. State,
explainer:
This case involved Dr. Muhammad Azam Kasi, a former Director-General of Livestock, whose bank accounts were frozen during a National Accountability Bureau (NAB) inquiry against him. NAB's Director-General froze five accounts in December 2011, and later that month a NAB prosecutor asked the Accountability Court to confirm the freeze, even though no formal reference (the actual corruption case) had yet been filed against him. The trial court rejected his objections and confirmed the freeze in February 2012, prompting this appeal.

The Balochistan High Court ruled in his favor. It explained that under Article 23 of the Constitution, people have a right to hold and dispose of property, and any restriction on that right must be reasonable and time-limited. The law only allows the Chairman of NAB to freeze property for 15 days, after which a reference must be filed in court for further confirmation. Since no reference had actually been filed here, confirming the freeze indefinitely meant the accounts could remain frozen forever without any real case being pursued—something the court found unlawful and unconstitutional. The court also noted that a person must be properly informed when their property is frozen, since the law gives only 14 days to object.

As a result, the High Court set aside the freezing order and directed that the appellant's bank accounts be released immediately, reinforcing that property rights cannot be suspended indefinitely without formal charges being filed.

title: Naseeb Gul v. Amir Jan,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal appeal under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which punishes dishonestly issuing a cheque that later bounces. The complainant, Naseeb Gul, accused Amir Jan of issuing a cheque worth over ten lakh rupees to repay a loan, which was dishonoured when presented to the bank. A trial court convicted Amir Jan, but on appeal the Sessions Judge acquitted him. Naseeb Gul then challenged that acquittal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. It explained that simply issuing a cheque that bounces is not automatically a crime — the law requires proof that the person acted dishonestly, meaning with fraudulent intent to cheat or humiliate the payee. In this case, evidence showed the complainant himself had physically confronted the accused and pressured him into writing the cheque, meaning it wasn't given voluntarily. A bank witness also revealed that the complainant had a signed blank cheque from the accused's account, filled it in himself, and submitted it despite being told there were no funds — suggesting the complainant was trying to trap the accused rather than being defrauded. No witnesses were produced to show dishonest intent, nor were the loan's terms disclosed.

The judgment matters because it clarifies that dishonesty is an essential element for a cheque-bouncing conviction, protecting people from being criminally punished merely because a cheque failed to clear.

title: Niaz Muhammad v. Muhammad Amin,
explainer:
This case involved a petition challenging the eligibility of a Member of the Balochistan Provincial Assembly, who had also served as a provincial minister. Under the election rules then in force, candidates needed a bachelor's degree to contest elections. The petitioner alleged that the respondent had not actually taken his B.A. exams himself; instead, another person impersonated him in the examination hall and sat the papers on his behalf, allowing him to fraudulently obtain the degree used to qualify for office.

The Balochistan High Court examined records from the University of Balochistan, including examination forms and certificates, which showed the photograph of the other individual (not the respondent) on the official documents. The court also noted that after being elected, the respondent had rewarded this individual with a government job, reinforcing suspicion of collusion. The court concluded that the degree was indeed obtained through impersonation and fraud, making it invalid, and ruled that the respondent could not be considered a graduate.

As a result, the court declared his election null and void, ordered the Election Commission to remove him from office, hold a by-election, and file a criminal case against him. He was also directed to return salaries and benefits received during his time in office, and the university was told to cancel the fraudulent degree and take action against those involved.

This case matters because it shows courts can intervene under constitutional jurisdiction to ensure only genuinely qualified individuals hold public office, especially when fraud is clearly documented.

title: Balochistan Public Service Commission v. National Accountability Bureau (NAB),
explainer:
Balochistan Public Service Commission went to court after officials of the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) raided the Commission's office and seized examination records related to postings. The Commission argued that NAB had no authority to act this way because, under the Balochistan Public Service Commission Act, 1989, only the Governor can initiate an inquiry against the Commission's Chairman and members, following a specific procedure involving a High Court judge. It also claimed no proper inquiry had been sanctioned before the raid took place, making the raid illegal.

NAB argued that Commission officials, being permanent government employees, fall under the category of "persons holding public office" and are therefore subject to NAB's jurisdiction under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999, which covers corruption and misuse of authority.

The Balochistan High Court agreed that Commission employees do count as holders of public office, and that NAB generally has power to investigate such persons. However, the court found that no inquiry had actually been sanctioned by the competent authority before NAB conducted the raid. Since the law requires that such actions follow a proper authorized process, the court ruled the raid was illegal and without jurisdiction because it happened without the required sanction.

The case matters because it reinforces the principle that even bodies with wide investigative powers, like NAB, must strictly follow the legal procedure and obtain proper authorization before taking action against public officials, protecting institutions from unauthorized raids.

title: Abdul Haleem and others V. Mir Zahid and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between landlords and tenants over eviction proceedings in Loralai, in Balochistan's tribal areas. Eviction applications had been filed under an old colonial-era law called the British Balochistan Rent Control Regulation of 1945, and the trial court allowed the evictions, rejecting the tenants' objection that this old law no longer applied.

The tenants challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing the 1945 Regulation had been superseded by the West Pakistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959. The landlords and the government countered that since the 1959 Ordinance had never been formally extended to tribal areas, the old 1945 Regulation must still govern those areas.

The High Court traced the history of the law and found that the 1945 Regulation was tied to the office of the Chief Commissioner and to courts that existed under British Balochistan administration, both of which had ceased to exist after Pakistan's creation and the formation of Balochistan province. With no one left with authority to apply or administer it, the Regulation had effectively become defunct. The court also noted the courts currently handling such cases were not properly empowered to hear rent matters under this obsolete law, making the earlier proceedings legally void.

The court ruled that no court could proceed under the 1945 Regulation anymore, allowed the petitions, and directed the provincial government to extend the 1959 Ordinance to tribal areas within thirty days, so residents there would have a proper legal mechanism for rent disputes.

title: Muhammad Rabani and 5 others V. Agha Arshad through Imran Ali and another,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute where the plaintiff (Agha Arshad) sued for specific performance of a 2007 agreement and recovery of a large sum of money, also seeking an interim injunction to restrain the defendants from certain actions while the case was pending. The trial court granted this restraining order. The defendants, however, argued that since there was an arbitration clause in their agreement, the matter should be referred to an arbitrator, and filed an application under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act seeking to stay the court proceedings. They then appealed against the interim injunction, arguing the trial court should not have issued it while their request for arbitration was pending.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the appeal. It held that merely filing an application to stay proceedings and refer a dispute to arbitration does not stop a trial court from separately deciding an injunction application, since arbitrators have no power to grant such interim relief under the law. The court clarified that the legal phrase barring a party from taking "any other step in the proceedings" after invoking arbitration refers only to steps in the main case, not to actions taken regarding interim applications like injunctions.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that courts retain authority to protect the subject matter of a dispute through interim orders even when arbitration is sought, ensuring one party cannot cause irreversible harm to the other while arbitration proceedings are being arranged.

title: Moula Bakhsh and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Muhammad Ibrahim and Moula Bakhsh, who were caught driving a tanker truck that customs officials intercepted. Hidden compartments in the vehicle were found to contain hashish. Ibrahim was the driver, while Bakhsh was a passenger sitting beside him. Both were convicted by a trial court under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act and sentenced.

On appeal, a two-judge bench disagreed about Bakhsh's guilt, so the matter went to a third judge to break the tie. That judge examined whether the prosecution had proven that both men knowingly possessed the drugs, since narcotics law places a heavy burden on the accused to prove innocence, but does not eliminate the prosecution's basic duty to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt.

The judge reasoned that because Ibrahim was driving the truck, he necessarily had control over it and could not credibly claim ignorance of drugs hidden inside. However, there was no similar evidence linking Bakhsh to the truck, its ownership, or the hidden compartments. The prosecution failed to show he was involved in transporting the drugs or connected to the vehicle in any meaningful way.

As a result, the court upheld the driver's conviction and sentence but acquitted the passenger, Moula Bakhsh. This case highlights that mere presence near contraband is not enough for conviction; the prosecution must establish a genuine link between each accused person and the crime, especially given the severe punishments narcotics offenses car

title: Syed Taj-Ud-Din V. Akhtar Muhammad and another,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute between a landlord and his former tenant over commercial shops in Quetta. The landlord had earlier won an eviction case against the tenant, which was upheld all the way to the Supreme Court, and possession of the shops was handed back to him in 2004. More than a year later, the former tenant applied under section 13(4) of the Rent Restriction Ordinance, claiming the landlord had illegally re-let one of the shops to someone else instead of using it himself, and asked to be reinstated as tenant. The Rent Controller partly agreed and ordered the shop restored to the former tenant.

The landlord appealed to the Balochistan High Court. The Court found that the former tenant had not proven his case: he did not show when the alleged new tenant took possession, produced no rent agreement or reliable documentary proof, and his own witnesses did not support his claims. Instead, the landlord showed the shop occupant was actually his business partner, not a new tenant, through a partnership deed. The Court also noted the application was filed after a long, unexplained delay, which cast doubt on the claim.

The High Court set aside the Rent Controller's order and accepted the landlord's appeal, ruling that the ex-tenant had failed to meet the legal conditions required under section 13(4) to reclaim possession. The case clarifies that mere allegations of re-letting are not enough; concrete evidence of a new tenancy and timely action are required.

title: Mir Baz Muhammad Khan V. Naz Bibi and 9 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a long-running property dispute in Balochistan. The respondents' predecessor had won a civil suit for declaration, possession, and permanent injunction against the petitioner back in 1998, and since no appeal was filed, that decree became final. When the respondents later filed an execution application in 2003 to enforce the decree, the petitioner repeatedly filed objections trying to block execution—first in 2005 (rejected), again in 2006 (dismissed for non-prosecution), and a third time, which was also dismissed. The petitioner then appealed to the District Judge, who upheld the dismissal, leading to this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition, holding that once the first objection was rejected and not challenged, the matter attained finality, and there was no legal basis to keep filing fresh objections against the same decree. The court found the petitioner had fraudulently mutated the property in his own name and had deliberately dragged the respondents through prolonged litigation since 1991, causing them financial and emotional hardship.

Importantly, the court awarded actual litigation costs of Rs. 175,000 plus Rs. 25,000 as compensation for frivolous litigation, emphasizing that courts have discretion to make losing parties pay real costs incurred by those wrongfully forced into litigation. This case matters because it reinforces that decrees, once final, cannot be endlessly relitigated, and it signals that courts can penalize parties who abuse the legal process to delay justice.

title: Ashfaque Ahmed and 4 others V. National Accountability Bureau through Chairman and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved civil servants who had been penalized departmentally for embezzlement. They appealed to the Balochistan Service Tribunal, which upheld findings against them and directed that the matter be referred to the National Accountability Bureau for action. Based on this direction, NAB investigated and filed a corruption reference against them before the Accountability Court. The petitioners later challenged the Tribunal's order before the Supreme Court, which sent the matter back for fresh departmental inquiry. Separately, they asked the Accountability Court to drop the NAB case, arguing that under the National Accountability Bureau Ordinance, only the NAB Chairman could initiate proceedings, and that acting merely on a Tribunal's direction made the reference invalid. When the trial court rejected this argument, they approached the High Court.

The High Court dismissed their petition. It held that NAB can lawfully start proceedings whenever it learns of an offence from any source, including a court or tribunal judgment, a government reference, or a complaint. Such information from a Tribunal's order can be treated as a complaint, and the NAB Chairman still exercises independent judgment before sanctioning investigation and filing the reference. Since the Chairman did examine the material and found sufficient evidence before filing the reference, the proceedings were valid and not "coram non judice." This matters because it clarifies that NAB's power to act is not limited to formal government references or complaints but extends to any credible source of information, including judicial findings.

title: The Bank of Punjab through Regional Chief, General Manager, Quetta V. Khan Muhammad and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between the Bank of Punjab, which rented commercial premises in Quetta, and the property owners, over whether increased rent applied after the original lease expired.

The bank had leased the premises for nine years starting in 2000, with rent set to increase by 15% every three years under the rental agreement. When the nine-year term ended in July 2009, the bank did not vacate the property. Legal proceedings followed, and the parties eventually reached a court-approved consent arrangement extending the bank's occupation until September 2010, on condition it kept paying rent regularly.

The owners argued that since the lease was extended by mutual consent, the original agreement's terms, including the 15% rent increase, still applied to the extended period. The bank argued the original lease had expired and the extension was essentially a new arrangement without any agreed rent increase.

Lower courts (the trial court and the appellate court) both ruled in favor of the property owners, ordering the bank to pay the increased rent. The Balochistan High Court upheld these decisions, reasoning that the original agreement itself allowed for extension of the lease term, and since the extension was granted by mutual consent, the original terms - including the rent escalation clause - continued to govern the tenancy.

This case matters because it clarifies that when a lease is extended with mutual agreement rather than simply overstayed unilaterally, the original contractual terms, including rent increases, remain binding unless the parties agree otherwise.

title: Shaan Sher Tareen V. Registrar, Allama Iqbal Open University, Islamabad and 2 others,
explainer:
The petitioner, a Regional Director at Allama Iqbal Open University's Quetta campus, was accused of corruption after forwarding travel expense vouchers worth Rs.38,380 submitted by a part-time tutor. Following inquiries, the University's competent authority imposed the major penalty of compulsory retirement on him in 2007. He appealed to the University's Executive Council, but the appeal was delayed and eventually decided against him by a three-member committee rather than the full Council. He then challenged this in the Balochistan High Court.

The University argued the petition was not maintainable, claiming the dispute was a service matter barred from High Court review under Article 212 of the Constitution, and that only the Service Tribunal had jurisdiction. The Court rejected this, holding that Article 212's bar does not apply to University service matters, and since the University's own law provided no further remedy against the appellate authority's order, the High Court could step in under Article 199.

On the merits, the Court found no evidence that any money was actually drawn using the vouchers, meaning the University suffered no loss, and no proof existed that the petitioner failed to verify the vouchers or attempted embezzlement. Since the inquiry committees never established wrongdoing, the compulsory retirement was ruled unjustified and set aside. The Court ordered the petitioner's reinstatement with full back benefits from the date his service was ended, recognizing the years of hardship he faced during the prolonged proceedings.

title: Mcb Bank Ltd. through Attorney V. Muhammad Imran Bhatti and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a bank employee, Muhammad Imran Bhatti, who worked at MCB Bank and was dismissed for alleged embezzlement after departmental proceedings found him guilty. Instead of filing a grievance notice with the bank, he filed a departmental appeal, and later took his case to the Labour Court through a grievance petition. The Labour Court ruled in his favor and ordered his reinstatement with back benefits, and the Labour Appellate Tribunal upheld this decision. The bank then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The bank argued that since the employee had been promoted to Officer Grade-III, he was performing managerial duties and no longer qualified as a "worker" under labour law, meaning the Labour Court had no jurisdiction over his case. The bank also argued he should have issued a formal grievance notice before going to court.

The High Court disagreed. It held that a person's status as a "worker" depends on the actual nature of duties performed, not job title or grade. Since the employee was still doing routine clerical work rather than genuine managerial work, he remained a "workman" entitled to use the Labour Court. The Court also clarified that issuing a grievance notice before filing a petition is optional, not mandatory, under the law. Since two lower forums had already agreed on the facts, the High Court said it could not interfere with these findings in its constitutional jurisdiction. The petition was dismissed, meaning the employee's reinstatement stood.

title: Abdul Rasheed V. The State through Deputy Prosecutor-General NAB, Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Rasheed, a government officer (Assistant Director, Food Department) in Kalat, who was accused of corruption under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999. When the trial court's warrants of arrest could not be served on him at his office or residential addresses, the court declared him an absconder after publishing notices in newspapers. It then proceeded under section 88 of the Criminal Procedure Code and, on the very next hearing, convicted him in his absence under section 31-A of the NAB Ordinance, sentencing him to three years' rigorous imprisonment.

The Balochistan High Court found this conviction illegal. It held that only one failed attempt to serve the warrant was not enough - the prosecution should have repeated the attempt or checked with his department whether he was actually on duty or absent. The accused's claim that he was never absent from work was never disputed by any evidence. The court also found that the mandatory legal steps for declaring someone an absconder - publicly reading and affixing the proclamation at his residence, town, and the courthouse - were never properly completed.

Because these procedural safeguards were ignored, the court ruled the trial court's orders declaring him an absconder and convicting him were invalid. The appeal was allowed, the orders were set aside, and the accused was directed to appear regularly before the trial court to continue facing his case. This case highlights the importance of following proper legal procedure before convicting someone in absentia.

title: Mrs. Elsa Marri and 7 others V. Phillips M. Irani,
explainer:
This is a property dispute decided by the Balochistan High Court on appeal. The original plaintiff claimed his father had set up a charitable trust over a property in Quetta, appointing the plaintiff's brother as trustee. The brother in turn appointed a man named Mir Khuda Bakhsh Marri as his attorney to look after the trust property. Marri later tried to claim ownership of the property himself through two separate lawsuits based on "adverse possession" (a legal claim that long-term occupation can create ownership rights), but both of those earlier cases were dismissed or withdrawn. When Marri still refused to vacate the property, the trust's beneficiary (the plaintiff, son of the original owner) sued for possession, declaration of ownership, and related relief. The trial court ruled in the plaintiff's favor, finding that Marri's occupation was unlawful since he had only been holding the property as an attorney/agent on behalf of the trustee, not as an owner, and ordered him to vacate and pay rent for the period of occupation. Marri's heirs appealed.

The High Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the trial court's decision. It held that possession by an agent or appointee legally belongs to the person who appointed him, so Marri could not claim ownership just because he physically occupied the property. The court found the plaintiff's evidence stronger and saw no legal errors in the original judgment. The case reinforces the principle that agents holding property on someone else's behalf cannot convert that possession into ownership claims against the true owner or trust.

title: Rukhsana Hidayatullah and 9 others V. Syed Bahauddin and another,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Balochistan over who was responsible for repaying a large sum of "pagri" (premium money) paid by a tenant.

The original owners of a building called Asmat Plaza received Rs. 5,50,000 from a tenant as pagri for a shop, then rented it to him at a nominal Rs. 500 per month. The owners later sold the entire building, including this shop, to a new buyer. The new owner then sought to evict the tenant. Eviction proceedings went all the way to the Supreme Court, which upheld the eviction and confirmed that the tenant had indeed paid the pagri, but left it to the tenant to separately sue for recovery of that money. The tenant then filed a recovery suit against both the original sellers and the new owner. The trial court ordered the original sellers to repay the amount, prompting this appeal.

The Balochistan High Court held that when the new owner bought the property, he took it with full knowledge of the pagri liability, which is why he paid a reduced price. Under the law governing sale of property, a buyer who purchases with knowledge of encumbrances becomes responsible for them once ownership transfers, and the sellers cease to have any further liability. Since the new owner also benefited from evicting the tenant, he alone was liable to repay the pagri, not the original sellers.

The court partly accepted the appeal, ruling that the new owner must pay the tenant, not the original sellers. This case clarifies how liabilities attached to a property pass to a buyer who knowingly purchases with encumbrances.

title: Mir Shah Nawaz Marri V. Sub-Registrar, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a power of attorney allegedly signed by a woman authorizing someone else to act on her behalf regarding property. She later sued to have the document cancelled, claiming it was based on fraud and misrepresentation and that she never actually signed it or appeared before the Sub-Registrar to have it registered. The trial court and the first appellate court both ruled in her favor, cancelling the power of attorney. The person who relied on the document then challenged these decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' rulings. It explained that while registered documents normally carry a presumption of correctness, this presumption weakens once the person disputes having signed it. In such cases, the party relying on the document must properly prove its execution, including producing the attesting witnesses who saw the signing happen, not just witnesses who can identify a signature. Here, the side defending the power of attorney failed to produce the Sub-Registrar as a witness, failed to bring both marginal witnesses, and could not prove the woman actually appeared before the Sub-Registrar or signed the document herself. Because of these gaps, the court found the document unproven and upheld its cancellation.

This case highlights how important proper proof and witness testimony are for validating legal documents like powers of attorney, and it reinforces protections against fraudulent use of such documents, especially in family property disputes.

title: Rossmere International Ltd. through Authorized Representative V. Sea Lion International Shipping Inc and 6 others,
explainer:
This case involved a company, Rossmere International, which had won a money award from a London arbitration tribunal against a shipping company (defendant No.1) and related "Fal Group" entities, after a failed vessel sale deal. Rossmere had already gotten this award recognized and turned into a decree by an English court. It then filed a fresh suit in the Balochistan High Court, seeking to enforce the same award in Pakistan, and additionally asked the court to attach and eventually sell another vessel, m.t. "ZETA" (renamed "MALIN"), which had since been sold to a different company, defendant No.7, and was reportedly beached in Balochistan.

The court rejected the plaint. It held that arbitration awards are enforceable only against parties who agreed to arbitrate, and defendant No.7 was never part of that arbitration or agreement. The vessel itself was never the subject matter of the original award, which was purely a money award. For enforcing a money award, the case should be filed where the defaulting party's bank account or assets are located, and none were found within the Balochistan High Court's jurisdiction. Since the vessel had already been sold before enforcement was attempted, it no longer belonged to the award debtor. The court also noted that since an English court had already recognized and decreed the award, it was for that court to enforce its own order, and a second enforcement suit elsewhere was not proper unless the first was shown unenforceable.

This ruling clarifies limits on cross-border enforcement of arbitral awards and protects third parties who were not part of the arbitration agreement.

title: Messrs Khan Gul Government Contractor V. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary/Chairman, Federal Board of Revenue, Islamabad and another,
explainer:
This case is about six vehicles imported by a government contractor that were held back by Customs authorities, who claimed the vehicles were older than five years, exceeding the age limit allowed under Pakistan's Import Policy Order, 2016 for specialized vehicles used in construction, mining, oil, gas and petroleum sectors. The importer had submitted an inspection certificate from an approved company confirming the vehicles met the age requirement, paid all duties and taxes, but Customs still refused to release the vehicles, relying instead on a certificate from a different source and a notice issued under Section 171 of the Customs Act.

The Balochistan High Court found that under Section 168 of the Customs Act, once goods are seized, authorities must prepare a seizure memo and issue a formal show-cause notice within two months, unless the Collector of Customs formally extends that deadline in writing with reasons. In this case, Customs did neither. The court ruled that a notice under Section 171 is not a legal substitute for the mandatory show-cause notice required under Section 168, and that failing to follow this procedure meant Customs no longer had the authority to keep holding the vehicles.

The court ordered the vehicles released. The case matters because it reinforces the principle that government agencies must strictly follow procedures set out by law, and citizens benefit when authorities fail to meet legally mandated deadlines and requirements.

title: Collector of Customs through Additional Collector Custom, MCC Gwadar, Gaddani V. Messrs BYCO Petroleum Pakistan Ltd. and others,
explainer:
This case is about whether import duties and taxes could be demanded on tug boats that a company had brought into Pakistan only temporarily, to help offload oil tankers, with a promise to re-export them later.

The company had imported three tug boats and given bank guarantees, declaring clearly that these were temporary imports meant for re-export, as allowed under the Import Policy Order, 2013. Customs authorities later issued show-cause notices accusing the company of violating provisions of the Customs Act by allegedly making false statements and evading duties, treating the import as a permanent, taxable one.

The Collector of Customs (Adjudication) withdrew the show-cause notice, finding it lacked jurisdiction, and the Customs Appellate Tribunal upheld that decision. Customs then approached the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the customs department's reference. It held that the show-cause notices were defective because they did not contain specific allegations of false statements, which is required under Section 32(3) of the Customs Act. It also found that since the goods declarations clearly showed the tugs were imported temporarily for re-export, and proper bank guarantees were furnished, this was not an ordinary import attracting full duties. If customs disputed the exemption, it should have used the specific remedy under the relevant SRO rather than issuing show-cause notices.

The ruling matters because it reinforces that legal procedures must be followed exactly as prescribed, and that goods imported temporarily for re-export, with proper guarantees, cannot be taxed as permanent imports.

title: Rahim Khan and 8 others V. Station Commander, Station Headquarter, Zhob Cantt. and another,
explainer:
This case is about a land dispute between local residents (the appellants) in Zhob and the Pakistan Army over land used for military exercises like field firing and artillery practice. The appellants claimed they owned the land, inherited from their forefathers, and said the Army was wrongfully interfering with their possession and stopping them from using it. The Army relied on government notifications issued under a 1938 law that allowed the land to be used for military maneuvers and firing practice, and argued the appellants had no right to be there.

The trial court had dismissed the appellants' suit, but the Balochistan High Court overturned that decision. The court held that lack of formal government land-settlement records does not mean the land has no owner; ownership can be proven through other evidence, including prior court rulings and long possession. Importantly, the court clarified that the government notification only allowed temporary, limited use of the land for military exercises - it did not transfer ownership or create permanent rights for the Army. Once the exercises were over, residents were entitled to resume normal use of their land, and any continued interference by authorities after that would be illegal.

This ruling matters because it protects the property rights of local landowners against overreach by military or government authorities, clarifying that special-purpose land-use notifications cannot be used to permanently dispossess people of their land.

title: Tufail Ahmed v. Joint Estate Officer,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a government flat in Quetta's Customs Colony. Tufail Muhammad claimed he was a lawful allottee of the flat, that rent was regularly deducted from his salary, and that the Joint Estate Officer (representing the Federal Government) had no authority over the property since it was never formally handed over to the government's housing pool. When he received a notice in 2003 ordering him to vacate within 24 hours, he filed a civil suit seeking to have the notice declared illegal and to stop his eviction.

Both the trial court and the appellate court ruled against him, finding that he could not produce any actual allotment order proving he was the lawful occupant, while records showed the flat had indeed been placed under the Federal Government's control. The Balochistan High Court, hearing his revision petition, upheld these decisions. It noted that Tufail Muhammad's claim to the flat had already been rejected in earlier litigation up to the Supreme Court, and that he had concealed this fact from the courts. The judge found this showed bad faith, and criticized him for misusing court proceedings to prolong his unauthorized occupation for over ten years.

The court dismissed the petition, finding no legal error in the lower courts' decisions, and directed authorities to recover possession using the proper legal procedure under the 1965 Ordinance. The case illustrates how courts scrutinize claims of government property occupation and penalize litigants who misuse judicial processes to delay lawful eviction.

title: Jaffar Khan v. the State,
explainer:
This case involved Jaffar Khan, who was convicted in two separate criminal cases arising from incidents of house-trespass and theft reported on the same day in 2008. In one case, he was sentenced to two years for lurking house-trespass and three years for theft, with fines, and the trial court ordered these two sentences to run concurrently. In the second case, he received similar sentences, which were also ordered to run concurrently within that case. However, no court had specified whether the sentences from the two separate cases should run concurrently with each other or one after the other (consecutively). Since the law defaults to consecutive sentencing unless a court specifically orders otherwise, this meant Khan faced a combined total of six years in prison.

Khan filed an application asking the Balochistan High Court to direct that the sentences from both cases run concurrently, arguing he was innocent and had already been denied this benefit by lower courts.

The High Court examined the relevant legal provisions and noted that no explicit concurrency order existed between the two cases. However, considering Khan's youth, poor financial background, and lack of any prior criminal record, the judge decided a lenient approach was warranted. The court allowed the application, directing that the sentences from both cases run concurrently. It clarified, though, that additional jail time imposed for failure to pay fines could not be included in this concurrent arrangement, since such default sentences aren't treated as ordinary imprisonment under the law. This case matters because it shows courts can exercise discretion to reduce effective prison time based on an offender's circumstances, even after conviction.

title: Lal Muhammad v. the State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Lal Muhammad who was convicted for possessing an unlicensed rifle, a crime weapon linked to a separate murder case, under Pakistan's Arms Ordinance of 1965. He was sentenced by a trial court to three years imprisonment, a fine, and confiscation of the rifle. He appealed, arguing the rifle was licensed, that the trial court lacked jurisdiction (claiming only a Magistrate could hear such cases), and that the judgment was not properly reasoned.

The Balochistan High Court rejected all these arguments. It found that the rifle's license had expired back in 1999, meaning he had been possessing it illegally for years, so it was correctly treated as unlicensed. The court also ruled that since the same weapon was tied to a murder case being tried by the Sessions Court, it made sense for that same court to handle the arms charge too, to avoid conflicting rulings.

Importantly, the court discovered that the appellant had concealed from his appeal that he had also been convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. Because of this, the court found he was not eligible for leniency under the Probation of Offenders Ordinance, which might otherwise have allowed a lighter, rehabilitative approach given the relatively short sentence.

The appeal was dismissed, and the original conviction and sentence were upheld. The case illustrates how courts scrutinize honesty in appeals and link related criminal proceedings for consistency.
