title: Government of Balochistan through Secretary Board of Revenue v. Raheem Badshah,
explainer:
This case was about a land dispute in Balochistan over property in Mouza Balan Northern, also known as Choot Dasht. The respondents claimed their mother, Mst. Mah Ganj, had owned the land since their forefathers' time, and that the government wrongly recorded the property in its own name while the family was away abroad. The trial court dismissed their suit, finding they had failed to prove ownership and that the case was filed too late, beyond the legal time limit. On appeal, the appellate court reversed this and ruled in favor of the family, declaring them owners and finding the suit was filed on time. The government then challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court sided with the government. It found that the respondents had produced only two oral witnesses and gave evidence through an attorney, but no title deed or documentary proof of ownership was ever presented. No one explained how the land had passed down to Mst. Mah Ganj, nor was there any account of when the disputed revenue entries were made. The appellate court, the High Court said, had simply accepted oral testimony without properly examining the record, and wrongly concluded the suit was filed on time despite a long, unexplained delay.

The High Court set aside the appellate court's decision and restored the trial court's ruling, dismissing the family's claim. The case underscores that in property disputes, mere oral claims of ancestral ownership are insufficient without documentary evidence and a clear explanation of how title was transferred, and that courts must properly justify findings on limitation periods.

title: Abdul Karim Mengal v. Sultan Badshah,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over Rs.80,00,000 that Sultan Badshah claimed was owed to him by Abdul Karim Mengal following the settlement of accounts from a partnership business. Badshah filed a recovery suit based on a dishonoured cheque, using a special fast-track procedure under Order XXXVII of the Civil Procedure Code, meant for cases involving negotiable instruments like cheques.

Mengal sought permission to defend the suit and also challenged whether the Quetta court had jurisdiction, arguing the cheque was issued and delivered in Kalat. The trial court rejected his jurisdiction objection, granted him permission to defend the case, but only on condition that he furnish security equal to the suit amount. When Mengal asked the court to reduce this security requirement, that request was also denied. He then challenged all three trial court orders before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court first decided it did have authority to review this type of order, since such interim orders are not listed among those subject to regular appeal, meaning revision was the correct legal route. On the substance, the Court found that trial courts have discretion under the law to grant permission to defend a suit either freely or with conditions, including requiring security. Since Mengal failed to show any specific error or misuse of this discretion by the trial court, the High Court dismissed his revision petition, upholding the security requirement.

A complaint was filed under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, alleging that Ahsan Raza and others had forcibly occupied the school building and flat, taking the resident family hostage. The trial court took up the case, found the occupier unable to justify his possession beyond a suspicious document, and ordered the property attached with a court official appointed to manage its accounts while the case proceeded.

Later, the original complainant tried to withdraw the complaint, and the trial court allowed this withdrawal, reasoning that ordinary criminal procedure permitted such withdrawal. This decision was challenged before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled that the Illegal Dispossession Act is a special law with its own procedure, and it contains no provision allowing withdrawal of a complaint once filed. Since the trial court had already taken up the case under this special law, it was obligated to decide it according to that law's specific procedure, not general withdrawal rules. The High Court therefore set aside the withdrawal order, ruling the complaint would be treated as still pending.

On the separate question of attaching the property, the court upheld the attachment, noting both sides claimed ownership and the school was generating significant income, so preserving the property under court supervision protected everyone's interests. The case was sent back to the trial court to continue proceedings properly under the Act.

title: Hazoor Bakhsh v. the State,
explainer:
This case involved an application for pre-arrest bail by Hazoor Bakhsh, who was named as an accused in a criminal case involving an armed ambush and firing that injured several people. He was booked along with several others under charges including attempt to commit murder and rioting with deadly weapons.

Bakhsh remained a fugitive from justice for months after the FIR was filed, only surfacing after four of his co-accused were acquitted by the trial court. He claimed he had been unaware of the case against him and came forward voluntarily once he learned of it, and argued he should get the same benefit of acquittal as his co-accused.

The Balochistan High Court rejected his explanation as implausible, noting he lived in the same area as the other accused who had participated in the trial, making it unlikely he genuinely didn't know about the proceedings. The court also found his conduct improper because he tried to secure bail from the High Court without first surrendering to the trial court unconditionally, and he could not simply piggyback on his co-accused's acquittal.

The court withdrew the earlier ad-interim bail it had granted him and ordered his arrest. This case illustrates that courts are reluctant to grant pre-arrest bail to persons who deliberately evade the judicial process for extended periods, and that absconding from trial, followed by attempts to secure bail only after favorable developments for co-accused, will generally be viewed unfavorably by courts.

title: Samiullah v. the State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Samiullah who was convicted by a Sessions Court in Quetta for illegal possession of a pistol under the West Pakistan Arms Ordinance, and sentenced to two years of rigorous imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the evidence against him was weak, that police procedures were not properly followed, and that contradictions in witness statements were ignored.

During the appeal, his lawyer shifted strategy, asking the court not to decide the case on its merits but instead to simply reduce his sentence to the time already served, since he had completed about a third of his punishment.

The High Court refused to take this lenient approach. It pointed out that this was not simply a case of illegal weapon possession, the accused had actually been caught in the act of snatching a motorcycle along with an accomplice who escaped, meaning the more serious crime of Haraabah (robbery) under the Hudood laws was also involved. The recovered pistol was loaded and in working condition. Because of this larger criminal context, the court held that leniency was not appropriate.

The court also found that the appellant failed to point out any actual contradictions in the evidence or any legal errors in the original judgment. As a result, the appeal was dismissed and the conviction and sentence were upheld. The case shows that courts are reluctant to reduce sentences merely on grounds of partial completion when the underlying crime is serious.

title: Miss Asma Gulistan v. Taraqee Foundation through Chief Executive,
explainer:
This case involved a woman who worked for Taraqee Foundation as a Credit Officer. The organization sued her for recovery of about Rs. 11,96,207, alleging she had misappropriated funds and abused her position. After earlier proceedings and an appeal that sent the case back to the trial court for a decision on the merits, the woman failed to appear despite being served through newspaper publication. As a result, the trial court proceeded against her ex parte (without her participation) and ultimately decreed the suit against her.

Ten months later, she applied to have the ex parte decree set aside, claiming she never knew about the case because she believed her lawyer was handling it and was busy working in another district. She also asked the court to excuse the long delay in filing her application. The trial court rejected this request, finding no merit in her explanation, and she appealed to the High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It held that negligence by one's own lawyer is not a valid excuse for such a long delay, and that a person who neglects their own legal rights must bear the consequences. Since she failed to prove a genuine reason for both her absence and the delay, the appeal was dismissed.

This case reinforces an important principle: courts expect litigants to stay informed about their own cases and to act promptly, and blaming one's lawyer alone will not justify years-long delays in seeking relief.

title: Eid Muhammad v. Abdul Wahab,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court in Quetta, concerned a dispute over possession of a government quarter (house) in Khuzdar's Civil Colony.

The plaintiff, Abdul Wahab, claimed he was the lawful allottee of the quarter based on an official allotment order issued by the D.C.O. Khuzdar in July 2008. When he tried to take possession, the occupants (Eid Muhammad and another) refused to vacate. They argued that the quarter had originally been allotted to one of them, and later reallotted to their brother, Taj Muhammad, who they claimed was in possession and should have been made a party to the case.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, ordering possession to be handed over to him. The occupants then filed this revision petition before the High Court, arguing procedural defects and misreading of evidence.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the allotment order in favor of the defendants' brother had actually been officially cancelled, and neither the brother nor the defendants had ever challenged that cancellation. The defendants failed to produce any valid title document proving their right to possession, and could not show that the lower courts had ignored or misread any evidence.

The court held that merely occupying a property, without lawful allotment, does not create a right to retain possession. This case reinforces that formal, uncancelled government allotment orders determine lawful possession, and unchallenged cancellations remain valid and binding.

title: Manzoor Ahmed v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Manzoor Ahmed and Taj Muhammad, who were convicted by a Sessions Judge in Lasbela for robbery under sections 392/34 of the Pakistan Penal Code. They were each sentenced to three years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 10,000. The complainant, Gul Hassan, alleged that three men had forcibly entered his home during Friday prayers and stolen gold ornaments, cash, and a mobile phone.

On appeal, the appellants' lawyer did not argue the case on its merits but simply asked for a reduced sentence. However, the Balochistan High Court chose to examine the evidence itself. It found serious problems: the complainant's statements about the incident and recovery of stolen items were contradictory and had changed over time. Key eyewitnesses, including the complainant's wife and family members, were never questioned by police or listed in the charges. Most strikingly, the accused were identified only through a vague process involving tracker dogs, without clear evidence linking the dogs' search to the appellants' homes.

The High Court ruled that these contradictions created reasonable doubt, and under law, that doubt must benefit the accused. Rather than merely reducing the sentence as requested, the court set aside the conviction entirely and acquitted both men. This case highlights how courts can overturn convictions when police investigations are sloppy and evidence is unreliable, even when the defense doesn't strongly contest the facts.

title: Muhammad Rasool v. Abdul Ghafoor,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute in Quetta over a small plot of land. Abdul Ghafoor (the plaintiff) claimed he was the rightful owner of the land but was forcibly deprived of possession by Muhammad Rasool and other defendants in 1998. He sued for a declaration of ownership, recovery of possession, and an injunction stopping the defendants from transferring or altering the property. The defendants argued that the plaintiff had actually sold the property to one of them, with part payment made and possession handed over, and they also raised technical objections about the suit's valuation, lack of a valid legal cause of action, and improper joinder of parties.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, rejecting the defendants' claims and technical objections. The defendants then filed a revision petition before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that evidence had been ignored and that the judgments were flawed.

The High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the lower courts' decisions. It found that the defendants failed to identify any specific evidence that had been overlooked, could not prove the alleged sale, and had no real basis for challenging the valuation of the suit. The court reaffirmed that a plaintiff's stated valuation is presumed correct unless disproved.

This case illustrates how courts handle disputes over property ownership and possession, and reinforces that vague, unsubstantiated objections cannot overturn concurrent findings of lower courts.

title: Jalil Khan Dotani v. Dawood Ahmed,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a property dispute in Quetta over a house and shops. Jalil Khan Dotani had filed a lawsuit for specific performance of a sale agreement, claiming Tahir Ahmed Dar had agreed to sell him the property. Dar denied ever signing such an agreement, calling it forged, and separately sued Dotani for declaration, possession, and injunction. The two cases were being heard together.

The key dispute here was about evidence. Dotani claimed the original sale agreement had been in his possession but got lost when he brought it to court, so he asked permission to prove the agreement using secondary evidence, like the photocopy already attached to his case. The trial court rejected this request, finding no sufficient proof that the document was actually lost. Dotani challenged that rejection in this revision petition.

The High Court explained that under Pakistan's evidence law (the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order), documents must normally be proved through the original itself, with secondary evidence like copies allowed only in specific situations, such as when the original is genuinely lost through no fault of the party. However, the court noted that Dotani only reported the document as lost more than two years after the fact, and had not first established that the agreement was validly executed before claiming it was lost.

The court upheld the trial court's decision, ruling that Dotani had failed to justify why secondary evidence should be allowed, and dismissed his petition. The case illustrates the strict evidentiary standards required before courts will accept copies instead of original documents.

title: Noor Muhammad v. Noor-ud-Din,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Balochistan over water and pathway rights. The plaintiffs claimed that for over 100 years they had used a watercourse and a passage running through land now owned by the defendants, to irrigate their fields and reach their property. When the defendants allegedly began blocking this watercourse and path, the plaintiffs sued for a declaration of their rights and a permanent injunction preventing interference. The trial court ruled in the plaintiffs' favor, and the first appellate court upheld that decision. The defendants then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious flaws in how the lower courts handled the case. The plaintiffs had not proven that the watercourse and passage actually existed as they claimed, especially since these were not recorded in the official land settlement records from 1958. The plaintiffs' own pleadings were also defective, since despite titling the suit for declaration, they never actually asked the court for a formal declaration of their rights. Additionally, the trial court had ignored important legal objections raised by the defendants, such as improper court fees and failure to include necessary parties. The appellate court, despite noticing these problems, still upheld the flawed decision without proper reasoning.

Because both lower courts failed to properly evaluate the evidence and legal issues, the High Court set aside their judgments and dismissed the plaintiffs' suit entirely. The case underscores that claims of long-standing property rights must be backed by solid evidence and proper legal procedure, not just assertions of tradition.

title: Abdul Ghaffar v. the State,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Ghaffar, who was convicted by an Additional Sessions Judge in Quetta for possessing an unlicensed TT pistol and three live cartridges, an offence under the West Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965. He was sentenced to three years imprisonment plus a fine, with additional imprisonment if the fine went unpaid.

Ghaffar appealed to the Balochistan High Court, but his lawyer did not contest the conviction itself. Instead, he asked the court to reduce the sentence, arguing that the trial court had been one-sided in weighing the evidence and ignored contradictions favorable to the accused.

The High Court noted that although this argument was raised, no specific contradictions were actually pointed out to support it. More importantly, the court observed that the weapon recovered from Ghaffar appeared to be linked to two other serious pending cases against him, one for robbery (Haraabah) and another for attempted murder and using criminal force against police officers. Since there was no evidence that he had been acquitted in those cases, the court found no justification for leniency.

Relying on Section 423(1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows an appellate court to reduce a sentence without disturbing the trial court's findings, the judge decided there was no valid basis to do so here. The appeal was dismissed, and the original conviction and sentence were upheld.

title: Nasir Hayat v. Qamar Raza Rizvi,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta. Nasir Hayat had won a court decree in October 2002 ordering the other party, Qamar Raza Rizvi, either to pay him a large sum of money under three agreements, or, failing that, to transfer a house to him along with possession. When Hayat later tried to have this decree enforced through an execution application, the trial court dismissed his application in August 2007, ruling that it was filed too late, beyond the legal time limit.

Hayat appealed, arguing that he had actually filed an earlier execution application within the proper time limit back in 2004, which was dismissed only because no one appeared to pursue it, and that his 2006 application should be treated as a continuation, not a fresh late filing. He also argued that since the decree was based on the other side's admission of his claims, he shouldn't be denied justice on a technical point about deadlines.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the appeal. Despite being given multiple opportunities, Hayat could not produce reliable proof of the earlier 2004 application, and the document he provided contradicted the court's own record of proceedings. He also failed to show any fraud, misrepresentation, or valid reason justifying the delay. The court held that without such proof, the six-year limitation period for executing a decree could not be extended, and upheld the dismissal.

The case highlights how strictly courts enforce time limits for executing decrees, even when the underlying claim was never disputed.

title: Faiz Muhammad v. the State,
explainer:
Faiz Muhammad was convicted under the West Pakistan Arms Ordinance for allegedly possessing an unlicensed Kalashnikov, two magazines and 39 live cartridges, and was sentenced to three years' imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed, arguing he was falsely implicated, that no independent witnesses were involved, and that the recovered weapon was never sent for forensic analysis.

The Balochistan High Court found serious problems with the case. The trial court's version of events, that police recovered the weapon while raiding the accused's house after learning of a murder, did not match the FIR at all. The FIR instead said police found the accused standing armed in an open plot near someone else's house late at night. There was no explanation for why he was there at that hour, nor any clear account of where the weapon and magazines were at the time of recovery. Crucially, while the Kalashnikov was produced in court, the alleged magazines and cartridges never were. Witness statements also contained contradictions that the trial court failed to notice.

Because the prosecution could not prove the recovery beyond reasonable doubt, and the accused was entitled to benefit of that doubt, the High Court set aside the conviction and acquitted Faiz Muhammad, ordering his release. The case highlights how inconsistencies between an FIR and trial testimony, plus missing evidence, can undermine a criminal conviction.

title: Kala Khan Tareen Coal Company Duki v. Mehrab Khan,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a coal mining lease in Loralai, Balochistan. The petitioner, Kala Khan Tareen Coal Company, claimed it held a mining lease and had been illegally dispossessed by the respondents, who allegedly moved onto the leased area and began extracting coal without authorization. The company filed a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, a special law designed to provide quick relief to people forcibly and unlawfully removed from property they possess. The trial court dismissed the complaint after investigation, and the company challenged that dismissal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It explained that under this Act, the only real question is whether someone in possession was wrongfully deprived of that possession without lawful excuse; disputes about ownership or title are not meant to be resolved through this fast-track process. Here, the complainant failed to specify exactly when the dispossession occurred, the precise boundaries or area involved, or whether the entire leased area was affected. It also waited more than a year to file the complaint without explanation, undermining its claim of urgent, wrongful dispossession. Since a civil suit and constitutional petition over the same property were already pending, the court held those proceedings were the proper venue to determine rights and ownership.

The case illustrates that the Illegal Dispossession Act is meant only for clear-cut, prompt dispossession claims, not for resolving long-running property or title disputes better suited to civil courts.

title: Secretary Government of Balochistan, irrigation Department v. Chandiazai Mengal Tribe through Malik Ghulam Qadir,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over water rights on a Bore Nala (water channel) in Balochistan. The Chandiazai Mengal Tribe sued the Irrigation Department and other government officials after they demolished a bund (embankment) that the tribe had built on the Nala in 1999, allegedly without notice or legal authority. The tribe based their claim on a 1921 arbitration award, upheld by the Political Agent in 1922, which had settled an earlier water-sharing dispute among four tribes using the Nala. Both the trial court and the appellate court had ruled in favor of the tribe, ordering the government to restore the bund at its own expense.

The Balochistan High Court overturned these rulings. It found that both lower courts had relied too heavily on the old 1921-22 award without properly examining more recent facts, particularly that a formal government irrigation scheme had been constructed in 1962. The plaintiff tribe failed to prove it still had a legal right, after 1962, to build a private dam on the Nala. The court held that the authorities were within their rights to remove unauthorized construction that affected water flow to thousands of other landholders in the area. Since the lower courts misread the evidence and ignored these key facts, the High Court set aside the decree and dismissed the tribe's suit.

This case matters because it clarifies that old customary or arbitration-based water rights do not automatically override government irrigation schemes and regulatory authority established later, especially when public interest and shared water resources are involved.

title: Abdul Ghafoor v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved four men, Abdul Ghafoor and three others, who were convicted of house-trespass under the Pakistan Penal Code for allegedly breaking into the house of a man named Lal Bakhsh, beating him, and humiliating him in front of his sons. A magistrate convicted them, sentencing each to 15 days imprisonment and a fine, and a Sessions Judge upheld this on appeal. The men then challenged both decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found serious problems with the case. There was an unexplained delay of nearly eleven hours between the alleged incident and the filing of the police report, with no reason given by the complainant. The court also found significant contradictions between the complainant's written report and the testimony given in court, including disputes over whether the accused carried sticks, how the complainant was beaten, and what his rescuing sons actually did or said. Despite claims of being beaten, the complainant and his witness admitted he suffered no injuries. The lower courts had failed to properly examine these inconsistencies, and the appellate court had simply rubber-stamped the trial court's findings without independently assessing the evidence. The High Court also noted evidence of a pre-existing enmity between the parties, including a separate counter-case.

Given these unresolved doubts and the courts' failure to apply the principle that such doubt should benefit the accused, the High Court set aside both judgments and acquitted all four petitioners.

title: Amanullah v. Rohi Muhammad,
explainer:
Amanullah v. Rohi Muhammad is a decision of the Balochistan High Court dealing with a landlord's request to evict tenants from a shop for non-payment of rent and because he genuinely needed the property for his own use.

The landlord said he bought the shop through a registered sale deed in 2004 from its previous owners, and that the existing tenant was informed of this change. When the landlord asked for the shop back, the tenant requested and got six months, on condition of paying rent, but then stopped paying. The tenants disputed this: they claimed to have earlier purchased the shop themselves from a prior owner in 1996 through an unregistered agreement, with part of the price still unpaid, and denied being tenants of the current landlord at all. They had also filed a separate civil suit over that disputed sale.

The court ordered immediate eviction and directed that rent be paid up until possession is actually handed back to the landlord. The case illustrates that rent disputes are decided on tenancy facts, not on unresolved ownership litigation pending elsewhere.

title: Bibi Shah Gul v. Saadia,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute in Quetta. Saadia sued relatives of her late father, Noor Muhammad, claiming her rightful inheritance share after they allegedly got his property mutated (transferred) in their own names, cutting her out. The courts found she was indeed his legal heir and entitled to half share of a specific property, while ruling that a will supposedly favoring another relative was forged. This decision went through several rounds of appeals, including to the Balochistan High Court and Supreme Court, which ultimately confirmed her half-share entitlement.

Once the decree was final, Saadia applied to have it executed, meaning the property was actually to be divided and transferred according to the court's ruling. One of the other heirs, Bibi Shah Gul, objected to how execution was carried out, arguing the executing court exceeded the decree by allowing Saadia to receive more valuable land than her fair share, and that her own portion had been ignored.

The High Court dismissed her revision petition. It held that under Section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code, disputes about executing a decree must be resolved by the executing court itself, not through a fresh lawsuit. Since Bibi Shah Gul had failed to object earlier despite having knowledge of proceedings, and could not clearly show any error in the property measurements or mutation, her objections had no merit. The lower courts' orders executing the decree were upheld, reaffirming that execution courts have authority to settle such disputes directly.

title: Siraj-ud-Din v. Haji Muhammad Zarif,
explainer:

He also claimed he spent years trying to recover the money through community elders, complaints to authorities, and a legal notice, but was unsuccessful due to the defendants' influence. He finally filed a court case in 2004, eleven years after the transaction.

The buyers denied any business dealings with him and argued the suit was hopelessly time-barred, since claims like this must be filed within three years under the Limitation Act, 1908. The court also noted he had made contradictory statements that undermined his own case. Since he could not show valid grounds to excuse the delay, his revision petition was dismissed.

The case highlights how important it is for plaintiffs to file lawsuits within the legally prescribed time limits, and to provide concrete, credible explanations if seeking condonation of delay.

title: Government of Balochistan through Secretary Revenue Board v. Rashid,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land in Turbat, Balochistan, between private individuals claiming ancestral ownership and the Balochistan Provincial Government, which claimed the same land as state property. The respondents said their ancestor had bought the land in 1931 and that it had remained in their family's possession, later being wrongly recorded in the government's name in the revenue record. They sued for a declaration of ownership, a permanent injunction, and correction of the revenue entries. Both the trial court and the appellate court had ruled in their favor.

The government challenged this in the High Court, arguing the lower courts had not properly examined the evidence. The High Court agreed. It found that although the respondents claimed a sale deed existed proving the 1931 purchase, they never actually produced this document in court. Instead, both lower courts had relied only on oral testimony to decide a matter of land title, which the High Court held was legally insufficient, especially since the land was officially recorded in the government's name.

Because the lower courts' decisions were based on inadequate evidence and were legally flawed, the High Court ruled they were void, meaning the usual time limits for filing an appeal did not strictly apply. It therefore excused the government's delay in filing, overturned both earlier rulings, dismissed the original lawsuit, and restored the land record in favor of the government. The case highlights that ownership claims, especially against government land records, must be proven with solid documentary evidence, not just witness statements.

title: Abdul Nasir v. Bibi Janatora,
explainer:

The plaintiffs claimed to own three-quarters of a property and argued that the remaining one-quarter share, originally belonging to two individuals named Sufi and Mandak, should pass to them because Sufi and Mandak had died without children, making the plaintiffs their closest surviving relatives. The defendants disputed this, claiming the land had legitimately passed through inheritance to a grandson and then to them through official mutation entries in the land records. The trial court and first appellate court both dismissed the plaintiffs' suit.

The High Court found that neither side could actually prove their claimed relationship to the deceased original owners. However, it agreed that Sufi and Mandak likely died without children, since the land records showed no heirs were ever properly recorded after their deaths, and the inheritance mutations were only entered nearly a century later without any explanation of who requested them. This meant the mutation entries were fraudulent.

Despite finding fraud, the lower courts had refused to cancel the mutations because the plaintiffs failed to prove their own title. The High Court ruled this reasoning was flawed: fraudulent entries should be struck down regardless of whether the plaintiffs proved ownership. It restored the original ownership entries in the names of Sufi and Mandak and directed the revenue authorities to reexamine the matter from scratch and proceed according to law. The plaintiffs, however, were not granted ownership themselves, since they failed to establish their own title.

title: Bhawal Khan v. the State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Bhawal Khan who had been convicted under Section 337-H(ii) of the Pakistan Penal Code (causing hurt through a rash or negligent act) and fined Rs. 5,000, with a default sentence of two months imprisonment if unpaid. He paid the fine through the jail superintendent while pursuing his appeals.

Later, the complainant and Khan reached a compromise, with the complainant forgiving him and giving up any claim to Arsh or Daman (forms of compensation under Islamic criminal law equivalents recognized in Pakistani law). The Balochistan High Court accepted this compromise, set aside the earlier convictions from the trial and appellate courts, and acquitted Khan of the charge.

Following his acquittal, Khan asked the court to return the Rs. 5,000 fine he had already paid, arguing that since the case was compromised and he was acquitted, the money should come back to him.

The High Court rejected this request. It clarified an important legal distinction: Arsh or Daman (compensation paid to a victim) can be returned if the victim waives their right to it as part of a compromise, since that money belongs to the victim. However, a fine is different because it is paid to the State, not to the victim. Even when a conviction is set aside due to compromise and acquittal, fines already deposited with the State cannot be refunded. The application was dismissed.

title: Syed Ahmed Ali Shah v. Raja Muhammad Akhtar Khan,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over agricultural land in Mouza Baroot, Hub, Balochistan. The petitioner claimed the land belonged to his late father and, after his father's death in 1991, passed to him, his brothers, and mother as legal heirs. He alleged that the respondents fraudulently got the land entered in their names in official revenue records without the family's knowledge, and later began claiming ownership and threatening to take possession.

The respondents countered that they had legally purchased the property from the petitioner's father during his lifetime, through the father's attorney, who happened to be the petitioner's own brother. They produced registered sale deeds and the attorney's own statement confirming the sale.

Both the trial court and the appellate court examined the evidence and ruled against the petitioner, finding that the respondents had validly acquired ownership through the sale transaction, while the petitioner failed to prove his claim of fraud or establish a superior right to the land.

The Balochistan High Court, hearing the petitioner's revision petitions, held that he had not shown any legal error or illegality in the lower courts' decisions. Since both courts had already thoroughly examined the facts and reached the same conclusion, the High Court found no grounds to interfere and dismissed the petitions.

This case illustrates how courts assess competing claims of inheritance versus prior sale transactions, emphasizing that clear documentary evidence of a registered sale can override claims of inherited title when the seller had authority to sell during their lifetime.

title: Abdul Wali v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a robbery that occurred at a home in Quetta in September 2007, where armed men broke in, assaulted the complainant, and stole cash, bonds, and jewelry. The complainant reported the crime the same day but could not name the attackers, saying only that he might recognize two of them since their faces briefly became visible during the struggle.

More than a year later, the complainant spotted one of the alleged robbers, Abdul Wali, at a bus stand and had him arrested. Wali was tried and convicted under Section 392 of the Pakistan Penal Code for robbery, receiving seven years' imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, Wali argued that he was wrongly convicted because no formal identification parade was conducted after his arrest, and that the trial court had misread or ignored evidence in his favor.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that since the accused was arrested directly on the complainant's own identification at the bus stand, a formal identification parade was unnecessary. The court also noted that three eyewitnesses had identified Wali as one of the culprits, with no significant contradictions in their testimony, and that the defense had not shown any specific evidence that was overlooked or misused by the trial court.

The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction upheld. The case illustrates how courts assess eyewitness identification and when procedural steps like identification parades are considered necessary.

title: Abdul Haleem v. Syed Ahmed Ali Gilani,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta. The petitioner, Abdul Haleem, had filed a civil suit claiming ownership of a piece of property, alleging he had been wrongfully dispossessed and that the structure on the land was demolished by the defendants under the cover of a decree they had obtained through misrepresentation.

During the litigation, it emerged that the original defendants had sold the disputed property to six other people while the ownership dispute was still pending in court. The petitioner then asked the trial court to add these six buyers as defendants in the case, arguing that no meaningful court decision could be made without including the people who now held the property. The trial court refused, saying the request was late and that adding these new parties would change the nature of the suit.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that since the ownership question was still unresolved between the original parties, and the property had admittedly been transferred to new owners during the case, those new owners had effectively "stepped into the shoes" of the original defendants. This made them necessary parties, because any final court order would directly affect their rights. The court also noted that including them helped avoid multiple, separate lawsuits over the same property.

The High Court therefore set aside the trial court's order and allowed the six buyers to be added as defendants, directing the petitioner to file an amended plaint. This decision highlights how courts ensure that all parties whose rights are affected by a dispute get a chance to participate, so that judgments are fair and enforceable.

title: Abdul Qadir v. Sher Muhammad,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Balochistan between two groups of people, the Abdul Qadir side and the Sher Muhammad side, over land in the Nailant Kappar and Kulanchi areas. The plaintiffs (Sher Muhammad and others) had filed a civil suit asking for a declaration of their ownership, a permanent injunction, and correction of revenue records, claiming that the defendants had wrongly gotten the land registered in their own names through collusion with a revenue official.

Before evidence could be recorded, the trial court (Qazi Pasni) threw out the entire suit at a preliminary stage, citing many technical defects: unclear prayer for relief, missing property boundaries, wrong type of suit given that defendants were allegedly in possession, an earlier pending suit over the same land, lack of proper valuation, and failure to include certain parties. On appeal, the Majlis-e-Shoora set aside this dismissal and sent the case back for a full trial on the merits.

The Balochistan High Court, hearing a further revision petition, upheld the appellate court's decision. It ruled that technical defects like unclear property description, undervaluation, or missing parties are not grounds to dismiss a suit outright without giving parties a chance to fix them or without recording evidence. Disputed facts such as who is actually in possession must be decided through evidence, not assumptions. The court emphasized that cases should be decided on their merits rather than technicalities, and dismissed the petition, restoring the order for a full trial.

title: Haji Mullah Dad v. Mir Assa Gul,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a procedural dispute about a civil suit concerning property. During the lawsuit, the defendants argued that the case should be dismissed because it was barred by the legal principle of res judicata, meaning the same issue had already been decided in another case. The trial court first examined this argument and rejected it, finding no evidence that the property dispute had previously been decided elsewhere. Later, while deciding separate applications about adding parties to the case, the same trial court reversed itself and dismissed the suit on the very same res judicata ground, this time concluding the property was the same as in another pending case. This second ruling was upheld on appeal.

The petitioners challenged both decisions, arguing that once a court decides a legal question, it cannot revisit and reverse that same decision later in the same proceedings. The High Court agreed. It held that since the trial court had already ruled on the res judicata issue and found against it, the court lost jurisdiction to reconsider and decide the same question differently afterward. The second order was therefore not just wrong, but legally invalid for lack of jurisdiction. The appellate court had failed to notice this problem even though it was raised.

As a result, the High Court set aside both the trial court's and appellate court's orders, restored the original suit, and sent it back for a proper hearing on its merits. The case highlights an important principle: courts cannot reopen and change their own final rulings on the same legal question within the same case.

title: Mst: Zeba v. Sher Muhammad,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over ancestral property in Pakistan. The respondents (plaintiffs) filed a lawsuit asking the court to declare their ownership rights in a jointly-held, unpartitioned family property, seeking an injunction and division of the property among the co-owners. The defendants opposed the suit, arguing it should be thrown out on technical grounds - claiming the property wasn't clearly described, necessary parties were missing, the case was filed too late, the shares claimed were vague, and there was no valid basis for the lawsuit.

The trial court agreed with the defendants and dismissed the suit early on, without even formally framing the legal issues or hearing evidence. The plaintiffs appealed to the Majlis-e-Shoora (an appellate forum), which overturned that dismissal and sent the case back for a full hearing on the merits.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It found that the trial court had wrongly dismissed the case based on technical objections without properly examining evidence or framing issues. The judge emphasized that cases should be decided on their merits rather than dismissed over technicalities, and that problems like unclear property descriptions or missing parties could often be fixed rather than used to kill a case outright. Since no real legal error was shown in the appellate court's order, the High Court dismissed the defendants' petitions and sent the case back for proper trial.

title: Baz Muhammad v. the State,
explainer:
This case involved a man whose licensed pistol was stolen from his car in 2000 while his brother was driving it. His brother reported the theft to police, who simply recorded it in a daily diary rather than opening a formal case. Seven years later, in 2007, the petitioner learned that his pistol had actually been recovered from another man, who was arrested for illegally possessing it and convicted, with the court ordering the pistol confiscated by the state. Only then did the petitioner approach the trial court asking for the pistol to be returned to him as its rightful licensed owner. Both the trial court and the sessions court refused his request, and the sessions court went further, cancelling his firearms license entirely.

The Balochistan High Court upheld these decisions. It found the petitioner had been seriously negligent, doing nothing beyond the initial diary entry to pursue his stolen weapon for seven years despite legal rules requiring prompt reporting to authorities. The court noted that licensing authorities have the power to cancel licenses, and the petitioner could not point to any law that would allow the confiscation order to be reversed. It also observed that the lower court had already taken a lenient approach by not imposing an additional penalty available under the law.

This case illustrates that gun owners bear responsibility for promptly and properly reporting lost or stolen firearms to authorities, and that unreasonable delay in doing so can result in permanent loss of both the weapon and one's license, regardless of original lawful ownership.

title: Haji Saleh Muhammad v. Abdul Wadood,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land in Quetta. The plaintiffs (Haji Saleh Muhammad and another) claimed they had bought a piece of land in 1995, paid the full price, had the land mutated in their names, and taken possession. In 1998 they built a boundary wall, but in 2000 the seller, Abdul Wadood, allegedly demolished it with tractors, causing damage. The plaintiffs sued for an injunction to stop interference with their possession and for damages, but did not ask the court to formally declare their ownership title.

The defendant denied the plaintiffs had valid title or possession, saying he had instead made a separate deal with a third person (Naseem), who he claimed fraudulently arranged the mutation in the plaintiffs' favor without paying him fully. The trial court sided with the plaintiffs and awarded Rs. 100,000 in damages.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found that since ownership of the land was seriously disputed and the key middleman, Naseem, never testified, the plaintiffs could not simply seek an injunction and damages without first asking the court to formally declare their legal title. Without such a declaration, an injunction had no basis, and damages could not be awarded either. The court ruled the suit was not properly framed and dismissed it as not maintainable, setting aside the lower court's decision. The case highlights that in property disputes, proving legal title is a necessary first step before seeking injunctions or damages.

title: Muhammad Yaqoob v. Abdul Aziz,
explainer:
This case concerned a dispute over land and the extent to which a court can revisit a final judgment through a "review" application.

Muhammad Yaqoob had sued Abdul Aziz for specific performance of a 1992 sale agreement to transfer property to him. The dispute was not contested, and the trial court (Qazi Kalat) issued a consent decree in 2004 describing the property's boundaries, including its southern boundary as adjoining a water well. Both parties were present when this decree was passed.

Later, Abdul Aziz filed a review application claiming the southern boundary was actually a public lane, the sole passage for the public, and that this had been improperly altered or cut out of the original agreement. The trial court, after physically inspecting the property, accepted this review and changed the boundary description in the decree. An appellate body, the Majlis-e-Shoora, upheld this change. Yaqoob challenged both decisions before the High Court.

The High Court ruled in Yaqoob's favor. It held that a review application has a narrow scope under the Civil Procedure Code, it cannot be used to introduce new evidence, conduct fresh inspections, or make major changes to a decree as if it were a new trial. Since the original decree was made by consent, with the defendant present, he could not later claim alleged alterations in the sale deed to change the boundaries. The court found no cutting existed at the disputed portion of the original agreement, and no public right could be transferred to benefit a private party's personal claim. Both lower orders were set aside, and the review application was rejected.

title: Imtiaz Shah v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Imtiaz Shah, an employee in charge of a Utility Store in Quetta, who was convicted by a Special Anti-Corruption Court of criminal breach of trust, cheating, and corruption for allegedly submitting fake bank deposit slips and causing stock shortages worth several hundred thousand rupees. He was sentenced to six years in prison and a heavy fine. Shah appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing he had been falsely implicated after he reported a dacoity (robbery) at the store and refused illegal demands from a regional manager, and that the audit implicating him was conducted while he was already in police custody, without his presence.

The High Court examined the evidence and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. No proper investigation was conducted into the reported dacoity. The stock audit and discovery of allegedly forged deposit slips both occurred while the accused was in police custody, meaning he had no opportunity to be present or respond. No money or stock was ever recovered from him, and the prosecution failed to show the shortages were actually caused by his actions. The court found this raised doubts about the prosecution's good faith and concluded that both the breach of trust and cheating charges were not proven beyond reasonable doubt.

The High Court set aside the conviction, acquitted Shah, and ordered his release. This case highlights the importance of proper investigation and giving the accused a fair opportunity to respond before being convicted on corruption charges.

title: Syed Sohbat Shah v. Muhammad Khan,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running property dispute in Noushki, Balochistan, over agricultural land described by certain khasra and khatooni numbers and specific boundaries. The original plaintiffs (later petitioners) claimed the land was their ancestral property, in possession of a tenant, and sought declaration of ownership, an injunction, and recovery of possession. During the trial, a Local Commissioner (the Tehsildar) inspected the site with consent of both parties and submitted a report. Based on that report, and with the consent of both sides, the trial court passed a decree in the plaintiffs' favor without objection to the report.

Later, when the decree-holders tried to execute the decree and obtain physical possession of land they claimed fell within the boundaries mentioned in their plaint, the executing courts refused. Both the trial court and the appellate court found that the decree did not actually cover the additional land being claimed, and that the decree-holders were already in possession of the specific plots awarded to them. The courts even warned them against filing frivolous litigation.

The High Court upheld these findings, ruling that a court executing a decree cannot go beyond or reinterpret what the decree actually says, and that parties who consented to a decree based on an inspection report cannot later go back on that agreement to claim more land than was granted. The revision petition was dismissed.

The case matters because it reinforces two settled principles: consent decrees bind the parties who agreed to them, and execution proceedings are not an opportunity to expand or relitigate the scope of what was originally decreed.

title: General Manager, WTR, PTCL, Quetta v. Daily Meezan,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between PTCL (the telephone company) and Daily Meezan, a newspaper subscriber, over unpaid telephone dues. PTCL had issued notices under Section 81 of the West Pakistan Land Revenue Act, 1967, demanding that Daily Meezan pay outstanding dues of over Rs. 5.7 lakh on its telephone connection within 15 days. When the dues were not paid, PTCL disconnected the phone. Daily Meezan claimed the old telephone number had simply been changed to a new one, that its bills were fully paid, and that the disconnection was illegal. It sued for a declaration that it was the lawful subscriber and for an order restoring its phone connection.

The trial court ruled in favor of Daily Meezan, but the appellate court partially reversed that decision. Both sides then filed revision petitions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence and found that Daily Meezan had, in its own letters, admitted owing money and had asked to pay in installments and to avoid disconnection. This contradicted its court claim that nothing was due. The Court held that Daily Meezan was in fact a defaulter and could not deny liability merely to escape payment. It concluded that Daily Meezan failed to prove its case, while PTCL had proven its claim of unpaid dues.

The case matters because it shows courts will rely on parties' own written admissions and conduct over their later claims in litigation, and that customers cannot escape valid debts through inconsistent legal arguments.

title: Khaliq Dad v. Noor Bibi,
explainer:
This case involves a property dispute over a residential plot of land in Kharan, Balochistan. The plaintiff, Khaliq Dad, claimed he had lawfully purchased the land in 1992 from a man named Mandost, who he said had been officially allotted the land by the government in 1983. He sought a court declaration confirming his ownership and an order stopping the legal heirs of another man, Qadir Bakhsh, from interfering with the property, since they claimed the same land belonged to them.

The trial court initially ruled in the plaintiff's favor, but the appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora) reversed this decision and dismissed his suit. The plaintiff then challenged that reversal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision. It found that the plaintiff's sale document made no mention of the original 1983 allotment or any leasehold rights, and there was no explanation for the long gap between the alleged 1983 allotment and the 1992 sale. Since the land was government-owned, no valid transfer to a private party could occur without official sanction from the competent authority. The plaintiff could not prove he held valid legal title to the land, and the physical description of the land he claimed did not match what actually existed at the site.

This case highlights that when disputing ownership of state land, a claimant must produce clear, unbroken documentary proof of lawful allotment and transfer - unsupported claims of possession or informal sales are insufficient to establish ownership.

title: Haji Muhammad Azam v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Haji Muhammad Azam, who was convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Khuzdar for possessing explosives and illegal arms. The charges arose after police were attacked by unknown gunmen in Hub, and a subsequent raid on a house linked to the appellant uncovered hand grenades, explosive material, weapons, ammunition, and bomb-making equipment. He was convicted under section 4(b) of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 and sentenced to seven years rigorous imprisonment, and under section 13(e) of the Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965, sentenced to three years with a fine.

On appeal to the Balochistan High Court, his lawyer did not challenge the conviction itself but only asked for a reduction in sentence. The court noted that the law for the explosives offense mandates a minimum sentence of seven years (or life imprisonment), and since the trial court had already given the lowest possible term, no further reduction was legally possible. For the arms offense, the maximum sentence allowed was seven years, but he had only received three years, already a lenient sentence. Given the serious nature of the offenses, the High Court refused to reduce the punishment further and upheld the conviction and sentences.

This case matters because it illustrates how courts apply mandatory minimum sentencing laws strictly, especially in terrorism-related and explosives cases, and shows that appeals seeking leniency alone, without contesting guilt, have limited scope when statutory minimums have already been applied.

title: Haji Abdul Bari v SDO Sub Division QESCO,
explainer:
This case involved a property owner in Chaman who sued the local electricity supply company (QESCO/WAPDA) over disputed electricity bills. He owned shops, a hotel, and an inn that had been rented to various tenants. Electricity connections at these premises had been billed under different names, including tenants, and eventually disconnected. The owner argued he should not be held responsible for bills issued in his former tenants' names, claimed the charges were based on estimated rather than actual meter readings, and asked the court to order correction of records, restore his electricity connection, and stop demands for disputed dues until the billing was fixed. The trial court and the appellate court both dismissed his suit, partly on the basis that the law barred courts from hearing such matters.

The High Court clarified that the law only prevents courts from intervening in disconnection and restoration of electricity supply, not in other disputes against the supplier, so the lower courts were wrong to dismiss the entire suit as not maintainable. However, on the merits, the High Court found that as the property owner, the petitioner qualified as the "consumer" under the law and was responsible for outstanding charges regardless of tenancy arrangements. It also found he had unlawfully extended electricity to disconnected areas, violating supply conditions. Since he had not paid his dues and could not prove the billing was incorrect, the court upheld dismissal of his suit, including his request for reconnection.

title: Siraj Ahmed v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Siraj Ahmed, who was convicted by an Additional Sessions Judge in Lasbella for possessing an unlicensed dagger under the Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965, and sentenced to three years' rigorous imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed from jail, seeking acquittal and claiming he had been falsely implicated.

The background was that Ahmed had allegedly walked into a police station holding a dagger and confessed to killing a man named Ghulam Muhammad and injuring another person, surrendering himself. Since he could not produce a license for the dagger, a separate case was registered against him for illegal weapon possession. Separately, the victim's family had also filed a murder case naming him as the accused.

The Balochistan High Court found a critical contradiction: the murder case FIR recorded the incident as happening at 11:30 p.m., while the weapons case FIR (based on his alleged confession) stated the incident occurred at 11:30 a.m. the same day. This meant, oddly, that Ahmed appeared to confess before the murder had even been reported. Additionally, key witnesses to the weapon recovery were never produced in court, weakening the evidence.

The Court ruled that these unexplained inconsistencies created reasonable doubt, and this doubt must benefit the accused. It found the trial court had failed to properly consider these facts. As a result, the High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted Ahmed, ordering his release. This case underscores how contradictions in police records can undermine

title: Siraj Ahmed v. The State,
explainer:
This is an appeal decided by the Balochistan High Court against a murder conviction. Siraj Ahmed had been convicted by a trial court of killing Ghulam Muhammad and injuring Abdul Hafeez with a dagger, receiving a life sentence plus additional punishments for the attempted murder and injury charges. He appealed, claiming he was falsely implicated, that witnesses were biased relatives, and that police had pressured him into making a confession before a magistrate by threatening him with torture and falsely promising his release if he confessed.

The High Court examined the evidence closely, particularly the confession recorded under Section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code. It held that while such confessions are strong evidence, they cannot be fully relied upon unless proven to be truly voluntary. The court found problems with the prosecution's case: the only eyewitness's account involved a motorcycle that no other witness mentioned and that was never recovered by police, undermining his claim to have clearly seen the attacker at night. The court also found the confession lacked proper corroboration from other evidence, and that the trial court had failed to properly address contradictions between witness statements and medical evidence.

Because of these unresolved doubts, the High Court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. It accepted the appeal and acquitted Siraj Ahmed of all charges, reinforcing the principle that confessions and eyewitness testimony must be credible and corroborated before they can support a conviction.

title: Faizullah v. Atta Muhammad,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute over shared agricultural property in Balochistan. An earlier suit between two sets of respondents over the property had been decided by compromise, resulting in a decree. Some individuals who were not part of that suit later claimed they were also shareholders and owners of the same property, and that the decree had been obtained fraudulently and in collusion between the parties, without their knowledge, specifically to deprive them of their rights. They said they only found out about the situation in 2003, when their tenant farmers refused to hand over their share of the produce. They asked the court to set aside the earlier judgments and decrees and to be added as parties so the case could be reheard on its merits.

The trial court and appellate court had already rejected this request, and the applicants brought the matter to the High Court.

The High Court dismissed the application. It found that the applicants were closely related by blood to one set of respondents and shared common households with them, making their claim of genuine ignorance about the ongoing litigation unbelievable. More importantly, the applicants failed to produce any documents proving their ownership or share in the property, could not even name their tenant farmers, and gave no evidence of the extent of their claimed share. Since they failed to establish even a basic case of fraud or misrepresentation, or show any real title to the land, the court held they were not entitled to have the case reopened or sent back for further evidence.

The case highlights that claims of fraud used to reopen final decrees must be backed by concrete evidence, not vague or unsupported assertions.

title: Shabbir Ahmed v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by Shabbir Ahmed, who was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine for possession of narcotics under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. He was apprehended along with three others during a routine checkpoint at Waricha Landhi, Balochistan, where about 19 kilograms of suspected heroin were found hidden in a vehicle he was riding in.

The appellant argued that the investigation was flawed because a Naib Risaldar, an officer below the rank required by law, conducted the seizure and recovery proceedings, and that these proceedings happened at a military fort rather than at the actual spot of recovery. He also claimed he was merely a passenger who had boarded the vehicle to collect his father's belongings and had no connection to the narcotics.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that the officer had acted with proper permission from a Judicial Magistrate in the absence of his superior, so no illegality occurred. The court also ruled that procedural irregularities during investigation do not automatically invalidate a case unless they cause real prejudice to the accused, which was not shown here. Since witness testimony was consistent and the appellant's presence in the vehicle was undisputed, the burden fell on him to prove he was an innocent hitchhiker, which he failed to do.

The court upheld the trial court's guilty verdict and dismissed the appeal, reinforcing how courts evaluate procedural objections and burden of proof in narcotics cases.

title: Ghulam Jillani v The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man convicted for possessing 19 kilograms of heroin found in a vehicle he was driving, under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. He and three others were arrested during a routine patrol near the Pakistan-Iran border, with heroin recovered from one vehicle and a satellite phone from another that was allegedly guiding it. After trial, one co-accused was found to be a minor and tried separately, two others were acquitted before trial for lack of evidence, and the appellant alone was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, his lawyers argued the investigation was flawed because the investigating officer wasn't properly authorized, never visited the crime scene, and didn't prepare a site plan, and that procedural requirements under the law weren't followed.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that the investigating officer had been properly authorized by a judicial magistrate, and no bad faith by police was proven. Importantly, the accused never denied owning the vehicle or the drums containing the drugs, nor claimed he was merely transporting them for someone else. This meant he was in conscious, knowing possession of the narcotics. Finding no major contradictions in the prosecution's case and considering the sentence appropriate for such a serious crime, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld his life sentence.

title: Syed Abdul Jabbar v. The State,
explainer:
Syed Abdul Jabbar was convicted by a Special Judge under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997 and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine, after police allegedly recovered a huge quantity of charas (about 42 kilograms, made up of 1978 rods and 67 cubes) from bags he was carrying at a bus stop in Quetta. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the evidence was unreliable, that witnesses contradicted each other, and that proper procedure was not followed in testing the recovered material.

The High Court agreed with him. It found that although a very large quantity of narcotics was allegedly recovered, the investigators only sent a small sample of 100 grams to the forensic laboratory for testing, without identifying or separating which specific rods or cubes the sample came from. Given the huge number of individual pieces, the law required proper sampling from each item to confirm that all of it was actually a narcotic drug. The witnesses also contradicted each other on important points. The court held that this carelessness and failure to follow proper procedure by the investigating agency created real doubt about whether the narcotics were genuinely recovered from the accused as claimed.

Because of this reasonable doubt, the court ruled that the benefit of doubt must go to the accused. It set aside the trial court's judgment and acquitted him, highlighting how sloppy police investigation and evidence handling can undermine even serious drug prosecutions.

title: Fateh Khan v Sher Khan,
explainer: This Balochistan High Court judgment addresses a property dispute between Fateh Khan (appellant/defendant) and Sher Khan (respondent/plaintiff) over a shop in Muslim Bagh City. The plaintiff's father had inherited a share of property jointly owned with his brother, and had rented a shop to the defendant. When the defendant repeatedly sublet the shop without permission, the father sought eviction. During those proceedings, the defendant produced a 1990 sale agreement claiming he had purchased the property from the plaintiff. The Rent Controller accepted this and dismissed the eviction case, but the High Court later ruled that dispute over ownership should be resolved by a civil court. The plaintiff then sued for cancellation of the allegedly forged sale agreement, plus declaration and injunction. The trial court ruled in the plaintiff's favor, and the defendant appealed, arguing that a mere declaratory suit without seeking possession was not legally maintainable since the plaintiff was out of possession. The High Court rejected this argument, finding that the plaintiff never claimed ownership of the property (which belonged to his father) and therefore was not required to seek possession as additional relief. The court also found the defendant failed to prove the plaintiff had legal authority to sell the property, especially since the actual owner was alive when the agreement was allegedly made. The appeal was dismissed, though the plaintiff was directed to pay proper court fees. The case clarifies when declaratory suits are legally valid without seeking possession.

title: Khaliq Dad v. Bibi Sahira,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over land ownership between family members. The petitioner, Khaliq Dad, claimed he was the sole rightful owner of certain properties because his brother Qahir had died without children, and another brother Zahir had already separated his share. The respondents, represented by an attorney, claimed to be the real daughters and other legal heirs of Qahir and therefore entitled to a share of the property.

A trial court initially dismissed the respondents' claim, finding they had not proven they were Qahir's legal heirs. However, an appellate court reversed this decision and ruled in favor of the respondents, granting them ownership rights. Khaliq Dad then challenged this appellate decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence and found serious problems with the respondents' case: their identity as Qahir's daughters was based only on oral, hearsay testimony, with no reliable documentary proof. There was no original documentation proving the identity of other claimed sisters living in India, only photocopies, which were not acceptable. There was also no evidence that Qahir had ever married. Additionally, the attorney representing the respondents could not even produce his power of attorney.

title: Mehran v. The State,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves an appeal by a man named Mehran, who had been convicted under the West Pakistan Arms Ordinance for possessing an unlicensed Kalashnikov rifle and live cartridges. He was sentenced to three years in prison and fined Rs.10,000.

The weapon was allegedly recovered from Mehran's house after he made a disclosure to police while in custody for a separate murder case. Police claimed he led them to his home and produced the rifle and 20 cartridges from under bedding.

On appeal, the High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The witnesses gave contradictory accounts about the timing of events and who handled the recovered items. Most tellingly, the court discovered that the number of cartridges recorded in one witness's statement had been altered from "3" to "20" through overwriting, without any initials confirming the change was authorized. The disclosure leading to the recovery was also made on the last permissible day of police remand, raising suspicion. No independent witnesses from the neighborhood were included in the recovery process, and the house wasn't shown to be under Mehran's exclusive control.

Given these serious doubts and contradictions, the High Court ruled that the trial court had wrongly ignored inconsistencies that should have benefited the accused. The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted Mehran, reinforcing the principle that criminal convictions require evidence free from reasonable doubt, and that altered or contradictory evidence cannot support a safe conviction.

title: Muhammad Saleem v. Muhammad Ehsan-ul-Haque Ghauri,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over an ex parte decree, meaning a court judgment issued against defendants who did not appear in court. The respondent had sued the appellants for recovery of money and damages related to a coal supply contract. When the appellants could not be served through normal means, the court ordered service by publication in a newspaper. The trial court eventually decreed the case in the respondent's favor without the appellants participating.

Years later, when the respondent tried to execute the decree and attach the appellants' property, the appellants claimed they had never known about the case. They argued the respondent had deliberately arranged for the newspaper notice to appear in a publication with poor circulation in their area, amounting to fraud, and that they only learned of the decree when the execution proceedings began. They asked the court to set aside the decree and allow a retrial.

The Balochistan High Court rejected this argument. It found that the appellants had used the same address in other lawsuits they filed against the respondent in another city, showing they were already aware of the decree and had deliberately delayed acting on it. The court held that under the Limitation Act, the clock for challenging such a decree starts once the party becomes aware of it, and the appellants had failed to prove any fraud. Since the trial court had properly evaluated the facts, the appeal was dismissed, upholding the original decree.

title: Aurangzeb v. The State,
explainer:
Aurangzeb was convicted by the Anti-Terrorism Court in Quetta and sentenced to life imprisonment, plus confiscation of his property, over an alleged incident where two women and a man were abducted at gunpoint and held for ransom in a garden, with police later arresting Aurangzeb after a car chase and collision.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found the prosecution's case riddled with problems. The firearm supposedly recovered from Aurangzeb was never actually seized at arrest or through any later disclosure. A private witness's presence at the crime scene was unexplained and unsupported by police witnesses, making the recovery evidence doubtful. There were also major contradictions between witness statements that the trial court had ignored. The court noted the garden belonged to Aurangzeb, which reasonably explained his presence there, and found the story of him releasing a hostage who then helped police catch him to be implausible. It also seemed odd that he would try to escape by car rather than on foot, as his co-accused had done. One alleged victim did not identify him, and another key witness was never even produced in court without explanation. Finally, the investigating officer failed to bring in any independent local witnesses.

Because the prosecution could not prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the High Court gave Aurangzeb the benefit of that doubt, overturned his conviction and sentence, and acquitted him. The case highlights how weak evidence and sloppy investigation can undermine even serious terrorism-related convictions.

title: Abdul Razzaq v. Jameel Ahmed,
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant dispute in Quetta over a house on Gurdat Singh Road. The original owner, Noor Ahmed, had rented the house to Abdul Razzaq. After Noor Ahmed's death, his son Jameel Ahmed sought to evict the tenant, claiming rent default and that he personally needed the house.

The tenant admitted he was a tenant but disputed the rent amount and claimed the landlord's father had refused to accept rent, so he had been depositing it in court since 1999. He also tried to argue there had been a sale transaction giving him ownership, though the trial court rejected this, and the High Court agreed it could not decide ownership questions in rent proceedings.

The Balochistan High Court ruled in favor of the tenant. It found that the son, as heir, did qualify as "landlord" under the law, but since the property was residential, the landlord needed special permission from the Rent Controller to convert it for commercial use, which he had not obtained—so the claim of "personal need" failed. Crucially, the court also found the landlord never gave the tenant formal notice of the change of ownership after his father's death, as required by law. Without such notice, the tenant could not be blamed for not paying rent to the new owner, so there was no legal default.

As a result, the eviction order was set aside and the appeal was accepted. The case highlights that landlords must follow proper legal procedures—like notifying tenants of ownership changes and obtaining permission before converting property use—before seeking eviction.
