title: Aurangzeb v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Aurangzeb, who was convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Quetta for illegal possession of a loaded Kalashnikov magazine with 30 live cartridges, under the West Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965. He was sentenced to three years' rigorous imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that no firearm was actually recovered from him and that the trial court had wrongly mixed up evidence from a separate, related case.

The High Court examined the prosecution's evidence closely and found serious problems. The police witnesses gave conflicting accounts of the timing of the incident and the recovery, with unexplained discrepancies between their oral testimony and the written report. The name of the person who delivered the report to the police station was also inconsistent. Crucially, the investigating officer admitted he did not conduct an independent investigation, merely taking custody of a carbon copy of the recovery document and statements already prepared by others. A private witness listed in the recovery memo was never brought to court, and there was no explanation for why he was even present at the scene, since he did not live nearby.

Given these unexplained contradictions and gaps, the court ruled that the prosecution had failed to prove the weapon was actually recovered from Aurangzeb's possession. Since recovery itself wasn't established, the question of licensing became irrelevant. The court set aside the conviction and acquitted him, highlighting how sloppy investigation and inconsistent evidence can undermine a criminal case.

title: Muhammad Azam v. The State,
explainer:
This case arose from a murder trial involving the killing of two young men. Two eyewitnesses, Mst. Rubina and Mst. Afsana, had given earlier statements to a Judicial Magistrate before the trial began, but when they testified in court, they changed their accounts, effectively contradicting their previous statements. Despite this, the Assistant District Attorney handling the prosecution failed to declare them hostile witnesses or confront them with their earlier statements. The complainant then asked the trial court to recall these two witnesses so they could be properly questioned and cross-examined about the inconsistencies. The trial court refused, reasoning that the prosecution should not be allowed to fix its own mistakes at this late stage.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed and overturned that decision. It held that Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code gives courts wide powers to summon, recall, and re-examine witnesses at any stage of a trial if their evidence is essential to reaching a just decision. The court found that since these two women were key eyewitnesses to a serious crime, and their statements appeared to have changed, fairness required that they be recalled and confronted with their earlier statements so the truth could be established.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that trial courts have a duty to actively ensure justice is done, not just to rely on the lawyers' conduct, especially when key witnesses in serious criminal cases like murder appear to contradict themselves.

title: Nasir Hameed v. Rais Muhammad Akram,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute where the original plaintiffs (Rais Muhammad Akram and others) had filed a lawsuit seeking a court declaration of their ownership title, a permanent injunction, and correction of entries in official revenue records. The trial court dismissed their suit at an early stage, ruling it was filed too late (barred by limitation) without hearing full evidence from both sides.

The plaintiffs appealed, and the appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora Mastung) overturned that dismissal, sending the case back to the trial court with instructions to properly frame factual issues, take evidence from both parties, and then decide the case on its merits. The petitioners (who were defendants in the original suit) challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court, arguing the trial court had correctly handled the matter as a pure legal question that could be decided through arguments alone.

The High Court disagreed and upheld the appellate court's decision. It explained that under civil procedure rules, when a case involves purely legal issues, courts can decide them by hearing arguments alone. However, when legal questions are intertwined with disputed facts, such as whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed or whether limitation periods applied, courts must record evidence before ruling, since these are "mixed questions of law and fact." The court found no error in sending the case back for a full trial with evidence. This ruling matters because it clarifies that courts cannot shortcut factual disputes disguised as legal questions, protecting parties' rights to have evidence properly examined.

title: Nazar Muhammad v. Niaz Muhammad,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running property dispute over a pre-emption suit, where the buyers of land (respondents) sought to acquire it back from the original purchasers (petitioners) under pre-emption rights. The trial court decreed in favor of the respondents in 2004, and the appellate court upheld this but ordered them to pay the market price for the property. After several rounds of appeals, including to the Supreme Court, the case was sent back to determine the exact purchase price and payment deadline. While the amount of purchase money was still being contested before the Balochistan High Court, the executing court went ahead and ordered mutation of land records and possession transfer in favor of the respondents.

The petitioners challenged this, arguing the execution was premature since the purchase price hadn't been finally decided, and also that the execution application was filed beyond the legal time limit. The High Court agreed, holding that under the Civil Procedure Code and Limitation Act, a decree-holder must apply for execution within a specific timeframe, and more importantly, in pre-emption cases, ownership only transfers once the court-assessed purchase money is actually paid. Since the price itself was still under litigation, the right to execute the decree had not yet arisen. The Court found the lower courts erred in allowing execution prematurely and set aside their orders, ruling in favor of the petitioners. This case underscores that in pre-emption suits, execution cannot proceed until the purchase price is conclusively settled.

title: Ilyas v. The State,
explainer:
This appeal concerns two men, Ilyas and another accused, who were convicted by a Sessions Court in Turbat for robbery (theft with violence) under sections 392 and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code. They were sentenced to four years' rigorous imprisonment plus fines. The prosecution's case was that they had stopped the complainant and his uncle on a motorcycle, demanded the bike, assaulted the complainant with a pistol butt, and fled with the motorcycle.

The Balochistan High Court, however, found serious flaws in the prosecution's evidence. There was unexplained delay both in filing the police report and in recording witness statements, as well as delay in inspecting the crime scene. No stolen motorcycle or weapon was ever recovered. The medical evidence did not match the witnesses' account of events, and the sequence of events described by the prosecution did not make logical sense. The court also questioned why the complainant would pursue a compromise with the accused after suffering violent injuries during a robbery, finding this unexplained.

Because of these contradictions and gaps, the court held that the essential elements of the robbery offence had not been properly proven, and the trial court had failed to consider these discrepancies. Applying the principle that any reasonable doubt must benefit the accused, the High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted both men. The case illustrates how courts scrutinize inconsistencies and unexplained delays in criminal prosecutions before allowing a conviction to stand.

title: Muhammad Asif v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of house-breaking and theft under Pakistan's Penal Code, after being accused of stealing a carpet from a government official's residence in Naushki. A trial court and later a sessions court both found him guilty and sentenced him to imprisonment and fines. He challenged both decisions before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the prosecution's witnesses contradicted each other and that the lower courts had wrongly relied on his own statement rather than properly weighing the prosecution's evidence.

The High Court agreed with him. It found that the man said to have reported the crime, Saadullah, had not actually witnessed the incident himself but relied on secondhand information. Key witnesses gave inconsistent accounts, and one witness who claimed to be present at the scene could not properly explain his presence there, making him a "chance witness" whose testimony required extra caution. The court held that in criminal cases, the burden always remains on the prosecution to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, regardless of any weaknesses in the accused's defense. Since the witnesses failed to corroborate each other convincingly, the court ruled that both lower courts had failed to properly evaluate the evidence and should have given the accused the benefit of the doubt.

As a result, the High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the petitioner. The case reinforces the fundamental principle that suspicion or weak, contradictory evidence cannot substitute for proof beyond reasonable doubt in criminal trials.

title: Ganj Bibi v. Muhammad Younas,
explainer:
This case involved a mother, Ganj Bibi, who sought to be legally appointed as the guardian of her young son, Muhammad Yousaf, after her marriage to the child's father, Muhammad Younas, ended through khula (a form of divorce initiated by the wife). Although she already had physical custody of the child, who was only a few months old at the time of filing, she wanted formal recognition as his legal guardian.

The trial court dismissed her application, and she appealed to the Balochistan High Court. The High Court upheld the dismissal. It explained that under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, particularly Section 19(b), a court cannot appoint someone else as guardian of a minor if the child's father is alive and not shown to be unfit for the role. The judge noted that while a mother is entitled to custody of a young child under Islamic law, custody and legal guardianship are different matters. Since Ganj Bibi already had custody and had not presented any evidence that the father was unfit or had tried to take the child away from her, there was no legal basis to remove the father's guardianship rights or appoint her instead.

This case clarifies the distinction between custody and guardianship under Pakistani law, showing that having physical custody does not automatically entitle a parent to formal guardianship, especially when the father remains fit and willing to fulfill that role.

title: Abdul Zahir v. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a violent clash in Killa Saifullah, Balochistan, in February 2009, where a group of men attacked two brothers working in their fields, resulting in one brother's death and injuries to the other. The accused were armed with farming tools like spades and rods, not weapons. The trial court convicted Abdul Zahir of murder under Section 302(c) of the Pakistan Penal Code, sentencing him to 25 years imprisonment, while another accused, Abdul Khaliq, was convicted of causing hurt. Both appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness testimony and medical reports, and found the trial court's overall assessment of guilt to be sound—the complaint was filed promptly, the accused were clearly named, and their three-month disappearance without explanation suggested guilt. However, the court disagreed with the murder conviction. It found no evidence of premeditation or intent to kill; the accused used farming tools, not weapons, and the death arose from a sudden fight rather than a planned attack. Therefore, the court reclassified the offense from qatl-e-amd (intentional murder) to a lesser category under Section 315 (qatl shibh-i-amd), reducing Abdul Zahir's sentence to 14 years imprisonment under Section 316.

This case matters because it illustrates how courts distinguish between different degrees of culpable homicide under Pakistani law based on intent, weapon use, and circumstances, ensuring punishment matches the true nature of the crime.

title: Mst. Parveen Akhtar v Syed Wasay Agha,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a dispute over property ownership between Mst. Parveen Akhtar (and another petitioner) and Syed Wasay Agha (and others). The petitioners had filed a civil suit seeking a declaration that they owned certain property, along with possession and an injunction against interference by the respondents. The trial court dismissed the suit without taking evidence, ruling it was not maintainable due to lack of a valid cause of action. The appellate court upheld this dismissal, citing insufficient court fees, vague dates for when the cause of action arose, and an unexplained earlier withdrawal of a similar suit.

The High Court found that both lower courts had misapplied the law. It held that the burden was on the defendants, not the plaintiffs, to prove the suit was barred due to an earlier withdrawal. It also clarified that under the Civil Procedure Code, a suit cannot be dismissed merely for non-joinder or misjoinder of parties, since courts have the power to add or remove parties at any stage. Additionally, the court noted that if there was an issue with court fees, the trial court should have given the plaintiffs a chance to correct it, rather than assuming failure and dismissing the case outright.

As a result, the High Court set aside both lower court orders and sent the case back to the trial court for a fresh decision. This judgment matters because it reinforces procedural fairness, ensuring that technical objections don't unjustly block legitimate claims from being heard on their merits.

title: Muhammad Ali v Branch Manager National Bank of Pakistan,
explainer:
This case involves a bank loan recovery dispute. National Bank of Pakistan sued a principal debtor and two guarantors, including the appellant Muhammad Ali, for recovery of over Rs.12.9 million. When the defendants did not appear despite notices sent through registered post, courier, and publication in two newspapers, the Banking Court in Quetta decided the case ex parte (without the defendants present) and ruled against them on 12 April 2008.

Muhammad Ali later found out about this decree only when he was arrested during execution proceedings on 24 July 2009. He then applied to have the ex parte decree set aside, claiming he was never properly served, that the newspapers used had no circulation in his area, and that the loan documents were fraudulently prepared without his knowledge or signature. The Banking Court rejected his application, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the rejection. It found that service by publication in newspapers was valid under the law governing bank recovery cases, and once such service is properly done, no further notice is required. The court noted Ali never denied his address was correct, that process servers had reported attempts to avoid service, and that he waited 21 days after his arrest to file his application without explaining the delay. Finding no evidence of fraud by the bank and no valid excuse for the delay, the court dismissed the appeal, reinforcing that defendants who evade court notices cannot later claim lack of proper service to escape decrees.

title: Dr. Muhammad Younas v. Government of Balochistan, Health Department,
explainer:
This case involved two doctors working in Balochistan's health department who challenged their transfer orders. They had been posted from Quetta to a District Headquarters Hospital in Zhob and argued that the transfer was improper for several reasons: it violated official rules and a 2003 Provincial Cabinet decision on transfer policy, it went against a 2010 ban imposed by the Chief Minister on postings and transfers, and they had not yet completed a required two-year minimum tenure at their previous posting.

The Balochistan High Court rejected their petition. The judge explained that under Section 10 of the Balochistan Civil Servants Act, 1974, every civil servant can be required to serve anywhere within or outside the province, unless they were specifically recruited for a particular area. Since the doctors did not fall into that exception, they had no automatic right to remain at their chosen posting. The court also found that while a two-year tenure was generally considered reasonable, it was not an absolute rule, and each case had to be judged on its own facts. The doctors failed to prove their transfer amounted to "frequent" transfer or that officials had acted with bad faith (mala fide).

The court dismissed the petition but directed the health department to promptly decide the doctors' pending administrative appeals. The case matters because it reaffirms that civil servants generally cannot use courts to block routine transfers unless they can show a legal right, established policy violation, or bad faith by the transferring authority.

title: Dr. Saba Durrazai v. Chairman House Allotment Committee/Secretary S&GAD Government of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a government-allotted residence in Quetta. Dr. Saba Durrazai had been officially allotted a house in May 2010, after it was cancelled from its previous occupant, Abdul Sattar Khajak. However, even after retiring, Khajak was allowed to retain the house for six months. When that period ended, instead of the house being handed over to Dr. Durrazai as the lawful allottee, the authorities extended his retention for a further year. She challenged this extension in the Balochistan High Court, arguing it violated the rules governing residential allotments and that as the rightful allottee she was entitled to possession.

The High Court did not rule on the merits of her claim. Instead, it dismissed the petition on a technical ground: under the Residential Accommodation at Quetta (Procedure for Allotment) Rules, 2009, an aggrieved person has the right to appeal an allotment-related order to the House Allotment Committee before going to court. Since Dr. Durrazai had not first used this internal appeal process, the court held that she had an adequate alternate remedy available, and that the High Court could not exercise its special constitutional jurisdiction while such a remedy remained unused.

This case illustrates an important principle in Pakistani administrative law: courts generally require people to exhaust available internal or departmental appeals before seeking judicial intervention, ensuring disputes are first addressed through proper administrative channels.

title: Peer Bakhsh v. Rasool Bakhsh,
explainer:
This case concerns a land dispute in Lasbella, Balochistan. The respondents (Rasool Bakhsh and others) had filed a civil suit claiming ownership and possession of a piece of land, seeking cancellation of a lease that had been granted to the petitioners (Peer Bakhsh and others), and asking for an injunction to stop them from occupying it.

The trial court dismissed the suit at an early stage without recording any evidence, ruling that it was barred by limitation (filed too late, after 30 years) and that the plaintiffs had no legal claim as owners or lessees. The plaintiffs challenged this before the District Judge, who accepted their revision petition, set aside the trial court's order, and sent the case back for a full trial with evidence from both sides, since it involved disputed facts as well as legal questions.

The petitioners then approached the Balochistan High Court, arguing the District Judge had wrongly interfered and that the original dismissal was correct. The High Court disagreed, holding that questions like limitation and ownership could not be decided merely on assumptions or written statements alone, especially when both sides disputed the facts. Such issues required proper evidence. The Court upheld the District Judge's order, dismissed the petition, and directed the trial court to involve the provincial government since the land's status appeared unsettled. This case underscores that courts should not dismiss suits on technical or factual disputes without allowing parties to present evidence.

title: Azizullah v. The State,
explainer:
This case is about whether a criminal complaint over a shooting should be tried in a regular Sessions Court or transferred to a special Anti-Terrorism Court. The complainant, Azizullah, reported that on 5 August 2009 armed men opened fire with a Kalashnikov on his brothers along the Quetta-Chaman Road, killing one and seriously injuring the other. The accused remained absconding, and the case was pending trial before an Additional Sessions Judge. Azizullah asked the High Court to transfer the case to the Anti-Terrorism Court, arguing that the crime happened on a main highway, caused public fear and panic, and therefore amounted to terrorism under the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, even though the police had not originally charged the accused under that law.

The Balochistan High Court examined the legal definition of terrorism under Section 6 of the Anti-Terrorism Act, which requires that an act not only cause death or injury but also be intended to intimidate, coerce or create fear among the government, public, or a section of society. The court found that although the incident tragically caused death and injury, it stemmed from personal enmity between the two families, as stated in the FIR itself. There was no evidence that the act was meant to spread fear or intimidate the wider public or any community. Since the essential element of terrorism—intimidation or overawing the public—was missing, the court dismissed the application to transfer the case, ruling it should remain a matter for the ordinary criminal court rather than a special anti-terrorism proceeding.

title: Mst. Shahzadi v. The State,
explainer:
Mst. Shahzadi's husband died, and she alleged that her stepsons forced her out of her home and took her cash, jewelry, vehicles, weapons, and other belongings. When she reported this to the police, they refused to register a First Information Report (FIR). She then approached the Sessions Judge, acting as Justice of Peace under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking that the case be formally registered and investigated. Instead of ordering registration of the FIR, the Justice of Peace directed the police to first conduct an inquiry under section 157(2) of the Code, and only register the FIR if that inquiry showed a crime had occurred.

The Balochistan High Court found this approach wrong. It held that the law does not allow for an inquiry to be conducted before an FIR is registered. Once information disclosing a cognizable offence (a serious crime the police can investigate without court permission) is received, the police must first record it as an FIR, and only afterward carry out an investigation and report to the court. By ordering an inquiry before registration, the Justice of Peace misunderstood and misapplied his powers under section 22-A.

The court set aside the earlier order and directed the police to register the FIR immediately and proceed with the investigation according to law. The case reinforces that citizens reporting cognizable crimes have a legal right to prompt FIR registration, without police or courts imposing extra preliminary screening.

title: Abdullah alias Lala v. The State,
explainer:
This case involves an appeal by Abdullah, who was convicted by a trial court for Qatl Shibh-i-Amd, a form of unintentional but culpable killing under Pakistan's Penal Code. He was sentenced to ten years in prison and ordered to pay Rs. 12,00,000 as Diyat (compensation) to the family of the deceased, Naimatullah.

While his appeal was pending before the Balochistan High Court, Abdullah reached a compromise with the deceased's legal heirs, his parents and brother, who forgave him and gave up their claim to compensation. The court examined this compromise carefully, noting that a settlement between parties does not automatically mean the accused walks free; the law requires courts to independently assess whether acquittal is appropriate, considering the nature of the offense and other circumstances.

The judge verified that the deceased's parents, who were alive, had genuinely pardoned Abdullah, and found that the killing appeared sudden and unpremeditated, not part of any pattern of criminal behavior by Abdullah, who was young. The State did not object to the compromise. Weighing all this, the court accepted the compromise and acquitted Abdullah, setting aside his conviction and ordering his release.

This case matters because it clarifies that under Pakistani law, courts have discretion, not an automatic obligation, to acquit based on compromise agreements in killing cases, and must weigh the circumstances before doing so.

title: Lasbella Industrial Estate Development Authority v. PRISM Printer (Pvt) Ltd.,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between Lasbella Industrial Estate Development Authority and Prism Printer (Pvt.) Ltd. over an industrial plot's electricity connection. Prism Printer had filed a civil suit seeking a declaration that it was the lawful allottee of the plot, along with a No Objection Certificate confirming no outstanding dues, and restoration of its disconnected electricity supply. The Authority had disconnected the electricity, claiming Prism Printer owed over a million rupees in unpaid charges. The trial court and the first appellate court ruled in favor of Prism Printer, but did so without properly examining evidence or the legal issues involved.

The Balochistan High Court overturned these decisions and dismissed the suit entirely. It held that the relationship between the parties was that of an electricity licensee and consumer, meaning any dispute over unpaid electricity charges had to be resolved through the Electricity Inspector under the Electricity Act, 1910, not through ordinary civil courts. The law specifically bars civil courts from deciding such disputes, and the prescribed procedure under the Electricity Rules had to be followed instead.

The court also found technical problems with how the decree was drafted, noting that a decree must match the judgment and clearly state the parties' details and relief granted.

This case matters because it clarifies that disputes over electricity charges and disconnections must go through the specialized regulatory process, not civil litigation, reinforcing the limits of civil court jurisdiction in specialized statutory matters.

title: Akhtar Muhammad v. Malik Abdul Hameed,
explainer:
This case is about a long-running dispute over a right of way. The petitioners claimed they had used a passage over land owned by the respondents for 27 years, and said the respondents blocked it by constructing something on it. The respondents denied any such right of way existed and argued the case should not proceed because it involved a "public nuisance" issue, which under the law requires prior written permission from the Advocate-General before filing suit, and also required following certain procedural rules for representative suits. Both the trial court and the appellate court agreed with the respondents and rejected the plaint without a full trial.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that the petitioners were claiming a private right of way for their personal use, not a right belonging to the general public over a recognized public road. Since no public right was involved, and only a private easement claim was being made, the case did not amount to a public nuisance, and therefore no special permission was needed to file the suit. The court noted that whether the easement actually existed still needed to be proven through evidence at trial.

The High Court set aside the lower courts' orders and sent the case back to the trial court to be decided properly, after hearing evidence. This matters because it clarifies that private disputes over rights of way don't automatically become "public nuisance" cases just because they occur on land others might use, and such technical objections shouldn't block a party from having their case heard on its merits.

title: Muhammad Imran Tehseen v Ejaz Lodhi,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with what happens to a court order attaching property when the underlying lawsuit is later dismissed. A recovery suit for over Rs. 41 lakh had been filed, and during the proceedings the trial court ordered the defendant's property to be attached, or alternatively required a bank guarantee, to secure the amount in dispute. This is a legal tool used before a final judgment to prevent a defendant from disposing of assets that might be needed to satisfy a future decree. While the petitioner's challenge to that attachment order was pending before the High Court, the trial court dismissed the original suit, and an appeal against that dismissal was filed.

The key legal question was whether the earlier attachment order survived the dismissal of the suit, especially since an appeal was still pending. The High Court held that under the law governing such attachments, once a suit is dismissed, the attachment automatically ends, even if the trial court does not explicitly say so in its order. The pendency of an appeal does not revive the attachment, and even if the appellate court later overturns the dismissal and sends the case back for further proceedings, the attachment does not automatically come back into effect. A party wanting the attachment reinstated must apply afresh for it at that stage.

This matters because it clarifies that protective measures like pre-judgment attachment are tied strictly to the life of the original suit and cannot be assumed to continue through appeals. The court accordingly dismissed the revision petition.

title: Mullah Gul Muhammad v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a tragic incident in April 2009 where a container truck traveling from Afghanistan to Pakistan was found parked near Quetta with dozens of Afghan nationals trapped inside, most of them dead from suffocation. The victims had allegedly been trafficked for forced labor. An FIR was registered, but the appellant, Mullah Gul Muhammad, was not named in it. He was implicated later, based on statements by surviving victims who identified him for the first time in court, allegedly as the owner of a hotel from which the victims had been loaded onto the container. The trial court convicted him under sections 322 and 337-L(2) of the Pakistan Penal Code, sentencing him to pay compensation (Diyat) to victims' families and to two years' imprisonment.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. The judge found that no identification parade had been conducted after his arrest, and the witnesses were not previously familiar with him, meaning their courtroom identification alone was unreliable and needed corroboration that was missing. The investigating officer had also failed to gather key evidence, and the prosecution never actually proved the appellant owned or ran the hotel in question. Given these serious gaps, the court held the prosecution failed to connect him to the crime and acquitted him, granting the benefit of the doubt.

This case highlights the importance of proper identification procedures and solid evidence in criminal trials, especially when an accused is not named in the original police report.

title: Akhtar Muhammad & Brothers v. Haji Muhammad Nabi & Brothers,
explainer:
This case is about a trade mark dispute over instant juice powder products called FRUTTI and TOP JUICES. The respondent, Haji Muhammad Nabi and Brothers, claimed to be the sole distributor of these products in Pakistan and said he had applied for and been allotted trade mark registration. He sued the appellant, Akhtar Muhammad and Brothers, for importing and selling similar products, arguing this infringed his trade mark rights. The trial court agreed and issued an interim injunction stopping the appellant from launching the FRUTTI product and stopping a related party from releasing it, provided the respondent posted a security bond.

The appellant challenged this order, arguing that no actual registration certificate had ever been issued to the respondent, only an application had been processed, and that without formal registration there could be no trade mark to infringe.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the appellant. It held that under the Trade Marks Ordinance 2001, infringement can only occur if a trade mark is actually registered, not merely applied for. Since no registration certificate existed, the respondent had no legal right to protect, meaning there was no strong case in his favor, no unfair disadvantage to him, and no risk of irreparable harm justifying an injunction. The court set aside the trial court's order and dismissed the injunction application, allowing the appeal. This matters because it clarifies that mere application for trade mark registration is not enough to claim legal protection against alleged infringement.

title: Barkat v. The State,
explainer:
This case is a criminal appeal before the Balochistan High Court by a man named Barkat, who was convicted of murdering his sister, Mst. Jamila, in what the case describes as an honour killing. The trial court had sentenced him to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay compensation to the victim's heirs. Barkat appealed, arguing the conviction was unjust and that the evidence against him was weak.

The prosecution's case relied heavily on a confession Barkat made before a magistrate, but there were problems: the confession was recorded six days after his arrest while he was in police custody, raising doubts about whether it was voluntary; the witnesses claiming to have seen the crime could not clearly establish they were actually present at the scene; and the complainant himself had not witnessed the killing. The court also noted the police investigation was poorly conducted.

Despite these weaknesses, the High Court upheld the conviction. It found that Barkat's own appeal letter, written from jail, actually supported and corroborated his earlier confession rather than contradicting it, and there was no evidence he had been coerced or mistreated. Because the confession appeared truthful and was backed by his own later statements, the court ruled the prosecution had sufficiently proven the case.

This judgment matters because it illustrates how courts evaluate confessions—especially delayed ones—and stresses that confessions need independent corroboration to be reliable, particularly in serious cases like honour killings.

title: Ali Akbar Zehri v. Syed Gul Shah,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over a government-owned residential house in Quetta. The house had originally been allotted to a retired government employee, Razia Begum. After her retirement, her husband, Syed Gul Shah, claimed he was entitled to the allotment as her spouse and filed a civil suit for declaration and permanent injunction to prevent his eviction. However, before the suit was filed, the house had already been allotted to another person, Ali Akbar Zehri. The government also argued that Gul Shah could not be accommodated since he worked in a different department, and that he had since been transferred to another district.

The Balochistan High Court held that under the relevant law and allotment rules, a transfer to another station automatically revokes a person's claim to official residence. Since Gul Shah had been transferred, his claim no longer held. The court also found that before going to civil court, a person must first pursue the remedy available under the allotment rules by approaching the designated authority (such as the Chief Secretary) with any grievance. Since Gul Shah had not done this, his suit was premature and not legally competent, so it was dismissed. The court clarified, however, that the law barring court intervention only restricts temporary injunctions, not the right to file a declaratory suit itself. This case highlights the importance of exhausting proper administrative remedies before seeking court relief in government housing allotment disputes.

title: Habib Bank Ltd v. Abid Hussain,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between Habib Bank Limited and its former employee, Abid Hussain, over the legality of his termination from service. The bank had terminated Hussain's employment while he was in jail facing a criminal case, without issuing a show-cause notice or holding any inquiry. Hussain challenged this termination before the Labour Court, which ruled against him partly on grounds of delay in filing his grievance petition. However, the Labour Appellate Tribunal later overturned that decision, ordering his reinstatement with back-benefits and setting aside the termination order. The bank then challenged the Tribunal's ruling before the Balochistan High Court.

The bank argued that Hussain's grievance petition was filed beyond the legally allowed time limit under the Industrial Relations Ordinance, and that since his termination was a straightforward termination (not a punishment for misconduct), no show-cause notice or inquiry was legally required. Hussain's side argued that he was terminated while still in jail, was never properly informed of the outcome of his grievance, and that basic principles of fairness required he be heard before such action was taken.

The court examined relevant law under the Industrial and Commercial Employment Ordinance, 1968, particularly the provisions dealing with termination simplicitor (termination without misconduct allegations). It clarified that in such cases, only one month's notice or pay in lieu of notice is legally required, not a show-cause notice or formal inquiry. This case matters because it clarifies employers' obligations when ending employment without alleging wrongdoing

title: Muhammad Illyas v. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Muhammad Ilyas who was caught driving a vehicle carrying 25 kilograms of hashish, hidden under bedding in the car. He was traveling with two other men, one a passenger and one a cleaner. A trial court convicted him under Pakistan's narcotics law and sentenced him to life imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the prosecution's case was weak because of delays in filing the police report, delays in sending drug samples for testing, lack of independent witnesses, and contradictions in witness statements. He also argued that a co-passenger had confessed that the drugs and bedding belonged to him, so Ilyas should not be held responsible.

The High Court rejected the appeal. It noted that Ilyas never denied that the drugs were found in his vehicle while he was driving it, so minor contradictions in witness testimony mattered less. Under the law, once possession is established, there is a legal presumption of guilt against the accused. The co-accused's confession only covered 4 kilograms of the hashish, leaving 21 kilograms unexplained. Since Ilyas offered no explanation for this remaining amount found in his vehicle, the court held he failed to prove his innocence. The court therefore upheld his life sentence, reinforcing how narcotics law places the burden on the person in control of a vehicle to account for drugs found in it.

title: Kamaluddin v Syed Muteebullah,
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant dispute over a commercial property in Pishin, Balochistan. Syed Muteebullah claimed he owned a property and had rented it to Kamaluddin and two others starting in 2006. He sought their eviction, alleging they had not paid rent, made unauthorized construction, sublet part of the premises without permission, and damaged the property, and he also wanted the premises back for his own business use.

The tenants denied ever being tenants at all. Instead, they claimed to be the actual owners of the property. The Rent Controller in Pishin sided with the landlord, ordering the tenants to vacate and pay overdue rent, without first resolving the more basic dispute over whether a landlord-tenant relationship even existed.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found this was a critical error. Since the tenants completely denied being tenants and asserted ownership themselves, the court held that the question of whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed had to be decided first, before any ejectment order could be made. The court noted there was no solid evidence of a rental agreement, and revenue records raised doubts about who actually owned the property. Because of this, the High Court set aside the Rent Controller's decision and dismissed the eviction application, ruling that ownership disputes like this should instead be resolved by a proper civil court.

title: Muhammad Musa v. Hamid Ali,
explainer:
This case was about a property dispute in which the petitioners claimed ownership of land, partly through a gift and partly through inherited rights. During the trial, they tried to submit will and gift deeds as evidence, but did so years after the lawsuit began and well past the stage required by law for filing documents. The trial court refused to allow these late documents, and the petitioners challenged that refusal before the Balochistan High Court through a revision petition.

The High Court first addressed whether such an interlocutory order could even be challenged through a revision petition. It ruled that revision is not limited only to final judgments or decrees, but can also apply to interim orders that affect the substantial rights of the parties, even if no appeal is available against them.

On the main issue, the court found that the petitioners failed to justify why they waited so long to produce the documents. They knew about these documents earlier but gave no reasonable explanation for the delay. Since procedural rules require timely submission of documents, and exceptions are only allowed when good cause is shown, the court held that the trial judge had rightly rejected the late submission.

The High Court therefore dismissed the revision petition, upholding the trial court's decision. The case clarifies that courts have discretion to reject late evidence unless a valid reason for delay is shown, and that such rulings can still be reviewed through revision.

title: Haji Tor Khan v Government of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute between private individuals (the petitioners) and the Government of Balochistan over ownership and possession of a piece of land. The government filed a suit claiming ownership of the land, arguing that the petitioners' possession was unauthorized and illegal. The petitioners argued they had rightfully purchased the land from previous owners, had been in possession for generations, built houses and shops on it, installed tube wells, and that the government's long silence about their occupation amounted to acceptance of their rights. They also raised technical objections, including that the suit was filed too late (barred by limitation), that not all persons in possession of the land were included as parties, and that the property description in the plaint was inadequate.

Lower courts (a Senior Civil Judge and an Additional District Judge on appeal) both ruled in favor of the government, and the petitioners then challenged this in the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the land was officially recorded in government revenue records, which was not disputed by the petitioners. While the petitioners claimed to have purchased the land, they failed to produce any valid title documents proving their sellers actually owned the land or had legal title to sell. Mere possession, without proof of legal title, was not sufficient to defeat the recorded ownership.

This case reinforces an important principle: physical possession of land alone does not establish ownership, and anyone claiming purchase-based title must prove their sellers had valid, provable ownership.

title: Haji Nizamuddin v. Haji Payo Din,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over ownership of a shop in Zhob, Balochistan. The petitioners (Haji Nizamuddin and others) filed a civil suit claiming the shop was jointly owned property and sought a declaration of their ownership share along with possession after partition. The respondent (Haji Payo Din) denied this, claiming exclusive ownership through an official allotment document (PATTA) from 1980.

The trial court and the appellate court both rejected the petitioners' suit, reasoning that the question of ownership had already been settled earlier by the Rent Controller during separate eviction proceedings, and that this earlier decision barred the new suit under the principle of res judicata (meaning the same issue cannot be litigated twice).

The Balochistan High Court disagreed and set aside both lower court orders. It held that a Rent Controller, acting under rent laws, only has jurisdiction to decide the relationship between landlord and tenant—not true ownership of property. The term landlord in rent law can include someone merely authorized to collect rent, not necessarily the actual owner. Since ownership is a substantive property right, only a regular civil court can determine it, through a full trial with evidence. The lower courts had wrongly decided the ownership question without even framing proper issues or recording evidence.

The case was sent back to the trial court to be decided properly, with issues framed and evidence taken. This judgment clarifies the limited authority of Rent Controllers and protects parties' rights to have ownership disputes fully tried in ordinary courts.

title: Rehmat Ali v. Abdul Samad,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute between family members in Turbat, Balochistan. Abdul Samad claimed he had lawfully purchased land and rooms from his father in 1984 and sought a court declaration confirming his ownership, along with eviction of relatives (the petitioners) who were living in some of the rooms. The petitioners denied his ownership, arguing the property belonged jointly to the family and that their father had allowed them to live there.

The trial court initially dismissed Abdul Samad's suit, but on appeal, the Appellate Court reversed this and ruled in his favor. The petitioners then challenged that appellate decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found a serious procedural flaw: during the trial, a key witness for Abdul Samad had been re-examined and asked about entirely new matters, not just clarifications of earlier cross-examination, without giving the opposing side a chance to cross-examine him again on those new points. This violated the proper legal procedure for re-examining witnesses under the law of evidence. Because of this defect, the witness's re-examination testimony could not be relied upon. The High Court also found that the Appellate Court had not properly evaluated the evidence and had reached conclusions inconsistent with the record.

As a result, the High Court set aside the Appellate Court's judgment and restored the trial court's original decision, with some modifications. This case highlights the importance of following fair procedure when examining witnesses, since violations can undermine the reliability of evidence and the fairness of a trial.

title: Azizullah v. Mst. Hameeda Begum,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute over two pieces of land in Quetta. The original owner, Mst. Hameeda Begum, claimed that her adopted son, working together with another person, fraudulently sold her land without her real consent. The land then changed hands multiple times through a chain of sales before finally being bought by Aziz Ullah and another buyer, the petitioners in this case. Hameeda Begum sued to have all these sales cancelled and to have her ownership and possession restored. Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled in her favour.

The petitioners then challenged these rulings, arguing they were innocent, good-faith buyers who had built houses on the land and invested money, and therefore should be protected under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, which shields genuine buyers who purchase from someone appearing to be the rightful owner, provided they took reasonable care to verify ownership.

The High Court rejected this argument. It explained that to claim this protection, buyers must prove the seller appeared to be the true owner with the real owner's consent, and that they themselves acted carefully and in good faith. Here, the buyers' own sale documents contradicted their court statements, and there was no proof they had verified ownership before buying. Since two courts had already agreed on the facts, and the buyers failed to show any legal error, the High Court dismissed their petition, upholding the original owner's title.

title: Syed Saeed Rehman v. Muhammad Azhar Jamal,
explainer:
This case involved a money recovery suit. A creditor (Muhammad Azhar Jamal) had won a decree against a debtor (Syed Saeed Rehman) for Rs.26 lacs. When the debtor failed to pay, he was sent to civil prison. He then appealed, and the High Court released him from prison on condition that he provide sureties and not leave the court's jurisdiction or dispose of property until sureties worth Rs.26 lacs were furnished. Two individuals agreed to stand as sureties, each bound for Rs.13 lacs, on the condition that they would produce the debtor before the court whenever required.

The debtor later failed to appear both before the executing court and during his appeal hearing. The creditor then asked the court to forfeit the sureties and recover the entire decretal amount directly from the two guarantors.

The High Court examined Section 145 of the Civil Procedure Code, which allows a decree to be enforced against a surety, but only to the extent that the surety personally agreed to be liable. Reviewing the actual wording of the surety bonds, the judge found that the two men had only promised to produce the debtor in court, not to pay the decretal amount themselves. Therefore, the court could not hold them liable for the Rs.26 lacs debt. The appeal itself was dismissed for non-prosecution since the debtor never showed up. This case clarifies that sureties can only be held liable strictly according to the specific terms they agreed to, not for obligations beyond what they promised.

title: Haji Attaullah Baloch v. Asadullah Baloch,
explainer:
This case involves a challenge to a 2008 Balochistan provincial assembly election. Haji Attaullah Baloch, who lost to Asadullah Baloch by a narrow margin, filed an election petition asking the court to void the results of one polling station, or the entire election, alleging serious irregularities.

The petitioner claimed that the winning candidate, a former District Nazim with local influence, had the original Presiding Officer at a key polling station replaced at the last minute with his own real uncle, without proper approval. He alleged this Presiding Officer then rigged the process: his polling agent was beaten and thrown out, unidentified people voted without identity cards, the officer himself allegedly stamped ballots in favor of the respondent, and vote counts didn't match up with other records.

The Election Tribunal, however, found that most of the petitioner's evidence was circumstantial rather than direct proof of wrongdoing. While the blood relationship between the winning candidate and the Presiding Officer was acknowledged, the court held that this alone doesn't invalidate an election unless it's proven the appointment was manipulated with intent to secure an unfair result. No witness testified to actual vote-rigging or manipulation of results, and the law itself states that a candidate's or agent's absence doesn't automatically invalidate election proceedings. Since the petitioner failed to prove corrupt practice or undue influence with sufficient evidence, the tribunal dismissed the petition, upholding the original election result.

title: Shah Wali v. Quetta Chamber of Commerce & Industry,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over elections at the Quetta Chamber of Commerce and Industry. A group of members (the appellants) challenged decisions made in September and December 2009 by the relevant authority under the Trade Organizations Ordinance, 2009. They alleged that the chamber's election process was flawed due to forged voter lists, false ID and tax numbers, improper membership decisions, and that sitting office-bearers had not completed their required two-year term, making the elections illegal.

The appellants first went to the Director-General of Trade Organizations, who is the final authority on election-related matters before an election is held. When that route failed to give them full relief, they appealed further, but this additional appeal was rejected as not allowed under the law, since the Ordinance clearly states no further appeal lies from the Director-General's decision on such pre-election matters.

The High Court also examined whether the appellants' appeal to it was filed too late. Although there was a 28-day delay beyond the 30-day limit, the court excused the delay because there was no clear proof of exactly when the order had been officially served on the appellants, making it unfair to strictly enforce the deadline.

However, on the core issue, the court ruled that the lower authority was correct to dismiss the appeal as not maintainable, since the law does not allow a further appeal in this type of election dispute. The appeal was therefore dismissed, reinforcing that decisions by the Director-General in pre-election matters are final and cannot be challenged further under this Ordinance.

title: Mohi-ud-Din v. Muhammad Iftikhar Siddique,
explainer:
Mohi-ud-Din bought a house in Quetta and took possession of it, claiming to be the lawful purchaser through a proper sale. Muhammad Iftikhar Siddique filed a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, alleging that he was the rightful heir and occupant of the same property since 1961, and that Mohi-ud-Din and another person had illegally broken the locks and taken over the house while he was away. The trial court (Sessions Judge, Quetta) accepted the complainant's request for interim relief and ordered the property restored to him, relying mainly on a police report that supported the complainant's version, and on the fact that the petitioner had not produced ownership documents.

Mohi-ud-Din challenged this order before the Balochistan High Court, arguing he was never given notice or a chance to be heard, that the trial had not even begun, and that the police report relied upon came from the wrong police station, one that had no jurisdiction over the area where the house was actually located.

The High Court agreed with the petitioner. It held that since he was in possession of the property, he had a right to be heard before being dispossessed, and that the trial court wrongly relied on a report from an unrelated police station whose officer was actually a party to the case. Because these legal requirements were ignored, the court set aside the restoration order and accepted the revision petition, sending the matter back for proper process.

title: Saleh Muhammad v. Muhammad Ishaque,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over government-allotted residential accommodation in Quetta. Muhammad Ishaque, the respondent, was formally allotted a government house through an official order in September 2009, but Saleh Muhammad, the petitioner, remained in illegal occupation despite ejectment notices. Ishaque filed a civil suit seeking a court declaration confirming his right as lawful allottee and asking for possession. The trial court decreed in his favour, especially since the government authorities themselves consented to the suit. Saleh Muhammad, who had been proceeded against ex parte (meaning the case went forward without his participation because he failed to respond to court notices), later appealed, but his appeal was dismissed as time-barred. He then filed this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court, arguing he was never properly served notice and that the appeal's limitation period was wrongly calculated.

The High Court rejected his arguments. It found that court notices had been properly affixed on his house's door after failed attempts at direct service, which counts as valid substituted service under the law, and that he clearly knew about the case but chose not to appear. The court also clarified that the correct limitation law (Article 152) gave him only thirty days to appeal, which he missed by six days without any valid explanation. Additionally, the court held that since Ishaque was simply enforcing a valid existing allotment order rather than challenging an allotment decision itself, his original suit was legally maintainable.

title: Ibrar Hussain v. Abdul Karim,
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant dispute over property in Quetta. Ibrar Hussain claimed he had bought the ground floor property from Abdul Karim, and that Abdul Karim and his wife, Mst. Qamar Begum, were his tenants living on the first floor. He filed for their eviction. The wife denied being anyone's tenant, insisting the property was actually purchased and built with her own money, though registered through her husband, who later sold it to the appellant without her consent. The husband never showed up in court to defend the sale or contest the case.

The Rent Controller dismissed the eviction application, and the High Court upheld that decision. The court explained that simply proving ownership was not enough - the appellant also had to prove an actual landlord-tenant relationship existed, meaning someone must be legally obligated to pay him rent. Mere physical occupation of a property does not make someone a tenant, since people can also occupy premises as owners, licensees, or trespassers. Since the wife claimed to possess the property in her own right as owner, not through her husband, she did not automatically become the new owner's tenant just because her husband sold the property. The court also noted the appellant should first get his ownership title legally confirmed by a court before seeking eviction, especially since the wife had separately filed a suit challenging the sale itself. This case highlights that ownership and tenancy are legally distinct, and eviction requires proof of both.

title: Liaquat v. Haji Allauddin,
explainer:
This case concerns a landlord-tenant dispute under the West Pakistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959. The landlord, Haji Alla-ud-Din, sought to evict his tenant, Liaquat, from a shop on two grounds: that the tenant had defaulted in paying rent since September 2004, and that the landlord genuinely needed the shop for his son to start a spare parts business. The Rent Controller ruled in the landlord's favor on both grounds, ordering the tenant to vacate. The tenant appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

On the rent default issue, the High Court agreed with the lower court. The tenant claimed he had tried to pay rent by money order, which was refused, so he deposited it in court instead, but he could not prove this refusal by producing postal officials or records, so the default finding was upheld.

However, on the claim of genuine personal need, the High Court disagreed. It found that the landlord had filed several nearly identical eviction cases against other tenants using the same grounds and even the same alleged default dates, suggesting a pattern of bad faith aimed at re-renting vacated shops at higher rents. Notably, the landlord's son, for whom the shop was supposedly needed, never testified to support the claim. The court ruled this showed the landlord's need was not genuine, and set aside that part of the eviction order. This case illustrates how courts scrutinize landlords' motives, not just tenants' compliance, in eviction disputes.

title: Jamaluddin v. Haji Gul Khan,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Balochistan between two groups of relatives claiming shares in agricultural land in Mouza Olyani, Tehsil Barkhan. The plaintiffs, who said they were joint owners in possession of the land, filed a suit asking that the land be declared joint property and divided among the co-owners according to their shares. The defendants argued they had already been in separate possession of a quarter share for twenty years following a private partition, and they challenged whether the local court (Majlis-e-Shoora) even had the power to hear this kind of case.

The trial court had ruled in favour of the plaintiffs and ordered partition. On appeal, the Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that since both sides agreed they were co-owners and there was no real dispute over title, the case was essentially about dividing shamilat (jointly owned) land. Under the West Pakistan Land Revenue Act, 1967, such partition matters must go through a Revenue Officer, not a civil court, unless a genuine question of title arises, in which case only that specific issue can go to civil court under Section 145 of the Act. Since this was a straightforward partition dispute, the civil court had no jurisdiction to decide it at all.

As a result, the High Court set aside the earlier judgment and dismissed the plaintiffs' suit entirely, sending the matter back to the proper revenue authorities. The case highlights the strict divide between revenue and civil court jurisdiction over land partition in Pakistan.

title: Muhammad Lal v The State,
explainer:
This is a jail appeal decided by the Balochistan High Court in a murder case. Muhammad Lal had been convicted by a trial court for killing Nadir Khan and sentenced to ten years imprisonment plus payment of diyat (compensation) to the victim's heirs. He appealed, arguing he was falsely implicated due to a personal grudge and tribal feud, and asked for his sentence to be reduced and to be excused from paying diyat because of his poor financial condition.

The prosecution's case relied mainly on the accused's confessional statement, since there were no direct eyewitnesses and the physical evidence, like the recovered knife and forensic reports, was not conclusively linked to the crime. The defense argued the confession was recorded after a suspicious seven-day delay and had been retracted, so it could not support a conviction.

The High Court examined whether the confession was voluntary and true, and whether it was corroborated by other evidence. It found that the accused never complained of torture or coercion when he had the opportunity before the magistrate, and that the confession matched the facts of the case and was supported by other evidence. The court upheld the conviction, ruling that a retracted confession can still support a conviction if it is voluntary, true, and corroborated. It also clarified that diyat payments must not be less than the value of 30,630 grams of silver, though courts can consider parties' financial circumstances in fixing the amount. The appeal was dismissed.

title: Jamaluddin v. Chief Justice Balochistan High Court,
explainer:
This case concerns a subordinate judiciary officer, Jamaluddin, who was reverted from the post of Senior Civil Judge to Judicial Magistrate and had his promotion withheld for three years through an order dated 21 July 2009 (notified 27 July 2009). He challenged this action before the Balochistan High Court, arguing he was never informed of the disciplinary proceedings against him, only learned of the penalty in early 2010, and was thus condemned without a fair hearing. He also argued the punishment was too harsh for what he called a minor procedural lapse in handling a confessional statement.

Before addressing these merits, the court first had to decide whether his departmental representation had been filed within the legally allowed time. Under the applicable rules, an employee has 60 days to file such a representation. The court found that Jamaluddin's application was filed roughly five months late, and that he gave inconsistent and unsupported explanations for the delay, failing to prove he genuinely lacked knowledge of the order earlier.

Because he could not justify the delay, the court held his representation was time-barred and upheld the department's rejection of it, dismissing his appeal without examining the substantive fairness of the reversion order.

This case illustrates how procedural deadlines for administrative appeals can prevent courts from even considering whether a punishment was justified, underscoring the importance of civil servants acting promptly when challenging adverse orders.

title: Mahmood Ahmed v. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man convicted of possessing an unlicensed pistol under the West Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965. The prosecution claimed that while the appellant was in custody for a separate murder case, he confessed and led police to a hidden pistol behind a cabin in Quetta, resulting in the recovery of the weapon along with cartridges. Because he could not produce a license for the pistol, he was charged, tried, and convicted by a trial court, receiving three years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious flaws in how the case was investigated and proved. The actual disclosure memo (the document recording the accused's confession and pointing out the weapon's location) and the seizure memo were never properly produced as evidence, and no witness verified them in court. The trial court had simply accepted the prosecution's assertions as fact without examining the actual record. Key witnesses did not properly support the recovery process, and evidence from a separate case file was relied upon without formally placing it on record, which the court said was legally impermissible.

Because of these gaps and contradictions, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Following the principle that any doubt in a criminal case must benefit the accused, the court set aside the conviction and acquitted the appellant, ordering his release. The case highlights the importance of proper evidence handling and documentation in criminal trials, especially regarding confessions and recoveries made during police investigations.

title: Mahmood Ahmed v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Mahmood Ahmed, who was sentenced to death by a trial court in Quetta for murder under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, and the case also came before the court as a Murder Reference for confirmation of the death sentence, as required by law in capital cases.

The High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's case. No one had actually witnessed the murder, and even the complainant was not an eyewitness. The accused was only named four days after the incident, based on secondhand information from someone who also had not seen the crime. The accused's confession came after four days of unexplained police custody, raising suspicion that it may have been obtained through pressure rather than given voluntarily. The court noted that a retracted confession cannot support a conviction unless proven truthful and corroborated by other evidence. Additionally, the alleged motive was never proven, the recovery of the murder weapon was questionable due to inconsistencies, and forensic evidence (crime shell casings) was sent for testing more than two weeks after being collected, further undermining reliability.

Given these gaps and unexplained inconsistencies, the court held that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It set aside the death sentence, acquitted Mahmood Ahmed, and ordered his release. The judgment underscores the importance of solid, corroborated evidence and proper procedure before convicting someone, especially in cases carrying the death penalty.

title: Issuance of Notice against money laundering allegation
explainer:
This case involved a challenge to a notice issued by the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) against a citizen under the Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010. The petitioner, Ahmad Bin Shahid, approached the Lahore High Court to contest a call-up notice dated 10.07.2024 through which the FIA had initiated an inquiry against him for alleged money laundering.

The petitioner argued that this notice violated the principles laid down by the same court in an earlier landmark case, Abdul Saboor v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2024 Lahore 244). That earlier ruling had held that under Section 9 of the Act, any notice issued to a person suspected of money laundering must, at minimum, clearly state the details of the alleged offence and the specific property said to have been acquired through proceeds of crime. This is necessary so the person can properly respond to the allegations. A notice lacking this information cannot be considered valid.

The court examined the notice issued to the petitioner and found that the FIA had failed to follow these requirements, making the notice invalid and issued without lawful authority. Accordingly, the court set aside the notice.

However, the court clarified that the FIA remains free to proceed against the petitioner following proper procedure, in line with the standards set out in the Abdul Saboor judgment. This case reinforces that investigating agencies must provide sufficient information in such notices to protect individuals' right to respond to serious allegations.

title: -If a convict has been sentenced to death as ta'zir then all legal heirs of deceased must enter into a compromise to enable compounding of offence u/S. 345(2) of Code
explainer:
This Supreme Court judgment dealt with three separate criminal appeals of men sentenced to death for murder (qatl-i-amd), whose convictions had been upheld by the Lahore High Court. In each case, at least one legal heir of the victim had forgiven the convict or entered into a compromise, but not all heirs had agreed to do so. The central question was whether such a partial compromise, by some but not all heirs, could justify reducing the death sentence to life imprisonment.

The Supreme Court clarified that under the law, a formal compounding of the offence requires agreement of all legal heirs of the deceased. Where only some heirs compromise, this cannot automatically result in a lesser sentence. However, the Court said such partial compromise is not irrelevant either it is one factor among many that courts may consider when deciding whether to impose death or life imprisonment, since the law requires courts to weigh all facts and circumstances of the case, even where all heirs have compromised, the court retains discretion to still impose punishment.

Applying this reasoning to the facts, the Court found the murders in question to be particularly brutal, premeditated, and violent, involving family members and repeated stabbings or shootings. Despite compromises by some heirs, the Court refused to reduce the death sentences, holding that the gravity and manner of the killings did not warrant leniency. The case is significant for clarifying how compromises by victims families interact with sentencing discretion in murder cases.

title: Custody of Minor Boy of Over 7 Years Age
explainer:
This case concerns a custody dispute over a young boy named Ali Raza, whose mother died when he was an infant. He was raised by his maternal grandmother, Mst. Jamila Bibi, until his father, Shabir Ahmad, applied to a Family Court seeking custody once the child had crossed the age of seven.

The trial court (Guardian Judge) and the appellate court both ruled in favor of the father, relying on the traditional principle from Muhammadan Law that a father is generally entitled to custody once a boy turns seven. However, they did not properly examine or record findings on whether giving custody to the father would actually serve the child's welfare, even though this was a specific issue framed for trial.

The Lahore High Court found this approach legally flawed. Citing a Supreme Court precedent (Sardar Hussain's case), the High Court held that a child's age crossing seven is not an automatic ticket to custody for the father - the paramount consideration must always be the welfare of the minor, based on evidence. Since neither lower court had properly assessed the evidence on this point, their judgments could not stand.

The High Court set aside both rulings and sent the case back to the Guardian Judge, directing it to hear both parties again and decide the matter specifically on the question of the child's welfare, within a set timeframe.

This case reinforces the principle that in custody disputes, courts must prioritize the actual best interests of the child over rigid age-based rules, even in disputes involving extended family members like grandparents.

title: Allah Almighty shows His love and affection with a person who speaks nothing except truth
explainer:
This case concerned Bilal Arshad, who was convicted by a trial court in Faisalabad of murdering his uncle Nadeem Aslam and wounding another uncle, Ijaz Ahmad, following a quarrel that began when the deceased objected to the appellant entering the family home while armed with a pistol. The trial court had sentenced him to death for murder, along with separate prison terms and fines for house trespass, causing hurt, and injuring another person. The case came before the Lahore High Court both as the appellant's appeal against conviction and as a murder reference required for confirming any death sentence.

The High Court found that the prosecution had proved its case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt, noting that when questioned during trial under Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the appellant admitted to the occurrence despite having contested the charges earlier. The court viewed this admission favorably, treating his eventual truthfulness as a mitigating factor. It also took into account that the appellant was a teenager at the time of the offense.

Based on these considerations, the court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment, declining to confirm the death penalty. The murder reference was answered in the negative. This case illustrates how appellate courts in Pakistan can reduce sentences by weighing factors like the offender's age and conduct during trial, even after affirming guilt, and shows the interplay between criminal appeals and the mandatory judicial review of death sentences.

title: Bail Granted in 17/22 Emigration Ordinance Case
explainer:
This case is about a man named Siddique who was accused of fraud related to overseas job placement. According to the police report, he and a co-accused allegedly took Rs. 960,000 from a complainant, promising to arrange police jobs in Bahrain for the complainant and his friends, but failed to deliver. He was charged under Sections 17 and 22 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1979, which deal with illegal recruitment practices for jobs abroad.

Siddique was arrested and sought post-arrest bail from the Lahore High Court. The court noted several weaknesses in the case against him: no passport, documents, or money were recovered from him during his arrest; he had no prior criminal record; the investigating officer admitted Siddique was not a licensed travel agent; and there was no documentary evidence of the alleged promise or the full amount supposedly received—only a cheque for Rs. 460,000, less than the claimed total.

Given these gaps, the court found the case required further inquiry into Siddique's actual guilt, which under Pakistani law is grounds for bail. The court also noted that while Section 22 carries a possible sentence of up to fourteen years, it allows for a fine as an alternative punishment, making continued detention less justified.

The court granted bail, requiring Siddique to submit bonds of Rs. 200,000 with two sureties. This case illustrates how courts weigh evidentiary gaps and possible alternate sentences when deciding pre-trial bail in fraud-related emigration cases.

title: Condition of Divorce Mentioned in Nikahnama
explainer:
This case concerns a couple whose marriage broke down, leading to multiple lawsuits over maintenance, dowry, dower (mahr), and money claimed under conditions written in their nikahnama (marriage contract). The husband, Muhammad Sajjad, challenged decisions by family courts and an appellate court in Punjab.

One key dispute involved a five-marla house promised as part of the dower. The court examined the marriage contract documents and testimony from the marriage registrar, finding that the property description had been legitimately amended with both parties' consent. The court upheld the lower courts' decision awarding the house to the wife.

The more significant legal question involved Rs. 500,000 that the wife claimed under a clause in the nikahnama stating the husband must pay this amount if he ever divorced her or took a second wife. The lower courts had ordered him to pay this sum. The High Court disagreed, ruling that under Islamic law, a husband holds an absolute, God-given right to divorce his wife, and no contractual condition can restrict or penalize the exercise of this religious right. The judge cited Quranic verses, Hadith, and Islamic legal scholarship to support this reasoning.

As a result, the court partly accepted the husband's petition, setting aside the part of the ruling that penalized him financially for divorcing or remarrying, while upholding the other financial awards to the wife. The case matters because it clarifies that marriage contract clauses cannot override or restrict a husband's fundamental right to pronounce divorce under Islamic law.
