title: Exemption from Goods Exit Tax
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over whether a local government body, Zila Council Jhang, could impose an export tax on crushed stone produced by Daewoo Corporation, a South Korean company building a section of the National Highway Authority's Motorway Project.

Daewoo had been authorized to excavate stone from hills near Rabwah for the road construction. It extracted the raw stone from a quarry located within the territory of Town Committee Rabwah, but transported it to crushing plants located within the jurisdiction of District Council Jhang, where the stone was mechanically processed into crushed stone. The District Council then imposed an export tax on this crushed stone as it left its territory, which Daewoo challenged, partly by arguing it deserved constitutional protection as an entity connected to a government project.

The Supreme Court rejected Daewoo's claim of exemption, finding it was a private foreign company with no government ownership, control, or funding, and therefore could not claim the special constitutional protections available to government bodies.

On the core tax question, the Court held that because the crushing process transformed the raw stone into a new commodity, this amounted to production, giving District Council Jhang lawful authority to tax its export. The Court also ruled that a government-issued "model schedule" of tax rates was only a guideline, not binding, so the Council's notified rate of Rs. 2 per quintal was valid.

The judgment matters because it clarifies when local councils can tax goods leaving their territory, and confirms that companies working on public projects don't automatically gain government-level legal immunities.

title: Ticket is a contract between airline and passenger
explainer:
This case involved a passenger, Daoud Shami, who sued Emirates Airlines for damages after he was prevented from boarding his connecting flight from Lahore to Dubai on his way to attend his graduation ceremony in Washington D.C. He claimed this caused him mental shock and financial loss due to breach of contract, since his onward flight from London to Washington had been cancelled by Virgin Atlantic Airlines, allegedly because he lacked a UK visa.

The trial court initially ruled in his favor, but the Lahore High Court overturned that decision, finding that the ticket was actually issued by Continental Airlines (not properly made a party to the case), that the original ticket showing the actual terms of travel was never produced as evidence, and that Emirates Airlines could not be held liable for damages it had no way of anticipating.

The Supreme Court examined international aviation law, including the Warsaw Convention and the Carriage by Air Act, 1966, confirming that an airline ticket serves as evidence of a contract between the airline and passenger, with its printed terms governing that relationship. The Court also reiterated basic contract law principles: a party can only recover damages that naturally flow from a breach, or special damages if the other party knew in advance about special circumstances that made such losses foreseeable.

This case is significant because it clarifies how ticket terms function as contractual evidence in air travel disputes, and reinforces that airlines cannot be held liable for losses they had no knowledge of or control over.

title: Delay in MLC shows Malafide
explainer:
This case comes from the Lahore High Court, Multan Bench, and deals with a request for pre-arrest bail. The petitioner, Hafiz Ghulam Haider, was accused in an FIR of assaulting a woman, outraging her modesty, and extorting Rs. 12,000 from her. He sought protection from arrest under Section 498 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The court examined the evidence and found several problems with the complainant's case. First, there was an unexplained delay of about eight days in filing the FIR, which courts generally view with suspicion since it allows time for fabrication or consultation. Second, while the FIR did not mention any weapon being used, the medical report (MLC) claimed a blunt weapon caused the injuries, an inconsistency the court found suspicious. Third, the medical examination itself was conducted eight days after the alleged incident, further weakening its reliability. Finally, the complainant never appeared before a radiologist to support her injury claims with additional medical evidence.

Based on these gaps, the court concluded there wasn't sufficient genuine evidence connecting the petitioner to the alleged crime, and that false implication was a real possibility. The court confirmed his pre-arrest bail, on condition of bonds worth Rs. 200,000.

This case matters because it illustrates how delays and inconsistencies in filing complaints and gathering medical evidence can seriously undermine a prosecution's credibility, and reaffirms that pre-arrest bail exists to protect people from misuse of the legal process,

title: PLJ 2018 Peshawar 1
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over dower and maintenance filed in a Family Court in Peshawar. A wife and her children (petitioners) had sued her husband (respondent) for recovery of dower, money she claimed to have given him, and monthly maintenance for herself and four children. While the case was pending, the trial court granted interim maintenance of only Rs. 5,000 per month for the youngest child, and refused any interim maintenance for the other three children, after the husband denied he was their biological father, claiming they were from the wife's first marriage.

The wife then approached the Peshawar High Court asking it to increase the maintenance amounts. The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that since the husband had specifically disputed paternity of three of the children in his written statement, this was a factual dispute that could only be resolved through evidence at trial, not through a writ petition. Courts exercising constitutional jurisdiction cannot decide disputed facts unless a party's right is clear beyond doubt. The court also noted the trial court had correctly rejected the husband's claim that the youngest child was illegitimate, since there was no evidence supporting his allegation of an undissolved prior marriage.

The judgment matters because it clarifies that interim orders in family maintenance cases, especially where paternity is contested, are provisional and not ordinarily open to challenge through writ petitions; such disputes must await full trial evidence.

title: Vendee has to prove Title, Consideration and Delivery of Possession
explainer:
This case involved a woman, Surraya Bibi, who owned about 15 kanals of land. A sale deed showed the land had been transferred to her nephews, the sons of her brother. She sued to cancel the sale deed, claiming she had only leased the land to her brother, who fraudulently used that arrangement to create a fake sale in his sons' favor, without her consent or any payment. The trial court initially decreed in her favor, but after remand and additional evidence, both the trial court and the appellate court dismissed her suit and upheld the sale.

She then approached the Lahore High Court. The Court ruled in her favor, setting aside the lower courts' decisions. It held that to prove a valid sale, the buyer must show three things: the seller had legal title, proper payment was made, and possession was actually handed over. Simply having a registered sale deed does not automatically prove these facts if the transaction is disputed - the burden falls on the buyer to prove it.

The Court also found a serious legal defect: the sale deed, being a document creating financial obligations, legally required at least two proper attesting witnesses. Here, one signatory was merely an "identifier" of the seller, not a true witness to the transaction, making the document technically inadmissible as evidence.

The Court explained that while it normally does not disturb matching findings by lower courts, it can and must intervene when those findings result from clear misreading of evidence or violate mandatory legal requirements, as happened here.

title: PLJ 2017 Islamabad 210
explainer:
This case involved Islamabad Law College's attempt to get affiliation with Islamia University, Bahawalpur (IUB) to run its LL.B program. Under the law, such affiliation required a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the Higher Education Commission (HEC). The college applied for the NOC, and HEC pointed out various deficiencies that needed to be fixed. Even though the college claimed to have addressed these issues, HEC did not issue the final NOC, and the college's requests and reminders went unanswered. Meanwhile, the college had already enrolled students for the 2015-16 academic session without having obtained the required NOC or affiliation, and it approached the Islamabad High Court seeking a direction for HEC to issue the NOC.

The court dismissed the petition on two main grounds. First, it held that the petition was not properly filed because Islamabad Law College, as a sole proprietorship, is not a legal entity capable of suing or being sued in its own name - only a sole proprietor could have filed the case. Second, on the merits, the court found no illegality or unfairness in HEC's refusal to grant the NOC, since real deficiencies remained unresolved. The court also criticized the college for admitting students without proper affiliation and without warning them of this risk, and noted that universities should decide on affiliation before, not during, an academic session. This case highlights the importance of institutions meeting regulatory requirements before enrolling students, and clarifies technical rules about who can legally bring a court case.

title: Provisions of CPC are not applicable before Family Court
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over dower and maintenance in Azad Jammu and Kashmir. A wife, Lubna Sadiq, had filed a suit before the Family Court seeking dower and maintenance from her husband, Rashid Shamim. While the case was ongoing, she gave birth and applied to add her newborn child, Falak, as an additional plaintiff in the maintenance suit, also seeking recovery of birth-related expenses. The husband objected, arguing that the Family Courts Act, 1993 has no provision allowing such amendments, and that adding a new party and new claims would improperly turn a family maintenance suit into something resembling an ordinary civil suit. The Family Court allowed the amendment, and the husband challenged this decision before the High Court through a writ petition.

The High Court upheld the Family Court's decision. It explained that the Civil Procedure Code does not strictly apply to Family Court proceedings, since the Family Courts Act is a special law meant to provide speedy relief to families. However, where the Family Courts Act is silent on a procedural matter, courts may still apply general principles of justice, equity, and good conscience, drawing on CPC principles when they don't conflict with the Act. Since there was no specific bar on allowing amendments or including a family member like a minor child in a maintenance suit, and since a father is legally obligated to support his children's genuine needs, the court found no illegality in allowing the child to be added as a plaintiff. The writ petition was dismissed, meaning the original amendment order stood.

title: PLJ 2015 Lahore 384
explainer:
This case involved a marriage dispute between Abdul Rafay Butt, an MBBS doctor, and his wife Faiza Meer, who had married in 2010 with dower fixed at gold bangles worth Rs. 350,000. Shortly after marriage, the husband went abroad for work, and the marriage broke down. The wife filed a suit seeking dissolution of marriage, return of dowry articles, dower, and maintenance. The husband agreed to end the marriage through khula (a wife-initiated divorce), and the Family Court dissolved the marriage but ordered separate proceedings on the other claims.

The Family Court ruled against the wife on maintenance and dower but partially awarded her dowry articles. On appeal, the Additional District Judge upheld the dismissal of the husband's appeal and partly allowed the wife's appeal, granting her maintenance for the iddat period (the mandatory waiting period after divorce) and dowry articles or their cash value.

The husband challenged these decisions in the High Court, arguing he shouldn't have to pay maintenance and that the wife should return the dower since the divorce was via khula. The High Court dismissed his petition. It held that factual findings by lower courts, reached through proper legal process, cannot be overturned unless there is serious injustice. The husband failed to prove he actually paid the dower at the time of marriage, as he didn't produce witnesses. The court also explained that under Islamic law, a divorced wife is entitled to maintenance during iddat, since she cannot remarry during this period

title: Father is financially responsible for his children
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute between divorced parents that turned into a criminal complaint. A mother, after her divorce, was granted custody of her young daughter by the Family Court, a decision upheld on appeal. While the custody case was ongoing, she moved to the United States with her daughter to pursue further studies, where the child, born in Texas, was also enrolled in school. The father then filed a police case (FIR) accusing the mother, her parents, and siblings of kidnapping the child under the Pakistan Penal Code, and separately sought Interpol assistance to have them arrested and extradited.

The Sindh High Court examined whether a mother could be criminally charged with kidnapping her own child from lawful guardianship. It ruled that both parents are natural guardians, and one natural guardian cannot accuse the other of kidnapping their shared child, especially when the mother's custody rights had already been affirmed by three courts. The court quashed the FIR, stressing that custody by the mother does not eliminate the father's guardianship status, financial responsibility for the child, or his visitation rights, all of which remained protected.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that custody disputes between parents should be resolved through family courts and guardianship laws, not criminal prosecutions for kidnapping, while affirming that fathers remain legally and financially responsible for their children even without custody.

title: Relief not prayed for can be granted
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over how the Pakistani government handled a special scheme allowing duty-free import of tractors. In 2005, the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) of the Cabinet decided to allow a one-time import of 10,000 tractors at zero tariff, intended to benefit companies willing to set up or install tractor manufacturing in Pakistan, subject to safeguards like bank guarantees. A committee was supposed to work out detailed rules for implementing this scheme.

The petitioners, including Facto Belarus Tractors Limited, challenged the way this scheme was actually carried out. They argued that the process used to invite and select companies for the import quota was not transparent, was arbitrary, exceeded the authorities' powers, and favored certain parties over others, since some companies were granted permission while the petitioners were refused.

The Sindh High Court agreed that the entire process lacked transparency and appeared arbitrary and favoritism-driven, and did not properly follow the ECC's original decision. It quashed all the proceedings related to the tractor import scheme. Rather than simply ending the matter, the Court directed the government committee to create a proper, detailed scheme with clear criteria, conditions, and safeguards, then re-advertise the opportunity and fairly select eligible companies.

The judgment is significant because it reaffirms that courts can grant appropriate relief even if not specifically requested, and it emphasizes that public authorities must act transparently and fairly, in line with principles of good governance and the rule of law.

title: Preference cannot be given British Citizen Father ordinarily
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute over a young boy, born in 2006, whose parents had married and lived in England. According to the mother, the father sent her back to Azad Kashmir with the child and later divorced her. Both parents subsequently remarried and had children from their second marriages. The father, living in England, applied to a Family Court in Kotli and was granted guardianship in proceedings held without the mother present. When the mother challenged this and sought custody herself, both the Family Court and the Shariat Court ruled against her, apparently reasoning that the father's residence in England made him the more suitable guardian.

The Supreme Court of Azad Jammu and Kashmir overturned these decisions. It held that the welfare of the child must be the paramount consideration in custody matters, not simply where a parent lives. The Court noted the father had never paid maintenance for the child and had remarried with children from that marriage, and found that awarding custody to him despite these facts was not in the child's best interest. Citing its own precedent, the Court ruled that when both parents have remarried, custody should generally go to the mother. The Court also emphasized that if a child is old enough to express an intelligent preference, that opinion should be considered in deciding custody.

This judgment reaffirms that in custody disputes, courts must prioritize the child's actual welfare over assumptions based on a parent's location or financial status, and that a father's foreign residence does not automatically entitle him to preference.

title: Mumtaz Qadri Case Judgment by Supreme Court of Pakistan
explainer:
This is the Supreme Court of Pakistan's judgment in the Mumtaz Qadri case, deciding two appeals arising from an Islamabad High Court decision. Mumtaz Qadri was an elite police guard assigned to protect Salman Taseer, then Governor of Punjab. On 4 January 2011, Qadri shot and killed Taseer using his official weapon and immediately surrendered to fellow guards. He was tried under anti-terrorism laws and murder provisions, and did not deny the killing, justifying it instead on religious grounds, claiming Taseer was an apostate for expressing sympathy toward a woman convicted under blasphemy law.

The Supreme Court emphasized that its role was to apply the existing law of the land, not to rule on religious or theological questions, which fall outside its constitutional jurisdiction and belong instead to specialized religious courts and bodies. The judgment opens by citing Quranic verses stressing the duty to verify information before acting on it, framing Qadri's actions as based on unverified assumptions rather than confirmed facts.

The text provided cuts off before the final verdict is stated, but it lays out the factual background, trial evidence (including ballistic matching, medical evidence, and a recorded confession), and the appellant's defense. The case is significant because it involved the assassination of a sitting provincial governor by his own security guard over an allegedly blasphemous political stance, raising major questions about the rule of law, religious extremism, and the justice system's handling of a religiously motivated killing.

title: Landlord cannot be deprived of his right
explainer:
Nadeem Asghar, a tenant, rented commercial space on the first floor of a building in F-7 Markaz, Islamabad from Dr. Sheikh Siraj-ul-Haque and two others under a lease that allowed a 25% rent increase after three years. When the landlords sought this increase, a dispute arose, and the landlords filed an ejectment petition citing several grounds: personal need (to set up a hospital), default in rent payment, damage to property, subletting, and expiry of the lease term.

The Rent Controller ordered the tenant's ejectment based on default and personal need. On appeal, the Additional District Judge overturned the default finding but upheld the personal need ground, meaning the tenant still had to vacate. The tenant then challenged both decisions before the Islamabad High Court, arguing the landlords had not properly specified how the space was needed and that sufficient vacant space already existed elsewhere in the building.

The High Court dismissed the petition, holding that it is the landlord's prerogative to reclaim premises for genuine personal use, and since the landlord (a doctor) intended to use the space to build a hospital for himself and his daughter, also a doctor, this personal need claim could not be denied. However, the court clarified an important safeguard: if the tenant is evicted but the premises are not actually used for the stated purpose, the tenant can apply to the Rent Controller under Section 17(6) of the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance to be reinstated. The father, Muhammad Saleem, later applied to a family court to be made the child's legal guardian, arguing that the mother had remarried a man unrelated to the child, which under Islamic law affects a mother's custody rights. The family court and appellate courts ruled in the father's favor, and the mother challenged this all the way to the Supreme Court of Pakistan.

The mother argued that the father had failed to pay maintenance for the child and had also remarried, so he should not get custody either. The Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice Iftikhar Muhammad Chaudhry, examined the evidence and found that the father had in fact been providing maintenance regularly, a claim the mother had not seriously disputed during the trial.

The court explained that while a father is generally the natural guardian, courts must always prioritize the welfare of the child above all else. Similarly, a mother's remarriage to someone unrelated to the child can cause her to lose custody rights, unless special circumstances show the child's welfare is still better served with her. title: Cancellation of Irrevocable Power of Attorney
explainer:
Case: Javaid Iqbal v. Pakistan Agricultural Storage & Services Corporation (PASSCO)
Court: Lahore High Court, 2003

What was it about: PASSCO, a government body, signed a contract to sell 25,000 metric tons of wheat to an exporting firm, allowing 60 days to lift the wheat and then three calendar months after lifting to submit export documents proving the wheat was actually exported. When the buyer could not lift the wheat in time, intervenors stepped in to save the deal, and the agreement was amended, reducing quantity and imposing a penalty. There was also an earlier irrevocable power of attorney that was cancelled. After a lawsuit, an interim injunction, and eventually a compromise between the parties, the court had already decreed the case according to that compromise, and PASSCO had acted on it. The petitioner then asked for more time to arrange exports, made arrangements to export wheat abroad, but PASSCO refused to accept his export documents, arguing the three-month deadline in the contract had passed.

What the court decided: The judge held that time was not "of the essence" of this contract, meaning strict deadlines were not so critical that missing them should void the petitioner's rights. Therefore PASSCO's refusal to accept the export documents could not be legally justified. The court gave the petitioner a fresh three-month period from the date of the judgment to export the wheat and submit the required documents, which PASSCO would then have to consider.

title: Bail can't be withheld if business transactions are admitted
explainer:
This case involved a bail petition before the Lahore High Court in a matter concerning a dishonoured cheque. The petitioner was accused under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with issuing a cheque without sufficient funds to cover it, after he allegedly failed to return money taken from the complainant for business purposes and a cheque issued to repay part of the amount bounced.

The petitioner argued that he and the complainant had an admitted business relationship, that the dispute was essentially civil in nature rather than criminal, that the offence did not carry a severe punishment barring bail, and that he was already granted bail in six similar cases filed by other business partners. The prosecution opposed bail, citing his involvement in multiple similar cases.

The court granted bail, relying on the established legal principle that when a business relationship and related transactions between parties are admitted, bail should not be denied. It also noted that the offence carried a maximum sentence of three years, which does not fall under the restrictions on bail found in Section 497 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Citing Supreme Court precedents, the court reaffirmed that for offences not punishable by death, life imprisonment, or ten years' imprisonment, granting bail is the rule and refusal the exception.

This case matters because it reinforces the principle that cheque-dishonour cases arising from acknowledged business dealings are generally treated as civil disputes for bail purposes, and reaffirms the broader rule favoring bail in less serious offences.

title: Matters of allotment or grant of lease of Government Lands

The plaintiff, an electric lamp manufacturers' association, had lawfully held and possessed a large plot of land since the 1950s, after acquiring it as evacuee property with official confirmation. The trouble began when the then Chief Minister of Sindh personally intervened to allot a portion of this land, about 35 Ghuntas, to a private individual (Defendant No. 3) at a drastically undervalued price, bypassing normal rules and relaxing conditions without justification. This person later occupied part of the plaintiff's land and eventually sold it to another party (Defendant No. 4). After a change of government, an inquiry into questionable land allotments named this individual as a beneficiary of improper allocation. The plaintiff sued to reclaim its land and cancel the allotment and sale documents.

The defendant sought dismissal of the case, arguing that Section 36 of the Colonization of Government Lands (Sindh) Act, 1912 barred civil courts from hearing such land allotment disputes, since the law provides its own departmental appeal process.

The Sindh High Court rejected this argument. It held that when a powerful government official or politician interferes directly and improperly in land allotment decisions, expecting a fair hearing through departmental appeals is unrealistic, since junior officials are unlikely to rule against their politically powerful superiors. title: Signature Verification by Handwriting Expert
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell property, dated 19.06.2004. The petitioner, Talib Hussain, claimed that Respondent No. 3 had sold him the property and signed and thumb-stamped the agreement after receiving full payment. Respondent No. 3 denied signing the document or placing his thumb impression on it. The petitioner asked the trial court to have the disputed signature and thumb impression compared with genuine specimens by handwriting and fingerprint experts. Both the Civil Judge and the Additional District Judge rejected this request, mainly because evidence had already been recorded and the case was close to final arguments.

The Lahore High Court disagreed and allowed the petition. It held that under Article 84 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, courts have clear power to order comparison of signatures and thumb impressions to reach a fair decision, especially since fingerprints are unique to each individual and expert reports assist courts in reaching accurate conclusions. Since this was a case of outright denial rather than a claim of fraud or coercion, the court found no valid reason to refuse the comparison. It ruled that forensic verification would not prejudice either party, since expert reports remain open to challenge, and that some delay is preferable to a hasty, potentially wrong judgment. The court set aside the lower courts' orders and directed that the comparison be carried out. This case affirms that courts should use available forensic tools to ensure just outcomes rather than rushing decisions on disputed documents

title: Report of Handwriting Expert is an opinion
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over agricultural land in Punjab. After Sardar Ali died, his legal heirs (the plaintiffs) discovered a mutation entry showing he had supposedly gifted his land to certain other heirs (the defendants) back in 1994. The plaintiffs went to court claiming no such gift had ever actually been made, and sought to have the mutation declared invalid. Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled against the plaintiffs, so they brought the matter to the Lahore High Court.

The High Court sided with the plaintiffs. It held that once heirs challenge a gift mutation and deny under oath that any gift occurred, the burden shifts to the people benefiting from the gift to prove it was genuine. They must show not just that the mutation was properly recorded, but that an actual gift took place, meaning a clear offer, acceptance, and handing over of possession. In this case, the defendants had not even pleaded these essential facts in their court filings, let alone proved them.

The court also addressed the two conflicting handwriting expert reports about disputed signatures on the mutation document. It ruled that expert opinions on handwriting are not binding on courts, and since the two reports contradicted each other, neither could be relied upon, leaving the witnesses' sworn testimony as the more credible evidence.

title: Benefit extended to one employee is for all employees
explainer:
This case involved seven employees of Allama Iqbal Open University who had been granted two advance salary increments back in 1986 for completing a Master's degree in Educational Planning and Management. Years later, an audit objection led the university to withdraw these increments and recover the money already paid. One affected employee, Muhammad Iqbal, challenged this withdrawal before the Federal Service Tribunal and won, on the grounds that the university had full authority over its own employees' pay and terms, and neither the Federal Government nor its Finance Division could override those decisions. The Supreme Court upheld this ruling when the matter was appealed. The petitioners in this case, who were in the same situation but had not been part of that original lawsuit, asked for the same treatment and refund, but the university refused, arguing they were not parties to the earlier case.

The Islamabad High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners. It held that once the Supreme Court decides a legal question, that ruling applies broadly and is binding on all courts, regardless of whether someone was an actual party to that specific case. The court also found that giving a benefit to one employee while denying the same benefit to other similarly situated employees violates the constitutional guarantees of equality and equal protection under the law (Articles 4 and 25). All seven petitions were accepted, meaning the employees were entitled to have their increments restored. This case matters because it reinforces that government and institutional bodies cannot treat similarly situated employees differently once a legal precedent has been set.

title: Appointment of a Civil Servant through Transfer
explainer:
This Supreme Court of Pakistan judgment is a review petition arising from an earlier 2013 decision concerning irregular appointments, promotions, and transfers of civil servants in Sindh, particularly involving police officers.

The core issue was whether civil servants could be appointed to different departments or cadres through transfer, and whether police officers could receive out of turn promotions. The Court clarified that under Sindh's civil service rules, a person can only be appointed by transfer if they are actually eligible and qualified for the new post, and must be screened by the proper selection bodies. Rule 9-A, meant to accommodate employees whose posts were abolished, could not be misused to bypass these eligibility requirements by artificially abolishing someone's post just to transfer them elsewhere.

On out of turn promotions, the Court upheld its earlier ruling that such promotions for police officers violated the Constitution's provisions on equality and fair treatment, since they lacked transparent, objective criteria. However, it ordered that officers who lost such promotions should still have their seniority fixed as if the improper promotion had never happened, alongside their original batchmates.

The Court also addressed whether its earlier judgment should apply only going forward. It held that benefits gained under laws later declared unconstitutional are void from the very beginning, so no rights survive from an invalid law, meaning such benefits must be withdrawn entirely.

This judgment matters because it reinforces merit-based, rule-following civil service appointments and prevents misuse of transfer and promotion rules for favorit

Under the Offence of Qazf (Enforcement of Hadd) Ordinance, 1979, anyone who makes such an accusation must prove it by producing four witnesses, as required for proving zina itself. The judges found that Ramzan had fabricated the allegation purely to grab property, without any evidence, and had failed to meet the legal standard of producing four witnesses to support such a serious accusation. title: Thumb Impression and Impersonation Case Law
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute where a suit for specific performance of a contract was filed over land based on an alleged agreement. During the case, the defendant (the petitioner in this writ petition) claimed that a written statement and a power of attorney filed on his behalf were forged, and that his thumb impressions on these documents had been fraudulently obtained through impersonation. He asked the trial court to cancel these documents, but his application was dismissed, and his subsequent appeal to the Additional District Judge was also rejected. Both lower courts had relied on the general legal presumption that documents filed in court proceedings are truthful.

The Lahore High Court disagreed with this approach. It found that neither court had actually investigated the fraud allegation properly, no issues had been framed, and no evidence had been recorded to check whether the documents were genuine. The court pointed out that under Article 84 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, courts have the power to compare disputed thumb impressions with genuine ones, or refer them to a forensic expert, to determine authenticity. Simply noting that the petitioner's CNIC number appeared on file was not enough to confirm his identity or rule out impersonation.

The High Court set aside the lower courts' orders, ruling that when serious allegations of fraud and impersonation are raised, courts must properly examine the evidence, including comparing thumb impressions, rather than dismissing such claims based on procedural presumptions alone.

title: Writ Petition under Article 199 against Order I Rule 10 Application
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Bahawalpur. Muhammad Yaqoob had filed a lawsuit claiming ownership and possession of 439 kanals of land, which he said he bought at an open auction. During the court proceedings, another person, Maqbool Ahmad, applied to be added as a party to the case under Order 1 Rule 10 of the Civil Procedure Code. Maqbool Ahmad claimed he had been cultivating 100 kanals of that land as a tenant since 1978 and was seeking ownership rights over it.

The trial court allowed Maqbool Ahmad to be added as a party. Yaqoob challenged this decision through a revision petition before the Additional District Judge, but that was dismissed too. He then approached the Lahore High Court through a constitutional petition, arguing that both orders were illegal and that Maqbool Ahmad had no real right to be included in the case.

The High Court disagreed. It held that given Maqbool Ahmad's long-standing possession of the land and his competing claim of ownership, he was at least a "proper party" whose inclusion would help fully resolve the dispute and avoid multiple lawsuits. The court also found no legal flaw, unfairness, or irrationality in the lower courts' orders. Since these were factual findings properly made by the lower courts, the High Court said it could not interfere in a constitutional petition. The petition was dismissed outright, meaning the lower courts' decisions stood.

title: Heirs of Victim and Heirs of Wali
explainer:
This case involved Ahmad Nawaz, who was convicted by a trial court in Hafizabad and sentenced to death for murdering Muhammad Mohsin in 2003, with an order to pay compensation. While his appeal was pending before the Lahore High Court, an application was filed seeking permission to compound (settle) the offence under Section 345 of the Criminal Procedure Code, based on a compromise with the victim's family.

The complication was that the murdered man's father had four wives, producing several children including daughters from earlier, divorced wives (called consanguine sisters) and a widow, Mst. Bushra Bibi, with her own children who were the deceased's full siblings. Bushra Bibi and her minor children agreed to pardon the accused and received diyat (blood money), but three consanguine half-sisters from the father's other marriages refused to compound the case.

The court had to determine who actually qualified as legal heirs entitled to grant pardon or compromise in a murder case. It ruled that only the direct heirs of the victim himself — not distant relatives or heirs of the victim's wali (guardian/next of kin) who might only inherit later — have the right to compromise under the law of qisas and diyat. Finding the compromise made by the victim's actual heirs genuine and voluntary, the court accepted it, set aside the conviction and death sentence, and allowed the offence to be compounded.

title: Adverse Remarks Effect in ACR's
explainer:
This case is about Abdul Rauf Khan, an Additional District and Sessions Judge in Dir Lower, who challenged adverse remarks in his Annual Confidential Reports (ACRs) for the years 2006 to 2009. These remarks, recorded by the Administration Committee of the Peshawar High Court, marked his integrity as "not above board," his overall performance as "below average," and declared him "not fit" for promotion. He appealed to the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Subordinate Judiciary Service Tribunal, arguing the remarks were communicated years late without explanation, no warning or counseling was given beforehand as required, and one committee member had not even been a judge during the relevant years. He also pointed out he had earned twelve good reports before 2006 and two more afterward, with no disciplinary action ever taken against him.

The Tribunal ruled in his favor, finding that adverse remarks—especially those touching integrity—must be backed by clear reasons and evidence, which the High Court failed to provide. It held that unexplained delays of three to four years in communicating such remarks caused serious prejudice to the officer, and that vague, unsupported adverse entries cannot stand. The Tribunal also emphasized that promotion should be based on seniority-cum-fitness, and denying promotion is effectively a punishment that cannot be imposed without proper charges and inquiry. The adverse entries were expunged.

title: Right of Pre-emption is activated on Talb-e-Muasabat
explainer:
This case is about a legal dispute over "pre-emption," which under Pakistani law gives certain people (such as neighbors or co-owners) the first right to buy a property before it is sold to someone else. To exercise this right, the law requires the claimant to immediately assert his intention to purchase upon hearing of the sale, a step called "Talb-e-Muwathibat," and later prove in court exactly how, when, and from whom he learned about the sale, including naming the person who informed him.

In this case, the petitioner (Gull Bad Shah) had filed a pre-emption suit and initially won in the trial court. However, he never named the person who informed him about the sale, either in his written claim or his list of witnesses, and never tried to produce that informer as a witness during the trial. The appellate court reversed the trial court's decision and ruled against him. He then approached the Peshawar High Court, seeking permission to introduce this missing evidence at a very late stage.

The High Court refused, holding that such a fundamental gap cannot be fixed later, especially not for the first time during a revision petition. It compared the pre-emption plaint to an FIR in a criminal case, meaning it must be complete and accurate from the start. Since the petitioner failed to establish this essential requirement early on, his case failed, and the revision petition was dismissed. This case reinforces strict procedural standards required in pre-emption lawsuits.

title: Wife is liable to return dower in case of Khula
explainer:
This case involved a couple whose marriage broke down after only about a month together. The wife filed a lawsuit seeking dissolution of marriage, claiming she was underage at the time of marriage, that her husband was much older and habitually drank, and that he treated her cruelly, including physical abuse, before throwing her out. The husband denied the allegations and separately sought restitution of conjugal rights. The family court in Kotli combined both cases and ultimately dissolved the marriage on the basis of khula, but without requiring the wife to return any dower or benefits she had received.

The husband appealed, arguing the wife had failed to prove cruelty or her other claims, and that since the marriage was being dissolved through khula, she should be required to return the gold ornaments given to her as dower.

The Azad Jammu and Kashmir High Court held that even when a wife cannot prove specific grounds like cruelty, a court can still grant khula if circumstances show the marriage cannot survive, which was true here given the age gap and mutual estrangement. However, the court disagreed with the lower court's decision to let the wife keep the dower. It ruled that under khula, a wife must return the dower or its equivalent value to the husband. Since the wife failed to prove she no longer had the ornaments, the court ordered her to return them, and the husband's appeal was accepted on this point.

title: If Dower is not paid, wife can refuse to live with husband
explainer:
This case involved a husband and wife whose marriage broke down after the wife left the marital home in 2010, alleging mistreatment. The wife sued for her unpaid dower (a sum promised to her at marriage), maintenance allowance, and dowry articles, while the husband sought restitution of conjugal rights, meaning a court order requiring his wife to return and live with him.

Lower courts had ordered the husband to pay the dower and maintenance but disagreed on whether he was entitled to restitution of conjugal rights. The husband challenged this outcome before the Islamabad High Court, claiming he had already paid the dower in cash on the wedding night and that his wife had left voluntarily.

The High Court rejected the husband's argument, ruling that simply stating in court that dower was paid is not proof, he needed actual evidence, which he failed to provide. The court explained that dower is essentially a debt owed by the husband, and if it remains unpaid, the wife has the right to refuse to live with him and is still entitled to maintenance.

However, since the allegation of cruelty against the husband was not proven, the court ruled he was entitled to restitution of conjugal rights, but only once he actually pays the dower. The petition was dismissed on the dower and maintenance issues but partly allowed on conjugal rights, conditional on payment.

This ruling reinforces that unpaid dower gives wives a legitimate right to withhold cohabitation and claim support.

title: Prosecution has to prove the case beyond any doubt
explainer:
This case involved four people arrested when police stopped their car on the G.T. Road near Peshawar, allegedly acting on a tip that charas (hashish) was being smuggled towards Punjab. On searching the vehicle, police claimed to have found 100 kg of charas hidden in the rear seat and boot. Two men were sitting in front, and two women, one elderly and one young, were in the back seat. All four were charged and convicted under the Control of Narcotics Substances Act, 1997, and sentenced to life imprisonment.

The two women appealed, arguing they were merely passengers travelling for medical treatment, had no knowledge of any hidden drugs, and that the contraband was not found on their persons but concealed in secret compartments not visible to them. The men's own statements supported the claim that the women had simply boarded the car for treatment in Rawalpindi.

The Peshawar High Court accepted this defense. It found that the prosecution failed to prove the women knew about the narcotics, since nothing was in plain view and the drugs were recovered from hidden parts of the car, not from their direct possession. The court held that mere presence in a vehicle where contraband is later found is not enough to establish guilt; knowledge and conscious possession must be proved. Since the prosecution could not meet this burden, the appeal was allowed and the women's convictions were overturned. The judgment underscores that criminal guilt requires proof beyond reasonable doubt, not mere association or presence.

title: Fauji Fertilizer V. NIRC .. Illegal lockout challenged in Judgement
explainer:
Fauji Fertilizer Company (formerly Pak Saudi Fertilizer) hired contractors over the years to bag, load, and handle its urea fertilizer. The contractors employed their own workers, who eventually formed a union recognized as the bargaining agent. When a dispute arose over a new contractor and reduced wages under a fresh settlement, the union alleged the workers were illegally locked out to pressure them into accepting worse terms, and sought reinstatement through the National Industrial Relations Commission (NIRC). The company argued there was no employer-employee relationship between it and the contractor's workers, so the lock-out provisions did not apply to them.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the company. It held that where a company retains control over how contracted work is actually performed, the workers are effectively its employees, even if hired through a contractor. Since these workers were directly supervised by the company and performed core functions like bagging and loading, they were considered company employees for legal purposes. The lock-out was therefore illegal, and the union had rightly challenged it. The Court upheld the Labour Appellate Tribunal's decision ordering reinstatement, though it clarified back-benefits would only apply until the relevant settlement's expiry, after which the workers had already attained permanent status by length of service. The appeals were dismissed.

This case matters because it protects contract laborers from being denied basic labor rights just because they're technically hired through a third party, when in reality they work under the direct control of the principal company.

title: NIRC V. UBL (Infructuous Petition Dismissed)
explainer:
This case was heard by the National Industrial Relations Commission (NIRC), Karachi Bench, and involved a bank employee, Hussain Bux Mallah, who filed a petition against United Bank Limited under the Industrial Relations Act, 2008. He claimed that during union election proceedings, the bank's management had threatened to victimize him because of his trade union activities.

The bank argued that the petition should be dismissed because, before it was even filed, the petitioner had already been dismissed from his job through an official dismissal order dated 7 October 2009, which he received on 8 October 2009. The petition itself was filed later, on 13 October 2009.

The Commission agreed with the bank. It found that since the petitioner was no longer an employee at the time he filed his case, the Commission could not grant the relief he sought, such as reinstatement, because such power only applies when someone is being punished for unfair labour practices, not when the person has been acquitted of charges. The Commission also noted that the union elections he complained about had already taken place, so there was no ongoing issue left to address.

As a result, the petition was declared infructuous, meaning it no longer served any real purpose, and was dismissed. The case illustrates that legal claims must be based on a live, current grievance, and courts or tribunals will not entertain petitions that have become moot due to intervening events.

They also claimed the order was discriminatory since it targeted only cellular operators and not other service providers, and that it wrongly banned even genuine, legitimate schemes along with fraudulent ones.

title: Un-explained delay favors the accused
explainer:
This case involved a pre-arrest bail petition before the Lahore High Court. Muhammad Hanif was accused of abducting a woman, Mst. Zubaida Bibi, for the purpose of illicit intercourse and of committing rape, along with stealing cash and gold ornaments, under Section 365-B PPC. The complainant filed the FIR nearly two months after the alleged occurrence.

The petitioner argued that the complainant was actually his relative who had voluntarily married him according to Islamic law on the same date as the alleged abduction, and produced a Nikah Nama as proof. He also showed that the complainant had appeared with him before a sessions court shortly after the alleged incident, that a union council official had certified their marriage, and that he had obtained a court decree for restitution of conjugal rights. The complainant, however, denied the marriage and had filed a separate suit disputing it.

The court found the unexplained two-month delay in filing the FIR suspicious, especially since no family member reported the incident immediately. Given the existing dispute over the authenticity of the marriage and the circumstances suggesting the allegations may not be genuine, the court held that the case against the petitioner was doubtful. Since an accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt even at the bail stage, the court granted him bail. This case illustrates how delay in reporting a crime, combined with conflicting evidence, can support a bail grant.

title: Can list of witnesses be changed?
explainer:
This case involved a wife who had filed a suit for dissolution of her marriage against her husband. As part of her case, she submitted a list of witnesses she intended to produce. When she was unable to produce those particular witnesses, she filed a second, revised list. The Family Court allowed this second list, and the witnesses named in it were examined, with only the wife's own statement remaining to be recorded.

The husband challenged the Family Court's order allowing the new witness list by filing an appeal before the Shariat Court, which accepted his appeal and set aside the Family Court's order.

The wife then approached the Supreme Court of Azad Kashmir, arguing that the Family Court's order was merely an interlocutory (procedural, non-final) order, not a final judgment or decree, and therefore no appeal against it could lie before the Shariat Court.

The Supreme Court agreed with her. It held that under the Family Courts Act, only final decisions or decrees of a Family Court can be appealed to the Shariat Court, not interlocutory orders like the one permitting a new witness list. The Court also found that the Shariat Court had wrongly treated the wife's application as a "review application" when it was simply a request to produce witnesses. Since the witnesses had already testified, the entire dispute had become moot. The Supreme Court therefore set aside the Shariat Court's judgment, reinforcing the principle that procedural orders during trial are not appealable.

title: Bail Petition Dismissed in Fraud Case
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by a man accused in a large-scale banking fraud involving fake auto loans. The prosecution alleged that a serious scheme was carried out in which vehicle registration numbers were misused to create forged documents, which were then used to obtain auto loans in the names of fictitious or fake persons. The accused, who worked as Branch Managers of the bank involved, were implicated in the scheme, with details of around 60 fraudulent vehicle loans presented in the police challan (charge sheet).

The accused were charged under several sections of the Pakistan Penal Code, including criminal breach of trust by a public servant, cheating by personation, forgery, and using forged documents as genuine. Their lawyer argued that no disciplinary action had been taken against them by the bank, suggesting they should be granted bail.

The Sindh High Court rejected this argument, holding that internal disciplinary proceedings by an employer and criminal proceedings in court are entirely separate matters, and the outcome of one has no bearing on the other. The court described this as a case of "white-collar crime," noting that such crimes are carried out through fabricated documents and often remain hidden until exposed by whistleblowers. Finding sufficient material connecting the accused to the alleged fraud, the court dismissed the bail applications, meaning the accused would remain in custody pending trial.

title: Article 199 and Article 35 of Constitution invoked
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute in which a wife sued her husband for recovery of dower money, maintenance during the Iddat period, and maintenance for their son. The Family Court and the Appellate Court both ruled in her favor. The husband then challenged these decisions before the High Court, disputing his son's legitimacy. He claimed the child was illegitimate because he was born only six months after the marriage, suggesting a premature birth that made him doubt paternity.

The husband's marriage to the woman was undisputed, as confirmed by the Nikah Nama (marriage certificate). However, apart from an ultrasound report that was never properly proven in court, he provided no credible evidence to support his claim that the child was illegitimate, despite having full opportunity to do so.

The High Court rejected his petition. It explained that under Islamic law, a child is presumed legitimate if born anywhere between 180 days (six months) and two years after marriage. Since the husband failed to prove otherwise, the child could not be branded illegitimate merely for being born early. The Court also invoked Article 35 of the Constitution, which obligates the State to protect marriage, family, mothers, and children. It emphasized that wrongly declaring a legitimate child illegitimate causes severe, lifelong harm and constitutes a grave injustice.

The Court upheld the lower courts' rulings, confirming the child's legitimacy and the father's duty to maintain him. This case highlights the judiciary's role in protecting children's rights and dignity under constitutional and Islamic law.

title: TIme period for filing suit in case of dispossession
explainer:
This case concerned a dispute over land ownership in Azad Jammu and Kashmir. The plaintiffs (respondents) filed a suit claiming they were the recorded owners of certain land and that their neighbors, the defendants, had encroached upon it by extending boundaries. The defendants argued the suit was filed too late, claiming that under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, a suit for possession must be filed within 12 years of dispossession, and they had been in possession since their forefathers' time.

The Supreme Court of Azad Jammu and Kashmir clarified an important legal distinction: Article 142's 12-year limitation applies only when a suit is based on the claim that the plaintiff was previously in possession and was later dispossessed. However, when a suit for possession is based on ownership title rather than prior possession, that time limit does not apply. Previously, Article 144 governed such title-based suits, but since that article was deleted from the law, there is now no fixed limitation period for a true owner to file a suit for possession based on title—it can be filed at any time.

Since the plaintiffs' suit was based on their ownership title (supported by revenue records), not on a claim of prior possession followed by dispossession, Article 142 did not apply and their suit was not time-barred. The court also rejected arguments about the need for a spot inspection, since ownership was largely admitted. Because lower courts had already reached consistent factual findings, the Supreme Court upheld those decisions and dismissed the appeal. This case is significant for clarifying limitation rules distinguish

title: Judgment against undue delay in criminal trials
explainer:
This case involves Shah Hussain, who along with two co-accused was tried for murder, causing injuries, and robbery (Haraabah) of a jeep. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to imprisonment for various offences, with sentences to run consecutively, totaling as much as 60 years. On appeal, the Peshawar High Court acquitted one co-accused but upheld Hussain's conviction and sentence. He then petitioned the Supreme Court of Pakistan.

The Supreme Court's judgment focuses heavily on Section 382-B of the Criminal Procedure Code, which requires courts to give convicts credit for time already spent in jail as an undertrial prisoner before sentencing. The Court held that this provision is mandatory, not optional, meaning judges must consider and usually deduct pre-trial detention time from a convict's sentence, and must explain their reasoning if they choose not to. The Court explained this rule exists because undue delays in trials, whether caused by court backlogs or procedural issues, should not unfairly prolong a person's total time in custody. It also ruled that stacking multiple sentences consecutively cannot exceed 14 years under Section 35 of the Cr.P.C., making the 60-year aggregate sentence unlawful.

title: Revision over revision is not possible
explainer:
This case involved a long-running property dispute over four marlas of land. During the trial, the petitioners asked the court to appoint a local commission to inspect improvements they claimed to have made on the disputed property. The trial court rejected this request, viewing it as a delaying tactic, and offered to consider it later if a final decree for dispossession was passed. The petitioners appealed to the Additional District Judge, who upheld the trial court's decision. They then filed this revision petition before the Peshawar High Court.

The High Court examined whether it had jurisdiction to hear the case. It ruled that an order rejecting the appointment of a local commission under Order 26, Rule 9 of the Civil Procedure Code is not something that can normally be appealed. Therefore, when the Additional District Judge heard the petitioners' appeal, he was actually exercising revisional powers under Section 115 of the CPC, not appellate powers. Since a district court had already exercised revisional jurisdiction, the law clearly barred the High Court from entertaining a further revision against that order, as Section 115(4) prohibits a "revision over a revision."

The court therefore dismissed the petition for lack of jurisdiction. This decision matters because it clarifies procedural limits: parties cannot keep escalating certain interlocutory orders through multiple rounds of revision, which helps prevent litigation from being needlessly prolonged, something the court itself noted had already happened for five years in this dispute.

title: Oral evidence is not sufficient to prove faith
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over inheritance property, turning on the religious faith of a deceased man, Imam Bakhsh. His nephews (through his sister) inherited his property through a mutation recorded under Shia inheritance law. Other relatives (collaterals) challenged this, claiming Imam Bakhsh was actually Sunni, which would have entitled them to a much larger share of the estate. The trial court dismissed their claim, but the first appellate court and initially the High Court sided with the collaterals. The Supreme Court then sent the case back, asking the High Court to determine two things: whether certain documents (a will, an affidavit, and a mutation record) were properly proved, and whether these documents plus a widow's statement to revenue officials were legally sufficient to establish that Imam Bakhsh was Shia.

On reconsideration, the High Court ruled in favor of the nephews. It held that the documents were genuine and executed by Imam Bakhsh well before the family dispute arose, making them reliable. It found that mere oral testimony from witnesses was not enough to prove someone's faith, but that written statements made by the deceased himself during his lifetime, along with his widow's statement recorded by revenue authorities, were legally sufficient evidence under the law of evidence. The court also clarified that a person's own declarations, family background, and conduct during life are more reliable indicators of religious faith than events after death, such as funeral prayers. The appeal was accepted, restoring the property to the nephews.

title: Maintainability of Civil Revision against High Court Decision
explainer:
This case involved a company, Techcorp Holding, that filed a lawsuit against another company, Konnect Holden, seeking recovery of over 22 crore rupees. Instead of responding to the lawsuit normally, Techcorp asked the court to reject the plaint outright. A single judge of the Islamabad High Court rejected this application. Techcorp then challenged that decision by filing a civil revision petition before a two-judge bench of the same High Court.

The key issue the court had to resolve was not the merits of the recovery suit, but a technical question: was a civil revision even the right legal tool to challenge this order? The respondent argued it was not, because the order was merely interlocutory (not a final decision) and such orders are appealable, not subject to revision.

The court agreed with the respondent. It explained that under Section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code, revision petitions can only be filed against decisions of courts subordinate to the High Court. A single judge of the High Court is not considered such a subordinate court. Instead, under Section 15 of the Civil Procedure (Amendment) Ordinance, 1980, interlocutory orders passed by a single High Court judge can be appealed to a two-judge bench through an Intra Court Appeal (ICA), not challenged via revision.

Since Techcorp used the wrong legal remedy, the court dismissed the revision petition as legally incompetent, without deciding the actual dispute over money. This ruling clarifies the correct procedure for challenging single-judge High Court orders in Pakistan.

title: Judgment under Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance 2001
explainer:
This case concerns a landlord-tenant dispute in Islamabad involving Shop No. 5 in the F-6/1 Farooqia Market. The landlords (respondents) filed an ejectment petition against the tenant, alleging he had defaulted on rent payments. The tenant denied there was a landlord-tenant relationship and argued the case was not valid, raising two key objections.

First, he argued the Rent Controller had no authority to hear the case because the ejectment petition was filed in January 2003, before the relevant notification bringing the area under the Islamabad Rent Restriction Ordinance took full effect in June 2004. Second, he claimed he was not actually occupying the shop himself; someone else was, so he shouldn't be liable.

The Rent Controller ruled against the tenant, and this was upheld by both the appellate court and later the Islamabad High Court. The Supreme Court, hearing the tenant's final petition for leave to appeal, also rejected his arguments. It held that since the Rent Controller gained jurisdiction while the case was still pending, and no unfairness resulted from this, the ejectment order was valid. It also found that the tenant himself was the one in possession of the premises, making him liable.

The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal, meaning the ejectment order against the tenant stood. The case clarifies how jurisdictional notifications under rent laws can apply to pending cases without causing injustice.

title: Judgment related with offense of Qazaf
explainer:
This case involves a dispute between a husband and wife over accusations of adultery. The husband made written and verbal statements accusing his wife of zina (adultery) and claimed that all three of their children were illegitimate. These accusations were made after the husband had already divorced his wife and executed a divorce deed, meaning their marital relationship had legally ended.

Under Pakistan's Offence of Qazf (Enforcement of Hadd) Ordinance, 1979, falsely accusing someone of adultery is a punishable offense under Sections 6 and 7. However, Section 14 of the same law provides an exception when such accusations happen between a husband and wife during their marriage, treating it differently since spouses have legal mechanisms like li'an (mutual imprecation) to handle such accusations within marriage.

The trial court initially refused to frame charges under Section 7, believing this was simply a marital dispute where Section 14 should apply. The Federal Shariat Court disagreed and ordered charges to be framed under Sections 6 and 7, reasoning that since the divorce had already occurred, the parties were no longer husband and wife but simply a man and a woman when the accusations were made.

The Supreme Court upheld this reasoning and refused the husband's request for leave to appeal, meaning the Federal Shariat Court's decision stood. This case clarifies that the special marital exception under the Qazf law does not protect a person who makes such serious accusations after the marriage has already ended through divorce.

title: Judgment on Rule of Consistency
explainer:
This case arose from a murder complaint filed by Muhammad Waryam after his son Riaz Ahmad was killed and his daughter injured. Three men, Daim, Aziz alias Ghazi, and Mehmood alias Mooda, were accused. The trial court had granted bail to Mehmood but refused it to Aziz, even though the FIR described both men as having played the same role in the incident. Two applications came before the Lahore High Court: one by the complainant seeking to cancel Mehmood's bail, and another by Aziz seeking bail for himself.

The complainant argued Mehmood's bail should be cancelled because he allegedly misused his freedom to intimidate a witness and commit further crimes, but the court found this claim did not hold up, especially since a related case against him had been withdrawn. On the question of Aziz, the court noted that investigation records showed both accused had been declared innocent by one investigating officer, with a difference of opinion among investigators making this a case fit for further inquiry.

Since the FIR placed both men in identical circumstances, the court held that treating them differently for bail purposes violated the rule of consistency, a principle requiring equal treatment for people in similar situations. The court therefore dismissed the request to cancel Mehmood's bail and granted bail to Aziz as well. This case highlights how courts ensure fairness by treating co-accused facing similar allegations and evidence in the same manner.

title: Interest is un-islamic as per the declaration of Supreme Court
explainer:
This case involved a man who had taken a loan from a government-linked finance corporation to build a house or buy equipment, agreeing to repay it in instalments. He had paid back nearly the full principal amount but the corporation was still demanding more money, which he argued was actually interest, something the Supreme Court of Pakistan had already ruled to be un-Islamic. He asked the Lahore High Court to intervene through a constitutional petition.

The court held that the petition itself was not maintainable, because the man had signed a loan agreement voluntarily and had other legal options available, such as approaching the corporation directly or filing a civil suit, instead of coming straight to a constitutional court. The court also noted it did not have authority to rule on whether interest violates Islamic law, since that falls under a special constitutional provision reserved for other forums. It also clarified that past, already-completed financial transactions could not be reopened even though interest had been declared un-Islamic.

Despite dismissing the petition on technical grounds, the judge directed the corporation to recalculate the man's dues fairly, apply any concessions or incentive schemes he might qualify for, and consider letting him pay in manageable instalments so he and his family would not be ruined. The judge also criticized finance institutions for aggressively pursuing poor borrowers while seemingly not acting against wealthy defaulters, calling this discriminatory, and asked the Ministry of Finance to create fairer recovery policies protecting both the institutions and poor borrowers.

title: Father's property cannot be given in Haq Mehr
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a father-in-law and his daughter-in-law over dower (haq mehr) after her husband died.

The marriage was solemnized in 2000, and the nikahnama listed gold ornaments and a house as dower for the wife. The house, however, actually belonged to the husband's father, not the husband himself. After the couple divorced and the husband later died, the wife sued for recovery of the dower, dowry articles, and maintenance for herself and her son. The family courts ruled in her favor regarding the house, dowry articles, and maintenance, though her claim for the gold ornaments was dismissed. The father-in-law challenged these rulings, arguing he never agreed to give away his own house and had not even signed the nikahnama.

The Lahore High Court held that, as a general rule, a husband cannot pledge someone else's property, such as his father's, as dower unless the father consented. However, consent need not be explicit or in writing—it can be implied from conduct. Since the father-in-law was present at the nikah, never objected when his house was listed as dower, and took no legal steps to have it removed from the nikahnama for years, the court found he had implicitly consented. The court also ruled that a grandfather is liable for his grandchild's maintenance, including past amounts, when the father is dead or unable to provide it.

The petition was dismissed, upholding the lower courts' decisions. This case matters because it clarifies how implied consent can bind a third party's property in dower arrangements and confirms grandparents' maintenance obligations to grandchildren.

title: Family suits can be consolidated
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute in the Lahore High Court, Rawalpindi Bench. A woman, after being divorced, filed a single consolidated lawsuit in the Family Court claiming dowry articles, maintenance, and dower (mehr) from her ex-husband. Her former mother-in-law, acting as attorney for her son, objected, arguing that under Section 17 of the West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964, such claims could only be combined into one suit if it was specifically a suit for dissolution of marriage—not otherwise. When the Family Court judge rejected this objection, the mother-in-law challenged that ruling through a constitutional petition in the High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition for two reasons. First, it held that a constitutional petition cannot be filed against a mere interim (temporary) order of a lower court—only final orders can typically be challenged this way. Second, on the merits, the court found nothing wrong with combining the claims. Since the woman was already divorced, she had no choice but to file one combined suit for all her claims. The court also noted that even if separate suits had been filed, the Family Court had the power to consolidate them anyway to serve justice and avoid delay.

This judgment matters because it confirms that Family Courts can combine related claims into a single case to make proceedings more efficient, and that parties cannot use technical objections or interim orders to stall justice. The petitioner was also ordered to pay costs for delaying the case.

title: Constructed building not to be demolished in case of contract
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a contractor, Kartar Masih, and the Municipal Committee of Okara. Under a contract, the petitioner had been given the job of collecting and disposing of dead animal carcasses within the committee's limits for a three-year period. He built a covered structure, spending over Rs. 25,000, to carry out this work, and there was also a resolution suggesting his contract would be extended for another three years at a higher rate.

While a formal lawsuit over his rights was still pending, the petitioner sought a temporary injunction to stop the Municipal Committee from interfering with his work. The trial court granted this interim relief, but the Municipal Committee appealed, and the District Judge overturned it, reasoning that a breach of contract only entitles a party to sue for damages, not for an injunction.

The Lahore High Court disagreed with the appellate court's decision and restored the trial court's injunction. It held that the petitioner had a strong, arguable case because he had invested significant money in constructing the building under permission from the committee, and losing the contract would cause him irreparable financial loss. The court found the balance of convenience favored the petitioner and that the appellate court had failed to properly consider these facts.

This ruling illustrates that courts may protect a party's investment and ongoing business interests through temporary injunctions when significant money has been spent in reliance on a contract, even while the main legal dispute remains unresolved.

title: Civil Revision of a case for declaration
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over inherited land in Peshawar. Two petitioners, claiming to be the son and widow of a deceased landowner named Ghulam Muhammad, filed a lawsuit asking the court to declare an inheritance mutation (an official land record transfer) invalid. That mutation, recorded in 1986, had transferred the deceased's property to other relatives without including the petitioners as legal heirs. The petitioners argued they had been left out due to fraud, that the son was a minor at the time, and that the widow was an illiterate, secluded woman (parda nasheen) who couldn't have knowingly given up her rights. The widow also separately claimed a portion of land as her dower (a marriage-related entitlement) based on a dower deed allegedly executed by her husband years earlier.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court rejected these claims, finding the evidence unconvincing. The dower deed lacked key legal formalities, was never officially registered, and its witnesses were never produced in court. Testimony about the petitioners' marriage and inheritance claims was inconsistent and based on hearsay rather than direct knowledge.

The Peshawar High Court, reviewing the case, agreed with the lower courts. It found no legal errors or misreading of evidence in their decisions and dismissed the petitioners' revision petition, upholding the original mutation. The case illustrates how courts require solid, direct evidence—not assumptions or secondhand claims—especially when disputing official property records long after the fact.

title: Circumstantial evidence matters a lot in murder case
explainer:
This case involved a man, Muhammad Ramzan, convicted of murdering his wife, Mst. Sakina Bibi, and sentenced to death by a trial court in Khanewal. The prosecution alleged that the killing happened at night in the bedroom of the wife's father, where the husband was living as a "ghar damad" (resident son-in-law). The father, an uncle, and another relative claimed to have witnessed the murder, saying the husband attacked his wife with a hatchet after a quarrel over gold ornaments, then escaped.

On appeal, the Lahore High Court closely examined the circumstances. It found that the couple had actually married for love against the father's wishes, and that the father had earlier filed (and later withdrawn) a criminal case accusing the husband of abducting his daughter. The court found it unbelievable that a father from a conservative rural background would let his daughter's love-marriage husband live in his own home, and equally implausible that the husband could kill her in a small, one-door room in front of three relatives and still escape unseen. Given the severe, multiple injuries and the fact that the killing was actually unwitnessed, the judges concluded this looked more like an "honour killing" by the family than a killing by the husband.

Since the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, the court acquitted the appellant, reaffirming that any genuine doubt must benefit the accused. The case highlights how careful scrutiny of circumstantial evidence and witness credibility can overturn even a death sentence.
