title: Appeal when time barred in Pakistan
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute in which the petitioners sued for a declaration of ownership rights over land, challenging a gift made by their relative to his daughters. During the trial, the petitioners repeatedly failed to produce their evidence despite being given eleven opportunities. On 18 July 2008, when their evidence was again absent, the trial court closed the evidence and dismissed the suit.

The petitioners tried to appeal this decision, but filed their appeal on 31 October 2008, well beyond the legally allowed period. Under the Limitation Act, appeals against such orders must be filed within thirty days, meaning their deadline had expired by mid-August 2008, even allowing for court summer vacations. The appellate court rejected their request to excuse the delay and dismissed the appeal as time-barred.

The petitioners then approached the High Court, arguing that the trial court's date-fixing process was flawed and that court staff, not the petitioners, caused the confusion over hearing dates, so the penalty of closing their evidence should not apply. They also argued the delay in filing their appeal should be forgiven.

The High Court disagreed. It found no sufficient cause for the delay, noted that the petitioners had obtained certified copies of the judgment only in October 2008, and held that the judgment was not void. Since the appeal was hopelessly late and lacked valid grounds for delay, the High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the lower courts' decisions. This case underscores how strictly limitation deadlines are enforced in Pakistani courts.

title: Abdul Ghafoor v. Sakhawat Khan,
explainer:
This case involved a criminal matter where the accused, Abdul Ghafoor and another, had reportedly reached a compromise with the family of a deceased victim over an offense involving injury or death under Pakistan's Penal Code (relating to Qisas and Diyat, the Islamic law concepts of retribution and compensation). The major heirs of the victim had waived their right to Qisas (retributive punishment), but the case involved minor heirs too, who needed compensation in the form of Diyat.

The accused asked the trial court to let them pay the Diyat amount owed to the minor heirs in the form of land rather than cash. The trial court rejected this request and instead ordered that the Diyat amount simply be deposited in a bank account for the minors, without ever formally deciding whether to accept the compromise, without fixing the actual Diyat amount, and without specifying each minor heir's share.

The Balochistan High Court found this was legally improper. It ruled that a trial court cannot just assume an automatic acquittal once a compromise is submitted; it must first examine the merits of the case and formally decide whether to accept or reject the compromise. Only after that should it determine the actual Diyat amount and how it should be paid. Since the trial court skipped these essential steps, the High Court set aside its orders and sent the case back, directing the trial court to follow the correct legal procedure this time.

title: Said Muhammad v. Chief Secretary Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved retired government employees in Balochistan who challenged how their Group Insurance benefits were being calculated. Employees had money deducted from their salaries during service for a Group Insurance scheme, along with General Provident Fund and Benevolent Fund contributions. While the Provident and Benevolent funds were refunded upon retirement, Group Insurance payouts were originally meant only for employees who died during service.

After employees complained about this policy, the Balochistan government issued an Ordinance in 2007 and related rules, followed by a notification that set new premium rates and insured amounts. This notification also stated that employees retiring between July 2007 and December 2008 would receive their actual contribution amount plus a modest increase capped at Rs. 50,000. The petitioners, who retired before this window, argued the notification made no distinction between old and newly retired employees, so they should also receive their contributions back as a matter of right.

The High Court declined to rule on the specific clause about the payment window, since that issue was already pending before the Supreme Court in a related case. Instead, the court found that the notification simply implemented enhanced insurance amounts under the 2007 Ordinance, which overrides other rules and notifications. Since the petitioners never legally challenged the Ordinance itself, they had no valid claim. The court dismissed the petitions.

This case matters because it clarifies that specific government notifications must be read alongside the governing law, and that challenging a notification without challenging the underlying ordinance is insufficient to succeed.

title: Mir Mitah Khan v. Government of Balochistan,
explainer:
A man applied for a government job (Microform Technician) in the National Assembly Secretariat, Islamabad, under Balochistan's reserved quota. When he wasn't appointed, he filed a civil suit in Quetta asking the court to declare him eligible and qualified for the post, to stop the post being re-advertised or given to someone else, and to direct his appointment.

The trial court in Quetta dismissed his suit at the outset, without examining its merits, ruling that it lacked territorial jurisdiction since the job, the advertisement's origin, the application submission, and the test were all connected to Islamabad. The appellate court agreed. The petitioner then challenged this before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court disagreed on the jurisdiction point, noting that since the job advertisement appeared in a Quetta newspaper and the petitioner applied from Quetta, part of the cause of action did arise in Quetta, so the courts below were wrong to say they had no jurisdiction.

However, the High Court still dismissed the case on a different ground: to seek a declaration under the Specific Relief Act, a person must show an existing legal right, not just a hope or candidacy for a job. Being a job applicant does not create a legal right to appointment, and appointment decisions rest solely with the hiring authority. Since no violation of law was shown, the suit was not legally maintainable regardless of jurisdiction.

This case clarifies that job applicants generally cannot sue for a declaration of entitlement to a government post merely because they applied and believe they are qualified.

title: Abdul Habib v. Fazal Muhammad,
explainer:
Abdul Habib and Fazal Muhammad were disputing over a piece of property. Fazal Muhammad had originally sued Abdul Habib for declaration of ownership, possession, and permanent injunction. However, when the trial court decided the case in 2008, its written judgment only granted declaration of ownership and an injunction stopping Abdul Habib from interfering—it never actually addressed or granted the claim for possession, even though possession had been asked for in the lawsuit. Neither side appealed that judgment, so it became final.

Later, Fazal Muhammad tried to enforce the decree by filing an execution application asking the court to hand him physical possession of the property. Abdul Habib objected, arguing that since the original judgment never granted possession, it could not be enforced at the execution stage. The executing court and the appellate court both rejected his objection and ordered him to hand over possession anyway.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It ruled that a decree must always match the judgment it comes from, and a court executing a decree cannot go beyond what the judgment actually granted. Since the judgment never granted possession, silence on that point meant the claim was effectively denied—not silently approved. Because the original judgment was never challenged and had become final, the missing relief could not be added later through execution proceedings. The High Court therefore set aside the lower courts' orders and dismissed the execution application, reinforcing that courts executing decrees cannot rewrite or expand what was originally decided.

title: Salahuddin v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Salahuddin and Wali Khan, who were named in a criminal FIR along with several co-accused. The FIR alleged that weapons had been recovered from two of their co-accused, who were also accused of firing shots, but no weapons were recovered from the petitioners themselves, and the FIR did not describe them performing any specific act in the alleged offence. Notably, the case against those co-accused was later allowed to be withdrawn by the prosecution, while the petitioners remained charged. The petitioners asked the trial court to acquit them early under Section 249-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows premature acquittal when there is no reasonable chance of conviction. The trial court refused, saying the case was at an advanced stage and that material witnesses still needed to be examined, without naming who those witnesses were.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence, including witness statements, and found that no witness placed the petitioners at the scene with any specific role in the crime, and one witness's testimony merely concerned recovery of empty shells. The court concluded there was no real evidence against the petitioners beyond mere presence, and that letting the more seriously implicated co-accused go free while pursuing the case against the petitioners suggested bad faith by the prosecution. The court allowed the petition and acquitted both men.

This case matters because it shows courts can end unjustified prosecutions early when evidence is clearly insufficient, protecting individuals from being kept unfairly on trial.

title: Mst. Faiqa Abdul Hayee v. Chairman BISE,
explainer:
This case is about a woman who asked a court to officially change her date of birth on her school records and secondary school certificate. She claimed her actual birth date was 25 December 1973, but her maternal uncle had mistakenly recorded it as 25 January 1970 when he enrolled her in school. She said she only discovered this error recently, after looking through her father's old diaries, and filed her lawsuit soon after finding out.

The trial court and the first appellate court both rejected her case, ruling that it was filed too late (barred by limitation law) and that she had not proven her claim with solid evidence. She then brought the matter to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed her case. It noted that she had waited 23 years without explaining why she or her parents stayed silent about the alleged error for so long. She also never produced the diaries she said revealed the mistake. While her parents testified in her favor, the court said parental statements about a child's birth date, though important, are not enough on their own—they need independent supporting evidence, such as municipal birth registration records, which she failed to provide.

This case highlights how Pakistani courts require timely action and solid documentary proof—not just family testimony—when seeking to correct official records like a birth date, and reinforces that delays in filing such claims can be fatal to a case regardless of the underlying facts.

title: The State v. Nawabzada Shah Zain Bugti,
explainer:
The case involved a criminal trial in Quetta arising from an FIR alleging that a large quantity of illegal arms and ammunition was recovered from Nawabzada Shah Zain Bugti and other accused persons. During the trial, the sole police eyewitness died. The prosecution then asked the trial court, under Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code, to allow two Army officers who were present at the scene and involved in the recovery to be brought in as additional witnesses, even though their names were not originally listed in the police challan.

The trial court refused, reasoning that similar evidence was already on record and questioning why these witnesses were not included earlier if they were so important.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed and set aside that order. It held that Section 540 gives courts wide power to summon any person whose evidence is essential for reaching a just decision, and this power must be exercised sensibly based on the case's circumstances. Since the only eyewitness had died, the court found it fair and necessary to let the prosecution bring forward the two remaining eyewitnesses. While acknowledging the prosecution had been negligent in not listing them earlier, the court stressed that some evidence needed to come on record to ensure a fair outcome for both sides. The prosecution was allowed to produce these witnesses without delay.

This case highlights how courts balance procedural lapses against the broader goal of ensuring justice is served through adequate evidence.

title: Syed Zia-Ud-Din and another V. Shabir Ahmed and others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a dispute over a car sold under an installment agreement. The buyer had agreed to pay Rs. 7 lac for a Toyota Corolla, paying only Rs. 50,000 upfront, with the remaining Rs. 6.5 lac due after two years, backed by a guarantor. When the balance was not paid, the seller sued and won an ex parte decree ordering the buyer and guarantor to pay the outstanding amount plus a fine, and barring the vehicle's registration from being transferred.

During execution of this money decree, the seller had police seize the vehicle from a third party, Shabbir Ahmed, who claimed he had legitimately purchased the car from someone else entirely. Ahmed argued he was a bona fide purchaser unconnected to the original defendants and sought to have the car returned to him.

The High Court found that the trial court's decree was only for recovery of money, not for handing over the vehicle itself, and it never authorized seizing the car from a third party. The execution court had failed to follow proper legal procedure for enforcing money decrees, which requires attaching and selling the judgment-debtors' own property, not simply seizing a vehicle from someone who wasn't a party to the original case. The court ruled that Ahmed's possession must be restored, while the decree-holder could still pursue proper execution methods within the actual terms of the decree. The ruling reinforces that courts must strictly follow prescribed legal procedures and cannot go beyond what a decree actually orders.

title: Muhammad Hassan Baloch v. Director Manpower Training,
explainer:
This case is about a government employee's right to keep living in an official residence after a department was split into two.

Muhammad Hassan Baloch was allotted a bungalow in Quetta in 1994 while working in the Labour and Manpower Department. Later, that department was bifurcated (divided) into separate departments, and he ended up working for one of the new departments while the property came under the control of the other. Authorities then ordered him to vacate, and the bungalow was allotted to someone else (respondent No. 2). Baloch sued, arguing he remained the lawful allottee and could not simply be evicted without due legal process. The trial court and the appellate court both dismissed his case, saying he had no cause of action.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that mere administrative bifurcation of a department does not automatically strip an employee of his lawful allotment status. The authorities, as owners, could reclaim the property, but only by following proper legal procedure - not by unilateral notice. The court declared that the letter demanding vacant possession and the fresh allotment to respondent No. 2 had no legal effect, and set them aside.

This matters because it reinforces that government employees have legal protections against arbitrary eviction from official housing, and that administrative reorganizations cannot bypass due process.

title: Syed Ain Ulah and 4 others V. Dilbar and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute between family members, Ain Ulah and others (petitioners) against Dilbar and others (respondents), over ownership and possession of agricultural land in Pishin, Balochistan. The petitioners had filed a civil suit seeking a declaration of ownership, cancellation of a mutation entry (land record change) in someone else's name, and a permanent injunction. The trial court dismissed the suit, saying it lacked jurisdiction under the West Pakistan Land Revenue Act, 1967, and that necessary parties had not been included in the case. The District Judge upheld this dismissal on appeal.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that while the Land Revenue Act does restrict civil courts from hearing certain revenue matters, this restriction has exceptions, and the lower courts wrongly focused only on the general bar without considering those exceptions. The court also noted that revenue authorities had never actually decided the dispute, but had instead told the parties to go to civil court. Since real questions about land possession and entitlement remained unresolved, a civil court was the proper forum. The High Court also found the dismissal for non-joinder of parties improper, since procedural law allows courts to add necessary parties rather than throw out a case entirely.

As a result, the High Court set aside the lower courts' decisions and sent the case back for a proper trial on the merits, with evidence. This case reinforces that civil courts cannot dismiss land disputes purely on technical or jurisdictional grounds without examining the substance of the claims.

The State through Assistant Advocate-General, Ex-Officio and Public Prosecutor
Balochistan, Quetta V. Abdul Wadood
,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by the State against the acquittal of Abdul Wadood, who was accused of leading an armed group that stormed Civil Hospital, Quetta in 1998 to forcibly free two prisoners under police custody, during which police officers were disarmed and hospital staff and patients were held at gunpoint. He was charged under section 17(3) of the Offences Against Property (Enforcement of Hudood) Ordinance, 1979, a serious offence known as Harabah.

During trial, after eighteen prosecution witnesses had already testified, the accused applied under section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows a court to acquit an accused early if there is no probability of conviction. The trial court granted this application and acquitted him before the trial was completed.

The State challenged this, arguing there was sufficient evidence on record and that the acquittal was premature. The Balochistan High Court agreed. It held that section 265-K gives courts discretion to acquit early, but this power must be used cautiously and only when there is clearly no chance of conviction, with reasons recorded based on the evidence. Since substantial evidence existed and the trial was nearly complete, the trial court should have finished the proceedings, examined the accused, allowed defence evidence, and decided the case on its merits rather than acquitting prematurely.

The High Court set aside the acquittal and sent the case back to the trial court for a proper decision on merits. This case clarifies that premature acquittals under section 265-K should not be used as a shortcut when a trial is far advanced

title: Malak Muhammad Noor through Attorney V. Mst. Bibi Rabia and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute between two sisters who jointly owned land in Quetta. One sister, Bibi Rabia, filed a lawsuit claiming that a general power of attorney used to sell her share of the property was fraudulent - she alleged it was prepared by affixing her thumb impression without her real consent, and that her signature-holder then sold her share to the petitioner. She asked the court to declare the sale invalid, cancel the power of attorney, and correct official land records to restore her ownership.

The trial court and the first appellate court both ruled in her favor, finding that the power of attorney and subsequent sale were fraudulent. The buyer of the property then challenged these decisions before the Balochistan High Court, arguing technical objections: that the burden of proof was wrongly placed on him, that the case was filed too late, and that a mere declaration suit was not valid without also seeking possession of the property.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It held that a co-owner does not need to include the other co-owner as a party when claiming her own share. It also ruled that when fraud is alleged against a registered power of attorney, the person alleging fraud carries the initial burden of proof, but strong evidence is needed to overturn such a registered document - and here the lower courts had properly found that burden was met. Importantly, the court emphasized that since both lower courts had already reached the same factual conclusions, the High Court could not disturb these findings in a revision petition. The petition was dismissed, and the sister's ownership claim was upheld.

title: Ghulam Hussain V. Chairman/Secretary S&GAD, Housing Allotment Committee, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a government-owned residential quarter (Quarter No. H-4, Wahadat Colony, Quetta) in Balochistan. The petitioner, Ghulam Hussain, a junior clerk, was occupying the house and claimed he was entitled to have it formally allotted to him, arguing the previous allottee had asked for it to be given to him when he vacated. He filed a civil suit seeking a declaration of his right to the property and challenging the later allotment of the same house to another government employee, respondent No. 3, asking that this allotment be cancelled and that he not be forcibly evicted.

The trial court dismissed his suit, finding he had no legal right or cause of action, and the appellate court upheld this decision. Ghulam Hussain then approached the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition, arguing the lower courts had not properly framed issues or considered evidence.

The High Court examined the relevant allotment rules and found that merely occupying a house without proper permission from the housing authorities does not create a legal right to that house. Someone in such a position is an illegal occupant, not someone with a valid claim, and authorities can lawfully order such a person to vacate. The court also clarified a procedural point: under the law, a court can reject a plaint for lacking a cause of action, but it cannot simply dismiss the entire suit on that basis. This distinction matters because it affects how such cases should be properly disposed of by trial courts.

title: The State and another V. Hameed and another,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murder (qatl-e-amd) and sentenced to death by a Sessions Court in Turbat, Balochistan. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court seeking acquittal. During the appeal, the family of the victim agreed to pardon him and filed a compromise application, waiving their right to demand qisas (retaliatory punishment equivalent to the death penalty) without asking for any diyat (compensation).

The High Court examined this compromise carefully because two of the nine legal heirs were minors (aged 14 and 17), and their mother tried to waive their right to qisas on their behalf without accepting any compensation. The court ruled this was not legally valid. Under Pakistani law, a minor's guardian cannot simply forgive the right to qisas for free; the law only allows the guardian to "compound" that right by accepting badal-e-sulh (compensation), which must be worth at least as much as the diyat (blood money) amount.

The court held that a valid compromise regarding minors requires a determined and accepted compensation amount, not a free pardon. It fixed badal-e-sulh at Rs. 32,00,000, to be deposited in National Savings accounts for the minors until they reach adulthood. The accused was acquitted of the murder charge under section 302(b) but would remain in custody until this amount was paid. The case clarifies that courts, not just guardians, must ensure minors' financial interests are protected in murder compromises.

title: Muhammad Naeem V. Orangzaib Khan,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over enforcing a court decree. The respondent had won an ex-parte judgment for specific performance from a Civil Judge in Abbottabad, ordering the appellant to fulfill an agreement. The respondent then sought to execute that decree, and the execution proceedings were transferred to a court in Quetta, since that is where the property and the appellant were located. Instead of simply objecting to how the decree was being executed, the appellant tried to challenge the original judgment itself, arguing that the Abbottabad court never had jurisdiction (since the property was in Quetta) and that the decree had been obtained through fraud. The Quetta court refused to entertain these objections, and the appellant appealed.

The Balochistan High Court upheld that refusal. It explained that under the law governing transferred decrees, a court merely executing a decree transferred to it cannot go behind that decree, cannot reverse or review the original judgment, and cannot rule on whether the original court had jurisdiction or acted properly. Its role is limited to deciding matters of execution, and only questions about its own jurisdiction to execute. The court also discussed the legal provision meant to let execution courts resolve disputes about carrying out a decree quickly, without forcing parties into separate lawsuits, but clarified that this doesn't extend to attacking the underlying judgment itself. The appeal was dismissed.

This case matters because it clarifies the limited powers of courts handling transferred decrees, preventing them from being used as a backdoor to challenge original judgments.

title: Muhammad Rafique and others V. Bibi Asifa and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over inherited property in Quetta. The plaintiffs, some legal heirs of the deceased Haji Pir Muhammad, sued for a declaration of their inheritance rights and a share of the estate. The defendants claimed the property had already been divided during the deceased's lifetime, based on a registered Will he had executed, and argued the plaintiffs had no remaining claim.

The Balochistan High Court examined two connected revision petitions. On the question of the Will and the alleged earlier partition, the court found the defendants had failed to prove their case. They did not produce the witnesses who had signed the Will, no one confirmed that a partition process had actually taken place, and the signatures on the Will were never verified. Because of this lack of solid evidence, the courts below were right to rule that the Will and partition were not proven, and the plaintiffs' suit for a share of the inheritance was upheld.

On the separate issue of mesne profits (compensation for use of property), the court held that a co-sharer who is in possession of joint family property is not automatically in "wrongful possession" just because other heirs are excluded from using it, unless there is proof of deliberate ouster. Since no such proof existed here, the appellate court's decision to award mesne profits to the plaintiffs was set aside.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the evidentiary burden needed to prove a Will and partition, and explains when co-sharers can be held liable for profits from shared property.

title: Muhammad Ishaque V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by Muhammad Ishaque, who was accused of murder along with several others under Pakistan's Penal Code provisions on qatl-e-amd (intentional killing) with common intention. The murder allegedly happened in 1998, and while two co-accused were arrested and tried soon after (eventually being acquitted in 2001), Ishaque remained a fugitive for about 15 years before being caught in 2013.

The Balochistan High Court refused to grant him bail. The judge reasoned that his 15-year absence from the law was deliberate, not accidental, especially since he was closely related to the two co-accused who had faced trial—making his claim of not knowing about the case against him unbelievable. The court also noted that the case was reported promptly and his name appeared in the original police report (FIR).

The court rejected his argument that he should get bail because the evidence used to acquit his co-accused also showed no case against him. The judge held that using that evidence for his bail would essentially decide his case before his own trial even began. The court also ruled that old age and physical weakness are not valid grounds for bail on their own.

This case matters because it reinforces the principle that fleeing from justice for a long time weakens a person's right to bail, and that evidence from a co-accused's trial cannot be used to pre-judge an absconder's case before he stands trial.

title: Muhammad Akram V. The State,
explainer:
In this case, a court employee (a "Naib Court," a junior court official) was accused of tampering with official court papers to help a convicted prisoner escape punishment. The prisoner, Zaman Khan, had been sentenced to 14 years in prison, but the appellant allegedly altered his remand papers to falsely show an acquittal instead of a conviction, and then got a judge to sign these fraudulent papers, leading to the prisoner's release. He was later re-arrested, exposing the fraud. The trial court convicted the appellant under Section 218 of the Pakistan Penal Code (dealing with public servants falsifying records to save someone from punishment), sentencing him to one year in prison plus a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious problems with how the case had been investigated and prosecuted. The court noted that other people who may have been involved—such as jail staff responsible for the prisoner's movement, or others connected to the fraudulent process—were never investigated or charged. The court felt that convicting only this one low-level official while letting other possibly responsible parties go free was unjust and incomplete justice.

Rather than deciding guilt or innocence, the High Court set aside the lower court's judgment entirely and sent the case back for fresh investigation, ordering police to identify and charge everyone potentially involved, and directing a full trial of all such persons, to be completed promptly. This case highlights the importance of thorough, fair investigations rather than scapegoating a single individual.

title: Abdul Hameed V. Mst. Shabnam Alias Shabana and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about which court should hear an appeal in a child custody dispute. A mother, Mst. Shabnam, had applied under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, for custody of a minor, and the Family Judge at Hub granted her custody. The father, Abdul Hameed, appealed to the Additional District Judge, but that judge dismissed the appeal, saying he had no jurisdiction and that such appeals should instead go directly to the High Court, based on Section 47 of the Guardians and Wards Act.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It explained that custody and guardianship matters cannot be decided by looking at the Guardians and Wards Act alone; they must be read together with the West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964, which gives Family Courts exclusive jurisdiction over such matters. Under this combined reading, appeals from a Family Court's custody decision normally go to the District Court, unless the Family Court itself was presided over by a judge of District Judge rank, in which case the appeal would go to the High Court. Since the case had been decided by a Family Judge without that status, the appeal should have gone to the District Judge, not the High Court.

The High Court found that the Additional District Judge had made an error and wrongly refused to hear the appeal. It set aside that order and directed the appellate court to decide the appeal on its merits. This clarifies the correct appellate path for custody cases decided by Family Courts.

title: Muhammad Ayub Khan and another V. Secretary, Board of Directors Hashim Khan Trust, Quetta and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over inheritance rights to land in Quetta originally belonging to Baz Muhammad Khan, who died in 1911. He left three sons and two daughters, but when the property was officially recorded in government revenue records, only the sons were listed as owners, excluding the daughters entirely. Decades later, descendants of one excluded daughter, Bibi Saeeda, sued for a court declaration recognizing their inheritance rights, seeking cancellation of the mutation entries, invalidation of a trust created in 1990 that they claimed was used to cut them out, and financial compensation. The trial court dismissed their suit, apparently on grounds that too much time had passed.

The Balochistan High Court reversed this decision. It held that inheritance rights vest automatically in legal heirs the moment a person dies, and mere passage of time does not extinguish that right. Entries in revenue records are only presumptive evidence of ownership, not actual proof of title, and can be challenged once a person becomes aware their rights were denied. The clock for filing a lawsuit starts running only when someone's inheritance claim is actually refused, not from when the original record entry was made. Since the daughters' descendants had been wrongly excluded, their claim was valid and not time-barred. The court sent the case back to the trial court for proper determination of shares, after adding the provincial government as a party. This case matters because it reinforces that inheritance rights, especially of women who are often historically excluded from land records, cannot be defeated simply by delay or bureaucratic omission.

title: Gohram alias Ali Gohar and another V. Mst. Zar Bano alias Zero through L.Rs. and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family land dispute in Balochistan. The petitioners, Gohram and Ali Akbar, claimed that their father and his brother had jointly purchased several pieces of land using their combined earnings, but the property documents were only put in the brother's name. They said that when their father moved away due to drought, he left the land in the care of a relative, Mst. Zar Bano, to cultivate on their behalf, and that they continued to receive a share of the proceeds for years. They later discovered that the revenue records showed the land registered in the names of Zar Bano and other relatives, and they claimed this was the result of fraud. They sued for a court declaration confirming their ownership and for possession of the land.

The lower courts dismissed the suit, and that dismissal was upheld on appeal. The petitioners then brought this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court also dismissed the case. It found that the petitioners had waited too long to sue, since a claim like this must be filed within six years of when the right to challenge the ownership first arose, and the petitioners could not show when their title was actually denied. More importantly, they failed to produce any real evidence proving their ownership: their names did not appear on the property agreements, no documents supported their claimed title, and they could not prove the old agreements were genuine. The court reaffirmed that revenue records don't create ownership by themselves but are simply presumed accurate until proven otherwise. Since the petitioners couldn't rebut that presumption, their case failed.

title: Muhammad Lal V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murder under Section 302(c) of the Pakistan Penal Code, sentenced by the trial court to ten years imprisonment plus payment of Diyat (blood money) to the victim's heirs. The Balochistan High Court had earlier upheld this sentence on appeal in 2012.

Later, while hearing an unrelated case, the same judges noticed a legal problem: Section 302 of the Penal Code only allows three types of punishment for murder—death as qisas, death or life imprisonment as tazir, or imprisonment up to 25 years—but nowhere does it allow imprisonment and Diyat to be imposed together. Realizing their earlier ruling may have imposed an unlawful double punishment, the court issued notices to reexamine its own 2012 judgment.

Both the defense lawyer and the prosecutor's office ultimately agreed that ordering both imprisonment and Diyat was not permitted by law. The court held that although judgments are normally final and cannot be reopened, an exception exists when a judgment is void, based on a patent illegality, or issued without jurisdiction. Since the earlier judgment imposed a punishment not recognized by law, the court ruled it must be corrected to prevent an illegality from continuing.

This case matters because it shows courts can revisit even their own final decisions to fix clear legal errors, and it clarifies that Pakistani law does not allow combining imprisonment with Diyat for murder convictions under Section 302(c).

title: Nawab Khan alias Dah Khan and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved a fight in Balochistan in which a man named Said Khan was injured, allegedly beaten with sticks and stones by four men, resulting in a fractured leg. Two of the accused, Nawab Khan and Fazal Khan, were tried and convicted by a Magistrate for causing hurt under the Pakistan Penal Code, receiving six months and two years imprisonment respectively along with fines (Daman) to be paid to the victim. Their appeal to the Sessions Judge was rejected, and the conviction was upheld. Both the convicted men and the complainant then approached the Balochistan High Court, the men seeking acquittal and the complainant seeking a harsher sentence.

The High Court examined whether there were serious legal errors or misreading of evidence by the lower courts that would justify overturning their decisions. It found that the explanation for a delay in filing the police report was reasonable and unchallenged, that family relationships among witnesses did not automatically make their testimony unreliable absent proof of bad faith, and that no major inconsistencies undermined the prosecution's case. The defense evidence had already been considered and found unconvincing.

The court therefore upheld the conviction and rejected both petitions, including the complainant's request for a harsher sentence, noting he had not raised that issue earlier before the appellate court. The judgment reinforces that revision courts should not reopen factual findings already properly considered by trial and appellate courts unless clear legal errors exist.

title: Abdul Majeed and 7 others V. Mst. Shah Bibi and 4 others,
explainer:
This case is about a family land dispute in Balochistan. Two sisters, Shah Bibi and Gull Bibi, claimed they had inherited land from their grandfather but had to leave the area due to drought. They alleged that while they were away, another family (the petitioners) wrongly got themselves recorded as owners in the revenue records. The sisters sued for a declaration that they were the rightful owners, correction of the land records, and a permanent injunction stopping the other side from interfering with the land. Notably, they did not ask for possession, claiming they already had it.

The case went through multiple rounds in the trial court, appellate forums, and even a previous revision before the High Court, with conflicting decisions along the way. Eventually, during these proceedings, the plaintiffs sought to amend their suit to add a claim for possession, since evidence suggested the other side was actually occupying the land with houses and a tube-well built on it.

The High Court ruled that courts have wide power to allow amendments to pleadings at any stage, including during appeals or revisions, as long as the amendment is necessary to resolve the real dispute and does not change the fundamental nature of the case. Since a plea for possession was closely tied to the original claim, the court allowed the amendment, subject to payment of costs, and sent the case back to the trial court to frame proper issues and decide the matter on merits. This ruling clarifies how flexible amendment rules can be used to ensure disputes are fully and fairly resolved.

explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a domestic gas consumer, Arbab Najeebullah, and Sui Southern Gas Company. The company disconnected his gas supply in 2007, alleging his domestic meter was being misused for commercial purposes, and filed a criminal case against him. He was acquitted in the criminal trial. He then sued the company in civil court, seeking a declaration that the disconnection and the resulting bill of Rs.110,105 were illegal, and asking for restoration of his gas connection. Both the trial court and the appellate court ruled in his favor, relying heavily on his criminal acquittal.

The Balochistan High Court overturned these decisions. It held that criminal and civil cases have different standards of proof, and evidence or findings from the criminal trial could not simply be transferred to the civil case without being properly presented as evidence there. More importantly, the court found that since this was a dispute between a gas consumer and a licensed utility company, it was governed by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority Ordinance, 2002, which provides a specific mechanism for resolving such disputes. The plaintiff should have used that regulatory remedy first instead of going straight to civil court. Because he bypassed this required process, his civil suit was not maintainable. The High Court set aside the lower courts' judgments and dismissed the suit, emphasizing that specialized statutory remedies must be exhausted before approaching ordinary courts.

title: Muhammad Qasim V. Ahsan Raza and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a property in Quetta housing a school, where the original complainant, Muhammad Naqi, had filed a case under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, alleging he was forcibly dispossessed by Ahsan Raza. Before the case could proceed to trial, Muhammad Qasim tried to have himself added as a co-complainant, claiming joint ownership of the property. The trial court repeatedly refused to include him and eventually allowed Naqi to withdraw his complaint after Naqi's lawyer said he did not intend to pursue the case and had no evidence to offer, with the court also noting the dispute seemed civil in nature. Qasim challenged this refusal, and after several rounds of litigation, including a Supreme Court remand, the matter came back to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found that Qasim's original complaint lacked essential details like witness names and a summary of evidence, and there was no proof the trial court had failed to summon witnesses despite being given proper information. The court held that the trial judge, despite poor drafting, had reached the right outcome by dismissing the complaint for lack of merit, though technically an order of acquittal should have been recorded for the accused. The High Court upheld the dismissal and acquittal, and separately directed the provincial government to look into the affairs of the school to protect the children studying there. This case clarifies procedural requirements for complaints under the Illegal Dispossession Act and reinforces that courts must properly record acquittals when dismissing such complaints.

title: Muhammad Ali and 21 others V. Abdul Jalil,
explainer:
This case concerns a civil revision petition filed in the Balochistan High Court by three women (Mehr Khatoon, Naz Bibi and Sharatoon) challenging earlier decisions of a local court and appellate forum that had rejected their property claim. The petition was filed in 2006 through an advocate who, instead of submitting a proper power of attorney (Wakalat Nama), merely gave an undertaking that he would file it later. That authorization never came.

Over the following years, the case dragged on, two of the original petitioners died, their legal heirs were added, and different lawyers appeared for the petitioners without ever formally proving they were authorized to represent them. When notices were finally sent directly to the petitioners, some heirs appeared and even claimed that certain original petitioners had never actually filed the suit or authorized any legal action at all.

The High Court examined the law on how advocates must be appointed, particularly Order III, Rule 4 of the Civil Procedure Code, which requires a written, signed authorization before a lawyer can act for a client. Since no such document was ever filed, the court held that the advocates who appeared were not properly authorized, meaning the petitioners were never legally represented before the court.

As a result, the court ruled that the revision petition, having been filed by an unauthorized person, was not maintainable and dismissed it. The case highlights the importance of formal, written authorization for lawyers to represent clients in court.

title: Abdul Haque V. Mir Ahmed and 6 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over agricultural land in Mastung district, Balochistan. The petitioner, Abdul Haque, filed a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, claiming he had been forcibly dispossessed of land he owned, that his tenants had been assaulted, standing crops destroyed, and that the respondents had illegally constructed houses on the property. The trial court dismissed his complaint at an early stage, before framing any charge, holding that the dispute was essentially civil in nature and did not amount to criminal illegal dispossession. Abdul Haque challenged this dismissal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court first addressed whether a revision petition was even allowed, since the Illegal Dispossession Act does not explicitly mention appeal or revision rights. The Court held that since the Act extends the Code of Criminal Procedure to its proceedings, the general right of appeal and revision under the Cr.P.C. applies, so the petition was maintainable.

On the merits, however, the Court found that the complaint lacked essential details, such as the exact area of land involved, when the alleged construction occurred, or how dispossession took place. There was no evidence the respondents were land-grabbers who forcibly seized the property. The investigation report showed only that respondents were in physical possession, which was not enough to prove criminal illegal dispossession. The Court therefore upheld the trial court's decision and dismissed the petition, emphasizing that vague allegations cannot substitute for specific proof of criminal wrongd

title: Mst. Aisha and 2 others V. Mst. Mah Gul and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a family dispute over a deceased government employee's unpaid dues (money owed to him by the Health Department in Balochistan, where he worked as a Ward Boy). His widow applied to a district court for a succession certificate, which would let her collect these dues. His mother, brother, and sister challenged this, saying they too were legal heirs entitled to a share under Islamic inheritance law. The trial court sided entirely with the widow, ruling she alone was entitled to the money and excluding the other relatives completely.

The Balochistan High Court overturned that exclusion. It clarified that a succession certificate under the Succession Act, 1925 does not decide who actually owns or is entitled to inherit the money involved. Its only purpose is to let someone collect a debt safely, while making the certificate holder legally responsible for later distributing the funds to all rightful heirs. The court explained that obtaining a certificate does not stop other heirs from later suing to prove their entitlement and claim their rightful share.

Because the trial court wrongly treated the certificate proceedings as if they settled inheritance rights, the High Court set aside that part of the decision and modified the order, allowing the appeal filed by the mother, brother, and sister.

The case matters because it reinforces an important legal principle: a succession certificate is a practical tool for debt recovery, not a final determination of inheritance rights, which must be decided through proper civil litigation if disputed.

title: Muhammad Anwar V. SHO and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a father, Muhammad Anwar, whose daughter Samina was found dead at her husband's house from a gunshot wound. A murder FIR was registered, and police investigated, recovering the pistol and other evidence from the scene. Unsatisfied with how the investigation was conducted, Anwar alleged the police acted with bias, failed to properly record a confession, and did not preserve evidence properly. He asked the Additional Sessions Judge, acting as Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace, to order a reinvestigation by transferring the case to the Crimes Branch. That request was denied on the grounds that the investigation was already complete and the case had moved to trial, so reopening it would serve little purpose. Anwar then challenged this refusal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition, ruling that Anwar had approached the wrong forum. It clarified that a Justice of the Peace only has power to order transfer of investigation before the police report is submitted and the trial court takes up the case. Once that happens, only the trial court can address concerns about evidence, missing witnesses, or forensic reports, using its powers under Section 540 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The court emphasized that the investigation process is never truly closed, since new facts can still be brought up during trial. This ruling clarifies the limited jurisdiction of Justices of the Peace and reinforces that trial courts are the proper venue for addressing investigative shortcomings once a case reaches trial.

title: Ghulam Mustafa and 4 others V. Evacuee Trust Property Board, Government of Pakistan through Chairman and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the transfer and posting of two employees (respondents 3 and 4) as Tehsildars in Balochistan's Revenue Department. Five civil servants already working in that department challenged these appointments, arguing that the two individuals were actually employees of the Evacuee Trust Property Board whose initial hiring had been irregular, and that placing them on deputation as Tehsildars violated civil service rules.

The evidence showed the two employees had first been appointed on a temporary work-charge basis, later "regularized," but the Board itself admitted on scrutiny that these appointments were bogus and illegal. Despite this, they were sent on deputation to the Revenue Department with government approval.

The Balochistan High Court ruled that since all parties involved were civil servants, the proper forum for resolving such disputes was the Service Tribunal, not a constitutional petition in the High Court. The petitioners had not pursued that remedy, so the petition was not maintainable in the High Court.

However, the Court still expressed concern that both the lending and borrowing government departments knew about the illegal appointments yet stayed silent for a long time. It ordered that the deputation should not be extended, directed that the two employees be sent back to their original department without delay, and instructed the parent department to take disciplinary action against them and against officials responsible for their improper appointment and transfer.

The case highlights how courts enforce proper civil service procedures while respecting jurisdictional boundaries between courts and specialized tribunals.

title: Abdul Bari Khadim V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a retired government employee, Abdul Bari Khadim, who had worked in Balochistan's Education Department since 1986 and retired in 2012. He also served as a Project Director in an education project and claimed he was owed reimbursement for various expenses. After retiring, he filed a departmental appeal in September 2012 seeking recovery of his salary and other dues, but the appeal remained undecided for years. He did not file an appeal before the Balochistan Service Tribunal within the required 120-day limitation period, for reasons he did not fully explain.

Instead, he approached the Balochistan High Court through a constitutional petition, asking it to direct the authorities to decide his pending departmental appeal, so that he could then potentially pursue a service appeal before the Tribunal. The government's lawyer argued that since the limitation period for filing before the Tribunal had already expired, no relief should be granted.

The High Court decided not to examine the deeper legal question of whether the petition was valid given the limitation issue, or whether the petitioner still had a right to approach the Service Tribunal. It left that question for the Tribunal itself to decide, since that was the proper forum for service-related disputes. The Court simply ordered the concerned authority to decide the petitioner's pending departmental appeal within one month.

This judgment matters because it shows courts sometimes issue narrow, practical orders (compelling a decision on a pending appeal) without ruling on broader legal questions, leaving those for the specialized tribunal meant to handle civil service disputes.

title: Muhammad Ayub and others V. Bibi Gull and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute in Quetta over land jointly purchased by two ancestors. The plaintiffs (petitioners) sued for a declaration that they owned specific shares of the property, wanted certain mutation entries in the revenue record cancelled, and claimed possession of their shares along with income from the property. The defendants claimed they were the sole owners.

After both sides had already presented their evidence in the trial court, the plaintiffs filed several applications, including requests to place additional documents on record and to call more witnesses. The trial court granted two minor procedural requests but refused to allow new documents and witnesses at that late stage, and also refused to strike out certain cross-examination. The plaintiffs challenged this refusal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the trial court's decision. It held that under the Civil Procedure Code, a party wanting to introduce late evidence or witnesses must show "good cause," and these rules are mandatory. Here, the plaintiffs had already closed their evidence without reserving any right to rebuttal, gave no real details of what they wanted to produce, and made their request only after the evidence stage was complete. The court noted such material could still be referred to and judicially noticed at final hearing.

This judgment clarifies how much discretion trial courts have to refuse late attempts to reintroduce evidence, reinforcing that procedural fairness requires timely and specific requests, not last-minute applications after evidence has closed.

title: Muhammad Ibrahim V. Niaz Muhammad,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a landlord-tenant dispute over a house in Quetta. Niaz Muhammad, claiming to be the owner, filed for eviction of his tenant Muhammad Ibrahim, citing non-payment of rent and his own need for the house. Ibrahim denied being a tenant at all, claiming instead that he had purchased the property from a different person, Baz Muhammad, and that a case for specific performance of that sale was already pending in court. The Rent Controller sided with the landlord and ordered eviction, prompting this appeal.

The High Court overturned that decision. It held that before seeking eviction, a landlord must first clearly prove two things: that he actually owns the property, and that the person he wants evicted is genuinely his tenant. Simply having some entries in revenue records (mutation) in his favor was not enough, especially when ownership itself was disputed and a separate ownership case was pending. The court found no solid evidence that Niaz Muhammad owned the house or that Ibrahim had ever paid him rent.

The court set aside the eviction order and dismissed the case, ruling that such ownership disputes must first be resolved in a proper civil court with full evidence, rather than through summary rent-eviction proceedings. This matters because it reinforces that eviction cases cannot be used to sidestep genuine ownership disputes—landlord status must be firmly established first.

title:
Hamayun Shah V. Secretary Home and Tribal Affairs, Government of Balochistan
and 4 others

explainer:
This case concerned a restaurant owner in Quetta who offered sheesha (water pipe) smoking to customers alongside his regular food business. The Balochistan government had issued an order in August 2014 banning sheesha at public places including restaurants, hotels, fast food centers, net cafes, and sheesha cafes. The petitioner was earlier charged over this but got acquitted in the criminal case. He then challenged the government's ban itself, arguing that tobacco used in sheesha was legally imported and available in the open market, that smoking sheesha wasn't defined as an offence under any law, and that the government had no legal authority to stop his lawful business, which he said violated his constitutional right under Article 18 to freely conduct trade and business.

The Balochistan High Court rejected his petition. It held that offering sheesha smoking violated the Prohibition of Smoking and Protection of Non-Smokers Health Ordinance, 2002, and that the legal importation of tobacco did not make its use in this manner lawful. The court also found that the provincial government's restraining order was validly issued under Section 144(6) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which specifically empowers provincial governments to issue such orders. Since Article 18 protects only lawful trade and business, and the petitioner's sheesha service was not lawful, no fundamental right had been violated. The petition was dismissed, meaning the ban on sheesha smoking at public places stood, reinforcing public health regulation over business claims.

title: Suleman Mehmood V. Anwari Begum and others,
explainer:
This case is about a legal dispute over which court had the authority to handle a deceased person's estate. Suleman Mehmood applied to a civil court in Quetta for a letter of administration, so he could manage the immoveable properties left behind by his late brother, Saqib Mashhood. The deceased had lived in Quetta, but his properties were located in different districts of Punjab (Sialkot, Multan and Sargodha). The trial court in Quetta refused to hear the case, saying it had no jurisdiction because the properties were outside its territorial limits, and returned the application.

Suleman appealed. The Balochistan High Court examined the relevant provisions of the Succession Act, 1925, particularly Sections 264 and 270 (which deal with jurisdiction for letters of administration) as opposed to Section 371 (which applies specifically to succession certificates). The High Court clarified that both the court where the deceased ordinarily resided and the court where the properties are located can have jurisdiction to grant a letter of administration. Since the deceased resided in Quetta, that court also had jurisdiction, and it was wrong to reject the application without properly examining the law.

The High Court set aside the trial court's order and sent the case back for a fresh decision. The judgment matters because it clarifies which courts can handle estate administration when the deceased's residence and property locations differ, ensuring people aren't wrongly denied access to the correct forum.

title: Mst. Parveen Khan V. Abdul Ghafoor and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a wife's claim for maintenance from her husband after their marriage broke down. Parveen Khan had sued her husband Abdul Ghafoor for unpaid dower money, dowry items, and maintenance for herself and their minor daughter, alleging she was mistreated and neglected. The husband denied cruelty, claimed she left his house on her own, said he had already divorced her, and disputed the dowry claims.

The trial court partly ruled in her favor, awarding her maintenance from 2010 through the divorce date and the Iddat period afterward. However, the husband appealed, and the appellate court reduced her maintenance entitlement, ruling she was only owed maintenance for the three-month Iddat period after divorce, not for the earlier years, since she failed to prove her husband had thrown her out of the house or treated her cruelly.

The wife then challenged this reduction before the Balochistan High Court, arguing an agreement between the couple entitled her to maintenance from whenever she left the house. The High Court disagreed. Under Islamic law principles (specifically Rules 277-278 of Muhammadan Law), a wife is only entitled to maintenance if she proves she was forced out due to her husband's cruelty. Since Parveen Khan couldn't prove this, the court upheld the appellate court's decision limiting her maintenance to the Iddat period only. Her petition was dismissed.

title: Ali Khan V. Superintendent Central Jail, Mach and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved Ali Khan, a prisoner at Central Jail Mach, who had been convicted decades earlier on ten counts of murder and offences under the Explosive Substances Act, arising from an FIR registered in 1987. He was originally sentenced to death, but this was later converted to life imprisonment on each count, with courts ordering that the sentences run consecutively rather than concurrently. Added together, this amounted to 239 years of imprisonment.

Ali Khan filed a petition in the Balochistan High Court arguing that he had already served more than 45 years including remissions, and that keeping him in custody any longer was unlawful. His lawyers relied on later Supreme Court judgments that had allowed similar relief to other prisoners.

The High Court found that Ali Khan's own case had already been specifically decided by the Supreme Court in 2011, which had considered and rejected exactly this request for concurrent sentencing and release, given the serious nature of his crimes involving bomb blasts and murders. Since the Supreme Court's decision is binding on all courts in Pakistan under Article 189 of the Constitution, the High Court held it could not override or go beyond that ruling, even in light of newer judgments in other people's cases.

The petition was therefore dismissed. The case illustrates how Supreme Court decisions bind lower courts, and that once an issue has been finally decided in a person's own case, later rulings in different cases cannot automatically be used to reopen it.

title: Muhammad Azhar Awan V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a petitioner, Muhammad Azhar Awan, who asked the Balochistan High Court to direct the provincial government to compensate his family for losses of life and property, which he claimed resulted from acts of terrorism linked to private respondents and certain officials of a cooperative bank and local revenue offices. He said his family had lawfully purchased ownership and tenancy rights to land in Dasht, Mastung, decades earlier, and that this ownership had already been upheld through civil court proceedings, appeals, and a revision petition. Despite this, he alleged that rival claimants had forcibly occupied the land, destroyed property including a house, tube well, and trees, and pursued fraudulent complaints against him and his family, warranting government compensation as victims of terrorism.

The High Court found that the dispute was essentially a factual and title controversy that had already been litigated extensively in civil courts, with the petitioner's ownership upheld and attempts to overturn it having failed. Allegations of fraud remained unproven in any forum. The court held that such factual disputes could not be resolved through constitutional petitions under Article 199, which are not meant to substitute for ordinary civil remedies, especially where alternate remedies exist or have already been pursued. The petition was therefore found not maintainable.

This case is significant because it reinforces the principle that constitutional jurisdiction is not a suitable avenue for resolving disputed facts or claims requiring evidence, particularly when alternate legal remedies are available or already exhausted.

title: Ali Bakhsh Baloch and others V. The State through D.G. NAB and others,
explainer:
This Balochistan High Court case involved three government officials—Ali Bakhsh Baloch, Abdul Wali Kakar, and Asfand Yar Khan Kakar—who had earlier held positions as Secretary of Food, Director Food, and Provincial Minister for Food in the Balochistan government. They sought pre-arrest bail after the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) filed a reference accusing them, along with an official named Muhammad Haseen Khan Afridi, of being involved in the embezzlement of government wheat worth nearly 293 million rupees from grain storage centers in Chaman and Pishin. The alleged offences fell under provisions of the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999, dealing with misuse of authority and corruption.

The petitioners argued they were falsely implicated due to mala fide (bad faith) on the part of the authorities. However, the court found that their petitions did not specifically spell out any such mala fide intent, which is a strict legal requirement for granting anticipatory bail in such cases. Instead, the allegations against them concerned genuine misuse of authority, negligence, and failure to perform their official duties, which collectively resulted in large-scale embezzlement and heavy financial loss to the government.

Given the seriousness of the accusations and the absence of proven bad faith, the court refused to grant pre-arrest bail and dismissed all three petitions. The case underscores that public officials cannot easily avoid arrest in corruption cases merely by alleging mala fide without concrete evidence

title: Bibi Humera V. Ghulam Dastagir and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a widow, Bibi Humera, whose husband, a government employee, died in the line of duty in 2011 and was declared "Shaheed." The government awarded compensation of two million rupees plus his monthly salary and pension benefits, meant for his widow and five children. A succession certificate was obtained by the deceased's brother, who then collected the compensation and salary, allegedly keeping most of it for himself and refusing to hand over the minor children or their share of the money to the widow. She approached the Balochistan High Court seeking custody of her children, return of the money, and protection.

During proceedings, custody of two of the five children was restored to the mother, while the older children preferred to stay with relatives. The Deputy Commissioner's office began paying school fees directly to the children's institutions to prevent misuse of funds. The court found that the brother-in-law, though granted the succession certificate as an attorney for the widow and children, was legally bound to properly distribute the funds under Section 375 of the Succession Act, 1925. It sent the matter back to the court that issued the certificate, directing it to recover the minors' shares from him. Regarding custody, the court held that since alternate remedies existed under the Family Courts Act, 1964, the mother should pursue custody through the family courts rather than through a constitutional petition. This case highlights the importance of protecting vulnerable widows and children from financial exploitation by relatives.

title: Principal, Bolan Medical College, Quetta V. Dr. Sharbat Khan and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a housing dispute at Bolan Medical College, Quetta. Dr. Sharbat Khan sued to be declared the lawful allottee of a government bungalow and sought to stop the college from allotting it to anyone else or handing over possession. The trial court ruled in his favor, declaring him the rightful allottee and restraining further allotment. It also ordered the Principal of the college to personally pay Rs. 25,000 in compensatory costs under Section 35-A of the Civil Procedure Code, reasoning that she had issued an illegal and unauthorized order that forced the plaintiff into unnecessary litigation.

The Principal challenged only this cost order, not the main decision. Her appeal was dismissed on a technicality (filed late), so she approached the High Court.

The High Court examined Section 35-A, which allows compensatory costs only when a party's claim or defence is shown to be false or vexatious to their own knowledge, when the opposing party specifically objected to it at the earliest opportunity, and when the trial court records clear reasons for such a finding. The judge found none of these conditions were met here: the plaintiff never objected that the defence was false or vexatious, and the trial court gave no reasons for imposing costs.

Therefore, the High Court set aside only the portion of the judgment imposing compensatory costs, while leaving the rest of the ruling intact. The case clarifies that courts cannot casually impose such penalties without following the specific procedural safeguards built into the law.

title: Akhtar Hussain V. Widow of Malik Naeem Ullah and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about whether a lawsuit filed against someone who was already dead can result in a valid court judgment.

Akhtar Hussain had filed a civil suit for property title and specific performance of an agreement against a man named Naeemullah. When Naeemullah did not appear in court, the trial court proceeded ex parte and eventually decreed the suit in Hussain's favour in 2010. Hussain then began executing the decree, transferring part of the disputed property into his name. Years later, it emerged that Naeemullah had actually died back in 2008, before the suit was even filed. His legal heirs applied to have the ex parte decree set aside, arguing the suit was filed against a dead person. The trial court accepted this, cancelling both the original decree and the execution proceedings. This decision was upheld on appeal.

Hussain challenged these rulings before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that at most the case should have been sent back for a fresh decision on merits, not dismissed outright, and that the heirs' application was filed too late.

The High Court rejected his arguments and dismissed the petition with costs. It held that a suit filed against a person who is already dead is fundamentally invalid from the start, and this defect cannot be fixed later by simply adding the deceased's legal heirs to the case. Since the original suit was void, everything built on it, including the decree and execution proceedings, was also invalid. The lower courts' decisions were therefore correct.

title: Naeem Sher Tareen V. Beenish Ali and others,
explainer:
This case involved a husband who challenged his wife's decision to seek dissolution of their marriage through khula (a wife's right to end a marriage) in a Family Court in Islamabad. The wife had left the matrimonial home with their daughter and filed for khula there. Instead of contesting the case on its merits, the husband filed a constitutional petition in the Balochistan High Court asking for two main things: first, to have the case transferred from Islamabad to Quetta, and second, to have Section 10(4) of the Family Courts Act, 1964 declared un-Islamic and unconstitutional, along with directions to the government to amend family laws according to Sharia.

The High Court dismissed the petition on two grounds. First, it held that questions about whether a law conflicts with Islamic injunctions fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Federal Shariat Court under Articles 203-D and 203-G of the Constitution, which specifically bar other courts, including High Courts, from deciding such matters. Second, since the Family Court in Islamabad was outside the territorial jurisdiction of the Balochistan High Court, it had no power to order the case transferred.

The judgment matters because it reinforces the constitutional boundary between ordinary courts and the Federal Shariat Court on religious-law questions, and confirms that High Courts cannot order transfers of cases pending in courts outside their territorial jurisdiction.

title: Naeem Sher Tareen V. Beenish Ali and 4 others,
explainer:
This case arose after a wife filed for dissolution of her marriage through khula in a Family Court in Islamabad, after leaving her husband's home with their daughter. The husband responded not by contesting the case on its merits, but by filing a constitutional petition in the Balochistan High Court. He asked the court to declare Section 10(4) of the Family Courts Act, 1964 (a provision dealing with khula proceedings) as illegal and un-Islamic, to stop Family Courts from applying it, to direct the government to make laws consistent with Islam, and to transfer his wife's case from Islamabad to Quetta. He named the President, National Assembly, and Senate as respondents, believing they were responsible for the law.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that the husband had misunderstood constitutional procedure: the President could not be sued due to constitutional immunity, and Parliament's houses are not legal entities that can be made parties in such petitions. More importantly, the court ruled that it had no jurisdiction to decide whether a law is repugnant to Islamic injunctions. Under Articles 203D and 203G of the Constitution, only the Federal Shariat Court has the power to examine such questions, and other courts, including High Courts, are barred from doing so. The court also refused the transfer request since it had no authority over courts in Islamabad.

The case is a reminder that challenges to laws on Islamic grounds must go to the Federal Shariat Court, not ordinary High Courts.

title: Tariq Hussain and others V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Education Department and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved 44 employees of the Balochistan Text Book Board who had been given leave encashment payments (cash payments for unused leave) for the years 2011 to 2015. Later, a Departmental Accounts Committee objected, saying the payments were calculated incorrectly, using gross salary instead of basic pay, and directed the employees to refund the overpaid amounts. The employees challenged these recovery notices in the Balochistan High Court, arguing the payments had been properly approved and that similarly placed employees in other provinces enjoyed the same benefit.

The court examined the relevant laws, including the Balochistan Text Book Board Ordinance and Revised Leave Rules. It found that the leave encashment rule cited only applied to employees retiring at superannuation, not to serving employees. It also found procedural problems: the body that had approved the payments, described as a "Board of Directors," did not actually exist under the law, only an Advisory Council did, and neither had the power to make binding rules. Only the Text Book Board itself had that authority, and government rules should have applied since the Board's own rules were not properly framed.

However, the court ultimately dismissed the petition not on these merits alone, but because the employees had not first used the available departmental remedy of filing a representation to a higher authority before approaching the court. Since an alternate remedy existed and was not used, the court held the constitutional petition was not maintainable.

title: Dost Muhammad V. Additional Sessions Judge Barkhan at Rakhni and another,
explainer:
This case concerns a criminal trial in Barkhan that was put on indefinite hold because two key prosecution witnesses, including the complainant, had stopped appearing in court after allegedly becoming fugitives in a separate murder case. The trial court had accepted the prosecution's request to place the case in "dormant" status, meaning it would remain paused with no further proceedings until these witnesses became available, while the accused remained on bail.

One of the accused challenged this order before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that a criminal trial could not simply be shelved indefinitely just because some witnesses were unavailable, especially when other witnesses were ready to testify.

The High Court agreed with the petitioner. It examined Section 344 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows courts to adjourn or postpone proceedings, but only for a definite, reasonable period, with written reasons, not indefinitely. The court also noted other relevant provisions dealing with absent complainants and discontinuation of prosecutions, finding that none of them justified simply parking the case in limbo.

The judges ruled that a trial, once begun, must continue and be brought to completion. The fact that some witnesses had absconded did not entitle the court to freeze the entire case indefinitely. As a result, the High Court struck down the trial court's order and directed it to proceed with the case according to law.

This decision matters because it reinforces that criminal trials cannot be left pending indefinitely due to witness unavailability, protecting the right of accused persons to a timely and continuing trial process.
