title: Dost Muhammad V. Additional Sessions Judge Barkhan at Rakhni and another,
explainer:
This case is about how criminal trials should be handled when key prosecution witnesses go missing. Dost Muhammad was one of several people accused in a 2012 case registered with local Levies police. During the trial, the complainant and two eyewitnesses repeatedly failed to appear despite being summoned, and it emerged that the complainant and one witness were themselves wanted, and hiding, in a separate murder case. Instead of proceeding, the trial judge accepted a request from the prosecutor to place the case "in dormant," effectively pausing it indefinitely while keeping the accused on bail without any fixed date for resuming proceedings.

Dost Muhammad challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that a case cannot simply be shelved because prosecution witnesses are unavailable, especially when other witnesses could still be examined.

The High Court agreed. It explained that under Section 344 of the Criminal Procedure Code, courts can adjourn trials for absence of witnesses or other valid reasons, but such adjournments must be recorded in writing and set for a definite, reasonable period, not left open-ended. The court held that witnesses who are themselves fugitives from the law lose the normal protection of having a case wait on their convenience, and their absence does not justify indefinite delay. The court therefore set aside the trial court's order, reinforcing that criminal trials must proceed with reasonable diligence rather than remain frozen indefinitely.

title: Muhammd Noor V. Government of Balochistan, S&GAD through Secretary and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a government employee, Muhammad Aslam, who was removed from service by the Balochistan government after being absent from duty for an extended period. His departmental appeals against this removal were rejected, and the removal order became final since he did not challenge it before the Service Tribunal. However, following recommendations from several provincial ministers, and on the direction of the then Chief Minister, the government reinstated him into service without following any proper legal procedure for reversing the earlier disciplinary order.

Muhammad Noor, who had a personal dispute with the reinstated employee (both were connected to a criminal case involving an alleged abduction), challenged this reinstatement through a writ petition, essentially asking under what legal authority the reinstatement was made.

The Balochistan High Court found that neither the Governor nor the Chief Minister had any legal power of review or revision to overturn a final disciplinary order under the relevant laws. The Court held that using ministerial recommendations to bypass proper legal channels was improper, that government employees are barred from seeking intervention from assembly members in such matters, and that following an illegal directive does not make it lawful. The Court concluded the Chief Minister had misused his authority, declared the reinstatement order illegal, and set it aside.

The case highlights that political influence cannot override final legal decisions made under proper statutory disciplinary procedures, and that executive officers must not blindly implement unlawful directions.

Concerned that the mother had resigned from her job and might take the child abroad, the father approached the High Court directly, asking it to order the child's recovery and to have his name placed on the Exit Control List to prevent him from leaving the country.

The court explained that the Family Court, acting as the executing court, already had full power under Section 25 of the Guardians and Wards Act to arrest the child and hand him over to the father, using powers similar to those given to magistrates under the Criminal Procedure Code. It could also penalize the mother for non-compliance under Section 45, and could order the child's name placed on the Exit Control List if needed.

title: Muhammad Yousaf Khan V. Haji Barat and another,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute in Quetta over ownership of a house and adjoining land with shops. Muhammad Yousaf claimed he owned the property through inheritance from his father, shared with his brother, and that it had been given to Haji Barat only as a licensee (with permission to use it, not own it) since 1969-70. When Yousaf later asked Haji Barat to vacate, Haji Barat refused, claiming he had actually purchased the property through written agreements executed in 1976, 1977, and 1982, for which he had paid money.

The trial court and the appeals court both sided with Haji Barat and dismissed Yousaf's suit, relying heavily on these purchase agreements. Yousaf then challenged both decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in Yousaf's favor. It held that simply placing documents like the agreements on record is not enough to prove a property sale - their execution must be properly proved through evidence, including signatures and witnesses. Since the agreement involved a financial transaction, at least two marginal (attesting) witnesses were legally required to prove it, but Haji Barat had produced only one. The court found that the lower courts had wrongly presumed the documents were valid without proper proof. Because Haji Barat, as the person relying on the agreements, failed to establish their authenticity, his claim of ownership could not stand. The court set aside the earlier judgments, declared Yousaf the rightful owner, and ordered Haji Barat to hand over vacant possession of the property.

title: Islam Hussain V. Election Commission of Pakistan through Secretary and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a candidate, Islam Hussain, whose nomination papers for a Senate seat reserved for Technocrats from Balochistan were rejected. The rejection was based on findings that he lacked the required experience in his field of study and that he had not shown proof of completing sixteen years of education recognized by the Higher Education Commission. An election tribunal upheld this rejection, and since the law made that tribunal's decision final, Hussain approached the Balochistan High Court, arguing his constitutional rights were being violated.

The court examined the legal definition of technocrat under the Elections Act, 2017, which requires a candidate to hold a degree representing at least sixteen years of education, recognized by the Higher Education Commission, plus twenty years of relevant experience with notable achievements. The court clarified that the twenty years of experience must be counted starting from when the candidate obtained the qualifying degree, and importantly, that experience must be connected to the field of the candidate's academic qualification, not just any work experience.

The court referred to earlier Supreme Court guidance distinguishing between different reserved categories, noting that for technocrats, both proper educational credentials and directly related professional experience are essential.

This case matters because it sets out clear criteria for who can qualify as a technocrat candidate for Senate elections, ensuring that reserved seats go to people with genuine, relevant expertise matching their educational background rather than unrelated work experience.

title: Jameel Ramzan Dehwar, Advocate, Supreme Court at Quetta V. Sadiq Sanjrani and 3 others,
explainer:
This case concerned a petition filed against Sadiq Sanjrani after he was elected Chairman of the Senate in March 2018. The petitioner argued that since the Chairman of the Senate can act as President of Pakistan when the President is absent, and the Constitution requires a President to be at least 45 years old, Sanjrani—who was 39 at the time—was not qualified to serve as Chairman either. He asked the Balochistan High Court to declare the election void and to bar Sanjrani from ever acting as President.

The court rejected this argument. It examined the relevant constitutional provisions and found that the qualifications for becoming a member of the Senate (Article 62) require only that a person be at least 30 years old, with no separate age requirement specified for the office of Chairman or Deputy Chairman (Article 60). The age requirement of 45 years applies specifically to someone standing for election as President (Article 41), not to the Chairman of the Senate. The court held that these provisions must be read together but should not be conflated—being unqualified for the President's post does not automatically disqualify someone from serving as Senate Chairman. Since no article of the Constitution imposed an age requirement on the Chairman's office itself, the petition was dismissed.

This ruling clarifies that constitutional offices carry distinct eligibility criteria, and qualifications for one office cannot be imported into another simply because one may temporarily perform functions of the other.

title: Obaidullah Jan Barat and 2 others V. Speaker, Balochistan Assembly and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a petition by three elected members of the Balochistan Provincial Assembly who were suspended from attending the remaining sittings of the 2018 budget session. The suspension was ordered by the Presiding Officer, who was chairing the session in the Speaker's absence, after disorder occurred during proceedings. The petitioners argued the Presiding Officer had no authority to adjourn and then reconvene the sitting, that proper procedure was not followed, and that the suspension was politically motivated to stop opposition members from participating in the budget debate.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It explained that under the Assembly's Rules of Procedure, a Presiding Officer nominated to chair in the Speaker's absence holds the same powers as the Speaker, including authority to adjourn sittings, reconvene them, and maintain order, even suspend members during grave disorder. The court clarified the difference between a "session" and a "sitting" and found the Presiding Officer acted within the rules. Importantly, the court held that under Article 69 of the Constitution, courts cannot question the internal procedural conduct of Assembly proceedings, only clear excess of jurisdiction, and the Presiding Officer enjoyed constitutional protection for regulating the House.

This ruling matters because it reaffirms the principle of parliamentary privilege and judicial restraint regarding internal assembly proceedings, limiting courts' power to interfere in how legislatures manage their own members and business.

title: Umer Daraz V. Judicial Magistrate-IX, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a man who had acted as a surety for an accused person to secure his bail. When the accused failed to appear in court, the trial court forfeited the surety bond and ordered the petitioner to pay the amount. When he didn't pay, the trial court directed the government department where he worked to stop his salary and deduct the forfeited amount directly from it. The petitioner challenged this in the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined Section 514 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which governs how courts can recover forfeited bond amounts, typically by attaching and selling a person's movable property. The court looked at how movable property is defined under Section 22 of the Pakistan Penal Code and found it covers tangible property that can be seen and taken possession of, not future income that has not yet been earned. Since unearned salary does not qualify as movable property, the court ruled that the trial court had no legal authority to order the attachment of the petitioner's future salary.

However, the High Court also found that the petitioner had been given multiple chances to pay in installments and had failed to do so, and that his petition concealed relevant facts. So the court did not reduce the forfeited amount further or allow fresh installments. Instead, it set aside only the salary attachment order and directed the trial court to recover the money through the proper legal procedure, such as attaching physical property or, if necessary, imprisonment. This clarifies limits on how courts can enforce bond forfeitures.

title: Aminullah Mandokhail V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Home and Tribal Affairs Department and 4 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a father, Aminullah Mandokhail, who won a custody order from the Family Court for his young son, Hamadan, after the mother, Dr. Shahista (Respondent No. 5), was granted only visitation rights. When she failed to hand over the child despite the court's directions, and reports suggested the child might not even be with her, the father approached the Balochistan High Court through a constitutional petition, seeking the child's recovery and action against the mother, fearing she intended to take the child abroad.

The High Court noted that an execution application was already pending before the Family Court and explained that the law already provides adequate tools to enforce such custody decrees. Under the Guardian and Wards Act, 1890, particularly Section 25, a court can order a child's return and even have him arrested and delivered to the rightful guardian, using powers similar to those a Magistrate has under Section 100 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Additionally, Section 44 of the same Act allows penalties against a guardian who removes a child from the court's jurisdiction without permission.

Since sufficient legal remedies existed through the Family Court's executing powers, the High Court held that invoking its extraordinary constitutional jurisdiction was unnecessary. It disposed of the petition, directing the father to pursue proper enforcement remedies before the executing court instead. This case clarifies that custody execution issues should generally be resolved within the specialized family law framework rather than through constitutional petitions.

title: Independent Media Corporation (Pvt.) Ltd. through Muhammad Azhar and 4 others V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and Secretary Law, Quetta and 9 ohters,
explainer:
This case involved a media company, Independent Media Corporation (owner of Geo News), its executives, and hosts of a current affairs show called Aaps Ki Baat. After the program discussed a news report about land allotted to a former army chief, multiple criminal cases (FIRs) were filed against them across Pakistan, including eight in Balochistan, all based on the same broadcast and containing nearly identical allegations of anti-state content.

The petitioners argued that since Pakistan's media regulator (PEMRA) had already fined them for violating licence conditions over the same broadcast, no separate criminal case should proceed. They also argued that having to defend themselves in numerous FIRs across different cities for the same incident was unfair, illogical, and violated their constitutional rights.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the argument that PEMRA's fine barred criminal prosecution, since the regulator only dealt with licence violations, not criminal liability. However, the Court agreed that filing multiple FIRs for a single incident was improper. It ruled that only the first FIR (registered in Karachi) should proceed to trial, while the other FIRs should be treated merely as witness statements under the law and quashed.

This matters because it reinforces the legal principle that one incident should result in only one FIR, protecting accused persons from being harassed through duplicate prosecutions in different courts, which the Court found to be an abuse of legal process and inconsistent with constitutional guarantees of fairness and due process.

title: Asimullah Vs The State,

This case involved a request to cancel bail that had already been granted to several accused men in a criminal case. The complainant, Asimullah, alleged that his younger brother was attacked by a group of men, including Haji Abdul Bari and others, who caused him serious injuries during what was said to be a civil dispute. After the accused were arrested, a magistrate granted them bail. The complainant challenged this decision, first before the Additional Sessions Judge and, after that failed, before the Balochistan High Court, seeking cancellation of the bail.

The complainant argued that the accused were specifically named in the police report, were misusing their bail, had caused serious injuries, and that the magistrate had not properly heard the case before granting bail.

The High Court rejected all these arguments. It noted that the police report itself had been filed with significant, unexplained delay, raising the possibility that the accused were named only after deliberation rather than immediate identification—so naming them alone did not disqualify them from bail. There was no proof, such as a formal complaint, that the accused had misused their bail; supporting affidavits alone were not enough. The court also found that the lower courts had properly heard all parties and exercised their authority correctly.

The court held that canceling bail already granted requires strong, exceptional circumstances, which were absent here. The application to cancel bail was dismissed, reaffirming that bail once properly granted should not be lightly withdrawn.

title: Rahim Bakhsh v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Rahim Bakhsh, who was booked by police in three separate criminal cases arising from a single incident on 6 November 2006, where he was accused of firing shots and creating panic while allegedly drunk, and of assaulting police officers who tried to arrest him. He was convicted by a magistrate on charges including assaulting a public servant, causing hurt through a rash act, and possessing an unlicensed firearm. His sentences were partly modified on appeal by the Sessions Judge, and he then approached the Balochistan High Court through criminal revision petitions.

The High Court examined the evidence closely and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. It noted that enmity between the accused and the police, especially the local police officer in charge, was admitted on record, suggesting possible bad faith in how the case was built. Witnesses had changed and improved their statements between the initial investigation and the trial. Crucially, the police never sealed the weapons they recovered at the scene, nor sent the firearm to a ballistic expert to confirm it was actually functional. Independent bystanders who were present were never involved as witnesses, and the police failed to produce their daily diary (Roznamcha) entry to prove they had even gone to the scene as claimed.

Given these fundamental lapses, the court ruled the prosecution's case could not be trusted and acquitted the accused entirely. The judgment underscores how sloppy police procedure and unverified evidence can be fatal to a criminal case, protecting individuals from convictions based on unreliable investigations.

title: Hasil Khan and another V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case involved Hasil Khan, who was convicted for possessing an unlicensed pistol under the West Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965. The background was that during investigation of a separate murder case, Khan disclosed information about a weapon and led police to his home, where a T.T. pistol was recovered from beneath his quilts. Since he could not produce a license for the weapon, a new case was registered against him, and he was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to two years' rigorous imprisonment plus a fine.

Khan appealed, arguing that the recovery was fabricated by police and that the mandatory procedure under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code (which normally requires independent witnesses to be present during searches and recoveries) had not been followed.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that when a recovery is made based on an accused person's own disclosure leading police to hidden evidence, strict compliance with Section 103 is not required. The court found the police witnesses' testimony consistent and credible, noting that despite extensive cross-examination, nothing emerged to discredit their accounts, and no enmity between the witnesses and the accused was alleged.

The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence were upheld. This case illustrates how courts treat "disclosure-based" recoveries differently from ordinary searches, and reinforces that consistent, unchallenged police testimony can be sufficient to sustain a conviction.

title: Abdul Qadir & others v. Nadeem Javed & others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a family dispute over ancestral property left by a man named Samandar Khan after his death in 1962-63. His daughter (from his first marriage) and her son filed a lawsuit against the children from his second marriage, claiming their rightful inheritance share in the property, which included several houses. The daughter also claimed she had transferred part of her share to her son.

The defendants argued that the plaintiffs had already been paid cash for their shares long ago and therefore had no more claim to the property. Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, ordering that the property be divided among all legal heirs.

The High Court, hearing this revision petition, upheld those decisions. It held that under Islamic inheritance law, legal heirs automatically become entitled to their share of a deceased person's property upon death, without needing any court order. Since the defendants admitted the property was ancestral but claimed they had already paid off the other heirs, the burden was on them to prove this settlement and payment actually happened with the heirs' free consent. They failed to provide convincing proof.

Because both lower courts had already carefully examined the evidence and reached the same conclusion, the High Court declined to interfere and dismissed the revision petition, reaffirming the plaintiffs' right to their inheritance share.

title: Malik Zaheer & others v. Muhammad Saleem & othr,
explainer:
This case involved four related civil revision petitions from Balochistan concerning a land dispute in Nushki/Dalbandin. The petitioners claimed they owned certain agricultural land, including areas with date-tree gardens, as ancestral property inherited from their forefathers, and said they had been in peaceful possession until the respondents began interfering. The trial court (Qazi, Dalbandin) initially ruled in favour of the petitioners, granting declaration and possession. However, on appeal, the Majlis-e-Shoora, Nushki, reversed this decision and dismissed the suit. The petitioners then challenged that reversal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision and dismissed all four revision petitions. It found that although petitioners claimed the land was ancestral property, none of their witnesses actually testified to this fact. The court held that mere possession of property does not automatically create a legal right to claim ownership through a declaration suit — specific legal ingredients must be proven, which were missing here. It also clarified that a plaintiff cannot win simply because the defendant failed to prove their own case; the plaintiff must independently prove their claim. The court further noted that once limitation begins running on a cause of action, withdrawing and refiling a suit does not restart the clock. This judgment reinforces the principle that possession alone is insufficient to establish ownership rights, and plaintiffs bear the burden of proving their own case with solid evidence.

title: Muhammad Anwar v. Abdul Hameed,
explainer:
This case involved a landlord, Muhammad Anwar, who filed four separate eviction applications against tenants renting properties in Quetta. He argued the tenants had defaulted on rent payments, altered the properties from residential to commercial use without permission, and that he needed the properties back for his own bona fide personal use, since he intended to return from the United States to Pakistan with his family. The tenants contested this, arguing the Rent Controller lacked jurisdiction since only open land had been rented, and claimed the landlord was well-settled abroad and did not genuinely need the properties.

The trial court (Rent Controller) dismissed the eviction applications, partly relying on testimony from witnesses who were themselves parties in related proceedings. The Balochistan High Court found this improper, holding that such interested witnesses' statements were inadmissible against the landlord.

More significantly, the High Court ruled that a landlord's decision to live abroad does not automatically defeat a claim of bona fide need for ancestral property in Pakistan. It held that owning other property, or being "well settled" overseas, cannot by itself disqualify a landlord from reclaiming his property—the choice of which property to live in is the owner's prerogative. The landlord's own statement was deemed sufficient proof of genuine need.

The High Court set aside the Rent Controller's dismissal, allowed the eviction applications, and allowed all four appeals. This case reinforces landlords' rights to reclaim property for personal use, even if they have alternative accommodations or reside abroad.

title: Abdul Qudoos v. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Abdul Qadoos, accused of attempted rape and criminal assault under Pakistan's Penal Code, who applied for bail after his initial request was rejected by a lower court. According to the First Information Report (FIR), the complainant, Mst. Maria, alleged that her neighbor forced his way into her home, attempted to rape her, and beat her when she resisted, until neighbors broke down the door and rescued her.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the case and granted bail, finding several problems with the prosecution's version of events. There was an unexplained three-hour delay in filing the FIR, raising suspicion of behind-the-scenes discussions before the complaint was formalized. The complainant never claimed her clothes were torn or removed, which the court felt weakened the claim of attempted rape. Additionally, witness statements were inconsistent — only one of several witnesses who allegedly entered the room described rescuing the complainant from the accused, while the others gave differing accounts, and oddly, none of the witnesses reported even attempting to physically restrain or strike the accused.

Given these inconsistencies and gaps, the court concluded that the case required further inquiry and that the essential elements of the alleged crimes were not clearly established. As a result, bail was granted. This case illustrates how courts scrutinize the internal consistency of prosecution evidence, especially in serious criminal allegations, before deciding on bail.

title: Attaullah Khan Buledi v Rustam Khan Jamali & othrs,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over a 2008 provincial assembly election in Balochistan (constituency PB-25 Jaffarabad-I). Attaullah Khan Buledi, who lost to Rustam Khan Jamali, filed an election petition alleging rigging, bogus voting, abduction of his polling agents, and intimidation of voters at several polling stations. He asked the tribunal to recount votes, declare the result void, and either declare him the winner or order re-polling.

While the petition was pending, the winning candidate, Rustam Khan Jamali, was killed in Karachi. His side then argued the petition had become pointless and should be dismissed as "abated," with the Election Commission asked to declare the seat vacant and hold a by-election instead.

The Balochistan High Court, sitting as an Election Tribunal, rejected that argument. It held that under the Representation of the People Act, 1976, an election petition does not automatically end just because the returned candidate has died; the tribunal must still proceed to decide the case, if necessary through ex parte proceedings against the deceased respondent's side. The court also noted that under the law, if a contesting candidate dies before polling day, the election is postponed - but that rule did not apply here since the death occurred after the election, not before.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that allegations of electoral fraud must still be examined and resolved even if the winning candidate later dies, rather than letting such deaths be used to sidestep scrutiny of the election's fairness.

title: Muhammad Iqbal v. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a bail application filed by Muhammad Iqbal, who was accused of robbing a man of his motorcycle and mobile phone at gunpoint in Quetta. According to the complainant's account, two men on a motorcycle stopped him, one showed a pistol and threatened him, and they took his motorcycle and phone. The applicant was later identified by the complainant during a police identification parade and was charged under robbery laws and a provision dealing with armed robbery (Haraabah) under the Offences Against Property Ordinance.

The applicant's lawyer argued that his client was falsely implicated, that the identification parade was improperly conducted by police and had no legal value, that the armed robbery provision didn't apply since there was no mention of a murderous attack, and that there was an unexplained delay in filing the police report.

The Balochistan High Court rejected all these arguments. It found no evidence of any prior enmity between the accused and complainant that might suggest false implication, held that using a pistol to snatch property clearly fit the definition of armed robbery, said it couldn't rule on the identification parade's legality at the bail stage since doing so might unfairly affect either side's case, and found no real delay in filing the complaint. Since the trial court had properly evaluated the evidence and used its discretion correctly, the High Court declined to interfere and dismissed the bail application, while allowing the applicant to reapply for bail later if new grounds emerged during trial.

title: Aijaz Ali v. Secretary Government of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved a government employee, Aijaz Ali, who worked as a Junior Clerk in Balochistan's Employees Social Security Institution (BESSI). When the department advertised for the post of Office Assistant in 2007, he applied and appeared for tests and an interview. A selection committee recommended two other candidates for the existing vacancies but placed Aijaz Ali on a waiting list, to be considered only if a new Office Assistant post became available in future. When such a post was later reportedly created, he sought court orders directing the department to appoint him, arguing that since he had qualified in the interview, the committee's recommendation was binding and the authorities were legally bound to honor it. His lawyer relied on the legal principle of locus poenitentiae, meaning that once an official decision is made in someone's favor, the authorities cannot go back on it.

The Balochistan High Court rejected this argument. It held that the selection committee had only been authorized to fill posts that already existed and were advertised at the time, not future or non-existent posts. Any recommendation about a future vacancy was beyond the committee's authority and had no legal effect. Since there was no valid, legally binding order in the petitioner's favor to begin with, the principle of locus poenitentiae did not apply. The court dismissed the petition, meaning Aijaz Ali had no enforceable right to appointment.

This case clarifies that recommendations exceeding a selection committee's mandate carry no legal weight, and administrative bodies cannot be forced to honor promises made outside their proper authority.

title: Moulvi Muhammad Ishaq V. Zubair Ahmed and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a father who filed a constitutional petition in the Balochistan High Court on behalf of his two sons, who had been convicted by a trial court and whose appeal had also been dismissed by the Sessions Judge. The father was not himself a party to the original criminal case against his sons. He was also upset that a Judicial Magistrate had refused to entertain his separate complaint accusing a prosecution witness of giving false evidence during the trial.

The High Court dismissed the petition, ruling it was not maintainable for two main reasons. First, to bring a constitutional petition under Article 199 of the Constitution, a person must be "aggrieved" and must have no other adequate legal remedy available. Since the father was not a party to the original case, he could not be considered an aggrieved person, and only his sons, as the actual convicts, had the right to challenge their convictions, which they could do through an ordinary appeal or revision petition, not through their father's constitutional petition.

Second, regarding the refused complaint about false testimony, the court explained that Section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code specifically bars courts from taking up complaints about offenses like giving false evidence unless the complaint comes from the court where the alleged false statement was made, not from a private individual. So the Magistrate was legally correct in refusing it.

The case illustrates important limits on who can seek constitutional relief and how procedural bars restrict private complaints about courtroom testimony.

title: Abdul Hadi v. Special Judge ATC,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Hadi, a police constable facing trial for triple murder in an Anti-Terrorism Court in Khuzdar. During the trial proceedings, a prosecution witness told authorities he feared for his life if he had to testify in Khuzdar, since he and several other witnesses were settlers from Karachi living amid tense local conditions. Based on this, the trial judge ordered that the accused's trial be conducted inside Central Jail Gaddani instead of the regular courtroom in Khuzdar.

The accused challenged this order in the Balochistan High Court, arguing it caused him financial hardship and inconvenience, since his lawyer had to travel further and only some witnesses had been examined in each location. He suggested the case be moved to Quetta instead, and cited past cases where courts considered convenience for both parties when deciding on trial locations.

The High Court rejected the petition. It held that the witnesses' fear for their safety, given the security situation in the area and their status as outsiders, was genuine and reasonable, and that this concern for witnesses' lives outweighed the accused's claims of financial inconvenience. The court distinguished the precedents cited by the petitioner as not applicable to these facts. It ordered that witnesses from Karachi and Hub be examined at Gaddani Jail, while the rest of the trial continue in Khuzdar.

This case illustrates how courts balance witness safety against the convenience of an accused when deciding where a criminal trial should be conducted.

title: Niaz Gul v. Malik Munir Ahmed,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a landlord and tenant over a rented shop. The landlord, Malik Munir Ahmed, filed an eviction application against the tenant, Niaz Gul, claiming the shop had been rented out at Rs.500 per month and that the tenant had stopped paying rent since July 2004, making him a defaulter. The tenant disputed the landlord tenant relationship, claiming a different, older tenancy arrangement at a much lower rent under a separate agreement, and argued he had been depositing rent with the court's Civil Nazir.

The Rent Controller initially dismissed the eviction case, but on an earlier appeal, the High Court sent the matter back for additional inquiry, including identifying the shop's actual number and the real rent amount. After further evidence, including a site inspection report showing the tenant had tried to alter the shop's number, and proof that rent receipts had been tampered with, the Rent Controller found that the tenant was depositing far less rent (Rs.150) than the actual amount owed (Rs.500), and ordered eviction for default in rent payment.

The tenant appealed again, but the Balochistan High Court upheld the eviction order. The court found no error, misreading of evidence, or legal flaw in the Rent Controller's decision, concluding that the tenant had deliberately underpaid rent and tampered with documents. This case highlights how courts scrutinize evidence carefully in rent disputes and uphold landlords' rights when tenants default or manipulate records to underpay rent.

explainer:
This case involved a landlord-tenant dispute in Quetta over a shop on Masjid Road. The landlord filed an eviction application against his tenant, claiming the tenant had stopped paying rent since December 2006, had illegally sublet the shop to a third party, and that the landlord genuinely needed the shop for his jobless son to start a garment business. The tenant disputed the landlord-tenant relationship and contested the claims.

After an earlier ex parte decision was set aside and the case sent back for a proper hearing, the trial court framed key issues and heard the landlord's witnesses. However, the tenant himself never appeared to give his own statement, despite being granted multiple adjournments. All proceedings were instead handled through his attorney, and no affidavit was filed explaining the tenant's absence. The trial court eventually closed the tenant's side and ruled in favor of the landlord, ordering eviction.

The tenant appealed, arguing he had been unfairly denied the chance to testify due to being abroad in Dubai and unable to get a flight. The High Court rejected this argument, finding that the repeated requests for delay without any supporting affidavit appeared to be a tactic to stall proceedings rather than a genuine difficulty. The court held that the trial court's judgment was thorough and well-reasoned, and dismissed the appeal, upholding the eviction order.

This case illustrates how courts scrutinize claims of unfairness when they appear to be delaying tactics, and reinforces that parties must act with good faith and provide credible evidence

title: Muhammad Akbar & others v. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a bail application by three men, Muhammad Akbar, Dost Muhammad, and Amir Muhammad, who were accused of attempted murder after a shooting incident. According to the prosecution, the applicants opened fire on a complainant and his son near a mosque, and the son was hit by a bullet in his eye.

Two eyewitnesses said all three accused fired indiscriminately, but the injured victim's own statement, given later, said that only Amir Muhammad had actually fired the shot that caused his injury. The court also noted an 18-hour delay in filing the police report despite the police station being only two kilometers away, and found that although police collected bullet casings from the scene, the site plan failed to clearly show where these were found or where the accused were actually standing.

The Balochistan High Court decided that Amir Muhammad, who was specifically identified as having fired the injuring shot, did not deserve bail. However, since the allegations against the other two applicants involved only ineffective firing (meaning they did not cause the injury) and the evidence linking them to the crime was weak, their situation warranted further investigation. The court granted bail to Muhammad Akbar and Dost Muhammad, subject to providing sureties, while rejecting bail for Amir Muhammad. This case illustrates how courts distinguish between defendants based on the specific harm they are alleged to have caused, even when they are jointly accused.

title: Obaidullah v. Haji Sher Muhammad,

title: Agha Pari Gul Syeda v. Kulsoom Parveen & others,
explainer:
This case was an election petition before the Balochistan High Court, acting as an Election Tribunal, challenging the result of the 2009 Senate election for a seat reserved for women from Balochistan. The petitioner, Agha Pari Gul Syeda, contested the seat and lost to Kalsoom Parveen. She alleged serious irregularities: that votes cast for her were wrongly counted in favor of the winning candidate, that the secret ballot process was violated, that voters cast more than the allowed transferable votes, and that the Returning Officer colluded with the winning candidate through corrupt and illegal practices to manipulate the result. She claimed the Returning Officer initially announced her as the winner but then changed the result after allegedly being contacted by the other candidate.

The Returning Officer had already rejected her request for a recount, but the court clarified that this rejection alone did not bar her from filing an election petition afterward.

To prove her serious allegations, the petitioner needed solid evidence, not just claims. She presented three witnesses and her own testimony, while the respondent relied only on her own statement. The court also rejected a last-minute request to summon another witness, finding it a delaying tactic filed months after evidence had closed without explanation.

The excerpt ends before the final ruling, but it shows the court's insistence that election fraud allegations must be backed by solid proof, and that procedural technicalities like a denied recount don't automatically stop a losing candidate from seeking justice through a full hearing.

title: Dr. Noor Jahan Panezai v. Zubaida Jalal & others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a National Assembly seat reserved for women from Balochistan, following the 2008 general elections. Dr. Noor Jehan Panezai and Zubaida Jalal were both listed as candidates for the reserved women's seat on the Pakistan Muslim League (Q) party's priority list, with Zubaida Jalal at number one and the petitioner at number two. However, Zubaida Jalal separately contested a general seat as an independent candidate and lost. After the deadline for submitting the official priority list had passed, the party president wrote to the Election Commission asking that Zubaida Jalal's name be removed and that the petitioner be declared the winner instead. The Election Commission rejected this request and declared Zubaida Jalal the returned candidate on the reserved seat, prompting this election petition challenging that decision.

The Balochistan High Court, acting as an Election Tribunal, dismissed the petition. It held that Zubaida Jalal had never resigned from the party, changed loyalty, violated party policy, withdrawn her candidacy, or been disqualified by any court. The party president had no legal authority to alter the priority list after the official deadline. The court also found no legal bar preventing a candidate from simultaneously contesting a general seat and being listed for a reserved seat. Since Zubaida Jalal remained validly at the top of the list on the relevant date, her declaration as the returned candidate stood, and the petition was dismissed.

title: Umash Kumar v. Engineer Basant Lal & others,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over Pakistan's 2008 general elections, specifically the reserved minority (non-Muslim) seat in the Balochistan Provincial Assembly. The petitioner, a candidate from the same political party (PML-Q) as one of the respondents, claimed that he had originally been placed first on his party's priority list of candidates for the reserved seat, and that this position was later illegally altered so that a rival candidate was moved to first place instead, allegedly through collusion with Election Commission officials. He asked the court to declare the results void and to have himself declared the returned candidate.

The Election Tribunal examined the official documents, including the priority list submitted to the Election Commissioner and Form-V, the list of validly nominated candidates prepared by the Returning Officer. It found that the petitioner's name appeared first in Form-V only because names were arranged alphabetically in Urdu, not because he held first priority on his party's actual priority list, where he was actually ranked fourth. The court also noted that a candidate is legally required to attach the party's priority list to the nomination papers.

Because the evidence did not support the petitioner's claim of being first in priority, and the process followed the applicable election laws, the tribunal dismissed the petition. The case highlights the technical distinction between alphabetical listing and actual party priority ranking in disputes over reserved minority seats.

title: Marduman-e- Mullazai v. Abdul Sadiq & others,
explainer:
This case is about how long a person has to apply for execution (enforcement) of a court decree, once it has been won.

A civil suit filed by the petitioners had been dismissed by the trial court, but on appeal the District Judge, Pishin overturned that decision and granted a decree in the petitioners' favor on 19-3-2003. The petitioners then filed their first application to execute (enforce) this decree on 16-6-2006, which was about three years and three months later. The opposing side argued this was too late, since the law generally allows only three years to file such an application. The petitioners countered that Section 48 of the Civil Procedure Code allows six years for executing decrees, so their application should be considered valid.

Both the trial court and the appellate court had rejected the execution application as time-barred, and the matter reached the Balochistan High Court by way of revision.

The High Court held that Section 48 CPC's six-year period only applies to "fresh" applications, meaning any application filed after an earlier execution application already exists. Since this was the very first execution application ever filed, it was governed by Article 181 of the Limitation Act, which sets a three-year limit. Because the application was filed after three years and three months, it was correctly dismissed as time-barred. The court relied on earlier Supreme Court rulings settling this exact question, and dismissed the revision petition, upholding the lower courts' decisions.

title: Mir Hazar Khan v. The State,
explainer:
Mir Hazar Khan was tried and convicted under section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, for possessing a large quantity of charas (140 kg baked and 19 kg raw), along with arms, ammunition, and walky-talkies, allegedly recovered from a hidden basement in his house in Killi Turkaman, Dasht, Balochistan, following a police raid based on informer tips. The Special Judge sentenced him to life imprisonment plus a fine, giving him benefit for time already served. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the recovery was actually from a house he didn't own or control, that his confessional statement was recorded after a suspicious 15-day delay, that police failed to get a search warrant despite prior information, and that the trial court wrongly ignored favorable testimony from a hostile witness.

The High Court rejected all these arguments. It found that the prosecution's witnesses were consistent and credible despite lengthy cross-examination, and that the combination of the accused's own disclosure statement, his recorded confession, and the physical recovery of drugs and weapons from his conscious possession proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The court also clarified an important evidentiary principle: testimony from a "hostile" witness (one who partly contradicts the prosecution) isn't automatically thrown out entirely - if parts of it are supported by other evidence, those parts can still be relied upon. The appeal was dismissed and the conviction upheld.

title: Jangi Khan v. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, a bus driver and conductor, who were convicted for possessing and smuggling a massive quantity of opium, roughly 298 kilograms, found hidden in secret cavities of their bus. The Anti-Narcotics Force intercepted the bus near Quetta based on prior intelligence, and during questioning the two men pointed out the hidden compartments where the drugs were concealed. A third person allegedly involved managed to escape. The trial court convicted both men under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, sentencing them to life imprisonment and fines, and they appealed to the Balochistan High Court arguing they had no knowledge of the hidden narcotics and that the bus itself was never produced as evidence at trial.

The High Court upheld the conviction. It ruled that information given by the accused leading directly to the recovery of the drugs can legally be used against them under Article 40 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order. Since the men were driver and conductor of the bus, the court said they had a duty to explain convincingly why they wouldn't have known about the hidden compartments, especially since they never testified under oath or presented any defense witnesses. The court also held that not physically producing the bus in court didn't hurt the prosecution's case, since the accused had already admitted being present in the bus and that drugs were recovered from it.

title: Haji Ghaibi Khan v. The State,
explainer:
Haji Ghaibi Khan was tried for shooting and killing Asal Khan and injuring a passer-by, Adel Masih, in Quetta in 2004. The prosecution's case, built on eyewitness accounts, medical evidence, and recovery of a licensed pistol from the accused shortly after the incident, led to his conviction by the trial court, which sentenced him to death under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and ordered him to pay compensation.

On appeal to the Balochistan High Court, the defence tried hard to raise doubts about the timing, date, and presence of witnesses at the crime scene, but failed. The court found the eyewitnesses' statements to be consistent, credible, and free of any personal grudge against the accused, meaning there was no apparent reason for them to falsely implicate him. Medical evidence and a positive chemical report supported their accounts, and the recovered pistol further strengthened the case. The court also clarified that prosecutors are not legally required to call every possible witness—they can choose which ones to present, as long as the case is proven.

Since the murder was committed in cold blood, in a public area of the city, against an innocent victim, the court held there were no grounds for leniency. It upheld both the conviction and the death sentence, finding the trial court's judgment sound and free of legal error.

This case reaffirms established principles in Pakistani criminal law: prosecutors have discretion over which witnesses to produce, and courts will uphold death sentences in clear-cut murder cases where evidence is strong

title: Haji Khair Bakhsh v. Allah Dad,
explainer: This case is about a decades-long dispute over rights to a water channel called Shandi Nadi in Khuzdar district, Balochistan. Back in 1982, a court ruled in favor of the respondents, granting them rights over the channel and permanently restraining the petitioners from interfering with it. Despite this, the petitioners repeatedly interfered with the channel over the years, leading to multiple rounds of litigation. In one earlier round, the petitioners' lawyer even gave a formal undertaking before the High Court promising they would not interfere with the water channel. Yet interference continued, prompting the respondents to file fresh execution applications seeking enforcement of the decree. The trial court ordered the petitioners to furnish a surety bond of Rs. 50,000 to guarantee compliance, and this was upheld on appeal. The petitioners then challenged this in the High Court, arguing that the court had no legal authority to demand a surety in a case involving a permanent injunction, and that they had already posted an earlier surety of Rs. 100,000. The High Court disagreed, finding that the petitioners were clearly determined to keep interfering with the channel and had shown no respect for their own prior undertaking. It held that every fresh instance of interference amounts to a breach justifying forfeiture of the surety, and that decree-holders facing recurring violations have the right to demand new sureties. The petition was dismissed, reinforcing that court orders protecting property rights like water access must be genuinely honored, not evaded through technical objections.

title: Muhammad & others v. Muhammad,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running property dispute over a piece of land in Balochistan. The plaintiffs claimed they owned and possessed the land, alleging that the defendant was unlawfully interfering with it. However, the plaintiffs own pleadings revealed a different story: the land had actually been given by their deceased brother to the defendant for cultivation, on condition that the defendant pay Rs.10,000 and build an embankment at his own cost. The defendant complied with these terms while the brother was alive but later stopped.

The case had gone back and forth multiple times between the trial court (Qazi Awaran) and the appellate forum (Majlis-e-Shoora Khuzdar), with several remands and reversals. Eventually, the trial court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, but the appellate court overturned that decision and dismissed their suit. The plaintiffs then challenged this in the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition.

The High Court dismissed the revision petition, agreeing with the appellate court. It found that since the plaintiffs case actually described a conditional arrangement or agreement rather than straightforward ownership, they should have filed a suit for specific performance of that agreement, not a simple declaration of title. The court also noted that the plaintiffs lawyer failed to properly produce or reference key witness statements from the later stages of the case.

This judgment highlights an important legal principle: when a claim is really based on an agreement with conditions, the correct remedy is to seek enforcement of that agreement, not a declaration of ownership.

title: Michael Nazir v. The State,
explainer:
Michael Nazir was tried for killing two people and wounding two others after a dispute at a church in Quetta. He had been removed from his position as church leader (Padri), and when church officials, including a lawyer and committee members, went to ask him to vacate church property, he allegedly opened fire on them with a pistol, killing Noor Muhammad Achakzai and Iqbal Masih instantly and injuring two others, Yousaf Masih and Saleem Raza.

The trial court had convicted him under anti-terrorism and murder laws but only sentenced him to life imprisonment, reasoning that he lacked clear criminal intent (mens rea). Nazir appealed his conviction, claiming he was falsely implicated because he had converted to Islam. Separately, the state appealed, seeking the death penalty instead of life imprisonment.

The Balochistan High Court found the prosecution's evidence—eyewitness accounts, medical reports, recovered weapon, and ballistic findings—consistent and convincing, and rejected the defense's claim as baseless. The court also disagreed with the trial court's finding that there was no intention to kill, holding that repeated firing at vital body parts by an educated person clearly showed intent to cause death.

As a result, the court dismissed Nazir's appeal against conviction, but allowed the state's appeal, enhancing his sentence from life imprisonment to death. The case illustrates how appellate courts can increase sentences when they find the original punishment too lenient given the evidence of deliberate intent.

title: M/s Lahore Dioceson Trust v. Shafi Jan,
explainer:
This case involves a property dispute in Chaman, Balochistan, where the Lahore Diocesan Trust Association and two members of the Christian community sued several people for declaration, injunction, possession, and recovery of money over church land and buildings they claimed were forcibly occupied and illegally built upon.

After evidence had been recorded, including statements from four of the trust's witnesses, the trust filed an application asking the court's permission to produce certain additional documents. The case was fixed for arguments on that application, but on the relevant date no one appeared for the trust and the matter was adjourned. On the next date, instead of deciding the pending application, the trial court dismissed the entire suit for lack of interest, treating it as if the suit itself, not just the application, was up for hearing.

The Balochistan High Court found this to be a serious error. The trial court had confused what was actually before it: only the application needed a decision that day, and at most that application could have been dismissed for non-appearance. The suit itself could not be thrown out under the procedural rules the trial court relied on. The High Court declared the trial court's order void and illegal, set it aside, and sent the case back for the pending application to be decided first, after which the suit should proceed to a proper decision on its merits within a set time. The case highlights the importance of courts correctly identifying what matter is actually scheduled before dismissing a case.

title: Mst. Hoora ors. v. Allah Dad.,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute involving the Islamic law right of pre-emption, which allows certain people (like adjoining landowners) to claim first right to purchase property before it is sold to someone else. To exercise this right validly, a specific legal procedure called Talbs must be followed, which requires the claimant to make formal demands at particular stages, with details of when, where, and in front of which witnesses these demands were made.

In this case, the respondent sued for cancellation of a property sale and asserted his pre-emption rights. The trial court and the appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora) both ruled in his favor, partly because the defendants had not seriously contested the claims in their written statement. The petitioners challenged this in the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the plaint itself was legally defective because it failed to properly plead the required Talbs.

The High Court agreed with the petitioners. It found that simply using the word "Shifa" was not enough, and that evidence about the Talbs could not be introduced later through witnesses if it was missing from the written pleadings. Since these details were essential prerequisites for a valid pre-emption suit, the plaint should have been rejected under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code. As a result, the High Court set aside the decisions of both lower courts and allowed the revision petition.

This case matters because it reinforces strict pleading requirements in pre-emption suits, emphasizing that courts must properly scrutinize plaints at the outset rather than allowing defective claims to proceed based on later testimony.

title: Bibi Amina & others v. Muhammad Iqbal & others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute over a shop and basement in Quetta. The plaintiffs (grandchildren of Nasrullah Khan) claimed their grandfather, originally a tenant, had entered into a sale agreement in 1999 to purchase the shop and basement for Rs. 25 lac, and that most of the price had been paid. They sued for a court declaration of ownership, enforcement of the sale agreement, possession, and an injunction, after the property owner allegedly refused to formally transfer the property despite payments.

The trial court sent the disputed sale agreement to a handwriting expert, who found that the signatures on it were forged. Based on this, the trial court dismissed the plaintiffs' suit. On appeal, the Balochistan High Court upheld that decision. It found that sending the document for expert examination was a reasonable and legally sound step. It also noted that the sale agreement was never registered, and under the Stamp Act, an unregistered, insufficiently stamped document could not even be admitted as evidence, let alone used to prove ownership of property worth Rs. 25 lac. The court concluded the plaintiffs' claims were fabricated and unsupported, and that no legal right to the property could arise from such a defective document. The appeal was dismissed, and the original ruling stood.

This case highlights how strict legal requirements—like proper registration and stamping of property agreements—can determine the outcome of ownership disputes, regardless of claimed payments or possession.

title: Murad Vs. Syed Muhammad & others.,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute in Balochistan. Murad filed a lawsuit claiming his rightful Islamic law share of ancestral property left by his grandfather, which was jointly owned by him and his relatives (the respondents). The respondents contested the case, disputing property boundaries and arguing the suit was time-barred, though they admitted the family relationship. They also claimed Murad's mother had waived her share in the property years earlier.

The trial court (Qazi, Pasni) heard evidence from both sides and ruled in Murad's favor, granting him his share. However, when the respondents appealed, the appellate body (Majlis-e-Shoora, Turbat) reversed this decision and dismissed the suit entirely.

Murad then took the matter to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the appellate court had not properly justified its reversal of the trial court's decision. The High Court agreed. It found that the appellate court had issued only a brief order without genuinely re-examining the evidence or explaining its reasoning, violating Order XLI, Rule 31 of the Civil Procedure Code, which requires appellate courts to give solid, evidence-based reasons whenever they overturn a lower court's decree.

The High Court ruled this failure made the appellate judgment legally unsustainable. It set aside the appellate court's decision and sent the case back for a proper, reasoned re-examination. This case reinforces that appellate courts cannot simply overturn decisions without demonstrating they seriously engaged with the evidence and legal issues involved.

title: I.G Police of Balochistan v. Ghulam Rasool,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Kalat, Balochistan. Ghulam Rasool claimed he was the lawful owner of a piece of land that the police department had allegedly occupied illegally in 1996. He sued for declaration of ownership, possession, and a permanent injunction against the Inspector-General of Police and other officials.

The case had a long procedural history, going back and forth between the trial court (Qazi Kalat) and the appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora), with the High Court itself remanding the matter once before for fresh evidence. Eventually, the trial court dismissed the suit, finding that the plaintiff failed to prove his ownership and possession claims with solid evidence. However, the appellate court reversed this and ruled in favor of Rasool, prompting the police department to file this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court sided with the police. It found that the appellate court had made serious errors: it relied on a document that was never formally tendered or proved in evidence, and it misread the record regarding possession, which actually showed continuous, uninterrupted control by the provincial government. The court also emphasized a broader legal principle—that a plaintiff's testimony must fully match the claims made in the written plaint; any inconsistency weakens the case.

As a result, the High Court set aside the appellate court's decision and restored the trial court's dismissal of the suit, ruling against Ghulam Rasool. This case underscores the importance of properly proving documents in court and maintaining consistency between pleadings and testimony.

title: M Afzal Alias Mazel & ors v. Haji Haq Dad & others.,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Pishin, Balochistan, over ownership and possession of a room and land in a residential area. The plaintiffs claimed they had bought a room from a man named Naik Muhammad, and that they were in possession of a piece of land, but the defendants disputed their ownership and even filed complaints with local authorities claiming the land for themselves. The plaintiffs sued for a declaration of ownership and an injunction to protect their rights.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs after examining witness testimony from both sides. The defendants then approached the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the lower courts had misread the evidence and failed to properly apply procedural rules under the Civil Procedure Code.

The High Court dismissed the revision petition. It held that the defendants had not shown any specific illegality, irregularity, or misreading of evidence in the lower courts' decisions—merely making general objections was not enough. The court reaffirmed the well-established principle that when two lower courts reach the same factual conclusion (concurrent findings), the High Court will not interfere unless there is clear proof that the evidence was misread or ignored.

This case is significant because it illustrates how Pakistani courts limit interference in revision petitions, protecting the finality of factual findings unless a genuine legal error is demonstrated.

title: Naimatullah v. State,
explainer:
This case is about a man convicted of drug trafficking under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. He was the driver of a vehicle intercepted at a checkpoint near Quetta, where police allegedly found 150 kilograms of charas (hashish) hidden in secret compartments. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to life imprisonment plus a fine, while acquitting a co-accused passenger who claimed he was merely hitching a ride.

On appeal, the driver argued that since the passenger was acquitted on the same evidence, he should be too. He also pointed to inconsistencies, such as the quantity of drugs remaining unchanged even after samples were removed for testing, and a five-day delay in sending samples for chemical analysis.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that the co-accused's acquittal was justified because there was no evidence linking him to the crime, unlike the driver who was in direct control of the vehicle and therefore in "conscious possession" of the drugs. The court found the delay in sample testing irrelevant since there was no evidence of tampering, and noted that at checkpoint arrests, independent witnesses are rarely available because the public is reluctant to get involved.

The court upheld the conviction and sentence, emphasizing that in narcotics cases, minor procedural discrepancies should not undermine an otherwise solid prosecution case. The appeal was dismissed.

title: Abdul Jabbar v. Mohammad Shareef & others,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal complaint filed by Abdul Jabbar against Muhammad Sharif and four others. Sharif had earlier filed a complaint against Jabbar under sections 107/151 of the Criminal Procedure Code, and in support of that complaint, three other respondents submitted affidavits. Jabbar then filed his own complaint claiming these affidavits were fake and fabricated, alleging offences under sections 193, 194 and 199 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deal with giving false evidence and fabricating false evidence.

The trial magistrate ordered a police inquiry, during which the respondents confirmed the contents of their affidavits. Based on this, the magistrate dismissed Jabbar's complaint, and a sessions judge upheld that dismissal on revision. Jabbar then approached the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It held that beyond the affidavits being confirmed as genuine during the inquiry, there was a more fundamental legal problem: under section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code, offences like the ones alleged can only be prosecuted if the complaint is filed by the concerned court or public authority, not by a private individual. This rule exists to prevent private citizens from misusing the legal process for personal revenge and to let courts decide when such prosecutions are truly necessary. Since Jabbar was a private complainant, his case was not legally permissible from the outset, regardless of its merits.

title: Fida Hussain v. Ghulam Mohammad & others,
explainer:
This case concerns a property dispute that reached the Balochistan High Court on a civil revision petition. The petitioner had originally filed a civil suit seeking possession, mesne profit, and injunctions, based on a 1984 sale agreement under which he had sold property to the respondent. The buyer had paid part of the price but allegedly failed to pay the remainder within the agreed nine-month period, meaning, according to the seller, the agreement stood rescinded and the earnest money forfeited. The trial court decided the case in the seller's favor without specifically framing an issue on limitation, even though the buyer had raised it in his written statement. On appeal, the Additional District Judge set aside that decision and sent the case back to the trial court, directing it to properly address the limitation question and give both sides a fair hearing before deciding again on the merits.

The seller challenged this remand order in the High Court, arguing it was unnecessary since enough evidence already existed to decide the case outright. The High Court disagreed and upheld the remand. It held that limitation is not simply a matter parties can raise or ignore through their pleadings; courts have an independent duty to examine it, since limitation law is mandatory and cannot be waived by the parties or overlooked by the court. Because this issue had not been properly examined below, sending the case back for a fresh, focused hearing on limitation was correct. The case illustrates the mandatory nature of limitation law in Pakistani civil litigation.

title: Haji Ghulam Mohammad v. Haji Anwar Jan & others,
explainer:
This case arose out of a civil dispute in which the petitioner, Haji Ghulam Muhammad, had earlier been allowed by the High Court, in an appeal, to produce a specific witness named Nazar Muhammad to support his case. However, Nazar Muhammad had become an absconder after being booked in a murder case, making it impossible to bring him to court. The petitioner then asked the trial court (Majlis-e-Shoora, Loralai) to let him produce a different witness who was already named in his original list of witnesses, and also to allow him to submit certain additional documents. The trial court rejected this request, and the petitioner challenged that rejection through a civil revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition, holding that it was not maintainable. It explained that under the law, decisions about whether to admit or refuse oral or documentary evidence do not qualify as a "case decided" under Section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code, which is the provision that allows revision petitions. Since the trial court's order was simply about evidence, it could not be challenged through a revision. The court also noted the documents in question had not been mentioned or attached to the original plaint, violating procedural rules.

This case matters because it clarifies that rulings on evidence-related matters during a trial generally cannot be immediately challenged in higher courts through revision petitions; they must wait for the final decision in the case.

title: Ghulam Mohammad v. The State,
explainer:
This is an explainer of a Balochistan High Court decision on Criminal Jail Appeal No. 40 of 2010, decided in September 2012.

The case involved Ghulam Muhammad, who was tried after an FIR was registered and a charge framed against him under the Offences Against Property (Enforcement of Hudood) Ordinance, 1979, specifically for "haraabah" (a form of armed robbery/dacoity under Hudood law). However, when the trial court found him guilty, it ended up sentencing him under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code (for murder), giving him life imprisonment, rather than sentencing him under the Hudood Ordinance itself.

This created confusion about which appellate court should hear his appeal: the High Court or the Federal Shariat Court, since different laws send appeals to different forums.

The High Court ruled that it is the charge originally framed against the accused - not the sentence eventually imposed - that determines which court has jurisdiction to hear the appeal. Since the FIR and the charge here were both framed under the Hudood Ordinance's haraabah provisions, the case belonged in the Federal Shariat Court, even though the trial judge had ultimately imposed punishment using a Penal Code section (which the law allows when Hudood standards of proof aren't met).

The court therefore transferred the appeal to the Federal Shariat Court rather than deciding it themselves.

title: Haroon-ur-Rashid v. Registrar High Court,
explainer:
This case dealt with recruitment to judicial posts in Balochistan—Additional District and Sessions Judges, Civil Judges/Judicial Magistrates, and Qazis—advertised by the Registrar of the Balochistan High Court in 2011-2012. Several groups of petitioners challenged different aspects of the recruitment process through constitutional petitions.

One group, Assistant District Attorneys, complained they were being wrongly barred from applying for the post of Additional District and Sessions Judge. The court held that under the applicable service rules, anyone who is a law graduate from a recognized university and has practiced as an advocate for at least five years is eligible, and Assistant District Attorneys meeting these criteria could not be excluded. Their petition was allowed.

Another set of petitioners challenged the reserved quota seats set aside for disabled persons, women, and religious minorities in the recruitment. The court rejected this challenge, holding that women and minorities form a reasonable class under the Constitution's equality provisions, and that reserving quota for them is neither illegal nor unconstitutional. Similarly, though disabled persons are not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution, they too qualify as a reasonable class, especially given the existing law protecting disabled persons' employment rights. The quota system was therefore upheld as valid.

The judgment matters because it clarifies eligibility rules for judicial recruitment and confirms that affirmative-action quotas for disadvantaged groups are constitutionally permissible in Pakistan.

title: Abdul Baqi v. The State,

The initial FIR named four suspects based on suspicion, but police investigation cleared three of them, leaving only Abdul Baqi to face trial. There was no eyewitness, so the case rested on circumstantial evidence: Abdul Baqi led police to the crime scene and to a blood-stained axe used as the murder weapon, which forensic testing confirmed was linked to the killing. He also gave a confession before a magistrate, though it was recorded about six days after his arrest.

The court found the chain of evidence—from pointing out the location, to recovering the axe, to the confession—was consistent and reliable, proving guilt beyond doubt.

title: Coll: of Customs Qta v. Custom Sale Tax & C. Excise,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over smuggled scrap iron and steel seized by Pakistan Customs officials near Quetta in 2004. Customs staff had intercepted three trucks carrying the goods without proper import documents, leading to confiscation of both the scrap and the vehicles, though the vehicle owners were given the option to pay a redemption fine to reclaim their trucks. The vehicle owners appealed, and the Collector (Appeal) allowed release of the vehicles on payment of the fine. Later, the Customs Appellate Tribunal set aside the original confiscation order entirely.

The Collector of Customs challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the Tribunal's single member did not have the legal authority to decide the case because, at the relevant time, single members could only hear cases where the value of goods was up to Rs.100,000 - but the seized goods here were valued at over Rs.500,000. The vehicle owners argued that a later rule change raised this limit to Rs.500,000, which should apply.

The High Court ruled that the higher monetary limit could not be applied retroactively, meaning the Tribunal's single member lacked jurisdiction to decide the case when it did. Because of this, the Tribunal's order was set aside, and the case was sent back for a fresh decision by a properly authorized bench. This case highlights the importance of tribunals staying within their legal authority based on the value of matters involved.

title: Ishaque v. Rasheed & others,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute in Turbat, Balochistan, where Ishaque accused Rasheed and two others of illegally occupying land he claimed to own, filing a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005. After charges were framed, the accused applied under Section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking the trial court to acquit them early because the evidence did not support a conviction. The trial court agreed and acquitted them, prompting Ishaque to appeal.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the acquittal. It found that Ishaque was not the officially recorded owner of the property and had not provided evidence to support his ownership claim. Notably, his own complaint admitted that his grandfather had gifted part of the land to one of the accused, undermining his case. The complaint also failed to specify when the alleged illegal dispossession occurred, which is essential because the Act does not apply to dispossession that happened before it came into force in 2005. The court also noted that a civil case over the same property was already pending, suggesting the criminal complaint might be an improper attempt to pressure the civil proceedings.

The court further clarified that there is no fixed stage in a trial when an accused must file a Section 265-K application; it depends on the judge's assessment of whether the existing evidence justifies an early acquittal. This ruling reinforces that weak or legally flawed criminal complaints, especially those overlapping with civil disputes, can be dismissed early rather than proceeding to a full trial.
