title: Rehmatullah & others v. Hameedullah & others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a long-running land and water dispute over property in Mouza "Narai Dag" near Loralai. The respondents had sued the petitioners, claiming their ancestors were co-sharers of the land and "lathband bazgars" (tenants) of the Provincial Government, and accused the petitioners of interfering with an irrigation water channel. A trial court (Qazi Bori/Sanjavi) ruled in the respondents' favor, and this was upheld on appeal. Later, when the petitioners allegedly violated that decree by using a tractor on the land, contempt proceedings followed, leading to further appeals and multiple connected petitions being heard together.

The High Court found a fundamental legal flaw: the disputed land actually belonged to the Provincial Government, yet the government was never made a party to the original suit, as required by law when government property is involved. Because of this, the original decree was declared void, and the court dismissed the suit, though it allowed the respondents to file a fresh case if they wished.

Since the contempt proceedings were based on that invalid decree, they too were set aside. The court also noted that only the High Court or Supreme Court have authority to convict someone of contempt—not a trial court—making those contempt convictions unlawful as well.

This case highlights the importance of including the government as a party in disputes over public land and clarifies which courts have power to punish contempt.

title: Merck (Private) Limited through Manager and others V. Member Labour Appellate Tribunal, Balochistan, Quetta and others,
explainer:
This case involved employees of Merck (Private) Limited who were terminated from their jobs and then filed grievance petitions before the Labour Court, claiming they were "workmen" entitled to protection under labour laws. The company argued they were actually officers, not workmen, and that their termination was based on agreed contractual terms rather than an industrial dispute, meaning the Labour Court had no jurisdiction to hear their case.

The Labour Court ruled in favour of the employees, ordering their reinstatement with full back-pay, and this decision was upheld by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The company then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found that the lower courts had made a critical error: they failed to properly examine whether the employees actually qualified as "workmen" under the law. The Court clarified that a person's job title or designation does not determine their status - what matters is the actual nature of the work performed. The employees had not adequately demonstrated in their applications that their day-to-day duties matched those of a "worker" rather than an officer.

The Court also held that reinstatement with full back-benefits contradicts the general principle of "no work no pay." Back-benefits should only compensate an employee for genuine hardship suffered due to job loss, not serve as punishment for the employer or a windfall for the employee.

Because both lower courts had misread the evidence on these points, the High Court set aside their judgments and sent the case back to the Labour Court to be decided afresh.

title: Bibi Rukhsana v. Abdul Malik Khan & others.,
explainer:
This case is about a pre-emption suit, a right recognized under Islamic law that allows a neighbouring property owner to buy land before it is sold to someone else, provided certain formal steps (called talbs) are strictly followed at the right time and in the right manner.

Bibi Rukhsana claimed she owned a house next to an open plot that had been sold by one respondent to another. She argued she had a right to buy that plot instead, and said her attorney had performed the required talbs (formal demands asserting the pre-emption right) immediately upon learning of the sale. The trial court believed her and ruled in her favour, but the Additional District Judge overturned that decision on appeal, finding her claim was not properly proven, and the case reached the Balochistan High Court on revision.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision and dismissed the suit. It found that the record showed a long, unexplained delay between when the pre-emptor's son learned of the sale and when the first talb was supposedly made, and that no proper witnesses or explanations were provided to support the claim. The court reaffirmed the settled principle that pre-emption rights must be exercised strictly and promptly according to Islamic law's exact requirements; sloppy or delayed conduct forfeits the right, since the law favours the vigilant, not the negligent.

This case matters because it reinforces that pre-emption claims are treated strictly by courts, and failure to follow the precise legal formalities and timelines can defeat an otherwise valid claim.

title: Muhammad Saleem v. Sui Southern Gas &,
explainer:
This case involved a customer, Muhammad Saleem, who ran a hotel and had a dispute with Sui Southern Gas Company over his gas bills. He complained that his gas meter had stopped working properly, but instead of fixing it, the company later accused him of tampering with the meter and demanded large sums of money for unpaid gas charges, first around Rs. 28,000, later escalating to over Rs. 7 lakh. Saleem claimed the real reason behind this was his refusal to pay a bribe demanded by the company's officials, after which they installed new meters and issued inflated bills.

The trial court had dismissed his suit but reduced the amount he had to pay from about Rs. 7.4 lakh to Rs. 3.1 lakh, without clearly explaining how it reached that figure. Both sides appealed, each dissatisfied with different parts of the decision.

The Balochistan High Court found that the trial court had failed to properly discuss or analyze the evidence presented by either side, as required under the Civil Procedure Code. It did not clearly accept or reject any evidence and gave no proper reasoning for its conclusions, making the judgment arbitrary and legally unsound.

As a result, the High Court set aside the trial court's decision and sent the case back for a fresh decision, this time requiring the trial court to properly examine the evidence and give clear, reasoned findings on each issue. The case highlights the importance of courts providing transparent, evidence-based reasoning in judgments, especially in consumer disputes involving utility companies.

The plaintiffs, relatives of the extended family, argued that Alam Khan was not really Baz Muhammad's son but had falsely gotten his name recorded as such, and later used a religious ruling (Fatwa) to transfer the property into his name and then into his heirs' names. The defendants, representing Alam Khan's heirs, argued he genuinely was Baz Muhammad's son and had lived his whole life acknowledged as such by the community and family.

The trial court dismissed the plaintiffs' suit, and the High Court upheld that decision on appeal. The judges found strong evidence—including Alam Khan's local certificate, identity card, and employment records—showing he was consistently recognized throughout his life as Baz Muhammad's legitimate son, both by Baz Muhammad himself and by others in the community. Since there was no error in how the trial court read the evidence, the appeal was dismissed.

title: Noor Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about Noor Ahmed, who was convicted of murder (qatl-e-amd) by a Sessions Court in Noshki and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine, for allegedly shooting a man who had merely asked for drinking water at a shop. Ahmed appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution relied mainly on two supposed eyewitnesses. However, the court found serious problems with their testimony. One witness, though named as an eyewitness in the original police report (FIR), gave only a vague description of the attacker and never actually claimed he could identify him—he also failed to pick out the accused in an identification parade and denied knowing the culprit beforehand. The second witness was not even mentioned as an eyewitness in the FIR, and his statement was recorded after an unexplained delay. Both witnesses' accounts contradicted each other in important ways.

Because of these gaps and contradictions, the High Court ruled that the prosecution had not proven guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It overturned the conviction, acquitted Noor Ahmed, and ordered his release.

The judgment reinforces an important principle in criminal law: even a single serious doubt in the prosecution's case entitles the accused to acquittal as a matter of right, not favor. The court also invoked the Islamic legal principle that it is better to mistakenly acquit a guilty person than to wrongly convict an innocent one, emphasizing the high standard of proof required before someone can be deprived of liberty or life.

title: Inam Khan and others V. Haji Abdul Rehman and others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court concerned a long-running property dispute over land in Kharan. The original plaintiffs (respondents in this appeal) claimed ownership of certain land, alleging that government officials had wrongfully conspired to allot their ancestral land to a private party (the petitioners). The trial court (Qazi, Kharan) had dismissed their suit, partly because the plaintiffs themselves never testified as witnesses, though several relatives and associates testified on their behalf. On appeal, the Majlis-e-Shoora, Kharan reversed this decision and ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, prompting the losing parties to file revision petitions before the High Court.

The petitioners argued that the plaintiffs had improperly changed their case through an amended plaint (introducing a new claim that the land was "Shamilat/Noutor" community land) without court permission, that the witness testimony was contradictory and unreliable, and that the plaintiffs' failure to testify personally was fatal to their case.

The court's key legal points included that evidence supporting claims never actually made in the original pleadings should be disregarded, that amending pleadings to introduce new claims without court approval is improper, and that while a party's failure to testify isn't automatically fatal if other evidence supports their case, it does prevent their own pleadings from being treated as evidence. The judgment also emphasized that courts have a special duty to protect public property and public rights against questionable administrative actions.

title: Haji Wahid Bakhsh V. Ahmed and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involves a property and money dispute from Gwadar. Haji Wahid Bakhsh sued three people, claiming the second and third respondents owed him Rs. 1,000,000 for a launch (boat) purchase and cash given to them. He alleged that the first respondent had guaranteed this debt through a 1997 agreement, promising to hand over two shops if the debt wasn't paid, and that he later took possession of the shops and was collecting rent from tenants.

The case went through multiple courts over many years, including the Qazi's court, a religious appellate body (Majlis-e-Shoora), and a previous round before the High Court, which had already sent the case back for the trial court to rewrite its judgment properly. Eventually, the Senior Civil Judge dismissed the suit, and the plaintiff appealed again.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the key agreement document was never properly proved: its author (the person who supposedly signed it) was alive but never brought to testify, only a photocopy was produced instead of the original, and the document required registration which had not been done. The court also found that the evidence given did not match the claims made in the plaint. Since there was no error in how the trial court had read the evidence, the appeal was dismissed with costs.

The case highlights how important it is to properly prove documents in court, especially originals and witness testimony, when claiming rights based on an agreement.

title: Hamid Ali v. Mst. Farzana,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved two related petitions between a husband, Hamid Ali, and his wife, Mst. Farzana, arising from a troubled marriage.

In the first case, the wife had filed a maintenance suit at the Family Court in Turbat, seeking monthly maintenance and medical expenses for their son. The husband argued the suit was not maintainable because an earlier maintenance dispute between the same parties had already been settled through a compromise, and also that the Turbat court lacked jurisdiction since he lived in Panjgoor. Both the trial court and the appellate court had ruled in the wife's favor.

In the second case, the husband had filed a suit in Panjgoor seeking restitution of conjugal rights and custody of their son, Talha, claiming the wife was being influenced by another respondent to avoid living with him. Both lower courts dismissed his suit.

The High Court found that since both parties actually resided in Panjgoor, the maintenance case should properly have been heard by the Family Court there, not in Turbat. It sent both cases back to the Panjgoor Family Court for fresh decisions. The court also clarified that principles of res judicata (Section 11, CPC) apply to family court proceedings, and emphasized that since the couple remained legally married, courts should make every effort to encourage reconciliation between spouses.

This case matters because it clarifies rules on territorial jurisdiction in family disputes and reinforces courts' duty to promote reconciliation in matrimonial matters.

title: Sayed Tayyab Ali V. Sayeda Nusrat Jahan and 12 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over inherited property. Sayeda Nusrat Jahan filed a lawsuit for partition, accounting, and injunction, claiming she was the legal daughter and heir of her late father, Sayed Mahboob Ali Naqvi, entitled to a share in his assets. The defendant, Sayed Tayyab Ali, disputed this, arguing she was only an adopted daughter and thus not entitled to inherit.

During the case, Nusrat Jahan asked the trial court to issue a preliminary order granting her possession of the property and mesne profits (compensation for use of the property). The trial court rejected that request but, with the consent of both parties' lawyers, ordered Tayyab Ali to furnish security of Rs. 10,00,000 based on estimated rental income from the property. Tayyab Ali later asked the court to reduce this amount, but that request was also denied, prompting him to challenge the order in the High Court.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed his petition for two main reasons. First, since the original order was appealable under the procedural rules, a revision petition was not the correct legal remedy. Second, because Tayyab Ali had agreed to the surety arrangement in court, he was legally estopped from later challenging its validity—he could not accept the order's terms while only disputing the amount, then try to have it thrown out entirely. The court found no illegality or unfairness in the trial court's decision and dismissed the case with costs.

This case highlights the legal principle that a party cannot "approbate and reprobate"

title: Dr. Abdul Raziq and 2 others V. Mst. Hameeda Begum and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over a house in Quetta. The plaintiffs (later appellants) had been living in the house but lost a long legal battle over ownership, which the Supreme Court ultimately decided in favor of a woman named Hameeda Begum, declaring her the owner and the plaintiffs mere tenants. After that ruling, Hameeda Begum reportedly forced the plaintiffs out, throwing their belongings into the street and causing property damage. The plaintiffs then sued for damages of over two crore rupees, alleging harassment, false criminal cases, defamatory statements in court filings, and breach of an undertaking to return possession of the house.

The trial court dismissed the suit, and the plaintiffs appealed. However, during the case, Hameeda Begum died before any final decree was issued against her, and her legal heirs were never properly brought into the case. The High Court found this fatal to the appeal: since the claim for damages was a single, joint claim against all defendants together and could not be split up, the death of one defendant before judgment meant the entire suit had to fail equally against everyone, not just her.

The court dismissed the appeal, upholding the trial court's decision. The case illustrates an important legal principle: when a claim is "indivisible," the death of one defendant during litigation, without properly continuing the case against their heirs, can cause the whole suit to collapse.

title: Syed Shahbuddin V. Haji Abdul Ghani and 5 others,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute over the right of pre-emption, which under Islamic law allows certain people, such as co-sharers, those sharing rights like a pathway, or adjoining property owners, to claim priority to buy property that has been sold to someone else, provided they follow specific legal steps and timing requirements.

The appellant, Syed Shahabuddin, claimed he had this right as an adjoining property owner and said he had properly announced his intention to exercise it. His pre-emption suit was dismissed by the trial court, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined whether the appellant had actually proven he qualified as an adjoining owner or in any of the other recognized categories entitled to claim pre-emption. It found that while the appellant claimed this status in his written complaint, his own testimony in court, describing the property boundaries, did not establish that he actually met the legal definition of a qualifying claimant. His witness's testimony was also found unreliable, since the witness admitted the property had already changed hands more than once before the transaction being challenged.

Because the appellant failed to establish his basic legal standing to claim pre-emption, the court held that other procedural requirements about how and when he announced his claim became irrelevant. The High Court found no error in the trial court's reasoning and dismissed the appeal, upholding the original decision against the appellant. This case illustrates how strictly courts require claimants to prove their qualifying status before pre-emption rights can even be considered.

title: Muhammad Arif and another V. Yar Muhammad,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a man (Yar Muhammad) and his former brother-in-law and another person over a written agreement supposedly made when Yar Muhammad's marriage to the sister of one of the petitioners ended through khula (a form of divorce initiated by the wife). Yar Muhammad claimed the agreement obliged the family to pay him Rs. 225,000 as compensation, with one relative acting as guarantor. When payment was not made, he sued for enforcement of the agreement.

The trial court dismissed his suit, finding the agreement was not properly proved, since key witnesses to the document were never produced in court. However, an appellate religious court (Majlis-e-Shoora) later ruled in his favor, issuing an ex parte decree without proper notice to the other side.

The Balochistan High Court found serious flaws in this outcome. It noted that the underlying claim made no legal sense, since khula and its financial terms only arise during a subsisting marriage, and this marriage had already been legally dissolved. The appellate court also failed to notice that no court fee had been paid, a mandatory requirement for filing the case.

The High Court set aside the appellate court's decision and restored the trial court's dismissal of the case, while also directing recovery of the unpaid court fees. The case highlights the importance of properly proving contested agreements and following procedural requirements like court fees before a court can decide a case.

title: Mrduman-e-Malle Zai Nida Kahol through Haji Saleh Muhammad and others V. Marduman-e-Killi Khudai-e-Rahim Sadezai (Shai) through their Elders and others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute between two tribal communities in Chaman, Balochistan, over a piece of land situated between properties belonging to Nida Kahool and Ahmed Kahool tribes. The appellants (Malezai Nida Kahool) claimed the land was theirs, citing an old 1945 judgment from the Additional District Magistrate that had ruled in favor of their predecessors and led to the respondents vacating the disputed land. They argued that the respondent tribe later re-encroached on the property while the appellants were away due to border tensions, and that a tribal jirga failed to resolve the matter, prompting the lawsuit for declaration, injunction, possession, and correction of revenue records.

The trial court dismissed the suit, and the High Court upheld that dismissal. The court found that the 1945 judgment did not specify the boundaries of the property or confirm it was the same land now in dispute, nor did it establish that possession had actually been handed over to the appellants. The appellants failed to prove exactly when they were dispossessed or that they had prior possession, which is required when seeking both declaration and possession under the law. Witness testimonies were also contradictory regarding measurements and timelines. Since the suit was filed too late under the Limitation Act and lacked basic details like property boundaries, the court ruled it was time-barred and unsubstantiated. This case reinforces that possession claims must be backed by clear, consistent evidence and filed within legal time limits.

title: Muhammad Saddique and others V. Secretary Forest through Executive Officer, Lasbella at Uthal and others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Lasbela, Balochistan, between the Forest Department and local residents (petitioners) over land recorded as government forest property. The Forest Department claimed ownership of the land based on a 1965 government notification allotting it forest land, later formally mutated in the department's name in 1980. It alleged that local residents had illegally cut trees and built structures on this land, and sued for declaration, injunction, and eviction. The residents argued they were in long-standing possession of part of the land, treating it as ancestral property, and that mere revenue records should not override their possession.

Both the trial court and the appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora) ruled in favor of the Forest Department, finding the land belonged to the government and had been properly transferred to the department. The residents then approached the Balochistan High Court through revision petitions.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions, ruling that courts should not disturb "concurrent findings of fact" by two lower courts unless those findings are clearly unreasonable or the evidence was misread. Since the residents' lawyer could not point to specific evidence that was overlooked or misinterpreted, the court dismissed the revision petitions.

The case is important because it reinforces limits on higher court intervention in factual disputes already decided consistently by two lower courts, and it clarifies how principles like res judicata apply when a party's claim has already been litigated and lost in an earlier related case.

title: Malik Mehboob V. Nazar Muhammad and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute in Quetta. The petitioner, Malik Mehboob, claimed he was in possession of a piece of land and filed a lawsuit seeking an injunction to stop the actual owners and a revenue official from entering the land or carrying out a demarcation (division) of the property. He argued that he had occupied vacant land in 1980 by building walls around it, and that no one had objected at the time.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court rejected his case, finding that he was not the owner and had essentially occupied the land as a trespasser without the owner's permission. The revenue record showed the respondents were the actual joint owners in possession, and they had lawfully asked a revenue officer to carry out demarcation of the land. The courts held that a revenue officer cannot be restrained from performing his lawful duties under the West Pakistan Land Revenue Act, and that mere illegal or unauthorized possession does not create a legal right against the true owner.

The Balochistan High Court, reviewing the case, agreed with the lower courts' findings. It found no error, unfairness, or misreading of evidence in their decisions and refused to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact. The revision petition was dismissed.

The case matters because it reaffirms that unauthorized possession alone does not defeat an owner's rights, and that courts will not block lawful actions by revenue officials or restrain rightful owners from accessing their own property.

title: Saadullah and another V. Secretary, Irrigation Department,

The petitioners claimed ownership of land in Ziarat district where the government intended to construct a Delay Action Dam. They filed a civil suit seeking a declaration of ownership and a permanent injunction to stop the department from taking the land without following proper legal acquisition procedures.

The trial court examined the case and, based on preliminary legal issues, dismissed the suit without allowing full evidence to be presented. This decision was upheld on appeal. The petitioners then approached the Balochistan High Court, arguing they were denied a chance to present evidence and that lower courts had ignored old revenue records supporting their ownership claim.

The High Court dismissed the revision petition, agreeing with the lower courts. It found that revenue records actually showed the land was registered in the name of the Provincial Government, not the petitioners. No formal allotment or ownership record existed in their favor. It relied on a Supreme Court precedent confirming that unclear or unsubstantiated ownership claims cannot support a suit for possession or declaration.

This case matters because it reinforces that courts can dismiss legally baseless claims at an early stage, and that unsupported ownership assertions cannot block public infrastructure projects like dam construction.

title: Ghous-Ud-Din V. Rashida and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a family property dispute in Quetta involving inheritance rights. After Jamal-ud-Din Kakar died, his children and widow were entitled to shares in his property. Two of his daughters filed a lawsuit seeking their rightful inheritance shares, along with partition, possession, and correction of property records. The defendants, who were other family members, admitted the relationship and that the property belonged to their late father, but claimed the daughters had already gifted away their shares to them. However, they had no written document proving this gift and relied only on oral testimony.

The trial court and the appellate court both ruled in favor of the daughters, rejecting the claim of an earlier gift. The Balochistan High Court upheld these decisions, dismissing the family members' revision petition. The court noted that during the case, one daughter did gift her share through a proper written compromise deed—which contradicted the defendants' claim that an earlier informal gift already existed. The court also held that new construction built by the defendants on the disputed property did not create any additional rights for them, since it was built at their own risk without the other heir's permission.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that Islamic inheritance shares pass automatically to heirs upon death and cannot be taken away through vague or unproven claims, especially affecting women's inheritance rights. It emphasizes that such rights require solid, credible evidence to override, not just oral assertions.

title: Abdullah V. Provincial Government through Secretary Board of Revenue and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a piece of land in Kharan, Balochistan. Abdullah, who ran a private school, claimed he had purchased a plot of land for Rs. 50,000 from one Javed Masih to build a school building. With government financial assistance, a school building was constructed, but the District Administration later refused to hand over the building to him, prompting him to file a civil suit for declaration and injunction.

The trial court (Qazi, Kharan) dismissed his suit, and his appeal to the Majlis-e-Shoora, Kharan was also dismissed. He then approached the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions. It found that Abdullah's claimed sale of the land was illegal and invalid, meaning no clear title had actually passed to him. Since he lacked proper title, he was not entitled to sue for declaration or possession of the property. The court also noted that a lease document he relied on had never been properly presented or exhibited as evidence during trial, so it could not now be considered.

The court emphasized that when lower courts have properly examined the evidence and reached consistent factual conclusions, the High Court's revisional powers do not allow it to reweigh that evidence simply because another view might be possible. Finding no legal errors or misreading of evidence, the court dismissed Abdullah's revision petition, meaning the school building remained outside his ownership claim.

title: Amir Muhammad V. Abdul Bari and 6 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta. Amir Muhammad had filed a civil suit seeking a declaration and cancellation of an inheritance mutation over shamilat (shared/communal) land, along with a permanent injunction. The trial court dismissed his suit in 2011 after hearing evidence from both sides. He then appealed, and while the appeal was pending, he asked the appellate court's permission to introduce two additional pieces of evidence that had not been presented at trial: an old revenue record (jama bandi) from 1950-51 and a pedigree table showing the family lineage connected to the land. The appellate court refused this request, so Amir Muhammad challenged that refusal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the appellate court's decision and dismissed the revision petition. It explained that Order XLI Rule 27 of the Civil Procedure Code allows additional evidence at the appeal stage only in limited situations: when the trial court wrongly refused to admit evidence that should have been admitted, when the appellate court itself needs the evidence to decide the case, or for some other substantial reason. Here, one document had already been part of the trial record, and the other was never mentioned in the original plaint or relied upon earlier, with no real explanation for the delay. The court stressed that such provisions exist to serve the court's own need for clarity, not to help a losing party patch up a weak case. This ruling reinforces strict limits on introducing new evidence late in litigation.

title: Ghulam Dastager V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a Toyota Hilux vehicle that was seized by police in Quetta in 2008, allegedly connected to explosives and arms recovered from persons using it. The three men arrested with the vehicle were tried under terrorism and explosives laws, but all were acquitted. However, the trial court, in its acquittal judgment, ordered the vehicle confiscated by the State. The appellant, Ghulam Dastageer, said the vehicle actually belonged to him, that it had been snatched from him, and that he was never accused in any of the cases. He fought through multiple rounds of litigation, including the Supreme Court, to recover his vehicle.

Eventually the Supreme Court allowed him to file an application before the trial court asking for custody of the vehicle, and directed the trial court to actually decide that application on its merits. Instead, the trial court dismissed his application again, reasoning that deciding it would amount to reviewing its own earlier judgment, which courts are generally not allowed to do.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that an order confiscating property is not the same as a full "judgment" under the law, so the rule against reviewing judgments did not apply. The trial court was legally required to examine Ghulam Dastageer's claim to the vehicle on its own merits, not dismiss it on a technical excuse. The High Court set aside the trial court's order and sent the matter back for a fresh decision, allowing the appeals. This shows courts must properly examine ownership claims over seized property, even after a criminal case has ended.

title: Muhammad Essa V. District Judge, Pishin and 14 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a pre-emption suit, a type of case where someone claims the legal right to purchase property that a family member or co-owner has sold to someone else, usually by matching the sale price.

The buyer of the disputed property (the petitioner) had purchased land, and the plaintiff filed a pre-emption suit to claim the property by offering to pay the same price, which was stated as Rs. 29,00,000 in the plaint. Later, the plaintiff sought to amend the plaint, apparently trying to alter details related to the sale consideration. The trial court refused to allow this amendment, but the plaintiff challenged that refusal before the District Judge, who reversed the trial court and permitted the amendment. The buyer then challenged the District Judge's order before the High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the buyer. It found that since the value of the suit property (Rs. 29,00,000) exceeded the monetary limit for the District Judge's revisional jurisdiction, the District Judge had no legal authority to even hear the case. Separately, the court also held that the plaintiff could not be allowed to change the sale price he had already committed to in the original plaint, since doing so would unfairly shift the fundamental nature of his claim after the fact, a legal principle preventing parties from taking contradictory positions.

The petition was allowed, the District Judge's order was set aside, and the amendment application was dismissed. This case reinforces the principles of jurisdictional limits and preventing inconsistent legal claims by litigants.

title: Abdul Haleem V. The State,
explainer:
Abdul Haleem was convicted under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997 after 24 kilograms of charas (cannabis resin) were allegedly recovered from the roof of a passenger van at a checkpoint near Quetta. The trial court sentenced him to life imprisonment and a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing the prosecution's evidence was weak, contradictory, and delayed.

The High Court did not rule on the merits of the conviction itself. Instead, it focused on a serious procedural flaw: the driver of the van, who had given a statement to police during investigation and was a key witness whose testimony went to the heart of the case, was never produced or examined at trial. The court found that only a token effort was made to secure his attendance, with no strong measures like bailable or non-bailable warrants used to compel him to appear. It held that the prosecutor had no legal justification to simply drop such a crucial witness, and that the trial court erred by allowing this to happen, since it deprived the defense and the court of essential evidence.

Because of this irregularity, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence and sent the case back to the trial court, directing it to secure the driver's testimony and the accused's statement, and then decide the case afresh on its merits. The judgment underscores that courts must ensure all material witnesses are properly examined before reaching a verdict, especially in serious narcotics cases carrying life imprisonment.

title: Abdul Hameed and 9 others V. Khursheed Ahmed and 12 others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute over agricultural land (Khasra Nos. 119 and 120) in Mouza Bhagyar, Balochistan. The plaintiffs sued for a declaration, correction, and cancellation of a land mutation entry, plus a permanent injunction, claiming the land was wrongly recorded in the government's name and later fraudulently transferred to certain defendants. The trial court (Qazi's court) ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, but the appellate body (Majlis-e-Shoora) reversed that decision and dismissed the suit. The petitioners then challenged this reversal before the Balochistan High Court.

However, the plaint itself revealed that the same subject matter had already been litigated: an earlier suit over the same land had been decreed in 1991, an appeal against it was dismissed, and a subsequent application to reopen the matter (under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code) had also failed all the way up to the Supreme Court. Given this, the High Court found that the fresh suit was not legally competent to begin with, since the matter had already been conclusively decided.

The Court held that when examining a plaint, courts must independently verify whether a suit is legally maintainable based solely on the plaint's own contents, and must reject it at the outset if it is barred by law. Since the trial court failed to do this, the suit should never have proceeded. The High Court dismissed the revision petition, emphasizing that courts must not allow relitigation of already-settled disputes.

title: Muneer Ahmed V. District and Sessions Judge, Lasbella at Hub and others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved disputes arising from local government council elections in Gaddani, District Lasbela, held in December 2013. Candidates who narrowly lost their contests filed election petitions before an Election Tribunal (the District and Sessions Judge, Lasbela), challenging vote counts, including allegations that certain votes were wrongly rejected or forcibly cast.

While these election petitions were still pending final decision, the Election Tribunal issued administrative letters or notifications instructing election authorities on how to treat certain contested votes, effectively deciding key factual issues without formally hearing the affected parties or issuing a proper judicial order.

The petitioners argued this was unfair and unlawful, since such consequential decisions were made behind their backs, through executive letters rather than a proper judicial process with notice and hearing.

The High Court agreed. It held that orders with such serious legal consequences cannot be passed through informal administrative communications while formal adjudication is still pending, and doing so violates natural justice. It ruled that such void orders cannot be allowed to stand, as illegality cannot be perpetuated. It also allowed additional affected persons to be added as parties to ensure everyone impacted had a chance to be heard. Ultimately, the Court set aside both impugned orders as illegal, without jurisdiction, and void from the outset.

The case highlights the importance of fair procedure and due notice before decisions affecting people's electoral rights are made, even by tribunals handling local government election disputes.

title: Muhammad Siddique Sherani V. Shahjahan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute where a buyer, Muhammad Siddique Sherani, sued to enforce an agreement to sell land. He claimed the sellers had signed an agreement, handed over possession to him, and that he had even built construction on the property, but the sellers later refused to formally transfer ownership (mutation) in his name. The trial court ruled in his favor, but the appellate court reversed that decision, questioning whether the agreement was properly stamped and registered, and whether the lawsuit was even legally valid.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the appellate court's ruling and restored the original decision favoring the buyer. It held that since the agreement had already been admitted as evidence without objection during trial, the appellate court had no legal authority to later question its validity based on stamp duty issues. The court clarified that stamp laws exist to collect government revenue, not to invalidate genuine contracts. It also found that since the buyer had taken possession and built on the land as part of fulfilling the contract, he was protected under property law principles even though the agreement wasn't formally registered. The court further ruled that the lawsuit was properly filed and should not have been dismissed on technical grounds.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that technical defects like unregistered or understamped documents cannot automatically defeat a genuine buyer's rights, especially when possession was taken in good faith and part performance of the contract is evident.

title: Rehmat Sanober V. Balochistan Public Service Commission through Chairman and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over age eligibility for a government teaching post in Balochistan. The petitioner, Rehmat Sanober, applied for a Lecturer (Urdu) position after the Balochistan Public Service Commission advertised the post in February 2013, offering a ten-year relaxation in the upper age limit under the government's policy then in effect. She was found eligible, passed the written test topping her zone, cleared the interview, and was officially declared successful through a press release. However, on the very same day, a second press release was issued cancelling her selection, claiming she was over-age based on a new notification issued later that reduced the age relaxation, and another candidate was declared eligible instead.

The High Court ruled in her favor. It held that the government could not apply the later notification retrospectively to undo rights she had already earned under the rules in force when she applied. Since she met the age criteria at the time of the advertisement, passed all stages of selection, and was recommended for appointment, a vested right had accrued to her that could not be taken away without giving her a hearing. The court also found the relaxation policy did not violate any law or fundamental rights.

The court set aside the cancellation press release and directed the government to issue her appointment letter immediately. This case underscores the principle that laws and policy changes generally apply prospectively, and that vested rights already earned through fair process cannot be arbitrarily withdrawn without due process.

title: Haji Zahir Ali, Advocate V. Xen/Executive District Officer, Public Health Engineering Department Kharan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case concerned a long-running property dispute in Kharan, Balochistan. A lawyer, Haji Zahir Ali, claimed that a large plot of land, measuring 160,000 square feet, had been allotted to him in 1980 by the Chairman of the Town Committee, and that he had remained in possession until others interfered while he was away pursuing his education. He sued for a declaration of ownership, an injunction, and partial possession. The case had a lengthy procedural history, moving between trial court, appellate forums (Majlis-e-Shoora), and even the Supreme Court, involving remands, a compromise decree that was later set aside, and multiple rounds of litigation over more than two decades.

The key legal question before the Balochistan High Court was whether the Chairman of the Town Committee even had the legal authority to allot this land in the first place. Examining government notifications from 1975, the Court found that only the Secretary of Local Government had power to allot such land, and only after a proper process involving a No Objection Certificate from the District Coordination Committee. Since this procedure was never followed, and the Chairman lacked jurisdiction entirely, the original allotment was void from the start. Local officials also confirmed no valid allotment had ever been made.

The High Court therefore dismissed the petitioner's revision petition, upholding the lower courts' rejection of his claim. The judgment reinforces that state land can only be allotted by officials with proper legal authority, protecting public land from improper transfers by unauthorized local officials.

title: Wali Muhammad V. Abdul Wahid and 3 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a dispute over an official government residential quarter in Zhob. Abdul Wahid claimed he was the lawful allottee of the quarter based on an allotment order from 1999. Government authorities later declared that order fake and tried to cancel it and evict him, but he sued and won a declaration from the trial court confirming his right to the property. Wali Muhammad, who had also been allotted the same quarter, challenged this decree, arguing it was obtained through fraud and misrepresentation, since the underlying allotment document had already been found bogus and a criminal case had been registered against Abdul Wahid. Lower courts rejected this challenge.

The High Court found serious problems with how the original suit was handled. It noted that since the suit involved the government, the law required a 90-day notice period before proceedings could continue, but the trial court decided the case within two months, violating this rule. The court also held that the government had no authority to permanently transfer ownership of official residential buildings to individuals, meaning the plaintiff never had a valid legal claim to begin with. The High Court set aside all the lower court decisions, dismissed the original suit, and directed the government to review the status of public buildings, prevent illegal permanent allotments, and hold responsible officials accountable for failing to protect public property during the case.

title: Inayatullah and 2 others V. Government of Balochistan through Senior M.B.R. and 3 others,
explainer:
This case concerned land in Quetta originally allotted by the government to two individuals, Allah Bakhsh and Shehnaz Akhtar, who later sold it to the petitioners. After the sale, the government cancelled the original allotment, and the petitioners sued for a declaration that they were lawful owners and could not be dispossessed. The trial court initially ruled in their favor, but the appellate court reversed this and dismissed the suit. The matter eventually went to the Supreme Court, which sent it back to the Balochistan High Court to be decided on merits.

The High Court dismissed the petitioners' case. It held that under the Balochistan Land Lease Policy of 1988, a government allotment or lease does not automatically create ownership rights. A lessee only gains ownership after remaining in possession for 45 years, and until then cannot legally sell, sublet, or transfer the land. Since the original allottees never had ownership, they could not pass valid title to the petitioners through sale. The court applied the principle that a seller cannot transfer better rights than they themselves hold, meaning the petitioners could not claim to be genuine "bona fide purchasers" of land that was illegally transferred. The court also noted that land on highways cannot be allotted or leased at all.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that government land allotments come with strict conditions, and buyers who purchase such land before ownership fully vests in the original allottee acquire no legal title, regardless of paperwork or possession.

title: Bolan Mining Enterprises through Site Incharge V. Ghous Baksh and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Balochistan. Bolan Mining Enterprises had been allotted about 9 acres of land by the government for mining, but claimed that certain individuals occupied part of that land and built structures on it. The company sued for declaration, injunction, possession, and removal of the encroachment. The trial court heard extensive evidence from both sides and ruled in favor of the mining company, ordering the land returned.

The opposing party appealed, and the appellate body (Majlis-e-Shoora) overturned the trial court's decision, throwing out the case entirely on the technical ground that the original complaint (plaint) did not clearly describe the property in dispute, as required under Order VII, Rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code.

The High Court disagreed with this approach. It held that a missing property description in the plaint is not, by itself, grounds to reject a case under the law's specific rejection rule (Order VII, Rule 11). Since sufficient evidence, including the specific plot number, was presented during trial to clearly identify the land, the trial court had correctly been able to decide the case. The High Court also noted that the appellate body had inconsistently decided some issues on merit while rejecting the plaint on a technicality, which was legally improper. The High Court set aside the appellate decision and sent the case back for a proper decision on the merits, reinforcing that minor pleading defects should not defeat justice when the underlying facts are clear from evidence.

title: Muhammad Abdullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns Muhammad Abdullah, who was convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Quetta and sentenced to life imprisonment under murder and terrorism charges, plus a separate three-year sentence under arms law. His appeals against these convictions were dismissed by the Balochistan High Court. He then approached the Supreme Court, which granted him leave to appeal (meaning it agreed to hear his case further). While that appeal was pending, he asked the High Court to suspend his sentences and release him on bail, arguing that since the Supreme Court had granted leave to appeal, he was entitled to this relief, especially since his case might take a long time to resolve.

The High Court rejected his request. It explained that under the law, getting leave to appeal from the Supreme Court is not enough by itself to suspend a sentence, the High Court still has discretion, and the applicant must show additional grounds, such as unreasonable delay or legal errors in the judgment. More importantly, the court ruled that the Anti-Terrorism Act contains a specific bar preventing bail during a pending appeal, and this special law overrides the general provision in the Criminal Procedure Code that might otherwise allow suspension of sentence. Since this bar applied fully to his case, his applications for bail were dismissed.

This ruling clarifies that convicts sentenced under anti-terrorism laws face stricter, non-negotiable restrictions on bail during appeals, even after the Supreme Court agrees to hear their case.

When the decree-holder tried to enforce the decree, the executing court ended up ordering the salary of a man named Naveed Ahmed to be attached, believing he was the same person as the company's CEO, whose name appeared in the case as Naveed Aftab.

Naveed Ahmed objected, saying he was a government servant with no connection to the company, that he was not a party to the original suit, and that the actual CEO was his brother, Naeem Aftab. He argued he was being wrongly targeted, possibly due to a personal family dispute after he divorced the decree-holder's relative. The executing court rejected his objections and upheld the attachment.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that merely sharing a similar name is not enough to make someone liable under a decree—the person must also share the same interest, character, or legal capacity as the actual judgment debtor (such as being a partner, guarantor, surety, or legal heir). Since none of this was shown for Naveed Ahmed, the court set aside the executing court's order and sent the case back for proper determination of the judgment debtor's true identity. This case highlights the importance of correctly identifying who is legally bound by a court decree before enforcing it against them.

title: Shafi Muhammad v. State,
explainer:
This case involved Shafi Muhammad, who had been convicted by a trial court of murder under section 302 of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to death, along with an order to pay compensation to the heirs of the deceased, Raheem Bakhsh. The case reached the Balochistan High Court in two ways: as an appeal filed by the convict challenging his conviction, and as a murder reference, which is a mandatory review that Pakistani law requires whenever a death sentence is handed down.

While the appeal was pending, the legal heirs of the victim informed the court that they had voluntarily compromised with the convict and forgiven him in the name of Allah, a practice recognized under Pakistani criminal law that allows victims' families to pardon an offender. The trial court verified this compromise, confirming that the heirs had acted freely, without pressure, and that no other family members existed who might object. The convict himself appeared before the High Court and showed remorse.

Finding the pardon genuine and seeing no reason to instead punish the convict under a separate provision allowing for state punishment despite forgiveness, the High Court accepted the compromise, set aside the conviction and death sentence, and acquitted the convict, ordering his release.

This case illustrates how Pakistani law permits victims' families to forgive those who killed their relatives, allowing courts to overturn even death sentences when such forgiveness is proven genuine and voluntary.

title: Qaim Khan v. State,
explainer:
This case involves a bail application before the Balochistan High Court, arising from a violent incident in Quetta in August 2009 where a dispute over a cricket match escalated into an armed attack. The complainant alleged that a group of armed men opened fire, killing one person and seriously injuring several others, and also caused damage using an iron rod. A First Information Report (FIR) was registered under charges including murder, attempted murder, and rioting.

The six applicants in this case were not named in the original FIR. They were only implicated later, when the complainant and two injured witnesses gave supplementary statements to police naming them as participants. No weapons, evidence, or recoveries linked the applicants to the crime during the police investigation.

The court noted that since the applicants were absent from the initial complaint and only surfaced in later statements, questions arose about how the witnesses came to know their identities, especially since the parties reportedly knew each other before the incident. The judge held that this raised the case to the level of "further inquiry," meaning there wasn't yet strong enough evidence to keep the applicants in custody without bail. The court also emphasized that any group/vicarious liability could only be properly assessed during trial, not at the bail stage, and that suspects shouldn't be jailed indefinitely as a form of punishment before their guilt is proven. Bail was therefore granted, with the court clarifying its remarks were tentative and would not affect the actual trial.

title: Muhammad Yaqoob Nasar v. Muhammad Israr Tareen,
explainer:
This case concerns an election petition challenging the results of a 2008 election in Balochistan, filed before the Election Tribunal at the Balochistan High Court. Before the merits could be examined, the winning candidate (respondent) filed an application arguing that the petition itself was legally defective and should be thrown out without further hearing.

The core issue was technical but important: under the Representation of the People Act, 1976, every election petition must be signed and "verified" by the petitioner in the manner required by the Code of Civil Procedure. This means the petitioner must clearly state which parts of the petition he knows to be true from his own personal knowledge, and which parts he believes to be true based on information from others. He must also properly swear this verification on oath before an authorized person, and any documents attached to the petition must likewise be signed and verified.

The judge examined the petitioner's actual verification statement and found it generic and incomplete—it did not distinguish between facts known personally and facts believed on information, and the oath was not properly attested as required. Relying on Supreme Court precedents, the judge held that this requirement is mandatory, not merely a technicality, and that failure to comply is a "fatal defect" leading to automatic dismissal.

As a result, the election petition was dismissed without examining whether the election result itself was actually flawed—illustrating how strict procedural compliance can determine the fate of election challenges in Pakistan.

title: Hassan v. State,
explainer:
This case involved Haji Hassan and his son, who were convicted by a Sessions Judge in Zhob for the murder of Hassan's wife, Mst. Zar Bakhat, and sentenced to life imprisonment. The prosecution's case was based on a First Information Report lodged by the victim's brother, who was not present at the time of the killing and only learned about it afterward. The evidence against the accused included an alleged extra-judicial confession by one appellant, recoveries of a rifle, magazine, and knife made during police custody, and reports from forensic and firearm experts.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence closely and found serious weaknesses in the prosecution's case. Neither the complainant nor other key witnesses had actually seen the crime take place. The extra-judicial confession was considered weak evidence, and in this case it lacked independent corroboration. The circumstantial evidence presented did not form a complete, connected chain proving guilt, and the prosecution's evidence was inconsistent in various respects. While it was undisputed that the death was unnatural, this alone was not enough to establish guilt.

Because the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, the High Court set aside the conviction and acquitted both appellants, ordering their release. This case illustrates the important legal principle that convictions, especially for serious offenses like murder, cannot rest on suspicion, weak confessions, or incomplete circumstantial evidence—guilt must be established with proof beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Shahnaz Parveen v. Abdul Aziz,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a house in Quetta. The respondents (plaintiffs) sued the predecessor of the petitioners, claiming that their family had purchased the house in 1939 and later allowed a man named Rahim Bakhsh Barfi to occupy two rooms as a licensee under an agreement. They alleged he later violated the terms of that arrangement and, after a earlier court petition was withdrawn, colluded with revenue department staff to fraudulently change property records in his own favor. They asked the court to cancel the 1982 agreement, declare their ownership, and restore possession of the house to them.

The trial court and, on appeal, the District Court both ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, relying on documentary evidence including the 1982 agreement (showing the occupant was only a licensee) and a 1939 registered sale deed proving the plaintiffs' grandfather had bought the property. The defendants then challenged these decisions before the Balochistan High Court, arguing the suit was time-barred and that the 1982 agreement was fraudulent.

The High Court dismissed the challenge. It found the limitation argument baseless, since the cause of action arose only after the revenue records were fraudulently altered, and the suit was filed well within time. It held that concurrent factual findings by lower courts cannot be disturbed in revision unless they involve jurisdictional error or serious illegality, which was not shown here. The case reaffirms the limited scope of revisional courts to interfere with settled factual findings of lower courts.

title: Ghulam Rasool v. Nasrullah,
explainer:
This case involved a family land dispute in Pishin, Balochistan. The plaintiffs (respondents in this appeal) sued their relatives for declaration of ownership, possession, cancellation of certain mutation (land record) entries, partition of jointly owned agricultural land, and a permanent injunction against interference. They claimed specific ownership shares in land that had been jointly purchased decades earlier, and argued that a mutation entry reducing their predecessor's share was fraudulent.

The defendants argued that the parties had already carried out a private partition of the land about 22 years earlier, with each side possessing and cultivating its own separate portion, including installing water boring and developing orchards.

The trial court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, granting the declarations sought and also ordering a fresh partition of the property by the authorities.

On appeal, the High Court rejected the defendants' complaint that the trial court had framed improper issues, noting they never objected to the issues during trial and could not now specify what better issues should have been framed.

However, the High Court agreed with the defendants on one key point: the trial court had contradicted itself. It had found that a private partition had already taken place and that both sides were already in separate possession of their respective shares—yet it still ordered a new partition, which was inconsistent with that finding.

The High Court therefore upheld the rest of the judgment but struck down the order for fresh partition, since one had already occurred privately. This shows courts will correct internally inconsistent rulings even while largely upholding a lower court's decision.

title: Adalat Khan v. State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, a driver and a cleaner of a truck, who were caught transporting 290 kilograms of hashish hidden inside onion bags on a highway in Balochistan. Coast guards, acting on secret information, stopped the vehicle and discovered the drugs concealed in ten bags. The men were arrested, tried under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and convicted by a Special Judge, receiving 14 years imprisonment each along with fines.

On appeal, their lawyer argued that the two were merely hired transport workers who had no knowledge that hashish was hidden in the onion bags they were carrying, and that the real culprits who arranged the shipment had already been acquitted by the trial court.

The Balochistan High Court rejected this argument. It found the prosecution witnesses credible and consistent, with only minor, natural discrepancies in their testimony. Importantly, the court explained that once possession of narcotics is not disputed, the law places a burden on the accused under Section 29 of the Act to prove their innocence with solid evidence, not just deny the charge. Since the appellants offered no evidence to support their claim of innocence, merely asserting they were unaware of the drugs, they failed to meet this legal burden. The court therefore upheld their conviction and sentence.

This case illustrates how narcotics law in Pakistan shifts the burden of proof onto the accused once possession is established, making a simple denial insufficient for acquittal.

title: Khayal Muhammad v. State,
explainer:
This case concerns the confiscation of a Mazda truck used to smuggle 290 kilograms of charas (a narcotic substance) in Balochistan. In 2007, Coast Guard officials intercepted the truck and found the drugs, leading to charges against two men, who were later convicted and sentenced to 14 years imprisonment each. The trial court also ordered the truck confiscated by the state.

Khayal Muhammad, claiming to be the truck's owner, appealed against the confiscation order. He argued that he had never been properly notified or given a chance to contest why his vehicle should not be confiscated.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with him. It held that under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, a vehicle can only be confiscated if it is proven that the owner knew the offence was being or was about to be committed. This knowledge, the court explained, is a factual matter that must be determined through proper legal process, which requires notifying the owner and giving them an opportunity to be heard. In this case, the trial court had failed to follow this procedure entirely and confiscated the vehicle without any inquiry into the owner's knowledge.

As a result, the High Court set aside the confiscation order and sent the matter back to the trial court to be decided properly, in accordance with the law. This case matters because it reinforces that property owners have a right to due process before losing their assets, even in serious narcotics cases.

title: Fateh Muhammad v. State,
explainer:
This case involved Fateh Muhammad, who was stopped during a routine police check in Quetta in 2003 while driving a vehicle that turned out to have a registration book later found to be forged. He was charged and convicted by the Sessions Judge under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with forgery and using a forged document as genuine, and sentenced to three years' imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, his lawyer argued that he had purchased the vehicle from another person and had no knowledge the registration book was fake, presenting a sale agreement to support this claim. The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence and found that the prosecution had not proven that the appellant himself prepared the forged document, or that he knowingly used it while aware it was forged. The court emphasized that simply possessing a forged document is not a crime unless it is knowingly and fraudulently used as genuine.

Since the prosecution failed to establish this knowledge or intent beyond reasonable doubt, the court held that the conviction could not stand. The appeal was allowed, and Fateh Muhammad was acquitted.

This judgment matters because it reinforces an important legal principle: criminal liability for forgery-related offenses requires proof of guilty knowledge and intent, not mere possession of a suspicious document. This protects innocent buyers who unknowingly come into possession of fraudulent paperwork through no fault of their own.

title: Fateh Muhammad v. State,
explainer:
This case is about Fateh Muhammad, who was caught with a suspected smuggled vehicle in Quetta in 2003. He was tried and convicted by a Special Customs Judge under the Customs Act for possessing smuggled goods, sentenced to two years in prison plus a fine, with the vehicle confiscated. Separately, he had also been named in the same FIR for offences of forgery and using forged documents under the Pakistan Penal Code. On appeal to the Balochistan High Court, his lawyer argued that being prosecuted twice from the same FIR violated the constitutional protection against double jeopardy (Article 13(a)) and Section 403 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which bars a second trial for the same offence.

The High Court rejected this argument. It explained that double jeopardy only applies when the offence being tried a second time is identical to the first. Here, the Customs Act offence (possessing smuggled goods) and the Penal Code offences (forgery and using forged documents) are legally distinct, even though they arose from the same set of facts and same FIR. Since they are different offences, they can be tried separately in different courts without breaching the law.

However, the court did show leniency on sentencing: since the appellant had already suffered the hardships of trial since his 2003 arrest and had no history of prior smuggling offences, his sentence was reduced to time already served. The case clarifies that facing multiple prosecutions from one incident is lawful when the charges involve genuinely separate offences under different statutes.

title: National Bank of Pakistan v. WASA,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a procedural dispute involving the National Bank of Pakistan and WASA (Water and Sanitation Agency). The bank had earlier filed a civil appeal against orders of a Senior Civil Judge in Quetta, but that appeal was dismissed in 2008 because the bank failed to pursue it properly (dismissed "in default"). The bank then tried to get the appeal restored, but did so about a year late and without asking the court to excuse the delay. This restoration request was also dismissed in July 2009.

Instead of accepting that outcome, the bank waited over eight months and then filed a "review application," asking the High Court to reconsider and set aside its own order. The bank argued that a longer limitation period (three years) should have applied to its case.

The High Court rejected this review application. It explained that under the law, a review can only succeed if there is a new and important piece of evidence that was not earlier available, or if there is an obvious mistake or error visible on the face of the original order. Neither condition was met here—the bank was essentially just repeating old arguments rather than pointing to any genuine error or new fact.

The judgment matters because it reinforces strict limits on when courts can revisit their own decisions, preventing review proceedings from being misused as a backdoor appeal.

The appellant claimed he was innocent, saying he was merely a mason waiting for a contractor near the checkpoint when police wrongly arrested him along with others who were later released, while he alone was falsely implicated.

title: Muhammad Qasim v. State,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Qasim, who was convicted by a trial court in Lasbella for causing an explosion in a public place, possessing explosives under suspicious circumstances, and keeping an unlicensed Kalashnikov rifle. He was sentenced to life imprisonment along with additional terms of rigorous imprisonment. The conviction stemmed from a nighttime police raid on a house in Jam Yousuf Colony, during which weapons, ammunition, a detonator, and other materials were allegedly recovered.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's case. The house raided was not exclusively occupied by the appellant, since another man, Khudai Rahim, was also arrested there but was later acquitted, raising doubts about who the seized items actually belonged to. Additionally, the house belonged to a person named Qurban Ali, who was never arrested or charged. The Kalashnikov and detonator were never sent to a weapons expert for verification. Crucially, the police search violated mandatory legal requirements under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which requires proper procedures like search warrants or independent witnesses.

Given these gaps and contradictions, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was accepted, and Muhammad Qasim was acquitted. This case highlights the importance of following proper legal procedures in searches and ensuring clear, reliable evidence before convicting someone of serious crimes.

title: Noor Ahmed v. State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by Noor Ahmed, who was accused of car theft under Section 381-A of the Pakistan Penal Code. According to the police report, the complainant's Alto car was stolen from outside his house, and after being alerted by children who witnessed the theft, he and a friend chased the suspects on a motorcycle. They caught the applicant as he was entering a house, while the other accused persons escaped. Police then arrived and arrested him.

The applicant's bail request had already been rejected by both a judicial magistrate and an additional sessions judge. He then approached the Balochistan High Court, arguing that he had been in custody since his arrest, the police investigation (challan) was already complete, and the offense did not fall under the category of serious crimes that automatically bar bail.

The court noted that the stolen car was not actually recovered from the applicant's possession, and the offense carried a maximum punishment of seven years, meaning it did not fall within the restrictive provisions of Section 497 of the Criminal Procedure Code that limit bail in serious cases. The court found the case required further inquiry.

As a result, the judge confirmed the applicant's earlier interim bail, granting it permanently on the condition that he provide sureties totaling Rs. 200,000. This case illustrates how courts weigh the severity of charges and evidence when deciding whether to grant bail before trial.

title: Jamshed Khan v. State,
explainer:
This case is about Jamshed Khan, who was stopped at a police checkpoint near Quetta in August 2007 while driving a car with an official-looking number plate. When signaled to stop, he sped away but was chased and caught. A search of the vehicle, conducted at the police station under the supervision of senior officers, uncovered 155 kilograms of charas (cannabis) hidden in secret compartments in the dashboard, seats, and other parts of the car. He was charged and convicted under Section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, his lawyer argued that certain senior officials present during the search were not called as witnesses, and that the search should have been conducted at the checkpoint rather than after moving the vehicle to the police station.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that the prosecution is not required to call every possible witness, and failing to do so does not weaken the case as long as other witnesses give consistent, credible testimony. It also ruled that conducting the search at the police station instead of the checkpoint was only a procedural irregularity, not serious enough to undermine the prosecution's case. Finding no contradictions in the evidence and no allegations of bias against the police, the court upheld the conviction and dismissed the appeal.

This case matters because it clarifies how much flexibility courts allow in narcotics prosecutions regarding witness selection and procedural technicalities, so long as the core evidence remains reliable.

title: Chakar Ali Khan Rind v. Govt; of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and deals with flood protection for villagers living near the Mirani Dam. The petitioner, representing residents of Kosh Kalat and nearby areas along the Kech River, asked the court to order authorities to build a protective wall, since heavy floods in June 2007 had caused major damage to homes and land. He argued that officials had promised to build such a wall but never did, and that the dam's spillway was too small to safely release floodwater.

The government responded that the damage was caused by an unprecedented cyclone-driven rainfall, not by any failure on its part, and that a flood protection project costing Rs. 84 million had already been approved and was partly completed.

The court first rejected the government's technical objection that the petitioner lacked proper authority to represent the community, noting he had consistently acted on their behalf. It held that the State has a constitutional duty under Articles 9 and 24 to protect people's life, liberty and property, and that residents facing flood threats were entitled to compensation and rehabilitation if harmed. However, the court said it could not, in this type of petition, calculate the exact compensation owed to the petitioner. It disposed of the case by allowing him to file a separate civil suit for compensation if he wished.

The ruling reinforces that constitutional rights to life and property include a government duty to protect citizens from disasters like floods, even though monetary claims must go through ordinary courts.

title: Muhammad Khan v. State,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Khan, who was stopped by Frontier Corps personnel near Quetta in 2009 and found in possession of a pistol, hand grenades, explosive material, a detonator, and other items. He was charged under laws dealing with illegal weapons and explosives, including the Anti-Terrorism Act. The trial court convicted him under the Arms Ordinance for unlawfully possessing an unlicensed pistol, sentencing him to three years imprisonment and a fine.

He appealed, arguing that the pistol recovered from him was not properly sealed at the scene and was never sent to a ballistics expert to confirm whether it actually worked. His lawyer suggested this undermined the prosecution's case.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It noted that the defence never actually challenged whether the pistol was functional when witnesses testified, and more importantly, the law does not require a weapon to be in working condition for its possession to be illegal—simply having an unlicensed weapon without proper authorization is the offence. The court held that failing to seal the weapon or send it for expert testing were mere procedural lapses by the investigating officer, not serious enough to undermine the conviction.

The court dismissed the appeal and upheld the original judgment, reinforcing the principle that technical or administrative omissions during investigation do not automatically invalidate a conviction when the core evidence of illegal possession stands unrefuted.
