title: Muhammad Adnan v. State,
explainer:
This case concerns a bail application filed by Muhammad Adnan, who was accused of murdering Ghulam Rasool along with a co-accused, in a case registered under section 302 (murder) read with section 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code.

The FIR was initially registered against unknown persons after the victim was found dead in his house. During investigation, a co-accused named Ali Khan was questioned and revealed the names of others involved, including the applicant. Based on Ali Khan's disclosure, police recovered a digital camera and prize bonds from Ali Khan's house, and recovered a mobile phone and prize bonds belonging to the deceased from the applicant's house.

The applicant's lawyer argued that there was no real evidence linking him to the crime, and that the only evidence was an inadmissible extra-judicial confession made to police.

The Balochistan High Court rejected this argument, ruling that the recovery of stolen items from the applicant's house, based on the co-accused's pointation, counted as "discovery of new facts" under Article 40 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (Pakistan's law of evidence). This meant the evidence was legally significant, not just an inadmissible confession.

Since the alleged offense carried the death penalty or life imprisonment, it fell under a legal category where bail is generally not granted except in special circumstances. Finding no such special circumstances, the court dismissed the bail application, while directing the trial court to proceed with the case quickly.

title: Commissioner Mekran v. Abdul Wahid,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a dispute over whether a government letter counted as a legally binding agreement. The respondents (plaintiffs) owned land at Koh-e-Murad and claimed that government officials had signed a letter in 2007 agreeing to install a temporary camp settlement on their land for ten months, after which water and electricity facilities would be handed back to them. When the government failed to honor this after more than two years, the landowners sued to enforce the letter as a contract. Both the trial court and the appellate court ruled in favor of the landowners, prompting the government officials to challenge these decisions before the High Court.

The High Court sided with the government. It found that the letter in question was not signed by the relevant government official, and the district officer who supposedly issued it lacked authority to do so. The court explained that under the Contract Act, 1872, a valid agreement requires two parties (a promisor and promisee) who freely consent to a lawful purpose with proper consideration. Since the letter only bore the signature of one of the plaintiffs and was not issued by anyone with proper authority, it could not qualify as an enforceable contract. The court set aside the lower courts' rulings and dismissed the original suit entirely.

This case matters because it clarifies that informal letters or documents, even if referenced as agreements, cannot be enforced as contracts unless they meet the basic legal requirements of a valid agreement, including proper authorization and mutual consent.

title: Nadir Shah v. State,
explainer:
This case involved Syed Nadir Shah, who along with his three sons was accused of defrauding two men, Syed Abbas and Altaf Hussain, by promising to send them to Australia for jobs. The complainants alleged they paid 5000 US dollars each to the accused for this purpose, but were never sent abroad, and the accused failed to return the money despite repeated demands. A stamp paper and receipt were produced as evidence during the investigation. The accused was charged under the Emigration Ordinance, 1979, which deals with illegal practices in arranging foreign employment, and this offence carries a punishment of up to 14 years imprisonment.

Shah applied for bail, arguing he was innocent, elderly and in poor health, that there was unexplained delay in filing the police complaint, and that no proper documents proved he received money from the complainants. The state opposed bail, arguing the delay was properly explained, sufficient evidence linked the accused to the crime, and that people involved in human smuggling typically do not issue receipts, so the absence of such documents was not significant.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the bail application, noting that the accused was named in the police complaint, the allegations were supported by witnesses, and the case was still at a preliminary stage where evidence could not be deeply examined at the bail stage. The court also directed the trial court to conclude the case within two months. This judgment illustrates how courts weigh evidence and the seriousness of alleged fraud in foreign employment scams when deciding bail matters.

title: Ghulam Akbar v. Abdul Raziq Khan,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court in 2011, involved a dispute among the heirs of a deceased man, Haji Abdullah Jan, over several properties he left behind. Some of his children and grandchildren sued other family members, seeking a declaration of their inheritance rights, cancellation of certain revenue mutations, partition, possession, and other relief. The defendants claimed the properties were not part of the inheritance because the deceased had gifted them to certain heirs before his death, and they relied mainly on entries in the land revenue record to prove this gift.

The trial court had partly decided in favour of the plaintiffs, and both sides appealed.

The High Court ruled largely in favour of the plaintiffs. It held that a claim of a preferential gift, which effectively cuts other legal heirs out of their inheritance, must be proved strictly and convincingly by those claiming the gift. Here, the persons claiming the gift did not appear in court themselves, and their attorney's testimony failed to establish the essential requirements of a valid Islamic gift—offer, acceptance, and delivery of possession. Mere revenue record entries, the court explained, are administrative formalities and do not by themselves prove ownership or transfer of property. Since the alleged gift was not properly proved, the court ordered that the properties be distributed among all the legal heirs according to their Islamic (Sharai) inheritance shares. The judgment reinforces that family members cannot be deprived of inheritance rights based on weak or unproven gift claims.

title: Hidayatullah Peerzada v. Khalid Zaman,
explainer:
This case involved a landlord-tenant dispute over a shop in Quetta under rent control law. The landlord had previously tried, unsuccessfully, to evict the tenant on grounds of needing the shop for demolition, reconstruction, and personal business use—that earlier attempt failed all the way up to the Supreme Court. Later, the landlord filed a second eviction application, this time claiming the shop was needed for his own personal use and for his son, who was said to be jobless. The tenant argued this second attempt was made in bad faith since a similar personal-need argument had already been rejected before, and claimed the landlord already owned other commercial properties suitable for his business.

The Rent Controller ruled in the landlord's favor, ordering the tenant to vacate. The tenant appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the landlord had proven the shop was genuinely needed for himself and his son, and that the tenant failed to disprove this. The court held that a landlord has the right to choose which of his properties to use personally, and running one business already does not bar him from starting another. Importantly, the court ruled that a second eviction application is legally permissible on new or different grounds if genuine need arises later, and such an application cannot be rejected merely because an earlier one on different grounds had failed, so long as there is no bad faith.

This judgment matters because it clarifies landlords' rights to file fresh eviction applications based on evolving personal needs, without being permanently barred by a prior unsuccessful attempt.

title: Ehsanullah v. State,
explainer:
This case involved two brothers, Ehsanullah and Khairullah, who sought bail from the Balochistan High Court after being arrested in Gwadar. Police, acting on a tip about planned target killings and terrorist activity, raided the house where they lived and, based on their alleged pointing out, recovered hand grenades, 36 detonators, and time pencils from a guest room, along with a revolver and cartridges linked to a co-accused. They were charged under the Explosive Substances Act, the Anti-Terrorism Act, and the Arms Ordinance for possessing illegal weapons and explosives.

Their lawyer argued for bail on two grounds: that police failed to follow proper search procedures under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code (which requires independent witnesses during searches), and that both applicants were minors, who are typically treated more leniently in criminal cases.

The court rejected these arguments and denied bail. It held that being a minor does not automatically entitle someone to bail in serious offences, and that each case must be judged on its own facts. It also noted that questions about the applicants' actual ages and whether search procedures were properly followed were issues for the trial court to sort out later, not at the bail stage. Since the offences were extremely serious and fell within the category of crimes where bail is generally restricted, and since there was sufficient evidence linking the applicants to the case, bail was refused. The court ordered the trial to be completed quickly, within three months.

title: Abdul Majeed v. Accountability Judge-I, Quetta,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted by an Accountability Court in Quetta for "abscondence"—failing to appear for trial—under section 31-A of the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999. He was originally accused, along with others, of benefiting from fraudulent vehicle registrations that caused financial loss to the government. When he did not appear in court, the trial proceeded without him, and he was sentenced to three years in prison. He was later arrested in 2012 and challenged both his conviction and sought bail.

His lawyer argued that he never deliberately avoided the court; he was a permanent resident of Rawalpindi, had not been properly served notice, and was arrested peacefully at his own home—showing he was not hiding from the law.

The Balochistan High Court agreed. It found no evidence that the trial court had sent notices to his actual address, and the process server who was supposed to confirm service never testified. Since the prosecution could not prove he had willfully or deliberately absconded, the court held that trying and convicting him in his absence violated his fundamental rights under Articles 9 and 10 of the Constitution (right to life, liberty, and fair trial safeguards).

The court set aside his conviction and sentence, sent the case back for a fresh trial where he could properly defend himself, and granted him bail. The case underscores that convicting someone in absentia requires solid proof that they deliberately evaded justice—not just procedural assumptions.

The delay in sending samples for testing did not matter because there was no claim that the evidence had been tampered with. Finally, the court ruled that sending the entire recovered substance for testing is not legally required - a small representative sample is enough to prove the whole quantity was contraband. title: Farheen v. State,
explainer:
This case is about a woman named Mst. Farheen who was stopped by police at a checkpoint on the Quetta-Chaman Road while traveling in a mini-wagon. Police said they had received a tip that two women were transporting charas (a form of cannabis), searched her bag, and allegedly found 7 kilograms of the drug hidden inside. She was charged and tried under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, and the trial court convicted her, sentencing her to seven years in prison plus a fine.

She appealed, arguing that she had been falsely framed by police, that the witnesses against her were police officials rather than independent bystanders, and that the evidence had been misread by the trial court.

The Balochistan High Court rejected her appeal. It found that the two police witnesses—the officer who prepared the recovery report and the officer who witnessed the recovery—gave consistent, matching accounts with no major contradictions. She was caught with the drugs on her at the scene, and the forensic laboratory confirmed the substance was indeed charas. Importantly, she never showed any personal enmity or motive that police might have had to falsely implicate her, and she did not present any evidence or testimony to support her claim of innocence. The court also reasoned that such a large quantity of narcotics was unlikely to have been planted. As a result, her conviction and sentence were upheld, showing how courts assess credibility of police testimony and the burden on defendants to substantiate defense claims in narcotics cases.

title: State v. Kalimullah,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by the State against the acquittal of a man, Kalimullah, who had been accused of murdering his wife, Mst. Bibi Jamila, under section 302 of the Pakistan Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that he brutally beat her, causing internal injuries that led to a miscarriage and eventually her death.

The trial court had acquitted him, and the State challenged this before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court examined the evidence and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. There were no eyewitnesses to the alleged beating, and the witnesses who testified were closely related to the complainant and the deceased, making them interested and potentially biased. Their statements also contradicted each other on important points and showed signs of dishonest exaggeration.

Crucially, medical evidence did not support the murder allegation. The deceased's medical history showed abdominal pain, vomiting blood, and diarrhea, and doctors determined she died from kidney failure and blood infection, not from injuries. A medical examination found no external wounds or bruises on her body, aside from some scratched hair, and evidence about the hair was never sent for forensic testing.

The High Court upheld the acquittal, reaffirming the legal principle that an acquitted person enjoys a strengthened presumption of innocence, which can only be overturned if the original decision was clearly perverse, arbitrary, or illegal. Since the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond doubt, the appeal was dismissed.

title: Collector of Customs, Federal Excise and Sales Tax, Quetta v. Ramzan,
explainer:
This case involved a bus intercepted near Gaddani carrying 5,100 liters of smuggled Iranian petrol in 75 plastic cans. Customs officials seized both the goods and the vehicle. The petrol was confiscated outright, but the vehicle's owner was given the option to get it back by paying a redemption fine set at 30% of the vehicle's customs value, as per the original Assistant Collector's order.

The vehicle owner appealed, and eventually the Customs Appellate Tribunal reduced this fine significantly, to a flat Rs. 30,000, regardless of the vehicle's value. The Collector of Customs challenged this reduction before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the Tribunal had ignored the legal framework requiring a percentage-based fine.

The High Court examined Section 181 of the Customs Act, 1969, which allows fines in lieu of confiscation, and a government notification (S.R.O. 574(I)/2005) which mandates that such fines must be at least 30% of the vehicle's customs value when it was used to transport smuggled goods. The court found that the original 30% fine imposed by the Assistant Collector was correct and lawful, in line with binding precedent from a similar case. However, despite finding merit in the Collector's legal argument, the court ultimately dismissed the reference application.

This case clarifies that fines for vehicles used in smuggling must follow the fixed percentage set by regulation, not be arbitrarily reduced, ensuring consistency in how customs penalties are applied

title: Inspector-General, Frontier Corps Balochistan v. Allauddin,
explainer:
This case involved a customs dispute over a Mitsubishi Pajero jeep that was seized in 2003 at a check post in Balochistan while allegedly being smuggled into Pakistan without proper import documents. The vehicle, along with two others, was confiscated by customs authorities. A man named Allauddin claimed ownership and appealed, and the Customs Appellate Tribunal ordered the vehicle released, allowing him to reclaim it by paying import duties and a redemption fine under a government scheme for smuggled vehicles.

The Frontier Corps, representing customs authorities, challenged this release before the Balochistan High Court, but filed their appeal (called a "Reference") late. They also filed a separate application asking the court to excuse the delay, citing bureaucratic delays in getting approval from the Central Board of Revenue and law-and-order problems in the city.

The High Court refused to excuse the delay. It explained that the Customs Act sets a specific 90-day deadline for filing such appeals, and this specific law overrides the general Limitation Act's provision allowing delays to be forgiven in certain circumstances. Since the Customs Act is a special law with its own limitation period, the general rule for condoning delays did not apply here.

As a result, the court dismissed the government's appeal simply because it was filed too late, without even examining whether the original decision to release the vehicle was correct. This case highlights how strict, specific deadlines in specialized laws like the Customs Act must be followed exactly, regardless of administrative difficulties.

title: Safi Ullah v. State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by 14 men accused in a violent clash between two rival groups over possession of a property (a bungalow) in Quetta. According to the police, cross-firing broke out between the groups, killing two people and injuring several others, including bystanders. The accused were arrested at or near the scene, and weapons and ammunition were recovered from some of them. They were charged with murder, attempted murder, rioting with deadly weapons, unlawful assembly, and offences under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

The accused argued they were falsely implicated, that the allegations against them were vague and general, that it wasn't yet clear which side started the violence, and that they should get bail since further investigation was needed to establish guilt.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the bail application. The judge held that when people are accused of murder as part of an unlawful assembly, the key legal question is whether they were members of that assembly and whether the offence was committed in furtherance of the assembly's common purpose. If a member knew that violence could occur in pursuit of that shared purpose, all members can be held responsible for what happened. Since witness statements, weapon recoveries, and medical reports supported the prosecution's version, the case fell under a category where bail is normally denied. The court therefore refused bail to all the accused.

title: Muhammad Amin v. State,
explainer:
This case involves three men, Muhammad Amin, Naik Muhammad, and Hazar Khan, who were accused of abducting a woman named Bibi Aliza from her brother's house at gunpoint, along with other serious charges including rioting and unlawful assembly. According to the First Information Report, the woman was already married to another man when she was allegedly forcibly taken away by the accused.

The accused sought bail after a trial court had rejected their application, reasoning that the woman was still in their custody, her marriage to one of the accused was disputed, she had not been recovered, and the alleged offences fell under a category of crimes where bail is normally restricted.

However, the Balochistan High Court found that the woman herself had appeared before a Judicial Magistrate and given a sworn statement saying she left her home voluntarily and married one of the accused by her own free choice. She specifically denied being abducted or forced, and denied any other marriage. The Magistrate had already allowed her to leave with her husband after recording this statement.

Based on this, the High Court concluded that no case of abduction was actually made out against the accused, despite the serious allegations in the original complaint. The court granted bail to all three applicants, requiring them to post surety bonds. This case illustrates how a woman's own sworn testimony affirming her consent and free will can undermine abduction charges brought by family members, even when the initial allegations were serious and specific.

title: Habibullah v. Managing Editor and Resident Director Daily Jang,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves a dispute between a construction contractor and a newspaper company that had hired him to build on its property. The contractor had completed about 80% of the work when the project stalled due to the owner's financial troubles. Years later, in 2008, the owner allegedly forced the contractor's watchmen off the site and took over possession by force. The contractor filed a police report and then sued for restoration of possession.

The trial court, without taking any evidence from either side, rejected the contractor's plaint (essentially dismissing the case at a preliminary stage) based on a claim by the owner that a later agreement between the parties had already settled the matter and required the contractor to hand back possession. This decision was upheld on appeal.

The High Court found this approach improper. It held that courts cannot reject a plaint based on the defendant's unproven claims and defenses, especially on a disputed factual issue like whether a settlement agreement existed and applied. Since no evidence had actually been presented to prove the alleged agreement, dismissing the case was premature and unfair to the contractor.

The High Court therefore declared the lower courts' orders illegal, and sent the case back to the trial court to be properly decided on its merits after both sides present evidence. This case reinforces the principle that factual disputes must be resolved through evidence, not shortcuts.

title: Qamar Gill v. Iram Nathaniel,
explainer:
This case involved a Christian couple whose marriage broke down. The wife, Iram Nathaniel, filed a suit seeking maintenance (alimony) for herself and her minor son against her husband, Qamar Gill, after she alleged she was thrown out of the house without proper support. The trial court in Quetta ruled in her favor, awarding monthly maintenance for both her and the child. On appeal, the amount was slightly adjusted but the core decision upheld.

The husband challenged these rulings before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to hear the case and that the lower courts had not properly weighed the evidence, including limits on alimony under the Christian Divorce Act, 1869.

The High Court dismissed the husband's petition. It held that he had never raised the jurisdiction objection in his original written statement, so he could not raise it for the first time later. It also found that, under the Divorce Act, 1869, a case like this could indeed be tried by a civil court where the spouses had resided together, which applied here. The court also upheld the maintenance amounts fixed by the lower courts as being properly calculated in line with the law's requirements.

This case matters because it clarifies how maintenance disputes among Pakistan's Christian community are handled under the Divorce Act, 1869, and reinforces the principle that legal objections not raised early in a case cannot be introduced later during appeals.

title: Abdul Baqi v. Attaullah,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta, Pakistan. Abdul Baqi claimed he owned a piece of land that he had purchased in 1997 and had been in possession of since then. He alleged that Attaullah had illegally occupied his plot, so he filed a criminal complaint against him under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, a law meant to protect people from being forcibly thrown out of property they possess.

The trial court examined the evidence, including witness testimony from both sides, and found that Attaullah was not actually in possession of the disputed plot. Instead, a house on the land was occupied by a different man, Noor Muhammad, who had lived there for fifteen years but was never made a party to the complaint. Because of this, the trial court dismissed the complaint and acquitted Attaullah.

Abdul Baqi appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing the evidence had been misread and that he should have been allowed to add Noor Muhammad as a respondent. The High Court disagreed. It held that since Attaullah was not in possession of the property, there was no question of him dispossessing or ousting Abdul Baqi, meaning the Illegal Dispossession Act simply did not apply. The court found this was really a civil property dispute, not a criminal matter, and upheld the acquittal, dismissing the appeal. This case illustrates that criminal dispossession laws cannot be used as a shortcut to resolve ordinary civil ownership or possession disputes, and that the person actually in possession must be properly named in such complaints

title: Balochistan Engineering Works Limited V. Jalal Khan,
explainer:
This case involved a worker, Jalal Khan, whose employment with Balochistan Engineering Works Limited was terminated in 2004 after he reached the age of 55, in accordance with a retirement clause in his original appointment letter from 1991. Khan challenged the termination, arguing he was still fit to work, that he had not actually reached 55, and that no law required retirement at that age. The Labour Court initially dismissed his case, and after an earlier round of appeals and a remand for fresh hearing, the Labour Court again ruled against him, prompting appeals to the Balochistan Labour Appellate Tribunal from both Khan and the company.

The Tribunal upheld the Labour Court's decision. It found that although the Industrial and Commercial Employment (Standing Orders) Ordinance, 1968 does not itself fix any mandatory retirement age, Khan had voluntarily accepted a contractual term at the time of hiring stating he would retire at 55. Since this term did not violate any provision of the Standing Orders, and Khan had accepted and acted under it for years, he could not later dispute it. The Tribunal distinguished the case law cited by Khan's lawyer, finding those precedents dealt with different facts, such as attempts to strip workers of pre-existing rights through later agreements, which was not the situation here.

The case matters because it confirms that a validly agreed contractual retirement age, even without statutory backing, is enforceable and binding on the employee who accepted it.

title: Said Akbar  V.  Gateron (Industries) Limited,
explainer:
This case involved a labour dispute between an employee, Said Akbar, and his employer, Gatron Industries Limited. When Akbar was hired, his appointment letter required him to work full-time for the company and barred him from taking up any other job, business, or profession during his employment. Despite this condition, Akbar took up work with another company, Ismail Industries, while still employed at Gatron. When this came to light, Gatron issued him a show-cause notice, conducted an inquiry, found the allegation of dual employment proven, and dismissed him.

Akbar challenged his dismissal, first through a grievance notice and then before the Labour Court, denying that he had worked for Ismail Industries. The Labour Court rejected his application and upheld the dismissal. He then appealed to the Labour Appellate Tribunal in Quetta.

The Tribunal dismissed the appeal. It held that since Akbar had voluntarily accepted the terms of his appointment, including the restriction against outside employment, he could not later argue that this condition was invalid or unenforceable. The Tribunal also found that this contractual condition did not violate any law, including the Industrial and Commercial Employment Standing Orders Ordinance, 1968. Therefore, his dismissal for violating the terms of his contract was justified, and the Labour Court's decision was upheld.

This case matters because it confirms that employees who accept specific contractual conditions, such as restrictions on outside employment, are bound by them, and violation of such agreed terms can justify dismissal.

title: Syed Muhammad Jawad  V.  Abdul Nabi,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court in 2011, involved a dispute over ownership and possession of a truck. The petitioner had originally sued for a declaration that he owned the truck, claiming he received it in a transaction involving his residential house, while the respondent argued the petitioner owed him a large sum of money and had failed to honor their agreement. The trial court initially ruled in the petitioner's favor, and he took possession of the truck. This decision was upheld on appeal, but the High Court later remanded the case back to the trial court due to a court-fee deficiency, without deciding the merits.

After remand, the trial court ordered the petitioner to return the truck or pay its value, and the petitioner's suit was eventually dismissed for non-prosecution. The respondent then sought restitution under Section 144 of the Civil Procedure Code, arguing he should get back the truck since the earlier judgments favoring the petitioner had been set aside. The lower courts agreed with him.

The High Court disagreed and set aside these orders. It held that restitution under Section 144 only benefits someone who lawfully lost something due to a court decree that was later reversed. Since the respondent had originally taken the truck illegally by force through the Truck Association rather than through lawful means, he was not entitled to restitution. This case clarifies that the law protects lawful possession gained through court orders, not those who take matters into their own hands.

title: Habibullah  V.  Ghulam Sarwar,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of a man accused of involvement in a bomb explosion that killed three children in Khuzdar, Balochistan, in 2007. The complainant, the children's father, initially named three men he saw fleeing the scene but did not name the respondent, Ghulam Sarwar. Two alleged eyewitnesses later gave statements to police, four days after the incident, claiming they saw six men on two motorcycles, including the respondent, and that one of them threw an explosive device into the house. The trial court acquitted the respondent, and the complainant appealed.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the acquittal. It found the eyewitnesses' account unreliable because they had not told the complainant the respondent's name, had not helped register the police report, had not assisted with the dead or injured, and admitted they only gave their statements after discussing and coordinating with the complainant beforehand. This raised serious doubts about whether they were actually present at the scene. The court also noted that other people supposedly present at the site were never produced as witnesses, which further weakened the prosecution's case.

The court emphasized that in cases involving the death penalty, evidence must come from trustworthy sources or be backed by strong circumstances. Finding no error in the trial court's reasoning, the High Court dismissed the appeal, reaffirming the principle that convictions cannot rest on doubtful or coached testimony.

title: Shah Nawaz  V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by two men, Shah Nawaz and Nadir Ali, who had been convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment by a trial court in Quetta for killing Muhammad Naeem in 2008. The complainant also filed a separate petition asking the court to increase their punishment.

The prosecution's version was that the two accused shot the deceased with a Kalashnikov for unknown reasons. However, the defense argued that the deceased had actually attacked the accused first with a knife, causing them serious injuries, and that the accused had registered their own police complaint about this attack before the murder case was filed against them.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence and found inconsistencies in the prosecution witnesses' accounts, noting they conveniently left out the injuries suffered by the accused. The court concluded there was no advance planning or shared intention (common intention) between the two accused to commit murder, so the legal provision holding both men equally responsible for a joint criminal act could not apply to Shah Nawaz. title: Shah Nawaz  V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Shah Nawaz and Nadir Ali, convicted by a trial court in Quetta for the murder of Muhammad Naeem, and sentenced to life imprisonment along with compensation payments. Both filed a criminal appeal seeking acquittal, while the complainant filed a separate revision petition asking for a harsher sentence.

The prosecution's case was that the two accused shot the deceased with a Kalashnikov. However, evidence also showed the accused themselves had sustained serious injuries, and a separate FIR about a quarrel involving injuries to the accused had been registered before the FIR in this murder case. Witnesses claimed the accused shouted a "Lalkara" (challenge/war-cry) before attacking, suggesting a preplanned, joint intention to kill, but the court found this claim unconvincing and inconsistent with the actual sequence of events.

The Balochistan High Court found no evidence of common intention or a shared plan to kill between the two accused. It held that the fight appears to have arisen spontaneously, with the deceased pulling out a knife and attacking the accused, and only then did one of the accused respond with fatal gunfire aimed at vital body parts rather than a less lethal shot. Because there was no proven common intention, the court ruled that one accused (Shah Nawaz) could not be held responsible for his co-accused's actions and acquitted him. However, it upheld the conviction of the co-accused who actually fired the fatal shots, finding his actions went beyond self-defense.

title: Khalique Dad alias Jan Agha  V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about an appeal by Khalique Dad, alias Jan Agha, who was convicted by the Special Judge for Control of Narcotic Substances (CNS) in Quetta for possessing large quantities of narcotics, including hashish and opium, discovered at his home. He received a life sentence and a fine. Police had acted on a tip-off, raided his house without a search warrant, and found the drugs hidden in a jute sack in a room. The appellant argued he was innocent, that the drugs actually belonged to another man, and that the police violated proper search procedures by not obtaining a warrant or including independent witnesses from the neighborhood, as normally required under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that Section 25 of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act specifically excludes the application of Section 103 Cr.P.C. in narcotics cases, meaning police don't need independent witnesses in the same way. The court also found that while Section 21 of the Act sets out search procedures, these are only directory guidelines, not mandatory requirements, so minor procedural lapses don't automatically invalidate a search. Since there was no evidence of ill will between the police and the accused, and no meaningful contradictions in witness testimony, the court upheld the conviction. This ruling clarifies that narcotics cases operate under different, more relaxed search-and-seizure rules than ordinary criminal cases in Pakistan.

title: Shaukat  V.  The State,
explainer:
This case involved a robbery appeal before the Balochistan High Court. The appellant, Shaukat, had been convicted by a Sessions Judge and sentenced to four years imprisonment plus a fine under Section 394 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with robbery. The prosecution's case was that Shaukat and an accomplice robbed the complainant, his nephew, and his brother of cash and mobile phones at gunpoint, and that the victims recognized Shaukat as their neighbour.

On appeal, the High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The complainant admitted he named Shaukat only on suspicion, after police pressured him to identify someone. There was also an unexplained two-hour delay before the police registered the case, during which the complainant appeared to have been kept waiting until a report implicating Shaukat was prepared. This raised concerns that the investigating officer had a personal interest in securing a conviction, especially since he was accused of bias against the accused. Additionally, no stolen property or weapon was ever recovered from Shaukat, and the brother who was also robbed was never called to testify, weakening the case further. The court noted that simply pointing out a location already known to police, without any recovery resulting from it, proved nothing.

Given these gaps and the unreliable identification process, the High Court acquitted Shaukat. The case highlights how courts scrutinize police conduct, delays in reporting crimes, and missing evidence to prevent wrongful convictions based on weak or manipulated testimony.

title: Akram V.  Nazar Ali,
explainer:
This case concerns a land dispute in Killa Abdullah district, Balochistan, where a group of plaintiffs claimed ownership of certain agricultural land, alleging that revenue records had wrongly recorded portions of the land in the names of the defendants due to errors during a settlement operation in 1963-64. The plaintiffs sought a court declaration confirming their ownership, cancellation of the disputed revenue entries, and an injunction preventing the defendants from transferring the land.

The defendants opposed the suit, pointing out that an earlier case involving the same parties and the same land had already been litigated and decided, including a prior civil revision before the High Court itself. The trial court rejected the plaint, holding that the matter was barred by the legal principle of res judicata, meaning the same issue between the same parties had already been conclusively decided in earlier proceedings and could not be relitigated.

The Balochistan High Court upheld this decision. It ruled that since the earlier suit had already determined the ownership and possession issues between the same parties over the same property, the new suit was barred under Section 11 of the Civil Procedure Code. The court noted this legal bar could be raised and decided at any stage of the case. Consequently, the plaintiffs' revision petition was dismissed.

This judgment reinforces the importance of the res judicata principle in preventing repeated litigation over settled property disputes, promoting finality and judicial efficiency.

title: Haji Sanaullah V. Khaliq Dad,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land in Kharan, Balochistan. Haji Sanaullah claimed he owned a piece of land, saying he had bought it through a chain of transactions originally from the family of Khaliq Dad. When he found Khaliq Dad, his wife, and two sons working on the land with a tractor, he filed a police complaint accusing them of criminal trespass under sections 447 and 147 of the Pakistan Penal Code.

A Judicial Magistrate examined the complaint and acquitted the accused early in the proceedings under section 249-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows a magistrate to dismiss a case if there is no reasonable chance of conviction. Sanaullah appealed this acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the magistrate's decision. It found that ownership and possession of the land were genuinely disputed, that it was unclear whether the chain of purchase Sanaullah relied on was valid, and that a civil suit over ownership of the same land was already pending in civil court. The court noted that at best Sanaullah had only symbolic, not actual, possession. Given this uncertainty, the court held that people with a legitimate claim to land cannot be criminally prosecuted for trespass simply for entering it, especially while ownership remains unresolved in civil litigation.

This case illustrates that criminal trespass charges should not be used to resolve what are essentially civil property disputes, and that criminal courts require clear proof of exclusive rights before convicting someone of trespass.

title: Murad Bukhsh  V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Murad Bukhsh who was convicted for forgery under Section 465 of the Pakistan Penal Code, after a Land Cruiser vehicle he claimed to own was found to have a fake number plate. The plate was actually registered to someone else. A trial court and then an appellate court both convicted him and sentenced him to one year's imprisonment plus a fine.

Bukhsh challenged this conviction before the Balochistan High Court. His lawyer argued that the evidence only showed a fake number plate existed, not that Bukhsh himself had made it, and that no witness could actually confirm the vehicle or plate was recovered from his possession.

The High Court agreed. It found that the complainant admitted he never personally saw or recovered the vehicle from Bukhsh, and the police recovery witness could not say from whom the vehicle was actually taken. The court also noted that there was no evidence the accused had personally created the forged plate, which is a key requirement for a forgery conviction under Section 465. The court even suggested the charge, if anything, should have been framed differently, under a provision dealing with using a forged document rather than making one.

Because the prosecution failed to produce solid evidence linking Bukhsh to the forgery, the High Court ruled that both lower court judgments were unsafe and unjust. It set them aside and acquitted him. The case highlights how criminal convictions require actual proof, not assumptions.

title: Syed Ahmed Jan V. Anjuman-e-Islamia, Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute between shopkeepers (tenants) in Quetta and Anjuman-e-Islamia, Balochistan, a welfare society that owned the land on which the tenants had built and operated shops since around 1967. The society filed eviction applications, arguing it needed the land to construct a multi-storeyed building and had obtained official municipal approval for this construction. The Rent Controller ordered the tenants to vacate within four months, but also directed the landlord to provide them equivalent-sized shops in the newly built plaza once completed. The tenants appealed, arguing they had spent decades building their shops and installing expensive machinery at their own cost, and that eviction would destroy their livelihoods without adequate compensation.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the tenants' appeals, finding that the landlord had genuinely established its need for the land and had properly obtained all necessary government permissions to build. The tenants had not disputed the landlord's ownership or its right to redevelop. However, recognizing that tenants would suffer real losses from having to demolish their existing shops and structures, and that the original order hadn't fixed fair rent for the new space, the Court added a protective condition: the landlord must charge tenants 30% less than prevailing market rent when they move into the new building.

This case matters because it balances a property owner's right to redevelop land against the practical hardships faced by long-term tenants, while confirming that appellate courts reviewing rent eviction orders have the same powers as courts hearing regular civil appeals.

His lawyer argued that although 200 grams of charas were recovered, only 5 grams had actually been sent for laboratory analysis, and even if he were convicted based on that small sample, he was unlikely to face more than a year's imprisonment. Since bail cannot be used as a form of punishment, he argued he deserved to be released pending trial.

The High Court agreed. It explained that while the law generally bars bail in cases carrying the death penalty, an exception exists for cases that are "fit" for bail, such as those needing further investigation or those involving a small quantity of narcotics. The court held that since only 5 grams out of 200 were sent for analysis, this qualified as a fit case, and the offence did not fall under the strict no-bail rule. The court granted bail, requiring a surety of Rs. 50,000.

This case matters because it clarifies how courts assess "meagre quantity" in narcotics cases and confirms that bail should not function as punishment before conviction.

title: Malik Sardar Muhammad Qasim V. Malik Haji Abdul Ghaffar,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute between two parties over land where one man had installed a flour grinding machine that allegedly damaged his neighbor's well. Rather than pursue lengthy litigation, the parties signed a written agreement to have their dispute settled by two private arbitrators outside the court system. The agreement stated that if either party failed to honor the arbitrators' decision, the other could sue them after paying a Rs.500,000 penalty. The arbitrators investigated the site, heard both sides, and ordered the machine's owner to remove it from the disputed land. Both parties signed the award accepting it, and a related criminal case was withdrawn as part of the settlement. However, the losing party later refused to comply and rejected the award. The winning party then sued in the Majlis-e-Shoora court to enforce the agreement, and won. The losing party appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing the suit was not maintainable and that proper court fees had not been paid.

The High Court dismissed the appeal. It held that although a private arbitration award is not the same as a formal award under the Arbitration Act, when parties voluntarily agree to resolve a dispute through arbitrators, participate in the process, and then accept the resulting decision by signing it, the legal principle of estoppel prevents them from later going back on that agreement. The court also found the required court fee had in fact been paid. This case matters because it reinforces that people who voluntarily submit to private dispute resolution and accept the outcome cannot later disown it simply because it wasn't issued through formal court arbitration proced

title: Shey Mureed  V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal before the Balochistan High Court by two men, including Shey Mureed, who had been convicted by a trial court for murder and abetment of murder under the Pakistan Penal Code, and sentenced to life imprisonment along with fines.

The background was that two brothers, Assa and Imdad, were shot dead by Nisar and Muheem during a family dispute. Shey Mureed, father of Muheem, was accused of abetting the murders because the deceased allegedly owed him money, and because he was said to have earlier threatened the victims' family along with the other accused, warning them not to leave the area.

The High Court found the case riddled with doubts. The main witnesses against Shey Mureed were the mother and sister of the deceased, whose testimony was uncorroborated by any independent evidence and was inconsistent with each other. The medical evidence did not support their version either. Crucially, no weapon, recovery, or direct evidence linked the appellants to the killing or showed they instigated, conspired, or otherwise aided the actual killers. Since the legal requirements for "abetment" were not met, the court held that the prosecution had failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Arshad Masih  V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Arshad Masih, who was convicted by a Sessions Court in Khuzdar for the murder of Samoil Anwar, a fellow member of a church congregation. During a quarrel that broke out among congregants, some of whom were reportedly drunk, Arshad struck the deceased with a flowerpot. The victim later died from the head injury. The trial court had convicted Arshad under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, treating it as qatl-e-amd (intentional murder), sentencing him to life imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence and found that the trial court itself had noted there was no evidence of premeditated intent to kill. The altercation happened suddenly, in front of a large crowd, and the accused used whatever object was at hand in the heat of the moment rather than a deliberate weapon. Since neither the prosecution nor the complainant had challenged this finding about lack of intent, the High Court held that the correct legal classification was qatl-e-shibh-i-amd (quasi-intentional killing) under section 315, punishable under section 316, rather than full intentional murder.

The court therefore set aside the life sentence and instead convicted Arshad under section 316, sentencing him to 10 years' rigorous imprisonment plus payment of diyat (compensation) to the victim's heirs. This case illustrates how Pakistani courts distinguish between different degrees of culpability in killings based on proven intent, even when a death results from violence.

title: Abdul Malik  V. The State,
explainer:
Abdul Malik was stopped at a Levies check post while driving a car, and 13 packets of charas weighing 13 kilograms were allegedly found hidden in the vehicle's secret cavities. A sample of 100 grams was sent for chemical analysis, and he was convicted by the Special Judge, CNS Khuzdar, under section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, his lawyer argued the case was weak because it wasn't clear the 100-gram sample truly represented all 13 packets (a mix of rods and slabs), the sample was sent for testing after a two-and-a-half-month delay, the drugs weren't weighed at the scene, and recovery paperwork wasn't prepared on site. He also claimed he was merely a paying passenger in a company vehicle, not the sole driver.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It found that prosecution witnesses consistently confirmed the accused was driving alone, he showed no proof of a bus ticket or company ownership, and there was no evidence of ill will by the police against him. The court held that delay in sending samples, or preparing paperwork away from a remote checkpost, did not automatically make the case false, especially since possession of the drugs and vehicle was clearly established. The conviction and life sentence were upheld, showing courts will maintain drug convictions despite procedural delays if the core evidence of possession remains credible and unchallenged.

title: Abdul Salam Khan  V. Muhammad Yaqoob Bangulzai,
explainer:
This case is about a legal dispute over a water supply order issued by a Judicial Magistrate in Sanjavi, Balochistan. The Magistrate had used Section 133 of the Criminal Procedure Code, a law meant to address public nuisances like blocked roads or health hazards, to order Public Health Department officials to continuously supply water to residents of Sanjavi bazaar and its surrounding areas. Officials were also told to post a surety bond of Rs. 200,000 each, forfeitable if they failed to supply water.

The Public Health official challenged this order directly in the High Court, which quashed it, ruling that the Magistrate had misused Section 133, a provision meant for removing physical nuisances or obstructions, not for compelling ongoing service delivery like water supply. The High Court called it an abuse of legal process.

The original complainant then filed this review application, arguing he was a necessary party who was never heard, and that the official had bypassed proper procedure by going straight to the High Court without his knowledge.

The High Court dismissed the review application. It held that not including the complainant did not violate his rights, since it was the official who was aggrieved by the Magistrate's order, and the State had already been made a party in the case. The Court reaffirmed its power to quash unlawful orders to prevent abuse of judicial process, even without hearing every affected party. This case clarifies the limited scope of Section 133 and reinforces courts' authority to correct jurisdictional overreach by lower courts.

title: State through Additional Prosecutor ATA V. Hashim Khan,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by the State against the acquittal of Hashim Khan and others, who had been accused of murder, attempted murder, and armed rioting under Pakistan's Penal Code and Anti-Terrorism Act. The incident stemmed from a property dispute, allegedly resulting in an ambush where the accused shot at a vehicle, killing one person and prompting a return of fire from the victims' side.

The trial court had acquitted the accused, and the State challenged this decision, arguing the trial judge had ignored important evidence, including eyewitness testimony from the complainant who was present at the scene.

The Balochistan High Court found a serious flaw in how the case had been handled: although the initial police report named eyewitnesses present at the scene, the investigating officer failed to include the most important witness in the list of prosecution witnesses presented at trial. The trial court also failed to summon this key witness on its own initiative, even though the law empowers judges to ensure all relevant witnesses are produced, regardless of whether their testimony might help or hurt the prosecution's case.

Because this crucial witness was never heard, the High Court ruled that a fair decision could not have been reached. It set aside the trial court's acquittal and ordered a retrial, directing that all necessary witnesses from both sides be called this time. This case highlights the importance of ensuring complete evidence is presented before a court reaches a verdict, especially in serious criminal cases.

title: Ishaq George V. The State,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved four men - Ishaq George and three others - accused of murder under sections 302/34 of the Pakistan Penal Code following the death of a man named Kashif Sardar. According to the prosecution, the accused had abused, dragged, and beaten the deceased with fists and kicks during an altercation near a church, after which he was taken to hospital but died.

The accused sought bail, arguing there was no evidence they intended to kill the deceased, no weapon was used, and medical records suggested he may have died from a heart condition rather than the beating itself. The doctor's report noted only minor injuries (swelling, bruises, a small wound) along with a history of heart problems, and stated the man died during first aid due to chest pain.

The court found that this evidence did not clearly establish the intentional murder charge under section 302, and instead raised the possibility that the case might fall under a different, lesser provision (section 315 PPC), which needed further investigation at trial. Applying the principle that any reasonable doubt should benefit the accused even at the bail stage, and noting that bail decisions require only a tentative, cursory assessment of evidence rather than a full trial-like analysis, the judge granted bail to all four applicants upon furnishing sureties. The ruling clarifies how courts weigh conflicting medical and circumstantial evidence when deciding bail in serious criminal cases.

title: Aurangzaib Shah v. State,
explainer:
This case is about three men convicted in connection with a robbery and separate weapons charges arising from the same incident in Mastung, Balochistan in 2006. All three had been convicted under section 395 of the Pakistan Penal Code (robbery) with sentences reduced on appeal to the Federal Shariat Court to five years each. They were also separately convicted under section 13-E of the Arms Ordinance, 1965 for illegal weapons recovered from them, receiving additional sentences of two to three years.

The trial court had ordered these sentences to run consecutively, meaning one after the other. The appellants argued this violated the law, since section 13-E of the Arms Ordinance caps punishment at seven years, but two of them would effectively serve eight years if their robbery and weapons sentences were added together. They relied on section 35 of the Criminal Procedure Code and section 71 of the Penal Code, which limit punishment in such situations and generally favor concurrent sentencing when offenses arise from the same transaction.

The Balochistan High Court, led by Chief Justice Qazi Faez Isa, agreed. It found that consecutive sentencing for two of the appellants exceeded the legal maximum. Even though the third appellant's combined sentence did not exceed the cap, the court noted it would be unfair for him to serve longer than the other two, so it extended the same relief to him.

The court ordered all three men's sentences to run concurrently rather than consecutively, ensuring consistent and lawful punishment across similar cases arising from one incident.

title: Abbas v. State,
explainer:
This case involved three men, Abbas and two others, who had been charged with robbery (section 392 of the Pakistan Penal Code) and causing injury (section 337-F). During the trial, the complainant forgave the accused and both sides reached a compromise. However, the trial magistrate and later the Sessions Judge in Kharan rejected this compromise entirely, reasoning that robbery under section 392 cannot legally be compounded (settled between parties).

The accused challenged this rejection before the Balochistan High Court. The Chief Justice, assisted by several lawyers acting as amicus curiae (friends of the court), agreed that robbery under section 392 indeed cannot be compromised since it is not listed among compoundable offences in the Criminal Procedure Code. However, the court found that the lower courts had made an error by failing to separately consider the injury charge under section 337-F, which the law does allow to be compromised with court permission.

The High Court accepted the compromise for the section 337-F charge and acquitted the accused of that offence, drawing on Islamic teachings about the value of forgiveness and mercy. Regarding the more serious robbery charge, the court left open the possibility that the accused could apply to the state for withdrawal of that case, and noted the state should consider such an application promptly.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that courts must examine each criminal charge separately when parties compromise, rather than rejecting an entire settlement just because one charge happens to be non-compoundable.

title: Ghulam Hussain v. Additional Sessions Judge,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted for gambling under Balochistan's Prevention of Gambling Ordinance, 1978. Police had raided his house based on a tip that gambling was occurring there, and he was subsequently convicted by a Judicial Magistrate and sentenced to prison and a fine. An appellate court upheld the conviction but reduced the fine. The man then challenged both decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The key legal issue was that the law required raids on private homes for suspected gambling to be conducted by a Magistrate, who must first inquire into the matter before authorizing entry. Police alone had no power to conduct such raids or initiate the case; their role was only to assist a Magistrate. In this case, no Magistrate had investigated the matter or been present during the raid, meaning the mandatory legal procedure was completely bypassed.

The Chief Justice ruled that this failure was not a minor technicality but a serious violation, since the privacy of one's home is a fundamental right protected under Article 14 of the Constitution. The judgment traced this right to religious and ethical traditions, citing Quranic verses and sayings of the Prophet Muhammad about respecting the sanctity of homes and not intruding without permission.

Because the raid violated mandatory legal safeguards, any evidence gathered during it was ruled invalid and inadmissible. As a result, the court set aside both lower court judgments and acquitted the accused, emphasizing that strict compliance with legal procedures is essential whenever the state intrudes into someone's private residence

title: Soorat Khan v. Anti- Terrorism Court,
explainer:
This case involved a father, Soorat Khan, whose son died after stepping on a landmine that had allegedly been planted to force employees of a government-run security force (Chamalung Security Force) to quit their jobs, and to discourage others from joining. An FIR was filed under explosives law, but the question arose over which court should try the case: an ordinary criminal court or the special Anti-Terrorism Court.

A trial judge initially decided the case did not qualify as terrorism and sent it back to be tried by an ordinary court. Soorat Khan challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the legal definition of terrorism under Section 6 of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, which requires both a harmful act (like causing death using explosives) and an intent to coerce, intimidate, or create fear among the public or the government. The court found that using a landmine to pressure security force employees into quitting and to intimidate others from joining fit squarely within this definition, since it created public fear and disrupted normal life, even though there was no personal enmity involved.

The court also clarified that ordinary criminal procedure rules about classifying offenses did not apply to Anti-Terrorism cases. As a result, the High Court set aside the earlier order and directed the Anti-Terrorism Court to proceed with the trial itself. This case matters because it helps define what counts as "terrorism" under Pakistani law, particularly in cases involving intimidation of workers or public institutions rather than personal disputes.

title: Noroz Khan v. Selection Committee,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a medical college admission in Balochistan. Noroz Khan applied for a seat reserved for District Gwadar at Bolan Medical College under the 2008-09 admission process. Although he ranked higher on the entrance test than another candidate who was ultimately admitted, the Selection Committee rejected his application because records showed he had held domicile certificates from two districts, Gwadar and Kech, at the same time. This violated Paragraph 32 of the college prospectus, which barred such candidates from reserved-seat admission unless specific conditions were met.

Khan argued he had gotten his Kech certificate cancelled before applying, leaving him with only the Gwadar certificate. The court found that even accepting this claim, admission could only be granted as a "special case" under the prospectus, which required three conditions: the extra certificate must have been cancelled at least two years before applying, the candidate must inform the Selection Committee of this at the time of admission, and the Committee retained discretion to allow it. Since Khan's cancellation had not occurred two years prior and he had not disclosed his prior dual certificates to the Committee, none of these conditions were satisfied.

The High Court ruled that the Selection Committee had acted lawfully in rejecting Khan's application and refused to interfere with its decision, dismissing the petition. This case illustrates how courts generally defer to institutional admission committees when they apply their own published rules correctly and fairly.

title: Muhammad Shoaib v. Project Director,
explainer:
This case involved a student, Muhammad Shoaib, who applied for a government-run scholarship under the National ICT Scholarship Program, administered by a company (National ICT R&D Fund) controlled by the Ministry of Information Technology. Applicants had to list universities in order of preference. Shoaib listed four universities in order, met the qualifying criteria after taking the required test, and was directed by the authorities themselves to move to his second-choice university when he did not meet the first university's entrance requirements, and then to his third-choice university when he did not meet the second university's requirements either. The authorities later claimed his transfer to the third-preference university was unauthorized.

The Balochistan High Court held that the authorities' objection was unjustified, since the petitioner had simply followed the process and instructions given to him at each stage. The court also emphasized that education is a state function, and under Articles 29 and 37(c) of the Constitution, the State is required to make technical and professional education broadly available and higher education accessible on merit. It further clarified that since the Company was substantially controlled by the Federal Government (through appointment and removal powers over its directors), it fell within the scope of constitutional writ jurisdiction under Article 199.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that government-linked bodies must act fairly and consistently with their own procedures, and highlights the constitutional importance of accessible education.

title: Giran Naz v. State,
explainer:
This case involved a woman who took shelter in a government-run women's shelter (Dar-ul-Aman) in Quetta because her brother opposed her wish to marry the man of her choice. She and her intended husband tried to get a court marriage arranged, but a Judicial Magistrate and later a Sessions Judge kept refusing, insisting instead that the matter be settled with her family first and that she be handed over to her relatives' custody as a precondition to marriage.

The couple then approached the Balochistan High Court, asking it to direct the shelter's superintendent to arrange their marriage and release the woman as the man's wife. The High Court ruled in their favor. It held that under Article 4 of the Constitution, no one can be stopped from doing something the law does not prohibit, and Pakistani law does not bar an adult woman from marrying an adult man she chooses. The court also invoked constitutional provisions protecting the institution of marriage and citing Islamic teachings on the sanctity and beauty of marriage. After personally confirming the woman was an adult who understood her decision, the judges found no lawful basis to block the marriage or make it conditional on family approval.

The court set aside the lower courts' orders, directed the shelter to arrange the marriage, and fixed a marriage dower (mehr) of Rs.100,000, given that the woman was an orphan. The case matters because it affirms that adult individuals, particularly women, have a constitutionally protected right to marry by their own choice, free from family or judicial interference.

title: Atta Muhammad v. State,
explainer:
This case involved a couple, Atta Muhammad and Mst. Shah Gul, who asked the Balochistan High Court to cancel a police case (FIR) filed against them under Pakistan's Hudood laws for alleged abduction. The woman's mother had filed the complaint claiming her daughter was abducted by the man with help from his brothers. However, the couple presented a marriage certificate (Nikah Nama) showing they had married voluntarily two days before the alleged abduction was reported.

When the case came before the court, the woman herself appeared and confirmed she had married of her own free will, was not abducted, and wished to remain with her husband. She also revealed she was pregnant. Even the State's own lawyer, after speaking privately with the woman, confirmed there was no coercion involved. The complainant mother later admitted in court that her real objection was that the marriage happened without her permission, and she offered to withdraw the complaint only if the husband's family provided a bride for her son in exchange—an offer the court did not endorse.

The Chief Justice ruled that since the alleged victim denied being abducted and confirmed a free, valid marriage, there was no actual offense to prosecute. Citing Supreme Court precedent, the court held that continuing the case would be an abuse of judicial process meant merely to harass the couple and settle personal scores. The FIR was quashed, and police were directed to ensure the couple's safety. This case illustrates how courts can intervene to stop misuse of criminal law in family disputes over marriage choices, particularly protecting adults

title: Ahmad Karam v. Director of Education,
explainer:
This case involved three petitioners who worked, or claimed to work, as Junior Arabic Teachers or Moallim-ul-Quran under the Education Department in Balochistan. They asked the High Court to declare that they were legitimately serving in the department, to let them perform their duties, and to order release of their withheld salaries.

The court found that the same dispute had already been raised in an earlier constitutional petition filed in 2007, which the petitioners themselves withdrew in January 2008 after seeing the government's response. Later, they filed a contempt application claiming the court's earlier order was being violated, and when that too was disposed of, they were told they could approach the appropriate forum for relief. They then filed this fresh petition, treating the contempt order as giving them a new right to litigate the same issue.

The Chief Justice rejected this approach, holding that a contempt order cannot revive or create new rights once the original petition was voluntarily withdrawn. Under the Civil Procedure Code, once a case is withdrawn, the person is barred from filing a fresh case on the same subject matter unless the court granted specific permission to do so, which had not happened here.

Additionally, the petitioners failed to prove their academic degrees came from a recognized institution, a point the government had specifically disputed.

For these reasons, the petition was dismissed. The case illustrates the legal principle that withdrawing a case has consequences, and litigants cannot use contempt proceedings to sidestep that bar and relitigate the same grievance.

title: Muhammad Rashid v. Irshad Begum,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a small shop and room in Quetta that had belonged to a deceased man, Muhammad Amiruddin. Earlier, the High Court had ruled that no one could occupy the property until the deceased's legal heirs were found or a court determined ownership. Muhammad Rashid filed a contempt application claiming that Irshad Begum, the deceased's divorced wife, had illegally taken possession of the property in violation of that earlier ruling, arguing she was not a legal heir since she was divorced before his death.

Irshad Begum's lawyer argued Rashid had no standing or personal interest in the property and wasn't a legal heir either. He noted she was an elderly woman caring for a mentally disabled son, and that she would vacate if a genuine legal heir came forward. The government's lawyer also opposed the contempt action, noting the property was unclaimed and the state technically owned such property, but had no objection to letting the woman and her son stay temporarily.

The court declined to punish her for contempt, given her circumstances and her lawyer's formal undertaking not to sell or transfer the property. It ruled she could keep living there until a legitimate heir appeared, provided she didn't dispose of the property, and that if she left, the state would take control of it. The court emphasized that supporting a vulnerable elderly woman and her disabled son served the public good.

title: Mashooq Ali v. S’r Member, Board of Revenue,
explainer:
This case concerns hiring irregularities in Balochistan's Board of Revenue. Petitioners challenged the appointment of Assistants and Stenographers, arguing the selections ignored merit. The Quetta High Court found serious problems: some candidates who failed or even skipped the written exam were still appointed. The Departmental Selection Committee never actually scored interviews, instead making vague notings against candidates, making it impossible to prepare a genuine merit list. Required skills like shorthand and typing speed were never properly tested for stenographer posts. When challenged, committee members initially denied wrongdoing and filed false affidavits, but later apologized to the court after the Senior Member of the Board of Revenue admitted merit had been violated.

The Court ruled the appointments illegal, unconstitutional, and void, holding they conferred no rights or benefits on those hired. It rejected an attempt by some petitioners to withdraw their case to protect the appointees' jobs, ruling that such large-scale fraud in public appointments was not a private matter to be settled between parties. The judges ordered disciplinary action against those responsible for the selection process and directed the provincial government to circulate the judgment's reasoning to all departments as a reminder.

This case matters because it reinforces that government hiring must be transparent and merit-based, and that courts will not tolerate corruption or favoritism in public sector recruitment, since such practices harm governance and taxpayers.

title: Saeedullah Jaffar v. Sr Superintendent of Police,
explainer:
This case concerns residents of Quetta who challenged the establishment of a local bus stand near their homes at the junction of Jinnah Road, Ramsay Road, and Adalat Road. They complained that the bus stand caused traffic jams, noise, filth, blocked access to their houses, and attracted crowds, vendors, and even public urination against their boundary walls, while also raising security concerns.

The dispute grew to involve a related issue: the old bus stand land, which had been acquired along with additional land for a new bus terminal, was instead being proposed for a massive commercial redevelopment by the Municipal Corporation, including nearly 786 shops, offices, a restaurant, and parking, with only a small portion left for actual bus operations.

The Balochistan High Court found this proposed redevelopment unlawful. It held that the tiny space left for buses would not have proper ventilation or room for buses to enter and exit safely, meaning the land's original public purpose as a transport amenity was being converted into private commercial use. The court ruled that public land acquired for a public amenity cannot be diverted for private profit by public authorities, and that such action violated local government laws and constitutional protections. The petition was accepted.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that government bodies cannot repurpose public land meant for essential services, like transport terminals, into private commercial ventures at the expense of public interest and residents' welfare.

title: Abdul Hameed v. Judicial Magistrate,
explainer:
This case is about illegal fishing off Pakistan's Balochistan coast. Fishermen aboard a trawler were caught fishing within four nautical miles of the shore using a prohibited fine-mesh net known as "gujja," which is banned because it harms marine life and fish populations. They were charged and pleaded guilty. The trial magistrate fined them Rs.15,000 and returned their trawler and equipment, but kept the banned fishing nets confiscated by the state. The fishermen challenged this, arguing the nets should also be returned, and their appeal to the Additional Sessions Judge was rejected. They then approached the Balochistan High Court, asking it to use its special inherent powers to overturn the confiscation.

The Chief Justice dismissed the petition. He held that confiscating equipment used for illegal fishing is not just permissible but mandatory under the relevant fisheries law, and that courts also have general power under the Criminal Procedure Code to order destruction or confiscation of items used to commit a crime. The judge noted that the accused had already received a lenient punishment (only a fine, no imprisonment) and had gotten their valuable trawler back, so there was no unfairness justifying court intervention. He went further, ordering that the confiscated nets be destroyed entirely, so they could never be reused for illegal fishing.

The case matters because it reinforces that courts can order destruction of tools used in environmentally harmful crimes, even without explicit legal provisions, to protect natural resources.

title: Atlas Cables (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Quetta Electric Supply Company Ltd,
explainer:
Atlas Cables, a manufacturer of electric cables and conductors, challenged a letter from Quetta Electric Supply Company (QESCO) that blacklisted it for allegedly breaching supply contracts and failing to deliver materials on time. Atlas argued this violated its fundamental right to conduct lawful business under Article 18 of the Constitution, since the blacklisting effectively barred it from doing business with power companies, its main customers.

QESCO argued the petition should not be heard because Atlas had also filed a civil suit for damages. The court rejected this objection, noting the constitutional petition was filed first, was disclosed in the civil suit, and did not overlap with the relief sought there (the suit did not ask for a declaration about the blacklisting itself). So both cases could proceed separately.

On the main issue, the court examined QESCO's own "Registration Procedures," which allow blacklisting only for serious causes like fraud, forgery, or bribery—not ordinary contractual breaches—and only after approval from a "Registration Committee" and a hearing for the affected party. QESCO could not show any such committee approval or that Atlas was given a hearing.

The court ruled that QESCO violated its own procedures and Atlas's fundamental right to business under Article 18. It declared the blacklisting letter unlawful and void, ordered its recall to everyone it was circulated to, and allowed the petition. This case reinforces that government bodies must follow fair procedure and proper legal grounds before blacklisting businesses.
