title: Abdul Malik v. Government of Pakistan,
explainer:
Two Ministers of the Balochistan government and two Senators went to the Balochistan High Court asking it to stop the national census being carried out in the province under the Census Ordinance, 1959. Their main arguments were that a large number of Afghan refugees were living in Balochistan, that law and order in the province was poor, and that some populations had migrated due to conflict or floods, making conditions unsuitable for an accurate census.

The High Court, led by Chief Justice Qazi Faez Isa, rejected these arguments. It noted that six general elections had already been held in Pakistan since the Afghan refugee influx began, without this issue being raised, and that refugee numbers had actually decreased over time compared to previous censuses in 1981 and 1998. The court pointed out that maintaining law and order was the government's own responsibility, and since two petitioners were sitting ministers, their plea effectively amounted to admitting their own government's failure. The court also observed that an accurate census could benefit Balochistan by increasing its representation in the National Assembly, since seats are allocated based on population. It held that deciding when to hold a census is a political decision for the Federal Government, not something courts should interfere with.

The petition was dismissed. The case matters because it reaffirms that courts will generally not intervene in political and administrative decisions like census-taking, and clarifies that census data serves broader planning purposes for governments at all levels.

title: Obaidullah v. Mir Muhammad Ali Rind,
explainer:
This case is about whether Senator Mir Muhammad Ali Rind was legally qualified to hold his Senate seat, given that he had earlier been convicted of corruption. In 2000, an Accountability Court found him guilty in two corruption references and disqualified him from holding public office for 21 years. He later struck a plea bargain, paying back the embezzled amounts, and this reduced his disqualification period to ten years, running from June 2001. Despite this, in 2009 he submitted nomination papers for a Senate seat and was elected, without disclosing his prior conviction, and while his ten-year disqualification period was still running.

The Balochistan High Court found that Rind had filed a false affidavit at nomination, hiding his conviction for corruption. The court held that under Article 62(1)(d) of the Constitution, which requires a member of Parliament to be of good character and not known to violate Islamic injunctions, disqualification for corruption and dishonesty is permanent, not time-limited like the ten-year bar under the accountability law. Since he had admittedly lied under oath and been convicted of stealing public funds, he failed this permanent character test.

The court declared Rind unqualified to hold the office of Senator, ordered him to return all salary and benefits he had received, and directed the government to enforce this and consider prosecuting him for submitting a false nomination form. The case highlights that convicted persons cannot circumvent constitutional character requirements simply because a specific statutory disqualification period has expired.

title: Ikramullah v. State,
explainer:
This case involved several people caught illegally possessing and transporting 190 cranes, a protected bird species under Balochistan's Wildlife Protection Act, 1974. After they pleaded guilty, a Magistrate fined each accused only Rs.1,000 and let them keep the birds. The Executive District Officer for Forest and Wildlife challenged this, and the Sessions Judge ordered the birds be seized and handed back to wildlife authorities. By the time the case reached the Balochistan High Court, however, all 190 cranes had died from a viral infection, making the seizure order impossible to enforce.

The Chief Justice found that the original fine was inadequate because the Magistrate had fined each person a flat Rs.1,000 regardless of how many birds they held, when the law actually treats possession of each bird as a separate offense. The court noted that Rs.1,000 was set as a maximum fine back in 1974 and had lost real value over 37 years, making it too weak a deterrent. Since the birds had died, the court imposed a fresh fine under a different section of the Act, calculated at Rs.500 per bird, totaling Rs.95,000, which the accused paid.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that wildlife protection laws must be enforced meaningfully, with penalties matching the scale of the offense, and it treats the killing or illegal capture of protected species as a serious matter deserving real consequences rather than token fines.

title: Students of Government Girls College Kuchlak v. Government of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case began when the Balochistan High Court took suo motu (on its own initiative) notice of a newspaper report saying that influential persons were encroaching on land set aside for the Government Girls College at Kuchlak. The court treated the news report as effectively a petition from the girls of the area who had no other practical way to seek legal help, and used its constitutional powers to investigate.

The land, about 14 acres, had been leased by the Balochistan government to the Education Department for 99 years specifically to build the college. Records showed a lawsuit by private individuals claiming ownership had already been dismissed by a civil court. The court found none of this created any legal right for those involved, since the land clearly belonged to the Education Department.

title: Rauf Khan Wazir v. Government of Pakistan,
explainer:
This case involved a candidate who took the 2009 Central Superior Services (CSS) examination and ranked 21st on Balochistan's merit list. When a higher-ranked candidate declined a position in the Military Lands and Cantonment Group, the petitioner argued he should have been offered that vacant post instead of having it carried forward to the next year's exam, as permitted under Rule 7 of the FPSC Competitive Examination Rules 2009.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the petitioner had not even completed the mandatory Common Training Program, and more importantly, he had unreasonably delayed nearly five months before challenging the decision, despite knowing about it. The court also noted that six other candidates who had taken the CSS exam the following year had a legitimate expectation of being considered for that same carried-forward vacancy, since results had already been published in newspapers before the petitioner filed his case. The petitioner failed to include these affected candidates as parties to his case, which was a procedural flaw. Given these facts, the court held that the government's decision to carry the vacancy forward was neither illegal nor unlawful.

This case matters because it illustrates how courts weigh delay and failure to involve all affected parties when deciding whether to intervene in civil service recruitment decisions, even when procedural rules are cited in support of a claim.

title: Chamber of Commerce and Industry v. Balochistan Director - General, QDA,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court concerned a public park in Quetta, built on the site of the old General Bus Stand, which had been named after the sitting Prime Minister. The Quetta Development Authority (QDA) planned to allot land around three sides of the park to build shops, with living quarters or upper floors that would overlook the park with no buffer distance. A chamber of commerce and, separately, a group of shopkeepers challenged this scheme.

The court held that the petitions were maintainable as public interest litigation, even without the petitioners being directly "aggrieved," because parks and similar public resources are held in trust for everyone. It found that surrounding the park with shops offering an unobstructed view into it would violate fundamental rights, including the right to dignity and limited privacy in public spaces, and would discourage women, families, and the poor and unemployed—who rely most on public parks—from using it. It also found that naming a public park after a living, sitting official was improper, amounting to self-promotion and misuse of official power.

The court ordered that no land be allotted or shops built around the park, that money already collected from prospective shop allottees be refunded, that the park's plaque and name honoring the living official be removed, and that the park be preserved permanently for public recreational use, with compliance reported to the court.

This judgment matters because it affirms that public spaces and natural resources belong to all citizens, restricts official misuse of power for self-glorification, and strengthens fundamental rights protections in the context of urban planning and public trust doctrine.

title: Muhammad Anwar Jaffar v. Govt. of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved a group of tribesmen from Tehsil Drug in Balochistan who claimed to be the rightful owners of land their ancestors had lived on for four to five hundred years. They objected to the government and a private company carrying out oil and gas exploration surveys on this land, arguing that under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, such surveys could not proceed without following legal procedures and paying compensation. They asked the Balochistan High Court to stop the exploration activities.

The court dismissed the petition. It found that the petitioners had failed to attach any actual order or notification showing that exploration had even taken place, despite being specifically asked to provide such documents years earlier. The only real evidence was a letter from the lead petitioner, styled as a tribal chief, asking a private company to negotiate with a tribal council rather than objecting to the exploration itself. The court noted this reliance on tribal chieftainship was questionable given that the System of Sardari (Abolition) Act, 1976 had formally abolished such tribal structures. The court also held that the petitioners had not proven their ownership of the land, that this was a disputed factual question unsuitable for resolution under constitutional jurisdiction, and that they were not "aggrieved persons" entitled to relief under Article 199. Instead, they had other legal remedies available to establish title and contest any encroachment. This case highlights the limits of constitutional petitions for resolving property disputes.

title: Abdul Malik v. Metropolitan Corporation,
explainer:
This case is about how public property in Quetta should be leased out. A government contractor challenged the way the Metropolitan Corporation Quetta (which took over from Zarghoon Town) had handed over the right to collect parking fees at Baldia Plaza. Instead of publicly advertising the contract and awarding it to the highest bidder, the Corporation appeared to have given it to another party through an agreement that was never properly verified, was not routed through the correct department, and whose signatory later denied signing it. That contractor also owed a large sum of money to the Corporation, and the Chief Minister had purportedly waived part of this debt.

The High Court found that no tender or public bidding process had been followed before granting the parking collection rights, which was legally required. It also held that there was no law allowing the Chief Minister to waive public dues owed to the Corporation, and that public money must be carefully protected and cannot simply be forgiven by executive discretion. As a statutory body, the Corporation had to follow its own rules.

The Court allowed the petition and directed the Corporation to immediately invite open bids for the parking fee collection rights and award the contract to the highest bidder. The judgment matters because it reinforces transparency and accountability in how local governments handle public assets and revenue, preventing informal or favoritism-based deals at the public's expense.

title: International Bunkering Middle East DMCC v. M.T. Tridonawati,
explainer:
This case concerns a dispute over unpaid fuel supplied to a ship. The plaintiff, a fuel supplier, claimed it had provided furnace oil worth over one million US dollars to the ship M.T. Tridonawati but received only a partial payment. It sued for the remaining balance, interest, and damages, and sought to have the ship arrested to secure its claim under admiralty law, which allows lawsuits directly against a ship (an action in rem) for debts like unpaid supplies.

The complication was that the ship had been sold to a new owner before the lawsuit was filed. The court examined whether this new owner, who claimed no knowledge of the outstanding debt and had genuinely paid for the ship, could be held responsible for the previous owner's unpaid bill.

The Chief Justice ruled that since the new owner had paid real, valuable consideration for the ship, held legitimate beneficial ownership, and had no knowledge of the fuel claim, he could not be made liable unless there was evidence he was part of a fake or sham sale designed to dodge the debt. No such evidence existed here.

This decision matters because it clarifies how admiralty claims interact with genuine ship sales, protecting innocent purchasers from inheriting a previous owner's debts, while reaffirming that such protection depends on the sale being real and the buyer being unaware of any hidden claims against the vessel.

explainer:
This case involved eight petitions filed in the Balochistan High Court challenging appointments made by the Director-General of Excise and Taxation, Balochistan to various government posts, including Inspectors, Assistants, Stenographers, Computer Operators, Clerks, Constables, Drivers and Naib Qasids. The petitioners argued that these appointments were made through nepotism and political influence, bypassing merit, and unfairly favoring candidates from particular areas, thereby denying other qualified applicants a fair chance to compete.

The Court found that the recruitment process was indeed non-transparent and violated applicable rules. The Departmental Selection Committee had failed to properly evaluate candidates' qualifications, did not conduct required tests for certain posts, and did not prepare proper merit lists before making appointments. The Court held that this violated the petitioners' fundamental rights to equality and equal opportunity under Articles 18 and 25 of the Constitution. As a result, the appointments were declared illegal, unconstitutional, and void, meaning they created no legal rights for those who had been appointed. The Court set aside these appointments and ordered the authorities to pay costs for each petition. It also clarified that the Balochistan Service Tribunal had no jurisdiction over these appointees' claims since the appointments were void from the start.

title: Saleh Muhammad v. Baz Muhammad,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land in Quetta. In 2007, Baz Muhammad claimed he had never signed a power of attorney dated 1977, which his father Ghulam Nabi had used to transfer property through official mutation entries. Baz Muhammad wanted these mutations cancelled, alleging forgery, even though the power of attorney was thirty years old, his father (the alleged attorney-holder) had died eighteen years earlier, and it had been duly registered.

Revenue officials initially rejected his complaint after confirming the document was properly registered. However, on appeal, the Land Commissioner accepted his claim, declared the power of attorney void, and cancelled the original mutation along with all subsequent mutations and sale deeds based on it. This was upheld by the Board of Revenue.

The Balochistan High Court found this to be a serious legal error. It held that revenue authorities like the Land Commissioner have no jurisdiction to declare a registered power of attorney forged or void, or to cancel mutations and sale deeds on that basis—only a competent civil court can do so. Mutation entries are for tax/fiscal record-keeping only and don't establish ownership. Since a thirty-year-old registered document enjoys a presumption of validity, only a civil court, after a proper trial, could decide whether it was genuine.

The High Court therefore intervened using its constitutional jurisdiction to correct this jurisdictional overreach, emphasizing that revenue officers cannot decide complex property title disputes reserved for civil courts.

title: Nasreen Khetran v. Government of Balochistan,
explainer:
Nasreen Khetran, a member of the Balochistan Provincial Assembly and provincial minister, challenged a 2009 government order creating 1500 new Junior Vernacular Teacher posts across Balochistan, complaining that her constituency, District Barkhan, received only 15 of these new posts. She argued this was unfair given the district's population and needs, and later also alleged schools in the area were closed or misused.

The government responded that Barkhan actually had a favorable teacher-student ratio (better than the recommended standard), already had 845 sanctioned teaching posts, and that the new posts were distributed based on need, not equally across districts. Court-ordered investigations by local officials found the schools were functioning properly and none were being misused, contradicting the petitioner's additional claims.

The Balochistan High Court noted that the petitioner, despite being an elected representative and minister, had to resort to litigation simply to get basic information about government performance and resource allocation. The judges emphasized that citizens and their representatives have a right to know how public money is spent and how government departments are performing, and that transparency laws already exist (like Pakistan's and Balochistan's Freedom of Information laws, and the constitutional right to information under Article 19A) to ensure this. The case highlights how lack of accessible public information can lead to unnecessary disputes and underscores the importance of transparency in government functioning.

title: Muhammad Abdullah v. Gov. of Pakistan,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court, where a routine constitutional petition against the federal government could not be heard on 1 October 2012 because no government lawyer showed up. The reason, revealed in a press statement, was that federal law officers across Pakistan had boycotted court proceedings that day in protest against an order passed by a judge of the Supreme Court, apparently over a personal grievance of the Attorney General.

The High Court sought explanations from the Attorney General, the Deputy Attorney General, and two Standing Counsel who had failed to appear. Their responses did not express regret but instead tried to justify the boycott, comparing it to past lawyers' strikes. The court rejected this comparison, holding that private lawyers protesting constitutional violations (such as judges being sacked by a dictator) is entirely different from state-paid law officers abandoning their duties over an individual's personal complaint. The court held that such intentional non-appearance obstructed judicial proceedings, violated the officers' statutory duties, wasted public money, and inconvenienced litigants.

Taking a lenient view since it was a first such incident, and acknowledging the officers may have felt pressured to show solidarity, the court ordered that one day's salary be deducted from the Deputy Attorney General and Standing Counsel who did not work that day, and recommended that other law officers across Pakistan who joined the boycott be treated similarly. The case underscores that public officials, especially law officers, are accountable to the public and cannot use strikes to settle personal grievances at the cost of justice.

title: Muhammad Saleem Khan v. Gov. of Pakistan,
explainer:
This case involved a government official, Muhammad Saleem Khan, who had been nominated by Balochistan's provincial administration to perform Hajj duty as part of a seasonal government staffing arrangement for 2012, with the Provincial Government agreeing to pay for his and other officials' Hajj expenses. The federal Ministry of Religious Affairs refused to accept the payment cheque, stating that the 2012 Hajj Policy contained no provision for Hajj to be performed at government expense, and citing a Supreme Court order which had said that no one may use government money without legal justification.

The petitioner argued that the Supreme Court order was only an interim order (not a final judgment) and did not actually prohibit performing Hajj at government cost, and sought a court direction ordering the Ministry to send him and other nominees for Hajj duty.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It held that even though the Supreme Court's order was interim, it could not be disregarded, since Article 189 of the Constitution makes Supreme Court rulings on points of law binding on all other courts. The Ministry had correctly relied on the principle that public money cannot be spent without legal justification, and no law existed requiring government-funded Hajj trips. The court also noted the petitioner failed to identify any fundamental right being violated, so he was not an "aggrieved person" entitled to file such a petition. The court added that Hajj is religiously obligatory only for those who can personally afford it, not something owed at public expense.

title: Asmatullah Khan v. Government of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Asmatullah Khan, who asked the Balochistan High Court to declare him head (sardar) of the Miankhail tribe and order the government to include him as a member of the Local Committee in Zhob district. He argued that without such recognition, members of his tribe faced difficulties obtaining local residency certificates, since these were issued based on Local Committee recommendations. He relied on certificates from local officials calling him "Sardar" and a government letter recognizing the Miankhail tribe as indigenous to the area.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that Pakistan's Constitution guarantees equality of all citizens under Article 25, and does not recognize anyone as superior due to titles like sardar, nawab, or malik. It noted that the "sardari" system was formally abolished by Parliament through the System of Sardari (Abolition) Act, 1976, and that Article 33 requires the state to discourage tribal and parochial prejudices. The court also explained that under Article 8, any custom inconsistent with fundamental rights is void, meaning claims to sardar status could not be enforced if they conflicted with equality principles. Finally, the court found the petitioner was not "aggrieved" as required by Article 199, since he wasn't denied legal protection or unequal treatment under the law.

This case matters because it reaffirms that Pakistan's constitutional framework does not permit special privileges based on tribal titles, reinforcing equal citizenship regardless of tribal hierarchy.

title: High Court Bar Association v. Government of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case is about the extent of the Balochistan High Court's power to protect people's fundamental rights, particularly when serious human rights violations occur but no formal petition is filed by an aggrieved individual.

The High Court Bar Association and others had approached the court, and the judgment addresses broader questions about the scope of the court's authority under Article 199 of the Constitution to intervene in matters affecting fundamental rights.

The court explained that under Article 4 of the Constitution, every citizen has an inalienable right to the protection of law and to be treated according to law. It held that the High Court's jurisdiction to enforce fundamental rights cannot be restricted or taken away, since the Constitution itself forbids such curtailment, and even constitutional amendments cannot abridge fundamental rights or the court's power to enforce them.

The judgment identifies three categories of petitions under Article 199: ordinary petitions requiring an aggrieved party, public interest petitions like habeas corpus or quo warranto where no personal grievance need be shown, and a third category involving serious or grave violations of fundamental rights where the High Court can act on its own initiative (suo motu), even without anyone approaching the court, because victims may be unaware of their rights, too frightened to come forward, or otherwise unable to do so.

The court also clarified that the Supreme Court's "public importance" requirement under Article 184(3) does not apply to the High Court's powers under Article 199, and that the High Court can act promptly and locally, making it well-suited to address urgent violations within its territory. This

title: Muhammad Hussain V. The Secretary, Government of Balochistan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a government job in Balochistan. The petitioner's father, a Sepoy in the Federal Levies, died while in service in December 1996. The petitioner claimed that under Levies rules, he was entitled to be appointed to his late father's post, but instead another man, respondent No.4, was given the job in 1998. The petitioner did not challenge respondent No.4's appointment as improper on its own terms, but argued he had a preferential right to the post as the deceased employee's son.

The problem was that the petitioner waited 18 years after his father's death, and about the same length of time after respondent No.4's appointment, before filing this petition in court. The Balochistan High Court held that this enormous, unexplained delay amounted to "laches," a legal principle where courts can refuse to grant relief if someone sits on their rights for an unreasonably long time, especially when others have relied on the existing situation in the meantime. The court noted that respondent No.4 had by then served 18 years, creating a settled legal position that could not simply be undone. The petitioner offered no explanation for the delay, and other family members had already been accommodated with similar jobs elsewhere.

The court dismissed the petition, emphasizing that such long, unexplained delays in service-related disputes will generally defeat a claim, even if it might otherwise have merit.

title: Adam V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court, deciding a criminal revision petition filed by Adam, a truck driver convicted of transporting liquor in violation of the Prohibition (Enforcement of Hadd) Order, 1979. Police had stopped his truck and found 52 sacks containing thousands of cans of beer and dozens of bottles of whisky. Two other men in the truck fled, but Adam, the driver, was arrested. He was convicted by a trial court and sentenced to two years' imprisonment plus a fine, and this was upheld on appeal.

The High Court reviewed the evidence and agreed that the prosecution had proven Adam was in possession of the contraband, since police witnesses gave consistent testimony, there was no evidence of a false implication motive, and lab tests confirmed the substances were alcoholic. However, the court noted a key flaw: although thousands of cans and bottles were seized, only one bottle of whisky and one can of beer were actually sent for chemical testing. Since the rest were never tested, the court held that only those two tested items could be legally treated as proven contraband for sentencing purposes.

Because of this gap in the evidence, the High Court reduced Adam's sentence from two years to time already served, while keeping the fine intact. This case matters because it illustrates an important evidentiary principle: prosecutors must scientifically test a representative and sufficient sample of seized contraband, not just a token portion, to justify a conviction for the full quantity.

The Balochistan High Court overturned their convictions and acquitted them, giving them the benefit of the doubt. Several serious problems undermined the prosecution's case. title: Balochistan Bus Owners Association (Regd.) through President V. Government of Balochistan Home and Tribal Affairs through Secretary and 4 others,
explainer:
This case was about a dispute between the Balochistan Bus Owners Association and provincial authorities over restrictions on night-time bus travel along the N-65 highway connecting Quetta with Sibi, Nasirabad, Dera Murad Jamali, and onward to Sindh and Punjab. The bus owners argued that local administration and police had stopped their coaches from traveling after sunset at checkpoints in Kolpur and Dera Murad Jamali, citing security concerns, leaving passengers stranded overnight without food or shelter. They asked the court to direct the government to let them run buses according to their official timetables and route permits without any restrictions.

The government and police responded that no buses were being outright stopped or banned; rather, due to law and order concerns, vehicles were being organized into escorted convoys with police and levies protection when crossing between districts, especially around sunset. They pointed out that this arrangement had actually been agreed upon in a joint meeting between the bus owners' representatives and the authorities, with the schedule and timing decided by mutual consent.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition, finding no evidence that authorities had issued any order banning night travel. Instead, the record showed the petitioners' own representatives had agreed to the convoy system for security reasons, and the bus owners were simply now reluctant to honor that agreement. The court held the petition baseless and ruled that security-driven convoy arrangements, agreed to by the industry itself, do not violate the owners' rights.

title: Shadi Khan V. The State ,
explainer:
This case is a criminal appeal decided by the Balochistan High Court in a matter involving murder charges linked to terrorism laws.

The appellant, Shadi Khan, was convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Quetta of murdering two people—his sister Yasmin and a man named Abdul Ghani Marri, whom he suspected was his sister's lover. A police patrol responding to noise at night found both bodies in the courtyard of Shadi Khan's house, with Khan standing nearby holding a pistol. He reportedly confessed on the spot, explaining he killed them because he found his sister in a compromising situation with the man. He was sentenced to life imprisonment.

On appeal, Khan's lawyers challenged the conviction, but the High Court upheld it. The court found the police witnesses' testimony consistent and credible, noting that police officers can be reliable witnesses even without independent civilian witnesses, especially since the crime occurred inside a house at 2 a.m. where outsiders were unlikely to see anything. The recovery of the weapon from Khan's possession, medical evidence matching the injuries described, and his judicial confession (even though recorded twelve days later and later retracted) all supported the prosecution's case. The court also accepted that Khan's stated motive—anger over his sister's relationship—was credible and proven.

This judgment matters because it reinforces legal principles about honor-related killings, the reliability of police testimony, and the validity of delayed or retracted confessions in Pakistani criminal law.

title: Waqas Ali V. The State ,
explainer:
Waqas Ali was convicted by a Special Judge in Quetta and sentenced to life imprisonment for allegedly possessing 275 kilograms of charas (cannabis) found in his vehicle, under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him, finding serious flaws in how the police and laboratory handled the case. The contraband samples were sent for chemical analysis 1 month and 24 days after seizure, far exceeding the 72-hour limit required by law, with no explanation of how the samples were safeguarded in the meantime. The Chemical Examiner's report itself was legally defective, missing a required second signature, failing to describe the testing method used, and not naming the officer who delivered the samples. Police also failed to seal or separate samples at the scene, instead sending the entire seized quantity to the lab, which the court saw as an attempt to cover up procedural lapses. Additionally, prosecutors could not prove Waqas Ali actually owned the vehicle, and his mere presence in it was not sufficient to prove he knowingly possessed the hidden drugs.

This case matters because it reinforces that in serious narcotics cases carrying harsh sentences like life imprisonment, courts require strict, error-free compliance with legal procedures for evidence handling. Sloppy police work or defective forensic reports can result in acquittal, regardless of the quantity of drugs allegedly involved.

title: Pervez Zaki V. The State through National Accountability Bureau, Balochistan, Quetta,
explainer:
This case is about a man accused, along with a colleague, of corruption while working at PTCL/WTR Quetta between 1991 and 1999. The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) alleged that funds meant for daily wage staff salaries were embezzled through his connivance with a co-accused who withdrew the money in cash. NAB filed a formal reference against him before the Accountability Court, and he sought pre-arrest bail from the Balochistan High Court.

His lawyer argued that the amount involved was too small to fall under NAB's jurisdiction, since NAB's own Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) restricts it to cases involving more than Rs. 100 million, and that he had already cooperated with the investigation, which was complete.

The High Court agreed. It held that NAB's SOP applies uniformly across the country, and treating this petitioner differently would violate Article 25 of the Constitution, which guarantees equality before the law. The court also noted that NAB was originally meant to tackle large-scale corruption, not petty cases, and that pursuing minor matters diverts resources and overlaps with other agencies like FIA and Anti-Corruption Establishment. Since investigation was complete and evidence already submitted to the court, keeping him in custody served no purpose. The court also emphasized the constitutional right to a speedy and fair trial. Accordingly, his pre-arrest bail was confirmed.

This case matters because it reinforces limits on NAB's jurisdiction and highlights equal treatment and fair trial rights

explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with an appeal by three men convicted of possessing unlicensed weapons and ammunition. Levies officials had stopped a vehicle carrying five rifles, a Kalashnikov, thousands of rounds of ammunition, and a revolver hidden in various parts of the car. The driver, Abdul Hayee, also had a separate revolver and live rounds on his person, along with a license belonging to someone else. All three occupants were tried; one, Muhammad Ayub, absconded during trial and was tried and convicted in his absence.

The court upheld the conviction of the driver, reasoning that since he was in control of the vehicle, he was legally responsible for what it contained, and the additional weapon found directly on him confirmed his role in concealing and transporting the arms. However, the court acquitted the other passenger, ruling that merely sitting in a vehicle where weapons are hidden does not prove knowledge or responsibility, and the prosecution had not shown he was aware of the concealed items.

Separately, the court set aside the conviction of the absconding accused, holding that trying and sentencing him without giving him a chance to be heard violated constitutional guarantees of due process and fair trial, as well as anti-terrorism law safeguards, amounting to condemning him unheard.

The case highlights important principles: possession/control determines criminal liability for concealed weapons, mere presence isn't guilt, and even absconders are entitled to a fair hearing before conviction.

title: Government of Balochistan through Secretary Board of Revenue and 2 others V. Muhammad Najmuddin Mengal and others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Balochistan over compensation for grape trees located on land acquired by the government for widening the Mastung Qambrani Road. The landowners' property was acquired, and while they were initially paid for the land itself, they later claimed compensation for grape trees growing on it. A survey found 1,061 grape trees, and the government paid Rs.1,300 per tree. The landowners accepted this payment under protest but disputed the rate, arguing the trees were worth much more, and took the matter to court.

A trial court sided with the landowners, awarding them Rs.16,199 per tree based on an expert report. The government appealed. Earlier, the Balochistan High Court had ruled in the government's favor, but the Supreme Court sent the case back for fresh decision, directing that the expert be examined as a court witness.

After re-examining the evidence, the High Court found that while the landowners successfully proved the correct number of trees, they failed to prove the much higher rate they claimed or their entitlement to interest. The court held that the government had properly assessed and paid a fair average rate consistent with payments made to other landowners, and that the landowners had already received full and final settlement. The court therefore ruled in favor of the government, setting aside the trial court's higher compensation award. This case illustrates how courts scrutinize expert evidence and government valuations in land acquisition compensation disputes.

title: Director General Nadra Through Deputy Manager (Legal) V. Popalzai and another,

Both the trial court and the appellate (revisional) court rejected NADRA's application. NADRA then approached the Balochistan High Court. The High Court found that the lower courts had focused on technicalities rather than examining the serious fraud allegations on record, and had not given the respondent a proper hearing on these issues. It ruled that the lower courts' decisions were flawed and speculative, set them aside, and sent the case back to the trial court to be decided afresh, with both sides given a fair opportunity to present their case. title: Sanaullah V. The State,
explainer:

The High Court overturned the conviction, finding the prosecution's case riddled with doubt. Given these serious contradictions and the requirement that guilt be proven beyond reasonable doubt, the court held that the benefit of doubt must go to the accused. title: Mohsin V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns Mohsin, who was convicted by a Special Judge in Quetta under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine, after 87 kilograms of heroin was allegedly recovered from a vehicle he was driving. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him. It found several serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, the prosecution failed to prove that Mohsin actually owned or possessed the vehicle at the time of the alleged recovery, and the investigating officer never bothered checking vehicle ownership records with the Excise Department. Second, and more importantly, the court found the prosecution had not shown that the seized heroin was kept safely or that the samples sent for chemical testing were protected from tampering during transit.

The court also examined the laboratory report itself and found it legally defective: it did not describe the testing protocol used, lacked signatures of two authorized officers as required by law, and did not name the police officer who delivered the samples to the lab. Since no such officer testified about safe custody of the samples, the report could not be treated as reliable evidence.

The court held that failing to follow the legally prescribed procedures amounts to a violation of law, and such a flawed report cannot support a conviction. This case matters because it reinforces strict procedural safeguards protecting the accused in narcotics cases, ensuring convictions rest on properly verified evidence rather than assumptions.

title: General Manager Pakistan International Airline and another V. Matiullah and 17 others,
explainer:
This case involved employees who worked as janitorial staff for Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), but who had been hired through a contractor. After working for anywhere between two and twenty years, they asked PIA to make their jobs permanent, since other workers doing similar work had already been regularized. When PIA did not respond, the workers filed a grievance case under Balochistan's labour law. The Labour Court initially rejected their claim, but the Labour Appellate Tribunal overturned that decision and ordered PIA to make their employment permanent after a three-month probation period, without back pay. PIA challenged this Tribunal decision in the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the workers were employees of the contractor, not of PIA, and therefore did not qualify as "workers" under labour law.

The High Court disagreed with PIA. It explained that courts use several tests to determine who a worker's real employer is, such as who controls the work, who pays wages, who has power to hire and fire, and whether the arrangement was genuine or simply designed to avoid labour law obligations. Applying these tests, the Court found that PIA exercised administrative control, paid the workers, and had power over their employment, even though a contractor was nominally involved. It ruled that a change of contractor did not change the employees' real employer. The Court held that the law recognizes indirect employment through contractors as still creating an employer-employee relationship. Finding no error in the Tribunal's decision, the High Court dismissed PIA's petition, meaning the workers were entitled to regularization.

title: Hidayatullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Hidayatullah, accused of murdering his wife after she stayed an extra night at her parents home. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to 20 years imprisonment plus payment of compensation (Diyat) to the victim's heirs. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him, citing serious weaknesses in the prosecution's case. Key problems included a 25-day delay in reporting the death to police, during which the body was buried without medical examination, raising suspicion that family members may have deliberated before naming the accused. No physical evidence like blood-stained items or the murder weapon was recovered because of this delay. When the body was later exhumed for autopsy, it was too decomposed for doctors to properly verify the injuries witnesses claimed to have seen, creating a conflict between medical and eyewitness evidence. Additionally, the accused's confession to a magistrate was recorded 13 days after arrest, and the magistrate had improperly allowed an outsider connected to the complainant's family to remain in the room during recording, undermining its reliability.

The court concluded that no one had actually witnessed the crime, the evidence was riddled with contradictions, and the trial court had failed to properly assess these facts. This case highlights how delays in reporting crimes, lack of timely medical examination, and improper procedure in recording confessions can create reasonable doubt sufficient to overturn a murder conviction, reinforcing the principle that guilt must be proven beyond doubt.

title: Noor Muhammad V. The State ,
explainer:
This case involved three men convicted for smuggling large quantities of foreign liquor and beer discovered aboard a vessel intercepted near Gwadar by Customs authorities and the Maritime Security Agency. The boat had thousands of bottles and cans of whiskey and beer, and after a chase, it was searched and the contraband seized. The trial court convicted the appellants under the Customs Act for possessing and transporting smuggled goods, sentencing them to five years' imprisonment plus fines.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court upheld the conviction itself, finding the prosecution's witnesses consistent and credible, with no contradictions or evidence of false implication, and a forensic lab report confirming the seized liquor was genuine contraband.

However, the court reduced the sentence significantly. It noted that only a small sample of the massive seizure, three bottles of whiskey and one can of beer, had actually been sent for chemical testing. The court held that an accused can only be held criminally responsible for the specific quantity that was scientifically tested and confirmed as contraband, not the entire seized stock, since without testing every portion, it cannot be presumed all of it was actually illegal liquor.

As a result, the court reduced the appellants' sentence from five years to time already served, while keeping other penalties intact. This case matters because it establishes an important safeguard: prosecutors must forensically test what they seize, and courts cannot punish someone for the full quantity of goods recovered if only a fraction was actually verified as contraband.

title: Abdul Ali V. Saath Muhammad and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a woman named Gul Makai who died under suspicious circumstances after allegedly being mistreated by her in-laws. Her father, Abdul Ali, and the police initially filed an FIR, but not all suspected persons were named. Unsatisfied, the family filed a private criminal complaint accusing the woman's husband and in-laws of murdering her, alleging she had repeatedly complained about cruelty and violence in her marital home, and that a ligature mark and injuries on her body suggested strangulation.

The trial court, after hearing witnesses, acquitted the accused, finding the evidence unreliable. The father appealed the acquittal to the Balochistan High Court. The High Court examined the record and found that the witnesses were not eyewitnesses, gave inconsistent accounts of how they learned of the death, and that key informants were never brought to testify. It rejected the argument that the accused should be presumed guilty simply because the death occurred in their home and because of their alleged conduct afterward, stressing that the burden remains on the prosecution to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

The Court also reaffirmed the well-established legal principle that an acquittal carries a "double presumption of innocence," meaning appellate courts should not interfere unless the acquittal was clearly arbitrary or against the evidence. Finding no such flaw, the High Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the acquittal. The case highlights how suspicion and family conflict alone, without solid evidence, cannot sustain a criminal conviction.

title: Muhammad Khan and another V. Additional Sessions Judge, Chaman and others,
explainer:
This case concerns a woman, Bibi Khatima, who died under suspicious circumstances after her marriage. Her family members, including her cousin and her father, believed she had been murdered by her husband and his relatives using firearms, and that she was buried hastily without informing her family. They approached an Additional Sessions Judge acting as an "ex-officio Justice of Peace" under the Criminal Procedure Code, asking him to direct the police (Levies) to register a First Information Report (FIR) against the accused. The Judge refused, partly because a separate FIR had already been registered against the deceased's own brother regarding the same incident. The family then challenged this refusal in the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners. It held that under the law, when someone reports a cognizable offence like murder, the police are legally obligated to record an FIR - they have no authority to first investigate whether the complaint is true before registering it. Similarly, a Justice of Peace's role is limited to checking whether the information describes a cognizable offence; if it does, they must simply direct the police to register the FIR, without assessing the truth of the allegations. The Additional Sessions Judge had wrongly gone beyond this limited role, so his order refusing registration was declared unlawful and set aside.

title: Muhammad Khan and others V. Additional Sessions Judge, Chaman and others,
explainer:
This case involved two related petitions concerning the death of a young woman, Bibi Khatima, allegedly murdered by her husband and relatives. Her cousin and later her father approached the police and Levies authorities asking them to register a criminal case (FIR) alleging murder, but the authorities refused, apparently believing the allegations were false. Both then went to an Ex-Officio Justice of Peace under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code seeking an order directing registration of the FIR, but the Justice of Peace dismissed their applications. They challenged that dismissal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners. It held that under the law, police or Levies officials have no authority to judge the truth or falsehood of a complaint before registering it—if the information discloses a cognizable offence (like murder), they are legally bound to record an FIR immediately and investigate afterward, not before. This case matters because it reinforces a fundamental principle of criminal procedure: authorities cannot refuse to register complaints of serious crimes based on their own assessment of credibility, protecting complainants' right to have allegations formally investigated.

title: Najeebullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Najeebullah, a 17-year-old shopkeeper who was running Al-Saif Medical Store in Quetta without a valid drug-selling license. A Drug Inspector, during a routine inspection, seized medicine samples from the store and issued a show-cause notice, which went unanswered. After sanction was obtained, a complaint was filed against him under the Drugs Act, 1976, along with the Pakistan Penal Code provision on common intention.

When charges were framed, Najeebullah pleaded guilty and asked for the court's mercy. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to two months' imprisonment plus a fine of Rs. 50,000 (or one month more in default of payment). He appealed, arguing that his young age, status as a student, and the fact that the seized medicines were not fake, substandard, or foreign-smuggled warranted leniency.

The Balochistan High Court noted that under the law, someone who pleads guilty cannot appeal their conviction itself, only the harshness of the sentence. Considering the appellant's juvenile age, his status as a student, the anguish and jail time he had already endured, and that the medicines involved were not counterfeit, the court reduced his prison sentence to the time he had already served. The fine and default sentence remained unchanged.

The case matters because it shows how courts can balance strict drug-law enforcement with compassion for young, first-time offenders, using sentence modification rather than overturning a guilty plea.

title: Messrs sino pak minerals private limited, islamabad through Law Associates Office V. Secretary Mines and Minerals, Government Of Balochistan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a mining company, Sino Pak Minerals, whose 30-year mining lease over land in Killa Saifullah, Balochistan, had been cancelled by the provincial Mines and Minerals authorities. The government accused the company of leaving the mining area idle, reporting no production, and failing to submit required quarterly progress reports under the Balochistan Minerals Rules, 2002.

The company challenged the cancellation, arguing it had never properly received the notices asking for progress reports or warning of cancellation, and so was never given a fair chance to respond before its lease was terminated. It cited genuine difficulties, including violent takeover of the mine site by armed men, deaths of foreign engineers during operations, and the illness of its managing director, as reasons for disruptions.

The Balochistan High Court found that the notices sent by the authorities had not been properly and verifiably served on the company. As a result, the company was "condemned unheard," meaning it was penalized without being given a genuine opportunity to explain itself, violating the basic legal principle of fair hearing (audi alteram partem).

The Court declared the cancellation orders void and of no legal effect, and directed the authorities to give the company proper notice and a fair opportunity before deciding the matter again. Separately, the Court rejected a rival claimant's request to be added to the case, since it had no ongoing legal interest in the lease after surrendering it earlier. This case underscores that government agencies must follow due process before cancelling valuable licenses or leases.

title: Govt. of Balochistan through Secretary Education Department, Civil Secretariat, Quetta V. M/s Campaigner Associates (Pvt.) Ltd. through Chief Executive and others,
explainer:
The case concerned a construction dispute between the Government of Balochistan's Education Department and a private contractor, Campaigner Associates, over a project to build workshops, classrooms, and a hostel at a Government Polytechnic Institute in Quetta. The contractor claimed it had completed the work satisfactorily but was not paid amounts owed, including payment for extra work, compensation for delayed payments, and losses from work stoppages. After earlier court intervention directed the parties to resolve the dispute through arbitration, an umpire was appointed by mutual consent and issued an award largely favoring the contractor, finding it had completed the work to the department's satisfaction and was entitled to most of its claims.

The trial court then made this arbitration award a formal rule of the court, essentially confirming it as legally binding. The government appealed, but the High Court noted that despite being given multiple opportunities, the government's lawyer failed to file any objections to the award before the trial court, and its right to object was eventually forfeited due to repeated delays.

The High Court dismissed the government's appeal, holding that its lawyer could not point out any real legal error in the trial court's decision, and that the government could not avoid its payment obligations simply because the project had since been wound up. This case illustrates how courts uphold arbitration awards when a party fails to properly contest them through available legal procedures, reinforcing the finality and enforceability of arbitration outcomes.

title: State Through Special Public Prosecutor, Anti Corruption Establishment V. Allah Dina,
explainer:
This case involved a criminal appeal by the State against the acquittal of a Patwari (revenue official), Allah Dina, who had been accused of colluding with a complainant's former business partner to fraudulently transfer land into other people's names. The complainant alleged that four land mutation entries were created using his forged signatures, and that the accused, a public servant, helped push through these fraudulent transfers. He was originally charged with criminal breach of trust, cheating, forgery, and corruption under the Pakistan Penal Code and the Prevention of Corruption Act, but the trial court acquitted him.

The State appealed this acquittal, but the Balochistan High Court upheld it and dismissed the appeal. The court found that the prosecution never got the complainant's disputed signatures examined by a handwriting expert, so there was no reliable proof the signatures were actually forged. It also noted that the disputed mutation entries had already been cancelled by revenue authorities on the complainant's own request, meaning the land transfers no longer had any legal effect. Additionally, a key witness who attested the mutation documents did not give evidence linking the accused to any wrongdoing.

The court reaffirmed that an acquittal carries a strong presumption of innocence, and appellate courts should not overturn it unless the decision is clearly unreasonable or contrary to evidence. Since the trial court's decision was well-founded, the acquittal stood. The case highlights how weak or incomplete evidence, especially the absence of expert verification, can be fatal to a corruption prosecution.

title: Habib Bank Ltd through Manager V. Haji Karim Dad and another,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running tenancy dispute between Habib Bank Limited, which had rented commercial premises in Quetta Cantonment since 1987, and the property's landlords who sought to evict the bank to use the space for their own business.

The landlords filed an eviction application claiming they genuinely needed the premises for personal use. The bank contested this, arguing it was a stable, long-term tenant with a good payment record, that evicting it would disrupt its established business, and that the landlords hadn't actually proven their need. The bank also argued the case should be barred because an earlier eviction attempt by the landlords had been dismissed back in 2010.

The Rent Controller rejected the bank's objections, finding that the earlier case was dismissed only due to non-prosecution (not decided on its merits) and concerned unpaid rent, whereas this new case was based on the landlords' personal need for the property—a different, fresh legal ground. The landlords presented convincing witness testimony supporting their claim, and the Rent Controller ruled in their favor, ordering the bank to vacate.

The bank appealed, but the Balochistan High Court upheld the eviction order. The Court emphasized that landlords have the right to reclaim their property for genuine personal use, and that a tenant—even one occupying premises for decades—cannot claim indefinite occupancy rights. The bank was ordered to vacate within six months. This case reinforces that long tenancy alone does not protect a tenant against a landlord's well-substantiated claim of personal need under rent laws.

title: Government of Balochistan through Secretary Education Department V. Messrs campaigner associates (pvt.) Ltd. through Chief Executive and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over an unpaid construction contract in Balochistan. A private company, Campaigner Associates, had been contracted to build workshops, classrooms and a hostel for a government polytechnic institute in Quetta. After completing the work, the company claimed the Provincial Education Department failed to pay amounts owed, including for extra work done beyond the original contract.

When the parties could not agree on arbitrators to resolve the dispute, the trial court appointed an independent umpire with the consent of both sides. The umpire heard both parties and issued an award in the contractor's favor. The government failed to file any formal objections to this award within the legal timeframe required under the Arbitration Act, 1940, despite being given multiple opportunities to do so. As a result, the trial court made the umpire's award a formal decree of the court.

The government appealed, arguing the contractor was not entitled to extra payments and that the award was unjustified. The Balochistan High Court rejected this appeal, finding that the government had not properly objected at the right stage, that the earlier court order allowing objections had never been challenged and become final, and that the contractor had completed the work to the department's satisfaction without any prior complaints. The court upheld the trial court's decision, dismissing the government's appeal.

This case matters because it reinforces that government bodies must follow procedural rules and deadlines just like any other party, and cannot avoid contractual payment obligations by raising objections late or without valid grounds.

title: Saeed Ahmad and another V. Mst. Anwar Sultana and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute among the children and widows of a deceased government health officer, Dr. Muhammad Abu Amar, who had three wives and several children. After his death, some of his heirs (from his first and third wives) claimed that he had, during his lifetime, gifted his properties to them, and had the revenue records transferred accordingly. Two other heirs, his son from a second wife and that wife herself, filed a suit for declaration, cancellation of the gift-related revenue entries, possession, and permanent injunction, arguing they were being unfairly excluded from their rightful share of the inheritance. The trial court dismissed their suit, accepting the respondents' claim of a valid gift.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the trial court's decision. The High Court held that every legal heir is entitled to a proportionate share of their predecessor's estate, and this right is not extinguished simply because the deceased gifted property to some heirs without the consent of the others. In other words, a gift made by a parent to some children cannot be used to completely deprive other legal heirs of their inheritance rights. The appeal was accepted, and the case was decided in favor of the appellants.

This judgment is significant because it reinforces the principle under Islamic inheritance law that all legal heirs have protected rights to their share of an estate, which cannot simply be bypassed through unilateral gifts to favored heirs.

title: Ibrahim Shah V. Pervez Rana,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and involved a civil dispute over damages for malicious prosecution. Ibrahim Shah had been accused in a criminal FIR filed by Pervez Rana, alleging that Shah and others had demolished a wall on Rana's property and committed related offences. Shah was tried and eventually acquitted by the criminal court, but only on the benefit of the doubt, not because he was found innocent outright. Following his acquittal, Shah filed a civil suit seeking Rs. 36,00,000 in damages, claiming the criminal case had been maliciously and falsely filed against him, causing him financial loss, mental torture, and damage to his reputation. The trial court dismissed his suit, and he appealed to the High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It explained that to win a malicious prosecution case, a plaintiff must prove three things: that the prosecution ended in his favor, that the defendant acted with malice, and that the defendant had no reasonable or probable cause for initiating the case. Simply being acquitted—especially on benefit of the doubt rather than a clean finding of innocence—is not enough to prove these elements. Since Shah failed to provide sufficient evidence of malice or absence of reasonable cause, his claim failed.

This case matters because it clarifies that acquittal in a criminal case does not automatically entitle a person to damages in a related civil suit; separate and specific proof of malicious intent and lack of cause is required.

The trial court dismissed his suit, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It explained that to win a malicious prosecution case, a plaintiff must prove three things: that the earlier criminal case ended in his favour, that the person who filed it acted out of malice, and that they had no reasonable or probable cause for filing it. Simply being acquitted, especially on benefit of the doubt rather than a clear finding of innocence, is not enough on its own. Ibrahim Shah failed to prove malice or lack of reasonable cause, so his case failed. The court found the trial court's judgment well-reasoned and free of errors.

This case matters because it clarifies that an acquittal alone does not automatically entitle someone to damages for malicious prosecution — malice and absence of reasonable cause must also be proven.

title: Syed Tahir Shah and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved the murder of a woman, allegedly killed by her husband with help from his brother. The prosecution's theory was that the husband strangled his wife and then staged the scene to make it look like she had hanged herself, concealing the true cause of death.

At trial, several witnesses testified, including the deceased's brother, her two sons, and her sister. They described a troubled marriage marked by ongoing physical abuse and threats against the deceased. One witness had even recorded a conversation in which the deceased described the torture she suffered. An independent witness placed the husband at the scene around the time of the killing. Medical evidence showed a two-inch wound on the deceased's neck caused by a sharp weapon, dust in her hair suggesting her body had been dragged, and a determination that death resulted from suffocation and homicide rather than suicide. The husband claimed his wife had killed herself due to depression, but he offered no explanation for his own suspicious behavior after finding her body, such as failing to question witnesses, involve her family, contact police, or arrange her funeral.

The High Court found the circumstantial and medical evidence, along with the husband's unnatural conduct, sufficient to uphold his conviction for murder. However, it acquitted the brother, ruling that no direct or indirect evidence proved he shared a common intention or participated in the killing. The judgment highlights how courts weigh circumstantial evidence, medical findings, and a suspect's behavior after a crime in murder cases, while insisting on distinct proof of guilt for each accused person.

title: Salahuddin and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a murder conviction, alongside a separate petition seeking a harsher sentence.

The incident occurred in November 2014 when the accused, Salah-ud-Din, and others allegedly attacked the complainant's brother at a medical store, resulting in his death from gunshot wounds. The trial court convicted Salah-ud-Din under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder) and sentenced him to life imprisonment, along with a compensation order. The convict appealed against his conviction, while the complainant filed a separate revision petition asking the court to enhance the sentence to death.

The Balochistan High Court examined several issues. First, it addressed the nine-hour delay in filing the police report, ruling this was not suspicious since the family first had to travel 25 kilometers to bury the body, and there was no evidence of deliberation or fabrication during that time. Second, the court found the eyewitness testimony credible and well corroborated by medical evidence about the injuries and timing, even though one witness was the deceased's brother, since mere family relationship doesn't automatically make testimony unreliable. Finally, on sentencing, the court noted that the complainant's own FIR mentioned prior enmity as the motive, which legally counts as a mitigating factor that rules out the death penalty.

As a result, the court upheld the conviction and dismissed both the appeal and the request for a harsher sentence, keeping the life imprisonment sentence intact.

title: Sadullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved the murder of a man named Khalil, who was shot outside a courthouse in Chaman on 14th May 2014 while going to inquire about a court hearing. His brother, the complainant, and cousins witnessed the shooting from a nearby car. The accused, Sadullah, along with two co-accused (who were declared proclaimed offenders and tried separately), allegedly ambushed the victim with pistols, firing shots that proved fatal. The trial court convicted Sadullah under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code for murder with common intention, sentencing him to life imprisonment and ordering compensation to the victim's family.

Sadullah appealed his conviction, while the complainant filed a separate petition seeking the death penalty instead of life imprisonment. The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness testimony from relatives of the deceased, medical evidence confirming death from firearm injury to the brain, forensic reports, and recovered weapons and bloodstained items. The court held that eyewitness accounts were credible despite being relatives, since it made no sense that real family members would falsely accuse innocent people while protecting the actual killers. The court also found sufficient evidence of common intention among the attackers.

The court dismissed both the appeal against conviction and the complainant's request for a harsher death sentence, ruling that since the main fatal shots were attributed to an absconding co-accused rather than Sadullah himself, this was a valid mitigating factor justifying life imprisonment rather than death. title: Shahid Dada V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Shahid Dada who was convicted by a trial court in Lasbella, Balochistan for possessing three kilograms of charas (hashish), a violation under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. He was sentenced to four years in prison plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned his conviction and acquitted him, citing several serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, although police claimed the drugs were found in a populated area, no independent or private witness was called to observe the recovery, as normally required. The court said police must at least show they tried to find such witnesses, which they did not. Second, there was an unexplained delay of nearly seven months before the seized drug sample was sent for chemical testing, far beyond the legally required 72 hours, raising doubts about whether the sample was tampered with or replaced. Third, the way samples were taken from three separate packets and mixed together made it impossible to know which packet the tested sample actually came from.

The court emphasized that even a single significant doubt in the prosecution's case is enough to acquit an accused person. Because of these combined problems, the court ruled that the prosecution had not proven its case beyond reasonable doubt, and set aside the conviction and sentence.

This case highlights the importance of proper procedure, chain of custody, and independent verification in narcotics prosecutions to protect against wrongful convictions.

title: Mazhar Ilyas Nagi and others V. Governor, State Bank of Pakistan and others,
explainer:
This case involved a State Bank of Pakistan officer, Mazhar Ilyas Nagi, who had served the Bank since 1975. In 1994, a major embezzlement was uncovered involving the then Chief Manager, who absconded. During the subsequent inquiry, the petitioner was issued a vague charge sheet and asked to respond, but when he sought to produce his own defence witnesses, the Inquiry Officer refused to summon them, assuring him informally that there was no solid evidence against him and that no defence was needed. Despite this assurance, the Inquiry Officer ultimately recommended serious penalties, including a permanent monthly salary deduction and denial of back benefits, based on findings of "contributory negligence." Notably, four other officers facing identical charges were exonerated, with their suspension periods treated as active duty.

The Balochistan High Court examined whether the State Bank, though governed by non-statutory staff regulations, could still be challenged through a constitutional petition, and found that it could, given its statutory establishment and public functions. On the merits, the Court held that the petitioner was denied a fair opportunity to defend himself, was misled by the Inquiry Officer's assurances, and was treated unequally compared to similarly placed colleagues. No finding had even been made on actual financial loss caused by his alleged negligence. The Court set aside the penalty as void from the start and allowed the petition, reinforcing that employees—even in institutions with non-statutory rules—are entitled to fair process and equal treatment.

title: Gul Mir V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a fatal shooting during a quarrel. According to the prosecution, the accused, Gul Mir, got into an argument with the deceased, Muhammad Azam, at a place called Killi Shah Nawaz. During the fight, Gul Mir allegedly fired a shotgun and killed Azam, after which people from both sides clashed and two more people were injured. The main evidence against the accused came from eyewitnesses who were relatives of the deceased.

The trial court had convicted the accused, but two judges of the Balochistan High Court disagreed on appeal - one favored acquittal, the other upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence from death to life imprisonment. Because of this disagreement, a third judge was asked to review the case and decide.

After examining the evidence, this judge found serious problems: the eyewitnesses were all closely related to the deceased, their accounts contradicted each other, and their behavior during the alleged attack did not make sense — none of them tried to intervene despite being present. No independent bystanders were presented as witnesses, even though people from the area had reportedly gathered at the scene. Additionally, police failed to recover the weapon or any shell casings, even though the accused was arrested at the scene, pointing to poor investigation.

Given these doubts, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and acquitted the accused, emphasizing that any reasonable doubt must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not just leniency.

title: Ghous-Ud-Din V. Abdul Manan alias Mano and another,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal appeal against an acquittal in the Balochistan High Court. The complainant, Ghous-ud-Din, had filed an FIR alleging that Abdul Manan, along with other accused persons, arrived at the scene armed with weapons (pistol, Kalashnikov, and Kalakov) in three vehicles and opened fire, killing one person and injuring others, following an earlier dispute. There was also a counter-FIR filed by the accused party, making it a "cross version" case where both sides accused each other of the same fight.

The trial court had acquitted the accused, but the High Court found this decision flawed. The judges noted that eyewitness testimony, including from an injured witness, was consistent and corroborated by medical evidence showing firearm and blunt-weapon injuries matching the accounts. Recovered bullet casings and an abandoned vehicle with a pistol further supported the prosecution's version. The defense failed to present evidence supporting their competing version of events.

The High Court held that the trial court had wrongly merged both cross-cases together instead of judging each on its own merits, and had misread or ignored key evidence. Finding the acquittal to be arbitrary and unsupported by the record, the High Court overturned it, convicting and sentencing the accused.

This case matters because it illustrates how appellate courts scrutinize acquittals for errors in evaluating evidence, especially in cases involving rival versions of the same incident, and reinforces that each case must be assessed independently on its own evidentiary merits.

title: Ashfaq Khalid etc V. State through D.G. NAB, Quetta etc.,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Ashfaq Khalid and Pervaiz Zaki, who worked as accounts officers at PTCL/WTR Quetta. The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) accused them of embezzling over Rs 1.94 crore between 1991 and 1999 by fraudulently recording payments to "daily wage staff" that either did not exist or were fewer than claimed, and pocketing the funds meant for their salaries. NAB had actually built four separate references (cases) against them on similar corruption allegations from the same period, but only sent three to trial while holding back the fourth.

After the three references went to trial, the accountability court convicted and sentenced both men, and the Balochistan High Court later ordered that their sentences in those three cases run concurrently (at the same time, not stacked one after another). NAB's own Chairman then acknowledged that pursuing the fourth reference separately would amount to double jeopardy—punishing the same people twice for essentially the same conduct—and NAB itself asked the trial court to close that fourth case. However, the trial court refused and pushed ahead with the trial anyway, also failing to decide the accused's request to dismiss the case.

The High Court found this improper. Citing Section 17(d) of the NAB Ordinance, which allows multiple similar offences committed over time to be tried together in a single trial, the court ruled that all four references should have been combined rather than prosecuted separately. Proceeding with a fourth, separate trial after conviction in the other three violated the rule against double jeopardy.

title: Read Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961
explainer:
This text is a Pakistani statute, the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961, not a court judgment. It is a law promulgated by the President of Pakistan following recommendations of the Commission on Marriage and Family Laws, setting out rules governing Muslim family matters such as marriage registration, polygamy, divorce (talaq), and inheritance.

The Ordinance establishes Arbitration Councils, made up of a Chairman and representatives of parties involved in disputes, to handle matters like requests for permission to contract a second marriage or attempts at reconciliation before a divorce becomes final. It requires all Muslim marriages to be registered through licensed Nikah Registrars, and imposes penalties for failing to report marriages for registration. It restricts polygamy by requiring a man to obtain written permission from an Arbitration Council before taking another wife, with penalties including fines, imprisonment, and immediate payment of dower if this requirement is violated. It also sets out procedures for talaq, requiring formal written notice to the Chairman and a 90-day waiting period intended to allow for reconciliation efforts before the divorce takes legal effect. Additionally, it changes inheritance rules so that grandchildren can inherit the share their deceased parent would have received.

Since this is legislative text rather than a judicial decision, there is no court ruling, legal dispute, or judicial reasoning to summarize as a "judgment."
