title: Mst. Sehat Bibi V. Bahar Khan and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over inherited agricultural land between a brother and sister, the only surviving children of their deceased father. The daughter, Sehat Bibi, sued for a declaration that a mutation (land transfer record) in her brother's favor was fraudulent, seeking partition, cancellation of the mutation, and her rightful share. She claimed her brother had transferred their late father's land into his own name and then sold it to a third party without her knowledge, depriving her of her inheritance. The brother argued the land had been gifted or willed to him by their father during his lifetime, and that the sister's claim was filed too late and undervalued. Both the trial court and the appeals court had ruled against the sister.

The Balochistan High Court overturned these decisions. It found that the brother had failed to prove the alleged gift or will with any credible evidence, no witnesses were produced, and the mutation document did not even bear the father's signature. The court held that under Islamic inheritance law, both siblings were entitled to their proportionate shares of their father's estate, and one heir cannot claim sole ownership over others through an unproven gift. Since the property had already been sold, the court ordered the brother to pay the sister her rightful share from the sale proceeds within three months, allowing her to pursue enforcement if he failed to comply.

This case matters because it reinforces that inheritance claims cannot be defeated by unproven gifts or wills, and that all legal heirs are entitled to their due share under Sharia-based succession law.

title: Muhammad Naeem V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murdering his wife by stabbing her with a knife (churri) in their home. A Levies official received information about the killing, went to the scene, and arrested the husband, who was later found to have already buried his wife's body. The prosecution's evidence included eyewitness testimony from the deceased's minor sister (aged eleven), corroborating testimony from the deceased's father, the accused's own judicial confession recorded before a Magistrate, and recovery of the murder weapon. The trial court convicted him under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced him to life imprisonment plus compensation to the victim's heirs.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court upheld the conviction. The court held that the minor witness's testimony was credible and reliable since she understood the questions and had no motive to lie, and her age alone did not disqualify her evidence. The confession was found to be voluntary and properly recorded. The court also ruled that the husband's silence and failure to explain how his wife died in his own house, combined with his conduct after the incident, worked against him under Article 121 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat, which places the burden on the accused to explain deaths occurring within his special knowledge. The court further held that neither the absence of a medical examination nor a three-day delay in filing the police report undermined the strong circumstantial and direct evidence. The appeal was dismissed, reaffirming how courts evaluate confessions, child witnesses, and circumstantial evidence in domestic murder cases.

title: Nazar Muhammad and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the alleged sale of vehicles. The complainant claimed he sold several vehicles, including a pick-up truck and two cars, to a father and his sons for over Rs. 47 lakh. He said he received partial payment plus a car in exchange, but the four cheques given for the remaining balance bounced when presented at the bank. He filed a criminal case accusing the buyers of cheating and dishonestly issuing bad cheques under the Pakistan Penal Code.

At trial, one accused, Nazar Muhammad, was convicted and sentenced to two years, while the other three family members were acquitted. Both sides then approached the Balochistan High Court: the convicted man sought to overturn his conviction, the complainant appealed the acquittals and also sought a harsher sentence.

The High Court examined the evidence closely and found major gaps. The complainant could not produce any documents proving the vehicle sale ever took place, gave no vehicle details, and had inconsistent testimony about where the deal happened. The bank confirmed cheques were dishonoured due to mismatched signatures, but no fraudulent intent was proven.

The court held that simply issuing a cheque that bounces is not enough to prove the crime of dishonest cheque issuance; deceitful intent must be shown. Since the prosecution failed to prove any genuine transaction existed, the court acquitted Nazar Muhammad too, setting aside his conviction, and rejected the complainant's appeals.

title: Saddar-Ud-Din V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about an appeal by a man named Saddar-ud-Din who had been convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment by a trial court in Sibi, Balochistan. The prosecution's case was that he and several others forced their way into a house and opened fire, injuring a man named Rehmatullah, who later died from his injuries.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence and found serious problems with it. The main witnesses who claimed to have seen the shooting were all close relatives of the victim, including his brother, father, and two uncles, making them interested witnesses whose testimony needed independent support. The court found this suspicious because none of these supposed eyewitnesses actually accompanied the injured victim to the hospital, raising doubts about whether they were really present during the attack. Additionally, no weapon was ever recovered from the accused, and a statement he allegedly gave to police that led investigators to evidence could not be used as proof because no actual recovery resulted from it, which made it inadmissible under evidence law.

Because of these unresolved doubts, the High Court ruled that the accused deserved the benefit of the doubt, a principle in criminal law meaning that if genuine uncertainty exists about guilt, the accused should not be convicted. The court overturned the trial court's decision, acquitted Saddar-ud-Din, and set aside his life sentence. This case highlights how Pakistani courts scrutinize eyewitness reliability and require solid, independent evidence before upholding serious criminal convictions.

title: Regional Election Commission, Naseerabad V. Abdul Ghafoor,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal complaint alleging that a politician, Abdul Ghafoor, submitted a false educational qualification document when he contested a Provincial Assembly election in Balochistan. He had used a religious seminary certificate, claiming it was equivalent to a bachelor's degree, to meet the minimum education requirement for candidates at the time. His opponent challenged this before an Election Tribunal, which ruled him unqualified and cancelled his election victory. He appealed unsuccessfully to the High Court and Supreme Court, with the Supreme Court reportedly making serious observations that he had submitted a false affidavit. Following this, the Regional Election Commission filed a criminal complaint against him for filing a false declaration, but the trial court (Sessions Judge) acquitted him.

The Election Commission appealed this acquittal to the Balochistan High Court. The High Court found serious problems with the trial court's handling of the case: it had failed to summon relevant official records from the Election Commission, and had not given both sides a fair and full opportunity to present their evidence. The High Court described the trial court's judgment as poorly reasoned, unjustified, and not sustainable in law.

As a result, the High Court set aside the acquittal and sent the case back to the trial court to be decided afresh, this time with proper evidence-gathering and fair opportunity for both sides. This case highlights the importance of thorough judicial process in election-related fraud cases, especially those involving candidates' qualifications and truthful declarations.

title: Abdul Majeed V. Special Judge Anti-Terrorism Court-I and another,
explainer:
This case concerns a road accident in Quetta involving a Member of the Provincial Assembly. According to the prosecution, the MPA was driving speedily when a Traffic Sub-Inspector signaled him to stop; instead of stopping, his vehicle hit the officer, then struck a car and a cyclist. The officer later died, and others were injured. The accused allegedly fled the scene and evaded arrest for several days before being caught due to public pressure. He was charged not only under ordinary Penal Code offences like murder and rash driving but also under the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997.

The accused asked the Anti-Terrorism Court to transfer his case to an ordinary criminal court, arguing this was simply a case of rash and negligent driving, not terrorism, and that terrorism charges were added later in bad faith to block a possible compromise between the parties. The trial court rejected this request, and he challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition, agreeing that this was not a simple accident case. It noted the accused had no valid license, did not help the injured, had a history of similar serious cases, and that the incident caused widespread media coverage and public fear, particularly among police officers. These factors, the court held, supported treating the act as terrorism. The ruling reinforces that when incidents create public fear and target law enforcement, they can be tried under anti-terrorism laws rather than ordinary courts.

title: Ali Bakhsh alias Ali dost V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Ali Bakhsh, who was convicted by a trial court for attempted murder and causing injury (hashimah) under Pakistan's Penal Code, after allegedly shooting his cousin's associate, Umid Ali, following an old dispute over harsh words exchanged a month earlier. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment along with fines and compensation (daman) to the victim.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court closely examined the prosecution's evidence and found it riddled with inconsistencies. The complainant did not witness the shooting himself and gave contradictory, vague accounts about how and when he learned of the incident. The FIR was lodged suspiciously fast, before timelines given by the complainant made sense. Key witnesses could not justify their presence at the scene, contradicted each other, and appeared to be giving false testimony due to their relationship with the victim. No independent witnesses supported the prosecution's version. Medical records confirming treatment were never produced, and the forensic report on recovered cartridges was delayed and did not even match the actual case evidence, making it worthless.

Given these serious gaps and contradictions, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt. Following established legal principles that benefit of doubt must go to the accused, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence, acquitting Ali Bakhsh.

title: Jaffar Khan V. Syed Moead Ahmed,
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant dispute in Quetta. The landlord filed a case seeking eviction, claiming he needed the house back for his sister's personal use and that the tenant had stopped paying rent since March 2014, making him a defaulter. The tenant denied these claims. The Rent Controller (trial court) ruled in favor of the landlord and ordered the tenant to vacate, partly because the tenant's lawyer missed several hearings, causing his right to cross-examine the landlord's witnesses and to present his own evidence to be closed one after another. The tenant then appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing he was never given a fair chance to defend himself or challenge the landlord's evidence.

The High Court agreed that fairness was compromised. It held that the right to cross-examine witnesses is a valuable constitutional protection (Article 10-A), and that if a party is denied this opportunity, the evidence given against them generally cannot be treated as reliable. Both sides must be tested through cross-examination to determine the truth of their claims. Applying the principle that no one should be condemned without a fair hearing, the court found that the tenant had not received proper opportunity to present his case.

As a result, the High Court partially allowed the appeal and sent the case back to the Rent Controller, directing that both parties be given a full and fair opportunity to produce their evidence before a fresh decision is made. This case highlights the importance of due process and the right to a fair hearing in eviction proceedings.

title: Sate through Prosecutor-General Accountability, NAB V. Ghulam Mustafa Randahawa and another,
explainer:
This case is about Ghulam Mustafa Randhawa, a former government officer in the Food Department who was accused by Pakistan's National Accountability Bureau (NAB) of acquiring properties and huge bank deposits far beyond what his official salary could explain. NAB alleged he used relatives and associates as "benamidars" (name-lenders) to hide plots, houses, a godown, and bank accounts worth over ten crore rupees, including holdings in his brothers' names.

The trial court had first convicted him, but after an earlier appeal the case was sent back for the charges to be properly reframed. After the retrial, the Accountability Court acquitted him, reasoning that the burden was on the prosecution to prove its case, rather than requiring the accused to explain his unusually large bank balance.

NAB appealed this acquittal to the Balochistan High Court. The High Court found that the trial court had made a mistake: under Section 14 of the National Accountability Ordinance, once assets disproportionate to known income are shown, the accused himself must justify them, not the other way around. The trial court had ignored this rule and instead focused on irrelevant, lengthy discussions.

The High Court set aside the acquittal and sent the case back to the trial court to be decided afresh, properly applying the law on burden of proof for unexplained assets. This case matters because it clarifies how corruption and illegal-wealth cases should be handled - placing the responsibility on public officials to explain unexplained riches.

title: Hassan Gul V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about an appeal against a death sentence handed down by a trial court in Balochistan. The appellant, Hassan Gul, had been convicted of murder and attempted murder after he and co-accused, armed with automatic weapons, allegedly opened fire on the complainant's group, killing one person and wounding another with multiple gunshot injuries.

The High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness accounts from the complainant and the injured survivor, both of whom gave consistent and detailed testimony that withstood cross-examination. Medical evidence confirmed the gunshot injuries, and the court found no reason to doubt the witnesses simply because they were related to the victims or had a personal stake in the case, since their accounts were credible and corroborated each other. The court also ruled that failure to recover the murder weapon did not weaken the prosecution's case, since direct eyewitness evidence was sufficient, and the accused had time to hide the weapon while he was a fugitive.

However, the court found that the trial court had been too harsh in imposing the death penalty, ignoring that there was a pre-existing land dispute and litigation between the parties, which served as a mitigating factor. As a result, the High Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence from death to life imprisonment.

This case illustrates how appellate courts balance strict evidentiary standards with considerations of context and mitigating circumstances when reviewing capital punishment cases.

title: Baz Muhammad and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved a violent clash between two groups over a land or passage dispute, which resulted in the deaths of two men, Dilbar Khan and Faiz Muhammad, and injuries to others. The prosecution alleged that several accused, armed with spades and at least one pistol, attacked the complainant's side after being confronted about laying stones and gravel on a shared passage. Following the incident, the trial court convicted two of the accused, Baz Muhammad and Sultan Muhammad, of murder and rioting, sentencing them to life imprisonment and fines. The convicted men appealed, while the complainant separately sought an even harsher sentence, the death penalty.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence presented by six eyewitnesses, including the complainant, and found serious problems. The witnesses gave accounts that contradicted each other and also contradicted their own earlier statements to police. Several witnesses could not convincingly explain why they were present at the scene, and all were closely related to each other, raising concerns about bias. Because of these inconsistencies and unexplained presence, the court could not trust the eyewitness testimony as reliable.

Applying the well-established principle that any reasonable doubt in the prosecution's case must benefit the accused, the court ruled that the prosecution had failed to prove the charges beyond doubt. As a result, it acquitted the appellants, overturning their convictions and sentences, and dismissed the complainant's request to increase the punishment.

title: Khair Muhammad Shah V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man convicted of causing another person's death by driving an oil tanker recklessly. In 2015, a truck driver, Khair Muhammad Shah, was involved in a road accident at Hub Bridge in Balochistan that killed a motorcyclist named Shafi Muhammad. Police charged him with rash and negligent driving that led to death, along with related offenses, and a trial court convicted him, sentencing him to one year in prison and ordering him to pay compensation (diyat) to the victim's family.

The accused appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing there was no real evidence that he had driven carelessly and that the accident might have resulted from the deceased's own actions, since the motorcycle was reportedly overloaded with goods at the time.

The High Court examined the evidence and found a major weakness: the only prosecution witness, the victim's uncle, had not actually witnessed the accident himself and arrived only after it happened. He could not explain how or why the crash occurred, and there was no other proof of reckless driving. The court held that a conviction cannot rest on guesswork or assumptions, and that the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

Because the evidence left real doubt about who was at fault, the court gave the benefit of that doubt to the accused, overturned his conviction, and acquitted him. The case highlights the importance of solid eyewitness evidence and the principle that suspicion alone cannot justify a criminal conviction.

title: Malik Mustafa and 6 others V. Secretary, Mines and Minerals, Govt. of Balochistan, Quetta and 4 others,
explainer:
This case dealt with a long-running dispute over marble mining leases in Chagai district, Balochistan, and how those leases should be divided among family members following a family partition and a related arbitration decree from 1979. The original leaseholders' successors argued that mining rights meant for them had, over the years, been improperly transferred or reassigned to other parties and companies (including firms called Pubni Minerals and Mir Marbles) without proper notice to them, sometimes even while related litigation was pending before the Supreme Court. Multiple petitioners filed constitutional petitions challenging various government orders, notifications, and allotment letters issued by the Balochistan Mines and Minerals Department, and one party also filed a contempt application. Because several connected cases raised overlapping facts and legal questions, the Balochistan High Court decided them together in a single judgment.

The court found that the dispute involved serious factual disagreements about who was entitled to which leases and shares, and that these disputed facts had not been properly examined by the mining authorities. It also found that the petitioners had not been given a fair opportunity to be heard before the disputed notifications and orders were issued. Rather than deciding the merits itself, the High Court set aside the impugned notifications and sent the matter back to the mining authorities, directing them to hear all the parties involved and decide the case afresh.

This judgment matters because it reinforces the basic legal principle that government authorities must provide affected parties a fair hearing before making decisions affecting their property or business rights, especially in cases involving complicated factual and family ownership disput

title: Syed Nasrullah V. The Director General Pakistan Sports Board, Islamabad and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a Sub-Engineer who was appointed to the Pakistan Sports Board in 2016 after clearing a written test and interview, and later being regularized. His appointment was initially challenged by a rival candidate in a separate petition, but that challenge was withdrawn after the rival found employment elsewhere. Despite this, the Sports Board later issued a show-cause notice claiming the petitioner's appointment was illegal and had been made on political grounds, wrongly citing the earlier court proceedings as support. Without holding a proper inquiry, the Board terminated his services. His departmental appeals went unanswered, prompting him to approach the Balochistan High Court.

The Board argued that the petition could not be heard because it was a non-statutory organization not governed by formal service rules, meaning constitutional petitions do not apply to its employment disputes, which are treated under ordinary "master and servant" principles.

The High Court agreed that since the Sports Board lacked statutory rules on appointments, promotions, and discipline, a constitutional petition against it was not maintainable. However, the judges noted that the petitioner appeared to have a strong case on the merits, since his termination was based on a misreading of the earlier court order. While dismissing the petition on maintainability grounds, the Court urged the Board to reconsider his case sympathetically and on humanitarian grounds. The ruling highlights limits on constitutional court intervention in disputes involving non-statutory public bodies.

title: Muhammad Akbar alias Akbar Ali V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a double murder in Lasbella, Balochistan, where a father and son were shot while riding a motorcycle. The complainant's brother and a young witness (aged eleven) both claimed to have directly witnessed the accused, Muhammad Akbar, and others chasing down the victims and opening fire with pistols. The father died at the scene, and the son later died from his injuries in hospital.

The trial court had convicted Akbar under section 302(b) read with section 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder with common intention), sentencing him to life imprisonment and ordering compensation to the victims' families. Two co-accused were acquitted. Akbar appealed to the Balochistan High Court challenging his conviction.

The High Court upheld the conviction. It found the eyewitness testimony credible and consistent, even though one witness was a child—the court held that a minor's testimony cannot be dismissed simply because of age, especially when the child answered cross-examination questions competently and showed no signs of being coached. The court also noted that eyewitness accounts were supported by medical evidence and an established motive (a matrimonial dispute involving the complainant's sister). It reaffirmed that testimony from relatives of the deceased ("interested witnesses") can still be relied upon if it is truthful and not shown to be biased, without needing independent corroboration.

This judgment reinforces important principles in Pakistani criminal law: child witnesses can give valid testimony if reliable, and family relationship to a victim does not automatically discredit a witness's evidence

The High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's evidence. The complainant, the injured victim, and the investigating officer gave conflicting accounts about basic facts, such as when the FIR was filed, who took the injured man to the hospital, and what time officials arrived at the scene. title: Abdul Hameed V. The State,
explainer:
This is a criminal appeal decided by the Balochistan High Court involving Abdul Hameed, who worked as Incharge of a government-run Utility Store in Khuzdar. He was accused of misappropriating store items worth over two hundred thousand rupees while in charge, and was convicted by a trial court under laws dealing with criminal breach of trust by public servants and corruption, receiving three years imprisonment along with fines.

On appeal, the High Court closely examined the evidence. It found serious gaps in the prosecution's case: when the store's locks were broken to inspect the alleged shortage, no proper record was made, no broken locks were preserved as evidence, and no signed inventory sheet listing the missing items was prepared. Additionally, financial records showed that Abdul Hameed had deposited a substantial amount into the bank, and when the accounts were tallied, the stock position actually matched between debit and credit sides. The prosecution's own witnesses admitted this reconciliation. This meant the claimed shortage was not actually proven through reliable evidence.

Because the prosecution failed to establish the alleged embezzlement beyond reasonable doubt, the High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted Abdul Hameed, setting aside his sentence.

title: Abdul Nafey V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and deals with a pre-arrest bail application in a murder case. The applicant, Abdul Nafey, was named in an FIR alleging that he and a co-accused fired shots that led to the death of a man named Zain-ud-Din, following a dispute between two groups from the same village. The applicant argued he was innocent and that his side had actually been attacked first, leading to a separate FIR filed by his group against the complainant's side just two years earlier. He also noted that other accused named in the case had already been granted bail.

The court first addressed whether the applicant could approach the High Court directly instead of the trial court, and ruled that this was permissible given the genuine tribal enmity and threat to life involved.

On the main issue, the court noted that both sides had filed cases against each other, both sides suffered injuries, and the incidents occurred within 45 minutes of each other. Since it was unclear which side was actually the aggressor, this could only be determined through a full trial. Because other co-accused had already received bail, the court applied the "rule of consistency" and confirmed the applicant's pre-arrest bail.

The judgment matters because it reinforces that people facing genuine threats can seek bail directly from a higher court, and that in cases involving cross-complaints between rival parties, courts may extend bail until trial clarifies who was truly at fault, especially where similarly placed co-accused have already been released.

title: Khair Muhammad and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about the murder of a young man named Abdul Hameed, allegedly by two neighbors, Khair Muhammad and Zahoor Ahmed, in Panjgoor, Balochistan in December 2015. According to the prosecution, the victim was called out of his house at night by the two accused, and shortly after, his father heard gunshots and saw the accused running away armed. The victim was later found dead from bullet wounds inside the accused's house.

The trial court convicted both men under Section 302(b) read with Section 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder with common intention) and sentenced them to life imprisonment, along with compensation to be paid to the victim's family. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the conviction. It found the eyewitness accounts credible and consistent, supported by medical evidence of bullet wounds, recovery of blood-stained earth and bullet casings from the accused's house, forensic matching of the recovered pistol to the casings, phone records showing contact between the victim and accused on the night of the murder, and one accused's confession leading to recovery of the weapon. The court also clarified that being related to the victim doesn't automatically make a witness's testimony unreliable, and that lack of a clear motive doesn't undermine a murder case if other evidence is strong.

The appeals were dismissed, and the convictions and sentences were upheld.

title: Lal Bakhsh and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Lal Bakhsh and others, who were tried and convicted by an Anti-Terrorism Court in Mekran, Turbat, for the brutal killing of a young man and woman, Jalal and Maryam. The killings arose from a so-called honour crime: Maryam's family disapproved of her relationship with Jalal, and after luring both to their home under the pretext of arranging a marriage (Nikkah), several family members attacked and slaughtered them. The trial court had sentenced one accused to life imprisonment and others to death, treating the killings as an act of terrorism under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

On appeal, the defense argued that this was actually a private family matter, not terrorism, and should have been tried by an ordinary criminal court rather than a special anti-terrorism court. The Balochistan High Court agreed. Relying on a Supreme Court ruling in Khuda-e-Noor v. The State, the High Court held that honour killings, even when committed violently, are private offences carried out for personal motives within the privacy of a home, and therefore do not meet the legal definition of "terrorism." As such, the Anti-Terrorism Court had no jurisdiction to try the case.

Without examining whether the accused were actually guilty, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence and sent the case back to be tried afresh by the ordinary courts. This decision clarifies that honour killings, regardless of their brutality, fall under ordinary criminal law rather than anti-terrorism law.

title: Ghulam Qadir and another V. Muhammad Ali and others,
explainer:
Two lawyers from Gwadar sued several people, including newspapers, for defamation, claiming Rs. 20 million in damages. They alleged that newspaper publications contained serious false allegations meant to damage their honor and reputation, motivated by jealousy and orchestrated by one of the defendants.

The defendants denied the allegations and countered that the plaintiffs were actually habitual, professional litigants and blackmailers with a poor reputation, pointing out that they had already been officially declared frivolous litigants by the local District Judge.

The trial court dismissed the suit, and the plaintiffs appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the published material did not actually contain anything that damaged the plaintiffs' reputation or caused them humiliation. It also noted that after the publications came out, the plaintiffs never tried to publicly rebut or respond to the allegations, which undermined their claim of harm. Additionally, the court noted that the plaintiffs and defendants had a history of other litigation between them, and that one of the plaintiffs' names appeared on an official list of advocates identified by the District Judge as being involved in frivolous litigation.

Because the legal requirement of proving actual damage to reputation was not met, the appeal was dismissed and the trial court's decision stood. The case illustrates that defamation claims require concrete proof of reputational harm, not just an allegation of unwanted publicity.

title: Abdul Ghafoor Kalmati V. Naguman and 15 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a dispute over land in Pasni. A group of plaintiffs had filed a civil suit (Suit No. 4 of 2016) seeking correction of mutation entries related to land they claimed was gifted and inherited from a deceased owner, Sher Jan. That suit was settled through a compromise, and the trial court issued a decree based on it.

Meanwhile, the petitioner, Abdul Ghafoor Kalmati, had filed his own separate suit (Suit No. 15 of 2016) over the same land against overlapping parties. He challenged the compromise decree in the other suit before the Majlis-e-Shoora, Gwadar, which set aside that decree and ordered the two suits to be consolidated and heard together.

After consolidation, Kalmati asked the trial court to formally add him as a party to Suit No. 4 of 2016 as well. The trial court refused, and he challenged that refusal in this revision petition before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision, reasoning that since both suits already covered the same subject matter and had been consolidated, there was no real prejudice to Kalmati. He still had his own pending suit in which he could fully argue his claims. The court found no legal error in the trial court's order and dismissed the revision petition outright.

The case illustrates how courts handle overlapping lawsuits over the same property: consolidation can make separate applications to be added as a party unnecessary, since litigants retain their right to be heard through their own existing suit.

title: Muhammad Hanif V. Seraj Ahmed and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Panjgur, Balochistan. Muhammad Hanif claimed he had purchased a piece of land 33 years earlier, in 1982, from several individuals through a sale deed. He filed a lawsuit seeking a court declaration of his ownership, an injunction, and cancellation of a separate sale deed through which one respondent had sold part of the land to another respondent. Hanif alleged this second sale was done without his knowledge and led to encroachment on his property. Both the trial court and the appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora) rejected his suit, so he brought the matter to the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the petition. It found that Hanif had failed to properly prove his ownership claim. He did not produce any marginal witnesses to the sale deed (as legally required), did not get the document formally exhibited as evidence, and could not produce any of the original sellers to confirm the transaction. The witnesses he did present had no direct connection to the actual signing of the sale deed, and the document itself was never verified by an Oath Commissioner or Notary Public.

The court concluded there was no error, misreading, or legal irregularity in the earlier rulings. This case highlights how important proper documentary proof and witness testimony are in property disputes in Pakistan—simply claiming ownership isn't enough; the law requires solid, verifiable evidence.

title: Ameer Bakhsh V. Assa and 2 others,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and deals with a procedural dispute in an ongoing civil lawsuit. The plaintiff, Ameer Bakhsh, had filed a suit for declaration, permanent injunction, and correction of revenue entries against the defendants back in 2014. The trial court framed nine issues for trial in 2016, and the case proceeded with the plaintiff producing three witnesses. Later, while still in the process of presenting evidence, the plaintiff filed an application asking the trial court to frame additional issues or correct the existing ones under the Civil Procedure Code. The trial court rejected this application, and the plaintiff challenged that rejection before the High Court through a civil revision petition.

The High Court dismissed the petition outright. It found that the plaintiff had not given any real justification for why additional issues were needed to properly decide the dispute. More importantly, the plaintiff had stayed silent for about a year and a half after the issues were originally framed, never objecting to them until this late stage. The court held that the trial court's decision to refuse the amendment was neither illegal nor improper.

This case matters because it reinforces that courts will not entertain last-minute attempts to reshape a case's legal questions without good reason, especially when a party had ample opportunity to raise objections earlier and failed to do so. It underscores the importance of timely diligence in civil litigation.

title: Raheem Bakhsh and another V. Bashir Ahmed and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute over land in Pakistan. The plaintiffs (Bashir Ahmed and others) filed a lawsuit seeking a declaration of ownership, an injunction, and correction of land records regarding property they claimed was ancestral and in their possession. The defendants (Raheem Bakhsh and another) contested the suit, denying the plaintiffs' claims in their written statement.

It later emerged that before the lawsuit was even filed, the defendants had secretly sold portions of the disputed land to third parties on three separate occasions. They did not disclose this sale in their written statement, effectively hiding it from the court. When the plaintiffs discovered this through revenue records, they applied to amend their suit and add the buyers as parties, which the trial court allowed. The trial court also issued a show-cause notice to the defendants for concealing facts, and since they failed to adequately respond, imposed a cost of Rs. 5,000 on them.

The defendants challenged this cost order before the High Court. The High Court dismissed their petition, finding no illegality in the trial court's decision. It held that hiding the prior sale amounted to misleading the court and could even be treated as contempt of court, but the trial court had already taken a lenient approach by only imposing a monetary penalty.

This case matters because it reinforces that parties must be honest and transparent with courts, and concealment of material facts can attract penalties or contempt proceedings.

title: Yasmeen Rehmat V. Secretary Balochistan Public Serivce Commission and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involves Yasmeen Rehmat, who applied for the post of Lecturer in Botany (Female, BPS-17) through the Balochistan Public Service Commission. She scored well in the written test and claimed to hold higher academic qualifications, including a PhD, which under the job advertisement should have earned her extra marks and preference. When the results were announced, she was not selected, and she believed a less qualified candidate had been chosen instead through unfair or biased selection.

She filed a petition before the Balochistan High Court asking it to declare the selection process illegal, direct authorities to produce written test papers for comparison, and stop the issuance of an appointment order until the matter was resolved.

However, the court found a critical flaw in her case: she never identified the actual candidate who had been selected for the post. The person listed as respondent No.4 in her petition was simply described as "successful candidate," with no name given. Despite being given two opportunities to amend her petition and name the selected candidate, her lawyer could not do so.

Because of this, the court ruled that the petition was vague, did not disclose a proper legal claim against anyone, and was therefore not maintainable. The court dismissed the case without examining its merits, but allowed Rehmat to file a fresh challenge later if she discovers the selected candidate's identity. This case highlights the importance of properly naming all necessary parties in legal challenges to administrative decisions.

title: Muhammad Saddique V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal revision petition filed by Muhammad Siddique challenging his conviction for kidnapping and sodomy. According to the prosecution, in June 2015, Siddique and a co-accused forcibly took a 12-year-old boy on a motorcycle from a market and brought him to a room near a fisheries pond, where they and another unidentified man sexually assaulted the child overnight before releasing him the next day. The boy's father filed a police report once his son returned home and explained what happened. Both the trial court and the appellate court had convicted Siddique and his co-accused under Pakistan's Penal Code sections dealing with kidnapping and unnatural offences (sodomy), sentencing them to prison terms and fines.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence and upheld the conviction. It found that the testimony of the father and the victim was consistent, detailed, and unshaken even after lengthy cross-examination, and was backed up by medical evidence confirming sexual assault. The court also addressed two common defense arguments: that a one-day delay in filing the police report should count against the case, and that testimony from a related witness (the father) should be less trusted. The court rejected both, ruling that such delays are natural given family embarrassment, and that a relative's testimony is credible unless there's proof of hostility or false motive. The court also confirmed that a victim's own credible testimony alone can be enough to convict in such cases. The petition was dismissed, and the conviction stood.

title: Muhammad Salah V. The State,
explainer:
Muhammad Salah was convicted by a trial court for murder and sentenced to life imprisonment after being accused, along with several co-accused, of shooting the complainant's brother Sachal during an alleged ambush on a road in 2012. The prosecution said the killing was motivated by an earlier declaration that the victim's family had committed "Siahkar" (a tribal honor-related accusation). Salah appealed his conviction, while the complainant separately sought a harsher sentence.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the accused. Reviewing the evidence, the judges found the two eyewitnesses, including the complainant himself, gave contradictory accounts on key details such as the road's condition, the distance from which shots were fired, the weapons used, and the reason for the alleged Siahkar declaration. The court also noted the prosecution withheld another witness without explanation, which allowed the court to presume that witness's testimony would have hurt the prosecution's case. Additionally, the recovery of the alleged murder weapon was suspiciously delayed by nearly two years, undermining its credibility, and medical evidence did not match the witnesses' account.

The court reaffirmed that weapon recovery alone cannot prove guilt and that any genuine doubt in a criminal case must benefit the accused. Because the prosecution's evidence was inconsistent and unreliable, the appeal was allowed, the conviction was set aside, and the accused was acquitted, while the complainant's request for a harsher sentence was rejected.

title: Saddam Hussain and another V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved a violent incident in which several accused allegedly opened fire with Kalashnikovs, killing the complainant's brother and a police official, and injuring others. The prosecution relied on eyewitnesses who were relatives of the deceased. One accused was convicted and sentenced by the trial court, while others were acquitted based on similar evidence; the case reached the Balochistan High Court through appeals and a revision petition.

The High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's case. The eyewitnesses gave contradictory statements at different stages, tried to hide the real motive (a prior enmity involving earlier killings between the two families), and failed to convincingly prove they were actually present at the scene. The FIR was delayed by two days without proper explanation, and investigation activities had suspiciously begun before the FIR was even registered. A key witness whose name appeared in the police record was never produced in court, and the court held that withholding this evidence created a presumption it would have been unfavorable to the prosecution. The court also noted it made no logical sense that the accused would kill two people in front of witnesses but spare those very witnesses.

Given these doubts, the court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and acquitted the appellant, setting aside his conviction. The judgment reinforces important principles: FIRs cannot be arbitrarily delayed, and withholding key witnesses or evidence works against the prosecution, with any reasonable doubt benefiting the accused.

title: Dur Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:

The prosecution's case rested mainly on a dying declaration recorded by police who arrived at the scene, supported by testimony from a police patrol member and the investigating officer.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found the prosecution's evidence riddled with contradictions. The dying declaration gave no motive for the killings. More importantly, the victim's widow, who was present during the attack, directly contradicted the police version, testifying that the actual attackers were the accused's absconding sons, not Dur Muhammad himself, and she exonerated him even under cross-examination. Another witness, the deceased woman's sister, similarly refused to support the prosecution and also cleared the accused. The court found it illogical that if the accused truly wanted to kill his relatives, he would leave eyewitnesses alive to testify against him. The accused's own explanation, that the real motive involved a dispute over an alleged irregular marital relationship, was found more plausible than the prosecution's unproven theory.

Concluding that the motive and events surrounding the killing remained unclear and unproven, the court held that the prosecution failed to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. title: Allah Dad V. Muhammad Nawaz and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute over a 3,000 square foot plot of land in Jaffarabad district, Balochistan. The petitioner, Allah Dad, claimed he had bought the land from one of the respondents and had it properly recorded in his name through official mutation records. He said the other respondents later tried to interfere with his ownership by fraudulently manipulating land records to claim a much larger portion of land for themselves. Allah Dad had filed an earlier lawsuit over this same interference, but withdrew it with court permission to file a fresh suit later. When the respondents again interfered with his construction plans on the land, he filed the present suit.

The trial court ruled in his favor, but the appellate court reversed that decision and dismissed his suit, partly on the basis that his claim was time-barred due to the earlier withdrawn lawsuit.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed with the appellate court. It found that the evidence, including admissions by the respondents themselves and revenue records, clearly supported Allah Dad's ownership claim. The court also held that since the interference by the respondents resumed after a period of peace following the earlier withdrawal, a fresh cause of action had arisen, meaning the case was not barred by limitation. The High Court ruled that the appellate court's judgment was flawed due to misreading of evidence, restored the trial court's original decision, and decreed the suit in favor of Allah Dad for the 3,000 square feet of land. This case illustrates how courts assess evidence and limitation issues in property ownership disputes.

title: Ghulam Ali V. Muhammad Azeem,
explainer:
This case involved a murder trial where the complainant, Ghulam Ali, asked the Balochistan High Court to move the proceedings from the Sessions Court in Sibi to a court in Dera Murad Jamali or Dera Allah Yar. His brother had been killed, and an FIR was registered against several accused persons, one of whom was arrested and put on trial. Ghulam Ali argued that he and his key eyewitnesses lived far away in Dera Murad Jamali, while the accused belonged to Sibi and were influential and had threatened the witnesses, making them afraid to travel to Sibi to testify. He backed this up with sworn affidavits from the witnesses describing these threats. The accused side denied any threats were made and argued the request was just a tactic to delay the trial, also claiming it was an unwitnessed murder with no direct evidence.

The court examined the law under section 526 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows transfer of a case when it serves the convenience and security of parties or witnesses. Since the affidavits describing threats were never challenged or rebutted by the other side, the judge treated them as reliable. Finding that the witnesses genuinely feared for their safety in appearing at Sibi, the High Court allowed the application and ordered the case transferred to the court at Dera Murad Jamali. This shows how courts can prioritize witness safety and willingness to testify over convenience of the original venue, which is important for ensuring fair trials in cases involving intimidation.

title: Khalil Ullah V. Mst. Sahib Bibi and another,
explainer:

She disputed this, alleging abduction and forced marriage. The Family Court dismissed his suit, and he appealed to a body called Majlis-e-Shoora at Loralai, which partly allowed his appeal and sent the case back to the Family Court for fresh proceedings.

The husband then challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that Majlis-e-Shoora had no legal authority to hear the appeal in the first place. He pointed out that under the Balochistan Family Courts Act, 1964, a special law governing family disputes, appeals against Family Court decisions must go to the District Judge, not to Majlis-e-Shoora.

The High Court agreed with him. It examined Section 14 of the Family Courts Act and confirmed that appeals from Family Court decrees are meant to go to the District Judge (or High Court in certain cases), and that Majlis-e-Shoora had no jurisdiction to entertain such appeals at all. Since Majlis-e-Shoora lacked authority, its order was declared void from the outset.

The High Court set aside Majlis-e-Shoora's order and directed it to return the appeal file to the husband, allowing him to file his appeal before the correct court. title: Noor Muhammad V. Special Judge Anti-Terrorism Court, Khuzdar and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved a murder in Mastung, where the victim was found shot and killed, and later it emerged that a woman was also killed in the same incident. Several accused were granted pre-arrest bail, and the complainant sought to have that bail cancelled. During the trial, four prosecution witnesses who had earlier given statements to police implicating the accused changed their testimony in court, essentially retracting what they had said. The complainant and the prosecutor asked the trial court to formally declare these witnesses hostile, so they could be cross-examined, but the trial court refused. The complainant also filed an application asking the court to recall these witnesses and summon others, arguing their testimony was crucial for a fair decision, but this too was rejected without any explanation.

The Balochistan High Court found that refusing these requests, especially without giving reasons, harmed the prosecution's case and was unfair. The court noted the witnesses' original statements were significant and that denying cross-examination opportunity was prejudicial. It partly allowed the petitions, set aside the trial court's orders, and sent the case back with directions to treat the recall application as still pending, allowing the prosecution the chance to cross-examine the witnesses who had changed their statements.

This decision matters because it reinforces the principle that courts must give reasons when denying such applications and must protect a party's right to challenge witnesses who reverse their statements, ensuring a fairer trial process.

title: Riaz Ahmed and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against convictions for murder. Two brothers had allegedly entered the complainant's house, where one held the victim while the other shot him in the face, killing him. The complainant, the victim's brother, was the only eyewitness. The trial court convicted the accused under section 302(b) read with 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder with common intention) and sentenced them to 25 years imprisonment plus compensation to the victim's family. The convicted men appealed, arguing the sole witness was unreliable because he was the victim's brother and therefore biased, that no weapon was recovered, and that the evidence had inconsistencies. Separately, the complainant filed a petition asking for harsher sentences.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the convictions and dismissed both the appeal and the request for enhanced sentences. The court held that being related to the victim does not automatically make a witness unreliable if the testimony is otherwise consistent and convincing. It also noted that the FIR was filed promptly, within two hours of the incident, which undercut any suggestion that the accusation was fabricated after deliberation. The lack of a recovered weapon was not fatal to the case, since the accused had months to dispose of it before arrest. The absence of a proven motive also did not weaken the prosecution's case. This judgment reinforces principles about evaluating eyewitness credibility and the limited weight given to missing physical evidence when other proof is strong.

title: Allah Bakhsh and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved three appeals arising from a violent incident in which a group of accused persons opened indiscriminate firing, killing the complainant's son and wounding his friend and a woman who was related to some of the accused. The accused were charged with murder, attempted murder, rioting, and related offenses under the Pakistan Penal Code. The trial had originally started in an anti-terrorism court before being transferred to a regular criminal court.

The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimony, including the injured woman herself, who described how the accused came to her house, accused her of misconduct, and shot her. Medical evidence confirmed the deceased died from multiple gunshot wounds and corroborated the injuries described by witnesses.

The defence argued the witnesses were "interested" because they were related to the accused, but the court rejected this, holding that relationship alone does not discredit a witness unless there is proof of prior enmity or motive to falsely implicate someone. The court found it especially credible that female witnesses, despite social pressures in a male-dominated society, came forward against their own relatives, making their testimony highly reliable.

The court upheld the convictions and dismissed the appeals, but noted a discrepancy: the same accused had received different sentences (ten years versus five years) under Section 324 for the same evidence in separate judgments. To remove this unfairness, the court reduced the harsher sentence to match the lighter one, ensuring consistent treatment for identical conduct.

This case is about an appeal against an acquittal in a murder case. Muhammad Jan had filed a complaint alleging that his brother-in-law, Muhammad Wazir, poisoned his sister, Hikmat Bibi, to death. He claimed that the accused used to beat and mistreat his sister during their marriage, and that shortly before her death she had complained about this mistreatment. When she was reported unwell, her family rushed to her home and found her dead, after which they filed a case against her husband under Section 302 of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder).

At trial, the prosecution presented nine witnesses, including relatives of the deceased, a medical officer, and investigating officers. However, the trial court acquitted the accused, finding the evidence insufficient. The complainant then appealed this acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the appeal, agreeing with the trial court's decision. It found that none of the witnesses had actually seen the crime occur; their testimony was based on assumptions about the accused's past behavior rather than direct evidence. Crucially, there was no medical or forensic evidence, such as a medico-legal certificate or chemical examination report, confirming poisoning or an unnatural death. The court emphasized that convictions cannot rest on suspicion alone and that acquittals carry a strong presumption of innocence, which should not be overturned unless the original decision was clearly unreasonable or unsupported by evidence. title: Quetta Metropolitan Corporation through Administrator (Successor of Administrator of Chilatan Town), Quetta V. Abdul Malik and 39 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over roadside cabins (khokhas) near the PWD/AG Office on Sariab Road, Quetta. A group of cabin owners claimed they had installed their stalls in 1984-85 with permission from the then Quetta Municipal Corporation and had been paying taxes ever since. Their cabins were destroyed during riots following the 2006 assassination of Nawab Akbar Bugti, after which the government allowed them to reinstall the cabins at their original locations. Later, following changes in the local government system, the Municipal Administration ordered them to remove the cabins. The cabin owners sued for a declaration and permanent injunction to stop this. The trial court decreed in their favor simply because the Tehsil Municipal Administration's written statement admitted their claims, without framing any legal issues or examining evidence. This decision was upheld on appeal.

The Quetta Metropolitan Corporation challenged this in the High Court, arguing there was no real permission on record for the cabins, that the case involved public interest since the disputed area was actually a footpath used by pedestrians, and that the municipal officer may have colluded with the cabin owners.

The High Court agreed, finding the lower courts had wrongly decided the case based only on an admission, without properly examining evidence or considering the public importance of the matter. It set aside the earlier judgments and sent the case back to the trial court, directing it to allow both sides to file proper written statements, frame issues, and decide the case after recording actual evidence.

title: Syed Aminullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by Syed Aminullah, who was accused in a case involving cheating, forgery, and violations of the Drugs Act for allegedly selling and stocking unlicensed, unregistered, and expired drugs. He had already been denied bail twice before, both by the trial court and by the High Court, on the merits of the case.

This time, he sought bail on different grounds: he had been in jail for about 18 months, but the trial had barely progressed, with only six witnesses examined out of many. The delay was partly because the position of Chairman of the Drugs Court, the judge meant to hear the case, was vacant, and no one had been appointed to fill it. He also argued that his co-accused in the same case had already been granted bail, so he should be treated the same way for consistency.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with him. It held that an accused cannot be kept in jail indefinitely while the trial drags on due to reasons beyond his control, especially when there is no clarity on when the case will be concluded. The court also emphasized that treating co-accused persons differently in similar circumstances would be unfair. As a result, the court ordered that Aminullah be released on bail.

This case matters because it reinforces the principle that prolonged pretrial detention without progress in the trial can violate an accused person's right to a timely and fair process, and that courts must apply bail decisions consistently among co-accused in similar situations.

title: Abdullah and 5 others V. Raheem Khan,

After Abdul Ghafoor died in 1995, leaving behind inherited property to be distributed among his legal heirs under Islamic law, various heirs filed lawsuits against each other. Some family members (the petitioners) later challenged these earlier decrees, filing applications under Section 12(2) of the Civil Procedure Code, which allows a decree to be set aside if it was obtained through fraud. They claimed that an attorney who represented some of them had given consent to the settlement without proper authorization, that facts were concealed from the courts, and that certain heirs had been left out of the proceedings entirely, making the whole process fraudulent.

The lower appellate court rejected these applications, and the matter came before the Balochistan High Court on revision petitions.

The High Court held that the lower courts had correctly examined and decided the fraud allegations. It found no evidence of actual fraud or misrepresentation in how the judgments and decrees were obtained. title: Muhammad Sadiq V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a serious criminal dispute arising from cross FIRs, meaning both sides had filed complaints against each other over the same incident. The complainant alleged that the petitioner, Muhammad Sadiq, along with associates, had demanded extortion money, then intercepted vehicles, kidnapped a person, and engaged in firing that caused injuries and a death. The petitioner denied involvement, claiming he was in Lahore at the time, and presented evidence, including CCTV footage, to support this alibi.

During investigation, the police officer accepted this alibi evidence and discharged the petitioner from the case under Section 169 of the Criminal Procedure Code, placing his name in a column of the police report reserved for persons not being sent to trial. Despite this, the trial court issued summons requiring the petitioner to appear in court. The petitioner challenged this, arguing the trial court had overstepped by overriding the investigating officer's decision.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition, ruling that investigating officers only have authority to assess whether there is enough evidence to justify prosecution, not to weigh defence evidence like alibi claims against prosecution evidence. That job belongs solely to the trial court, which can evaluate both sides through proper judicial process, including cross-examination. The court noted the petitioner could still seek acquittal later if the trial court found the prosecution's case weak.

This ruling clarifies the limited role of police in deciding guilt versus the trial court's broader authority to evaluate conflicting evidence before trial.

title: Muhammad Haseen Khan Afridi V. National Accountability Bureau thrugh Director General and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a bail petition filed by Muhammad Haseen Khan Afridi, a former District Food Controller, who was accused of embezzling over 100,000 bags of wheat worth around Rs. 292 million along with other officials, in a reference filed by the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) under Pakistan's accountability laws.

The petitioner had been in jail since November 2015, roughly two and a half years, without his trial being concluded. Out of thirty prosecution witnesses, only seventeen had been examined. He had previously sought bail twice from the High Court and once from the Supreme Court, all without success, though the Supreme Court had directed the trial court to finish the case within six months and proceed daily. This direction was not followed.

The Balochistan High Court held that the prolonged delay in concluding the trial, despite the Supreme Court's clear directions, violated the petitioner's fundamental right to a speedy and fair trial. The court emphasized that no accused, regardless of how serious the alleged crime, should be kept in jail indefinitely while trial proceedings stall, since such delay amounts to abuse of the legal process. Citing earlier Supreme Court precedents, the court ruled that unreasonable delay alone can justify granting bail. Accordingly, the court granted bail to the petitioner.

This judgment matters because it reinforces the principle that the right to a speedy trial is a constitutional protection, and that prolonged pretrial detention without progress in a case cannot be justified even in serious corruption cases.

title: Haleem V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about the murder of Muhammad Hayat, who was fatally shot when men knocked on his door at night. His cousin, who was also present and survived, filed a police report identifying Haleem as the shooter, along with two others, Abdul Ghaffar (who fled and was declared a proclaimed offender) and Ikram. A trial court convicted both Haleem and Ikram for murder under Pakistan's Penal Code, sentencing them to life imprisonment. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence carefully, including eyewitness testimony from two people present in the house, the promptness of the police report, and forensic evidence linking a recovered Kalashnikov rifle to bullet casings from the scene. The court found this evidence credible and sufficient to prove Haleem's guilt beyond doubt, even though the witnesses were relatives of the victim, since their testimony was consistent and trustworthy. The court upheld Haleem's conviction and life sentence.

However, the court found that while Ikram was present at the scene, there was no evidence he participated in the shooting or shared a common intention to kill. Since the law requires proof of active participation or shared criminal intent to convict someone as an accomplice, the court acquitted Ikram, ruling that merely being present as a bystander was not enough for conviction.

This case illustrates how courts weigh eyewitness credibility, forensic evidence, and the legal requirement of proving individual intent before convicting someone as a participant in a crime, even when they were present during the incident

title: Muhammad Naseem and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved two brothers, Muhammad Naseem and Muhammad Qasim, who were convicted of murder under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code for killing a man named Haji Nizam. The trial court had sentenced them to life imprisonment and ordered them to pay compensation to the victim's family. The convicts appealed, while the complainant separately sought a harsher sentence through a revision petition.

While these proceedings were pending before the Balochistan High Court, the accused reached a compromise with the deceased's family, who agreed to forgive them. Since murder under Tazir (discretionary punishment, as opposed to Qisas) is a compoundable offence under the law, the court sent the compromise documents back to the trial court to verify their authenticity. The deceased left behind a widow and seven children, most of whom were minors. The trial court recorded statements from the widow, the complainant, and the two adult children, all of whom confirmed they had genuinely and voluntarily pardoned the accused and waived their right to Diyat (blood money).

Satisfied that the compromise was genuine, the High Court accepted it under section 345(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, but ruled that Diyat must still be paid on behalf of the minor children who could not legally waive their share. Consequently, the court set aside the conviction and life sentence, acquitting the accused. This case illustrates how Pakistani law allows victims' families to pardon offenders in murder cases while still protecting the financial rights of minor heirs.

title: State through Special Public Prosecutor, Anti-Corruption V. Allah Dina,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by the state against the acquittal of Allah Dina, a Patwari (land record official), who was accused of corruption. The allegation was that while a former district official, Syed Aurangzaib Shah, was in judicial custody facing corruption cases, Allah Dina helped him illegally transfer his land to his sister through a mutation (land transfer record) dated 22 September 2008, falsely showing Aurangzaib Shah as present before revenue authorities on that date, even though jail records showed he was in custody from 8 to 30 September 2008.

The trial court had acquitted Allah Dina, and the state challenged this acquittal before the Balochistan High Court. On examining the record, the High Court found inconsistencies in the prosecution's case: although the mutation document was dated 22 September 2008, its contents showed it was actually prepared on 22 August 2008 and only signed and attested by the parties before the Naib Tehsildar on 14 October 2008, a date when Aurangzaib Shah was out on bail, not in custody. This meant the alleged fraudulent transfer may actually have occurred legitimately after his release, not during his detention as claimed.

Finding no solid evidence connecting Allah Dina to any criminal wrongdoing, the High Court upheld the acquittal and dismissed the state's appeal. The case highlights how careful scrutiny of documentary evidence and dates is essential in corruption prosecutions, and that convictions cannot rest on assumptions when the record itself contradicts the prosecution's

title: Abdul Baqi and another V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case is about a murder that took place inside a locked office in Quetta, where the accused was convicted based on circumstantial evidence, since no one witnessed the killing directly. The victim, Ameer Bacha, was found shot dead in his office. His nephew, the complainant, filed a case against unknown persons, and police investigation later led to the arrest of Abdul Baqi, who reportedly gave an extra-judicial confession while in custody, followed by police recovering the murder weapon and matching bullet casings to the crime.

The trial court convicted Abdul Baqi under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code for qatl-i-amd (intentional murder) and sentenced him to life imprisonment. Two things then happened: the convict appealed his conviction, arguing the confession was inadmissible and unsupported by real evidence, while the complainant filed a separate petition asking the court to increase the sentence to death.

The Balochistan High Court examined the extra-judicial confession, the recovery of the weapon, matching forensic evidence, and established motive, and found the prosecution had built a solid circumstantial case even though the crime was unwitnessed. The court upheld the life sentence, ruling that the lack of direct eyewitnesses was itself a mitigating factor that justified life imprisonment rather than execution. It therefore dismissed the complainant's request for a harsher sentence.

This case is significant because it clarifies how Pakistani courts evaluate extra-judicial confessions and circumstantial evidence in murder cases

title: Ghulam Muhammad V. Obaid-Ur-Rehman and 2 others,
explainer:
This is a criminal acquittal appeal decided by the Balochistan High Court concerning the killing of a man named Naqeebullah, who was shot while working in his agricultural field. The complainant, his father, had accused four men, including the alleged shooter Abdul Shakoor, of murder and attempted murder. Two of the accused, Obaid-ur-Rehman and Ameen Ullah, were acquitted by the trial court, while the main alleged shooter and another accused remained fugitives declared proclaimed offenders. The complainant appealed against this acquittal.

The High Court examined the evidence and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. The complainant himself faltered under cross-examination, and the supposed eyewitnesses contradicted each other, contradicted the complainant, and were even contradicted by the medical evidence. Crucially, none of the witnesses accused Obaid-ur-Rehman or Ameen Ullah of actually doing anything violent, they were merely present at the scene alongside the absconding main suspect. The court held that mere presence, without evidence of a shared intention or plan to commit murder, is not enough to convict someone of the crime.

The court reaffirmed the well-established legal principle that an acquittal carries a "double presumption of innocence," meaning appellate courts should not interfere unless the original decision was clearly arbitrary or unsupported by evidence. Finding no such flaw, the High Court upheld the acquittal, dismissing the appeal.

title: Muhammad Anwar and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about whether a violent incident stemming from a family property dispute should be tried as an act of terrorism or as an ordinary criminal offense. Two accused, Muhammad Anwar and another, were charged after a confrontation in which the complainant and his relatives were allegedly shot and stabbed by the petitioners, who were said to be armed with pistols and daggers. The case was initially registered under terrorism laws along with regular criminal charges of attempted murder and rioting. The Anti-Terrorism Court refused the accused's request to move the trial to an ordinary criminal court, so they challenged that refusal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the facts and found that the incident, while violent, arose from a personal dispute over ancestral property, not an attempt to spread fear among the general public. There was no evidence of aerial firing or any indication the attackers intended to terrorize the community at large. Since the core legal definition of terrorism requires actions meant to create fear and insecurity in society, and the complainant himself admitted the motive was a private property dispute, the court ruled that the case did not qualify as terrorism.

As a result, the High Court set aside the Anti-Terrorism Court's order and directed that the case be transferred to the Sessions Judge for trial as an ordinary criminal matter. This decision matters because it reinforces the principle that not every violent crime automatically qualifies as terrorism, and courts must carefully distinguish personal disputes from acts intended to terrorize the public.

title: Ghulam Habib V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murdering his own son and injuring his wife. According to the prosecution, the accused, Ghulam Habib, became enraged when his infant daughter cried and his wife could not quiet her. When his elder son entered the room, the accused pulled out a pistol and fired, wounding his wife in the arm and killing his son on the spot. He was tried and convicted by a Sessions Court in Pishin, sentenced to life imprisonment for murder along with additional punishment and compensation for the injury caused to his wife. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the evidence was misread, that a father could not be expected to kill his own son, and that his confession was obtained through coercion.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It held that the wife's testimony, given as both an eyewitness and an injured victim, was highly credible, especially since it made no sense that she would falsely accuse her own husband while letting the real killer of her son go free. Her account matched medical evidence, and the accused's confession before a magistrate was found to be voluntary, given without pressure, and driven by his own remorse. The recovered pistol further supported the case. Finding no merit in the appeal, the court upheld the conviction and dismissed it.

The case illustrates how courts evaluate the credibility of a sole eyewitness, particularly a family member, and how confessions and physical evidence are weighed together in murder trials.

The killing happened at night when armed men entered the victim's house; the victim's wife and daughter witnessed the attack, along with a neighbor. The trial court in Kalat convicted the appellant under sections dealing with murder, outraging a woman's modesty, house-trespass, and criminal force, sentencing him to death for the murder along with additional prison terms and fines for the other offences. The case was sent to the Balochistan High Court both as an appeal by the convict and as a mandatory reference to confirm or overturn the death sentence.

The High Court examined the evidence closely, including eyewitness testimony from the victim's widow and daughter, a neighbor's identification, recovery of the murder weapon based on the accused's own disclosure, and a confession he gave to a magistrate. The court found the witnesses credible and consistent, and rejected the defense's alibi claim, upholding the conviction.

However, the court reduced the death sentence to life imprisonment. It reasoned that multiple armed attackers had fired indiscriminately, the victim was hit by only two bullets, and it could not be established with certainty whose bullet actually caused the death—making the death penalty inappropriate. The conviction and other sentences, along with compensation to the victim's family, were upheld. This case illustrates how courts may maintain guilt findings while adjusting punishment when uncertainty exists about individual responsibility in a group attack.
