title: The Collector of Customs, through Additional Collector of Customs and others V. Akhtar Hussain and others,
explainer:
This case involved six trucks seized by Pakistan Customs authorities, allegedly used to smuggle Iranian diesel across the border, along with one truck (LEZ-7771) confiscated separately for having a tampered chassis number. Customs officials claimed drivers fled when confronted, and armed men later tried to tow away one stalled truck during an exchange of gunfire, but the culprits also escaped. Customs seized about 123,000 liters of smuggled diesel and the vehicles, and an Adjudicating Officer confiscated the trucks and fined the registered owners Rs. 50,000 each.

The truck owners appealed, and the Customs Appellate Tribunal ruled in their favor, ordering the trucks released upon payment of a 20% redemption fine and reducing the personal penalty to Rs. 20,000. The Collector of Customs then challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the Tribunal's decision and dismissed the Customs Department's references. It found that while smuggling by drivers or cleaners may have occurred, the prosecution failed to prove that the truck owners themselves were involved in or even aware of the smuggling activity. Since there was no evidence linking the owners to the crime, the Court held that confiscating their property outright was not justified, and only penalizing them with a reduced fine plus redemption fee was fair. This case highlights an important principle: vehicle owners cannot be punished for crimes committed by drivers or employees without proof of their knowledge or involvement.

title: Muhammad Naeem Khan V. Government of Balochistan Through Secretary and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a retired government employee, Muhammad Naeem Khan, who worked at the Balochistan Coastal Development Authority as an Accounts Officer (BPS-18). He sought promotion and, after his retirement in August 2013, the Authority's Governing Body approved promoting him retroactively to Director Planning (BPS-19) and then upgraded that post to BPS-20, with effect from dates before his retirement. He was also given a six-month contract job after retiring, during which he was paid BPS-20 salary. However, when he later sought arrears of salary and pension based on this higher grade, the Finance Department rejected his claim, stating no policy allowed promotions after retirement or upgrading posts during a ban on such upgrades.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed his petition. It found that the Director General's order promoting him and upgrading his post appeared illegal and without lawful authority, since there was no policy permitting promotion two weeks after retirement, there was an existing ban on upgrading posts, and the proper procedure had not been followed by the Governing Body when granting the promotion.

This case matters because it clarifies that retrospective promotions and post upgrades granted after an employee's retirement, without following proper procedure or policy, cannot be used to claim higher pension or salary benefits, reinforcing the importance of due process in civil service promotions.

title: Nabi Bakhsh V. The State,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with whether a person could face two separate FIRs (police cases) arising from the same incident, or whether that amounted to illegal double punishment.

The background: customs officials stopped a truck for checking and found smuggled foreign goods inside it. Before that, the petitioners arrived, stopped officials from checking the truck, abused and beat them, and blocked the road with a large crowd. Two FIRs were registered: one under the Customs Act for the smuggled goods found in the truck, and a second one under the Pakistan Penal Code for obstructing officials, assault, and rioting. The petitioners asked the court to quash the second FIR, arguing that being prosecuted twice over the same episode violated the constitutional protection against double jeopardy and related legal provisions.

The court rejected this argument. It held that the two FIRs covered different offences under two separate laws, each with its own distinct ingredients, procedure, and forum, even though both arose from the same overall incident. The smuggling offence was distinct from the offence of assaulting officials and obstructing their duty. The rule against double jeopardy only prevents someone from being tried twice for the exact same offence, not from being tried separately for different offences arising from connected facts. The petition was dismissed for lacking merit.

This case clarifies that people cannot escape prosecution under one law simply because they are also being prosecuted under another law for related but legally distinct conduct arising from the same event.

title: Muhammad Ibrahim V. Mera Jan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a property dispute in Quetta. Muhammad Ibrahim claimed he owned a house, which he had purchased and taken possession of. He said that while he was ill and away, another man, Mera Jan, along with associates, broke the locks and illegally occupied the house. Ibrahim filed a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, a law meant to protect property owners from forcible takeover by land grabbers.

However, when the police (SHO) investigated, they found the house was actually in the possession of a different person, Muhammad Azeem, who had rented it out to yet another individual. Ibrahim had not even named these two men as parties in his complaint. The trial court also found that there was a broader business dispute involving property, cash, and vehicles between Ibrahim, Mera Jan, and Azeem, and that civil court proceedings over the property were already ongoing. The trial court dismissed the complaint, ruling it was really a civil dispute, not a criminal case of illegal dispossession.

The Balochistan High Court agreed. It held that the case involved disputed facts requiring detailed evidence and inquiry, which is better suited to a civil court than to the special, fast-track remedy under the Illegal Dispossession Act. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the judge ruled that courts should not use extraordinary jurisdiction to resolve complicated factual disputes. The revision petition was dismissed, meaning Ibrahim must pursue his claim through ordinary civil litigation instead.

title: Suleman Shah V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about Suleman Shah, who was accused, along with two others, of murdering two people, Haji Sarwar and his son Asadullah, in a 2011 incident in Chaman, Balochistan. The dispute reportedly began when the deceased had stopped the accused party from throwing garbage in the street. According to the First Information Report, the actual shooting was carried out by the two co-accused, not by Suleman Shah, and the FIR did not even say whether he was carrying a weapon. He remained absconding for more than nine years before being arrested, after which he applied for bail.

The Balochistan High Court granted him bail. It reasoned that simply being present at the scene of a crime does not make someone guilty unless the prosecution shows he shared a common intention with the actual killers or helped them in some way. Since no specific violent act was attributed to him in the FIR, and the claim that he was armed and blocked the victims only appeared in witness statements recorded nine years later, the court found this raised serious doubts requiring further inquiry at trial. The court also held that long absconsion alone does not disqualify someone from bail if they otherwise have a strong case on merits.

This decision reinforces the principle that mere presence near a crime scene, without a clear active role, does not justify continued detention, and that bail decisions should focus on the strength of the evidence rather than an accused's absconsion alone.

title: Muhammad Zeeshan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a police constable, Muhammad Zeeshan, who had been issued an official Kalashnikov rifle for his duties. After being transferred to a different section, he did not immediately deposit the weapon back with the department. He later reported to police that his house had been broken into and the rifle, along with cash and jewelry, was stolen. However, investigation found no clear signs of a break-in, and a departmental inquiry concluded that he had actually embezzled the weapon and filed a false theft report to cover it up. Based on this, trial and appellate courts convicted him under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with giving false information to police, making a false charge, and criminal breach of trust by a public servant, sentencing him to prison terms and a fine.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the case and found the prosecution's theory was built on assumptions rather than solid evidence. It noted that both sides could be blamed for negligence, the constable for not returning the weapon promptly, and the department for not properly collecting it during his transfer. Importantly, the court held that since the constable himself reported the missing weapon to police, this showed he had no dishonest intent to embezzle it. Finding no proof of criminal intent, the court accepted his petition, set aside the lower courts' convictions, and acquitted him.

The case matters because it reinforces that criminal convictions require actual evidence of wrongful intent, not mere suspicion or administrative lapses.

title: Abdul Khaliq and 6 others V. Muhammad Anwar Nasir and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over inherited property in Loralai, Balochistan. The plaintiffs (applicants) had filed a civil suit in 2018 seeking their share of property left by their late maternal grandfather, which was in the possession of the defendants (respondents). While that suit was still pending, the plaintiffs asked the High Court to transfer the case to a different court, arguing that the defendants had become hostile toward them, had physically attacked their maternal aunt in December 2019, and were threatening them with violence if they pursued their legal claim.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the transfer request. It found that the criminal incident described was actually a separate matter between the defendants and the aunt, and that the plaintiffs were improperly trying to link this unrelated criminal incident to their civil case to gain an advantage and cause inconvenience to the defendants. The court noted the parties lived close to each other with no history of prior enmity, and that a criminal case had already been registered and was proceeding through the proper channels. It also pointed out that the plaintiffs' lawyer was himself one of the plaintiffs, so he could simply arrange another advocate if needed.

The court held that under Section 24 of the Civil Procedure Code, a party must show genuine, sufficient cause to transfer a case, and vague or opportunistic claims are not enough. Allowing such transfers without real justification would cause delays and unfairness to the other side. The application was therefore dismissed.

title: Muhammad Ibrahim V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of stealing electricity in Quetta. Officials from the electricity company (QESCO) and the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) raided his ice factory and accused him of illegally drawing power directly from a transformer to run his tube-well and service station, and of swapping in a larger unauthorized transformer. Based on an FIR filed by a QESCO official with the FIA, the trial court convicted him under section 462-K of the Pakistan Penal Code, sentencing him to time already served plus a fine.

On appeal, his lawyer argued that the entire prosecution was invalid because the law dealing with electricity theft offenses, specifically section 462-O of the Penal Code, requires a special procedure: courts cannot take up such cases based on an ordinary police-style FIR. Instead, a formal written complaint must be filed by a specifically authorized government or power-company officer of a certain rank, with documented reasons and full details of the offense. This requirement overrides the normal criminal procedure code.

The Balochistan High Court agreed, relying on a Supreme Court precedent, and found that since the case began with an FIR rather than the legally required complaint, the trial court never had proper authority to hear it in the first place. As a result, the entire proceeding was declared invalid, and the appellant's conviction was overturned.

The case highlights that when a law sets out a specific mandatory procedure for prosecution, skipping that procedure can void the whole case, regardless of the evidence involved.

title: Muhammad Nabi V. Bibi Malika,
explainer:
This case involved a civil dispute where a woman sued a man for recovery of money, roughly Rs. 245,000 plus monthly rent, related to a mortgage loan. When the defendant failed to appear in court, proceedings went ahead without him (ex parte), and after the plaintiff presented her evidence, the trial court ruled in her favor. The defendant later tried to have this decision set aside, arguing he was never properly notified of the case, but both the trial court and the appellate court rejected his request and upheld the judgment against him.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed with the lower courts. It found that the notices sent to the defendant were never actually delivered to him, and the court simply resorted to publishing a notice in a newspaper without properly verifying whether he was deliberately avoiding service or whether his address was even correct. The court noted that the process server never reported that the defendant had refused or evaded service, and the trial court failed to ask for a fresh address before jumping to public notification. This meant the defendant was never truly given a chance to defend himself, violating his constitutional right to a fair trial and due process under Article 10-A.

As a result, the High Court set aside both lower court decisions and sent the case back to the trial court to be decided fresh, with proper notice given to both sides. The judgment emphasizes that courts must ensure genuine fairness in service of legal notices, rather than deciding cases on technical shortcuts, especially when someone's rights are at stake.

title: Eid Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal appeal filed by Eid Muhammad, who had been convicted under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, by a Sessions Judge in Mastung and sentenced to seven years imprisonment, along with fines and compensation. The complainant claimed Eid Muhammad had forcibly taken over his inherited agricultural land four years earlier and started cultivating it.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. The court explained that the Illegal Dispossession Act was specifically designed to target professional land grabbers, mafias, and organized groups who forcibly seize others' property, not ordinary civil disputes between individuals. The judges noted several problems with the case: the complainant never actually accused the appellant of being part of a land mafia or qabza group, he offered no explanation for waiting four years before complaining, and he never described how the alleged dispossession actually took place. The court found that the appellant had been in long-standing possession of the land, which suggested this was a private property dispute rather than criminal land-grabbing.

The court concluded that such disputes, including those involving inheritance claims or competing ownership documents, belong in civil courts, not under this special criminal law meant for combating organized land grabbing. As a result, the appeal was accepted and the conviction set aside.

This case matters because it clarifies the limited scope of the Illegal Dispossession Act, preventing its misuse in ordinary property disputes that should be resolved through civil litigation rather than criminal prosecution.

title: Asmatullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a prisoner named Asmatullah who was convicted separately in two different criminal cases arising from two FIRs registered at the same police station. In one case he was convicted under Section 392 of the Pakistan Penal Code (robbery) and sentenced to three years' imprisonment. In the other, he was convicted under Section 380 (theft in a building) and sentenced to one year's imprisonment. Both cases were tried side by side by the same magistrate, and his appeals against both convictions were dismissed. Asmatullah then asked the High Court to order that his two sentences run concurrently (at the same time) rather than one after the other (consecutively), which would significantly reduce his total time in prison.

The Balochistan High Court examined Sections 35, 397 and 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, which deal with sentencing for multiple offences and courts' powers to combine sentences. The judge explained that courts have broad authority, even at the revision stage, to direct that sentences from separate trials run concurrently rather than one after another. The court also noted the principle that when two reasonable interpretations of the law are possible, the one favoring the accused's liberty should be preferred. Based on this reasoning, the court accepted Asmatullah's petition and ordered that his sentences in both cases run concurrently, meaning he would serve the longer three-year sentence rather than both sentences added together.

title: Syed Zahir Shah and another V. Habibullah alias Sabo and others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of eleven men accused of abducting the son of the complainant, allegedly at gunpoint, in an incident said to have occurred in March 2017 in Balochistan. The complainant claimed the accused forcibly took his son away in a vehicle, and the boy's whereabouts remained unknown for some time. After trial, the accused were acquitted by the Judicial Magistrate, and the complainant challenged that acquittal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal, finding serious weaknesses in the prosecution's case. There was an unexplained twenty-five hour delay in filing the police report, suggesting the complaint may have been prepared after deliberation rather than reflecting immediate facts. The complainant's account contained contradictions and unexplained details about how he learned of the incident, and he failed to identify the accused in court despite naming them earlier. Key witnesses, including people who allegedly received the victim after his abduction, were never brought to testify, weakening the case further. Most strikingly, the alleged victim himself gave a court confession contradicting the abduction story entirely, effectively clearing the accused.

The court reaffirmed the principle that an acquittal gives the accused a "double presumption of innocence," meaning courts should not overturn such acquittals unless the original decision was clearly perverse or unsupported by evidence. Finding no such flaw, the High Court dismissed the appeal, meaning the acquittal stood and the accused remained free.

title: Gul Marjan V Deputy Commissioner Loralai,
explainer:
This case concerns a political activist, Gul Marjan, who took part in a peaceful procession organized after obtaining a No Objection Certificate from the district administration in Loralai. The Deputy Commissioner had initially granted permission for the gathering but abruptly cancelled it the next day without properly informing the organizers. The procession went ahead as planned, and FIRs (police cases) were registered against the petitioner alleging inflammatory speech and other offences. Separately, and without issuing any notice to the petitioner, the Deputy Commissioner ordered cancellation of his arms license, his and his family's CNICs and local certificates, and also had his bank account frozen.

The Balochistan High Court found these administrative actions to be unlawful. It held that the Deputy Commissioner had no authority to cancel documents issued by other bodies, the arms license issued by the Ministry of Interior, the CNIC issued by NADRA, or to freeze a bank account, and that doing so without notice violated the petitioner's fundamental rights. The court concluded these orders were passed carelessly, without proper judicial reasoning, and appeared motivated by malice rather than lawful authority.

The court allowed the petition, struck down the Deputy Commissioner's orders, and restored all the cancelled documents to their original status. The case highlights limits on administrative power and protects citizens from arbitrary punitive measures targeting their identity documents and property in response to political activity.

title: Tayyab Raza V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by a man convicted of sexually abusing minor girls in his neighborhood, including filming and photographing the abuse. He was charged with rape, sodomy, obscene acts, and criminal intimidation, and had been sentenced to death by the trial court, which also referred the case to the High Court for confirmation.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence carefully. It found that the testimonies of the child victims were consistent with each other, with their earlier statements to police, and with the accused's own confession before a magistrate. Medical examinations of the victims supported the allegations, and the accused was found medically capable of the acts. Crucially, forensic analysis of his phone, computer, and USB drive recovered during a police raid showed genuine, unedited photos and videos of him abusing minor girls, further confirming his guilt.

The court upheld his conviction, rejecting the appeal against guilt, since the defence could not find any real contradictions or motive for false accusation. However, it noted that the prosecution had not produced all named victims in court, including one major victim, and that some victims had stayed silent until the accused's arrest. Because of these gaps, the court ruled that a death sentence was not justified, and instead converted it to life imprisonment. This case highlights how courts balance strong evidence of guilt against procedural shortcomings when deciding the severity of punishment.

title: Abdul Ghaffar and others V. Shinko and others,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court, concerned a dispute over agricultural land in Zhob district. The plaintiffs claimed that decades earlier their elders had exchanged a piece of land with the father of some of the defendants, with possession changing hands accordingly. They alleged that two of the defendants, in collusion with revenue department staff, later fraudulently transferred the land into their own names using fake sale documents and mutation entries.

The trial court dismissed the suit, finding no fraud proven. However, the appellate court reversed this and decided in favor of the plaintiffs, prompting the defendants to file this revision petition before the High Court.

On review, the High Court found that despite producing eleven witnesses, the plaintiffs failed to provide any concrete oral or documentary evidence proving that the mutation entries were fraudulently made. A key document they relied on, a 2006 agreement, was vague, did not specify property or mutation details, and made no mention of fraud. Witnesses were never even cross-examined on the fraud allegation. The Court also noted that neither the plaintiffs nor the original landowners had objected to the transfer for over 20 years.

Since the burden of proving fraud lay on the plaintiffs and they failed to meet it, the High Court set aside the appellate court's decision and restored the trial court's dismissal of the suit. The case highlights that mere allegations of fraud are insufficient in property disputes; they must be clearly proven with specific evidence.

title: Naseem Khan Kasi V. Station House Officer, Police Station Quetta and another,
explainer:
This case involved a businessman, Naseem Khan Kasi, who had launched a housing scheme called "Kasi Bahria Town" in Quetta after obtaining official approval. A dispute arose when revenue authorities and the Defence Housing Authority (DHA) accused him of encroaching on land and began demolishing his scheme's boundary walls, despite ongoing civil litigation over the matter, including a court order suspending the demolition notices. After the petitioner obtained a status-quo order from the High Court to stop the demolition, the complainant allegedly retaliated by filing a criminal case (FIR) against him, accusing him of interfering with government officials' duties and using abusive language.

The Balochistan High Court examined the FIR and found that the demolition was actually being carried out in the presence of police, making the allegation that the petitioner obstructed officials illogical. The court concluded that the FIR was essentially a criminal case arising out of what was fundamentally a civil property dispute, and that no real evidence existed to support a conviction. Using its inherent powers under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, the court quashed the FIR entirely.

This case matters because it reinforces that courts can step in to stop criminal cases from being misused as tools of pressure or harassment in what are really civil disputes, protecting citizens from abuse of the legal process even before trial.

title: Jannat Bibi and 2 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about the murder of a young man, Muhammad Jabbar, who worked as a night watchman in Quetta. He was shot dead in December 2018, but the initial police report named no suspects since the killers were unknown at the time. Twelve days later, the victim's father suddenly identified three people, Jannat Bibi, Muhammad Qasim, and Sardar Khan, as the killers through a supplementary statement. The trial court convicted them of murder with common intention and sentenced them to life imprisonment.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the convictions. The judges found the prosecution's case was built entirely on circumstantial evidence with no independent corroboration. They questioned why the accused weren't named immediately if witnesses truly recognized them, concluding the delayed identification looked like the result of guesswork and discussion rather than genuine knowledge. The court also distrusted the alleged extra-judicial confessions and formal confessional statements, noting a suspicious six-day gap before they were recorded, and pointing out the accused had complained of torture soon afterward, complaints the trial court had wrongly dismissed. Medical evidence, the judges noted, only confirms details like injury location, not who committed the crime.

Because of these unresolved doubts, the High Court acquitted all three appellants, reaffirming the basic principle that any genuine doubt in a criminal case must benefit the accused, and that convictions cannot rest on mere suspicion, however strong.

title: Dr. Shahid Amin V. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of National Food Security and Research and another,
explainer:
This case is about a government job selection process that was suddenly cancelled and restarted, apparently to favor different candidates. Dr. Shahid Amin applied for the post of Chief Executive Officer of the Livestock and Dairy Development Board (LDDB) after a public advertisement was issued in October 2020. Along with 22 other applicants, he went through a proper shortlisting process, was among 10 candidates selected for interview, and ultimately scored the highest marks, 87 out of 100, placing him first on the merit list. His name, along with two others, was recommended to the Board of Directors for final approval.

Before the Board could finalize the appointment, the petitioner learned through a newspaper report that the entire interview process had been scrapped and a new scrutiny committee would shortlist and interview candidates all over again. He also suspected that certain favored candidates were being added to benefit from this fresh process. The government argued that the Board had simply not approved the earlier recommendations.

The Balochistan High Court found that the decision to restart the process appeared to be motivated by bad faith, aimed at accommodating certain preferred candidates, since no genuine reasons were given for cancelling the original merit-based selection. The court accepted the petition, declared the fresh recruitment process illegal, and directed that the original selection process, in which the petitioner ranked first, be finalized instead. The judgment reinforces that merit-based public appointments cannot be arbitrarily reopened without valid justification.

title: Asfand Yar V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of killing two of his brothers and injuring his mother and another brother by shooting them inside their family home. The background was a family dispute: the accused had mistreated his wife, his brothers criticized him for it, he then divorced her, and he blamed his brothers and mother for the divorce, which led to the shooting.

The trial court had sentenced him to death, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence carefully, including eyewitness accounts from the complainant and two widows living in the house, medical reports confirming bullet injuries, forensic lab reports on blood-stained clothing, and the police inquest report. Although two injured witnesses later turned hostile and gave different accounts in court, the court found their testimony still partly supported the prosecution's version, and noted they likely changed their stories out of a mother's and brother's reluctance to see their remaining son/brother punished after already losing two family members. The court also rejected the defense argument that family witnesses were "interested" and unreliable, reasoning it was implausible that grieving relatives would falsely blame one of their own for such brutal killings.

The court upheld the conviction, finding the prosecution had proven its case. However, it reduced the sentence from death to life imprisonment, given the circumstances of the family dispute. The appeal was dismissed except for this modification in sentence.

This case matters because it shows how courts assess hostile witnesses, family testimony, and corroborating forensic evidence in serious criminal cases, while also exercising discretion in sentencing

title: Juma Khan and another V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murdering his wife after suspecting she was having an illicit relationship with another man. The complainant, the deceased woman's brother, along with another witness, saw the accused shoot her inside a relative's house during daylight hours. On the same day, the accused had also killed the man he suspected of the affair, for which he was separately tried and convicted, and that conviction was under a connected appeal.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness testimony, a confession recorded by a magistrate, an extra-judicial confession, and forensic evidence linking a recovered pistol to bullet casings found at the scene. The eyewitnesses were found credible since they were present at the scene and correctly identified the accused, and their accounts held up under cross-examination. The court found the confession voluntary, made after the magistrate ensured the accused was not pressured or coerced, and it also revealed the motive behind the killing.

The court held that an extra-judicial confession can be the sole basis for conviction if proven truthful and voluntary. It also treated the accused's conduct - his silence and failure to blame anyone else after his wife's death - as supporting evidence of guilt.

Finding no reasonable doubt, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction, reaffirming principles on evaluating eyewitness testimony, confessions, and circumstantial evidence in murder cases.

title: Mira Bakhsh V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal appeal before the Balochistan High Court. The appellant, Mira Bakhsh, had been convicted of murder, attempted murder, and causing injuries, along with others, in an attack rooted in old enmity between the families involved. A man's assistant was killed and his brother was injured during the incident.

The prosecution's case rested on eyewitness accounts from the complainant, his young brother (a minor witness aged 12-13), and the injured victim himself. The court examined whether this evidence was reliable enough to sustain the conviction. It found the minor witness competent to testify, since he answered questions correctly and showed no signs of being coached by adults, and his account matched the other witnesses. The injured witness's testimony was considered especially strong because injured witnesses are generally seen as credible and not likely to falsely implicate people while ignoring the real attackers. His account was also backed by medical evidence documenting his injuries. Additionally, the accused had led police to recover the weapon used in the crime, and forensic testing confirmed the pistol was functional and linked to shell casings found at the scene.

The court concluded that minor inconsistencies in testimony did not create real doubt about the accused's guilt, since the core accounts remained consistent. Finding no reasonable doubt, the High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction. The case reinforces how Pakistani courts weigh eyewitness, child, and injured-witness testimony alongside forensic evidence in serious violent crime cases.

After eleven consecutive missed hearings, the Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition for non-prosecution in November 2017.

More than three and a half years later, the petitioners applied to have the case restored, claiming they never knew about the dismissal because their lawyer failed to inform them, and that they only found out when the other side moved to enforce the decree against them.

The High Court rejected this request. It found the long, unexplained silence inexcusable, especially since the restoration application did not even include a request to formally excuse the delay. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the judge invoked the legal principle that the law assists those who are vigilant about their rights, not those who are negligent or indifferent. Since the petitioners had been inactive for years without justification, the court refused to reopen the case, and the application for restoration was dismissed.

This case illustrates that courts expect litigants to actively monitor their cases and act promptly, and that prolonged unexplained inaction can permanently forfeit legal remedies.

title: Shakirullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over who could take temporary custody of a vehicle involved in a fatal accident while a criminal case was pending. Shakirullah was accused of driving a coach negligently, causing the death of the complainant's son. Shakirullah applied for "superdari" - a temporary release of the seized vehicle into his custody - claiming he was its owner and last possessor. The trial court rejected his request, and he challenged that rejection before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the rejection. It explained that under the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1965, the legal "owner" of a vehicle is the person in whose name it is registered, or a properly registered transferee. Shakirullah's vehicle was registered in someone else's name, not his. He only possessed the vehicle's "return file" (a registration-related document), which the court said does not prove ownership or transfer title. The law required that if he had genuinely bought the vehicle, the transfer should have been formally registered within thirty days, which had not happened.

Since Shakirullah could not establish legal ownership under the law, the court ruled he was not entitled to have the vehicle released to him. The petition was dismissed, and the trial court's original decision was upheld.

This case matters because it clarifies that mere physical possession or informal documents are not enough to claim ownership of a vehicle in legal proceedings; formal registration under the law is required, especially when courts decide who can regain custody of property tied to a criminal case.

title: Muhammad Yaseen V. Wali Muhammad and 3 others,
explainer:

However, while his application was pending, a rival group (the defendant) separately applied to the Trade Organization regulator in Islamabad for a license under the Trade Organizations Act, 2013, followed proper advertisement and approval procedures, and was granted License No.171. The defendant then used this license to obtain a company incorporation certificate for the same name from SECP's Quetta office.

The plaintiff sued, asking the court to cancel both the incorporation certificate and the trade organization license, claiming they were obtained improperly and through political influence, and that his prior name reservation should have blocked the defendant's registration.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the suit. It found that the defendant's license application had been properly processed, publicly advertised, and approved according to law, and that having a name reserved with SECP was not actually a legal requirement for obtaining a trade organization license. The court also noted that the plaintiff had a proper legal remedy available under the Trade Organizations Act to challenge the license, but failed to pursue it.

This case matters because it clarifies that reserving a company name does not automatically confer rights over a trade organization license, and that parties must use the specific legal remedies provided by relevant laws rather than seeking court intervention directly.

title: Atta Muhammad and another V. Sarfaraz and 6 others,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over compensation for land taken by the National Highway Authority to build a road. The petitioners claimed they were rightful owners of a share in unpartitioned Shamilat (communal) land and wanted their share of the compensation award. The trial court partly ruled in their favor, declaring they were entitled to compensation according to their shares once the shares among co-owners were settled, based on old revenue records.

Unhappy that the decree did not grant them everything they wanted, the petitioners first tried to enforce it through execution proceedings, but then withdrew that execution application, saying the decree did not fully satisfy their claim. Only after withdrawing the execution application did they file an appeal against the original judgment, along with a request to excuse the delay in filing since the appeal was filed well past the normal deadline.

The High Court agreed with the appellate court, emphasizing the legal principle that the law protects those who act promptly, not those who delay. Since the petitioners failed to justify the delay properly, their revision petition was dismissed, and the original decree stood. This case highlights how strict courts are about deadlines and the need to explain delays fully when seeking condonation.

title: Abdul Razaq and others V. Hoor Jan and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the pension and service benefits of a government employee, Abdul Khaliq, who worked as a Valve Man in Pakistan's Public Health Engineering Department and died in 2020 without children. Two groups claimed entitlement to his pensionary dues, including leave encashment, commutation pension, group insurance, financial assistance, and provident fund amounts. His widow, Hoor Jan, filed for a Succession Certificate claiming these benefits. Separately, a group of distant relatives, described as cousins and descendants of the deceased's paternal aunt, also filed a claim, arguing that as his legal heirs under Islamic inheritance law they were entitled to a share of his pension.

The trial court in Mastung ruled in favor of the widow and rejected the relatives claim. The relatives appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the appeals, holding that pension is not inheritable property under Islamic law and therefore does not form part of a deceased person's estate or tarka. Instead, pension distribution is governed by the specific government rules and statutes that created the pension scheme, not by ordinary inheritance principles. The court relied on precedents from the Supreme Court and other high courts establishing that pension rights end at death and any benefits paid afterward are a statutory grant to specified next-of-kin, not inherited wealth.

This case clarifies that distant relatives cannot claim shares in a deceased government employee's pension simply through general inheritance law when specific rules designate who receives such benefits.

title: Ghulam Qadir and others V. Jam Ali Akbar and others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute in Balochistan that had already gone through the courts once before. The petitioners claimed they were owners in possession of about 1,100 acres of ancestral land since 1908, saying their forefathers had cultivated it as settlers, and that in 2007 the respondents, allegedly acting with police collusion, forcibly evicted them. Both the trial court and the appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora) had rejected their suit for declaration, possession, cancellation of mutation entries, and permanent injunction, and the petitioners then brought a civil revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence and found the petitioners' own witnesses gave contradictory statements about possession, ownership, and revenue entries. Crucially, official land settlement records from 1969 showed ownership registered in the respondents' names, not the petitioners'. Although the petitioners knew about this record, they never challenged it until filing this suit decades later, making the claim barred by limitation—delayed by roughly 37 years. The court reiterated that in ownership disputes, plaintiffs must prove their own case with solid evidence rather than relying on weaknesses in the other side's case. It also held that even if the case were sent back for retrial, it would serve no purpose since the limitation bar alone was fatal.

The court dismissed the revision petition, upholding the lower courts' decisions. The ruling underscores the importance of timely legal action and strong, consistent evidence when claiming land ownership against official government records.

title: Abdul Ghaffar V. Faizi Bibi and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over compensation money paid after a government employee's death. Din Muhammad, a Balochistan Traffic Police officer, died in 2010 after being struck by a vehicle while on duty. The government declared him a martyr and announced a compensation payment of Rs. 20,00,000 for his legal heirs. Since he had no children, his mother and two brothers obtained a succession certificate and received the compensation, but they did not include another brother, Abdul Ghaffar, as a legal heir in that process. Ghaffar sued, claiming he was also entitled to a share of the compensation as the deceased's brother. The trial court ruled in his favor, but the appellate court overturned that decision, so he brought the matter to the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It held that compensation or grant-in-aid money paid by the government after someone's death is different from Tarka, meaning the deceased's actual estate or inheritance under Islamic law. Tarka consists of property and assets the deceased owned and controlled during his lifetime. Since this compensation only arose after death and was essentially a government grant, it did not qualify as inheritable estate, and therefore could not be claimed as a matter of legal right by all heirs under succession law. The court relied on earlier Supreme Court and Lahore High Court rulings to reach this conclusion, ultimately upholding the appellate court's decision and rejecting Ghaffar's claim.

title: Abdul Ghaffar V. Faizi Bibi (Widow) and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over compensation money paid after the death of a Balochistan Traffic Police employee, Din Muhammad, who died in 2010 after being struck by a vehicle while on duty. The government declared him a martyr and announced Rs. 20 lakh in compensation for his legal heirs. Since he had no children, his mother and two brothers obtained a succession certificate and received the compensation, without including the petitioner, another brother, as a party. The petitioner sued, claiming his share of the compensation as an heir. The trial court ruled in his favor, but the appellate court reversed that decision, prompting the petitioner to file this revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The central legal question was whether government compensation for a deceased employee counts as "Tarka," meaning inheritable property left behind by the deceased, which would have to be divided among all legal heirs according to Islamic inheritance rules.

Relying on landmark Supreme Court Shariat Appellate Bench rulings, the High Court held that such compensation is not part of the deceased's estate because it was never the deceased's property during his lifetime, nor a right he could have claimed while alive. Instead, it is a form of government grant or goodwill gesture, and no heir can claim it as a matter of legal right. The court therefore upheld the appellate court's judgment and dismissed the petitioner's revision petition, meaning he was not entitled to a share of the compensation.

title: Muhammad Ayaz V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about the murder of Muhammad Afzal, who was shot dead while riding in a rickshaw with a witness after picking up children from school. The complainant, the deceased's brother, filed a police report alleging that the accused, Muhammad Ayaz, dressed in police uniform, intercepted the rickshaw and shot the victim with a 9mm pistol before fleeing on a motorcycle. The motive was said to be a matrimonial dispute: the accused's wife had left him and taken shelter with relatives, and the deceased was her maternal cousin.

The trial court convicted Ayaz of murder and sentenced him to life imprisonment plus compensation to the victim's family. He appealed, while the complainant filed a separate petition asking the court to increase the sentence to death.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence carefully, including eyewitness testimony, forensic reports matching the recovered pistol to bullet casings found at the scene, and the established motive. It found the eyewitnesses consistent and credible, noting that being related to the victim did not automatically make their testimony unreliable, especially since the crime occurred in daylight, making misidentification unlikely.

The court concluded that the prosecution had proven its case through direct, circumstantial, and medical evidence. It dismissed the appellant's appeal, upholding his conviction and life sentence. This judgment reinforces principles about how courts assess eyewitness credibility, forensic corroboration, and motive in murder cases.

title: Muhammad Ibrahim V. The State,
explainer:
This is an appeal decided by the Balochistan High Court concerning a man convicted of robbery under Pakistan's Penal Code. The appellant, Muhammad Ibrahim, had been sentenced to four years' imprisonment by a trial court after being accused of participating, along with four other masked men, in stopping a farmer on a road, kidnapping him briefly, and stealing his tractor, cash, mobile phone, and wristwatch.

The High Court overturned the conviction, giving the appellant the benefit of the doubt. It found several serious weaknesses in the prosecution's case. First, the complainant's own statements never described the physical appearance of the attackers or explained what specific role each accused person played, and he never actually identified the appellant as one of the culprits during his trial testimony. Second, although the complainant claimed to identify the appellant in an earlier police identification parade, the court found this suspicious and contradictory, since all the attackers had covered their faces and the crime happened at night, making it implausible that he could have recognized anyone. Third, the only other evidence was that the appellant was allegedly caught driving the stolen tractor, but the prosecution failed to connect him convincingly to the actual robbery, and since the main eyewitness account was unreliable, the supporting evidence collapsed too.

This case matters because it reinforces the principle that convictions cannot rest on inconsistent, vague, or implausible eyewitness identification, especially when identifying disguised attackers. The court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction.

title: Shabbir Ali V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Shabbir Ali who was convicted by a trial court in Quetta for using fake currency notes, a crime under Section 489-B of the Pakistan Penal Code. He was sentenced to three years in prison and fined Rs. 20,000. He appealed this conviction to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court reviewed the evidence and found serious problems with how the police handled the case. No recovery of the fake notes was done at the scene where the crime allegedly happened; instead, the accused was taken to a police station where his personal search was conducted, without any explanation for this unusual procedure. The witnesses also gave contradictory accounts about basic facts, such as how many fake notes were recovered, their denominations, and even the time of the incident. Additionally, the recovered currency notes were never properly presented as evidence in court, and the investigating officer admitted to significant lapses, including not conducting a proper inquiry.

Given these inconsistencies and poor investigation, the High Court concluded that the prosecution's case was doubtful and unreliable. It ruled that the accused was entitled to the benefit of the doubt, a fundamental right in criminal law, and that this benefit should not have been denied by the trial court. As a result, the High Court set aside the conviction and acquitted Shabbir Ali, accepting his appeal. This case highlights the importance of proper police procedure and reliable evidence in securing a criminal conviction.

title: Habibullah V. State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Habibullah who was convicted by a Special Customs Judge in Lasbella, Balochistan, for driving a coach that was found carrying smuggled goods, including betel nuts, mixed cloth, padlocks, salt, and cigarettes. Pakistan Coast Guard officials intercepted the coach during a routine patrol and claimed to have found the smuggled items hidden under the seats. Habibullah was sentenced to three years in prison and a heavy fine.

He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that his conviction was flawed. The High Court agreed with him. It found two major problems with the prosecution's case: first, neither the smuggled goods themselves nor the actual coach were ever produced as evidence in court, something a prosecution witness admitted under cross-examination. Second, none of the coach's passengers or its conductor were called as witnesses, even though they could have supported or contradicted the claim that the goods belonged to the driver.

The court held that these gaps created serious doubt about the prosecution's version of events, and under well-established legal principles, such doubt must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not mercy. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent on the benefit of the doubt, the High Court set aside the conviction and acquitted Habibullah entirely.

This case highlights how courts require solid, complete evidence, not just witness testimony, before convicting someone, especially in smuggling cases involving serious penalties.

title: Collector, Collectorate of Customs, Custom House, Gwadar V. Wali Muhammad and others,
explainer:
This case involved multiple appeals by Pakistan Customs against decisions favoring vehicle owners whose trucks had been used to smuggle Iranian diesel across the border. In each incident, customs officials or Frontier Corps troops intercepted trucks carrying large quantities of smuggled diesel oil, often in hidden or additional tanks, near border areas like Panjgoor, Turbat, Awaran, and Wadh. The drivers typically fled the scene when caught. Customs authorities seized both the diesel and the vehicles, confiscating the diesel outright and imposing redemption fines and penalties on the vehicle owners before allowing the trucks to be released.

Customs appealed further, but the Appellate Tribunal upheld the lower orders allowing the vehicles to be released upon payment of a 20 percent redemption fine, rather than fully confiscating them. Customs then challenged these Tribunal decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed all the customs department's references. It held that there was no evidence connecting the vehicle owners to the smuggling activities of their drivers. The court emphasized that confiscating a common carrier vehicle for transporting smuggled goods requires proof that the owner was directly involved or knowingly complicit, not just that the vehicle was used by a driver who smuggled goods. Since customs failed to prove the owners knew about or participated in the drivers' illegal actions, the lower courts had correctly allowed the vehicles to be released on payment of fines rather than confiscated out

title: Collector, Collectorate of Customs, Custom House, Gwadar V. Habib Ur Rehman,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a vehicle used to transport smuggled goods. Customs officials, acting with the Frontier Corps, intercepted a Toyota car near Hub in Balochistan and found it loaded with smuggled cigarettes, betel nuts, and gutka, along with a fake number plate. Both the goods and the vehicle were seized, and the driver was arrested. The Additional Collector of Customs ordered the smuggled goods and the vehicle to be confiscated outright.

The vehicle owner appealed, arguing he was an innocent public transport operator who had simply carried passengers and their luggage without knowing what was hidden inside, that no secret compartment existed in the car, and that proper legal procedure for seizure had not been followed. The Customs Appellate Tribunal agreed, finding no evidence of guilty knowledge (mens rea) on the owner's part, and ordered the vehicle released upon payment of a 20% redemption fine, while the confiscation of the smuggled goods themselves stood unchallenged and final.

The High Court upheld the Tribunal's ruling, agreeing that there was no proof the vehicle had a hidden cavity or had ever been used for smuggling before, and that it was the owner's only source of income. Finding no legal error in the Tribunal's judgment, the High Court dismissed the Customs Department's reference application, meaning the vehicle owner could recover his car by paying the fine.

title: Gul Zaman and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Gul Zaman and Imran, who were convicted for kidnapping a seven-year-old girl and keeping her confined. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court against their conviction under sections of the Pakistan Penal Code dealing with kidnapping for ransom or harm, wrongful confinement of an abducted person, and acting with common intention.

The prosecution's case rested heavily on the testimony of the child victim herself. Despite her young age, the court questioned her directly and found she understood the questions and answered consistently, even under cross-examination, showing she had not been coached by adults. She identified one accused as the man who took her on his bicycle, threatened to kill her if she revealed her identity, and slapped her. She was also recovered from a location linked to the accused. A judicial magistrate had recorded her statement soon after her rescue and conducted a formal identification parade, during which she correctly identified the accused. Additionally, one accused's confession led police to recover the victim from the other accused's house, and investigators noted he had prior involvement in child abduction cases.

The High Court found all this evidence—direct testimony, identification parade results, and the confession-linked recovery—consistent and credible, with only minor discrepancies raised by the defense that did not undermine the case. The court held that a child's testimony can be sufficient to convict if she is shown to be mentally sound and truthful. Both appeals were dismissed, and the convictions were upheld.

title: Ghulam Mustafa V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a rape conviction. Ghulam Mustafa had been convicted by a trial court in Hub, Balochistan, of committing rape under Section 376 of the Pakistan Penal Code against the sister of a complainant, and was sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction, granting the appellant benefit of the doubt. Several serious weaknesses in the prosecution's case led to this outcome. First, the FIR was lodged more than two days after the alleged incident, with no explanation for the delay, which meant crucial physical evidence was lost because the victim had washed her body before medical examination. Second, the complainant's testimony was based on hearsay, not firsthand knowledge, and he admitted under cross-examination that there was a pre-existing property dispute and rival criminal complaints between his family and the accused, raising the possibility of false implication. Third, the medical report showed no signs of violence, no blood or sperm traces, and no injuries, undermining the claim of forcible rape. Finally, two "last seen" witnesses only came forward 25 days later, and were personally produced by the complainant rather than found independently, casting doubt on their credibility.

Because the prosecution failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt, the court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction. The case highlights how delays, lack of independent evidence, and personal disputes between parties can undermine even serious criminal charges.

title: Abdul Haye V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of kidnapping and raping a five-year-old girl, the niece of the complainant. According to the prosecution, the accused lured the child and another young girl with ice cream, took them to his house, and raped one of them before letting them go. He was tried and convicted by an Additional Sessions Judge in Quetta, sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine for rape, plus five years for kidnapping. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the conviction. It examined the child victim's testimony carefully, first questioning her to confirm she understood the nature of truthful testimony despite her young age. She answered clearly and consistently, correctly identifying the accused and describing what happened, and her account held up even under cross-examination. The court also relied on medical evidence, including a doctor's examination showing signs of sexual assault and forensic lab results confirming seminal material on the victim's clothing, which matched her account. The FIR was also filed promptly, reducing the chance of fabrication.

The defence argued that a conviction should not rest solely on the child's testimony, but the court rejected this, holding that in rape cases the victim is often the only witness, and credible, confidence-inspiring testimony alone can support a conviction. This case matters because it reaffirms that children can be reliable witnesses if their mental capacity is properly tested, and that sole victim testimony, when credible and corroborated by medical evidence, is sufficient for conviction in sexual assault cases.

title: Sardar Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murdering his wife on allegations of illicit relations (siyakari), a charge based on eyewitness accounts from the victim's parents and sister, plus a judicial confession and an extra-judicial confession. The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him, finding serious problems with the evidence.

The court noted that the sister, who suddenly appeared as an eyewitness, was never mentioned as present at the scene in the original police report or in the initial statements of other witnesses. She was introduced into the trial over 16 months after the crime, right as the trial was nearly finished, which made her testimony unreliable and looked like an attempt to patch holes in the prosecution's case. The other witnesses admitted they hadn't actually seen the accused commit the murder, and past marital tension alone wasn't enough to prove guilt.

The court also found the confessions unconvincing. The accused's confession before a magistrate was recorded 16 days after his arrest, with no explanation for the prolonged illegal detention, raising doubts about whether it was voluntary or obtained through pressure. Similarly, an alleged extra-judicial confession made days earlier was never promptly reported to a magistrate, further undermining its credibility.

Because of these contradictions, unexplained delays, and lack of corroboration, the court ruled the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, granting the accused the benefit of the doubt and allowing his appeal, overturning his conviction and death sentence.

title: Jalat Khan and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved a violent clash between two groups that left three people injured, one of whom died. The accused men were tried for murder and causing hurt through common intention. The trial court had convicted them, and the matter came before the Balochistan High Court through a criminal appeal, a criminal revision, and an acquittal appeal.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the accused, giving them the benefit of the doubt. Several weaknesses in the prosecution's case led to this outcome. First, the FIR was not filed until roughly 27 hours after the incident, even though a police station was only 10 kilometers away, suggesting the complainant's side had time to consult and deliberate before framing their account, which cast doubt on its reliability. Second, the testimonies of the complainant, the two injured witnesses, and an alleged independent mediator contradicted each other on basic facts, such as who arrived at the scene and when, undermining their credibility. The mediator was also found to be closely tied by tribe and relationship to the victims, reducing his impartiality. Third, the investigation was flawed: the investigating officer failed to collect blood-stained soil, stones, or bullet casings, and never visited the hospital or spoke to the treating doctor for days. Finally, weapons recovered from the accused were not blood-stained or forensically tested, making their evidentiary value doubtful.

This case highlights how delayed FIRs, contradictory eyewitness accounts, and poor investigation can collectively defeat a criminal prosecution, even in serious murder cases.

title: Shah Wali V. The State,
explainer:
Shah Wali was convicted by an Additional Sessions Judge in Loralai of murdering Abdul Khaliq by shooting him, and was sentenced to death under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code. He appealed the conviction to the Balochistan High Court, and the trial court separately referred the death sentence for confirmation, so both matters were heard together.

The prosecution's case rested on eyewitness accounts from two people who saw the shooting, backed up by medical evidence showing gunshot wounds, recovery of three spent bullet casings and blood-stained earth from the crime scene, and the accused's own pointing out of the location during investigation. The defence argued the witnesses were unreliable because they happened to be nearby by chance and were related to the deceased, and suggested the killing was actually carried out by unknown persons due to a separate family dispute.

The High Court rejected these defence arguments. It held that witnesses who reasonably explain their presence at a crime scene are not disqualified as "chance witnesses," and that being related to the victim does not automatically make a witness unreliable unless there is a motive to falsely accuse someone. The court also noted that the accused had absconded for seven months, which it treated as evidence pointing to guilt, and that failure to prove a motive does not weaken a prosecution case when other evidence is strong.

Finding the eyewitness testimony credible and well-supported by physical and medical evidence, the court dismissed the appeal, upholding both the conviction and the death sentence.

title: Additional Prosecutor General, Balochistan, Quetta V. Abdul Qadeer and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over whether police could be ordered to register a second FIR (First Information Report) about the death of Abdul Majeed, a young man serving in the Airport Security Force who was killed on 13 March 2016 near Mastung.

Police had already registered one FIR describing the death as resulting from a botched motorcycle-snatching attempt, in which the deceased and his companions allegedly tried to rob a man named Ali Ahmed, who fired in self-defense. However, the deceased's father gave a completely different account, claiming his son was murdered by unknown persons while returning from training, and that police refused to record his version because a case was already registered. He approached the Sessions Judge acting as Justice of the Peace, who ordered a second FIR to be registered. The government's prosecutor challenged this order before the Balochistan High Court, arguing it was improper since investigation and a court challan already existed under the first FIR.

The High Court dismissed the challenge, holding that Pakistani law does not prohibit registering a second FIR when a different, genuinely conflicting version of the same incident is presented, so long as it is not merely repeating or embellishing the first account. Since the father's account described an entirely different scenario (murder by unknown people, not a robbery gone wrong), the court held it deserved independent investigation. The case reaffirms that competing narratives of the same crime can each generate separate FIRs, leaving it to trial to determine the truth.

title: Nazar Khan V. Tariq Khan and 6 others,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court, dealing with an application to cancel bail that had been granted to several accused persons in a serious criminal case. The accused were charged with murder, attempted murder, mischief, rioting, and terrorism offences after a Daewoo passenger coach was allegedly attacked with gunfire, resulting in the death of an FC (Frontier Corps) personnel and injuries to two passengers. The bus owner and complainant, Nazar Khan, had asked the court to cancel the bail earlier granted to the accused by an Anti-Terrorism Court, arguing that the offences fell within a category of crimes where bail should not normally be granted, and that granting it was illegal.

The High Court dismissed the application, refusing to cancel the bail. It explained that cancelling bail is different from deciding whether to grant it in the first place, and that courts should not interfere with bail once granted unless there are strong, exceptional reasons—such as the bail order being clearly illegal, factually wrong, or resulting in a miscarriage of justice, or the accused misusing their freedom by tampering with witnesses or making threats. In this case, there was no evidence that the accused had misused their bail. The court also noted that the trial had already begun, with two witnesses examined, and that courts should avoid commenting on the merits of a case while proceedings are ongoing. This ruling reinforces the principle that bail, once granted, deserves strong protection from being casually reversed.

title: Shakar Khan and 17 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a request for pre-arrest bail by Shakar Khan and 17 others accused of murder and terrorism-related offences in a violent incident in Jhal Magsi, Balochistan. According to the FIR, the accused allegedly attacked the complainant's group, fired rocket launchers causing panic, abducted three men, and later killed them, dumping their bodies near the complainant's house. The accused had earlier been granted temporary pre-arrest bail by the court and were now seeking to have it confirmed, arguing they were falsely implicated due to enmity with an influential complainant family.

The Balochistan High Court rejected their plea and cancelled the earlier bail. The judge explained that pre-arrest bail is an extraordinary remedy meant only to protect genuinely innocent people from malicious prosecution, not a routine alternative to regular bail. To get it, accused persons must show reasonable grounds to believe they are innocent and that the case against them is motivated by ulterior purposes. Here, the court found no evidence of malice by police or investigators, and the material on record showed reasonable grounds to believe the accused were involved in the killings, meaning the case fell under the legal bar against granting bail in serious offences.

This judgment reinforces that courts will not use pre-arrest bail loosely, especially in serious crimes like murder and terrorism, and that such relief requires strong justification rather than mere claims of false implication.

title: Shakeel Ahmed V. Abdul Jalil and others,
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant dispute in Quetta. The landlord had filed a petition asking a Rent Controller to evict a tenant, saying he needed the property back for his personal genuine use, specifically to combine it with other properties he owned to store construction material. The tenant contested this, and while the appeal was pending in the High Court, the landlord passed away, with his legal heirs taking his place in the case.

The tenant's lawyer argued that since the landlord died, his heirs couldn't claim the ground of "personal need" anymore, and that the property still hadn't been legally converted from residential to commercial use.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that once a court decree grants a right to someone, that right automatically passes to their legal heirs after death, and the heirs are entitled to defend the decree and pursue the case. The court also found that no separate permission was needed from the Rent Controller to convert residential property to non-residential use in this context, since the eviction petition itself covered that need. The court found the landlord's evidence credible and consistent, and the tenant's witnesses did not disprove the claim.

The appeal was dismissed, and the tenant was given two months to vacate. The ruling is significant because it clarifies that death of a landlord during litigation does not kill their case, and their heirs can still enforce an eviction based on the deceased's needs.

title: Zahid Hussain V. The Chairman Selection Committee/Chairman Balochistan Public Service Commission and 4 others,
explainer:
Zahid Hussain, a student seeking admission to MBBS, filed a constitutional petition in the Balochistan High Court against the Chairman of the Balochistan Public Service Commission's Selection Committee and other respondents, including the Quetta Institute of Medical Sciences (QIMS). He wanted the court to declare that another candidate's admission to QIMS for the 2015-16 academic year was illegal, and to direct that he himself be admitted instead.

The core legal question was whether a constitutional petition under Article 199 of the Constitution could even be brought against QIMS, since it is a private medical institution not governed by any statutory rules. The petitioner's lawyer struggled repeatedly, over several hearings, to justify why the petition should be allowed to proceed against a private body, eventually arguing that the government partly funds some students there.

The court held that constitutional petitions are a public law remedy meant to enforce fundamental rights against public functionaries or to ensure statutory bodies act within their powers. They cannot be used to resolve disputes with private institutions that are not backed by statutory rules or performing functions on behalf of the government. Since QIMS was purely private and unregulated by statute, the petition could not be entertained. The court therefore dismissed the case at the outset, without even examining the merits of the admission dispute. The ruling reinforces the limits of constitutional court jurisdiction over private entities.

title: Qurban Ali and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Qurban Ali and another accused, who were arrested near Sui, Balochistan, after police at a checkpoint acted on a tip-off and stopped them on a motorcycle. A search allegedly recovered forged Saudi Riyal notes worth about 60,300 rupees from their possession. They were charged under sections 489-B and 489-C of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deal with using or possessing forged currency notes. After a sessions judge refused them bail, they applied to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court granted them bail. It reasoned that the case, as it stood, was simply one of possession of forged currency, and it hadn't yet been established whether the men actually knew the notes were fake, or whether the more serious charge (489-B, using forged currency as genuine) or the lesser one (489-C, mere possession) applied. Since the facts suggested only possession, the offense fell under 489-C, which is not covered by the "prohibitory clause" of the bail law (meaning bail isn't automatically barred). The investigation was also already complete, so there was no need to keep them in custody further.

The court granted bail on surety bonds of Rs. 200,000 each, while clarifying that its comments were preliminary and would not influence the trial court's final judgment. This case illustrates how courts distinguish between possessing versus knowingly using counterfeit currency when deciding bail.

title: Abdul Ahad and 19 others V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary C & W and others,
explainer:
Twenty landowners in Quetta had their property acquired by the government to build and widen a road (old Mastung Road). The Deputy Commissioner, acting as Land Acquisition Collector, awarded them compensation at Rs.126.50 per square foot. Dissatisfied, the landowners objected, arguing their land was worth much more, and claimed Rs.400 per square foot instead. When the matter went to a District Judge acting as Referee, the landowners' claims were rejected, and they appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower court's decision and dismissed all 20 appeals. It explained that under the Land Acquisition Act, once the Collector fixes compensation, that amount is presumed correct unless the landowner proves otherwise with solid evidence. The burden of proof lies on the landowner seeking higher compensation, not on the government. The court emphasized that market value should reflect what a willing buyer would reasonably pay a willing seller, considering factors like location, future development prospects, and any impact on the remaining property.

In this case, the landowners failed to present any documentary evidence, such as sale records or comparable land prices, to show that the awarded rate was too low. They relied only on verbal claims, which the court said carry no legal weight. Because they failed to meet their burden of proof, their appeals were dismissed, and the original compensation amount stood. The case reinforces the principle that claimants seeking higher compensation must back their claims with concrete evidence, not mere assertions.

title: Larik Mal V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Larik Mal who was convicted for possessing an unlicensed Kalashnikov rifle. The weapon was allegedly recovered from a residential room after he pointed it out to police during investigation of a separate murder case. He was tried and convicted by a Sessions Judge in Jaffarabad, sentenced to five years imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, his lawyer argued that the recovery was doubtful because it happened in a populated area, yet the police did not bring in any independent witnesses from the public to observe and confirm the recovery, as required by law. Only police officials testified about finding the weapon.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with this objection. Under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code, police are generally required to have two independent members of the public witness such recoveries, unless they can show it was genuinely impossible to find such witnesses. Here, the investigating officer admitted no effort was even made to involve any local residents, despite the area being populated. The court relied on a Supreme Court precedent holding that such recoveries, made without independent witnesses, become highly doubtful and unreliable.

Because the prosecution failed to prove the recovery was genuine and failed to establish the case beyond reasonable doubt, the High Court acquitted Larik Mal, setting aside his conviction and sentence. The case highlights the importance of following proper procedure in evidence collection to protect individuals from potentially planted or fabricated evidence by police.

The Rent Controller ordered Saifullah to vacate the shop within thirty days. Saifullah appealed this decision to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the eviction order, giving Saifullah two months to vacate. The judge explained that questions of property title are not relevant in rent proceedings before a Rent Controller; what matters is only whether a landlord-tenant relationship exists. Once that relationship was proven, and Saifullah had denied it without valid evidence to back up his own version of events, the law left no option but to order eviction. The court also noted that if the landlord fails to occupy the property or re-lets it improperly, the tenant retains rights to reclaim possession later.
