title: Khudai Dad and 2 others V. Rahimuddin and 6 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between co-sharers (joint heirs) of agricultural land near Chaman, Balochistan, all descendants of the same original owner. The petitioners claimed that the respondents had illegally occupied 50,000 square feet of jointly-owned land by forcibly constructing a wall on it. They filed a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005, a special law meant to protect property owners from forcible dispossession by land grabbers, asking the trial court to direct authorities to investigate and act against the respondents.

The trial court dismissed the complaint, noting that a civil suit over the same property was already pending between the parties and directing them to seek relief through the civil courts instead. The petitioners appealed this dismissal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision. It found that the ownership of the land was genuinely disputed, litigation over title and possession was already underway in civil court, and the petitioners had even filed another civil suit seeking possession of the very same 50,000 square feet after their criminal complaint was dismissed. The court held that the Illegal Dispossession Act is meant to stop outside land grabbers, not to let co-sharers turn ordinary civil property disputes into criminal cases. Allowing this would be an abuse of the law. The appeal was dismissed, reaffirming that genuine ownership disputes between family co-sharers must be resolved by civil courts through evidence, not through criminal proceedings meant for illegal dispossession.

title: Abdul Malik V. Hazrat Ali alias Lalai and another,
explainer:
The case concerned the murder of Abdul Qadir, who was shot while sitting in his vehicle by unidentified assailants after being chased and intercepted by a Jeep. The complainant, Abdul Qadir's brother, accused Hazrat Ali and others of the killing, allegedly motivated by an old blood feud. The trial court acquitted the accused, and the complainant appealed against this acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness testimony from the complainant and another witness who was the deceased's nephew. It found that these witnesses had a close family relationship with the deceased, making them "interested witnesses" whose testimony required cautious scrutiny. Their statements also contained material contradictions on important points. Additionally, no weapon was recovered from the accused, which meant the prosecution failed to establish a direct link between the accused and the crime.

The court reaffirmed the principle that an accused who has been acquitted enjoys a "double presumption of innocence," and that appellate courts must be very cautious before overturning an acquittal. Since the trial court's findings were not shown to be perverse or illegal, the High Court upheld the acquittal and dismissed the appeal.

This case matters because it illustrates how Pakistani courts handle appeals against acquittals, emphasizing the heavy burden on the prosecution to prove guilt beyond doubt, and the special protection given to already-acquitted individuals.

title: Muhammad Umar and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Muhammad Umar and Ghulam Siddique, who sought bail after being arrested in connection with a shooting that occurred over a land dispute in Khuzdar, Balochistan. According to the FIR, seven armed men opened fire on a group of people, killing one man, Muhammad Ashraf, and seriously injuring four others. The applicants were named among those who fired the shots. Their bail plea had already been rejected by the Sessions Judge, prompting them to approach the Balochistan High Court.

Their lawyer argued that no specific role was assigned to them in the FIR and that witness statements recorded later did not clearly implicate them, so they deserved bail. The State opposed this, arguing that injured eyewitnesses had specifically named the applicants and that the charges (murder and attempted murder) were too serious for bail.

The High Court denied bail. It explained that at the bail stage, courts only make a tentative assessment of whether the accused appear prima facie connected to the crime, not a deep evaluation of evidence. Since the FIR was filed promptly, specific roles were attributed to the applicants, and multiple witness statements placed them at the scene, the court found strong grounds linking them to the crime. Because the offence fell under the serious/prohibitory category of the law, bail could not be granted. The court also reminded the trial court that these bail-stage observations should not influence the actual trial.

title: Ghulam Qadir V. Mst. Zainab alias Zeena and another,
explainer:
This case concerns a marriage dispute decided by the Balochistan High Court. Mst. Zainab had filed a suit for dissolution of her marriage on the ground of khula (a wife's right to seek divorce) before a Family Court in Lasbella. She claimed she had been married to Ghulam Qadir for about 22 years, that he lived abroad in Dubai, never paid her maintenance, tortured her, and eventually turned her out of the house, leaving her without support for around 15 years. Since Ghulam Qadir did not appear despite being served notice through his brother and a newspaper publication, the Family Court proceeded against him ex-parte and, based on the wife's evidence, granted the khula and dissolved the marriage in March 2014.

Ghulam Qadir challenged this decision before the High Court, arguing he was not given a proper hearing and that certain facts had been concealed when the suit was filed.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It explained that khula is a right granted to wives under Islamic law when spouses cannot continue living together within the limits prescribed by Allah, and that a husband's long-term failure to provide maintenance and support is a valid basis for finding that these limits cannot be maintained. Since the Family Court's decision was based on proper consideration of evidence and was not unlawful or without jurisdiction, the High Court found no reason to interfere. This case reaffirms that courts will uphold a wife's right to khula, especially where there is clear neglect of marital duties such as maintenance.

title: Tania Naseer V. Muhammad Zubair and 2 others,
explainer:
Tania Naseer sought dissolution of her marriage through khula, giving up her unpaid dower of Rs.300,000 as consideration. The Family Court granted the khula but ruled that the husband could not recover gold ornaments, clothes and shoes he had given her, since he failed to prove they were meant to be returned. On appeal, the Additional District Judge reversed this and ordered her to return 135.380 grams of gold ornaments to her ex-husband, treating them as "marriage benefits" tied to the khula settlement. She then challenged that appellate decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court accepted her petition, holding that the appellate court had erred. Under the Dowry and Bridal Gifts (Restriction) Act, 1976, gifts given by the husband or his family to the bride around the time of marriage qualify as "bridal gifts" and become the wife's absolute property—separate from dower (mehr) and not recoverable by the husband. The court noted that only the cash dower amount was recorded in the Nikah Nama, with no mention of gold ornaments as part of the marriage consideration. Since the wife had already given up her dower claim to secure the khula, that alone was sufficient consideration; she could not also be made to return bridal gifts.

This case matters because it clarifies that bridal gifts under Pakistani law belong exclusively to the wife and cannot be clawed back by husbands during divorce proceedings, protecting women's property rights in family law disputes.

title: Ghulam Qadir V. Mst. Zainab alias Zeena and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the dissolution of a marriage through khula, a wife's right under Islamic law to seek separation from her husband. Mst. Zainab had filed a suit before the Family Court in Lasbella, stating she had been married to Ghulam Qadir for about 22 years, that they had two children together, and that her husband, who lived abroad in Dubai, had not paid her maintenance for 15 years, had mistreated her, and had eventually turned her out of his house. Since the husband did not appear in court despite being served notice, the Family Court proceeded ex parte (without his participation) and granted the khula based on the wife's evidence.

The husband challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the judgment was based on a misreading of law and facts and that he had not been given proper opportunity to be heard.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It explained that khula can be granted when a court is satisfied that spouses cannot live together within the limits set by Allah, meaning a reasonably happy married life. Long-term separation combined with the husband's failure to provide maintenance was strong evidence that this standard was not being met. Since the wife had proven her case through unchallenged evidence, the Family Court's decision was lawful and did not warrant interference.

This case matters because it reaffirms that a wife's right to khula can be upheld even in ex parte proceedings when supported by credible evidence, and clarifies what "living within Allah's limits" means in practice.

title: Nabi Dad and another V. The State,
explainer: Two men accused of murder and other serious offences under the Pakistan Penal Code sought pre-arrest bail from the Balochistan High Court after already obtaining temporary protection from arrest. The case stemmed from a violent clash between rival groups on 4th November 2016, in which two people died and three were injured during a firing incident linked to an old enmity. Twenty-three people were named, but the two applicants said no specific role was assigned to them in the FIR. Crucially, their lawyer produced official High Court attendance records showing they were physically present at the High Court, over 300 kilometers from the crime scene, on the same day the murders occurred, making their involvement seem implausible. They had also cooperated with the investigation by appearing for questioning. The State opposed bail, arguing the accused should have first approached the trial court and that they were named in a promptly-lodged FIR. The High Court held that while normally an accused should first seek bail from the sessions court, this isn't an absolute rule, and direct High Court applications are allowed in compelling circumstances. Finding the case required further inquiry due to the enmity, lack of specific allegations, and the strong alibi evidence, the court confirmed the pre-arrest bail. The judgment reaffirms that at the bail stage, courts only make a tentative assessment of evidence rather than a deep evaluation, and that bail observations don't bind the eventual trial.

title: All Quetta Balochistan Arms Dealers Association and 9 others V. Secretary Home and Tribal Affairs, Civil Secretariat Quetta,
explainer:
This case involved a group of licensed arms dealers in Balochistan who challenged a government notification issued in December 2014 by the Home and Tribal Affairs Department. That notification increased the renewal fee for arms dealership licenses from Rs. 1,500 to Rs. 25,000, while also raising the initial licensing fee. The dealers argued the hike was unreasonable, inconsistent with fees charged in other provinces, and the result of the government misusing its authority.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed and dismissed the petition. It held that under Section 11(b) of the West Pakistan Arms Ordinance, 1965, the government has clear legal authority to fix and revise license fees, and the law sets no maximum limit on how much fees can be increased, only that the amount must be reasonable. The court found that a jump to Rs. 25,000 was not so excessive as to be unreasonable, especially since the fee had remained unchanged for a long time and dealers had benefited from low rates for years.

The court also emphasized that fixing fees is a policy decision belonging to the executive branch, not the judiciary. Citing Supreme Court precedent, it ruled that courts should not interfere with government policy choices under their constitutional writ jurisdiction unless the decision violates the Constitution, breaks the law, or is driven by bad faith. Since the petitioners failed to show any such illegality, the fee increase was upheld and the case was dismissed.

title: Naseer Ahmed V. Khair Bibi and 3 others,
explainer:
This case concerns Naseer Ahmed, who was accused by his mother-in-law of causing his wife Shazia's death, allegedly by poisoning her along with his brother and two other men. The wife's mother had approached the police to register a murder case, but police refused, saying the woman had committed suicide. She then went to an Additional Sessions Judge acting as Justice of the Peace, who ordered the police to register a criminal case against the husband. The husband challenged this order in the Balochistan High Court, arguing there was no evidence linking him to any crime and that his wife had died by suicide from poison, as shown in medical reports.

The High Court examined the police inquiry report and found that it failed to meet the legal requirements of Section 174 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which governs how police must investigate suspicious or unnatural deaths, including suicides. This section requires police to notify a magistrate, investigate at the scene with witnesses, prepare a detailed report, and refer the body for medical examination if there is any doubt about the cause of death. Since these mandatory steps were not properly followed, the court could not simply accept the police's suicide theory.

Finding that the Justice of Peace had issued a well-reasoned order based on the facts, the High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the direction to register a criminal case. This ruling highlights the importance of following proper legal procedures when investigating unnatural deaths before concluding they were suicides.

title: Khudai Noor V. District Judge, Pishin and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute between a husband and wife over dissolution of marriage, dower, dowry articles, and maintenance. The wife had filed a suit against her husband claiming these entitlements, alleging he abused her and eventually threw her out of the house without paying what she was owed. The Family Court ruled in her favor, and the District Judge upheld that decision on appeal. The husband then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The husband argued that an earlier arbitration had settled the dowry issue, that the wife failed to prove dower was still owed, and that her suit was technically invalid because she had not signed or affixed her thumb impression on the plaint and affidavit.

The High Court rejected all these arguments. It held that failing to sign the plaint was a minor, correctable irregularity, not grounds for dismissing the case. It found clear evidence, including the husband's own admissions, that the dower amount and certain dowry items were genuine. It also held that the wife's testimony and witnesses established cruelty, clarifying that cruelty need not be physical, mental abuse and disrespect also count. The court reaffirmed that a Muslim wife has a right to maintenance from her husband, and that even Khula (wife-initiated divorce) does not remove the husband's duty to maintain her during her Iddat period. Finding no legal error, the High Court dismissed the husband's petition and upheld the lower courts' decisions.

title: Balochistan Medical Association through President V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Health and others,
explainer:
This case was about a challenge to how doctors were selected for a postgraduate training program, the Master of Public Health course at the Institute of Public Health in Quetta. The Balochistan Medical Association, through its President, filed a petition asking the High Court to review the selection process used over the past five years, claiming that around 18 candidates had been selected without following proper rules, and asking the court to set aside those selections and order a fresh, rule-based selection.

The government and the selected doctors opposed the petition, arguing that the Association had no legal standing to bring the case because it was not even a registered or recognized body, and its President was not personally affected by the selections since he was not eligible for the program himself.

The High Court agreed with this objection. It explained that under Article 199 of the Constitution, only a person who is directly or personally affected, an aggrieved person, can file such a petition. The petitioner failed to prove it was a registered association, failed to show any personal or legal right had been violated, and its president had no personal stake in the outcome. Since these basic requirements were not met, the court held that the petitioner had no legal standing to bring the case, and dismissed the petition without examining the merits of the selection process itself.

title: Saeedan Bibi V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a woman named Saeedan Bibi who was arrested for allegedly possessing two kilograms of charas, a narcotic substance, found in her handbag while she was traveling on a bus from Quetta to Bahawalpur. Police said they acted on a tip from the bus company's clerk, who pointed her out as a suspected drug carrier. She was charged under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act and denied bail by the trial court, so she approached the Balochistan High Court seeking bail while her case was pending.

The High Court granted her bail. It found several weaknesses in the prosecution's case that made it one requiring further inquiry: the clerk who supposedly tipped off the police was never made a witness, her bus ticket was not taken into evidence, and the bus's registration number was not even mentioned in the police report. The court also noted that investigation was already complete and the formal charges had been filed in the trial court, meaning there was no longer any need to keep her in custody for investigative purposes.

The court emphasized that when deciding bail in narcotics cases, judges should also weigh the quantity of the drug involved against the likely punishment. Given the gaps in evidence and the completed investigation, the court ruled her case fell under a legal provision allowing bail in cases of doubt, and released her on bail bonds of Rs. 100,000. This case illustrates how courts scrutinize procedural gaps in narcotics prosecutions when deciding on bail.

title: Khudai Noor V. District Judge Pishin and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a husband challenging court decisions in a family dispute. His wife had filed a lawsuit seeking dissolution of marriage, maintenance payments, return of dowry items, and dower money, along with custody of their child. The Family Court in Pishin ruled in the wife's favor, and this decision was upheld on appeal by the District Judge. During the case, the husband had produced a divorce document showing he had already divorced the wife, which she did not dispute, so the marriage was formally dissolved on that basis.

The husband then challenged the rulings before the High Court, arguing mainly that the case should have been dismissed because his wife had not personally signed or placed her thumb impression on the lawsuit documents, and that the couple had already settled the dowry dispute through arbitrators before the case was filed.

The High Court rejected the technical objection about the missing signature, ruling that such procedural defects in signing or verifying court documents are minor irregularities that can be corrected later and do not justify dismissing an entire case. The court cited established legal precedents supporting this view.

The court also reaffirmed that cruelty justifying divorce isn't limited to physical violence but can include mental or emotional abuse, and clarified that even when a marriage ends through khula (wife-initiated divorce), the husband remains responsible for maintaining his wife during her iddat (waiting period) regardless of dower settlements.

This case is significant because it reinforces that courts should prioritize substantive justice over procedural technicalities in family law matters.

title: Bibi Zawar V. Sessions Judge Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a woman, Bibi Zawar, whose house was attacked in 2014, resulting in the deaths of two people, injuries to five others, and the abduction of her two sons. An FIR was registered under ordinary criminal law provisions dealing with murder, attempted murder, kidnapping, and rioting. The case was being heard in a regular Sessions Court in Quetta. The petitioner asked the Balochistan High Court to have the case transferred to a special Anti-Terrorism Court by adding Section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997 to the FIR, arguing that the violent nature of the attack qualified it as an act of terrorism.

The respondents and the state prosecutor opposed this, arguing the incident did not meet the legal threshold for terrorism.

The High Court ruled in favor of the petitioner. It explained that to decide whether an offence counts as terrorism, courts must look at the FIR's allegations, evidence gathered during investigation, and the surrounding circumstances, particularly the motive and effect of the act. If an act creates fear, panic, or a sense of insecurity among the public in an area, it qualifies as terrorism under the law, even if not motivated by political or religious extremism. Since the armed attack caused deaths, injuries, and abductions, and instilled fear in the community, the court found it met this standard. It ordered the investigating officer to add the terrorism charge to the FIR and transfer the case to the Anti-Terrorism Court, which would have exclusive jurisdiction

title: Rukhsana and others V. Asmatullah and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running property dispute in Quetta. The original plaintiff had sued for specific performance of a property sale agreement, asking the court to order the seller to accept the remaining payment and hand over possession of certain plots, along with a permanent injunction stopping the property from being transferred to anyone else. After multiple rounds of litigation, including an earlier appeal that sent the case back to the trial court, the defendants filed an application under Order VII Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code seeking rejection of the plaint. The trial court agreed and dismissed the suit again without a hearing on the merits, prompting this second appeal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the legal test for rejecting a plaint under this provision, which allows dismissal only in narrow situations: no cause of action, incorrect valuation of relief, insufficient stamp duty, or if the suit is clearly barred by law. The Court clarified that a plaint cannot be rejected piecemeal, it can only be thrown out if every single relief sought is legally barred; if even one prayer is maintainable, the suit must proceed. After reviewing the plaint, the judges found none of the specified defects present and ruled that the trial court had misapplied the law.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that courts must be cautious before shutting the door on a case early, protecting a plaintiff's right to have genuine disputes heard on their merits rather than dismissed on technical or premature grounds.

title: Rukhsana and 8 others V. Asmatullah and 3 others,
explainer:

The original plaintiff had sued for specific performance of a property sale agreement, asking the court to order the defendant to accept the remaining payment and hand over possession of the land, along with a permanent injunction against transferring the property. After the original defendant died, his legal heirs were brought into the case. They later filed an application under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Civil Procedure Code, technically asking that their names be removed from the case as defendants. Instead, the trial court used this application to reject the entire plaint and dismiss the suit.

The Balochistan High Court found this to be an error. It explained that a plaint can only be rejected under this rule in limited situations, such as when it discloses no cause of action, is undervalued, is improperly stamped, or is clearly barred by law. None of these applied here. The court emphasized that even if just one prayer in the suit was legally maintainable, the whole plaint could not be thrown out. Given the serious factual disputes between the parties, the case deserved full examination through evidence, not summary dismissal.

The High Court set aside the trial court's order, restored the case, and sent it back for proper framing of issues and a full trial on the merits. This decision reinforces that courts must not misuse procedural rules to avoid deciding genuine property rights disputes.

title: Abdul Rasheed and 2 others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved three men, Abdul Rasheed, Kangar Khan, and Saddam Hussain, who were accused of dacoity (armed robbery) under sections 395 and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code after a motorcycle was allegedly snatched at gunpoint from a student near Mastung. The applicants had been denied bail by the Sessions Judge, Mastung, and approached the Balochistan High Court seeking post-arrest bail.

The High Court granted them bail. The judge noted several weaknesses in the case against the accused: there was an unexplained delay of about 21 to 22 hours between the incident and the filing of the police report (FIR), which raised doubts about possible deliberation or manipulation before naming suspects. Additionally, the accused were not named in the original FIR, no incriminating evidence was recovered from them, and there was no direct evidence linking them to the crime—only a statement made by a co-accused implicating them.

The court held that such disclosure statements' reliability should be tested at trial, not used to justify continued detention beforehand. Since the case file had already been submitted to the trial court but no real progress had occurred, keeping the accused in custody served no purpose. Citing Supreme Court precedents, the judge reaffirmed that bail is generally a right unless exceptional circumstances exist, and this case warranted "further inquiry." The accused were released on bail bonds of Rs. 200,000 each, with the court clarifying its observations were preliminary and would not affect the trial's outcome.

title: Muhammad Azeem Kakar V. Sessions Judge, Zhob and another,
explainer:
This case involved a Deputy Commissioner, Muhammad Azeem Kakar, who was summoned to face trial in a criminal case originally registered against a levies official for allegedly wrongfully confining three men in a lock-up without lodging an FIR. The matter began when a father filed an application before the Sessions Judge of Zhob seeking recovery of his illegally detained son and two others. During the inquiry, it emerged that the detainees had been held by an in-charge of the Levies Squad, leading to registration of an FIR against him. Later, while deciding an acquittal application filed by a co-accused, the Sessions Judge reviewed the evidence and concluded that the Deputy Commissioner also appeared to have played a role similar to the main accused, and therefore summoned him to stand trial as well.

The Deputy Commissioner challenged this summoning order before the Balochistan High Court, asking that it be quashed. However, by the time the case was heard, he had already appeared before the trial court, obtained bail, and had formal charges framed against him.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It held that quashing criminal proceedings is an extraordinary remedy to be used only when no other remedy exists. Since the petitioner still had the option to seek acquittal from the trial court itself under Section 265-K of the Criminal Procedure Code, he could not bypass that avenue and directly approach the High Court. The case reaffirms that criminal proceedings should ordinarily continue and be decided on their merits rather than being cut short prematurely by higher courts.

title: Muhammad Sadiq and others V. Special Judge, Anti-Terrorism Court-II, Quetta and another,
explainer:
The case involved Muhammad Sadiq and other petitioners who were accused of confronting Frontier Corps personnel at a checkpoint on a main road in Quetta in September 2016. They were overpowered, and various weapons and ammunition were recovered from them. They were charged under several sections of the Pakistan Penal Code along with the Anti-Terrorism Act.

The accused sought to have their case moved from the Anti-Terrorism Court to an ordinary criminal court, arguing that their actions did not amount to terrorism under Section 6 of the Anti-Terrorism Act. The trial court rejected this request, and they challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision, dismissing the petition. It explained that determining whether an act counts as terrorism requires looking at the nature of the offence, the circumstances, and whether it created fear or insecurity among the public. Since the incident occurred on a public road, targeted security personnel, and involved serious violence, the court found it fell within the special categories covered by the Anti-Terrorism Act. Therefore, the Anti-Terrorism Court retained jurisdiction to try the case, reaffirming how courts assess whether violent incidents qualify as terrorism.

explainer:
This case involved a young woman named Abrira who was allegedly killed by her relatives in what her mother described as an honour killing, after Abrira had earlier been abducted and later returned. A criminal case was initially filed under ordinary murder and rioting charges, but a private complaint was later lodged and the case ended up being tried by the Anti-Terrorism Court, with charges that included terrorism offences alongside murder.

The accused challenged this, arguing their case should not be tried by a special anti-terrorism court but by an ordinary criminal court, since the killing did not amount to terrorism as defined by law. The trial court had rejected this request, so the accused approached the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined how courts should decide whether a case belongs in the Anti-Terrorism Court: by looking at whether the act had a real connection to terrorism, such as creating widespread fear, panic, or insecurity in the public, rather than just being a serious personal crime. Relying on a Supreme Court ruling that honour killings do not fall within the scope of the Anti-Terrorism Act, the High Court found that this case lacked the necessary elements of terrorism. It allowed the petition, set aside the lower court's order, and transferred the case to an ordinary criminal court.

The judgment matters because it clarifies that not every violent or shocking crime, including honour killings, automatically qualifies as terrorism, and helps define the proper boundary of the Anti-Terrorism Court's jurisdiction.

title: Muhammad Shafiq V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Shafiq, who ran a medical store in Quetta and was caught by a Drug Inspector selling medicines without a valid drug sale license. When his case went to trial, Shafiq pleaded guilty to the charge, admitted he had stocked and sold drugs without a license, and offered no defense evidence. The trial court convicted him under the Drugs Act, 1976 and sentenced him to five months imprisonment plus a fine of Rs. 50,000, with additional jail time if the fine went unpaid.

Shafiq appealed to the Balochistan High Court, not to contest his guilt, but hoping for a reduced sentence, arguing he was a first-time offender and his family's sole breadwinner.

The High Court dismissed the appeal. It held that under the law, once an accused person voluntarily pleads guilty and confesses, he cannot later challenge his conviction through an appeal; he can only challenge whether the sentence itself was excessive or illegal, which Shafiq had not done. The court found that the trial court had already been lenient given the confession, and the punishment matched what the law prescribed. Citing a similar 1985 Supreme Court ruling, the judges emphasized that a person who freely pleads guilty must accept responsibility for that choice.

This case illustrates an important legal principle: pleading guilty carries serious consequences, significantly limiting one's right to appeal, and courts will not second-guess a conviction based on a voluntary confession.

title: The State through Prosecutor General, Balochistan V. Abdul Nafay and another,
explainer:
This case concerns a legal challenge over the registration of a criminal case. A man named Abdul Nafay had filed an application under Section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code after his brother was found dead. Police had told him his brother was killed while committing theft, but they refused to register a formal criminal case (FIR) against the accused persons he identified. He approached the Sessions Judge, acting as Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace, who ordered the police station to register the case and investigate impartially.

The State, through the Prosecutor General of Balochistan, challenged this order in the Balochistan High Court, arguing it should be set aside. However, the High Court focused on a preliminary question: was the State actually an "aggrieved party" with the right to challenge this order at all?

The court explained that an aggrieved person is someone whose personal, legal, pecuniary, or property rights have been directly and adversely affected by a court's decision. Since the order simply directed police to register a case involving a private dispute between private individuals, the State's own rights were not harmed in any way. The Prosecutor General therefore had no legal standing to file this petition.

As a result, the court dismissed the case, ruling it was filed by someone without the authority to do so. This decision matters because it clarifies who can legally challenge court orders and reinforces that only genuinely affected parties can seek judicial remedies.

title: Habib Qadir V. Station House Officer, Sadar Khuzdar and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a father, Habib Qadir, who filed a petition asking the Balochistan High Court to order police to register a criminal case (FIR) against a relative and a school official. He alleged that while he was away performing Umrah, the relative enticed away his wife and children and got his sons admitted into a Karachi school using fake school-leaving certificates prepared by a school official. When the police station refused to register an FIR, he approached the Sessions Judge acting as Ex-Officio Justice of Peace, who also refused. He then challenged that refusal before the High Court.

The High Court explained that police are legally bound to record an FIR whenever information discloses a cognizable offence, and a Justice of Peace's role is limited to checking whether the complaint discloses such an offence, not to judge whether the allegations are true. However, the court noted that Habib Qadir waited about fourteen months after learning of the alleged incident before even approaching the police, and gave no explanation for this delay. Such unexplained delay, the court held, casts doubt on the genuincess of a complaint, since prompt reporting is what supports the credibility of an FIR.

Concluding that the facts suggested the complaint arose from a family dispute rather than a genuine grievance, and finding no legal error in the Justice of Peace's reasoned decision, the High Court dismissed the petition. The case illustrates how delay in reporting crimes can undermine an FIR request, and clarifies the limited scope of a Justice of Peace's powers under the law.

title: Muhammad Alam V. Nazish Qazi and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute over a minor girl, Ilsa Khan, following the divorce of her parents through khula. The trial court had granted the divorce but denied the mother custody, allowing her only scheduled visits. On appeal, the district court reversed this and awarded custody to the mother instead. The father then challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

A key fact emerged during proceedings: the mother had remarried a man named Abdul Mueez Khilji, who had no blood relation to the child. The father argued that under Islamic personal law, a mother who remarries someone unrelated to her child (a "stranger") forfeits her right of custody (hizanat). The mother's side argued that remarriage alone should not automatically disqualify her, especially since the father had also remarried, and that the child's welfare should be the deciding factor.

The High Court held that while the welfare of the minor is always the paramount consideration in custody matters, Islamic law also protects the moral and social environment of a female child. Since the mother had married a person who was a stranger to the minor, she lost her entitlement to custody. The court set aside the appellate court's decision and restored the trial court's ruling giving custody to the father, while maintaining visitation rights for the mother. This case reinforces how remarriage to a non-relative can legally affect a mother's custody rights over daughters under Pakistani family law.

The complainant was not actually an eyewitness. One eyewitness was himself later charged and convicted as a co-accused. None of the accused were named in the original police report, and no proper identification parade was held after their arrest.

The recovered motorcycle was equally unreliable, with contradictory and incomplete accounts of how and where it was found. Additionally, the crime weapons and empty cartridges were sent to the forensic lab only after a long, unexplained delay, weakening the value of that report.

title: Ghulam Shabbir etc.. V. State,
explainer:
This case concerns three men, Ghulam Shabbir, Ejaz Ali and Munir Ahmed, who were convicted by a Sessions Court in Quetta for the murder of Habib Jalib, who was shot dead at his shop in 2010. The trial court had sentenced them to life imprisonment and ordered compensation to the victim's family. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the convictions and acquitted the appellants, giving them the benefit of the doubt. The judges found serious weaknesses in the prosecution's case: none of the accused had been named in the original police report, meaning no witness recognized them at the time of the crime. No proper identification parade was held, and one witness identified an accused for the first time only in court, without describing what role he played, which the court said was too weak to rely on. The medical evidence could confirm the injuries but could not identify who caused them. Witnesses also contradicted each other about the recovery of a motorcycle allegedly used in the crime. Additionally, the weapons and bullet casings were sent for forensic examination after an unexplained delay of over a month, casting doubt on that evidence too. The court also noted that the alleged recovery of weapons had not actually followed from the accused's disclosures to police, further weakening that evidence.

The case highlights how Pakistani courts require solid, corroborated proof beyond reasonable doubt before convicting someone of murder, especially regarding identification and evidence handling.

The alleged loss to the government was calculated at over 404 million rupees. Their appeals against conviction were dismissed by the High Court, though sentences were reduced for some, and the Supreme Court refused to hear further appeals, making the convictions final.

Later, the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) tried to recover the unpaid fine amounts by filing a fresh application in the trial court. However, this application was dismissed because it was filed too late. Under the law, authorities have six years from the date of sentencing to recover an unpaid fine, but NAB's application was filed nine months after this deadline expired, and NAB could not provide any reasonable explanation for the delay.

The High Court upheld the dismissal, ruling that the recovery request was time-barred. This case matters because it shows that even government bodies pursuing corruption cases must follow strict legal deadlines, and courts will enforce limitation laws even when large sums of public money are involved.

title: Muhammad Humayun V. The Station House Officer (SHO) Police Station Jinnah Town, Quetta and another,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Muhammad Humayun, whose father had been booked in an FIR by the FIA for offences under the cybercrime law (PECA) and related sections. The petitioner claimed that when he appeared before the Investigating Officer after being summoned, he was beaten and abused. He said he complained to a Judicial Magistrate, was referred for a medical examination, and later tried to get an FIR registered against the Investigating Officer for assaulting him. When the police allegedly refused to register his complaint, he approached the Sessions Judge acting as Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking for an FIR to be ordered. That application was dismissed, and he challenged this dismissal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the petitioner's application lacked basic details, such as the date, time, and location of the alleged beating, or which part of his body was injured. More importantly, the court noted that he had never first approached the local police station (SHO) with his complaint before going to the Justice of Peace, which the law requires. Only if the SHO refuses to act can a person turn to the Justice of Peace, and even then, they should typically first escalate to higher police officials.

The judgment reinforces that courts will not order FIR registration unless a complainant has followed the proper procedural sequence and provided sufficient factual detail, and that a well-reasoned order by a Justice of Peace will not be disturbed without clear illegality.

title: Muhammad Farooq Shah and another V. The State through National Accountability Bureau Balochistan, Quetta,
explainer:
This case involved a father, Muhammad Farooq Shah, an Assistant Excise and Taxation Officer, and his son, who were accused by Pakistan's National Accountability Bureau (NAB) of accumulating assets worth over 107 million rupees far beyond their known legitimate income, through corruption. The father allegedly also hid some properties in the names of his sons as "benamidars" (nominal owners holding assets on someone else's behalf). Both were arrested and sought post-arrest bail from the Balochistan High Court while the NAB reference case was pending trial.

The court examined the evidence separately for father and son. For Muhammad Farooq Shah, the main accused, investigators had prepared a detailed breakdown of his income versus assets showing suspicious deposits and unexplained wealth clearly linking him to the alleged corruption. The court found this evidence strong enough that no bail was justified for him, and dismissed his petition.

However, for the son, Suleman Shah, the court took a different view. Since the properties in his name were allegedly purchased and controlled by his father, and his personal involvement in the transactions was not clearly established, the court held that his liability needed to be determined through evidence at trial. This uncertainty meant his case required "further inquiry," a legal standard that permits bail. The court therefore granted bail to the son while keeping the father in custody.

The case illustrates how courts assess bail differently based on the strength and directness of evidence against each accused, even within the same corruption case.

title: Saifullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Saifullah, who was convicted of robbery under Section 392 read with 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code for allegedly helping snatch a motorcycle, CNIC, and mobile phone from a complainant at gunpoint. He was sentenced to three years' imprisonment with a fine by a trial court, and his appeal was rejected by an Additional Sessions Judge. He then filed a revision petition before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence and found it seriously lacking. There was no direct eyewitness testimony properly implicating the petitioner - one witness who was supposedly present did not say anything against him. The prosecution relied on a confession the accused allegedly made while in police custody, but the court held such confessions are legally inadmissible and carry no weight. It also relied on an identification parade, but this was conducted eleven days after arrest with no explanation for the delay, making it unreliable. Additionally, the Judicial Magistrate who supervised the identification parade was never called to testify, and the court held that this failure to produce a material witness allowed a legal presumption that his testimony would have gone against the prosecution.

Given these gaps, the court found the prosecution's case did not form an unbroken chain of proof and created reasonable doubt. Since any single reasonable doubt must benefit the accused, the High Court acquitted Saifullah, setting aside his conviction and sentence. The judgment reinforces strict standards for confessions, identification parades, and the prosecution's burden to prove guilt independently.

title: Ghulam Sabir through Special Power of Attorney V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Mines and Minerals Development and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a mining prospecting license in Balochistan. Back in 1989, a person (respondent No.3) was granted a prospecting license for coal near Shahrag. In 1996, the government cancelled that license through an official notification. The license holder did not challenge this cancellation for about 20 years, finally filing an appeal in 2016 under the Balochistan Mineral Rules, 2002, which allow only 30 days to appeal such a decision. Surprisingly, the appellate authority (the Secretary of Mines and Minerals) accepted this massively delayed appeal and restored the prospecting license in 2017.

Another party, Ghulam Sabir, who had an interest in the area, challenged this restoration before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the appeal should never have been entertained because it was filed 20 years too late without any valid explanation for the delay.

The High Court agreed with the petitioner. It held that the law of limitation exists to protect public policy and ensure an orderly legal system, and that when someone misses a deadline by such an enormous margin, each day of delay must be properly explained. Since no credible justification was given for the 20-year delay, the appellate authority had wrongly exercised its jurisdiction in condoning it. The Court therefore set aside both the order accepting the late appeal and the subsequent restoration of the prospecting license, ruling in favor of the petitioner. The case underscores that limitation periods must be respected and cannot be waived without proper cause, even by government authorities.

title: Mst. Fahmida Bibi V. Abdul Bari and another,
explainer:
This case is about custody of two children after their parents' marriage ended. The mother had earlier gone to court seeking divorce, dowry articles, and maintenance. The family court dissolved the marriage through khula and awarded maintenance for the children, but rejected her claims for dowry and personal maintenance. Both her appeal and the father's contest were decided at earlier stages.

Later, the mother remarried another man through Nikah (though the formal move to her new husband's house had not yet happened) and asked the family court to direct the father to take custody of both children, since she felt she could no longer keep them. The family court refused this request, so she challenged that refusal before the High Court.

The High Court examined Islamic family law principles: normally a mother keeps custody of a son until age seven and a daughter until puberty, even after divorce, but this right ends if she remarries someone unrelated to the child, a "stranger." The father then generally becomes entitled to custody, especially since he is the natural guardian, provided it serves the child's welfare.

Applying this, the Court found that since the son was already about 13, the custody question over him differed, but for the daughter, the mother's remarriage meant she lost her right to keep custody. The Court accepted the petition, effectively ruling in the mother's favor to have custody arrangements reconsidered in light of these principles.

title: Ghulam Haider V. Additional District & Sessions Judge and others,
explainer:
This case concerns a property dispute in Balochistan where the petitioner, Ghulam Haider, claimed ownership of ancestral land and Shnay fruit trees that he and his brothers jointly possessed. He alleged that two men, along with six armed accomplices, forcibly stole two bags of fruit from his workers. When he tried to get a criminal case registered, the local Tehsildar refused. He then approached the Additional Sessions Judge acting as an Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace, asking for a direction to register an FIR, but this request was also rejected after the judge reviewed reports from local revenue officials. Haider then challenged that rejection before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It explained that a Justice of the Peace's role under the law is limited to checking whether the facts described amount to a criminal offense, and if so, directing police to register a case, without weighing the truth of the allegations. In this instance, official reports showed the land was actually subject to a competing ownership claim between the parties, making it a civil dispute rather than a criminal matter. The court held that Justices of the Peace should not mechanically order FIR registration in every case, and that determining who truly owned the disputed land required factual inquiry beyond the scope of this constitutional petition. title: Juma Gul V. Government of Pakistan Model Customs Collectorate through Collector Customs House, Quetta and others,
explainer:

Since the Customs Act already provided a proper appeal process that the petitioner had not used, the court could not step in. It also noted that the case involved factual disputes that needed evidence and inquiry, which is not something a constitutional petition can resolve. This case reinforces the principle that courts expect people to exhaust proper legal channels before seeking constitutional intervention.

title: Mst. Fahmida Bibi V. Abdul Bari and another,
explainer:
Fahmida Bibi divorced her husband, Abdul Bari, and they had two children, a boy (Ahmedullah) and a girl (Bibi Mariam). After the divorce, Fahmida remarried, and while the marriage's rukhsati (formal transfer to the new husband's home) had not yet happened, she asked the family court to order the father to take custody of the children, arguing she was poor and could no longer properly care for them, while the father was financially better off. The family court and the appellate court rejected her request, and she challenged that decision in the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court referred to Islamic law principles (as recognized in earlier Supreme Court rulings) stating that a mother normally keeps custody of her children after divorce, but she loses that right over a daughter if she remarries someone unrelated to the child, since living with a stranger husband is seen as compromising the child's welfare. Since Fahmida had already contracted a new nikah, the court ruled she lost her right to custody of her daughter, though the son, being about 13, was old enough that this rule mattered less for him. The High Court set aside the family court's order and allowed the petition, meaning custody arrangements had to be reconsidered in light of these principles.

This case matters because it clarifies how courts balance a mother's remarriage against a child's welfare in custody disputes under Pakistani family law.

title: Ghulam Haider V. Additional District and Sessions Judge/Justice of Peace, Dalbandin and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over land and fruit trees in Balochistan. The petitioner, Ghulam Haider, claimed that he owned ancestral land and Shnay fruit trees, which were in his and his brother's possession. He alleged that two named individuals, along with six unknown armed men, forcibly looted fruit from his property. When he tried to get a police case (FIR) registered, the Tehsildar refused. He then approached the Additional Sessions Judge acting as Ex-Officio Justice of the Peace under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, asking that the case be registered, but this request was also rejected.

Haider then challenged that rejection before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court examined the record and found that the underlying dispute was actually a civil disagreement over land ownership, with both parties claiming the same property, and the land in question fell outside recognized boundary lines. The court held that a Justice of the Peace's role under the law is limited to checking whether the facts presented describe a criminal offence, not to resolve ownership disputes or verify the truth of allegations, and should not act automatically to order FIR registration in every case. Since resolving this dispute would require detailed factual investigation, which isn't appropriate for the High Court's special constitutional jurisdiction, the court dismissed the petition, upholding the earlier rejection. This shows how courts distinguish between criminal complaints and civil property disputes.

title: Akhtar Jan V. Shah Murad through Levies Thana, Harnai and another,
explainer:
This case involved a challenge to a criminal acquittal, brought by the complainant, Akhtar Jan, before the Balochistan High Court. The original case concerned the alleged murder of one Zaitullah, who was reportedly shot dead on 17 February 2014 by the accused, Shah Murad, and others, allegedly over a family dispute. The trial court had acquitted the accused, and the complainant appealed against that acquittal.

The High Court upheld the acquittal, dismissing the appeal. It found significant problems with the prosecution's case. First, there was an unexplained two-day delay in filing the police report (FIR), even though the police station was only about eight kilometers away, raising suspicion that the accusation was the product of deliberation rather than a spontaneous complaint. Second, the three eyewitnesses gave contradictory and inconsistent accounts of the incident, undermining their credibility. Additionally, no post-mortem examination or inquest report was conducted to establish the cause of death, and a recovery witness admitted there was no sign of a bullet on the deceased's blood-stained clothes. No weapon or evidence was recovered from the accused either.

The court reaffirmed the legal principle that appeals against acquittals are treated differently from appeals against convictions, since an acquitted person enjoys a stronger presumption of innocence. Such acquittals can only be overturned if they are clearly unreasonable or arbitrary, which was not the case here.

However, an appellate court overturned these orders, ruling that meetings should instead take place within court premises, supervised through the Civil Nazir's office.

The father challenged these appellate decisions before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court ruled in his favor, holding that meeting a young child only inside court premises was not conducive to her wellbeing, since such settings lack a homely, comfortable atmosphere. It stressed that both children and fathers need real bonding time together, not just brief supervised encounters, since deprivation of parental affection can harm a child's emotional and intellectual growth. Since the father had continued paying maintenance and there was no serious misconduct disentitling him from access, the Court restored a more flexible schedule, allowing meetings at the father's residence on Saturdays and special occasions, arranged through court officials to safely transport the child between parents.

The case matters because it reinforces those courts must prioritize a child's genuine emotional welfare, not administrative convenience, when deciding custody and visitation matters.

title: Salam Din V. Mst. Sameena and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a custody dispute over three children between their father, Salam Din, and their mother, Sameena. After the couple divorced, the mother filed an application seeking custody of the children under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890. The Family Court at Hub granted her custody, allowing the father limited visitation rights, and this decision was upheld on appeal by the Additional District Judge, Lasbela. The father then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the record and found that the three children had been living happily with their father, were enrolled in a good school, and had told the Family Court during earlier proceedings that they loved their father and did not want to live with their mother, whom they accused of being careless and abusive toward them. The court also noted that the mother, during cross-examination, admitted she had no independent income and was financially dependent on her brothers after the divorce, while the father was a government servant capable of properly supporting the children.

Relying on Section 17 of the Guardians and Wards Act, the High Court emphasized that custody rights are never absolute but must always be decided based on the welfare of the child. Finding that the children's welfare favored remaining with their father, the court set aside the earlier judgments and accepted the father's petition, meaning custody was awarded to him instead of the mother.

title: Abdul Rehman V. The State,
explainer:
Abdul Rehman was tried for the murder of Rozi Khan, who died from knife wounds inflicted on 30 November 2014 after a group of men, including the appellant, went to his house. Rozi Khan was initially injured and later died in hospital two days later, so the case was upgraded to murder. The trial court convicted Rehman under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced him to death, along with a fine payable to the victim's heirs. He appealed, and the case also came before the High Court as a mandatory murder reference.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence, including eyewitness testimony from the deceased's son, medical evidence, and arguments about a five-hour delay in filing the police report and the absence of a recovered weapon. The court found the delay understandable given the urgent need to get the injured man to hospital, and ruled that a missing weapon does not automatically weaken a case when reliable eyewitness testimony exists. It held that the son's detailed, consistent account, corroborated by medical findings, proved the prosecution's case beyond doubt, and that a witness's relationship to the victim doesn't by itself make their testimony unreliable. The court also said that even without a clear motive, strong evidence can still justify conviction.

The High Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence. The case matters because it clarifies how courts evaluate delays in reporting crimes, witness credibility, and the weight of medical versus eyewitness evidence in murder trials.

title: Momin Khan V. Special Judge Anti-Terrorism Court-II, Quetta and another,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court, deciding a petition filed by Momin Khan, who had been accused in a criminal case involving recovery of a large quantity of illegal arms and ammunition from his house. He was charged under the Arms Ordinance, the Explosive Substances Act, and the Anti-Terrorism Act.

After the investigation and framing of charges, the government's Special Public Prosecutor filed an application asking the trial court to withdraw the case against him. However, key government officials, including the Secretary Home and Tribal Affairs, Secretary Prosecution, and Chief Secretary of Balochistan, had actually opposed this withdrawal. The trial court refused to allow the withdrawal, and Momin Khan then challenged that refusal before the High Court.

The High Court dismissed his petition. It explained that under Section 494 of the Criminal Procedure Code, only the Public Prosecutor can apply to withdraw a case, and even then, the court's consent is required and is not automatic. Courts must independently assess whether such a withdrawal genuinely serves justice or is being sought for improper reasons. Here, since senior officials had opposed the withdrawal and no real justification was given, the court found the attempt suspicious, possibly influenced by improper motives linked to the Chief Minister. Importantly, since the accused himself has no legal right to demand withdrawal of his own case, his petition was ruled not maintainable. The trial court was directed to proceed with the case.

title: Naseebullah V. The State,
explainer:
Naseebullah was convicted by a trial court in Killa Saifullah of murdering his wife, Bibi Ruqaya, and a man, Ain-ud-Din, sentencing him to life imprisonment under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, which deals with intentional murder. The bodies were found in his baithak (guest room), and he had given a confessional statement saying he killed them after finding his wife and the other man together in a compromising position in his home.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined whether this amounted to murder committed under grave and sudden provocation, even though the accused had not formally raised this defence during trial. The court found that his confession, along with medical evidence of gunshot wounds, recovered weapons, and forensic reports, supported his account that he acted in a sudden loss of self-control upon discovering the couple together, rather than through cold, premeditated intent.

The court laid out general principles for assessing claims of provocation, including that the triggering act must be serious enough to provoke an ordinary person, there must be no time to cool down, and the retaliation should be roughly proportionate to the provocation.

Applying these principles, the court concluded this was a case of grave and sudden provocation. It therefore reduced the conviction from clause (b) to clause (c) of section 302, and reduced his sentence from life imprisonment to fourteen years' rigorous imprisonment, dismissing the appeal only to that limited extent.

title: Syed Abdul Nabi V. Baz Muhammad and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of four men accused of murdering Muhammad Rafiq, whose body was found near Jagda Dam in Pishin district in 2015. The victim's brother filed a complaint, and police recovered bullet casings from the scene. The trial court acquitted the accused, and the victim's father appealed against that acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. It noted that the murder was unwitnessed, meaning there was no direct evidence linking the accused to the crime. The prosecution relied mainly on disclosure statements made by the accused while in police custody, but the court held that such statements are legally inadmissible and carry little weight, especially without independent corroboration. The court also explained that extra-judicial confessions are inherently weak evidence and cannot support a conviction unless strongly backed by other proof. Recovered bullet casings and medical evidence about the cause of death were considered merely supportive evidence that cannot substitute for direct proof or identify the actual killers.

The court emphasized an important principle: once a person is acquitted by a trial court, a "double presumption of innocence" applies, meaning appellate courts should not overturn such acquittals unless the decision was clearly arbitrary or against the evidence on record. Finding no such flaw, the High Court dismissed the appeal, keeping the accused acquitted. This case illustrates how Pakistani courts protect the presumption of innocence and set high standards for evidence in murder convictions.

title: Gul Hassan V. State,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Gul Hassan who was convicted by a trial court in Quetta for possessing heroin, under Pakistan's narcotics law, and sentenced to six years in prison plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the prosecution had not proven its case properly.

The main problem the court found was a serious delay: although the drugs were allegedly recovered on 1 January 2016, the sample was not sent to the government chemical laboratory until 26 January 2016, twenty-five days later. The law required this to happen within 72 hours, and the prosecution gave no explanation for the delay. The court also noted that the police officer who actually carried the sample to the laboratory was never brought forward as a witness, so there was no way to verify who held the sample and how it was kept safe during those twenty-five days.

Relying on earlier Supreme Court rulings, the High Court held that this broken chain of custody made the laboratory report unreliable, since the whole case depended on proving the sample was not tampered with. Because the prosecution failed to establish safe custody and transmission of the evidence, the court gave Gul Hassan the benefit of the doubt, overturned his conviction, and accepted his appeal, acquitting him. The case highlights how procedural lapses in handling evidence can be decisive in narcotics prosecutions.

title: Shah Nazar and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court, deciding an appeal by two men, Shah Nazar and Aziz Ahmed, who were convicted for possessing and transporting narcotics.

The background: anti-narcotics officers stopped a Suzuki Mehran car near Quetta after receiving a tip. Shah Nazar was driving, with Aziz Ahmed sitting beside him. On questioning, they allegedly disclosed that charas (a form of cannabis) was hidden in secret cavities of the vehicle. Officers recovered 80 kilograms of charas, took samples for laboratory testing, and the lab confirmed the substance was hashish. Both men were charged and convicted under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, sentenced to life imprisonment and fined.

On appeal, their lawyers argued the case was fabricated, that no independent witness was present during the search as required by law, and that statements made to police were not admissible as evidence.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It held that the driver of a vehicle is presumed responsible for anything transported in it, and a passenger sitting beside him could not escape responsibility either, especially since he offered no explanation for being there. The court noted the lab report confirmed the drugs, the recovery process was properly documented, and there was no evidence of enmity between the accused and the police witnesses that might suggest they were falsely implicated. Since the accused failed to disprove the prosecution's case as required under the law once the initial burden was met, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the convictions

title: Faqir Dad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a bail application before the Balochistan High Court by a man named Faqir Dad, who had been arrested in connection with a 2009 murder case registered under sections 302 and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code (murder and common intention). He was seeking post-arrest bail after a trial court had already denied it.

Key facts: Faqir Dad was not named in the original police report (FIR). He was only implicated later, based on a supplementary statement given by the complainant nine days after the FIR was filed, raising the possibility that this statement was the product of deliberation rather than immediate, reliable identification. The only evidence against him was his own disclosure statement, which was not backed up by other evidence. Additionally, two co-accused in the same case had already been acquitted by the trial court. He had also been absconding for about ten years before his arrest.

The High Court granted him bail. It reasoned that where a case calls for "further inquiry" into guilt due to weak or uncorroborated evidence, bail should be granted as a right, not a favor. The court also held that the acquittal of co-accused in similar circumstances cannot be ignored when deciding bail, and that a long period of absconding does not automatically disqualify someone from bail if the case is otherwise fit for it. This judgment reinforces important bail principles: evidentiary weakness and co-accused acquittals matter, and absconding alone isn't an absolute bar to bail.

The defendants did not appear, so the trial court proceeded ex parte and eventually dismissed the suit. SCD appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

title: Taqveem Shah V. Government of Balochistan and 2 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a challenge to the government's decision to hire a retired civil servant, Abdul Wahid Kakar, on a two-year contract as Senior Coordination Officer for CPEC (China-Pakistan Economic Corridor) in the Chief Secretary's Office. The petitioner, Taqveem Shah, filed a constitutional petition seeking what is known as a writ of quo warranto, essentially asking the court to question the legal authority behind this appointment.

The central issue the court examined was whether Shah had the legal standing to bring this challenge at all. Under Pakistan's Constitution, only an "aggrieved person" can file such a petition. The court explained that to qualify as aggrieved, a person must show that some personal right or interest of theirs was directly affected by the decision being challenged, not just a general objection to how government business is conducted.

The court found that Shah failed to demonstrate any personal stake in the matter. He could not show that the appointment violated any right belonging to him or caused him any personal loss, disadvantage, or harm. Citing several precedents from Pakistani and Indian courts, the judges emphasized that constitutional courts exist to resolve real disputes affecting genuine rights, not to entertain challenges from parties with no direct connection to the issue.

Because Shah did not meet this threshold, the court dismissed his petition outright, without going into the merits of whether the appointment itself was proper. The case underscores the importance of legal standing as a gatekeeping requirement in public interest lit

title: Messrs Iqra Anwar-Ul-Quran Lil Itefal through Director V. Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation, Headquarter Islamabad through Station Director BPS, Quetta,
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant dispute over four flats in Quetta rented to a religious teaching trust by the Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation (PBC). PBC filed for eviction, claiming it needed the flats back to house its own employees, and also alleged the tenant had defaulted on rent payments. The tenant contested this, denying the claims.

The trial court (Rent Controller) ruled in favor of PBC, ordering the tenant to vacate the flats and pay outstanding rent. The tenant appealed, but the Balochistan High Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the eviction. The tenant then went to the Supreme Court, which sent the case back to the High Court for a fresh, more detailed review of the evidence.

On reconsideration, the High Court again ruled against the tenant. It found that PBC's witnesses gave consistent testimony about needing the flats for staff accommodation, and the tenant failed to disprove this during cross-examination. The court held that when a landlord's sworn statement about genuine personal need matches the eviction application and survives cross-examination, that is enough to prove the need is real. The court also emphasized that under Pakistan's Constitution, property ownership rights are a protected fundamental right that takes precedence over a tenant's lesser right of occupancy, meaning a tenant cannot second-guess whether the landlord's need is sufficient.

This case matters because it clarifies how courts assess a landlord's "bona fide need" in eviction cases and reinforces that ownership rights generally

title: Bahadur Khan V. The Vice-Chancellor, Balochistan University of Medical And Health Sciences, Quetta,
explainer:
This case involved a student challenging the admission policy of Bolan Medical College, Quetta, run by the Balochistan University of Medical and Health Sciences. The petitioner had passed his matriculation exam in 2012 but then pursued Islamic religious education before completing his intermediate (F.Sc) exam in 2017, six years later. When he applied for an MBBS/BDS seat, the university deducted five marks per year for the six-year gap between his matriculation and intermediate qualifications, as required by the prospectus's merit formula. He argued this deduction was unfair and unconstitutional, and also complained that he was denied 20 bonus marks awarded to religious scholars or those with madrasa qualifications, even though marks were deducted for his religious studies gap.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the petitioner had not submitted a certificate proving he was a Hafiz-e-Quran or met the specific madrasa qualification requirements needed to claim the 20 bonus marks, so he was not entitled to them. On the marks deduction issue, the court held that admission eligibility criteria are policy matters set by the college, and courts cannot act as an appellate body over such policy decisions unless they are shown to be unconstitutional, illegal, arbitrary, or made in bad faith. Since no such flaw was shown here, the court refused to interfere and dismissed the petition outright, reaffirming that courts generally defer to institutions on academic policy matters.

title: Azizullah V. The Inspector General of Police Balochistan, Central Police Office and 18 others,
explainer:
This case concerns Azizullah, who applied for the post of Inspector Police in the Home and Tribal Affairs Department after an advertisement was issued in 2019. He passed the written test and qualified, but during the physical measurement stage, he was declared unfit due to short height. Police Rules, 1934 require a minimum height of 5 feet 7 inches for recruits, and his measured height fell short of this requirement, first recorded at 5 feet 6 3/4 inches, and later, after an inquiry into his complaint, found to be even shorter at 5 feet 6 inches and 2 soot.

The petitioner argued he had separately been measured and found fit for the post of ASI, and challenged his rejection for the Inspector post. An inquiry was conducted, which found inconsistencies in how his height had been measured by different committees using different scales, and even recommended disciplinary action against officials who had wrongly recorded his height for the ASI post.

The Balochistan High Court held that meeting the minimum height requirement is a mandatory condition for appointment, and can only be relaxed with special sanction from the Deputy Inspector General of Police, which had not been granted in this case. Since the petitioner did not meet the height standard, the court dismissed his petition, while directing authorities to continue the recruitment process on merit. The case underscores that physical eligibility rules in police recruitment are strictly enforced unless properly relaxed by the competent authority.

title: Sheikh Abdul Aziz V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a pre-arrest bail application before the Balochistan High Court. The applicant, Sheikh Abdul Aziz, was accused in an FIR alleging that he and others, armed with a pistol, set fire to machinery belonging to a coal company using petrol. He faced charges including mischief by fire, criminal intimidation, and rioting.

The court noted several important facts: the FIR was lodged with an unexplained 20-hour delay even though the police station was only 3 kilometers from the crime scene; no specific individual role was attributed to the applicant, only a general collective one; and notably, the applicant himself had filed an earlier FIR against the coal company's laborers over an incident where machinery was damaged, mines were set on fire, and one person died with another injured. This made the case against the applicant look like a "counterblast" - a retaliatory complaint filed to undermine his original FIR.

The judge explained that pre-arrest bail is meant to protect people from false or malicious prosecution, and that courts can examine the merits of a case when deciding such applications. Given the delay in filing the FIR, lack of specific allegations against the applicant, and the suspicious timing suggesting retaliation, the court found sufficient grounds to grant pre-arrest bail. This case illustrates how courts scrutinize delayed FIRs and counter-complaints to guard against misuse of the criminal justice system for personal disputes.
