title: Before Muhammad Kamran Khan Mulakhail, Chairman and Gul Hassan Tareen, Member Nazir Ahmed V. Chief Justice High Court of Balochistan through Registrar and another,
explainer:
This case involved a Court Assistant working at the Balochistan High Court who, after completing 27 years of qualifying service, applied for and was granted Leave Preparatory to Retirement (LPR) for 365 days, from August 2022 to July 2023. Near the end of this leave period, he suddenly changed his mind and applied to withdraw his LPR, wanting to continue working instead of retiring. The Chief Justice, as the competent authority, rejected his request.

The employee appealed, arguing that under the applicable leave rules, he was entitled to withdraw his LPR option before it expired. The Tribunal disagreed and dismissed his appeal. It held that once he exercised his option for LPR and it was accepted and acted upon (including drawing salary during that period), the matter became final and could not be undone, based on the legal principle of locus poenitentiae (no right to change one's mind after a decision has taken effect). The Tribunal also found that the specific rule he relied on for withdrawal did not apply to High Court staff, since it required approval from a higher authority than the one who granted the leave, and in the High Court, the Chief Justice has no superior authority to approve such withdrawal. Additionally, that rule was never adopted into the High Court's own service rules.

This case clarifies that government employees who opt for retirement leave generally cannot reverse that decision once it's been approved and enacted, reinforcing certainty and finality in retirement decisions within the civil service.

title: Shazia Jaffar and 4 others V. General Public and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a letter of administration, which is a legal document that allows someone to manage the property of a deceased person. After Fozia Jaffar died, her husband applied to a Civil Judge acting as a District Delegate to get authority over her property. Her relatives objected, arguing that the husband had actually divorced her about 35 years earlier and that his application was dishonest, especially since a related civil suit was already pending in court.

Despite this objection, the District Judge (acting as District Delegate) went ahead, framed formal legal issues, held proceedings, and granted the husband the letter of administration.

The Balochistan High Court found this to be improper. It explained that under the Succession Act, 1925, a District Delegate only has power to handle uncontested cases. Once someone formally opposes an application, it becomes a contentious case, and the law requires the District Delegate to either send the case back to the applicant to present to the District Judge, or forward it directly to the District Judge himself. The District Delegate has no authority to decide contested matters on his own.

Because the objection here clearly made the case contentious, the District Delegate had no jurisdiction to frame issues and rule on the matter. The High Court therefore declared his order void, set it aside, and sent the case back to be handled correctly under the proper legal procedure. This ruling clarifies the limits of a District Delegate's authority in succession matters.

title: Syed Muhammad Qasim V. Syed Bashir Ahmed,
explainer:
Court judgment summary needed on the given case.

This case involved a dispute between a property seller (Syed Muhammad Qasim) and buyer (Syed Bashir Ahmed) over a 2020 sale agreement worth 9.1 million rupees. The buyer had allegedly paid 1.6 million rupees as advance, with the remaining 7.5 million due within a year. When the seller allegedly refused to complete the sale, the buyer sued for specific performance, asking the court to force the sale through.

The trial court dismissed the buyer's case, but an appellate court reversed this and ordered the sale to proceed. The seller then challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court sided with the seller. It found that although the written contract mentioned the advance payment, the seller could still argue in court that he never actually received that money, since acknowledgment of payment is merely a factual claim, not a binding contract term. More importantly, the buyer failed to prove he had ever paid the advance or tried to pay the remaining balance on time. He also never showed genuine willingness to pay by depositing the money in court during the trial. Since specific performance is a discretionary remedy requiring the buyer to prove readiness and willingness to fulfill his side of the deal, the court ruled he wasn't entitled to it. The High Court therefore overturned the appellate court's decision and restored the trial court's dismissal of the case, emphasizing that both parties in a sale must be ready to perform their obligations for such relief to be granted.

title: Saeed Ahmed and 4 others V. Bibi Khourd and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over jointly-owned family property in Chaghi, Balochistan. The petitioners had filed a civil suit seeking a court declaration that certain lands were jointly owned and should be divided among the family members through partition. While the suit was pending, they filed an application asking the trial court to allow amendments to their original plaint.

The trial court rejected this amendment application, and when the petitioners challenged that decision through a revision petition before the Additional District Judge, that too was dismissed. They then approached the Balochistan High Court under Article 199 of the Constitution, asking it to set aside both lower court orders and allow their proposed amendments.

The High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the decisions of both lower courts. It held that anyone seeking to amend pleadings under Order VI, Rule 17 of the Civil Procedure Code must clearly and specifically state exactly what changes they want to make and where in the document those changes should go. Vague or general requests for amendment cannot be granted. In this case, the petitioners had not clearly specified what they wanted added or changed. The court also noted this was effectively a second attempt at amendment, repeating facts already covered in an earlier amendment that had been allowed, suggesting the petitioners were delaying the case rather than genuinely needing changes.

This ruling reinforces that amendment applications must be precise and specific, not open-ended, to prevent misuse of procedural rules to stall litigation.

title: Umar Farooq and another V. Muhammad Usman and 7 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between neighbors over the right to use a street. The petitioners bought a house from one branch of a family that had inherited two adjoining properties. They claimed that a rear street behind the properties belonged exclusively to their house, based on how the family had earlier divided the land between two brothers, and sought to stop the respondents, who owned the neighboring house, from using it. They filed a lawsuit asking for a declaration of rights, possession of a disputed strip of land, and an order stopping the government land authority from delaying transfer of the property in their name.

Both the trial court and the appellate court ruled against the petitioners, finding that the respondents also had a legal right to use the street. The petitioners then approached the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions. It explained that under Section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act, when property is transferred, everything permanently attached to it, including rights like easements, passes along with it, based on the legal principle that an accessory follows the main property. Since the petitioners had originally sold part of the property to the respondents' predecessors, that transfer included the right to use the connecting street. The court also noted that when two lower courts agree on the facts, higher courts are usually reluctant to interfere. The revision petition was dismissed, meaning both families retained shared rights to use the street.

title: Azmat Ali and another V. Chaman Ali and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a house in Quetta. Chaman Ali claimed that the previous owner, whose legal heirs became the petitioners, had orally agreed to sell him the house for Rs. 1,700,000. He said he paid off two mortgages on the property worth Rs. 850,000 and paid the remaining Rs. 850,000 directly to the owner, but the owner never formally transferred the property and later tried to evict him. The trial court dismissed his suit, finding he failed to prove the oral sale and that his claim was time-barred. However, an appellate court reversed that decision and ruled in his favor. The petitioners then challenged that appellate ruling in the High Court.

The High Court sided with the petitioners, restoring the trial court's dismissal. It found that Chaman Ali had not properly proven the essential elements of the oral contract, could not produce a receipt for the payments he claimed to have made, and failed to call the witnesses who signed the mortgage documents to verify their authenticity, as required by evidence law. The court also criticized the appellate court's reasoning as vague and legally unsound.

This case matters because it reinforces that claims of oral property sales must be backed by solid, specific evidence, including proper witnesses and documentation, especially when large sums of money and property ownership are at stake.

title: Muhammad Ameen and others V. Munawar Ali and others,
explainer:
This case is about how appellate courts should handle situations where evidence on record is already sufficient but a trial court judgment left a question unresolved.

The petitioners had won at trial, but the respondents appealed to the District Judge, who partly allowed the appeal and sent the whole case back to the trial court, asking it to decide an additional issue about whether the disputed land had earlier been mortgaged to a bank. The petitioners challenged this remand order in the Balochistan High Court, arguing that since both sides had already produced all their evidence, the Appellate Court itself should have decided the case, including the mortgage issue, rather than sending it back down.

The High Court agreed with the petitioners. It explained the difference between various remand rules in the Civil Procedure Code: some allow sending a case back only when evidence is incomplete or a suit was decided merely on a preliminary point, while another rule requires the appellate court to decide the case itself once full evidence is already available, even if it needs to reframe or add issues. Since the record showed the trial court had already recorded findings on the mortgage question and all evidence existed, the High Court held that remanding the whole case was a jurisdictional error.

The High Court set aside the Appellate Court's remand order and directed the District Judge to decide the appeal itself, including the mortgage issue, based on existing evidence. This case clarifies when appellate courts may send cases back for retrial versus when they must decide matters themselves, promoting quicker, more efficient resolution of civil disputes.

title: Shoukat Das and others V. Shazia Riaz alias POLY and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over plots in the Bashirabad Christian Welfare Housing Society in Quetta. The society had been formed on land originally purchased and donated by a Christian politician for poor Christian community members, and plots were allotted under contracts that restricted allottees from ever transferring or selling their plots to non-Christians. When some plot and shop holders sold their properties to other buyers, members of the society sued, arguing the sales violated these contractual restrictions and that the land was religious endowment (waqf) property meant only for the Christian community.

Both the trial court and the appellate court dismissed the suit, and the matter reached the Balochistan High Court by way of revision petition. The High Court upheld the dismissal. It held that a condition permanently barring an owner from selling or transferring property is void, since it conflicts with a property owner's basic right to dispose of their own property under the Transfer of Property Act, and with constitutional protections including the right to own and dispose of property and the right against being deprived of property. The court also found the petitioners failed to prove the land was actually waqf property, and noted evidence that non-Christians already lived in houses in the society.

This judgment matters because it reaffirms that contractual clauses permanently restricting how an owner can deal with their own property are legally unenforceable, even when tied to community or religious housing schemes.

title: Huafa Urban Operation Gwadar (PVT.) Limited V. Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan,
explainer:
This case involved a company called Huafa Urban Operation Gwadar, which was set up to work on infrastructure projects. Its parent company in China had promised to invest a large amount of capital, but because of financial difficulties caused by the Covid-19 pandemic, it could only pay in a smaller portion of the originally planned share capital. As a result, the company wanted to formally reduce its paid-up capital to match what had actually been invested, changing it from over two billion rupees to about 552 million rupees.

Under company law, such a reduction requires shareholder approval through a special resolution and, ultimately, confirmation by a court. The company held a special meeting, passed the required resolution, registered it with the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP), and published public notices inviting objections. No one objected, and SECP itself raised no concerns after reviewing the company's financial position, which showed it could easily cover its existing liabilities.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed whether the reduction was fair to shareholders, transparent, and did not harm public interest or unpaid creditors. Finding all legal requirements met and no unfairness involved, the court approved the reduction of capital as proposed.

This judgment matters because it illustrates how courts oversee corporate capital restructuring to protect shareholders and the public, while still allowing legitimate business adjustments—especially those necessitated by real economic hardships like the pandemic.

title: Dr. Sadaf Usman V. Ahmed Yar,
explainer:
This case concerns a medical negligence lawsuit filed by a husband after his wife died following childbirth complications. The wife, who was pregnant and had a declining platelet count, was under the care of the petitioner doctor at a hospital in Quetta. The husband alleged that the doctor failed to properly review blood test results, failed to advise necessary platelet and blood transfusions, and after surgery to remove the uterus due to severe bleeding, abandoned the patient in a critical condition overnight without arranging proper follow-up care. The patient was later transferred between hospitals and eventually died.

The trial court and the first appellate court both found the doctor negligent and awarded the husband 50 million rupees in damages. The doctor challenged this in the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition.

The High Court upheld the finding of negligence, agreeing that the doctor's conduct caused the death and that the lower courts' findings were not legally flawed. However, it found that the huge damages award of 50 million rupees was not properly justified or explained, and appeared punitive rather than compensatory, especially since no specific financial losses had been claimed or proven. The court clarified that general damages for pain and grief are meant to compensate, not punish, and cannot be awarded arbitrarily. As a result, it partly allowed the revision, keeping the negligence finding intact but sending back the damages amount for reconsideration under proper legal principles.

title: Mst. Farzana (widow) and another V. Abid Khan and 2 others,
explainer:
Mst. Farzana and another petitioner (the widow and a co-defendant) challenged a decision that revived a civil suit against them. The dispute began when a suit was filed in a court that later turned out to lack territorial jurisdiction. On the petitioners' own request, the plaint was returned so it could be filed in the correct court. Instead of filing a brand-new suit, the plaintiff (respondent 1) simply presented the same returned plaint, along with all prior proceedings and evidence, to the court that did have jurisdiction. The petitioners took part in these proceedings, cross-examined witnesses, and never objected to this procedure until later, when they applied to have the plaint rejected, arguing a fresh suit should have been filed from scratch.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed their revision petition. It held that under the Civil Procedure Code, when a plaint is returned for lack of jurisdiction, the same plaint and record should be presented to the correct court, which then continues from where proceedings left off rather than restarting entirely. Since the petitioners had actively participated without objection and showed no actual prejudice, they were barred by the doctrine of waiver/estoppel from later challenging the process. The court upheld the lower appellate court's order sending the case back for trial on merits.

This ruling clarifies that parties who participate in proceedings without timely objection cannot later use procedural technicalities to escape a case, reinforcing fairness and efficiency in civil litigation.

title: Naimat Ali Shah V. Anjum Shagufta and another,
explainer:
This case concerns a landlord-tenant dispute in Quetta. The property owner, Anjum Shagufta, sought eviction of her tenant, Naimat Ali Shah, claiming he had not paid rent since the tenancy began in 2020 and that she needed the house for her own personal use. The Rent Controller ordered eviction and recovery of unpaid rent, and the tenant appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The tenant argued that the landlady had failed to prove non-payment of rent and personal need, and claimed he had actually paid her Rs.550,000, which created a "charge" on the property that would block eviction unless repaid. He also, at points, claimed to have purchased the house outright.

The High Court rejected these arguments. It found the tenant's positions contradictory: he could not simultaneously claim to be a buyer, a charge-holder, and admit paying rent as a tenant. He provided no documentary proof of any sale price or payment, and no evidence that the money was given as a loan secured against the property, which is what a legal "charge" requires. Since he had originally been let into possession as a tenant and later acknowledged the landlady's ownership, the law presumes that relationship continues unless clearly disproven. The court invoked the principle "once a tenant, always a tenant" and held that his denial of the landlord-tenant relationship was baseless. The appeal was dismissed, upholding the eviction order.

title: Faizullah V. Senior Member Board of Revenue Balochistan, Quetta and 5 others,
explainer:
Faizullah sued in the Civil Court claiming he was the lawful lessee of government land in Quetta, based on a 2015 deed of transfer and assignment executed in his favour by a woman who had earlier taken over a private company that originally leased the land from the Deputy Commissioner in 1993. When the Board of Revenue later leased the same land to government offices in 2019, Faizullah asked the courts to cancel that new lease and confirm his rights, including specific performance of the transfer deed. The trial court dismissed his suit, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the original 1993 lease was invalid because the Deputy Commissioner had no authority to lease out government property without prior approval from the Board of Revenue. Since that lease was legally ineffective and unregistered, the woman who later transferred rights to Faizullah never actually held valid leasehold rights herself, and could not pass on something she never had. The court also noted the transfer deed to Faizullah lacked any consideration, making it unenforceable under contract law. As a result, Faizullah had no legal standing to bring the suit.

This case matters because it reinforces the principle that no one can transfer better rights than they possess, and that government land transactions require proper official authorization to be legally valid.

title: Abdul Khaliq and another V. Muhammad Ismail and others,
explainer:
This case involved a land dispute where two brothers, Abdul Khaliq and another, claimed ownership of unsettled land based on a 2011 purchase agreement, while another group claimed ownership based on an earlier 2003 purchase and long-standing possession as hereditary tenants. Lower courts had dismissed the petitioners' lawsuit for declaration and possession, and the Balochistan High Court reviewed that decision.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It found that the petitioners never actually proved they held possession of the land, and their own witnesses admitted that the respondents were the ones physically occupying and cultivating it, including operating tube-wells there. The petitioners also failed to explain why they bought land without taking possession of it, and they had concealed important facts from the trial court, including the existence of a religious scholar's prior decision on the matter.

The court applied the legal principle that possession is strong evidence of ownership, and when both sides are equally at fault, the law favors whoever is actually in possession. It also emphasized that remedies like declaration and injunction are discretionary and equitable, meaning courts only grant them to parties who come with clean hands and full honesty—something the petitioners failed to do. Since they weren't in possession and hadn't disclosed key facts, they weren't entitled to relief. The court also noted unresolved court-fee deficiencies. The petition was dismissed, reinforcing that hiding facts and lacking possession can defeat even a seemingly valid ownership claim.

title: The Secretary B&R Department, Government of Balochistan Civil Secretariat, Quetta and others V. Sardar Sikandar Hayat Khan Jogezai,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute over unpaid fuel bills. A petrol pump owner sued the Balochistan Building and Roads Department for recovery of about Rs. 12.6 lakh, claiming the department had failed to pay for fuel supplied to its vehicles and machinery, causing him financial loss because he had borrowed money from a bank to cover the shortfall. His first suit was dismissed and, after appeals, he was permitted to file a fresh suit on the same cause of action. This second suit was decreed in his favor by both the trial court and the appellate court, prompting the government to challenge those decisions before the High Court.

The government's revision petition was itself filed late, and it tried to get the delay excused. The High Court found the delay unexplained and refused to condone it under the normal rules. However, the Court held that when it exercises its own suo motu revisional powers, ordinary limitation restrictions do not apply. Using this power, the Court examined the case and ruled that the second suit was actually time-barred, because the time spent on the earlier withdrawn suit could not be excluded when calculating the limitation period, despite permission having been granted to refile.

As a result, the High Court set aside the judgments and decrees of both lower courts and allowed the revision, emphasizing that limitation law is mandatory and courts must dismiss suits filed beyond the prescribed time limit, regardless of whether parties raise the issue themselves.

title: Abdul Razzaq V. Muhammad Shafiq and others,
explainer:
This case is about a long-running property dispute in Quetta. Abdul Razzaq claimed he had bought a piece of land in 1995 from a man named Rozi Khan, who he said had himself bought it from the family of Respondent 2, the recorded owner. Razzaq said the owner's father and uncle had promised to formally transfer the land into his name once he paid them money, which he claimed to have done. When he later tried to build on the land, Respondent 2 objected and claimed ownership himself, leading to a legal battle.

The trial court initially ruled in Razzaq's favour and ordered the transfer of the land to his name. However, on appeal, the Additional District Judge overturned this decision, finding that Razzaq had failed to prove the alleged sale chain: Rozi Khan was never actually the legal owner of the land, so any deal between him and Razzaq could not bind the real recorded owner, Respondent 2. There was no proof that Respondent 2 himself agreed to transfer the land or received the payment.

The Balochistan High Court, reviewing the case, agreed with the appellate court's reasoning and dismissed Razzaq's revision petition, upholding the dismissal of his suit.

This case matters because it reinforces an important legal principle: a buyer cannot claim rights to transfer land title from someone who did not have proper ownership or authority over that property, and unproven sale claims cannot override official land records.

title: Ghulam Nabi and others V. Bibi Tahira and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family land dispute in Balochistan. The petitioners claimed that they and some of the respondents had agreed to settle a land disagreement through arbitration in 2002. An arbitration award was issued, which awarded certain land to the petitioners in exchange for other land. The petitioners then filed a civil suit asking the court to declare them owners of the land based on this award and to order transfer of the land records into their names. Both the trial court and the appellate court rejected their case, and they brought the matter to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It explained that under the Arbitration Act 1940, an arbitration award has no legal effect on its own, it must first be formally made a rule of the court through proper legal procedure. Since the petitioners never took this step, they could not use the award to claim ownership through an ordinary civil suit. The law specifically bars using a regular lawsuit to enforce or validate an arbitration award outside the procedures set by the Act.

The court also found that one of the female respondents, who was the recorded owner of part of the land, was never a party to the arbitration agreement and had not authorized anyone to represent her in it. Therefore the award could not bind her or force her to transfer her land.

This ruling reinforces that arbitration awards need formal court validation to be enforceable, and that no one can be bound by an arbitration they never agreed to join.

title: Mrs. Razia Amir Sultana and others V. Al Amir Paper Mills (Pvt.) Limited and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over shares in Al-Amir Paper Mills, a company incorporated in 1993. The applicants and one respondent (Respondent No. 2) were siblings who inherited shares from their late father. Several siblings moved abroad to Canada and the USA around 1999-2000, leaving Respondent No. 2 to run the company. The applicants alleged that while they were away, Respondent No. 2 fraudulently removed their names from the company's register of members, took over their shares along with their deceased father's shares, and later transferred these shares to another party in violation of the company's rules. In 2021, the applicants petitioned the Balochistan High Court to correct the shareholding register and restore their names as rightful shareholders.

The court sided with the applicants. It found that Respondent No. 2, as the person who benefited from the disputed transfer, bore the burden of proving he had legitimately purchased the shares—but he provided no evidence of any sale, payment, or properly executed transfer documents as required by law. The court also ruled that no time limit applies to such rectification petitions, especially between co-heirs disputing inherited property, so the case was not too late to file. The court ordered the company's shareholding register to be corrected to reflect the applicants as rightful shareholders. This case matters because it clarifies that claims to correct company ownership records among family co-owners aren't barred by limitation periods, and that whoever benefits from a disputed share transfer must prove its legitimacy.

title: Shakar Khan through Legal Heirs V. Muhammad Ali and others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running land dispute over correction of a revenue record and cancellation of certain contracts dating back to 1965, 2010, and 2013. During the proceedings, an appellate court had earlier sent the case back to the trial court and directed the plaintiffs to amend their claim to include cancellation of the 2013 contract. The plaintiffs repeatedly failed to file this amended plaint despite being given many chances, including opportunities granted on payment of costs, and even citing the Covid-19 pandemic as an excuse. As a result, the trial court dismissed the entire suit, and the first appellate court upheld that dismissal.

The Balochistan High Court found that both lower courts had made a legal error. It explained that under the Civil Procedure Code, when a party fails to file an amendment within the allowed time, the correct consequence is simply that they lose the right to amend—not that their whole case gets thrown out. Additionally, the court noted that the rule used to dismiss the suit only applies once a case reaches the hearing stage with issues framed, which had not happened here since the case was still at the pleadings stage.

The High Court allowed the revision, set aside both lower court orders, and sent the case back to the trial court to proceed using the existing (unamended) pleadings, with instructions to decide the suit within four months. This case matters because it clarifies that procedural defaults in amending pleadings should not result in a case being dismissed outright if the correct legal remedy is narrower.

title: Messrs National Bank of Pakistan Attorney/Officer/Manager V. Messrs Bismillah Maritime Breakers through Partners and others,
explainer:
This case involved two connected civil suits filed in 2009 in the Balochistan High Court. National Bank of Pakistan sued Bismillah Maritime Breakers, a partnership firm, along with its partners and their guarantors, to recover about Rs. 431 million. The bank had provided the firm with import and finance facilities that were repeatedly enhanced over the years, from Rs. 62 million to Rs. 500 million, secured by mortgaged properties, pledged stock, and personal guarantees. When the firm defaulted on repayment and its renewal request was declined due to poor performance, the bank discovered that pledged stock worth millions had disappeared from the site, allegedly with the involvement of the stock custodian.

The court held that the guarantors were liable along with the principal debtor, since they had signed guarantee documents and title-deed deposits that provided sufficient legal consideration for their guarantees. Under the Contract Act, a guarantor's liability is equal to that of the principal debtor. The court also ruled that the bank was entitled to recover cost of funds and other charges under the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001, from the date the finance agreement expired and default occurred.

The judgment reaffirms important banking law principles: guarantors cannot escape liability once they've signed valid guarantees, special damages must be specifically proven, and even an acquittal in a criminal case doesn't remove civil liability for unpaid debts. The bank's suit was decreed in its favor.

title: Muhammad Waseem V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns the rape of a four-year-old girl, Maryam, allegedly committed by the appellant, Muhammad Waseem, a neighbour of the victim's family. The incident was reported by the child's father, and after medical examination, an FIR was registered. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 376-A of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced him to life imprisonment with a fine, while extending credit for time already served.

On appeal, the defence raised several objections, including that the investigation did not follow the special procedures required under the Anti-Rape (Investigation and Trial) Act, 2021; that the FIR was lodged by the father rather than the victim; that there was delay in reporting and in sending forensic samples; and that a pending civil suit gave the family a motive to falsely implicate the appellant.

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence, focusing particularly on statements made by the victim to a witness and to her parents shortly after the assault. The court explained the legal doctrine of res gestae, which allows spontaneous statements made at or near the time of an event to be treated as reliable evidence, even though they would normally be considered hearsay. Since the victim disclosed the abuse almost immediately to those around her, and her account was consistent and corroborated by medical evidence, the court found the prosecution had proven its case beyond doubt. The conviction and life sentence were upheld, and the appeal was dismissed, with the court noting that the sentence was already lenient compared to the maximum penalty of death.

title: Behzad Hussain V. Bibi Ansa and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a husband and wife over dowry articles and maintenance payments. After their marriage in 2016 and the birth of three children, the couple separated, with the wife alleging she was mistreated, denied maintenance, and eventually divorced. She sued for recovery of her dowry items (jewelry, crockery, household goods) and monthly maintenance until the end of her waiting period (iddat). The Family Court ruled in her favor, a decision upheld on appeal. The husband then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the courts had misread evidence, particularly disputing gold purchase receipts that were dated before the wedding, which he claimed proved they were fake.

The High Court rejected his petition. It found that the wife had proven her dowry items were genuinely brought to the marital home, noting that receipts predating a wedding are common since parents often buy jewelry in advance. The Court explained that under the Constitution's Article 199, its power to overturn lower court decisions is limited, especially when two courts have already agreed on the facts after examining evidence. It can only step in if there is clear misreading of evidence or a shockingly unjust outcome—not simply to reweigh evidence itself. Finding no such flaw here, the Court dismissed the petition, leaving the wife's entitlement to dowry recovery and maintenance intact. The case illustrates how family courts prioritize practical justice over rigid technicalities, and how limited high courts' review powers are once lower courts agree on facts.

title: Rukhsana V. Muhammad Khan and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a family maintenance dispute from Quetta. A wife filed a suit seeking monthly maintenance for herself and her two daughters, plus recovery of the daughters' educational documents, from her husband, whom she said was wealthy and earning substantially but had failed to support them. The husband denied this, saying the separation was the wife's own doing and that he had been regularly paying maintenance for the daughters.

The Family Court partly ruled in the wife's favor: it ordered the husband to pay maintenance for the two daughters, with a yearly increase, but dismissed her personal claim for maintenance and for the documents. The Appellate Court upheld this decision. The wife then challenged both rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the evidence and found that the wife had left the husband's house on her own accord, without justification such as cruelty or non-payment of dower. Under Islamic law principles cited by the court, a husband is not obligated to maintain a wife who is disobedient or who leaves his home without lawful cause. Since both lower courts had already reached the same factual conclusion, the High Court declined to interfere with these "concurrent findings of fact." The petition was dismissed, meaning the wife was not granted personal maintenance, though the daughters' maintenance award remained intact. The case illustrates how courts assess a wife's conduct and reasons for separation when deciding maintenance entitlement.

title: Rozi Khan alias Chako alias Dolat Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about Rozi Khan, also known as Chako or Dolat Khan, who appealed his conviction under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. He had been caught by police near a graveyard trying to flee, and a search found him carrying 1020 grams of hashish. A trial court convicted him and sentenced him to one year of rigorous imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, his lawyer argued that the chain of custody for the narcotics sample was broken, that there were contradictions in the evidence, and that the police had the wrong name for him, claiming he was actually Dolat Khan son of Abdullah, not Rozi Khan son of Gul Muhammad.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It found that the police witnesses gave consistent testimony about his arrest, the search, and the recovery of the drugs. title: Khaliq Dad and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Khaliq Dad and Basharatullah, who were caught at a checkpoint in Khuzdar, Balochistan, driving a car in which police allegedly found 2 kilograms of heroin and 25 kilograms of opium hidden in secret cavities inside the dashboard. They were tried under Pakistan's narcotics law and convicted, receiving life imprisonment and fines. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted both men, giving them the benefit of the doubt. The court found serious flaws in the prosecution's case: the police witness and the investigating officer gave contradictory accounts of basic facts, like who received the initial report and when the officer arrived at the scene. The dashboard, which supposedly contained the hidden drugs, was never produced in court despite being key evidence, and no one explained how it was taken apart. The prosecution also failed to show that the drug samples were properly handled and transported to the laboratory for testing, as required by law. Additionally, there was no evidence that the passenger, Basharatullah, knew drugs were hidden in the car.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that criminal convictions, especially those carrying life sentences, must rest on consistent, credible evidence and strict compliance with legal procedures for handling evidence like narcotics samples. Gaps or contradictions in the prosecution's story can be enough to overturn a conviction.

title: Haider Khan V. Sher Khan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case dealt with a property dispute where a citizen, Haider Khan, filed a civil suit involving a piece of land, naming the revenue department (a government body) as one of the defendants. The Qazi Court initially hearing the case sent the plaint back to him, ruling that under a special 1976 regulation for tribal areas, such courts could not hear cases where the government was a party. An appellate body upheld this decision. However, neither court told the petitioner which court he should actually approach instead, leaving him without a clear path forward.

The Balochistan High Court examined the situation and noted a major legal change: the 25th Constitutional Amendment of 2018 had merged Pakistan's tribal areas (like the Provincially and Federally Administered Tribal Areas) into the regular provinces. This meant the old system of tribal courts, including Qazi Courts and the Majlis-e-Shoora operating under the 1976 regulation, no longer had a special legal basis. A High Court notification from 2019 had already formally transferred all pending cases from these tribal forums to the ordinary Civil Courts.

The court ruled that since the tribal areas no longer exist as a separate legal category, disputes like this one must now go to the regular Civil Courts. It dismissed the petition but clarified that Haider Khan could refile his property case before an ordinary Civil Court, effectively resolving the confusion about jurisdiction after the tribal areas' merger into Balochistan province.

title: Abdul Khaliq V. The State,
explainer:
This is a criminal appeal decided by the Balochistan High Court concerning a fatal attack in Mastung. According to the prosecution, the appellant, Abdul Khaliq, along with several co-accused, attacked a group of men returning from their fields. One man, Mir Shadain, died after being shot by a co-accused who fled and was declared a proclaimed offender, while two others were injured, including one struck by the appellant with an axe. The trial court had convicted Abdul Khaliq of murder under Sections 302 and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code, sentencing him to life imprisonment plus compensation payments, on the theory that he shared a common intention with the shooter.

The High Court reviewed the evidence, including eyewitness testimony from the complainant and injured witnesses, and medical evidence. It found the witnesses credible and consistent, but concluded that the prosecution had not proven that the appellant shared any common intention or plan with the actual shooter to kill the deceased. The court found the incident happened spontaneously, not as part of a coordinated murder plan, and noted the appellant only used an axe against one victim rather than lethal force. Therefore, the court held he could not be convicted of murder, but only for the specific injuries he caused. It set aside the murder conviction and instead convicted him under injury-related provisions (337-A(ii) and 337-L(2)), reducing his sentence accordingly. The case highlights how courts distinguish between direct participation in a killing and mere presence during a group assault.

title: Nazeer Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Nazeer Ahmed, who was stopped by police on a motorcycle in Killa Abdullah, Balochistan, and allegedly found with two large quantities of opium and a black flag resembling that of the proscribed organization "Daesh" (ISIS). He was convicted by a trial court under section 11-F(6) of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, which deals with membership in or support of a banned organization, and sentenced to 18 months imprisonment plus a fine.

He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that no real evidence tied him to the banned organization beyond the flag itself. The High Court agreed. It found that the prosecution's key evidence, a "disclosure" the accused supposedly made to police, was actually inadmissible because it amounted to a confession made to a police officer rather than one leading to actual recovery of evidence, which is barred under the law of evidence. The court also noted that a government notification simply listing Daesh as a banned group did nothing to prove the accused's link to it.

Crucially, the court ruled that merely possessing a flag resembling that of a proscribed organization is not, by itself, enough to prove the terrorism-related charge. Without independent, strong corroborating evidence, the conviction under the anti-terrorism law could not stand. The court set aside his conviction and sentence and acquitted him, ordering his release. This case matters because it clarifies that symbolic items alone cannot establish serious terrorism charges without solid supporting evidence.

The trial court had convicted them under Pakistan's Penal Code for murder, rioting, and rioting with deadly weapons, sentencing them to life imprisonment plus fines.

The appellants challenged their conviction before the Balochistan High Court. The prosecution's case rested on eyewitness testimony from the complainant (the victim's brother) and two other witnesses who were present at the scene. The defense failed to offer any alternative explanation suggesting false implication.

The court upheld the conviction, ruling that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt through direct eyewitness accounts, even though medical evidence alone cannot identify culprits, only confirm injury details. The court also noted that lack of a proven motive doesn't automatically benefit the defense. Additionally, since it wasn't clear which specific shooter caused the fatal wound, this uncertainty was treated as a mitigating factor, but it only affected sentencing considerations, not the conviction itself. title: Nabi Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Nabi Khan, who was accused of transporting 22 kilograms of charas (a narcotic) hidden in the spare tyres of a trailer vehicle he was driving in Mastung, Balochistan. He was tried under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, convicted by the trial court, and sentenced to life imprisonment along with a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the prosecution's evidence closely and found serious contradictions between key witnesses. The complainant claimed no levies staff were present during the search and recovery, while the investigating officer (a Tehsildar) said he rushed to the scene immediately and personally prepared the parcels and extracted samples—directly contradicting the complainant. Another witness gave a different account of where the vehicle was actually searched. There were also gaps in proving how the narcotic samples were safely stored and transported to the laboratory for testing, and the person who carried the samples for testing was never produced as a witness to confirm the chain of custody.

Because of these unexplained contradictions on basic facts—who conducted the search, where it happened, and how the evidence was handled afterward—the court ruled that the prosecution had failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction was set aside, and Nabi Khan was acquitted.

This case highlights how contradictory witness testimony and broken chains of evidence custody can undermine even serious narcotics prosecutions, safeguarding the principle that guilt must be proven beyond reason

title: Muhammad Ismail and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Muhammad Ismail and Muhammad Musa, who were convicted by an Anti-Rape Court in Quetta for sodomizing two young boys, aged 15 and 13, and sentenced to life imprisonment along with heavy fines. The prosecution's case relied on the victims' testimony, medical examinations, a test identification parade, and forensic reports.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious flaws in the evidence. The court noted that for a test identification parade to carry evidentiary weight, the witnesses must have given a detailed description of the perpetrators' features soon after the incident, before the parade takes place; this had not properly happened here. The court also emphasized that identification parades are only corroborative evidence, not proof on their own, and that medical evidence can only confirm that an assault occurred, not identify who committed it. Crucially, the forensic laboratory reports on blood and swab samples came back negative, undermining the prosecution's case. One of the accused had not even been put through an identification parade or medical examination, making the case against him even weaker.

Given these gaps, the High Court concluded that the prosecution failed to properly connect the accused to the crime, and that the trial court had wrongly appraised the evidence. The convictions and life sentences were set aside, and both men were acquitted. The case highlights how convictions cannot rest on weak identification procedures or inconclusive forensic evidence, especially in serious criminal charges.

title: Ihsan Ali V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murdering his wife and attacking his cousin, both accused of infidelity (siyakaari), after he attacked them with a hatchet. The trial court sentenced him to death for murder and ten years imprisonment for the attempted murder. The Balochistan High Court reviewed the case on appeal, along with the mandatory reference for confirmation of the death sentence.

The court examined the evidence carefully, including testimony from eyewitnesses who lived on the same premises as the accused and victims. Despite lengthy cross-examination, the witnesses' accounts remained consistent and credible. Medical evidence confirmed the injuries matched the alleged attack, and a bloodstained hatchet recovered from the accused was scientifically confirmed to have human blood on it, further supporting the prosecution's case.

However, the court noted that the prosecution never actually proved the claimed motive - that the killing was due to alleged infidelity - with solid, independent evidence. This failure to establish motive was treated as a "mitigating circumstance."

As a result, while the court upheld the conviction, finding guilt proven beyond doubt, it reduced the death sentence to life imprisonment. The appeal was dismissed except for this change in sentencing.

This case matters because it shows how appellate courts scrutinize both the strength of evidence and the completeness of prosecution's case, and how gaps in proving motive can affect sentencing even when guilt itself is clearly established.

title: Jaffar Khan V. Federation of Pakistan, through Secretary, Ministry of Interior, Islamabad and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a father seeking help for his son, who was stranded in the UAE. The son had been working there as a laborer, but when he tried to renew his travel documents at the Pakistani Consulate, he was refused because his name had been placed on a control list, linked to a criminal case (an FIR under section 496-A PPC) pending against him in Dera Ismail Khan. The petitioner argued this violated his family's constitutional rights and asked the court to remove his son's name from the list so he could return to Pakistan.

The government clarified that the son was actually on the Passport Control List (not the Exit Control List, which only applies to people trying to leave Pakistan), placed there under court orders in connection with the criminal case. Officials suggested the son could get Emergency Travel Documents from the Pakistani Consulate in UAE to travel back and face trial.

The Balochistan High Court agreed this was the right solution. Citing Article 15 of the Constitution, which guarantees citizens the right to enter, move through, and reside in Pakistan, the court held that since the son was willing to return and face the charges against him, he could not be denied entry to his own country. The court directed authorities to issue him Emergency Travel Documents so he could come back and participate in the criminal proceedings. The petition was allowed.

This case matters because it reaffirms that Pakistani citizens have a constitutional right to return to their own country, even while facing criminal charges, and that administrative travel restrictions cannot be used to block that fundamental right.

title: Collector of Customs (Enforcement), Custom House Airport Road Quetta V. M/s. Abdul manan and another,
explainer:

Customs authorities accused him of illegally trafficking foreign currency, seized the money and vehicle, and issued a show-cause notice. Manan explained that the money came from selling ancestral property in Afghanistan and that he was heading to the State Bank in Quetta to exchange it, since there was no facility at the border to declare or convert foreign currency. Initially, customs authorities confiscated the currency and vehicle, but the Customs Appellate Tribunal reversed this decision and ordered everything returned to him. Customs then challenged that reversal before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the Tribunal's decision and dismissed the customs department's case. It found multiple problems with the original seizure: there was no facility at the border for declaring currency, a State Bank notification actually permits people to bring unlimited foreign currency into Pakistan, and the seizure itself was legally invalid because it was carried out by a low-ranking clerk temporarily given inspector powers, when the law requires seizures to be made by a properly authorized senior officer. The court also noted the seizure happened far from the border, weakening the smuggling allegation.

title: Pervaiz V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves an appeal from a murder conviction. The appellant, Pervaiz, was found guilty of murdering Ghulam Rasool and injuring another man, Amanullah, by stabbing them with a dagger during a late-night altercation at a hotel over a dispute involving a Ludo game and closing time. The trial court had sentenced him to death for the murder and additional imprisonment for the injury charge.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence, including eyewitness testimony from the injured complainant, medical reports confirming the fatal stab wounds, and the recovery of the blood-stained dagger based on the accused's own disclosure. The court found this evidence credible and sufficient to prove Pervaiz's guilt beyond doubt. It also clarified an important legal point: while a confession made to police is generally not admissible as evidence, the part of the accused's statement that led to recovering the weapon is admissible under the law of evidence.

However, the court decided the crime lacked premeditation and appeared to result from a sudden quarrel rather than a planned killing. Because of this mitigating factor, the judges reduced the death sentence to life imprisonment, while upholding the conviction itself and dismissing the appeal with this modification.

This case matters because it shows how courts balance strong evidence of guilt against circumstances that may lessen the severity of punishment, particularly distinguishing spontaneous violence from premeditated murder.

title: The State through Additional Attorney General V. Muhammad Juma,
explainer:
This case involved a raid by the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) on a shop in Quetta, where large amounts of Pakistani and foreign currency were seized from Muhammad Juma. He was charged under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, for illegal possession of foreign currency. The trial court acquitted him of the criminal charge but still ordered the confiscation of the seized currency. Separately, an FIA request to attach his properties under anti-money laundering law was dismissed. Both the State and Juma challenged different parts of these decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined whether the raid and seizure were lawful. It found that FIA officials had entered and searched Juma's shop without first obtaining a search warrant from a magistrate, as required under Section 19(3) of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act. The prosecution's own witness admitted ignorance about any such warrant, and no one could show that one had been obtained. The court held that this made the entire search and seizure illegal, since the law's procedural requirements had not been followed at all.

The court emphasized the basic legal principle that when a law prescribes a specific manner of doing something, it must be done exactly that way, not otherwise. Because the raid was conducted without proper authorization, the acquittal was upheld, and the State's appeal against it was dismissed. The judgment underscores the importance of following proper legal procedure, especially search warrant requirements, to protect individuals from unlawful searches and seizures.

title: M/s. R.L Papers Board Mills and others V. M/s. Sui Sothern Gas Company Limited etc.,
explainer:
This case involved several companies accused by Sui Southern Gas Company of gas theft through illegal means such as direct connections, tampered meters, and unpaid bills. SSGC filed multiple recovery suits before the Gas Utility Court at Lasbela seeking large sums of money, ranging from around six lakh to over eight crore rupees, under the Gas (Theft Control and Recovery) Act, 2016. The Gas Utility Court refused the companies leave to defend and decreed the suits in favour of SSGC, prompting the companies to appeal to the Balochistan High Court.

The appellants argued that once written statements were filed, issues framed, and evidence directed, leave to defend should be considered implied, and that disputed facts required proper evidence before any decree could be passed. They also raised jurisdictional objections, including a pending application to reject the plaint that was never decided.

The High Court found that the trial court had failed to decide the jurisdictional objection and had left important legal and factual questions unaddressed. Because of this failure, the judgments and decrees could not stand. The High Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the lower court's decisions.

This case matters because it clarifies that Gas Utility Courts, despite having special expedited procedures for recovery suits, must still properly address preliminary objections and jurisdictional questions before deciding a case, ensuring fairness even in specialized recovery proceedings.

title: Messrs R.L. Paper Board Mills through Manager and others V. Messrs Sui Southern Gas Company Limited,
explainer:
This case involved several factory owners in Balochistan who were sued by Sui Southern Gas Company for large unpaid gas bills, allegedly arising from illegal gas use, meter tampering, and installation of fake meters. The gas company had filed suits before the Gas Utility Court under a special law, the Gas Theft Control and Recovery Act, 2016, which allows expedited recovery of dues from consumers. The trial court refused to grant the factory owners "leave to defend" themselves and instead issued judgments and decrees ordering them to pay the claimed amounts, based mainly on documents rather than full evidence.

The factory owners appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing that proper legal procedure had not been followed - specifically, that required notices in a prescribed legal form had never been issued, and that serious factual disputes (about meter installation, tampering, and disputed calculations) could not fairly be decided without allowing both sides to present evidence.

The High Court agreed. It found that the case had not followed the mandatory procedure from the start, and that important factual and legal questions remained unresolved. Because such disputes require proper evidence rather than being decided solely on paperwork, the High Court set aside the lower court's judgments and sent the cases back for a fresh decision, this time following correct procedure. This ruling reinforces that even under special recovery laws, consumers facing serious factual disputes are entitled to a fair chance to defend themselves through evidence.

title: Messrs Friends Coal Company through Director V. The Government of Balochistan, Civil Secretariat through Secretary Mines and another,
explainer:
A coal mining company in Balochistan had been granted a mining lease for 20 years in 2014, but after just six years, the government's Director General of Mines and Minerals cancelled the lease in 2018, citing the company's failure to submit required documents like a lease deed, exploration scheme, and demarcation certificate on time. The company appealed to the Secretary of Mines, but the appeal was dismissed. The company then challenged both decisions before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found that under the Balochistan Mineral Rules, 2002, before cancelling a lease for delay, the licensing authority must first satisfy itself that the delay was not the applicant's fault or was due to circumstances beyond their control. This requires proper inquiry and giving the affected party a chance to be heard. In this case, no notice was given to the company and no such inquiry took place before the lease was cancelled. The appellate authority also failed to address this failure and dismissed the appeal without giving reasons.

The court ruled that cancelling the lease without a hearing violated the fundamental right to fair trial and due process under Article 10-A of the Constitution, as well as basic principles of natural justice. It declared both the cancellation notification and the appellate order null and void, and sent the matter back to the mining department to hold a proper hearing and decide the case afresh on its merits. This case reinforces that government authorities cannot cancel licenses or take away rights without following fair procedure and giving affected parties a chance to be heard.

title: The State through Regional Director V. Farooq Khan,
explainer:
This case is about who gets custody of a car seized during a drug trafficking arrest, while the criminal case is still ongoing. The Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF) stopped a Toyota Corolla and found 1.5 kg of charas (hashish) hidden under the driver's seat. The driver, Amanullah, was charged with the crime. However, the car actually belonged to Farooq Khan, who ran a rent-a-car business and had rented the vehicle to Amanullah for an out-of-city trip. Khan was never charged in the case. He applied to the trial court to have the car released to him under section 516-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, and the trial court agreed. The ANF appealed this decision.

The High Court upheld the release of the vehicle. It explained that while the Control of Narcotic Substances Act generally bars returning a seized vehicle to an accused or associates before the case concludes, courts can make an exception for an innocent owner who had no knowledge that his vehicle would be used for smuggling drugs, following earlier Supreme Court rulings. Since Khan was the legitimate registered owner, had financed the car through a bank loan, and swore he was unaware of any drug activity, the court found no fault on his part. It ruled there was nothing wrong with the trial court's order and dismissed the ANF's appeal, allowing Khan to keep temporary custody of his car.

title: Ali Sher V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Ali Shair, convicted by a trial court for possessing 3000 grams of charas (cannabis), an offense under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. The trial court sentenced him to nine years imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 80,000, applying a stricter penalty scheme introduced by a 2022 amendment to the law.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court upheld the conviction, finding that the evidence—including testimony from police witnesses about the recovery, safe custody, and chemical testing of the drugs—clearly proved the appellant's guilt.

However, the High Court found the sentence itself unlawful. The 2022 amendment that increased penalties was enacted about three months after the offense actually occurred. Applying this harsher law retroactively violated Article 12 of Pakistan's Constitution, which protects against retrospective punishment. The court also noted the appellant was a first-time offender with no prior criminal record, making the nine-year sentence excessively harsh.

As a result, the High Court reduced his sentence from nine years to three years imprisonment and lowered the fine from Rs. 80,000 to Rs. 30,000, while giving him credit for time already served in custody.

This case matters because it reinforces a fundamental legal principle: laws that increase punishment cannot be applied to offenses committed before those laws existed. It also shows courts exercising discretion to ensure sentences remain proportionate, especially for first-time offenders.

title: Abdul Rauf Kasi V. Syed niza-ud-din and another,
explainer:
This case is about a landlord-tenant dispute in Quetta over two shops. The landlord, Abdul Rauf Kasi, wanted to evict his tenant, alleging that the tenant had illegally sublet the shops to another person without permission and had defaulted on rent payments. The tenant denied subletting, claiming the other person was actually his business partner in one shop and his employee in the other.

The Rent Controller initially dismissed the landlord's eviction application. The landlord then appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned that decision and ruled in favor of the landlord. It noted that the alleged sub-tenant never appeared at any point to contest the case, which suggested he had no real defense. More importantly, the tenant himself repeatedly failed to show up for cross-examination despite being given several chances, even though he had submitted a written affidavit. The court held that an affidavit not tested through cross-examination carries little weight, and that mere written claims in pleadings mean nothing without supporting evidence or testimony.

Since the tenant could not produce any documents, accounts, salary records, or written partnership agreement to back up his story, and avoided being questioned in court, the judge found the landlord's version of events credible and unchallenged. The court ordered the tenants to hand over vacant possession of the shops to the landlord, allowing the appeal.

title: Messrs Salam International and others V. Secretary Ministry of Law and Parliamentary Affairs, Government of Balochistan, Civil Secretariat, Quetta,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved a group of businesses, mainly ship breakers and a textile manufacturing company, challenging a provincial law called the Balochistan Development and Maintenance of Infrastructure Cess Act, 2021. This law allowed the provincial government to charge a "cess" (a type of levy) on goods being imported or exported through Balochistan.

The petitioners argued that the provincial assembly had no authority to pass this law, claiming it amounted to a customs duty, which under the Constitution only the federal Parliament can impose. They said the provincial legislature had overstepped its constitutional powers.

The government defended the law by explaining that the cess was actually a fee charged for services provided to importers and exporters, such as building and maintaining infrastructure to facilitate trade, which falls within the province's legislative authority.

The High Court found the government's explanation reasonable and did not strike down the law entirely. Instead, it ordered that only 50% of the cess be collected, reflecting the actual services the government provides, while noting that a similar law was already being examined by the Supreme Court in other cases. The court's decision was made subject to whatever the Supreme Court eventually decides in those related cases.

This matters because it affects how much businesses importing and exporting goods through Balochistan must pay, while leaving the broader constitutional question of provincial versus federal taxing power unresolved until the Supreme Court rules.

title: Naqeebullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court, deciding a criminal appeal by Naqeebullah, who had been convicted by a trial court under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine, after police allegedly recovered 20 kilograms of charas (hashish) hidden in secret cavities of the car he was driving.

On appeal, the High Court found serious flaws in the prosecution's evidence. First, neither the police officer who seized the drugs nor the recovery witness could describe where or how the cavities were built into the car, and the car itself was never shown to the trial judge or examined in court to verify how the drugs were actually concealed. This made the entire recovery claim doubtful. Second, the court found gaps in the chain of custody: witnesses failed to explain who handed the seized drugs to the investigating officer, when samples were sent to the police storage facility (Malkhana), and how they were later retrieved and sent to the laboratory for testing. These unexplained gaps raised doubt about whether the substance tested was actually the same substance recovered from the appellant.

Because the prosecution could not prove the recovery was genuine or that the drugs were safely and traceably handled from seizure to lab testing, the court ruled that the appellant deserved the benefit of the doubt. The conviction was overturned and the appeal was allowed, highlighting how strict evidentiary standards protect the accused when police investigation and evidence-handling procedures are sloppy or incomplete.

title: Muhammad Naeem V. The State,
explainer:
Muhammad Naeem was arrested during an Anti-Narcotics Force operation near Quetta after his vehicle was intercepted, with 9 kg of powdered charas found between his legs and another 4 kg found concealed in the rear seat. His companion, who was driving, fled the scene. The trial court convicted Naeem under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act for possession of all 13 kg and sentenced him to life imprisonment, and additionally convicted him under the Anti-Money Laundering Act for related currency and weapons recoveries.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found that the prosecution had reliably proven recovery, safe custody, and forensic transmission of the 9 kg found directly on Naeem, but could not attribute the additional 4 kg hidden in the rear seat to him, since that recovery was not linked to his own disclosure and was more plausibly connected to the escaped driver. Because of this, his sentence was reduced from life imprisonment to ten years.

Separately, the court ruled that the Special Judge trying narcotics cases had no legal authority to also try and convict Naeem under the Anti-Money Laundering Act, since that law requires cases to be handled by a specially constituted court. That part of the conviction was declared void, and the case was sent back so a proper Anti-Money Laundering court could decide whether it could even take up the matter.

This case highlights the importance of correctly linking evidence to individual guilt and respecting jurisdictional boundaries between specialized courts.

title: Mst. Nazeerah V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns a bail application filed by Mst. Nazeerah, a woman arrested at Quetta Railway Station on 8 May 2023 during a police snap-check. A search allegedly recovered 560 grams of heroin and 1590 grams of Ice (methamphetamine) from her possession, leading to charges under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997.

Her lawyer argued she was falsely implicated and, since investigation was complete and she was a woman, she deserved bail as a matter of law. The state opposed, saying she was caught red-handed with no evidence of bad faith by police.

The Balochistan High Court refused bail. It held that the heroin recovery attracted Section 9(6)(c) of the Act, punishable by 10 to 14 years imprisonment, which falls within the "prohibitory clause" of Section 497(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, normally barring bail. Although the law generally allows women accused of serious offences to be granted bail as a concession, the court noted that women are increasingly used as couriers in organized narcotics trafficking, making such crimes different from ordinary offenses. It also found she was from Shikarpur and might abscond. The claim of false implication couldn't be examined deeply at this bail stage.

This case illustrates how courts balance statutory bail concessions for women against concerns about organized drug trafficking and flight risk, emphasizing that such concessions aren't automatic.

title: Imran Munir V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man convicted of transporting 40 kilograms of charas (hashish) found hidden in a car he was driving, for which the trial court sentenced him to 20 years imprisonment and a heavy fine under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction after finding serious flaws in how the prosecution handled the evidence. First, instead of taking a separate sample from each of the 40 packets of charas for laboratory testing, officials mixed small amounts from all packets into one combined sample. The court ruled that under proper procedure, if samples aren't drawn separately from each packet, only the amount actually tested in the lab (in this case, just 1 kilogram) can legally count as recovered narcotics, not the full 40 kilograms.

Second, the court found major gaps in the chain of custody, the process of proving the drugs were securely stored and transported to the laboratory without tampering. Witnesses could not clearly say who they handed the evidence to or when, and the malkhana (evidence storage) register produced in court did not match records or show proper entries. The vehicle allegedly used was also never produced as evidence.

Because these failures created serious doubt about whether the drugs were properly seized, stored, and tested, the court ruled the prosecution failed to prove its case and acquitted the appellant, overturning his conviction and sentence. The case highlights the importance of strict evidence-handling procedures in narcotics prosecutions.

title: Jaffar Mehmood V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Jaffar Mehmood, who was convicted by a trial court in Kuchlak, Balochistan, under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine. The prosecution alleged that police intercepted a bus and found 24 kilograms of charas (hashish) in a bag held in the appellant's lap.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him. The court found two major flaws in the prosecution's case. First, it was not convincing that the appellant would simply wait to be caught red-handed with the narcotics in his lap when he had ample opportunity to push the bag away and distance himself from it. Since the drugs were not recovered from his direct physical possession, the court held that the prosecution failed to prove he had exclusive possession of the narcotics, a key requirement for conviction.

Second, the court found serious gaps in how the evidence was handled after recovery. The narcotics were allegedly seized on 4 February 2022, but the samples only reached the forensic laboratory on 7 February 2022, with no explanation for the three-day gap. This raised doubts about whether the samples were kept safely and whether the laboratory results could be trusted.

Because both possession and safe custody/transmission of the evidence were not proven beyond doubt, the court set aside the conviction and acquitted the appellant, highlighting how gaps in evidence handling can undermine even serious narcotics cases.

title: Samiullah V. SHO Police Station Airport Quetta and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute between two neighbors or acquaintances involving a violent altercation. Abdul Haq filed a police report (FIR) accusing Samiullah of shooting him in the leg and, along with his brother, assaulting Abdul Haq and his guest. Samiullah claimed he was also injured in the same incident and tried to get his own FIR registered against Abdul Haq, but the police refused, and so did the Justice of Peace, a judicial officer who can order police to register cases. Samiullah then challenged that refusal in the Balochistan High Court.

The court dismissed his petition. It explained that under the law, two separate FIRs generally cannot be registered for the same single incident. Instead, the accused's version of events should be recorded by the investigating officer as part of the evidence, rather than through a competing FIR. The court also noted that a Justice of Peace can refuse to order registration of a case if the facts do not amount to a "cognizable offence" (a serious crime that police can act on without needing court permission first). Here, Samiullah's medical report showed injuries that only qualified as a minor, non-cognizable offense. The court said his remedy was to file a private criminal complaint directly before a magistrate instead. This ruling reinforces the principle that rival versions of the same incident are handled through investigation, not duplicate FIRs.

title: Gulshan Bibi V. The State,
explainer:
This Balochistan High Court judgment concerns a woman convicted of possessing 2300 grams of charas (a narcotic) under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. She had been sentenced by a trial court to ten years imprisonment and a fine after police claimed to have found the drugs in a bag she was carrying on a roadside near Loralai.

On appeal, the High Court examined whether the prosecution had properly proven the case, particularly regarding two critical requirements in narcotics cases: the actual recovery of the contraband and its safe custody from the point of seizure to laboratory testing. The court found serious gaps in the evidence. No witness explained how the seized drugs were transferred from the police officers at the scene to the investigating officer, breaking the chain of custody. Additionally, there was an unexplained three-day delay between the recovery (January 14) and when the laboratory received the sample (January 17), with no evidence showing who held the parcel during that gap or when it was handed over for testing.

Because narcotics cases carry heavy punishments, the court held that the evidence proving guilt must be correspondingly strong and reliable. Since the prosecution failed to establish an unbroken, verified chain of custody for the drugs, the court ruled that the case had not been proven beyond reasonable doubt. The appeal was allowed, and the conviction was overturned. This case highlights how procedural lapses in handling evidence can be fatal to a prosecution, even in serious drug cases.
