title: Muhammad Ishaq V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of possessing 25 kilograms of charas (a narcotic substance) allegedly found hidden in the spare wheel of the truck he was driving, under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act. He was sentenced by a trial court to over seven years in prison. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction, finding serious flaws in how the prosecution handled the evidence. First, samples of the narcotic were supposed to be sent for chemical testing, but the testimony revealed that during testing, 300 grams of the sample was consumed and the rest returned, yet the key witness never mentioned this in court, raising doubts about what was actually tested. Also, samples from different packets were mixed into one consolidated parcel instead of being kept separately, meaning only a small portion could reliably be linked to the appellant.

Second, the court found the prosecution failed to prove the "safe custody and transmission" of the narcotic, meaning the chain of custody from seizure to laboratory testing was not properly documented. Witnesses could not confirm dates of handover, failed to produce required registry records, and no receipt was obtained when the sample was deposited at the testing laboratory.

Because of these gaps, the court ruled the prosecution had not proven the case beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant. The judgment highlights how strict evidentiary standards, especially around chain of custody in drug cases, protect individuals from wrongful conviction based on unreliable procedures.

title: Akhtar Ali and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a murder charge arising from a shooting on 26 March 2021, in which the complainant's nephew was killed and another person injured. Three accused men were said to have opened fire following a prior verbal altercation with the complainant's side. Two of the accused were convicted by the trial court, while the third was also found guilty largely based on a supplementary statement (an affidavit filed days after the incident) naming him for the first time.

The Balochistan High Court, hearing the appeal and a related revision petition, examined the evidence carefully. It found the direct eyewitness accounts of the complainant and injured witness credible and consistent, and this was supported by medical evidence confirming the fatal and non-fatal firearm injuries. Recovery of a rifle used by one accused was also found reliable since it matched forensic reports on bullet casings collected the same day. However, the recoveries linked to the other two weapons were considered unreliable because samples had been sent for testing improperly, together rather than separately, weakening their evidentiary value.

Crucially, the court ruled that the third accused could not be convicted, since he was never named in the original complaint or identified through a proper identification parade, and his identification in court came only after he had visited the court repeatedly. His implication via a later affidavit was treated as an unreliable afterthought.

The court upheld the convictions of two accused but acquitted the third, showing how courts scrutinize evidence reliability, identification procedures, and forensic handling in murder trials.

title: Hazoor Bakhsh V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between the Chief Engineer of Pakistan Public Works Department, Quetta, and a construction company that had been awarded a contract to build a road linking Musakhail and Zhob. The company claimed the project could not be completed on time because the government failed to release adequate funds, revised cost estimates were not honored, the project was excluded from the development program, and it was later shifted to Punjab without notice. The company sought arbitration under the Arbitration Act, 1940, and a sole arbitrator was appointed with the consent of both parties. The arbitrator ruled in the company's favor, awarding over 136 million rupees. Trial and appellate courts both upheld this award as binding.

The government challenged the award before the High Court, alleging misconduct by the arbitrator. The High Court dismissed the challenge, holding that since the arbitrator had been appointed by mutual consent and no objection was raised until after the award was issued, the government was legally barred (estopped) from objecting at that late stage. The court emphasized that an arbitration award can only be overturned if there is proven misconduct, invalidity, or procedural defect - none of which were substantiated here. It also reaffirmed that courts reviewing lower court decisions should not interfere unless there is clear illegality or serious error.

This judgment reinforces the finality of arbitration awards and the principle that parties cannot object to an arbitrator's appointment after accepting it throughout the proceedings, especially only after losing the case.

It found that the police witnesses gave consistent and credible testimony about the recovery of the drugs, and that the chain of custody—from recovery to storage to laboratory testing—was properly proven. This case highlights the importance of proper forensic sampling procedures in narcotics cases—prosecutors must test each seized packet individually, or risk having convictions and sentences significantly

title: Muhammad Murad V. Jameel Ahmed and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a petition to cancel bail that had been granted to two men accused of murdering Mir Nabi Bakhsh Khan, the father of the complainant, Muhammad Murad. According to the FIR, the victim was shot dead during a dinner visit after an earlier verbal dispute, with several armed men allegedly involved, including the two respondents.

A trial court in Naseerabad had granted bail to both accused, mainly because they were said to have been at Frontier Corps checkpoints (shown by call data records and register entries) at the time of the murder, suggesting they weren't at the crime scene, and because no weapon was recovered from them.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed this decision and split the outcome. For the first accused, Jameel Ahmed, who was specifically named as having fired the fatal shot from close range, the court found the evidence too strong and the alibi unproven, since the people who supported his alibi never appeared before the court to be questioned. His bail was cancelled. For the second accused, Dil Murad, who was only accused of standing at the scene with a weapon and making threats but not of directly attacking anyone, the court found the weaker evidence justified keeping him on bail.

The case illustrates how courts assess bail differently based on the specific role attributed to each accused, and how unverified alibi evidence like phone records or affidavits cannot automatically override serious murder allegations.

title: Niaz and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved two related criminal appeals arising from a violent clash at a market in Manjhoo Shori Bazar in May 2021, in which one person died from a gunshot wound and several others were injured. Two rival groups each filed their own police report (FIR) accusing the other side of attacking first, and after trial, an Additional Sessions Judge convicted accused persons from both sides of murder, attempted murder, and rioting-related offences.

On appeal, the High Court examined the evidence closely and found serious problems. The eyewitnesses gave vague accounts that did not identify which specific accused caused which injury, and their claim that five people fired guns did not match medical evidence showing only one gunshot wound on the deceased. The court also found the recovery of weapons (a pistol and knives) from the accused unreliable and suspicious, given the timing and circumstances of these recoveries.

Most importantly, the court concluded that the incident was actually a sudden, unplanned "free fight" that erupted from an argument, rather than a premeditated attack by one side. Since both parties were armed and injured, and it was impossible to determine clearly who was the aggressor, the court held that guilt could not be fairly pinned on either side based on the weak evidence presented.

As a result, the court allowed the appeals and set aside the convictions, emphasizing that criminal convictions must rest on truthful, reliable evidence, not mere probability or suspicion.

title: Nazir Ahmad V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a murder appeal from Balochistan. Nazir Ahmad was convicted by a trial court under Pakistan's Penal Code for the murder of a man named Lal Jan, allegedly shot during an armed group attack. He was sentenced to life imprisonment plus additional terms for related offences of rioting and unlawful assembly, and ordered to pay compensation to the victim's family.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. The judges found serious problems with the prosecution's case. The claimed motive, old family enmity, was weak and inconsistent, since even the complainant's own brother described it as minor. The medical evidence did not match the eyewitness account, since witnesses claimed a barrage of gunfire but the victim had only one bullet wound. The recovery of the alleged weapon was unreliable because of contradictions about where the accused lived, and because forensic testing of bullets and the weapon was delayed for months, making the forensic report meaningless as corroboration. Finally, a key eyewitness, the complainant's nephew, was never actually presented to testify in court despite appearing once, and the law says withholding such evidence creates a presumption that it would have hurt the prosecution's case.

Given these gaps and contradictions, the court ruled the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant, allowing the appeal. The case illustrates how courts scrutinize motive, forensic timing, and witness evidence before upholding a murder conviction.

title: Nazeer Ahmad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Nazeer Ahmad, who was convicted under the Balochistan Arms Act for allegedly possessing an unlicensed Kalashnikov rifle, a magazine, and nine live rounds. The weapon was supposedly recovered on his pointing out the location during investigation of a separate murder case (registered under sections 302, 147, 148, and 149 of the Pakistan Penal Code), after it had allegedly been buried under the ground in his house wrapped in plastic. He was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to five years imprisonment plus a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. The court found serious flaws in the prosecution's case: the address listed for the appellant did not match the location where the weapon was recovered, and the investigating officer failed to establish any connection between the appellant and that house, whether as owner or tenant. No supporting documents or neighbor testimony were provided to prove he actually lived there. Notably, in the related murder case from which this weapons case originated, the same recovery evidence had already been disbelieved, leading to the appellant's acquittal in that case.

Given these gaps, the High Court ruled the prosecution had failed to prove its case and acquitted Nazeer Ahmad, ordering his release. This judgment highlights how courts scrutinize the reliability of recovery evidence and the importance of establishing a clear, documented link between an accused person and the location of an alleged recovery before convicting someone based on such evidence.

title: Chief Engineer (West) Pakistan Public Works Department, Quetta V. M/s nip construction and engineering construction builders and Manufacturers through Karim Dad,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a criminal conviction from the Balochistan High Court. The appellant, Hazoor Bakhsh, had been convicted by a Trial Court for causing the death of a man named Habib-ur-Rehman and injuring another person, and was sentenced to pay compensation (diyat and daman) and serve jail time.

The prosecution's story was that the appellant and his co-accused stopped the deceased and another man on a road, and this led to the deceased being hit by a motorcycle and dying, while his companion was injured. However, the High Court found major problems with the evidence. The complainant admitted he had not actually witnessed the incident himself. The original police report told a different story than what witnesses later testified in court, and it suggested an unknown motorcyclist caused the accident. Crucially, the prosecution never called this unknown motorcyclist as a witness, even though he was identified and medically examined. The court said failing to produce him meant the missing testimony would likely have supported the defense, not the prosecution. The court also found that the Trial Court had wrongly convicted the appellant under legal provisions different from what he was originally charged with.

Because of these serious doubts and procedural errors, the High Court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and it overturned the conviction, allowing the appeal. This case highlights the importance of consistent evidence and proper adherence to criminal charges in ensuring fair trials.

title: Shamasullah V. Additional Sessions Judge-I, QUETTA and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a murder trial in Quetta. The petitioner, Shamsullah, had accused respondent Naguibullah and a co-accused of killing his sister. During the trial, one of the prosecution's own witnesses, Samiullah, gave testimony in court that contradicted the statement he had earlier given to police under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The prosecution asked the trial court to declare Samiullah a "hostile witness" so they could cross-examine him about the contradiction, but the trial court refused, reasoning that since Samiullah's police statement wasn't signed or thumb-marked by him, it couldn't be used to challenge him this way.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It ruled that the trial court's approach was legally wrong. Under the law, a witness can be declared hostile when they clearly show they're not being truthful or when their courtroom testimony conflicts with earlier statements, even if the earlier statement was unsigned—since police statements under Section 161 are never signed by law. Since Samiullah directly denied making his earlier statement, the trial court should have treated him as hostile and allowed cross-examination, subject to certain safeguards recognized in law for such witnesses.

The High Court set aside the trial court's order and directed it to reconsider whether Samiullah should be declared hostile. This case clarifies the correct legal standard for declaring prosecution witnesses hostile, which matters because it affects how contradictory testimony is handled and how fairly criminal trials are conducted.

title: Messrs Usman Ship Breakers through Proprietor V. Government of Balochistan through Secretary Ministry of Planning and Development, Balochistan and 4 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a ship-breaking company that had been allotted two plots at Gaddani Shipbreaking Yard by the Balochistan Development Authority, first in 2012 and then renewed for five more years in 2017 through lease agreements. Under the Balochistan Ship Breaking Industry Rules, 1979, a plot could not be left without a ship for more than four months (extendable to eight months only with prior written approval), and failure to comply meant the lease would automatically terminate.

The company beached several ships successfully until 2017, but after that stopped bringing in vessels, citing severe financial difficulties following a fire on a related company's ship. It later informed the authorities it intended to resume operations, but before that happened, the authorities cancelled its allotment and gave the plots to another company. The petitioner challenged this cancellation in the High Court, alleging it was done secretly and improperly, using backdated orders.

The court found that the petitioner had not beached any ship since 2017, well beyond the permitted period, and had provided no solid evidence of financial hardship to justify the delay. It also noted that the plots had already been leased to a new company, which had acquired vested rights, yet the petitioner failed to include that company in the case. Additionally, the original lease term had already expired by 2022. Finding no proof of any wrongdoing by the authorities, the court dismissed the petition, upholding the cancellation and reallocation of the plots.

title: Imran V. The State through Prosecutor General,
explainer:
This case is about a man named Imran who was convicted by a trial court in Balochistan of raping a 14-year-old girl and committing an unnatural offence, and was sentenced to life imprisonment plus additional jail time and fines. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court challenging his conviction.

The prosecution's case relied on the complainant mother's account (which was based on what her daughter told her, not what she witnessed herself), the victim's testimony, a rickshaw driver's statement, medical evidence, and a DNA report. The High Court found serious problems with all of this evidence. The victim's own testimony suggested she went with the accused willingly rather than being forced. The rickshaw driver refused to identify the accused in court and his earlier statements were never properly used to challenge his testimony. There was also an unexplained four-day delay in filing the police report, suggesting the story may have been discussed and shaped beforehand. Medical evidence showed no signs of force and old, not fresh, injury. The DNA sample reached the forensic lab 17 days late with no explanation, and its safe handling wasn't proven, and even then, it didn't conclusively match the accused.

Because of all these doubts, the High Court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and it overturned the conviction, allowing the appeal. This case highlights how delays, weak evidence handling, and inconsistent testimony can undermine a criminal conviction, even for serious charges.

title: Sajjad Ahmed and 3 Others V. Gul Sima and 5 others,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court in 2023, involved a family dispute over inheritance and dower rights. Gul Sima, the widow of Abdul Razzaq (deceased), had filed a suit against her late husband's sons from another marriage, seeking maintenance, possession of a house that she claimed had been given to her as her dower (Haq Mehr), household items, and money. Her stepsons argued that the marriage document (Kabin Nama) proving this arrangement was forged, and that their father had actually divorced her before his death, meaning she wasn't entitled to these claims.

Both the Family Court and the District Court (on appeal) sided with the widow, finding that the house was indeed given to her as dower and awarding her possession along with custody of her minor daughters.

The stepsons then challenged these rulings in the High Court through a constitutional petition. The High Court dismissed their petition, explaining that when two lower courts have already examined the facts and reached the same conclusion, higher courts should not interfere unless there's a clear legal error, arbitrariness, or an obvious mistake. Since no such flaw was found here, the concurrent findings favoring the widow were upheld.

This case matters because it reinforces an important principle: courts generally respect factual findings made by trial and appellate courts in family matters, and will only overturn them in exceptional circumstances of serious legal error, providing stability and finality to family court decisions.

title: Gohar Khan Luni V. Returning Officer, PB-6 Duki General Elections 2024 and 5 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a challenge to the arrangement of polling stations ahead of Pakistan's 2024 General Elections. The petitioner, a candidate for a provincial assembly seat (PB-6 Duki), was unhappy with a polling scheme issued by election authorities on 4th January 2024. He argued that this scheme repeated certain problems that had earlier been flagged and supposedly resolved through a letter from the District Election Commissioner dated 16th November 2023. He asked the court to strike down the polling scheme and order authorities to implement the earlier letter's recommendations.

The Election Commission's representatives countered that the November letter merely contained recommendations for a draft scheme, and that a final polling scheme had since been issued on 20th January 2024, which the petitioner never actually challenged.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It found that the petitioner had only contested the earlier draft scheme, not the final one, and had not shown the kind of exceptional circumstances required under election law to justify altering an already-finalized polling scheme, especially with only about two weeks remaining before polling day. The law only allows changes to a finalized polling scheme in very exceptional circumstances.

This case matters because it shows how courts balance individual grievances about election logistics against the practical need for stability and finality in election arrangements close to polling day.

title: Sabira Asad V. Saad Bin Abdullah and another,
explainer:
This case involves a woman who wanted to run for a reserved women's seat in the National Assembly through her political party, the National Party. She submitted two nomination papers to the Returning Officer for her local constituency (NA-262, Quetta-I): one for a general seat and one for the reserved women's seat. The Returning Officer accepted her general seat nomination but rejected her nomination for the reserved seat.

The problem was that this particular Returning Officer only had authority to handle nominations for general constituency seats. Under election law, nominations for reserved seats for women and non-Muslims must be submitted to and decided by the Provincial Election Commissioner, who acts as the Returning Officer specifically for those seats. The local Returning Officer had no legal power to accept or reject her reserved-seat nomination at all.

The Balochistan High Court found that the constituency Returning Officer should have either forwarded her papers to the correct authority or returned them to her so she could refile properly. Instead, he wrongly rejected them, leaving her without a remedy through normal channels.

The court ruled that this rejection was null and void due to lack of jurisdiction, and ordered the nomination papers to be sent to the Provincial Election Commissioner, who must now properly review them and decide the matter according to law. This case highlights the importance of following correct procedural authority in election matters, especially for reserved seats meant to ensure women's representation.

title: Dawood Shehzad and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved the kidnapping and murder of a young boy for ransom. The complainant's son was abducted, and the family received ransom calls demanding three crores of rupees. Several accused were charged with murder, kidnapping for ransom, and terrorism-related offences, and faced the death penalty at trial.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court carefully examined the evidence, which was largely circumstantial. This included phone call records tracing the ransom calls, statements recorded before a magistrate, disclosures made by accused persons leading to recovery of the victim's shoes, tape used to bind him, tablets allegedly given to him, and DNA evidence linking some accused to items found at the crime scene. Medical evidence confirmed the boy died from strangulation and his body was later burned.

The court found that evidence strongly and consistently connected two of the accused to the crime, so their convictions were upheld, though their death sentences were reduced to life imprisonment due to mitigating circumstances. However, for three other accused, the only evidence was that their names came up in the confessions of the convicted men—without independent, reliable corroboration. The court held this was legally insufficient to sustain a conviction, since one accused's statement cannot alone be used to convict another. Their appeals were allowed and they were acquitted.

This judgment reinforces the principle that circumstantial evidence must form an unbroken chain directly linking the accused to the crime, and that confessions of co-accused cannot substitute for independent proof against others.

title: Imran V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Imran who was arrested in Quetta after police, acting on a tip-off, found him carrying a black polythene bag containing 1090 grams of baked charas (hashish). He was charged under Pakistan's narcotics law, specifically a provision that applies to larger quantities of drugs and carries harsher, non-bailable treatment. His initial bail request was rejected by the trial court.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the case and noticed a key flaw in the prosecution's evidence: the charas had been weighed together with the polythene bag it was found in, rather than separately. This meant nobody could say what the actual net weight of the drug itself was. Since the total weight of 1090 grams was only slightly above the threshold separating a lesser offense (which allows bail) from a more serious one (which does not), the court found this discrepancy significant enough to require further investigation at trial.

Because the case sat right on the borderline between the two categories of offense, and the lower one does not fall under the law's bail-restricting provisions, the court ruled that the presumption should favor granting bail rather than denying it. The court therefore granted Imran bail upon furnishing security of Rs. 50,000, while clarifying that its observations were preliminary and would not affect the actual trial's outcome.

title: Sanaullah V. Inspector General of Police Balochistan, Quetta and 7 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over 16 postdated cheques worth over 32 million rupees, allegedly issued under an agreement for the sale of truck tyres. When the cheques bounced, the complainant, Khair Muhammad, lodged multiple criminal cases (FIRs) against the petitioner, Sanaullah, in different police stations across Balochistan and even in Karachi, all essentially based on the same set of facts and the same dishonored cheques.

The petitioner argued he was not even a signatory to the cheques and that he was being harassed through repeated FIRs to pressure him into meeting demands, especially since a related civil case (a summary suit) was already pending in court over the same matter.

The Balochistan High Court held that the law does not allow multiple FIRs to be registered for the same incident or offence, even if the opposing party frames it differently each time. Doing so violates the constitutional protection against double jeopardy (being tried twice for the same offence) under Article 13 of the Constitution. Since the FIRs were based on identical allegations and transactions, the court found them to be an abuse of the legal process, aimed at keeping the petitioner in continuous legal jeopardy despite securing bail.

The court quashed the duplicate FIRs, though it left the first FIR and the civil suit unaffected. This case reinforces the principle that police and complainants cannot misuse the criminal justice system by filing repeat cases over the same dispute.

title: Sami Ullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Sami Ullah, who was convicted by a trial court in Quetta for sodomizing a four-year-old boy, the son of a shopkeeper. According to the prosecution, the child went to the accused's shop to buy firecrackers, where he was forcibly undressed and sexually assaulted. The boy told his father he was bleeding, leading the family to file a police report the same night. Medical examination and forensic DNA testing on swabs and clothing confirmed evidence supporting the assault, and the child himself testified in court, identifying the accused as his abuser. The defense argued an alibi and suggested the case stemmed from a property dispute between families, but produced witnesses whose testimony did not hold up or actually undermined their own case.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the appeal against the trial court's conviction and life sentence. The judges found the prosecution's evidence—the child's testimony, supporting witness accounts, and forensic reports—credible and sufficient to prove guilt beyond doubt. They upheld the conviction under Section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code (dealing with unnatural sexual offenses) read with the Anti-Rape Act.

However, the court reduced the sentence from life imprisonment to five years, citing "peculiar circumstances," including that the accused was only 13 years old at the time and had no prior criminal record.

This case matters because it shows how courts balance strong evidence of guilt with considerations of a young offender's age and background

title: Muhammad Waqas V. The State,
explainer:

The Balochistan High Court examined the evidence and found serious problems with each piece. The complainant was not an eyewitness, and the two witnesses he named did not actually testify against the accused. The accused's confession described shooting both the husband and wife with a single bullet, but medical evidence contradicted this: the wife had actually been strangled, not shot, and the entry/exit wound details for the husband did not match what doctors observed. The court noted that a confession must not only be voluntary but also true and consistent with other evidence to support a conviction, especially in a capital case.

The recovery of the rifle was also found doubtful, since the house where it was found had already been searched earlier without success, suggesting the recovery was staged. Additionally, there was an unexplained 24-day delay in sending the weapon and cartridge to the forensic laboratory, undermining the reliability of the forensic report.

title: Abdul Qayum V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about Abdul Qayum, who was sentenced to death by a trial court in Quetta for allegedly murdering his brother-in-relation (the complainant's brother) based on an FIR from November 2021. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, which reviewed the entire case and overturned the conviction, acquitting him.

The court found serious problems with every piece of evidence used to convict him. The sole eyewitness was the deceased's cousin whose presence at the crime scene was doubtful, and he never described the attacker in detail; plus the accused was never put through a proper identification parade before being identified in court. The accused's confession to a magistrate was ruled unreliable because required legal safeguards weren't followed - for instance, he wasn't warned he wouldn't be sent back to police custody if he refused to confess, and a police officer's presence during the process raised doubts about voluntariness. The pistol supposedly recovered based on the accused's disclosure was sent for forensic testing 20 days late with no explanation, undermining its value. CCTV footage was never forensically verified. Medical evidence only confirmed how the victim died, not who did it.

Because the prosecution's case had major gaps and unreliable evidence, the court applied the principle that it's better to acquit ten guilty people than convict one innocent person, and set Qayum free.

title: Ghulam Murtaza and 4 others V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about whether the Balochistan government's recruitment policy for teachers, which reserved posts based on region, zone, district, and union council quotas, violated Article 27 of the Constitution, which prohibits discrimination in government service based on race, religion, caste, sex, residence, or place of birth. The petitioners, who were job applicants, challenged a March 2023 job advertisement issued under this 2019 policy, arguing that all government appointments should be made purely on merit at the provincial level without any area-based quotas.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It held that Article 27 itself permits an exception to the general rule of equality: posts may be reserved for people from specific classes or areas for up to forty years to ensure their adequate representation in government service. The court explained that deciding how to structure such quotas is a policy matter for the executive branch, not the judiciary, and courts should not interfere unless the policy is shown to be made in bad faith or through misuse of authority. The court found the 2019 recruitment policy was designed to ensure fair, transparent, merit-based hiring while giving balanced representation to candidates from different union councils, districts, and zones.

This judgment matters because it reaffirms that area-based quotas in public sector recruitment are constitutionally valid tools for ensuring balanced regional representation, and that courts will generally defer to the executive's policy choices in this area.

The court upheld the conviction, finding the prosecution proved custodial torture led to death. title: Muhammad Arif V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of possessing 10 kilograms of charas (cannabis resin) under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act. Police claimed they stopped him while on patrol and found ten packets of charas, each weighing one kilogram, wrapped in his shawl. He was tried, convicted by a Special Judge, and sentenced to 20 years in prison plus a fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction due to serious inconsistencies in the prosecution's evidence. The officer who seized the drugs and the police constable who witnessed the recovery both said the packets were prepared at the scene of arrest. However, the police station record-keeper (Moharar) testified that the accused, complainant, and investigating officer arrived at the police station hours later, and that the parcels were made there, not at the arrest site. This contradiction made it unclear whether the evidence was properly packaged at all, raising doubts about tampering or fabrication.

Additionally, the court found that the prosecution failed to establish a clear chain of custody for the drug samples sent for chemical testing. No witness clearly explained who handled the samples between seizure and their delivery to the forensic laboratory, which is essential to prove the substance tested was actually what was recovered from the accused.

Because of these gaps and contradictions, the court ruled that the prosecution had not proven its case beyond reasonable doubt, and acquitted the appellant. The case highlights how procedural lapses in evidence handling can undermine even serious criminal

title: Sher Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Sher Muhammad, who was convicted of murdering his wife and two daughters and attempting to murder a third daughter by shooting them with a Kalashnikov rifle at their home in Zhob, Balochistan, in April 2022. The trial court had sentenced him to death.

The key evidence came from his injured daughter, who survived the attack and testified that her father came home during an argument among the women of the household, locked the door, fetched a rifle, and opened fire, killing her mother and two sisters and wounding her and her brother. Her account was supported by medical evidence and was not seriously undermined during cross-examination. The Balochistan High Court found her testimony credible and sufficient to prove the appellant's guilt.

However, the court reduced his sentence from death to life imprisonment for several reasons: there was no evidence of premeditation, suggesting the shooting happened in a sudden rage during a domestic dispute rather than as a planned killing; the prosecution failed to produce the injured brother as a witness even though he could have confirmed part of the account, which counted against the prosecution; and the appellant and his family had already suffered greatly.

The case matters because it shows how Pakistani courts distinguish between guilt and sentencing, converting death sentences to life imprisonment when mitigating circumstances like lack of premeditation or incomplete evidence exist, even after guilt is firmly established.

title: Khuda Bakhsh alias Baboo V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Khuda Bakhsh, who was convicted under the Pakistan Arms Ordinance for illegally possessing a 9mm pistol. The weapon was allegedly recovered when he was being questioned in an unrelated murder case, after he pointed police to a location near Mastung where the pistol and an empty magazine were found. He was sentenced to three years in prison plus a fine by the trial court.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious flaws in how the prosecution built its case. The two witnesses who supposedly watched the police recover the pistol were never brought to testify in this arms case. The pistol itself was never formally presented as evidence during the trial. Instead, the prosecution simply relied on a copy of the recovery document that had been prepared for the separate murder investigation. The court held this was not enough to prove guilt, since the actual witnesses to the recovery needed to testify, and crucially, no one gave evidence that the accused was ever asked to produce a weapons license and failed to do so, which is a key element of the offense.

Because these basic evidentiary requirements were not met, the court ruled the conviction could not stand. It set aside the trial court's judgment, acquitted Khuda Bakhsh, and ordered his release. The case highlights how convictions must rest on solid, properly presented evidence, not shortcuts or borrowed paperwork from other cases.

title: Ghulam Sarwar V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case is about a murder allegation arising from a firing incident at an orchard in Mastung, Balochistan, in May 2023, in which Sami Ullah was killed. His brother, the complainant, accused Shair Ali and others of shooting the deceased. During the trial, Shair Ali was granted bail by the Sessions Judge, Mastung. The complainant then approached the Balochistan High Court asking for that bail to be cancelled.

The High Court explained that the legal standards for granting bail and for cancelling bail already granted are very different. Once bail has been granted by a competent court, it can only be cancelled on strong, exceptional grounds, such as the order being clearly illegal or contrary to the record, misuse of bail, tampering with evidence, risk of the accused fleeing, repeating the offense, or new evidence showing guilt.

Examining the facts, the court noted that it was unclear who fired the fatal shot, since multiple people were shooting and the deceased wasn't hit in vital body parts. There was also a background of enmity and multiple cross-FIRs between the parties, raising the possibility of false implication, and the accused had presented an alibi defense. Since other co-accused had already been granted bail on similar facts, consistency also favored bail for this accused. Finding no legal error in the original bail order and no valid grounds for cancellation, the High Court dismissed the application, allowing the accused to remain on bail during trial.

title: Collector, Model Customs Collectorate, Custom House, Gawadar at Gaddani V. Messrs Byco Petroleum Pakistan Limited and another,
explainer: This case is about a dispute between Pakistan's Customs authorities and Byco Petroleum Pakistan Limited over an import of furnace oil brought in on a partially empty oil tanker from the UAE. Because the tanker was not fully loaded, the company paid extra charges known as dead freight for the unused space, and its import declaration was cleared and assessed by the proper customs officer at the time. Later, an audit officer objected that the freight amount declared was too low compared to normal market rates, leading to a show cause notice and an order demanding the company pay additional duty and taxes of over 2.4 million rupees. The company argued that the audit officer had no legal authority to reopen an already finalized assessment, since only the Collector of Customs can do so, and only within two years, under section 195 of the Customs Act. The Customs Appellate Tribunal agreed and cancelled the demand, prompting the Collectorate to challenge that decision before the Balochistan High Court. The High Court upheld the Tribunal's decision, ruling that the original assessment was valid, the audit officer lacked authority to reopen it, and that factual disputes about freight rates should have been resolved during adjudication, not through a High Court reference. This case reinforces limits on customs officials' power to reopen settled assessments and protects importers from arbitrary re-assessment after the legal deadline has passed.

title: Latif and others V. Abdul Nabi and others,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court, involved a dispute over a property between petitioners who claimed to have bought and legally received possession of land in 2016, and the respondents, who admitted the sale but argued the petitioners were trying to unlawfully occupy an additional portion of jointly owned family property. The petitioners sued for declaration, possession and permanent injunction. Both the trial court and the appellate court dismissed their case, ruling that the dispute was really about land demarcation and should instead be handled by Revenue authorities under the Balochistan Land Revenue Act, not by a civil court.

The High Court disagreed and allowed the petitioners' revisions. It explained that while the law does give Revenue Officers exclusive power over certain matters, such as boundary or partition disputes, it specifically excludes cases where the real issue is one of property title or ownership. Since the two sides were making conflicting factual claims about ownership and possession that could only be resolved by examining evidence, the matter was not a simple demarcation issue for Revenue authorities to decide. Instead, it required proper judicial determination, which only a civil court could provide.

This ruling matters because it clarifies the boundary between the powers of Revenue courts and civil courts in Pakistan, ensuring that genuine ownership disputes are decided through full evidentiary trials in civil courts rather than being wrongly redirected to administrative revenue forums.

title: Hotak alias Sapak V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Hotak alias Sapak, who was convicted of murdering a woman by shooting her outside her house in 2014. The motive was that she had refused to marry him. The trial court in Killa Saifullah had sentenced him to death, and the case came before the Balochistan High Court both as his appeal against conviction and as a mandatory reference to confirm or reject the death sentence.

The prosecution's case rested on eyewitness testimony, medical evidence, and a confessional statement recorded by a judicial magistrate. One witness saw the accused approaching the victim's house with a gun and heard shots fired; another was present when the victim was shot and had earlier been warned by the accused that he intended to kidnap or kill her. Medical evidence confirmed she died from a gunshot. The court also examined the accused's confession, finding it voluntary, properly recorded, and consistent with the witnesses' accounts. However, the recovery of the weapon was rejected as evidence because the witnesses to that recovery were never produced in court.

It therefore reduced the sentence from death to life imprisonment, while dismissing the appeal otherwise. This shows courts’ careful distinction between proving guilt and justifying the harshest punishment.

title: Aziz Ahmed V. The State,

The court also noted that trial delays were partly caused by the accused himself, so he could not claim bail on that basis yet. The bail application was dismissed, though the court directed the trial to be completed within three months, clarifying that its observations were preliminary and should not affect the actual trial's outcome.

title: Muhammad Rafiq V. The State through Prosecutor General Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Rafiq, who was convicted by a trial court in Balochistan and sentenced to life imprisonment plus a fine for possessing 30 kilograms of charas (a narcotic), allegedly recovered from the trunk of the car he was driving. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction after finding serious flaws in the prosecution's evidence. Key witnesses gave contradictory accounts of basic facts, such as who received the recovered drugs at the scene, whether the police record-keeper (Moharar) was even present during the recovery, and who prepared the official documents. There were also unexplained gaps in the chain of custody: the drugs were allegedly handed over on one date but received at the forensic laboratory a day later, with no explanation for where they were in the meantime. Additionally, important entries in the police malkhana (storage) register were left blank, violating police rules, and the forensic lab report failed to include a required declaration confirming proper testing protocols were followed.

The court held that these contradictions and gaps created reasonable doubt about whether the drugs were genuinely recovered from the appellant and properly preserved and tested. Citing established legal principle, the court ruled that even a single reasonable doubt must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not leniency. As a result, the appeal was allowed and the conviction set aside.

This case highlights how courts scrutinize procedural safeguards in narcotics cases, ensuring evidence handling meets legal standards before someone can be deprived

title: Mst. Zainab Bibi V. Muhammad Rizwan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a wife, Zainab Bibi, who filed a family court suit against her husband seeking recovery of her dower (haq mehr), dowry articles, and maintenance for herself and their daughter after their marriage broke down and he divorced her. The Family Court partly granted her claims, awarding her the house promised as dower, monthly maintenance for her and the child, and her dowry articles, but rejected her claim for 3 tola of gold that had also been specified as dower, as well as gold ornaments she said her mother had given her. She appealed to the Additional District Judge, but that appeal was dismissed too. She then approached the Balochistan High Court under its constitutional jurisdiction, asking it to overturn the lower courts and award her the gold as well.

The High Court dismissed her petition. It held that since both the trial court and the appellate court had already examined the evidence carefully and reached the same factual conclusions, the High Court should not re-examine the facts or substitute its own view for theirs. Relying on a Supreme Court precedent, the judges explained that constitutional petitions are meant to correct clear jurisdictional errors or serious procedural illegality, not to give a third chance to re-argue facts already properly decided twice. Since there was no such error here, the concurrent findings of the lower courts were upheld.

This case matters because it reaffirms the limited role of the High Court in reviewing family court decisions, promoting finality in litigation and discouraging repeated appeals over factual disputes already fairly decided.

A wife (respondent) had filed a suit before the Family Court seeking past and future maintenance for herself and her minor son, after her marriage to the petitioner broke down due to alleged maltreatment. She had left the matrimonial home while her older son stayed with the father. The Family Court ruled in her favor, ordering maintenance payments. This decision went through two rounds: first the Appellate Court sent it back for the trial judge to properly address all legal issues, and after the Family Court re-decided in the wife's favor again, the Appellate Court upheld that decision on appeal.

The husband then approached the Balochistan High Court, asking it to overturn both lower court rulings and dismiss the wife's suit entirely.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It explained that when both the trial court and the appellate court have already examined the evidence and reached the same factual conclusions, the High Court cannot re-examine those facts under its constitutional jurisdiction (Article 199). Citing a Supreme Court precedent, the judges emphasized that constitutional petitions are not a backdoor way to get a second appeal, and that finality of factual findings by lower courts is necessary to prevent endless litigation. Since the wife had proven her claim with evidence and the husband failed to rebut it, the maintenance order stood. The case reinforces that High Courts should not reopen settled factual disputes, especially in family law matters where quick resolution is important.

title: Naimatullah and others V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case concerns the murder of a young man named Aminullah, allegedly by Niamatullah over a money dispute involving a loan of three million rupees. According to the prosecution, the complainant, who was the deceased's maternal uncle, witnessed the accused arrive by jeep, exchange heated words with the deceased, and then shoot him fatally in the chest. The accused remained a fugitive for years before being arrested in Punjab on an unrelated case and brought back to Quetta for trial. The trial court convicted him under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code for murder, sentencing him to life imprisonment and a fine payable to the victim's heirs. He appealed the conviction, while the complainant separately sought enhancement of the sentence to the death penalty.

The Balochistan High Court examined the eyewitness testimony of the complainant, which remained consistent despite lengthy cross-examination, and found it credible even though he was related to the victim. This testimony was corroborated by medical evidence confirming death by firearm, as well as forensic reports. The prosecution also successfully proved motive through witness testimony about a threatening phone call and a dishonored cheque linked to the money dispute.

Finding the evidence solid and unshaken, the High Court dismissed the appeal against conviction, upholding the life sentence. This case illustrates how Pakistani courts evaluate eyewitness credibility, corroborating medical/forensic evidence, and proof of motive in murder trials.

title: Sardar Hafeez Loni and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute between a tractor company owner and a buyer who paid for tractors and machinery with a large post-dated cheque that later bounced. After the initial cheque case, the parties settled through arbitration, reducing the outstanding debt, and the buyer issued multiple new post-dated cheques as installment payments. Several of these cheques also bounced, leading to separate FIRs (police cases) being filed against him under cheque-dishonour law.

The accused challenged these cases in multiple petitions before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that since he had already been acquitted once over the original cheque, prosecuting him again over the new cheques amounted to double jeopardy. He also challenged a trial court order allowing the complainant's statement to be recorded through a court-appointed commission at his residence, instead of in person, due to technical issues with video recording.

The High Court rejected all these arguments. It held that each dishonoured cheque was a separate transaction on a different date, so there was no double jeopardy, and the dismissal of his application to quash the case had no legal error. It also upheld the trial court's decision to record the complainant's statement at his home through a commission, since the accused could not show any actual unfairness caused by this arrangement. The court directed police protection during that recording. All the petitions were dismissed, meaning the criminal cases against the accused will continue.

title: Bibi PATO and another V. Government of Pakistan, through Secretary Ministry of Interior, Islamabad and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a woman, Bibi Pato, and her son who challenged NADRA's refusal to issue them corrected identity documents. Bibi Pato had a valid CNIC and passport (she had even performed Hajj using it), and applied to correct her date of birth from 1970 to 1950. NADRA's own Zonal Board recommended the correction, and the change was formally approved by NADRA's higher authority. Despite this approval and after she paid the required fee, NADRA delayed issuing her a new corrected CNIC. It also refused to renew her son's CNIC. NADRA's stated reason was a Ministry of Interior policy requiring documentary evidence of identity from before 1978, which the family could not provide.

The Balochistan High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners. It noted there was no allegation that they were ineligible for CNICs, had obtained multiple cards, tampered with documents, or used forged cards. The family had a long documented history with NADRA and its predecessor system, including identity cards issued to the petitioner's husband and grandfather-in-law decades earlier. The court held that under Section 18 of the NADRA Ordinance, cards can only be cancelled or withheld if there is concrete evidence of wrongdoing, which NADRA failed to prove here. The pre-1978 evidence requirement did not apply to this family's situation. The court ordered the corrected CNIC and renewal to be issued, reinforcing that citizens' documented rights cannot be denied without genuine cause.

title: Hajj Organizers Association of Pakistan (HOAP) Balochistan Zone through Executive Body Member V. Government of Pakistan through Federal Secretary, Ministry of Commerce, Islamabad and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns the Hajj Organizers Association of Pakistan (HOAP), Balochistan Zone, which challenged notices issued by the Director General Trade Organization requiring it to hold elections for its office bearers within a set schedule, and barring current Executive Committee members from contesting again. HOAP argued that these directives violated Article 17 of the Constitution, which guarantees citizens the right to form associations. It claimed elections could not be held on time because of Hajj operational duties, and that preventing sitting members from re-contesting was unfair and unconstitutional.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments and dismissed the petition. It held that while Article 17 protects the right to form associations, this right is subject to reasonable legal restrictions. Timely elections for representative bodies are themselves a fundamental requirement that cannot be delayed without lawful justification. The court further explained that the Trade Organizations Act, 2013 empowers the regulator to supervise elections, and Rule 21(15) of the Trade Organizations Rules, 2013 clearly states that outgoing office bearers cannot contest for the next term. This provision directly defeated HOAP's claim that such a bar was unconstitutional.

The judgment matters because it clarifies that regulatory oversight of trade body elections, including term limits for office bearers, is lawful and does not infringe the constitutional right to association. It reinforces that democratic accountability within trade organizations takes precedence over incumbents' desire to retain power indefinitely.

title: Muhammad Yousaf V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by Muhammad Yousaf and two co-accused before the Balochistan High Court. They were accused of embezzling over Rs. 25 million from a development account of the Municipal Committee, Kohlu, through fraudulent cash withdrawals allegedly carried out between 2019 and 2024 using forged signatures. The accused included an ex-Chief Officer, a sweeper, and a cashier of the Municipal Committee, and were booked under provisions relating to criminal breach of trust, cheating, forgery, and corruption.

The trial court had earlier rejected their bail plea, so they approached the High Court. The court noted that during the relevant period, several different officers had served as Chief Officer or Administrator of the Municipal Committee, making it difficult at this stage to pin sole responsibility on the applicant who held that post. Regarding the sweeper, although a large sum was traced to his bank account, there was no clear evidence he personally withdrew it, and he claimed his cheque book had been misused by someone else. The court held that mere presence of funds in an account isn't proof of guilt without further evidence at trial, and since the case relied on documentary evidence already collected, continued detention served no purpose.

The court granted bail to all applicants, emphasizing that it is better to wrongly grant bail than wrongly deny it, since a conviction can later correct that error, but wrongful detention cannot be undone.

title: Bashir Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Bashir Ahmed, who was convicted by a Special Judge in Khuzdar under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act for allegedly possessing large quantities of opium, heroin/crystal, and sheesha (ice) found hidden beneath the rear seat of a pickup truck he was driving. He was sentenced to lengthy prison terms, including life imprisonment, along with heavy fines.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined the evidence closely and found serious problems with the prosecution's case. Witnesses gave contradictory accounts: the complainant claimed a road blockade was set up to check vehicles, but the recovery witness said no other vehicle was checked that day, and no blockade was mentioned in the original police report. The recovered packets were not properly sealed or labeled with the case number or accused's name. There were also major gaps in how the narcotics were handled afterward - no proper record-keeping of when evidence was stored, and an unexplained eight-day delay before samples were sent to the forensic laboratory, with conflicting testimony about logbook entries.

Given these contradictions and the failure to prove safe custody and secure transmission of the narcotics, the court ruled that the prosecution's case was too doubtful to sustain a conviction. Citing the principle that serious punishments require strong evidence, and that any reasonable doubt must benefit the accused as a matter of right, the court set aside the conviction and allowed the appeal.

title: Muhammad Qaseem V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man convicted of possessing and transporting 40 kilograms of charas (hashish) under Pakistan's narcotics law, sentenced to life imprisonment and a heavy fine by a trial court in Quetta. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing his conviction was unsafe.

The High Court agreed and acquitted him, finding serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, no witness explained who the drugs were handed to immediately after recovery or how they reached police storage, breaking the required "chain of custody." Second, officials never explained the technical details of how the drugs were hidden inside a CNG cylinder's cavities or how they were extracted, and the cylinder itself was never produced as evidence. Third, and most critically, prosecution records meant to prove safe custody of the samples were incomplete (blank entries in an official police register), and there was an unexplained two-day gap between the seizure date and when the laboratory received the samples for testing.

The court held that even a single reasonable doubt entitles an accused to acquittal as a matter of right, not leniency. Since the prosecution failed to prove an unbroken, reliable chain from seizure to laboratory testing, the conviction could not stand. This case matters because it reinforces strict standards for handling drug evidence, ensuring convictions rest on solid proof rather than procedural shortcuts by investigators.

title: Mushtaq Ahmed and 6 others V. Fouzia Nawaz and 14 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute among the legal heirs of a deceased man, Muhammad Nawaz. One of his heirs, Fouzia Nawaz, filed a suit asking for a declaration of her share, partition of the inherited properties, possession, an accounting of income, mesne profits (compensation for being kept out of use of the property), and a permanent injunction. Evidence showed that other family members were collecting rent from shops, a flour mill, and a mobile phone tower on the inherited land, without giving her any share since 2014, even though her right to inherit was never seriously disputed.

The trial court ruled in her favor, ordering partition of the properties and awarding her mesne profits from January 2019. The appellate court upheld this decision. The family members opposing her then challenged the ruling before the Balochistan High Court, mainly objecting to the mesne profits award.

The High Court explained that normally one co-owner cannot claim mesne profits from another co-owner in joint possession, since each co-owner has rights over the whole property. However, an exception applies when one co-owner excludes others from enjoying their share. Since the lower courts had not properly calculated the actual amount of mesne profits owed, the High Court held that part of the decree could not be enforced. It therefore upheld the rest of the judgment confirming her inheritance share and ordering partition, but set aside only the unspecified mesne profits award.

title: Najeeb Ullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Najeeb Ullah and Shah Mureed, who were convicted by a trial court in Khuzdar, Balochistan, and sentenced to 20 years imprisonment plus a fine after police allegedly recovered 10 kilograms of charas (hashish) hidden in the switchboard cavities of their car. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing the evidence against them was unreliable and full of contradictions.

The High Court agreed and acquitted both appellants. It found serious inconsistencies between the complainant's account and the recovery witness's testimony, including disagreement over the car's color and how the drugs were actually found and weighed. The court also found the chain of custody for the seized narcotics was broken and unexplained delays occurred before the samples reached the forensic laboratory, undermining confidence that the substance tested was actually what had been recovered from the accused.

Crucially, the court also found that the forensic lab had wrongly treated a preliminary screening test (Thin Layer Chromatography) as a confirmatory test, contrary to international scientific guidelines and prior Supreme Court directions, meaning the chemical analysis report itself was unreliable.

Given these doubts, the court applied the well-established legal principle that even a single reasonable doubt must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not favor. The conviction was overturned and the appeal allowed, highlighting the importance of proper evidence handling and forensic testing standards in drug prosecution cases.

title: Muhammad Ismail V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Muhammad Ismail who was arrested after police allegedly found 1200 grams of baked charas (a narcotic substance) wrapped in a polythene bag in his waistband in Quetta. He was charged under a provision of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act that carries harsher penalties for larger quantities of drugs, and his initial bail request was denied by a trial court.

The key issue before the Balochistan High Court was the actual weight of the drug itself. The police had weighed the charas together with the polythene bag it was wrapped in, but never determined the net weight of the charas alone. This mattered because the law sets different punishment brackets depending on quantity, and the total recorded weight was only slightly above the threshold separating a lesser offense from a more serious one. Since the exact quantity of pure charas remained unclear, the court found this was a borderline case requiring further investigation at trial to determine which legal provision actually applied.

Because the lesser offense category does not fall under the law's "prohibitory clause" (which normally makes bail harder to get), and given the ambiguity about the true weight of the drug, the court ruled that bail should be granted as a matter of course rather than refused. The applicant was released on bail after furrishing sureties, with the court clarifying that its observations were preliminary and would not affect the eventual trial outcome.

title: Osama and another V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case involved two men, Osama and another accused, who were convicted for the murder of the complainant's brother. According to the prosecution, the accused had invited the victim for dinner and to repay a loan, after which he disappeared. When he did not return, his family reported the matter, naming the appellants. One accused, after arrest, disclosed details of the murder and led police to recover the victim's dead body, along with blood-stained items, a weapon, and cash.

The Balochistan High Court examined the reliability of "last seen" evidence, meaning testimony that the victim was last seen with the accused. The court explained that such evidence is generally weak on its own but becomes strong when it fits into an unbroken chain of circumstances connecting the accused to the crime. Here, the court found that the recoveries of the body, weapons, and blood-stained articles, all made based on the accused's disclosures, formed a consistent and reliable chain, satisfying legal requirements for admissibility under the law of evidence.

Based on this, the court upheld Osama's conviction and sentence for murder. However, for the second appellant, the court found the evidence insufficient to prove direct involvement in the killing, but sufficient to show he helped conceal evidence. His conviction was therefore reduced from murder to the lesser offense of destroying evidence, with a seven-year sentence.

This judgment matters because it clarifies how courts should evaluate circumstantial and "last seen" evidence, and it distinguishes between guilt for murder and guilt for merely helping conceal a crime.

title: Mir Hassan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Mir Hassan who was convicted under Pakistan's Arms Ordinance of 1965 for possessing a knife that police said was recovered from his home during a murder investigation. The law makes it illegal to possess certain weapons, including knives with blades of four inches or more, but specifically excludes kitchen knives or knives used in good faith for carrying on a profession from this definition.

During the murder investigation, Hassan reportedly led police to a knife hidden beneath blankets in a room of his house. Based on this recovery, a trial court convicted him and sentenced him to three years of rigorous imprisonment.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. The court found that the prosecution never proved the knife was NOT a kitchen knife or was NOT used for legitimate professional purposes, an essential element the law requires prosecutors to establish. Additionally, the trial court had failed to specifically ask Hassan to explain whether the knife was a kitchen knife when questioning him after the prosecution's evidence closed. Because he was never given this chance to respond, that gap in evidence could not be held against him.

The High Court concluded the prosecution failed to prove its case and that the trial court had misread the evidence. As a result, the appeal was allowed, the conviction was set aside, and Hassan was acquitted and ordered released. This case highlights that prosecutors must prove every legal element of a crime, including exceptions written into the law, and that defendants must be properly questioned about specific evidence used against them.

title: Mir Hassan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against a murder conviction from the Balochistan High Court. Mir Hassan had been convicted by a trial court and sentenced to life imprisonment for murder under Pakistan's Penal Code, based largely on circumstantial evidence since there were no eyewitnesses to the killing.

The prosecution's case rested on several pieces of evidence: medical/autopsy findings, a video clip allegedly showing the deceased with an unknown person and a knife that had been posted on Facebook, a confessional statement made by a co-accused, and a bloodstained knife recovered based on the appellant's disclosure to police.

The High Court found serious problems with each piece of evidence. The medical report was contradictory and confusing about the actual cause of death and weapon used. The video clip's source and authenticity were never verified, and it was never sent for forensic analysis to rule out tampering or AI manipulation—a significant gap given the case involved a possible death sentence. The co-accused's confession was ruled involuntary due to unexplained delays, police mistreatment, and procedural lapses. Finally, the recovered knife's forensic report couldn't confirm the blood belonged to the victim.

The court explained that circumstantial evidence must form an unbroken chain connecting the crime to the accused; if any link is missing, conviction cannot stand. Finding multiple broken links here, the High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the appellant. This case highlights how courts must rigorously scrutinize weak, contradictory, or unverified evidence

title: Naimatullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Naimatullah who was convicted of robbery under Section 392 of the Pakistan Penal Code after being accused, along with a co-accused, of snatching Rs. 23,00,000 and cheque books from a complainant at gunpoint. He was sentenced to three years imprisonment with a fine by a trial court, and both his appeal and the complainant's request for a harsher sentence were rejected by an appellate court.

The Balochistan High Court overturned the conviction. It found that the identification evidence was unreliable because neither the complainant nor the eyewitness had described the culprits to police beforehand, and although they picked out Naimatullah during a formal identification parade, they did not assign him any specific criminal role or actually identify him as one of the robbers. The court held that simply being picked out in a parade, without more, was not enough to prove guilt.

The court also rejected the recovery of cash as meaningful evidence, since the complainant never specified the serial numbers or denominations of the stolen money, making it impossible to confirm the recovered cash was actually the stolen amount. The cheque books, which could have been crucial evidence, were never recovered at all. Since recovery evidence only supports an already-proven case and cannot stand alone, the court found the prosecution's case unproven and acquitted Naimatullah, highlighting the importance of rigorous identification procedures in criminal trials.

title: Daroo Khan and 2 others V. Haji Abdul Zahir and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and involves a civil dispute over ownership of a shop in Quetta. The plaintiff, Haji Abdul Zahir, filed a suit for declaration, possession, and permanent injunction, claiming he was the lawful owner of a shop that had been illegally occupied by the defendants (Daroo Khan and others). While the trial was ongoing, the defendants filed an application asking to have the case transferred to a different judge, alleging that the trial judge was biased against them. They based this claim on remarks the judge had made while deciding a separate, unrelated application about the authenticity of an agreement, arguing these remarks suggested the judge favored the other side. The District Judge rejected this transfer request, and the defendants challenged that rejection before the High Court.

The High Court dismissed the petition, upholding the lower court's decision. It explained that bias must be proven through concrete evidence, not just suspicion or apprehension, and that a judge's comments on a preliminary evidentiary matter do not necessarily indicate prejudgment of the whole case. The court noted that the trial judge must still decide all the main issues in the final judgment. Since the petitioners could not demonstrate genuine bias or improper interest, their fear of an unfair trial was insufficient grounds for transfer.

This ruling matters because it reinforces the legal principle that transferring a case away from a judge requires solid proof of bias, not merely a party's subjective distrust, protecting the integrity and continuity of judicial proceedings.

title: Muhammad Asad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a Hino truck that was seized by police in 2021 after 574 kg of charas and 7 kg of opium were found hidden in its secret compartments. The driver, Abdul Qadir, was convicted and sentenced (later reduced to life imprisonment), and the trial court also ordered the truck confiscated as part of that judgment.

Muhammad Asad, the registered owner of the truck since November 2020, was never named as an accused in the case and was not accused of knowing about the drugs. He later applied to the trial court for return of his vehicle, claiming he had simply rented it out to the convicted driver and had no knowledge of any narcotics being transported in it. The trial court rejected his request, so he appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court noted that under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, a vehicle used to transport drugs can only be confiscated if the prosecution proves the owner knew the offence was being or would be committed. Since Asad was never implicated as a co-accused or shown to have such knowledge, the prosecution had failed to meet this legal requirement. The court also found the trial court's order rejecting his application was poorly reasoned and unlawful.

As a result, the High Court set aside the confiscation order and directed that the truck be returned to Asad after verification. The case highlights that innocent vehicle owners cannot lose their property merely because it was misused by someone else without their knowledge.

title: Muhammad Afzal V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application filed by Muhammad Afzal, who was accused of murdering Jamal Khan and injuring two others in a firing incident that occurred in 2023 in Loralai, allegedly along with his brother and father over a land dispute. The prosecution claimed Afzal tried to shoot the victims on his father's instructions but his pistol malfunctioned, after which his brother fired the fatal shots.

Afzal had earlier absconded and was declared a proclaimed offender before surrendering and seeking bail, which lower courts had refused.

The Balochistan High Court granted him bail. The judge noted a key contradiction: while the prosecution said Afzal's gun failed to fire, a forensic report showed the pistol was actually in working condition, undermining the prosecution's own narrative. The court also found it too early to determine whether Afzal truly shared a "common intention" to kill with his co-accused, saying this could only be properly decided after a full trial. Since his father, accused of instigating the attack, had already been granted bail, the court held Afzal's situation was different and less serious.

The court further ruled that simply having absconded earlier is not, by itself, a valid reason to deny bail, since fear of arrest or mistreatment can explain such behavior.

This case matters because it clarifies that bail can be granted when forensic evidence contradicts the prosecution's story and when an accused's exact role or intent remains unclear pending trial.

title: Muhammad Hamayun V. Shamsullah and 5 others,
explainer:
This case is about a criminal complaint arising from a violent street altercation in Quetta in 2019, where several people were attacked with knives and other weapons, leaving multiple people injured, including the complainant Muhammad Hamayun who suffered a stab wound to his abdomen. The accused were charged with serious offences including attempted murder (Section 324 PPC) and rioting with deadly weapons.

The case had bounced back and forth between the Sessions Court and a Judicial Magistrate's court multiple times over jurisdiction disputes. The Sessions Court eventually sent the case back to the Magistrate, reasoning that since the injuries weren't on "vital parts" of the body, the attempted murder charge didn't apply, meaning the case belonged in a lower court.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed and overturned this transfer order. It found that stab wounds to the abdomen and chest are indeed on vital body parts capable of causing death, so the Sessions Court's reasoning was factually wrong. The High Court also noted that under the law, once a magistrate commits a case involving offences exclusively triable by the Sessions Court, it shouldn't be sent back and forth like this, especially after charges had already been formally framed years earlier.

The Court ordered the case be transferred back to the Sessions Court to proceed with a full trial. This decision matters because it clarifies how courts should determine whether injuries are serious enough to warrant a full sessions trial, and it prevents cases from being repeatedly shuffled between courts, ensuring victims
