title: Muhammad Khan V. Amanullah,
explainer:
Muhammad Khan was Chairman of the District Zakat and Ushr Committee in Sibi. Wanting to contest the upcoming local council elections, he resigned from this position on 30 October 2013, shortly before submitting his nomination papers for a seat on the Municipal Committee, Sibi. A returning officer initially accepted his nomination papers, but a rival candidate appealed, and the District and Sessions Judge, acting as Appellate Authority, rejected the papers on the ground that six months had not passed since Khan's resignation, as required by law.

Khan challenged this rejection before the Balochistan High Court, arguing the Zakat Committee post was unpaid and part-time and that he had resigned merely to avoid political criticism, so no disqualification should apply.

The High Court disagreed. It held that anyone administering Zakat funds is legally considered a "public servant," and such officials are barred from taking part in political activity. Since local council elections count as political activity, and the law requires a six-month gap after leaving such public service before running for office, Khan remained disqualified. The court reasoned this waiting period exists precisely to prevent any lingering influence from the office affecting election results. Since Khan himself resigned specifically because he knew he could not otherwise contest while holding that post, the court found the Appellate Authority's decision lawful and dismissed his petition, upholding the rejection of his nomination papers.

title: Haider Ali Khan Jamali V. Returning Officer/Adc Jaffarabad,
explainer:
This case involved a candidate, Haider Ali Khan Jamali, who wanted to contest a local government election from Ward No. 2 of Municipal Committee Usta Muhammad in Balochistan. He had originally submitted nomination papers from multiple constituencies, including one where his name actually appeared on the electoral roll, but withdrew from those and sought to contest from a ward where his name was not registered as a voter. His nomination was initially accepted by the Returning Officer, but on appeal by another candidate, the Appellate Authority rejected his papers because his name was not on the electoral roll for that ward. He then approached the High Court seeking a direction that he be included in the list of validly nominated candidates.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that under the Balochistan Local Government Act, 2010, a candidate must be a registered voter in the electoral roll of the relevant ward to qualify for election there. It also relied on Section 20 of the Electoral Rolls Act, 1974, which bars any correction or revision of electoral rolls once an election schedule has been announced. Since the petitioner had over five months before the election schedule was announced to correct his voter registration but failed to do so, the court found the electoral roll could not be corrected at this late stage.

This case matters because it clarifies that candidates must ensure their voter registration is accurate well before elections are announced, and courts cannot override statutory deadlines for correcting electoral rolls once the election process has begun.

title: Ejaz Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
Ejaz Ahmed was accused, along with an absconding co-accused, of shooting and killing Muhammad Anwar in Quetta in October 2011. He was already in custody and had also been charged in the murder case, and applied for post-arrest bail after a sessions judge had earlier rejected his request.

His lawyer argued that two other co-accused, alleged only of instigating the crime, had already been acquitted in the same trial, so the applicant deserved similar treatment. He also argued the eyewitnesses were the deceased's relatives and thus biased, that there was an unexplained delay in reporting the crime to police, and that the case needed further investigation.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the bail application. It held that the acquittal of the co-accused did not help the applicant, because they were only accused of encouraging the crime while he was accused of actually carrying it out, so the cases were not comparable. The court also said the legal principle that lying about one part of a case discredits the whole case does not apply in criminal justice, and courts must separate reliable evidence from unreliable evidence. Being related to the victim did not automatically make witnesses unreliable. The court also found that the applicant had been a fugitive for over two years, which, combined with other evidence, suggested guilt, and that the reporting delay of just over an hour was not significant. Bail was therefore refused.

title: Abdul Lateef and 13 Others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved fourteen people from Zhob, Balochistan, who were accused of beating relatives during a family dispute in November 2011. The complainant said he and three others were attacked with spades and sticks while trying to help his cousin, who was being beaten. All fourteen accused were convicted by a magistrate for causing injuries, and this conviction was upheld on appeal by the Sessions Judge. They then challenged their convictions before the Balochistan High Court.

The defense argued that the case stemmed from a land dispute among relatives, that elderly family members had been wrongly implicated, that witnesses gave contradictory statements about motive, and that the charge sheet did not clearly specify what role each accused person played.

The High Court found that while the motive (land dispute) was proven and the injuries were confirmed by medical evidence, only five of the fourteen accused had been given specific roles in the incident by witnesses. The other eight were vaguely implicated simply because they belonged to the same family, apparently to humiliate the opposing side. The court held that injured witnesses do not always tell the complete truth, and doubtful cases must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not mercy.

The court acquitted eight of the fourteen accused for lack of clear evidence, while upholding convictions for five people who were specifically identified as participants, with punishments including fines instead of harsher terms given their clean records. This case highlights the importance of assigning individual responsibility rather than convicting entire family groups collectively.

title: Collector of Customs, through Additional Collector of Customs V. Messrs Haji Ballow Khan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the internal procedures of the Customs, Excise and Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal. The Customs Department challenged an order passed by the Tribunal's Chairman, arguing that he had decided the case sitting alone as a single member without properly constituting a two-member bench, as generally required under Section 194C of the Customs Act, 1969.

The Balochistan High Court examined the law governing how the Tribunal organizes its benches. It held that while the Chairman has administrative discretion to distribute cases among Tribunal members, this discretion is not unlimited. Before assigning a case to a single member, the Chairman must record reasons and can only do so for matters already allotted to a two-member bench, using a member who was part of that bench. The Chairman cannot simply retain and decide a case himself without following this process, except in genuine situations of urgency, and even then he must record his reasons.

Since the Chairman had decided the matter without properly constituting a bench or justifying single-member adjudication, the Court ruled his order was "coram non judice" (issued without proper jurisdiction) and therefore invalid. The Court set aside the order and directed the Tribunal to reconstitute a proper bench and rehear the case from scratch.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the limits of a tribunal chairman's administrative power and reinforces that procedural safeguards ensuring fair, properly constituted adjudication cannot be bypassed even for convenience or urgency.

title: Gelcaps Pakistan Employees Union through General Secretary V. Province of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and another,
explainer:
This case involved a labour union at a private company, Gelcaps Pakistan, which filed a constitutional petition in the Balochistan High Court fearing that the company would shut down operations and terminate workers, particularly union office-bearers, in retaliation for submitting a charter of demands. The union asked the court to declare such possible actions as unfair labour practice and to bar the company from closing down or dismissing employees.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It found that no application to close the establishment or terminate workers was actually pending before the Labour Court, meaning the union was acting on a mere apprehension rather than an actual, existing grievance. Courts cannot intervene based on fears about what might happen in the future. The judges also noted that questions of "unfair labour practice" involve disputed facts requiring evidence, which cannot be resolved through constitutional petitions. Instead, the Balochistan Industrial Relations Act, 2010 already provides a complete mechanism, including Section 41 on redressal of grievances, for workers or unions to challenge terminations or unfair treatment once they actually occur. Since this adequate alternate remedy existed, and since the employer was a private company rather than a state authority, the constitutional petition was not maintainable.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that courts will not pre-emptively intervene in labour disputes based on speculation, and that workers must first pursue remedies under labour laws before approaching the High Court under its constitutional jurisdiction.

title: Nazeer Ahmed V. Abid Ahmed and another,
explainer:
This case is about who is allowed to appeal against a criminal acquittal and within what time limit. A man was tried for allegedly beating his wife and divorcing her, causing injury. The trial court acquitted him, giving him the benefit of the doubt. The complainant, the injured woman's brother, then filed an appeal against the acquittal, but he filed it four days late, explaining this was due to a miscalculation of dates, and asked the court to excuse the delay.

The Balochistan High Court refused to excuse the delay and dismissed the appeal. It explained that the law gives only 30 days to appeal an acquittal, and once that period passes, the acquitted person gains a valuable right to their liberty that courts should not disturb lightly. Simple mistakes in calculating dates are not good enough reasons to excuse a late filing.

The court also ruled that the brother was not the proper person to file the appeal. Even though the victim was a woman observing purdah, she had personally appeared and testified in court, including facing cross-examination, showing she was capable of pursuing the case herself. Since she was an adult, sane, and alive, only she - not her brother acting merely as the original complainant - qualified as the "aggrieved person" entitled to appeal. This case clarifies strict rules on appeal deadlines and who has legal standing to challenge an acquittal.

title: Muhammad Hanif V. S.H.O. Police Station New Sariab, Quetta,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Muhammad Hanif, who was injured along with his cousin in an attack. His cousin later died from the injuries. When Hanif tried to report the incident to police, the SHO (Station House Officer) refused to register his complaint (FIR), because the police had already recorded their own FIR about the same incident, in which Hanif himself was named as an accused. Hanif then approached the Sessions Judge acting as Justice of the Peace to compel registration of his version of events, but that application was dismissed.

The Balochistan High Court examined whether a second FIR could be recorded when there were two completely conflicting versions of the same incident. The court ruled that police have a legal duty to record any report of a cognizable offence and investigate it, without judging guilt or credibility at that stage—that job belongs to magistrates and trial courts. Importantly, the court held that when two versions of an incident are genuinely different and not just a defense narrative, a separate FIR should be registered for each so that the trial court can compare both accounts and fairly determine what actually happened.

Finding that the SHO had wrongly refused to register Hanif's complaint, the High Court directed that his application be processed in accordance with the law. This case matters because it reinforces citizens' right to have their version of events officially recorded, ensuring fair investigation even in cases involving rival claims from opposing sides.

title: Mst. Shugafta V. Chairman Federal Public Service Commission, Islamabad and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a woman who applied for two teaching positions—Assistant Head Mistress and Vice Principal—advertised by the Federal Public Service Commission (FPSC). The advertised eligibility criteria required candidates to have a Master's degree in any discipline plus a separate B.Ed. (Bachelor of Education) degree. The petitioner held only one degree: an M.A. in Education, a two-year postgraduate qualification. She argued that the Higher Education Commission had officially recognized her M.A. Education as equivalent to an M.Ed. (Master of Education), so she should be considered qualified. She also argued that since she had already been allowed to sit for the written test, she had earned a right to be interviewed, even though the FPSC later rejected her candidacy for lacking the required qualifications.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that the advertised post required two separate degrees—a Master's degree in any subject AND a B.Ed.—not one combined qualification. Since the petitioner had only one degree, she did not meet the criteria, regardless of any equivalence recognition for her single degree. The court emphasized that being allowed to take a written test does not create a permanent right to proceed further if a candidate is later found ineligible on proper scrutiny. It ruled that the government has the authority to set qualification requirements for jobs, and courts should not create eligibility where the criteria are clearly not met. title: Mirza Luqman Masud V. Government of Pakistan, Establishment Division through Secretary and 14 others,
explainer:
This case involved a petition filed in the Balochistan High Court by Mirza Luqman Masud, a former Senior Investigating Officer at the National Accountability Bureau (NAB), Quetta. He challenged the appointments of ten NAB officials (respondents 6 to 15), claiming they were retired army officers appointed in violation of the NAB Ordinance and its rules on qualifications, since many allegedly held only intermediate-level education. He asked the court to issue a "writ of quo warranto" - a legal order requiring these officials to justify the authority under which they held their posts - and to declare their appointments void, along with recovering benefits they had received.

The court examined whether it had jurisdiction to hear this case, since almost all the respondents were appointed by NAB headquarters in Islamabad and served outside Balochistan, except for one. It ruled that under Article 199 of the Constitution, a High Court's power to issue a writ of quo warranto is limited to persons holding public office within its own territorial jurisdiction. Since the respondents were neither appointed nor working within Balochistan, the court could not compel them to justify their positions, as doing so would exceed its constitutional authority. The court also noted that the petitioner failed to show a prima facie case regarding the respondents' lack of qualifications. Consequently, the petition was dismissed. This case clarifies the geographic limits on High Courts' power to question public appointments through quo warranto petitions.

title: Sanaullah V. The State,
explainer:

Since he could not produce registration documents, police contacted the Citizen Police Liaison Committee in Karachi, who claimed the motorcycle had been reported stolen in an earlier robbery case. Sanaullah was charged and convicted under Section 411 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which criminalizes dishonestly receiving or keeping stolen property while knowing or having reason to believe it was stolen. He was sentenced to two years imprisonment plus a fine, and this conviction was upheld on appeal.

The Balochistan High Court, however, overturned the conviction. It found that the prosecution's claim that the motorcycle was stolen relied only on hearsay - a phone call the complainant received from CPLC - which was never properly proven with reliable evidence. The court also noted that the earlier robbery the motorcycle was allegedly linked to occurred when Sanaullah was just 10 years old, so he could not have committed that robbery himself. Since the prosecution failed to even establish that the motorcycle was actually stolen property, it could not prove the essential elements of dishonesty and knowledge required for a conviction under Section 411.

title: Malik Munir Ahmed V. Sardar Khair Muhammad Tajik and others,
explainer:
This case is about a family property dispute in Quetta over a building called Kabir Building, which was constructed by the father of the parties. After his death, the property was informally divided among his children into different blocks. The petitioner, Munir Ahmed, claimed exclusive ownership of certain rooms and storage spaces (godowns) in his allocated block, saying he had only temporarily allowed relatives to use them, and that he held a 99-year lease from the Cantonment Board for the land beneath the structure. When the relatives who were occupying the space started renting it out for profit instead of returning it to him, he sued for possession and a permanent injunction.

Both the trial court and the appellate court ruled against him, finding that he failed to prove he ever built the structure or actually possessed it, and that his lease deed and record entries did not establish real ownership. The other family members had shown long-standing possession since their father's time.

The Balochistan High Court, hearing his revision petition, upheld these findings. It explained that a lease deed or mutation entry alone does not create ownership; actual proof of transfer and possession is required. It also noted that a court reviewing a case under its revisional powers cannot overturn concurrent factual findings already agreed upon by two lower courts. The petition was dismissed, meaning the property remained undivided among the family as before.

title: Abdul Qayyum and 8 others V. Abdul Ghaffar and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a shop in Bombay Shopping Centre, Quetta. The appellants, claiming to be landlords as successors of the original owner, filed an eviction application against a tenant, alleging non-payment of rent since 2005, illegal subletting to two other men, and personal need for the shop. The tenant admitted renting the shop but said he had been paying rent to one of the other respondents, who claimed to be the actual owner of the entire shopping centre and denied any landlord-tenant relationship with the appellants. That respondent pointed out that ownership of the property was already being litigated in a separate civil suit between him and the appellants' predecessor.

The Rent Controller dismissed the eviction application, finding no landlord-tenant relationship existed between the appellants and the tenant, given the unresolved ownership dispute. The Balochistan High Court upheld this decision on appeal. It held that when the very existence of a landlord-tenant relationship is disputed, and ownership of the property is genuinely uncertain and already subject to pending civil litigation, the Rent Controller cannot decide issues like eviction, since rent tribunals are not the proper forum to determine title. The landlords were told to wait for the civil court's final decision on ownership before pursuing eviction. The appeal was dismissed, reinforcing that eviction proceedings cannot substitute for resolving genuine ownership disputes through civil courts.

title: La Guardia Group of Companies through Assistant Manager Terminal V. Abdul Nafey and another,
explainer:
This case involves a dispute over commercial property in Quetta used as a truck terminal. The property owner, Abdul Nafey, filed an eviction application against the tenant, La Guardia Group of Companies, claiming unpaid rent since 2011. Because notices could not be delivered to the tenant directly, they were served on a watchman at the property instead. When the tenant did not appear, the Rent Controller proceeded ex parte (without the tenant present) and ultimately ordered eviction and payment of a large sum in back rent.

The tenant later challenged this, arguing it never received proper notice and only learned of the case during separate execution proceedings, where its correct Karachi address was used. The Balochistan High Court examined whether service of notice had been properly carried out under the law, particularly the rules on substituted service.

The court found that the trial court had not followed the proper legal procedure for serving notice when the tenant's address was unavailable, and that service on the watchman did not meet legal requirements for effective service. Because proper service was lacking, the court held the tenant's appeal was filed within the allowed time limit, not late.

The High Court set aside the ex parte judgment and sent the case back for a fresh decision on the merits, emphasizing that both sides must get a fair hearing and that cases should be decided on substance rather than technical procedural defects. The appeal was allowed.

title: Haji Inayatullah Bazai V. Muhammad Ayub and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta over a piece of land. The plaintiff, Muhammad Ayub, claimed he was the recorded owner of a specific plot and had been running a brick kiln on it since 1992. He filed a suit seeking a court declaration confirming his exclusive ownership and a permanent injunction to stop interference with his possession. The defendant, Haji Inayatullah Bazai, argued that the land was part of a larger jointly-owned property with multiple shareholders, that no formal partition had taken place, and that the plaintiff's suit could not succeed without all co-owners being made parties to the case.

The trial court initially dismissed the plaintiff's suit, but the appellate court reversed that decision and ruled in the plaintiff's favor, finding that the land the plaintiff possessed and claimed was distinct from the land the defendant was referring to, and that the plaintiff had been in possession since he purchased it.

The Balochistan High Court, hearing the defendant's revision petition against the appellate court's ruling, upheld the appellate court's decision. It found that the defendant's evidence didn't match what he had claimed in his written statement, and that parties cannot present evidence departing from their own pleadings. The court also held that the trial court had failed to properly understand the dispute, while the appellate court's reasoning was sound. The revision was dismissed, meaning the plaintiff's ownership declaration stood confirmed. This case highlights the principle that courts hold litigants strictly to what they actually plead in their court papers.

title: Muhammad Rafiq and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with two men convicted under Section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code, which criminalizes sodomy, along with Section 34 covering common intention. They had been sentenced to three years' rigorous imprisonment and a fine by a trial court, and this conviction was upheld on appeal. Both the convicted men and the complainant filed revision petitions before the High Court, the men seeking acquittal and the complainant seeking a harsher sentence.

The complainant alleged that the accused had committed sodomy with his minor son a week before the police report and had also filmed a nude video, later using it to threaten and beat the boy again. However, the High Court found serious problems with the prosecution's case. The victim's own father, in his testimony, never actually mentioned the sodomy allegation, only the video recording. The court also found that the police relied on inadmissible evidence, namely a "joint disclosure" and "joint recovery" from both accused together, which is not legally permissible. The medical examination did not follow proper procedure, and no forensic comparison of semen was conducted to link the accused to the crime, making the doctor's opinion unreliable.

Because the prosecution failed to prove its case with credible evidence, the High Court acquitted both accused men, dismissed the complainant's request for a harsher sentence, and refused to allow a compromise since sodomy is a non-compoundable offence under the law.

title: Muhammad Sabir and 3 others V. Mst. Janat Khatoon,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over inherited land in Kharan, Balochistan. Mst. Janat Khatoon sued claiming to be the sole surviving legal heir of her deceased father, seeking declaration, injunction and partition of twelve pieces of land. She argued that her brother and sister had died before their father, and since her brother's children (the petitioners) were grandchildren rather than direct children, they were not entitled to inherit under the law of inheritance. The defendants disputed this, claiming their grandfather had already gifted the land to one of them in lieu of dower at the time of marriage.

Both the trial court and the appellate court (Majlis-e-Shoora) ruled in favor of the plaintiff. The defendants then challenged these rulings before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court found a fundamental problem: the suit never properly described the land in dispute. There were no boundaries, measurements, or revenue records identifying the twelve properties, and evidence showed the land wasn't even officially settled or recorded in anyone's name. The court held that a suit for partition or inheritance cannot succeed without clearly identifying the property involved, and no decree can be enforced based on vague or uncertain property descriptions.

The High Court set aside both lower court decisions and dismissed the suit entirely. It also clarified that while it normally would not disturb factual findings of lower courts, it can intervene when those findings rest on unclear or legally flawed reasoning. This case underscores that clear property identification is essential for any land dispute to succeed in court.

title: Noorullah and others V. Additional District and Sessions Judge and others,
explainer:
This case dealt with a technical but important question in criminal procedure: what is the correct legal way to challenge an order passed by a Justice of the Peace (usually a Sessions or Additional Sessions Judge acting in that separate role) under sections 22-A and 22-B of the Criminal Procedure Code, which deal with matters like directing police to register FIRs or conduct investigations.

Several petitioners had approached the Balochistan High Court through constitutional petitions against such orders, raising the question of whether these orders could instead, or additionally, be challenged under section 561-A of the Cr.P.C., which allows courts to use their inherent powers to prevent abuse of process.

The High Court, referring to precedent including a Lahore High Court full bench decision and Supreme Court rulings, held that a Justice of the Peace does not exercise judicial power under Pakistani law. Their role is purely administrative and ministerial, not judicial, since no law classifies them as a court or magistrate empowered to adjudicate. As a result, their orders cannot be treated as judicial orders open to challenge under section 561-A, which applies only to judicial proceedings. Instead, since such orders are administrative or executive in character, they can only be challenged through a constitutional petition under Article 199 of the Constitution.

This ruling clarifies the correct legal remedy available to citizens dissatisfied with decisions of Justices of the Peace, ensuring consistency in how such matters are pursued in Pakistani courts.

title: Abdul Rehman V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns Abdul Rehman, a civil servant, who sought review of a Balochistan High Court order that had earlier dismissed his constitutional petition. His original petition asked the court to enforce a mutual transfer/posting arrangement with another officer, which had reportedly been approved by the Chief Minister but not implemented by the Secretary of Secondary Education. He also raised complaints about junior officers being given higher-grade duties, sought a declaration against a notification posting another person, requested his own appointment as Deputy Director, and asked for contempt proceedings against government officials.

The High Court held that matters of transfer, posting, and promotion of civil servants are governed by service rules and fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Service Tribunal, not the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction, which is barred by Article 212 of the Constitution. It also explained that transfers are a government prerogative, and no civil servant can dictate his own posting through mutual arrangements. On the review application itself, the court emphasized that review is a limited remedy meant only to correct clear errors, not to reargue or reopen a case on its merits. Since the petitioner failed to show any new evidence or apparent error justifying review, the court dismissed the review application, upholding its earlier decision to reject the constitutional petition. The case reaffirms the limited scope of judicial review and the boundary between High Court and Service Tribunal jurisdiction over civil service matters.

title: Abdul Rehman Kehtran V. The State,
explainer:
This case is a bail application from the Balochistan High Court decided in 2014. The applicant, Abdul Rehman Kehtran, a sitting member of the Provincial Assembly, was arrested after police raided a bungalow linked to him and recovered an enormous cache of illegal arms, ammunition, and explosives, including rocket launchers, grenades, mortar shells, and thousands of rounds of ammunition. He was charged under Pakistan's Arms Ordinance and Explosive Substances Act. His lawyers argued he had no connection to the bungalow, was not present during the raid, and that the case involved politically motivated false implication, asking the court to treat it as needing further inquiry and grant bail.

The court rejected these arguments. It found clear evidence that the applicant was present and arrested at the scene, that witnesses' statements were recorded promptly, and that he never actually denied the recovery of the weapons. The court also noted it was implausible that local residents, including police officers, would falsely implicate a powerful sitting legislator whose party had controlled the province, especially since authorities had seemingly been reluctant to arrest him despite other pending cases against him. Since the offenses were non-bailable and fell under a legal provision restricting bail in serious cases, the court dismissed the bail application.

This case matters because it shows how courts assess bail requests in serious weapons cases, weighing political influence claims against physical evidence and witness testimony, and reinforces that political status does not automatically entitle someone to bail in grave offenses.

title: Muhammad Aalam V. Mehmood Khan and another,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves a dispute over agricultural land in Jaffarabad district. The landowner, Mehmood Khan, had leased 24 acres of land to Muhammad Aalam in 2001 under an arrangement called "Ijara." After the lease period ended in 2013, the landowner claimed Aalam refused to vacate and was illegally occupying the land, so he filed a complaint under the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005 — a special law meant to protect property owners from land grabbers. The trial court accepted this complaint and issued an order stopping Aalam from farming the land.

Aalam challenged this order, arguing that the land had actually been sold to him after the lease, not just leased, and that he had filed a separate civil suit for enforcement of that sale. He also argued that since the landowner himself admitted a tenancy relationship existed, the dispute should be handled under the Balochistan Tenancy Ordinance, 1978, which specifically deals with landlord-tenant disputes and ejectment procedures, not the Illegal Dispossession Act.

The High Court agreed with Aalam. It held that the Illegal Dispossession Act is meant to target professional land grabbers, not tenants in lawful occupation. Since the complainant admitted Aalam was his tenant, the dispute properly belonged under the Tenancy Ordinance. The Court ruled the trial court's proceedings were legally void and quashed them, allowing the landlord to pursue proper remedies elsewhere. This

title: Rozi Khan V. Muhammad Asif And Another,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of a man accused of assault. The complainant, Rozi Khan, had filed a police report alleging that during a quarrel, one brother, Muhammad Arif, fired a pistol and injured the complainant's brother, while the other brother, Muhammad Asif, attacked the complainant and his brother with a knife. After trial, the sessions court convicted Muhammad Arif on charges of causing bodily harm but acquitted Muhammad Asif, giving him the benefit of the doubt. The complainant appealed, arguing that witness testimony clearly implicated both brothers equally and that the acquittal resulted from a flawed reading of the evidence.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the appeal and upheld the acquittal. It found that the medical evidence did not match the witnesses' account of how the injuries were caused, particularly noting that a knife could not have produced the type of wound (a lacerated injury) described by doctors, which typically results from blunt trauma rather than a cutting weapon. This contradiction between the eyewitness testimony and the medical findings created real doubt about whether the acquitted man was responsible for those injuries.

The court also reaffirmed important legal principles: an acquitted person enjoys a double presumption of innocence, and appellate courts should be reluctant to overturn acquittals unless the original decision was clearly unreasonable or ignored the evidence. Since the trial court's decision was well-reasoned, the High Court declined to interfere, keeping the acquittal intact.

title: Ikhtiar Khan V. Muhammad Hassan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involves an appeal against the acquittal of four respondents who had been accused of forgery in a private criminal complaint filed by Ikhtiar Khan. The dispute originated from a civil suit filed by the respondents against the appellant, based on what the appellant claimed was a forged power of attorney. When the appellant challenged the document's validity in the civil case, the respondents withdrew their suit. The appellant then filed a separate criminal complaint accusing them of forgery and related offences under the Pakistan Penal Code.

The trial court had acquitted the respondents at an early stage, relying on Section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which restricts private individuals from directly filing criminal complaints about forged documents connected to ongoing civil proceedings. Under this law, only the court where the document was produced (or a superior court) can file such a complaint, not a private litigant.

The Balochistan High Court examined this legal bar in detail, reproducing Section 195 and affirming that its purpose is to prevent parties in civil litigation from using criminal complaints as a tool against opponents over documents contested in that litigation. The judgment reinforces that such criminal prosecution can only proceed if initiated by the concerned court itself, not by a private party.

This decision matters because it clarifies the limits on private litigants seeking criminal action over document disputes arising from civil cases, ensuring court processes for forgery allegations are properly controlled by the judiciary rather than opposing parties

title: Ella-Ud-Din and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about two men, Ella-ud-Din and Jalal-ud-Din, convicted of drug trafficking under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. Police stopped their car at a checkpoint on the Quetta-Sibi road and found 82 packets of charas (cannabis), weighing 82 kilograms total, hidden in secret compartments of the vehicle. Ella-ud-Din was driving while Jalal-ud-Din sat beside him. Both were arrested and later convicted by a trial court, sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine.

On appeal, their lawyer argued the case was flawed: the drug samples were sent to the forensic lab two months late instead of within the required 72 hours, witness statements contained contradictions, no independent witnesses were present during the search, and there were inconsistencies in how the packets were weighed.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It ruled that a delay in sending samples to the lab does not automatically invalidate a trial, and that only major contradictions—not minor inconsistencies—can undermine a prosecution's case. The court held that since the drugs were found in secret cavities of the car, the driver could reasonably be presumed to have knowledge of them, and so could his passenger. Finding the prosecution's evidence—witness testimony, the recovery, and the lab report—convincing and unshaken, the court upheld the conviction and dismissed the appeal, keeping both men in prison for life.

title: Aurangzaib V. Division Superintendent Pakistan Railways and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved two employees of Pakistan Railways, working as Ticket Controllers, who wanted to be promoted to a higher position called Special Ticket Examiner (STE). They claimed that other employees were wrongly promoted ahead of them in violation of a reserved quota policy that set specific percentages for promotion from different job categories. The petitioners asked the Balochistan High Court to cancel the promotions given to two other employees and order the railway authorities to promote them instead.

The High Court dismissed the petition without even examining whether the quota rules were actually violated. Instead, it focused on a legal bar found in Article 212 of the Constitution, which generally prevents High Courts from directly hearing disputes involving civil servants' terms and conditions of service, such disputes are meant to go through special service tribunals or departmental remedies first. The court noted that Pakistan Railways is a federal government department, so its employees count as being "in the service of Pakistan." Since the dispute here was about promotion based on a service quota, not about any employee's basic fitness for a job, it counted as a "terms and conditions of service" matter falling under this constitutional bar. The court also noted that the employees had not properly exhausted departmental remedies like appeal or review before rushing to court.

The case matters because it reaffirms that civil servants generally cannot bypass service tribunals and go straight to the High Court over promotion disputes.

title: Abdul Razzaq V. The State,
explainer:
Abdul Razzaq was convicted by a trial court in Balochistan and sentenced to death for murdering his wife, Kaz Bano, whose body was found at their home with gunshot injuries. The case relied on circumstantial evidence rather than eyewitnesses: he had phoned the complainant (his wife's brother) admitting he killed her, accusing her of illicit relations with another man; he never explained how she died despite being in the house; he did not report the death to police or attend her funeral; and he was arrested more than eight months later. The High Court examined this evidence and agreed that the circumstances, taken together, formed an unbroken chain pointing to his guilt, since there was no other explanation and no motive for anyone else to kill her.

However, the court found the death sentence unwarranted. It noted there was no evidence the couple was unhappy or that the accused had any prior reason to kill his wife, suggesting the killing arose from a sudden provocation rather than cold, premeditated murder. Applying principles about mitigating circumstances, the court downgraded the offense from section 302(c) to section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, replacing the death sentence with life imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 100,000. This case illustrates how Pakistani courts evaluate circumstantial evidence in murder cases and how mitigating factors, like apparent sudden provocation, can lead to reduced sentencing even when guilt is established.

title: Muhammad Ismail and another V. The State,
explainer:

An FIR was registered under the Drugs Act, 1976. However, when the seized liquid was chemically tested, the Government Analyst identified it not as liquor but as Hydrochloric Acid (HCL), a chemical used in laboratories and industry.

The accused's lawyer argued that since the substance was actually HCL, it did not qualify as a narcotic drug, psychotropic substance, or controlled substance under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, and asked the trial court to change the charge to Section 16 of that Act, which covers offences for which no specific punishment is otherwise provided. The trial court refused, reasoning that HCL still counted as a "controlled substance" requiring a licence to transport.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It examined the Act's definitions of narcotic drug, psychotropic substance, and controlled substance, and found that HCL, being a general laboratory chemical, did not fit any of these categories. Therefore, the trial court's order rejecting the accused's application was set aside. The High Court directed the trial court to alter the charge to one under Section 16 of the CNS Act and proceed with the case accordingly. This case matters because it clarifies that not every chemical substance automatically qualifies as a controlled narcotic substance under the law.

title: Sohail V. Mst. Nazia Amin and 3 others,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and deals with a dispute over payment of dower (haq-e-mehr) following a divorce. A wife had filed a family court suit against her former husband, seeking recovery of Rs. 300,000 and 70 miscal of gold that had been fixed as her dower at the time of marriage in 2008. Only part of the gold had been given to her at the time of the nikah; the rest of the gold and the cash amount remained unpaid. After the couple separated, the family court decreed in her favour, ordering the husband to pay the remaining dower in full. The husband did not challenge this decree, so it became final.

When the wife sought to enforce the decree, the husband asked to pay in small monthly installments due to his financial situation, and the executing courts allowed this, gradually increasing the installment amounts on appeal. The husband still felt this was too harsh and challenged the arrangement before the High Court.

The High Court dismissed his petition, holding that since he never appealed the original decree, it had become final and could not be reopened or reduced through execution proceedings. The Court also emphasized the Islamic legal principle that dower is a debt owed by the husband to the wife as a mark of respect and a legal right, due as soon as the marriage is consummated. The ruling reinforces that dower obligations must be honestly fulfilled and cannot be diluted at the execution stage.

title: Abdul Hafeez Luni V. The State through NAB,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted under the National Accountability Ordinance for corruption, who was sentenced to ten years in prison along with a heavy fine of over 50 million rupees, with an additional two and a half years' imprisonment if the fine went unpaid. His conviction was upheld on appeal, and he did not challenge it further before the Supreme Court. He served his full prison sentence, including the extra time for non-payment of the fine, and was released. Afterward, the National Accountability Bureau applied to recover the unpaid fine as arrears of land revenue, and the Accountability Court accepted this request. The convicted man challenged that order before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled against him, holding that serving the additional prison term imposed for defaulting on a fine does not erase the obligation to pay the fine itself. Relying on Supreme Court precedent and relevant provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code and Pakistan Penal Code, the court held that if someone has the means to pay a fine but chooses imprisonment instead, authorities can still recover the fine afterward as arrears of land revenue. The court found the law under the National Accountability Ordinance to be similarly structured, and upheld the recovery order.

This case matters because it clarifies that completing a prison sentence for non-payment of a court-imposed fine does not discharge the actual debt, and the state retains the right to pursue recovery of unpaid fines even after release from custody.

title: Abdul Salam V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Abdul Salam, who sought bail after being accused of kidnapping and murdering a taxi driver, Khuda-e-Rahim, in Balochistan. According to the FIR, the victim was hired by five men for a trip, later kidnapped for a ransom of Rs. 20 lakh, and killed when the ransom was not paid, with his body dumped in a mountainous area, found handcuffed with iron shackles. The applicant and a co-accused were arrested shortly after the incident, and the case was eventually transferred to the Anti-Terrorism Court because the offence was classified as falling under terrorism laws.

The applicant argued for bail mainly because there was no eyewitness and because the trial had been delayed for reasons not his fault, invoking the rule that prolonged pretrial detention without conclusion of trial can justify bail.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the bail application. It found that the FIR was filed promptly, named the accused specifically, and was corroborated by later evidence, including the manner in which the body was recovered. The court held that since the case involved terrorism-related charges punishable by death or life imprisonment, a special legal provision barred granting bail based merely on delay, as such offenders are excluded from that benefit under the law.

This judgment reinforces that in terrorism-related cases, courts apply stricter bail standards, denying the usual relief granted for trial delays when serious charges like terrorism are involved.

title: Allah Dina and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court and concerns whether a fine imposed on convicted persons can still be recovered even after they have served their full prison sentence, including any additional jail time ordered for failing to pay the fine.

The petitioners had been convicted in a National Accountability Bureau reference and sentenced to imprisonment along with fines. Their appeals against the conviction were dismissed, and they did not challenge the matter further before the Supreme Court. After completing their prison terms, the accountability authorities applied to recover the unpaid fines as arrears of land revenue, a mechanism used to collect government dues. The accountability court accepted this application, and the petitioners challenged that decision before the High Court.

The petitioners argued that a similar legal question was pending before the Supreme Court but could not provide any supporting precedent. The prosecution relied on an earlier Balochistan High Court ruling and a Supreme Court decision establishing that serving extra jail time for not paying a fine is treated merely as punishment for non-payment, not as a substitute for actually paying the fine.

The High Court agreed with this reasoning and held that simply serving the default imprisonment does not free a convicted person from the obligation to pay the fine. The fine remains recoverable as arrears of land revenue. The court found no fault in the accountability court's order and dismissed the petition, meaning the recovery process against the petitioners could proceed.

title: Abdul Qadeer V. The State,
explainer:
Abdul Qadeer, a truck driver, was arrested by Anti-Narcotics Force personnel after 4650 kg of poppy straw was found in the truck he was driving. He was charged under the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. He had already been refused bail once by the trial court, and he approached the Balochistan High Court seeking bail a second time.

His lawyer argued that no independent witnesses were present during the raid, that a Soobedar should not have been the complainant, that the FIR did not mention weighing the drugs, and that a co-accused had already been granted bail on similar evidence, so he deserved the same treatment.

The High Court rejected all these arguments. It held that as the driver in charge of the truck, the accused was in conscious possession and control of the narcotics, and knowledge could reasonably be inferred from his role. It found no personal enmity with the ANF to suggest false implication. The court explained that the law specifically excludes the requirement of private witnesses in such cases, and that procedural provisions about investigation and rank of officers are directory, not mandatory, so their breach does not automatically invalidate a case. It also ruled that the consistency argument didn't apply because the evidence against him differed from that against the co-accused who got bail. The bail application was dismissed, meaning he remained in custody pending trial.

title: The State through Regional Director Anti-Narcotics Force, Quetta V. Abdul Hameed,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by the Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF) seeking to cancel the pre-arrest bail granted to Abdul Hameed. Hameed had been named by the driver of a vehicle caught with 87 kg of heroin near Turbat, Balochistan, who claimed during on-the-spot questioning that Hameed was a partner in the drug operation. Hameed was not present at the scene and was not directly arrested with the drugs; his name surfaced only through this alleged confession by the co-accused.

The Balochistan High Court refused to cancel his bail. The judges noted that no independent witness was present when the co-accused supposedly named Hameed, making that disclosure legally equivalent only to a police statement, not solid evidence of guilt. They also noted that documents, including Hameed's passport, showed he was actually abroad when the drugs were seized, undermining the claim that he was hiding from the law. The court emphasized that while narcotics cases generally restrict bail, this restriction cannot be used to punish someone before trial. To cancel bail, the prosecution needed to show the original bail order was legally flawed, that Hameed was tampering with evidence, or that he might reoffend—none of which was proven. The court found the prosecution's case still needed further investigation and dismissed the application, allowing Hameed to remain free on bail pending trial. This shows courts' role in balancing anti-narcotics enforcement with individual rights when evidence is weak.

title: Nisar Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a man named Nisar Ahmed who was convicted by a Sessions Court in Sibi under Section 489-C of the Pakistan Penal Code for possessing a forged currency note. He was sentenced to two years of rigorous imprisonment and fined Rs. 5000. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution's case relied heavily on a certificate from the State Bank of Pakistan stating that the seized currency note was examined and found to be forged. However, the High Court found this certificate seriously deficient: it was a single line, did not name the currency officer who examined the note, and did not explain what procedure was used to determine it was forged. The officer who supposedly examined the note was never brought to court to testify, and since he was not officially recognized as a government expert, he could not be exempted from appearing. As a result, the report itself was not even legally admissible as evidence.

Beyond that problem, the court noted that simply having a forged note in one's possession is not automatically a crime. The law requires proof that the person knew or had reason to believe the note was fake, and intended to use it as if it were genuine. The prosecution provided no such proof.

Because the evidence was weak and legally flawed, the High Court overturned the conviction and ordered Nisar Ahmed's immediate release. The case highlights how courts require solid, properly presented expert evidence and clear proof of criminal intent before convicting someone.

title: Sikandar Ali and another V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a bank loan under the Prime Minister's Youth Business Loans Scheme. The complainant, a bank customer, filed a private complaint against two bank officials, alleging they demanded a bribe and mishandled his loan application, particularly around the requirement to provide a guarantor. Instead of following the proper legal procedure, the trial court magistrate at Dera Allah Yar sent the matter to the bank for a report, and after receiving the bank's reply, directly ordered police to register a criminal case (FIR) against the two bank officials under charges of taking illegal gratification, criminal breach of trust, and cheating.

The accused officials challenged this, arguing the magistrate had no authority to order registration of an FIR in this manner and had effectively conducted an investigation himself instead of following the law.

The Balochistan High Court agreed. It held that under the law, a magistrate receiving a complaint must either order a formal inquiry or transfer the matter to the Sessions Court -- not investigate and then directly order an FIR. The court also found no actual evidence of bribery or breach of trust in the record. Since continuing the criminal case would amount to misuse of legal process without any supporting evidence, the court used its special powers to quash the FIR entirely. This case highlights the importance of magistrates following correct procedure before criminal cases can be launched against individuals.

title: Bakhtiar Ali and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved two men, Bakhtiar Ali and Meer Gul, who were convicted by a trial court of murder under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code for shooting a man named Muhammad Farooq during an incident involving old enmity between families. The trial court found them guilty and sentenced them to life imprisonment along with a fine, rather than the death penalty.

The High Court's focus was not on whether the men committed the murder, but on how the trial court decided the punishment. Under Pakistani law, murder classified as qatl-i-amd under Section 302(b) normally carries a default sentence of death, though judges have discretion to impose life imprisonment instead if there are genuine mitigating circumstances, and they must clearly explain those reasons in the judgment. The High Court found that the trial judge had misunderstood the law, mistakenly relying on conditions from a different section (Section 304) that only apply to death sentences imposed as qisas (retribution), not to sentencing decisions made under Section 302(b). Because the trial court failed to properly justify why it chose life imprisonment over death, its reasoning was legally flawed.

As a result, the High Court set aside the sentencing portion of the judgment and sent the case back to the trial court, instructing it to rewrite its decision with proper legal reasoning. This case matters because it clarifies how judges must exercise sentencing discretion in murder cases and ensures decisions about such serious punishments are made transparently and correctly under the law.

title: Sher Dil V. Mst. Sharifa and 2 others,
explainer:
This case is about a man, Sher Dil, who had filed an appeal against a court decision but lost it because he and his lawyer repeatedly failed to show up for hearings over more than two years. The Balochistan High Court dismissed his appeal in September 2012 for non-prosecution, meaning the court concluded he had lost interest in pursuing it.

More than a year later, Sher Dil applied to have his appeal reinstated (re-admitted), claiming he never got proper notice when his case was transferred between court branches, and that his absence was accidental rather than deliberate.

The court rejected this request. Under the law, an application to reinstate a dismissed appeal must normally be filed within thirty days. Sher Dil filed his roughly fourteen months late, and the court found he had not acted diligently even after learning his appeal was dismissed—he took no prompt steps to fix the situation. The court also noted that by the time he filed this application, the winning party had already been enforcing the original judgment, including taking possession of disputed land, and Sher Dil had been present and contesting those enforcement proceedings, undermining his claim of not knowing about the case.

The court held that special exceptions to the limitation rules require solid justification, and simply citing human error is not enough, especially for such a long, unexplained delay. This case reinforces the principle that courts favor people who actively protect their legal rights over those who delay, and that missing filing deadlines can permanently cost you your case.

title: Fareedullah V. Muzaffar Ali,
explainer:
Fareedullah, the complainant, sought cancellation of bail granted by a trial court to Muzaffar Ali, an accused in a murder case registered under sections 302/34 of the Pakistan Penal Code for the fatal shooting of the complainant's brother.

The accused had earlier applied for pre-arrest and post-arrest bail, both of which were rejected by the trial court, and a subsequent bail application before the High Court had been withdrawn without being argued on merits. Later, the trial court granted him bail, citing discrepancies in addresses on CNICs of the deceased and witnesses, and the fact that no specific violent act was attributed to him, treating these as matters requiring further inquiry.

The Balochistan High Court found that these same grounds had already been available and considered at the time of the earlier bail rejections, and were not new or fresh grounds. Since the accused had previously withdrawn his bail plea without pressing it on merits, he could not later rely on the same old grounds to secure bail. The court held that while successive bail applications are not barred by law, they can only succeed if based on genuinely fresh grounds. Finding none here, the court ruled that the trial court's order was an improper exercise of judicial discretion, set it aside, and cancelled the bail granted to the accused.

This case is significant because it reinforces the principle that repeated bail applications cannot be used to relitigate the same points already rejected, protecting the integrity of the judicial process in serious criminal cases.

title: Abdul Sattar Khan Durrani and others V. Province of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved public prosecutors in Balochistan who were working on contractual appointments and wanted the government to make their jobs permanent (regularized). They pointed to earlier government decisions, including a Cabinet-level policy encouraging regularization of contract and ad hoc employees across departments, and a specific summary approved by the Chief Minister in 2013, which they argued obligated the government to regularize their posts. They also challenged a committee's recommendations, arguing the committee had exceeded its mandate and that its findings should be treated as invalid.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition. It held that the prosecutors had been hired through a competitive process involving the Public Service Commission, but strictly on contract, with appointment orders stating their jobs would last only until the Commission completed a formal recruitment process. The court emphasized that contractual or ad hoc employment does not create any vested legal right to permanent status, and employees who accept such terms are bound by them and cannot later challenge their validity. Since the recruitment process was already underway, the petitioners could not claim regularization.

However, the court criticized the government's slow and inattentive handling of the matter, warning that such delays undermine the justice system, and directed the authorities to resolve the issue promptly.

This case matters because it reaffirms the legal principle that contract employees in government service have no automatic right to permanent employment, even amid broader regularization policies.

title: Saadullah V. The State,
explainer:
This is a bail application decided by the Balochistan High Court (Sibi Bench). The accused, Saadullah, had been named in a first information report (FIR) for a dacoity (armed robbery) in which a shepherd was killed and another man was injured. He was accused, along with several others, of firing on the victims, looting cattle, and stealing gold and cash from women during the raid. Under the law, everyone who jointly takes part in such a crime can be held equally responsible for what happens, even if only one person's shot caused the death.

Saadullah argued he deserved bail because he had earlier been granted bail in a similar, separate case with almost identical facts, and because there was an eight-hour delay in filing this FIR, no clear motive was stated, and recovery of weapons from him after his arrest was not possible since he had been absconding for 18 months.

The court rejected these arguments. It held that the delay in filing the FIR was adequately explained, that the seriousness of the accusation (dacoity leading to murder) itself supplied sufficient motive, that recovery of cartridges matched the complainant's account, and that unexplained absconding supported his likely involvement. It also ruled that consistency in one case doesn't automatically apply to a different case. Since the offense was non-bailable and no reasonable grounds favored bail, the application was dismissed. The case illustrates how courts weigh evidence, absconding, and procedural delays when deciding bail in serious criminal matters.

The petitioner sought bail, arguing the case was built on assumptions rather than solid evidence. title: Naimatullah Khan and others V. The National Accountability Bureau, Balochistan through Chairman and another,
explainer:
This case involved government officials from the Prosecution Department of Balochistan who served on a Departmental Selection Committee responsible for recruiting staff to various vacant posts in 2011-12. The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) investigated allegations that the committee members misused their authority to select favored candidates by bypassing merit, and filed a corruption reference against them under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999.

The petitioners sought pre-arrest bail, fearing arrest and humiliation, arguing they had cooperated with the inquiry, that many originally accused candidates had already been cleared, and that the case needed further investigation to determine whether their actions truly amounted to criminal misconduct or were simply routine official duties.

The Balochistan High Court noted that the actual beneficiaries of the allegedly improper recruitment—the candidates who got the jobs—had already been granted pre-arrest bail by the same court in a related case. Applying the legal principle of consistency (treating similarly situated people alike), and noting that all relevant evidence had already been collected and was part of the filed reference, the court found no purpose would be served by denying bail and jailing the petitioners while their alleged beneficiaries remained free on bail.

The court therefore confirmed pre-arrest bail for the petitioners, allowing their petitions. This case illustrates how courts apply fairness and consistency principles when deciding bail in corruption cases involving multiple accused persons.

title: Babul alias Babu V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a bail application in a murder case in Balochistan. The victim, Ali Bakhsh, was found dead with bullet wounds, and the initial police report (FIR) was registered against unknown persons, since no one witnessed the killing. The applicant, Babul alias Babu, was never named in the original FIR. His name only came up 45 days later, through a supplementary statement given by the victim's brother, who himself had not witnessed the murder. No weapon or incriminating evidence was recovered from Babul, and no clear link was established between him and the alleged motive (an old tribal enmity involving a kidnapping).

The trial court had earlier refused him bail, but the Balochistan High Court took a different view. It held that at the bail stage, courts should not deeply examine evidence, only assess whether the case appears to need further inquiry. Since the only evidence against Babul was a delayed, secondhand statement with no direct proof, the court found this was enough doubt to justify bail under Section 497(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code, which allows bail when further inquiry into guilt is needed.

The court also clarified that the common practice of avoiding bail decisions once a murder trial is imminent is not an absolute legal bar—an accused with a genuine right to bail cannot be denied it. Babul was therefore granted bail.

title: Banners Store Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd. through General Manager V. Malik Zafar Iqbal and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of two employees, Malik Zafar Iqbal and Shafeh Muhammad Morijo, who worked as operations/administrative manager and accountant at a branch of Banners Store, a departmental store chain. They had been accused of embezzling and misappropriating large sums of company money, including cash shortages, unexplained expense payments, and missing stock, and were charged under sections 409 and 406 (criminal breach of trust) read with section 34 (common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code. The trial court acquitted them, finding the prosecution's evidence insufficient, and the company appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed the appeal on two grounds. First, it held the appeal was not properly filed because it came from the company's General Manager, who did not qualify as an "aggrieved person" entitled to challenge the acquittal, and the appeal lacked a required affidavit, being signed only by counsel. Second, on the merits, the court found the prosecution had failed to prove the essential elements of criminal breach of trust — there was no evidence showing the money was actually encashed or misappropriated, no clear figures on what was entrusted versus what was allegedly stolen, and no proper accounting records or vouchers. The documents relied upon were also inadmissible.

title: Faqeer Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Faqeer Muhammad, who had been convicted for two separate crimes arising from an incident at the Officers Club in Dera Murad Jamali. During a nighttime robbery there, a chowkidar (night watchman) was murdered and property was stolen. Faqeer Muhammad was convicted of haraabah (robbery) with murder under the Offences Against Property (Enforcement of Hudood) Ordinance and originally sentenced to death, later reduced to life imprisonment by the Federal Shariat Court. He was also separately convicted of possessing an unlicensed weapon under the Pakistan Arms Ordinance and given a further prison term.

Faqeer Muhammad filed this application asking the Balochistan High Court to order that his two sentences run concurrently (at the same time) rather than consecutively (one after the other), which would mean spending less total time in prison.

The court explained that under Section 35 of the Criminal Procedure Code, when someone is convicted of multiple offences in one trial, sentences normally run consecutively unless the court specifically orders otherwise. Since the robbery-murder and the weapons offence involved distinct criminal objectives at different points, the court found no justification for treating them as connected offences deserving concurrent sentences. It also noted that courts cannot use their inherent or supervisory powers to substitute concurrent sentencing where offences are unrelated. The court further observed that being involved in multiple such cases reflected a "desperate character" on the applicant's part.

The application was dismissed

title: Said Muhammad V. Station House Officer, Police Station, Shalkot, Quetta and another,
explainer:
This case is about a businessman, Said Muhammad, who supplied fruit and vegetables to a buyer who agreed to pay him money and issued two cheques as payment. When Said Muhammad presented these cheques at a bank in Quetta, both bounced. He asked the local police station to register a criminal case (FIR) against the buyer for dishonestly issuing bad cheques, an offence under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, but the police refused. He then approached a Justice of Peace (an Additional Sessions Judge) under Section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code to order registration of the FIR, but that application was also dismissed on the ground that the offence did not occur within that police station's jurisdiction, since the buyer and the bank issuing the cheque were located elsewhere.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that under Section 179 of the Criminal Procedure Code, when dishonouring a cheque completes the offence, the case can be tried where the cheque was actually dishonoured, which was Quetta. The court also ruled that a Justice of Peace has no power to decide jurisdiction questions or examine the merits of a case at this stage; their only job is to check whether a complaint about a cognizable offence was properly recorded. The High Court set aside the lower court's order and directed the police to register the FIR, allowing the criminal case to proceed. This clarifies limits on judicial power at the FIR stage and protects complainants from being turned away on technical jurisdiction grounds.

title: Habibullah V. Irshad Ahmed and 2 others,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involves a dispute over two rival criminal cases arising from the same violent incident. Rahim Gul first lodged an FIR accusing Irshad Ahmed (respondent) and others of assaulting his nephews and causing serious injuries. Weeks later, Irshad Ahmed, who was named as an accused in that FIR, applied under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, presenting a medical certificate showing that one of his own companions had also been injured during the same clash. Based on this, a Justice of the Peace directed the local Naib Tehsildar to register a separate, counter FIR against Habibullah (the petitioner) and others. Habibullah challenged this order in the High Court, arguing it was passed without proper evidence, without hearing him, and was essentially a retaliatory move to build a counter-case.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that when both sides in a single violent incident claim injuries, it is legally proper and necessary to record both versions of events as separate FIRs, rather than treating one as merely a defense to the other. Both accounts should then go before a trial court for evidence and judicial scrutiny. The court also refused to accept an affidavit from someone who was avoiding arrest and hadn't submitted to the court's authority. This ruling reinforces the principle that competing versions of the same incident can each result in an FIR, leaving final determination of truth to trial, not to preliminary constitutional petitions.

title: Badost V. The State,
explainer:
This case comes from the Balochistan High Court and involved a bail application filed by a man named Badost, who was accused of being involved in an attack on police and levies personnel in Kharan in 2014. According to the police report, officials had raided a house in search of a suspect when the accused and others allegedly opened fire and threw grenades at the raiding party, killing one levies official. Badost was charged under several sections of the Pakistan Penal Code, the Explosive Substances Act, and the Anti-Terrorism Act.

Badost sought bail after a trial court had already refused it. Notably, his own lawyer failed to appear in court on numerous scheduled dates, but the judge decided to proceed anyway, noting that criminal cases should not be dismissed simply due to non-prosecution.

The court examined the evidence, particularly a confessional statement Badost had given before a magistrate, in which he admitted his role in obtaining weapons and cash for the crime. Although this confession was later retracted, the court held that such questions could not be settled at the bail stage and that a retracted confession, if credible, could still be used to assess whether there was enough evidence to justify continued detention.

Finding sufficient incriminating material connecting Badost to the offence, the court dismissed the bail application, while clarifying that its remarks were tentative and would not affect the final trial.

title: Obaidullah V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves a man named Obaidullah who was convicted by a trial court in Loralai for possessing an unlicensed Kalashnikov rifle, under Pakistan's Arms Ordinance. He was sentenced to four years of rigorous imprisonment and fined. He appealed this conviction to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him, giving him the benefit of the doubt. The judgment identified several serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, the recovered weapon was never sent to a forensic or ballistics expert to confirm its nature, caliber, or whether it even worked. Second, although the arrest happened in a busy, populated commercial area, police made no genuine effort to have independent members of the public witness the recovery, as required by law under Section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Third, prosecution witnesses gave contradictory accounts of exactly where the weapon was found. Finally, the weapon was never properly sealed at the scene, raising the possibility that evidence could have been tampered with.

The court emphasized that while police officers can be credible witnesses, extra caution is needed when they are the only eyewitnesses, since there's a risk of overzealous conduct in securing convictions. Because these lapses were not minor technicalities but fundamental to a fair trial, the court ruled the entire process was legally flawed, and acquitted the appellant. title: Muhammad Naeem V. Siraj-U-Din and 6 others,
explainer:
This case is about a long-running family land dispute in Quetta, Balochistan. The petitioner, Muhammad Naeem, wanted revenue records from decades ago (Jamabandi entries from the 1940s-50s and a 1960 mutation) corrected, claiming he had rightful cultivating possession of the land. A Settlement Officer initially ordered corrections in his favor, but a rival claimant challenged this, and the Additional Commissioner eventually sent the matter back to the Settlement Officer for fresh review, citing unresolved issues like limitation, questionable authority, and possible tampering with mutation records. title: Hazoor Bakhsh and 2 others V. Mir Nasrullah Khan,
explainer:
This case was about a defamation and damages claim. Three landowners sued a local political figure, the Nazim of Union Council Noor Pur, seeking one crore rupees in compensation. They alleged he had, in connivance with his brother, filed a fake police application falsely accusing them of causing the death of a worker who died while cleaning a water course, and that he then held a press conference repeating these false allegations, which was published in a newspaper and damaged their reputation and caused them mental distress. The trial court dismissed their suit, and they appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the dismissal. It clarified an important legal point: even though Pakistan has a specific Defamation Ordinance, 2002, that law does not remove the ordinary civil courts' jurisdiction to hear defamation claims, so people can choose to sue either under that Ordinance or as a regular civil suit. However, on the facts, the court found the appellants had failed to prove the respondent actually filed the application against them, and that merely providing information about a possible crime to authorities is not defamation but a civic duty. The court also stressed that claims of damaged reputation or mental agony must be proven with solid evidence, not just personal feelings of resentment. Since no such proof existed, the appeal was dismissed.
